## Front Matter

### Series Title Page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with a number of manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by those possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in what passages of their works. This is the most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself: a single, methodical, chronological assemblage of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

SECOND SERIES, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Saint Isidore

Bishop of Seville

Printed at Rome in the year of the Lord 1797, under the supervision of Faustino Arévalo, who prefixed his Isidoriana (Isidorian studies); he collected the prefaces, notes, and collations of various scholars, some previously published and others to be published for the first time; compared earlier editions and Roman manuscript codices; and presented the work in a new and more accurate edition, enlarged by the most valuable monuments. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [The Complete Works of Saint Isidore]

## [Col. 0009]

# Notice from the Editor of the Patrology

If anyone should ask why we have appended the following collection of canons to the works of Saint Isidore, we shall readily admit that, among the most learned men, there has until now been vigorous controversy over identifying the author of this collection, and that for this reason an easy opportunity was available to us to pass over a monument of uncertain origin. Yet two considerations prevented us from doing so. First, we judged that this dispute was not unworthy of being submitted to the judgment of the reader. Second, since we intend in our course of Patrology to embrace the immense chain of Catholic tradition, we considered it a matter of conscience not to deprive the reader of such precious remains of ecclesiastical antiquity. In any case, at the end of the volume we shall present the very learned dissertation of Charles de la Serna Santander on this collection of canons.

## [Col. 0009]

# To the Benevolent Reader

Whatever the Church and the Spanish commonwealth most justly claimed for themselves; whatever the most learned men had earnestly sought for the past three centuries; whatever the common wishes of all the best men had long desired; whatever the honor of holy religion and the sound discipline of morals seemed especially to require—all of this we consider today to have been perfected and completed in this one legitimate collection of canons, drawn from the most approved and most ancient codices and now published for the first time.

For when men who had rendered the republic of letters the greatest services—Ambrosius de Morales, Juan Bautista Pérez, Juan Vázquez de Mármol, García Loaysa, and very many others—had begun to clear a path toward revealing this hidden treasure of truth, it is certainly astonishing that their studies should have been so completely disregarded that no one attempted, until the end of the preceding century, to open that treasure and place it in the full light of day.

The Church, spread throughout the whole world, ought to have gathered abundant fruits from it. For while false things were published as true, apocryphal as genuine, and spurious monuments as legitimate, innumerable injuries were inflicted upon the Christian people, very many upon moral rectitude, and the greatest upon the purity of the faith. The Spanish nation, too, could have secured for itself a greater advantage and ornament while it was being cleansed of the stain wrongly and unjustly branded upon it by certain foreigners, who asserted that Spain had introduced apocryphal decretal letters into canon law, promulgated them, and supported them.

How many and how great were the errors in transmitting moral discipline to the faithful! How many abuses in almost everything relating to the Church and the worship of the true God! How great the negligence in the administration of the sacraments! The mind shudders to recall it, and it will not cease to attribute all these things—from the ninth century down to our own memory—to forgers and corruptors, or rather inventors, of apostolic writings.

So that this distinguished work may be examined with all due diligence and usefulness, both by day and by night, we shall merely taste, as it were, with the tips of our lips whatever may shed light for learned men who wish to look into its inner chambers. Learned people may dispute over other matters; we, acting only in the capacity of editors, have resolved to fulfill the task undertaken and to give an account of everything we have examined and of what the most ancient codices present.

The Greeks possessed ancient collections of canons; somewhat later, the Latins obtained several. The Greeks collected their canons, and down to the ninth century they count five collections, the last of which circulated under the name of Photius and is called the Nomocanon. It is clear that they had many commentators, among whom John Balsamon, John Zonaras, and Alexius Aristenus deserve special mention.

The Latins assembled the canons of Nicaea and Sardica. It is sufficiently probable that these alone were observed by them until the Council of Chalcedon. After that council had been celebrated, whatever canonical regulations were contained in the Eastern collections were rendered into Latin. In the codices edited by Justellus and Paschasius Quesnellus, we miss the characteristics and marks of this first collection.

Dionysius, commonly called Exiguus, by birth a Scythian but a Roman citizen, undertook and published, at the request of a friend—as he himself says—the making of another collection at the beginning of the sixth century. To it he appended another work, in which he reviewed with the utmost diligence all the letters of the pontiffs that could be brought forth from the archives of the Roman Church. This collection afterward acquired such authority in the Catholic Church that it was almost universally called the Book of Canons.

The Gallican Church embraced it; the German and Italian Churches received it. The English Church, however, while it followed with great enthusiasm the collection published under the name of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, after that man’s death also followed the collection called Irish.

Let us now come to Spain. In the earliest centuries of the Christian religion, so many and such furious storms of persecution arose and raged in this region that no one who has even crossed the threshold of the volumes of ecclesiastical history can recall their memory without trembling and lamenting. But after almighty God appeared willing to drive that most destructive devastation away to the ends of the earth, Spain began to shine through the strictness of its doctrine and morals, the celebration of synods, and the holiness and learning of very many men.

Only three councils are certainly known to have been celebrated in the fourth century: the Council of Elvira, the Council of Zaragoza, and the First Council of Toledo. Nevertheless, it is probable that other councils also existed at that time. The Fathers of the First Synod of Toledo hint at a certain council of Lusitania; a synodical booklet edited by Justellus presents another, assembled at Córdoba by Hosius; D. Juan de Ferreras, supported by the authority of Saint Athanasius, commends another held in the year 362; and the very learned Father Enrique Flórez endeavors to demonstrate, with many and weighty arguments, that yet another was held at Toledo four years before the synod now called the First.

Who would dare to call into doubt that Spain, distinguished by fervent zeal for the observance of ecclesiastical discipline, provided whatever seemed necessary and most suitable for preserving it intact? Would Hosius—Hosius, famous throughout the world—and those Spanish bishops who attended the Nicene and Sardican synods have failed to publish in their own sees and dioceses the acts and decrees of those councils, as well as of the preceding councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, and Laodicea, insofar as they concerned the whole Church?

While the Spanish bishops were then assembled at Elvira, Zaragoza, and Toledo and issued many most righteous decrees, anyone would be thought to have gone beyond the bounds of probability who supposed that a book of canons was compiled from the statutes of our councils, and shortly afterward from the decrees of foreign or Eastern councils. It is known, moreover, that the neighboring Gauls aimed at the same goal, since certain Spanish subscriptions are read in the First Council of Arles.

We infer that this was the earlier collection of canons in our region, and we think that it was afterward enlarged in succeeding years, contained in a single volume, and deposited in the treasuries of the churches. Are the monuments of this opinion of ours lacking? Let anyone read the many sanctions in our councils that agree most closely with the decrees of Nicaea, Sardica, Riez, and Valence in Gaul.

Let every learned person compare, if he wishes, the twentieth canon of the First Synod of Braga with the thirteenth canon of Sardica. Let him consult the teaching of the Council of Lérida concerning monks, drawn from the statutes of Agde and Arles. Let him examine, we ask, the eleventh title of the Council of Tarragona, and he will encounter these words placed at the end: “The constitution of the Gallican canons concerning these matters having been observed above all.”

A richer harvest, however, may be gathered by anyone who examines the language of the First Council of Braga: “The canons both of general synods and of local ones were reread from the Codex before the council,” and so forth.

In the year 540 Spain knew the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, as is revealed with the greatest clarity by the tenth canon of the First Council of Barcelona; the preface of the Second Synod of Braga should also be consulted. Numerous testimonies from our councils affirm that no cleric was permitted to be ignorant of the canons.

But in what way could men enrolled in the ecclesiastical army have learned the canons, worked at understanding them, and kept them readily at hand, unless codices from which they might be instructed had existed in abundance? “Let the deacon, clothed in white, bring forth the Book of Canons into the midst and pronounce the chapters concerning the holding of councils,” it is written in the Fourth Council of Toledo.

“While we were discussing ecclesiastical discipline and rereading the ancient canons,” the Council of Valladolid records in title 1. Why should we mention more? Let it remain beyond all doubt that the Spaniards enjoyed their own collection of canons from the most remote times.

Yet there were those who said that the earlier collection of which we boast was the collection of Dionysius Exiguus. But some of the monuments that we have drawn from the councils themselves preceded this man’s time; moreover, an attentive investigator will notice, at a single glance, a great difference between them.

Our collection rejected the apostolic canons as apocryphal; the Dionysian collection extols them with the highest praises as legitimate. Our collection possessed a version of the Greek councils peculiar to itself; Dionysius had used another version. The nations that adopted the Dionysian collection attempted to compile no other before the ninth century, whereas we accepted, toward the end of that century, the collection published by Martin, bishop of Tours and metropolitan of Braga.

Why Saint Martin undertook to produce a collection of this kind, which acquired the name of the Excerpts, appears with complete certainty from the words of the preface inserted in the Second Council of Braga and delivered by the bishop himself. It consists of eighty-four titles. Sixty-eight of them, occupying the first place, discuss bishops and clerics; the remainder discuss laypeople.

Do not seek in those collections or excerpts the exact wording of the Greek canons, or a translation word for word. You will find only their meaning and sense, together with many ecclesiastical regulations contained under a single title.

Spain finally acquired another collection of canons, written in the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo, as all learned men agree. Whether its author was Isidore of Seville, who presided over the synod, is still under judgment, since critics have produced many grounds both for affirming and for denying it.

Nevertheless, the opinion that appeals to us above all is that which attributes to the holy Doctor the method by which it was to be compiled, the order to be observed in writing down councils and decretal letters, and the plan for its enlargement in every succeeding age. In this way we endeavor to reconcile the differing opinions of all the learned.

Thus the collection of canons became genuine, legitimate, and in a certain sense proper to the Church of Spain. Subsequent decrees issued by the Fathers in synods and by the pontiffs in letters enlarged it. In later times ecclesiastical discipline was augmented by ordinances committed to writing. Hence codices were preserved in almost all our churches, and neither the Moorish invasion, over so many centuries, nor the necessary corruption of morals, nor ignorance—the inevitable companion of wars—nor the negligence of archivists, nor time itself was able completely to destroy their great number.

It is plainly evident that this was not the collection which Justellus published under the rather inappropriate title of the Book of the Universal Church; nor that which Cajetan Cenni honored with the very grand title of the Most Ancient Book of the Church of Spain; nor finally that which the most eminent Joseph Saenz de Aguirre attributed to the holy bishop of Seville, Saint Isidore, and which contains merely excerpts from the canons or an index. None of these was our genuine and true collection. If testimony is needed, let us bring forward one witness above all: the very exemplar that we are publishing.

We cannot sufficiently marvel that the most eminent cardinal, bearing the title of Saint Balbina, attached to the learned bishop and outstandingly devout Isidore of Seville the collection circulated under the name of Isidore Mercator, or Peccator, which we see encumbered with very many counterfeit and spurious letters, and that, in explanation of his opinion, he amassed only conjectures and flimsy arguments.

Again we marvel that he undertook to refute the weightier arguments of the opposing view with this one claim: namely, that whatever in the collection of canons was later than the time of the holy Doctor, or indecorous, or engraved by an unskilled hand, had been written by some other author.

If that eminent man had both read through and investigated our codices, his entire proposal would have collapsed. Was it easier to assert, together with the most learned men, that the collection completed in the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo was the proper work of the holy bishop, and that a certain copy of it was afterward corrupted by a forger?

What else, we ask, was Aguirre compelled to imply when he testified that the decrees of councils and letters had been collected by the holy Doctor up to the era of the Synod of Seville, but that whatever is subsequently found in the canon had been inserted by another?

The collection of Isidore Mercator neither originated in Spain nor was it the work of a Spaniard. No writer of the eighth or ninth century, whether Spanish or foreign, is found to mention this Mercator, or rather this seller of false wares. In the German chronicles and in those accepted among the Spaniards there is no trace of that Isidore; nor is there any trace of him in Isidore of Beja (Pacensis) from the year 511 to 754.

Who would believe that a man and bishop of such authority among our people, who undertook and completed a collection of canons at the request of eighty bishops and other priests, could have been passed over in silence by every writer of his age? Nor could those eighty bishops have been present in Spain, which was being harassed by continual disaster and persecution. Therefore the collection cannot properly be attributed to the aforementioned Isidore of Badajoz, who is said to have written that brief Chronicle of the Gothic and Saracen kings.

It is not permissible to claim that any ancient codex, marked by the characteristics of a genuine work, exhibiting the collection of Isidore Mercator, can be found in our region. So said our illustrious predecessor D. Francisco Pérez Bayer in his notes to the old Library of Nicolás Antonio; the very learned Father Andrés Burriel maintained the same; and after many most diligent investigations we openly affirm it ourselves.

Almost all the Churches preserved the genuine collection of our homeland, but all the writings of that spurious collection perished? Where, among the most ancient monuments, does any memory of it persist? What judgment did the eighty bishops, by whose authority its inventor was supposedly compelled, render concerning it? In what ecclesiastical assembly, under what titles, and in what city or province of Iberia was it made public?

Why is it that, from the beginning of the ninth century to the end of the tenth, many codices of our legitimate collection survived the ruins of so many wars, while not a single volume of the collection woven from his fabrications is found anywhere? We do not wish to linger longer over a matter clearer than sunlight. Whoever wishes to gather more should consult foreign scholars: Baluze, in his preface to the Dialogues of Antonio Agustín; Blondel, in the prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore; and among our own writers, Domingo López de Barrera, Andrés de Burriel, and others whose writings have been approved by the laws of criticism.

But the opinion that the author of this collection was Isidore, bishop of Setabis, also collapses under its own weight.

> **[Note: [Col. 0013]** This Isidore had been called Setabian by the most eminent Aguirre, Ramírez, and other learned men. Anyone who reads the subscriptions of the Spanish councils attentively will find our correction sufficiently appropriate. **[Col. 0014]**]

This bishop, using the assistance of a certain monk, compiled and published that work around the end of the eighth century and finally died in the year 805, as the illustrious D. Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado seems to indicate in almost these very words in a work called the Chronicle, which he published under the name of Julian of Toledo.

What madness! Julian succeeded Quiricus in the episcopate in the year 680, and was giving testimony concerning the works and death of the aforementioned Isidore of Setabis 115 years after that man had been buried?

That Isidore, then, was fictitious—the Mercator of an unwarranted glory, and certainly a Peccator—who was adorned with the name of the holy Doctor of Seville; who corrupted and engraved in his own metal the preface taken from chapter 16 of Book VI of the Etymologies; and who brought a certain correct exemplar of the canons from Spain into Gaul, corrupted it, and disfigured it.

There was no place in that age to which the teaching, virtues, and fame of our outstanding Doctor had not reached. The true depraver of ecclesiastical antiquities seized the opportunity. The opportunity made patrons and Maecenases into credulous and upright men, especially Riculphus of Mainz, who is said to have been the first to bring into Germany a collection laden with false monuments.

The circumstances of public affairs, the ignorance of the age, wars, the destruction of empires, the sordid profits of certain men, and in others an excessively eager and lamentable ambition for honors all favored the opportunity. The Pseudo-Isidorian fabrications attracted people by their flatteries; no one undertook their refutation. The peoples remained silent, the clergy entered them into the canon, and the prelates of the Churches seemed to have fallen mute.

No one, therefore, will cease to marvel that this collection acquired such authority among so many nations and so many otherwise upright men, after so many centuries, if he does not refuse to consider the miserable condition of the ninth century.

Did Germany hold it? Italy hold it? Gaul hold it? Did almost the entire East hold it? And did fortunate Spain finally hold it after many centuries?

Spain certainly would never have taken it into her bosom if she had wished to search through the precious treasures of her churches and shake moth and dust from the most ancient parchments. Let all those, then, who have been able either to assert or to imagine that the compilation of Isidore Mercator was produced in Spain or was the work of a Spaniard depart, alas, into the darkness.

Our region was so observant of the canons, and so tenacious of them, that at the beginning of the eleventh century it arranged for them to be translated from Latin into Arabic. For when the Moors had occupied almost the whole of Hesperia, when its vernacular language had perished after centuries, and when ecclesiastical discipline was rushing headlong to ruin, the diligence of a certain priest Vincent was so great that he rendered the collection of canons into the Arabic language and completed it for the use of the most noble bishop John Daniel on the seventeenth day of October, in the era 1087, or A.D. 1049, so that Christians oppressed under the Moorish yoke might more easily retain in memory the sound teaching of faith and morals.

D. Miguel Casiri found in the library of El Escorial a parchment exemplar of this Arabic collection, written in Kufic letters, mutilated or obliterated in certain places by its very age and consisting of 435 leaves. We ourselves saw and examined it. Casiri rendered it into Latin, furnished it with notes, and brought a transcript of it to this library in Madrid.

D. Elias Scidiac, a Maronite Syrian, and D. Pablo Lozano afterward compared this version. Seeing that leaves, titles, and entire periods were missing from the autograph, they did not disdain to supply them from the Codex Vigilano. May God grant that this Arabic collection of canons—which is in reality ours—although laborious and requiring enormous expense, may at last one day see the light of public publication.

For it will display in the clearest arguments Spain’s devout and righteous zeal and enthusiasm for learning the canons, and, if further confirmation is still necessary, it will strengthen and reinforce the collection that we are publishing.

Joseph El-Sahir bil-Tabib al-Merxum al-Messii wished to imitate the efforts of the priest Vincent. He was prefect of the Church of Alexandria and was promoted to the honor of the priesthood in the year 1398. He rendered a paraphrase of the Greek canons into Arabic, though not very successfully. In it one encounters an uncultivated style, tedious repetitions, and meaning that is not sufficiently clear.

But the genuine Spanish Collection of Canons now being published calls our discourse back to our own subject. We recently affirmed that it received its form and method from the Fourth Council of Toledo. There can be no doubt that it was afterward enlarged by the addition of other sanctions issued in subsequent councils and in the letters of the Roman pontiffs.

Hence it has happened that one may read in certain codices some things that are missing in others, while everything down to the era of that same council is contained in all of them, as the reader will observe from the note made at each place in our edition.

Those codices, however, preserved with the utmost accuracy, formerly served for the transcription of others. Thus it came about that, although no transcript from the ninth century is found to have survived down to our own times, we nevertheless have before our eyes codices written in the tenth century.

Most devout men grieved that the discipline of faith and morals, committed only to ancient parchments, should be erased from human memory. Their piety added spurs to their efforts: they studied and acquired copies of the codices. Monasteries kept them; churches retained them; no one thought of searching them out.

What then? At last the truly golden sixteenth century dawned for us, when the Spaniards cultivated every branch of learning and the arts, explored the most ancient monuments, and desired to climb, as it were, to the highest summit of an everlasting fountain of erudition.

Here we judge that the greatest honor should be shown to Pedro de Marca, who was the first, in his minor works, folio 206, at the second chapter after the Council of Chalcedon, to write these words concerning our Book of Canons:

> “Here we explain that earlier collection, hitherto unknown, which, with God’s favor, we have drawn from two manuscript codices of the monastery of Ripoll in Catalonia.”

He certainly explained it. Yet we cannot at all agree with this most illustrious archbishop of Paris when he asserts that the collection itself was not merely proper to the Church of Spain, but common also to the Roman, Gallican, and African Churches.

Our authority for this is Pierre Coustant, in his preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 134. Since the Parisian bishop had asserted that it was customary among the Latins publicly to recite the Constantinopolitan Creed, if we show that no Church except the Spanish Church preached it from the years 589 and 636, shall we not rightly and properly conclude that the collection was made in this region and received into daily use?

There is no difficulty in demonstrating this. It is established that the Gauls adopted this rite in the eighth century, and the Romans much later. Concerning the Gauls, Walafrid Strabo bears witness when, in chapter 22, he testifies that they embraced the practice of singing this Creed neither before the age of Charlemagne nor until after the condemnation of Felix of Urgel.

Concerning the Romans, Berno of Reichenau, himself an eyewitness, gives evidence in Book I, On Matters Pertaining to the Mass, chapter 2. No monuments inform us what custom the Africans followed; but that they did not use our collection, filled as it is with Gallican and Spanish synods, is clearer than it could need proof.

The preface placed at the beginning of the collection itself therefore demonstrates that it belonged to Spain. Apart from other considerations, Iberia alone at that time reckoned the days by eras; no decree relating to Hesperia is found to have been omitted; and nowhere are such numerous and highly commendable ancient exemplars found.

While the magnificent and never sufficiently praised monastery of Saint Lawrence of El Escorial was being erected; while rarer books were being sought for the construction of its library; while Ambrosius de Morales and Benito Arias Montano were exploring the most hidden hiding places, exemplars of this genuine collection of our canons appeared, by an almost auspicious fate, as though sent down from heaven.

The zeal especially of Ambrosius will always be worthy of praise among posterity. He undertook a description of the Codex Alveldensis, or Vigilano—which we now see in autograph—and wrote it out in his own hand, judging that by this means that most precious volume would reach public knowledge.

Yet, O deceptive hopes of men! O uncertain prayers! Foreign nations spread the claim that the Spaniards were the authors of the Pseudo-Isidorian compilation, or that it had originated in this region. We were branded with this mark.

Ambrosius de Morales, Juan Bautista Pérez, Juan Vázquez del Mármol, and many other outstanding men carried a torch before them to expose the common error. We, alas, extinguished it by our silence. Extinguished it? Rather, we seemed to confirm the unjust and detestable stain.

The study of antiquities began to be cultivated more eagerly in the preceding century. As more hidden corners were explored, more codices of the canons were discovered, beyond everyone’s expectation.

Their discovery immediately stirred the mind of our most learned predecessor, D. Blas Nasarre. He committed to writing a transcription of all that could be obtained, illuminated them with his own observations, and resolved to compare them with one another. Death, however, prevented him from completing the task. We have examined all his annotations and commend them.

In the year 1798, our likewise illustrious predecessor D. Pedro Luis Blanco was also planning an edition of this collection, and he set forth its plan and form in a specimen committed to the press.

He was planning, I say, a magnificent edition, engraved with copperplate figures and decorated with engraved representations of all the kings, writers, trees, winds, and so forth that appear in the Codex Vigilano. The immense resources of the treasury would scarcely have sufficed to complete it.

He was also considering publishing exactly as they are read in the codices all the words, the errors arising from the ignorance of scribes, and all the capital letters—as they are called—wherever they are written, whether in the middle of a sentence or even in the middle of a word, with graphic precision and the utmost exactitude for public use.

We praise the man’s fidelity. Nevertheless, we do not believe that we violated it in any way when we did not hesitate to substitute correct orthography, division of sentences, and letters suited to the words.

Our view and counsel were the same as those of the most excellent and illustrious D. Pedro de Silva y Meneses, a man praised by all good people and one who rendered the greatest services to the military, ecclesiastical, and literary commonwealth.

In printing books that must be consulted continually, we thought that the common good and economy should be served by giving readers volumes that were as faithful as possible, complete in every respect, closer to the archetype, not excessively costly, not filled with errors, and not confused or entangled.

Accordingly, in the year 1806 the Madrid library undertook the collation of the autograph codices that had been brought here by royal command. It marked their variant readings that deserved notice; examined the annotations already anticipated by our predecessors; searched through the commentaries; and restored ecclesiastical sanctions that in certain codices were either mutilated or mixed together to their true form by comparison with readings in other codices.

Meanwhile at Toledo, by order of the most eminent Cardinal de Scala, two ancient codices preserved in that metropolitan church were compared with the transcript sent from here by the very learned D. Manuel Ipola, the reverend Father Fray Lorenzo Frías of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, D. Raimundo Fernández de Loaysa, and D. Baltasar Fernández.

When certain doubts arose, we traveled to the city of Toledo. Supported by the assistance and learning of the same Reverend Father Frías, we examined those codices again and endeavored to bring whatever had been obscure and uncertain into the clear light.

Then the Gothic—or rather Spanish and ancient—collection of canons containing the statutes of the councils was committed to the royal press in the year 1808. That part of the collection, however, which contains the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and is now printed, remained in manuscript until the present time because of the well-known changes in public government and sovereignty.

If you should wish to examine the method and arrangement of the decrees, the division of the councils of each province or region, and the single intention of the writers, you will nowhere discover any substantial or noteworthy variation in the Codices. You should observe with care the errors produced by time, ignorance, or negligence. After examining one ancient Codex of the canons, the most experienced men in criticism and learning boasted that they had acquired the entire body of canon law, a discovery more precious than gold and a very rare pearl. What now remains for the Spaniards to desire, when it has fallen to their lot to see, handle, inspect, compare, and publish several ancient Codices?

Would that, while we write these words, we could show that we had originated in some other region of the earth, so that we might congratulate this most fortunate Iberian land with the greatest respect, and remove from ourselves every odious suspicion of undeserved praise. But truth knows no fatherland; we place ourselves before the irrefutable tribunal of the Codices. Their antiquity commends their authority and excellence, and no greater antiquity has yet appeared. The reader will note their mutual agreement with one another in the principal matters.

We cannot, however, pass over in silence the fact that our Codices were preserved not in one or two provinces of this kingdom, but in separate regions of the same land, in archives differently maintained: some in free communities, others in towns subject to the yoke of oppression. Learned men have recorded that the Codices of Rivipull, which Peter de Marca saw, as well as those of the church of Soissons and finally those of the churches of Laon, Noyon, and Beauvais—if one excepts the three spurious letters printed in the workshop of Isidore Mercator in those three—are in almost every respect like the Spanish Codices.

From this we have drawn clear testimony in proper and just commendation of our collection. In cities situated far apart, amid so many and such great changes, amid the shifting boundaries of dynasties ruling now here, now there, and amid divergent human opinions, the Codices have remained unharmed, uniform, consistent, and intact. O wondrous marvel on every side! Surely no one will henceforth anywhere doubt their reliability.

We set out in the following articles the method we followed in collating and editing the Codices.

1. The Alveldense, or Vigilano, Codex was the principal exemplar, or archetype. The variant readings of the others, distinguished by their own numbers, have been recorded at the foot of the pages.

2. Whenever the reading of the Alveldense Codex was found to be mutilated, excessive, ambiguous, obscure, or erroneous, the correct reading was taken from other Codices and regularly recorded at the foot of the page.

3. Scribes readily confused letters belonging to the same organ, and among the vowels they changed *e* into *i*, *i* into *e*, *o* into *u*, and *u* into *o*. Thus they wrote *babtisma*, *subscribtionem*, *nubtias*, *neglegentiam*, *elegatur*, *catechumini*, *Aurilianense*, *adolatores*, *pecodum*, *adulescentuli*, and many similar forms. Diphthongs were unknown to them. The division of periods is often scarcely visible; few or no orthographic marks are supplied. The letters and marks that belonged to the original text will be found reproduced in our edition.

It is also worth noting that a single Codex is not always consistent with itself. The one that now has *babtisma* later writes *baptisma*; the one that earlier wrote *intelligendum* subsequently displays *intellegendum*. It is therefore certain that we have sometimes taken the correct spelling from the Codices themselves.

4. The Codices almost always write *mici* for *mihi*, *catecizati* for *catechizati*, *nicilominus* for *nihilominus*, *inrationabiliter* for *irrationabiliter*, *conlatio* for *collatio*, *comunicare* for *communicare*, *anticus* for *antiquus*, and very many forms of this kind. We have restored all these and similar forms to correct orthography, as the character of the work required. Moreover, in the Codices themselves—even within a single Codex—we have repeatedly found the correct spelling of words, and we proclaim this three and four times over.

5. Titles were sometimes inserted into the canonical decrees themselves; we separated them. At other times no division was made between the decrees; we supplied one. Repeated words occur in certain places through the copyist’s drowsiness; we removed them. In other places decrees had been transposed; we restored them to their proper position. Yet we did none of these things on our own authority: the Codices themselves supplied the basis. Those who consult our notes will see this.

The *Excerpta Canonum*, which others have called the *Index*, are set out in ten books in the Codices. Since the eminent Aguirre and Cajetan Cenni had left these works published for posterity, it was not our intention simply to repeat them. But when, in comparing their text with ours, we observed excessive differences between the two, we were compelled to issue them publicly a third time, corrected and revised.

The rough and discordant verses, the title of synods held much later, a certain disorder in the words and subject matter, the inelegance of the decrees, and the occasionally obscure sense reveal that the author of the *Excerpta* lived many years after Saint Isidore.

The preface was taken from chapter 16 of book VI of Saint Isidore’s *Etymologies*, whether by the holy doctor himself or by some other compiler. The whole of that sixth chapter, almost in its entirety, appears as the preface; but the scribe removed from it whatever words seemed unsuitable to the subject.

Among learned men there has been a dispute concerning the words, “whose acts also are contained, deposited in this body”: whether the preface preceded that chapter of the *Etymologies*, or the chapter preceded the preface, so that one might determine from which source the words were transferred to the other. We abstain from uncertain matters. We have established, however, that the particle “also” is absent from the most ancient Codices of the works of the bishop of Seville.

You will find only one variant reading, in Vatican exemplar no. 5764, according to Arevalo’s statement in his edition of Saint Isidore’s works, where he reads: “whose acts, begun in this body, are contained.” What if we wished to compare the preface placed before our Codices with the one Isidore Mercator set before his work? Let those who undertake the comparison determine the result.

So that the reader may more easily find the canonical decrees of synods and decretal letters, we have prepared and compiled, for the public benefit, a most complete table of contents or index of all the subjects and matters included in the Spanish collection of canons.

It is now fitting, as the crown of this preface, to undertake an exact description of the most distinguished Codices. Let us begin with the most beautifully executed of all. The Alveldense is so called from the monastery of Albelda, not far from Lucronium, a celebrated city of the province of Ruconia or Rivogia. It is also commonly called the Vigilano, because it was written by a monk named Vigila.

Since we recently stated that Ambrosius de Morales had elucidated it, and since we wish our reliability to be commended to the reader in every respect, we reproduce from the autograph that scholar’s judgment concerning this remarkable volume:

> “This Codex must certainly be esteemed highly for many reasons and carefully preserved as a great treasure. Above all, even on account of its antiquity alone—which everywhere deserves veneration—it should be received with reverence. For it was written in the year 976 from the Lord’s Nativity and completed on the twenty-fifth day of May. The scribe himself bears witness to this at the end of the Codex, in more than one place and in more than one manner. The acrostic letters of the Asclepiad poem placed there, by which the verses come to an end, report the same fact; the poem itself recalls it; the following iambic poem repeats it; and the periods of the kings Sancho, Ramiro, and Urraca, who are named, confirm it. The Greeks call those letters acrostics which, when they begin or end verses, also perform the special function of signifying something by themselves. Thus, in the present year—1571 from the Lord’s Nativity, on the twenty-fourth day of May—five hundred and ninety-five years have elapsed since the Codex was completed.
>
> “Vigila wrote the Codex, a priest of the monastery of Saint Martin at Albelda, inhabited by two hundred monks. This is demonstrated in the same Asclepiad poem. He had as fellow scribes the priest Sarracino and also his disciple Garcia. The verses beginning with the acrostic letters of the same poem show this, and the picture placed at the end of the Codex, together with its inscriptions, also indicates it.
>
> “The contents of the entire book greatly increase its immense value. There is no doubt that many things in it are written with the greatest accuracy and that, if someone should undertake the labor—a pious task above all and very necessary for writings of such importance—it would wonderfully assist in correcting printed Codices. I could not express in a few words how greatly this Codex might benefit our own history, that is, the history of the Spaniards. But among its other exceptional features, and one that can never be sufficiently celebrated according to its worth, is this: it contains certain councils that have not yet been printed and perhaps will be found nowhere except here. Such are the council of Gundemar, king of the Goths, who succeeded Witteric; the Council of Zaragoza under King Egica; and certain others contained in the index we have appended.

> “It also contains the book of Gothic laws commonly called the *Forum of Judges*. Although not a few handwritten copies of that book are found throughout Spain, this one, on account of its great antiquity, easily surpasses all the others.
>
> “The painting itself, however deformed and however inelegant, can nevertheless teach us something: it allows us to understand, at least in part, what dress and adornment kings, bishops, priests, and monks wore in the scribe’s time, in what order everyone sat in council, and certain matters of a similar kind.

> “Index of everything contained throughout the book.
>
> “The second page of the first folio contains a picture of Vigila in the act of writing. Above it is written how greatly he was deterred by the difficulty of writing and with what spirit he finally began.
>
> “The following verses are trochaic; in them Vigila implores God’s assistance.
>
> “The next two folios contain an interwoven and self-returning form of writing, such as is seen in the epitaph of King Silo at Oviedo. The same text can be read if you proceed forward, retreat backward, follow the lower letters, follow the upper ones, or inspect the sides and corners across one another. In Vigila’s time this was regarded as an extraordinary display of ingenuity, and many people adopted and used it.
>
> [Col. 0019] “A brief Chronicle from the beginning of the world, with certain pictures.
>
> “A Computus, such as the holy Church customarily uses, extensively described and enlarged with many documents, with tables arranged for many years.
>
> “A discussion of the winds, with a picture.
>
> “Trees of consanguinity and affinity, with their explanations.
>
> “An index of all the councils, with certain pictures. The final one is almost an exact representation of the cross made at Oviedo by angels.
>
> “A summary of all the councils, written in ten books in heroic verse and arranged by commonplaces for the instruction of clergy and laity alike.
>
> “Up to this point everything seems to be, as it were, preliminary material and supplementary matter. What follows is the principal content of the entire book: the sacred councils, distributed not chronologically but by nations, with the councils held in each province brought together at the same time. Our own councils, that is, the Spanish ones, occupy the final place.
>
> “There are also many decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs.
>
> “The book of the blessed Isidore against the Jews.
>
> “A brief Chronicle up to Ramiro III.
>
> “An epitome of the books of the blessed Jerome, Gennadius, the blessed Isidore, and the blessed Ildefonsus concerning illustrious men.
>
> “A little book on the order for celebrating a council in Spain; but here it is not attributed to the blessed Isidore, as it is in printed books.
>
> “The *Forum of Judges*, containing the laws of the Goths. Here the book finally ends. What follows has been added as a conclusion.
>
> “A picture displaying Vigila and his assistants, together with the kings who ruled Spain in their time.
>
> “An Asclepiad poem in which Vigila prays to God both for himself and for his monastery, that is, the monastery of Saint Martin at Albelda. The acrostic letters, beginning and ending the verses, which we cited at the beginning, contain an iambic poem of almost the same subject, and the acrostic has almost the same writer. End.”

The Aemilianense parchment Codex imitates the Alveldense. It received this title or name because it was preserved several centuries ago in the monastery of Saint Aemilianus of La Cogolla. The clear form of its letters, the vivid colors of its painted images, and the inscription of more treatises than in most other Codices, as well as its antiquity itself, greatly commend it.

Sisebutus and Velasco wrote it. If you seek its era, you will find at the beginning a note that might allow you to assign it to the year 1000; but we do not place complete confidence in this inscription. It was not written by the same hand as the Codex, nor at the same time, nor in the fold of the leaf, but in the margin.

We judge this most distinguished Codex to be a few years later than the Alveldense, enriched with a greater number of ancient monuments, possessing the same order in the representation of figures, and finally written in the year 994, according to a note attached to it at the end. Here is a description of the contents of this exemplar.

At the beginning there is a very brief description of the ages of the year, the world, and the ages of history, or a concise chronology from the creation of the world up to the death of Jesus Christ the Savior.

A Computus for finding the moon at the beginning of Lent and Easter, adapted both to the Hebrews and to Christians.

A description of the art of arithmetic and its divisions.

A brief account of the origin of the world and of the leap year.

A very short treatise in which the etymology, direction, origin, and courses of the winds are represented by various human and fanciful figures at the author’s discretion.

A quadrant-shaped painting, represented in brilliant colors that have remained undimmed through so many centuries, which we suppose was made for ornament and without any meaning.

Twenty hendecasyllabic or heroic verses, containing, among other things, a prayer for the eternal salvation of Bishop Sisebutus and his nephew, called Velasco, on account of the highly useful books on imperial law that they composed.

An image of the Most High God, written with the mystical words Alpha and Omega, together with figures of the cherubim and seraphim and of the archangels Gabriel and Michael.

A representation of the tree of knowledge and of the first parents of the human race at the very giving of the noxious fruit.

A very brief ancient division of the world into Asia, Europe, and Africa.

A description of the earthly paradise and a little wheel indicating the four regions of the world.

A cross with an inscription that cannot be understood appropriately.

An excerpt of the canons and a most complete Codex of all the councils and decretal letters.

The book of the blessed Isidore on the kinds of ecclesiastical offices.

A letter of the blessed Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, to Laudefredus, bishop of Córdoba.

His book of prefaces concerning the books of the New and Old Testament.

The order for celebrating a council.

A catalogue of the bishops of the sees of Seville, Toledo, and Illiberis: of the church of Seville, from Marcellus to David Julianus; of Toledo, from Pelagius to John, who died in the era 964; and of Illiberis, from Caecilius to Gupius.

The Council of Aachen.

An ancient division of the Spanish lands, in which the provinces of Gallaecia, Lusitania, Baetica, Carthaginensis, Tarraconensis, and Gaul are represented.

The book called the *Register*, which contains certain letters and rescripts of Gregory the Great.

A Chronicle of the history of Spain, also including information about Muhammad, the false prophet.

The *Forum of Judges*, on whose final folio the figures or portraits of the nobles and kings who compiled it are represented.

Counsels and precepts that can be gathered from sacred Scripture concerning marriages between blood relatives, together with trees showing the degrees of agnation and cognation.

A table by which the beginning of Lent and Easter may be determined, together with another concerning the annual festivals. This completes the entire and most distinguished Codex.

It remains to note that this exemplar was copied by Garcia Loaisa under the name “the Sevillian.” That distinguished man wrongly called it Sevillian, for this Codex never belonged to Seville. The Codex that truly bore that name and title was burned and disappeared in the monastery of El Escorial on 7 June 1671.

We have seen a summary, in our vernacular language, of all the treatises of the Aemilianense Codex, made by Ambrosius de Morales.

Let us proceed to describe the very ancient canon-law exemplars of the Church of Toledo. The first and older of them is a parchment Codex of 315 folios, consisting of three columns on each folio, written in rounded Gothic characters by a certain priest named Julianus.

Although on the edge or margin of the first folio one may read that it began to be written on 19 January in the era 986, we do not think it should in any way be assigned to that date. We place greater confidence in the following note preserved in the text at the end of the Codex:

> “This book ends twenty-four days before the Kalends of April, in the era 1072. Julianus, an unworthy priest, wrote it in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Genesius, etc.”

No treatise other than the decrees of councils and letters may be observed in this Codex.

The second proper canon-law exemplar of the Church of Toledo, written in two columns and in letters not equally bright, was being copied in the city of Alcalá in the era 1133 by another Julianus, as is clear from the following final note:

> “This book of canons ends . . . happily. Thanks be to God. Julianus, an unworthy priest, wrote it—he to whom it belongs—with the Lord’s assistance, while living in Alcalá, which is situated above the Laudable Field, on Wednesday, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the era 1133.”

Father Andreas Merino discussed this Codex in his *Palaeography*, p. 136, though his account is not correct in every respect. We show that it contains only the acts of councils and the decrees of letters. Other monuments also exist in the Toledo treasury of Codices that could testify to our collection, but we omit their description because we have found that they belong to much later times.

A canon-law Codex is preserved in this public library of Madrid. It is mutilated at the beginning and end, marked with the letter P and the number 21, consists of 345 folios, and is written in extended Gothic characters. The form of its letters clearly shows that it was written at the end of the tenth or the beginning of the eleventh century.

We learned the following noteworthy fact about this distinguished Codex: although it is, like the others, full of common and easily recognizable errors, whenever the words containing the canonical decrees do not fit together properly, or the sense appears obscure and confused, it corrects and emends the other Codices.

On the back of the first folio one reads a letter of the blessed Pope Boniface, who was fourth after Gregory, in which it is asserted that monks may everywhere celebrate the priestly office.

A specimen of a labyrinth, decorated with various colors, is displayed at the front. Within it, through 187 little globes, the following words are inscribed and repeated many times through all the corners: “To the superior abbot the book.” We think the dedication of the Codex is contained in these words, although the reading may be *superiori*.

Several folios are missing from this volume; their absence is always noted in its proper place in our edition. This very ancient Codex contains excerpts of canons, synods, and decrees of the Roman prelates. Its scribe is entirely unknown to us. It is established, however, that the Codex belonged to D. Garcia Loaisa and was brought to this library from the monastery of the Friars Preachers of Saint Vincent at Plasencia.

We have assigned the designation “Third Escurial Codex”—because it belongs to the monastery of Saint Laurence—to another parchment canon-law Codex belonging to the same monastery after the Vigilano and Aemilianense. Since it is mutilated at the beginning and end, it gives us no indication by which we can determine when it was written.

Considering the form of its letters, we believe that we would not be far wrong if we assigned the writing of this volume to the final years of the tenth or the early years of the eleventh century. After incomplete excerpts of the canons, the tenth and eleventh councils of Toledo have been removed from their proper places; in all other respects anyone may see in this exemplar the sequence preserved by all the Codices.

We also examined another volume belonging to the library of the same monastery of Saint Laurence, which we have more conveniently designated “Fourth Escurial Codex.” It is written in clear letters, consists of 135 folios, is mutilated in every part, and we conjecture that it was written after the middle of the eleventh century.

Apart from the councils held in Spain, you will seek in vain for anything else in this Codex. You will likewise search in vain for all the decrees of the Roman prelates that are written in the other Codices.

A parchment volume also belonging to the Church of Urgel, consisting of 292 folios, contributed great authority to this collection. In its first four folios the careful investigator will read a letter of Saint Clement to James, the brother of the Lord, deserving of the fullest and most attentive examination by any learned man; a decree of the blessed Gregory issued in the basilica of the Apostle Peter in the presence of twenty-three bishops and thirty-three priests; and canon four of the twelfth Council of Toledo.

He will immediately notice, however, that these four folios were newly sewn in and placed before the rest. The whole Codex does not appear to have been written by one hand. Nevertheless, it contains the complete collection of canons, except for certain omissions that are always noted in their proper places.

Although no trace of the era in which it was committed to writing can be found in it, anyone who considers the form of its letters and compares it with other distinctive and ancient monuments of the same church will not be far from certainty if he assigns it to the end of the tenth or the beginning of the eleventh century.

A Codex belonging to the Church of Girona, bound in parchment and consisting of 389 folios, was available to us. Its first folio, added later and better described as the volume’s wrapper, contains the confirmation of the peace and truce established at the Council of Girona in the year 1068.

The second folio—in reality the first folio of the Codex—displays the division of the provinces and metropolitan sees. The titles of the councils, letters, and canons are found shining in vivid red colors. But the scribe’s name could nowhere be discovered.

Anyone who wishes to compare the Urgel Codex with this one and read through our more extensive notes will recognize that they are exceedingly similar. We therefore conjecture that the Girona Codex was written not long afterward, certainly in the latter half of the eleventh century. Certain collections have been added to it after the decretal letters.

We stated long ago that the Sevillian Codex and, in addition, the Lucense Codex had passed from the hands of learned men into the devouring flames that ravaged the library of El Escorial in 1671; but neither their memory nor their writings have perished.

With the greatest gratitude and affection we can express, we honor Juan Bautista Pérez and Juan Vázquez del Mármol, who took care to leave to posterity a complete description of everything contained in those exemplars. Father Fr. Emmanuel Risco made this publicly available in volume 40 of *Sacred Spain*.

In 1807 we were permitted to see and compare the autograph written by Juan Mármol in the library of R. Flórez. We now grieve—and grieve bitterly—that it has perished through the vicissitudes of human affairs and adverse fortune.

A different Codex belonging to the library of El Escorial, which appears to have belonged to Hieronymus Zurita according to a note engraved in his own hand, was seen and compared with the Alveldense by the learned D. Blasius Nasarre. We have also examined his observations for this edition.

That exemplar contained only seventeen councils of Toledo and the decrees of King Ferdinand I. The Sevillian and Lucense Codices were wholly harmonious, uniform, and entirely consistent with the exemplars that survived the fire. The most learned men testify that the former was written at the beginning of the tenth century and the latter after the year 1031.

We have designated the Codices we used in the body of the work or in the notes by initial letters, as the following table shows:

| Siglum | Meaning |
|---|---|
| A | The Alveldense, or Vigilano, Codex |
| Ae | The Aemilianense |
| T. 1 | The First Toledo Codex |
| T. 2 | The Second Toledo Codex |
| B. R. | A Codex of the Royal Library |
| E. 3 | The Third Escurial Codex |
| E. 4 | The Fourth Escurial Codex |
| U | The Urgel Codex |
| G | The Girona Codex |

[Col. 0023]

These, then, are the most ancient, celebrated, and most carefully preserved Codices. From them, as from the purest springs, we have attempted to issue the ancient canonical doctrine of the Spanish Church into the public domain.

We hope that our labor will be pleasing to pious and learned men, salutary to faithful peoples, highly useful for fostering uprightness, and finally most honorable to the Iberian region.

Written at Madrid, on the day before the Ides of September, in the year of the Lord 1821.

[Col. 0024] Franciscus Antonius Gonzalez, prefect of the Public Library of Madrid.

[Col. 0023]

## IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER AND OF THE SON AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, THE BOOK OF CANONS BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0023C] Aem., Toledo I: “The Book of Canons begins in the threefold, simple divine name.”] (C, G)*

## A VERSE DIALOGUE AND QUESTIONING OF THE READER CONCERNING THE CODEX

[Col. 0023A]

**I.** [Note: This sign indicates the reader’s question.]

You Codex, who are set in a lofty, fearsome seat—  
who are you?

**R.** [Note: This sign designates the Codex’s response.]

The vital order.

**I.** What name belongs to you?

**R.** I am called the heavenly rule of the saints.

**I.** Who are those by whom you are commanded to be designated under this title?

**R.** Those who hold the imperial law of the whole world.

**I.** You, whom the judgment of so many powerful nobles forms,  
what are you able to decree? What power lies beneath your authority?

**R.** O slender client, wavering in a tender heart!  
Fame has made me renowned throughout the whole world.

**I.** And why does this pitiable old age shelter you in concealment?

**R.** If you wish to know me, turn wholly toward me,  
and readily immerse yourself wholly in my mysteries.

Listen now to what my signs can bring forth;  
and if you possess the ability to recognize what is right in this way,

[Col. 0023B]

I announce to earth the truth held in heaven.  
I send earthborn people to heaven, commanding them to leave the earth.

Standing on high, I lower the necks of those who stand erect,  
while I command that lofty laws be arranged against sins.

Stationed on a height, I am carried aloft from a lofty citadel,  
while, strong in sacred order, I press down all things placed beneath me.

It is fitting that a truthful assembly should proclaim me with distinction,  
while, as I resound, all things soon fall silent together.

All things tremble while I impose laws of trembling upon all.  
The powerful fear me; the great are commanded to obey me.

Schism perishes, error recoils, deceit is absent.  
The obscene flees, the impure falls, the ungodly is cast out.

Gluttony falls; there will be no drunkard; pomp withdraws.

I command that heads not be bowed to stones,  
nor incense offered to demons.

There will be no other creator of things,  
nor will a creature give the Creator’s work its honor.

I arrange all things in order; I govern all things in order.  
Strong in orders, I make everything beautiful according to order.

[Col. 0024A]

I proclaim the holy faith; I bestow the holy mysteries:

the altar, the temple, the vestment, the vessel, the honor of the seat;  
the chrism, the sacred flesh and blood, the consecrated baptism;

the doorkeeper, acolyte, reader, and melodious psalmist;  
the powerful exorcist, and the lesser-ranking levite;

the levite strong in voice, the bishop and the priest;  
the blessed Virgin, the yoke of the married woman,  
and the celibate, reclining widow;

and all those who are considered to possess the faith and name of God.

Distinguished by my orders, they remain most renowned  
and preserve their form, marked off by my boundary.

Although all these could exist, complete in their own causes,  
nevertheless all are ordered by my commands.

**I.** I ask you: allow me to tell, by myself, what I desire,  
if you grant me the right to speak.

[Col. 0024B]

**R.** Say whatever you wish, and hold your vows firm in your heart.

**I.** After I wished to know you and was able to understand you,  
and after you granted me knowledge of your sublime power,

I plainly desire enough to turn your commands over with you.  
And if God grants me the ability to know, to search out the depths,

so that I may gather into my recesses you who are scattered like seed through the world of words,

and, taking you up with the sharpness of my mind,  
compress you, though extended through a body of many parts,

and, gathering the scattered discussions, bind them into one,

so that, while a divided opinion seeks judgment,  
agreement may provide everything that anyone desires;

and thus, filling a new body with its original limbs,  
I may fashion brief summaries for slow-witted minds—

**R.** [T. 1: “great one”; the reading is uncertain.] As you please, unknowing one, proceed swiftly; let no leisure delay you.

[Col. 0024C]

If you accomplish it fully, you will do what is beneficial everywhere.  
May God be with you as, through me, you gather together these scattered things,  
so that you may fashion in me summaries worthy of many.

# EXCERPTS OF THE CANONS CONTAINED IN TEN BOOKS

## BOOK ONE: ON THE INSTITUTIONS OF CLERICS

[Col. 0025]

## TITLE I. Those Who Are Not to Be Ordained Clerics

[Col. 0025A]

Concerning eunuchs who mutilate themselves. Council of Nicaea, title 1, chapter 1.

Likewise, concerning those who mutilate themselves or are mutilated by others. In Martin’s *Excerpts*, title 21, chapter 64.

Likewise, concerning those who mutilate themselves. Second Council of Arles, title 7, chapter 22.

Likewise, concerning those who mutilate themselves. General Decree of Gelasius 82, title 5.

If anyone, willingly, cuts off a part of his own body, he cannot be a cleric. Letter of Innocent to Felix 9, title 5.

Concerning those who do not know letters and those who have lost a bodily part. General Decree of Gelasius 82, title 18.

A layman whose wife is adulterous shall not be a cleric. But if the husband of an adulterous wife is a cleric, let him either repudiate her or withdraw from the clergy. Council of Neocaesarea, title 8, chapter 3.

Concerning those whose wives commit adultery, that they should not be clerics. [Col. 0025B] In Martin’s *Excerpts*, title 28, chapter 64.

A bishop who promotes into the clergy the husband of a widow or a divorced woman shall be deposed. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 69, chapter 15.

Laymen who, after their wife, have had relations with any other woman shall not be admitted to the clergy. Council of Girona, title 8, chapter 60.

Concerning those who marry widows or divorced women, or who have been involved in evil counsels. In Martin’s *Excerpts*, title 26, chapter 64.

That those who profess virginity, if they commit adultery, are to be counted among the twice-married. Council of Ancyra, title 18, chapter 2.

That if a layman marries a widow, he shall not be a cleric. Letter of Innocent to Victor 7, title 5.

He who marries a second wife shall not be a cleric. Letter of the same to the same, title 6.

That men married twice cannot be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Innocent to Felix 9, title 2.

That a man married twice, or the husband of a widow or a corrupted woman, shall not be a cleric. Synodal Decree of Hilary 74, title 2.

Concerning men married twice and almost all persons who are not to be clerics. General Decree of Gelasius 82, title 5.

Concerning men married twice, that they are not to be consecrated into the clergy. Council of Valence, title 3, chapter 45.

That if a priest or anyone from the clergy marries a widow or a repudiated woman, he is neither to be admitted to the clergy nor to remain in it. Letter of Innocent to Rufus 26, title 1.

Concerning clerics who marry a widow or a second wife, that they are to be deprived of every dignity. Letter of Siricius to Himerius 3, title 11.

That anyone promoted to the priesthood who is the husband of a widow or has contracted numerous marriages is to be barred from ecclesiastical offices. Letter of Leo to all the bishops throughout Campania and the various provinces, 64, title 2.

Concerning those who were found incontinent before they were ordained. Council of Orange, title 24, chapter 27.

[Col. 0025D] That if a monk becomes a cleric, he should preserve his profession; and that no monk or cleric who, after baptism, has become defiled may have both a wife and ecclesiastical rank. [Col. 0026A] Letter of Innocent to Victor 7, title 10.

He who had a wife before baptism and married another after baptism shall not become a cleric. Letter of Innocent to all those in Toulouse 27, title 6.

Men of unexamined life, or those who take a corrupted wife, shall not be clerics. Letter of Siricius to Himerius 3, title 8.

A catechumen who takes another wife after the washing shall not be a cleric; and in baptism sins alone are forgiven, not the number of wives erased. Letter of Innocent to Victor 7, title 6.

Concerning the discernment of penitents: who may be advanced to ecclesiastical honors and who may not. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 54, chapter 49.

Concerning the discernment of freedmen: who may attain ecclesiastical honors and who are forbidden promotion. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 73, chapter 49.

Concerning freedmen belonging to the households of the Church: whether and how they are to be promoted to the priesthood, and what is to be done with their property. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 74, chapter 49.

A cleric ordained from among the penitents shall be deposed. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 68, chapter 15.

That men married twice, penitents, or husbands of divorced women are not to be promoted to the clergy. Third Council of Arles, title 3, chapter 23.

A penitent shall not be a cleric. A deacon likewise shall not minister, nor shall a priest consecrate the altar. Council of Agde, title 43, chapter 30.

Concerning penitents [Note: From these words the Codex of the Royal Library begins.] or men married twice or husbands of widows: they are not [Note: The Royal Library and Toledo Codices 1 and 2 read *ne*, “not.”] to be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Siricius to Himerius 3, title 15.

That penitents who are ignorant of letters, or who have bodily defects, amputations, or some other deficiency, shall not be clerics. Synodal Decree of Hilary 74, title 3.

That after penance no one can be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Innocent to Agapius and the others, in full, 11.

That those involved in other people’s affairs are not to become [Col. 0026C] clerics before rendering an account. Council of Carthage I, title 8, chapter 12.

That no one may make a person bound to another a cleric without the consent of his master or patron. Council of Toledo I, title 10, chapter 46.

Concerning those bound by conditions, who are not to be ordained without the consent of their master or patron. In the Excerpts of Martin, title 46, chapter 64.

Those who were patrons in the world are not to be advanced to the clergy. [Note: [Col. 0026D] In A., Ae., and Bib. R., this and the following title are absent. They are taken from T. 1.] Letter of Innocent to Victor, 7, title 11.

A person of servile origin is to be ordained without his master’s consent. Decree of Gelasius, general, 82, title 16.

Those from the municipal curiae, or those who hold assigned public functions, are not to be clerics, because of the pleasures of the devil. Letter of Innocent to Victor, 7, title 11.

Concerning faithful laymen who have conducted lawsuits or administered them. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, 8, title 3.

Advocates, members of the municipal curiae, and those devoted to secular military service are not to be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Innocent to all [Col. 0026D] in Toulouse, 27, title 2.

Those baptized immediately after baptism are not to be attached to the clergy; [Col. 0027A] and those who previously committed a mortal sin are not to be clerics. Council of Nicaea, title 2, chapter 1.

Those rebaptized are not to be advanced to any clerical rank. Council of Carthage V, title 11, chapter 16.

Concerning those baptized or rebaptized by heretics, so that they may not attain to ecclesiastical service. Letter of Felix to the bishops throughout Sicily, 79, title 5.

Neophytes, that is, the newly baptized, are not immediately to become clerics. In the Excerpts of Martin, title 22, chapter 64.

Those who after baptism have taken up the belt of secular military service are not to be clerics. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 7, title 2.

Concerning magistrates and duumvirs, that they are not to be advanced to the clergy. Council of Eliberis, title 56, chapter 38.

Seditious persons and usurers are not to be clerics, nor are they to become such in any way. Council of Carthage IV, title 67, chapter 15. [Note: [Col. 0027D] B. R., “are ever to become so.”]

Concerning heretics, that they are not to be advanced to the clergy. Council of Eliberis, title 51, chapter 38.

[Col. 0027B] Concerning criminals, that they are not to be advanced to the clergy. Decree of Gelasius, general, chapter 82, title 20.

The possessed, that is, those who have been openly seized, and likewise those who are found [to be so], are to be rejected. Council of Orange, title 16, chapter 27.

Those baptized abroad are not to be clerics. Council of Eliberis, title 24, chapter 38.

That demoniacs and others entangled in afflictions are not permitted to handle the sacred ministries. Decree of Gelasius, general, 82, title 21.

Concerning nearly all the persons who are not to be clerics. Letter of Innocent to all in Toulouse, 27, title 4.

Concerning the reproach of the Spaniards who appoint clerics irregularly. Letter of Innocent to all in Toulouse, 27, title 1.

## TITLE II. Concerning the profession and marriages of clerics

That clerics, when they reach puberty, are to profess either marriage or chastity. Council of Carthage III, title 19, chapter 14.

[Col. 0027C] That a cleric may not take a wife of another sect, unless perhaps he has promised that he will come to the true faith. Council of Chalcedon, title 14, chapter 11.

Concerning those whom their parents have dedicated from infancy to the clerical office, if afterward they wish to marry. Council of Toledo II, title 1, chapter 47.

Concerning the kinds of women whom clerics may suitably marry, and what is to be done if a cleric takes a wife without the bishop’s knowledge. Council of Toledo IV, title 44, chapter 49.

Concerning the wives of clerics. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 3, title 9.

That clerics are to be joined to virgins and are not to take either a widow or a rejected woman. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 7, title 4.

## TITLE III. Concerning the wives of clerics

Concerning adulterous wives of clerics. Council of Eliberis, title 65, chapter 38.

[Col. 0027D] That a cleric whose wife has sinned has power, apart from killing her, to discipline her, and is not to eat with her. Council of Toledo I, title 7, chapter 46.

## TITLE IV. Concerning the children of the entire clerical order

The children of clerics are not to attend public spectacles. Council of Carthage III, title 12, chapter 14.

The children of clerics of any order are under no circumstances to be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics. Council of Carthage III, title 12, chapter 14.

Clerics of any order are not to allow their children to leave their authority unless their age and conduct have been tested and approved. Council of Carthage III, title 14, chapter 14.

The children of clerics are not to be baptized or reside among heretics. Council of Chalcedon, title 14, chapter 11.

If the religious daughter of a priest or deacon has sinned, she is to receive communion only at the end of life. [Col. 0028A] Council of Toledo I, title 19, chapter 45.

Concerning the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been consecrated and has sinned. Council of Braga II, title 30, chapter 64.

Concerning the condemnation of children proven to have been born of priests and ministers. Council of Toledo IX, title 10, chapter 54.

## TITLE V. Concerning the inheritances of clerics

Clerics of every order are not to transfer any of their property in writing to unbelievers, even if they are relatives. Council of Carthage III, title 13, chapter 14.

Concerning bishops who leave their possessions to heirs outside their family, or to heretical or pagan relatives: if they have contributed nothing to the Church, their names are not to be recited at the altar, and after their death an anathema is to be pronounced against them. For they will have no excuse from receiving condemnation even if they have died [Col. 0028B] intestate, because at the time of their consecration they did not make an arrangement of their own property appropriate to their profession. Council of Carthage V, title 14, chapter 16.

## TITLE VI. Concerning the widows of clerics

If the widow of a presbyter or deacon joins herself to anyone, either they are to be separated after correction, or they are to be punished with excommunication. Council of Orléans I, title 9, chapter 31.

If the widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon marries, she is not to live with any Christian and is to receive communion only at the end of life. In the Excerpts of Martin, title 29, chapter 64.

If the widow of a priest or Levite takes a husband, she is to receive communion only at the end of life. Council of Toledo I, title 18, chapter 46.

## TITLE VII. Concerning the service of the Church and of clerics

That the servants of the Church or of clerics are not to be harassed with any forced labor by judges or officials. [Note: [Col. 0028D] Ae., “exactors.”] [Col. 0028C] Council of Toledo III, title 21, chapter 48.

## TITLE VIII. Concerning the emancipation and freedom of freeborn and servile clerics

Concerning the release of freeborn clerics from labor or undifferentiated obligations. Council of Toledo IV, title 47, chapter 49.

That no one from the fiscal estates is ever to be requested by the king from the clergy; and if anyone has received such a person, the donation is to remain invalid. Council of Toledo III, title 8, chapter 48.

That bishops are to grant freedom to servile clerics. Council of Toledo IX, title 11, chapter 54.

## TITLE IX. Concerning the stipends of clerics

Clerics, however learned, are to seek their livelihood by a craft. Council of Carthage IV, title 51, chapter 15.

How clerics are to seek their food and clothing. [Col. 0028D] Council of Carthage IV, title 52, chapter 15.

That the stipends of clerics are to be distributed according to merit. Council of Agde, title 36, chapter 30.

## TITLE X. Concerning clerics not to be ordained absolutely

That no clerics whatsoever ought to be ordained absolutely except for a particular church. Council of Chalcedon, title 6, chapter 11.

That a person is to remain where he has been ordained. Council of Arles I, title 2, chapter 21.

## TITLE XI. Ordinations of clerics not to be performed without testimony

Clerics are not to be ordained unless they are approved by the testimony of the bishop and the people. Council of Carthage III, title 22, chapter 14.

Clerics are not to be ordained without the testimony and consent of [Col. 0029A] the clerics and citizens. Council of Carthage IV, title 22, chapter 15.

## TITLE XII. Concerning the election, times, and ranks of clerics

Concerning those whom their parents have dedicated from infancy to the clerical office: at what time they are to begin being raised to honors, and whether, if they violate their professed continence, they are to be regarded as sacrilegious. Council of Toledo II, title 1, chapter 47.

Concerning those who do not undertake public penance but receive only viaticum, so that they may be advanced in the clergy. Council of Gerona, title 9, chapter 40.
