If women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious women. In the work cited above, title 4.

A wife is one thing and a concubine another; and anyone who gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine must not err. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 66, title 4.

It is not a duplication of marriage when a slave woman is dismissed and a wife is taken. In the work cited above, title 5.

## TITLE II. Concerning the right to marry and those who impede chastity

Concerning widows and virgins: those who wish to do so should maintain continence, while those who choose to marry may marry whomever they wish; and concerning the excommunication of those who impede a resolve to chastity. Third Council of Toledo, [Col. 0074D] title 10, canon 48.

## TITLE III. Concerning abductors

Concerning betrothed girls who have been violated by others: they are to be restored to their betrothed, even at the cost of their modesty. Council of Ancyra, title 11, canon 2.

Concerning those who abduct wives for themselves or provide them assistance. Council of Chalcedon, title 27, canon 11.

Concerning abductors who take refuge in a church. First Council of Orléans, title 2, canon 31.

Concerning abductors of widows and virgins. Letter of Symmachus to Caesarius, 85, title 3.

## TITLE IV. Concerning broken marriages

Concerning laypeople: without the judgment of a bishop, they must not leave culpable spouses. Council of Agde, title 25, canon 30.

[Col. 0075A] Neither a dismissed husband nor a dismissed wife may join themselves to another. Council of Milevis, title 17, canon 19.

If someone’s wife has committed adultery, he must not take another. First Council of Arles, title 10, canon 21.

Concerning women who leave their husbands and marry others. Council of Elvira, title 8, canon 38.

Concerning women who leave adulterous husbands and marry others. In the work cited above, title 9.

That those who, after a repudiation, have undergone divorce, if they bind themselves in another marriage, are shown to be adulterers. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius of Toulouse, 8, title 6.

## TITLE V. Concerning second and repeated marriages

Second marriages are not to be denied to laypeople, although such persons are by no means to be admitted to the clergy. General decree of Gelasius, 82, title 24.

A priest may not pray over a second marriage. [Col. 0075B] Council of Neocaesarea, title 7, canon 3.

Concerning priests: they must not enter into second marriages. In the excerpts of Martin, title 38, canon 64.

Concerning those who rush into many marriages. In the excerpts of Martin, title 80, canon 64.

Those who marry lawfully for a second time are not to communicate unless they repent. Council of Laodicea, title 1, canon 7.

## TITLE VI. Concerning secular virgins who commit adultery and must not live with other men

Concerning secular virgins if they commit adultery. Council of Elvira, title 14, canon 38.

Concerning girls who wish to live with certain men. Council of Ancyra, title 19, canon 2.

## TITLE VII. Concerning those who repeatedly commit adultery

Concerning one who, while having a wife, repeatedly commits adultery. Council of Elvira, title 47, canon 38.

[Col. 0075C] Concerning married men who afterward fall into adultery. Council cited above, title 69.

If one who has a wife keeps a concubine, he must not communicate. First Council of Toledo, title 17, canon 46.

Although husbands do not consort with adulterous wives, the Christian religion condemns adultery in both sexes. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, 8, title 4.

Concerning those who, after baptism, have at all times been devoted to the pleasures of incontinence and seek repentance at the end of life. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, 8, title 2.

## TITLE VIII. Concerning adultery, separation, and the procuring of sexual relations among married people

A layman whose wife has committed adultery must not take another wife. First Council of Arles, title 20, canon 21.

Concerning laypeople who abandon their wives. Council of Agde, title 25, canon 30.

Concerning the wife left by a catechumen if he takes another; but if the woman being taken is a believer and knows that the man is leaving an innocent wife, she may communicate at the end of life. Council of Elvira, title 10, canon 38.

Concerning women who act as procurers. Council cited above, title 12.

Concerning women who commit adultery with other men until death. Council of Elvira, title 64, canon 38.

A faithful female catechumen must not have long-haired men or hairdressers (*cinerarii*). Council cited above, title 67.

Concerning women who commit adultery with the knowledge of their husbands. Council cited above, title 70.

Concerning married believers if they commit adultery with Jews or gentiles. Council cited above, title 78.

If someone’s wife has committed adultery, he shall do penance for seven years. In the excerpts of Martin, title 76, canon 64.

## TITLE IX. Concerning reciprocal affection between parents and children

No one should neglect his children on account of continence. Council of Gangra, title 15, canon 4.

[Col. 0076A] Children should not despise their parents on the pretext of religion. Council cited above, title 16.

## TITLE X. Concerning parents who kill their children

Concerning women who, having committed fornication, kill their offspring. Council of Ancyra, title 21, canon 2.

Concerning an adulterous female catechumen who kills her son. Council of Elvira, title 68, canon 38.

If anyone kills his children, he is to be restrained by priests or judges. Third Council of Toledo, title 17, canon 48.

Concerning fornicating women who cause abortion or act against conception. In the excerpts of Martin, title 77, canon 64.

Concerning wives who kill children conceived in adultery. Council of Elvira, title 63, canon 38.

Concerning those who cause abortion or destroy their newborn children. Council of Ilerda, title 2, canon 44.

## TITLE XI. Concerning exposed infants

[Col. 0076B]

Whoever finds an exposed child must notify the church. First Council of Vaison, title 9, canon 28.

Whoever reclaims an exposed child before the prescribed time is to be regarded as a murderer. Council cited above, title 10.

Concerning exposed children who are found: the established rule is to be observed. Council of Agde, title 24, canon 30.

## TITLE XII. Concerning incestuous marriages

Concerning incestuous marriages. Council of Agde, title 61, canon 30.

Concerning incestuous unions: they are to be excommunicated. First Council of Orléans, title 14, canon 31.

Concerning those who are joined to two sisters. Council of Elvira, title 61, canon 38.

Concerning incestuous persons: as long as they remain in their crime, they are to be counted among the catechumens. Council of Ilerda, title 4, canon 44.

[Col. 0076C] Concerning those who join themselves to close relatives: they are to be separated from the communion of Christ. Second Council of Toledo, title 5, canon 47.

Concerning a woman who has two brothers in marriage, or a man who has two sisters. In the excerpts of Martin, title 79, canon 64.

Concerning those who marry their stepdaughters. Council of Elvira, title 66, canon 38.

A woman may not marry two brothers, nor a man two sisters. Council of Neocaesarea, title 3, canon 3.

## TITLE XIII. Concerning corrupters of boys

Concerning corrupters of boys. Council of Elvira, title 71, canon 38.

## TITLE XIV. Concerning those who have intercourse with animals

Concerning those who have mingled themselves with animals. In the excerpts of Martin, title 81, canon 64.

[Col. 0076D] Concerning those who have lived irrationally. Council of Ancyra, title 16, canon 2.

Concerning those who have lived like dumb animals: they are to pray among the demoniacs. Council cited above, title 17.

## TITLE XV. Concerning the observance of vanities

Concerning those who observe omens, auspices, dreams, and other such things according to the custom of the gentiles. Council of Ancyra, title 24, canon 2.

Concerning those who serve omens, incantations, or Jewish superstitions. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 89, canon 15.

Concerning diviners and those who observe omens: they are to be separated from the Church. Council of Agde, title 42, canon 30.

Concerning diviners and sorcerers. In the excerpts of Martin, title 71, canon 64.

Christians may not attend to various observances. Council cited above, title 72, canon 64.

[Col. 0077A] Concerning the fact that it is not permitted to observe the Kalends. Council cited above, title 73.

Concerning the fact that it is not permitted to gather medicinal herbs with any observance. Council cited above, title 74.

Concerning the fact that Christian women may not observe anything in their weaving. Council cited above, title 75.

Concerning religious and secular persons who attend to divinations. First Council of Orléans, title 26, canon 31.

## TITLE XVI. Concerning involuntary killings

Concerning those who have committed homicide unwillingly. Council of Ancyra, title 23, canon 2.

If a mistress kills a female slave out of jealousy, intentionally or by accident. Council of Elvira, title 5, canon 38, and in the excerpts of Martin, title 78, canon 64.

## TITLE XVII. Concerning voluntary murderers and false witnesses, adulterers and thieves, and those who take refuge in a church

[Col. 0077B]

Concerning those who have committed homicide intentionally. Council of Ancyra, title 22, canon 2.

Concerning murderers and false witnesses: they must not communicate. Council of Agde, title 37, canon 30.

Concerning those who kill their slaves without a judge. Council cited above, title 62.

Concerning murderers, adulterers, and thieves if they take refuge in a church. [Col. 0078A] First Council of Orléans, title 1, canon 31.

If anyone kills a person through sorcery. Council of Elvira, title 6, canon 38.

Concerning those who inflict death upon themselves through any negligence: their commemoration is not to be made in the offering; likewise concerning those who are punished for their crimes. First Council of Braga, title 16, canon 63.

Concerning intentional and unintentional homicide. In the excerpts of Martin, title 78, canon 64.

## TITLE XVIII. Concerning those who take refuge in a church, and concerning clerical slaves, who are not to be seized on their behalf

Concerning slaves who take refuge in a church: after an oath, if they refuse to leave, it is permitted to seize them. First Council of Orléans, title 3, canon 31.

Concerning those who take refuge in a church: they must not be handed over. Council of Orange, title 15, canon 27.

No one may seize the slaves of clerics in exchange for his own slaves who have taken refuge in a church. Council [Col. 0078B] cited above, title 6.

If a cleric drags a slave or pupil from a church so that he may do penance. Council of Ilerda, title 8, canon 44.

Concerning those who, although ordered by the bishop, contemptuously refuse to leave the church after their guilt has been set aside. Council cited above, title 10.

Concerning those who take refuge in a church. Twelfth Council of Toledo, title 10, canon 57.

# BOOK SIX. CONCERNING THE GENERAL RULES OF CLERICS AND OTHER CHRISTIANS, AND PRINCELY GOVERNMENT

[Col. 0077]

## TITLE I. Concerning the instruction of the people

[Col. 0077B]

[Col. 0077C] The people are to be taught, not followed. Letter of Celestine to the bishops throughout Apulia, 35, title 3.

The petition of the people must not be thought decisive, and the will of the Lord is to be sought. Letter of Hilary to Ascanus and all the people of Tarragona, 75, title 4.

A layman must not teach in the presence of clerics. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 98, canon 15.

## TITLE II. Concerning assembling at church

Concerning those who, neglecting the church, go to spectacles. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 88, canon 15.

Concerning those who arrive at church late. Council of Elvira, title 21, canon 38.

The greater solemnities are to be celebrated by laypeople in the cities without exception. Council of Agde, title 21, canon 30.

Concerning laypeople who do not come into the city on the greater solemnities. Council cited above, title 63.

No citizen may celebrate the greater festivals in a village. [Col. 0077D] First Council of Orléans, title 21, canon 31.

No one may withdraw from the church during the three weeks before Epiphany. First Council of Zaragoza, title 4, canon 41.

Concerning the times at which laypeople ought to communicate. Council of Agde, title 18, canon 30.

Concerning those who, upon entering the church, abstain from the sacrament because of excessive indulgence. In the excerpts of Martin, title 83, canon 64.

## TITLE III. Concerning certain rules

Concerning not permitting laypeople to command religious persons. Tenth Council of Toledo, title 3, canon 55.

That, out of necessity, the sin of the people is customarily allowed to pass unpunished in the church. Letter of Innocent to Rufus, 26, title 6.

Concerning those who place defamatory libels in a church. Council of Elvira, title 52, canon 38.

[Col. 0078B] No Christian is permitted to bathe together with women. Council of Laodicea, title 30, canon 7.

Concerning men and women who have given their garments to adorn the pomp [Col. 0078C] of the world. Council of Elvira, title 57, canon 38.

Concerning those who play board games. Council cited above, title 79.

Concerning the fact that Christians are permitted to carry meals to tombs. In the excerpts of Martin, title 69, canon 64.

Concerning the continent and the use of cloaks. Council of Gangra, title 12, canon 4.

Christians who are laypeople, no less than clerics, ought not to exact interest. Letter of Leo to all, 64, title 3.

Those who throw down their weapons in peacetime are to be excommunicated. First Council of Arles, title 3, canon 21.

Charioteers are to be excommunicated while they are driving. Council cited above, title 4.

Those who assemble in theaters are to be excommunicated. Council cited above, title 5.

Concerning the excommunication of faithful charioteers and theatrical performers. Second Council of Arles, title 20, canon 22.

Concerning charioteers and pantomimes if they convert. Council [Col. 0078D] of Elvira, title 62, canon 38.

## TITLE IV. Concerning discord and the offerings of clerics and laypeople

If bishops are in disagreement and the fear of God does not reconcile them, a synod shall do so. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 25, canon 15.

Bishops must compel dissenting clerics or laypeople to make peace. Council cited above, title 26.

Concerning those who, out of hatred, do not return to peace. Council of Agde, title 31, canon 30.

Concerning those who bind themselves by oath not to return to peace. Council of Ilerda, title 7, canon 44.

The offerings of brothers who are in disagreement are not to be received. Fourth Council of Carthage, title 93, canon 15.

## TITLE V. Concerning the discernment of abstinence from meat

Clerics may abstain from meat, not as something accursed but after having tasted it, if they wish. In the excerpts of Martin, title 58, canon 64.

[Col. 0079A] Concerning clerics of every rank abstaining from meat. Council of Ancyra, title 14, canon 2.

Concerning those who condemn anyone who eats meat other than that sacrificed to an idol, strangled meat, and blood. Council of Gangra, title 2, canon 4.

Concerning clerics abstaining from eating meat. First Council of Braga, title 14, canon 63.

Concerning the condemnation of the Priscillianists, who abstain from meat. Letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, 96, title 1.

One should abstain from the flesh of birds and animals not as something accursed but for the chastisement of the body. First Council of Toledo, from the rules of the Catholic faith, title 17, canon 46.

### Rules for women

[Col. 0080A]

Concerning letters from women. Council of Elvira, title 81, canon 38.

Faithful women must separate themselves from gatherings of unrelated men. First Council of Zaragoza, title 1, canon 41.

A woman must not assume male dress for the sake of continence. Council of Gangra, title 13, canon 4.

A woman may not shave her head. Council cited above, title 17.

Women must not keep vigil in cemeteries. Council of Elvira, title 35, canon 38.

[Col. 0079]

## TITLE I. Concerning the reverence to be shown by princes to God’s priests

[Col. 0079B]

Concerning the address of the emperor Marcian to the holy Council of Chalcedon. Beginning of this council, canon 11.

Address of the prince Reccared to the holy Council of Toledo. Beginning of the Third Council of Toledo, canon 48.

A reference to the address of the prince Sisenand to the Council of Toledo. Beginning of the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 49.

A reference to the address of the prince Chintila to the Council of Toledo. Beginning of the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 50.

Address of the prince Receswinth to the Council of Toledo, together with an exposition of the holy faith and the remedy of piety brought forward against the institution of parental severity. Beginning of the Eighth Council of Toledo, canon 53.

## TITLE II. How princes are to be chosen

[Col. 0079C] Concerning the election of princes. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 75, canon 49.

Concerning praise of the prince Reccared, because through him the Gothic people were converted to the Catholic faith. Letter of Gregory to King Reccared, canon 100, title 1.

Concerning the constitution of the same prince, that it was not corrupted by gold. Letter of the same to the person mentioned above, title 3.

Concerning the favor granted to princes by the acclamation of the council. Fifth Council of Toledo, title 9, canon 50.

Concerning thanksgiving offered to God and the prince at the confirmation of the council. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 19, canon 51.

That princes should have humility of heart. Letter of Gregory to King Reccared, canon 100, title 4.

[Col. 0079D] That princes should pursue bodily chastity. Letter of the same to the person mentioned above, title 5.

That princes should be moderate and gentle toward their subjects. Of the same to the person mentioned above, title 6.

Where the emperor is admonished to obey the decrees of the apostolic see, with an evident rebuke. Letter of Anastasius to Anastasius Augustus, 84, title 6.

That the emperor should admonish the Alexandrians to return to sincere faith and Catholic peace. Letter of Anastasius to Anastasius, 84, title 5.

Concerning the clemency reserved by princes for wrongdoers. Fifth Council of Toledo, title 8, canon 50.

Concerning the safeguarding of the kings’ welfare and the defense of their offspring. Fifth Council of Toledo, title 2, canon 50.

Concerning the protection of the princes’ lives and the defense of preceding [Col. 0080B] kings against those who follow them. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 18, canon 51.

Concerning those who presume to curse princes. Fifth Council of Toledo, title 5, canon 50.

That at the celebration of all councils the synod of Toledo held in the time of the prince Sisenand must be read out. Council cited above, title 7.

Concerning the safety of the royal offspring and the affection to be shown toward them. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 16, canon 51.

## TITLE VI. Concerning the judgments and punishments of princes

Concerning the admonition of princes regarding how they should judge. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 75, canon 49.

Concerning the vengeance against princes who judge wickedly. In the same place.

Concerning the condemnation of Suintila, his wife, and his offspring, and of Geila and their possessions. In the same place.

## TITLE VII. That the people must not offend the prince

[Col. 0080C] Concerning the admonition of the people, that they must not offend princes. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 75, canon 49.

## TITLE VIII. Concerning the inviolability of the faith pledged to princes

Concerning the violation of the faith that is promised to princes. Fourth Council of Toledo, title 75, canon 49.

Concerning the non-violation of oaths given for the safety of the realm. Tenth Council of Toledo, title 2, canon 55.

Concerning those who, while the king is alive, flatter themselves with hope of the kingdom. Fifth Council of Toledo, title 4, canon 50.

Concerning the rejection of persons who are forbidden to obtain the kingdom. Council cited above, title 3.

Concerning those who, while the king is alive, make provision for a future kingdom either for themselves or for others, and concerning persons who are forbidden to approach the kingdom. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 17, [Col. 0080D] canon 51.

## TITLE X. Concerning the faithful of kings

That the king’s faithful should not be deprived by the successors to the kingdom of their rightful possessions as the reward of their service. Fifth Council of Toledo, title 6, canon 50.

Concerning the honor of the palace officials. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 13, canon 51.

Concerning the remuneration granted to the king’s faithful. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 14, canon 51.

## TITLE XI. Concerning those who flee to enemies

Concerning those who flee to the enemy. Sixth Council of Toledo, title 12, canon 51.

Concerning refugee and treacherous clerics or laypeople. Seventh Council of Toledo, title 1, canon 52.

# BOOK EIGHT. CONCERNING GOD AND THE THINGS THAT ARE TO BE BELIEVED ABOUT HIM

[Col. 0081]

## TITLE I. That there is one God who made all things and who gave the Law and the Gospels

[Col. 0081A]

That God alone made both the world and all its instruments. First Council of Toledo, On the Rule of Faith, title 1, canon 46.

That the one God alone made the world, of whom it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” In the work cited above, title 9.

That nothing exists which can extend itself outside the divinity. In the work cited above, title 14.

That the same God is the God both of the ancient Law and of the Gospels. In the work cited above, title 8.

## TITLE II. That there is one God in the Trinity

That the Trinity is both to be believed and proclaimed. Second Council of Carthage, title 1, canon 13.

Rule of faith concerning the Trinity against the Priscillianists. First Council of Toledo, [Col. 0081B] canon 46.

That the Father is not the same as the Son or the Paraclete. In the work cited above, title 2.

That the Son is not the Father or the Paraclete. In the work cited above, title 3.

That the Paraclete is not the Father or the Son. In the work cited above, title 4.

Concerning the unity of the Trinity. Letter of Damasus to Paulinus, 1, title 2.

Against the Priscillianists, who distinguish the holy Trinity not by persons but only by names. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 61, title 1.

Concerning the mystery of the Trinity: what is designated by “person” and what by “substance.” Letter of Hormisdas to the emperor Justin, 86, title 2.

## TITLE III. Concerning the mystery of Christ’s incarnation
On the two natures of Christ and the mystery of the Trinity. [Col. 0081C] Letter of Hormisdas to Epiphanius 93, § 2.

On the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Letter of Hormisdas to the emperor Justin, 86, title 3.

Against the claim that Christ is called “only-begotten” because he alone was born of a virgin. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 61, title 3.

That the Son of God assumed both flesh and a soul. Council of Toledo I, from the rule of faith, title 5, canon 46.

That Christ was born. In the same source above, title 6.

That Christ’s deity is changeable and passible. In the same source above, title 7.

That there is not one nature of Christ’s deity and flesh. In the same source above, title 13.

Many testimonies of the Fathers concerning the two natures and one person in Christ. Council of Seville II, title 13, canon 67.

It must be confessed that God is truly Emmanuel, and that Mary the Virgin is Mother of God, who gave birth according to what is written: “The Word became flesh.” Sent by Cyril and the assembled synod to Nestorius, title 1, canon 10. [Col. 0081D]

It must be confessed that the only-begotten Word of God the Father was so united to his own flesh that there is one Christ, namely God and man at once. In the same source above, title 2, canon 10.

It must be confessed that the two substances in Christ, after the union, are joined not by power alone but by a natural conjunction effected through the union. In the same source above, title 3, canon 10.

What is said about Christ in the apostolic and evangelical writings must not be divided in such a way that what is worthy of God is assigned solely to the nature of God, and what is worthy of man solely to the nature of man. In the same source above, title 4, canon 10.

[Col. 0082A] It must be confessed that Christ is not man in the sense of being a *Theophoros*, that is, one who bears God, but is truly Son by nature; and that, according to the Word becoming flesh, he shared flesh and blood in the same way as we do. In the same source above, title 5, canon 10.

It must be confessed that Christ is God not only in that he is the Father’s Word, but also in that the Word became flesh: God and man are one Christ, God. In the same source above, title 6, canon 10.

Christ must not be confessed as though he were a man joined to the Word by God’s operation, so that the glory of the only-begotten Son might be attributed to someone else existing apart from him. In the same source above, title 7, canon 10.

It must not be confessed that the man in Christ is worshiped together with God, as though one were worshiped with the other; rather, by one supplication and glorification, the Word made flesh—the one Christ—is to be worshiped and glorified. In the same source above, title 8, canon 10.

It must not be confessed that this Jesus worked miracles through the Holy Spirit as though he had employed an alien power, but that he truly completed through his own Spirit the signs he willed. In the same source above, title 8, canon 10.

It must be confessed that this same Jesus, who is the Word made flesh, became the high priest and apostle of our confession—not another man specially born from a woman apart from him. It must also be confessed that he offered sacrifice only for us and not for himself. In the same source above, title 10, canon 10.

It must be confessed that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, according to his nature as life and as God who gives life. In the same source above, title 12, canon 10.

## TITLE IV. Against the doctrine of Eutyches concerning the incarnation of Christ

Against the claim that they believe the Lord God was with the Father as Father. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 65.

[Col. 0082C] That Christ assumed a complete man without sin, and that one Christ existed before the ages from the Father and was born in time from the Virgin. Letter of Damasus to Paulinus I, titles 1 and 2.

Against those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons. Letter of Leo to Bishop Flavian, 38, title 2.

Against those who dare to assert that the divinity of the only-begotten Son is passible. In the same source above, title 3.

Against those who argue for mixture or confusion in Christ’s two natures. In the same source above, title 4.

Against those who, in their madness, assert that the form of a servant which the Lord assumed from us was heavenly or derived from some other substance. In the same source above, title 5.

Against those who rave that the Lord had two natures before the union but invent one after the union. In the same source above, title 6; and the letter of Peter, bishop of Ravenna, to Eutyches, where he answers his errors with an appropriate example, 39.

That in the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ a twofold nature, of deity and humanity, must be affirmed. Letter of Leo to Leo Augustus, 60, § 2.

On the chapters of faith collected from the books of the holy Fathers concerning this same subject. In the same source above, § 3.

Letter of Pope Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, in which he asks why Eutyches, holding an opinion contrary to the Catholic faith, was separated by him from communion with the Church. In full. 37.

On the plots of the deceitful enemy. Rescript of Flavian to Pope Leo, title 1, p. 51.

[Col. 0083A] On the fraudulent subtlety of heretics. In the same, title 2.

On the blasphemies of Eutyches. In the same, title 3.

On his entirely just excommunication. In the same source above, title 4.

Where he signed the sentence of Eutyches’s exile, so that he might transfer him to more remote places, because where he had been placed he was still teaching perverse doctrines. Letter of Leo to Marcian Augustus, 59.

On the blasphemies and anathema of Nestorius and Eutyches. Letter of Leo to Leo Augustus, 69, §§ 1 and 2.

A statement of faith in which Nestorius, Eutyches, and the blasphemies of the remaining heretics are anathematized. Letter, or statement of faith, of Saint John, translated from Greek into Latin and sent to Hormisdas, 88.

Against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches. Letter of Hormisdas to the emperor Justinian, 86, title 1.

Where Bishop Leo calls upon the assembled bishops to condemn the blasphemies of Eutyches. Letter of Leo [Col. 0083B] to the synod of Ephesus, 40.

On the Second Synod of Ephesus, in which the heresy of Eutyches was supported by the perverse understanding of certain bishops; hence Bishop Leo urges Theodosius Augustus that the decree of the ancient faith not be violated by them until the priests of the whole world are assembled. Letter of Leo and of the entire synod to Theodosius Augustus, 41.

Against that same Second Synod of Ephesus, so that its errors may be reconsidered in another synod. Letter of Leo to Pulcheria Augusta, 42.

On that very matter. Letter of Leo to Pulcheria Augusta, 43.

On the condemnation of the Second Council of Ephesus. Letter of Leo to the presbyters Martin and Faustinus, 44.

Where Leo writes that, concerning what is preached about the incarnation of the Son of God by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, he should acknowledge it, and that a universal council should be held in Italy. Letter of Leo to Theodosius Augustus, 45.

Where he asks Pulcheria Augusta for what he earlier requested from Theodosius Augustus. Letter of Leo to Pulcheria Augusta, 46.

On the commendation of those who were sent to the emperor with the authority of the Fathers. Letter of Leo to Faustus and Martin, and the other presbyters, 47.

## TITLE V. Against the Arians, concerning the faith of the holy Trinity

The faith and communion deriving from Arius must not be retained. Council of Toledo III, from the chapters against the Arians, title 1, canon 48.

That our Lord Jesus Christ, begotten without beginning from the Father’s substance, is equal and consubstantial with him. Council of Toledo III, from the chapters against the Arians, title 2, canon 48.

It must be believed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is coeternal and coessential with them. Council of Toledo III, from the chapters against the Arians, title 3, canon 48.

In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the persons must be distinguished and the substance of one divinity acknowledged. In the same source above, title 4.

Our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit must absolutely not be said to be lesser than the Father or separated from him by degrees, or called creatures. In the same source above, title 5.

It must be believed that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, omnipotence, and eternity. In the same source above, title 6.

It must not be said that the Son of God, as God, is ignorant of what the Father knows. In the same source above, title 7.

No beginning must be assigned to the Son of God or to the Holy Spirit. In the same source above, title 8.

The Son of God must not be declared visible or passible in his divinity. In the same source above, title 9.

It must be believed that the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is true God and omnipotent. In the same source above, title 10.

[Col. 0084A] The Catholic faith and communion outside the universal Church—which is upheld by the decrees of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—must not be accepted. In the same source above, title 11.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must not be separated or distinguished in the honor and glory of divinity. In the same source above, title 12.

The Son of God and the Holy Spirit must be glorified and honored together with the Father. In the same source above, title 13.

Glory and honor must be declared to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the same source above, title 14.

## TITLE VI. Against the Priscillianists

It must not be denied that human bodies can rise again after death. Council of Toledo I, from the rules of faith, canon 46.

It must not be believed that the human soul is a portion or substance of God. In the same source above, title 11.

Astrology and *mathesis* must not be believed. In the same source above, title 15.

[Col. 0084B] The sect of Priscillian must not be followed, nor may anything be done in saving baptism contrary to the see of the apostle Peter. In the same source above, title 18.

On the Lord’s Nativity, during which the Priscillianists observe fasts. Letter of Pope Leo to Thuribius, bishop of Astorga, 61, title 4.

Against the claim that the human soul is of divine substance. The same letter, title 5.

Against the claim that the devil derives from himself or from chaos and possesses a nature of his own. The same letter, title 6.

Against the claim that marriage and the procreation of children are sin. The same letter, title 7.

Against the claim that human bodies are the devil’s creations and are formed by demons in the womb. The same letter, title 8.

Against the claim that the children of the promise are conceived from the Holy Spirit. The same letter, title 9.

Against the belief that souls sin in the heavens and, according to the quality of their sin, receive in this world either a good or an evil lot. The same letter, title 10.

Against the claim that human souls are bound by the stars of fate. The same letter, title 11.

Against the claim that the parts of the soul are assigned to some powers and the members of the body to others. The same letter, title 12.

Against the claim that the names of the patriarchs are distributed among the individual members of the body. The same letter, title 13.

Against the claim that the twelve signs observed by astrologers are distributed throughout the entire body. The same letter, title 14.

On the apocryphal writings of those same Priscillianists. The same letter, title 15.

On those who read the treatises of the Priscillianists. The same letter, title 16.

## TITLE VII. Against the Pelagians, concerning free will

[Col. 0084D] Against the Pelagians, who say that Adam could also have died without sin. Council of Milevis, title 1, canon 19.

That, according to the testimony of the Apostle, even infants who have not yet committed any sin are all baptized for the remission of sins. The same council, title 2.

That the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps prevent them from being committed. The same council, title 3.

That by the grace of God we know what we ought to do, and love it so that we may do it. The same council, title 4.

That the grace of God enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, that difficult things can easily be fulfilled as though without the grace of God. The same council, title 5.

That, according to the judgment of John the Evangelist, no one exists who can be without sin. The same council, title 6.

That everyone, even the righteous, ought to say not only for others but also for himself: “Forgive us our debts.” The same council, title 7.

That the saints truly say: “Forgive us our debts.” The same council, title 8.

[Col. 0085A] On Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain presbyters of Gaul of being followers of Pelagius. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 33, title 1.

On Saint Augustine, a remarkable assertion of praise. The same letter, title 2.

Authorities of the former bishops of the apostolic see concerning the grace of God. The same letter, title 3.

That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ. The same letter, title 4.

That no one is good by his own powers except through participation in him who alone is good. The same letter, title 5.

That unless we are continually helped by the grace of God, we cannot avoid the snares of the devil. The same letter, title 6.

That through Christ we use free will well. The same letter, title 7.

That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God. The same letter, title 8.

That every holy thought and movement of a devout will is from God. The same letter, title 9.

[Col. 0085B] That the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps prevent them from being committed, and enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, that it can be fulfilled easily, as though without the grace of God it could be fulfilled only with greater difficulty. The same letter, title 10.

## TITLE VIII. On the condemnation of heresies and heretics

On the condemnation of certain heretics. Letter of Damasus to Paulinus II, title 1.

On the fact that a great number of Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome through the vigilance of Pope Leo. Letter of Pope Leo to the bishops throughout Italy, 62.

Against Jovinian the heretic and his associates, who are to be removed from the unity of the Church; here a bishop and a presbyter are also called fellow-presbyters. Letter of Siricius sent to various bishops, 4.

On Bubalius and Taurianus, condemned by the provincial bishops, whose judgment the apostolic see took care to reconsider. Letter of Innocent to Rufus and the others in Macedonia, 12.

On the Bonosians, who are to be compared with the Jews. Letter of Innocent to Laurentius of Siena, 25.

On the condemnation of the Sabellian and Priscillianist heresies. From the chapters against the most wicked sects, First Synod of Braga, title 1, canon 63.

Condemnation of heresies and confirmation of the confession of faith. Edict of King Reccared in the Third Council of Toledo, canon 48.

Confession of faith by the priests and the entire Gothic people, together with the chapters condemning heresies. Third Council of Toledo, canon 48.

The detestable booklet published in the time of Leovigild, which contains the transfer of the Goths to the Arian heresy from the Romans, must in no way be accepted as true. Third Council of Toledo, against the Arians, title 16, canon 48.

The Council of Ariminum must be rejected and condemned with all one’s heart. In the same source above, title 17.

## TITLE IX. On the condemnation of those who do not receive the councils of the Fathers

[Col. 0086B]

Let anyone to whom the holy faith of the Catholic Church is displeasing be anathema. Third Council of Toledo, from the chapters against the Arians, title 18, canon 48.

Let anyone who despises the faith of the Council of Nicaea be anathema. In the same source above, title 19, canon 48.

Let anyone who says that the faith of the Council of Constantinople is not true be anathema. In the same source above, title 20.

Let anyone who does not uphold the faith of the First Synod of Ephesus and of Chalcedon and takes delight in this be anathema. In the same source above, title 21.

Let anyone who does not receive the concordant councils of all orthodox bishops—the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—be anathema. In the same source above, title 22.

Declaration in confirmation of the Catholic faith and in condemnation of every heretical perversity. In the same source above, title 23.

# BOOK NINE. ON THE RENUNCIATION OF HERETICS AND THEIR PRACTICES

[Col. 0085]

## TITLE I. On avoiding heretics and their practices

[Col. 0085C]

Catholics must not enter those places which heretics call their martyr shrines. Council of Laodicea, title 9, canon 7.

Christians must not Judaize or observe the Sabbath. The same council, title 29.

Blessings must not be received from heretics, because they are curses. The same council, title 32.

One must not pray with heretics or schismatics. Council of Laodicea, title 33, canon 7.

One must not go to false martyrs. The same council, title 34.

Christians may not, after abandoning the Church, gather at assemblies of angelolatry. The same council, title 35.

It is not permitted to receive from heretics or Jews the festival gifts that are sent, or to celebrate feast days with them. The same council, title 37.

It is not permitted to receive unleavened bread from Jews. The same council, title 38. [Col. 0085D]

It is not permitted to celebrate festivals with pagans. The same council, title 39.

The gathering of heretics is to be called not a church but an assembly. Council of Carthage IV, title 71, canon 15.

One must neither pray nor sing psalms with heretics. The same council, title 75.

Unbelievers are to remain in the church until the dismissal, in order to hear the reading. The same council, title 84.

Concerning the fruits of the faithful, that they must not be blessed by Jews. Council of Elvira, title 49, canon 38.

## TITLE II. On avoiding banquets with heretics

[Col. 0086C]

Christians are to avoid banquets with Jews. Council of Agde, title 40, canon 30.

On Christians who eat with Jews. Council of Elvira, title 50, canon 38.

The faithful and devout must not share food with those who have been rebaptized. Council of Lérida, title 14, canon 44.

On the prohibition against Catholic clerics or laypeople receiving *eulogiae* from heretics or praying with them or with schismatics. In Martin’s excerpts, title 70, canon 44.

## TITLE III. On the marriages of the faithful and of heretics

Catholics must not be joined in marriage to heretics. Council of Laodicea, title 10, canon 7.

On not mixing marriages with heretics, nor giving them the children of Christians, nor accepting their children. [Col. 0086D] The same council, title 31.

On guarding against marriages with heretics. The same council, title 31.

Faithful women who have joined themselves to pagans are to be excommunicated. Council of Arles I, title 11, canon 21.

On Catholics, that they must not be joined in marriage to heretics. Council of Agde, title 67, canon 30.

Christian girls may be given in marriage to pagans because of the danger of adultery. Council of Elvira, title 15, canon 38.

[Col. 0087A] On faithful girls, that they must not be joined to unbelievers. The same council, title 16.

On those who join their daughters to priests of the pagans. The same council, title 17.

## TITLE IV. On the faith of the Jews and those who agree with them against the faith

On distinguishing which Jews are not to be compelled to believe and which are to be compelled. Council of Toledo IV, title 57, canon 49.

On guarding the faith of the Jews. Council of Toledo VI, title 3, canon 51.

On Jews who were formerly Christians and later returned to their former rite, and on the circumcision of their slaves or children. Council of Toledo IV, title 59, canon 49.

On those who, contrary to the faith of Christ, offer a gift or favor to Jews. The same council, title 58.

## TITLE V. On the wives and children of Jews, and that they must not own Christian subjects whom they have purchased or hold public offices

[Col. 0087B] On the marriages of Christians and Jews and their children. Council of Toledo IV, title 63, canon 49.

Jews may not have or acquire Christian wives or concubines, purchase Christian slaves, Judaize, or perform public offices. Council of Toledo III, title 4, canon 48.

On the children of Jews, that they must be separated from their parents and assigned to Christians. Council of Toledo IV, title 60, canon 49.

On the children of Jews, that after their parents have transgressed and been condemned, they must not become exiles from their parents’ property. The same council, title 61.

Jews, or anyone descended from Jews, must not perform public offices. The same council, title 65.

Jews must not possess any Christian slave under any title whatsoever. The same council, title 66.

On baptized Jews who associate with unbelieving Jews: the former are to be given to Christians, and the latter assigned to corporal punishments. [Col. 0087C] Council of Toledo IV, title 62, canon 49.

Baptized Jews are to celebrate feast days with the bishops. Council of Toledo IX, title 17, canon 54.

## TITLE VI. On heretics to be received by the Church

On how the Novatians are to be received into the Catholic Church, and with what honor or rank priests and ministers coming from them are to be received. Council of Nicaea, title 8, canon 1.

On the rebaptism of the Paulianists and Cataphrygians, and how those among them who were clerics are to be received into the clergy. Also, concerning the deaconesses found among them, they are to be counted among the laywomen. Council of Nicaea, title 19, canon 1.

Heretics who remain in heresy must not enter the church. Council of Laodicea, title 6, canon 7.

On how the Novatians and Quartodecimans are to be received. The same council, title 7.

On the baptism of the Cataphrygians who come to the Church. The same council, title 8.

[Col. 0087D] On how those baptized by the Donatists are to be received. Council of Carthage III, title 48, canon 14.

Novatians are not to be received into communion unless they have accepted the belief in penance and condemned their error. [Col. 0088A] Council of Arles II, title 9, canon 22.

Photinians and Paulianists are to be baptized. The same council, title 10.

On anyone who wishes to separate himself from heretics, so that he may be received by the Catholic Church. Council of Turin, title 5, canon 25.

# [COUNCILS]

[Col. 0091]

## PREFACE

The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. In the preceding years, while persecution was raging, no opportunity was given for teaching the peoples; afterward [Note: [Col. 0091] T. 1, 2: *inde*, “thereafter.”] Christianity was split into various heresies, because the holy bishops had no permission to assemble in one place except in the time of the aforesaid emperor. He himself granted Christians the freedom to gather. Under him also, the holy Fathers, assembling at the Council of Nicaea from every part of the world, handed down, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic faith, the creed that followed the Apostles.

There are, moreover, four principal councils [Note: [Col. 0091] For correct syntax a verb is lacking: “it is clear,” “it is established,” “it is certain,” or something similar.], from which the Church holds the fullest teaching of the faith, both concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and concerning the incarnation of the aforesaid Son and our Savior.

The first of these is the Council of Nicaea, held under the rule of Constantine Augustus by three hundred and eighteen bishops [Note: [Col. 0091] From Ae., T. 1, 2. In A and the other manuscripts: “held by bishops under the rule of Constantine Augustus.”], in which the blasphemy of Arian [Note: [Col. 0091] In the manuscripts: *Arrianae*, as elsewhere *Arrianus* and [Col. 0092] *Arrius*. The doubling of the letter reflects the pronunciation of the Spanish language.] perfidy was condemned. Since that same Arius asserted the inequality of the holy Trinity, the holy synod defined through the creed that the Son, God from God the Father, is consubstantial with him.

The second council was the gathering of one hundred and fifty Fathers at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it demonstrated that the same Paraclete is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and it gave a fuller form to the creed that all Greece and the Latin-speaking world proclaim in their churches.

The third council was the First Council of Ephesus, consisting of two hundred bishops, held under the younger Theodosius Augustus. It condemned Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, with a just anathema, demonstrating that one person of the Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

The fourth council was the Council of Chalcedon, held under the emperor Marcian by six hundred and thirty priests. In it, by one judgment of the Fathers, it condemned Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh have one nature; Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, his defender; and Nestorius himself again, together with the remaining heretics. The same council proclaimed that Christ God was born from the Virgin in such a way that we confess in him the substance of both the divine and the human nature.

These are, as we said above, the four principal and venerable councils embracing the whole faith [Note: [Col. 0092] In Ae. and E. 3, “embracing the Catholic faith.”]. But whatever councils there are that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, decreed remain firmly established after the authority of these four; their acts too are contained in this work.

At the beginning of this volume, however, we have placed the Council of Nicaea because of the authority of that great council; thereafter we shall place, within the scope of this volume, the various Greek and Latin councils—whether held earlier or later—distinguished in their respective chapters according to the order of their numbers and dates [Note: [Col. 0092] At the completion of the sentence, the word *gesta* or *acta* is missing.]. We shall also append the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, in which, because of the eminence of the Apostolic See, there is an authority no less than that of councils, so that the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, collected and arranged by us into one body, may both instruct holy prelates by the rules of their fathers and imbue ministers or peoples obedient to the Church with particular examples.

As for the canons that are called apostolic: since neither the Apostolic See receives them nor the holy Fathers granted them their assent, because they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the apostles, although some useful things are found in them, their acts are nevertheless clearly removed from canonical and apostolic authority and reckoned among the apocrypha.

In Greek, *canon* is called in Latin *regula*, “rule.” It is called a rule because it leads along what is straight and never draws elsewhere. Others have said that it is called a rule either because it rules, or because it provides a standard for living rightly, or because it corrects something distorted and wrong. They say that *synod* is interpreted from Greek as “company” or “assembly”; the name *council* (*concilium*) is derived from a common intention, because all direct the gaze of their minds toward one point. For the *cilia* are the eyelashes, and therefore those who disagree among themselves do not hold a council, because they do not share one judgment. An assembly (*coetus*) is a meeting or gathering, from *coire*, that is, from coming together into one; hence it is called a *conventus*, because people come together there, just as an assembly or council derives from the association of many into one.

[Col. 0093]

# COUNCILS OF THE GREEKS (C, S)

## I. THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA, HELD IN THE TIME OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE BY THREE HUNDRED AND EIGHTEEN BISHOPS IN THE CITY OF NICAEA, THE METROPOLIS OF BITHYNIA, UNDER THE CONSULS PAULINUS AND JULIANUS, ON THE THIRTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY, IN THE YEAR 362 OF THE ERA

[Col. 0093A] 1–2 When this holy and great council had assembled at Nicaea, a city of the province of Bithynia, the following provisions were established by them, translated from Greek into Latin [Note: [Col. 0093C] In B. R., the leaves containing this entire council are missing.].

### I. Concerning eunuchs who mutilate themselves

If someone has been operated on during an illness by physicians, or has been castrated by barbarians, it has been decided that such a person is to remain in the clergy [Note: [Col. 0093C] Ae., E. 3, U., “such a person is to remain.”]. But if someone, while healthy, has mutilated himself, even if he is in the clergy, he must cease from it, and from that time no such person ought to be ordained. Just as the provisions stated above have been established concerning those who either desired or dared to mutilate themselves, so also, if some have been mutilated either by barbarians or by their masters and are of approved conduct [Note: [Col. 0093C] T. 1, 2, G., “and have proved themselves of approved conduct”], ecclesiastical rule admits such persons to the clergy.

### II. Concerning those who immediately after baptism apply for the clergy

[Note: [Col. 0093C] In the manuscripts the forms *babtisma*, *babtismus*, *babtizare*, and *rebabtizare* are consistently found. We consider this spelling to be repeated from the analogy of letters produced by the same organ.]  
[Note: [Col. 0094C] From Ae. and E. 3. In A. and the remaining witnesses: “they will be appointed.”]

[Col. 0093B]

Since many things have been done contrary to rule, whether from necessity [Note: [Col. 0094C] U., “because of necessity.”] or for whatever reason, so that people who had only recently come from pagan life and had been catechized [Note: [Col. 0094C] U., “recently catechized.” In the manuscripts: *catazizati*.] or instructed immediately came to spiritual baptism and, as soon as they had been baptized, were advanced also to the episcopate or presbyterate, it has rightly seemed good that henceforth nothing of this kind should occur. For time is needed for someone to be a catechumen, and after baptism much testing is required. The apostolic command is clear, saying: “Not a novice, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.” But if, at an earlier time, he has committed some mortal offense [Note: [Col. 0094C] Ae., E. 3, T. 2, U., “has committed some sin”], and has been convicted by two or three witnesses, a person of this kind shall cease from the clergy [Col. 0093C]. If anyone acts otherwise, he too, as one acting contrary to the decrees of the holy council, will endanger his clerical status.

### III. Concerning women introduced into the household

The holy synod absolutely forbids an arrangement whereby a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever is permitted to have with him a woman from outside, unless she is perhaps his mother, sister, or aunt (*thia*) [Note: [Col. 0094C] The words “or aunt” (*aut thia*) are taken from the remaining witnesses, since they are absent from A.], that is, a paternal or maternal aunt. For suspicion arising from women is avoided only in the case of these persons [Col. 0094A] and those similar to them. Whoever acts otherwise will endanger his clerical office.

### IV. How bishops ought to be ordained

A bishop ought to be ordained by all the bishops who are in his province, if this can be done. [3] But if this should be difficult, whether because of pressing necessity or the length of the journey, certainly three bishops ought to be gathered together [Note: [Col. 0094C] Ae., E. 3, U., “ought to be gathered”], so that they may also possess in writing the consent of the others who are absent, and may then carry out the ordination. Authority or confirmation shall belong, in each province, to the metropolitan bishop.

### V. Concerning excommunicated clerics or laypeople

Let this decision also be observed: those who are excommunicated [Col. 0094B] by some must not be admitted to communion by others. Inquiry must certainly be made lest perhaps persons have been excluded by the excommunication of their bishop because of some indignation, dispute, or any such stirring of anger. Therefore, so that these matters may be investigated through a proper examination, it has rightly seemed good that in every province, twice each year, a council of bishops should be held. Thus, assembling together from the whole province, they may examine such questions, so that those who have deservedly incurred the offense of their bishops on account of their faults may likewise be considered rightly excommunicated by the others until either the communion itself or their own bishop judges it appropriate to pronounce a more humane judgment concerning them. One council is to be held before the days [Col. 0094C] of Lent, so that, once all hostilities have been cut away, a pure solemn offering may be presented to God; the second council is to be held around the time of autumn.

### VI. Concerning the primacy of metropolitan bishops

Let the ancient custom remain in Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, namely, that the bishop of Alexandria have authority over all these regions, since the same custom also belongs to the bishop of Rome. Likewise, [Col. 0095A] in the region of Antioch and in the other provinces, let each Church retain its proper honor. It is altogether clear, however, that if anyone has been ordained against the will and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, this great and holy council has judged that he ought not to be a bishop. If, on the other hand, an ordination has been reasonably approved by the common consent of all according to ecclesiastical rule, and two or three, driven by hostility, oppose it through contention, let the judgment of the greater number of priests prevail.

### VII. Concerning the honor of the bishop of Jerusalem

Since ancient custom and an old tradition have prevailed—that the bishop of Aelia, that is, of Jerusalem, should be accorded honor [Note: [Col. 0095D] U., “honor should be accorded to the bishop.”]. Let him consequently [4] have honor, while the proper dignity of the metropolitan city nevertheless remains.

### VIII. Concerning the Novatians

[Col. 0095B]

If some of the Novatians wish to come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy council that they be ordained and remain in the clergy. Above all, however, a written confession must be required from them, in which they acknowledge that they will observe the decrees of the Catholic Church by common agreement—that is, that they will communicate also with those who have perhaps experienced a second marriage, and with those who fell during the time of persecution. For those who fell, a manner and period of penance have nevertheless been assigned, so that in all things they may follow what is observed in the Catholic Church. Thus, wherever they are found—whether in villages or in cities—let them be ordained by the Catholics who are present, and let each remain in the clergy in his own rank [Note: [Col. 0095D] U., “so that everywhere all of them may be found.”].

But if there is a bishop [Col. 0095C] or presbyter of the Catholic Church to whom some of these persons come, it is certain that the Catholic bishop shall retain his dignity, and likewise the presbyter and deacon shall retain theirs. Those who come from the Novatians, however, if one of them is a bishop, shall have the dignity of a presbyter, unless the Catholic bishop should also choose to grant him the honor of the episcopal title. If he does not choose to do so, let him find him a place, so that he may be in the clergy in the district as a bishop or presbyter, provided that two bishops are not seen to exist in the city and that he nevertheless clearly remains in the clergy in every respect.

### IX. Concerning presbyters appointed without examination

If some have been promoted to the presbyterate without examination, and afterward, when examined, have confessed their sins, and after they had confessed, men, acting contrary to rule, rashly laid hands upon them, the ecclesiastical order does not receive them. For in all things the Church defends what is blameless [Note: [Col. 0095D] T. 2, “what is reprehensible.”].

### X. Concerning clerics who fell and were ordained

Whoever among those who fell has been ordained either through ignorance or through the contempt of those who ordained him—this does not prejudice ecclesiastical rule; when the matter has been discovered, they shall be deposed [Note: [Col. 0096D] T. 1, 2, U., “let them be deposed.”].

### XI. How those who fell voluntarily ought to do penance

It has pleased the holy synod, although they are unworthy [5] of mercy [Col. 0096A], nevertheless to show some humanity toward them. If, therefore, some repent sincerely, let them be counted among the hearers for three years; if they are faithful, let them then spend seven further years among the penitents; and for two more years let them participate with the people in prayer alone, outside communion.

But if some, called first through the grace of faith [Note: [Col. 0096D] Ae., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., “through the grace of God,”] displayed their faith by laying aside the military belt and afterward returned to their own vomit, so that they gave money and sought to return again to military service, let these spend ten years among the penitents after the first three years during which they were among the hearers. Above all, let this be observed by everyone: that attention be paid to their disposition and to the fruit of their penance.

For whoever demonstrates his way of life with all fear and tears and perseverance and good works—not by words alone, but by deed and truth—[Col. 0096B] once the appointed period has also been completed by them and they have already begun to participate in prayers, may receive from the bishop a more humane consideration. But those who have treated their fall with indifference and think it sufficient for them that they have entered the church shall in every respect complete the prescribed periods.

### XII. Concerning those excommunicated who are departing from this life

With regard to those who depart from the body, the rule of the ancient law shall still be observed, so that, if someone is perhaps departing from the body, he is not deprived of the necessary provision for his journey through life. But if someone who seemed hopeless, after receiving communion, survives, let him be counted among those who participate in prayer alone. In the case of all who depart from the body, however, let the bishop exercise care and judgment [Col. 0096C] in administering communion to them.

### XIII. Concerning fallen catechumens

It has pleased this holy and great council, concerning catechumens who have fallen, that they remain for only three years among those who hear the word; after that, let them pray with the catechumens.

### XIV. Concerning deacons, that they neither give the body of Christ to presbyters nor receive communion before presbyters

It has come to the holy council’s attention that in certain places and cities deacons administer the sacraments to presbyters. Neither rule nor custom has handed this down: that those who do not possess the power of offering the sacrifice should give the body of Christ to those who offer it. It has also become known that some deacons receive the sacraments even before bishops [Col. 0096D]. Let all these practices therefore be cut away, and let deacons remain within their own proper measure [6], knowing that they are ministers of bishops but are lower than presbyters. Accordingly, let them receive in due order after the presbyters, from the bishop or presbyter. If neither bishop nor presbyter is present, then let the deacon himself bring it forth and give it.

But deacons must not even be permitted to sit among the presbyters. It is outside rule and outside order for this to happen. If anyone does not wish to be satisfied with these provisions, let him cease to be a deacon after this definition.

### XV. Concerning clerics who rashly depart from the Church

[Note: [Col. 0097D] U., “who depart from the Church or from their own city.”]

[Col. 0097A]

Because of the many disturbances and frequent riots of seditions that commonly arise, it has been decided that this practice, which is contrary to rule, must be completely cut off wherever it occurs—namely, that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon should pass from one city to another. If, after these statutes of the holy council, anyone should attempt such a thing, every such effort shall be thwarted in every way [Note: [Col. 0097D] U., “shall be invalidated.” G., “let it be thwarted.”], and he shall be restored to his own Church, in which he was ordained.

### XVI. Concerning presbyters, deacons, or clerics who pass to other cities

If some act without regard for God, do not have the fear of God before their eyes, and do not observe ecclesiastical statutes, and depart from their own Church—whether they are presbyters, [Col. 0097B] deacons, or placed in any ecclesiastical order—they must not be received in another church. Rather, they must be compelled by every necessity to return to their own Churches; or, if they remain, they ought to be excommunicated.

### XVII. Concerning foreign clerics who are not to be ordained by another into his Church without the consent of their own bishop

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Ae., “of his bishop.”]

If anyone dares to ordain in his own Church someone who belongs to another, without possessing the consent of the bishop from whom the cleric departed [Note: [Col. 0097D] Ae., “of his own bishop”], let such an ordination be invalid.

### XVIII. Concerning clerics who receive interest or excessive increase

Since many clerics, pursuing shameful profits out of greed [Note: [Col. 0097D] U., “shameful profit,” singular], have forgotten the divine command that says [Col. 0097C], “Who has not given his money at interest,” and, when lending money, demand hundredfold returns, this holy council decrees: if anyone is found after this definition [7] to accept interest, or to pursue shameful profits from any such transaction, or even to lend measures of grain at sixfold return, anyone who has devised such a thing for gain shall be expelled from the clergy and considered alien to the ecclesiastical order.

### XIX. Concerning the rebaptism of the Paulianists and Cataphrygians

If anyone from the Paulianists or Cataphrygians [Note: [Col. 0097D] E. 3, T. 1, *Cataphrygibus*.] takes refuge in the Catholic Church, let it be decreed that they must in every respect be rebaptized [Note: [Col. 0097D] U., “baptized.”]. If some were clerics among them, then, provided they are found blameless and irreprehensible, after being rebaptized they shall again be ordained by the bishop of the Catholic Church. But if, when examined, they are found less suitable and are reproved [Col. 0097D] [Note: U., “are found out”], they ought to be deposed. The same procedure shall likewise be observed concerning deacons and all who are found in that clergy.

We shall also mention the deaconesses found in this order. They have no laying on of hands [Col. 0098A] whatsoever, and are therefore to be counted entirely among the laywomen. Likewise, deaconesses who are not found in the Catholic canon are to be assigned to the same status, that is, as laywomen and as though unconsecrated.

### XX. Concerning Sundays and Pentecost, that we should pray standing on those days

[Note: [Col. 0097D] In the manuscripts, *Pentecosten*, since they often render this noun as indeclinable.]

Since some kneel in prayer on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, the holy synod has therefore decreed that, because a harmonious and suitable custom is to be observed in all Churches, we should offer our vows to the Lord while standing in prayer [Note: [Col. 0097D] T. 2, “standing for prayer.”].

## CREED OF FAITH

Issued by the same great Council of Nicaea through the three hundred and eighteen Fathers.

[Col. 0098B]

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord, Jesus Christ, our Lord, the Son of God, born from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, consubstantive [Note: [Col. 0098D] T. 2, “consubstantial.”] with the Father, that is, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*; [8] through whom all things were made, both those in heaven [Note: [Col. 0098D] T. 1, 2, “in the heavens.”] and those on earth; who for us human beings [Note: [Col. 0098D] Ae., E. 3, T. 1, 2, “for human beings”] and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, and became human; he suffered and died; he rose again on the third day; he ascended into the heavens; he will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and “Before he was born he was not,” and that he was made from things that did not exist, or from some substance or nature, saying that he is mutable and subject to alteration, and asserting that he is the Son of God—these the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes and condemns.

This is the faith that the Fathers set forth: first, against the blasphemous Arius, who said that the Son of God was a creature; and against every heresy of Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Mani, Valentinus, and Marcion; and against every heresy whatsoever, should any arise against the Catholic and Apostolic Church. All these the three hundred and eighteen bishops assembled at Nicaea condemned; their names and provinces are recorded. But most of the devoted servants of God took greater care to record the names of the Eastern bishops, because the West had not conducted an inquiry into heresies in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0098D] In all the manuscripts except the Urgelitan and Gerundan, the words and subscriptions written here occur, followed later by *The Faith of Saint Gregory the Great*. We have transferred them to a more appropriate position, after the subscriptions.].

[Note: [Col. 0098D] The subscriptions of the bishops who attended this great council are lacking in most manuscripts. In the Urgelitan manuscript, however, it is permitted to read a great many of them. Although we recognize them as corrupt and removed from the correct reading, we nevertheless judged it more reverent to incorporate them as they are presented, together with the variant readings of the Gerundan manuscript [Col. 0099D–0100D].]

And the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who had assembled at that council subscribed.

Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba in the province of [Col. 0099A] Hispania [Note: [Col. 0100D] In the manuscripts, *Spania*.], said: “I believe as it is written above.” Victor and Vincentius, presbyters of the city of Rome, subscribed.

## The Faith of Saint Gregory the Great

[Col. 0104A]

One God, the source and Father of the living Word, of existing Wisdom, of Power, and of his own image; perfect Father of the Perfect One begotten, Father of the only-begotten Son; and one Lord from one Lord; God [Note: [Col. 0104B] Ae., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., “from one, God.”] from God; the figure of the Father’s substance; the image of God; God the living Word and maker of the whole substance; Wisdom containing all things that exist; and the power of the whole creature capable of creation; true Son from a true Father; invisible from the invisible; incorruptible from the incorruptible; immortal from the immortal; and eternal from the eternal.

And one Holy Spirit, perfect, the perfect life of the living, holiness and the source of holiness, and the minister of sanctification; through whom God is in all believers [Col. 0104B] and above all, and the Son is through all. A perfect Trinity, glory and eternal kingdom, indivisible and inalienable. Therefore there is in the Trinity neither anything created and servile or enslaved, nor anything adventitious or introduced from outside, as though something that had not existed before had entered last. For the Son was never lacking to the Father, nor the Holy Spirit to the Son; rather, this same Trinity is always immutable and unchangeable.

## II. THE COUNCIL OF ANCYRA, HELD BY TWELVE BISHOPS

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103C] 17–18 These canons, or rules, are earlier than the Nicene canons, but the Nicene canons are written first because of the authority of the great and holy council held at Nicaea. The following men assembled in the aforesaid synod of the city of Ancyra: Marcellus of Ancyra, Agricolaus of Caesarea, Lupus of Tarsus, Vitalius of Antioch, Basilius of Amasea, Philadelphius of Juliopolis, Festulus of Nicomedia, Heraclius of Zela, Petrus of Iconium, Nunecius of Laodicea, Sergianus of Antioch in Pisidia, and Narcissus of Neroniada.

### I. Concerning presbyters who fell during the persecution

As for presbyters who sacrificed and afterward entered the contest again, if they did this from faith itself and not by preparing the matter for themselves through some stratagem, so that they might appear to be seized again [Col. 0103D] [Note: From the words “might appear” the manuscript B. R. begins: “so that they might be subjected to torments”], so as to be subjected to tortures, as though they were thought to have acted unwillingly; if therefore they struggled from faith and did not themselves arrange the matter for display, so that they might be offered up, it has pleased the council that they retain the honor of their proper seat, but that they not be permitted to offer, address the people, or perform any priestly functions.

### II. Concerning deacons who sacrificed

[Col. 0104C]

[The supplied source ends here, with this heading and column reference.]

Deacons likewise who have sacrificed, but afterward again entered the struggle [Note: [Col. 0103D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2: “resisted again.” U.: “they resisted again; some others, however, ought to be ordained.”], should indeed retain some honor, but ought to cease from every sacred ministry, so that they may neither offer the bread nor the cup [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “they should offer neither the bread nor the cup, nor pronounce anything except …”], unless perhaps some bishops have been aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness, and have wished to grant or assign them something more. The authority in these matters, therefore, shall rest with those bishops.

### III. On clerics or laymen whose hands others forcibly placed upon the sacrifices of idols

Those who, fleeing during the persecution, were captured or betrayed by relatives or members of their household, and either lost their property, endured tortures, or were even confined in prisons, yet proclaimed themselves Christians [Col. 0104D]—and, while the violence continued, were driven to the point that their seized and forcibly drawn hands were placed upon the sacrifices, while they themselves persisted in the faith and cried out that they were Christians [Note: Ae., B. R., U.: “persisting in the faith and proclaiming themselves Christians”—let this act, therefore, which happened against their will and under compulsion by others, be judged as follows: if they show that they bear it bitterly, with grief and sorrow of heart, and, walking in humble [Col. 0105A] conduct through a good manner of life, demonstrate that they grieve because they were compelled against their will, such persons, as blameless, are not to be barred from communion [Note: U.: “it was decided that they should not be barred.”].

But if some have already been excluded from communion by others—whether for the sake of greater diligence and investigation, or through the ignorance of certain persons—they ought immediately to be received. This is also to be observed concerning all clerics and laymen: laymen, in particular, who have fallen into similar necessities, as persons who have committed no sin, especially if a reputable life commends them, are to be admitted to ordination; so it was decided.

### IV. On those who dined in the temples of idols

Concerning those who were compelled to sacrifice, and also concerning those who dined in the temples of idols: if any of them were led to the temples wearing more elegant clothing, and there, after changing into still more costly garments, were made participants in the meal [Note: U.: “after changing their clothing, they also became participants in the meal”] of the idols [Col. 0105B], indiscriminately consuming everything that had been set before them, it was decided that they should be placed for one year among the hearers, should do penance for three further years, should share in prayer alone for two years of that three-year period, and in the third year should be reconciled to the sacraments.

### V. On those who performed pagan rites through fear

But all who went up to the temples in mournful clothing and, reclining among the others, ate while weeping—if they complete the three-year period of penance—are to be received into communion without the offering; that is, they themselves are not to present the offering. But if, after being led to the temples, they did not eat, they are to remain in penance for two years; in the third year they are to communicate, but without the offering, as stated, so that in the fourth year they may recover their full standing [Col. 0105C]. The bishop ought therefore to have permission, after examining each person’s conduct, to assign a rule and standard for his conduct: either, acting more humanely according to the manner of life, to shorten the period for someone, or also to add a longer period wherever he sees this necessary for correction. The earlier and later life of all these persons is to be examined, and priestly humanity is accordingly to be tempered in dealing with them.

### VI. On those who ate in places dedicated to idols

Concerning those who yielded merely to threats, or sacrificed because they were deterred by the surrender of their property or by the punishment of transportation, and have not yet repented or turned back, but now—that is, at the time of this synod—have presented themselves, resolving upon their conversion: it was decided that they should be received among the hearers until the great day, should do penance for three years, and afterward should communicate for two further years without the offering, finally reaching perfection after the completion of six years. If some were admitted to penance before this council, the beginning of the prescribed six-year period shall be reckoned for them from that earlier time. If any danger of death should befall one of them—whether through illness or any other cause—communion is not to be denied to them as their viaticum.

### VII. On those who frequently sacrificed to idols

Concerning those who on the festival days of the pagans attended banquets in their remote places, and nevertheless brought their own food there and ate it [Col. 0106A], it was decided that they should be received after two years of penance. Nevertheless, each bishop is to examine whether they should be received with the offering or admitted to communion alone, taking into consideration their former and present life.

### VIII. On those who were forcibly compelled to sacrifice to idols

Those who sacrificed a second and third time after being compelled by force are to submit themselves to penance for four years; for two further years they are to communicate without the offering; and in the seventh year they are to recover the fullness of communion.

### IX. On those who gave others cause to sacrifice
