But all who not only deviated from the Lord’s faith [Col. 0106B], but also rose up against others, persuaded their brothers, and became responsible for their persuasion, are to be kept among the catechumens for three years; for another six years they are to occupy the place of penitents; in the following year—that is, the tenth—they are to receive communion without the offering, so that, when the ten years have been completed, they may enjoy perfection. During that same period, however, their life and conduct are also to be examined.

### X. On deacons

Whatever deacons, when they are ordained, declare at the very time of their ordination that they wish to have wives and cannot remain continent: if afterward they enter into marriage, they are to remain in the ministry, because the bishop gave them permission. But those who remained silent and accepted the laying on of hands while professing continence, and afterward entered into marriage, must cease from the ministry.

### XI. On betrothed girls carried off and violated by others

It was decided that betrothed girls who were afterward carried off by others should be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it were established that they had lost the flower of their modesty at the hands of their abductors.

### XII. On those who sacrificed to idols before baptism

It was decided that those who sacrificed before baptism and afterward received baptism could be promoted to ordination, as having been cleansed from every crime by the sanctification of the saving bath.

### XIII. On rural bishops

The deputies of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi*, are not permitted to ordain presbyters or deacons, nor to command anything further to the city’s presbyters without the bishop’s instruction, nor to do anything in any parish without his written authorization.

### XIV. On presbyters who abstain from meat

Concerning those in the clergy who are presbyters or deacons and abstain from meat, it was decided that they should not despise it as unclean, although they may refrain from touching it; if they wish to abstain, they have permission. Nevertheless, if meat is ever cooked together with vegetables, they must not judge those vegetables to have been polluted by the meat, but may eat them even though they abstain from meat [Col. 0107A]. If they judge meat so unclean and abominable that they consider even vegetables cooked with meat unfit to eat, they must cease from their ministry and order, as persons who do not consent to this rule [Note: T. 1, 2: “they must cease.”]. If anyone, after being admonished concerning this rule, does not obey [Note: U.: “does not observe it”], but judges meat, as stated, to be unclean and abominable, he must cease from his order.

### XV. Presbyters must not sell ecclesiastical property

If presbyters sell anything belonging to the Church while the bishop is absent, it was decided that, after the contract has been annulled, the property must be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It shall be for the bishop to determine judicially whether the price should be accepted or not, since it often happens that the proceeds of property sold have yielded a greater sum than the price received.

### XVI. On those who have lived irrationally

[Col. 0107B]

The Greek words in this heading are: **Περὶ τῶν ἀλογευσαμένων ἢ καὶ ἀλογευομένων**, which we can render in Latin as: “On those who have behaved irrationally or are behaving irrationally.” The sense of this statement may be twofold, as is inferred from the matters in question: either it concerns those who have had intercourse with animals, or those who, after the manner of animals, have committed incest with blood relatives.

Therefore, all who committed such a crime before their twentieth year are, after completing fifteen years in penance, to begin sharing only in prayer; after remaining for another five years in communion of prayer alone, they are to be received into communion with the offering after their twentieth year. Their conduct during the time of penance is also to be examined, and they are to receive this humane treatment accordingly [Col. 0107C]. But if any have persisted more obstinately in abusing themselves through this crime [Note: U.: “they themselves are to be admitted to communion of prayer only after a longer period, namely after completing twenty years of penance”], they are to undergo penance alone for a longer period—that is, twenty years.

But those who, after reaching the age of twenty and having wives, fell into this crime are, after doing penance for twenty-five years, to be admitted to communion of prayers. After remaining in this communion of prayers for another five years, they are to receive full communion with the offering [Note: Ae., B. R.: “receive.”]. If some, while having wives and having passed their fiftieth year, have fallen into this crime [Col. 0107D], they are to deserve communion only at the end of life.

### XVII. On those who lived like dumb animals

It was decided that not only these same persons, made lepers by such a crime [Note: All the codices contain the word *idem* (“the same”), which seems superfluous; perhaps *item* (“likewise”).], but also others who have filled others with their own disease, should pray among those who are tossed about by the storm—by which expression we understand the possessed.

### XVIII. On bishops who are not received after their ordination

If any bishops have not been received by their own diocese, in which they had been designated [Note: Ae., E. 3, T. 1, 2: “named”], they are to be compelled by judicial decree to return to it. But if they wish to occupy other churches and use force against other bishops whom they find there [Col. 0108A], raising seditions against them, they must be segregated. If they wish to reside as presbyters in the church where they formerly served as presbyters, they are not to be deprived of their proper dignity. But if they are also proved to stir up seditions there against the bishops established in that place, they must be segregated and, nonetheless, deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate.

### XIX. On those who profess virginity

All who have promised virginity but have violated their profession after despising it are to be counted among the twice-married, that is, among those who have passed to a second marriage. But we prohibit virgin girls who wish to live as sisters with certain men from associating with them.

### XX. On adulterers

[Col. 0108B] If anyone has committed adultery, after completing seven years in penance he is to be restored to perfection according to his former degrees.

### XXI. On women who fornicate and kill their children

Concerning women who fornicate and kill their offspring, and also concerning those who act against themselves in order to expel what has been conceived in the womb: the ancient decree indeed removed them from the Church until the end of their lives; but now we define more humanely that they should be assigned a period of ten years of penance.

### XXII. On those who committed murder intentionally

Those who have committed voluntary homicide are to devote themselves continually to penance; but toward the end of life they are to be considered worthy of communion, and they are to do penance for ten years [Note: In B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., G., these words are absent: “and let them do penance for ten years.”].

### XXIII. On those who committed murder unintentionally

[Col. 0108C]

As for those who committed homicide not intentionally but by accident, the earlier rule joined them to communion after seven years of penance, according to the prescribed degrees. But this more humane decree assigns a period of five years [Col. 0108D] [Note: From T. 2 and U. In A., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, G.: “a period of time.” In Ae.: “periods.”].

### XXIV. On those who live according to pagan custom

Those who observe omens, auspices, dreams, or any kinds of divination according to pagan custom [Col. 0108D], or introduce such people into their homes to inquire into things by magical art, or to purify their houses [U. adds: “things”], must, after confessing, perform five years of penance according to the ancient rules that have been established [Note: U.: “to purify their houses; whoever confesses must perform five years of penance.”].

### XXV. On the man who violated his fiancée’s sister

[Col. 0108D] If anyone, having a fiancée, has perhaps violated her sister and attached himself to her as though she were his own, and as though a union with her ought to be sought, and, after deceiving her, has afterward married the woman to whom he was betrothed [Note: U.: “has promised himself to her in marriage as one to be sought, and after deceiving her …”]; but the woman who suffered the violation has perhaps taken her own life: all who were aware of this deed are to be reduced to ten years of penance according to the established canons.

## III. COUNCIL OF NEOCAESAREA, HELD BY NINETEEN BISHOPS

[Col. 0109]

[Col. 0109A] These canons are indeed second to those set forth at Ancyra and Caesarea, but they are found to precede the Nicene canons. The following persons assembled in the aforementioned synod of the city of Neocaesarea: Vitalis, Germanus [Note: Ae.: “Germanus, Iristrius.”], Sedus, Eristius, Lupus, Gerontius, Leontius, Sanctus, Basiliscus [Note: Ae.: “Gerentius, Sanctus.” U.: “Gerontius, Leontius, Basiliscus.”], Valentinus, Stephanus, Gregorius, Salaminus, Narcissus, Leontius, Longinus, Decasius, and Heraclius Alipius. From them these rules were issued, which are written below.

### I. Presbyters may not marry

If a presbyter marries, he must be deposed from his order. But if he has fornicated or committed adultery, he must be cast out of the Church and reduced to penance among the laity.

### II. A woman may not marry two brothers

If a woman marries two brothers, she must be cast out until the day of her death; but, in the interest of humanity, she ought to be reconciled in her final sacraments [Note: Ae.: “be reconciled”], provided that, if she recovers her health, she is admitted to penance after the marriage has been dissolved. If the woman dies while living in such a union, the penance of the man who remains will be difficult. This judgment must apply equally to men and women.

### III. On those who have entered into many marriages

Concerning those who frequently marry wives and those who marry repeatedly: it is clear that they must observe the period prescribed for them [Note: Ae.: “must be observed”]; but their conduct and faith will shorten the period [Col. 0109C].

### IV. On desire that has not been consummated

If anyone has desired a woman and, even though he has desired intercourse with her, the act has not followed, it is clear that he has been delivered by divine grace.

### V. On sinful catechumens

A catechumen—that is, a hearer—who enters the church and stands with the catechumens, if he is seen to sin, shall hear the word while kneeling, but must abstain from the sin he committed. If he persists in it, he must be cast out altogether.

### VI. On baptizing pregnant women

Concerning pregnant women: since they ought to be baptized whenever they wish—for nothing in this sacrament is shared between the woman who is about to give birth and the one who is born from her womb [Col. 0109D] [Note: U.: “between the woman who is about to give birth and the one who has been brought forth from her womb, because the freedom of each person’s will is declared in that confession; therefore the child, once born, will be baptized separately.” Ae.: “the one conceived”]—because the freedom of each person’s will is declared in that confession [Col. 0110A].

### VII. On presbyters: they may not attend second marriages [Note: From T. 2. In A. and the other codices: “may not pray.”]

A presbyter ought not to attend a feast celebrating a second marriage, especially since he is being asked to impose penance for a second marriage. What presbyter, therefore, would consent to such a marriage for the sake of a feast?

### VIII. A cleric may not be made from the husband of an adulterous wife

[Note: U.: “If it is established that someone’s wife committed adultery while he was still a layman, and this has been proved …”] If it has been established that someone’s wife committed adultery while he was a layman, he cannot be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry. But if she committed adultery after he had already been established in the clerical state [Note: U.: “if she has committed adultery”], he must dismiss her after granting her a bill of repudiation. If he wishes to retain her companionship, he cannot enjoy the ministry he has received.

### IX. On presbyters previously guilty of a bodily sin

[Col. 0110B]

If anyone committed a bodily sin and was afterward ordained presbyter, then, if he confesses that he sinned before his ordination, he is not to offer; but he is to remain in the other offices because of the usefulness of his zeal. For many have judged that even other sins result in deprivation of ordination [Note: Ae.: “that he be deprived because of …”]. But if he has not confessed these matters and cannot be openly convicted by anyone, authority over himself must be left to him.

### X. On deacons previously guilty of a bodily sin

Likewise, if a deacon has been entangled in the same kind of fault [Note: Ae.: “if deacons have been entangled in …, they will restrain themselves …”], he must restrain himself from the ministry.

### XI. A presbyter under thirty years of age is not to be ordained

A presbyter is not to be ordained before the age of thirty [Col. 0110C], even if his life is exemplary; he must wait until the appointed time. For the Lord was baptized in his thirtieth year, and then preached.

### XII. On those baptized during illness

If anyone was baptized while suffering from illness, he ought not to be ordained presbyter. For his faith was not the voluntary faith of a son but arose from necessity—unless afterward his zeal and faith prove exemplary, or scarcity of men compels it.

### XIII. On presbyters from another region

Presbyters who are not from the same region cannot offer in a church when the bishops or presbyters of the city are present, nor give the bread; but in prayer they may give the cup. If the city’s priests are absent and the presbyter has been invited, he may give it in prayer alone [Col. 0110D]. But the deputies of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi* [Col. 0111A], have been established after the example of the seventy elders; nevertheless, as fellow priests, they are to offer for the sake of their care and attention toward the poor and are to be held in honor.

### XIV. On the seven deacons

[Col. 0112A]

There must be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is large [Note: B. R.: “of which”], and the authority for this rule is the Book of the Acts of the Apostles.

## IV. COUNCIL OF GANGRA, ISSUED AFTER THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA BY FIFTEEN BISHOPS

[Col. 0111]

[Col. 0111A] [27–28] To the venerable lords and fellow priests established in Armenia: Eusebius, Eulalius, Olympius [Ae., [Col. 0111B] “Olympus”], Philetus [T. 1: “Piletus”; T. 2: “Philestus”], Pappus, Basilius, Bithynicus [Ae.: “Binicus”], Hieracius, Hipatius [Ae.: “Ipanus”; U.: “Lipacius”], Bassus, Eugenius, Gregorius, Aelianus, Presius [B. R., T. 1: “Proesius”], and Eugenius, who assembled in the council of Gangra, greetings in the Lord.

Since the holy synod of bishops, assembled in the church of Gangra to investigate certain ecclesiastical and necessary matters and to ascertain what had been done according to Eustathius, found many indecent practices being carried out by those very people who followed this same Eustathius, it necessarily decreed that, once everything had been made public [U.: “once all things had been made public”], all the things wrongly committed by him should be cut away.

For it was made clear that these same persons accused marriage and taught that no one living in the married state could have hope in God. Hence it happened that many women, deceived, abandoned their own husbands, and men, deprived of their wives, dissolved the marital bond; and, while professing continence, they committed adultery when they could not maintain it.

They were also found to teach dissension and separation from the Lord’s established institutions of the Churches of God—that is, that ecclesiastical traditions and the things done in churches ought to be despised—establishing private gatherings and presuming to perform and celebrate everything in imitation of what is done in the house of God.

Furthermore, despising ordinary clothing, they adopted new and unusual forms of dress. They also claimed for themselves the firstfruits of the harvest and the offerings that the institution of the ancients assigns to the churches [Col. 0111D], saying that, by their own reasoning [T. 2, U.: “reason”] about doctrine, these ought to be offered to them as holy things and distributed among them.

They taught that slaves who withdrew from their masters, and who, under the guise of religion, despised their masters through this unusual custom of their region [Note: From Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G. In A. and E. 3: “religion”], were acting properly.

Women, contrary to custom and to the adornment proper to their sex, also adopted masculine clothing, believing that they were thereby justified; and many of them, on the pretext of religion, cut off entirely the hair that belonged to their natural beauty.

By despising the fasts preached in the church, they served their bellies. Some of them also rejected foods of meat as unlawful [Col. 0112A] [Ae., T. 2: “considered them”]. They persuaded people that not even prayers ought to be celebrated in the houses of married persons [Col. 0112B], to such an extent that they prohibited them and decreed that no one should share in the offerings made in those houses.

They say that presbyters who have contracted marriages ought to be despised, and that one should not touch the sacraments made by them. They despise the places of holy martyrs and the basilicas, and criticize all who gather there and celebrate the sacraments.

They claim that wealthy believers who do not renounce everything they possess have no hope [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “have no hope in God”]. They also establish many other practices, too numerous for anyone to enumerate, each according to his own judgment [T. 2, U.: “each of them”].

For each of them, departing from the ecclesiastical canon through such an institution, has made laws for himself as though they were his own. Nor is there one common and united opinion among all of them: each, as it seems and pleases him, strives to accuse the Church, adding or diminishing decrees as though he were its ruler.

For these reasons, this council was convened in the church of Gangra to set forth these canons, by which the aforesaid persons will be proved to be outside [Ae., B. R., E. 3, U.: “inside”] the Church. If, however, through penance, they condemn all these things which they have wrongly held, acknowledging that they were not properly uttered by them, they may become acceptable; and the synod believed that each of the things which they ought to condemn should be set forth individually [Ae., B. R., E. 3, U.: “believes”].

But if anyone refuses these things established today, he is to be anathematized and condemned as a heretic and cast out; he shall be not only excluded from communion [Col. 0112D], but also regarded as an exile from the Church, until he begs the bishops for pardon and declares, concerning all the things discovered and exposed among them, which of these he has undertaken to observe [Note: From Ae., B. R., U. In A. and the other codices: “which of these things”; T. 2: “to obey.”].

### I. On those who condemn marriage

If anyone has condemned marriage and has considered a faithful and religious woman sleeping with her husband to be abominable or even blameworthy, as though married persons could not enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

### II. On those who condemn people who eat meat

[Col. 0113A]

If anyone believes that a person who eats meat in faith and with religion—apart from blood, meat sacrificed to an idol, and what has been strangled—is to be condemned, as though he had no hope because he eats it [Note: U.: “as though he had no hope in God because he eats it,”] let him be anathema.

### III. A slave must not despise his master on the pretext of religion

If anyone, on the pretext of religion, teaches another person’s slave that he ought to despise his master and abandon his service, and does not rather teach him to serve his master in good faith and with all honor, let him be anathema.

### IV. On the offering of a married presbyter

If anyone distinguishes against a married presbyter on the ground of his marriage, asserting that he ought not to offer, and for that reason abstains from his offering [Col. 0113B] [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, U.: “abstains”], let him be anathema.

### V. The prayers of the Church must not be despised

If anyone teaches that the house of God and the assemblies held in it ought to be treated with contempt, let him be anathema.

### VI. It is not permitted to assemble outside the Church

If anyone privately gathers people outside the Church and despises the ecclesiastical ordinances [Note: Ae.: “gathers people and despises them”] and the Church itself, while conducting affairs among himself and with presbyters without the bishop’s counsel [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “with a presbyter”], let him be anathema.

### VII. On giving the fruits to the Church and nowhere else

If anyone wishes to receive or give outside the Church the offerings of fruits or the firstfruits owed to the Church [U.: “assigned to the Church”], without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not rather think that these matters should be handled with that person’s counsel [Col. 0113C], let him be anathema.

### VIII. On offerings assigned for the use of the poor

If anyone gives or receives offerings of fruits outside the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy [T. 1: “payment”] to the poor, both the giver and the receiver are to be anathema.

### IX. A person devoted to virginity must not curse marriage

If anyone who has professed virginity or continence judges marriage to be abominable, and not merely because continence and virginity are a good and holy purpose, let him be anathema.

### X. On those who take pride in virginity

If anyone who has professed virginity for God’s sake arrogantly reviles those living in marriage [Col. 0113D], let him be anathema.

### XI. The brothers’ love-feast must not be despised

If anyone considers those who hold a love-feast and summon poor brothers for the Lord’s honor to be contemptible, and refuses to share in their invitations, treating what is done as nothing [Note: Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “treating it as nothing”] [Note: B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “judging it”], let him be anathema.

### XII. On those who practice continence and the use of cloaks

[Col. 0114A]

If any man thinks that, because of his holy purpose—that is, continence—it is appropriate for him to wear a cloak [Ae., B. R., U.: “a pallium”], as though he would thereby obtain righteousness, and reproaches or judges others who respectfully wear the *birrus* and other ordinary clothing that is in common use, let him be anathema.

### XIII. A woman must not assume masculine clothing for the sake of continence

If any woman, judging masculine clothing useful for this purpose [Note: U.: “If any woman, judging the purpose of continence useful …”], wears men’s clothing in order to imitate the dress of men, let her be anathema.

### XIV. A woman who condemns marriage must not leave her husband

If any woman, abandoning her husband, wishes to leave him and dissolve the marital bond by condemning marriage, let her be anathema [Col. 0114B].

### XV. No one may neglect his children for the sake of continence

If anyone abandons his own children and does not support them, nor provide what piety requires, but, on the pretext of continence, considers them worthy of neglect [Note: From U. In A. and the other codices: “If anyone abandons his own children, does not support them, and does not provide them with what is necessary according to piety”], let him be anathema.

### XVI. Children must not despise their parents on the pretext of religion

If any children abandon their parents, especially faithful parents, on the pretext of religious observance [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “on the pretext of the worship of God”], judging this to be right, and do not instead render their parents the honor that is due, venerating in them the very fact that they are faithful, let them be anathema.

### XVII. A woman may not shave her head

[Col. 0114C] Whatever woman, judging it suitable for religious devotion, cuts off her hair, which God gave her as a covering and as a reminder of subjection, thereby undoing the rights of subjection, let her be anathema [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3: “Whatever woman …”].

### XVIII. It is not permitted to fast on Sunday

If anyone fasts on Sunday, judging this appropriate to continence, in contempt of that day, let him be anathema.

### XIX. It is not permitted to reject the common fasts

If any of those who are committed to the purpose of continence, apart from bodily necessity, become proud and consider the common fasts of the whole Church contemptible, claiming for himself, in his own knowledge [Ae.: “conscience”], a perfect rationale [U.: “judgment”], let him be anathema.

### XX. Communion is to be received in the basilicas of the martyrs

[Col. 0114D]

If anyone, through pride, considering himself perfect, either condemns the assemblies held in the places and basilicas of the holy martyrs, or believes that the offerings celebrated there ought to be despised, and that the memorials of the saints ought to be held in contempt [Note: U.: “if anyone, being proud, considers …”], let him be anathema.

We have written these things, however, not cutting off those who, according to the Scriptures, choose the holy purpose of continence in the Church of God [Col. 0115A], but condemning those who esteem its outward form and are lifted up in pride against those who live more simply [Ae.: “who are simple”]. We also condemn those who exalt themselves against the Scriptures and the ecclesiastical canons and introduce new precepts [Note: Ae.: “And we also condemn these.” B. R., U.: “But we also condemn these.”].

We admire virginity together with humility; we declare continence, joined with chastity and religious devotion, most acceptable to God; and we approve and praise the renunciation of worldly affairs and activities [U.: “a suitable”] together with a humble withdrawal. We honor the bond of marriage that endures with chastity. We do not reject the wealthy when they possess justice and good works. We do not condemn frugality accompanied by humble clothing.

Likewise, we praise adornment applied without cosmetics for the care of the body, but we do not accept loose and dissolute behavior in dress [Note: U.: “in the wearing of clothing”]. We honor the houses of God and accept the assemblies held in them as holy and useful, not confining piety to private houses. We honor every place built in the name of God and accept the assembly held in the church for the common benefit. We bless, according to ecclesiastical traditions, the good works performed for poor brothers even beyond one’s means, and we desire that everything consistent with apostolic traditions and the precepts of the Holy Scriptures be done in the Church.

## V. COUNCIL OF SARDICA, OF THREE HUNDRED BISHOPS, AND THE CANONS ESTABLISHED THEREIN

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115B] [33–34] In the sixth year of the emperor Constantius [Note: Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “Constantine.” In the Lucchese codex the same emperor was identified as Constantine.], in the consulship of Leontius and Sallustius, in the era 371 [Note: Ae.: era 372. U., G.: era 381.], the Sardican synod was assembled. There all the Arian bishops throughout the East were condemned; summoned to the council, they refused to attend because of the guilt of their conscience [Note: Ae.: “to assemble at the council because of the guilt of their conscience.”]. In that council, among other matters, the following rules were established for ecclesiastical discipline.

### I. A bishop must not transfer himself to another city

Osius the bishop said: “A custom no less evil than it is pernicious must be eradicated from the roots, so that no bishop may be permitted to move from his own city to another. For the reason why they attempt this is obvious: no bishop has ever been found in this matter to have moved from a larger city to a smaller one [Col. 0115C] [Note: B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: ‘has moved.’]. Hence it is apparent that they are inflamed by the ardor of avarice, serve ambition, and seek to exercise domination. Therefore, if it please everyone that such ruin be punished more severely, let one who is such have not even lay communion.” All said: “It pleases us.”

“If such a man should prove so rash as perhaps to offer the excuse that he has received letters from the people, when it is clear that he has been able to corrupt by reward and payment a few persons who do not possess the sincere faith, so that they might cry out in the church as though they wished to ask for him as bishop, I judge that these frauds must altogether be condemned, so that such a person may not receive even lay communion at the end. If this pleases you all, decree it.” All said: “It pleases us.”

### II. A bishop must not pass from province to province unless invited

[Col. 0116B]

Osius the bishop said: Let this also be decreed, that a bishop may not pass from his own province to another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps he has been invited by his brethren [Note: [Col. 0116D] B. R., “has been invited by his brethren”], lest we seem to have closed the door of charity.

### III. Concerning two bishops of one province who are in dispute with one another

Osius the bishop said: Provision must also be made that, if in some province a bishop should happen to have a lawsuit against his brother bishop, neither one of the two should summon bishops from another province to give judgment.

### IV. Concerning a bishop whose case has been adjudicated

[Col. 0116C] Osius the bishop said: But if a bishop has been adjudged in some case, and thinks that he has a good cause, and wishes the judgment to be reopened [E. 3, U., “so that the judgment may be reopened”], if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter, so that a letter may be written to the Roman bishop either by those who conducted the inquiry or even by other bishops [Ae., “those bishops”] who reside in the neighboring province. If he judges that the judgment ought to be reopened, let it be reopened, and let him appoint judges [Note: [Col. 0116D] Ae., “let him give the judgment’s decision”]. [Note: [Col. 0116D] T. 2, “to the bishop, so that if.”] But if he determines that the case is such that the proceedings already completed should not be reconsidered [Note: [Col. 0116D] In the remaining codices, except A., “should not be renewed”], whatever the Roman bishop decrees shall stand confirmed. Therefore, if this pleases everyone, let it be enacted.

The synod replied: It pleases us.

### V. Concerning bishops deposed by a synod

Gaudentius the bishop said: If it pleases you, an addition should be made to this sentence, which you have pronounced with complete holiness [Col. 0116D], [Col. 0117A] namely, that when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who reside in the neighboring districts, and he declares that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome, no other bishop should be ordained to the same see 35 after the appeal of the man who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

### VI. Concerning the foregoing matters

Osius the bishop said: If it should happen that in one province in which there are two bishops one bishop alone should remain [Note: [Col. 0117D] In the other codices, except A., “several”], and, through negligence, he should be unwilling to ordain a bishop, while the people assemble, the bishops of the neighboring province must first summon that bishop who resides in the same province and show him [Note: [Col. 0117D] From U. In A. and the remaining witnesses: “the bishop of the neighboring province ought first to be summoned by the bishops who reside in the same province and shown”] that the people are asking for a ruler, and that it is just that he himself should come and ordain a bishop together with them. But if, after being summoned by letter, he remains silent and ignores the matter and sends no reply, then the people must be satisfied: they should come from the neighboring province and ordain a bishop [Note: [Col. 0117D] U., “the people must be satisfied; and so they should come”]. Yet permission must not again be granted indiscriminately. For if some village or small town, for which one presbyter is sufficient, should suddenly wish a bishop to be ordained for it, so that the name and authority of a bishop may be cheapened, those invited from another province must not make a bishop for them, except either in cities which have had bishops, or in a city or place so populous that it deserves to have a bishop.

The synod replied: It pleases us.

### VII. Concerning accused bishops

Osius the bishop said: It was also agreed that, if a bishop has been accused [Col. 0117C], and the assembled bishops of that region judge him and remove him from his rank [Note: [Col. 0117D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U., “of that very region”], and the man who appears to have been removed appeals and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, wishing to be heard, then, if he considers it just that the inquiry be reopened, the Roman bishop should deign to write to the bishops who are in a neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the faith of truth [Note: [Col. 0117D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “so that”].

But if the man who asks that his case be heard again [Note: [Col. 0118D] U., “who wishes his case to be heard again and has appealed to the Roman bishop”] moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send presbyters from his own side [Note: [Col. 0118D] Ae., B. R., “a presbyter”], it shall be in the Roman bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and considers appropriate. If he decrees that men should be sent to judge in person together with the bishops, so that they may also possess the authority of the person by whom they were sent [Col. 0117D], this shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the provincial bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.

36 ### VIII. That bishops should not indiscriminately go to the imperial court

Osius the bishop said: The excessive frequency of our importunity and our unjust petitions [Note: [Col. 0118D] Ae., E. 3, T. 1, 2, “unjust requests”] have caused us not to possess as much favor or confidence, since certain bishops do not cease going to the imperial court [Col. 0118A], especially the Africans, who, as we have learned, disregard and despise the salutary counsels of our most holy brother and fellow bishop Gratus. They bring to the imperial court not only many different cases that will not benefit the Church, as is customary or perhaps necessary, so that the poor, widows, or orphans may be helped, but also ask for secular dignities and offices to be granted to certain persons.

This depravity has therefore long aroused not only murmuring but also scandals. It is honorable, however, for a bishop to offer his intercession for those who are oppressed by some unjust force, or when a widow is afflicted or an orphan despoiled—provided, nevertheless, that these matters have a just cause and petition.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if it pleases you, decree that bishops should not approach the imperial court, except perhaps those who have either been invited or summoned by letters of the most religious emperor [Col. 0118B]. But since it often happens that those who suffer injury flee to the mercy of the Church, and that those who have sinned are condemned to exile or to the islands, or indeed that anyone receives a sentence, assistance must therefore be given to them, and without hesitation pardon must be sought for them through the Church. If this pleases you, let it be enacted.

All said: It pleases us, and let it be established.

### IX. Concerning the foregoing matters

Osius the bishop said: Your prudence must also address this matter: since you have decreed that a bishop’s impropriety should not be marked by his going to the imperial court, let anyone who has or has received the sorts of petitions mentioned above send them through his deacon. The person of the minister will not be regarded with envy, and he will be able to report more quickly what he has obtained [Col. 0118C].

It also seems fitting that anyone who has a petition should send it to our brothers and fellow bishops who reside in the chief city—that is, in the metropolis—and that they should send it through their deacons, granting letters of recommendation in the same manner to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in the regions and cities in which the fortunate and blessed Augustus governs the state.

But if one of the bishops has 37 friends in the palace from whom he wishes to obtain something that is nevertheless honorable, he should not be forbidden to ask and inform them through his deacon—those whom he knows can kindly provide intercession for him in his absence [Note: [Col. 0118D] Ae., B. R., U., “kindly”; Note: [Col. 0118D] U., “can arrange it for him in his absence”].

Whoever comes to Rome, as has been said [Col. 0118D], should hand over to our most holy brother and fellow bishop of the Roman Church the petitions he has, so that he himself may first examine whether they are honorable and just, and may diligently and carefully arrange for them to be carried to the imperial court [U., “may arrange it”].

All said that this counsel pleased them and was honorable.

### X. Concerning the foregoing matters

Alipius the bishop said: If, on behalf of orphans and widows or of those suffering who have just causes, they undertake the hardships of a journey [Note: [Col. 0119D] Ae., “arduous journeys”], they will have some reasonable justification. But when they ask for things that cannot be obtained without provoking everyone’s envy and criticism, it is not necessary for them to go to the imperial court.

### XI. Concerning the foregoing matters

Gaudentius the bishop said: The measures you have prudently provided—measures acceptable to everyone and pleasing both to God and to human beings—can retain their force up to this point if fear is joined to this sentence. For we ourselves know that, very often, because of the shamelessness of a few, the sacred and religious name of the priesthood has been criticized.

Therefore, if anyone, contrary to the judgment of everyone, strives to please ambition more than God, he must know that, after an accounting has been rendered, he will lose his honor and dignity. This can be known and discovered if each one of us who is stationed along the route, when he sees a bishop proceeding [U., “emerging”], inquires about his journey, examines his reasons, and learns where he is going. If he discovers that the man is going to the imperial court, he should ask whether the provision stated above applies—whether, perhaps, he has been invited [U., “has been”]—so that permission may be granted him to go.

But if, as your holiness mentioned above, he has attempted to go to the imperial court because of desires and ambitions, neither his letters should be countersigned nor should he be received into communion [Note: [Col. 0119D] U., “his letters should not be written; no”].

If this pleases you, it ought to be confirmed by the judgment of everyone.

All said that this was honorable and that the decree pleased them [Note: [Col. 0119D] Ae., “that this decree pleased them”].

### XII. Concerning the foregoing matters

Osius the bishop said: But moderation is also necessary, dearest brothers [Col. 0119C], lest some, still 38 unaware of what has been decreed in the synod, should suddenly come to the cities that are along the route. The bishop of that city must admonish and instruct him, so that he may send a deacon from that place; but, after being admonished, he himself must return to his own parish.

### XIII. That no one should be ordained bishop from the laity

Osius the bishop said: I think it necessary that this be considered with the greatest care [Note: [Col. 0120D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U., “that you consider”]. If perhaps a wealthy man, a lawyer from the forum, or an administrator is requested as bishop, he should not be ordained beforehand unless he has first discharged the office of lector and the ministries of deacon and presbyter. Thus, if he is worthy, let him ascend through the individual ranks to the summit of the episcopate.

For through these promotions, which necessarily occupy a lengthy period [Col. 0119D], it can be tested with what faith, modesty, seriousness, and reverence he acts, so that, if he is proved worthy, he may be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that a neophyte should be rashly and lightly ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon—especially since the most blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have warned and forbidden this. Rather, those should be ordained whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been approved.

All said that this pleased them.

### XIV. That a bishop should not remain in another province

Osius the bishop said: You must also decree this [Col. 0120A]: when a bishop comes from another city to another city, or from his own province to another province, and serves ambition more than devotion, so that he wishes to remain for a long time in a foreign city, and it happens that the bishop of that city is neither so well instructed nor so learned, while the newcomer begins to despise him and frequently preach in such a way as to dishonor and weaken his person, thereby coming to feel no hesitation about abandoning the church assigned to him and moving to another [Note: [Col. 0120D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., “a foreign one”]—then set a definite period.

For it is inhuman not to receive a fellow bishop, but it is harmful for him to remain longer than he should. Therefore provision must be made to prevent this [Note: [Col. 0120D] T. 1, 2, U., “it must be prohibited”].

I remember that at the preceding council our brothers decreed that, if a layman in the city where he resides failed to hold an assembly for three Sundays—that is, for three weeks—he would be deprived of communion. If this was decreed concerning laymen, how much more is it neither lawful nor fitting for a 39 bishop, unless he has some very serious necessity or an exceptionally difficult case, to be absent from his church for so long and distress his people? [Col. 0119B]

All said that this pleased them.

### XV. Concerning bishops who have possessions in another province

Osius the bishop said: Since nothing ought to be overlooked, there are certain brothers and fellow bishops who do not own property in the city in which they appear to have been appointed bishops, or who have only a small amount of property there where they reside, while they are known to possess suitable estates elsewhere, or the interests of relatives whom they may favor.

They should therefore be permitted, up to this point, to go to their estates, manage them, and arrange the produce of their labor, so that, if it is necessary to remain after three Sundays—that is, after three weeks—they may remain rather on their own farms. [Col. 0120C] If there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, let them go there, so that they do not appear to celebrate the Lord’s Day without a church. In this way, neither will their household affairs suffer loss through their absence, nor will they incur suspicion of ostentation and ambition by coming frequently to another city in which there is a bishop.

All said that this pleased them.

### XVI. Concerning the excommunication of clerics

[Col. 0120D] Osius the bishop said: If this also pleases everyone: whether a deacon, a presbyter, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his bishop and has gone to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was rejected by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, he should know that, after the bishops have been summoned, he will have to give an account of the reasons.

All said: This decree will preserve peace and guard harmony.

### XVII. That clerics, if unjustly excommunicated, may approach neighboring bishops

Osius the bishop said: I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps being angry—which he ought not to be—should quickly or harshly become enraged against his presbyter or deacon and wish to expel him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.

Therefore, the man who has been removed must have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, since a petitioner ought not to be denied a hearing [Note: [Col. 0121C] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, G., “of petitioning”]. The bishop who removed him, whether justly or unjustly, must patiently accept that the matter 40 be investigated, so that his sentence may either be confirmed by many or corrected [Note: [Col. 0121C] U., “the bishop who removed him must patiently accept that the matter be investigated, and that his sentence, if harsh, be corrected by many”].

Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no other person should presume to receive the man who had been separated from communion and associate him with communion.

If those who have assembled to hear the case see contempt and arrogance on the part of the clerics—for it is not fitting that a bishop should suffer either injury or insult—they should rebuke them with sterner words, so that they obey the bishop who gives honorable commands. For just as he ought to show sincere love and charity toward the clerics, so in turn the ministers ought to show their bishop unfeigned obedience.

### XVIII. That a bishop may not ordain another bishop’s cleric in his own Church

Januarius the bishop said: Let your holiness also decree this: no bishop may solicit an ecclesiastical official of another city and ordain him in his own diocese, because discord commonly arises from such disputes. Therefore, by the judgment of everyone, let it be forbidden that anyone dare to do this [B. R., U., “let it be forbidden”].

### XIX. Concerning the foregoing matters

[Col. 0122A]

Osius the bishop said: We have also unanimously decreed this: if anyone from another parish wishes to ordain another bishop’s minister without the consent of that bishop and without his will, his ordination shall not be valid. Whoever usurps this authority must be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow bishops.

### XX. That foreign clerics should not remain long at Thessalonica

Aetius the bishop said: You are not unaware how great and important the city of the Thessalonians is. Presbyters and deacons often come to it from other regions, and they are not content to remain or reside there for a short time; indeed, they can scarcely be compelled to return to their own places except after a long time [Note: [Col. 0122C] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, “to their own”].

All said: The periods established concerning bishops must also be observed with regard to these persons.

### XXI. Clerics who have suffered violence or persecution, if they come to another city, should not be forbidden to remain there as long as they are unable to return

Osius the bishop said: At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius [T. 2, Alipius], this too was agreed: if anyone has suffered violence and been unjustly driven out for the sake of discipline, the Catholic defense, 41 or the confession of truth, and, while fleeing danger as an innocent man, has come to another city in distress, he should not be forbidden to remain there as long as he is unable to return or until his injury has received a 42 remedy. For it is harsh not to receive one who is suffering persecution. Rather, generous goodwill and humanity must also be shown to him.

## VI. COUNCIL OF ANTIOCH: THIRTY-ONE BISHOPS

[Col. 0121]

[Col. 0121D] The holy and most peaceful synod, gathered together as one, sends greetings in the Lord to the unanimous holy and fellow priests throughout the individual provinces.

The grace and truth of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, visiting the holy Church of Antioch and joining it together through the concord of the most peaceful Spirit, has accomplished many things and others besides. In everything, however, with the holy and peaceful Spirit suggesting it, it also accomplished this: that the matters which appeared rightly to be established, after very careful consideration and judgment, by all of us bishops gathered together at Antioch from different provinces, should be brought to your knowledge.

We trust in the Lord’s grace and in the holy Spirit of peace that you too will join with us as though you had been gathered into one power [Note: [Col. 0121D] Ae., “as though you had been gathered into one strength”], and, strengthened by striving together with us in prayers [Col. 0122D], will be present in the Holy Spirit, consenting to the very things that have been defined and, with the agreement of the Holy Spirit, confirming those matters which appeared right.

The ecclesiastical canons established are the following. The bishops present at the synod were: Eusebius, Niceta, Antiochus, Archelaus, Isicius [Note: [Col. 0121D] Ae., B. R., U., “Hesychius”], Jacobus, Aeneas, Bassus [Note: [Col. 0121D] U., “Passus”], Moses, Macedonius, Theodorus, another Theodorus, Paulus, Eustachius, Manicius, Agapius, Alexander, Patritius, Petrus, Theodorus, Narcissus, Syricus [Note: [Col. 0121D] T. 1, 2, “Siricius”], Manicius [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ae., B. R., U., “Mocimus”], Aetherius, Magnus, Alipius [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ae., B. R., U., “Alphius”], Tarcodius [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ae., U., “Tharcordi”; T. 2, “Tarchodimantus”], Mantus, Petrus, Anatolius, and Chirion [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, “Cyrion”; U., “Sirion”], from the provinces of Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, ancient Arabia, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, and Isauria. They established the following matters.

### I. It is not permitted to celebrate Easter at a different time or to celebrate it with the Jews

[Col. 0123A]

All who dare to dissolve the rule of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, which was celebrated in the presence of God and the most beloved Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0123D] Ae., “in the presence of the most beloved lord”], concerning the holy and saving festival of Easter of our Savior, ought to be excommunicated and cast out from the Church, especially if they persist out of a contentious desire to overturn what has been excellently established. These statements concern laymen.

But if anyone among the leaders of the Church—that is, a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition should dare, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the churches [Note: [Col. 0123D] Ae., E. 3, U., “in the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the churches”], to maintain [Note: [Col. 0123D] U., “to resist in these matters and with the Jews”; G., “strive to maintain”] and wish to celebrate Easter with the Jews, the holy synod has judged him to be from that very moment alien to the Church [Col. 0123B], as one who is guilty not only of his own sin but has also become a corrupter of others in mind and conduct.

Not only must such a person be deposed from the priesthood and ministry, but those who dare to communicate with them after their condemnation must also be deposed. Those who have been deposed must likewise be deprived of the external honor which the holy canon and the priesthood of God had merited for them.

### II. It is not permitted to despise the Church’s communion or to communicate with the excommunicated

All who enter the church of God and hear the sacred Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer, 43 also oppose the holy reception of the Lord’s sacrament according to some personal discipline [Col. 0123C]. Such persons must be cast out from the Church until, by confessing, they demonstrate the fruit of repentance and, after making supplication, have shown themselves worthy to be received when pardon has been granted.

It is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated, nor to enter their homes, nor to pray with those who do not participate in the Church’s prayer, nor to receive into one Church anyone excommunicated by another. If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or even anyone enrolled in the canon is seen communicating with the excommunicated, he too must be deprived of communion, as one who confuses the rules of the Church.

### III. A cleric who migrates to another Church must not remain there

If any presbyter, deacon, or any cleric, abandoning his own Church, believes that he ought to move to another and gradually attempts to remain permanently in the place to which he has migrated, he must no longer minister, especially if his bishop has urged him to return [T. 1, “asked him to return”]. If, even after being summoned by his bishop, he does not obey but persists, he must in every way be deposed from his office and must never have hope of restoration.

But if another bishop receives a man deposed for this fault, he too shall deserve a penalty of rebuke from the common synod [Col. 0124A], as one who dissolves ecclesiastical rights.

### IV. A bishop or any cleric who has been removed from office may not minister

If a bishop has been deposed by a synod [Note: [Col. 0124D] T. 1, 2, “by his own synod”], or a presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, and has presumed to undertake anything belonging to the priesthood or sacred ministry, he may no longer have hope of restoration or any place for making a defense in another synod. All who communicate with him must also be cast out from the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against him, they have stubbornly communicated with him.

### V. Clerics may not gather privately while despising their bishop

[Col. 0124B] If any presbyter or deacon, despising his bishop, separates himself from the Church and, having privately gathered people [U., “presbyters”] around him, dares to erect an altar, and nevertheless remains disobedient when his bishop urges him and recalls him once and again [44], he must by every means be deposed, and must not hope ever to obtain healing or recover his former honor.

If he also persists in disturbing and stirring up the Church outside, he must be punished as a seditious person.

### VI. Concerning the excommunicated

If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he must not first be received by others unless he has been received by his own bishop, or unless a council has been convened at which he appears, gives an answer, satisfies the synod, and is ordered to be received under another sentence [Col. 0124C]. This is also to be observed concerning laymen, presbyters, deacons, and all who belong to the clergy.

### VII. No stranger should be received without a letter

No foreign cleric should be received without a *formata*, which the Greeks call an *epistolium* [Note: [Col. 0124D] From the remaining witnesses, except A., which has “letter”].

### VIII. Only chorepiscopi may issue *formatae*

Nor may presbyters give *formatae*—that is, canonical letters—to distant regions; they may send only ordinary letters to neighboring bishops. But the vicars of bishops [Note: [Col. 0124D] B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “the vicar-bishops”], whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi*, may issue *formatae*.

### IX. Concerning metropolitan bishops

[Col. 0124D] Throughout each province, each bishop must know that the metropolitan bishop who presides has undertaken the care and concern of the entire province. Therefore those who have cases must without hesitation go to the metropolitan city.

Accordingly, it has pleased us that he should take precedence in honor, and that the other bishops should do nothing beyond this without him, in accordance with the ancient canon that has prevailed among our fathers, except for matters belonging to each individual church within its own diocese [U., “belonging to each individual church”].

For every bishop ought to have authority over his own diocese, in order to govern it according to the respect due to him and to provide for the region situated under his city. Thus it is also permissible for him, after suitable judgment, to ordain presbyters and deacons and to deliberate concerning individual matters with moderation and due weight.

Beyond this, nothing may be done without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, nor may the metropolitan undertake anything without the counsel of the other priests.

45 ### X. Concerning chorepiscopi

The chorepiscopi who are established in villages and rural districts, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops, should, in the judgment of the holy synod, know that they must retain their proper measure and govern the neighboring churches entrusted to them [Col. 0125B], and be content with the care and governance they have received.

They are permitted to appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, who need receive authorization only for these grades. But they must not dare to ordain a presbyter or deacon without the knowledge of the bishop of the city or of the church beside which either they themselves or the region over which they are known to preside is situated.

If anyone dares to violate these decrees, he must be deposed and deprived of the dignity with which he is endowed. A chorepiscopus, however, must be ordained by the bishop of the city or place to which he is attached [U., “of the place which is adjacent”].

### XI. Concerning bishops or clerics who go to the emperor without letters from the bishops

[Col. 0125C] If any bishop, presbyter, or absolutely anyone subject to ecclesiastical discipline goes to the emperor without the counsel or letters of those bishops who are within the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he must be repudiated and expelled not only from communion but also deprived of his own dignity, as one who causes trouble and annoyance to imperial ears contrary to ecclesiastical decrees.

But if necessity compels someone to hasten to the emperor for some action, he must go with deliberation and the counsel of the bishop of the metropolitan province and with the knowledge of the others who are in the same province, carrying letters.

### XII. Concerning deposed bishops or clerics

[Col. 0125D] If anyone deposed by his own bishop—whether a presbyter or deacon—or any bishop removed from office by a synod, presumes to bring trouble to imperial ears, he must instead turn to the greater synod of bishops, state in their council the matters which he thinks just [U., “attach what he considers just to their council”], and await from them whatever judgment is pronounced concerning him.

But if, overcome by faintheartedness, he refuses to do this and becomes such an annoyance to the emperor, he shall receive no pardon, nor any opportunity for that assertion of his [T. 1, 2, “of that complaint”], nor hope of recovering his rank in the future.

46 ### XIII. Bishops may not ordain clerics in another province

[Col. 0126A]

No bishop should dare to travel from one province to another and ordain anyone in its churches or promote anyone to sacred ministry. Nor should he attract other bishops there with him [U., “to attract”], unless perhaps he has gone after being requested by letter, not only by the metropolitan but also by the bishops of the province who are with him.

If, however, he arrives disorderly, with no one inviting him, and presumes either to ordain anyone or attempts to usurp for himself any acts belonging to that church and not pertaining to him [Ae., E. 3, U., “which do not pertain”], everything he has done shall indeed be empty and void. He himself, however, must bear the appropriate consequences of this undisciplined daring and unreasonable undertaking [Note: [Col. 0125D] B. R., E. 3, “seek”; U., “await”], as one deposed by the holy synod and already condemned on account of such presumption [Col. 0126B].

### XIV. Concerning accused bishops

If a bishop is accused before a judgment of bishops on some criminal charges, and it happens that the bishops of the province who have assembled hold differing opinions—some declaring him innocent and others guilty—then, in order to remove such a controversy, it has pleased the holy synod that the metropolitan bishop of a neighboring province should be summoned, together with some other bishops, so that, sitting together, they may resolve whatever the question may be. This is so that the judgment pronounced by the bishops of one province may be firm.

### XV. Concerning the foregoing matters

[Col. 0126C]

If a bishop criminally accused has received one unanimous sentence from all the bishops within the province, he may not thereafter be judged by others. Rather, the sentence pronounced by everyone must remain firm and valid concerning him, as one that is agreed upon.

### XVI. Concerning bishops without a see [T. 1, “wandering bishops”]

If a bishop without a see [T. 1, “wandering bishop”] comes upon a vacant church and secretly believes that he ought to seize it [Note: [Col. 0125D] From B. R. T. 1, 2. In A. and the remaining witnesses, “while it is being seized”; U., “suddenly”] without a full synod, he must be cast out, even if the people whom he has seized wish to retain him as their bishop.

A synod shall be called 47 full when the metropolitan bishop is also present.

### XVII. Concerning bishops who, after receiving the laying on of hands, refuse to undertake their ministry

[Col. 0126D]

If a bishop, after receiving the laying on of hands [Note: [Col. 0126D] U., “refuses, after the people assigned to him have been designated, to preside over them and so does not accept”], does not accept the priestly ministry and preside over the people assigned to him, nor consent to go to the church in which he was ordained, he must be regarded as excluded from communion until he consents under compulsion to receive the people assigned to him, or until the full provincial synod of bishops makes some decision concerning him.

### XVIII. Concerning the foregoing matters

If an ordained bishop does not go to the parish for which he was ordained [Col. 0127A], not through his own fault [Note: [Col. 0127D] U., G., “if it is not through his own fault”] but perhaps because of the opposition of the people, he must retain the honor he received and exercise the priesthood, provided that he causes no trouble to the church in which he had been appointed.

He must, however, await the full provincial synod until a decision is made concerning what is appropriate in his case.

### XIX. It is not permitted to ordain a bishop without the counsel of the metropolitan bishop

A bishop must not be ordained without the counsel and presence of the metropolitan bishop. It would be better if bishops from the entire province were assembled. If this cannot be done, those who cannot be present should indicate their consent concerning the candidate in letters of their own; only then, after the agreement of the majority has been expressed either by presence or by letters, should he be ordained.

If this is done otherwise than has been decreed [U., “than has been decreed”], such an ordination shall have no validity. But if the ordination is carried out according to the defined rules and some oppose it because of personal and domestic quarrels, their opposition must be disregarded, and the judgment of the majority concerning him shall prevail.

### XX. That a synod should be held twice a year

For ecclesiastical matters and for resolving disputes that arise, it has seemed sufficient that a council of bishops be held twice a year in each province. Once, indeed, after the third week of the Easter festival, so that the council may be completed in the fourth week that follows—that is, at mid-Pentecost. The provincial bishops should be summoned by those who reside in the larger cities, that 48 is, in the metropolitan cities [Col. 0127C] [Note: [Col. 0127D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, “the bishops of the province”].

The second council should be held on the Ides of October, a date which among the Greeks falls on the tenth day of the month Hyperberetaeus.

At these councils, presbyters and deacons must also be present, as well as all who consider themselves injured, and they must await the synodal judgment. Nor may anyone hold councils on his own, without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishops, to whom judgment concerning all matters has been entrusted.

## XXI. A Bishop Must Not Transfer from One Diocese to Another

A bishop must not transfer from one diocese to another, neither if he has intruded on his own initiative, nor if he has been forcibly drawn there by the people, nor even if this is advised to him by bishops. Rather, he must remain in the Church of God which he received by lot from the beginning and must not depart from it elsewhere, according to the rule established by the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0127D] U.: “according to the rule formerly established by the Fathers concerning this matter.”].

## XXII. A Bishop Must Not Invade Another City

A bishop must not invade another city which is demonstrably not subject to him, nor a region which is clearly not assigned to his care, in order to ordain anyone there; nor may he establish presbyters [Col. 0128A] or deacons belonging to other bishops, unless perhaps with the counsel of the bishop of that region. If anyone should attempt such a thing [Note: [Col. 0127D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, U.: “dare”], such an ordination shall indeed be invalid [E.: “must be rejected”], and the man who has wrongly usurped this authority shall be reproved by the synod.

## XXIII. A Bishop May Not Appoint His Own Successor

A bishop may not appoint another as though he were to be his future successor, even when he is near death. If anything of this kind has been done, the ordination shall be invalid. He must observe the ecclesiastical constitutions, which state as follows: a bishop cannot be appointed in any other way except in a council and with the consent of the bishops—namely, those who, after the death of the bishop who preceded him [Note: [Col. 0128D] T. 2: “of another who preceded him”], have authority to advance the man who is worthy.

## XXIV. Ecclesiastical and Episcopal Property

Whatever belongs to the Church must be preserved with every diligence and good faith—that faith, namely, which is owed to God, who foresees and judges all things. Such property must be governed and administered with the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the souls of the entire people appear to have been entrusted.

The property belonging to the Church must be made known to those presbyters and deacons [Note: [Col. 0128D] U.: “to the presbyters and deacons”], that is, to those who are around him, so that they themselves may not be ignorant and nothing belonging to their own Church may be concealed from them. Thus, if the bishop should happen to depart this life, the ecclesiastical possessions, being manifest and known, will not be lost or perish.

Nor should the bishop’s private property, as though liable, suffer injury on account of ecclesiastical property [Note: [Col. 0128D] U.: *rebus ecclesiasticis*, for *rerum ecclesiasticarum*.], whether that injury [Note: [Col. 0128D] Ae., B. R., T. 2: “any injury”]. For it is just and fitting before the Lord [Ae.: “God”] that the bishop’s own property be left to those persons to whom he himself has judged it should be left, while whatever belongs to the Church should be preserved for it. In this way neither will the Church be afflicted by any loss, nor will the bishop be deprived under the pretext of ecclesiastical property, nor will those belonging to him become involved in lawsuits by which his memory after death might be burdened with curses of some kind [U.: “dishonored”].

## XXV. A Bishop Has Authority to Administer Ecclesiastical Property

A bishop has authority over ecclesiastical property, in order to distribute it to all who are in need, with complete fear and reverence toward God. He himself may also receive from it and use whatever he needs, provided that he truly needs it, whether for his own necessities or for the expenses of the brethren who stay with him for the sake of hospitality, so that they may not in any respect be defrauded through want, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Having daily food and bodily covering, with these we are content” [U.: “let us be content”].

But if, not content with these things and finding them insufficient, he transfers ecclesiastical property or any of the Church’s revenues to domestic necessities, or gathers into his own possession the produce of ecclesiastical fields without the knowledge of the presbyters or deacons [U.: “those dwelling with him”], and grants his household members—or even his relatives, brothers, or sons—authority over such property, so that through their secret administration the other ecclesiastical members appear to be harmed, he must render an account for this fault, such as it is, before the metropolitan of the province.

If the bishop, or the presbyters who are with him, should be accused in this way [T. 2: “detected”]—that they are said to be appropriating to themselves what belongs to the Church, whether fields or any other ecclesiastical possessions, while the poor are oppressed by need and deprivation, and that because of this not only the Church’s administration but also its administrators are increasingly subjected to curse [Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2: “curses”] and reproach—then such men must receive the correction they deserve, as the holy synod shall determine.

Eusebius subscribed in person to all that was established [B. R., E. 3: “that they established.”] Theodorus, Nicetas, Macedonius, Anatolius, Tharcodius [T. 1, 2: “Tarchodimantus”], Mantus, Aetherius, Narcissus, Alipius, Archelaus, Bassus, Syricus, Eustachius, Mauricius, Hesychius, Manicius, Paulus, and the others, whose names are already contained above in Greek [Note: [Col. 0129A] From all the codices. In A.: “are contained in writing,”]—we have consented.

# VII. THE COUNCIL OF LAODICEA, ISSUED BY THE PRIESTS OF LAODICEA [Note: [Col. 0129D] In the codices: “Laudocia.”]

[Col. 0129]

[Col. 0129B] The holy synod of Laodicea in Phrygia Pacatiana, summoned from various provinces of Asia, set forth ecclesiastical rules, as written below.

### I. Concerning Those Married Twice

Concerning the fact that, according to the ecclesiastical canon, those who have freely and lawfully entered a second marriage, without engaging in secret intercourse, should devote themselves for a short time to prayer and fasting, and thereafter be restored to communion by way of pardon.

### II. Concerning Those Who Fall into Various Sins

For those who fall into various sins and devote themselves earnestly to prayer, confession, and penance, demonstrating a complete turning away from their evil deeds, a period of penance is to be assigned according to the character of the sin, because of the mercy and goodness of God. Therefore, those who are such must be recalled and admitted to communion.

### III. Neophytes Are Not to Be Promoted to the Priesthood [Note: [Col. 0129] Many of the titles of these canons are absent in A. They have been taken from B. R.]

A neophyte must not be promoted to the priestly order.

### IV. Clerical Ordination Must Not Be Performed in the Presence of Catechumens

The laying on of hands over those being ordained must not be performed in the presence of catechumens.

### V. Clerics Must Not Take Interest or Sixfold Profit

Those serving at the altar, or those constituted in the priestly order, must not lend at interest or receive interest or profits called “sixfold.”

### VI. Heretics Must Not Enter the Church

[Col. 0129D] Heretics who remain in heresy must not be granted entry into the house of God.

### VII. Concerning Novatians and Quartodecimans

Novatians, and also Quartodecimans, whom the Greeks call Τεσσαραδεκατίτας [U.: Τέσσαρες καὶ δεκάτερες], that is, those who celebrate Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the first month, as well as their catechumens or faithful, must not be received until they condemn every heresy, and above all the one in which they were held. Then those who among them are called faithful must be taught the creed; and, after they have been anointed with holy chrism, it will be appropriate for them to share in the divine sacrament.

### VIII. Concerning Cataphrygians Coming to the Church

Those who convert from the heresy called “According to the Phrygians” (*Secundum Phrygas*) and consider themselves members of the clergy, even if they are called eminent, must be carefully instructed as catechumens and baptized by the bishops and presbyters of the Catholic Church.

### IX. Catholics Must Not Enter What Heretics Call Their Martyria

[Col. 0130C] Catholics must not enter the cemeteries or places called *martyria* of heretics for the sake of prayer or seeking healing. Those who do go there, if they are faithful, must be excluded from communion and assigned to penance for a certain period; but when they have repented and confessed that they have erred, they must be received.

### X. Catholics Must Not Be Joined in Marriage with Heretics

Those who belong to the Church must not indiscriminately join their own children in marriage with heretics.

### XI. Concerning the Canonical Women of the Church

Women whom the Greeks call *presbytides*, but whom we call elder widows, women who have had one husband, and *matriculariae* (women enrolled on the church register), must not be established in the church as though they had been ordained.

### XII. Bishops Are to Be Ordained with the Counsel of Metropolitans and Neighboring Bishops

[Col. 0130D]

Bishops must not be appointed to the leadership of the Church without the judgment of the metropolitans and neighboring bishops. Nor may any be chosen except those whose commendable life has recommended them long beforehand and who, moreover, have been proved by their conduct in the word of faith and in sound reasoning.

[Col. 0131A] [Note: [Col. 0131D] [ [Col. 0131] This note is printed at the foot of column 131, but its callout letter, “a,” does not appear in the text.] From all the codices. In A.: “having been admitted.”]

### XIII. The People Must Not Elect Ministers of the Altar

Concerning the fact that the people must not be permitted to make the election of those who are to be assigned to the ministry of the altar.

### XIV. Holy Offerings Must Not Be Sent to Other Provinces as Eulogies at Easter

[U., G.: “sent across.”]

Holy offerings must not be sent to other parishes during the Easter season in place of eulogies.

### XV. Concerning Psalmists

No one other than the canonical psalmists [Note: [Col. 0131D] In the codices: “psalms.” U.: “psalms which are sung publicly and read from the codex, another,”] who ascend the pulpit and read from the Codex may sing in the church.

### XVI. The Holy Gospel Is Also to Be Read on Saturdays

The Gospels are to be read on Saturdays together with the other Scriptures.

### XVII. Psalms Must Not Be Confused by Being Scattered Together

In processions, different verses and meanings from various books must not be connected [T. 1: *conjugere*, for *conjungere*]—that is, joined into a single song—but a reading must duly be made after each psalm.

### XVIII. Concerning Daily Prayers

Concerning the fact that prayers of supplication must always be celebrated at the ninth hour and in the evening.

### XIX. Concerning the Order of the Prayers of Catechumens and the Faithful, and Concerning Communion

[Col. 0131C] Since the prayer of the catechumens must be celebrated separately and first, after the address of the bishops, when they have departed, those who are undergoing penance must also pray. After the laying on of hands, when these too have withdrawn, then the faithful must pray. Three prayers are to be made by them: one, namely the first, in silence; the second and third with spoken words. Only then is the kiss of peace to be given [T. 2, U., G.: “the giving of the kiss of peace.”] After the presbyters have given peace to the bishop, the laypeople too are to give it, and thus the offering is to be presented. Only the ministers of the altar may enter the altar and receive communion.

### XX. Concerning the Discipline and Modesty of Clerics

A deacon must not sit in the presence of a presbyter, but must sit at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, the deacon is to be honored by the lower ministers and by all the clergy.

### XXI. Concerning the Ministry of Subdeacons

Ministers must not be permitted to enter the secretarium or sacrarium, which the Greeks call the *diaconicon* [U.: *diaconion*], or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

### XXII. Concerning the Minister: He Must Not Use an Orarium

A minister must not use an orarium, nor leave the doors.

### XXIII. Readers and Psalmists Must Not Use an Orarium

[Col. 0132A]

Readers and psalmists must not use an orarium and thus read or sing psalms.

### XXIV. Concerning Readers and Psalmists: They Must Not Enter Taverns

Those serving at the altar [Ae., B. R., U.: “serving diligently”], from the presbyters down to the deacons and thereafter all the ecclesiastical orders down to the ministers, as well as readers, psalmists, exorcists, doorkeepers, and even those who have undertaken a life of continence, must not enter taverns.

### XXV. Ministers Must Not Give Bread or Bless the Chalice

Ministers must not give bread or bless the chalice.

### XXVI. Concerning Exorcists

[Col. 0132B] No one may perform exorcisms who has not yet been advanced by the bishops, whether in churches or within houses.

### XXVII. Clerics or Laypeople Invited to an Agape Must Not Take Away Portions

Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, or even laypeople invited to an agape, must not take away portions, because of the injury which on this occasion might be attributed to the ecclesiastical order.

### XXVIII. It Is Not Permitted to Spread Couches or Hold an Agape in Churches

It is not fitting [Note: [Col. 0131D] T. 1: “It is not permitted.” T. 2: “It is not proper.”] to hold an agape and eat inside the churches of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0132D] Ae.: “in the houses of the church”], or to spread couches there.

### XXIX. Christians Must Not Judaize by Keeping the Sabbath
