Christians must not Judaize and cease work on the Sabbath [Col. 0132C], but must work on that day. On the Lord’s Day, however, giving it precedence, let them cease from work, if they wish, as Christians. If they are found Judaizing, let them be anathema.

### XXX. No Christian May Bathe with Women

Christians must not use common baths with women—neither ministers of the altar, nor any clerics, nor those who practice continence, but absolutely no Christian at all [Note: [Col. 0132D] From Ae., U. In A. and the others: “must use common baths.”]—for this is the first reproach among the pagans.

### XXXI. Concerning Avoiding Heretical Marriages

One must not contract marriages indiscriminately with all heretics, nor give sons or daughters in marriage to them, but rather receive them, provided that they profess that they will become Catholic Christians.

### XXXII. It Is Not Permitted to Receive Eulogies from Heretics

One must not receive the blessings of heretics, since these are curses rather than blessings.

### XXXIII. One Must Not Pray with Heretics or Schismatics

One must not pray with heretics or schismatics.

### XXXIV. One Must Not Go to False Martyrs

No Christian must abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs, for these are alien to God. Whoever wishes to go shall be anathema.

### XXXV. Christians Must Not Abandon the Church and Gather Assemblies for Angels [U., G.: “corners”]

Christians must not abandon the Church of God and go to angels [U., G.: “corners”], forming assemblies of idolatry, all of which things are forbidden. Whoever is found secretly devoting himself to this idolatry shall be anathema, because, abandoning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, he has approached idols.

### XXXVI. Clerics Must Not Be Magicians or Enchanters, or Make Phylacteries

Ministers of the altar or clerics must not be magicians or enchanters, nor make what are called phylacteries, which are great bonds of souls. We have ordered that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

### XXXVII. It Is Not Permitted to Receive Festival Gifts Sent by Heretics or Jews

[Col. 0133D] One must not receive from Jews and heretics the festival gifts that are sent, nor keep festival days with them [T. 2: “holy days.” G.: “festival gifts.”].

### XXXVIII. It Is Not Permitted to Receive Unleavened Bread from Jews

One must not receive unleavened bread from Jews [T. 1: *azyma*], or share in their impieties.

### XXXIX. It Is Not Permitted to Celebrate Festivals with Pagans

One must not celebrate festivals with pagans or have fellowship with their impiety.

### XL. Bishops Summoned to a Synod Must Not Despise It

[Col. 0133C]

Bishops who have been summoned to a synod must not despise it, but must go and either teach or be taught what pertains to the correction of the Church and of the others. If one despises it, he will appear to have accused himself, unless perhaps he is unable to go because of illness.

### XLI. A Cleric or Layperson Must Not Travel Without a Letter

A minister of the altar, or even a layperson, must not depart anywhere without canonical letters, that is, a *formata* [Note: [Col. 0133D] T. 1, 2, G.: “anywhere.”].

### XLII. No Cleric May Travel Without the Bishop’s Command

[Note: [Col. 0133D] This canon is absent in U.]

A minister of the altar or any cleric must not depart for a foreign place [T. 2: “for a journey”] without the bishop’s command.

### XLIII. Ministers Must Not Withdraw from the Doors

Ministers, that is, doorkeepers, must not be absent from the doors even for a short time in order to devote themselves to prayer.

### XLIV. No One Is to Be Received for Baptism After Two Weeks of Lent

No one is to be received for baptism after the second week of Lent.

### XLV. Women Must Not Enter the Altar

Women must not enter the altar.

### XLVI. Those to Be Baptized Must Learn and Recite the Creed

[Col. 0134A]

Those to be baptized must learn the creed of the faith [Note: [Col. 0133D] From Ae., T. 1, 2, U., G. In A. and the others: “recite it”] and recite it to either the bishop or the presbyter on the Thursday of the final week.

### XLVII. Concerning Those Baptized in Illness

Those who received baptism while afflicted by illness, after becoming well, must be taught the creed of the faith, so that they may know what gift they have been deemed worthy to receive [U.: “may recognize.”].

### XLVIII. Chrism Must Be Given After Baptism

Those who have been baptized must, after baptism, also become participants in heavenly chrism and in the kingdom of Christ.

### XLIX. During Lent, Offerings Are to Be Made Only on Saturday and Sunday

Bread must not be offered during Lent except on Saturday and Sunday alone.

### L. It Is Not Permitted to End the Fast on the Thursday of the Final Week

[Col. 0134B]

The fast must not be ended on the Thursday of the final week, thereby dishonoring the whole of Lent. Rather, one must fast throughout all the days and use foods appropriate to abstinence, that is, drier foods.

### LI. During Lent, the Birthdays of Martyrs Are to Be Celebrated Only on Saturday and Sunday

The birthdays of the martyrs must not be celebrated during Lent; rather, their commemoration is to be made only on Saturday and Sunday.

### LII. It Is Not Permitted to Hold Weddings During Lent

During Lent one must not celebrate weddings or any birthdays.

### LIII. Christians Going to Weddings Must Not Sing or Dance

[Col. 0134C]

Christians going to weddings must neither dance nor leap [Note: [Col. 0134D] B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G.: “sing”], but must dine or take lunch chastely, as befits Christians.

### LIV. Ministers of the Altar Must Not Attend Spectacles

Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, must not attend spectacles displayed at weddings or dinners [Col. 0134D], but must rise from the banquet and depart before the theatrical performers [Note: [Col. 0134D] T. 1, 2, G.: “the theatrical performances”] enter.

### LV. Clerics or Christian Laypeople Must Not Hold Banquets from Contributions

Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, or even Christian laypeople, must not hold banquets from shared contributions, called by the common people *commissalia*.

### LVI. Presbyters Must Not Enter Before the Bishop

Presbyters must not enter before the bishop’s entrance or sit in the tribunals, but must enter with the bishop, unless perhaps the bishop is ill [U.: “should be ill”] or it is established that he is abroad.

### LVII. Bishops Must Not Be Ordained in Villages or Rural Districts

Bishops must not be ordained in villages or rural districts. Instead, visitors are to be appointed, that is, men who make the rounds. Those who have previously been ordained, however, must do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city. Likewise, presbyters must do nothing without the bishop’s command and counsel.

### LVIII. Bishops or Presbyters Must Not Make Offerings in Houses

Offerings must not be made in houses by bishops or presbyters.

### LIX. Psalms Composed by Unlearned Persons Must Not Be Sung in Church; and Which Books Are Canonical

Psalms composed by unlearned persons and intended for common use must not be sung in churches, nor may books outside the canon be read, but only the canonical books of the New and Old Testament. The books which ought to be read and received as authoritative are these:

[Col. 0135B] Genesis of the world; Exodus from Egypt; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; Joshua son of Nun; Judges; Ruth; the four books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0135B] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2: “of Kingdoms”]; the two books of Chronicles; the Book of Ezra [U.: “Ezra”]; the Book of Psalms, numbering 150; the Proverbs of Solomon; Ecclesiastes; the Song of Songs; Job; Esther; the books of the sixteen prophets, namely: Hosea, Amos, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.

Likewise, of the New Testament: the four books of the Gospels, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; the Acts of the Apostles; the seven canonical Epistles: one of James; two of Peter, the first and the second; three of John, the first, second, and third; and one of Jude. The fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul: one to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Ephesians; two to the Thessalonians; one to the Galatians; one to the Philippians [Col. 0136B]; one to the Colossians; two to Timothy; one to Titus; one to Philemon; and one to the Hebrews.

# VIII. THE FIRST COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE. HELD AGAINST THE HERESY OF MACEDONIUS [Note: [Col. 0135D] U.: “Macedonian heresy.”] BY 150 BISHOPS UNDER THEODOSIUS THE GREAT, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF SIAGRIUS AND EUCHERIUS, IN ERA 418 [Note: [Col. 0135D] T. 2: “era 409.”]

[Col. 0135]

[Col. 0135B] The rules, or definitions, set forth by the 150 bishops who assembled together at Constantinople when the blessed Nectarius was ordained bishop, after Maximus the Cynic had been condemned [Note: [Col. 0135D] Ae.: “the wicked one,” and likewise below in the sixth canon]. Their names and provinces are contained in Greek.

### I. The Faith of the 318 Fathers Is to Be Guarded

[Col. 0135C]

The faith of the 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia must not be rejected. Rather, it must remain confirmed, and every heresy must be anathematized, especially that of the Eunomians—or rather, the Anomians, who in Latin are called “lawless”—and of the Arians or Eudoxians, and of the Semi-Arians, as well as of the Pneumatomachi [Note: [Col. 0136D] T. 1, 2, G.: *Pneumatematicorum*.], that is, those who fight against the Holy Spirit; and of the Sabellians, Marcellians, Photinians, and Apollinarists.

### II. Bishops Must Govern Their Own Dioceses and Must Not Enter Those of Others

Bishops who are outside their own diocese must not go to Churches outside their boundaries, nor confuse or intermingle Churches. Rather, according to the rules, the bishops of Alexandria shall govern only what is in Egypt; the bishops of the East shall care only for the East, while preserving the primatial honors of the Church of Antioch contained in the rules of the Council of Nicaea. The bishops of the Asian diocese shall govern what is in Asia and what belongs only to the Asian diocese; the bishops of Pontus shall have care only of the diocese of Pontus [Col. 0136B]; and those of Thrace only of Thrace itself.

### III. Bishops Who Are Not Invited Must Not Enter Beyond Their Dioceses

Bishops who have not been invited must not enter beyond their diocese [Note: [Col. 0136D] B. R.: “must not enter beyond their own diocese”] for the ordination of anyone or for arranging any ecclesiastical affairs [Col. 0136C], while the rule written above concerning each diocese is preserved. For it is clear that, in each individual province, the provincial synod must administer and govern all things according to what was defined at Nicaea.

### IV. Concerning Churches Situated among Barbarian Peoples

The Churches of God established among barbarian peoples must be governed and administered according to the custom which is known to have prevailed from the time of the Fathers.

### V. Concerning the Honor of the Bishop of Constantinople

The bishop of the city of Constantinople must have the honor of primacy after the Roman bishop, because it is New Rome.

### VI. Concerning Maximus the Cynic Philosopher

Concerning Maximus the Cynic philosopher and all his indiscipline, which arose in Constantinople, it has been decreed that Maximus must no longer be considered to have been or to be anything, nor may those ordained by him hold any rank of the clergy. Everything done concerning him or by him is declared invalid.

### VII. The Creed Established at Constantinople by the Same 150 Holy Fathers

[Col. 0137A]

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord [Note: [Col. 0137B] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “the Lord Jesus Christ”], Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made; who for us and for our salvation came down and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and became man; who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0137B] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “at the right hand of the Father”], and will come from there with glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom will have no end; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life [Note: [Col. 0137B] Ae., B. R.: “the Lord and the life-giver.” U.: “and the life-giver”], who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son is to be worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets; in one Catholic and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

### Names of the 150 Bishops

[Col. 0138A] Nectarius of Constantinople; Timothy of Alexandria; Dorotheus of Oxyrhynchus; Cyril of Jerusalem; Galasius of Caesarea; Macher of Jericho; Dionysius of Diospolis; Priscianus of Nicopolis; Saturninus of Sebaste; Ausentius of Ascalon; Helianus of Tamnis [Note: [Col. 0138B] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2: “of Jamnia”]; Zenon of Tyre; Paul of Sidon [G.: “of Sidon”]; Nestabus of Ptolemais; [Col. 0138B] Philippus of Damascus; Beracus [Note: [Col. 0138B] Ae.: “Baracus.” B. R.: “Baracius”] of Palead [T. 2: “of Piliad”]; Timothy of Beirut; Basilides of Ibbo; Mocimus of Aradus; and the other 130 [Note: [Col. 0138B] Since 150 bishops took part in this council, one name is missing from the catalogue of subscriptions, since only nineteen names are listed in it; twenty, however, ought to have been recorded, so that, joined with the other 130 Fathers, they would complete the number 101].

# IX. THE COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE: 163 BISHOPS, EXCLUDING ELEVEN VICARS WHO SUBSCRIBED ON BEHALF OF THEIR OWN BISHOPS, IN THE TIME OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE, IN ERA 720

[Col. 0137]

[Col. 0137C] [Note: [Col. 0137D] [ [Col. 0137] This note is printed at the foot of column 137, but its callout letter, “a,” does not appear in the text.] This council is absent from A., Ae., and E. 3. It has been taken from Codex B. R., with the variant readings of the others. It was also present in the Lucca Codex, as it is found in B. R.]

[Col. 0137C] 63–64 The holy, great, and universal synod, assembled according to the grace of God and the most pious decree of the most clement and faithful great emperor Constantine in this royal Constantinople, the New Rome preserved by God, in the secretarium of the divine palace called the Trullus, decreed the matters set forth below.

The only-begotten Son and Word of God the Father, who in every respect became man like us except for sin, our true God Christ, clearly proclaimed [U.: “preached”] through the evangelical voices: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life”; and again: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.”

Walking in this divinely uttered teaching of peace, our most gentle emperor, who was also a propagator [T. 1: “defender”] of the right faith but a conqueror of false doctrine, assembled this holy universal council from among us and united the structure of the whole Church.

Therefore, this holy and universal synod of ours, casting far away the error of impiety which has existed among certain persons through the ages and even until now [Note: [Col. 0138D] From U. In B. R. and the others, the verb “has existed” is absent], and following without deviation the path of the holy and approved Fathers, agreed piously in all things with the five holy and universal synods:

with the 318 holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea against the madness of Arius;

then with the 150 God-inspired men at Constantinople against Macedonius, the opponent of the Spirit, and the impious Apollinaris;

likewise with the 200 venerable men who first assembled at Ephesus against Nestorius of Jewish understanding;

and with the 630 God-inspired Fathers at Chalcedon against Eutyches and Dioscorus, hateful to God;

and, beyond these, with the last of the five holy synods, assembled here against Theodore of Mopsuestia [Note: [Col. 0138D] From all the others except B. R., which has “Mopsuetenus”], Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius; against the writings of Theodoret directed against the twelve chapters of the praiseworthy Cyril; and against the letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian.

Restoring in all things the pious decrees unimpaired, but casting out the profane doctrines of impiety [Col. 0139A], this synod, holy, universal, and inspired by God, also confirmed the creed set forth by the 318 Fathers, as well as that confirmed by the 150 God-inspired men, which the other holy synods likewise readily received and held firm for the destruction of every deadly heresy.

### The Creed of the Council of Nicaea: 318 Fathers

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible [T. 1, 2: “maker”]; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was born from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the essence of the Father—God from God, light from light, [Col. 0139B] true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate and made human, suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say that there was a time when he was not [Note: [Col. 0139D] In the others except B. R.: “there was a time when he was not, and before he was born he was not, and because…”], and that he was made from nothing or from another substance or essence, and who say that the Son of God is subject to change or alteration—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

### The Creed of the 150 Holy Fathers Assembled at Constantinople

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, [Col. 0139C] maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, became human, was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried, rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom will have no end; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified together, who spoke through the prophets; and in one holy, Catholic, and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We hope for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen [Note: [Col. 0139D] The word “Amen” has been taken from the other codices, since it is absent in B. R.].

It was indeed sufficient for perfect knowledge and confirmation of the orthodox faith: this pious and orthodox symbol of divine grace. But because the inventor of ancient wickedness did not cease—finding in the serpent a collaborator for himself [Note: [Col. 0140D] U., G., “finding collaborators for themselves through the serpent”]—through him to inflict poisonous death upon human nature, so now also, finding instruments suited to his own will, namely Theodore, bishop of Pharan [U., “of the Pharanites”], Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, who were bishops of this royal city, and in addition Honorius, who was pope of ancient Rome, and Cyrus, who held the episcopate of Alexandria, as well as Macarius, who was recently bishop of Antioch, and his disciple Stephen, he did not cease through them to stir up scandals of error against the fullness of the Church, consonantly disseminating among the orthodox people the heresy of one will and one operation in the two natures of Christ, one of the holy Trinity, our true God—a heresy corresponding to the insane and malicious sect of the impious Apollinarius, Severus, and Themistius. This sect attempted to extinguish the perfection of the humanity of the one and same Lord Jesus Christ our God through a certain crafty invention, blasphemously introducing the claim that his intellectually animated flesh existed without will and without operation.

Therefore Christ our God raised up a most faithful emperor, a new David, finding in him a man after his own heart. He did not give, as it is written, sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids until, through this sacred assembly gathered by God, he found the perfect proclamation of the right faith itself. For according to the voice uttered by God: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

This present holy and universal synod therefore faithfully received and embraced with outstretched hands both the petition made by the most holy and blessed Agatho, pope of ancient Rome, to our most pious and most faithful emperor Constantine, which expressly rejects those who taught or preached, as stated above, one will and one operation in the dispensation of the incarnation of Christ our true God, and also the other synodal petition sent by the sacred council of one hundred and twenty-five God-loving bishops, held under that same most holy pope, to his God-instructed serenity. These accord with holy Chalcedon and with the tome of the most sacred and blessed Leo, pope of that same ancient Rome, sent to holy Flavian and called by this synod a statement (*titulus*) of the right faith. It likewise embraced the synodical letters written by blessed Cyril against the impious Nestorius and to the Eastern bishops.

Following the five holy universal councils and the holy and approved Fathers, and defining that our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, one of the holy, consubstantial Trinity that gives origin to life, is to be confessed concordantly as perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, the same consisting of a rational soul and a body, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and the same consubstantial with us according to humanity, in all things like us except for sin; begotten before the ages from the Father according to divinity, but in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same begotten from the Holy Spirit and Mary the virgin, properly and truly Mother of God according to humanity; one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, with the distinction of these natures nowhere abolished because of the union, but rather the property of each nature preserved, the two converging into one person and one substance; not divided or separated into two persons, but one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, in accordance with what the prophets of old taught concerning him, what the Lord Jesus Christ himself taught us, and what the symbol handed down to us by the holy Fathers teaches.

We likewise proclaim, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, two natural wills and two natural operations in him, without division, without change, without separation, and without confusion. The two natural wills are not contrary—far be that from us, as the impious heretics assert—but his human will follows and does not resist or struggle against his divine and almighty will; rather, it is subject to it. For the will of the flesh had to be moved but subjected to the divine will, according to the most wise Athanasius. Just as his flesh is called and is the flesh of God the Word, so the natural will of his flesh is called and is properly the will of God the Word. As he himself says: “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” [Note: In the other witnesses, except BR., “the will of my Father”]. By “my own will” he means the will that belonged to his flesh, for his flesh also became properly his own.

For just as his most holy and immaculate, animated flesh, having been deified, was not destroyed but remained in its own proper state and nature, so the will of his humanity, having been deified, was not destroyed; rather, it was preserved, according to the God-speaking Gregory, who says: “For that willing which is understood in the Savior was not contrary to God, being wholly deified.”

We likewise glorify two natural operations, without division, without change, without confusion, and without separation, in the same Lord Jesus Christ, our true God—that is, a divine operation and a human operation—according to the most explicit statement of Leo, herald of divine things [Note: In the other witnesses, except BR., “inquiring”]. For he says:

“Each form performs what properly belongs to it in communion with the other: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. For we shall in no way attribute one natural operation to God and creation, so that we neither raise what is created into the divine essence nor cast down what is exalted in the divine nature to the level proper to creatures. We recognize that the miracles and the sufferings alike belong to one and the same person, according to the one and the other of the natures from which he consists and in which he has his being,” as the admirable Cyril says.

Therefore, preserving everywhere what is without confusion and without division, we proclaim all these things with a clear voice, believing that our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, is one of the holy Trinity even after the incarnation. We say that his two natures shine forth in one subsistence, in which throughout the whole course of his dispensation he truly displayed both miracles and sufferings, not according to appearance; the natural distinction being recognized in the same one substance, in that, in communion with the other, each nature wills and operates its own things without division and without confusion. Accordingly, we confess two natural wills and operations, converging appropriately for the salvation of the human race.

Having therefore defined all these matters with complete diligence and care on every side, we decree that no one may bring forward, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith. But those who presume either to compose or put forward another faith, or to teach or hand down another symbol to those wishing to turn from paganism to the knowledge of the truth, or from Judaism, or from any heresy, or who introduce some novelty of expression or invention of speech in order to subvert what has now been determined by us—if they are bishops or clerics, they are to be excluded: bishops from the episcopate, clerics from the clergy. But if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized.

And the subscriptions.

Theodore, humble presbyter of the holy Church of Rome, representing Agatho, most blessed universal pope of the city of Rome, have subscribed. [Col. 0142C] George, humble presbyter of the holy Church of Rome, as above. John, humble deacon of the holy Church of Rome, as above. Likewise George, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, having defined, have subscribed. And we have read and agreed in the same manner with the others.

The holy synod exclaimed: “Many years to the emperor! Many years to the emperor beloved by Christ! We all believe orthodoxly. Lord, preserve the illuminator of peace. Eternal memory to the new Marcian Constantine; likewise eternal memory to the new Justinian Constantine, who deposed the heretics: Lord, preserve him. Anathema to Nestorius, Eutyches, and Severus; anathema to those who think like them. Anathema to Theodore of Pharan. Anathema to Sergius and Honorius. Anathema to Pyrrhus and Paul. Anathema to Cyrus and Paul [U., G., Peter]. Anathema to Macarius and Stephen. Anathema to Polychronius, the new Simon. Anathema to all heretics. Anathema to those who have preached or preach and hope to teach one will and one operation in the dispensation of the incarnation of Christ our true God.”

To all the most beloved brothers, the bishops of the Churches of Christ established throughout Spain, Leo.

Although the pursuits of human beings, by which human life is believed to be ordered, are diverse, there is nevertheless one duty of piety that can lead to the gain and reward of eternal life. It is right for every companion in the Christian faith to strive for this duty; the gracious favor of the Holy Spirit inspires the desire for it and makes the unimpeded effect of good works evident. For, as the Lord teaches, “the Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice,” and because his grace is incomprehensible, it joins things together and bears witness to them, while you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.

Knowing and being assured, therefore, that zeal for the Christian religion also burns within you, and that you embrace the seeds of heavenly teaching with spiritual arms; and that the fervor and purity of evangelical and apostolic tradition bear fruit among you—for the sake of which this holy apostolic see, the mother of the Churches, has always labored and still labors even unto sacrifice, and, if the divine majesty should so determine, prefers for its soul temporarily to be separated from the body [T. 1, 2, “to depart”] rather than, through sacrilegious betrayal, to be separated from the true confession by temporal pleasure or affliction—for apart from this confession, just as the reward of eternal blessedness that the Lord has prepared for his saints cannot be attained, so, grievously lamentable as it is, whoever is made an exile from the living and true God through the error of a deceitful doctrine is delivered over to eternal torments.

But now, by the grace of God, while our most Christian and most pious son, the emperor Constantine, reigns—the one whom heavenly clemency chose and preferred for this duty of piety—the radiance of the right confession and apostolic tradition, after the darkness of heretical depravity had been expelled, has shone like a brilliant ray throughout the whole world. Peace and concord in the truth reign among all the bishops of the Churches of Christ, descending from the peaceful confession of Christ, who is the true and saving peace, through whom we are reconciled to God.

Let your sincerity know, and let it become known to all Christians, what wondrous things the almighty God has done: in the city of Constantinople, our most clement emperor—indeed, the son of blessed Peter the apostle—armed with zeal for God and inflamed by the desire for piety, having gathered bishops from every region of the world, fulfilled, during the recently elapsed new indiction, what he had long and faithfully desired, when heavenly majesty so determined [G., “he fulfilled the ninth indiction”].

Thus the holy Sixth Universal Council was celebrated. For its celebration, presbyters and deacons were sent in the person of our predecessor, the lord Agatho, pope of apostolic memory. From the various councils subject to this holy apostolic see, whose ministry we exercise, we sent archbishops, who, together with the pious prince and all the bishops of the Churches who had assembled at his command, presided and sat in council. First they reread and reviewed the five holy universal councils and the venerable Fathers of the Church, whose books and testimonies had been sent from here, together with the dogmatic letter of our predecessor, the lord Agatho, pope and pontiff of apostolic memory, and with the responses of our entire synod, for the confirmation of the two natures and the two natural wills and operations in our one Lord Jesus Christ, and for the condemnation of those who taught or believed otherwise.

And because they searched out the things of God with his fear and love, the sincerity of the true confession was demonstrated and confirmed through them by his will. Accordingly, the synodal definition bears witness that it agrees with the statements of the apostolic men; from these, we trust, your love will receive satisfaction.

But all who rebelled against the purity of apostolic tradition have departed under the sentence of eternal condemnation: Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople, together with Honorius, who did not extinguish, as he ought to have done, the flame of heretical doctrine when it first began through apostolic authority, but by neglecting it fed it instead.

Those survivors who refused to turn or return to the confession of the truth through the remedy of repentance were removed from the episcopal and priestly rank: Macarius, bishop of Antioch, together with Stephen, his disciple, a former abbot and presbyter, indeed the kindler [T. 1, 2, U., G., “kindler”] of heretical error; and a certain old man, Polychronius, a former abbot and presbyter, the new Simon. They were deservedly expelled from the Churches of Christ as faithless hirelings, whose harmful successors [T. 1, 2, U., G., “successors”] and corrupters they proved to be, and were brought here into exile so that they might recognize the guilt of their own blasphemies against God, placed under the contempt and denunciation of all the faithful.

And because the proceedings conducted and celebrated in the universal council held in the city of Constantinople, on account of the diversity of languages, were written in Greek and have not yet been carefully translated into our language [Note: T. 1, 2, “for they were written down, and have not yet been translated into our language”], we have sent to your love, through the bearer of this letter, Peter, regional notary of our holy Church, the definition of that same holy Sixth Council and the acclamation made by the whole council to the most pious prince, called the *prophoneticus*, together with the edict of our most clement emperor, translated from Greek into Latin and sent everywhere for the knowledge of all. We shall also send the acts of the entire venerable council when they have been smoothly translated, if your charity, fervent in good works, is pleased by this.

We therefore exhort your concord, devoted to the divine ministries, in the truth of the faith, to give the greatest diligence and effort and to gird yourselves for equal labors, out of love and fear of God, for the advancement of the Christian religion and the purity of apostolic preaching. Thus, through all the bishops, priests, and peoples of your province, this matter may become known and be salutarily proclaimed through our religious zeal; and let subscriptions from all the reverend bishops, together with you, be appended to the same definition, as though each bishop of the Churches of Christ, hastening toward the book of life, were writing his name in it and, through the confession of his subscription, were spiritually present with us and with the holy universal synod in the harmony of the one evangelical and apostolic faith.

Then, when our Lord Jesus Christ comes in glorious and terrible power to judge, let each one meet him bearing the title of orthodox confession and demonstrate, through the seal of his own hand, that he is a companion of apostolic tradition, so that he may enjoy blessed fellowship with the apostles of Christ, whose confession he embraces with zeal for true piety, always turning over in the secret places of his heart the saying of the Lord who declares: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” [G., “who is in the heavens”].

For we too, although unequal to them, nevertheless exercise the office of the prince of the apostles. When, with God’s protection, we have received the pages of your subscriptions through the bearer of this letter, we shall place them at the confession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that through him and by his intercession—from whom the true tradition of the Christian faith descended—they may be offered to the Lord Jesus Christ as a testimony and glory from those who faithfully confess and subscribe to his mystery. The proclamation of the true confession concerning him, which for so long had been oppressed by the snares of heretics, has now, through the inspiration of the diligent zeal of the pious prince, been granted to shine everywhere with the clear rays of truth.

Since an opportunity for salvation has been offered, we exhort you to show by effective diligence that this truly divine gift is fruitful, so that glory before God may increase for you through purity of conscience. May God keep you safe, most beloved brothers.

To the most beloved brother Quiricus, Leo.

We bring to the knowledge of your love that we have hastened to send there the bearer of this letter, Peter, regional notary of our holy Church, with a circular letter to all the bishops of the Churches of Christ together with you, and also to our most excellent and most Christian son, the king, and to the glorious count. We have likewise entrusted to him, written on linen, the responses [Note: In B. R., “responses on a vessel.” In the other manuscripts: “inside the response.” Let the reader consult the word *linteum* in our glossary], the definition of the venerable synod celebrated in the city of Constantinople, with God’s protection, during the recently elapsed new indiction [T. 1, U., G., “the ninth”], for the stability of our orthodox faith; also the acclamation of the most reverend bishops assembled there; and the edict of our most pious son and most clement emperor [Col. 0145D]. For the sake of the ministry of God which we have undertaken [T. 2, U., “mystery”], and of the uprightness of apostolic faith through which we await the salvation both of ourselves and of the souls entrusted to us, may your love in Christ offer every care and assistance, so that, through your fervent zeal for the evangelical and apostolic faith, you may deserve to share eternal blessedness with the blessed princes of Christ’s apostles. May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.

As a gift of blessing, therefore, we have sent your love a cross bearing a key, made from the sacred chains of our founder, blessed Peter the apostle, so that episcopal dignity and love of God and neighbor may bind you, and so that, through the standard of the saving cross, the members of the whole body may be fastened by the nails of the divine commandments to Christ, who was suspended upon it. Thus fortified by such a seal, may the prince of the apostles receive you, with the doors of the heavenly kingdom opened, to enjoy eternal blessedness with him.

To the glorious lord, our son, the count Simplicius, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

Since the true confession of God, descending from apostolic tradition, is the unique remedy of our salvation, and since the blessed martyrs, contending for it in temporal life, deserved the rewards of eternal life; since, for its sake, the most approved [Note: T. 1, 2, “most blessed”; U., G., “most ready”] Fathers and teachers of the holy Church endured various struggles and immeasurable afflictions and chose to surrender their souls rather than betray the true faith [U., “preferred”]; since, from their authoritative teaching—which this holy Church of Christ, preserved and established by the prince of its apostles, is known to proclaim even now—the saving instruction has, by God’s grace, reached us through the apostolic successors; and since our predecessors also labored exceedingly for its stability—after so many struggles and innumerable afflictions inflicted at various times by the enemies of the true faith, heavenly clemency at last stirred the imperial heart with heavenly grace [U., G., “instructing it”] and kindled it with the fervor of its grace to investigate the integrity of true piety, and recently arranged for a universal council to be gathered from different parts of the world.

At that council, the legates of this holy apostolic Church, whose administration we have received by divine favor, and the representatives of the councils subject to it, assembled together with our serene son, the emperor, crowned with the insignia and emblems of piety. From the pontifical writings of the holy Fathers, strengthened by testimonies, they proved with all their efforts that the rule of apostolic tradition, on which this holy Church rests with divine assistance, must be proclaimed and preserved in its entirety.

For the tome of the lord Agatho, of apostolic memory, our great pontiff and predecessor, which he had sent to the most serene emperor, was so thoroughly furnished with the definitions of the holy councils and the testimonies and assertions of the blessed Fathers that it most clearly revealed the integrity of the apostolic faith and exposed the hiding places of heretical error. From its unconquerable statements, after the darkness of heretical doctrine had been removed from human hearts by the grace of God, the light of the true confession shone forth.

In this matter the labor of the most gentle prince for the piety of the right faith shone forth, worthy to be praised throughout all ages, so that, with his favor and with God’s protection, the truth of the apostolic faith might receive the prize of victory, and the empire divinely granted to him might be adorned with the insignia of piety.

Therefore, most glorious sons of the Church of Christ, in whom the desire for piety is strong, extend a helping hand to evangelical and apostolic preaching, so that the radiance of the sincere faith that you love may also illuminate your Christian regions. By favoring and assisting apostolic preaching, may you deserve to have fellowship with the faithful before God, to whom the integrity of the true confession concerning him is directed [U., “is brought”].

Since it belonged to our office, to which the administration of souls has been entrusted, we have hastened, with paternal affection, to send through the bearer of this letter, Peter, regional notary of our holy Church, to your provinces as well the definition of the holy Sixth Council celebrated in the city of Constantinople during the recently elapsed indiction, together with the acclamation of all the most reverend bishops, which is also called the *prosphoneticus* [T. 1, 2, G., *prosphoneticos*], and the edict of our most pious Augustus, our serene son, concerning the faith, sent here, so that you may rejoice unanimously with us in the progress of evangelical and apostolic preaching, as true companions of the faith [T. 1, 2, “with you”].

We have also urged the reverend bishops of all the Churches to append their subscriptions to the same apostolic and synodal definition, and, as fathers on behalf of and together with their sons, to inscribe their names in this book of life, for the praise of those who faithfully participate, labor together with the Gospel of Christ, and commend themselves to God. May we then deserve to have him favorable to us, when we preserve the truth of his faith unaltered to the end [T. 1, 2, “unchanged”; Note: From G. In B. R., “that we may preserve it to the end.” T. 1, “we preserve it to the end.” T. 2, “we preserve the end.” U., “as far as faith”]. May heavenly grace preserve your glory in safety.

For the perpetual protection of your glorious Christianity, we have therefore sent through the present bearer a venerable cross bearing a key, made from the saving chains of our founder Peter, the prince of Christ’s apostles, so that you, who cherish his sincere love, faithfully care for his lamps, and truly embrace the uprightness of his tradition, may continually be saved under his apostolic protection. Amen [Note: From U. and G.; this word is absent in B. R., T. 1, and T. 2].

Benedict, presbyter and, in the name of God, elect of the holy apostolic see, to Peter, regional notary.

In accordance with the arrangement by which Leo, pope of apostolic memory, determined to send your energetic self to the province of Spain, to the most excellent and most Christian king, to the most holy archbishops and all the bishops of the Churches established there, and likewise to the glorious count, carry out with the greatest zeal for piety the ministry entrusted to you, so that the definition of the venerable Sixth Synod may become known, together with the acclamation—also called the *prosphoneticus*—of the most reverend bishops who assembled in that God-gathered council and addressed the most clement prince, and with the edict of that same most pious prince, sent generally everywhere, for the firmness of our apostolic faith.

Also take the greatest care and exercise the utmost vigilance to ensure that the subscriptions of the most reverend bishops are appended after the same synodal definition, so that both those most reverend bishops and the whole religious province through them may be shown to be companions with us in the catholic and apostolic tradition and faith; and so that before God, to whose glory the praise and stability of the Christian faith are directed, commendation and acceptance may result for them unto the salvation of souls.

Therefore hasten to complete the office of piety you have undertaken, adorning it with vigilance and skill [U., “vigilant skill”], because you are also storing up for yourself the fruit of good work, and providing for those who receive it that they may attain the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom and the perfect confession of apostolic faith.

I, Benedict, presbyter by the grace of God and chosen of the holy apostolic see, have subscribed.

To the lord and excellent son Ervig, king, Leo.

Since there is one [U. adds: “and eternal”] king of all, God, who created everything and governs and sustains what he created out of nothing, who is truly King of kings and Lord of lords, he, in the balance of his incomprehensible providence [Col. 0148B], appoints different men to reign on earth both temporally and locally. Although their kingdoms are divided [U.: different], he nevertheless requires an equal account of administration from each of them and expects from them all one sacrifice of praise consisting in the true confession of him. His immense majesty is pleased with the human race by this one service alone: that a true confession concerning him [T. 1, 2: concerning God] is proclaimed by all, so that, although there appears to be a diversity in temporal arrangements, harmony in unity may be maintained regarding the rectitude of faith in him.

The Savior of the world, the Son of God, also established this among his holy disciples. He appointed blessed Peter as chief in his place among his disciples. Through Peter’s saving preaching and tradition, proceeding from this holy apostolic Church of Christ [Col. 0148C] as from the fountain of preaching, all the regions over which your highness presides have been led to knowledge of the truth and the way of life; this preaching also illumines the summit of your kingdom. While you reign through the grace of God in piety, you acquire from your temporal kingdom the kingdom of eternal blessedness. To attain that kingdom more perfectly, just as we earnestly pray, so, while by God’s condescension we discharge the office of the fathers and, though unequal to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, fill his place by divine aid in the ministry entrusted to us, we endeavor through preaching and admonition to advance you toward the merit of blessed life.

The beginning of attaining eternal blessedness is the rule of right apostolic preaching. Although certain men formerly attempted to undermine it [Col. 0148D], striving to introduce heretical errors into the Church of Christ, evangelical truth prevails. For its stability and preservation without mutilation, this apostolic Church of Christ has always endured, and continues to endure, various treacherous afflictions; and, with heavenly grace assisting it, it remains unharmed.

Now, however, with thanksgiving and rejoicing in God, we proclaim that during the recently elapsed new indiction 76 [T. 1, U., G.: the ninth indiction] our most pious and most Christian emperor—indeed, a son of the Church of God—sent imperial letters to our predecessor of apostolic memory, Agatho, pope and pontiff, earnestly urging him to send from this holy Church of the apostolic see [T. 1, 2: our holy Church] [Col. 0149A], and from all the venerable councils adjoining it, legates to the royal city of Constantinople, both from among the prelates of the Churches and from the other ecclesiastical orders, equipped with dogmatic letters and with the books and testimonies of the venerable Fathers.

This was accomplished and brought to completion by God’s will. When the legates arrived there for this purpose, His Piety assembled a council from different parts of the world. Setting aside for a short time the cares of the commonwealth entrusted to him, he took his place in the venerable council of the bishops and Fathers [T. 1, 2: brothers] and caused the truth of apostolic tradition and the rectitude of the faith to be examined carefully and attentively through the holy synods, the testimonies of the venerable Fathers, and the declarations of our predecessors, the apostolic pontiffs [Col. 0149B]. He also caused the sincerity of the true faith to be demonstrated by the legates of this holy apostolic see. By God’s grace, with the support of the empire, this undertaking was begun and completed.

The truth of our true faith became perfectly clear, in accordance with the venerable councils and the teachings of approved Fathers. In our one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who is the same true and perfect God and the same true and perfect man, just as we confess two natures inseparably and without confusion, namely, the divine and the human, so we proclaim that he possesses two natural wills and two natural operations, according to the qualities and properties of the natures that converge in him. For we believe him to be one Christ and one person of the holy Trinity in such a way that we proclaim that he possesses both the divine and the human nature [Col. 0149C], together with the properties of those natures, without confusion, division, or diminution.

The most pious emperor, inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit and voluntarily enduring labor for the purity of the Christian faith, strove with the utmost effort to cleanse the Catholic Church of God from the stain of heretical error. Whatever could generate offense among Christian peoples, he caused to be removed from the midst of God’s Church. All the authors of heretical teaching, condemned by the venerable council’s judgment [U.: with the council’s consent], were expelled from the proclamation of the Catholic Church: Theodore, bishop of Pharan; Cyrus of Alexandria; Sergius; Paul; Pyrrhus; and Peter, formerly prelates of Constantinople [Col. 0149D]; and, together with them, Honorius of Rome, who consented [U.: conceded] to the stain being placed upon the unstained “wrinkle” of apostolic tradition that he had received from his predecessors.

Macarius of Antioch was likewise punished with eternal condemnation, together with Stephen, his disciple—or rather, the teacher of heretical perversity—and with a certain Polychronius, an insane old man, a new Simon, who, relying on the confidence of heretical preaching, promised to carry it through [the object is unstated] and not to return, even in confusion, to the way of the true confession.

All these men, together with Arius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Severus, Theodosius, and Themistius [Col. 0150A], tried shamelessly to defend the heretical teaching that there was one will and one operation in the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ. They did not demonstrate this, as priests of God ought to have done, by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures and the Fathers; rather, through worldly sophistries they cunningly contrived to pervert the Gospel of Christ.

Divine judgment cast all of them, together with their errors, out of God’s holy Church. Now, with heavenly assistance favoring us, all the prelates of God’s Churches everywhere agree in one harmony of the true faith. There has become one mouth and one speech, one flock and one shepherd, Christ the Son of God, who is unanimously and sincerely proclaimed by all his priests [U.: equally sincerely].

Therefore let the highness of your Christian kingdom [Col. 0150B] undertake the duty of piety, so that this may be proclaimed to all the Churches of God, to prelates, priests, clerics, and peoples, both for the praise of God and for the stability of your kingdom and the salvation of all. Thus may almighty God be glorified and praised unanimously by all peoples.

Accordingly, we have arranged to send through Peter, the regional notary of our holy Church, the definition of the holy council, the acclamation of the most reverend bishops—called the *prosphoneticus*—addressed to the most pious emperor, and the edict of the most clement emperor written and promulgated everywhere for the confession of the true faith [Col. 0150B]. We have sent them so that, in accordance with the definition of the sacred synod sent there by us, all the most religious bishops of the Churches of your kingdom, like fathers on behalf of spiritual sons [Col. 0150C], may each append their subscriptions, writing them—as though in the book of life—as the seal of their confession.

May peace and concord in the Churches of God flourish and endure during the times of your exalted kingdom, with God granting it and your Christianity assisting, so that he who appointed your highness to reign may grant you, supported by the stability of his faith, to administer prosperously and acceptably to him the people entrusted to you for very many years. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] The word “Amen” is taken from U. and G., since it is absent from B., R., and the other witnesses.]

## On those who try to bark insolently against the prelates of the Churches of God

[Note: [Col. 0149D] At this point only Codices U. and G. present the reading of this canon; from the former we have taken the text, together with the variant readings of the latter [Col. 0150D].]

[Col. 0150D] It pleased this holy synod, in accordance with the sanction of the earlier canons, that those who persist in despising the Church of Christ or its sacred prelates should be excommunicated from the assembly of the faithful for three years, until perhaps, coming to their senses and making satisfaction through repentance, they might at last be admitted to communion.

Certainly, if their wicked insolence should continue and dare unceasingly to revile what it has begun [G.: should finally dare to revile such things] [Col. 0150D], it was decreed that not even at the end should they be given viaticum, so that perhaps through punishments [G.: so that, if somehow, through punishments] they might perceive what, dull in understanding here, they neglected, as the Holy Spirit says through the prophet: “Only affliction will give understanding to the ear” [Col. 0151A]. And as a certain outstanding teacher bears witness in harmony with this prophecy, saying: “No wicked person knows the evil he is doing until he has begun to be punished for those same evils” [Col. 0152A].

# X. The Council of Ephesus

A council of two hundred bishops held against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that a mere man was born from the holy Virgin Mary, so as to make one person of the flesh and another of the divinity, and who did not understand one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but proclaimed separately and distinctly one Son of God and another of man.

[Col. 0151]

[Col. 0151A] This synod was held under the consulship of Theodosius the Younger for the thirteenth time [U.: fourteenth] and Valentinian for the third time, in the year 469 of the era [Note: [Col. 0152D] From Ae., T. 2, and U. A., and the other witnesses have 468]. The blessed Cyril, formerly bishop of Alexandria, presided over the synod [Col. 0151B]. Together with the entire council, he sent the following synodal decrees to the same Nestorius.

## Cyril, or the synod assembled at Ephesus, to the religious and God-beloved fellow priest Nestorius

When our Savior expressly declares, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me,” what shall we suffer, since your religious office demands that we love you more than Christ, the Savior of all? What benefit will this bring us on the day of judgment, or what satisfaction will we be able to offer for such prolonged silence concerning the blasphemies you have uttered against him?

If you alone were harmed by teaching or holding these things, our concern would be less [Col. 0151C]. But since you have scandalized the whole Church and mixed the leaven of unfamiliar perversity and a new heresy among peoples—not only those present there, but those established everywhere, since the books of your interpretations have been circulated throughout the world—what further reason or word of excuse can suffice for our silence? How could it not be necessary to remember Christ the Lord, who says: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword; for I have come to separate a man from his father and a daughter from her mother” [Col. 0151D]?

When faith is injured, reverence for parents is despised as useless and dangerous, and love for children and brothers is avoided. Finally, even death is preferred to life by devout men, so that, as it is written, they may attain a better resurrection.

Behold, therefore, we summon you for the third time in this synodal letter, together with the holy synod assembled at the great city of Rome under the presidency of our most holy and venerable brother and fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop. We advise you to abstain from such perverse and distorted doctrines, which you are known both to hold and to teach. Instead, receive the right faith handed down from the beginning to the Churches through the most blessed apostles and evangelists, who themselves saw these things with their eyes and are shown to have been ministers of the Word.

If your religious office delays doing this, in accordance with the deadline established in the letter of our most holy and venerable fellow priest Coelestine, bishop of the Roman Church [Col. 0152A], know that you have no share with us [T. 1: no part], nor will you obtain a place or conversation with the priests and bishops of God [Col. 0152B].

For it is not lawful for us to disregard Churches so troubled, peoples so scandalized, and the most upright faith so violated; nor may we disregard the flock that you ought to have guarded, if you had truly been, together with us, a lover of right doctrine and had piously followed the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

Therefore, all those whom your religious office has removed from communion or deposed from their order on account of the faith, whether laymen or clerics, we receive into our communion [T. 1, 2, G.: we receive them]. For it is not just that your decrees should oppress those who know how to think rightly and who, even while doing good, wisely resisted you. You yourself took care to indicate this very matter in the letter you sent to our holy fellow bishop Coelestine, prelate of the great city of Rome [Col. 0152C].

It is not sufficient for your religious office merely to confess the creed expounded at that time through the generosity of the Holy Spirit by the venerable and great council assembled at Nicaea. You neither understood nor correctly interpreted it; indeed, you interpreted it perversely, although you uttered the same words in sound. It is also necessary, and rightly so, for you to confess under oath that you anathematize your polluted and profane doctrines, while holding and teaching what we, all the bishops, teachers, and prelates of the peoples throughout East and West, believe and teach.

Both the holy synod assembled at the city of Rome and all of us gave our assent to the letters sent from Alexandria to your religious office, as having been written rightly and irreproachably [Col. 0152D]. We have appended to this letter what you ought to hold and teach and from what you ought to abstain. For this is the faith of the Catholic Church, to which all orthodox pontiffs throughout East and West give their assent.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the Father as only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father [B. R., E. 3, U.: from the Father’s substance]—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousios* with the Father, that is, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth [Col. 0153A] [Note: Ae.: “all things that are in heaven and all things that are on earth”]. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, was incarnate, and became man; he suffered and, rising on the third day [B. R., T., 2: rose again], ascended into heaven. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead [Col. 0153B]; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was born he was not,” and who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or that he is from another substance or essence, or call the Son of God convertible or changeable [E. 3, T. 1, 2: “and changeable”] [Col. 0153D]—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

Following in every respect, therefore, the confessions of the holy Fathers [Note: T. 2: substance; U.: justice], which they uttered while the Holy Spirit spoke in them, adhering with equal steps to the intention present in their understanding [Col. 0153B] and walking along the royal path, we confess that the only-begotten Word of God was born from the very essence of the Father: true God from true God, light from light. Through him all things were made, whether in heaven or on earth [T. 1: on earth]. For our salvation he descended and graciously stooped to self-emptying.

When he was incarnate and became man—that is, when he received flesh from the holy Virgin and made it his own—he endured our birth from the womb, coming forth as man from a woman [Ae.: proceeding], without abandoning what he was. For although he came to be in the assumption of flesh and blood, even so he remained what he was: God by nature and in truth.

We do not say, therefore, that the flesh was changed into the nature of the divinity, nor that the substance of the flesh was transformed into the ineffable essence of the Word of God. For he is unchangeable and immutable, remaining continually the same, according to the Scriptures.

He was also seen as a little child, still lying in a cradle and placed in the bosom [U.: “in the bosom,” singular] of the Virgin who bore him; yet, as God, while remaining undivided from his Father, he filled all creation. For what is divine is understood to be without quantity or bulk and is contained within no limits.

Therefore, confessing the Word of God as united to flesh according to subsistence [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “then also”], we adore one Son and Lord Jesus Christ. We do not set apart and define a man and God as joined to one another by a unity of dignity and authority; this is merely a novelty of expression and nothing more. Nor do we name separately as Christ the Word who is God and from God, and similarly name separately as another Christ the one born from a woman; but we recognize only one Christ, the Word of God the Father, together with his own flesh.

For, according to us, he was then anointed, although he himself gave the Spirit to those worthy of it, and not according to measure, as the blessed evangelist John asserts [Col. 0153C]. Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt in the holy Virgin as in an ordinary man born from her, lest Christ the man be believed to possess God as an inhabitant [U., G.: “had dwelt”].

Although the Word dwelt among us and it is said that the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, we understand that, because he became flesh, this did not mean that he dwelled in him as he is said to dwell in the saints. Nor have we attempted to define such a dwelling in him. Rather, united according to nature and not wholly changed into flesh, he made for himself the kind of dwelling that the soul of a man is also believed to have in its own body.

There is therefore one Christ, Son and Lord—not as though he possessed some conjunction in a unity of the dignity and authority of a man with God. For equality of dignity alone cannot unite natures. Peter and John, after all, are equal to each other in dignity, for which reason they are shown to be apostles and holy disciples; nevertheless, the two are not one [Col. 0154A].

Nor do we understand the mode of conjunction according to comparison or connection. That is insufficient for natural unity, nor is it according to the effect of participation [E., B. R.: affection], as when we cling to the Lord and become one spirit with him. Indeed, we avoid the term “conjunction” as unsuitable to signify the mystery of unity [Note: From the other codices. In A.: “as existing.” Certain leaves of this codex are found transposed at this point] [Col. 0154B].

Nor do we assert that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ [U.: “Christ, the Word of God the Father”], lest we once again divide the one Christ, Son and Lord, more manifestly into two, and fall into the crime of sacrilege by making God and Lord for him. For, as we said above, the Word of God, united to the flesh according to subsistence [Ae., B. R.: according to substance], is indeed God of all and rules the universe [Col. 0154C].

Nevertheless, he is not himself his own servant or his own lord, since it is foolish, or rather impious, to think or say this. Although he called his Father his God, while he himself is also God by nature and from his Father’s essence, we nevertheless in no way fail to understand that, while remaining God, he also became man, existing under God according to the law appropriate to human nature. How, then, could he himself be God or Lord for himself?

Therefore, as man, insofar as it suitably corresponds to the measure of self-emptying, he declared that he was with us under God. In this same way he was made subject to the law, although he himself promulgated the law and existed as God the lawgiver.

We take care not to say of Christ: “I venerate the assumed because of the one assuming, and I adore the visible because of the invisible.” It is even more dreadful to teach this: “The one who was received is not named God together with the one who received him” [Note: Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “to say this”] [Col. 0154D]. Whoever says this again divides the one Christ into two, setting the man apart in one part and God likewise in another. For he clearly denies the unity according to which one is not adored or named God together with the other; rather, one Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, is understood and is to be venerated with one service together with his own flesh.

We also confess that the same one who was born from God the Father, the only-begotten Son, is God. Although by his nature he was impassible, nevertheless, according to the Scriptures, he suffered in the flesh for us; and, while in the crucified body of his own flesh, he impassibly referred the suffering to himself [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “sufferings”] [Col. 0155A].

By the grace of God he tasted death for all, giving up his own body, although by nature he is himself life and the resurrection of the dead. In order to overthrow death by ineffable power, to become firstborn from the dead in his own flesh, and the first fruits of those who sleep, and to make a way for human nature toward incorruption [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “a return”] [Col. 0155D], by the grace of God, as was said above, he tasted death for all; and, rising on the third day, he stripped the underworld.

Therefore, although it is said that the resurrection of the dead came through a man, we understand that the Word who is from God became man and that through him the dominion of death was destroyed [Col. 0155B].

At the appointed times he will come, as the one Son and Lord, in the glory of the Father, to judge the world in righteousness, as Scripture testifies [Note: From Ae., B. R., U. A. and the other witnesses have “he comes”] [Col. 0155B].

We must necessarily add this as well: proclaiming according to the flesh the death of the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the bloodless service of sacrifice. Thus we also approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, our redeemer.

We do not receive them as common flesh—far be it from us—nor as of a sanctified man joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as though he possessed a divine indwelling. Rather, we receive them as truly life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word. For since he exists naturally as life, as God, and is united to his own flesh, he declared it to be life-giving.

Therefore, although he says to us, “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” we must not regard it as the flesh of an ordinary man, one of us. For how could the flesh of a man be life-giving by its nature? Rather, we must regard it as truly made his own—the flesh of him who became and was called, for our sake, the Son of Man [Col. 0155C].

We do not at all divide among two subsistences or persons the words that our Savior spoke in the Gospels. For the one and only Christ is not double [Note: From the other witnesses except A. and E. 3, which have “the one, although…”] [Col. 0155D], although he is recognized as having come together into an indivisible unity from two different realities, just as a man, consisting of soul and body, is not rather two but one from both.

Thus, observing that both human and divine words were spoken by one Christ, we think rightly. When he speaks most fittingly about God and says of himself, “Whoever sees me sees the Father,” and, “I and the Father are one,” we understand his divine and ineffable nature, according to which he is one with his Father because of one and the same substance, existing as his image, character, and radiance of glory [Col. 0156A].

But when, fully aware of the measure of human nature, he addresses the Jews and says, “Now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you,” we recognize him no less as the true God, who is in the likeness and equality of the Father, even within the measures of his humanity [Ae.: “the true Word”].

If it is necessarily believed that God by nature became flesh, or rather a man endowed with a rational soul [T. 1, 2: “a reasoning soul”], why should anyone be ashamed of any of his words if he uttered words appropriate to man? If he rejects words fitting for man, who, according to us, compelled him to become man? When he mercifully inclined himself for our sake toward voluntary self-emptying, for what reason would he have avoided words worthy of self-emptying?

We therefore ascribe all his words in the Gospel to one person, to one subsistence—namely, that of the incarnate Word—because there is one Lord Jesus Christ. As it is written, he was called “the apostle and high priest of our confession,” as one offering to God and the Father the confession of our faith, which is continually offered by us and through him to God and the Father [Col. 0156B].

Again, we say that he who is by nature the only-begotten Son from God is the one to whom the name and office of priesthood belong, and we assign them to no other man besides him. For he became mediator between God and human beings and reconciler to peace, offering himself to God and the Father for us as a fragrance of sweetness. Therefore he said:

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; burnt offerings for sin did not please you. But you prepared a body for me. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the heading of the book it is written about me, to do your will, O God.”

For he offered his own body, not for himself, but for us, as a fragrance of sweetness [Col. 0156C]. What offering or sacrifice would he need for himself, since as God he was free from every sin? If all have sinned and lack the glory of God, since human nature has become more prone to exceed the limits of mutability and has been weakened by sins, but he was not so, and therefore we are overcome by his glory, why should there still be any doubt that the true Lamb was sacrificed for us?

Whoever says that he offered himself both for himself and for us [T. 1, 2: “that he had offered”] will in no way escape the charge of impiety, since he committed absolutely no offense and made no sin whatsoever. What offering, then, would he need, when he had no crime of his own for which an offering would be suitably required?

When he also says of the Spirit, “He will glorify me,” we rightly understand this and confess one Christ and Son—not as though he needed glory from another, but as having received glory from the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit is neither better nor higher than he. Rather, because he used the power of his own Spirit in performing marvelous works for the demonstration of his divinity, he is said to be glorified by that Spirit, just as one might say of a human being that his own ability or some discipline makes him renowned.

Although the Spirit exists in his own subsistence and his property is understood in his person, according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son [Col. 0157A], nevertheless he is not alien to the Son [Ae., B. R., E. 3: “nevertheless”]. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth. Hence the Spirit proceeds from him as likewise from God the Father.

Indeed, this same Spirit, performing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified the Lord Jesus Christ after he had ascended into heaven. Christ, who exists by nature as God, was believed to perform mighty works through his Spirit; therefore he said, “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you.”

The same Spirit is not said to be wise or powerful through participation in another, since he is perfect in every respect and wholly lacks nothing good. He is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s power and wisdom—that is, of the Son—and therefore he is shown in reality and in subsistence to be power and wisdom [Col. 0157B].

Since the holy Virgin physically gave birth to God united to flesh according to subsistence, we therefore confess that she is the Mother of God. This does not mean that the nature of the Word received from flesh the beginning of its existence. For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God, and the Word was with God”; he is himself the creator of the ages, coeternal with the Father, and creator of the universe.

Rather, as we said above, by uniting the human nature to himself according to subsistence, he endured birth from the bodily womb itself. He did not require this birth of necessity or on account of his own nature—for it took place at the final times of the world—but in order to bless the first fruits of our substance. When a woman gave birth to him united to flesh, the curse pronounced against the whole human race ceased, and our bodies were no longer consigned to death [Col. 0157C].

By himself abolishing what had been said, “You will give birth to children in sorrow,” he showed true what had been foretold in the prophet’s voice: “Death has been swallowed up in victory,” and again, “The Lord has removed every tear from every face” [Col. 0157D].

For this reason we say that he providentially blessed even those marriages when he deigned to attend the wedding at Cana of Galilee, having been invited there with the holy apostles.

We have been taught to think these things by the holy apostles and evangelists and by every divinely inspired Scripture, as well as by the blessed confessions of the Fathers, grounded in truth. It is now necessary for your religious office to agree with all these things and to consent without deception. The matters that your religious office must anathematize are appended to this letter.

### I

If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God and therefore does not confess that the holy Virgin is Mother of God [Note: U.: “the holy Virgin Mary”], for she bore according to the flesh the Word of God who became flesh, according to what is written, “The Word became flesh” [Note: From Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, and G. A. and E. 3 have: “the Virgin, and that she bore him.” U.: “the Virgin who bore him according to the flesh”], let him be anathema.

### II

If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father was united to the flesh according to subsistence, and that there is one Christ with his own flesh, namely, the same one who is at once God and man, let him be anathema.

### III

[Note: This canon is absent from U. and G.]

If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a connection according to dignity, or even authority or power, and not rather by the coming together effected through natural unity, let him be anathema.

### IV

If anyone divides between two persons or subsistences the words contained in the apostolic and evangelical writings, or the words spoken about Christ by the saints or by Christ himself about himself, and applies some of them as though to a man understood separately from the Word of God, while assigning the others as appropriate to God alone to the Word of God the Father, let him be anathema.

### V

If anyone dares to say that Christ is a man who bears God—that is, a “God-bearer”—and does not rather confess that he is truly God, as the Son by nature, according to the statement, “The Word became flesh,” and that he shared in flesh and blood as we do, let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that the same one is at once God and man, because the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone says that Jesus the man was assisted by the operation of the Word of God, and attributes the glory of the only-begotten Son as though to another existing separately from him, let him be anathema.

### VIII

If anyone dares to say that the assumed man must be worshiped together with God the Word, glorified together with him [Note: From Ae., U., and G.
