A. and the other witnesses have “glorified”], and named God together with him as one distinct from another—for the added *co(n)-* syllable always compels this meaning—and does not rather venerate Emmanuel with one worship and render him one glorification, according to the statement, “The Word became flesh,” let him be anathema.

### IX

If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as one who used an alien power through him and received from him the ability to act against unclean spirits and to perform divine signs among human beings, and does not rather confess that it is his own Spirit, through whom he performed the divine signs, let him be anathema.

### X

Holy Scripture commemorates that Christ became the high priest and apostle of our confession; he offered himself for us as a fragrance of sweetness to God and the Father.

If anyone therefore says that our high priest and apostle was not the Word of God himself when he became flesh and, according to us, man, but rather another man separately understood, distinct from him and born from a woman; or if anyone says that he offered himself as an offering for himself as well as for us, and not rather for us alone—for he who knew no sin whatsoever had no need of an offering—let him be anathema.

### XI

If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and the very own flesh of the Word of God the Father, but regards it as belonging to another joined to him by dignity, or as though to one possessing a divine indwelling, and does not rather confess, as we have said, that it is life-giving because it was made the very own flesh of the Word, who is able to give life to all things, let him be anathema.

### XII

If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, according to the fact that he is life and, as God, the giver of life, let him be anathema.

## Another decretal letter to the same Nestorius
Therefore the holy and great synod says:

He who is naturally begotten from God the Father, the only-begotten Son, true God from true God, light from light, through whom and with whom the Father made all things—he descended, became incarnate, and was made man; he suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended once more [Col. 0159B] into heaven. These words we must follow; these doctrines we must obey, considering what it means for the Word of God to become incarnate and to be made man.

For we do not say that the nature of God was changed or transformed into flesh, nor that it was transformed wholly into the man consisting of soul and body. Rather, we say that the Word united to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, and that he became man substantially, ineffably, and irreproachably, and was also called the Son of Man—not by bare will alone, nor by the assumption of a person alone, but because different natures came together into one. Yet one Christ and Son arose from both [Note: [Col. 0159D] Ae., B. R., U.: “from both of them.”], without the difference of the natures being emptied or removed by their conjunction; rather, because divinity and humanity together made for us one God, Christ, and Son [Col. 0159C] through that secret and ineffable union unto unity.

Thus he who before all ages was born from the Father is also said to have been physically begotten from a woman—not because his divine nature took its beginning from the sacred Virgin, nor because, for his own sake, he needed to be born a second time after the birth which he had from the Father. For it is foolish and absurd to say that he who is coeternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to exist. Rather, because for our salvation he united a human nature to himself and proceeded from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born physically.

For a common man was not first born from the holy Virgin and only afterward did the Word dwell in him. Rather, in the very virginal womb and uterus he united himself with the flesh [Note: [Col. 0159D] B. R.: “he united the flesh to himself”] and endured physical generation, making the birth of his flesh his own birth.

Thus we say that he both suffered and rose again—not because God the Word suffered in his own nature wounds, blows, the piercing of nails, or other injuries, for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering, but because that body which had become his own [Col. 0160A] suffered. Therefore he himself is said to have suffered all these things for us; for God, who could not suffer, was present in the body that suffered.

In the same way we understand his death. The Word of God is naturally immortal and incorruptible, life itself and life-giving. But because his own body, by the grace of God, as Paul says, tasted death for everyone, he is therefore said to have suffered death for us—not because he himself experienced death with respect to his own nature, for it is madness either to think or to say this, but because, as we said above, his true flesh tasted death.

Likewise, when the flesh rose again, we speak of his resurrection—not because it had fallen into corruption, God forbid, but because his body rose. In the same way we confess one Christ [Col. 0160B] and Lord, not worshiping a man together with the Word as though they were separate, lest some appearance of division be introduced, but worshiping one and the same person; for his body is not foreign to the Word, with whom it also sits beside the Father.

Nor do we say this as though two sons were seated beside him, but one Son with the flesh through the union. For [Note: [Col. 0159D] From the Greek exemplar; for all the codices incorrectly read: “as though.”] if we refuse to accept such a substantial union, regarding it as either impossible to suffer or somehow dishonorable, we fall into the position of saying that there are two sons.

It is necessary to distinguish and say that a man was separately honored with the title of son, and again that the Word who is from God is, both in name and in truth, the Son of God. But we must not divide our one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons. For this does not assist [Note: [Col. 0160D] T. 1, 2, U., G.: “helps.”] the right account of the faith, even though some assert some sort of union of persons. For Scripture did not say that the Word of God assumed a human person, but that he became flesh.

This means that the Word of God, like us, shared in flesh and blood, made our body properly his own, and proceeded as a man from a woman, without casting aside or laying down either his divinity or the generation which he had from the Father, but remaining, even in the assumption of flesh, the God that he was.

The right account of the faith proclaims this everywhere. We find that the holy Fathers held this understanding; therefore they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin *Theotocon*—“Mother of God”—not because the nature and divinity of the Word took their beginning in the holy Virgin, but because from her was born that sacred [Col. 0160D] body, animated by a rational soul, to which the Word of God was substantially united and is said to have been physically born.

I write these things out of love [Note: [Col. 0160D] T. 1, 2: “in preference to love.” U.: “through love”] in Christ [Note: [Col. 0160D] From the Greek exemplar; all the codices incorrectly read: “I wrote.”], appealing to you as a brother and calling God and the elect angels to witness, so that you may think and teach these things together with us, so that the peace of the churches may be preserved and the indissoluble bond of concord and love may remain among priests.

## XI. THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON

Of six hundred and thirty bishops, held against all heresies, and especially against Eutyches and Dioscorus, in the consulship of Valentinian for the seventh time and Avienus, in the year [Note: [Col. 0161D] Ae., E. 3: “in the year 488.” T. 1, 2: “in the year 484.”] 489.

[Col. 0161]

At the command [Note: [Col. 0161D] From B. R., T. 1, 2. In A. and the others: “in the consulship.”] of the most devout and Christ-loving emperor, Flavius Marcianus, perpetual Augustus, on the Ides of October, a synod was held in the city of Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, by decree of the most devout and faithful emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

The most glorious officials assembled in the church of the holy and triumphant martyr Euphemia: namely, the magnificent and most glorious master of the soldiers, former prefect, former consul, and patrician Anatolius; the magnificent and most glorious prefect of the sacred praetorium, Palladius; the magnificent and most glorious prefect of the city, Tatianus; the magnificent and most glorious master of the divine offices, Vincomalus; the magnificent and most glorious count of largesses [U., G.: “of the largesses”], Martialis; and the most glorious [Col. 0161B] and magnificent count of the household troops, Sparocius [Note: [Col. 0161D] Ae., B. R., U.: “Sparatius.”]; and the magnificent count of the imperial private property, Genetholius [Note: [Col. 0162D] T. 1, 2, G.: “Genethlius.”].

Members of the glorious senate were also present: namely, the magnificent and most glorious former prefect, former consul, and patrician Florentius; the magnificent and most glorious former consul and patrician senator; the magnificent and most glorious former master, former consul, and patrician Nomo; the magnificent and most glorious former prefect, former consul, and patrician Protogenes; the magnificent and most glorious former prefect Zolius; the magnificent and most glorious former prefect of the city, Theodorus; the magnificent and most glorious former prefect of the city, Apollonius; and the magnificent and most glorious former praepositus, Artaxerxes.

The holy council of the whole world also assembled in Chalcedon according to the divine command, namely, the bishops Paschasius and Lucentius and the presbyter Boniface, representing the place of the venerable and holy archbishop of ancient Rome, Leo; and the holy archbishop of the magnificent New Rome of Constantinople, Anatolius; together with the remaining six hundred and thirty most holy and reverend bishops.

All were seated before the railings of the holy altar with the magnificent and most glorious [Note: [Col. 0162D] B. R.: “the most glorious of the distinguished senate”] members of the senate. The most devout emperor Marcianus also arrived in the aforementioned most holy basilica, and the most devout and faithful queen Augusta Pulcheria, inflamed with divine zeal and the ardor of faith, was present as well. The most devout emperor Marcianus addressed the holy synod as follows [Ae., U.: feminine “addressed”]:

“When we first entered upon the kingdom by election and by God’s decree, amid so many public concerns no business bound us more than making known to all the upright and true faith of the Christians, in which holiness and truth reside.

“For it is evident that, whether through greed or empty ambition, many of those who in former times thought and taught different things led the people astray according to what benefited themselves, not according to what was fitting or what the truth and the teaching of the Fathers required. Therefore many were led into error [Ae., B. R.: ‘were brought into error’].

“Accordingly, we approved the holding of this holy synod and considered it necessary to impose this labor upon you, so that, when every darkness of error has been removed, our faith—which is pure and holy—may enter the souls of all and shine with the light of its own truth, according to the way in which the Godhead itself wished to reveal itself to humanity and according to what the teaching of the Fathers has demonstrated.

“From now on, let no one dare to argue about the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ in any way other than what the proclamation of the apostles and the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, whose teaching is consonant with this, are known to have handed down. The same is attested by the letters of the most holy Pope Leo, who governs the apostolic throne, written to Flavianus, of sacred memory, formerly bishop of the imperial city of Constantinople.

“Therefore, when such defenses have been removed and cut off, and greed has ceased, let the whole truth be revealed. We have devised our presence at the synod for the confirmation of the faith, not to display power, and following the example of the emperor Constantine; but we have come lest in the future the multitude of the people be found to disagree with the teachings. For the simplicity of some has hitherto easily been deceived by the inventions of talkative men. It is evident that discord and heresies have arisen from the wicked teachings of different persons.

“We must devote all our attention to attaching the people, who hold the same view because of the true and holy teaching, to the one upright Church. Therefore let your reverence hasten to set forth the true catholic faith according to the teaching of the Fathers, with your minds in agreement, so that just as from the Council of Nicaea until this time the true faith has been known to all after error was cut away, so now also, through this holy synod, the cloud may be removed which, as we said above, appears to have arisen during these few years from the depravity and greed of certain persons.

“If what has been established is always preserved, it will indeed be a work of divine providence to preserve forever in the Church what we devoutly wish to accomplish.” [T. 1, 2, [Col. 0162D]: “in the Church.”]

After these royal words, all the bishops cried out:

“Many years to Marcianus, the new Constantine! Many years to the king! Many years to the queen of the orthodox! Many years to Marcianus, the Christ-loving king! May his reign endure forever! Worthy lovers of the orthodox faith and of Christ, may envy be far from you!”

After these acclamations, Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, New Rome, and chief secretary, said:

“Since, by the will of heavenly grace and through the divine zeal of your serenity, most devout emperors, to whom God has granted rule over all [U. adds: ‘human beings’], this holy and great synod of the whole world has assembled around your decree, it has, with the extensive leisure of many days and divine diligence, driven away by the word of truth all the discord that previously arose against our upright and inviolable catholic faith, banishing every innovation, as the acts that follow demonstrate in writing in each detail.

“It has established a simple rule, fortified by the power of the divine Scriptures, preserving within it the judgment of the holy and blessed Fathers for the true recognition of those who sincerely seek it. May the long-lasting crown of your empire endure. I have it before me, and, if it pleases your serenity, I shall read it.”

The most devout and faithful emperor said: “Read it.” And the same archdeacon read it.

The holy and great universal synod, which by the grace of God and by decree of the most devout emperors Valentinian and Marcian, Augusti, was assembled in the city of Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the basilica of the holy and triumphant martyr Euphemia, established the provisions written below.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, [Col. 0163C] strengthening his disciples in the recognition of the faith, said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you,” so that no disagreement of faith might arise among those who are close to one another, but that the preaching of the truth might be shown equally.

But because the evil one does not cease to plant his tares among the very seeds of piety and always to devise something new against the truth, our Lord, desiring as usual to provide for the human race, raised up this most devout and faithful emperor to heaven, who summoned to himself from every direction the leaders of the priests, so that, with the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ cooperating, he might remove every pestilence of falsehood from Christ’s sheep and refresh them with the shoots of truth.

This too we have completed by common decree: rejecting the sects of error, renewing the upright faith of the Fathers, proclaiming to all the creed of the three hundred and eighteen, and designating as household members of these Fathers another one hundred and fifty Fathers who agreed with this most devout title. These latter, afterward assembling in this most splendid city of Constantinople, also themselves confirmed the same faith.

We therefore establish and preserve the order and all the formulas of the faith, as well as our holy synod formerly held at Ephesus, whose leaders were Celestinus, the priest of the city of Rome, and Cyril, the priest of the church of Alexandria, both of venerable memory. Thus the exposition of the upright and blameless faith of the three hundred [Col. 0164A] and eighteen holy and blessed Fathers who assembled at Nicaea under the pious emperor Constantine of blessed memory may shine forth.

Also included is the decree of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers in the city of Constantinople, intended to destroy the sects then springing up, but to confirm [Note: [Col. 0163D] U.: “springing up; it also contains the confirmation” [Col. 0164D]] our catholic and apostolic faith itself.

## Creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, *homousion* with the Father—that is, of the same [Col. 0164B] substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us and for our salvation descended, became incarnate, was made man, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was born he was not,” and who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or that he is from another subsistence or substance, or that the Son of God is changeable or mutable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

## And likewise that of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, *homousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us and for our salvation descended, and became incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, was made man, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life [U.: “life-giving”], who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets; in one catholic and apostolic Church; we confess one baptism for the remission of sins; we await the resurrection of the dead and the life [Ae.: “and the life”] of the age to come. Amen.

This careful and salutary symbol of divine grace would indeed have sufficed for the fullest recognition and confirmation of piety. For it teaches the perfect doctrine concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and faithfully reveals the incarnation of the Lord to those who receive it.

But because those who strive to destroy the proclamation of the truth bring forth innovations of their own heresy—some daring to corrupt the mystery of the divine dispensation accomplished for us and denying the Virgin that designation of divine childbirth; others introducing mixture and confusion and senselessly composing one nature of flesh and divinity, monstrously proclaiming the divine nature of the only-begotten to be subject to suffering through such confusion—therefore the holy and great universal synod, wishing to exclude every contrivance they might set against the truth, while teaching the ancient proclamation to remain unshaken, decreed above all that the undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers should remain intact.

And because of those who oppose the Holy Spirit, it confirms the doctrine concerning the substance of the Holy Spirit handed down by the one hundred and fifty Fathers who assembled somewhat later in the city of Constantinople. They too made the same understanding known to all—not adding anything that was lacking in what had previously been stated, but more fully manifesting by testimonies from the Scriptures the same understanding concerning the Holy Spirit against those who strive to deprive his divinity of lordship.

Moreover, because of those who attempt to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation and shamelessly proclaim that the one born from the holy Virgin Mary was merely a man, it received the synodical letters of the most blessed Cyril, formerly priest of the church of Alexandria, both those addressed to Nestorius and those addressed to the others throughout the East, appropriate and agreeing with one another, for the refutation of Nestorian madness and for the interpretation of those who, with religious zeal, desire the understanding of the salutary symbol.

To these it clearly added the letter of the holy and most blessed archbishop of the chief see, Leo, written to Flavianus, archbishop of sacred memory, for the destruction of the wickedness of Eutyches and in agreement with the confession of the great Peter, together with a certain common document directed against those who do not glorify rightly, for the confirmation of the catholic religion.

For it both curses those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons, and excludes from the council of priests those who dare to assert that the divinity of the only-begotten Son is subject to suffering. It opposes those who argue for a mixture or confusion of Christ’s two natures, and casts far away those who madly assert that the form of a servant which he assumed from us is heavenly or of some other substance. It anathematizes those who rave that the Lord had two natures before the union but fabricate one nature after the union.

Therefore, agreeing with the holy Fathers, we are likewise taught with one harmonious voice to confess one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, the same consisting of a rational soul and body; according to divinity, of one nature with the Father, and according to humanity, the same of one nature with us, like us in all things [Col. 0166A] except sin; before the ages begotten from the Father according to divinity, and in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same begotten from Mary the Virgin, the Mother of God, according to humanity—one and the same Christ, Son, [Note: [Col. 0165D] U., G.: “only-begotten Son of God”] Lord, only-begotten, to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation.

The distinction of the natures is in no way abolished because of the union; rather, the property of each nature is preserved, and the two come together in one person and one status. He is not divided or separated into two persons, but is one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ, just as the prophets from the beginning taught concerning him, as he himself instructed us, and as the symbol of the Fathers handed down to us.

Having therefore established all these matters with the utmost precision and diligence on every side, the holy and universal synod decreed that no one may present, write, publish, hold, or teach any other faith. Whoever dares either to set forth another faith, or to present, teach, or transmit another creed to those wishing to turn from the Gentiles, the Jews, or any heretics whatsoever to the knowledge of the truth—if they are bishops or clerics, they are to be deprived of their episcopate and clergy; but if they are monks or laymen, they are to be anathematized.

# Ecclesiastical regulations established by the aforementioned council

## I. On preserving the canons of each council

We decree that the regulations issued by the holy Fathers in every synod up to the present be observed.

## II. That bishops or any members of the clergy should not be ordained for money

If any bishop, having accepted money, performs an ordination and turns the priceless grace into a commercial transaction, and ordains a bishop, or a rural bishop, or a presbyter, or a deacon, or anyone else counted among the clergy; or if, having accepted money, he ordains an administrator of property, a defender, or a *paramonarius*; whoever attempts such things, or is convicted of them, shall himself undergo the penalty affecting his rank [Note: [Col. 0165D] From Ae., B. R., U. In A. and the others: “shall be subject to”]. The person so ordained shall gain no benefit from such commerce [Note: [Col. 0166D] U.: “from such commerce, but shall be excluded from it as from a shameful curse”] and shameful appointment, but shall be excluded both from the dignity and from the responsibility which he obtained through money.

The person who acted as intermediary in such disgraceful [Col. 0166D] and illicit profits, if he is a cleric, shall fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.

## III. That bishops, clerics, and monks should not undertake secular estates or lawsuits

It has come to the holy synod’s attention that some of those counted among the clergy, for the sake of shameful gain, undertake the leases of other people’s estates and secular lawsuits. They thereby separate themselves through negligence from the holy ministries, but run to the houses of secular persons and, out of greed, undertake the administration of their property.

Therefore the holy and great synod decreed that henceforth none of these—whether a bishop, cleric, or monk [Note: [Col. 0167D] Ae.: “of bishops, clerics, or monks”—] may lease estates or involve himself in secular administrations, except those who are necessarily drawn by the laws into guardianships or curatorships of minors, or to whom the bishop of the city himself has entrusted the administration of ecclesiastical property, or of orphans and widows who are defenseless [Note: [Col. 0167D] U., G.: “who are already exhausted”], or of those persons who especially need ecclesiastical assistance [Note: [Col. 0167D] From U. In A. and the others: “who need ecclesiastical assistance”], for fear of God.

Whoever transgresses these decrees shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction.

## IV. On the honor due to monks, and that none of them should disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs or receive another’s slave without the master’s knowledge

Those who truly and purely choose the solitary life are worthy of appropriate honor. Yet because some, using the monastic habit, disturb ecclesiastical and civic affairs, wandering indiscriminately through cities and monasteries and entrusting themselves to their own presumption, it has been decided that no one may build or establish for himself a monastery or a house of prayer [Ae.: “build”] without the knowledge of the bishop of that city.

Those who are subject to monasteries in the various cities or estates are to be subject to the bishops, remain quiet [Note: [Col. 0168D] From U. In A. and the others: “be quiet”], devote themselves to their duties, and observe fasts and prayers in the places where they once dedicated themselves to God, remaining there. They are not to engage in ecclesiastical or secular business, abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps they are ordered to do so by the bishop of that city because of urgent necessities.

No slave is to be received into a monastery to become a monk among them without the knowledge of his own master.

We decree that anyone who transgresses these provisions is to be excluded from communion, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. It is fitting, however, that the bishop of the city provide the monasteries with the necessary care and supervision.

## V. That a bishop or any member of the clergy may not move from one city to another

Because of those bishops or clerics who move from city to city, it has been decided that the regulations issued by the holy Fathers shall retain their proper force.

## VI. That no one should be ordained absolutely, except for a specific place

No one is to be ordained absolutely as a presbyter or deacon, or as anyone else established in an ecclesiastical order, unless it is expressly for the church of a city or estate, a martyr shrine, or a monastery, and the person ordained is to receive the designation of a publicly assigned ordination.

For those ordained absolutely, the holy synod decreed that the laying on of hands is void and that no such act has validity, to the injury of the person who ordained him.

## VII. On clerics and monks who do not remain in their chosen state

Those who have once been enrolled in the clergy or in monasteries, we decree, are not to enter military service or secular offices. Those who dare to do so and prefer not to repent of it, or who return to that same course which they had previously set before themselves, not on the pretext of God, are to be anathematized.

## VIII. On clerics in poorhouses [Note: [Col. 0168D] This word is written corruptly in the codices. In A., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, U., G.: *tociis*. In Ae.: *thociis*. In T. 2: *toicis*], monasteries, and martyr shrines under the authority of the bishop of each city

Clerics established in poorhouses, monasteries, or martyr shrines are to be under the authority of the bishop of the city in which they are located, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers. They are not to withdraw presumptuously from their bishop.

Those who dare to sever this arrangement in any way, or who refuse to submit to their own bishop, if they are clerics, shall be subject to the condemnations of the ancestral regulations; [Col. 0168B] but if they are monks or laymen, they shall be excommunicated.

## IX. That clerics should not go to secular courts while bypassing the bishop

If a cleric has a dispute with another cleric, he is not to abandon his bishop and hasten to secular courts. The dispute must first be heard before his own bishop; then, if it is the bishop’s judgment [reading uncertain; U.: “contrary to the bishop’s judgment”], the case is to be heard before arbitrators chosen by both parties.

Whoever acts against these provisions shall be subject to the corrections prescribed by the canons.

If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or another bishop, he shall bring his complaint before the hearing of the synod of that province [Ae.: “shall investigate”]. If a bishop or cleric has a dispute against the bishop of that province and its metropolitan [Col. 0168C], he shall go either to the bishops of that diocese or, certainly, to the see of the imperial city of Constantinople, and there pursue his own case [B. R.: “investigate it”].

## X. That a cleric may not serve in two churches

A cleric may not be ordained [T. 2: “serve”] in the churches of two cities, but only in the church in which he was ordained from the beginning and to which he had previously sought refuge.

If, out of a desire for empty glory, he has fled to a larger church, we order that he be restored to his own church—that is, to the place where he was originally ordained—and serve there alone.

If someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he is to have no connection with the former church, whether with the martyr shrines, poorhouses, or guesthouses established under that church, or with their affairs.

The holy synod decreed that those who dare, after the promulgation of this great and universal synod, to do what has been forbidden shall fall from their own rank.

## XI. That letters of passage should be given to the poor, while persons of higher standing should be authenticated by letters of recommendation

We decree that all poor persons and those in need of ecclesiastical assistance may travel only with a verified letter of passage or peace letter, called an ecclesiastical *irenic* letter [Col. 0169A], and not with letters of recommendation.

For it is fitting that those whom we call letters of recommendation be given only to persons of greater distinction, so that such letters may be provided solely to them.

## XII. That a province should in no way be divided between two metropolitans

It has come to our attention that certain persons, desiring power contrary to ecclesiastical regulations, divide one province into two by an imperial administrative enactment, and consequently two metropolitan bishops are found in one and the same province.

Therefore the holy synod decreed that henceforth no bishop should attempt anything of this kind, and that those who attempt it shall fall from their own rank.

If any cities were previously honored with the title of metropolitan by an imperial administrative enactment [Col. 0169B], they are to enjoy the name only; and the person who governs its Church—that is, the bishop—shall retain by his own right the privilege belonging to a metropolitan bishop.

## XIII. That foreign clerics should not minister without letters of recommendation

A foreign cleric or lector may never minister outside his own city without letters of recommendation from his own bishop [Note: [Col. 0169D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, U., G.: “nowhere,” rather than “never”].

## XIV. That a cleric should not take a wife from another sect unless she has promised to come to the true faith

Since in certain provinces psalmists [Note: [Col. 0169D] From Ae., B. R., U., G. In A. and the others: “psalmists, that is, lectors and singers”] and lectors are permitted to take wives, the holy synod decreed that they may in no way take a wife from another sect.

If someone has acted beforehand and already has children from such a marriage, and they have perhaps previously been baptized among heretics, he must offer them to the catholic Church so that they may commune there. Those who have not yet been baptized may in no way be baptized in a heretical church, nor may a person marry a heretic, a Jew, or a pagan, unless the latter has first promised to come to the orthodox faith while being joined to the orthodox person.

Whoever transgresses this definition of the holy synod shall be subject to the condemnations of the regulations.

## XV. On women deacons, and that they may not be ordained before the age of forty

A woman deacon is not to be ordained before the age of forty, and this only after careful examination.

If she receives ordination, observes the ministry for any length of time, and afterward gives herself to marriage [Col. 0169D], thereby insulting the grace of God, she is to be anathematized, together with the man who entered into her marriage.

## XVI. On monks and virgins dedicated to God, and that they may not marry

If a virgin has dedicated herself to God, and likewise a monk, they may not marry.

If they are found doing so, they are to remain excommunicated. We decree, however, that mercy may be shown toward them if the bishop of the place approves it.

## XVII. On churches in parishes held by a bishop for thirty years, or on restored cities
Through the individual rural churches and parishes, or on estates, they are to remain undisturbed with those bishops who hold them, especially those who have already held and governed them without violence for thirty years. If, however, within thirty years a dispute has arisen or should arise concerning them [Ae., B. R.: “below thirty years”], those who say that they have been wronged on their account may bring the matter before the provincial synod. If anyone thinks that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him bring judgment before the ruler of that diocese or before the see of the city of Constantinople, as has already been stated. But if any city has been restored by imperial authority, or if it should hereafter be restored through civil and public administrative measures, the organization of the parish churches is likewise to follow that arrangement.

### XVIII. Concerning the conspiracy of clerics, which the Greeks call *fratria*

[Col. 0170B]

The crime of conspiracies and plots, which among the Greeks is called *fratria*, is also expressly prohibited by the public laws; much more, therefore, ought it to be rejected lest it occur in the holy Church of God. If any clerics or monks are found swearing conspiratorial oaths or forming any *fratriae* or factions against their bishops or against other clerics, they are in every respect to fall from their own rank.

### XIX. That a council ought to be held twice a year in each province

It has come to our ears that the councils of bishops established in the provinces are scarcely being celebrated, and that consequently many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are being neglected. Therefore this holy synod decrees, according to the regulations of the Fathers, that in each province the bishops meet together twice a year [Col. 0170C], wherever the metropolitan approves, and correct individually whatever matters may have arisen. If bishops established in their own cities refuse to attend, especially when they are in good bodily health and free from all other pressing and unavoidable business, they may be rebuked by admonitions of fraternal charity.

### XX. That clerics may not migrate to another city, except those who have lost their own cities

As we have already decreed, clerics established in individual churches may not be ordained in the churches of another city, but must remain in the city in which they first began their ministry [Note: [Col. 0170D] T. 1, 2, U., G.: “acquiesce”]—except for those who have lost their own cities and have migrated by necessity to other churches. If, after this definition, any bishop receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, the holy synod has decreed that both the one who received him and the one who was received are to remain excommunicated until that cleric returns to his own church.

### XXI. Concerning the accusers of bishops or clerics, and what sort of persons are to be admitted to accusation

A cleric or layman who accuses bishops or clerics is not to be admitted rashly and indiscriminately to bring an accusation [Col. 0171A], unless his reputation has first been investigated.

### XXII. That clerics may not seize property belonging to their bishop after his death

Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, seize property belonging to him, as has already been established by the preceding regulations. If they do so, they must know that they endanger their own rank.

### XXIII. Concerning clerics, monks, or excommunicated persons who come to the royal city against the will of their bishop

It has come to the ears of the holy synod that certain clerics and monks, without having received any assignment from their own bishop—and sometimes even those who have been excommunicated by him—come to this royal city of Constantinople and, remaining there for long periods [Col. 0171B], bring disturbances upon ecclesiastical peace and corrupt the households of various people. Therefore the holy synod decrees that these persons are first to be admonished by the defender of the Church of Constantinople to leave the royal city. But if they persist shamelessly in the same purpose, they are to be expelled against their will by that same defender, so that they may return to their own places.

### XXIV. That monasteries may not be turned into secular lodging houses

Monasteries that have once been consecrated are to remain permanently so, by judgment of their bishop, and the property belonging to them is to be preserved for the monastery itself [Note: [Col. 0171D] U.: *monasteria, quae consecrata sunt, diversoria* (“monasteries that have been consecrated, lodging houses”).]. They may not thereafter be made into secular dwellings. Those who permit this to happen are to be subject to the condemnations established by the canons [Col. 0171C].

### XXV. That after the death of a bishop the ordination of another bishop ought not to be long delayed

Since, as has been reported to us, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay the ordinations of bishops, it has pleased the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops be carried out within three months, unless perhaps an unavoidable necessity compels the time of ordination to be extended further [Ae.: “postponed”]. If any bishop fails to observe this, he himself is to be subject to ecclesiastical condemnation. The revenues of the same widowed Church, however, are to be kept intact with the steward of that Church.

### XXVI. Concerning stewards—that is, administrators—to be appointed for each church

[Col. 0171D]

Since, as has reached us, in certain churches bishops administer ecclesiastical property without a steward, it has pleased the synod that all Churches having bishops should also have stewards from their own clergy. These are to administer the Church’s property with the discretion of their bishop, so that the administration of those ecclesiastical goods may not take place without witnesses [Note: [Col. 0171D] U.: “so that the administrators of those goods may exist”], and so that the property of the same Church may not consequently be scattered and reproach brought upon the dignity of the priesthood. If anyone fails to observe this, let him be subject to the divine regulations.

### XXVII. Concerning those who abduct wives for themselves

The holy synod decrees that those who abduct women as wives for themselves, and those who assist them [Note: [Col. 0172D] U.: “those who cooperate with or connive at women being taken under the pretext of living together, or those who…”], are to fall from their own rank if they are clerics; if they are laymen, they are to be anathema.

Paschasius, bishop of the city of Lillibitana, acting in place of the most blessed Bishop Leo, subscribed to the definition. Lucensius, bishop of the city of Asculum, likewise acting in place of the most holy Bishop Leo, subscribed to the definition. Boniface, presbyter of the city of Rome, acting in place of the apostolic see, subscribed to the definition. Anatolius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, New Rome, subscribed to the definition. Maximus, bishop of Antioch, subscribed to the definition. Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, subscribed to the definition [Col. 0172B]. Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, subscribed to the definition. Quintilius, bishop of Heraclea in Macedonia, acting in place of the most holy Bishop Anastasius of the city of Thessalonica, subscribed to the definition. Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, subscribed to the definition. Lucian, bishop of Byzus, acting in place of the most holy Bishop Cyriacus of Heraclea in Thrace, subscribed to the definition. Eusebius, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, subscribed to the definition. Diogenes, bishop of Cyzicus, subscribed to the definition. Peter, bishop of Corinth, subscribed to the definition. Florus, bishop of Sardis [T. 2: “of Sardica”], subscribed to the definition. Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, subscribed to the definition. Anastasius, bishop of Nicaea, subscribed to the definition. Eleutherius, bishop of Chalcedon, subscribed to the definition. Likewise all six hundred and thirty bishops subscribed to the definition.

After it had been read aloud, the most pious emperor said to the holy council:

“Let the holy council declare whether the definition that has now been read was issued with the consent of all the bishops.”

All the most reverend bishops replied [Col. 0172D]:

“We all believe this: with one faith, with one judgment, we all think the same thing; all consenting, we subscribed; we are all orthodox. This is the faith of the apostles; this is the faith of those who believe rightly; this is the faith that has saved the whole world.” [Ae., B. R.: “will save.”]

“Life to Marcian, the new Constantine, the new Paul, the new David, the emperor; life to the most pious lady Augusta.”

After these acclamations, the most pious and faithful emperor said to the holy synod:

“The venerable Catholic faith has been made manifest by the holy universal synod according to the exposition of the Fathers. And if we have caused labor and insult to your Reverence, we give the greatest thanks to almighty God” [Note: [Col. 0173D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “to almighty God the Savior”], “because the discord of many who were wandering concerning the faith has been cut away, and now we have all come together into one and the same faith, hoping that through your prayers God will soon grant us a better peace above all others.”

The holy synod again cried out:

“These things are worthy of your empire; these things are proper to your empire; this is the correction of your empire—worthy of the faith, worthy of Christ, worthy of empire, worthy both of empire and of faith. Therefore the whole world is made peaceful.” [Note: [Col. 0173D] From the other codices. In A.: “of empire with dignity and of faith; therefore.”]

After these acclamations, the most pious and faithful emperor said to the holy synod:

“The venerable Catholic faith, manifested by the holy and universal synod according to the exposition of the Fathers, has been shown by our tranquility to be in accordance with the law; and it is fitting that every occasion for future contention concerning its faith be cut away. Therefore, if any civilian, soldier, or cleric publicly gathers a crowd concerning the faith under the pretext of discussion and causes an uproar, then, if he is the aforesaid civilian, he is to be expelled from the royal city; but the soldier or cleric will suffer the loss of his rank and will be subject to other penalties.”

## Edict of the emperors in confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon

The emperors Valentinian and Marcian, Augusti, to all peoples.

At last what we desired with our highest prayers and efforts has come to pass: contention concerning the orthodox law of the Christians has been removed. At last remedies for culpable error have been found, and the discordant judgment of the peoples has come together in one agreement and harmony. For the most religious priests came from various provinces to Chalcedon in accordance with our commands [Col. 0173C], and by a clear definition they taught what ought to be observed in religion.

Profane contention has therefore now departed, for he is truly impious and sacrilegious who, after the judgment of so many priests, leaves anything of his own opinion still to be considered. It is the height of madness to seek a fabricated light in the midst of clear daylight; for whoever discusses anything further after the truth has been found is seeking a lie.

Therefore no one—whether cleric, soldier, or of any other condition—shall hereafter attempt publicly to discuss the Christian faith, which has been definitively settled, in an assembled gathering and before listeners, seeking from this an occasion for disturbance and impiety. Whoever attempts to reopen and publicly debate matters once judged and rightly arranged insults the judgment of the most religious synod, since the matters now established concerning the Christian faith are known to have been defined according to the apostolic expositions and the institutions of the holy Fathers—three hundred and eighteen and one hundred and fifty.

There will be no shortage of punishment for those who despise this law, because they not only oppose a faith rightly established but also profane the venerable mysteries before Jews and pagans through such disputation. Therefore, if the offender is a cleric who has dared publicly to discuss religion, he shall be removed from the company of the clergy. If he is a soldier, he shall be stripped of his military belt. Others guilty of this crime shall likewise be expelled from this most holy city [Col. 0174A] and subjected, with judicial force, to the appropriate punishments.

For it is clear that the beginnings and fuel of heretical madness are supplied when certain people publicly dispute and contend. Therefore all shall observe what was established by the holy Council of Chalcedon [U.: “Chalcedonian Council”], without thereafter doubting anything.

Having thus been admonished by this edict of our sincerity, abstain from profane speech and cease hereafter to dispute about divine matters, which is unlawful. For we believe that this sin will be punished not only by divine judgment but also restrained by the authority of the laws and judges [Note: [Col. 0174D] From the remaining codices except A., which has “of judgment”].

7th day before the Kalends of February, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Sporacius.

## Sacred edicts of the Augusti Valentinian and Marcian after the Council of Chalcedon, in affirmation of that council and condemnation of the heretics

[Col. 0174B]

The emperors Valentinian and Marcian, Augusti, to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium.

Thanks must always be given and rendered to the divine power, because it neither permits the authors of heresy to remain hidden nor allows them to continue unpunished: one of these evils has great power to harm, while the other provides the rest with an example of prevention. That divine power is concerned with human acts, and especially with reverence for religion, has recently appeared clearly in the confirmation of the Catholic faith: it neither allowed Eutyches, a follower of criminal doctrines, to remain concealed as he had long remained concealed, nor, once his crime had been exposed, permitted him to escape punishment for his crime.

Thus condemned by divine and human judgments, he received the synodical decree as he deserved—guilty before the divinity whom he had insulted, and guilty before the human beings whom he had attempted to deceive. Recently, innumerable most blessed bishops from almost the entire world assembled at Chalcedon and expelled the wicked inventions of the aforesaid Eutyches, together with the case of his synod, following the definitions of the holy Fathers: those established at Nicaea by three hundred and eighteen, those later declared in this venerable city by one hundred and fifty bishops, and those established at Ephesus when the error of Nestorius was excluded, under the presidency of Celestine, bishop of the city of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

We have therefore judged, and continue to judge, that those things defined at Chalcedon by the venerable synod according to the ancient discipline are to be observed in every respect with the faith by which we worship God. For it is altogether fitting to preserve with the greatest veneration the definitions of six hundred and thirty priests who worship God with pure minds, which proceeded as sacred matters for the orthodox faith according to the regulations of the Fathers.

Since it belongs to princely foresight to suppress every evil at its beginning and to cut out a poisonous disease by the medicine of the laws, by this law we decree that those who are deceived by the error of Eutyches, following the example of the Apollinarians whom Eutyches followed, and whom the venerable regulations of the Fathers—that is, the ecclesiastical canons—and the most sacred enactments of the divine emperors condemn, shall have no bishop, no presbyter, and shall create or appoint no clerics. Eutyches himself is to be entirely deprived of the title of presbyter, of which he is both unworthy and has been stripped.

If, nevertheless, any persons dare, contrary to our definitions, to create bishops, presbyters, or other clerics, we order that both those created and those creating or presuming to assume clerical ranks be punished by loss of property and held in perpetual exile. We order that they have no license to meet, gather, or assemble monks, or to build monasteries. The places in which they may at any time dare to assemble are to be confiscated, if they met with the knowledge of the owner of the place. But if they assembled without the knowledge of the owner, tenant, or manager of the place, we decree that they be beaten with rods and undergo deportation.

Furthermore, they may receive nothing from anyone’s will, nor may anything be left to them by testament by those who share the same error. We do not permit them to enter any military service except the *cohortal* or frontier forces. If anyone is found serving outside those forces, whether because his religious perversity was unknown or because he fell into this error after acquiring his military belt, then, once released from military service, he shall have this as the fruit of his infidelity: he shall be deprived of the society of respectable men and of the palace, and shall reside nowhere except in the village or city in which he was born. If any of them were born in this venerable city—which it is wicked even to suppose—and were condemned, they shall be excluded both from this venerable city, from the most sacred imperial entourage, and from every metropolitan city.

These provisions we establish generally concerning all who have been or shall be stained by this pollution.

But those who were formerly clerics of the orthodox faith, and monks who lived in the lodging house of Eutyches—for it must not be called a monastery, since it harbored enemies of religion—and who have proceeded further into madness, abandoning the worship of venerable religion and the synodical decree defined by the priests of almost the whole world assembled at Chalcedon, and follow the accursed assertion of Eutyches because they believed that darkness ought to be chosen after abandoning the true light, we order to be held under all the penalties established either by this law or by earlier laws against heretics. Indeed, they are to be expelled beyond Roman soil, just as the preceding most religious enactments provided concerning the Manichaeans, lest innocent or weak minds be deceived by their poisonous frauds and wicked inventions.

Moreover, we have learned that they lied in certain matters to the insult of religion and to the discredit of the venerable synodical definition, and that, after composing books and volumes of writings, they fabricated many things that openly marked their madness against the true faith [Note: [Col. 0175D] From T. 1, 2. In the other codices: “pure faith”; and so afterward]. We therefore order that wherever writings of this sort are found, they be burned in the fire. Those who have either written them or handed them to others to read, whether for the purpose of teaching or of learning, we decree are to be punished by deportation. This accursed heresy must be destroyed, as was formerly provided by the edicts of our serenity; we deprive everyone of the power to do so, because whoever attempts to teach unlawful things shall be restrained by the ultimate penalty.

But those who listen, out of a desire to learn, to someone discussing the accursed heresy we restrain by a fine of ten pounds of gold [Note: [Col. 0175D] Ae.: “fine”; and likewise afterward]. Thus the material for error will be removed if there is neither a teacher nor a hearer of crimes.

Palladius, our dearest and most beloved father, your illustrious and magnificent Authority shall, by posting edicts, make known to all what we have ordered, so that the governors of the provinces and their officials, as well as the defenders of the cities, may know it. If they neglect or permit to be violated what we have judged must be guarded with true faith and holy purpose, they shall be punished by a fine of ten pounds of gold, as betrayers of religion and the laws, and shall also suffer loss of status.

Issued on the 15th day before the Kalends of August at Constantinople, in the consulship of Sporacius and of the one who was announced [Note: [Col. 0176D] T. 1, 2, U., G.: “Issued”].

## Another edict of the August Emperor Marcian against the heretics mentioned above

The Emperor Marcian Augustus to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium.

Although it has already been provided and decreed in the most sacred constitution of my clemency what severity ought to be exercised against those who, following the heretical perversity of Eutyches or Apollinaris [U.: “depravity”], have deviated from religion and the Catholic faith, nevertheless the citizens and inhabitants of the city of Alexandria are so infected with the poisons of Apollinaris that it has been necessary to decree again by the present law what we previously sanctioned.

For where license for offenses is frequent, the severity of sanctions must be numerous and vigilant. Moreover, the care that my serenity must devote to the orthodox faith ought to be all the more zealous because divine matters precede human affairs.

Therefore, whoever, whether in this sacred city, in the city of Alexandria, throughout the diocese of Egypt, or in various other provinces, follows the profane perversity of Eutyches and does not believe as the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers handed down when they founded the Catholic faith in the city of Nicaea, nor as the other one hundred and fifty venerable bishops who later assembled in this venerable city of Constantinople taught, nor as Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril, bishops of the city of Alexandria and of holy memory, believed [T. 1, 2: “which”]—the Council of Ephesus also followed them in all things, the council presided over by the blessed Cyril, in which the error of Nestorius was expelled [Col. 0176D], and which the venerable Council of Chalcedon recently followed, with the earlier councils of priests agreeing in every respect, taking nothing away from the most sacred creed and adding nothing to it, but condemning the deadly doctrines of Eutyches—let them know that they are heretical Apollinarians. For Eutyches and Dioscorus, with sacrilegious minds, followed the most criminal sect of Apollinaris [Note: [Col. 0176D] From U. In A. and the others, the words “they followed” are absent].

Therefore all who follow the perversity of Apollinaris or Eutyches must know that they are to be punished by those penalties decreed by the constitutions of the former divine emperors against the Apollinarians, by the later enactment of our serenity against the Eutychians, or by this very august law against the same persons.

Accordingly, the Apollinarians—that is, the Eutychians—although their names differ, are joined in the depravity of their heresy; their name is different, but their sacrilege is the same. Whether they are in this venerable city, in various provinces, in the city of Alexandria, or within the diocese of Egypt, if they neither believe what the venerable Fathers mentioned above believed nor communicate with the most reverend Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, who holds the orthodox faith, then, according to the most sacred constitutions of the former divine emperors promulgated concerning the Apollinarians, they shall have no power to make a testament or to establish a final disposition of their property, nor shall they acquire what has been left to them by anyone’s testament. They shall receive nothing from any donation. If anything has been conferred upon them through the generosity of a living person or the will of a dying person, it shall immediately be assigned to our treasury. They themselves may not transfer anything from their property to anyone under the title or right of donation.

They may not create or have bishops, presbyters, or other clerics [Note: [Col. 0177D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G.: “also”]. Both those Eutychians or Apollinarians who dare to confer upon anyone the name of bishop, presbyter, or cleric, and those who attempt to retain the priestly name conferred upon them, must know that they will suffer the penalty of exile together with the loss of their property.

Those who were formerly clerics of the churches of Catholic Rome or monks of the orthodox faith, and who, abandoning the true and orthodox worship of almighty God, followed or shall hereafter follow the heresy of Apollinaris or Eutyches and their abominable doctrines, we order to be held under all the penalties established by the earlier laws against heretics and to be expelled even beyond Roman soil, just as the enactments of the preceding laws sanctioned concerning the Manichaeans [Ae.: “statutes”].

Furthermore, no Apollinarian or Eutychian is to establish churches or monasteries for himself, nor are they to form *parasynaxes* or gatherings by day or night. The agents of that most deadly sect are not to assemble in anyone’s house, estate, monastery, or any other place [Note: [Col. 0177D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “in any other person’s place”].

If they do so, and it is established that the act took place with the owner’s consent, then, after the matter has been confirmed in the judge’s examination, the house or estate in which they assembled shall without delay be joined to our treasury. The monastery, however, shall be assigned to the orthodox church of the city in whose territory it lies.

But if the forbidden *parasynaxes* and gatherings have taken place without the owner’s knowledge, though with the knowledge of the person who collects the rent of the house, or of the tenant, agent, or manager of the estate, then the tenant, agent, manager, or anyone else who has received them into a house, estate, or monastery and allowed unlawful *parasynaxes* and gatherings to be held there shall be punished. If they are of low and degraded status, they are to be publicly beaten with rods [Note: [Col. 0178D] Ae.: “publicly with rods, one hundred [times]”], both as their own punishment and as an example to others. If they are respectable persons, they shall be fined ten pounds of gold and compelled to pay it into our treasury [T. 2: “to discharge it”].

Furthermore, no Apollinarian or Eutychian is to enter any military service except the *cohortal* or frontier forces. If any are found serving outside the *cohortal* or frontier forces, once their military belt has been removed [Ae., T. 1, 2: “once they have been deprived of their belt”], they are to be deprived of the society of respectable men and of the palace, and may reside in no city, village, or district except that in which they were born. If any were born in this venerable city, they are to be expelled both from the most sacred imperial entourage and from every metropolitan city in the province.

No Eutychian or Apollinarian is to be granted the power, publicly or privately, to form groups or circles, to discuss heretical error, or to assert the perversity of the criminal doctrine. Nor may anyone dictate, write, read, or publish anything against the venerable Council of Chalcedon, or produce the writings of others on the same matter. No one may possess books of this kind or dare to preserve the sacrilegious monuments of such writings.

If any are discovered in these crimes, they shall be condemned to perpetual deportation. Those who listen, out of a desire to learn, to persons discussing the accursed heresy shall suffer a loss of ten pounds of gold, to be paid into our treasury. All writings and books of this kind that contain the deadly doctrine of Eutyches—that is, of Apollinaris—shall be burned, so that the traces of criminal perversity may perish, consumed by the flames. For it is just that monstrous sacrilege should be struck by a punishment of equal magnitude.

Palladius, our dearest and most beloved father, your illustrious and magnificent Authority shall, by the customary posting of edicts, make known to all what we have decreed in this most sacred constitution, in this venerable city, in the various provinces, and especially in the city of Alexandria and throughout the entire diocese of Egypt, so that the full severity established against those found guilty may immediately be exercised, and so that the governors of the provinces and their officials, as well as the defenders of the cities, may know it.

If they neglect what we have decreed must be guarded by the most religious sanction of this law, or permit it to be violated through any rashness, they shall be fined ten [Note: [Col. 0178D] The weight or value is perhaps missing. B. R.: “denarii”] pounds of gold and compelled to pay it into the treasury; moreover, they shall suffer the loss of their status.

The provisions that we decreed by our perpetual law concerning pagans, to have equal force throughout the Roman Empire, are also to be most vigorously enforced against those found to celebrate profane rites, the impious worship of images, and sacrileges forbidden to them.

Issued under the date of the Kalends of August at Constantinople, in the consulship of the most divine Valentinian for the eighth time and of the most illustrious Anthemius.

## Formal letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 0179A]

No one who has even a slight knowledge of the Greek language is unaware that the Greek letters also express numbers. Therefore, lest any fraudulent falsification be rashly attempted in the composition of canonical letters—which Latin usage calls *formatae*—this was most beneficially devised and established by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers assembled at Nicaea: that formal letters should observe the following method of calculation or reckoning.

That is, in the reckoning there are to be taken first the Greek letters of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, namely Π, Υ, Α. These letters signify the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one [Col. 0180A]. There is also to be taken the first letter of the apostle Peter, namely Π, which signifies the number eighty; then the first letter of the bishop who writes, the second letter of the bishop to whom it is written, the third letter of the bishop who receives it, the fourth letter of the city from which it is written, and the number of the indiction, whatever it may be at that time.

When all these Greek letters—which, as we have said, express numbers—have thus been brought together, the letter is to contain whatever total has been obtained. The person who receives it must carefully look for this expression. In addition, the letter is separately to include the number ninety-nine, which the Greek letters signify [the source supplies no sign or continuation].

[Col. 0179]

# Councils of Africa (C)

## XII. First Council of Carthage, of fifty bishops

[Note: [Col. 0179D] The number of bishops was missing in the Lucensian Codex; in the other codices it agreed with A.]

[Col. 0179B]

When Gratus, bishop of Carthage, had taken his seat in council together with his colleagues, and those who had come to Carthage from the various African provinces—Felix of Bajana, Fortunatianus of Capsa, Crescentius of Baga, Vindicius of Lacubaca, Abundantius of Hadrumetum, Privatus of Bejeisel, Gaudentius of Turretamallus, Epartius of Sicca, Quietus of Utica, Romulus of Theveste, and the rest whose signatures are included [Note: [Col. 0179D] In Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, the names of the bishops are placed in the ablative case: *Felice, Fortunatiano*, etc.]—the same Gratus, bishop, said:

“Thanks be to almighty God and to Christ Jesus, who has brought an end to evil schisms [Note: [Col. 0179D] T. 1, 2: “to an evil schism”] and has looked upon his Church, so that he might raise all its scattered members into its bosom; who commanded the most religious Emperor Constantius [Note: [Col. 0180D] T. 1, 2: “Constantine”] to undertake the cause of unity and to send the servants of God, Paul and Macarius, as ministers of this holy work.

“By God’s will, therefore, we have been gathered for unity, so that we might celebrate councils throughout the various provinces, and so that the whole province of Africa might come to Carthage on this day for the sake of the council. Therefore, with you considering these matters together with my modest self, let the necessary headings be addressed—those matters concerning which we must, mindful of the divine commands and the teaching of the holy Scriptures, contemplating this time of unity, define each point in such a way that Carthage neither weakens the force of the law nor, in this time of unity, establishes anything excessively harsh.”

### I. That baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated

Therefore, if it pleases you, let us first consider the heading concerning rebaptism [Note: [Col. 0180D] In the codices: *rebaptidiationis*. Elsewhere certain codices customarily write *rebaptizatio*, others *rebaptidiatio*; and in one and the same codex one may properly find different spellings of this word]. I ask your Holiness to express the judgment of your minds: whether a person who has descended into the water, been questioned concerning the Trinity according to the faith of the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, and confessed a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ may be questioned again in the same faith and immersed again in water.

All the bishops said [Note: [Col. 0180D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G.: “They said: ‘God forbid, God forbid’”]:

“God forbid. For we decree rebaptism to be unlawful, and altogether foreign to sincere faith and Catholic discipline.”

### II. Concerning the tombs and honor of the martyrs

Bishop Gratus said:

“Great blessedness has been granted by God the Father through Christ the Lord to our time, so that it may be permitted to impress ecclesiastical discipline upon religious minds, so that hearers, receiving the right rule, may both please God and obtain the rewards of good merits, and so that God may be honored in them in all things and for all things.

“The necessary heading concerning rebaptism has been discussed, in which the rage of the schismatics lay concealed to a greater degree, and with moderation having been applied, the force and authority of the law have been preserved. I strive to impress this upon your very wise minds—although your prudence is instructed and taught by God, and deserves to receive abundant gifts from above in peace and unity. Nevertheless, I too, as one of you and as one who shares an equal concern with you for ecclesiastical order, shall take care to make this point known.

“Let no profane person dishonor the dignity of the martyrs. Nor should they designate as martyrs the bodies that have merely been entrusted to burial out of ecclesiastical mercy [Col. 0181A], bodies of those who have been cast down by madness or separated by some other kind of sin, without regard to the appropriate reason or proper time at which memorials of the martyrs are celebrated. If anyone, to the injury of the martyrs, joins madmen to their glory, it is decreed that, if they are laymen, they be brought to repentance; but if they are clerics, they are, after admonition [Note: [Col. 0181D] From Ae., T. 2, U., G. In A. and the others: “after communion”] and investigation, to be deprived of their honor.”

All said:

“Your Holiness has rightly decreed this; this too has been established in the individual councils.”

### III. That clerics or women devoted to religious observance may not live with unrelated men or women
Gratus, the bishop, said: “And especially this, if it seems good to your charity, must be guarded against: that royal providence should, as much as it ought and can, fully prearrange the pastor’s care, so that no men or women abstaining from carnal affection may be permitted to live together indiscriminately with outsiders. For opportunities for sins must be cut off, and every suspicion removed, by which the devil’s cunning habitually ensnares unwary or ignorant souls under the pretext of charity and affection. Therefore, no man or woman devoted to holiness and virginity should, for the blasphemy of the Church, if it pleases you, live at all in the same house.”

All said: “Those who do not wish to marry and choose the better part of chastity must avoid not only living together but also having anyone come to them. Thus the law commands, and your holiness commends it; this also has been established by us in each of the councils.”

[Note: U., G.: “thus confirmed or established by us.”]

Gratus, the bishop, said: “Thus persuasion sometimes keeps the prudent away from sins, whereas fear of this kind ought to restrain the imprudent when they reject sound counsel and a saving command. Therefore, if they are laypeople, after admonition, if they despise it, let them be excluded from communion; if they are clerics, let them be deprived of their rank.”

All said: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

## IV. That outsiders should not live with widowers or widows

Gratus, the bishop, said: “Although there are innumerable matters prescribed by law that advance discipline, and each one of us, through continual discussion and frequent admonition, will be able to make known to the peoples every individual matter that promotes discipline, nevertheless some of these must be brought forward by us and established in council on account of the blasphemy involved. If it seems good to you, let the same rule and judgment also apply to those who live with widowers and are related to them by no family bond.”

All said: “The same law and judgment shall remain concerning widowers and widows.”

## 117 V. That clerics and laypeople should not be ordained from another church

Privatus, bishop of Bejeisela, said: “I suggest to your holiness that you establish that no one should receive a cleric from another bishop without letters from his own bishop, or retain him with himself; nor should a layman seize someone from another’s flock and ordain him without the knowledge of the bishop whose flock he belongs to.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “Observance of this rule preserves peace. I also remember that the most holy Council of Sardica established similarly that no one should seize for himself a man belonging to another’s flock. But if ordination should happen to be necessary, so that a suitable man from a neighboring place is needed, let him ask his colleague and obtain his consent.”

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1, U., G.: “obtain permission.”]

## VI. That clerics should not undertake secular affairs or household management

Nicasius, bishop of Culusis, said: “I believe that my suggestion will please your holiness, and that you will disapprove of those who serve God and have devoted themselves to the clergy taking up the affairs, administration, or management of households.”

[Note: In the manuscripts: “should not take up.”]

Gratus, the bishop, said: “The statutes of the apostles also say: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business.’ Therefore, either let clerics remain without the management of households, or let managers remain without clerical office.”

All said: “Let us observe this.”

## VII. That clerics or laypeople should not communicate in another’s church without letters from their own bishop

Cassianus, bishop of Usula, said: “Let your dignity establish that no cleric or layperson should communicate in another’s congregation without letters from his own bishop.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “Unless this is observed, communion will become passive. For if someone is received with letters, harmony is preserved among the bishops, so that no cunning person, fleeing the communion of one bishop, may secretly approach another.”

[Note: U.: “and no one [lacuna] will approach.”]

All said: “You provide for everyone, caring for both clergy and laypeople.”

[Note: This reading is taken from the remaining manuscripts. In A.: “caring for clerics and layperson.”]

## VIII. That those involved in other people’s business should not be ordained clerics unless they have first rendered an account

Magnus, bishop of Astuaga, said: “What does your affection think? Should managers and agents, and also guardians or curators of orphans, be ordained?”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “If, after all their affairs have been laid down and their accounts rendered, their conduct of life has been found satisfactory in every respect, they should be honored with the dignity of the clergy, and with praise, if they are sought for it. For if someone has been ordained without consideration before being freed from business or official responsibilities, the Church is disgraced.”

[Note: From U.; in A. and the remaining manuscripts: “ratiocinia si actus” (“accounts, if [their] conduct”); the added *si* therefore appears redundant.]

All said: “Your holiness has established everything rightly. Therefore, what is your judgment is also ours.”

## IX. That laypeople should not appoint clerics as their managers or accountants

[Col. 0182D]

Mettun, bishop of Cannæ,

[Note: Aem.: “Mettucanensis.” T. 2: “Metun canonensis.” U., G.: “Met Tuncanensis.”]

said: “It has rightly been established that those burdened with other people’s business should not be ordained. Nevertheless, if they have been released, they ought to give thanks and refrain from injuring clerics; nor should they themselves or their masters be permitted to choose our clerics as storekeepers or accountants.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “No one doubts that all masters, managers, and whoever else is in charge, when they hear the council’s most wholesome statutes and understand that provision has been made for them rather than obstruction, will restrain their own injury against our clerics. But if they should think that our clerics may be harassed in violation of the imperial constitution, ecclesiastical defense will not be lacking, and public shame will be avenged.”

All said: “Such salutary provisions ought to have been enacted by so great a council.”

## X. That no bishop should usurp the congregations or boundaries of another bishop

Felix, bishop of Baga, said: “No one ought to injure a colleague. For many overstep their own congregations and usurp those of others against their will.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “No one doubts that the desire for avarice is the root of all evils.”

[Note: U., A.: “avarice and desire.”]

[Note: From Aem. In A. and the remaining manuscripts: “who does not doubt?”]

“Therefore, it must be prohibited that anyone usurp another’s boundaries or overstep his fellow bishop and usurp another’s congregations without his request, because all the other evils arise from this.”

All said: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

## XI. Concerning contumacious clerics, and the number of judges who are to hear a bishop, presbyter, or deacon

Elpidephorus,

[Note: Aem.: “Elipidephorus.”]

bishop of Cuicul, said: “Let your holiness establish that clerics who are proud or contumacious be restrained, and that those who are junior, if they inflict injuries on their seniors, should fear discipline.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “It is clear that the one who condemns humility is not of God but of the devil, who is the inventor and prince of pride. Therefore, if anyone proves haughty or insulting toward an elder, or has some case to bring, let him be heard by three neighboring bishops if the person accused is a deacon; by six if he is a presbyter; and by twelve fellow priests if he is a bishop.”
