All the bishops said: “Contumacy must be subdued and pride broken in all things; but cases should be heard according to the established number, proportionate to the persons involved.”

## XII. That agreements made between bishops should be observed

Antigonus,

[Note: T. 2, U.: “Antigonius.”]

bishop of Maginus,

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1: “Magirensis.” U.: “Margiensis.”]

said: “I am suffering a grave injury, and I believe that your holiness grieves over my humiliation and counts it as a common injury.”

[Note: From the remaining manuscripts except A., in which the words “and counts it as a common injury” are absent.]

“When Optantius presented himself, he had an agreement with me, and we divided the congregations between us. Our signatures and written agreements are held; yet, contrary to this agreement, he goes around the congregations assigned to me and whispers to the peoples that they should call him ‘Father’ and me ‘stepfather.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “This deed is grievous, since by it he incites the minds of ignorant peoples against discipline, against evangelical tradition, and against the settlements of peace. For if anyone thought he could do such a thing with impunity, no one would ever have sinned against a brother. Therefore, either let agreements that have been made retain their force, or, if he does not restrain himself when summoned, let him experience ecclesiastical discipline.”

All said: “Let peace be preserved; let agreements be observed.”

## XIII. That clerics should not lend at interest

Abundantius, bishop of Hadrumetum, said: “It was established in our council that clerics may not lend at interest. Let what your holiness and this council think also be set forth in the present decision.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “This is a new proposal. Matters that are obscure or concealed under a general category will receive their form when examined by us. But concerning matters on which divine Scripture has spoken most plainly, judgment is not to be pronounced; rather, its command is to be carried out. Therefore, what is found among laypeople must be condemned in advance all the more strongly among clerics.”

All said: “No one acts against the prophets or against the Gospels without danger.”

## XIV. That laypeople who despise the canons should be excommunicated and clerics deprived of their rank

Gratus, the bishop, said: “In accordance with the statutes of the council and the judgment of my mediocrity, it pleases me to bring all matters to a conclusion. Let all the designated and arranged headings retain their judgments. Surely you remember that rebaptization has been condemned by many councils of our fathers and by tradition, and that its impiety must be punished. I believe that these matters have also now received their settlement in our council.

“We must observe the remaining matters, whether deeds or words, included above or found written in other councils in accordance with the law. But if anyone oversteps or violates the statutes, or considers them worthless, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his rank.”

All said: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

Gratus, the bishop, said: “It remains now for you to confirm by your own subscription the decisions of all of us that have been written with your agreement.”

All said: “The writings of this council bear witness that we have agreed, and our agreement will be declared by our subscription.”

And they subscribed.

# Thirteenth Council of Carthage, the Second, of Sixty-One Bishops, in the Era 428, on the Sixteenth Day before the Kalends of July

[Col. 0183]

[Col. 0183D] In the consulship of the most glorious emperor Valentinian Augustus for the fourth time and of the most illustrious man Neoterius, at Carthage, in the Basilica Perpetua Restituta, when Geneclius the bishop had taken his seat together with Victor of Abdirita, another Victor of Puppiana, and his other fellow bishops from the various provinces.

[Note: In A. the word “various” is absent; it is supplied from the remaining manuscripts.]

## 121 I. That the Trinity should both be believed and preached

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “I give thanks to almighty God, who permitted you, in accordance with the common council held in the past and according to the tenor of my letter of petition, to come to Carthage for the faith and ecclesiastical welfare—not all of you, but since charity persuades us all, those who are absent in body may nevertheless be seen to be joined with us in spirit.”

[Note: U.: “since the entire bond of charity persuades us.”]

“Therefore, by God’s favor, since you are present, the ecclesiastical faith handed down through us must first be confessed in this glorious assembly by a common profession. Then the ecclesiastical order must be established with the agreement of each and the consent of all, to strengthen the minds of our recently promoted brothers and fellow bishops concerning the matters to be proposed, which we have received from our fathers as firmly established.

“Thus, the Trinity which we retain as consecrated in our minds—the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which is known to have no difference—just as we have learned,

[Note: U.: “as we are learning.”]

so must we instruct God’s peoples.”

All the bishops said: “We have plainly received it thus; we hold it thus; we teach it thus, following the apostolic faith.”

## II. That chastity should be observed by Levites and priests

Epigonius, bishop of the regions of Bulla,

[Note: T. 2: “of the regions of Hulla.”]

said: “When the previous council was treating of continence and chastity, these three ranks, joined by a certain bond of chastity through their consecrations—I mean the bishop, presbyter, and deacon—should be instructed through fuller discussion to preserve purity.”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “As was said above, it is fitting that the holy bishops and priests of God, as well as the Levites and those who serve the divine mysteries, should be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain from the Lord what they ask, and that we too may observe what the apostles taught and antiquity itself preserved.”

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “so that.”]

All the bishops said: “It pleases everyone that the bishop, presbyter, and deacon, guardians of purity, should also abstain from wives, so that purity may be preserved in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

## III. That chrism, the consecration of girls, and the reconciliation of penitents should not be performed by presbyters

Numidius, bishop of Maxula, said: “If your holiness commands it, I offer this suggestion, for I remember that previous councils established that chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and likewise the consecration of girls should not be performed by presbyters. But if anyone should arise who does this, what should be established concerning him?”

Geneclius, the bishop,

[Note: U.: “the bishop said to everyone.”]

said: “Your dignity has heard the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Numidius. What do you say about these matters?”

All the bishops said: “Let the making of chrism and the consecration of girls not be performed by presbyters; and let it be permitted to no presbyter to reconcile anyone at a public Mass. This pleases everyone.”

## IV. That a presbyter should reconcile a penitent when ordered by his bishop

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled at the divine altars, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter must of course consult the bishop and, according to his command, reconcile the person in danger. This matter ought to be strengthened by a salutary decision.”

All the bishops said: “What your holiness has deemed it necessary to teach us pleases everyone.”

## V. That a diocese which has never had a bishop should not have one

Felix, bishop of Selemsela, said: “If this also pleases your holiness, I suggest that dioceses which have never had bishops should not have one, whereas a diocese which once had one should retain its own. If, with time and the growth of faith, the people of God should multiply and desire to have their own ruler, let it have a bishop with the consent, naturally, of the one in whose authority the diocese has been constituted. According to this proposal,

[Note: T. 2: “according to this proposition.”]

it is for your holiness to determine what should be done.”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “If the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Felix pleases you, let it be confirmed by all.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

## VI. That those involved in crimes should not accuse clerics

Numidius, bishop of Maxula, said: “Furthermore, there are very many people of poor conduct who think that elders or bishops should be dragged indiscriminately and recklessly into accusations. Should such persons be so readily admitted against the apostolic rule, or not?”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “Does it therefore please your charity that one who is entangled in some crimes should have no voice to accuse an elder?”

All the bishops said: “If he is a criminal, it pleases everyone that he should not be admitted.”

## VII. That whoever receives another’s excommunicate should be excommunicated

Felix, bishop of Selemsela, said: “I also offer this suggestion to your holiness: concerning those who are expelled from the Church for their crimes and dare either to go to the imperial court, or rush to the public courts, or perhaps attempt to approach the thresholds of the Catholic Church—what is your judgment concerning any bishop or cleric of any congregation who receives them?”

Epigonius, bishop of the regions of Bulla, said: “If any bishop who remains in Catholic communion should approach such a person with empty flatteries, let him know that he has been corrupted together with those rejected persons and has passed into their lot.”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “Therefore our brothers and fellow bishops rightly suggest that, if those expelled from the Church because of their crimes are received into communion by any bishop or cleric, that person too should be held liable to the same crime as they are.”

All the bishops said: “This pleases everyone.”

## VIII. That an excommunicated presbyter who presumes to offer sacrifice should be anathematized

Felix, bishop of Selemsela, said: “Nor should this be omitted: if some presbyter, corrected or excommunicated by his bishop, should, inflated with arrogance or pride, think that sacrifices ought to be offered to God separately, or believe that another altar should be set up,

[Note: Aem.: “some other altar.”]

and that action should be taken contrary to ecclesiastical faith and discipline, he must not go unpunished.”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “What our brother Felix has set forth is necessary for ecclesiastical discipline and accords with the faith. Therefore, state what seems good to your charity concerning it.”

All the bishops said: “If a presbyter has been excommunicated or corrected by his superior, he must, of course, bring his complaint before neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his own bishop. But if he does not do this and, inflated—God forbid—with pride, decides to separate himself from communion with his bishop and, making a schism with certain others, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be regarded as anathema, having lost his position. Moreover, let him be driven far from the city in which he has been, so that he may not deceive either the ignorant or those living simply by serpent-like fraud.

“According to the Apostle: ‘There is one Church, one faith, one baptism.’ But if he has a just complaint against his bishop, it must be investigated.”

## IX. That if a presbyter celebrates the *agenda*—that is, Mass—without consulting the bishop, he should be deprived of his rank

[Note: U.: “celebrates the *agenda*, that is, celebrates Mass.”]

Numidius, bishop of Maxula, said: “In certain places there are presbyters who, either simply through ignorance or boldly through dissimulation, celebrate the *agenda* in many homes while the bishop is present and without consulting him. Your holiness recognizes that this is contrary to discipline and improper.”

[Note: U.: “it is recognized; your holiness, what does this signify here?”]

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “Let our brothers and fellow bishops not delay in responding suitably to your worthy suggestion.”

All the bishops said: “Any presbyter who wishes to celebrate the *agenda* in any place without consulting the bishop acts against his own dignity.”

## X. How many should judge a priest and a Levite

Felix, bishop of Selemsela, said: “I also add this, according to the statutes of the ancient councils: if any bishop—which we do not wish—should incur some fault and be under such great necessity that many cannot be assembled, so that he does not remain in his offense, let a bishop be heard by twelve bishops, a presbyter by six bishops, and a deacon by three, together with his own bishop.”

[Note: T. 1, 2: “we wish this to happen.”]

[Note: B. R., T. 1, 2: “many bishops cannot be assembled, so that …”]

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “What does your holiness say to this?”

[Col. 0187D]

All the bishops said: “It is right that we should preserve the statutes of the ancient councils.”

## XI. That no one should presume to exercise another’s parish

[Note: T. 1: “should presume to exercise another’s parish.”]

[Col. 0188A]

Victor, bishop of Abdiritana,

[Note: In all the manuscripts: “Abziritanus,” although earlier they had written “Abdiritanus.”]

said: “Ecclesiastical discipline must be strengthened, so that no bishop may attempt, through his importunity, to harass another’s congregation or diocese, or try to exceed the boundaries assigned to him. How should anyone who attempts this be restrained?”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “The holy law prohibits it, and truth itself does not permit anyone to covet what belongs to another. Therefore, let each of you signify by his own voice what pleases you all.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us that, according to the authority of the divine law, none of us should cross another’s boundaries.”

## 125 XII. That no bishop should be ordained without consulting the metropolitan

[Note: U., G.: “without consulting the metropolitan.”]

Numidius, bishop of Maxula, said: “Certain bishops, by a kind of usurpation, think that, after disregarding the primate of their own province, they may ordain a bishop at the people’s request, without letters proceeding from the chief see and without having received authority.”

[Note: B. R., T. 1, 2: “without letters proceeding from it.”]

“What does your holiness establish concerning this?”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “Since the honor that ought to be preserved for each person is common to all, it is for you, brothers, to pronounce judgment on this matter.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases everyone that no one should so readily presume, without consulting the primate of any province, to ordain a bishop anywhere, even with many others present, without his command, as has been said. But if necessity should arise, three bishops, wherever they may be, must ordain with the primate’s command.”

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “must ordain the bishop.”]

## 126 XIII. That a bishop who acts against his profession made in council should be deposed

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “Does it therefore please everyone that all the matters established by this most glorious assembly should be observed?”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us; let them be observed by all.”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “If—which we do not suppose—they are violated by anyone, what do you establish?”

All the bishops said: “Whoever acts against his own profession or subscription has himself separated from this assembly.”

Geneclius, the bishop, said: “I give thanks that, by the favor of our God, we have resolved by salutary counsel that all things concerning the state of the Catholic Church must be observed. Therefore, what has been said by all must be strengthened by our own subscription.”

[Col. 0188D]

All the bishops said: “Let it be done; let it be done.”

And they subscribed.

# Fourteenth Council of Carthage, the Third, Held by Forty-Seven Bishops

[Note: Aem.: “forty-eight in number.”]

Era 436

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1, 2: “Era 435.”]

In the consulship of the most illustrious men Caesarius and Atticus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0189]

[Col. 0189A] At Carthage, in the secretariat of the restored basilica, when Aurelius the bishop had taken his seat together with his fellow bishops, with deacons also standing by, the following matters were established and defined in the present council.

## I. That the provincial bishops should inquire of their primate concerning Easter

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “fellow-provincial bishops.”]

At the outset, therefore, it was decided, because of the error that often tends to arise, that all the bishops of the African provinces should take care to receive from the Church of Carthage the observance of the day of Easter.

## II. That a council should be held every year

Likewise, it was decided that, because of ecclesiastical matters which often grow old to the destruction of the congregations, a council should be convened every year. To it, all the provinces that have chief sees should send from their own councils two bishops as legates, or as many as they choose,

[Col. 0189B]

so that they may be less subject to envy and less burdensome in expense to their hosts, and so that full authority may be possible in the assembled gathering. From Tripoli, however, one bishop should come because of the scarcity of bishops there.

[Note: G.: “one bishop or cleric should come.”]

## III. That a bishop should know the canons before he is ordained

Likewise, it was decided that, before bishops or clerics are ordained, the decrees of the councils should first be impressed upon their ears by those ordaining them, so that they will not have cause to regret having done anything contrary to the council’s statutes.

## IV. That Levites and virgins should not be consecrated before the age of twenty-five

Likewise, it was decided that before twenty-five years of age neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated, and that readers should not greet the people.

## V. That the sacrament should not be given to catechumens

Likewise, it was decided that even during the most solemn days of Easter the sacrament should not be given to catechumens, except the customary salt; for if the faithful do not change the sacraments during those days, neither ought catechumens to change them.

## VI. That baptism or the Eucharist should not be given to the dead

Likewise, it was decided that the Eucharist should not be given to the bodies of the dead. For the Lord said: “Take and eat”; corpses, however, can neither take nor eat. Furthermore, care must be taken lest the weakness of the brothers should even come to believe that the dead can be baptized, when it has observed that the Eucharist cannot be given to them.

## VII. If a bishop is accused, where and within what period his case should be examined

[Col. 0189D]

Aurelius, the bishop, said: “Whenever a bishop is accused, the accuser shall bring the case before the primates of that province, and the person against whom the charge is made shall not be suspended from communion unless, summoned by letters from the chief see to state his case, he fails to appear on the appointed day—that is, within the period of one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letters.

“But if he proves some genuine causes of necessity by which it is clear that he could not appear, he shall have the full opportunity to state his case within another month. Nevertheless, after the second month he shall not communicate for as long as he remains unpurged.

“But if he is unwilling to appear even at the universal annual council, so that his case may be settled there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation against himself. During the period in which he does not communicate, he shall not communicate even in his own church or parish.

“As for his accuser, if he has never been absent on the days appointed for stating the case, he shall not be removed from communion. But if he has at any time been absent, withdrawing himself, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself shall be removed from communion. Even so, he shall not be deprived of the opportunity to pursue the case if he proves that he did not refuse to appear on the appointed day but was unable to do so.

“It was also decided that, once he has begun to act before the judgment of the bishops, if the accuser is a culpable person, he should not be admitted to bring an accusation, unless he wishes to assert his own causes, though not ecclesiastical ones.”

## VIII. Concerning presbyters and deacons: how many bishops should hear them

But if presbyters or deacons are accused, their own bishop, joined by a legitimate number of colleagues from neighboring places, shall investigate their case together with them: six bishops in the case of a presbyter and three in the case of a deacon. The same procedure shall be observed concerning the days allowed, delays, removal from communion, and examination of the persons of the accusers and the accused.

But the cases of the remaining clerics may be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.

## IX. That clerics should not appeal to public courts

Likewise, it was decided that if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric, when a charge has been brought against him in the Church or a civil case has been initiated, should abandon ecclesiastical judgment and wish to clear himself before public courts, he shall lose his position even if a judgment has been issued in his favor. This applies in a criminal action; in a civil case, he shall lose what he has won if he prefers to retain his position.

For when the authority of the whole Church is open to him everywhere for the selection of judges, he judges himself unworthy of fellowship with the Church if, by thinking ill of the universal Church’s judgment, he seeks help from a secular judgment, when the Apostle even commands that the cases of private Christians be brought before the Church and decided there.

## X. If someone appeals from one set of ecclesiastical judges to another, the earlier judges should not be disadvantaged if a different judgment is issued

[Col. 0191A]

This also was decided: if an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, it should not harm those whose judgment has been set aside if they cannot be convicted of having judged with an inimical intention or of having been corrupted by some desire or favor. But if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, it shall not be permitted to appeal even from a smaller number than the number established.

## XI. That the children of clerics should not attend spectacles

The sons of priests or clerics should not put on secular spectacles, nor should they watch them, since all laypeople are also prohibited from watching them. For this has always been forbidden to all Christians, so that they should not go where there are blasphemies.

## XII. That the children of clerics should not marry unbelievers

Likewise, it was decided that the sons or daughters of bishops or of any clerics should not be joined in marriage to Gentiles, heretics, or schismatics.

## XIII. That clerics should give nothing from their possessions to unbelievers

Bishops or clerics should not confer anything from their possessions by donation upon those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are blood relatives.

## XIV. That clerics should not allow their children to leave their authority unless their age and conduct have been tested

Bishops or clerics should not allow their children to leave their authority through emancipation unless they are assured concerning their conduct and age, so that the children may already be capable of bearing responsibility for their own offenses.

## XV. That clerics should not be tenants or business agents

Likewise, it was decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or clerics should not be tenants or agents of private persons, nor should they seek their livelihood through any shameful or dishonorable business, because they ought to heed the statement: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business.”

## XVI. That no cleric should be a usurer

No cleric should receive more than what he has lent to anyone: if he lent money, let him receive money; if a commodity, a commodity; let him receive as much as he gave; and whatever else he gave, let him receive only as much as he gave.

## 130 XVII. That outsider women should not live with clerics

[Col. 0191D]

Outsider women should not live with clerics at all, except mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, sisters, and the daughters of brothers or sisters; and except any women who, because of household necessity, were already living with them before they were ordained; or women whom their sons married after their parents had been ordained; or, where there are slaves who have no women in the household whom they can marry, women whom necessity requires them to bring from elsewhere.

## XVIII. That clerics should not be ordained unless all those living with them are faithful

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons should not be ordained until they have made all those who are in their household Catholic Christians.

## XIX. That when clerics reach puberty they should profess either marriage or chastity

[Col. 0192A]

It was decided that readers, when they reach the age of puberty, should be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.

## XX. That no bishop should usurp another’s congregations

It was decided that no bishop should usurp another’s congregations, nor should any bishop overstep into the diocese of his colleague.

[Note: Aem., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “into the diocese of his colleague.”]

## XXI. That no bishop should dare to retain or ordain another’s cleric

No one should dare to retain or promote in the church entrusted to him a cleric belonging to another bishop, unless that bishop grants permission. The designation “clerics” also includes readers, psalmists, and doorkeepers.

## XXII. That no one should be ordained a cleric unless his life has been found worthy

[Col. 0192B]

No one should be ordained a cleric unless he has been approved either by examination by the bishops or by the testimony of the people.

## XXIII. Concerning prayers and intercessions

No one should name the Father in place of the Son or the Son in place of the Father in prayers; and whenever one stands at the altar, the prayer should always be directed to the Father. Whoever copies prayers for himself from elsewhere should not use them unless he has first discussed them with the brothers who are teachers.

## 131 XXIV. That bread and the cup should be offered in the sacrifice

[Note: U.: “in the sacrament.”]

In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing more should be offered than the Lord himself handed down: that is, bread and wine mixed with water.

[Note: B. R.: “thoroughly mixed with water.”]

Nor should anything more be offered in the first fruits than what comes from grapes and grain.

## XXV. That clerics or those practicing continence should not visit virgins or widows alone

Clerics or those practicing continence should not visit widows or virgins except by order or permission of bishops or presbyters. They should not do so alone, but with fellow clerics or with those whom the bishop or presbyter has ordered to accompany them. Nor should bishops or presbyters themselves visit such women alone, but only where either clerics are present or certain respected Christians are present.

## XXVI. That the bishop of the chief see should not be called chief of the priests

The bishop of the chief see should not be called “chief of the priests,” “high priest,” or anything of this sort,

[Col. 0192D]

but only “bishop of the chief see.”

[Note: U., G.: “only the bishop of the chief see.”]

## XXVII. That clerics should not enter taverns

Clerics should not enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking, except when necessity during a journey requires it.

## XXVIII. That a bishop should not travel far without a formal letter from the metropolitan
The bishops should not travel overseas unless they have consulted the bishop of the primatial see of their respective province, so that they may especially receive from him a credential letter or letter of recommendation.

**XXIX. That the Mass be celebrated by fasting persons.**

That the sacraments of the altar be celebrated only by fasting persons; for if a commendation is to be made in the afternoon [Col. 0193A] [In the codices, *promeridiano*, “afternoon”], for some of the dead, whether bishops or others, it shall be done with prayers alone, if those who are to perform it are found already to have eaten.

**XXX. That no one hold a feast in the church.**

That no bishops or clerics hold banquets in the church, unless perhaps travelers, because of the necessity of lodging, refresh themselves there; the people, too, should be prohibited as far as possible from such banquets. 132

**XXXI. That a measure of penance be assigned to penitents according to their sin.**

That for penitents the bishops, according to the different kinds of sins, determine the periods of penance.

**XXXII. That a presbyter not reconcile a penitent without the bishop’s command or in his absence.**

That a presbyter not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless the bishop’s absence makes it necessary; but if the crime of any penitent is public and notorious and has disturbed the whole Church, hands shall be laid upon him before the apse [Note: [Col. 0193D] In A. and E. 3 there is a marginal note: “that is, the altar.”].

**XXXIII. Concerning the safeguarding of consecrated virgins.**

That if consecrated virgins are deprived of the parents by whom they were being guarded, they shall, through the provision of the bishop—or, when the bishop is absent, of the presbyter—be entrusted to a monastery [Note: [Col. 0193D] From U. In A. and the others: “instead of a monastery.”] of virgins or to more respectable women, so that, living together, they may guard one another and not, by wandering about indiscriminately, damage the Church’s reputation.

**XXXIV. Concerning the baptism of sick persons who can no longer speak.**

That the sick, if they cannot answer on their own behalf, shall be baptized when their relatives have given testimony to their will [Col. 0193C] [Note: [Col. 0194D] U.: “when their relatives, at their own risk, have given testimony to their wishes, they shall be baptized.”].

**XXXV. That reconciliation not be denied to converted apostates and actors.**

That grace or reconciliation not be denied to actors, stage performers, and other persons of this kind, or to apostates who have converted or returned to God.

**XXXVI. That the presbyter not prepare the chrism.**

That the presbyter, without consulting the bishop, not consecrate virgins; but that he never prepare the chrism.

**XXXVII. That clerics not remain in another city without necessity.**

That clerics not remain in another city unless the bishop of the place or the presbyters of the places have judged their reasons just.

**XXXVIII. That translations of bishops may not take place.**

133 [Col. 0193D]

We report this matter as having been entrusted to us, and as having also apparently been established in the full council at Capua: that rebaptisms, reordinations, or translations of bishops may not take place. For Crisconius, bishop of Villaregius, abandoned his own people and seized the church of Tubunium [T., 2: *Tugunium*]; although he has now been admonished according to what had been established, he has scorned to leave the same people whom he had seized. We have indeed heard that the judgments pronounced against this man were confirmed; but we ask, according to what has been entrusted to us, that you deign to give us assurance that, when necessity itself compels it, we may be free to approach the governor of the province against him, in accordance with the statutes of the most glorious emperors, so that the man who refused to heed the mild admonition of your holiness and to correct his unlawful conduct may immediately be excluded by judicial authority.

Bishop Aurelius said: “If the discipline’s procedure is preserved, the desire will not be considered excessive if, after being courteously summoned by your charity, he refuses to withdraw, since he will have been summoned because of his contempt and defiance, and also by judicial authority.”

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “Does this therefore please everyone?”

All the bishops said: “It is just; it pleases us.”

**XXXIX. That two bishops not presume to ordain a bishop.**

[Col. 0194B]

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “This, too, has been entrusted to us: because recently two of our brothers in Numidia presumed to ordain a bishop, you should decree that ordinations be celebrated only by twelve bishops.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “The ancient procedure shall be preserved, so that no fewer than three bishops who have been appointed by the metropolitan shall suffice to ordain a bishop. This is because in Tripoli and perhaps in Arzuge [T. 2: *Arzure*] barbarian peoples appear to lie between the churches; and in Tripoli, as is reported [Ae.: ‘as is said’], there are only five bishops, and perhaps two of that number may be occupied by some necessity. It is difficult for all of any given number to be able to attend. Should this itself be allowed to impede the usefulness of the Church? For in this Church, to which your holiness has deigned to assemble, we frequently, almost every Sunday, have persons to be ordained. Shall I often be able to summon twelve or ten bishops, or not many fewer? It is easy for me to add two of my neighbors to my own small number. 134 Therefore your charity sees with me that this cannot be observed.”

**XL. That when a bishop is being elected and has opponents, five priests should assemble.**

And this must be established: whenever we assemble to elect a bishop, if some opposition arises—for such things have occurred among us—those responsible should not presume to clear the person to be ordained with only the three already mentioned, but two or three more should be requested, bringing the number up to that stated above. In the same people over whom he is to be ordained, the persons of the opponents should first be examined, and finally the matters brought forward against him should also be investigated. When he has been cleared in the presence of the public, only then shall he be ordained. If this accords with the mind of your holiness, let it be confirmed by your gracious response.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us sufficiently.”

**XLI. That the bishops who assemble each year for council should also be informed by their primate concerning the Paschal solemnity.**

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “Since it is known that certain matters have been discussed concerning the council, we add that we have also been instructed concerning the day of Easter: we are always to be informed by the Church of Carthage, as was stated above, and not within too short a period of time.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “If it seems good to your holiness—for we remember that we promised above that we would assemble each year for discussion—then, when we have gathered together, the holy day of Easter will be announced through the envoys who have attended the council.”

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “For the present assembly, we ask that you deign to inform our province by letter concerning this day.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “It must be done.”

**XLII. That a people which has always been subject to a diocese should not receive another bishop.**

Bishop Epigonius said: “It has been established by many councils, by an assembly of priests, that peoples held within dioceses by bishops, which have never had bishops of their own, should receive their own leaders—that is, bishops—only with the consent of the bishop under whom they are held. But because some, after attaining a kind of domination, shun communion with their brothers, or, when they have been corrupted, claim domination for themselves as though in a tyrannical fortress, many proud and foolish presbyters raise their necks against their bishops, either winning the people over by banquets or, at any rate, by wicked persuasion, so that they wish to have the same men unlawfully installed as their leaders—I remember, religious brother Aurelius, the notable intention of your mind in this matter, since you have often suppressed such attempts by refusing to attend to such petitioners—I say this because of their evil [Col. 0195C] thoughts and perversely contrived consultations: the people that has always been subject to a diocese and has never had a bishop of its own ought not to receive a leader. Therefore, if this statement of mine pleases the entire holy assembly, let it be confirmed.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “Our brothers and fellow priests, I do not oppose your proposal; rather, I profess that I have done this and will continue to do it.”

**XLIII. That those who disdain their own people and refuse to come to council should lose both their people and their honor.**

With regard to those who should be united not only with the Church of Carthage but with the entire fellowship of priests: there are many who conspire with their own peoples, whom they deceive, as has been said, by tickling their ears, being flattering in order to seduce them, men of vicious life, or at any rate puffed up and separated from this fellowship. They think they should remain attached to their own people, and sometimes, when summoned, refuse to come to council, perhaps fearing that their crimes will be exposed. I say, if it pleases you, that in their case not only should the dioceses not be preserved for them, but every effort should also be made to have them rejected by public authority from their own Church, which has wrongly favored them [B. R., T. 1: “has been”], and removed from the principal sees themselves. For the one who clings to all his brothers and to the entire council ought to possess not only his own see in full right but also the dioceses; but those who think their own peoples sufficient for them, scorning brotherly love, should lose not only the dioceses but, as I have said, even their own sees through public authority, as rebels.”

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “Your holiness’s supreme prudence has accorded with the minds of each of us, and I think that what you have deigned to propose should be strengthened by the response of all.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us, it pleases us.”

**XLIV. That no bishop should presume to claim another’s cleric.**

Bishop Epigonius said: “It has been established in many councils, and must now also be confirmed by your wisdom, most blessed brothers, that no bishop should seize for himself another’s cleric against the will of the bishop to whom the cleric belongs. I speak of Julianus, who is ungrateful for the benefits of God bestowed upon him through my insignificance and has proved so reckless and audacious that he seized, without consulting me, a man whom I baptized and who, as a boy, had been entrusted to me by that same Julianus; a man whom I nourished and raised for many years; a man whom, as I have said, I baptized in my Church through the ministry of my poverty; and who had begun to serve as a lector in my diocese of Appalius—indeed, he had read there for nearly two years. With what contempt for my humility I do not know, that same Julianus seized him, claiming that he had baptized him as though he were a citizen of his own place, Babtizaritanus [Note: [Col. 0195D] B. R., T. 1, 2, G., *Vazaritanus*]. He also ordained him deacon. Let it be clear, most blessed brothers, whether such license is permitted to us: unless so imprudent a man is restrained, he must not intrude himself into anyone’s communion.”

Bishop Numidius said: “If Julianus appears to have done this without requesting or consulting your dignity, we all judge that it was done unjustly or unworthily [Note: [Col. 0196D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2: ‘and improperly’]. Therefore, unless Julianus corrects his error and, with satisfaction, returns to your people the same cleric whom he had dared to ordain, since he has acted against the statutes of the council, he shall, separated from us because of his defiance, receive judgment.”

Bishop Epigonius said: “Our father in age, most senior in promotion, the praiseworthy man, our brother and colleague Victor, wishes this petition to be made general for all.”

**XLV. That a bishop who has more clerics should give one to a bishop who requests one for ordination.**

Bishop Aurelius said: “Hear my speech, brothers. It sometimes happens that churches lacking leaders, whether presbyters or bishops, make requests; nevertheless, mindful of the statutes, I follow this procedure: I approach the bishop concerned and impress upon him that his cleric is being requested by some church. At present they perhaps did not resist, but lest they ever resist, when I have been asked in this matter—as you know that I bear responsibility for many churches and for those who are to be ordained—it is just that I approach any fellow priest with two or three witnesses from our fellowship. But if he proves unwilling, what does your charity think should be done? For, as you know, brothers, by God’s favor I bear responsibility for all the churches.”

Bishop Numidius said: “This see has always had the right to ordain a bishop wherever it wished and from whatever person it had summoned, according to the desire of any church.”

Bishop Epigonius said: “Goodness restrains possibility; for you presume less, brother, when you show yourself good and kind [Note: [Col. 0197D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U.: ‘kind to all’]. You have this power at your discretion. It is enough that you satisfy each bishop’s personal claim at the first summons only. But if he should judge that what is permitted to this see must be claimed for himself, you must support all the churches. Therefore we do not give you authority [U.: ‘capacity’], but assign it to your judgment, so that it may be permitted to your will always to retain whomever you wish, in order to appoint as leaders over peoples or churches those who have been requested, and from wherever you wish.”

Bishop Postumianus said: “Then, if someone has only one, should that one presbyter himself be taken away from him?”

Bishop Aurelius said: “There can be one bishop through whom, by divine favor, many presbyters can be appointed; but it is difficult to find a single bishop to appoint. Therefore, if someone has a presbyter whom he needs as a bishop, and has only one, as you said, brother, he must give that one also for promotion.”

Bishop Postumianus said: “Then, if someone else has clerics in abundance [Ae.: ‘abundantly’], should another people come to my aid?”

Bishop Aurelius said: “Certainly. Just as you have helped another Church, that man who has more clerics will be persuaded to give one to you for ordination.”

**XLVI. That a bishop appointed in a diocese should retain only the people among whom he was ordained.**

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “We have heard it established that dioceses should not receive bishops except with the consent of the bishop under whom they were constituted. But in our province, when some men have perhaps been ordained bishops in a diocese with the consent of the bishop in whose jurisdiction that diocese had been constituted, they also claim the dioceses for themselves. This must be corrected by the judgment of your charity and prohibited from now on.”

Bishop Epigonius said: “For each bishop, this rule has been preserved as was fitting: none of the mass of dioceses should be taken as his own if it had had its own bishop, unless he himself had given consent. It is enough if he has consented that the same permitted diocese should have only its own bishop; he should not claim for himself the other dioceses, which, having been taken out of the bundle of many, alone deserved to receive the honor of the episcopate.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “I do not doubt that it pleases your charity and everyone that the man who, with the consent of the bishop who held the principal see, has been appointed in a diocese should retain only that same people among whom he was ordained.”

**XLVII. That nothing except the canonical Scriptures be read in church under the name of divine Scripture.**

The canonical Scriptures are as follows:

1. Genesis.  
2. Exodus.  
3. Leviticus.  
4. Numbers.  
5. Deuteronomy.  
6. Joshua.  
7. Judges.  
8. Ruth.  
9. The four books of Kingdoms.  
10. The two books of Chronicles.  
11. Job.  
12. The Psalter of David.  
13. The five books of Solomon.  
14. The twelve books of the prophets.  
15. Isaiah.  
16. [Col. 0198A] Jeremiah.  
17. Ezekiel.  
18. Daniel.  
19. Tobit.  
20. Judith.  
21. Esther.  
22. The two books of Ezra.  
23. The two books of Maccabees.  
Of the New Testament:  
24. The four books of the Gospels.  
25. One book of the Acts of the Apostles.  
26. Thirteen Epistles of the apostle Paul, and one to the Hebrews.  
27. Two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; one of James; one book of the Apocalypse of John.

Thus there are twenty-seven books, with the overseas churches to be consulted concerning the confirmation of this canon. It is also permitted to read the passions of the martyrs when their anniversaries are celebrated.

**XLVIII. Concerning those baptized by the Donatists.**

Concerning the Donatists, it was decided that we should consult our brothers and fellow priests Siricius and Simplicianus only about infants who are baptized among them, lest, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a salutary purpose, the error of their parents prevent them from being advanced to the ministry of the sacred altar, although they did not commit what their parents did [Note: [Col. 0198D] From U. In A. and the others: “although they committed it in judgment.”].

After these matters had been inserted, bishops Honoratus and Urbanus, envoys of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, said: “A little while ago, when we were presenting our written submissions before your holiness, we were delayed out of consideration that our brothers might arrive as envoys from Numidia. But since they have not come, although they have been awaited for many days, we ought not to postpone any longer the matters entrusted to us by our fellow bishops. Therefore, brothers, receive our proposal willingly. We have heard about the faith expressed in the Nicene proceedings, and also about prohibiting sacrifices after the meal, so that they may be offered by fasting persons, as was said; and this was confirmed then and is confirmed now.”

**XLIX. [Note: [Col. 0198D] This canon is absent from codices B. R., T. 1, 2, and U.] Concerning those who are ordained in the churches while possessing nothing.**

It was decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, but who during the time of their episcopate or clerical office acquire fields or any estates in their own name, shall be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those very possessions to the Church. But if something comes to them personally through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from relatives, let them dispose of it in a way consistent with their purpose. If they deviate backward from their purpose, let them be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, as reprobates. 139

**L. That the acts of the council be confirmed by the bishops’ subscriptions.**

[Col. 0198D]

Bishop Aurelius said: “Since I think that everything has now been discussed, if all these matters accord with your minds, strengthen them all by your speech.”

All the bishops said: “All these things have pleased us, and we shall confirm them by our subscription.” And they subscribed.

I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was reread, have subscribed.

I, Epigonius, bishop of the people of the region of Bullis, have subscribed.

[Col. 0199A] I, Augustine, bishop of the people of the regions of Hippo, have likewise subscribed.

[Col. 0200A] Likewise, all forty-four bishops subscribed.

**THE FIFTEENTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, THE FOURTH, HELD BY TWO HUNDRED FOURTEEN BISHOPS, IN THE YEAR 436 OF THE ERA, UNDER THE FOURTH CONSULSHIP OF HONORIUS AUGUSTUS AND THE CONSULSHIP OF EUTYCHIANUS, ON THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF NOVEMBER.**

[Col. 0199]

[Col. 0199A] When Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat in the general council at Carthage, in the secretariat, with all his fellow priests, all those who were present in that holy synod agreed with him to establish the following matters, which are necessary for the canonical discipline of ecclesiastical orders. At the beginning, the following was established.

**I. What sort of men should be ordained bishops.**

[Col. 0199B]

The man who is to be ordained bishop must first be examined: whether he is naturally prudent [Note: [Col. 0199D] U.: “first let him be examined, whether he is naturally prudent”]; whether he is teachable; temperate in conduct; chaste in life; sober; always attentive to his own affairs; approachable to people; merciful; learned; instructed in the law of the Lord; cautious in his understanding of the Scriptures; trained in ecclesiastical doctrines; and, above all, whether he sets forth the propositions of the faith in simple words—that is, affirming that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, proclaiming the entire Godhead in the Trinity to be of one essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; affirming that each individual person in the Trinity is fully God, and that all three persons are one God; believing that the divine incarnation took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0199C] but in the Son alone, so that the one who was the Son of God the Father in divinity himself became, in humanity, the son of a human mother [Note: [Col. 0199D] Ae.: “in the human nature of a mother”], true God from the Father and true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul simultaneously in himself; so that of both natures—that is, human and divine—there is one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, both author and lord of all creatures that exist, and creator with the Father and the Holy Spirit of all creatures; who truly suffered the passion of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0199D] U.: “the true death of the flesh”], died the true death of his body, rose again in the true resurrection of his flesh and the true recovery of his soul, and in that same flesh and soul will come to judge the living and the dead.

He must also be asked whether he believes that the New and Old Testaments—that is, the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles—have one and the same author and God; whether the devil became evil not by creation but by his own choice; whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh that we bear and not of another; whether he believes that judgment will come and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done in this flesh; whether he does not condemn marriage; whether he does not condemn second marriages; whether he does not criticize the eating of meat; whether he communicates with penitents after they have been reconciled; whether in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both original sin contracted and those voluntarily committed; and whether he believes that no one is saved outside the catholic Church.

When he has been found, upon examination in all these matters, to be fully instructed, then, with the consent of the clerics and laity, from the assembly of all the bishops of the province, and especially through the authority or presence of the metropolitan, he shall be ordained bishop. Having received the episcopate in the name of Christ, he must submit not to his own affection [Col. 0200B] [Note: [Col. 0200D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G.: “delight”] or to his own character [Note: [Col. 0200D] Ae., E. 3, U.: “impulses”], but to these definitions of the Fathers. At his ordination, the age required by the holy Fathers, following the example of the Savior in the selection of bishops, must also be demanded.

Next it is determined how ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered.

**II. How bishops are consecrated.**

When a bishop is ordained, two bishops shall place and hold the Book of the Gospels over his head and neck, and while one pours the blessing over him, all the other bishops who are present shall touch his head with their hands.

**III. How presbyters are ordained.**

When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hand over his head, all the presbyters who are present shall also hold their hands over his head alongside the bishop’s hand.

**IV. How deacons are appointed.**

When a deacon is ordained, only the bishop who blesses him shall place his hand on his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to the ministry.

**V. How subdeacons are appointed.**

When a subdeacon is ordained, since he does not receive the laying on of hands, he shall receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice; from the archdeacon’s hand he shall receive a small vessel [U.: *urceolum*, “pitcher”] with water, a ewer, and a towel. 142

**VI. How acolytes are appointed.**

When an acolyte is ordained, he shall indeed be taught by the bishop [Col. 0200D] how he ought to conduct himself in his office, but he shall receive from the archdeacon a candle-bearing stand with candles, so that he may know that he is assigned to light the Church’s lamps. He shall also receive an empty small vessel for supplying wine for the eucharist of Christ’s blood.

**VII. How exorcists are appointed.**

When an exorcist is ordained, he shall receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, the bishop saying to him: “Receive this, entrust it, and have the power [Note: [Col. 0200D] Ae.: “and have the power entrusted to you”] to lay hands upon the possessed, whether baptized or catechumen.”

**VIII. How lectors are appointed.**

[Col. 0201A]

When a lector is ordained, the bishop shall speak about him to the people, indicating his faith, life, and ability. After this, with the people watching [Note: [Col. 0201D] T. 2, U.: “waiting”], he shall hand him the book from which he is to read, saying to him: “Receive this, and be a bearer of the word of God. If you faithfully and usefully fulfill this office, you will have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.”

**IX. How doorkeepers are appointed.**

When a doorkeeper is ordained, after he has been instructed by the archdeacon how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, the bishop, at the archdeacon’s recommendation, shall hand him the keys of the church from the altar, saying: “Act as though you will have to give God an account for the things that are locked away by these keys.”

**X. How psalmists are appointed.**

[Col. 0201B]

A psalmist, that is, a cantor, may undertake the office of singing without the bishop’s knowledge, solely at the command of the presbyter, the presbyter saying to him: “See that you believe in your heart what you sing with your mouth, so that you may prove by your works what you believe in your heart.”

**XI. How a consecrated virgin is appointed.**

When a consecrated virgin is presented to her bishop for consecration, she shall be brought in such clothing as she will always wear, suitable to her profession and consecrated state.

**XII. What widows or consecrated women should be appointed for the ministry of baptism.**

143 Widows or consecrated women who are chosen for the ministry of baptizing women shall be instructed for the office, so that they can explain in clear and sound speech to uneducated and rustic women, at the time when they are to be baptized, how they should answer the questions put to them by the baptizer and how they should live after receiving baptism.

**XIII. How bridegrooms and brides are blessed.**

When a bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by a priest, they shall be presented by their parents or by the wedding attendants. After they have received the blessing, they shall remain virginal that same night out of reverence for the blessing itself.

**XIV. Concerning the priest’s lodging.**

That the bishop have a small lodging not far from the church.

**XV. Concerning the priest’s food and clothing.**

That the bishop have modest furnishings, a modest table, and poor food, and seek the authority of his dignity through faith and the merits of his life.

**XVI. That the bishop not read the books of the Gentiles.**

That bishops not read the books of the Gentiles, but may read those of heretics when necessity and circumstance require it.

**XVII. That the bishop not personally undertake care of the needy.**

That the bishop administer the care of widows, orphans, and travelers not personally, but through the archpresbyter or archdeacon.

**XVIII. That the bishop not provide guardianship through a will.**

That the bishop not undertake the guardianship of wills.

**XIX. That the bishop not litigate over secular matters.**

[Col. 0202A]

That the bishop not litigate even when provoked over transitory matters.

**XX. That the bishop should be devoted only to spiritual matters.**

That the bishop not take upon himself any care of household affairs, but devote himself solely to reading, prayer, and preaching the word of God. 144

**XXI. That a sick bishop send a representative to the synod on his behalf.**

That if a bishop is prevented by sufficiently serious necessity from going to the synod, he should nevertheless send a representative in his own person, and accept, while preserving the truth of the faith, whatever the synod shall decree.

**XXII. That a bishop not appoint clerics without the testimony of the clerics and people.**

[Col. 0202B]

That a bishop not ordain clerics without the counsel of his presbyters, and that he seek the assent and testimony of the citizens [Note: [Col. 0201D] Ae.: “that assent and testimony be required”].

**XXIII. That the bishop hear cases in the presence of the clerics.**

That a bishop hear no one’s case without the presence of his clerics; otherwise the bishop’s judgment shall be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of his clerics [Note: [Col. 0201D] U., G.: “of the clerics and peoples … unless it is confirmed by the presence of the clerics [Col. 0202D] and peoples.”].

**XXIV. That no one leave when the bishop is delivering a sermon.**

When a priest is delivering a sermon in the church, anyone who leaves the congregation shall be excommunicated.

**XXV. Concerning bishops who are at odds.**

If bishops who are in disagreement are not reconciled by fear of God, let the synod reconcile them. [Col. 0202C]

**XXVI. That the bishop compel those who are at odds to come to agreement.**

The bishop must strive to urge brothers who are at odds, whether clerics or laypeople, toward peace rather than judgment.

**XXVII. Concerning a bishop or cleric being transferred to another place.**

A bishop shall not move from an obscure place to a distinguished one through ambition, nor shall any cleric of a lower order do so. But if the usefulness of the Church should demand that this be done, he shall be transferred by the judgment of the synod after a decree concerning him has been presented to the bishops by the clerics and laity; nevertheless, another bishop shall be substituted for him in the other place. Priests of a lower rank and other clerics may, with the permission of their own bishops, migrate to other churches.

145 **XXVIII. Concerning the reconsideration by the synod of the condemnation of bishops.**

The condemnation of bishops, if unjust, is to be considered invalid; therefore it must be reconsidered by the synod.

**XXIX. Concerning a bishop who has charged someone with a crime.**

If a bishop brings a charge against a cleric or layperson [Note: [Col. 0202D] Ae., B. R., U.: “has brought a charge against”], he shall be brought before the synod for proof.

**XXX. That the judgment of bishops against an absent person is invalid.**

Let the judges of the Church beware of pronouncing judgment in the absence of the person whose case is being examined, because the judgment will be invalid; indeed, they will also give the case to the synod as an offense. [Col. 0203A]

**XXXI. How bishops should possess the Church’s property.**

That a bishop use the property of the Church as property entrusted to him, not as his own.

**XXXII. Concerning invalid alienations by bishops.**

A bishop’s gift, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property without the assent and subscription of the clerics shall be invalid.

**XXXIII. Concerning bishops and presbyters, that they be received according to their rank.**

If bishops or presbyters come to the church of another bishop in order to visit that church, they shall be received according to their rank, and shall be invited both to deliver a sermon and to consecrate the offering.

**XXXIV. Concerning the private seating of a presbyter with the bishop.**

[Col. 0203B]

Wherever he is seated, the bishop shall not allow a presbyter to remain standing.

**XXXV. Concerning the seating of a presbyter with the bishop in church.**

The bishop shall sit in the church assembly in a place higher than the presbyters; within the house, however, he should recognize himself as a colleague of the presbyters.

**XXXVI. That parish presbyters receive the chrism either personally or through their sacristans.**

Presbyters who govern churches throughout the dioceses shall request the chrism before the Paschal solemnity, not from just any bishops but from their own, and not through a junior cleric but either personally or through the one who keeps the sacristy. 146

**XXXVII. Concerning the obedience of deacons toward presbyters.**

[Col. 0203C]

A deacon should recognize that he is the presbyter’s minister just as he is the bishop’s.

**XXXVIII. That a deacon distribute the Eucharist at the presbyter’s command.**

That a deacon, when a presbyter is present, distribute the Eucharist of Christ’s body to the people, if necessity compels it, when ordered to do so.

**XXXIX. That a deacon sit when ordered by a presbyter.**

That a deacon sit wherever the presbyter orders him to sit.

**XL. That a deacon answer when questioned before a presbyter.**

That a deacon speak when questioned in an assembly of presbyters.

**XLI. That a deacon wear the white garment only during the office.**

[Col. 0203D]

That a deacon use the white garment only during the offering and the reading.

**XLII. Concerning clerics who have been tested for the faith.**

A cleric who remains devoted to his office amid trials [Note: [Col. 0203D] From U. In A. and the others: “a cleric who, amid trials, remains away from his office”] should be promoted through the ranks.

**XLIII. Concerning those who have suffered persecution from unbelievers for the faith.**

A catholic Christian who suffers affliction for the catholic faith is to be honored by the priests with every honor; daily sustenance shall also be provided for him.

**XLIV. Concerning the tonsure of clerics.**

[Col. 0204A]

A cleric shall neither grow long hair nor shave his beard [Note: [Col. 0203D] From B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., G. In A.: “for he should shave the beard from the roots.” In Ae.: “he should neither shave the beard [Col. 0204D] from the roots.”].

**XLV. Concerning the clothing of clerics.**

A cleric should demonstrate his profession through his clothing and bearing; therefore he should seek elegance neither in garments nor in footwear.

**XLVI. Concerning the continence of clerics.**

A cleric shall not live with unrelated women.

147 **XLVII. Concerning the conduct of clerics.**

A cleric shall not walk through streets and passageways except for a definite and very serious necessity of his office.

**XLVIII. Concerning clerics who go to markets without necessity.**

A cleric who strolls through the market or marketplace without going there to buy something shall be degraded from his office.

**XLIX. Concerning the vigils of clerics.**

[Col. 0204B]

A cleric who is absent from vigils without bodily infirmity shall be deprived of his stipend and excommunicated.

**L. Concerning clerics who withdraw from their office.**

A cleric who withdraws from his office amid trials or performs it negligently shall be removed from that office.

**LI. Concerning the craft of a cleric.**

A cleric, however learned in the word of God [Note: [Col. 0204D] From Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G. In A., E. 3: “whatever his learning”], shall seek his livelihood through a craft.

**LII. Concerning a cleric’s clothing and food.**

A cleric shall provide himself with food and clothing through a craft or agriculture, provided that this causes no detriment to his office.

**LIII. Concerning clerics who are physically incapable.**

[Col. 0204C] All clerics who are incapable of working shall learn both some small craft and letters.

**LIV. Concerning envious clerics.**
A cleric who envies the advancement of his brothers shall not be promoted so long as he remains in this vice.

### LV. On clerics who are accusers

Let bishops excommunicate those who accuse their brothers; and if they amend their fault, let them receive them into communion, but not into the clergy.

### LVI. On clerics who are flatterers and betrayers

A cleric who is found to devote himself to flattery and betrayal shall be degraded from office.

### LVII. On clerics who use abusive language

A cleric who uses abusive language, especially if he is among the priests, [Col. 0204D] shall be compelled to ask pardon; if he refuses, he shall be degraded and shall never be restored to office without making satisfaction.

### LVIII. On clerics who frequently engage in litigation

No one shall accept the testimony of a person who frequently quarrels and is readily inclined to bring accusations without a serious examination.

### LIX. On clerics who are at odds

The bishop shall draw clerics who are at odds into agreement, whether by reason or by authority; those who disobey shall be condemned by the synod after a hearing.

### LX. On clerics who use obscene language or wander about

[Col. 0205A]

A clownish cleric who jokes with obscene words shall be removed from office.

### LXI. On clerics who swear by created things

A cleric who swears by created things shall be severely rebuked; if he persists in the vice, he shall be excommunicated.

### LXII. On healthy clerics who violate the fasts

A cleric who breaks the fast during an appointed fast without unavoidable necessity shall be regarded as inferior and strictly restrained.

### LXIII. On clerics who sing during meals

A cleric who sings during meals shall be severely rebuked [Note: [Col. 0205D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “A cleric who sings during meals shall be restrained with the severity of the foregoing sentence.”]; if he persists in the vice, he shall be excommunicated.

### LXIV. On those who deliberately fast on the Lord’s Day

One who deliberately fasts on the Lord’s Day shall not be believed to be Catholic.

### LXV. That Easter is to be celebrated at one time

The solemnity of Easter is to be celebrated on one day and at one time.

### LXVI. That a cleric should have recourse to the synod

A cleric who considers the discipline exercised by his bishop toward him unjust shall have recourse to the synod.

### LXVII. On seditious clerics

Seditious persons are never to be ordained as clerics, just as neither usurers nor those who avenge their own injuries are to be ordained.

### LXVIII. On penitents who have been ordained [Note: [Col. 0205D] In the others, except A.: “That a cleric ordained from among the penitents be deposed.”]

Although he may be a good cleric, no one who has been a penitent is to be ordained. If he has been made a cleric through the bishop’s ignorance, he shall be deposed from the clergy, because at the time of his ordination he did not disclose that he had been a penitent. But if the bishop knowingly ordained him, the bishop himself shall likewise be deprived solely of the power of ordaining in his episcopate. [Col. 0205C]

### LXIX. On bishops who are condemned [Note: [Col. 0205D] In the others, except A.: “That a bishop who promotes to the clergy the husband of a widow or of a divorced woman be deposed.”]

A bishop shall be subject to a similar sentence if he knowingly ordains as a cleric a man who has had a widow, a divorced woman, or a second wife.

### LXX. On the banquets of clerics [Note: [Col. 0206D] In the others, except A.: “That a cleric avoid the banquets and associations of heretics.”]

A cleric shall equally avoid both the banquets and the associations of heretics or schismatics.

### LXXI. On the gatherings of heretics

The gatherings of heretics are not to be called churches but assemblies of conspirators.

### LXXII. Nor are psalms to be sung with heretics

One must neither pray nor sing psalms with heretics.

### LXXIII. On those who have communicated with an excommunicated person

[Col. 0205D]

Whoever communicates or prays with an excommunicated person, whether cleric or layman, shall be excommunicated.

### LXXIV. On the law concerning penitents

Let a priest, without respect of persons, impose the laws of penance upon one who seeks penance.

### LXXV. On more negligent penitents

Let more negligent penitents be received later.

### LXXVI. On those who seek penance and later become speechless

[Col. 0206A]

If a person who, while lying ill, asks for penance should, by chance, become speechless through the severity of his illness or be overcome by delirium while the priest summoned to him is coming, those who heard him shall bear witness, and he shall receive penance; [150] and if he is believed to be immediately dying, he shall be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist shall be poured into his mouth. If he survives, the witnesses mentioned above shall inform him that his request has been fulfilled, and he shall be subjected to the prescribed laws of penance for as long as the priest who granted the penance determines.

### LXXVII. On penitents

Penitents who are ill shall receive the viaticum.

### LXXVIII. Likewise on penitents

[Col. 0206B]

Penitents who have received the viaticum of the Eucharist while ill shall not consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands if they survive.

### LXXIX. On penitents who die by some accident

If penitents who are carefully fulfilling the laws of penance die by chance while traveling or at sea, where no assistance could be given them, their memory shall be commended in prayers and offerings.

### LXXX. On the laying on of hands over penitents

At every time of fasting, priests shall lay hands upon penitents.

### LXXXI. That penitents should carry out and bury the dead

Let penitents carry out and bury the dead of the Church.

### LXXXII. That penitents should always kneel

[Col. 0206C]

Penitents shall kneel even on days of remission.

### LXXXIII. On honoring the elderly of the Church

The poor and the elderly of the Church are to be honored more than the rest.

### LXXXIV. On unbelievers attending the reading in church

Let the bishop prohibit no one from entering the church and hearing the word of God—whether a Gentile, a heretic, or a Jew—up to the dismissal of the catechumens.

### LXXXV. That those who are to be baptized should give their names

Those who are to be baptized shall give their names; and while they are repeatedly examined under abstinence from wine and meat and with the laying on of hands, they shall receive baptism.

### LXXXVI. That the newly baptized should live chastely

Neophytes shall for some time abstain both from luxurious banquets and from spectacles and marital relations [Note: [Col. 0206D] Ae.: “from spectacles and marital relations.”].

### LXXXVII. On Catholics who bring cases before unbelievers

A Catholic who brings a case, whether just or unjust, before a judge of another faith shall be excommunicated [Note: [Col. 0206D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G.: “his case.”].

### LXXXVIII. On those who neglect the church and go to spectacles

[Col. 0207A]

Whoever, on a solemn day, neglects the assembly of the church and goes to spectacles shall be excommunicated.

### LXXXIX. On auguries and incantations

A person devoted to auguries or incantations is to be separated from the assembly of the church; likewise one who adheres to Jewish superstitions or festivals.

### XC. On the possessed

Every day exorcists shall lay hands upon the possessed.

### XCI. Likewise on the possessed

Let the possessed sweep the pavements of the houses of God.

### XCII. On the food of the possessed

For the possessed who sit in the house of God, the exorcists shall provide daily food at the appropriate time.

### XCIII. On the offerings of those who are at odds

The offerings of brothers who are at odds are not to be received either in the sacristy or in the treasury.

### XCIV. On oppressors of the poor

The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by priests.

### XCV. On those who defraud the churches of offerings for the dead

Those who either withhold offerings for the dead from the churches or return them with difficulty shall be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.

### XCVI. On an accuser or an accused person

In court, inquiry must be made into the conduct and faith of both the accuser and the accused. [Col. 0207C]

### XCVII. On religious women

The man who is to be placed over religious women must be approved by the bishop of the locality.

### XCVIII. On lay teachers

A layman shall not presume to teach in the presence of clerics unless the clerics themselves approve.

### XCIX. On learned women

A woman, however learned and holy, shall not presume to teach men in the assembly.

### C. That women should not presume to baptize

A woman shall not presume to baptize.

### CI. On young widows

Young widows who are physically infirm shall be supported at the expense of the Church to which they belong as widows.

### CII. On clerics and widows

It shall be reckoned to the guilt of the bishop, or of the priest who presides over the parish, if younger widows or nuns are subjected to the familiar associations of clerics for the sake of maintaining their present life.

### CIII. On widows

Widows who are supported by the Church’s allowance must be so diligent in the work of God that they assist the Church by both their merits and their prayers.

### CIV. On widows who have violated their professed continence

[Col. 0208A]

Just as the reward of chastity is good, so too it must be established with greater observance and injunction [Note: [Col. 0207D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U.: “guarded”] that if any widows—however young in years and left by a husband at an immature age—have devoted themselves to God, cast off secular dress, and appeared in religious attire under the testimony of the bishop and the Church, but afterward have entered into secular marriage, they shall, according to the Apostle Paul, incur condemnation, because they dared to invalidate the pledge of chastity [153] that they had vowed to God.

Such persons, therefore, are to be excluded from the communion of Christians and are not to share a banquet with Christians. For if adulterous wives are liable to their husbands on account of their guilt, how much more will widows who had vowed religious devotion to God be branded with the crime of adultery if they corrupt by lustful pleasure the devotion that they spontaneously offered to God and enter into a second marriage? Even if such women have been carried off by force by someone, and afterward consent, through the pleasure of lust, to remain in marriage with their abductor or with the man who violated them, they are to remain subject to the condemnation described above. For concerning such women the Apostle says: “When they have become wanton, they wish to marry, bearing condemnation because they have annulled their first faith.”

### CV. On those who despise the Church [Note: [Col. 0207D] This canon has been taken from U. and G.; it is absent from the other manuscripts.]

It is indeed found that schismatics often arise from among Christians—men without reason—who, while these build as Catholics, persist in destroying as heretics. Some adorn the churches of the Lord with most faithful devotion and ready contrition, while others diminish them by establishing seditions. Of these the prophet rightly speaks through the Holy Spirit: “Blessed are those who build you forever, and cursed are those who destroy your walls, or certainly those who overthrow your dwellings, or who now have attempted to diminish your holy things. But you, house of God, rejoice with the children of the righteous.”

In accordance with this ordinance of the Lord, it pleased all the Fathers assembled throughout the province of Carthage that, if any cleric or layman should rise up against the Church of God, sowing schisms through seditions and failing to direct his attention toward the summit of its charity, but wishing to undermine its foundations—which are the stability of all Christians—then, if he is a cleric, he shall fall from his proper rank; if a layman, he shall be separated from the Church of God that he despises and from the assembly of the whole Christian religion, and shall remain excluded from holy communion. [Col. 0208D]

I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have subscribed. I, Donatian, bishop of Telepte, bishop of the first see, have subscribed. I, Augustine, bishop of the region of Hippo, have subscribed [Note: [Col. 0208D] T. 2: “bishop of the region of Hippo”; U.: “bishop of royal Hippo.”]. Likewise all the bishops subscribed [Note: [Col. 0208D] U.: “Four hundred and fourteen subscribed together with these.”].

## XVI. FIFTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, HELD BY SEVENTY-THREE BISHOPS, IN THE YEAR 438 OF THE ERA, AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF FLAVIUS STILICHO, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, ON THE SEVENTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY

[Col. 0209]

[Col. 0209A] At Carthage, in the secretary’s office of the restored basilica, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with his fellow bishops, with deacons also standing by, the following matters were established, which were defined in the council that follows [Note: [Col. 0209D] U.: “were defined in the councils that follow.”]. [155]

### I. On clerics not being summoned to give testimony

At the outset it is to be established that, if anyone should wish to pursue any case in a church under the apostolic right imposed upon churches, and if perhaps the decision of the clerics displeases one party, it shall not be permitted to summon to court as a witness the cleric who was the investigator or was present [U.: “who is or was present”], so that no member of the clergy whatsoever may be summoned to give testimony.
