### II. On clerics condemned for their crime

It is also to be established that, if a cleric of whatever rank has been condemned by the judgment of the bishops for any crime, no one shall be permitted to defend him, whether from the churches over which he presided or from any other person, under penalty involving the loss of money and honor; and they shall prescribe that neither age nor sex is to be accepted as an excuse.

### III. On priests and Levites abstaining from their wives

Moreover, since it had been reported that certain clerics were incontinent even toward their own wives, it pleased the council that bishops, priests, and deacons should, in accordance with the earlier statutes, abstain also from their wives. If they do not do so, they shall be removed from ecclesiastical office. The remaining clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but are to observe the practice according to the custom of each individual.

### IV. On not alienating Church property without consulting the metropolitan bishop

[Col. 0209C]

It also pleased the council that no one sell Church property. If some necessity compels this, the matter is to be brought to the primate of the province, so that, together with the appointed number of bishops, he may determine whether it ought to be done. If such a great necessity presses upon the Church that consultation cannot take place beforehand, he shall at least take care to do this immediately afterward, or to notify the neighboring bishops beforehand and refer the same needs of the Church to the council. If he does not do so, the seller shall be held liable before the council, having lost his rank [Note: [Col. 0209D] In Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., the words “having lost his rank” are absent.].

### V. That no bishop should reside in a diocese after leaving his see

Again, it pleased the council that no one should have the power, after leaving his principal see, to transfer himself to a church established in the diocese, or, while remaining in his own property longer than is proper, to neglect the care of or attendance upon his own see. [156]

### VI. On those who know from no testimony that they were baptized, and are therefore to be baptized

[Col. 0210A]

It also pleased the council concerning infants that, whenever wholly certain witnesses cannot be found to testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and the infants themselves, because of their age, are not capable of answering concerning the sacraments entrusted to them [Note: [Col. 0209D] The words “to testify … and the infants themselves” are taken from the other manuscripts; they are absent from A.], they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation deprive them of the cleansing of the sacraments. For this reason our brothers, the envoys of the Moors, consulted us, since they redeem many such children from the barbarians.

### VII. On the time of Easter and of the council

It also pleased the council that the venerable day of Easter be announced to all by a written notification bearing signatures, while the day of the council be observed on the tenth day before the Kalends of November; and that a letter be sent to the primates of each province, [Col. 0210B] so that, whenever they assemble a council in their own provinces, they do not interfere with this day.

### VIII. On intercessors not retaining the see of a deceased bishop for long

It has also been decreed that no intercessor may retain the see to which he has been appointed as intercessor through any popular zeal or sedition, but must take care to provide them with a bishop within a year. If he neglects this, after the year has elapsed another intercessor shall be appointed.

### IX. On requesting a defender of the churches from the emperor

It was unanimously decided that a request should be made to the emperor, on account of the affliction of the poor, by whose troubles the Church is incessantly harassed, that defenders be appointed for them against the power of the rich, with the provision of the bishops. [Col. 0210C]

### X. That bishops should attend on the day of the council

It also pleased the council that, whenever a council is to be assembled, bishops who are hindered neither by illness nor by another more serious necessity should attend in due form [Note: [Col. 0210D] The words “should attend in due form,” absent from A., are taken from the other manuscripts]. The primates of their provinces are to be notified that all the bishops be divided into two or three groups, and that, from each group in turn, as many as have been chosen should attend the day of the council with the greatest urgency. If they are unable to attend, they shall record their excuses in the official summons [Note: [Col. 0210D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “in the official summons … in the official summons.”]. Or, if some necessity should suddenly arise after the arrival of the summons, they must give an account of the reason for their absence to their primate; otherwise they are to be content with the communion of their own church. [157]

### XI. That the hands of fallen priests should not be laid upon them as upon laymen

[Col. 0210D]

It was thus confirmed that, whenever priests or deacons are convicted of some more serious fault for which it is necessary to remove them from the ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them either as upon penitents or as upon faithful laymen. Nor is it ever to be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.

### XII. On excommunicated clerics, and how long they may be permitted to defend themselves

It has again been established that, whenever clerics who have been convicted and have confessed to some crime are spared either out of regard for their shame or because of the reproach to the Church or the insolent attacks of heretics and Gentiles, if they should wish to appear on behalf of their case and assert their innocence, they must do so within the year of their excommunication. But if they disdain to clear their case within the year, no statement of theirs shall afterward be heard at all.

### XIII. On clerics or monks ordained by another bishop

[Col. 0211B]

It also pleased the council that, if anyone should wish either to promote to the clergy a person found in another’s monastery or to appoint him as head of a monastery in his own monastery, the bishop who does this shall be separated from communion with the other bishops and shall be content with communion with his own people; and the man in question shall continue as neither cleric nor superior.

### XIV. On bishops who leave their property to unbelievers

It has also been established that, if a bishop prefers to the Church heirs unrelated to him by blood, or even heretics related to him by blood, or pagans, at least after his death an anathema shall be pronounced against him, and his name shall in no way be recited among the priests of God. Nor can he be excused if he dies intestate, since, having become a bishop, he certainly ought not to have delayed arranging his property in a manner appropriate to his profession. [Col. 0212A]

### XV. On basilicas dedicated without the relics of martyrs

It also pleased the council that the altars established here and there through fields or along roads as memorials of martyrs, in which no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, should, if possible, be overturned by the bishops who preside over those places. If popular disturbances prevent this, the people are nevertheless to be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held there by any superstition.

In general, no memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as credible unless there is a body or some relics there, or unless the origin of some habitation or martyrdom has been transmitted with the utmost reliability. For altars established everywhere on the basis of dreams and empty, supposedly revealed visions of various people are to be rejected in every respect. [Col. 0212B]

### XVI. On destroying idol shrines

It also pleased the council that a request be made to the most glorious emperors that the remnants of idolatry be utterly destroyed, not only in images but also in every place, grove, and tree.

I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have subscribed to the statutes set forth above in our council.

Likewise, seventy-three bishops subscribed.

## XVII. SIXTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, HELD BY TWO HUNDRED AND SEVENTEEN BISHOPS, IN THE YEAR 457 OF THE ERA, AT WHICH IT WAS DECIDED THAT THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA SHOULD BE REQUESTED FROM THE EASTERN BISHOPS; THE LEGATION OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, NAMELY BISHOP FAUSTINUS AND THE PRIESTS PHILIPPUS AND ASELLUS, WAS PRESENT AT THIS SYNOD, AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EMPERORS HONORIUS XII AND THEODOSIUS VIII, AUGUSTI, ON THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JUNE

[Col. 0211]

[Col. 0211C] At Carthage, in the secretary’s office of the basilica of Faustus, when Pope Aurelius had taken his seat together with Valentinus, bishop of the first see of the province of Numidia, and Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church for the Italian province of Picenum and the Church of Potentia, and also with legates of the various African provinces—that is, the two Numidias, Byzacena, Mauretania Sitifensis, Mauretania Caesariensis, and Tripolitania—and with Vincentius of Culusitana, Fortunatianus, and the other bishops of the proconsular province, two hundred and seventeen in number, as well as with the priests Philippus and Asellus and the legates of the Roman Church, and when the deacons were standing by, Bishop Aurelius said: [159–160]

### I. Address of Bishop Aurelius to the synod [Note: [Col. 0211D] Here and in the following titles, the headings are written in the margin in A.; sometimes, however, when inserted into the text, they seem to interrupt the sentence.].

After the appointed day of the council, as you remember, most blessed brothers, many matters were requested while we awaited our brothers who have now arrived as legates for the present synod. These matters must be joined to the records; concerning this, we give thanks to our Lord for the gathering of so great an assembly.

It remains that both the copies of the Council of Nicaea that we now possess and its decrees established by the Fathers, as well as the material here established by our predecessors in confirmation of that same synod and the salutary regulations made according to its form throughout all the ranks of the clergy, from the highest to the lowest, be brought forward.

The whole council said: “Let them be brought forward.”

Daniel the notary read: “The profession of faith and the decrees of the Council of Nicaea are as follows.”

### II. Response of Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, concerning matters established in the Church partly by canon and partly by custom

When Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church from the people of Potentia in the Italian province of Picenum, had heard this, he said:

“Some matters have been entrusted to us by the apostolic see in writing and some also in oral instructions, to be discussed with Your Beatitude, just as we also recalled in the preceding records [Note: [Col. 0212D] Ae., B. R., U., “When he had said this, Faustinus.”]. This concerns the canons of Nicaea, so that both their ordinance and their custom may be preserved, since some matters are held by established order and canon, while others have been confirmed by custom.

“Therefore, if it pleases Your Beatitude, let us discuss these matters, so that you may also inform the venerable see by your written reply, and so that it may clearly appear that we have brought a reminder before the venerable pope, although the chapters of the proceedings have already been inserted into the records. Concerning these matters, then, as I said above, we must determine what it pleases Your Beatitude to do.

“Let the memorandum therefore be brought forward, so that Your Beatitude may know what it contains and a response may be given to each point.”

### III. On the reading of the memorandum of the Roman pope

Bishop Aurelius said: “Let the memorandum be brought forward [Col. 0213B] which our brothers and fellow priests recently cited in the proceedings, together with the other matters that have been done or are to be done.”

Afterward the notary Daniel read the memorandum [Note: [Col. 0213D] Ae., B. R.: “the matters that are to be done shall follow. Daniel.” U.: “the matters that are to be done shall follow. Daniel.”]:

“Bishop Zosimus to his brother Faustinus and to his sons, the priests Philippus and Asellus.

“The affairs entrusted to you are not unknown to you. Conduct everything as though our presence were there—or rather, because our presence is there in you—as we especially entrust to you this mandate of ours. We have also inserted into this memorandum the words of the canons for fuller confirmation.

“For thus the beloved brothers said in the Council of Nicaea when they decreed concerning the appeal of bishops:

“‘It was decided that, if a bishop has been accused, and the assembled bishops of that region have judged him and deposed him from his rank, and he appears to have appealed and fled to the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and that bishop wishes him to be heard and considers it just that the examination be renewed, he should deign to write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the faith of truth.

“‘But if someone asks that his case be heard again, and by his petition moves the Roman bishop to send a priest from his own side, it shall be in the power of the bishop to determine what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. If he decides that men should be sent who will sit in judgment with the bishops present, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, the matter shall lie within his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the affair to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.’”

### IV. Response of Bishop Alipius concerning the search for authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea

[Col. 0213D]

When this had been read, Bishop Alipius of the Church of Tagaste, legate of the province of Numidia, said:

“We have already replied concerning this in earlier letters of our council, and we profess that we shall preserve what was established in the Council of Nicaea. Nevertheless, I am still troubled [Note: [Col. 0214D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2: “nevertheless, it still troubles me”], because, when we examined the Greek copies of this Council of Nicaea, we found none of these things there, I do not know for what reason.

“Therefore we ask Your Holiness, holy Pope Aurelius, since this authentic Council of Nicaea is said to be in the city of Constantinople, to deign to send certain persons with writings from Your Holiness [Col. 0214A], not only to our holy brother, the bishop of Constantinople, but also to the venerable priests, the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, so that they may send us this council with the endorsement of their letters. In this way all subsequent ambiguity may be removed, since we have not found it as our brother Faustinus reported.

“Nevertheless, as I said before, we profess that we shall observe these provisions for a little while, until complete copies arrive. The venerable bishop of the Roman Church, Boniface, should also be requested by our letters to deign to send certain persons to the aforesaid churches, so that they may bring the same copies of the Council of Nicaea according to his written instructions [T. 2: “present”]. For now, however, we join to these proceedings the copies of the aforesaid Council of Nicaea that we possess.” [Col. 0214B]

### V. Where Bishop Faustinus says that the synod should notify the Roman pope in order to investigate the truth of the Council of Nicaea

Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said:

“Nor does Your Holiness prejudice the Roman Church either concerning this chapter or concerning others, because our brother and fellow bishop Alipius has been pleased to say that the canons are doubtful. But deign to write these very matters to our holy and most blessed pope, so that he too, while investigating the complete canons, may discuss all the decrees with Your Holiness.

“It is enough that the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome himself investigate the matter, just as Your Holiness discusses it here, so that no contention may appear to arise between the churches, but rather so that you may deliberate in fraternal charity, with him writing back concerning what ought better to be observed [Note: [Col. 0214D] In the other manuscripts except A.: “what ought to be renewed.”].”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“In addition to the matters that we have brought forward in the proceedings, it is necessary that we also inform our holy brother and fellow priest Boniface, by a letter from our unworthiness, of each matter that we are discussing in the fullest detail. Therefore, if our proposal pleases everyone, let us learn this from the mouth of all.”

The whole council said: “It pleases us.”

### VI. On the reading of the sentence of the Council of Sardica at the request of Bishop Novatus

Bishop Novatus, legate of Mauretania Sitifensis, said:

“We now remember that the memorandum read at this present council also contained something concerning priests and deacons, namely how they ought to be heard by their own bishops or by neighboring bishops, which we have by no means read in the Council of Nicaea. Therefore, let Your Holiness order this very matter to be read to us.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “Let the requested passage also be read at the appropriate place.”

The notary Daniel read:

“Concerning the appeals of clerics—that is, of those of lower rank—and the definite response of the synod, we believe that we should insert what you are going to do in this matter. It was stated as follows from the Council of Sardica (Title 17):

“Bishop Hosius said: ‘I must not conceal what still troubles me. If some bishop should, perhaps in anger—which ought not to happen, but can happen—become quickly or harshly enraged against his priest or deacon and wish to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent person be condemned or lose communion. The expelled man shall have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, since a hearing ought not to be denied to one who requests it. That bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, must patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that either the expelled man's innocence may be proved or the bishop's judgment corrected.’ And so forth.”

### VII. Where Bishop Augustine promises, together with the synod, to preserve the Council of Nicaea

When this was read, Bishop Augustine of the Church of Hippo Regius, legate of the province of Numidia, said:

“We also profess that we shall preserve this, subject to a more careful investigation of the Council of Nicaea.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “If this also pleases the charity of all of you, confirm it by your response.”

The whole council said: “Everything established in the Council of Nicaea pleases us all.” [Col. 0215B]

Bishop Jucundus of the Church of Sufetula, legate of the province of Byzacena, said:

“What has been established in the Council of Nicaea can in no way be violated by anyone.”

### VIII. Where Bishop Faustinus finds that a letter should be written to the Roman pope concerning the uncertainty of the chapter read

Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said:

“Still, according to the profession of Your Holiness, I believe that some things have been confirmed by both the holy Alipius and our brother Jucundus, while some have been weakened—something that ought not to happen—since the canons themselves have now become doubtful.

“Therefore, as it pleases both us and Your Beatitude, may Your Holiness deign to write to the holy and venerable bishop of the Roman Church, so that he too may deliberate upon what holy Augustine has deigned to establish: whether this too ought to be established and retained, namely, the matter of appeals from a lower rank.

“If, therefore, this chapter has again become doubtful, it is right that the bishop of the most blessed Roman see should be informed, if you can find this in the approved canons [Note: [Col. 0215D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, U.: “if this can be found”; T. 2: “if it can be found.”].”

### IX. Where the synod decreed that copies of the Council of Nicaea should rather be requested from the Eastern bishops

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Permit us now also to bring forward the copies of the statutes of the Council of Nicaea that we mentioned to Your Charity some time ago, as well as the matters salutarily established here by our predecessors according to the form of that same council and those that we have now ordered, and to have them read and inserted into the proceedings.”

The whole council said:

“The copies of the faith and the statutes of the Council of Nicaea that were brought to our council by Caecilianus, bishop of blessed memory and the predecessor of Your Holiness who was present at that council, together with those things that the Fathers established here while following those copies [Ae., B. R., U.: “examples”], and those that we now establish by common deliberation, shall remain inserted in these ecclesiastical proceedings.

“Thus, as was said above, may Your Beatitude deign to write to the venerable bishops of the churches of Antioch and Alexandria, and also of Constantinople [U., G.: “of the Church”], so that they may send the most authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea with the endorsement of their letters. Once the truth has been made clear, the chapters that our present brother and fellow bishop Faustinus and the fellow priests Philippus and Asellus brought with them in the memorandum will either be confirmed by us if they are found there, or, if they are not found, we shall discuss the matter in an assembled synod at a later time.”

The notary Daniel read the profession of faith and the statutes of the Council of Nicaea in the African council.

### X. Profession of faith of the Council of Nicaea

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*; through him all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, and was incarnate and became human; he suffered and rose again on the third day; he ascended into the heavens; he sits at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And we believe in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten he did not exist,” and who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or from some substance or nature, and who say that the Son of God is mutable and subject to change—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

### XI. Letter to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, sent by Aurelius and the other bishops of the African province through the aforesaid legates of the Roman Church concerning that very council [Note: [Col. 0216D] In all the manuscripts: “concerning that same council.”]

[Col. 0216C]

To the most blessed and honorable brother Boniface, Aurelius, Valentinus, bishop of the first see of the province of Numidia, and the rest of us who were present, two hundred and seventeen in number, from the entire council of Africa.

Because it pleased the Lord that, concerning the matters which our holy brothers, our fellow-bishop Faustinus and the fellow-presbyters Philippus and Asellus, conducted with us, our humility should reply not to the bishop of blessed memory, Zosimus, from whom they brought us instructions and letters, but to your veneration, who by divine appointment have been established in his place, we ought briefly to make known those matters which were settled by the agreement of both sides—not those contained in the lengthy volumes of the proceedings, in which, while preserving charity, we nevertheless spent time amid no small labor of dispute, deliberating from the acts [Col. 0216D] what now pertains to the case. Although he too, if he were still alive, would more gratefully accept this, lord brother, seeing it brought to a more peaceful conclusion.

The presbyter Apiarius, whose ordination, excommunication, and appeal had occasioned no slight scandal not only to the Church of Sicca but also to the whole Church of Africa, was restored to communion after asking forgiveness for all his errors. Our former fellow-bishop Urbanus of Sicca corrected without hesitation whatever in his conduct had seemed in need of correction. But because the peace and tranquility of the Church had to be safeguarded not only for the present but also for the future, since many such events had preceded this one, so that similar or even more serious matters ought thereafter to be prevented, it pleased us that Apiarius should be removed from the Church of Sicca while retaining the honor of his rank, and that, after receiving a letter of release, he should exercise the office of presbyter wherever else he wished and was able. We granted this to him without difficulty when he himself requested it by his own letters.

Before this case was closed with that conclusion, however, among the matters over which we were engaged in lengthy [U., “protracted”] discussions, reason itself required that we ask our brothers, the fellow-bishop Faustinus and the fellow-presbyters Philippus and Asellus, before the ecclesiastical records, to disclose whatever instructions they had been given to conduct with us. Some matters they pursued orally, without any writing; but when we pressed them especially about what they carried in their letters, they produced a memorandum which, after being read to us, was also attached to the proceedings that they were carrying with them to you. In it they were instructed to conduct four matters with us:

1. Concerning appeals by bishops to the priest of the Roman Church;

2. That bishops should not sail importunately to the imperial court;

3. Concerning the rehearing of cases of presbyters and deacons before neighboring bishops, if they had been improperly excommunicated by their own bishops;

4. Concerning excommunicating Bishop Urbanus or even summoning him to Rome, unless he corrected what seemed to require correction.

Regarding the first and third of these matters—that is, that a bishop should be permitted to appeal to Rome, and that the cases of clergy should be concluded before the bishops of their own provinces—we had already taken care, in the previous year, to make our position known in letters sent to the same bishop Zosimus of venerable memory, so that we might permit these arrangements to be observed for a short time without any injury to him, until the statutes of the Council of Nicaea could be investigated. And now we ask your holiness that, just as those matters were enacted or established by the fathers at Nicaea, you cause them to be observed for us, and that you cause those matters which they brought in the memorandum to be put into practice among you.

The following is also stated [Note: [Col. 0217D] From the Council of Sardica, title 7.]:

“If a bishop has been accused, and the assembled bishops of that region have judged him and deposed him from his rank, and he appears to have appealed and has taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and he has wished to be heard and has considered it just that the examination be renewed, let him write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the faith of truth. But if the one who asks that his case be heard again should move the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send presbyters from his side [Note: [Col. 0217D] Ae., B. R., presbyterum], it shall be in the power of the bishop to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. And if he should decide that those who are to be sent ought to sit in judgment with the bishops present, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, it shall be at his discretion. But if he should believe that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he has judged by his most prudent counsel.”

Likewise concerning presbyters and deacons [Note: [Col. 0218D] From the Council of Sardica, title 17.]:

“If any bishop—who ought not to be so—should be irascible and become quickly or harshly [Col. 0218A] angered against his presbyter or deacon and should wish to expel him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. The expelled man shall have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and his case shall be heard and examined more carefully, for the one who asks ought not to be denied a hearing. And let the bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that either his judgment may be proved right or corrected.”

These provisions were inserted into the proceedings pending the arrival of the most reliable copies of the Council of Nicaea. If they were observed there in the manner in which they were established, and in the manner in which our brothers sent from the apostolic see alleged that they were contained in the memorandum, and if they were observed among you in Italy in that same order, we would in no way be compelled either to recall or tolerate such matters as those we have mentioned, nor would we suffer what is intolerable.

But, with the help of the mercy of our God, we believe that, with your holiness presiding over the Roman Church, we shall no longer endure this arrogance; and we trust that, with brotherly charity, those provisions will be observed toward us which ought to be observed even when we are not in disagreement, according to the wisdom and justice which the Most High has given you. You yourself also perceive that they must be observed, unless perhaps the canons of the Council of Nicaea are otherwise.

For although we have read very many copies, nowhere in the Latin copies have we read in the Council of Nicaea what was sent from there in the aforesaid memorandum. Since we could find these provisions in no copy, we desire all the more that copies be brought to us from the Eastern Churches, where the same decrees are said to be capable of being found in an authentic form. For this reason we also earnestly beseech your veneration to write to the priests of those regions—the bishops of the Churches of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople—and, if it should please your holiness, to others as well, so that from there the same canons established by the fathers at the city of Nicaea may come to us, with you above all, by the Lord’s help, conferring this benefit upon all the Western churches.

For who could doubt that these are the most genuine copies of the council assembled at Nicaea in Greece, since they were brought from such widely separated places and from distinguished Greek churches and agree with one another?

Until the matters which we have alleged above from the memorandum—concerning appeals by bishops to the priest of the Roman Church and the settlement of clerical cases before the bishops of their own provinces—are accomplished, we declare that we shall continue to observe them until they are verified; and we trust that your blessedness, in accordance with God’s will, will assist us in this.

As for the remaining matters conducted or confirmed in our synod, since the aforesaid brothers of ours, Bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philippus and Asellus, have brought them with them, they will make them known to your holiness, if you deign to receive them.

And in another hand:

May our Lord preserve you for many years for us, most blessed brother [Note: [Col. 0218D] Ae., E. 3, U., “brother. Amen.”]

Aurelius, bishop of Carthage; Alipius; Augustinus; Possidius; Marinus; and the remaining two hundred and seventeen signed.

## XII. Replies to the African Council from Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, by which authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea, translated from Greek by the presbyter Innocentius, were sent; these letters, together with the same Council of Nicaea, were also sent through the aforementioned presbyter Innocentius and Marcellus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, to the holy bishop Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

To the honorable lords, holy brothers and fellow-bishops Aurelius and Valentinus, and to the entire holy congregation assembled in the synod at Carthage, Cyril sends greetings in God to your charity.

We received the writings of your veneration, full of many complaints, with complete joy through our son Innocentius the presbyter [Col. 0219B]. In them you ask us to present to your love, under our profession of faith, the most genuine copies from the archive of our Church, from the authentic synod established and confirmed by the holy Fathers at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia.

Therefore, honorable lords [Ae., “venerable”] brothers, with the greeting preceding them, I found it necessary through this bearer, our son Innocentius, to send to your charity the most trustworthy copies from the authentic synod held at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia. You will also find them when you consult ecclesiastical history. As for Easter, concerning which you write, we inform you that we shall celebrate it on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May in the coming indiction.

And in another hand:

May our God and Lord preserve your congregation, as we desire, dearest [Col. 0219C] brothers. Amen.

### Letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople

To the most blessed brothers [Note: [Col. 0219D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “To the holy and deservedly most blessed lords and brothers”] and fellow-bishops Aurelius, Valentinus, and the other beloved men established in the synod held at Carthage, Atticus, bishop.

Through our son Marcellus, your subdeacon, I received the writings of your love with every expression of joy, giving thanks to the Lord that I have deserved to enjoy the blessing of such great brothers, most blessed lords and brothers.

You write that I should send the most genuine canons established by the Fathers at the city of Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, with the attestation of faith. Who is there who would deny to his brothers the common faith or statutes confirmed by the Fathers? Therefore, through the same son of mine, Marcellus, your subdeacon, who was hastening greatly, I sent the complete canons, as they were established at the city of Nicaea by the Fathers, just as you ordered, asking that your holy congregation command many prayers to be offered for me.

And in another hand:

May our God preserve your holiness, as we desire, most holy brothers [Note: [Col. 0219D] Ae., B. R., U., “brothers. Amen.”]

## XIII. Copies of the Council of Nicaea sent on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0220D] Ae., T. 1, 2, G., “the seventh day”; B. R., “the sixth day”], after the consulship of the most glorious emperors, the Augusti Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time, to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not created, of the same substance [Note: [Col. 0220D] Ae., “not made, homousion with the Father, that is, of the same substance”] as the Father, through whom all things were made, things heavenly and earthly [U., G., “terrestrial”] [Note: [Col. 0220D] Ae., “all things in heaven and all things on earth”], who for us human beings and for our salvation descended [Note: [Col. 0220D] Ae., “who for our salvation descended”], and was incarnate and became human, suffered, and rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” or that he was made from nothing, or that the Son of God is from another substance or essence, or mutable or changeable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

To this confession of faith copies of the statutes were also attached, which were established at the great and holy synod held at Nicaea, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, and translated from Greek by Philo and Evaristus of Constantinople.

### I. Concerning those who have mutilated or castrated themselves

If anyone has been cut by physicians because of illness, or castrated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while healthy, has castrated himself, he must abstain from the clergy, and thereafter no such person is to be promoted.

Just as this is clearly stated concerning those who devise such a thing and dare to castrate themselves, so the canon admits to the clergy those who have been castrated by barbarians or by their masters and are found worthy.

### II. Concerning those who, coming from paganism, are immediately admitted to the clergy after baptism

Because many things have been done, either from necessity or otherwise, by people in haste, contrary to ecclesiastical canon—for example, people newly coming from a pagan life to the faith and catechized for only a short time being immediately brought to the spiritual bath, and, as soon as they have been baptized, being promoted to the episcopate or presbyterate—it has seemed good that nothing of this kind be done in the future.

For the one being catechized requires time, and after baptism a more extensive period of testing is necessary. The apostolic Scripture clearly says: “Not a novice, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.” But if, as time proceeds, some sin of the soul is found in such a person and he is convicted by two or three witnesses, let him cease from the clergy.

If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, as though attacking the great council, he himself will be in danger regarding the clergy.

### III. Concerning women living in the household of clergy [Note: [Col. 0221D] In the other copies, except A.: “Concerning women cohabiting with clergy”]

[Col. 0221A]

The holy council altogether forbade a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy to have a woman living with him in his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or maternal aunt, or only such persons as entirely avoid suspicion [Note: [Col. 0221D] In the other copies, except A.: “an aunt or those women alone”].

### IV. Concerning the ordination of bishops

A bishop ought above all to be ordained by all the bishops within the province. But if this is difficult, either because of urgent necessity or because of the length of the journey, then at least three bishops must assemble together, with the absent bishops consenting and responding in writing [Note: [Col. 0221D] From Ae. In A., B. R., E. 3: “with the absent bishops giving the prescribed response.” T. 1, 2: “by letters.” G.: “in writing”]; then the laying on of hands is to take place.

Confirmation of what has been done must be given to the metropolitan bishop of each province.

### V. Concerning the excommunicated

Concerning those who are excommunicated, whether they belong to the clergy or to the laity, let the judgment of the bishops in each province prevail according to the canons: those rejected by some are not to be received by others. It must, however, be investigated whether they were excommunicated through the bishop’s weakness, obstinacy, or some other annoyance.

Therefore, so that this may be investigated more appropriately, it has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that, with all the bishops assembled together, such questions may be examined; and so that those who have plainly offended the bishop may be considered reasonably excommunicated by all, for as long as it should please the community or the bishop to issue a more merciful judgment regarding them.

One council is to be held before Lent, so that, with all weakness removed, a pure offering may be presented to God; the second is to be held around autumn.

[Note: [Col. 0221D–0222D] In this passage, all copies improperly divide the phrase “it has seemed good” as though it belonged between the fifth and sixth numbers, because the marginal heading “Concerning the holding of a council” was introduced into the text.]

### VI. Concerning the primacy of metropolitan bishops

Let the ancient customs that prevail in Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis remain in force: that the bishop of Alexandria have authority over all, since a similar custom also exists with respect to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in the region of Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges proper to the metropolitan churches be preserved.

It is altogether clear that if anyone is made a bishop without the consent of the metropolitan, the great council has defined that he ought not to be a bishop. But if, by the common decision of all, two or three oppose the appointment reasonably and according to ecclesiastical canon on account of their own personal enmities, let the decision of the majority prevail.

### VII. Concerning the bishop of Aelia, that is, of Jerusalem

Since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed that the bishop of Aelia be honored, let him have the order of honor, while the dignity of the metropolitan of that same province remains intact [U., G., “with the dignity … preserved”].

### VIII. Concerning those who call themselves Cathars

[Col. 0222A]

When some of them come to the catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that those who have been ordained should remain in the clergy in this manner. Above all, however, they must make this profession in writing: that they consent to and follow the catholic and apostolic doctrines. This means that they are to communicate with bigamists and with those who have fallen during persecution, for whom a period and a fixed day have been established, and that in all matters they are to follow whatever pleases the bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church.

Wherever all of them, whether in villages or in cities, are found to be the only ordained clergy, let those who are found among the clergy remain in the same rank. But whenever they come to a place where there is a bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church, it is clear that the bishop of the Church shall have the dignity of bishop, while the one who is called a bishop among them shall have the honor of a presbyter, unless the bishop should wish him to enjoy the title of honor. If he does not wish this, he shall provide him with a place either as a chorepiscopus or as a presbyter, so that he may plainly remain in the clergy, and so that there may not be two bishops in one city.

### IX. Concerning those who have been promoted to the priesthood without examination

If any persons have been promoted to the presbyterate or episcopate without examination, and, when questioned, have confessed the sins they committed, or if they are convicted by others who testify against them, and men, contrary to canon, have laid hands upon them after their confession, the canon does not admit such persons but rejects them. For the catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.

### X. Concerning those who denied the faith during persecution and were later promoted to the clergy

Those who were ordained through the ignorance or concealment of the ordainers, if they had fallen, are not thereby protected from ecclesiastical canon [Note: [Col. 0222D] U., G., “this does not prejudice ecclesiastical canon”]. Once discovered, they are deposed [T. 2, “let them be deposed”].

### XI. Concerning those who denied the faith and remain among the laity

Concerning those who transgressed without necessity, without the surrender of their possessions, without danger, or without some similar circumstance—such as occurred under the tyranny of Licinius—the holy council decided that, although they are unworthy of humaneness, they should nevertheless receive assistance.

Accordingly, as many as sincerely repent shall spend three years among the hearers; those who have fallen shall remain bowed down for seven years; and for two years they shall communicate in prayers with the people without an offering.

### XII. Concerning those who renounced the world and returned again to secular life

Those who were called to grace and, at the beginning, displayed good works and laid aside the military belt, but afterward returned to their own vomit, so that some even paid money and sought to reenter military service through influence, shall remain bowed down for ten years after the three-year period of hearing.

In all these cases, however, the intention and the character of the repentance must be examined. Those who demonstrate their conversion in deed, not in pretense, through fear, tears, perseverance, and good works, shall, when they have completed the appointed period of hearing, rightly communicate in prayers; afterward the bishop may decide to treat them more humanely.

But those who have acted indiscriminately and have considered merely entering the church sufficient for conversion shall complete the entire period.

### XIII. Concerning those who request communion at the point of death

Regarding those who are departing from the body, the ancient and canonical law is now also to be preserved, so that those who are preparing to die are not deprived of the final assistance. But if those who were thought to be dying, after receiving communion and partaking of the offering, recover again, they shall be counted among those who communicate only in prayers.

In every case, whenever a dying person asks that grace be given to him, the bishop should reasonably grant him the offering.

### XIV. Concerning catechumens who have fallen

It has pleased the holy and great synod that they should spend three years only as hearers; after that, they should pray with the catechumens.

### XV. Concerning clergy who move from one city to another

Because of the great disturbances and seditions that have occurred, it has seemed entirely necessary to abolish the custom that is contrary to canon. If clergy are found migrating from one city to another, it must not be permitted for a bishop, presbyter, or deacon [U., G., add: “to be”] to do so.

If anyone, after the definition of the holy and great council, attempts anything of this kind or engages in such a matter, this sort of scheme shall be entirely nullified, and he shall be restored to the Church in which he had been ordained as bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

### XVI. Concerning those who do not remain in their own churches in which they were promoted

If any persons, readily exposing themselves to dangers, having neither the fear of God before their eyes nor knowledge of ecclesiastical canon, depart from the Church—whether they are presbyters, deacons, or anyone else established in the canon—they must in no way be received by another Church. Every compulsion ought instead to be imposed upon them so that they return to their own parishes. The obstinate ought to be excommunicated.

But if anyone should rashly steal away someone belonging to another Church and ordain him in his own Church, without the consent of the bishop from whom the cleric belonging to the canon had departed, such laying on of hands shall be invalid.

### XVII. Concerning clergy who receive interest

Since many among those established in the canon pursue greed and shameful profits, forgetting the holy Scripture which says, “He who has not given his money at interest,” while, when they lend at interest to others, they demand a hundredfold, the holy and great council rightly decreed that if anyone is found, after this definition, receiving interest or devising anything else for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be rejected from the clergy and excluded from the canon [Note: [Col. 0223D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U., G., “or”].

### XVIII. Concerning the privileges of presbyters

It has come to the attention of the holy and great council that in certain places or cities deacons give the Eucharist to presbyters [E., T. 2, “the Eucharist”], although neither canon nor custom has handed down that those who do not have the authority to offer should give the body of Christ to those who do offer.

It has also become known that certain deacons touch the Eucharist even before the bishops. Let all these practices therefore be abolished. Let the deacons remain in their own order, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops but inferior to the presbyters. Let them receive the Eucharist in its proper order after the presbyters, with the bishop or presbyter giving it to them. Nor may they sit among the presbyters, for if this happens it is contrary to canon and order.

If anyone refuses to obey after this definition, let him cease from the diaconate.

### XIX. Concerning those who come to the Church from Paul of Samosata

A definition has been issued concerning the Paulianists who flee to the catholic Church: they must be rebaptized without exception.

If any of them previously belonged to the clergy, then, if they have been without accusation or reproach, they are to be ordained by the bishop of the Church after baptism. But if examination finds them less suitable, they ought to be deposed.

The same procedure shall be observed concerning deacons and, in general, concerning all who belong to the same order.

We also remember the deaconesses, who are in the same condition, since they receive no laying on of hands: they are to be counted altogether among the laity.

### XX. Concerning kneeling

Since there are some who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, in all places, everyone should pray to the Lord standing, with one accord and in agreement.

Here end the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

Furthermore, it is decreed in this council that deaconesses who do not receive the laying on of hands are to be counted among the laity.

Accordingly, after the bishops had decreed all these matters as the reverence owed to the divine laws required, and after the holy council had handed down, concerning the observance of Easter, an ancient canon by which no further variation would arise among the churches, peace and faith were preserved properly and identically among the Churches of the East and West, with everything duly arranged.

We believe that these matters must necessarily be inserted from ecclesiastical history.

## Letter of the African council to Caelestine, bishop of the city of Rome

To the beloved and honorable lord and brother Caelestine, Aurelius, Valentinus, Antonius, Tutus, Servus Dei, Terentius, Fortunatus, Martinus, Januarius, Optatus, Celticius [T. 1, 2, “Celesticius”], Donatus, Theasius, Vincentius, Fortunatianus [Ae., “Fortunatus”], and the others who were present at the universal African council at Carthage.

[Col. 0225A]

We would have wished that, just as your holiness informed us through letters sent by our fellow-presbyter Leo that you had rejoiced at the arrival of Apiarius, so we too might send these writings with joy concerning his purification. In that case, both our eagerness and yours would certainly be more securely grounded, and yours would not seem premature, since what preceded still concerned hearing the case rather than having heard it.

When our holy brother and fellow-bishop Faustinus arrived among us, we assembled a council. We believe that he was sent with him for this reason: just as through his efforts Apiarius had previously been restored to the presbyterate, so now, through his labor, he might be purified from the many crimes charged against him by the people of Tabraca.

But the examination conducted by our council found such great and monstrous offenses in him that the advocacy of the aforesaid man prevailed more than judgment, and the work of a defender surpassed the justice of an examiner.

First, consider how he obstructed the entire assembly by inflicting various injuries, as though asserting the privileges of the Roman Church and wishing us to receive into communion a man whom your holiness, believing that he had appealed—although he could not prove it—had restored to communion, even though this was by no means permitted. You will learn this more accurately from reading the proceedings.

After a most laborious three-day trial had been conducted, while in our deep distress we investigated the various charges brought against him, God, the just, strong, and long-suffering judge, cut short with great efficiency both the delays of our fellow-bishop Faustinus and the evasions of Apiarius himself, by which he was trying to conceal his unspeakable crimes.

For when his grim and foul obstinacy had been crushed—an obstinacy which, through the shamelessness of denial, wished to bury such a mass of lustful filth—our God constrained his conscience [U., G., “encouraging”] and revealed to human beings the hidden things which he was already condemning in that man’s heart as in a pit of crimes. The deceitful denier suddenly burst into confession of all the offenses alleged against him, and at last, of his own accord, convicted himself of all the incredible disgraces.

Thus he turned even the hope which we had both held and desired—that he might be cleansed from such shameful stains—into lamentation, except that he mitigated our sorrow with this one consolation: his confession released us from the labor of a prolonged investigation and provided some kind of remedy for his wounds, even though his conscience resisted and gave this confession unwillingly, lord brother.

Accordingly, after offering the greeting owed to you, we earnestly beseech you henceforth not to admit so readily those who come from here to your ears, nor to wish to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated. For your veneration will easily perceive that this too was defined by the Council of Nicaea.

Although it appears that provision was made there concerning lower clergy or laity, how much more did it wish this to be observed concerning bishops, lest those suspended from communion in their own province should appear to be restored to communion by your holiness prematurely or improperly.

Let your holiness also repel, as is worthy of you, the improper refuges of presbyters and other clergy. For no definition of the Fathers has deprived the African Church of this right, and the decrees of Nicaea have most plainly entrusted both lower-ranking clergy and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans.

For they saw with the greatest prudence and justice that whatever matters arise in their own places ought to be concluded there, and that the grace of the Holy Spirit would not be lacking to each person’s care, by which equity might be perceived wisely and held most firmly by the priests of Christ.

Above all, everyone has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those who examined his case, to appeal to the councils of his own province or even to a universal council. Unless perhaps someone believes that our God can inspire the justice of judgment in just any individual while denying it to countless priests assembled in council.

Or how will an overseas judgment be valid, when the necessary witnesses cannot be brought to it because of their sex, the weakness of old age, or many other intervening obstacles [Note: [Col. 0225D] From Ae., B. R. In A. and the other copies: “could not be brought”]?

For we have found no synod of the Fathers that established that some persons should be sent as though from your holiness’s side.

As for that matter which you formerly sent through our fellow-bishop Faustinus as though it came from the Council of Nicaea, we could find nothing of the kind in the more reliable councils accepted as Nicene—those sent from the authentic records by our fellow-bishop Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, and by the venerable Atticus, bishop of Constantinople. These copies had also previously been sent through the presbyter Innocentius and the subdeacon Marcellus, by whom they were transmitted to us from them, and through those same men we sent them to your predecessor, Bishop Boniface of venerable memory.

Do not send your clerical agents at the request of certain persons; do not grant them this authority, lest we seem to be introducing into the Church of Christ the smoky arrogance of the world, whereas the Church reflects the light of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see the day of the Lord.

As for our brother Faustinus, now that Apiarius has sorrowfully been removed from the Church of Christ because of his unspeakable wickedness, we are confident that Africa will no longer endure him in his depravity [Note: [Col. 0226D] All copies: “in depravity”; perhaps “his,” or “in integrity,” as in the printed editions and the Greek version], under the moderation of your holiness and while preserving brotherly charity.

And in another hand:

May our Lord God preserve your holiness, praying for us for a long age, lord brother.

## XVIII. EIGHTEENTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, THE SEVENTEENTH OF EIGHTEEN BISHOPS, HELD IN THE SAME YEAR AS ABOVE, AT WHICH THE AFOREMENTIONED LEGATION OF THE ROMAN CHURCH WAS ALSO PRESENT, AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF THE MOST GLORIOUS EMPERORS, THE AUGUSTI HONORIUS FOR THE TWELFTH TIME AND THEODOSIUS FOR THE EIGHTH TIME, ON THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY

[Col. 0227]

At Carthage, in the secretariat of the Basilica Restituta, a delegation of the Roman Church attended this council. Bishop Aurelius sat together with Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church for the Church of Potentia in the province of Picenum in Italy; Vincentius of Culusi; Fortunatianus of Neapolis; Maurianus of Uzipara; Adeodatus of Simidicus; Pentadius of Carpis; Rufinianus of Muza; Praetextatus of Sicilibba; Quodvultdeus of Ucres [Note: [Col. 0227D] From Ae., B. R. In A., “Ugrensis.” T. 2, “Verensis.”]; Candidus of Abbir; Gallonianus of Utica [Note: [Col. 0227D] From Ae., B. R., E. 3, U., and G.: “Uticensis.” In A., “Utenensis.” In T. 1, 2, “Utinensis”], legates of the proconsular province; Alipius of Thagaste, Augustinus of Hippo Regius, and Possidius of Calama, legates of the province of Numidia; Maximianus of Aquae Regiae, Jucundus of Sufetula, Maximianus of Sufes, and Hilarius of Orreocelium [Note: [Col. 0227D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U., G., “of Orreocelium”], legates of the province of Byzacena; Novatus of Sitifis and Leo of Opta, legates of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis; Ninellus of Rusurrus, Laurentius of Icosium, and Numerianus of Rusguniae, legates of the province of Mauretania Caesariensis, chosen as judges by the universal council.

When the deacons were standing by and some matters had been completed, many bishops complained that they could not endure the delays in completing the remaining matters and were hurrying to their own churches. It therefore pleased the universal council that, from each of the several provinces, men should be chosen who would remain because other matters still had to be completed. Thus those whose signatures attest their presence remained in attendance.

### I. Concerning the excommunicated, so that they may not be admitted to accuse clergy

It therefore pleased everyone that, although the earlier decrees of the councils had already established which persons are to be admitted to the accusation of clergy, they had not expressly stated which persons were not to be admitted. For this reason we define that a person is not rightly to be admitted to an accusation if, after having been excommunicated, he remains in that excommunication—whether he is a cleric or a layman—and seeks to accuse…
will have wished.

## II. On the Persons Who Are Forbidden to Bring an Accusation against Clerics

It was likewise decided that no slaves or personal freedmen be admitted to bring an accusation, nor any whom the public laws do not admit to accuse of public crimes; nor, moreover, those stained by the mark of infamy—that is, actors and persons subject to dishonorable occupations—nor heretics, whether Pagans or Jews. Nevertheless, for all those to whom the right of accusation is denied, permission to bring an accusation in their own cases is not to be refused. [Col. 0227D]

## III. On Those Who Have Not Proved the First Charge, So That They Are Not Admitted to the Others

It was likewise decided that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, and they are unable to prove one of those charges—the one they addressed first—they are thereafter not to be admitted to bring the others. [Col. 0228A]

## IV. On the Persons Who Are Forbidden to Give Testimony against Clerics

Witnesses are not to be admitted to give testimony if they have been ordered not to be admitted to bring an accusation, nor those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household. They are also not to be admitted to give testimony before they have reached fourteen years of age.

## V. On the One Whom a Bishop Presumes to Excommunicate on the Basis of His Sole Testimony

It was likewise decided that if at any time a bishop says that someone confessed a particular crime to him alone, and that person denies it, the bishop must not consider it an insult to himself that the person is not believed solely on his testimony. If, because of the scruple of his own conscience, he says that he is unwilling to communicate with the one who denies it, then, for as long as that bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, the other bishops are not to communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may be more cautious about saying of anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence. And they subscribed:

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage. Faustinus, of Potentia in the province of Picenum. Alipius, of Tagaste, legate of the province of Numidia. Augustine, of Hippo Regius, legate of the province of Numidia. Possidius, bishop of Calama, legate of the province of Numidia. Novatus, of Sitifis, legate. Leo, of Optensis [Note: [Col. 0228D] Ae., B. R., T. 1: Moptensis], legate of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis. Maurianus, of Uzipara [Note: [Col. 0228D] Ae., B. R.: Aziparitanus]. Rufinianus, of Muzensis. Quodvultdeus, of Ucres. Candidus, of Abbir Germaniciana. Gallonianus, of Utica. Maximianus, of Aquae Regiae, legate of the province of Byzacena. Jucundus, of Suffetula, legate of the province of Byzacena. Hilary, of Orreocella, legate of the province of Byzacena. Maximianus, of Suffetanum, legate of the province of Byzacena. Ninellus, of Rusurrus [Note: [Col. 0228D] U., G.: Nunellus], legate of the province of Caesariensis. Laurentius, of Icosium, legate of the province of Caesariensis. Numerianus, of Rusguniae [Note: [Col. 0229A] T. 2: Rusugumensis; U., G.: Gunmensis], legate of the province of Caesariensis. Philip, presbyter, legate of the Roman Church. Asellus, presbyter, legate of the Roman Church.

# XIX. Council of Milevis of Two Hundred Fourteen Bishops, in Era 440

Under the most glorious emperors Arcadius, consul for the fifth time, and Honorius Augustus, consul for the fifth time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0229]

In the city of Milevis, in the secretariat of its basilica, when Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, had taken his seat in the universal council, with the deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

“Since the holy Church is one body and there is one head of all the members, it has come about, with the Lord’s will, that we should come to this Church, invited for the sake of love and fraternity. Therefore I ask your charity—for it must be believed that our coming to you is neither superfluous nor unpleasant to anyone—that matters concerning the faith, especially since the question of the Pelagians now threatens us, should first be discussed in this most holy assembly; thereafter, let some matters necessary to ecclesiastical discipline also be taken up.”

## I. Against the Pelagians, Who Say That Adam Could Have Died Even without Sinning

Therefore all the bishops who were present in this holy synod decided to establish the following, defined in the present council: whoever says that the first man Adam was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die bodily—that is, depart from the body—not on account of the merit of sin but by necessity of nature—let him be anathema.

## II. That, in Accordance with the Apostle’s Testimony, Even Infants Who Have Not Yet Committed Any Sin Are Truly Baptized for the Remission of Sins

It was likewise decided that whoever denies that newborn infants are to be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing from Adam’s original sin that is cleansed through the washing of regeneration—so that consequently the form of baptism “for the remission of sins” in them is understood to be not true but false—let him be anathema. [Col. 0229D]

For what the Apostle says—“Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned”—is to be understood in no other way than that in which the Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, has always understood it. For on account of this rule of faith, even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sins in themselves, are baptized for the remission of sins, so that through regeneration what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed in them.

## III. That God’s Grace Not Only Forgives Sins but Also Assists So That They Are Not Committed

It was likewise decided that whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as assistance so that they may not be committed, let him be anathema. [Col. 0230A]

## IV. That through God’s Grace We Know What We Ought to Do and Love It in Order to Do It

It was likewise decided that whoever says that this same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled to do what we have recognized ought to be done, let him be anathema.

For when the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up,” it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have Christ’s grace for that which puffs us up, but not for that which builds us up, since both knowing what we ought to do and loving in order to do it are gifts of God, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. Just as it is written of God, “He who teaches a human being knowledge,” so it is also written, “Love is from God.” [Col. 0230B–C]

## V. That God’s Grace Enables the Law to Be Fulfilled, Not Merely, as Pelagius Says, Making It Easier

It was likewise decided that whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us so that we may more easily fulfill through grace what we are commanded to do by free choice—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema.

For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing.” [Col. 0230D]

## VI. That, According to the Judgment of John the Evangelist, No One Can Exist without Sin

It was likewise decided that whoever thinks that what the holy apostle John says—“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” [U., G.: “we seduce ourselves”], “and the truth is not in us”—should be understood to mean that, out of humility, we ought not to say that we have no sin, but not because it is true, let him be anathema.

For the Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.” Here it is sufficiently clear that this is to be said not only humbly but also truthfully. For the apostle could have said, “If we say that we have no sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he sufficiently shows that the one who says he has no sin is speaking not truth but falsehood.

## VII. That Every Just Person Ought to Say, Not Only for Others but Also for Himself: “Forgive Us Our Debts”

It was likewise decided that whoever says that the saints say “Forgive us our debts” in the Lord’s Prayer for this reason: not to say it for themselves, because this petition is no longer necessary for them, but for the sinners who are among their people—and that therefore each saint does not say, “Forgive me my debts,” but “Forgive us our debts,” so that the just person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself—let him be anathema.

For the apostle who said, “In many things we all offend,” was himself holy and just. Why was “all” added, unless so that this statement might agree with the Psalm where it says, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight”; and with the prayer of the wisest Solomon, “There is no human being who does not sin against you”; and with the Book of holy Job, “He marks the hand of every human being, so that every human being may know his own weakness”?

For this reason, when the holy and just Daniel said in his prayer in the plural, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly,” and the other things that he there confesses truthfully and humbly, lest it be thought—as some understand it—that he had spoken not of his own sins but rather of the sins of his people, after saying, “When I prayed and confessed my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God,” he did not wish to say “our sins,” but spoke both of the sins of his people and of his own, because, like a prophet, he foresaw those who would later understand this so badly. [Note: [Col. 0231] In the remaining manuscripts, except A, which lacks the words “in prayer.”]

## VIII. That the Saints Truly Say: “Forgive Us Our Debts”

It was likewise decided that whoever wishes the very words of the Lord’s Prayer—when we say, “Forgive us our debts”—to be said by the saints in such a way that they say this humbly but not truthfully, let him be anathema.

For who could tolerate someone praying and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself, saying with his lips that he wishes to be forgiven, while saying in his heart that he has no debts requiring forgiveness?

Thus far, the chapters on the faith against the Pelagians. Now the ecclesiastical regulations are treated.

## IX. That a General Council Ought to Be Convened for Common Church Matters, but a Special Council of Each Province for Private Matters

It was first decided that the brothers should no longer be wearied by the necessity of an annual gathering, but that whenever a common matter—that is, a matter concerning all Africa—requires it, wherever letters have been sent to this see requesting a council, a synod is to be convened in the province where circumstances make it expedient. Matters that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces. [Col. 0231D]

## X. That the Metropolitan Should Sign and Send the Letters Convening the Council

It was also decided, at the request of all the bishops, that Your Holiness alone should sign all letters issued concerning the council.

## XI. That Whatever Is Established in Council concerning Heretics or Unbelievers Should Be Sought from the Emperor

It was decided that envoys sent by this glorious council against heretics and Pagans, or against their superstitions, should obtain from the most glorious emperors whatever they foresee to be useful. [Col. 0232A]

## XII. That Composed Prayers or Orations May Not Be Said Unless They Have Been Approved in Council

It was also decided that prayers or orations, or Masses, or traditions [Ae., B. R., U., G.: “prefaces”], commendations, or the laying on of hands that have been approved in council should be celebrated by all. None of these is to be said at all in the Church unless it has been considered and approved by the more prudent persons in synod, lest something be composed against the faith, whether through ignorance or zeal. [Col. 0232B]

## XIII. That Later Bishops Should Defer to Earlier Bishops and Presume to Do Nothing without Consulting Their Primates

Bishop Valentinus said:

“If your good patience permits, I shall pursue those matters that are necessary to ecclesiastical discipline. We know that in this Church of Carthage ecclesiastical discipline has always remained inviolate, so that no brother ever dared to place himself before his predecessors; rather, the lawful honors due to predecessors have always been rendered by those who came afterward, as was reasonably expected. May Your Holiness order this arrangement to be strengthened more firmly by your pronouncements.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“It would not have been fitting for us to repeat these matters unless perhaps there existed the thoughtlessness of certain persons, which would sharpen our minds to establish them. But this is a common matter, as our brother and fellow bishop [Ae., B. R., U.: ‘fellow priest’] has indicated: each of us must recognize the established rule clearly enough that later bishops defer to earlier ones and presume to do nothing without consulting their primates. For this reason, those who think that something may be presumed after disregarding their superiors ought properly to be restrained by the entire council.” [Col. 0232C–D]

All the bishops said:

“This order has been observed by our fathers and by our elders, and, with God’s favor, it will be observed by us.”

## XIV. That Bishops Should Receive Letters from Their Ordainers Giving the Date of Their Consecration

It was then decided that all who are ordained thereafter should receive from their ordainers letters signed by their hands, containing the name of the consul and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning those who are later or earlier. [Col. 0232D]

## XV. That Wherever Someone Has First Read, There He Should Remain a Cleric

It was likewise decided that anyone who has first or once read in a church is not to be taken by another church into the clerical order. [Col. 0233A]

## XVI. That Executors or Advocates Should Be Requested from the Emperor for the Affairs of the Churches

It was further decided that executors should be requested from the emperor for all the needs that the Church has, and that they should be assigned to individual churches.

It was also decided that the most glorious emperors should be asked to order the judges to provide defenders—trained advocates—whom they have requested for themselves, who are active in or hold office in the defense of ecclesiastical cases, so that, following the custom of the priests of the province, those who have undertaken the defense of the churches may have authority, whenever necessity demands it, either to resist intruders or to bring forward what is necessary, to enter the judges’ secretariats. [Col. 0233A–B]

## XVII. That Neither a Divorced Man nor a Divorced Woman May Be Joined to Another

It was also decided, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic discipline, that neither a man who has dismissed his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may be joined to another, but that they should remain as they are or be reconciled to one another.

If they disregard this, they are to be subjected to penance; in this matter, the promulgation of an imperial law is to be requested. [Col. 0233B]

## XVIII. On Those Who Do Not Communicate in Their Own Province but Communicate Elsewhere

It was decided that whoever, while not communicating in his own province, slips into other provinces or overseas regions in order to communicate is to suffer the loss of communion or of his clerical office. [Col. 0233B]

## XIX. On Clerics Who Have Sought Secular Judgment from the Emperor or Appealed to a Synod

It was decided that whoever asks the emperor to hear a public judicial case is to be deprived of his own rank. But if he requests an episcopal judgment from the emperor, this is not to harm him [U.: “benefit him”]. [Col. 0233B–C]

## XX. That No One May Travel to the Imperial Court without a Formata, and How Formatae Are to Be Made

It was decided that any cleric who wishes, because of his own necessity, to go somewhere to the imperial court must receive a *formata* from his bishop. Whoever wishes to travel without a *formata* is to be removed from communion.

If a sudden necessity arises somewhere requiring him to go to the imperial court, he must present that necessity to the bishop of the place and carry with him a written response from that bishop.

The *formatae* issued by primates or by the individual bishops of the persons concerned are to contain the date of Easter. If the date of Easter in that same year is still uncertain, the preceding date is to be added, just as it is customary to record dates after the consulship in public documents. [Col. 0233C–D]

## XXI. On Bishops Who Have Seized What They Could Have Reclaimed by Proceeding through a Synod

It was likewise decided that bishops who think that certain churches or congregations belong to their see but have not reclaimed them in such a way as to conduct their cases before judging bishops, and instead have rushed in while another person retained them—whether the congregations wished it or not—are to suffer harm in their own case.

Whoever has already done this, if the dispute among the bishops has not yet been concluded but they are still contending about it, is to withdraw if it is established that he rushed in after disregarding the ecclesiastical judges.

No one should flatter himself if he has obtained letters from the primate authorizing him to retain the church. Whether he has such letters or not, he must approach the person who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may appear that he has held peacefully the church belonging to him.

If that person raises some objection, the case is to be concluded by episcopal judges—either those whom the primate has appointed for them or those whom they themselves, with the primate’s advice, have chosen from among the neighboring bishops. [Col. 0233D–Col. 0234A]

## XXII. On Clerics Who Complain about the Judgments of Their Bishops

It was likewise decided that presbyters, deacons, or other lower clerics who have complaints in their cases against the judgments of their bishops are to be heard by neighboring bishops, and that whatever matter exists between them is to be settled by those bishops, appointed with the consent of their own bishops.
