If they think that they should appeal from those bishops as well, they may appeal only to African councils or to the primates of their provinces. Those who think that they should appeal overseas are not to be received into communion by anyone within Africa. [Col. 0234A–B]

## XXIII. On How Those Who Have Received Penance among Heretics Are to Be Received by the Church

It was decided that whenever someone converted from the heretics says that he received penance among them, each Catholic bishop must inquire where and for what reason he received penance among those same heretics. When he has demonstrated this to the bishop with reliable evidence, the Catholic bishop is to determine the period of penance or reconciliation according to the nature of the sin, as seems appropriate to him. [Col. 0234B]

## XXIV. On Bishops Who Are Negligent toward Heretics

It was likewise decided that bishops who neglect to win to Catholic unity the places belonging to their see are to be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, so that they do not delay in undertaking this.

If within six months of the day on which they were summoned they have not accomplished this, whoever is able to win those places is to have them assigned to him. This is subject to the following provision: if the bishop to whom they appeared to belong can prove that the other bishop’s negligence had been deliberately chosen by the heretics so that they might remain there with impunity, and that his own diligence had been forestalled so that his more vigilant care might thereby be avoided, then, once the episcopal judges have learned this, they are to restore the places to his see.

If the bishops between whom the case is disputed belong to different provinces, the primate in whose province the disputed place lies is to appoint the judges [U., B.: “judge the case”]. If, by common agreement, they choose neighboring judges, they are to choose either one or three. If they choose three, they must follow either the judgment of all or that of two.

No appeal may be made from judges chosen by common agreement. Whoever is proved, through contumacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been reported to the bishop of the principal see, is to give letters ordering that none of the bishops communicate with him until he obeys. [Col. 0234C–D]

## XXV. On the Matter Mentioned Above

If a bishop in the chief sees is negligent toward the heretics, he is to be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, and his negligence is to be demonstrated to him so that he cannot excuse himself.

If, within six months from the day on which he is summoned, enforcement has taken place in his province and he has not taken care to convert them to Catholic unity, communion is not to be extended to him until he fulfills this duty.

If it is proved that he has lied about their communion, saying that persons communicated whom it is established, with his knowledge, did not communicate, he is also to lose his episcopate. [Col. 0234D–Col. 0235A]

## XXVI. On Virgins Who, under the Pressure of Necessity, Are Veiled before the Age of Twenty-Five

It was likewise decided that if any bishop, because the chastity of a virgin is endangered—when either a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared, or when she has been troubled by scruple because of some danger of death, lest she die without being veiled—or at the insistence of her parents or of those responsible for her care, veils a virgin before she reaches twenty-five years of age, the council’s decree concerning that number of years is not to prejudice him. [Col. 0235A]

## XXVII. On the Bishops Who Were Retained after the Acts of the Council of Carthage in Order to Complete the Remaining Business

It was likewise decided that all the bishops who had assembled for the council should not be detained longer. The whole council therefore chose three judges from each province.

From the province of Carthage: Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and Clarus.

From the province of Numidia: Alipius, Augustine, and Restitutus.

From the province of Byzacena, together with the venerable elder Donatianus, the primate: Cresconius, Jucundus, and Aemilianus.

From Mauretania Sitifensis: Severianus [T. 1, G.: Severinianus], Casiatticus, and Donatus.

From the province of Tripolitana: Plautius, who was sent as the one legate according to custom.

All these, together with the venerable elder Aurelius, are to investigate everything. The whole council asked Aurelius himself to sign all the acts that had already been completed and all the letters.

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, subscribed.

Donatianus, of Telepte, of the principal see, subscribed.

Likewise all the bishops subscribed.

# XX. Council of Telepte, after the Second Consulship of the Most Glorious Honorius and Constantius

After the second consulship of the most glorious Honorius and Constantius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. [Note: [Col. 0235D] This council is taken from Codex Ae., since it is absent from A. and the remaining manuscripts. It has also been compared with a manuscript of excellent quality preserved in the Royal Library under the title *Works of Saint Martin of Dumio*; its variant readings will be marked with the letter D.] [Note: [Col. 0236D] D: “under the second consulship of the most glorious Honorius and Constantius.”]

[Col. 0235]

When the council had assembled in the Church of the Apostles of the congregation of Telepte, and the blessed Father Donatianus, bishop of the principal see of the city of Telepte, had taken his seat, with Januarius, Felix, Secundus, Cyrius, Victorius, Secundianus, Geta [D.: Zeta], Eunomius, Maximianus, Donatus, Cresconius, Jucundus, Sopatrus, Restitutus, Julianus, Maximianus, Tertiolus, Milicus, Maximus, Donatianus, Basilius, Papinianus, Januarius, Porphyrius, another Porphyrius, Donatus, Julianus, Tutus, Fortunius, Quintianus, Capio, and the other bishops seated with him, and also Vincentius and Fortunatianus, legates of the proconsular province sent to the council at Byzacena [D.: Byzantium], together with the rest, Vincentius and Fortunatianus said:

“Even when we were at Thusdrus, as your memory recalls with me, and when we delivered letters of the holy Siricius, bishop of the apostolic see, to be read—one of which our brother, Bishop Latonius, began to read—the indication given to us now suggests that we should present both of them. Permit them to be read.”

The bishops said:

“Let the letters of the venerable memory of holy Siricius be read, so that we may know what their text contains.”

When they were handed over, Privatus the notary said:

“Copy of the letter of Siricius, bishop of the city of Rome:

“To our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa, Siricius.

“Although various matters [Note: [Col. 0236D] From D. In Ae.: ‘Various’], when we brothers had gathered together at the relics of the holy apostle Peter, through whom the beginning of both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ originated, it pleased us—because of the many matters that had arisen, some of which were not merely cases but crimes—that henceforth each person in the Church should take care to address matters of this kind, as the apostle Paul proclaims: that a Church should be presented to God such as has neither spot nor wrinkle, lest our conscience appear contaminated by the breath of some diseased sheep [D.: ‘by the breath of a diseased sheep’].

“Therefore, after better counsel, it was decided, especially for those who could not be present because of their current bodily illness or the weariness of age, that letters of this kind should be issued, so that this form might be preserved perpetually—not letters presenting something new [D.: ‘pretending something new’], but letters by which we wish those things to be observed that have been neglected through the negligence of certain persons, although they have been established by apostolic and ancestral constitution, as it is written: ‘Stand firm and hold to our traditions, whether by word or by letter.’

“Certainly, this ought to stir your minds more intensely, most beloved brothers: that we may come before God’s presence free from every stain of this world and secure. For we who preside over congregations will not be free from guilt, since it is written: ‘From the one to whom much has been entrusted, more will be required.’

“Therefore, since we must give an account not only for ourselves but also for the people entrusted to us, we ought to instruct the people with divine discipline in humility. For certain persons have arisen who, not holding to the statutes of their predecessors, have violated the chastity of the Church through presumption, following the will of the people and not fearing God’s judgment.

“Therefore, lest we seem by silence to connive at and consent to such persons, and thereby incur the punishments of Gehenna, as the Lord says, ‘You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers,’ these are the matters which, henceforth, in view of divine judgment, it is expedient for all Catholic bishops to observe.”

## I.

No one is to dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see—that is, of the primate—for the judgment that follows the opinion of the majority is sound.

## II.

No single bishop is to presume to ordain a bishop out of arrogance, lest the benefit conferred appear stolen; for this is established as having been defined at the Council of Nicaea.

## III.

Likewise, if someone, after the remission of sins, has held a military belt of secular service, he must not be admitted to the clergy. [Col. 0237A]

## IV.

A cleric is not to take a woman, that is, a widow, as his wife.

## V.

A layman who has married a widow is not to be admitted to the clergy.

## VI.

No one is to usurp the right to ordain a cleric from another church.

## VII.

Another church is not to admit a cleric who has been rejected.

## VIII.

Those coming from the Novatians or Montanists are to be received by the laying on of hands, because they rebaptize.

## IX.

Moreover, because it is worthy, chaste, and honorable, we advise [D.: “we strive”] that priests and Levites not have intercourse with their wives, because ministers engaged in ministry are occupied with daily necessities.

For Paul writes thus to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” If, then, abstinence is commanded to lay people so that their prayers may be heard, how much more must a priest be ready at every moment, so that, secure in the purity of cleanliness, he may offer the sacrifice or be compelled to baptize?

If he has been defiled by carnal desire, what will he do? What excuse will he offer? With what shame, with what state of mind, will he presume to do this? With what conscience, with what merit, will he believe that he will be heard, when it is said, “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

Therefore I exhort, admonish, and entreat that this reproach be removed—a reproach which even the Gentiles may rightly bring against us.

Perhaps someone believes that this is permitted because it is written, “The husband of one wife.” But he did not speak of one who remains in the desire to beget children; he spoke with regard to future continence. For the one who said, “I wish that all people were as I am,” did not exclude those who were sound in body; and he declares it more openly when he says, “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit.”

Therefore, brothers, if all these matters are observed by everyone with full vigilance, ambition will cease, dissension will subside, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no place to rage, unanimity will remain, iniquity will be overcome and trampled down, love will burn with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will [D.: “delight”] of the soul.

This is indeed the peace of our God, which the Savior himself, already near his passion, commanded to be preserved and left to us as an hereditary right, saying, “My peace I leave you.” And the Apostle says that we should remain of one mind, thinking one thing in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through contention or empty glory, but pleasing not human beings but our God and Savior.

If we faithfully wish to obey all these commands, the Lord will guard our bodies and our souls on the day when he will repay each person according to his works.

If anyone, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, wishes to wander from the rule of this canon, let him know that he will be excluded from our communion and will suffer the punishments of Gehenna.

Moreover, mercy must be exercised with judgment. For hands ought to be extended to such persons, provided that they do not drag one who is thus running into ruin.

Given at Rome in the council of eighty bishops, on the ninth day before the Ides of January [D.: “the Kalends of January”], after the consulship of Honorius Augustus and Bauto. [Col. 0238B–C]

# Councils of Gaul (C)

# XXI. First Council of Arles, Held by Numerous Bishops in the City of Arles, under Bishop Marinus, in the Time of the Emperor Constantine, at the Same Time as the Council of Nicaea, at Which Three Hundred Eighteen Bishops Were Present

To the lord and most holy Bishop Silvester, the assembly of bishops who were gathered in the town of Arles sends word of what we have decreed by common counsel, so that all may know what they ought to observe in the future.

## I. That Easter Be Celebrated on One Day and at One Time

Concerning the observance of the Lord’s Pascha: it is to be observed throughout the whole world on one day and at one time, and, according to custom, you are to send letters to all. [Col. 0237D–Col. 0238D]

## II. That Everyone Remain Where He Is Ordained

Concerning those who have been ordained as ministers in any places whatsoever: they are to remain in those places.

## III. That Those Who Lay Down Their Arms in Time of Peace Be Excommunicated

Concerning those who lay down their arms in time of peace, it was decided that they be kept from communion. [Col. 0239A]

## IV. That Charioteers Be Excommunicated While They Drive

Concerning charioteers who are faithful: it was decided that, for as long as they drive, they be separated from communion.

## V. That Those Who Assemble in Theaters Be Excommunicated

Concerning theatrical performers, it was likewise decided that, for as long as they practice their profession, they be separated from communion.

## VI. That Converts in Illness Receive the Laying on of Hands

Concerning those who wish to believe while suffering from illness, it was decided that hands ought to be laid upon them.

## VII. On Governors, That They Communicate with the Knowledge of Their Bishop

Concerning governors who are faithful and advance to the governorship, it was decided that, when they have been promoted, they receive ecclesiastical letters of communion, with the provision that, in whatever places they exercise office, the bishop of that place is to care for them, so that they are excluded from communion only when they begin to act against public discipline. The same is to apply to those who wish to administer public affairs. [Col. 0239B]

## VIII. That Converts from Heresy Who Have Been Baptized in the Trinity Receive the Laying on of Hands

Concerning the Arians, who follow their own rule by rebaptizing, it was decided that if some people from this heresy come to the Church, they are to be asked about the Creed. If it is found that they were baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, hands alone are to be laid upon them so that they may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, they do not confess this Trinity, they are to be baptized. [Col. 0239B–C]

## IX. That Those Who Carry Letters from Confessors Receive Other Letters

Concerning those who bring letters from confessors, it was decided that, once those letters have been taken from them, they receive other letters of communion.

## X. That If Someone’s Wife Commits Adultery, He May Not Take Another Wife

Concerning those who discover their wives in adultery, if they are themselves young faithful men and are forbidden to marry, it was decided that, as far as possible, counsel should be given to them not to take another wife while their own wives are still alive, even if those wives are adulteresses. [Col. 0239C]

## XI. That Faithful Women Who Join Themselves to Pagans Be Excommunicated

Concerning faithful girls who join themselves to Pagans, it was decided that they be separated from communion for some period of time. [Col. 0239D]

## XII. That Clerics Who Lend at Interest Be Excommunicated

Concerning ministers who lend at interest, it was decided that they be kept from communion according to the divinely given rule.

## XIII. That Traitors against Their Brothers, Sacred Vessels, or the Scriptures Be Deposed with Beatings

Concerning those who are said to have handed over the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0239D] Ae., B. R., E, 3, T. 1, 2, U.: “the holy Scriptures”], or the Lord’s vessels, or the names of their brothers, it was decided by us that whoever among them is detected in the public records is to be removed from the clerical order, not merely by bare words.

For if it is discovered that the same persons ordained others, and if the status of those whom they ordained remains valid, their ordination is not to be prejudiced.

Since there are many who appear to oppose the Church and think that they ought to be admitted under an excuse through bribed witnesses, they are absolutely not to be permitted to do so unless, as we have said above, they have proved their case through public records. [Col. 0239D–Col. 0240A]

## XIV. That False Accusers of Their Brothers Be Excommunicated until Death

Concerning those who falsely accuse their brothers, it was decided that they not communicate until death, since, according to Scripture, a false witness may not remain unpunished.

## XV. That Levites Are Not to Offer Sacrifice
Concerning deacons, whom we have learned to make offerings in many places, it was decreed that this must by no means be done.

## XVI. That penitents should communicate where they receive prayer

[Col. 0240B] Concerning those who are separated from communion for their offense [Note: [Col. 0239D] Ae., B. R., E, 3, T. 1, 2, U., “the Holy Scriptures.”], it was decreed that wherever they have been excluded, in that same place they are to receive communion.

197

## XVII. That no bishop should trample upon another bishop

No bishop is to trample upon another bishop.

## XVIII. That a deacon should offer nothing without a priest

[Note: [Col. 0239D] T., 2, U. 1, G., “should act.”]

Concerning urban deacons: they are not to presume too much for themselves, but must reserve honor for priests, so that they do nothing of this kind without the latter’s knowledge.

## XIX. That a place for offering sacrifice be given to a visiting bishop

Concerning visiting bishops who customarily come to the city, it was decreed that a place be given to them so that they may offer sacrifice.

## XX. That no bishop be ordained without three bishops

[Col. 0240C] Concerning those who arrogate to themselves the right to ordain a bishop alone, it was decreed that no one presume to do this unless he has taken seven other bishops with him; if he cannot have seven, he must not dare to ordain with fewer than three.

## XXI. That a cleric transferring elsewhere be excommunicated

Concerning priests or deacons who customarily abandon the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves to other places, it was decreed that they are to minister in those places, so that if, having abandoned their own places, they wish to transfer themselves elsewhere, they are to be deposed.

## XXII. That apostates who return late not be received except through worthy penance

Concerning those who apostatize and never present themselves to the Church, nor even seek to do penance, and who later, seized by illness, request communion, [Col. 0240D] it was decreed that communion not be given to them unless they recover [U., G., “gain strength”] and produce worthy fruits of penance.

[Note: [Col. 0239D] At the beginning of the Second Council of Arles, all the manuscripts contain the names of the bishops who attended this first Synod of Arles; therefore both the number of bishops and canon eighteen of the following council clearly prove that they must be transferred to this place.]

From Sicily: Sixtus, bishop of Syracuse, and Florus, deacon; from the province of Campania, Protinus, bishop of the city, and Agrippa and Tutila, deacons; from the province of Apulia, Pardus, bishop, and Crescens, deacon; from the province of Dalmatia, Theodorus, bishop, and Agathon, deacon; from the city of Rome, whom Sylvester, bishop, sent: Claudianus and Avitus, priests, Eugenius and Cyriacus, deacons; from the province of Italy, Orosius, [Col. 0241A] bishop, and Nazareus, lector; from the province of the Viennenses, from the city of Arles, Marinus, bishop, Salamas, priest, Nicatius, Afer, Ursinus, and Petrus, deacons; from the province mentioned above, that of the Viennenses, Verus, bishop, and Beclas, exorcist; from the city of Vaison, Damnas, bishop, and Victor, exorcist; from the city of Orange, Laustinus, priest; from Porta, Innocentius, deacon, and Agapius, exorcist; from the province of Gaul, from the city of Rheims, Imbethausius [B. R., Bethausius], bishop, and Primigenius, deacon; from the city of Rouen, Avidianus, bishop, and Nicetius, deacon; from the city of Autun, Petius, bishop, Amandus, priest, and Philomatius, deacon; from the city of Leudona, Votius [Note: [Col. 0241B] Ae., Notius. BR., U., G., Nuvotius.], bishop, and Petulius, exorcist; from the city of Cologne, Maternus, bishop, and Marinus, [Col. 0241B] deacon; from the province of Aquitaine, from the city of Vagalum, Genialis, bishop; from the city of Bordeaux, Orientalis, bishop, and Flavius, deacon; from the city of Trier [U., Treverorum], Agricius, bishop, and Felix, exorcist; from the city of Toulouse, Martinus, bishop, and Leoncius, deacon; from the province of Britain, Eburius, bishop; [Col. 0242A] from the city of Lyon, Restitutus, bishop; from the city of Clunia, Adelphus, bishop, and Soter, priest; from the city of Rheims, Liberius, bishop, and Florentius, deacon; from the province of Baetica, Sabinus, priest; from the city of Ursulentum, Natalis, priest, and Cytherius, deacon; from the city of Tarragona, Probatius, priest, and Castorius, deacon; from the city of Zaragoza, Clementius, priest, and Rufinus, exorcist; from the city of Bastigentum, Termarius, priest, and Victor, lector; from the province of Caesarian Mauritania, Fortunatus, bishop, and Deuterius, deacon; from the province of Sardinia, Quintus [T. 2, Quintinus], bishop, and Aumonius, priest; from the province of Africa, Caecilianus, bishop, and Sperantius, deacon; from the city of Onina, Lampadius, bishop; from the city of Utica, Victor, bishop; from the city of Beneventum, [Col. 0242B] Anastasius, bishop; from the city of Turbustum, Faustus, bishop; from the city of Cocofeltum, Surgentius, bishop; from the province of Numidia, Victor, bishop; from the city of the Virenses, Vitalis, bishop; from the harbor of the city of Rome, Gregorius, bishop; from Centumcellae, Epictetus, bishop; from the city of Ostia, Leontius and Macarius, priests.

## XXII. SECOND COUNCIL OF ARLES

[Col. 0241]

199

### I. That neophytes not be ordained clerics

[Col. 0241C]

A neophyte is not to be ordained to the office of deacon or priest.

### II. How married men are to be advanced to the priesthood

No one bound by marriage may be admitted to the priesthood unless a conversion of life has first taken place.

### III. That no cleric or deacon keep a strange woman in his household

If any cleric from the rank of deacon onward presumes to have a woman in his household, other than a grandmother, mother, sister, daughter, granddaughter, or a wife who has converted with him, he is to be regarded as excluded from communion; the same penalty is also to strike the woman if she refuses to separate from him.

### IV. That no cleric admit a girl into his storeroom or private quarters

[Col. 0241D]

No deacon, priest, or bishop is to admit a girl, whether freeborn or enslaved, into the private quarters of his storeroom.

### V. That when a bishop is ordained, three bishops ordain him with the metropolitan’s consent

A bishop may not be ordained without the metropolitan, or without a letter from the metropolitan, or without three bishops of the same province, in such a way that the other provincial bishops are informed by letters and indicate by their reply that they have given their consent. If any dispute should arise between the parties, the metropolitan is to agree with the larger number in the election.

### VI. Concerning a bishop ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge

Let this be clear above all: one who has been appointed bishop without the metropolitan’s knowledge is, according to the great synod, not to be regarded as a bishop.

200

### VII. Concerning those who mutilate themselves

Those who mutilate themselves because they do not know how to resist carnal desire are unable to attain the clerical office.

### VIII. Concerning those who receive another’s excommunicates

If anyone, after the prohibition, presumes to receive another’s excommunicated person, whether cleric or layman, let him know that he has made himself guilty against the brotherhood and will have to give an account before the council.

### IX. That Novatians not be received into communion

A Novatian is not to be received into communion unless, having embraced the faith of penance, he condemns his former error.

### X. Concerning those who compromised during the persecution

[Col. 0242D] Concerning those who compromised during the persecution: if they voluntarily denied the faith, the Council of Nicaea established the following regarding them: they are to spend five years among the catechumens and two among those admitted to communion, but they are not to presume to receive communion while among the penitents. Nevertheless, it is to remain in the bishop’s power and judgment that, if he sees them sincerely mourning their error and practicing penance, he may receive them into communion out of ecclesiastical mercy.

### XI. Concerning those who, overcome by punishment, were compelled to sacrifice

But if some, overcome by suffering and the weight of persecution, were compelled to deny the faith or sacrifice, they are to remain suspended from communion for two years among the catechumens and three years among the penitents.

### XII. Concerning those who died while doing penance

[Col. 0243A]

Concerning those who died while doing penance, it was decreed that no one should be dismissed without communion; rather, because he honored penance, his offering is to be accepted.

201

### XIII. That no one abandon his own church for any necessity

No cleric of any order—neither deacon, priest, nor bishop—is to abandon his own church for any reason whatsoever. Instead, he is either to be excommunicated by every means or compelled to return. If, after spending some time elsewhere, a cleric is ordained by the bishop of that place while residing in another church against the will of his own bishop, such an ordination is to be considered invalid.

### XIV. That a cleric not accept interest

[Col. 0243B] If any cleric lends money at interest, or wishes to become a tenant of another’s property, or practices any kind of business for the sake of shameful profit, he is to be deposed from the clergy and excluded from communion.

### XV. That a deacon neither sit before a priest nor distribute the Eucharist

A deacon is not permitted to sit among the priests in the sacristy, nor may he presume to distribute the body of Christ in the presence of a priest. If he does so, he is to withdraw from the office of deacon.

### XVI. That Photinians and Paulianists be baptized

Photinians, or Paulianists, ought to be baptized according to the regulations of the Fathers.

### XVII. Concerning baptized heretics

But the Bonitians, who come from the same error and whom it is clear are baptized in the Trinity like the Arians, need only be received into the Church with chrism and the laying on of hands, provided that, when questioned, they confess our faith with their whole heart.

### XVIII. That the synod be convened at the metropolitan’s discretion

A synod is to be convened at the discretion of the bishop of Arles. We read that, in the time of Saint Marinus, a council and assembly was held in that city from all parts of the world. If anyone, after being notified, is absent on account of illness, let him send a representative in his place.

### XIX. That no bishop be permitted to depart from the synod

If anyone neglects to attend, or thinks that he should leave the assembly of the brothers before the council is dissolved, let him know that he has separated himself from communion with the brothers; nor may he be received unless he has been absolved at the following synod.

202

### XX. Concerning charioteers and theatrical performers who are believers

Concerning charioteers and theatrical performers who are believers, it was decreed that, for as long as they practice those professions, they are to be separated from communion.

### XXI. If someone marries after receiving penance

Women doing penance who presume to marry another man after their husband’s death, or who live with an outsider in a suspicious or forbidden relationship, are to be barred from the thresholds of the Church together with that man. The same was decreed to be observed regarding a man placed under penance.

### XXII. That penance be given to married persons with consent

Penance is not to be given to married persons except with their consent.

### XXIII. Concerning priests who have not destroyed pagan worship

If, in the territory of any priest, unbelievers light torches or venerate trees, springs, or stones, and he neglects to eradicate this [T. 2, “overturn it”], let him know that he is guilty of sacrilege. The owner or originator of the practice, if admonished and unwilling to correct it, is to be deprived of communion.

### XXIV. Concerning accusers of the brothers

Those who are convicted of having falsely brought capital charges against their brothers [Note: [Col. 0243C] U., “convicted of having brought capital accusations against them”] are not to receive communion until death, as the great synod previously established, unless they repent with worthy satisfaction.

### XXV. Concerning apostates if they do not return

Those who, after making a holy profession of religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, are not to receive communion at all without penance. We also order that they not be admitted to the clerical office, and that none of them presume, after penance, to wear secular dress. If he does presume, he is to be regarded as separated from the Church.

## XXIII. THIRD COUNCIL OF ARLES, OF TWELVE [Note: [Col. 0243D] In the remaining manuscripts, except A., “fourteen”] BISHOPS, HELD IN ERA 461, UNDER THE REIGN OF THE EMPEROR MARCIAN, WITH OPILIO AND VINCOMALO AS CONSULS, ON 8 JULY

[Col. 0243]

[Col. 0243D] Since, by the will of God, the Lord’s priests had assembled in the city of Arles for the dedication of the basilica of Saint Mary, it seemed fitting and reasonable to them first to examine, with the greatest care, the observance of the canons, and to determine by salutary counsel how the ecclesiastical rule might be maintained by them.

### I. That a deacon not be ordained before twenty-five years of age, nor a priest before thirty

And because it is recognized that the regulations of the ancient Fathers concerning the ordination of clerics have not been observed in their entirety, as would be fitting, lest the Lord’s priests perhaps be wearied by the importunate and disorderly petitions of certain people and compelled to transgress what has so often been commanded, they define among themselves that the following is to be observed: no bishop is to presume to ordain a deacon before he has completed twenty-five years. No layman is to receive the honor of the episcopate or priesthood before the previously mentioned conversion [Ae., BR., U., “conduct of life”] or before thirty years of age.

### II. That a layman not be ordained before one year of conversion

Although the ancient Fathers prescribed longer periods to be observed for laymen, nevertheless, because the increasing number of churches makes it necessary for us to ordain more clerics, we have established this among ourselves, without prejudice to the ancient canons: no metropolitan is to grant the dignity of the episcopate to any layman, nor may the other bishops presume to confer the honor of the priesthood or diaconate, unless a full year of conversion has first been completed.

### III. That bigamists, penitents, and husbands of divorced women not be advanced to the priesthood

No one is to dare to ordain to the aforementioned honors a penitent, a bigamist, or a husband of a woman who has remarried. Although nearly all the canons already contain these provisions [T. 1, “all the canons”], nevertheless, lest the importunity or unjust urging of supplicants—as we have already said—should insinuate itself upon any priest, it was necessary that the Lord’s priests now impose a stricter rule upon themselves. Therefore, whoever from this day forward presumes to ordain a cleric contrary to the provisions stated above is not to presume to celebrate Masses for a full year from the day on which this can be proved against him [T. 2, “to conduct them”]. If anyone refuses to observe this and, acting against the agreement of the brothers, presumes to celebrate Masses, let him know that he is estranged from the charity of all the brothers; for it is fitting that one who scorns to observe what the holy Fathers salutarily established should feel the severity of ecclesiastical discipline.

### IV. Concerning foreign clerics who are defended by others

[Col. 0246A]

And if some cleric, evading the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, should wander away, whoever receives him and not only fails to reconcile him with his own bishop but also presumes to defend him is to be deprived of communion with the Church.

Caesarius, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have reread and signed this definition of my holy brothers and myself. Contumeliosus, bishop: I have consented and signed. Florentius [E. 3, Florentinus], bishop: I have signed. [Col. 0246B] Cyprianus, bishop: I have signed. 206 Montanus, bishop: I have signed. Florentius [Note: [Col. 0245C] The names Florentius and Cyprianus appear to have been repeated. Therefore, we correctly stated from manuscript A. that twelve bishops attended this council, although the other manuscripts report that fourteen attended.], bishop: I have signed. Cyprianus, bishop: I have signed. Coelestinus [Ae. BR., Coelestius], bishop: I have signed. Porcianus, bishop: I have signed. Eucherius, bishop: I have signed. Cataphronius, priest, sent by my lords Agricius and Severus, bishops: I have consented and signed. I, Desiderius, priest, sent by my lord John, bishop: I have consented and signed. Leontius, priest, sent by my lord Constantinus [Ae. T. 1, Constantius], bishop: I have signed. [Col. 0246C] I, Hemeterius, sent by my lord Gallicianus, bishop: I have consented and signed.

## XXIV. COUNCIL OF VALENCE, OF TWENTY BISHOPS, HELD IN ERA 413, UNDER THE EMPERORS THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER AND VALENTINIAN, WITH THEODOSIUS FOR THE SEVENTEENTH TIME AND FESTUS AS CONSULS, ON 12 JULY

[Col. 0245]

[Col. 0245D] To the most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Gaul and the five provinces: Faegadius [Note: [Col. 0245] From Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, U. In A. and the remaining manuscripts: Egadius. In T. 2: Fegatius.], Eumerius, Florentius, Artemius [Ae., Anthemius], Aemilianus, Britto, Justus, Euphodius [Ae., Euphrodius; U., Eufomius], Rhodamius, Eortius, Cretus, Concordius, Constantius, Paulus, Antherius, Felix, Neoterius, Urbanus, Simplicius, and Vincentius, bishops, greeting in the Lord.

When all the matters at Valence that had begun as causes of division had been concluded and, in God’s name, settled in a better condition, some of the Fathers made a useful and religious proposal: that we should reconsider matters which, because of the Church’s holiness, we can neither accept, nor yet condemn merely because of an established custom. For the seed of such vices has so grown throughout all the churches that recourse to complete remedies is not easy—certainly not without embarrassment to those whom the matter concerns. Therefore, brothers, after long and measured deliberation, a policy of caution was maintained that would both remove scandals and preserve the holiness of the Church.

207

### I. Concerning bigamists: that they not be consecrated

It was therefore resolved that, after this synod—which comes late to the aid of such unlawful practices—no bigamist or husband of a woman who has remarried may be ordained as a cleric. Nor is it to be investigated whether they stained themselves with this unhappy condition after having received the divine sacraments or while still pagans.

### II. That a woman who, after vowing herself to God, marries or commits adultery be assigned penance

Concerning girls who have vowed themselves to God: if they voluntarily turn to earthly marriage, we have decreed that the following is to be observed: penance is not to be given to them immediately, and when it has been given, their communion is to be deferred until they have fully satisfied God, to the extent that the matter requires [Ae., BR., E. 3, “of those same women”].

### III. That those who, after baptism, worship idols or have been polluted by incest do penance

Concerning those who, after the one holy washing, have polluted themselves either with profane sacrifices to demons or with incestuous intercourse, we have judged that the following form of discipline should be observed: according to the Council of Nicaea, access to satisfaction is not to be denied them, nor is the door of consolation to be closed to their unhappy tears through despair. They are to do penance until the day of death, yet not without hope of remission, which they must fully hope to receive from the One who alone possesses the right to grant it [Col. 0247B] and is so rich in mercy that no one should despair. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.

### IV. That a priest or deacon be deposed if he confesses a crime against himself

Nor did we consider it foreign to the Church’s welfare to write the following, brothers, so that you might know that anyone under the order of the diaconate, priesthood, or episcopate who says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime is to be removed from the aforementioned orders, whether he is guilty because of a true confession or because of a falsehood. For in such cases he cannot be absolved unless they have spoken against themselves, so that what was said against others might be punished, since anyone who is the cause of his own death is a greater murderer. May divine mercy guard you forever, most beloved brothers.

### Another letter of the same bishops mentioned above

To the most beloved brothers, the clergy and people of the church of Fréjus: Faegadius, Eumerius, Florentius, Artemius, Aemilianus, Britto, Justus, Euphodius, Rhodamius, Eortius, Constantius, Paulus, Cretus, Concordius, Antherius, Neoterius, Nicetius, Urbanus, Felix, Simplicius, and Vincentius, bishops, greeting in the Lord.

Although our brother Benedictus proposed matters concerning the most holy Acceptus that are worthy of a prudent and Christian man, and although he declared with what eagerness all of you were requesting his elevation to the honor of the priesthood, nevertheless, since a synod had already decreed that such ordinations were to be excluded because they could not occur without scandal, we could not grant to one person what was denied to the others. Although we were not unaware that many, out of embarrassment, and some, through fear of undertaking the priesthood—signs which are certainly signs of holiness—had falsely accused themselves in order to reject the honor, nevertheless, since almost everyone’s judgment is inclined toward what is worse and material for disputes is sought through the disparagement of God’s priests, the synod resolved that whoever had said either true or false things about himself should be believed on the basis of his own testimony and immediately removed from the rank that ought to be free from every scandal. May divine mercy protect you forever.

[Note: [Col. 0247] U., “Council of Turin of eighty bishops.” G., “Council of Turin of seventy bishops.”]

## XXV. COUNCIL OF TURIN

[Col. 0247]

[Col. 0247C] To the most beloved brothers established throughout Gaul and the five provinces: the holy synod that assembled in the city of Turin.

209–210 When, at the request of the provinces of Gaul, we priests had assembled in the city of Turin and, with the Lord as author and mediator, had taken our seats in that city’s church, after hearing the allegations of the bishops—namely, those who had been gathered for our judgment—the following form of decision proceeded concerning each matter [Note: [Col. 0247D] U., “this decision of ours proceeded”], so that the canons’ provisions might be preserved for the sake of peace and useful medicine might be applied to the intentions of many.

### I. That whoever proves his city to have been a metropolis retain the primacy

At the outset, the holy man Proculus, bishop of the city of Marseille, said that he ought to preside as metropolitan over the churches that appeared to be situated in the second province of Narbonensis and that the ordinations of the chief priests in that province ought to be carried out by him. He asserted that those churches had either been his own parishes or that their bishops had been ordained by him in those same churches. The bishops of that region, on the other hand, defended a different position and maintained that a priest of another province ought not to preside over them.

The holy synod therefore judged, in consideration of peace and harmony, that deference should be shown not so much to his city—which is situated in another province, whose extent we did not fully know—as to Proculus himself, so that he might stand before them like a father before his sons, with the honor of primacy. For it seemed fitting that, although they were not at all bound by the unity of a single province, they should nevertheless be united by an affection of piety.

This arrangement is to be observed for him alone during his lifetime: in the churches of the second province of Narbonensis that are shown either to have been his parishes or to have had their bishops ordained as his disciples, he is to hold the dignity of primacy. The parties are to observe the following provision, which, although perhaps superfluous, is nevertheless usefully recalled: Saint Proculus himself, like a pious father, is to honor his fellow priests as sons, and the priests of the aforementioned province, like good sons, are to regard him as their parent and show one another an affectionate regard, fulfilling what the blessed Apostle says: “Going before one another in honor, not setting your minds on high things, but consenting to humble things.”

Furthermore, concerning the bishops of the cities of Arles and Vienne, who were disputing before us over the honor of primacy, the holy synod decreed that whichever of them proves his city to be a metropolis is to obtain the honor of primacy over the whole province and, according to the command of the canons, is to have authority over ordinations. [Col. 0249A] Certainly, to preserve the bond of peace, this more useful arrangement was decreed: if it pleases the bishops of the aforementioned cities, each may claim for itself the cities within the province that are nearer to it and may claim those churches [Note: [Col. 0249C] Ae., B. R., U., “visit”] that are shown to be closer to its towns, so that, mindful of unanimity and harmony, neither may disturb the other by appropriating at a greater distance what properly belongs to the other.

### II. That bishops who act contrary to the regulations be deprived of their honor

It was also decreed that, for perpetual discipline, a written record be made of what the holy synod decided concerning the bishops Octavius, Ursio, Remigius, and Tryferius, who were accused of having arrogated to themselves authority over the ordination of priests. Until now, it appears that indulgence had been granted to them on the understanding that, having been warned by this authority, they would henceforth attempt no such usurpation, since they had defended themselves in this matter by claiming that they had not previously been summoned.

Accordingly, the synod judged that if anyone from now on acts against the statutes of the elders, he is to know that the person ordained will be deprived of the honor of the priesthood, and that the one who ordained him will retain no authority whatsoever in ordinations or councils. This decision will prevail not only concerning the bishops mentioned above, but also concerning all who, deceived by a similar error, commit such ordinations.

### III. Concerning laymen who bring accusations against clerics

Concerning Palladius, a layman who had brought a serious accusation against the priest Spano, between whom the bishop Tryferius testified that he had investigated the circumstances of the same accusation, the authority of the council decreed that Palladius should remain under the same sentence by which he had been punished by the priest Tryferius at the time of the investigation. The council showed him this mercy: Tryferius himself is to have the power to release him whenever he wishes.

### IV. Concerning clerics who are excommunicated by their bishop because of misconduct

[Col. 0250A]

The holy synod also made the following decision concerning the priest Exuperantius, who had committed many serious offenses against his holy bishop Tryferius and had provoked him with frequent insults, even doing certain things against ecclesiastical discipline, for which reason he had been deprived by him of the Lord’s communion: his restoration is to lie in the power of the one who had authority over his expulsion. That is, he is to receive the grace of communion when either Exuperantius has made satisfaction or Bishop Tryferius has deemed it appropriate.

211

### V. Concerning one who wishes to separate from heretics in order to be received into the Catholic Church

The holy synod further decreed that, since the bishops of Gaul who are in communion with Felix had sent envoys, if anyone wishes to separate himself from Felix’s communion, he is to be received into our fellowship of peace according to the letters previously issued by Ambrose, of venerable memory, bishop and priest of the Roman Church, which were read aloud in the presence of the envoys at the council.

### VI. That one person neither promote another’s cleric nor receive one who has been expelled

Nor was it to be omitted that the synod’s decision established the following: according to the canonical regulations, no one is to receive another’s cleric, nor dare to ordain him in another rank for his own church, nor receive into communion one who has been expelled.

### VII. Concerning those who have been ordained contrary to a prohibition or have fathered children while in office

[Col. 0250C] Concerning those who have been ordained contrary to a prohibition or have fathered children while in the ministry, the authority of the synod decreed that they not be permitted to advance to the higher ranks of orders.

May our Lord deem it worthy to preserve you unharmed for a very long age, most beloved lords and brothers.

## XXVI. COUNCIL OF RIÈZ, OF THIRTEEN BISHOPS, HELD IN ERA 477, UNDER THE EMPERORS THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER AND VALENTINIAN, WITH THEODOSIUS FOR THE SEVENTEENTH TIME AND FESTUS AS CONSULS

[Col. 0249]

[Col. 0249D] When, by the will of the Lord, we had assembled at the church of Rièz and a remedy was being sought for the transgression committed at the church of Embrun—where it was clear that, with the sacred canons of the Church and the revered constitutions of the Fathers neglected in every respect, an invalid semblance of ordination had been rashly presumed by two men meeting together without the presence of three bishops, without letters from the provincial bishops, and without the metropolitan’s authority—the matter was discussed at length in the hearts of all, with no less grief at the fall of those who had presumed than at the upheaval of the church itself.

First, because, by the Lord’s will, a desire not for vengeance but for remedy had taken firm possession of everyone’s heart through priestly counsel, and because the exact force of the canons had been examined in every statement, it was decreed [Note: [Col. 0249] From B. R., T. 1, 2. In A. and the other manuscripts: “it was evident”] that, just as the unlawful acts that had been presumed were to be annulled, so charity might absolve those who had presumed them, although discipline compelled their disgrace. This was especially so because those who had fallen into such perversity had, from the very first day of their fall, offered prayers in every direction, repented of their fault, and attributed it either to ignorance or to deception. For even if it seemed incredible that a priest could have been ignorant of priestly statutes, it was nevertheless less serious than if he had admitted with shameless lips that he had trampled upon what he knew.

213

### I. That one ordained by two bishops not be regarded as a bishop

[Note: [Col. 0251D] The manuscripts contain a double title: the one printed here and another reading, “Concerning the punishment of the two who presumed to perform the ordination”; the latter has been deleted to avoid repetition.]

[Col. 0251A]

Accordingly, it was decreed that those who had arrogated to themselves such disorderly and unstable acts should, through an encounter with mercy and charity, be received into communion and affection, but in such a way that they would know that, according to the recent and most salutary definition of the Council of Turin [T. 2, “of Turin”], to their perpetual disgrace during this life, they would henceforth take part in no ordinations and attend no ordinary councils, since nothing salutary could be expected from those who had offered such detestable examples of such great corruption.

Above all, it seemed necessary to provide carefully for the church of Embrun, which, having been deprived of a lawful priest for four months short of two years, had been made more seriously ill. Its innocent clergy, as has been established, mindful of discipline, had been harassed by the insolence and varied disturbances of certain laymen and had recently endured, among its priests and ministers, threats and quarrels, the most bitter violence, and a dangerously destructive slaughter. The expectation of the good and of those mindful of discipline could not be postponed, lest the wishes of the obstinate and restless should appear to be indulged. Their conspiracies and schemes, insofar as they could be detected, had to be punished by ecclesiastical correction for the past and forestalled for the future.

Therefore, we too judged that the ordination which the canons define as invalid must be annulled, since the presence of three bishops had been omitted, letters from the provincial bishops had not been sought, and the metropolitan’s will had likewise been disregarded; in short, nothing had been demonstrated that could make the man a bishop.

### II. Concerning the removal of the man whom two men rashly presumed to ordain improperly

[Note: [Col. 0251D] The manuscripts contain a double title: the one printed here and another reading, “That one ordained by two bishops may at some time be a bishop”; the latter was deleted because it is irrelevant.]

Accordingly, it was resolved, by the will of the Lord, that this man who had improperly been made bishop should be removed and that an entirely proper arrangement of the brothers should be established, with ecclesiastical tradition preserved.

Yet because this holy synod cared not only for discipline but also for mercy, the following considerations arose. Armentarius had recently returned to that church with much insolence and flattery; nevertheless, it was also noted that he had departed before being admonished, that some priests had encouraged him in this very matter, and that he had returned to a private household. He had sent letters to the clergy themselves in which he announced his desire for the episcopate, although he acknowledged that he had not obtained it, asking that his name be erased and affirming that the very act rashly presumed upon him would from that time be disordered and invalid.

The decision therefore inclined rather in this direction: for a young man brought up in the fear of the Lord, it was more favorable that he had sometimes shown sound judgment in a thoroughly corrupt undertaking than that he had yielded in some respect to youthful impulses. Accordingly, setting aside the matters that, upon his return, implicated him in guilt without any possibility of excuse, the Lord’s priests who were present at this council preferred to pass over the same man as innocent and free from condemnation, under the concession to him of the title of a visiting bishop or fellow bishop.

### III. Concerning heretical and schismatic bishops who come to the Catholic faith, and what they are to observe
What, therefore, the Council of Nicaea established concerning the reception of certain schismatics—that each person should observe this within his own territory—the present assembly likewise decrees that all must observe it: namely, that any one of the brethren whom charitable counsels may have prompted to do such a thing may cede one of his parish churches [T. 2: grant] in which he might enjoy, as the same canon says, either the title of co-bishop [Note: [Col. 0252D] From all the manuscripts. In A., “bishops.”] or, as they call it, communion as a stranger [Col. 0252B] [Ae., “may enjoy”].

First, therefore, it is decreed that this be permitted in any province except Alpes Maritimae. If he should intrude into any part of that province, he shall, as an instigator of evils and one impatient of peace, undergo the condemnation that he has provoked against himself. Moreover, if anyone communicates with him while he transgresses any of the provisions established, he shall be excluded from communion with everyone.

Next, this is to be done in any place except in public, so that no place may be assigned to him that is ennobled by the appearance or rank of a court or city. It is further added that he must never presume to offer in cities or in the absence of bishops; nor ordain even the lowest cleric; nor do so in that church which the mercy of anyone may have granted to him. Nor may any bishop, or anyone later appointed to the episcopate, yield to him in any respect during his beginnings, as though out of reverence for his age. Nor may he anywhere usurp anything belonging to episcopal functions, except in the church which someone’s mercy has allowed him to obtain. In that church alone he may confirm neophytes and offer before presbyters.

If at any time, prompted by another’s charity, he changes his residence, he shall not receive a place of rest in another church unless he has renounced the former one; nor shall he ever hold the governance of two churches. In the church ceded to him, its ministers must be ordained by the bishop of the city.

Since mention has been made of ministers, and some were said to have been discovered by him and rashly advanced in the clergy although excommunicated, it has been decreed that those who were so appointed are to be deposed. Those against whom no stain of conduct prejudiced their case are, according to the judgment of the priest of Embrun who is to be appointed, either to be retained in the ministry of their own church or transferred to him wherever he may have lived. They may bless the people whom they receive by permission of this constitution; as determined above, they may confirm neophytes in one and the same church; and in castles and villages, wherever he may come, he may do everything before presbyters. This is entirely forbidden to him in cities [Note: [Col. 0252D] T. 2: “he must in no way presume to do this.”].

## IV. That a presbyter should both bless and confirm [T. 2: sanctify] a neophyte [Note: [Col. 0253D] In the manuscripts there is a double title: the one given here and another reading, “That presbyters should privately bless the faithful who desire it”; the latter has been deleted so that it may not be repeated.]

[Col. 0253A]

Amid these brief deliberations, it seemed right to open to every presbyter the power of blessing in households, in the countryside, and in private homes, according to the desire of the faithful—a practice already found in some provinces. It also seemed right that this same power be granted in the parish churches, though more in rural places than in cities. In the church in which he was ordained, he shall also have the right to consecrate a virgin, just as he has the right to confirm a neophyte. In every respect, as though giving evidence of the greatest indulgence, he must always conduct himself as inferior to a bishop and superior to a presbyter. Let him live in the fear of the Lord, following the commands and wishes of all the saints; let him cultivate peace and serve God; let him give thanks for the synod’s benevolence toward him [Col. 0253B]; and let him always acknowledge that he is unworthy of the concessions granted to him and unequal to those denied him.

## V. That the bishop who buries a bishop should take charge of his church [Note: [Col. 0253D] In the manuscripts there is a double title: the one given here and another reading, “Regarding the church to be organized after the death of a bishop”; the latter has been deleted so that it may not be repeated.]

All the priests who had assembled jointly judged that they should guard against scandals of this kind. Accordingly, provision was made against such rashness by this definition, so that henceforth it should be observed that no one should approach the church that had lost its bishop unless the bishop of a neighboring church came at the time of the funeral. He must immediately assume the strictest care of that church, so that before the ordination no opportunity might be given for discord and the overturning of the clergy amid innovations [Col. 0253C]. Thus, whenever such an event occurs, the inspection, description, and inventory of the neighboring churches are entrusted to the neighboring bishops.

## VI. That no bishop be ordained without the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0253D] In the manuscripts there is a double title: the one given here and another reading, “That no one should come to an ordination unless invited by letters from the metropolitan”; the latter has been deleted so that it may not be repeated.]

All these matters shall be carried out from the time of the funeral until the seventh day after the deceased’s death, with the mandate of the metropolitan being reported to the distinguished church. He shall be buried together with all the holy [Ae.: associate] bishops. No one should approach the church that has lost its chief priest unless invited by letters from the metropolitan, lest he be deceived by the people and appear to have wished to employ force.

## VII. Regarding those who have been seditious toward churches or their ministers, that is, priests [Note: [Col. 0253D] This canon and the next are taken from U.; they are absent from the other manuscripts.]

It has come to this holy synod’s attention that certain unknown persons, through the arrogance of pride, are attempting to mutilate the published institutions of the canons [Note: [Col. 0254D] Baluzius says perhaps “more fully edited”; we, however, consider this word superfluous.] by the counsel of the ancient enemy. These are not humble but proud, and persist in sedition against the churches of God or his priests. The whole synod decreed that such persons be separated from the Church of God and from the assembly of Catholics, and that, after being excommunicated, they be banished into exile, so that, once corrected through the satisfaction of repentance, they may be admitted again to holy communion, though not to the clergy.

## VIII. That a council be held twice a year

[Col. 0254A]

It seemed sufficient that a council of bishops be held twice a year in each province: once after the third week of the Paschal festival, so that the council might be completed in the fourth week thereafter, that is, at mid-Pentecost. The bishops of the province who reside in the larger cities, that is, the metropolitan cities, shall admonish the others.

The second council shall be held on the Ides of October, at the time of the vintage. Among the Greeks this day is found to be the tenth day of the month Hyperberetaeus. At these councils presbyters, deacons, judges or curials, and private persons ought all to be present; and all who consider themselves wronged should state their cases and await the synodal judgment.

Nor should it be permitted for anyone to hold councils among themselves without the presence of the metropolitans [Note: [Col. 0254D] The passage is certainly corrupt; the words “without the presence of the metropolitans” appear to be redundant.], or to act without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishops, whose judgment is established as having issued a truthful and wholly reliable decision concerning every case.

I, Hilary, bishop, in accordance with what pleased all the holy bishops who subscribed with me, following the statutes of the Fathers, have subscribed to these definitions on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0254D] B. R., T. 1, 2: “the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.”], in the seventeenth consulship of the Emperor Theodosius and the consulship of Festus, an honorable man [Note: [Col. 0254D] Ae., B. R., U.: “Festus, a most illustrious man”; “the honorable consuls.”].

I, Severianus, bishop, was present at this definition and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above [Note: [Col. 0254D] Ae., B. R.: “on the day and in the consulships written above”; and likewise in all the subscriptions. T. 2: “on the day of the council written above.”].

I, Audentius, bishop, was present at these statutes on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Julius [T. 2: Julianus], bishop, was present at these statutes and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above [Col. 0254C].

I, Arcadius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Auspicius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Severus, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Valerianus, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Nectarius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Asclepius, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Theodorus, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

I, Maximus, bishop, was present at these definitions and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above [Col. 0254D].

I, Vincentius, presbyter of Constantianus, ordained by him, was present [Note: [Col. 0254D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U.: “I was present during his lifetime.”] and subscribed on the day of the consulship written above.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] B. R., T. 1, 2: “Arausian.” In the other manuscripts: “Aurasiac.”]

# XXVII. COUNCIL OF ARAUSIO, OF SIXTEEN BISHOPS, HELD IN THE YEAR 479, IN THE TIME OF THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER, ON THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF NOVEMBER, DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF CYRUS, IN THE CHURCH OF JUSTINIANUS

[Col. 0255]

## I. Regarding heretics who are converted when in danger of death

[Col. 0255A]

If heretics placed in danger of death desire to become Catholics, and a bishop is unavailable, it is decreed that they be signed by a presbyter with chrism and blessing.

## II. That no minister depart without chrism

None of the ministers who undertake the office of baptizing should ever proceed without chrism, because it has been agreed among us that a person is chrismated only once. If, because of some necessity, someone has not been chrismated at baptism, the priest shall be reminded of this at confirmation. Since among us there is only one blessing of the chrism itself, the chrismation is not to be repeated as though anything were thereby prejudiced, but is to be regarded as unnecessary.

## III. Regarding penitents who depart from the body [Note: [Col. 0256D] T. 2: “Regarding un-reconciled penitents who depart from the body.”]

[Col. 0255B]

Those who depart from the body after accepting penance are to be admitted to communion without the imposition of the hand of reconciliation. This is sufficient consolation for the dying, according to the definitions of the Fathers, who appropriately called such communion viaticum. If they survive, they are to remain in the order of penitents, so that, once the necessary fruits of penance have been demonstrated, they may receive legitimate communion with the imposition of the hand of reconciliation.

## IV. Regarding clerics who wish to do penance

Penance is not to be denied to clerics who desire it.

## V. Regarding those who take refuge in a church so that they may not be handed over

Those who have taken refuge in a church ought not to be handed over, but should be defended through reverence for the holy place and through intercession.

## VI. Regarding slaves who take refuge in a church

[Col. 0255C]

If anyone believes that the slaves of clerics who have taken refuge in a church should be seized as his own slaves, let him be struck with the strictest condemnation throughout all the churches.

## VII. Regarding freedmen entrusted to the church, that they not be oppressed

If anyone attempts to impose servitude, service, or a tenant’s condition upon those who were manumitted in the church or entrusted to the church by testament, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment.

## VIII. Regarding those who presume to ordain another’s cleric

[Col. 0255D]

If anyone thinks that a cleric established elsewhere should be ordained, he must first determine that the man will live with him; even then, this must not be done without consulting the bishop with whom he previously lived. He must not presume to ordain someone who perhaps, and not without cause, has long remained unordained by another.

## IX. Regarding those who have ordained citizens of another place

[Col. 0256A]

If anyone has ordained citizens of another place or persons established elsewhere, lest they be accused of being irregular in any respect, let them either recall those persons to themselves or obtain the favor of those with whom they live.

## X. Regarding bishops who have built a basilica not on their own property but in another’s diocese

If any bishop plans to build a church in the territory of another city, whether for the convenience of his own estate or of an ecclesiastical property, or for any other convenience of his own, once permission to build has been granted—for it is impious to prohibit such a vow—he must not presume to conduct the dedication. That is reserved in every way to the person in whose territory the church rises.

The bishop who built it is granted this privilege: that the bishop whose territory it is may ordain whichever clerics he wishes to see in the builder’s property, or, if they have already been ordained, may consent to his retaining them. The entire governance of that church shall belong to the bishop in whose city’s territory the church has arisen [Col. 0256B].

If, moreover, any secular person builds a church and thinks that someone other than the bishop in whose territory he builds should be invited, both the person whom he wishes to favor contrary to constitution and discipline, and all the bishops who are invited to such a dedication, shall abstain from the assembly. If anyone exceeds these limits, he shall be called to account; if anyone exceeds them, let him recognize the proper order.

## XI. Regarding bishops who receive another’s excommunicated person

It has been decreed that a bishop shall incur liability if, after being warned that someone has been excommunicated, he presumes to communicate with that person without the reconciliation of the one who excommunicated him. Thus, if reconciliation should intervene, all matters concerning the justice or injustice of the recent excommunication are to be reserved for the next synod.

## XII. Regarding those who suddenly become mute, and that they may receive both baptism and penance

A person who suddenly becomes mute may, as has been established, be baptized or receive penance if he has either testimony of his will or of the past expressed in the words of others, or testimony of his present will in his own sign.

## XIII. Regarding those who are mentally deranged

Whatever belongs to piety is to be bestowed upon the mentally deranged.

## XIV. Regarding baptized demoniacs

Baptized demoniacs, if they take care about their purification, entrust themselves to the care of the clergy, and obey their admonitions, are in every way to share in the power of the sacrament—whether for protection against the attack of the demon [U., G.: demons] by which they are afflicted, or for purification, the greater purity of whose life is already being displayed [Col. 0256D].

## XV. That demoniacs and catechumens be consulted regarding baptism [Note: [Col. 0257D] This canon, absent from A., is taken from the other manuscripts.]

[Col. 0257A]

Demoniacs and catechumens are to be consulted regarding baptism insofar as necessity demands or opportunity permits.

## XVI. That demoniacs not be advanced to the clergy

Those who have at any time been publicly seized by such an affliction are not only not to be admitted to any clerical order; if some have already been ordained, they are to be removed from the office imposed upon them.

## XVII. That the sacramental offering be consecrated together

When the chest [or pyx] and chalice are brought in, they are to be consecrated with the addition of the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 0257D] From all the manuscripts. In A.: “when the chalice and paten are to be brought in.”].

## XVIII. That catechumens hear the Gospels

Henceforth it has been decreed that the Gospels be read to catechumens [Col. 0257B] in every Church of our provinces.

## XIX. That catechumens not approach the baptistery

Catechumens are never to be admitted to the baptistery.

## XX. That catechumens not receive the blessing with the faithful

Catechumens are to be separated, insofar as this can be guarded against, even during the private prayers of the faithful, and instructed to withdraw themselves and to present themselves separately to be signed or blessed [Note: [Col. 0257D] The word “catechumens” is taken from U.; it is absent from A. and the other manuscripts.].

## XXI. That two bishops must not make a bishop [Note: [Col. 0257D] In the manuscripts there is a double title: the one given here and another reading, “Regarding the rejection of one whom two men have presumed to ordain as bishop”; the latter has been deleted so that it may not be repeated.]

In our provinces it has been decreed concerning presumptuous persons that, if it should happen that two bishops make someone a bishop against his will, the authors being condemned, the person who suffered the force should himself be substituted in one of their churches. If, however, his life is suitable [Col. 0257C], he is nevertheless to be ordained in place of the other who has been deposed. If two men have done this voluntarily, he too shall be condemned, so that the ancient statutes may be observed with greater caution.

## XXII. That married clerics must not become deacons unless they profess continence

But it was further decided [Note: [Col. 0258D] Ae.: “It was further decided”] that henceforth married men are not to be ordained deacons [Note: [Col. 0258D] U.: “we decree that married men are not to be ordained unless…”], except those who have first professed chastity with the intention of conversion.

## XXIII. Regarding those found incontinent after receiving the diaconate

If anyone, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found to be incontinent with his wife, he shall be removed from office.

## XXIV. Regarding incontinent clerics

[Col. 0257D]

Regarding those who, having previously been ordained, have fallen into this same offense, the judgment of the Council of Turin is to be followed, by which they are ordered not to be advanced any further [T. 2: “of the Council of Turin”].

## XXV. Regarding proven men

As for suitable and especially proven men, whom the seriousness of their life compels to be bound to the clergy [Note: From B. R., T. 1, 2. In A., Ae., E. 3: “whom grace will have favored.” In U.: “whom gratuitousness compels.”], if they have happened to enter into a second marriage, they are not to receive any rank beyond that of subdeacon or any ecclesiastical dignity [Col. 0258A].

## XXVI. Regarding women deacons, who are not to be ordained

Women deacons are in no way to be ordained. Those who already exist are to submit their heads to the blessing that is bestowed upon the people.

## XXVII. Regarding women who have professed widowhood before a bishop

A profession to preserve widowhood, made before a bishop in the secretarium and accompanied by the bishop’s imposition of the widow’s garment, must not be violated. Anyone who abducts such a woman, or she herself if she abandons such a profession, is rightly to be condemned.

## XXVIII. Regarding those who have professed chastity, if they violate their profession

In either sex, those who abandon professed chastity are to be regarded as violators of their profession, and all such persons are to be helped through legitimate penance.

## XXIX. That no bishop leave the council without consent or excuse himself from going to the council

We wish and decree that the matters we subscribe, together with the agreement of those who gave their consent, henceforth be regarded as ratified among us and our people. We do not pass over those who refuse to be present at a synod, whether in person, through their consent, or by sending legates in their place. Let it not be that those who despise the statutes of the Fathers should please themselves above us—statutes by which it has been made sacred for us to assemble twice a year, difficult though that is for us because of the circumstances of the times.

We add that we wish to append similar provisions in future documents for the welfare and remedies of the churches [Col. 0258C], so that no assembly may be dissolved without notice of another assembly. Accordingly, in the following year, if it is granted by the permission of the Lord and our God Jesus Christ, we shall hold an assembly on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, at Justinianus’s place in the territory of Arausio. It is announced so far in advance through this assembly so that there may be neither freedom to make excuses nor compulsion to issue invitations.

We shall notify each of you ourselves of the day and place, reporting in copies the matters established by us. Those who were absent we leave to the care of our most blessed brother Hilary, so that they may be notified by copies of these decisions sent to them [Col. 0258D].

After all this, the matter of human frailty arose: if any bishop should fall into illness, weakness, or some dullness of understanding, or lose the use of speech, he must not permit presbyters to conduct matters that are performed only by bishops in his presence; instead, he must summon a bishop and entrust to him whatever must be done in the church.

I, Hilary, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Claudius, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Constantianus, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Audentius, bishop, have subscribed [Col. 0259A].

I, Agrestius, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Julius, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Auspicius, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Theodorus, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Maximus, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Eucherius, bishop, have subscribed, awaiting the assent of my fellow provincial holy priests concerning these matters.

I, Nectarius, bishop, have subscribed [Col. 0260A].

I, Justus, bishop, have subscribed.

Gevetius, bishop, has subscribed.

I, Augustalis, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Ingenuus, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Superventor Solonius, bishop, have subscribed.

I have subscribed and reviewed this on behalf of my father, the bishop Claudius.

# XXVIII. FIRST COUNCIL OF VASIO, HELD IN THE YEAR 480, UNDER AUSPICIUS, BISHOP OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH, IN THE TIME OF THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER, DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF DIOSCORUS, ON THE IDES OF NOVEMBER

[Col. 0259]

## I. That Gallican bishops not be investigated within Gaul

[Col. 0259B]

After deliberation, it pleased us that bishops coming from the Gallican provinces into Gaul should not be investigated, but that it should be sufficient if no one has forbidden them communion with anyone. For among those living nearby and almost mutually known, the upright require testimony less than the corrupt require denunciation and formal accusation.

## II. Regarding penitents who die suddenly, that their offerings be received

For those who, having accepted penance, live in the good course of life with satisfactory contrition, but are sometimes overtaken by an unexpected death in the fields or on journeys without communion, their offering is to be received, and their funerals and subsequent memory are to be honored with ecclesiastical affection [Col. 0259C]. It is impious to exclude from the saving sacred rites the commemoration of those who, striving toward those same rites with faithful devotion, declare themselves unworthy of the life-giving mysteries by considering themselves guilty for a longer time and desiring to be restored in greater purity, yet are intercepted without the sacramental viaticum—though perhaps a priest would not have thought it right to deny them the fullest reconciliation.

## III. That no one receive chrism from another bishop

In each territory, presbyters or ministers are to request chrism from their own bishops every year as the Paschal solemnity approaches, not from nearer bishops according to their pleasure, nor through just anyone belonging to the clergy. If there is some necessity or the ministers are occupied, it may be sent through a subdeacon, because it is dishonorable to entrust the highest matters to inferiors [Col. 0259D].
