It is best, however, that the person who will use it in administering it should himself receive it; if something prevents this, then at least the person whose duty it is to arrange the sacrarium and receive the sacraments.

## IV. That those who retain the offerings of the dead be excommunicated

Those who retain the offerings of the dead and delay handing them over to the churches are to be expelled from the Church as faithless persons [Note: [Col. 0259] The manuscripts contain the words “Regarding their condemnation,” which have been deleted because they are redundant]. It is certain that this aggravation of divine piety reaches the emptying out of faith: the faithful who depart from the body are deprived of the fullness of their vows, and the poor of food contributed and necessary support [Col. 0260B]. Such persons are to be regarded as killers of the needy and as people who do not believe in the judgment of God. Hence one of the Fathers inserted in his writings the following apt judgment: “To steal something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege.”

## V. That one who does not submit to his bishop’s judgment should appeal to the synod

If anyone does not submit to the judgment of his bishop, let him appeal to the synod.

## VI. That an excommunicated person humble himself so that he may be reconciled more quickly

Whatever useful things are necessary for the churches in the present time are to be brought forward honorably from the letter of Saint Clement and received reverently by all the faithful, especially the clergy. Among these matters, one particular point has pleased us, apart from the venerable antiquity, and we strengthen it by our present statutes. The blessed martyr mentioned above recalls it as an institution of the most blessed apostle Peter, saying:

“But you ought also to understand certain things yourselves, if there are matters which he himself, because of the plots of evil men, cannot state more openly and clearly. For example, is he hostile to someone because of his deeds? Do not wait for him to say to you, ‘Do not be friends with that man.’ Rather, you ought prudently to observe and comply with the will of the one who has charge of the Church, without communion; withdraw from the one toward whom you perceive him to be hostile, and do not speak with those with whom he does not speak. Thus, when each person who is at fault desires to recover the favor of all of you, he may hasten more quickly to be reconciled to the one who presides over all, and through this return to salvation when he begins to obey the admonitions of the ruler.”

And so forth, including the matters set out below concerning the friends of those who are hostile to the truth. Let the clergy henceforth know that it will be charged against them, and the people of the faithful that it will be counted as their fault, if anyone is recognized as an opponent of evils and a subverter of discipline in this matter.

## VII. That accusers not be heard in trivial cases, but be examined in criminal cases

It further pleased us to restrain the license to accuse, even if any such levity exists among our order. If a bishop judges that someone should be kept from communion, and if he rises for the humiliation and correction of a brother, let the others entreat him and let him yield to the brother concerned, after applying correction and warning [Col. 0261A].

But if he thinks someone should be condemned for a crime, he must understand that he himself is to be examined by his accuser. For it is right that matters proved to one person should be proved to everyone.

## VIII. That a bishop rebuke another’s cleric when he sins

If a bishop knows himself to be aware of another’s crime but cannot prove it, he must say nothing. Rather, he should work privately with that person toward contrition through secret admonitions. If, after being admonished, the person becomes more obstinate and publicly thrusts himself into communion, then, even if the bishop who judges him guilty lacks proof when rebuking him, the man may nevertheless be ordered, for a time and because of the greater authority of his position, to withdraw from those who know nothing of the matter [Col. 0261B]. Meanwhile, so long as he can prove nothing, he remains in communion with everyone except the bishop who judges him guilty.

## IX. That whoever finds an exposed child should notify the church

Regarding exposed children, since a widely voiced complaint has arisen that they are now exposed not to mercy but to dogs, and since the human mind, though bent by the commandments of mercy, hesitates to take them in for fear of accusations [Note: [Col. 0261B] In the manuscripts: “unfortunate through the commandments”], it seemed right that the following be observed.

In accordance with the statutes of the most faithful, most pious, and most august emperors, whoever takes up an exposed child must notify the church and record the notification. Nevertheless, on the Lord’s Day the minister shall announce from the altar that an exposed child has been taken in, so that the church may know. Within ten days from the day of exposure, the child is to be reclaimed if anyone proves that he recognizes it. For the collector, in return for the mercy shown during those ten days, gratitude is to be rendered according to his preference, either immediately by the person or perpetually with God.

## X. That anyone who reclaims an exposed child contrary to the established procedure be regarded as a murderer

[Col. 0262B]

If, after this most careful sanction concerning exposed children collected according to this procedure, anyone should become a reclaimer or accuser, he is to be regarded as a murderer.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] This council is absent from E. 3.]

# XXIX. SECOND COUNCIL OF VASIO

[Col. 0261]

## I. Regarding the conduct of presbyters

[Col. 0261B]

It has been decided that all presbyters established in parishes, according to the custom which we know is observed with considerable benefit throughout all Italy, should receive into the house where they themselves appear to live as many young readers as they have who are unmarried [Col. 0261C]. Like good fathers, they should strive to nourish them spiritually, teach them to prepare psalms, devote themselves to divine readings [U.: instruct them], and educate them in the law of the Lord, so that they may provide worthy successors for themselves and receive eternal rewards from the Lord.

When they have reached mature age, if any of them wishes to have a wife because of the weakness of the flesh, he must not be denied the power to marry.

## II. How homilies are to be recited by deacons

For the edification of all the churches and the benefit of the entire people, it has also pleased us that we grant presbyters the power to preach the word not only in cities but also in all parishes. If a presbyter is prevented by some illness from preaching in person, the homilies of the holy Fathers are to be recited by deacons [Col. 0261D]. If deacons are worthy to read publicly what Christ spoke in the Gospel, why should they be judged unworthy to recite publicly the interpretations of the holy Fathers? [U., G.: “are they unworthy?”]

## III. That “Kyrie eleison” and “Sanctus” be said frequently

Because a sweet and exceedingly salutary custom has been introduced not only at the apostolic see but also throughout the eastern provinces and those of Italy—namely, that “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) be said more frequently, with great devotion and contrition [Col. 0262B]—it has pleased us also that this most holy custom [Note: [Col. 0262D] T. 1, 2: “this holy statute”] be introduced into all our churches, God willing, at morning prayer, at Mass, and at Vespers.

At every Mass, whether at morning prayer, during Lent, or at those celebrated in commemoration of the dead [Col. 0262C], “Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus” (“Holy, Holy, Holy”) is always to be said in the order in which it is said at public Masses. For so holy, sweet, and desirable a voice, even if it could be said day and night, could not produce weariness.

## IV. That the pope’s name be recited in the churches

It also seemed right to us that the name of the lord pope, whoever presides over the apostolic see, be recited in our churches.

## V. That it be said: “As it was in the beginning”

Because, on account of the cunning of heretics who blaspheme by saying that the Son of God was not always with the Father but began to exist at a particular time, the words “As it was in the beginning” are said after the Gloria not only at the apostolic see but also throughout the entire East, Africa, and Italy [Col. 0262D], we too have decreed that this be said in all our churches.

Caesarius, rereading this Catholic rule of our definition in the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 0262D] B. R., T. 1, 2: “Caesarius, bishop, in the name of Christ,”], have subscribed.

And it was made known on the ninth day before the Ides of November, during the consulship of Decius the Younger, a most illustrious man. Seventeen bishops subscribed to this constitution.

Because we know that the matters written below are also sufficiently necessary for all the churches [Col. 0263A], it seemed just and reasonable that we join them to the titles of the canons written above [Col. 0264A], among other provisions of the synodal constitution of the apostolic see.

# XXX. COUNCIL OF AGDE, OF TWENTY-FIVE BISHOPS, HELD IN THE YEAR 544 [Note: [Col. 0263D] Ae.: “in the year 543”]

[Col. 0263]

[Col. 0263A]

In the twenty-second year of the reign of King Alaric, on the third day before the Ides of September, when we had assembled in the name of the Lord in the city of Agde, in the basilica of Saint Andrew, we sat down to deliberate concerning the discipline and ordination of clerics and bishops, and concerning the interests of the churches. First, it pleased us that the canons and statutes of the Fathers should be read in order. After they had been read [Note: [Col. 0263D] U.: “after they had been read, they defined.” In A. and the other manuscripts, the words “the canon of the first decision pleased us” must be added to complete the sentence.].

## I. Regarding clerics married twice, that they not minister

[Col. 0263B]

It has been decided that, regarding men married twice or husbands of women who had been married before, although the statutes of the Fathers decreed otherwise, those who have been ordained up to this time, out of consideration for mercy, may retain only the title of presbyter or deacon. Such presbyters must not presume to consecrate, nor such deacons to minister.

## II. Regarding contumacious clerics and those slow to perform their office

Contumacious clerics are to be corrected by the bishops according to what the order of their dignity permits. If any, inflated by the pride of their former rank, should perhaps despise communion, neglect frequenting the church, or fail to fulfill their office, let them be granted communion as strangers. When penance has corrected them, they shall be restored to the register and recover their rank and dignity.

## III. Regarding bishops who excommunicate the innocent or those guilty of only minor offenses

[Col. 0263C]

If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons or those culpable of only minor offenses, and perhaps refuse to receive them when they hasten toward reconciliation, they are to be admonished by letters from the neighboring bishops of whatever province. If they refuse to comply [BR., T. 1, 2: “to spare them”], communion is not to be denied them by the other bishops until the time of the synod [Note: [Col. 0264D] From T. 1, 2. In A. and the other manuscripts: “communion is to be denied them by the bishops.”], lest those who have been excommunicated, through the sin of the excommunicator, perhaps be overtaken by death after a long time.

## IV. Regarding those who defraud the church of their own offerings or those of their relatives

Clerics and secular persons who persist in retaining offerings of their parents, whether donated or left by testament [Col. 0263D] [U.: “presume to retain”], or who think that what they themselves have donated to churches or monasteries should be taken away, are to be excluded from the churches as killers of the poor, just as the holy synod has decreed, until they restore it.

## V. If a cleric commits theft from the church

If any cleric commits theft from the church, he shall be granted communion as a stranger.

## VI. If anything has been left to a bishop by anyone

[Col. 0264A]

The bishops, moreover, to whom, once established in the highest priesthood, something is left or donated by outsiders—whether jointly with the Church or separately—shall reckon it among the Church’s assets, not as their own property but as something left to the Church, since the donor is evidently offering it for the redemption of his soul, not for the benefit of the priest. For just as it is right that the priest should possess what has been left to the Church, so also the Church should possess what is left to the priest. Yet whatever is perhaps left by fideicommissum, whether to a priest or to the Church, for the future benefit of someone else, the Church will not be able to reckon or retain among its own assets.

### VII. Concerning Church property: how bishops are to possess it, and how Church slaves are to be manumitted by a bishop

As the ancient authority of the canons has commanded, bishops shall possess the small houses and little slaves of the Church, or the vessels used in the ministry, entrusted to their faithful care, with the Church’s full right intact; that is, they must not presume either to sell them or to alienate, through any kind of contract, property from which the poor live. But if a definite necessity should compel the disposal of something for the Church’s necessity or advantage, whether by usufruct or indirect sale, the matter requiring the sale must first be verified before two or three neighboring or provincial bishops; and, after priestly examination, the sale that has been made must be confirmed by their signatures. Otherwise, the sale or transaction will have no validity.

If a bishop should grant freedom to certain deserving Church slaves, it was decided that the freedom bestowed should be safeguarded by his successors, together with what the manumitter conferred upon them into freedom [Note: [Col. 0264D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2: “in freedom”]. Yet we order that this be limited to twenty solidi, a small plot of land, a little vineyard, or a modest lodging. Whatever more has been given, the Church shall reclaim after the manumitter’s death. We permit small or less useful possessions of the Church to remain in use by pilgrims or clerics, without prejudice to the Church’s right.

### VIII. Concerning clerics who take refuge with secular persons

It was also decided that if a cleric, abandoning his office because of discipline, should perhaps take refuge with a secular person, and the person to whom he appeals should provide him the protection of support, both shall be expelled from communion with the Church.

### IX. Concerning priests and deacons who return to marital intercourse

It was also decided that if married deacons or priests should wish to return to the bed of their wives, the ordinance of Pope Innocent or the authority of Bishop Siricius shall be observed. But if that ecclesiastical rule of life and discipline which was sent by Bishop Siricius to the provinces is found not to have reached certain people, forgiveness shall be granted for their ignorance [U., G.: “for their ignorances”], so that thereafter they may begin to abstain completely and retain the ranks in which they were found, without being permitted to rise to higher ones. It should be counted as a benefit to them that they do not lose the very position they retain.

But if any are discovered to have known the manner of life sent [U., G.: “dispatched”] by holy Bishop Siricius, yet not to have immediately cast away the desires of lust, they must by every means be removed—those who, after learning the admonition, judged pleasure preferable to what ought to be put first.

### X. That no cleric may live with unrelated women

Also, for the preservation of life and reputation, we specifically command that no cleric be joined to an unrelated woman by any association or familiarity. Not only must no unrelated woman enter his house, but he himself must not have permission to visit an unrelated woman. He may have the freedom to live only with his mother, sister, daughter, or granddaughter, if he has or wishes to have such relatives. Concerning these relationships, it is impious to suspect anything other than what nature has established.

### XI. That no cleric admit a woman into the storeroom or private quarters

It was decided that female servants or freedwomen be removed from the storeroom, from the private ministry, and from the same residence in which the cleric lives.

### XII. That fasting be observed on Saturdays throughout Lent

It was also decided that all the Churches, except on Sundays during Lent, should fast even on Saturday, by priestly ordinance and under threat of strict discipline.

### XIII. That the Creed be preached to the candidates eight days before Easter

It was also decided that the Creed be publicly delivered by all the Churches on one day—that is, eight days before the Lord’s Resurrection—to those preparing for baptism in the church.

### XIV. That the altar be both anointed and blessed

It was decided that altars be consecrated not only by anointing with chrism but also by priestly blessing.

### XV. How the older and how the younger [B. R., T. 2: “the younger persons”] are to receive penance

When penitents seek penance, they shall receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon the head, as has everywhere been established. If they have not cut their hair or changed their clothing, they shall be rejected; and unless they have performed penance worthily, they shall not be received. Penance should not readily be entrusted to young people because of the weakness of their age. Nevertheless, the viaticum must not be denied to anyone at the point of death.

### XVI. At what age deacons are to be ordained

A bishop must not by any means entrust the blessing of the diaconate to anyone under twenty-five years of age. But if married young men agree to be ordained, the consent of their wives must also be sought, so that, after a separate bedroom has been assigned and a religious commitment made, they may be ordained once they have adopted this common way of life.

### XVII. At what age bishops and priests are to be consecrated

No metropolitan shall presume to ordain a priest or bishop before the age of thirty—that is, before he has reached the age of a mature man—lest, because of age, they be blamed for some error, as has happened more than once.

### XVIII. Concerning laypeople and the times when they ought to receive communion

Laypeople who have not received communion at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, or Pentecost must not be regarded as Catholics or counted among Catholics.

### XIX. At what age nuns are to receive the veil

Nuns, however approved their life and conduct may be, shall not receive the veil before their fortieth year.

### XX. Concerning clerics who grow their hair long

Clerics who grow their hair shall be forcibly shorn by the archdeacon, even against their will. They shall not be permitted to wear or possess clothing or footwear except what is suitable for religious observance.

### XXI. That the greater solemnities be celebrated in the cities

If someone wishes to have an oratory in the countryside, outside the parishes in which the lawful and customary assembly is held, we permit Masses to be celebrated there on the other festivals, by proper arrangement, for the sake of the household’s exertions. But Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, and any other days regarded as especially great festivals must be celebrated only in cities or in the parishes.

If any clerics wish to celebrate or hold services in these oratories on the festivals mentioned above without the bishop’s command or permission, they shall be expelled from communion.

### XXII. That a priest or cleric may not sell or donate Church property

Although it is superfluous to define again a matter that is known and prohibited by the ancient canons, nevertheless, so that greed or dishonesty may more easily be restrained, we decree what all the authorities command: city or diocesan priests and clerics shall hold Church property, preserving the Church’s right, insofar as the bishops have permitted; they must by no means presume to sell or donate it.

If they do so, the sale shall be invalid, and they shall restore the Church’s loss from whatever private property they possess, and shall be deprived of communion.

### XXIII. That a younger cleric not be placed before an older one

A bishop shall not place a later-appointed person before an earlier-appointed one whose life is not blameworthy, unless the latter, perhaps carried away by pride, refuses to fulfill what the bishop has ordered for the Church’s necessity. If, however, because of his simpler nature, he is unable to perform or manage the office of archdeacon, he shall retain the title of his position, while the person whom the bishop has chosen shall be placed before him in the Church’s administration.

### XXIV. Concerning exposed infants who are found

Regarding exposed infants, the rule established long ago by the holy synod is to be observed.

### XXV. Concerning laypeople who abandon their wives

Those laypeople who abandon or have abandoned the marital union because of a serious fault, and who, without presenting credible grounds for separation, leave their marriages in order to presume upon illicit or alien relationships, shall be excluded from the Church’s communion and from the holy assembly of the people because they defile faith and marriage—if, before stating the grounds for separation before the bishops of their province, they have cast away their wives before they have been condemned by judgment.

### XXVI. That if a cleric voluntarily harms the Church, he must make satisfaction and be excommunicated

If any clerics, with blameworthy and punishable obstinacy, should presume to steal, suppress [Note: [Col. 0267D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2: “suppress”], deny, or perhaps hand over to adversaries documents by which the Church’s possession is secured, they shall restore from their own property whatever loss the Church has suffered through the absence of the documents, and shall be deprived of communion. The same applies to those who, to the Church’s detriment, have impiously received Church documents after being solicited by betrayers.

### XXVII. That no one establish a monastery without consulting the bishop, and concerning monks

No one shall presume to begin or establish a new monastery without the bishop’s permission or approval. Wandering monks shall not be ordained in cities or parishes for clerical office unless their abbot has given them a testimonial.

No abbot shall presume to receive or retain a monk who transfers to another monastery without the permission or consent of his abbot. Wherever such monks may be found, they shall be recalled to their own abbot by the authority of the canons. If it should be necessary to ordain a cleric from among the monks, the bishop shall do so only with the abbot’s consent and approval.

### XXVIII. That a monastery for girls be built far from monasteries of monks

Monasteries for girls shall be situated at a considerable distance from monasteries of monks, either because of the devil’s snares or because of human reproaches.

### XXIX. Concerning freedmen, that the Church protect them in necessity

The Church shall protect freedmen who have been lawfully made free by their masters if necessity requires it. If anyone presumes, before a hearing, to seize or despoil such a person [Ae.: “to persuade”], he shall be rejected by the Church.

### XXX. That prayers be said after the antiphons

Since it is fitting that the order of the Church be observed equally by all, care must be taken that, as is done everywhere, after the antiphons the collects be said in order by bishops or priests; that morning or evening hymns [Ae.: “a morning or evening hymn”] be sung every day; that, at the conclusion of the morning or evening Masses, brief passages from the Psalms [U.: “chapters”] be recited after the hymns; and that, after a collected prayer, the people be dismissed at evening by the bishop with a blessing.

### XXXI. Concerning those who do not return to peace because of hatred

It was also decided that whenever, as often happens, people have become estranged from one another through hatred or prolonged litigation and cannot be recalled to peace after a long effort, they should first be rebuked by the priests of the city. If they refuse, with destructive intent, to lay aside their enmities, they shall be expelled from the Church’s assembly by the most just excommunication.

### XXXII. That a cleric not go to a secular judge without consulting the bishop

A cleric must by no means presume to summon anyone before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission. If he is summoned, however, he may answer; but he must not initiate, nor dare to bring, a criminal case before a secular court.

If any layperson should attempt, through false accusation, to harass the Church or a cleric, and is convicted [T. 1, 2: “defeated”], he shall be barred from the thresholds of the Church and from communion with Catholics, unless he performs worthy penance.

### XXXIII. If a bishop without heirs does not make the Church he governed his heir

If a bishop who has no sons or grandsons leaves an heir other than the Church, anything he has presumed to dispose of from the Church’s property, whether by sale or donation, for a purpose unrelated to the Church’s cause or necessity, shall be considered invalid. But if he has sons, the Church’s indemnity shall be secured from the heirs regarding whatever property he left behind.

### XXXIV. How Jews who desire conversion are to be received

Since the perfidy of Jews frequently returns to its vomit, if they wish to come to the Catholic law [T. 1, 2: “Church”], they shall enter the Church’s threshold among the catechumens for eight months. If they are recognized as coming with pure faith, only then shall they receive the grace of baptism [Note: [Col. 0268D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, T. 1, 2: “be deemed worthy of it”]. But if anyone should incur the danger of illness within the prescribed period and be considered beyond hope, he shall be baptized.

### XXXV. If a bishop, summoned by the metropolitan for a synod or episcopal ordination, delays coming

If a metropolitan bishop sends letters to the bishops of his province inviting them either to the ordination of a chief bishop or to a synod, they must set everything else aside and not delay being present on the appointed day, except in the case of serious bodily illness or a royal command. If they are absent, then, as the ancient authority of the canons has commanded, they shall be deprived of the brothers’ charity and of communion with the Church until the next synod.

### XXXVI. That clerical stipends be distributed according to merit

All clerics who faithfully and vigilantly serve the Church shall receive from the priests the stipends due for their holy labors, according to the merit of their service and the prescriptions of the canons.

### XXXVII. Concerning murderers and false witnesses

Accordingly, we have decreed that murderers and false witnesses be removed from ecclesiastical communion, unless they purge the crimes they have committed through the satisfaction of penance.

### XXXVIII. That a cleric or monk may not travel without a letter from his bishop, and concerning monks and abbots

Clerics shall not have permission to wander without letters of recommendation from their bishop. The same rule of the present sentence shall be observed for monks. If verbal rebuke does not correct them, we decree that they also be restrained by beatings.

The rule concerning monks is likewise to be observed: they may not leave the community for solitary cells, unless perhaps, after approved labors have been completed, or because of the necessity of illness, a harsher rule is relaxed for them by the abbots. Even then, this shall be done in such a way that, while remaining within the same monastery enclosure, they may be permitted to have separate cells under the abbot’s authority.

Nor shall individual abbots be permitted to have different cells or several monasteries, except that, for the sake of receiving guests, they may establish shelters within the walls.

### XXXIX. That clerics avoid wedding banquets

Priests, deacons, subdeacons, and those of the subsequent grades who have no permission to take wives must also avoid the banquets of other people’s weddings. They must not join gatherings in which love songs and obscene songs are sung, or where shameful bodily movements are displayed in choruses and dances, lest hearing and sight, dedicated to the sacred mysteries, be polluted by the contagion of disgraceful spectacles and words.

### XL. That Christians avoid the banquets of Jews

Henceforth all clerics and laypeople shall avoid the banquets of Jews, and no one shall receive them at a banquet. Since they do not use common foods among Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to eat their foods, when they judge unclean the things that we consume with the Apostle’s permission. Thus Christians would begin to be inferior to Jews if we used what they set before us, while they despised what is offered by us.

### XLI. That drunkenness be forbidden to clerics

Above all, drunkenness must be forbidden to clerics, since it is the fuel and nourisher of every vice. Therefore, if someone is shown to have been drunk, we decree that, as the order of his rank permits, he either be removed from communion for thirty days or subjected to bodily punishment.

### XLII. Concerning diviners and those who observe omens, that they be separated from the Church

And lest it appear that something has been omitted which especially attacks faith in the Catholic religion: certain clerics or laypeople devote themselves to omens and, under the name of a false religion, call them “the lots of the saints” and profess a knowledge of divination, or promise the future through examination of writings of whatever kind. Any cleric or layperson who is discovered either consulting or teaching such practices shall be regarded as outside the Church.

### XLIII. That no cleric be ordained from among penitents, and that a priest not erect an altar

Concerning penitents, it was decided that the rule established by our holy Fathers in their synodal judgment be observed: no one from among them shall be ordained a cleric. Those who have already been ordained through ignorance shall hold the status either of bigamists or of husbands of remarried women.

A priest shall not presume to ordain deacons [Note: [Col. 0269D] E. 3, U.: “to minister”; Ae., B. R.: “a deacon shall minister”] or to consecrate an altar.

### XLIV. That a priest not presume to give a blessing or impose penance in church [Note: [Col. 0269D] U.: “That a priest, in the presence of the bishop, not give a blessing,” etc.; “[Col. 0270D] It shall by no means be permitted for a priest to bless in the bishop’s presence.”]

A priest shall by no means be permitted to pronounce a blessing over the people in the church or to bless a penitent in the church.

### XLV. That a bishop may dispose of something small without even the tacit agreement of the clerics

A bishop shall have the power, if necessity requires it, to dispose of small plots of land or little vineyards that are of little use to the Church or are situated far away, without the advice of his brothers.

### XLVI. That a bishop may sell fugitive Church slaves

Fugitives who abandon their houses or households, and who cannot be kept even if they have been recalled, may likewise be disposed of by bishops, if they wish or if such persons have deserved it.

### XLVII. That the people not presume to leave before Mass is completed

We specially command that laypeople attend the whole Mass on Sunday, so that the people may not presume to leave before the priest’s blessing. If they do so, they shall be publicly disgraced by the bishop.

### XLVIII. Concerning the bishop’s own or acquired property

Whatever a bishop possesses as his own private property, he may leave to his heirs if he wishes. Whatever he has from the Church’s provision—whether from fields, crops, or offerings—we have decreed must all be preserved under the Church’s right.

### XLIX. Concerning the non-alienation of Church property by a bishop, and concerning freedmen

Deacons or priests established in a parish must not dare to exchange, sell, or donate anything from the Church’s property entrusted to them, since it is known to be consecrated to God. Similarly, priests must not presume to diminish anything from the Church’s property entrusted to them, as has been stated above [B. R.: “alter”]. If they wish to do so, once convicted in council and deposed from their honor, they shall restore from their own property an equal amount to what they are seen to have presumed to take.

If anyone wishes, for any reason, to alienate something from the Church’s property, it may stand only if he first contributes from his own property to the Church as much as he is seen to have taken.

We order that freedmen whom priests, presbyters, or deacons wish to create from the Church entrusted to them must continue to perform the Church’s functions. If they refuse to do so, it was decided that they be returned to their former servitude.

### L. Concerning clerics who commit a capital crime

If a bishop, priest, or deacon commits a capital crime, falsifies a document, or gives false testimony, he shall be deposed from the honor of his office, confined in a monastery, and there receive only lay communion for as long as he lives.

### LI. Concerning bishops who leave something from Church property by testament

If a bishop, having drawn up a testament, bequeaths anything from property belonging to ecclesiastical right, it shall not be valid unless he supplements it with an equal amount from his own property.

### LII. Concerning clerics who travel without letters from their bishop

No one shall grant communion to a priest, deacon, or cleric traveling without letters from his bishop.

### LIII. Concerning parish priests who dispose of Church property

Whatever a parish priest disposes of from property belonging to ecclesiastical right shall be regarded as null and void, with an action lying against the seller for the purchaser [Note: [Col. 0271D] From U. In A.: “against the seller”; in the other witnesses: “against the person selling”].

### LIV. That the same persons make whatever they purchase in the Church’s name

While a priest holds a diocese, he shall draw up a document in the Church’s name for whatever he purchases; otherwise, he must withdraw from the administration of the Church he has held.

### LV. That priests and Levites not use dogs for hunting or hawks

Bishops, priests, and deacons may not keep dogs or hawks for hunting. If anyone of these persons is discovered engaged in such a pursuit, then, if he is a bishop, he shall suspend himself from communion for three months; a priest shall abstain for two months; and a deacon shall cease from every office and from communion for one month.

### LVI. Concerning sales that abbots presume to make

In sales that abbots presume to make, this rule shall be observed: whatever is sold without the bishop’s knowledge shall be recalled to the bishop’s authority. Slaves donated to monks may not be manumitted by abbots. For we consider it unjust that, while monks perform daily rural labor, their slaves should enjoy the leisure of freedom.

### LVII. That one abbot not preside over two monasteries

We prohibit one abbot from presiding over two monasteries.

### LVIII. That a monastery not be built without the bishop’s knowledge

We prohibit the establishment of new cells or small communities of monks without the bishop’s knowledge.

### LIX. Concerning Church property granted for use, that it not be protected by lapse of time

Whatever clerics have possessed from the Church’s remuneration, even for however long a period, must not be claimed as their own property by prescription of time, provided that it is clear that the property belonged to the Church. Otherwise, bishops might appear, when they were ordained, to have been required to make long-term or temporary administrations, or to be able to transfer long-retained assets into their own ownership.

### LX. Concerning those who fall away from the Catholic faith into heresy

For those who have fallen away—that is, those baptized in the Catholic faith [B. R.: “Church”] who, through blameworthy apostasy, have afterward passed into heresy—antiquity established great difficulty in returning. We, shortening the number of years, impose upon them a two-year penance under the following conditions: throughout the prescribed two years they shall fast every third day without relaxation and diligently attend church. They shall understand that they must stand and pray humbly in the place of penitents, and that they must leave when the catechumens are instructed to depart.

If they are willing to observe this, then, at the appointed time, the discipline may be relaxed so that they may be admitted to the altar. But if they consider the requirement too arduous or harsh, they must fulfill the statutes of the earlier canons.

### LXI. Concerning incestuous unions

We reserve absolutely no pardon for incestuous unions unless they have remedied the adultery by separation. Incestuous persons are not to be counted under any name of marriage, and it is disastrous even to identify them. We judge the following to be incestuous: if anyone violates carnally his brother’s widow, who had previously been almost a sister; if anyone takes his brother’s lawful wife; if anyone marries his stepmother; if anyone joins himself to a female cousin or niece—something we prohibit for the present in such a way that we do not dissolve arrangements established before our time; if anyone joins himself to his uncle’s widow or daughter; or if anyone is polluted by intercourse with his father’s daughter or his stepdaughter.

Those, however, whose illicit union is prohibited shall have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.

### LXII. Concerning those who kill their slaves without a judge

If anyone kills his own slave without the judge’s knowledge, he shall cleanse the guilt of bloodshed through excommunication or two years of penance.

### LXIII. Concerning laypeople who do not come to the city on the greater solemnities

If, as stated above, citizens neglect to attend with the bishop the aforementioned festivals of Easter and the Nativity of the Lord, in the cities where they know that they are established, in order to receive communion or a blessing [Note: [Col. 0271D] In the manuscripts: “of the solemnities.” The word *natalium* is taken from another manuscript text of Ae. and B. R., in which, under the title *Sentences*, twenty-three canons of this Council of Agde are repeated], those who neglect to do so shall be deprived of the Church’s communion for three years.

### LXIV. Concerning clerics who are absent from the Church’s service on solemn days

If anyone belonging to the clergy is absent from his church on solemn days—that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, the holy Epiphany, Easter, or Pentecost—while devoting himself instead to secular profits rather than obeying his service, it is fitting that he be suspended from communion for three years [Note: [Col. 0272D] Ae.: “at Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John or of Saint Mary, while instead…”]. Likewise, if a deacon or priest is absent from his church for three weeks, he shall suffer the same condemnation.

### LXV. Concerning Levites, that they not sit without the priest’s command

Since a deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a priest, he shall sit only at the priest’s command. Likewise, the deacon shall be honored by lower ministers and by all clerics.

### LXVI. Concerning ministers, that they not enter the sacristy

Since ministers ought not to have permission to enter the sacristy—which the Greeks call the *diakonikon*—or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

### LXVII. Concerning Catholics, that they not enter into marriages with heretics

Since it is not proper to form marriage alliances with all heretics, or to give them sons or daughters, but rather to receive children from them only if they profess that they will become Catholic Christians.

### LXVIII. Concerning Levites and clerics, that they not be magicians or enchanters

Since ministers of the altar and clerics ought not to be magicians or enchanters, or make what are called *phylacteria*—great bonds upon souls—we have ordered that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

### LXIX. Concerning seditious persons

Seditious persons are never to be ordained clerics, nor are usurers or those who avenge their own injuries.

### LXX. Concerning buffoonish and jesting clerics

A cleric who is buffoonish and makes jokes with disgraceful words must be removed from office.

### LXXI. Concerning the synod to be assembled every year

It was also decided, according to the decrees of the Fathers, that the synod be assembled every year. And because, after all salutary provisions have been established in the Lord’s name, the synod is dismissed in peace, we give thanks to God, praying for his mercy that we may be able to carry out these same things for the honor of the Lord for many years.

I, Caesarius, bishop, in the name of Christ, following the institutions of the Fathers and assenting to these definitions, subscribed on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in accordance with what was pleasing to all my holy fellow bishops who subscribed with me.

## XXXI. The First Council of Orléans, of Twenty-Eight Bishops

### I. Concerning murderers, adulterers, and thieves who take refuge in a church

When, with the Lord as author [T. 1, 2: “teacher”], a council of the highest bishops had been assembled in the city of Orléans, it was agreed by the common deliberation of all that what they had established orally should also be confirmed by written testimony.

We decree that the following be observed, as the ecclesiastical canons have decided and Roman law has established: it is altogether unlawful to drag accused persons from the atria of a church or from the bishop’s house, or to hand them over to anyone else, unless, after oaths have been sworn upon the Gospels, they have been guaranteed safety from death, bodily harm, and every kind of punishment. The person against whom the accused has committed the crime must be satisfied by an appropriate settlement.

If the accused is convicted of violating his oaths, as guilty of perjury he shall be separated not only from communion with the Church and all clerics but also from the banquets of Catholics. If he is unwilling to make a settlement with the person against whom he is accused, because of the latter’s insistence, and the accused himself leaves the church through fear, the Church’s clerics must not pursue him.

### II. Concerning abductors who take refuge in a church

We have judged that the following must be established concerning abductors: if an abductor comes to a church with the woman he has abducted, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she shall immediately be freed from the abductor’s power. The abductor, after being granted immunity from death or punishment, shall be subjected to servitude, or shall have the freedom to redeem himself.

But if it is established that the abducted girl has a father and that she consented to the abductor, she shall be returned, with pardon, to her father’s authority, while the abductor shall be liable to make satisfaction to the father according to the superior status of the latter.

### III. Concerning slaves who take refuge in a church

If a slave who has taken refuge in a church for any offense receives an oath from his master after the offense has been set aside [B. R.: “after the offense has been assigned”], he shall immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service. But after he has been handed over to his master upon the giving of an oath, if it is proved that he has suffered any punishment for the same offense from which he had been excused, then, for contempt of the Church and violation of faith [Note: [Col. 0275D] U., G.: “through contempt of the Church and violation of faith”], he shall be regarded as excluded from communion and from the banquet of Catholics, as stated above.

But if, after the Church has defended a slave on account of his offense, he has received from the clerics an oath from his master guaranteeing immunity, the master may seize the slave if he refuses to leave.

### IV. That someone who brings a claim against a bishop not be deprived of communion merely for making the claim

If anyone believes that he has a claim against a bishop, or against the Church, or concerning his own lawful right, he must not be removed from communion with the Church merely for bringing the claim, provided that he makes no insult or accusation.

### V. If a bishop makes another person’s slave a cleric

If a slave is ordained deacon or priest while his master is absent or unaware, and the bishop knows that he is a slave, the bishop shall compensate the master with double satisfaction, while the slave remains in the clerical office. But if the bishop did not know that he was a slave, those who gave testimony or petitioned for his ordination shall likewise be liable to make restitution.

### VI. If a deacon or priest commits a capital crime

If a deacon or priest commits a capital crime, he shall be expelled both from office and from communion.

### VII. Concerning those who violate their penance

Those who, after undertaking penance, forget the religious commitment they professed and relapse into secular life shall be suspended from communion and separated from the banquet of all Catholics. If anyone presumes to eat with such a person after the prohibition, he too shall be deprived of communion.

### VIII. If a priest or deacon has suspended himself from the Eucharist because of some offense

If a priest or deacon, because of his offense, has removed himself from communion at the altar under a profession of penance, nevertheless, if others are absent and a genuine necessity arises, he may baptize someone requesting baptism.

### IX. If the widow of a priest or deacon joins herself to another man

If a woman joins herself to anyone else after having been the widow of a priest or deacon who had been married twice, they shall either be separated after correction, or, if they persist in the criminal intention [Note: [Col. 0275D] B. R.: “persist or wish to remain in marriage”], they shall be punished by equal excommunication.

### X. Concerning what is offered on the altar
Reading the ancient canons anew, we have judged that the earlier provisions should be renewed, so that, from the offerings of the faithful presented at the altar, the bishop may claim one half, while the clergy receive the other half for distribution among themselves according to their rank, with the estates remaining under the bishop’s authority together with all their revenues.

[Note: Ae.: “we decreed.”]

### XI. Concerning what is offered by the faithful in parish basilicas

Concerning whatever faithful persons have offered to parishes in the form of lands, vineyards, slaves, or livestock, the provisions of the ancient canons shall be observed, so that everything remains under the bishop’s authority. Of whatever has been added at the altar, however, one third shall faithfully be delivered to the bishop.

### XII. That the bishop should protect the poor and the sick

The bishop shall provide food and clothing, insofar as his means allow, to the poor and the sick who, because of physical weakness, cannot work with their own hands.

### XIII. That basilicas remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated

It has been decided that all basilicas built in various places, or built each day, shall remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated, according to the rule of the earlier canons.

### XIV. Concerning incestuous unions, that they be excommunicated

A surviving brother must not take to the bed of his deceased brother, nor may anyone dare to join himself to his wife’s sister after losing his own wife. If they do so, they shall be punished with ecclesiastical discipline.

### XV. That abbots be under the authority of the bishops, and concerning wandering monks

For the benefit of religion, abbots shall remain under the authority of the bishops, and if they do anything contrary to the rule, they shall be corrected by the bishops. Once a year, at the place chosen by the bishop, they shall assemble when summoned.

Monks, however, shall submit to their abbots with complete obedience and devotion. If anyone proves disobedient through obstinacy, or presumes to wander about in various places or to possess anything as private property, everything he has acquired shall be taken from him by the abbots for the benefit of the monastery, according to the rule. Those who have wandered away shall be brought back under guard, wherever they are found, with the help of the bishop, as fugitives. Let that abbot know that he will be held guilty who fails to discipline such persons with regular severity, or who receives another man’s monk.

[Note: Ae., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “humility.”]

### XVI. That monks not wear the orarium or zancas

A monk may not have an orarium or zancas in the monastery.

### XVII. If a monk marries

If a monk, after having entered the monastery or having been proved to have received the monastic pallium, subsequently joins himself to a wife, then, as guilty of such great transgression, he shall never obtain office in an ecclesiastical rank.

### XVIII. That a monk not build a cell for himself without the permission of the bishop or abbot

No monk, after abandoning the monastery’s community, shall presume, driven by ambition and vanity, to build a cell for himself without the permission of the bishop or the will of his abbot.

### XIX. If a bishop has granted little plots of land to anyone for cultivation, they shall be held without prejudice to the Church’s rights

If a bishop, out of human consideration, has granted little slaves, small vineyards, or little plots of land to clerics, monks, or anyone else for cultivation or temporary possession, even if it is established that long periods of years have passed, the Church shall suffer no prejudice, nor shall a prescription under secular law that obstructs anything belonging to the Church be brought against it.

### XX. That Lent be observed before Easter

All the priests have decreed that before the solemnity of Easter the period observed shall be the forty-day fast, not the fifty-day period.

### XXI. That no townsman celebrate the greater festivals in the countryside

No townsman may celebrate the solemnity of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost in the countryside, unless illness is proved to have kept him there.

### XXII. That the people not leave the Mass before the priest’s blessing

When the people assemble in God’s name to celebrate Masses, they shall not depart before the solemnity of the Mass has been completed. Where the bishop is absent, they shall receive the priest’s blessing.

### XXIII. That litanies be celebrated after the Lord’s Ascension

It has been decided that the Rogations—that is, the litanies—be celebrated after the Lord’s Ascension, so that the three-day fast previously announced may be ended after the solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension. During those three days, male and female servants shall be released from every task, so that the whole people may assemble more readily. During those three days, everyone shall abstain and use the foods proper to Lent.

### XXIV. Concerning clerics who refuse to come to the service

Clerics who refuse to be present for the sacred work shall receive ecclesiastical discipline according to the bishop’s judgment.

### XXV. Concerning intimacy with foreign women

Both bishops and presbyters or deacons shall observe the provisions of the earlier canons concerning intimacy with foreign women.

### XXVI. Concerning religious and secular persons who attend to divinations

If any cleric, monk, or layperson observes divinations, omens, or lots—which they falsely claim to be those of the saints—and believes that these should be reported to anyone, let him be expelled from communion with the Church together with those who have believed them.

### XXVII. That the bishop should not be absent from church on Sunday

If the bishop is not prevented by illness [Note: Ae.: “if he has not suffered illness,”] he may not be absent on Sunday from the church nearest to him.
