[Note: This council is absent from E. 3.]

## XXXII. SECOND COUNCIL OF ORLÉANS

[Col. 0277]

When we had assembled in the city of Orléans for a synodal council in the name of God, we renewed, while preserving the authority of the earlier canons, the old provisions concerning matters that had been neglected for a long time because their observance had ceased, and we judged that new provisions should be added according to the circumstances of the cases and the times.

### I. Concerning the metropolitan council

First, each metropolitan in his own province shall hold a synodal council with his fellow provincials every year, at a suitable time. If illness or some definite necessity prevents him from being able to attend at another appointed place, he shall summon his brothers to his own city.

If, within two years, after divine providence has granted peaceful times and the fellow provincials have been admonished, the metropolitan has not called a synod, the metropolitan himself shall not presume to celebrate Masses for a full year because of his delay in summoning them.

If those who have been summoned, without being detained by any bodily illness, disdain to attend through their own fault, they shall be subject to the same sentence. Let them know, however, that this excuse has been removed from them if they think to excuse their absence by alleging a division by lot.

### II. Concerning married priests

No cleric from the rank of subdeacon upward, who is forbidden to take a wife as part of his profession, shall have intercourse with his own wife, if he happens already to have one. If he does so, he shall be deposed from office, remaining content with lay communion, according to the provisions of the earlier canons.

If his bishop, knowingly admitting that he is living in this disgraceful presumption, should later admit him to office, that bishop himself shall be separated from his office for three months in order to perform penance.

[Note: T. 1: “living presumptuously in this disgrace.”]

### III. Concerning the ordination of metropolitans

Concerning the ordination of metropolitans, it has been decided that metropolitans shall be ordained by a metropolitan, with all the provincials present if this can be done. The privilege of ordaining shall remain with the metropolitan himself, as the custom of ordination requires.

Nevertheless, the metropolitan shall be elected by the provincial bishops, as the decrees of the apostolic see state, with the consent of the clergy and the citizens. For, as the apostolic see itself has said, it is just that the one who is to be placed over all should be chosen by all.

For provincials who are to be ordained, the will and choice of the clergy and citizens shall likewise be sought with the consent of the metropolitan, according to the provisions of the earlier canons.

[Note: Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “fellow provincials.”]

### IV. Concerning intimacy with foreign women

Although many provisions that ought to be observed have already been established by numerous canonical decisions, what is recognized as being frequently transgressed ought to be repeated. Therefore we decree that no bishop or any cleric shall have permission to keep anyone within his house except those related women whom the earlier canons mention.

They are also specifically forbidden to do the following: if any cleric should perhaps incur adverse suspicion or the people’s accusation concerning any woman, he shall immediately dismiss her if he has her within his house. If she is in fact a foreign woman and legally independent, he shall take care by every means to avoid her, so that the infamy that has arisen may be removed.

If any bishop or cleric refuses to avoid what has been written above, he shall be punished with excommunication for three years because of his disobedience. If adulterous intercourse has been established, the provisions of the earlier canons concerning degradation from office shall be observed. In these admonitions, the metropolitan shall be disciplined by the fellow provincials, and the fellow provincial by the metropolitan together with the remaining fellow provincials.

[Note: Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U.: “re-graduation” rather than “degradation.”]

### V. Concerning the property of parishes

If offerings of any kind or substance have been presented to basilicas established in cities, they shall be brought under the bishop’s authority, and it shall be at his discretion what is assigned for the repair of the basilica or for maintaining its resources there.

Concerning the property of parishes or basilicas established in the rural districts of cities, the custom of each place shall be observed.

[Note: From Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U. In A. and the remaining manuscripts: “statute.”]

### VI. Concerning the excommunication of a bishop

The following shall be observed in every respect concerning the prior conversion of clerics: no one from among the laity shall be ordained before the annual period of conversion or the legitimate age—that is, before the age of twenty-five for a deacon and thirty for a presbyter.

Moreover, in the case of those who are to be ordained as clerics, careful attention must be paid to the rule, so that neither a man with two wives, nor the husband of a remarried woman, nor one who has professed penance, nor a physically mutilated person, nor anyone who has at some time been publicly arrested, is promoted to the orders mentioned above.

If a bishop knowingly believes that he ought to act contrary to these provisions, the man ordained shall be deprived, in accordance with the earlier canons, of the office he has received; but the bishop, because of the rashness of the ordination, shall be separated from celebrating the offices for six months.

If he presumes to celebrate Masses during the appointed period, he shall be deprived for a full year of the charity—that is, communion—of all the brothers.

If any cleric or citizen has testified concerning the promotion of such men—and by their testimony the bishop’s ignorance is frequently forestalled—then, when it has been recognized that an illicit ordination has taken place, they shall be expelled from communion for a full year. Nevertheless, if they should incur a dangerous illness, viaticum communion shall not be denied them.

[Note: T. 2, G.: “warnings” (*promonitionibus*) rather than “promotions” (*promotionibus*).]

### VII. Concerning a bishop who presumes to ordain someone unwilling or protesting

Clerics who, although they have had no wives, have believed that marriages should be chosen after receiving the blessing, and who have been ordained at the legitimate age willingly and without any protest, shall be expelled from communion together with the women whom they have taken.

If someone has been ordained unwillingly or while protesting, he shall indeed be deposed from office, but he shall not be expelled from communion. The bishop who has presumed to ordain someone unwilling or protesting shall be subjected to a year of penance and shall not presume to celebrate Masses.

### VIII. Concerning adultery by honored clerics

[Note: U.: “clerics to be honored.”]

Concerning the adultery of honored clerics, the following shall be observed: if anyone has committed adultery, confessed it, or been convicted of it, he shall be deposed from office, granted communion, and confined in a monastery for the whole duration of his life.

### IX. Concerning theft or falsification by honored clerics

If any cleric commits theft or falsification, since these too are capital crimes, he shall be degraded from his rank, while communion is granted to him.

Concerning perjury, we have judged that the following shall be observed: if any cleric gives an oath in cases that must be settled under oath, and afterward is exposed by evident facts as having sworn falsely, he shall be punished by two years of excommunication.

[Notes: T. 1, 2, U., G.: “re-graded.” B. R., U., G.: “must be concluded.” T. 2: “by events that occur.”]

### X. Concerning those who have children by concubines

Concerning those who have children by concubines and have had legitimate wives, or who, after their wives’ deaths, have publicly believed that concubines should be joined to them, we decree that the following shall be observed: just as we do not remove those who have already been ordained as clerics through ignorance, so we establish that such men shall not be ordained in the future.

### XI. Concerning incestuous unions

Concerning incestuous unions, the provisions already established shall be observed in this way. Those who are now coming to baptism, or to whom the provisions of the Fathers have not previously been made known through priestly preaching, should, because of the newness of their conversion and faith, receive the following concession: marriages of this kind that have already been contracted shall not be dissolved, but in the future the prohibition concerning incestuous unions established in the earlier canons shall be observed.

That is, no one shall presume to join himself in marriage to his father’s widow, his wife’s daughter, his brother’s widow, his wife’s sister, a *consobrina* or *sobrina* (two distinct kinds of female cousin), his maternal uncle’s widow, or his paternal uncle’s widow.

If any persons have been joined in this incestuous adultery rather than in marriage, they shall be excluded from ecclesiastical communion for as long as they do not separate from one another. We have also judged that the following should be added: they shall remain subject to the examination of their bishop.

Concerning those who reside in their own city or territory and have entered into such a union, it must be determined whether they came to illicit marriages through ignorance or whether, through obstinacy, they presumed upon what had been forbidden.

Just as assistance is given to those who have fallen through ignorance, so, for those to whom the provisions of the Fathers had previously been made known and who nevertheless persist in such a union against the prohibition of the priests, all the provisions of the earlier canons shall be observed. They shall not be received into communion until they have healed their incestuous adultery by separation, as it is written.

For it is plainly read in the law of the Lord: “Cursed is the one who has lain with his father’s wife, with his stepdaughter, or with his wife’s sister,” and other things of the same kind. Thus, those whom God has cursed we cannot bless unless they have been corrected.

[Note: From the words “that is” through the end of the canon, the remainder is written in the margin of A.]

### XII. Concerning clerics who refuse to fulfill their office

[Note: This canon and the following canons of this council are absent from A. and E. 3. They have been taken from manuscript B. R., together with the variant readings of the other manuscripts.]

If any clerics refuse, for whatever reason, to perform the ministries they have undertaken as the others do, and offer the protection of various persons as an excuse for not fulfilling their office, and under such a pretext think that priests may be despised through disobedience, they shall in no way be counted among the other canonical clerics, lest others be corrupted by this license. Nor shall they receive any stipends or gifts from ecclesiastical property together with the canonical clergy.

### XIII. Concerning ecclesiastical property not to be alienated

The provisions of the earlier canons concerning little estates and other ecclesiastical properties, which priests must neither alienate nor bind by useless contracts, shall be observed, so that we may not alienate ecclesiastical property or uselessly bind it by any contracts.

Whatever is known to have been alienated by predecessors from ecclesiastical property, or bound by any instruments to the Church’s disadvantage, and for which recovery remains possible within thirty years, shall be restored through a public judgment or the judgment of chosen judges, with justice supporting the action.

If the person who holds the ecclesiastical property, after being admonished, avoids judgment, he shall be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until he comes to examination and restores the property.

[Note: Ae.: “until either he comes to examination or restores the property,” and so forth.]

### XIV. Concerning Christian slaves held in Jewish service

If Christian slaves held in Jewish service are subjected by their masters to something forbidden by the Christian religion, or if their masters perhaps presume to afflict or beat those whom the Church has removed as exempt from an offense that has been forgiven, and those slaves flee again to the church, they shall not be returned by the priest unless a price is offered and paid equal to what the slaves themselves are established to be worth, according to an assessment.

[Note: Ae.: “the fair assessment has declared them to be worth.”]

We also forbid all Christians to marry Jews. If they do so, whoever the person may be shall be expelled from communion until separation has taken place.

Likewise, we forbid Christians to attend Jewish banquets. If they are proved to have been present at such banquets, they shall be subject to a year of excommunication for this defiance.

### XV. Concerning the celebration of Masses

Concerning the celebration of Masses, it shall be observed on the principal solemnities alone that the celebration of Masses begin at the third hour in the name of God, so that, once the service has been completed within the appropriate hours, the priests may more easily assemble for the evening offices, that is, at evening time. For on such days it is neither proper nor fitting for a priest to be absent from the evening offices of the church.

### XVI. That a bishop not intrude into another’s diocese

Bishops must not intrude into another’s diocese to ordain another’s clerics or consecrate altars. If they do so, those whom they have ordained shall be removed, while the consecration of the altar remains; and the transgressors of the canons shall abstain from celebrating Masses for a year.

### XVII. That clerics not reside in another city

Clerics who, under any pretext or condition, have decided to reside in the cities or territories of others shall not be promoted to the highest honor of the clergy without a written document from their own bishop.

[Note: Ae.: “without a written document and consent.”]

### XVIII. Concerning clerics who wander without letters of recommendation

In accordance with the earlier provisions, no one shall grant communion to a presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon who travels without letters from his bishop.

### XIX. Concerning the abduction of consecrated virgins

Concerning the abductors of consecrated virgins or of women living in a profession of devotion, we decree that if anyone presumes to use force against a consecrated or devoted woman—that is, one who has professed religion—he shall be excluded from ecclesiastical communion until death, with only viaticum reserved for him in the danger of illness.

If a woman said to have been abducted consents to live with her abductor, she too shall be struck with the same excommunication. The same rule, under ecclesiastical severity, shall be maintained concerning penitents and widows who remain in their profession.

If any priest knowingly grants communion to such persons, he shall not have the peace of the Church for a full year.

### XX. Concerning the gifts of priests

[Note: This canon is taken from Ae.; the other manuscripts read “it is fitting,” and therefore the numbering of the remaining canons has been corrected.]

Concerning the gifts of priests, the following shall be observed: whatever is currently held or possessed through the gifts of deceased clerics shall in no way thereafter be taken away by their successors.

Those who enjoy the generosity of their predecessors shall provide the Church’s services, obedience, and affection to the priests. If the bishop should wish, for a useful reason, to exchange some of the gifts that they currently possess, as has been said, let it be exchanged for property in other places without loss to the recipient.

Concerning current gifts that each person judges should be granted to clerics for their service out of his own favor: just as it lies within the giver’s discretion to bestow them on whomever he wishes, so, if disobedience or obstinacy should arise in the recipient, once the fault has been recognized it shall lie within the discretion of the superior whether and how the gift should be recalled.

### XXI. Concerning clerics who undertake the administration of monasteries, dioceses, or basilicas

Concerning those clerics who, from the office of a city church, undertake the administration of monasteries, dioceses, or basilicas situated anywhere—that is, whether in territories or in the cities themselves—it shall be in the bishop’s power to decide whether they are to retain some or none of what they previously had from the ecclesiastical office. For the resources of the monastery, diocese, or basilica undertaken by each person ought fully and reasonably to suffice for him.

[Note: U., G.: “remain.”]

### XXII. Concerning contumacious clerics

If anyone, lifted up by pride, refuses out of any indignation to fulfill his office, then, in accordance with the earlier provisions, he shall be deposed from his rank and remain excluded, content with lay communion, until he has made satisfaction through worthy penance and supplication, as it is written, in the presence of the bishop.

Nevertheless, regular charity shall be provided to them in full, and whatever stipends are customarily returned to them shall be supplied outside the office according to their status. If a complaint arises concerning these matters, the person exercising the office shall have recourse to the synod.

### XXIII. That clerics oppressed by a bishop have recourse to the synod

If any cleric thinks that the severity or treatment of his bishop toward him is unjust, he shall have recourse to the synod according to the ancient customs.

### XXIV. Concerning conspiracies of clerics to be punished in the synod

If any clerics, as has recently become evident in many places through the instigation of the devil, gather together with rebellious authority and with a conspiracy intervening among them, and it becomes clear that oaths have been exchanged among them or a written document has been drawn up, this presumption shall not prevail through any excuses.

When the matter has been brought before the synod, the bishops then assembled together shall punish the offenders according to the status and rank of the persons involved.

For just as charity is to be displayed according to the Lord’s commandments in the heart, not by writing on a document or by conspiracies, so what is admitted contrary to the sacred Scriptures must be restrained by episcopal authority and discipline.

[Note: U., G.: “judged.”]

### XXV. Concerning ecclesiastical offerings not to be retained

If anyone, driven by dreadful greed, seizes or retains property owed to or belonging to the Church or to a priest, or obtains it from the authority through a claim, he shall have no excuse if he fails to restore it.

If, after recognizing the Church’s right, he does not immediately restore it to the Church or priest, or delays coming to the judgment of chosen judges so that he may establish the right itself, he shall be suspended from ecclesiastical communion until, after the property has been restored, both the Church and the priests have been indemnified.

The same form of ecclesiastical discipline shall be observed, according to the earlier canons, against those who delay assigning in any manner or presume to retain offerings legally left by the dead.

He shall likewise be subject to the same sentence if anyone, in whatever manner, presumes to reclaim what he has given to churches out of his devotion.

### XXVI. Concerning ecclesiastical property not to be alienated without the bishop’s consent

Abbots, presbyters, and the other ministers may not alienate or bind any ecclesiastical property or sacred ministry without the permission and subscription of their bishop.

Whoever presumes to do so shall be degraded, while communion is granted to him, and whatever has been rashly presumed upon and alienated shall be restored by the bishop’s decision.

[Note: Ae.: “re-graded.”]

### XXVII. Concerning penance for young persons and married persons

Concerning the conversion of penitents, no one shall presume to confer the blessing of penance upon young persons.

Certainly, in the case of married persons, no one shall dare to grant it except with the consent of both parties and when they have reached full maturity.

[Note: Ae. adds “persons.”]

### XXVIII. Concerning those who return to secular life after undertaking penance

If anyone, after receiving the blessing of penance, presumes to return to secular dress and military service, he shall be punished by excommunication until death, with viaticum granted.

[Note: Ae.: “secular surroundings” rather than “secular dress.”]

### XXIX. Concerning slaves not to be ordained

No one bound by servile or tenant status shall, according to the provisions of the apostolic see, be admitted to ecclesiastical honors unless it has first been legally established that he has been freed either by a will or by written documents.

If any bishop, knowing the status of the person being ordained, should perhaps wish to transgress by carrying out a forbidden ordination, he shall not presume to celebrate Masses for the space of a year.

### XXX. Concerning clerics who lend money

A cleric from the rank of deacon upward shall not lend money at interest. Nor shall he expect anything more from benefits granted than what is given. Nor, in conducting business like public merchants who pursue trade in response to the people’s needs, shall he engage in the desire for shameful profit; nor shall he dare to conduct forbidden business under another person’s name.

If anyone presumes to act against these provisions, he shall be re-graded from his rank, while communion is granted to him.

[Note: T. 1, 2, U., G.: “That a cleric or a deacon and above shall not lend money at interest.”]

### XXXI. Concerning observance of the Lord’s Day

Since the peoples have been persuaded that on the Lord’s Day they ought not to travel with horses, oxen, or vehicles, nor prepare anything for food, nor perform anything pertaining to the adornment of a person or a house—practices that are proved to belong more to Jewish than to Christian observance—we decree that whatever was previously permitted may be done on the Lord’s Day.

With regard to rural work, however—that is, plowing, work in the vineyard, cutting, threshing, clearing, or fencing—we have judged that people should abstain, so that those who come to the church may more easily devote themselves to the grace of prayer.

If anyone is found engaging in the works listed above, which are forbidden, how he should be corrected shall lie not under lay discipline but under the priest’s chastisement.

[Note: Ae.: “mules” instead of “oxen.”]

### XXXII. Concerning hearing the Mass in its entirety

No layperson shall leave the Masses before the Lord’s Prayer has been said. If the bishop is present, his blessing shall be awaited.

No one shall attend the morning or evening sacrificial Masses with weapons intended for use in warfare. Whoever does so shall remain under the priest’s authority as to how he should be punished by that priest’s discipline.

### XXXIII. Concerning the days on which Jews may not go among Christians

Since, by God’s favor, we live under the rule of catholic kings, the Jews shall not presume, from the day of the Lord’s Supper until Easter Sunday—that is, during those four days—to go out among Christians or to mix with catholic peoples in any place or on any pretext.

### XXXIV. Concerning a judge who does not punish those who rebaptize

If a judge of a city or place learns that a heretic, a Bonosian, or a person of any other heresy has rebaptized someone from among Catholics, and, since it is clear that we have catholic kings, does not immediately constrain the rebaptizers and bring them to be disciplined according to the king’s faith and justice, he shall be subjected to a year of excommunication.

### XXXV. That a cleric not drag a layman, nor a layman a cleric, before a secular court

No cleric of any rank shall presume, without the permission of his bishop, to drag anyone before a secular court. Nor may a layman, without consulting a priest, bring a cleric before a secular court.

### XXXVI. Concerning observance of these canons

Therefore, if any of the bishops now living, or any of those whom God may appoint as their successors, neglects to preserve and fulfill these provisions, abandoning the integrity of their observance, let him know that he will be guilty both before the judgment of God and before that of the brotherhood. For no one is permitted either to be ignorant of his canons or to disregard them—that is, to pass them over.

[Note: These subscriptions are found in A. and E. 3.]

Lupus, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have agreed and subscribed.

[Note: Ae.: “I have agreed and subscribed, in the fourth year after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger, in the second indiction.”]

Pantagathus, bishop: I have agreed and subscribed.  
Leocadius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Theobades [Ae.: Theudovades], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Asterius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Lausto [Note: Ae., T. 1: Lauto; T. 2: Leuto], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Rustinus [Ae.: Rusticius], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Agrippinus, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Passius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Paulinus [Note: T. 1, 2: “Paulinus the Younger, unworthy bishop”], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Leo, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Placidius [Note: T. 2: Placidus; T. 1: Placitus], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Eleutherius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Arcadius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Amelius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Lucinus [Ae.: Licinius], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Flavius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Ursolus, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Albinus, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Campanus, presbyter, sent by my lord Gregorius [Ae.: Injuriōsus], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Aulus, presbyter, sent by my lord Agricola [Ae.: Agroegula], bishop: I have subscribed.  
Obtardemus, presbyter, sent by my lord Gallus, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Marcellianus, presbyter, sent by my lord Eumerius, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Baudastis, presbyter, sent by my lord Perpetuus, bishop: I have subscribed.  
Vincentius, presbyter, sent by my lord Subtrasius, bishop: I have subscribed.

[Note: The subscriptions of Baudastis and Vincentius are taken from Ae., since they are absent from B. R. and the other manuscripts.]

## XXXIII. COUNCIL OF EPAON, OF TWENTY-FOUR BISHOPS

[Note: The number of bishops, absent from A. and the other manuscripts, has been taken from B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G.]

### I. Bishops, presbyters, and deacons may not keep dogs for hunting or hawks

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons may not keep hunting dogs or hawks. If anyone among such persons is discovered to have this inclination, then, if he is a bishop, he shall suspend himself from communion for three months; a presbyter shall abstain for two months; and a deacon shall cease from every office and from communion for one month.

### II. Concerning presbyters or deacons traveling without letters

No one shall grant communion to a presbyter or deacon traveling without letters from his bishop.

### III. Concerning presbyters who have alienated property belonging to ecclesiastical right

Whatever presbyters of parishes have alienated from property belonging to ecclesiastical right shall be considered null and void. The purchaser’s action against the seller shall be reserved.

[Note: B. R., T. 1, 2: “shall be returned.”]

### IV. Concerning a presbyter who has held a diocese

While a presbyter holds a diocese, concerning whatever he has held, he shall either draw up a written document in the name of the church or withdraw from the administration of the church he has held.

The same rule shall also be observed concerning sales that abbots have presumed to make: whatever has been sold without the knowledge of the bishops shall be restored to the bishop’s authority.

An abbot may not free slaves given to monks. For we consider it unjust that, while monks perform daily rural labor, their slaves should enjoy the leisure of freedom.

[Note: B. R., U., G.: “purchased.” Note: In the other manuscripts apart from A., “given” is written.]

### V. That one abbot not preside over two monasteries

We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

### VI. Concerning new cells and small communities

We forbid new cells or small communities of monks to be established without the bishop’s knowledge.

[Note: T. 1, 2: “small cells.”]

### VII. That clerics not presume to approach a public court without their bishop’s authorization

Clerics shall not presume, without the authorization of their bishop, to approach or address a public court. But if they have been summoned, they shall not delay in following the summons to a secular court.

### VIII. Concerning ecclesiastical property not to be alienated

No bishop shall have the power to sell anything belonging to his own Church without the knowledge of his metropolitan, although a useful exchange for the benefit of all is permitted.

[Note: U., G.: “shall have the power”; “although a useful exchange for all is permitted.”]

### IX. Concerning clerics convicted of false testimony

If any cleric is convicted of false testimony, he shall be considered guilty of a capital crime.

### X. Concerning the generosity of the Church
Whoever, having obtained something from the munificence of the Church [Col. 0288A] which he had served, has been or is ordained to the highest priesthood of another city shall return what he received or will have received as a gift; but what he is proved to have purchased, whether for use or as property, according to the wording of the document, he may retain.

### XI. On banquets with heretics or Jews

If a cleric of a higher rank attends the banquet of any heretical cleric, he shall have no share in the Church’s bread [T. 1, *spatio*: “for the space of a year”; B. R., T. 1, 2, *pacem*: “peace”] for the space of one year; and if junior clerics presume to do so, they shall be flogged. Our constitution has also prohibited laypeople from Jewish banquets, and whoever has been defiled by a Jewish banquet shall not eat the Church’s bread with any of our clerics.

### XII. On giving chrism

[Col. 0288B] For the salvation of souls, which we desire in all things, we permit priests to assist heretics who are in despair or lying ill with chrism, if they suddenly request their conversion; but all who are to be converted, if they are healthy, must know that chrism is to be sought from the bishop.

### XIII. On a bishop’s testament

If a bishop, having made a testament, bequeaths anything from property belonging to ecclesiastical right, it shall not be valid unless he has made it good from resources belonging to his own right.

### XIV. On those who have possessed ecclesiastical remuneration

Whatever clerics have possessed, even without petitions, for however long a period from the Church’s remuneration, shall not, with the authority of our most glorious lord and prince, be summoned into proprietary ownership [U., “into their own ownership”] by prescription of time, provided that it is clear that the thing belonged to the Church.

### XV. On a deacon or priest who has committed a capital crime

If a deacon or priest has committed a capital crime, he shall be removed from the honor of his office and confined in a monastery; there he shall receive communion only for as long as he lives.

### XVI. On renewed profession

If anyone, having accepted and professed penance, forgetful of the good, falls back into worldly affairs, he shall be entirely unable to communicate unless the profession [B. R., “to the profession”] which he had unlawfully abandoned is renewed.

### XVII. On laypeople who bring charges against clerics

[Col. 0288D] We permit laypeople to bring forward accusations if they are preparing to charge a cleric of any rank with a criminal offense, provided that they report the truth.

### XVIII. Where the relics of saints are to be placed

The relics of the saints shall not be placed in rural oratories, [Col. 0289A] unless perhaps it happens that clerics of some neighboring parish are present who may serve the sacred ashes by frequent chanting of psalms. If such clerics are absent, no one shall be appointed to serve them until suitable means of food and clothing have been assigned to them.

### XIX. Altars shall not be anointed unless they are of stone

Altars that are not of stone shall not be consecrated with the anointing of chrism for the celebration of divine services. The provincials shall observe the order maintained by their metropolitans.

### XX. On the absolution of the condemned

If a bishop is carried off by death before the absolution of a condemned person, his successor may absolve the person who has been corrected or has performed penance.

### XXI. On those who have fallen from the faith

[Col. 0289B] For those who have fallen—that is, those who, having been baptized as Catholics, have afterward passed into heresy through damnable treachery—antiquity established great difficulty in returning. For them we, having shortened the number of years, impose a two-year penance under the following discipline: throughout the prescribed two years, they shall fast on the third day without relaxation; they shall strive to attend church; they shall know that the humility of standing and praying in the place of penitents must be observed; and they are also to be instructed to leave together with the catechumens when they depart. If they are unwilling to observe this, [265] once the appointed period has elapsed, the discipline for admitting them to the altar shall be relaxed. If they should perhaps consider this too arduous or severe, they shall be required to complete the provisions established by the earlier canons.

### XXII. On incestuous unions

[Col. 0289C] We reserve absolutely no pardon for incestuous unions, unless they have remedied the adultery by separation. We judge those to be incestuous—and not to be overcome by any name of marriage—apart from those whom it is dreadful even to name, as follows: if anyone violates by carnal union his brother’s widow, who had previously been almost like a sister; if a brother takes his wife’s full sister; if anyone marries his stepmother [Note: [Col. 0289D] B. R., T. 1, “marries his stepmother, his father’s second wife”]; if anyone joins himself to a female cousin or niece. Just as we prohibit these things from the present time, so we do not dissolve unions previously established. Likewise, if anyone has intercourse with his maternal uncle’s widow, or is defiled by intercourse with his paternal uncle’s widow or with his stepdaughter. Certainly, those to whom an illicit union is forbidden shall have the freedom to enter a better marriage.

### XXIII. On the penance of homicides

[Col. 0289D] Concerning the penance of homicides who have escaped the laws of the world, it has pleased us to observe among ourselves, with the greatest reverence, what the ancient Nicene canons decreed concerning them.

### XXIV. On the basilicas of heretics

[Col. 0290A]

We disdain to apply the basilicas of heretics to holy uses. We hate them with such great abhorrence that we do not consider their pollution capable of purification. Nevertheless, we may reclaim those which they had taken from us by force.

### XXV. If anyone kills his own slave

If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, he shall expiate the shedding of blood by two years’ excommunication.

### XXVI. No one shall be expelled from the Church without remedy or hope of pardon

No one shall be expelled from the Church without remedy or hope of pardon, nor shall access to returning for forgiveness be closed to anyone if he has repented or corrected his conduct; but [Col. 0290B] if the danger of death should perhaps threaten someone, the prescribed periods of condemnation shall be relaxed. If the sick person, having received the viaticum, should perhaps recover, he ought to observe the periods of the appointed time.

### XXVII. On the ordination of laypeople

A layman shall not be ordained a cleric unless religious commitment has first been undertaken.

### XXVIII. On monasteries of girls

No one shall be permitted to enter a monastery of girls except a person of tested life and advanced age, and only for whatever necessities or services of theirs may arise. Those who enter to celebrate Masses shall hasten to return immediately after completing their ministry. Otherwise, neither a cleric nor a young monk shall have any access to the community of girls unless paternal or sisterly kinship is demonstrably shown to warrant his admission.

### XXIX. On slaves fleeing to a church

If a slave guilty of a grave offense flees to a church, he shall be excused only from corporal punishments. With respect to cutting his hair or any other work, it has pleased us that oaths not be exacted from his masters.

### XXX. On the observance of these canons

Therefore, if any of the holy bishops who have confirmed these present statutes by their own subscriptions, or any successors whom God may appoint to them, should depart from the integrity of their observance, let him know that he will be judged guilty both before God and before the brotherhood.

[Col. 0290C] Avitus, bishop, reread and subscribed our constitutions—that is, the holy constitutions [Note: [Col. 0290D] In A., “in the holy constitutions.”] of the priests of the province of Vienne—on the day and at the time of the tenth day before the Kalends of the eighth month, during the consulship of Agapetus [B. R., Agapius]. Twenty-three bishops subscribed in this synod [Note: [Col. 0290D] B. R., T. 1, 2, “twenty-four.”].

## XXXIV. COUNCIL OF CARPENTORATE

[Col. 0289]

[Col. 0289D] 267–268 When we had assembled at Carpentorate, a complaint of the following kind reached us: that the things contributed by any of the faithful to the parishes are appropriated by certain bishops in such a way that little or almost nothing is left for the churches to which they had been contributed.

This seemed just and reasonable to us: if the church of the city over which the bishop presides [U., G., “of this city”] is so well supplied that, by Christ’s favor, it lacks nothing, whatever has been left to the parishes shall be reasonably distributed to the clerics serving those parishes or for the repair of the basilicas. But if it is established that the bishop has many expenses or fewer resources [Note: [Col. 0291A] Ae., but B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G., “and fewer resources”], then, from the parishes to which a more generous amount of property has been contributed, only as much as is reasonably sufficient for the clerics or builders shall be reserved. Whatever is left beyond that, the bishop may reclaim for his greater expenses, but only in such a way that he himself has no permission to diminish anything from the small resources [Note: [Col. 0292A] B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G., “from the resources themselves”] or from the ministry of the clergy of that place.

It also pleased us that this be observed: in the following year the council shall be assembled in the village of Vaison.

Fifteen bishops subscribed this constitution.

## XXXV. FIRST COUNCIL OF ARVERNUS

[Col. 0291]

### I. What is to be treated first in a synod

[Col. 0291B]

First of all, it pleased us that whenever a holy synod is assembled according to the statutes of the Fathers, none of the bishops should dare to bring forward any other matter before the matters concerning the correction of life, the strictness of the rule, and remedies for the soul have been concluded.

### II. On bishops to be ordained

It also pleased us that no one should seek the sacred dignity of a bishop by gifts but by merits, so that he may not seem to purchase the divine office with possessions but with character, and may ascend the summit of the highest dignity through the election of all, not through the favor of a few. Let there be the greatest care in choosing priests, since those who must preside over people needing correction ought to be irreproachable. Let each person carefully examine the value of the Lord’s flock, so that he may know what merit is suitable for appointing a priest. Therefore, whoever desires the episcopate shall be ordained bishop through the election of the clergy or citizens and also with the consent of the metropolitan of the same province. He shall not employ the patronage of powerful men; he shall not, by crafty deceit, urge some to draw up the decree with rewards or compel others through fear. Whoever does this shall be deprived of communion by the Church over which he disgracefully desires to preside.

### III. On the coverings of the church; that clerics not be stirred up by powerful men; and on plunderers of church property

It must be observed concerning the coverings or sacred vessels of the church that the bodies of the dead are not wrapped in them. Clerics must in no way be stirred up by powerful men of the world against their bishops. Those who wish to take away even a small thing belonging to the Church or its modest property [Col. 0291D] shall be excluded.

### IV. That Christians shall not marry Jews

If anyone enters into a marital union with Jewish depravity—that is, if either a Jewish woman has intercourse in a carnal union with a Christian man, or a Christian woman with a Jewish man—whichever of them is known to have committed such great wickedness shall immediately be separated from the Christian assembly and banquet and from communion with the Church.

### V. On the covering of the Lord’s body

The body of a priest shall never be covered with the cloth used for the Lord’s body when it is carried to the tomb; and when the sacred cloth has been returned to its proper use, the altars must not be polluted while the bodies are being honored.

### VI. That sacred vessels and services shall not be supplied for wedding adornment

[Col. 0292B]

Sacred vessels and services shall not be supplied for the adornment of weddings, lest, when polluted by the touch of the wicked or by the pomp of worldly luxury, they appear unworthy of the functions of sacred ministry.

### VII. That Jews shall not be placed over Christians

Jews shall not be appointed as judges over Christian peoples.

### VIII. That another bishop shall not invade a bishop’s parishes

Let no bishop of another city, violating the canons, invade the parishes of any bishop, and, inflamed by the torches of mad greed, seize what belongs to another, as though he were not content with his own.

### IX. On not receiving another’s clerics

No bishop shall dare to receive another bishop’s cleric against the will of that cleric’s bishop or to promote him to the priesthood.

### X. On incestuous unions

If anyone believes that his brother’s widow, his wife’s sister, his stepdaughter, his cousin, his niece, or likewise the widow of his paternal or maternal uncle may be violated through carnal intercourse, and by sacrilegious boldness transgresses the authority of divine law and the rights of nature, and attempts to use force against one to whom he ought to have offered the support of charity and devoted affection, as an enemy of his own family and an assailant of chastity, let him be struck by the judgment of the apostolic constitution. As long as he remains in such a crime, he shall be deprived of the Christian assembly and banquet and likewise of communion with the mother Church.

### XI. On the continence of clerics

[270] When priests and deacons are advanced to the lofty summit of dignity, let them wholly renounce worldly activities and, being chosen for the sacred mystery [Ae., B. R., “ministry”], reject carnal association and exchange their former cohabitation for the affection of brotherhood. Whoever he may be, a priest or deacon, after receiving the blessing by divine gift, shall immediately become a brother to his former wife instead of a husband.

### XII. On the incontinence of priests

We have found certain men inflamed by the heat of lust who, having cast aside the belt of their service, returned to their former vomit and resumed the marriages that had been forbidden, thereby in a manner violating the priesthood by the crime of incest; their children also revealed the fact. Whoever is known to have done this shall be deprived forever of every dignity that he lost when he committed the crime.

### XIII. On defrauders

If anyone, by wicked cunning, defrauds, seizes, retains, or suppresses any gift contributed to the sacred Scriptures [or “to sacred Scripture,” depending on the reading], and, immediately after being admonished by a priest, does not return what was given to God, he shall be expelled from communion with the Catholic Church.

### XIV. On celebrating the principal feasts with the bishop in the city

[Col. 0293B] If a priest or deacon is recognized as belonging canonically neither to the city nor to the parishes, but lives in villages and celebrates the divine mysteries while serving in oratories, he shall celebrate the principal feasts—the Lord’s Nativity, Easter, Pentecost, and whatever other principal feasts remain—in no other place than with his bishop in the city. All citizens who are older in age shall likewise come in the cities to their bishops on the aforesaid feasts. If any, in wicked boldness, despise this, they shall be expelled from communion on those same feasts on which they disdain to be present in the city.

### XV. On the good reputation of clerics

[Col. 0294A]

A bishop, priest, and deacon should shine with the light of a holy conscience in such a way that, through the integrity of their conduct, they avoid the slanders of the malicious. Let them strive to fulfill in themselves the divine testimony that the Lord said: “Seeing your good works, they will glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

### XVI. That clerics shall not live with unrelated women

[271] Therefore, by canonical authority and by a constitution that shall endure forever, we decree that all clerics must flee the blameworthy freedom of living with unrelated women. They may live only with a grandmother, mother, sister, or granddaughter, if necessity requires it. Regarding these relationships, as the sequence of the earlier canons states, it is wrong to suspect anything other than what nature has established. In their bedroom, storeroom, or any household service, there shall be neither a nun nor an unrelated woman; nor shall a female servant be admitted in any way. If anyone, forgetful of God’s commands, believes this may be disregarded, let him know that, by canonical authority, he will undoubtedly suffer the loss of communion.

## XXXVI. LETTER OR COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF ARVERNUS SENT TO KING THEUDOBERT

[Col. 0293]

[Col. 0293C] To the most illustrious and pre-eminent lord and son, King Theudobert: Honoratus, Hilary, Gregory, Soricius, Nicetius, Flavius, Domitius, Dalmatius, Lupus, Sperius, and Desideratus [Note: [Col. 0293D] Ae. has “Domitianus, Deuterius, Gallus, Dalmatius, Venantius, Gramaticus, Lupus, Sperius, Desideratus, bishops.”].

While we, the bishops of your churches and your servants, were sitting together in the city of Arvernus to review the statutes of the canons and to clarify ecclesiastical law for those who were perhaps burdened by uncertainty about the regulation of their own lives, a crowd of many people who sought from us a remedy for their despair gathered before us. They hoped that our humility would entreat your piety no less for the prosperity of your kingdom than for their own consolation, so that, through our petition, justice and your piety might now be made known to your ears: that your piety would permit no one to be deprived of his own property or small possessions; that, while each person is subject to the power and dominion of one king, he would not lose through another’s claim property situated in another’s realm, as commonly happens.

Trusting in the justice and piety of your highness, we do not believe that you will refuse this, so that, while we attend through what we believe to be a just and God-pleasing petition to the needs of many, you may have prosperity for your kingdom and a return from the heavenly Lord through the granted grace of your compassion [Note: [Col. 0293D] T. 1, “through the compassion granted”; T. 2, “through the indulgence of compassion”]. [Ae., “may you increase it.”]

Therefore, with the greatest reverence, as is fitting, we beseech you: may your piety, out of regard for God, not deny this request of ours, so that you may not permit the governors of your churches, all the clerics, and even the laypeople remaining under the condition of your kingdom—and likewise those belonging to the dominion of the kingdoms of your fathers, who are outsiders in the portion assigned to you—to be deprived of what they have always appeared to possess as their own. Let anyone who securely possesses his property pay the due taxes to the lord in whose realm his possession has come to lie.

We judge this to be altogether more useful for your treasuries as well, if preserved possession continues to bring your piety its customary revenue. Your clemency also affords us particular consolation if, through the granting of this petition, it causes us too to rejoice in your enactments.

By God’s favor, the synod recorded below [Note: [Col. 0294D] This letter presupposes the transmission of a copy to King Theudobert. Although it is placed before the Second Council of Arvernus in the manuscripts, both the context and the date demonstrate that it must be assigned to the First Council of Arvernus] was held at the Church of Arvernus on the sixth day before the Ides of November, after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger.

## XXXVII. SECOND COUNCIL OF ARVERNUS

[Col. 0295]

[Col. 0295A] 273–274 Since blessed Peter, inspired by God and, through his confession, destined to benefit all believers, says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he is rightly pronounced blessed by the Lord. And, beginning with the ruler, it must be ascribed to divine grace when the wishes of princes accord with the minds of priests, so that, since it is a pontifical council, its rule of life may follow the ancient summary of the canons, or, as place and time require, a new constitution of enactments adhering to whatever ancient headings are applicable.

Accordingly, when the most merciful prince, Lord Childebert, king unconquered in the titles of triumph [Note: [Col. 0295] U., “the prince and unconquered lord Theudobert.”], had assembled the priests of God in the city of Orléans through love of the sacred faith and concern for the stability of religion, wishing to hear from the mouth of the Fathers what is sacred and what is set forth with pastoral authority for ecclesiastical order, so that it might be a rule for those to come and a discipline for those present, and so that the things fitting to be observed henceforth might, with God’s help, be expressly set out under headings [U., “set apart”]:

### I. On the confirmation of the condemnation of the sects of Eutyches and Nestorius

We anathematize and condemn the revived wicked sect which its author Eutyches, sacrilegiously conscious of his guilt and departing from the living fountain of the holy Catholic faith, once founded, and likewise whatever was advanced by the similarly impious sorcerer Nestorius. Since the holy Apostolic See also condemns these sects, we too, execrating those same sects together with their authors and followers, anathematize and condemn them with the force of this present constitution, proclaiming in Christ’s name the upright and apostolic order of the faith.

### II. That excommunication shall not be imposed for minor matters

No priest shall suspend anyone of correct faith from communion for small or minor causes, except for those offenses on account of which the ancient Fathers ordered offenders to be excluded from the Church.

### III. That clerics shall not live with unrelated women

No bishop, priest, or deacon shall presume to keep the companionship of unrelated women within his house. Nor shall anyone, even for his own benefit, entrust a woman to such a cleric to be governed more familiarly. We likewise prohibit this with respect to female relatives at indecent hours, lest, under the permission granted to him on the pretext of kinship, either the life or reputation of those mentioned be polluted by their attendants.

If bishops should now wish, under some presumption, to make use of what is forbidden, they shall be removed from office for one year by their metropolitan or by their fellow provincials [Ae., B. R., T. 1, “suspended”]. Clerics, however, shall be corrected by their own bishops in the manner written above.

### IV. On married clerics

If any cleric, after receiving the blessing of any position or order, should presume to return again to the marriage bed, now illicit for him, he shall, as the ancient canons of the Fathers prescribe, be removed for the rest of his life from the rank of the order he received and from his office, with communion alone granted to him.

### V. That a bishop shall not promote another’s cleric

No one shall dare either to promote another’s cleric or lector, or to claim him for himself under any conditions, without the permission of his bishop. If anyone transgresses this constitution under any pretext, the person in question, having been recalled from him to whom he belongs either by ecclesiastical right or by private right, shall be suspended from the office or honor he received according to the judgment of his own bishop, because he departed through an unlawful calling away [B. R., T. 1, “vocation”]. The bishop who ordained him, however, shall not presume to celebrate Mass for six months.

### VI. That slaves shall not be ordained

[Col. 0296B]

No bishop shall dare to ordain as a cleric a slave who has not received freedom from his own masters, or even a free person, without the consent of the one whose slave he is or who is recognized as having freed him [U., “as having been freed”]. Whoever does this shall have the one ordained recalled by his master; and the one who conferred the order, if proved to have done so knowingly, shall not presume to celebrate Mass for six months.

If, however, the person is proved to be the slave of a layman, the one who has been ordained, with his blessing preserved, shall render service to his master in an honorable order. If the lay master wishes to subject him to further service, so that he appears to inflict an injury on the sacred order, the bishop who ordained him shall restore two slaves, as the ancient canons also prescribe, to the lay master [Col. 0296C]; and the bishop shall have the power to recall to his own Church the person whom he ordained.

### VII. On those freed in a church

Since we have learned from the report of many that those who, according to the custom of the parishes, had been freed from service in churches are again recalled to service at the pleasure of various persons, we have judged it impious that what is freed from the bond of slavery in the Church of God through consideration should be treated as void. Therefore, by common counsel, it has pleased us to establish this as a rule: whatever slaves are released from servitude by freeborn masters shall remain in the freedom which they then received from their masters. If such freedom is challenged by anyone, the churches shall defend it with justice, except in the cases for which the laws ordered that freedoms granted to slaves be revoked.

### VIII. That no one shall seize the property of a deceased bishop

In a city where a bishop has died according to the condition of human nature, no bishop shall dare, before the successor has been duly appointed in his place, either in the city or throughout the parishes, to ordain clerics, consecrate altars, or presume to take anything from the property of the Church beyond what humanity requires.

If anyone should transgress these statutes with reckless boldness, once summoned by the appointed bishop, he shall restore what he took without delay, having regard for his own shame [Ae., “with the delay removed”]. But if, acting on his own free will or at the entreaties of others, he should presume either to promote any person or to act against this prohibition, he shall not presume to celebrate Mass for an entire year.

### IX. No layman shall be ordained bishop without a year of conversion

No layman shall be ordained bishop without first completing a year of conversion, so that during the space of a year he may be more fully instructed by learned and approved men in spiritual disciplines and rules [U., G., “instructed”]. If any bishop should presume to exceed this under any pretext [Note: [Col. 0297D] In the manuscripts: “should presume to ordain one”; the word “to be ordained” is omitted, as in U.], he shall for an entire year be regarded as a stranger both to office and to the charity of the brethren.

### X. No one shall obtain the episcopate by money or rewards

No one shall be permitted to obtain the episcopate by any arrangement through rewards or purchase. Rather, as is written in the ancient canons, a bishop shall be consecrated by the metropolitan, or by someone whom he has authorized to act in his place, with the consent of the clergy and people and together with the bishops of the province. If anyone violates this rule in contempt of this holy constitution, we decree that the person ordained through rewards shall be removed.

### XI. No unwilling person shall be ordained bishop

Likewise, as the ancient canons decreed, no one shall be given as a bishop against his will [Col. 0297C] [Note: [Col. 0297D] B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “shall be ordained bishop against his will”]. Nor shall citizens or clerics—something wicked even to say—be bent toward giving their consent by the oppression of powerful persons. If this should happen, the bishop himself who is ordained more by force than by a legitimate decree shall be removed forever from the episcopal honor he acquired.

### XII. No one shall be appointed while a bishop is alive

No other bishop shall be appointed or placed over a living bishop, except perhaps in the place of one whom a capital offense has overthrown.

### XIII. On gifts of charity not being alienated

No one shall be permitted to retain, alienate, or remove property or resources assigned to churches, monasteries, or hospices as any form of charitable gift [Note: [Col. 0298D] B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “assigned”]. Whoever does this shall be excluded from the thresholds of the church, bound by the judgment of the ancient canons as a murderer of the poor, for as long as he fails to return to the Church what he has taken or retained.

### XIV. No one shall presume to accept the property of another Church

No bishop, cleric of any rank, or any other person, wherever situated—whether in one kingdom or another—shall under any conditions request or presume to accept the property of another Church. If he does so, he shall be considered suspended from communion at the altar and from the charity of all the brothers and sons until he restores to the Church itself what was taken from it, since it belongs to it by direct legal right.

[277] [Note: [Col. 0298D] This canon is taken from the Ae. manuscript; it is absent from the other manuscripts.]

### XV. On preserving the hospice of Lyon

Regarding the hospice which the most devout King Childebert and his wife, Queen Guldragota, founded in the city of Lyon at the Lord’s inspiration, and whose institutional order and expenditure we confirmed by the subscription of our hands when they themselves requested an accounting, it seemed right, for the sake of God’s consideration, that we gathered together and decreed with enduring authority that whatever is attempted or contributed to the aforesaid hospice—whether through the offering of the aforementioned kings or through the charity of any of the faithful—whether in goods or persons, the bishop of the Church of Lyon shall never at any time claim any of it for himself or transfer it into the right of the Church.

Nor shall the priests who succeed one another over time merely refrain from diminishing anything from the established resources of the hospice or from its constitution; they shall also take care that the stability of its property suffer no harm or diminution in any respect. Let them provide, with a view to eternal reward, that capable and God-fearing superintendents are always appointed when their predecessors depart, and that care for the sick and the number or reception of travelers remain forever in inviolable stability according to the institution originally established.

If anyone, whatever his power or rank, attempts to act against this institution of ours, removes anything from the custom or resources of the hospice, or—God forbid—causes the hospice to cease to exist, let him be struck by irrevocable anathema as a murderer of the poor.

### XVI. On offerings of churches not being taken away

Whoever, whether of high or moderate rank, presumes afterward to take away any gifts or resources contributed to priests, churches, or any holy places by any benefaction, out of zeal for reward and for the sake of God’s consideration, or anything known to have been donated by parents, shall, under the preceding judgment, be deprived of communion as a murderer of the poor.

### XVII. How the cases of churches are to be settled

It also pleased us that if any person believes he has a matter against a bishop or the administrators of a Church, he should first have recourse to him in a spirit of charity, so that, strengthened by a private conference, he may heal the matters brought forward in complaint. If he wishes to delay this matter, only then should he come to the hearing of the metropolitan.

When the metropolitan has sent his letter concerning the matter to his fellow-provincial bishop, and the case between the two has not been settled by any agreement through friendly intermediaries, so that it becomes necessary for the metropolitan to repeat his written order in the same matter, and, after being admonished a second time, the bishop delays either healing the matter, sending a response, or coming in person, let him know that he is suspended from the charity of his metropolitan until he comes into his presence and renders an account of the case for which the response is requested.

If it becomes clear that the bishop himself was harassed contrary to justice, and that the person who harassed him pressed him with an unjust appeal, that person shall be suspended from ecclesiastical communion for one year.

If a metropolitan has twice been appealed to by a fellow-provincial bishop in his own case and has delayed hearing him, the bishop shall have permission to pursue his case at the next synod that is convened. Whatever his fellow provincials determine in accordance with justice, he shall strive to ensure is observed [Note: [Col. 0299D] T. 1, 2, U., G., “to observe.”].

### XVIII. [Note: [Col. 0299D] This and the following canons are taken from the Ae. manuscript; they are absent from A. and the other manuscripts.] Fellow-provincial bishops summoned to a council must come

We believe this too should be inserted into the decree: if any of the fellow-provincial bishops is summoned by his metropolitan to a council within his province, and, apart from evident illness, delays coming to the council, or should perhaps presume to leave the synodal assembly before everything has been concluded without the council’s permission, he shall, as established by the preceding rules, be suspended from the office of celebrating Mass for six months.

If some necessity should delay the holding of the council, he shall ask pardon from his metropolitan and be restored to the privilege of celebrating Mass.

### XIX. On the offering of girls to monasteries

Whatever girls either seek a monastery of their own will or are offered by their parents shall remain for one year in the clothing in which they entered. In monasteries where they are not kept permanently enclosed, they shall remain for three years in the clothing in which they entered, and afterward, according to the statutes of the monastery in which they choose to remain, they shall receive the garments of religious life.

If thereafter, abandoning the sacred places, they transgress their holy purpose through worldly ambition, or if those who have converted in their own homes—whether girls or widows—change their clothing, they shall be deprived of communion with the Church together with those to whom they are joined in marriage. But if they remedy their fault by separation, they shall be restored to the grace of communion.

### XX. On visiting prisoners

[279] We have also judged it equitable, out of regard for mercy, that those who are assigned to prisons for whatever offenses be visited every Sunday by the archdeacon or the rector of the church, and that the needs of the prisoners be mercifully relieved according to the divine command. The bishop shall appoint a faithful and diligent person to provide what is necessary, and suitable food shall be supplied to them from the resources of the Church.

### XXI. On supporting lepers

Although, with God’s favor, this care may belong to all priests of God or to any of the faithful, namely, that they should provide what the needy require, it is nevertheless especially appropriate, as an act of mercy, concerning lepers: each bishop shall supply from the resources of the Church, according to its capacity, what is necessary for food and clothing to those whom he recognizes as inhabitants of both his territory and his city who have contracted this illness [Col. 0300A], so that the care of mercy may not be lacking to those whom intolerable poverty constrains through severe illness.

### XXII. On the annual celebration of the provincial synod and the observance of earlier canons
Having thus established these provisions, with the Lord’s favor, we solemnly decree by an appropriate definition what is chiefly recorded in all the councils of the Fathers: within the course of each year, every metropolitan bishop shall take care to hold a council within his province, bringing together his fellow-provincial bishops in one place, so that either any matters that have arisen may be corrected through the pursuit of charity, or, if peace has continued by God’s help through the rules and disciplines imposed, they may rejoice in the love and presence of God, the author of all good. Therefore, steadfastly and unanimously observing these definitions made with God’s favor, we also decree concerning the statutes of earlier canons that henceforth all of them shall be kept inviolate under Christ’s authority, so that, while the harmony divinely inspired remains, the provisions soundly defined at the present time may henceforth possess force and preserve charity.

In the name of Christ, I, a priest of the Church of Lyon, have reread and subscribed to our constitution.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] The subscriptions of all the bishops have been taken from Codex Ae. In A. and the other codices only ten bishops are enumerated: Hesychius, Nicetius, Desideratus, Aspasius, Agricola, Urbicinus (T. 1, 2: Urbicus), Rufus, Basilius, Avolus, and Hilarius.]
