# XLIII. THIRD COUNCIL OF ZARAGOZA, HELD ON THE DAY OF THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER, IN THE FOURTH YEAR OF THE ORTHODOX AND MOST SERENE LORD KING EGICA, ERA 729

[Col. 0317]

[Col. 0317D]  
[Note: [Col. 0317] [ [Col. 0317] This note is printed at the foot of column 317, but its callout letter, a, does not appear in the text.] This council is absent from codices B.R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, U., and G.]

307–308 The priests of the Lord, whom divine goodness not only raises to the sacred office of teaching but also appoints as watchers over the peoples, ought to equip themselves with such an authoritative judgment that they may persist without interruption in the divine commandments and direct the entire people by worthy examples. And therefore, because the divine majesty commanded us, by order of our most excellent, most pious, and great worshiper of God, our lord Prince Egica, to assemble in this city of Zaragoza, and established us here with every particularity so that, as the sickle of justice cuts away, the structure of equity might be strengthened, and whatever the indiscriminate destructiveness of anyone has torn away from the holy institutions of the Fathers concerning ecclesiastical orders might, with God’s help, be brought into the light of truth through our laboriously prepared judgments: for this reason, while during three days we had mutually conferred concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity according to the formula of the Council of Nicaea, carefully and attentively examining the matters that had presented themselves to our assembly for the edification of the entire people, we defined in brief and continuous chapters everything that proved necessary, with Christ’s help—whose concern for our salvation moved us to this undertaking—and we took care to strengthen for their enduring validity, by the writing of our own hands, the matters enacted or defined by us.

## I. That bishops not perform church consecrations except on Sundays

While we were seated in the holy and sufficiently venerable council, it was reported to us that certain bishops, neglecting the rule of truth, consecrate churches built by the faithful with pious devotion on days other than Sundays. If, therefore, whenever one of us mortals is promoted to the priestly office, we by no means permit those deemed worthy of this honor to be placed in ecclesiastical rank on other days except the festivals of Sunday, how much more must holy temples, made divine and considered worthy of honor by faithful people, be proclaimed consecrated only on Sundays? We are compelled to prohibit the presumptions of such bishops not only by the judgment of the holy Fathers but also by our own deliberation; accordingly, we decree that no bishop appointed in any province shall henceforth be permitted to consecrate holy churches except on designated Sundays.

## II. That neighboring bishops annually inquire concerning the date of the sacred Easter solemnity from their primate

Although the holy institution of the Fathers concerning the Easter solemnity commands that all neighboring bishops, in annual rotation, inquire from their primate at what time they are to celebrate the feast of Easter, nevertheless, because we have learned that certain bishops transgress the judgment of the Fathers—even though for this reason they ought to have remained constantly vigilant—it has pleased all of us that henceforth all neighboring bishops, offering themselves no excuse and taking no precaution on account of the length of the journey, shall annually inquire, at the appropriate time concerning the Easter festival, from the primate under whose authority they remain, so that they may celebrate the feast of Easter with attentive reverence on the day and at the time he announces to them.

## III. That monasteries not become lodging houses for secular people

The judgment of the holy Fathers decreed that monasteries must not become lodging houses for secular people. Since we know that certain abbots, to whom the care of governing souls has been regularly entrusted, grant secular persons access to monasteries in a seemingly patronal spirit, they introduce various insolences among the monks serving God there: they observe their conduct, by which the monks eagerly and zealously display themselves as pleasing to divine goodness, and, with a certain destructive perversity of mind, they do not cease to defame and disgrace their life and morals. Again—and this is the worst matter—when outsiders are indiscriminately given access to stay within the monastery enclosure, a serious vice grows up among the monks: they degenerate by pursuing their life through worldly profits and separate themselves from their own monastery through shameful indulgence.

This matter moves our hearts with paternal compassion to establish provisions that both offer assistance and consolation to holy souls and remove the presumptions of secular people. Therefore it pleased, or rather it was defined by, our entire assembly that henceforth no secular person, whether by authority, or even with the permission of an abbot or of any monk, shall have a lodging or dwelling within the enclosure of monasteries, except those whom the abbot’s inspection recognizes as persons of worthy life, needy, or oppressed by poverty. These we permit by every means to be received with goodwill in the monasteries and supported by alms.

As for the other secular persons, as we have stated above, we absolutely do not permit them to have lodging within the monastery enclosure. However, if somewhere more privately or separately from the monastery a dwelling constructed for newcomers is available, the abbots or monks ought to receive them there, so that their life, removed from the disturbances of the world, may be found worthy in every godly work, and so that they may not be dishonored by anyone’s most empty slanders—or, what is dishonorable, so that through receiving such persons they may not incur laxity and make their own lives alien to their good purpose.

## IV. Concerning freedmen manumitted by bishops from the Church’s household

[Col. 0320B]

There is no doubt that the holy Fathers defined that all freedmen whom bishops manumit from their own ecclesiastical households and register for the sake of manumission must, after the death of the deceased bishop, as soon as another bishop succeeds, present their instruments of freedom within the space of a year, so that, according to the judgment of the canon, through their own declarations they may acknowledge the condition of their due origin.

But because the holy synod decreed in a special manner that if those freedmen neglect to present the documents of their freedom to their succeeding bishop within the space of a year, they are immediately to be reduced to their former condition of slavery—and although this matter has been reconsidered in a more appropriate and sufficiently clear manner—we nevertheless judge this point to be especially important: not only do we arrange the estates of the churches with due authority, but we also extend pious assistance to the oppressed, by which both priestly greed may be frustrated and the weakness of the poor relieved.

Since, therefore, we have discovered that certain bishops, striving rather to enlarge their own profits than to please the Lord through the work of their reward, immediately reduce to their former slavery the freedmen whom they find manumitted by their predecessors from the Church’s household, on the grounds that they have not presented the documents of their freedom within the prescribed time, we substitute this benefit as a general provision out of a spirit of piety: if those freedmen should perhaps be ignorant of the order of the canons, or if, as commonly happens, they have been slow to present their instruments of freedom, the bishop himself, as soon as he has succeeded to the see entrusted to him, shall take care, through the clergy or household officials, to seek out those whom deceased bishops registered for manumission from the Church’s households. Then, with that same bishop giving prior notice, the freedmen themselves shall present the documents of their freedom, so that neither the freedmen of the Church may claim that they are ignorant of the provisions of the canons, nor may the priest’s crafty intention become apparent, whereby those who have been manumitted are reduced contrary to the proper order to their original slavery.

But if, after being warned by the bishop, they disdain within the space of a year to disclose their freedom to the bishop of their own see, it shall be lawful for him, according to the sanctions of the canons, to reduce them to servitude under the right of his Church.

## V. That after the death of the prince, the surviving queen immediately lay aside secular dress and be committed to a convent of virgins, where she is to remain

[Col. 0321A]

Although the Council of Toledo had established very fully concerning the widows of princes that no one was permitted to take a surviving queen in marriage or defile her with sordid contact, and that neither succeeding kings nor any other person was permitted to do so, it is nevertheless proper to our order that we very frequently direct the attention of our mind to matters that we perceive can advance the soul.

Therefore, because in former times we know and have learned that many widows of princes, after their summons from this life, were shown no respect for the dignity which they had held in every way while governing at the height of royal power, but that it was commonly established that various persons, under various pretexts, not only secretly plotted against them but also—contrary to the truth—insolently subjected them to insulting words in the presence of many people; and, what is abhorrent and dreadful to every form of religion, did not permit people to refrain from slandering those whom they saw living among the crowd, we have been moved by paternal compassion and, with due foresight concerning so great a dignity, have decided through the page of this decree not only that the provisions concerning the wives of princes written in the aforementioned council are to remain perpetually and firmly preserved, but also to add what is clearly necessary for propriety.

Accordingly, while all the sanctions of the entire Council of Toledo concerning the widows of princes—those known to have been promulgated and defined—are preserved, henceforth the widow of the prince, faithfully and chastely observing the foregoing judgment with an undefiled spirit, shall immediately, after the prince has been summoned from this world, lay aside secular dress and eagerly assume the religious habit. We further decree that she is immediately to be committed to a convent of virgins, so that, removed from every storm of the world, no opportunity may be granted to anyone by which insult might be inflicted upon so great a power [Note: [Col. 0321C] Ae., “public insult might be inflicted upon so great a power”], or by which it might become apparent that she remained subject to the people whose mistress she is known to have been until recently. Instead, persisting within the monastery enclosure in continual devotion and living the life of a consecrated woman, may she deserve, with divine assistance, to pass from temporal sovereignty to the kingdom of eternity.

Whoever, therefore, violates the preceding constitutions, which are known to have been defined by us after salutary deliberation, or attempts or permits them to be cursed by any faction, shall know that he will receive the sentence of excommunication and also incur, for a long period, the loss imposed by condemnation to exile.

312 After we had completed what was appropriate concerning ecclesiastical orders, we first offer immense praises to almighty God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whose care it is to provide peace and unity for his holy Catholic Church. Then we render manifold thanks to our orthodox and most serene lord, King Egica, at whose prompting and through whose most devout initiative we have been permitted to assemble in this synodal gathering. He not only stirred our minds to correct ecclesiastical orders but also freed the people, through the gracious command of his royal authority, from the payment of tribute. For this beneficent concern, through which he has bestowed such great gifts upon his people, we implore the Lord Jesus Christ—who has adorned us by the power of his might and redeemed us through the precious and proper outpouring of his blood—that he himself may establish his kingdom in peace through many courses of years, preserve the nation and the whole country in tranquility, and always make it victorious against the enemy through the victorious right hand of Christ. Thus, when the extended periods of this life have been completed, may he deserve to reach unharmed the eternal reward of blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor, supreme power, and authority forever and ever. Amen.

# XLIV. COUNCIL OF LLEIDA, OF EIGHT BISHOPS, HELD IN THE ERA 534, IN THE FIFTEENTH YEAR OF KING THEODORICUS  
[Note: [Col. 0321D] B. R., G., “Teudi.” U., “Theudericus.”]  
ON THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST

[Col. 0321]

## I. Concerning those who minister at the altar, that they abstain from all blood

[Col. 0321D]

Concerning clerics who have been placed in the necessity of a siege, this has been established: those who minister at the altar, deliver the blood of Christ, or handle vessels assigned to sacred service must abstain from all human blood, even that of an enemy. If they fall into this offense, they are to be deprived for two years both of office and of communion, so that during those two years they may atone, according to the strength that the Lord grants, through vigils, fasts, prayers, and almsgiving. Only then are they to be restored to office or communion, with this condition observed: they are not thereafter to be promoted to higher offices. But if, within the prescribed period, they prove negligent concerning their salvation, it shall remain in the power of the priest to prolong the period of that penance [Ae., “to add to that penance”].

## II. Concerning those who cause abortions or kill their own newborn children

Those who strive to kill children conceived or born from adultery, or who in the wombs of their mothers destroy them by some potion, whether male or female, are to be granted communion after the course of seven years, provided that throughout the whole time of their lives they persist in tears and humility; they are not permitted to recover the ministry of office. Nevertheless, from the time they receive communion, they are to attend among the choir of psalm-singers. Communion is to be granted to those who practice poisoning only at the point of death, provided that they have mourned their crimes throughout the whole time of their lives.

## III. Concerning monks, that they be ordained clerics with the abbot’s consent; that offerings made to the monastery not be taken away; and concerning basilicas built by laymen

Concerning monks, it has pleased us that the provisions known to have been decreed by the Synod of Agde or Orléans [B. R., Arles] be observed. Only this is to be added: for the benefit of the Church, those whom the bishop approves are to be ordained to the clerical office with the consent of the abbot. Whatever is offered from property under the legal control of the monastery is not to be touched by bishops under any diocesan law.

But if any layman wishes a basilica built by him to be consecrated, he must not dare to remove it from diocesan jurisdiction under the pretext of a monastery where no community is gathered or rule established by a bishop.

## IV. Concerning incestuous persons, that as long as they remain in the crime they be held among the catechumens

Concerning those who defile themselves with the pollution of incest, it has pleased us that, for as long as they persist in that detestable and unlawful carnal cohabitation, they be admitted in the church only as far as the Mass of the catechumens. No Christian ought to take food with them, just as the Apostle says or commands.

## V. Concerning those who serve at the altar, if they suddenly fall through the weakness of the flesh

[Col. 0323C]

If those who serve at the altar of God suddenly fall through the lamentable weakness of the flesh and, with the Lord looking upon them, repent worthily, so that, having mortified the body, they offer to God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, it shall remain in the power of the bishop either not to suspend those who are genuinely afflicted for long, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer period. Yet they are to recover their places in their offices in such a way that they cannot thereafter be promoted to higher offices. But if they return again, like dogs, to their vomit, they are not only to lose the dignity of their office but also are not to receive holy communion except at the point of death.

## VI. Concerning those who violate a penitent widow or a consecrated virgin

[Col. 0323D]

Whoever uses force to commit sexual violation against a penitent widow or a consecrated virgin, if he refuses to separate himself from her, is likewise to be separated both from communion and from the fellowship of Christians. But if the woman who suffered the violence returns to holy religious life, the sentence is to remain in force against him alone until he publicly performs penance.

## VII. Concerning those who bind themselves by oath not to return to peace

Whoever binds himself by oath that, while in dispute with someone, he will in no way return to peace is, on account of perjury, to be separated from communion of the body and blood of the Lord for one year and to absolve his guilt through almsgiving, tears, and as many fasts as he is able to undertake [Ae., T. 2, “to cleanse it”]. Let him hasten to return to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

## VIII. If a cleric drags a servant or disciple away from the church, that he perform penance

No cleric may dare to drag away or presume to beat his servant or disciple who has taken refuge in the church. If he does so, he is to be separated from the place to which he has not shown honor until he performs worthy penance.

## IX. Concerning those who have been rebaptized, how they are to perform penance

Concerning those who, in apostasy, have slipped into rebaptism without any necessity or compulsion, it has pleased us that the provisions established by the Council of Nicaea concerning apostates be observed in their case: namely, that they pray among the catechumens for seven years and among the Catholics for two years, and afterward, by the moderation and mercy of the bishop, communicate with the faithful in the offering and the Eucharist.

## X. Concerning those who, when ordered by the bishop, disdain to leave the church for an offense

Those who, when ordered by the priest to leave the church for any offense, refuse to do so are to be received more slowly into pardon, on account of the offense of their defiance.

## XI. Concerning clerics who rush into mutual slaughter

If clerics rush into mutual slaughter, the bishop shall punish the offense with greater severity in proportion to the dignity of the offices that have suffered insult through such an excess.

## XII. Concerning those ordained contrary to the canons, that they be deposed

May the Lord or holy ecclesiastical charity forgive those who until now have indiscriminately ordained clerics contrary to the decrees of the canons. But henceforth, if they venture into such conduct, the canonical decree established concerning their persons is to be observed: namely, that they dare ordain no one; and those who are ordained thereafter are to be deposed. Those who have so far been ordained in this manner are never to be promoted [Ae., T. 2, “removed”].

## XIII. Concerning Catholics who have given their children to be baptized by heretics

If a Catholic presents his children to be baptized in heresy, his offering is in no way to be received in the church.

## XIV. Concerning Catholics, that they not associate with the rebaptized

The devout faithful are not to share food with the rebaptized.

## XV. That clerics not live with unrelated women

[Col. 0324D]

Familiar association with foreign women, although the holy Fathers in their ancient admonitions entirely forbade it to the churches, we nevertheless now judged that whoever is proved to have such an association, if after a first and second admonition he neglects to amend, should be deprived of the dignity of his office for as long as he persists in the fault. But if, with God’s help, he corrects himself, he shall be restored to the holy ministry.

**316 XVI. If a priest dies, what is to be observed concerning the property of the church.**

Although the ancient authority of the canons has by no means been silent concerning this matter, which we decree should be established by a salutary ordinance, but has expressly commanded that, when the bishop of any church has died, no one should indiscriminately rush at will to seize the property he left when he died or overturn his house, rather, the priest who is present at the time of the funeral should carefully secure everything pertaining to its usefulness and preservation; nevertheless, because this very sanction—which is worse—is known to be violated by many clerics, so that, driven by unbridled desire and setting aside every severity of discipline, when a priest dies they savagely invade and strip whatever is found in the bishop’s house, it has now pleased all of us to safeguard the force of this agreement and decree among us:

When a bishop has died, or is even still in his final illness, no cleric—whatever his order, office, or rank—may presume to take anything from the house, or attempt to seize any useful property known to belong among the household’s equipment, whether movable or immovable ecclesiastical property; he must suppress, take away, or conceal nothing by theft, force, or fraud. Rather, the person entrusted with the house, after associating with himself, with the counsel of the clergy, one or two men of complete fidelity, must preserve everything until a successor to the bishop has been appointed, or provide the clerics found in the house with their customary provisions.

The succeeding bishop, having received these things, shall use them according to what his predecessor ordered, or according to what God shall have commanded him [U., “inspired him”], together with those whom he recognizes as having faithfully obeyed the discipline and charity of his predecessor.

But if thereafter any cleric of whatever order, as stated above, is proved on any pretext to have taken anything from the church’s house or from its entire property, or perhaps to have fraudulently concealed something, he shall be condemned as guilty of sacrilege to a prolonged anathema, and even communion as a stranger shall scarcely be granted to his soul. For it is harsh that those who are known to have labored in the service of the Lord with the bishop of the chief see should in any way be tormented by the contempt of those who are known to have been intent upon and occupied with appropriating his property or serving their own interests.

Sergis [U., “Sergius”], bishop, in the name of Christ, reread and subscribed these constitutions, according to what, with God’s inspiration, pleased us together with our brothers.

Justus, bishop in the name of Christ, was present at these constitutions and subscribed.

Carontius, bishop in the name of Christ, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. **317** [Col. 0326B]

John, bishop in the name of Christ, was present at these constitutions and subscribed.

Paternus, bishop in the name of Christ, bishop of the Catholic Church of Barcelona, agreed and subscribed.

Maurilio [B. R., T. 1, U., G., “Maurulio”], bishop in the name of Christ, of the Catholic Church of Tortosa, agreed and subscribed.

**318** Taurus [U., “Maurus”], bishop in the name of Christ, of the Church of Egara [in the manuscripts, “Agarensis”], was present at these definitions and subscribed.

Februarius, bishop in the name of Christ, of Lérida, was present at these constitutions and subscribed.

Gratus, priest in the name of Christ, sent by my lord Bishop Staphylus [T. 2, U., “Stabilius”], was present at these constitutions and subscribed.

# XLV. Council of Valencia, of six bishops, held in the year 587 of the era [Note: [Col. 0325D] Ae., B.R., T. 1, 2, U., G., “era 584”], in the fifteenth year of King Theuderic [U., “Theudericus”], on 4 December.

[Col. 0325]

## I. That the Gospel be read after the Apostle.

[Col. 0325C]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We who had assembled at Valencia in council, while discussing ecclesiastical regulation and rereading the ancient canons, judged among other things that this should be observed: that the sacred Gospels be read after the Apostle, in the order of the readings, before the presentation of the gifts or the Mass of the catechumens, so that not only the faithful but also catechumens and penitents, and even all who are outsiders, may be permitted to hear the saving commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ and the priest’s sermon. For we clearly know that, after hearing the preaching of bishops, some have been drawn to the faith.

## II. That after the death of a bishop no one presume anything concerning his property or that of the Church.

[Col. 0325D] This also pleased us: when a bishop has been summoned from this world by the Lord, the clerics must keep their grasping hands entirely away from all the furnishings or anything whatsoever in the house of the Church or of the bishop—books, valuables, utensils, vessels, crops, flocks, animals, or absolutely any other thing—and must not plunder anything in the manner of thieves. If they are not restrained even by the authority of the canons, they shall be compelled, through the strictness of the metropolitan or of all the priests of the province, to restore everything they have seized to its former condition, so that under this just constitution nothing necessary may be lost to the bishop or future administrator.

To ensure that this is observed with greater confidence while justice remains intact, according to the decrees of the Council of Riez, when a bishop has departed from the body, the bishop who is nearest to him shall approach and, after the customary funeral rites have been performed, immediately assume the strictest care of that Church, so that before the future bishop is ordained nothing may be permitted to the covetous clerics for the destruction or plunder of the church [Col. 0326D]. Thus, if possible, a careful inventory and a most trustworthy description of everything found shall be made under the supervision of the present bishop within the octave of the deceased [Col. 0327A]. Thereafter the arrangement or inventory shall be conveyed to the metropolitan’s knowledge, so that by his choice a person may be appointed to administer the church’s household who will be able to distribute the customary stipends to the clerics and, if delay should occur in ordaining the bishop, render an account to the metropolitan at suitable times of the property entrusted to him.

Thus, under this salutary constitution, clerics, fully content with their stipends, will not plunder the labors of the departing bishop, and the future bishop will not enter the empty house of the Church with grief; rather, he may himself rejoice in what his predecessor left behind and distribute it to others.

## III. That the relatives of a dying bishop appropriate nothing from his property without the knowledge of the metropolitan and the bishops of the province.

[Col. 0327B] In the same way, the parents and relatives of a deceased bishop, if he has died intestate, must be warned not to attempt to seize anything from the dead man’s property without the knowledge of the metropolitan or of the priests of the province, lest among the hereditary goods they also appropriate or mingle something belonging to the Church. Rather, they should either wait until the future bishop is ordained or, if this should take a long time, have recourse, as stated, to the metropolitan’s arrangements.

But if any cleric or layman, forgetful of divine fear, attempts with wicked intent to act against these synodical decrees, he shall be deprived both of communion and of fellowship with the Church, since it is harsh that he should approach the Church which he did not fear to strip—unless perhaps, seized by a better spirit, he abandons his presumption and thereby recovers pardon [Col. 0327C]. If, however, someone reasonably and modestly seeks what is legally owed to him, neither the matter nor the legal claim shall be denied him by the metropolitan or by whoever he appoints, without any penalty.

All those who in the past seized and plundered the property of the Church or of a bishop shall also be bound by this canon.

## IV. How the funeral of a dying bishop is to be conducted.

With prudent counsel we also decree this: because the funerals of holy bishops are often delayed through the absence of the bishop responsible for them, so that the venerable remains of the bishop, being buried too late, suffer every indignity, the bishop who is customarily invited to come and bury his brother after his death should not delay, once notified, visiting him while he is ill and still in the body. In this way he may either rejoice more fully in the recovery of his fellow bishop or, at least, advise his brother concerning the administration of his household and bring his worthy wishes into effect. After a sacrifice has been offered to God for his commendation, the departing man should then be most diligently committed to burial, and the canonical provisions established above should not be delayed.

But if, as often happens, the bishop departs through a sudden death, and the neighboring priests are unable to arrive from afar, the lifeless body of the priest shall be kept for one day and one night only, not without the attendance of brothers and religious persons or the vigil of psalm-singers. It shall be placed with every care by the priests in a coffin, but shall not immediately be buried separately; rather, it shall be honorably entrusted until, without delay, a bishop has been invited from wherever possible and the body has been solemnly buried by him, as is fitting. Thus an opportunity for indignity will be removed and the ancient custom in burying priests will be preserved.

## V. Concerning wandering and disobedient clerics.

This also pleased us: if a wandering and unstable cleric—even one established in the ministry of a deacon or the office of a priest—does not obey the commands of the bishop by whom he was ordained, namely, that he carry out his office continually in the Church entrusted to him, he shall, for as long as he remains in the fault, be deprived both of communion and of honor.

## VI. That no one ordain another’s cleric, and that no one be a cleric who has not promised the place to which he is assigned.

No one may presume, according to the decrees of the canons, to ordain another’s cleric without the consent of his own bishop [Col. 0328C]. Nor may any of the holy priests ordain a man who has not first promised that he will remain in the place to which he is assigned [G., “shown himself local”], so that no one may be permitted to deviate from ecclesiastical rule or discipline with impunity.

Celsinus, bishop in the name of Christ, subscribed [Note: [Col. 0327C] Ae., E. 3: “I, Celsinus, bishop, subscribed these chapters,” [Col. 0327D] and similarly in the remaining subscriptions. B.R.: “I, the bishop, subscribed [Col. 0328C] these decrees,” and likewise thereafter in the others.]

Justinian [T. 1, “Justinus”], bishop in the name of Christ, subscribed.

Reparatus, bishop in the name of Christ, subscribed.

Setabius, bishop in the name of Christ, subscribed.

Benagius, bishop in the name of Christ, subscribed.

Ampelius, bishop in the name of Christ, subscribed.

Sallustius, archdeacon in the name of Christ, vicar of my lord Marcellus, bishop, subscribed.

# XLVI. Council of Toledo, of nineteen bishops, held in the times of Arcadius and Honorius, on 7 September, with Stilicho as consul, in the year 435 of the era [Note: [Col. 0327D] Ae., U., “era 438”; B.R., “era 436”; T. 1, 2, “era 430”].

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327D] **321–322** When the bishops had assembled in the church at Toledo—namely, Patruinus, Marcellus, Aphrodisius, Alacianus [Note: [Col. 0328D] Ae., U., G., “Licinianus”; B.R., “Lucianus”; T. 2, “Licianus”], Jucundus, Severus, Leonas, Hilarius, Olympius, Florus, Orticius, Asturius, Lampius, Serenus, Leporius, Eustochius, Aurelianus, Lampadius, and Exuperantius of Gallaecia, of the Lucensian conventus, from the municipality of Celenis—all nineteen are those who, in other proceedings as well, sent a written judgment against the followers of Priscillian and against the heresy he had constructed. With the priests seated, the deacons standing by, and the other participants assembled at the council, Bishop Patruinus said:

“Since each of us has begun to do different things in our churches, and from this have arisen such great scandals that they reach even to schism, if it pleases you, let us decide by common counsel what all bishops must follow in ordaining clerics. For my part, I approve that the decrees first established by the Council of Nicaea be observed perpetually and that we not depart from them.”

The bishops said: “This pleases us all, so that if anyone, having learned the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, presumes to do anything other than what has been established, and does not think that it must be adhered to, he shall be regarded as excommunicated, unless he corrects his error through the rebuke (*correptionem*; Ae., *correctionem*, “correction”) of the brothers” [Col. 0329B].

## I. Concerning priests and deacons who father children after ordination.

It pleased us that deacons, whether married or unmarried, should be upright, chaste, and of continent life, and should be established in the ministry even if they have wives. Nevertheless, if any have lived incontinently with their wives even before the prohibition established by the bishops of Lusitania, they shall not be advanced to the honor of the priesthood. If any priest has fathered children before the prohibition, he shall not be admitted from the priesthood to the episcopate [T. 1, “permitted”].

## II. That a penitent, if necessity requires, may become a lector or doorkeeper.

It also pleased us that a penitent not be admitted to the clergy, unless necessity or practical need requires that he be assigned among the doorkeepers or among the lectors, and even then he shall not read the Gospels or the Apostle. Those who were previously ordained as subdeacons shall remain among the subdeacons, but shall not lay on hands or touch the sacred things.

By “penitent” we mean one who, after baptism, having undertaken public penance for homicide or for various grave crimes and sins, has been reconciled to the divine altar while wearing sackcloth [Ae., “while undertaking penance”].

## III. Concerning those who have married widows, that they are not to become deacons.

The holy synod also decreed that if a faithful lector has taken another man’s widow as his wife, he shall hold no higher office, but shall always remain a lector, or perhaps a subdeacon.

## IV. That a subdeacon who marries another woman after his wife’s death is to become a doorkeeper.

[Col. 0329D]

If a subdeacon, after his wife’s death, marries another woman, he shall be removed from the office in which he was ordained and placed among the doorkeepers or lectors, so that he may not read the Gospel or the Apostle, lest one who has served the Church appear to serve in public offices. But if he takes a third wife—which ought neither to be said nor heard—he shall abstain for two years and thereafter, reconciled among the laity through penance, shall receive communion.

**323 V. That if a cleric of any order comes late to the church, he is to be deposed.**

If a priest, deacon, subdeacon, or any cleric assigned to the Church is in the city or in a place where there is a church, fortress, village [Col. 0330A], or estate, and does not come to the church for the daily sacrifice, he shall not be regarded as a cleric if, after being disciplined, he refuses to earn pardon from the bishop through satisfaction.

## VI. That a religious girl is not to have the companionship of men.

Likewise, no girl of God may have familiar association with a confessor or with any layman, whether unrelated by blood or otherwise, nor dine alone, except where there is a gathering of elders, respectable persons, or honorable widows, where any confessor may honorably attend the meal in the presence of many witnesses. She is not to be admitted at all into the houses of lectors, nor seen by them, unless perhaps she is the lector’s sister by the same father or by the same mother.

## VII. That a cleric whose wife has sinned, except by killing her, has authority to discipline her and is not to eat with her.

[Col. 0330B]

It pleased us that if the wives of any clerics sin, lest they thereby have greater license to sin, their husbands shall receive the authority to guard them and bind them in their house, except by killing them, compelling them to salutary, not deadly, fasts. Thus clerics shall assist one another if they should perhaps have no servants. They shall not eat with the wives who have sinned [Note: [Col. 0329D] From the word *peccaverint* onward, Codex E. 4 begins], unless they return after having performed penance in the fear of God.

## VIII. Concerning one who has served in the army after baptism, that he is not to be promoted to the diaconate.

If anyone has served in the army after baptism and has taken the military cloak or belt, even if he has committed no grave offense, and has been admitted to the clergy, he shall not receive the dignity of the diaconate.

## IX. That no professed woman or widow, in the absence of a priest, perform priestly or lamp-lighting rites in her house.

No professed woman or widow, in the absence of a bishop or priest, may perform antiphons in her house with a confessor or with her servant. The lamp-lighting service is not to be read except in a church; or, if it is read in a village, it is to be read in the presence of a bishop, priest, or deacon.

**324 X. That no one make an obligated cleric a cleric without the consent of his master or patron.**

Clerics who are bound, whether by an agreement or by belonging to the household of someone, are not to be ordained unless they have proved themselves of good character and the consent of their patrons has been obtained.

## XI. That if a powerful man strips anyone of his property and does not restore it when admonished by the bishop, he is to be excommunicated.

[Col. 0330D] If any powerful person [Note: [Col. 0330D] E. 4, T. 1, “one of the powers”] strips a cleric, or anyone poorer, or a religious person of his property, and the bishop sends word to him that he should hear the matter, but he refuses, letters shall immediately pass among all the bishops of the province and all whom they can reach, so that he may be regarded as excommunicated until he is heard and restores what belongs to another.

## XII. That no cleric depart from his bishop and transfer himself to another.

Likewise, no cleric may freely depart from his bishop and communicate with another bishop, unless perhaps he is someone whom another bishop willingly accepts as departing from the schism of heretics and returning to the Catholic faith [Col. 0331A]. But if anyone departs from the Catholics and is found, openly or secretly, in communion with those who are excommunicated or have already been marked by sentence, let him share even in the condemnation of those to whom he wished to go.

## XIII. Concerning those who enter the church and do not receive communion, that they are to be excommunicated.

Those who enter the church and are found never to receive communion are to be admonished: if they do not receive communion, let them approach penance; if they do receive communion, let them not continually abstain. If they do not do this, let them abstain.

## XIV. Concerning one who receives the Eucharist but does not consume it, that he is to be rejected as a sacrilegious person.

If anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from the priest, let him be driven away as a sacrilegious person.

## XV. Concerning those who are excommunicated by priests, that no one approach them.

[Col. 0331B]

Whenever a layman is under abstention, no cleric or religious person may approach him or his house. Likewise, if a cleric is under abstention, he is to be avoided by clerics [Note: [Col. 0331D] Ae., B.R., E. 3, 4, T. 1, 2, G., “avoided”]. If anyone is discovered speaking with him or dining with him, he too shall be placed under abstention. But this applies to the clerics who are under the authority of his bishop and to all who have been warned concerning the person under abstention, whether he is a layman or a cleric.

**325 XVI. That if a devoted woman commits adultery, she do penance for ten years; if she marries, she is not to be admitted to penance unless her husband departs.**

A devoted woman who has sinned is not to be received into the Church unless she has ceased to sin and, after ceasing, has performed suitable penance for ten years [Col. 0331C]. Let her receive communion. Before she is admitted to prayer in the church, however, she is not to attend the banquet of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, the woman who received her is also to be regarded as under abstention. The corrupter is likewise to be bound by an equal penalty.

But a woman who has taken a husband is not to be admitted to penance unless, while that husband is still alive, she begins to live chastely, or after he has departed.

## XVII. Concerning a married man who has a concubine, that he is not to receive communion.

If a faithful man who has a wife keeps a concubine, he is not to receive communion. But a man who has no wife and keeps a concubine in place of a wife is not to be barred from communion [Col. 0331D]. Let him be content with the union of only one woman, whether wife or concubine, whichever he prefers. But if he lives otherwise, let him be cast out until he ceases and returns through penance.

## XVIII. If the widow of a priest or deacon marries, she is to receive communion only at the end of life.

If the widow of a bishop, priest, or deacon takes a husband [Col. 0332A], no cleric or religious woman is to dine with her. She is never to receive communion; only when she is dying are the sacraments to be given to her [T. 2, “nevertheless”] [Note: From Ae., B.R., U., G. In E. 3, T. 2: “let the sacrament come to her aid.” In A. and the others: “let assistance be given by the sacrament,” perhaps for “let her be assisted.”]

## XIX. If the religious daughter of a priest or deacon sins, she is to receive communion only at the end of life.

If the daughter of a bishop, priest, or deacon has been devoted to God, sins, and takes a husband, and her father or mother receives her back affectionately, they are to be regarded as excluded from communion. The father must know that he will have to give an account of the matter in the council. The woman, however, is not to be admitted to communion unless, after her husband’s death, she has performed penance. But if she leaves him while he is still alive [Note: [Col. 0331D] Ae., B.R., E. 4, “withdraws”] **326**, performs penance, and asks for communion, she is to receive communion on the last day of her life, as she is dying.

## XX. That no one except a bishop prepare the chrism.

[Col. 0332B]

Although it is observed almost everywhere that no one may prepare chrism without a bishop, nevertheless, because in certain places or provinces priests are said to prepare chrism, it pleased us that from this day no one except a bishop prepare chrism [Note: [Col. 0331D] B.R., E. 4, “make it”] and send it through the dioceses. Thus, from each church, deacons or subdeacons are to be sent to the bishop before Easter [Note: [Col. 0331D] Ae., “the feast day of Easter”; U., “the holy day of Easter”], so that the chrism prepared and sent by the bishop may arrive by Easter.

It is certainly established that a bishop may prepare chrism at any time; but absolutely nothing is to be done without the bishop’s knowledge. It has been decreed, however, that a deacon is not to chrismate, but a priest may do so in the bishop’s absence, and in his presence if he has been instructed to do so by the bishop.

Let the archdeacon always remember to recommend this constitution, whether bishops are present or absent, so that either the bishops may observe it or the priests may not neglect it.

Patruinus, bishop, subscribed.

Marcellus, bishop, subscribed.

Aphrodisius [Note: [Col. 0332D] Ae., T. 1, 2, “Aphrodius,” although at the beginning of the council they wrote “Aphrodisius”], bishop, subscribed.

Licinianus [Note: [Col. 0332D] “Let the scribal negligence be considered: the manuscripts that wrote ‘Alacianus’ in the preface to the council now write ‘Licinianus’; those that earlier had ‘Lucianus’ later have ‘Lucinianus’; and those that earlier had ‘Licianus’ have ‘Lucianus’ in the subscriptions”], bishop, subscribed.

Jucundus, bishop, subscribed.

Severus, bishop, subscribed.

Leonas, bishop, subscribed.

Hilarius, bishop, subscribed.

Olympius, bishop, subscribed.

Orticius, bishop, subscribed.

Asturius, bishop, subscribed.

Serenus, bishop, subscribed.

Florus, bishop, subscribed.
