# Rules of the Catholic Faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, drawn up by the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Baetica, and sent, at the command of Pope Leo of the City [Note: [Col. 0333D] B.R., T. 2, “of the city of Rome, Leo”; E. 4, “of the city to Balconius”], to Balconius [B., R., “Balaconius”], bishop of Gallaecia.

These same bishops also established the twenty canon chapters written above in the Council of Toledo.

[Col. 0333A]

**327** We believe in one true God, the Father and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, maker of visible and invisible things, through whom all things were created in heaven and on earth. We believe that this is one God and that this is the one Trinity of the divine substance; that the Father is not the Son himself, but has a Son who is not the Father; that the Son is not the Father, but is the Son of God, of the Father’s nature; and that the Spirit, the Paraclete, is neither the Father himself nor the Son, but proceeds from the Father and the Son [Col. 0333B]. [Note: [Col. 0334D] This sentence is lacking in BR.]

Thus the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Paraclete not begotten but proceeding from the Father and the Son.

The Father is he whose voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” The Son is he who says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world from God.” The Spirit, the Paraclete, is he of whom the Son says: “Unless I go away to the Father, the Paraclete will not come to you.”

We believe this Trinity to be distinct in persons, united in substance, indivisible, undifferentiated in power, authority, and majesty. Apart from this, we believe that there is no divine nature, whether of an angel, spirit, or any power believed to be God.

We believe, therefore, that this Son of God, God born from the Father before every beginning whatsoever, sanctified the womb of the Virgin Mary and received from her a true human being, generated without male seed. Only two natures—that is, divinity and flesh—came together in one person, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ. His body was neither imaginary nor some phantasm, but solid and true. He both hungered and thirsted, suffered and wept, and endured every bodily affliction. Finally, he was crucified and buried by the Jews and rose again on the third day. Afterward he lived with his disciples and, on the fortieth day after the resurrection, ascended into heaven.

This Son of Man is also called the Son of God, and the Son of God, God, is called the Son of Man.

We believe that there will be a resurrection of human flesh. But we say that the human soul is not a divine substance or a part of God, but a creature created by the divine will.

## I.

If anyone says or believes that this world was not made by almighty God, together with all its structure, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0334A] **II.** If anyone says or believes that God the Father is the same as the Son or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

**328 III.** If anyone says or believes that the Son of God is the same as the Father or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

**IV.** If anyone says or believes that the Paraclete is the Father or the Son, let him be anathema.

**V.** If anyone says or believes that the Son of God assumed flesh only, without a soul, let him be anathema.

**VI.** If anyone says or believes that Christ is unbegotten, let him be anathema.

**VII.** If anyone says or believes that Christ’s divinity was changeable or passible, let him be anathema [Col. 0334B].

**VIII.** If anyone says or believes that there is one God of the ancient Law and another of the Gospels, let him be anathema.

**IX.** If anyone says or believes that the world was made by another God and not by the one of whom it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” let him be anathema.

**X.** If anyone says or believes that human bodies do not rise again after death, let him be anathema.

**XI.** If anyone says or believes that the human soul is a portion of God or is God’s substance, let him be anathema.

**XII.** If anyone says or believes that writings other than those which the Catholic Church receives are to be held authoritative or venerated, let him be anathema [Col. 0334C].

**XIII.** If anyone says or believes that divinity and flesh are one nature in Christ, let him be anathema.

**XIV.** If anyone says or believes that there is anything which can extend beyond the divine Trinity, let him be anathema.

**XV.** If anyone thinks that astrology or the mathematical arts are to be believed, let him be anathema.

**XVI.** If anyone says or believes that human marriages which are regarded as lawful according to divine law are accursed, let him be anathema.

**XVII.** If anyone says or believes that the flesh of birds or cattle, which has been given for food, is not merely to be abstained from for the chastening of the body but is to be execrated, let him be anathema [Col. 0334D].

**XVIII.** If anyone follows or professes the sect of Priscillian in these errors, so as to do anything else in saving baptism [Note: [Col. 0334D] From T. 1. In A. and the others: “in the salvation of baptism”] contrary to the see of Saint Peter, let him be anathema.

# XLVII. Second Council of Toledo, of eight bishops, held on 18 May, in the fifth year of the reign of our lord King Amalaric, in the year 565 of the era.

[Col. 0335]

[Col. 0335A] **329–330** When, by the will of the Lord, we had assembled in the city of Toledo in the presence of the holy bishops, and a discussion was being held concerning the institutions of the Fathers and the decrees of the canons, this pleased us when gathered together: that if anything has not been mentioned at all in the ancient canons, it should be established through salutary deliberation and careful consideration; but if anything was decreed in earlier councils and has until now been neglected through the abuse of the times, it should receive the authority of a renewed ordinance. Thus, while we devote ourselves to religious observance in matters pertaining to the worship of the faith, we may more easily obtain the mercy of our God.

## I. Concerning those whom their parents have devoted to the clerical office from infancy, if they later wish to marry.

[Col. 0335B] Concerning those whom the will of their parents has devoted to the clerical office from the earliest years of infancy, we establish that this must be observed: as soon as they have been tonsured or, having been assigned to the ministry of the chosen [BR., “readers”], have been handed over to the church’s household, they are to be taught by the person placed over them in the presence of the bishop. When they have completed their eighteenth year, however, their desire for marriage is to be examined by the bishop before the sight of all the clergy and the people.

If, by God’s inspiration, they prefer the grace of chastity and promise that they will preserve their profession of chastity without the necessity of marriage, they are to be placed under the Lord’s very gentle yoke as seekers of the strictest way of life [Note: [Col. 0335D] Ae., B.R., E. 3, 4, U., G., “way”], and, after their profession has been tested, they are to undertake the ministry of the subdiaconate from their twentieth year [Col. 0335C]. If they have completed their twenty-fifth year without blame or offense, they may be promoted to the office of the diaconate, provided the bishop has established that they can fulfill it competently.

They must nevertheless beware lest, forgetting their promise, they ever again return to earthly marriages or secret sexual unions. If they do so, they are to be condemned as guilty of sacrilege and regarded as strangers to the Church.

But to those whom their own desire, at the time of questioning, persuades toward marriage, we cannot deny the judgment granted by the apostles: when, having reached mature age and living in marriage, they promise by mutual consent that they will renounce the works of the flesh, they may aspire to the sacred orders.

## II. Concerning a cleric who transfers to another church and the one who receives him.

[Col. 0335D]

It likewise pleased us to ensure that none of those who are educated in this manner, compelled by any circumstance, should presume to leave his own church and transfer to another [Col. 0336A]. The bishop who perhaps presumes to receive him without the knowledge of his own priest must know that he is guilty before the whole brotherhood, since it is harsh that one should presume to receive or claim a man whom another has stripped of the rustic ignorance and squalor of infancy.

## III. That no one from the subdiaconate upward live with a foreign woman.

We further decreed by a special ordinance [Note: [Col. 0335] From all the manuscripts except A., which has “by order”] what the ancient councils have not been silent about in almost all their canons: that no cleric from the rank of subdeacon upward may keep in familiar companionship any woman, whether freeborn, freedwoman, or enslaved. If he has such servants, he must entrust them to his mother, sister, or another female relative, and whatever they produce by their labor must be delivered to their proper master.

If the relatives mentioned are lacking, another household is to be sought for their residence, provided that no opportunity is allowed for a woman to enter the cleric’s house, where she might either fall into a snare or perhaps bring a harmful reputation upon an innocent man.

If thereafter, following this admonition, anyone wishes to enjoy the companionship of such women, he must know that he will not only be removed from the clerical office and expelled from the church doors, but also deprived of communion with all Catholic clerics and laypeople, with absolutely no consolation even of conversation left to him. Thus the rust of a bad custom, once scraped away, cannot spread among posterity with the poison of its root.

## IV. That whatever clerics hold by right of the Church return to the Church after their death.

[Col. 0336C]

If any cleric is proved to have made little fields or vineyards for himself on Church lands for the purpose of sustaining his life, he may possess them until the day of his death. After his departure from this light, however, he must restore his right to the holy Church, according to the constitutions of the earlier canons, and may not leave it to any heir or heir’s heir by testamentary or hereditary right—unless perhaps the bishop wishes to grant it to someone for services rendered and benefits provided to the Church.

## V. Concerning those who unite themselves to their relatives, that they are to be separated from the communion of Christ.

For we decree that this too must prudently be forestalled: no member of the faithful may desire to marry a close blood relative, for as long as the lines of kinship can be recognized through the succession of their lineage, since it is written: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relative to uncover his nakedness.” Nor is this without a declaration of the sentence, for shortly afterward it adds and says: “The soul who does any of these abominations shall be cut off from the midst of his people.” Therefore, if anyone should prove to be a transgressor of this decree of ours and presume to violate what is forbidden, let him recognize that he must be punished by a sentence all the more severe, the nearer he does not deny that the person to whom he chose to be joined is to him in origin; and let him be separated from the body of Christ and from the fellowship of the brethren for a period of excommunication all the longer, the more polluted he has been by the contagion of near blood relationship. We who sign the regulation of this institution pledge, with irrefragable authority, that we shall observe it. But if anyone, whether among us or among those who are now absent from this holy synod from this province, should presume to oppose this highly salutary ordinance or negligently fail to fulfill it, once convicted, let him for a time be regarded as a stranger to all fraternal charity.

Indeed, in accordance with the decrees of the earlier canons, we announce that a council is to be held, if the Lord wills, with our brother Bishop Montanus, so that our brother and fellow bishop Montanus, who is in the metropolitan see, may in due time send letters to our fellow provincial priests of the Lord summoning the approaching synod. Now, therefore, having completed in the Lord’s name the matters that came before the assembly, we give thanks to almighty God; then, asking divine clemency for the glorious lord King Amalaric, we pray that throughout the innumerable years of his reign he may grant us permission to carry out whatever pertains to the worship of the faith. Amen.

Montanus, bishop in the name of Christ, have assented to these enactments, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

Pancarius, bishop, have assented to these enactments, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

Canonius, bishop, have assented to these enactments, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

Paulus, bishop, have assented to these enactments, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

Domitianus, bishop, have assented to these enactments, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

Marcianus, bishop in the name of Christ, assigned to exile in the city of Toledo on account of the Catholic faith, attended the enactments of my holy brothers, reread them, and subscribed them on the day and in the year stated above.

[Note: Ae., B.R., Marrucinus. E. 3, 4, T. 1, 2, U., Marracinus.]

Nibridius, bishop in the name of Christ of the Catholic Church of Egara, having arrived after some time, reread, approved, and subscribed this enactment of my fellow priests, held in the city of Toledo, without prejudice to the authority of the ancient canons.

Justus, bishop in the name of Christ of the Catholic Church of Urgell, having arrived after some time, reread, approved, and subscribed this enactment of my fellow priests, held in the city of Toledo, without prejudice to the authority of the ancient canons.

[Note: These letters are absent in A., Ae., and E. 2. They are taken from B.R., with variant readings from the other witnesses.]

To the most beloved lords, brothers and sons of the territory of Palencia, Montanus, bishop, eternal salvation in the Lord God.

[Col. 0338A]

That terrifying admonition addressed to the foremost bishops of all the Lord’s churches through the prophet Ezekiel, under the name of the watchman, strikes them, saying: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Therefore, when you hear a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. When I say to the wicked, ‘Wicked man, you shall surely die,’ and you do not announce it to him or speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that man shall indeed die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood at your hand”—and the rest, which the order of this passage shows must be considered concerning the soul of the admonisher and the one admonished.

Moved, therefore, by this warning, and not unaware that I had undertaken the necessity of this office, I took care to apply myself diligently, lest Christ should require from my hand the soul of anyone who had been lost [T. 1, 2: “lest Christ should inquire after the soul of anyone lost”]. This was especially so because ancient custom has conferred metropolitan privilege upon the city of Toledo, and the care not only of parishes but also of cities places the responsibility for this city upon its bishop.

Therefore, as the Apostle says, “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and in a spirit of gentleness?” A new presumption on the part of the priests presiding over you has struck our ears—if indeed it can be called merely new, and not detestable—which is shown never to have crept in from the beginning of the Catholic faith until now: that a priest ignorant of discipline should presume to prepare chrism himself which the invocation of the Trinity, through the hands of the supreme pontiff, has been accustomed to sanctify.

If this is due to negligence, such a priest ought not to have been so foolish; if it is due to presumption, who does not know that he is a schismatic, when such a transgressor introduces, now that the world is already growing old, something unheard-of and contrary to religion? Let the most sacred Book of Numbers be turned over in your hands, O priests, in which the honor of your office began with the persons of the seventy elders, and you will find what duties have been granted to you by privilege. God willed you to be helpers in our labor, in the second rank of dignity; he did not permit you to be transgressors with respect to certain sacred matters.

Thus Nadab and Abihu, offering strange fire—that is, fire not belonging to their office—were consumed by divine fire. Thus Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, envying Moses, who enjoyed the grace of God and divine utterances, and saying, “God has not spoken only to you, for the whole congregation is holy,” met the destruction of a new perdition as new schismatics, so that the earth, with fasting mouth, might insatiably swallow those whom divine indignation had condemned.

Why should I mention Uzziah? Not content with royal authority, he attempted to perform the priestly office as well. Against right and divine law, he donned the buskin of authority and prepared to offer the expiatory offering reserved for priests alone; then he was so covered with leprosy by heavenly vengeance that, hated both by the priesthood and by the kingdom, he remained so until his death.

Likewise Uzzah, who, as far as he was concerned, was preparing in devoted service to support the ark of God lest it slip when the oxen stumbled, was struck by a divine blow and destroyed. This plainly showed that under no circumstances, not even under the pretext of humility, may those who presume to do so touch divine offices and heavenly sacraments when the office does not belong to them.

Let those who think it lawful for themselves what they do not fail to know is unlawful for others beware—indeed, let them beware—lest a punishment like that of those whom we have mentioned strike them. Or perhaps you are ignorant of the rules of the holy Fathers and the synodal constitutions, which prescribe that parish priests should request chrism annually from the bishop presiding over them, not through inferior persons, but either in person or through the administrators of the shrines? I believe that those who ordered it to be requested entirely removed the authority to consecrate it.

Your Charity must therefore take care that, after this prohibition issued in our humility, until the customary bishop is prepared for you by the Lord, no one presumes to repeat what is forbidden [E. 4: “what is old”] and thus begins to undergo the more severe censure of ecclesiastical discipline. Let each person use the privilege granted to his rank, which he knows belongs to the order of the priesthood; let no wicked minister assume what belongs to the supreme pontificate.

Anyone who, after this warning, is discovered in any way to have engaged in such matters must know that he is to be condemned by the unbreakable bond of anathema. Yet in this very matter a considerable measure of humaneness is now being granted him, since we allow him to pass unpunished.

Indeed, if the Lord wills, when the time of the Paschal feast arrives, if it is impossible for you to come to request it, you must inform us by sending your letters, and we shall be able voluntarily to transmit the grace of this sacred liquid, provided that nothing unlawful is presumed.

In the same way, we have learned that bishops from another jurisdiction are invited by you for the consecration of basilicas. Although they are joined to us in Christ by the bond of one faith, this is nevertheless known to be contrary both to the privileges of the province and to the interests of the Lord’s possessions, since report of such a matter has already reached him. Therefore, by a salutary ordinance, we have judged that whenever such a necessity arises you must inform us by letter, so that either we, or whichever of our brothers and fellow bishops seems suitable to us, may celebrate the consecration of the churches, with God’s blessing.

Moreover, we know that the most depraved sect of the Priscillianists is honored among you, especially not so much in its deeds [Note: E. 4, T. 1, 2: “the sect in its deeds”] as in its name. I ask: what madness is this, to drift needlessly into love for one whom you do not wish to imitate in practice? To bring a few of his filthinesses to your attention, apart from the things in which he profanely broke out against the Godhead and blasphemed with sacrilegious mouth, a heap of every vice flowed together in him as though into a cesspool of filth, so that an unashamed adulterer might deprive his female followers of their modesty; and, to reach more easily the outcome of his unspeakable crime, his deeds are identified by the practice of magic.

Yet what in all this does the soul of any faithful person revere as consistent with religion? He was not only rejected by holy priests, but worldly rulers also condemned him by the justice of their laws in proportion to the crime mentioned.

Anyone who reads the books published by the blessed and most religious Bishop Thoribius to the holy Pope Leo of the city of Rome will learn more fully what he was like. In those books he explained and exposed this filthy heresy and brought into the open the faithlessness hidden beneath its darkness and cloud of deceit. From those very books the devout reader will learn how he may guard against sacrilegious people and what he may answer them.

Therefore, I ask you, while condemning and anathematizing the faithlessness together with its author, to hold fast to the rule of the true faith and to make yourselves more cautious concerning all the matters written above. In this way I may more easily avoid condemnation for silence, and you may secure for yourselves the greatest fruit of obedience before God our Savior. The peace of the Lord be with you all. Amen.

To the distinguished and foremost worshiper of Christ, my lord and son Thoribius, Montanus, bishop.

[Col. 0340B]

We have both greatly recognized and approved you as a pupil of the Catholic faith and a friend of holy religion, even while you have conducted yourself in public affairs. For while you still flourished in the world, the life of your distinction shone forth so clearly that, according to the Lord’s command, you did not refuse to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and you rendered to God what belongs to him with devoted mind.

I shall rightly call you the author of divine worship in this province in particular. Do you suppose how great a reward remains for you with God, by whose diligence or inspiration both the error of idolatry has departed and the detestable and shameful sect of the Priscillianists has withered? [Note: E. 4, T. 1, 2: “shameful” instead of “pudenda,” “disgraceful.”]—provided that they cease still to honor his name, whose works they know have collapsed through your admonition.

For what should I say about the faith of the earthly lords? You devoted your labor to them in such a way that you brought the fierce dispositions of those dwelling with you to a salutary rule and the standard of regular discipline. Divine clemency will grant that what you attempted with the greatest labor you may accomplish through prayers and supplication.

I have taken care to inform your Excellency of what has reached us from the assembly of Palencia, so that, through your rebuke, this wicked presumption may more easily cease in the future. As it has been reported to us, certain priests, with reckless audacity, presume not so much to consecrate sacred things as to violate them. They unquestionably assume—whether I should call it some delusion or madness I do not know—the right of consecrating chrism, which has been unfamiliar to men of their order throughout all the centuries from the beginning of the Catholic faith and is owed only to the supreme pontiffs.

I do not believe that the sacrilegious character of this can be hidden from your most devout conscience. I therefore hope that you will use the authority of a most severe priest to weaken this very excess, and that you will restrain the transgressors of so great a matter by stern rebuke. If, after the warning has been given, they presume to repeat this impiety, their obstinacy will be condemned by an appropriate sentence.

In the same way, we have learned that, because of the need to consecrate basilicas, our brothers, bishops from another jurisdiction, are invited and assemble in these places. Although throughout the whole world there is one bridal chamber of Christ’s Bride, and her bishops are joined together in the same clasp of charity and unity of faith, we have sent to your Charity, as examples, the privilege that your fellow bishop granted to our predecessor and also to our lords and brothers, the bishops of Carpetania and Celtiberia, so that you may know what result such an improper request might have had.

Certainly, we granted to him the municipalities—that is, Segovia, Brittablo, and Cauca—not indeed reasonably, but out of regard for the dignity of the name, lest the blessing conferred should be cheapened by the wandering of the person. Know that this was granted to him only while he was assisting.

We therefore wish you to take care that you in no way neglect the ancient custom. If this warning of ours accomplishes nothing in you, it will be necessary for us thereafter to report the matter to the ears of our lord, and likewise to bring it to the attention of our son Ergani. Such an attempt will be punished with the utmost severity, by the commands of his high authority or by the rigor of the judge, and not without harm to you. For, by the Lord’s grant, his piety is so great that he will not permit anything to be altered from what he is shown to have preserved as the ancient right.

May the divine Trinity protect you. Amen.

XLVIII. THE THIRD COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, OF SIXTY-TWO BISHOPS, AT WHICH THE ARIAN HERESY IS CONDEMNED IN HISPANIA.

[Col. 0341]

[Col. 0341B] 337–338. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fourth year of the reign of the most glorious, most pious, and most faithful-to-God lord King Reccared, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the era 627, this holy synod was held in the royal city of Toledo by the bishops of all Hispania and Gaul who are written below [Note: Ae., B.R., T. 1: “are about to subscribe.” E. 3, T. 2: “are about to write.” E. 4: “are subscribed.”].

When that most glorious prince, on account of the sincerity of his faith, had commanded all the bishops of his realm [BR., E. 4: “kingdom”] to assemble together, so that they might rejoice in the Lord both over his conversion and over the renewal of the Gothic people, and might give thanks to divine favor for so great a gift, that same most holy prince addressed the venerable council as follows:

“I do not think it is unknown to you, most reverend priests, that I have summoned you into the presence of our Serenity in order to restore the form of ecclesiastical discipline. Since, in past times, the heresy that threatened the whole Catholic Church prevented synodal business from being conducted, God, who was pleased through us to remove the obstacle of that same heresy, admonished us to restore the ecclesiastical institutions according to custom.

“Therefore, let it be a source of delight and joy to you that, by God’s providence and through our glory, canonical custom is being brought back to the boundaries of our fathers. First, however, I jointly admonish and exhort you to devote yourselves to fasts, vigils, and prayers, so that the canonical order which long and lasting forgetfulness had removed from priestly minds—and which our age admits that it does not know [BR., ‘admits that it is growing old’]—may once again be revealed to you by the gift of God.”

In response, they gave thanks to God and to the most religious prince, and, while the entire council acclaimed him with praises, a three-day fast was then proclaimed. But when, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, the priests of God were present in one assembly, and, after prayer had been offered, each priest had taken his seat in the appropriate place, behold, the serene prince appeared among them. Sharing in prayer with the priests of God and thereafter filled with the divine Spirit, he began to speak as follows:

“I do not believe that it is hidden from your Holiness how long Hispania labored in the error of the Arians, and we believe that, not many days after the death of our father, when your blessedness learned that we had been joined to the holy Catholic faith, you experienced a great and eternal joy. Therefore, venerable fathers, we determined [T. 2: ‘commanded’] that you should assemble to conduct this synod, so that you yourselves might offer eternal thanks to the Lord for the people recently coming to Christ.

“Whatever it was necessary for us to do in words before your priesthood concerning the faith and hope that we possess, we have made known in this volume, written down and presented. Let it be read in your midst, and, once examined by synodal judgment, let our glory shine throughout all succeeding time, adorned by the testimony of that same faith.”

[Col. 0342C]

The volume of the sacred faith, offered by the king, was received by all the priests of God, and, when the notary had proclaimed it, it was read aloud as follows:

“Although almighty God has granted us to assume the height of kingship for the benefit of peoples and has entrusted the governance of not a few nations to the care of our royalty, we nevertheless remember that we are constrained by the condition of mortals, and that we cannot otherwise earn the happiness of future blessedness unless we devote ourselves to the worship of the true faith and please our Creator at least with the confession that he himself deserves.

“Therefore, the more highly royal glory exalts us over our subjects, the more provident we must be in matters concerning God, whether to increase our hope or to care for the nations entrusted to us by God.

“For what can we offer almighty God in return for the bestowal of so many benefits [Note: In A. and the remaining manuscripts: ‘consolations’], since everything belongs to him and he needs nothing of our goods, except that we believe in him with complete devotion as he himself wished to be understood through the Holy Scriptures and commanded to be believed? That is, we must confess that there is a Father who begot from his own substance a Son equal and coeternal with him—not, however, that the same person is both begotten and begetter, but that the Father who begot is one person and the Son who was begotten another, although both subsist in the divinity of one substance.

“The Father is the one from whom the Son is; the Son, however, is from no other, although he has the Father, but subsists without beginning and without diminution in that divinity in which he is coequal and coeternal with the Father.

“Likewise, we must confess and proclaim that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is of one substance with the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit is the third person in the Trinity, yet he shares with the Father and the Son the essence of divinity.

“For this holy Trinity is one God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. By his goodness every creature was created good; yet through the Son’s assumption of the form of human guise, we are restored from our condemned ancestry to our former blessedness.

“But just as the sign of true salvation is to perceive the Trinity in unity and unity in the Trinity, so it will be the completion of righteousness if we hold this same faith within the universal Church and observe the apostolic instructions, established upon the apostolic foundation.

“Yet you, priests of God, must remember how greatly the Catholic Church of God throughout Hispania has until now suffered from the troubles caused by the opposing party, while the Catholics steadfastly held and defended the truth of their faith, and the heretics, with more stubborn determination, tried to vindicate their own faithlessness [Note: T. 2: ‘their own faithlessness’].

“The Lord also aroused me, as you see in reality, kindled by the fervor of faith, so that, after the obstinacy of unbelief had been driven away and the fury of discord removed, I might recall to the knowledge of the faith and fellowship of the Catholic Church the people who, under the name of religion, had been enslaved to error.

“For the entire illustrious nation of the Goths is present—renowned for the native manliness of almost all peoples. Although, through the perversity of its teachers, it has until now been separated from the faith or from the unity of the Catholic Church, it is now united with me in complete agreement and shares in the communion of that Church which receives multitudes of diverse nations into its maternal embrace and nourishes them at the breasts of charity. Of this Church the prophet says: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations.’

“Nor has only the conversion of the Goths been added to the fullness of our reward. There is also the countless multitude of the Suevic nation, which we have subjected to our kingdom by heavenly aid. Though it had been led into heresy through another’s fault, we have nevertheless recalled it, through our own zeal, to the origin of truth.

“Therefore, most holy Fathers, I offer these most noble peoples, who through us have been won for the Lord, to eternal God through your hands as a holy and acceptable sacrifice. It will be for me an unfading crown, or joy in the recompense of the just, if these peoples, who through our diligence have hastened to the unity of the Church, remain founded and established in it.

“For just as by divine will it was our care to draw these peoples to the unity of Christ’s Church, so let it be for your teaching to instruct them in Catholic doctrines, so that, taught in the knowledge of the truth in every respect, they may know solidly to reject the error of the destructive heresy, retain the path of the true faith in charity, and embrace the communion of the Catholic Church with more eager desire.

“Furthermore, just as I confidently believe that it is easy to obtain pardon for so illustrious a people because until now it was ignorant and had gone astray, so I do not doubt that it will be more serious if, after recognizing the truth, they hold it with hesitant heart and—God forbid—turn their eyes away from the light that has been made manifest.

“Therefore, I have judged it highly necessary that your blessedness should assemble together, trusting in the Lord’s sentence, which says: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.’ For I believe that the blessed divinity of the holy Trinity is present at this holy council.

“Therefore, as though before the sight of God, I have set forth my faith in your midst, fully conscious of the divine sentence that says: ‘I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from a great congregation.’ I have also heard the Apostle Paul commanding Timothy his disciple: ‘Fight the good fight of faith; take hold of eternal life, to which you were called, and make the good confession before many witnesses.’

“For true is the sentence of our Redeemer in the Gospel, by which he says that he will confess before the Father the one who confesses him before human beings, and will deny the one who denies him.

“It is necessary for us to confess with our mouth what we believe in our heart, according to the heavenly command that says: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’

“Therefore, just as I anathematize Arius, with all his doctrines and accomplices, who asserted that the only-begotten Son of God was degenerate from the substance of the Father, and said that he was not begotten by the Father but created from nothing, and just as I anathematize all the councils of the wicked that arose against the holy Council of Nicaea, so, to the honor and praise of the holy faith of the Council of Nicaea, I observe and honor the faith that the holy synod of three hundred and eighteen bishops wrote against that same plague of true faith, Arius.

“Accordingly, I embrace and hold the faith of the one hundred and fifty bishops assembled at Constantinople, which destroyed Macedonius, who diminished the substance of the Holy Spirit and separated the unity and essence of the Father and the Son, striking him down with the sword of truth.

“I likewise believe and honor the faith of the First Synod of Ephesus, which was issued against Nestorius and his teaching. Similarly, with the whole Catholic Church, I reverently receive the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, which it set forth, full of holiness and learning, against Eutyches and Dioscorus.

“I also observe with equal veneration the councils of all the orthodox and venerable priests that do not differ in the purity of faith from the four synods written above.

“Let your Reverence therefore hasten to apply this faith of ours to the canonical records, and carefully hear from the bishops, the religious, or the leading men of our people the faith that they have believed in God within the Catholic Church. Preserve this faith, recorded in writing and strengthened by their subscriptions, for future times as a testimony before God and humanity.

“Thus, if any of these peoples, over whom we excel by royal power in God’s name, and who, after wiping away their ancient error, have received the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, within God’s Church through the anointing of the most holy chrism and the laying on of hands—confessing him to be one and equal with the Father and the Son and being placed by his gift in the bosom of the holy Catholic Church—should in no way wish to believe this right and holy confession of ours, let them receive the wrath of God together with eternal anathema, and let them be a source of joy to the faithful in their destruction and an example to the unbelieving.

“To this confession of mine I have appended the constitutions of the holy councils written above, and with complete simplicity of heart I have subscribed my testimony before God.”

The faith issued by the holy Council of Nicaea.

“We believe in one God, the almighty Father,” and the rest.

[Note: The complete Nicene Creed is written in the other manuscripts except A., in which this marginal note is read: ‘You will find this in the Nicene synod.’]

Thus King Reccared gave testimony, as it was established in the Council of Nicaea by the holy bishops.

The faith expounded by the 150 Fathers, consonant with the great Synod of Nicaea.

[Col. 0345B]

“We believe in one God, the almighty Father,” and the rest.

[Note: The faith of the Council of Constantinople is found in all the manuscripts except A.; in A. the following is written in the margin: “Likewise, you will find this in the Council of Constantinople.”]

The Treatise of the Council of Chalcedon.

“Indeed, it would have been sufficient for the fullest piety,” and the rest.

[Note: This treatise is expressed at greater length in the other manuscripts except A. and Ae., in which the following words are displayed in the margin: “You will investigate this in full in the Council of Chalcedon.”]

Thus the aforementioned king spoke:

“I, King Reccared, retaining in my heart and affirming with my mouth this holy and true confession of faith, which the one Catholic Church throughout the whole world confesses, have subscribed it with my right hand, God being my protector.”

“I, Baddo, glorious queen, have subscribed with my own hand, from my whole heart, this faith which I have believed and received.”

Then the entire council acclaimed God’s praises and the prince’s favor:

“Glory to God the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, whose care it is to provide peace and unity for his holy Catholic Church.

“Glory to our Lord Jesus Christ, who gathered the Catholic Church from all nations at the price of his blood.

“Glory to our Lord Jesus Christ, who joined so illustrious a people to the unity of the true faith and established one flock and one shepherd.

“To whom is eternal merit from God [Ae.: ‘joy’] if not to the true Catholic King Reccared?

“To whom is an eternal crown from God if not to the truly orthodox King Reccared?

“To whom belong present and eternal glory if not to the God-loving King Reccared?

“He is the gatherer of new peoples into the Catholic Church.

“May he truly deserve apostolic merit who fulfilled an apostolic office.

“May he be beloved by God and human beings who so wondrously glorified God on earth, through the favor of the Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Ae., T. 2: ‘our Lord Jesus Christ’], who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

Confession of faith of the bishops, priests, and nobles of the Gothic people who subscribed below.

At the command and direction of the entire venerable council, one of the Catholic bishops addressed the bishops, religious persons, and elders who had been converted from the Arian heresy, beginning as follows:

“The care of our office and the admonition of our most faithful and glorious prince compel us carefully to inquire of your Charity what you condemn in the heresy and what you believe within God’s holy Catholic Church. For, as we have learned from the Psalmist’s words, ‘Begin with confession to the Lord,’ it is best and conducive to your salvation openly to confess what you believe and, in the hearing of all, to anathematize what you reject.

“Then you will be able most fully to become participants in the evangelical and apostolic faith if you begin from a Catholic confession to profess this same Catholic faith, or confirm it by your own subscription. Just as you are already known to God by the good agreement of your conscience, so you should show yourselves to your neighbors by your assent to the holy faith.

“In this way you will signify that you are members of Christ’s body, and our insignificance will never suspect anything doubtful or faithless concerning your brotherhood, once it is clear that you condemn in advance the rot of Arian faithlessness, with all its doctrines, rules, offices, communion, and books, and, stripped of the contagion of this detestable heresy [Note: Ae., B.R.: ‘attested heresy’], shine within God’s Church, renewed as though in the splendid clothing of the true faith.”

Then all the bishops, together with their clergy, and the nobles of the Gothic people, spoke with one accord:

“Although we already did what your brotherly and fatherly authority now wishes to hear or see us do, at the time of our conversion, when we followed our most glorious lord King Reccared and passed over to the Church of God and jointly anathematized and rejected the Arian faith with all its superstitions, nevertheless, on account of the charity and devotion that we remember we owe either to God or to the holy Catholic Church, we hasten most willingly to do not only these things that you request, but also, if you see anything else that is suitable to the faith, persuade us of it in charity.

“For the love of the true faith once led us into such devotion that whatever your brotherhood may more truly reveal to us, we shall hold and confess with a willing profession.”

**I.** Whoever desires still to hold the faith and communion that came from Arius and has until now been retained by us, and does not condemn it with the full intention of his heart, let him be anathema.

**II.** Whoever denies that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, was begotten without beginning from the substance of the Father, and that he is equal or consubstantial with the Father, let him be anathema.

**III.** Whoever does not believe, or shall not have believed, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and does not say that he is coeternal and coessential with the Father and the Son, let him be anathema.

**IV.** Whoever does not distinguish the persons in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and does not acknowledge the substance of one divinity, let him be anathema.

**V.** Whoever asserts that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit are lesser than the Father, separates them by degrees, and says that they are creatures, let him be anathema.

**VI.** Whoever does not believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, omnipotence, and eternity, let him be anathema.

**VII.** Whoever says that the Son of God does not know what the Father knows, let him be anathema.

**VIII.** Whoever assigns a beginning to the Son of God and to the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

**IX.** Whoever dares to profess that the Son of God, according to his divinity, is visible or subject to suffering, let him be anathema.

**X.** Whoever does not believe that the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is true God and omnipotent, let him be anathema.

**XI.** Whoever believes that the Catholic faith and communion exist anywhere outside the universal Church—by “Church” we mean the Church that likewise holds and honors the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—let him be anathema.

**XII.** Whoever separates and divides the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in honor, glory, and divinity, let him be anathema.

**XIII.** Whoever does not believe that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are to be glorified and honored together with the Father, let him be anathema.

**XIV.** Whoever does not say, “Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,” let him be anathema.

**XV.** Whoever believes, or shall have believed, that the sacrilegious act of rebaptizing is good, or does, or shall have done, such a thing, let him be anathema.

**XVI.** Whoever regards as true the detestable booklet issued by us in the twelfth year of King Liuvigild, which contains the transfer of the Romans to the Arian heresy and in which the doxology “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit” was wrongly formulated by us, let him be anathema forever.

[Col. 0347D] **XVII.** Whoever does not reject and condemn with all his heart the Council of Ariminum, let him be anathema.

### XVIII

For we confess that we have been converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic Church with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. No one doubts that we and our predecessors went astray in the Arian heresy, and that we have now learned the evangelical and apostolic faith within the Catholic Church. Therefore, we likewise hold, confess, and receive the holy faith which our aforementioned most religious lord set forth in the midst of the council and subscribed with his own hand; and we promise to preach and teach it among the peoples.

This is the true faith which, because the whole Church throughout the world holds it, is believed and recognized to be Catholic. Whoever does not approve, or shall not approve, this faith: let him be anathema—*Maran atha* (“Our Lord, come!”)—at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### XIX

Whoever rejects the faith of the Council of Nicaea: let him be anathema.

### XX

Whoever does not declare the faith of the Council of Constantinople, of the one hundred and fifty bishops, to be true: let him be anathema.

### XXI

Whoever does not hold and delight in the faith of the First Synod of Ephesus and of Chalcedon: let him be anathema.

### XXII

Whoever does not receive the councils of all orthodox bishops, harmonious with the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon: let him be anathema.

### XXIII

Therefore, with our own hands we have subscribed this condemnation of the treachery and communion of the Arians, and of all the councils that fostered the Arian heresy, together with their anathema. But the constitutions of the holy councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, which we heard with the greatest gratitude and judged to be true by our assent, we have subscribed with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, considering nothing more illuminating for the knowledge of the truth than what the authorities of the aforesaid councils contain.

Concerning the Trinity and the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, nothing truer, nothing more illuminating, ever can or will be demonstrated than what is found here. Concerning the mystery of the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God for the salvation of the human race—that is, whereby both the true assumption of human nature without the taint of sin is proved and the fullness of incorruptible divinity remains in him, while neither nature is destroyed and one person is made from both natures, that of our Lord Jesus Christ—the truth is sufficiently and fully shown to be revealed in these councils, and we believe it without any doubt.

If anyone at any time should attempt to pervert, corrupt, or change this holy faith, or should wish to depart from, separate himself from, or dissociate himself from that same faith or Catholic communion which, by God’s mercy, we have recently obtained, let him be eternally liable before God and the whole world for the crime of unbelief.

But may the holy Catholic Church flourish throughout the whole world in profound peace, and may she excel in teaching, holiness, and power. If there are within her those who have believed and shared in communion, let them hear, placed at the right hand of the Father:

> Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.

But if there are those who have withdrawn from her, disparaged her faith, and rejected communion, let them hear from the divine mouth on the day of judgment:

> Depart from me, you accursed; I do not know you. Go into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] Ae., B.R., E. 4, T. 1 read *praeparatus* (“prepared”) for *paratus* (“prepared”).]

Therefore, whatever is condemned through this Catholic faith, let it be condemned in heaven and on earth; and whatever is accepted through this faith, let it be accepted in heaven and on earth, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

Ugnas, bishop, in the name of Christ, anathematizing the doctrines of the Arian heresy condemned above, have subscribed with my own hand, with all my heart, this holy Catholic faith which I believed when I came into the Catholic Church.

Likewise, all the elders of the Goths subscribed.

After the confession and subscription of all the bishops and of the elders of the entire Gothic people, our most glorious lord, King Recared, for restoring and at the same time confirming the practices of ecclesiastical discipline, addressed the priests of God as follows:

“Royal care ought to be extended and directed to the point at which it is evident that it can embrace a complete understanding of truth and knowledge. For just as royal power shines more gloriously in human affairs, so also its concern and foresight for the welfare of those who share the province ought to be greater.

“But now, most blessed priests, we do not devote our diligence solely to those matters by which the peoples placed under our rule may be governed and live in the greatest peace. With Christ’s assistance, we also extend ourselves to think about heavenly things, and we strive not to remain ignorant of those things that make peoples faithful.

“Moreover, if all human strength must be exerted to set a limit to human wrongdoing and to restrain the madness of the insolent by royal power; if we ought to contribute aid to the promotion of quiet and peace; much more must care be applied to desire and contemplate divine things, to long for sublime realities, and to show truth in serene light to peoples recalled from error. For thus acts the one who trusts that God will reward him with manifold good; thus hears the one who increases what has been entrusted to him, when it is said to him: ‘Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.’

“Therefore, because your blessedness has now reviewed at full length the form of our faith and confession, and because the faith and confession of our priests and nobles has likewise been made evident to your holiness, our authority has decided, still supplicating God, to establish the following necessity for the strengthening of the Catholic faith: that all the churches of Spain and Gaul observe this rule for strengthening the recent conversion of our people. At the time of the sacrifice, before communion of the body or blood of Christ, all are unanimously and in a clear voice to recite the most sacred creed of the faith according to the custom of the eastern regions, so that the peoples may first confess what they hold by belief and thus, with their hearts purified by faith, present themselves to receive the body and blood of Christ.

[Note: Ae., B.R., E. 3, 4, U.: *communicationem* (“communion/participation”) for *communionem* (“communion”).]

“For when this decree has been perpetually preserved in the Church of God, the belief of the faithful is firmly strengthened, and the unbelief of the faithless, refuted, is readily inclined toward what it recognizes as having been repeated so often. No one will then excuse himself from guilt on the ground of ignorance of the faith, when he learns from the mouth of all what the Catholic Church holds and believes.

“Therefore, among all the chapters which are still to be added to the ecclesiastical rules through your holiness, set this forth, out of reverence for and firmness of the holy faith, which our serenity, God teaching us, has decreed concerning the proclamation of the creed.

“As for the rest, to restrain insolent behavior, with my clemency consenting to you, conclude matters with stricter judgments; prohibit by firmer discipline what ought not to be done; and strengthen by immovable decree what ought to be done.”

# Chapters Established by the Holy Synod in the Name of God

## I. That the Decrees of the Councils and the Decisions of the Roman Bishops Be Observed

After condemning the Arian heresy and setting forth the holy Catholic faith, this holy council decreed the following. Since in some churches throughout Spain the canonical order had been neglected because of either heresy or pagan necessity, while permission to transgress had abounded and the choice of discipline had been denied, and while every excess had been encouraged by the patronage of heresy, therefore, so that strict discipline may restrain the abundance of evil, now that peace has been restored to the Church of Christ by mercy, everything prohibited by the authority of the ancient canons shall be forbidden through the revival of discipline, and everything they command to be done shall be carried out.

Let the constitutions of all the councils remain in force, together with the synodal letters of the holy Roman bishops. Henceforth let no unworthy person aspire to ecclesiastical honors contrary to the prohibitions of the canons. Let nothing be done that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, decreed ought not to be done; and whoever presumes to do so shall be restrained by the severity of the earlier canons.

[Note: From the other manuscripts except A. and E. 3, in which this reading is present: “And let the strictness of discipline temper the abundance of evil.”]

## II. That the Creed Be Recited on Sunday in All Churches

[Col. 0351D]

Out of reverence for the most holy faith, and to strengthen the frail minds of human beings, the holy synod, at the counsel of our most devout and glorious lord, King Recared, decreed the following: throughout all the churches of Spain, Gaul, and Galicia, according to the practice of the eastern churches, the creed of the Council of Constantinople—that is, of the one hundred and fifty bishops—shall be recited, so that before the Lord’s Prayer is said, it may be proclaimed aloud by the people.

[Note: T. 1, 2: “recited.”]

Thus the true faith may have manifest testimony, and the hearts of the people, purified by faith, may approach to partake beforehand of the body and blood of Christ.

## III. That No One Alienate Church Property Except in Necessity

This holy synod grants no bishop permission to alienate the property of the Church, since this is also prohibited by the ancient canons. If, however, they should give something that does not burden the Church’s resources, for the support of monks belonging to their parish, let it remain valid. They are permitted, while the rights of the Church are preserved, to provide for the needs of travelers, clerics, or the poor for as long as they are able.

## IV. That a Bishop May Make One of the Parish Basilicas a Monastery

If a bishop wishes to dedicate one of his parish churches as a monastery, so that a regular community of monks may live there, he has permission to do this with the consent of his council. If he should also donate to that place something from the Church’s property for their support, provided that it does not cause loss to the Church, let the gift remain secure. For the holy council gives its assent to establishing a good work.

[Col. 0352B] [Note: U., G.: “enrich.”]

## V. That Priests and Levites Live Chastely with Their Wives

It has been discovered by the holy council that bishops, priests, and deacons coming from heresy are still joined to their wives by carnal desire. Therefore, so that this may not happen henceforth, the following is prescribed, as it is also established by the earlier canons: they are not permitted to live in lustful companionship, but, while marital fidelity remains between them, they shall have a common benefit; they shall not live together in one room, or, if strength permits, he shall have his wife live in another house, so that chastity may have a good testimony before God and human beings.

If anyone, after this admonition, chooses to live shamefully with his wife, let him be treated as a reader. But those who have always remained under ecclesiastical canon, if, contrary to the commands of the ancients, they have women in their cells whose association can generate disreputable suspicion, shall indeed be disciplined canonically; the women themselves, sold by the bishops, shall have the proceeds distributed to the poor.

[Note: B.R., E. 4, T. 1: “they shall be corrected by the bishops and assigned to a convent of girls, where they shall serve all.”]

## VI. That a Church Slave Manumitted by a Bishop Never Withdraw from the Church’s Protection, and That the Freedpersons of Others Be Defended by the Bishop

[350]

Concerning freedpersons, the priests of God prescribe the following: if any have been freed by bishops according to the measure permitted by the ancient canons, they shall be free, yet neither they nor their descendants shall withdraw from the protection of the Church. Those also who have been given freedom by others and entrusted to churches shall be governed by episcopal protection, and the bishop shall ask the ruler that they not be given away to anyone.

## VII. That the Divine Scriptures Be Read at the Bishop’s Table

Out of reverence for the priests of God, the entire holy synod decreed the following: since idle stories are frequently introduced at meals, at every priestly banquet a reading from the divine Scriptures shall be included. Through this, souls are built up toward goodness and unnecessary stories are prohibited.

[Note: Ae.: “rejected.”]

## VIII. That a Cleric from the Fiscal Household Not Be Given Away by the Ruler

By the command and consent of our most devout lord, King Recared, the priestly council prescribed the following: no one shall dare to seek from the ruler clerics belonging to the fiscal household as gifts. Instead, after rendering the tribute owed for their persons to the Church of God to which they are bound, they shall administer their duties regularly for as long as they live.

[Note: F. 1: “with the indication.”]

## IX. That the Churches of the Arians Belong to the Catholic Bishop in Whose Diocese They Are

By decree of this council it is established that the churches which were in the Arian heresy but are now Catholic shall belong, together with their property, to those bishops to whose dioceses the parishes in which those churches are located appear to belong.

## X. That No One Inflict Violence on Widows for the Sake of Chastity, and That a Woman Not Take a Husband Against Her Will

For the promotion of chastity, which ought especially to advance through the encouragement of the council, and with the assent of our most glorious lord, King Recared, this holy council affirms the following: widows who wish to preserve chastity shall not be compelled by force to marry again. If, before professing continence, they choose to marry, let them marry whomever they wish to have as husbands of their own free will.

Let a similar condition apply to virgins: they shall not be compelled to accept husbands against the will of their parents or their own will.

[Note: B.R., E. 4, T. 1: “short of.”]

But if anyone obstructs the purpose of chastity of a widow or virgin, let him be excluded from holy communion and from the thresholds of the church.

## XI. That a Penitent Perform Penance

Because we have learned that in certain churches of Spain people perform penance for their sins not according to the canon but in the most shameful manner, asking to be reconciled by a priest as often as they wish to sin, therefore, to restrain such detestable presumption, the holy council commands the following.

[Note: T. 2 reads *fidissime* (“most faithfully”) for *foedissime* (“most shamefully”); all manuscripts except A. read *libuerit* (“it has pleased [them]”) for *voluerint* (“they wish”).]

Penance shall be imposed according to the canonical form of the ancients. That is, the person who repents of his deed shall first be suspended from communion and repeatedly return among the other penitents for the laying on of hands. When the period of satisfaction has been completed, the priest, in accordance with his judgment, shall restore him to communion.

Those who relapse into their former vices either during the period of penance or after reconciliation shall be condemned according to the severity of the earlier canons.

## XII. Concerning Those Who Seek Penance: A Man Shall First Be Shorn; a Woman Shall First Change Her Garb

Whoever, whether healthy or ill, asks a bishop or priest for penance, the bishop and priest shall observe the following above all: if he is a man, whether healthy or ill, he shall first have him shorn and then give him penance. If she is a woman, she shall not receive penance unless she has first changed her clothing.

For when penance is carelessly granted too often to laypeople, they relapse after receiving penance into crimes for which they must again lament.

## XIII. That Clerics Who Seek Secular Judges Be Excommunicated

Long-standing indiscipline and the entrenched presumption of license have opened the way to unlawful attempts to such an extent that clerics drag their fellow clerics before public courts, abandoning their own bishop. Therefore, we decree that no one henceforth presume to do this. If anyone presumes to do so, let him both lose his case and be excluded from communion.

## XIV. Concerning the Jews

[352]

At the council’s suggestion, our most glorious lord ordered this to be inserted into the canons: Jews are not permitted to have Christian wives or concubines, nor to purchase a Christian slave for their own use. If children have been born from such a union, they are to be brought to baptism.

They shall not hold public offices through which an opportunity might be given them to inflict punishment on Christians. If any Christians have been defiled by them through the Jewish rite, or even circumcised, they shall return to freedom and the Christian religion without payment of a price.

## XV. That Fiscal Slaves Who Build Churches Establish an Endowment, and That It Be Confirmed by the Ruler

If any fiscal slaves should happen to build churches and enrich them from their own poverty, the bishop shall arrange through his petition that this be confirmed by royal authority.

## XVI. That Bishops, Together with Judges, Destroy Idols, and That Masters Prohibit Idolatry to Their Slaves

Since the sacrilege of idolatry has become established throughout almost all Spain and Gaul, the holy synod, with the consent of the most glorious ruler, ordered the following: every priest, in his own locality and together with the territorial judge, shall diligently investigate the aforesaid sacrilege and shall not delay in exterminating whatever is found.

The people who resort to such error shall be restrained by whatever punishment is possible, with their lives preserved from danger. If they neglect this, let them know that both of them will incur the danger of excommunication.

If any masters neglect to root out this evil from their estates or refuse to prohibit it among their household, they too shall be expelled from communion by the bishop.

[Note: T. 2: “let them certainly know.”]

## XVII. That Bishops, Together with Judges, Correct with Stricter Discipline Those Who Kill Their Children

While many complaints were being brought to the ears of the holy council, among other matters an act of such great cruelty was reported that the ears of the assembled priests could not endure it: in certain regions of Spain, parents, eager for fornication and ignorant of compassion, kill their own children.

If they find it burdensome to increase their children in greater number, they ought first to chastise themselves for fornication.

[Note: In the other manuscripts, except A. and E. 3: *agere* (“to do, perform”) for *augere* (“to increase”).] For while they undertake marriages for the purpose of propagating offspring, those who kill their own fetuses are guilty both of parricide and of fornication; they show that they have joined themselves not for children but for lust.

Therefore, this enormous crime was brought to the attention of our most glorious lord, King Recared, whose glory deigned to command the judges of those regions to investigate this horrifying deed carefully together with the priest and, after applying severity, prohibit it.

[Note: In the others except A. and E. 3: “investigate.”]

Thus this holy synod more sorrowfully admonishes the priests of those places to seek out the same crime with the judge more carefully and to prohibit it with stricter discipline, without capital punishment.

## XVIII. That a Synod Be Held Once a Year and That Judges and Fiscal Officials Be Present

This holy and venerable synod prescribes that, while the authority of the earlier canons remains,

[Note: In the other manuscripts, except A. and E. 3: *veneranda* (“venerable”) for *venerabilis* (“venerable”).] which commanded councils to be assembled twice a year, and taking into account the length of the journey and the poverty of the churches of Spain, the bishops shall assemble once a year at a place chosen by the metropolitan.

The local judges and administrators of the fiscal estates shall, by decree of our most glorious lord, assemble together with the priestly council in the autumn, on the first day of November, so that they may learn how piously and justly they ought to act toward the peoples, lest they burden either private persons or the fisc through forced labor or excessive tasks.

The bishops shall be inspectors, according to the royal admonition, of how the judges treat the peoples, so that they may either correct them after warning them or make their insolence known to the ruler’s ears. If they are unable to amend those who have been corrected, let them suspend them both from the Church and from communion.

The priest and the elders shall deliberate what service the province ought to provide without detriment to itself. The council shall not be dissolved until they have first chosen the place where they will come together again for council at the succeeding time, so that the metropolitan bishop will no longer need to send letters to convene the council if the time and place have been announced to everyone at the preceding council.

[Note: B.R.: “inspectors”; E. 4, T. 1: “inspectors of Christ.”]

## XIX. That the Church, Together with Its Property, Belong to the Bishop’s Administration

Many people, contrary to the provisions of the canons, demand that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they consider the endowment they have bestowed on the church not to belong to the bishop’s administration. This has displeased us in the past and is prohibited for the future. Rather, according to the ancient constitution, everything shall belong to the bishop’s administration and authority.

## XX. That a Bishop Not Impose Forced Labor or Assessments in His Diocese

The complaints of many people demanded this constitution, because we have learned that bishops rage through their parishes not priestly but even cruelly. Although it is written, “Be examples to the flock, not lording it over the clergy,” they inflict exactions or losses upon their diocese.

Therefore, except for what the constitutions of the ancients command bishops to receive from their parishes, let the other things that have hitherto been presumed be denied. That is, let them not weary priests or deacons with forced labor, nor with any assessments, lest we appear in the Church of God to be exactors rather than pontiffs of God.

[Note: Ae., 4, T. 1, 2: “serve.”]

[Note: From the other manuscripts except A., which has “be wearied.”]

Those clerics, both local and diocesan, who recognize that they are being burdened by the bishop shall not delay in bringing their complaints to the metropolitan. The metropolitan shall not hesitate to restrain such presumptions strictly.

## XXI. That Judges Not Occupy Clerics or Church Slaves in Their Forced Labor

Because we have learned that in many cities the slaves of churches and of bishops or of all clerics are wearied by judges or public officials in various forced labors, the entire council asked the piety of our most glorious lord to prohibit such attempts henceforth.

Instead, the slaves of the aforementioned offices shall labor for their own uses or for the Church. If any judge or official wishes to occupy a cleric, or the slave of a cleric or of the Church, in public or private business, let him be excluded from ecclesiastical communion, which he obstructs.

## XXII. That the Bodies of Religious Persons Be Carried to Burial Only with Psalmody

The bodies of all religious persons who depart this life by divine calling ought to be carried to their graves only with psalms and the voices of those singing psalms. For we entirely prohibit the funeral song which is commonly sung for the dead, or the giving over of relatives or household members to sinners [sense of this clause uncertain].

Let it be sufficient that, in the hope of the resurrection, the service of divine songs is offered to the bodies of Christians. For the Apostle forbids us to mourn our dead, saying:

> Concerning those who sleep, I do not want you to grieve like the rest, who have no hope.

And the Lord did not weep for Lazarus as a dead man, but wept over the afflictions of this life, in order that he might be resurrected. If the bishop can enforce this, let him not delay in prohibiting all Christians from doing otherwise. Nevertheless, we judge that it is entirely improper for religious persons to be treated in any other way. Thus the bodies of deceased Christians ought to be buried throughout the whole world.

## XXIII. That Dances Be Prohibited at the Feasts of the Saints

The irreligious custom which the common people are accustomed to practice during the solemnities of the saints must be entirely eradicated: people who ought to attend to divine services keep vigil over dances and shameful songs, harming not only themselves but also disturbing the offices of religious persons.

The care of ensuring that this is driven out of all Spain is entrusted by the holy council to the priests and judges.

## The King’s Edict Confirming the Council

Our most glorious and most devout lord, King Recared:

“Divine truth, making us lovers of all who exist under the power of our kingdom, has principally inspired our royal mind so that, for the restoration of the faith and ecclesiastical discipline, we ordered all the bishops of Spain to be presented before our majesty.

“After careful and prudent deliberation, it is evident that the matters pertaining to the faith and those concerned with the correction of morals have been arranged with complete maturity of judgment and seriousness of understanding.

“Therefore, our authority commands all people belonging to our kingdom that, if anything has been defined in this holy council held in the city of Toledo in the auspicious fourth year of our reign, no one may despise it and no one presume to pass it over.

“For the chapters written by the present synod, approved by our judgment and consonant with discipline, shall be observed and remain in full authority by clerics, laypeople, and all other persons. They are as follows:

### I. Concerning the Observance of the Earlier Canons

### II. Concerning the Proclamation of the Creed by the Peoples in the Church

[Col. 0357B]

### III. Concerning Bishops, That They Not Be Permitted to Alienate Church Property

### IV. That a Bishop Be Permitted to Make One of the Parish Churches a Monastery

### V. That Bishops, Priests, and Deacons Converted from Heresy No Longer Be Permitted to Associate with Their Wives; and That Those Who Have Always Been Catholic Not Live in Their Cells with Strange Women

### VI. That Freedpersons Made Free by Bishops or Others and Entrusted to Churches Must Remain Free

### VII. That a Reading Be Given at All Priestly Tables

### VIII. That No One Ever Ask the King for Clerics from Our Fiscal Households, and That Any Such Gift Remain Invalid

[Col. 0357C]

### IX. Concerning Churches Transferred from Heresy, That They Belong to the Bishops in Whose Parishes They Are

[356]

### X. Concerning Widows: That Those Who Wish Shall Preserve Continence, and Those Who Choose to Marry Shall Marry Whomever They Wish; and the Same Concerning Virgins

### XI. That Penitents Must Perform Penance According to the Measure of the Ancient Canons

### XII. That Those Who Wish to Perform Penance Must First Be Shorn or Change Their Garb

### XIII. That Two Clerics May Not Bring a Case against One Another in a Public Forum

### XIV. That Jews May Not Have Christian Wives or Concubines, Purchase Christian Slaves, Judaize, or Perform Public Offices

### XV. That It Must Remain Valid If the Slaves of Our Treasury Build Churches and Enrich Them from Their Own Property

[Col. 0357D]

### XVI. That the Practice of Idolatry Must Be Investigated and Eradicated by Priests and Judges

### XVII. That Those Who Kill Their Children Must Be Disciplined by Priests and Judges

### XVIII. That Priests, Judges, and the Administrators of Our Estates Must Assemble for Council Once a Year

### XIX. That the Endowments of All Churches Must Belong to the Bishop’s Administration

[Col. 0358A]

### XX. That Priests Must Act Moderately throughout Their Parishes

### XXI. That Church Slaves or the Slaves of Clerics Must Not Be Wearied by Judges or Our Officials in Any Forced Labor

### XXII. That the Bodies of Religious Persons Be Carried to Their Graves Only with Hymns and Songs

### XXIII. That Dances and Shameful Songs Be Prohibited at the Solemnities of the Saints

“We decree that all these ecclesiastical constitutions, which we have briefly and summarily outlined, shall remain with perpetual stability, as they are contained more fully in the canon.

“Therefore, if any cleric or layperson refuses to obey these enactments, then, if he is a bishop, priest, deacon, or cleric, let him be subject to excommunication by the entire council. If he is a layperson and a person of higher status, let him lose half of his property, to benefit the resources of the fisc. But if he is a person of lower status, let him be punished by the loss of his possessions and assigned to exile.”

Flavius Reccared, king, confirming this deliberation which we defined together with the holy synod, have signed it.

## Homily of Saint Leander, issued in praise of the Church because of the conversion of the people, after the council and the confirmation of the canons

[Note: [Col. 0360D] This homily is absent from A. and E. 3. It has been taken from the B.R. manuscript, with the variant readings of the other witnesses.]

The very novelty of this celebration indicates that it is more solemn than all other celebrations, since, just as the conversion of so many peoples is new, so the Church’s joys are newer than usual. The Church celebrates many solemnities throughout the course of the year, and although it possesses its customary joys in them, it has none new as it has in this one. For one rejoices differently over things long possessed and over great gains recently discovered.

For this reason we too are lifted up by greater joys, because we suddenly behold the Church having brought forth new peoples, and because we now rejoice in the faith of those whose harshness we once lamented. Thus the cause of our joy was the occasion of our former tribulation. We groaned when we were burdened, when we were reproached; but those groans brought it about that those who through unbelief had been a burden to us should, through their conversion, become our crown.

Indeed, the Church expresses this thankfully in the Psalms, saying: “In tribulation you enlarged me.” And Sarah, while she is repeatedly desired by kings and suffers no stain to her chastity, makes Abraham rich because of her beauty; for Abraham is enriched by those very kings by whom Sarah is desired.

Accordingly, the Catholic Church fittingly leads to the gains of her Bridegroom—that is, Christ—the peoples whom she has felt to be rivals of her faith’s beauty, and through those kingdoms by which she has perceived herself disturbed she makes her husband rich. Thus, while she is attacked from the beginning or gnawed by the teeth of the envious, while she is oppressed, she is instructed; and while she is persecuted, she is enlarged, because through her endurance she either overcomes or wins over her rivals.

For the divine word says to her: “Many daughters have gathered riches, but you have surpassed them all.” It is no wonder that heresies are called daughters, but it must be observed that they are placed in the position of thorns. They are daughters because they are generated from Christian seed; they are thorns because outside God’s paradise—that is, outside the Catholic Church—they are nourished. This is proved not by the conjecture of our own understanding but by the authority of divine Scripture, Solomon saying: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.”
