Therefore, lest it seem a great matter to you that I have called heresies daughters, he immediately names them thorns. Heresies, I say, are found operating either in some corner of the world or among a single people; but the Catholic Church, just as it extends throughout the whole world, is constituted by the fellowship of all peoples. Rightly, therefore, heresies gather riches in the caves in which they hide, each in its own part; but the Catholic Church, situated in the watchtower of the whole world, [Col. 0361D] surpasses them all [Note: [Col. 0361D] E. 4, T. 1, 2, *enriched*.].

Rejoice, therefore, and be glad, Church of God; rejoice and rise up, one body of Christ; clothe yourself with strength and shout for joy, because your sorrows have been changed into joy and the garment of your sadness has been turned into an apparel of gladness.

Behold, having suddenly forgotten your barrenness and poverty, in one birth you have brought forth countless peoples for your Christ; for you prosper through your losses and grow through your damage. So great, finally, is your Bridegroom, by whose command you are governed, that while he allows you to be plundered for a little while, he again brings your spoil back to you and wins your enemies for you.

Thus the farmer, thus the fisherman [Ae., *shepherd*], while he considers future gains, does not count as losses what he sows or what he pursues with the hook. Therefore, do not now weep; do not mourn temporally for those who have departed from you, whom you see returning to you with great gains.

Rejoice, therefore, in the confidence of faith and, by the merit of your head, be strong in faith, while you now see those things which you recall as having long ago been promised [Note: [Col. 0362D] Ae., “promised, now see accomplished in deed.”] fulfilled.

For Truth itself says in the Gospel: “It was necessary for Christ to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered.” You proclaim this in the Psalms, saying to those who hate peace: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.” And again: “In gathering peoples together, and kingdoms, that they may serve the Lord.”

Knowing how sweet charity is and how delightful unity is, through prophetic predictions, evangelical oracles, and apostolic teachings, you proclaim nothing except the joining together of peoples; you sigh for nothing except the unity of nations; you sow nothing except the goods of peace and charity.

Rejoice, therefore, in the Lord, because you have not been defrauded of your desire. For those whom you conceived for so long with groaning as witness and with unceasing prayer, now, after the ice of winter, after the hardness of cold, after the severity of snow, you have suddenly brought forth in joy, like the delightful fruit of fields, the glad flowers of spring, and branches smiling upon the vine-stakes.

Therefore, brothers, let us exult in the Lord with complete gladness of heart and let us shout for joy to God our Savior. Through what has already been fulfilled, let us henceforth believe that what is still expected will truly be fulfilled.

For the things foretold by the Lord are these: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and them also I must bring in, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.” Behold, we see these things fulfilled. For this reason let us not doubt that the whole world can believe in Christ and come together into one Church, since again, on the testimony of Christ himself, we have learned in the Gospel: “And this Gospel of the kingdom,” he says, “will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then,” he says, “the end will come.”

If, therefore, any part of the world or any barbarian people should remain which the faith of Christ has not illumined, let us in no way doubt that it will believe and come into one Church, if we hold that what the Lord said is true.

Therefore, brothers, goodness has been set in the place of wickedness, and truth has confronted error, so that, because pride had separated the peoples from unity through the diversity of languages, charity might gather them again into the embrace of kinship; and just as the Lord is the one possessor of the whole world, so his possession might have one heart and one mind.

“Ask of me,” he says, “and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.” For this reason the whole human race was propagated from one man, so that those who proceeded from that one man might have one understanding, seek unity, and love it.

The natural order therefore demands that those who derive their origin from one man maintain mutual charity, and that one who is not separated by natural descent should not dissent from the truth of the faith. Heresies and divisions, however, flow from the fountain of vices. Thus whoever comes to unity returns from vice to nature; for just as it belongs to nature to form unity from many, so it belongs to vice to turn away from the sweetness of brotherhood.

Let us therefore rise with our whole mind into joy, so that, because the peoples had perished through their zeal for strife, Christ might establish one Church for them in friendship, in which the harmony of charity would bring them back together.

Of this Church the prophet plainly prophesies, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations.” And again he says: “It shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

For the mountain is Christ, and the house of the God of Jacob is his one Church, to which he declares that the rush of the nations and the gathering of peoples will flow.

Again, in another place, the prophet says of it: “Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.” And he says: “The nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising. Lift your eyes round about and see: all these have been gathered together and have come to you.” And he says: “The sons of strangers shall build your walls, and their kings shall serve you.”

To make known what would happen to the nation or people that had fallen away from the communion of the one Church, he continued: “For the nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish.” Elsewhere he likewise says: “Behold, you shall call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you shall run to you.”

For there is one Christ the Lord, whose holy possession is one Church throughout the world. He is the head, and it is the body; of them Genesis says in the beginning: “The two shall be one flesh,” which the Apostle understands of Christ and the Church.

Since, therefore, Christ wills to have one Church from all nations, whoever is outside it, even if he is called by the Christian name, is nevertheless not held within the structure of Christ’s body.

For heresy, which rejects the unity of the Catholic Church because it loves Christ with adulterous affection, occupies the place not of a wife but of a concubine, since Scripture truly says that two are one flesh, namely Christ and the Church; in this arrangement there is no place for a third, a prostitute.

“For there is one,” says Christ, “my beloved; one is my bride; one is the daughter of her mother.” Concerning this the same Church also declares, saying: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.”

Let the heresies now seek to discover by whom they have been violated or whose brothel they have become, since they have withdrawn from Christ’s immaculate marriage-bed. And the more precious we know the bond of charity to be, the more let us praise God in this celebration, because he did not allow the peoples for whom the blood of his Only-Begotten was poured out to be devoured outside the one fold by the teeth of the devil.

Let the lethargic robber, therefore, mourn that he has lost his spoil, because we see fulfilled what we heard the prophet foretell: “Indeed,” he says, “the captive is taken from the strong, and what had been seized is rescued from the mighty.”

For Christ’s peace destroyed the wall of hostility that the devil had built, and the house that, through division, was engaged in mutual slaughter is now joined together by the one cornerstone, Christ.

Let us all say, therefore: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” For no reward is equal to charity. It is preferred above every joy because peace and charity have come to be, and they hold primacy among all virtues.

It remains, however, that, made altogether one kingdom with one accord, we should all approach God with prayers, both for the stability of the earthly kingdom and for the happiness of the heavenly kingdom, so that the kingdom and the nation that glorified Christ on earth may be glorified by him not only on earth but also in heaven. Amen.

# FORTY-NINTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO: SIXTY-SIX BISHOPS OF HISPANIA AND GAUL, IN THE THIRD YEAR OF THE REIGN OF OUR MOST GLORIOUS LORD AND PRINCE SISENAND, ON THE NONES OF DECEMBER, IN THE ERA [Note: [Col. 0363D] E. 4, T. 1, *era DCLXX*.] 671

[Col. 0363]

[Col. 0363C] When, moved by zeal for the love of Christ and by the devotion of the most religious Sisenand, king of Hispania and Gaul, we priests had assembled at the city of Toledo in the name of the Lord, so that, in accordance with his commands and orders, a common discussion might be conducted by us concerning certain matters of Church discipline, we first gave thanks to our Savior, almighty God. After this we gave thanks to the aforesaid, most excellent and glorious servant of his, the king, whose devotion toward God is so great that he remains concerned not only with human affairs but also with divine matters.

For when the assembly of all of us had already gathered together in the basilica of the most blessed and holy martyr [Note: [Col. 0363D] Ae., B.R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G., *confessor*.] Leocadia, he entered with the most magnificent and noble men, as befitted his faith, and first prostrated himself on the ground before the priests of God, asking with tears and groans that they intercede with God for him [Note: [Col. 0364D] In the other witnesses, except A. and E. 3, “for the Lord.”]. Then, in a religious address, he exhorted the synod to remember the decrees of the fathers and to devote itself to preserving the rights of the Church among us, and to correcting those practices which, having come into use through negligence, had arrogated to themselves a license contrary to ecclesiastical custom.

Rejoicing, therefore, at such exhortations from him, it became necessary, in accordance with his desire and ours, to discuss what was appropriate, both in the divine sacraments that are celebrated in the churches of Hispania in diverse and illicit ways and in those matters of conduct known to have been wrongly usurped. And since we are holding a general council, it is fitting that the first words of our discourse should concern God, so that, after the profession of faith, the subsequent aims of our work may be arranged as upon the firmest foundation.

## 1. On the evident truth of the Catholic faith

[Note: [Col. 0365D] From Ae., B.R., E. 3, T. 1, 2, all the titles of the canons of this council have been supplied; they are absent from A. and the other witnesses.]

According to the divine Scriptures and the teaching that we have received from the holy Fathers, we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one deity and substance. Believing in a Trinity in the distinction of persons, we proclaim unity in the divinity; we neither confuse the persons nor separate the substance.

We say that the Father was made by no one and begotten by no one. We assert that the Son was not made by the Father but begotten. We confess that the Holy Spirit was neither created nor begotten but proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself, the Son of God and Creator of all things, was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages and descended from the Father in the last time for the redemption of the world; he never ceased to be with the Father. For he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and from the holy and glorious virgin Mary, Mother of God, and was born from her alone.

The same Christ, the Lord Jesus, one of the Holy Trinity, assumed a perfect human being, consisting of soul and flesh and without sin; remaining what he was, he assumed what he was not. He is equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity, possessing in one person the properties of two natures.

For there are two natures in him, God and man, but not two sons and not two gods; rather, the same person is one in both natures. He endured passion and death for our salvation, not in the power of divinity but in the weakness of humanity. He descended [Col. 0365C] to the underworld to free the saints who were held there, and, having conquered the dominion of death, he rose again.

Then, taken up into heaven, he will come in the future for the judgment of the living and the dead. By his death and blood we have been cleansed and have obtained the forgiveness of sins. He will raise us on the last day in the flesh in which we now live and in the form in which the same Lord rose. From him some will receive eternal life according to the merits of their righteousness, while others will receive the sentence of eternal punishment according to their sins.

This is the faith of the Catholic Church. We preserve and hold this confession; whoever guards it most firmly will have everlasting salvation.

## II. On celebrating one order in ministries and offices in all churches

[Col. 0365D] After the confession of the true faith, which is preached in the holy Church of God, it pleased us that all the priests who are united in the unity of the Catholic faith should perform nothing further in the ecclesiastical sacraments that is different or discordant, lest any diversity among us appear to outsiders or worldly people to display the error of schism, and lest the variety of the churches become a cause of scandal to many.

Therefore, one order of praying and psalm-singing shall be preserved by us throughout Hispania and Gaul; there shall be one manner in the solemn celebrations of the Mass, one in the evening and morning offices; and there shall no longer be differing ecclesiastical customs among us who are held together by one faith and one kingdom.

For the ancient canons also decreed this: each province is to maintain an identical custom both in psalm-singing and in ministering.

## III. On the character of councils, and why or when they are to be held

Hardly anything has driven discipline and good conduct from the Church of Christ more than the negligence of priests, who, disregarding the canons, neglect to hold a synod for correcting ecclesiastical conduct. For this reason it has been universally determined by us that, since the difficulty of the season does not permit a council to be held twice a year, according to the ancient decrees of the Fathers, it should at least be celebrated once a year.

Nevertheless, if the matter concerns the faith or any other common concern of the Church, a general synod of all Hispania and Gaul shall be summoned. But if the discussion concerns neither the faith nor the common welfare of the Church, it shall be a special council of each province, to be held wherever the metropolitan chooses.

All who are known to have causes against bishops, judges, powerful persons, or anyone else shall likewise come to that council. Whatever is found by synodal examination to have been wrongly usurped by anyone shall, through the diligence of the royal executor, be restored most justly to those who possess the rights, so that, in order to compel judges or secular men to attend the synod, the metropolitan may request the same executor from the prince.

The synod in each province is to be assembled on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, because of the spring season, when the earth is clothed with grass and the pasture of new growth is found.

## IV. The procedure according to which the holy synod is to be held in the name of God

[Col. 0366C]

At the first hour of the day, before sunrise, everyone is to be expelled from the church. After all the doors have been closed, doorkeepers shall stand at one entrance through which the priests must enter. All the bishops shall enter together and take their seats according to the time of their ordination.

After all the bishops have entered and permission has been granted, the presbyters whom the matter requires to enter shall then be summoned; no deacon shall intrude among them. After these, the approved deacons whom the order of proceedings requires to be present shall enter. A circle being formed from the bishops’ seats, the presbyters shall sit behind them, while the deacons shall stand in the bishops’ sight.

Then the laymen who have deserved to attend by the council’s election shall enter. The notaries whom the order of proceedings requires for reading or recording shall also enter, and the doors shall be closed.

When the priests are seated in prolonged silence and have their whole heart directed toward God, the archdeacon shall say: “Pray.” Immediately all shall prostrate themselves on the ground and pray silently for a long time, with tears and groans. [Note: It would correctly have been written: *sedentibus . . . sacerdotibus . . . habentibus . . . orantibus* (“with the priests seated … having … praying”).] One of the senior bishops shall rise and openly pour out a prayer to the Lord while all are still lying on the ground.

When the prayer has ended and all have answered, “Amen,” the deacon shall again say: “Rise.” Immediately all shall stand, [Col. 0367A] and, with complete fear of God and discipline, both bishops and presbyters shall sit. When everyone has silently taken his place, the deacon, clothed in a white garment, shall bring the Book of Canons into the midst and proclaim the chapters concerning the conduct of councils.

When the titles have been completed, the metropolitan bishop shall address the council, saying: “Behold, most holy priests, the judgments of the ancient Fathers from the canons concerning the celebration of a council have been read. If, therefore, any matter moves any one of you, let him bring it forward before his brothers.”

Then, if anyone brings before the priestly hearing any complaint whatsoever concerning an action contrary to the canons, they shall not pass to another chapter until the matter first proposed has been settled.

Moreover, if any presbyter, deacon, cleric, or layman among those standing outside should think that the council ought to be appealed to for any matter, let him notify the archdeacon of the metropolitan church of his case, and the archdeacon shall announce it to the council. Permission shall then be granted to that person both to enter and to present his case.

No bishop shall withdraw from the common assembly before the general hour of withdrawal arrives. Nor shall anyone dare to dissolve the council until everything has been determined, so that whatever is concluded by common deliberation may be signed by the hands of each bishop.

For then God is to be believed present among his priests, when, with all tumult cast aside, ecclesiastical affairs are concluded carefully and peacefully.

## V. On inquiring among the bishops about announcing Easter before Epiphany

[Col. 0367C] It is customary in Hispania for diversity to arise in the proclamation of the Easter solemnity. For differing observance of the Easter tables sometimes produces error. Therefore it pleased us that, three months before Epiphany, the metropolitan priests should inquire of one another by letter, so that, instructed by common knowledge, they may make known the day of Christ’s resurrection to their fellow provincials and announce that it is to be celebrated at one time.

## VI. On triple and single immersion in baptism

Concerning the sacrament of baptism, because in Hispania some priests perform triple immersion and others single immersion, this is regarded by some as a schism, and the unity of the faith appears to be divided. For, while the parties act in different and almost contrary ways, some insist that others have not been baptized.

Therefore, we should be instructed by the commands of the Apostolic See concerning what ought to be done [B.R.: *finiendum*, “brought to an end”] by us in this diversity regarding the sacrament, following not our own institution but that of the Fathers.

Accordingly, Gregory of blessed memory, pontiff of the Roman Church, who not only illumined the regions of Italy but also thoroughly instructed distant churches by his teaching, was asked by the most holy bishop Leander about the diversity in Hispania and what should preferably be followed. Among other things he wrote to him as follows:

“Concerning triple immersion in baptism, I can answer nothing more truly than you yourselves have perceived: because there is one faith, a diversity of custom does not harm the holy Church.

“When we immerse three times, we signify the mysteries of the three-day burial, so that, when the infant is brought out of the water for the third time, the resurrection after three days may be expressed. But if someone thinks that this is also done for the veneration of the most high Trinity, this too does not prevent immersing the person to be baptized once in the water. Since there is one substance in three subsistences, it can in no way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, since in the three immersions the Trinity of persons can be signified, and in the single immersion the unity of the divinity.

“But if until now an infant has been immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the divinity; and, while continuing to do what they have done, they boast that they have overcome your custom.”

Therefore, since concerning both aspects of the sacrament performed in holy baptism so great a man has given an explanation by which both are held to be right and both irreprehensible in the holy Church of God, nevertheless, to avoid the scandal of schism or the practice of heretical doctrine, let us retain single immersion in baptism.

Otherwise, those among us who immerse three times may appear to approve the assertion of the heretics while following their custom. And lest anyone perhaps doubt the mystery of this single sacrament, let him see in it the death and resurrection of Christ signified. For immersion in the waters is like a descent into the underworld, and rising again from the waters is resurrection.

Let them also see in it the unity of the divinity and the Trinity of persons: unity when we immerse once, and Trinity when we baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

The mystery of this singular baptism is also disclosed by examples from the holy Scriptures, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.”

The Red Sea signifies baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ, through which the people of God passed once, although the whole Trinity was present there: a pillar of fire and a cloud going before the people. In the fire the Father was signified, in the pillar the Son, and in the cloud the Holy Spirit.

The people of God also crossed the waters of the Jordan once with the ark. This signifies the single immersion of baptism, by whose sacrament the Church is washed and, through baptism, enters from the labors of this world into the land of the heavenly promise, as though through the Jordan.

## VII. On celebrating the office on Good Friday

We have learned that in certain churches, on the Friday of the Lord’s Passion, the doors of the basilicas are closed, and neither is the office celebrated nor is the Lord’s Passion preached to the people, although our same Savior commands his apostles, saying: “Preach my passion, death, and resurrection to all.”

Therefore, on that same day it is necessary to preach the mystery of the cross, which the Lord himself wished to be announced to all, and aloud to seek forgiveness of sins for the whole people, so that, cleansed by the compunction of repentance, we may deserve to receive the venerable day of the Lord’s resurrection with our sins forgiven, and may receive the sacrament of his body and blood cleansed from sin.

## VIII. On not breaking the fast on Good Friday

Some, on the day of the Lord’s Passion, break their fast from the ninth hour, indulge in banquets, and, while the sun itself on that day, clothed in darkness, has withdrawn its light, and while the elements themselves, thrown into disorder, have displayed the grief of the whole world, pollute the fast of so great a day and devote themselves to feasting.

Since the universal Church spends the whole of that day in mourning and abstinence because of the Lord’s Passion, whoever on it, except children, the aged, and the sick, breaks the fast before the prayers for forgiveness have been completed shall be excluded from Easter joy [Ae., E. 4, “shall be rejected”] and shall not receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, because he does not honor the day of his Passion through abstinence.

## IX. On blessing the candle and lamp at the Easter vigils

In certain churches the lamp and candle are not blessed at the Easter vigils, and they ask why we bless them. Because of the glorious mystery of that night, we solemnly bless these things, so that we may receive, in the blessing of sanctified light, the mystery of Christ’s holy resurrection, which arrives during the time of this votive night.

And since this observance is commended in the churches throughout many lands and regions of Hispania, it is fitting that, for the sake of the unity of peace, it be preserved in the churches of Gaul as well.

No one, however, will go unpunished who despises these statutes [Col. 0369C], but will be subject to the regulations of the Fathers.

## X. On publicly reciting the Lord’s Prayer every day
Some priests throughout Spain are found who recite the Lord’s Prayer, which our Savior taught and commanded, not every day but only on Sunday. And since the Apostle taught us to pray without ceasing, while Christ prescribed how we should pray, saying, “But when you pray, say: Our Father, who are in heaven,” how then is that prayer not said every day which is commanded to be said without ceasing? Indeed, this prayer must be said daily to the extent that it bears this very title, since it is called the “daily prayer”; thus the holy Fathers named it, as is also found among teachers renowned for their distinguished learning.

For Saint Cyprian says:

> Accordingly, in the Lord’s Prayer we ask that our daily bread—that is, Christ—be given to us every day, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not withdraw from his sanctification and body.

Saint Hilary says:

> “Give us this day our daily bread.” For what does God desire so greatly as that Christ, who is the bread of life and the bread from heaven, should dwell in us every day? And since it is a daily prayer, we also pray every day that it may be given.

Saint Augustine says:

> As for daily and lesser sins, without which this life is not lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction; for it belongs to them to say: “Our Father, who are in heaven”—they who have already been reborn as children of such a Father from water and the Holy Spirit. Therefore this daily prayer wipes away these minor daily sins; it also wipes away those sins from which the lives of the faithful depart after repentance has changed even their sinful deeds for the better.

Therefore, just as Christ commanded, just as the Apostle urged, and just as the ecclesiastical teachers instructed, since every day we sin either in thought, word, or deed, we must pour out this prayer daily in God’s presence. Accordingly, any priest or subordinate cleric who, through pride, omits this Lord’s Prayer every day, whether in public or in private worship, shall be condemned and deprived of the honor of his order.

### XI. That the Alleluia Is Not to Be Sung in Lent

[Column 0370B] We have likewise learned that certain priests in Spain sing the Alleluia during the days of Lent, except in the final week before Easter. Henceforth we forbid this, decreeing that throughout all the aforesaid days of Lent—since it is a time not of joy but of mourning—the Alleluia is not to be sung. For then it is necessary to devote oneself to weeping and fasting, to clothe the body in sackcloth and ashes, to humble the mind with grief, and to turn joy into sadness, until the time of Christ’s resurrection arrives, when the Alleluia ought to be sung in gladness and mourning changed into joy.

The universal consensus of the Church has established this throughout all parts of the provinces [Variant in B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., and G.: “lands”], and it will be necessary for all of us to preserve it throughout the provinces of Spain and Gaul. During the remaining calendar days of January as well, which are observed because of the error of the Gentiles, the Alleluia is absolutely not to be sung. On those days, too, abstinence is practiced from all meats except fish and vegetables, as during those forty days, and some do not even drink wine. [Note: In Ae., B. R., E. 4, U., and G., everything from “in those times” through “If anyone, therefore” is absent.]

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone belonging to the clerical order is found to consider his own judgment preferable to this decree, he shall be compelled to forfeit the office of his order and be deprived of communion at that Easter.

### XII. That the Lauds Are to Be Said after the Gospel, Not Immediately after the Apostle

In certain churches of Spain, lauds are sung after the Apostle has been read, before the Gospel is proclaimed, although the canons prescribe that after the Apostle it is not lauds but the Gospel that must be announced [Variant: proclaimed]. It is presumptuous to place first what ought to follow. Lauds follow the Gospel for this reason: the glory of Christ is proclaimed through that same Gospel.

Henceforth, therefore, let this order be observed by all priests. Those who disturb this order shall incur the penalty of excommunication.

### XIII. That the Singing of Hymns Is Not to Be Rejected

We have examples of the singing of hymns both from the Savior and from the Apostles. The Lord himself, as the evangelist Matthew bears witness, is said to have sung a hymn:

> And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

The Apostle Paul also wrote to the Ephesians, saying:

> Be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.

And since certain hymns are known to have been composed by human effort in praise of God and for the triumphs of the Apostles and martyrs—for example, those published by the most blessed teachers Hilary and Ambrose—some nevertheless reject them specifically because they do not derive from the Scriptures of the sacred canon or from apostolic tradition. Let them, then, reject that hymn composed by human beings which we say every day, in public and private worship, at the end of all the psalms:

> Glory and honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

For even that hymn which the angels sang at the birth of Christ in the flesh—

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will,

—and the rest that follows there, was composed by ecclesiastical teachers. Therefore it too should not be sung in the churches, because it is not found in the books of the sacred Scriptures. [Variant: Therefore these hymns too should not be sung in the churches, because they are not found in the books of the sacred Scriptures.]

Hymns are therefore composed, just as Masses, petitions, prayers, commendations, and the laying on of hands are composed. If none of these were said in the Church, all ecclesiastical offices would be empty. The Apostle urges and admonishes Timothy that these things be done, saying:

> I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions.

Therefore, just as no one rejects prayers composed in praise of God, so let no one henceforth reject hymns; rather, let Gaul and Spain celebrate them alike. Those who dare to reject hymns shall be punished by excommunication.

### XIV. That the Hymn of the Three Young Men Is to Be Sung at Every Solemn Mass

The hymn of the three young men, in which every creature of heaven and earth praises God together, and which the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world celebrates, is neglected by certain priests, who do not sing it at Sunday Masses or at the solemnities of martyrs. Therefore this holy council decrees that throughout all the churches of Spain and Gaul that same hymn be sung from the pulpit at every solemn Mass. Those who violate the ancient custom concerning this hymn and our present decree shall lose communion.

### XV. That “Glory and Honor to God” Is to Be Said at the End of the Psalms

[Column 0371D]

At the end of the psalms, let it not be said, as some have hitherto said, “Glory to the Father,” but “Glory and honor to the Father,” since the prophet David says:

> Ascribe glory and honor to the Lord.

And the evangelist John heard in the Apocalypse the voice of the heavenly host saying:

> Honor and glory to our God who sits upon the throne.

Accordingly, these two words ought to be spoken on earth just as they resound in heaven. We impose this observance upon all ecclesiastical persons; whoever neglects it shall suffer the loss of communion.

### XVI. Concerning the Proper Use of “Glory” at the End of Responsories

[Column 0372A]

There are some who do not say “Glory” at the end of responsories because it sometimes sounds unsuitable. But the proper distinction is this: in joyful passages, “Glory” is to follow; in more mournful passages, the beginning is to be repeated.

### XVII. That the Book of the Apocalypse Is to Be Accepted by All

The authority of many councils and the synodical decrees of the holy Roman bishops declare the book of the Apocalypse to belong to John the Evangelist and have established that it is to be received among the divine books. Since there are many who do not accept its authority and refuse to proclaim it in the Church of God, anyone who henceforth either fails to accept it or does not proclaim it in the church during the celebration of Masses from Easter to Pentecost shall receive the sentence of excommunication.

### XVIII. That Priests Should Receive Communion after the Blessing Has Been Given to the People

Some priests receive communion immediately after saying the Lord’s Prayer and afterward give the blessing to the people. Henceforth we forbid this. Instead, after the Lord’s Prayer and the joining of the bread and chalice, the blessing is to be given to the people; only then is the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood to be received. The order is to be as follows: the priest and levite receive communion before the altar, the clergy in the choir, and the people outside the choir.

### XIX. Concerning the Ordination of Bishops

A harmful practice must by no means be passed over in silence, for, transgressing the decrees of our ancestors, it has disturbed the whole order of the Church. Some seek priestly offices through canvassing and intrigue; others assume the episcopate after offering gifts; still others, entangled in crimes or devoted to secular military service, have reached the honor of the highest and sacred order despite being unworthy. A ruling ought indeed to have been made concerning their fall and removal, but the Church would have been thrown into very great disturbance.

Leaving the past aside, we believe it necessary henceforth to insert into the canonical regulations those who are not to be promoted to the priesthood. These are: those discovered to have committed any crime; those stained by a mark of infamy; those who have confessed, through public penance, to having committed some crimes; those who have fallen into heresy; those known to have been baptized or rebaptized in heresy; those who have castrated themselves; those who are known to lack any part of their limbs either by natural defect or through amputation; those who have entered into a second marriage or contracted numerous marriages; those who have married a widow or a woman abandoned by her husband, or who have been husbands of corrupted women; those who have kept concubines for fornication; those subject to servile status; those who are unknown; neophytes or laymen; those devoted to secular military service; those bound by obligations to a municipal curia; those ignorant of letters; those who have not yet reached the age of thirty; those who have not advanced through the ecclesiastical degrees; those who seek honor through canvassing; those who strive to obtain honor by gifts; and those elected to the priesthood by their predecessors.

Nor shall he henceforth be a priest whom neither the clergy nor the people of his own city have elected, and whose election has not been sought with the agreement of the metropolitan or of the bishops of the neighboring province. [Note: In the other copies, except A., “provincialium” appears instead of “comprovincialium.”]

Therefore, whenever anyone is henceforth presented for the priestly order, if, after examination, he is found free of all the matters mentioned above (*praedicta*; variant *praedicata*) and is judged to possess a reputable life and teaching, then, according to the synodal or decretal provisions, he shall be consecrated to the priesthood on Sunday by all the bishops of the province—or at least by three—with the consent of all the clergy and citizens, while the others who are absent signify their agreement by letter, and especially with the authority or presence of the one established in the metropolitan city.

A bishop of the province is to be consecrated wherever the metropolitan chooses; but a metropolitan is to be consecrated only in the metropolitan city, with the bishops of the province assembled there. Whoever henceforth attempts, contrary to these canonical prohibitions, to aspire unworthily to the priestly rank shall, together with those who ordain him, be subject to the danger of losing the honor he has obtained.

### XX. Concerning the Number of Years at Which Priests and Levites Are to Be Ordained

In the old Law, levites are commanded to serve the tabernacle from the age of twenty-five, and the holy Fathers followed its authority in the canons. We, forgetful of the commands both of the divine law and of the councils, make infants and boys levites before the lawful age and before they have experience of life. Therefore, to prevent this from happening among us any longer, we admonish in accordance with the judgments of divine law and the canons that levites be consecrated from the age of twenty-five and presbyters ordained from the age of thirty. They are first to be tested, according to the apostolic command, and then to serve, having no crime to their account.

### XXI. Concerning the Chastity of Priests

All who have been placed in the priesthood of God must be irreproachable, as the Apostle Paul testifies:

> It is necessary for a bishop to be irreproachable.

Therefore God’s priests ought to be blameless and undefiled, and not be polluted by any contagion of fornication; rather, living chastely, they should present themselves pure for the celebration of the sacraments. Let us therefore abstain from every evil deed and remain free from every defilement of the flesh, so that, pure in body and cleansed in mind, we may approach the sacrifice of Christ worthily and entreat God on behalf of the sins of all.

### XXII. That a Bishop Is to Have Suitable Testimony in His Private Residence

Although we ought to have a pure conscience before God, it is nevertheless proper also to preserve an excellent reputation among human beings, so that, in accordance with the apostolic command, we may have testimony of a holy life not only before God but also before people. For up to now certain priests have created no small scandal by being accused of sexual misconduct and by having a reputation for an unworthy manner of life.

Therefore, so that every shameful suspicion or incident may henceforth be excluded, and so that secular persons may no longer be given an opportunity for slander, bishops ought to have in their private residence the testimony of reputable persons, so that they may please God through a pure conscience [Variant: through good conduct] and the Church through an excellent reputation.

### XXIII. That Presbyters and Deacons Are to Have Testimony Concerning Their Lives

It has likewise been decided that, just as bishops do, presbyters and levites—whom weakness or the burden of age may prevent from remaining in the bishop’s private residence—should have witnesses to their lives in their own cells, and should maintain their life not only in name but also in conduct.

### XXIV. Concerning the Reformation of Clerics: That They Are to Live in One Residence

[Column 0374B]

Every age, from adolescence onward, is inclined toward evil; for nothing is more uncertain than the life of adolescents. It was therefore necessary to decree that, if there are mature youths or adolescents among the clergy, they should all live together in one residence within the episcopal compound, so that they may spend the years of their unstable age not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines. They are to be entrusted to a most approved elder, whom they will have both as a teacher of doctrine and as a witness to their life.

If any of them are orphans, they are to be supported under priestly protection, so that their lives may remain untouched by crimes and their property safe from the wrongdoing of wicked people. Those who resist these commands are to be assigned to monasteries, so that their wandering and proud dispositions may be restrained by a stricter rule.

### XXV. That Priests Are to Possess Knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and the Canons

[Column 0374C]

Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must be avoided especially among the priests of God, who have undertaken the duty of teaching the people. For Scripture admonishes priests to read, as the Apostle Paul says to Timothy:

> Attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching; remain always in these things.

Therefore priests must know the holy Scriptures and the canons, so that all their work may consist in preaching and teaching, and so that they may edify everyone both through knowledge of the faith and through discipline of conduct.

### XXVI. Concerning an Official Booklet to Be Given to Parish Presbyters

When presbyters are ordained for parishes, they are to receive an official booklet from their own priest, so that they may enter the churches assigned to them with proper instruction and not offend even in the divine sacraments through ignorance. Thus, whenever they come to the litanies or to a council, they are to give their bishop an account of how they celebrate the office entrusted to them and how they baptize.

### XXVII. Concerning the Profession of Parish Presbyters

When presbyters or deacons are appointed throughout the parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop, promising to live chastely and purely [Variant: chaste and pure] in the fear of God, so that, while such a profession binds them [Variants: obliges them; binds them anew], the discipline of a holy life may restrain them.

### XXVIII. Concerning the Manner in Which Those Who Have Been Deposed Are to Be Ordained Again

If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been unjustly expelled from his rank and is found innocent at a second synod, he cannot be what he was unless he receives back the rank he lost. If he was a bishop, he is to receive before the altar, from the hands of the bishops, the orarium, ring, and staff; if a presbyter, the orarium and planeta; if a deacon, the orarium and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. The remaining ranks likewise are to receive, as restoration of their status, the objects they received when they were ordained.

### XXIX. Concerning Clerics Who Consult Magicians or Diviners

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone belonging to the clerical order is discovered consulting magicians, haruspices, diviners, augurs, or sorcerers, or persons who profess any art whatsoever, or anyone practicing similar activities, he shall be deposed from the honor of his dignity and undergo the punishment of a monastery. There, devoted to perpetual penance, he shall atone for the sacrilege he has committed.

### XXX. Concerning Priests Who Send Messages to a Foreign People

Priests living near the borders of enemies, except those who have received permission from the royal authority, must not presume secretly to receive or send any message to a foreign people. Anyone who is discovered and convicted of doing so shall be denounced to the prince at the council and punished with a fitting penalty.

### XXXI. Concerning the Distinction to Be Made among Cases

Princes often entrust their affairs to priests concerning persons liable to charges against the majesty of the ruler. But since priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, they should agree to act as judges for kings only where leniency from punishment is promised by oath, not where a sentence involving danger is being prepared.

If, therefore, any priest, contrary to this common decree, acts as an examiner in the dangers of others, he shall be guilty before Christ of bloodshed and shall lose his own rank before the Church.

### XXXII. Concerning Care for Peoples [Variant: Orphans] and the Poor

Bishops must not doubt that God has imposed upon them the duty of protecting and defending the people [Variant: orphans]. Therefore, when they see judges and powerful persons acting as oppressors of the poor, they should first rebuke them with priestly admonition. If they refuse to amend, the bishops should report their insolence to the king’s ears, so that royal power may restrain in wickedness those whom priestly admonition does not bend toward justice. If any bishop neglects this, he shall be answerable to the council.

### XXXIII. That a Bishop Is Not to Take Anything from the Property of the Churches Except a Third of the Offerings

Avarice is the root of all evils, and its thirst takes possession even of the minds of priests. Many of the faithful, out of love for Christ and the martyrs, build basilicas in the dioceses of bishops and record offerings; the priests take these offerings and convert them to their own uses. Hence worshipers fall away when they lose their support; hence the ruins of collapsing basilicas are not repaired, because priestly avarice takes everything away.

For this reason the present council has decreed that bishops govern their dioceses in such a way that they presume to take nothing from their lawful property, but, according to the authority of earlier councils, receive a third both of the offerings and of the revenues and crops. If they presume to take anything more, it is to be restored through the council, at the appeal either of the founders themselves or, if they have already departed from this world, of their relatives.

The founders of basilicas should know, however, that they have no authority over the property they confer upon those churches. In accordance with the canons, just as the Church itself belongs to the bishop’s administration, so does its endowment.

### XXXIV. Concerning the Thirty-Year Period and the Limitation of Cases to a Province

[Column 0376B]

If any bishop has possessed the diocese of another bishop for thirty years without any challenge, since under the force of law that diocese now appears to belong to him, an action for its recovery is not to be admitted against him. This applies only within one province; outside it, it applies in no way, lest, while a diocese is being defended, the boundaries of the provinces become confused.

### XXXV. To Which Bishop Newly Built Basilicas Belong

Just as possession for thirty years takes away another’s diocese, so it does not take away the jurisdiction of a district. Therefore newly founded basilicas will undoubtedly belong to the bishop whose jurisdiction the district is shown to be.

### XXXVI. Concerning the Annual Inquiry to Be Made by Bishops in the Parishes

[Column 0376C]

A bishop ought to go every year throughout all his dioceses and parishes, to inquire what each basilica needs for its repair. If he is unable to do this because he is held by illness or entangled in other occupations, he should send reputable presbyters or deacons to investigate the revenues of the basilicas, their repairs, and the lives of those who minister in them.

### XXXVII. Concerning the Fulfillment of Promises from Church Property

Whoever, with the support of any bishop, has provided something for the benefit of the Church and promised him some—even small—remuneration in return must fulfill the promised payment, so that it may be brought before the provincial council and confirmed with the bishops’ consent. For, as the Apostle Paul says:

> The laborer is worthy of his wages.

### XXXVIII. Concerning Assistance to the Founders of Churches or Their Children

Priests must provide the support of life to those in need, and especially to those to whom a return is owed. Therefore, if any of the faithful have given something from their property to the Church out of personal devotion, and if they themselves or their children should subsequently be reduced to poverty, they are to receive from that same Church assistance for their livelihood, according to the needs of the time.

For if ecclesiastical property is generously given for the use of clerics, monks, pilgrims, or anyone suffering need, solely out of regard for religion, how much more ought provision to be made for those to whom a just repayment is owed?

### XXXIX. Concerning the Distinction between Presbyters and Deacons, So That They Stand in Both Choirs

[Column 0377A]

Some deacons burst forth into such great pride that they place themselves before presbyters and presume to stand first in the first choir, while the presbyters are placed in the second choir. Therefore, so that they may acknowledge presbyters as superior to themselves, both groups are to stand in both choirs.

### XL. That Deacons Are to Use One Orarium, Plain and Unadorned

It is not permitted even to a bishop or presbyter to use two oraria; how much less to a deacon, who is their minister? Therefore a levite ought to wear one orarium on his left shoulder, because from it he speaks—that is, preaches—while the right side ought to remain free, so that he may move unimpeded in priestly service.

Henceforth, therefore, let levites beware of using a double orarium. They are to use only one, plain and unadorned by any colors or gold.

### XLI. Concerning the Form of the Tonsure to Be Maintained by All Clerics and Readers

All clerics and readers, like levites and priests, are to have the entire upper part of the head shaved, leaving below only a circular crown. They are not to follow the practice hitherto seen among readers in parts of Galicia, who, with long hair like laymen, shave only a small circle at the crown of the head. For this custom was the practice of heretics in Spain. Therefore, to remove a scandal from the Church, this sign of disgrace must be taken away, and there must be one tonsure and one form of dress, as is the custom throughout Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.

### XLII. Concerning the Removal of Women from Association with Clerics

No unrelated woman is to live with clerics, except a mother, sister, daughter, or aunt. In the case of these persons, the bond of nature permits nothing criminal to be suspected. This was also decreed by the constitution of the ancient Fathers.

### XLIII. Concerning the Sale of Women Known to Be Associated with Clerics

Certain clerics, lacking a lawful marriage, seek the forbidden association of unrelated women or of their own female slaves. Therefore, any women who are associated with clerics in this manner are to be taken away and sold by the bishop. The clerics whom these women have infected with their lust [Variant: destroyed] are to be confined for a time to penance [Variants: bound; sent away].

### XLIV. Concerning the Classes of Women with Whom Clerics Ought Not to Be Joined

Clerics who, without consulting their bishop, have taken wives, or who have received a widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute in marriage, ought to be separated from their own bishop.

### XLV. Concerning Clerics Who Take Up Arms

If clerics willingly take up arms, or have taken them up, in any sedition and are discovered doing so, they shall lose the rank of their order and be handed over to a monastery for penance.

### XLVI. Concerning Clerics Who Demolish Tombs

[Column 0378A]

If any cleric is discovered demolishing tombs, since this crime is punished by the public laws with bloodshed as sacrilege, one exposed in such a crime ought to be removed from the clerical order and assigned to three years of penance.

### XLVII. Concerning Exemption of Freeborn Clerics from Forced Labor and Assessments

At the command of our lord and most excellent King Sisenand, this holy council decrees that all freeborn clerics, on account of the office of religion, are to be exempt from every public assessment and forced labor, so that they may serve God freely and not be drawn away from ecclesiastical offices by any hindering necessity.

### XLVIII. Concerning the Appointment of Stewards

Those whom the Greeks call *oikonomoi*, that is, those who manage ecclesiastical property in place of bishops, ought, as the holy Synod of Chalcedon established, to be appointed by every bishop from his own clergy to govern the churches. Whoever henceforth neglects this shall be answerable to that great council.

### XLIX. Concerning the Profession of Monks

A monk is made either by parental devotion or by his own profession. Whichever of these has occurred will bind him. Therefore, we close the way for them to return to the world and forbid every return to secular life.

### L. Concerning Clerics Who Seek the Monastic Calling

Clerics who seek the monastic calling because they desire to follow a better life ought to be granted by the bishop free access to enter monasteries. Their purpose must not be obstructed when they strive to pass over to the desire for contemplation.

### LI. Concerning the Limits of the Power Bishops May Exercise in Monasteries

It has been reported to the present council that monks are subjected to servile labor by episcopal command and that the rights of monasteries are usurped by unlawful presumption contrary to the canonical regulations, so that the monastery’s property is almost turned into personal possession and Christ’s illustrious portion is reduced to disgrace and servitude.

Therefore, we admonish those who preside over churches not to presume such things any longer. Priests are to claim for themselves in monasteries only what the canons prescribe: namely, to admonish monks toward holy conduct, appoint abbots and other officers, and correct actions committed outside the rule.

If they presume to do anything among the monks that the canons forbid, or attempt to usurp anything from the property of the monastery, a sentence of excommunication will not be lacking against those who henceforth do not withdraw from these unlawful practices.

### LII. Concerning Wandering Monks

Some monks, leaving the monastery, not only return to secular life but also take wives. These men, therefore, are to be brought back to the same monastery from which they departed and assigned to penance; there they are to mourn the crimes that caused them to leave. [Note: In A., everything from “there” to the end of the canon is absent.]

### LIII. Concerning Wandering Religious Men

[Column 0379A]

Religious men of a particular region who are found neither among the clergy nor among the monks, as well as those who wander about in various places [Variant: roam about], are to be restrained, at the discretion of the bishops in whose district they are known to reside, and assigned either to the clergy or to monasteries. This does not apply to those who have been released by their own bishop because of age or illness.

### LIV. Concerning the Distinction among Penitents

Those who, being in danger, receive penance without confessing any manifest crimes, but merely proclaiming themselves sinners, may, if they recover, even attain the ecclesiastical orders on account of the uprightness of their conduct.

Those, however, who receive penance in such a way that they publicly confess to having committed a mortal sin can in no way attain the clergy or ecclesiastical honors, because they have branded themselves by their own confession.

### LV. Concerning Penitent Men, Widows, and Virgins

Any layperson who, having received penance, has had his hair cut and then, rebelling, has become a layman again is to be seized by his bishop and recalled to the penance from which he withdrew. If any are irrevocably bound by penance (*poenitentiam*; variant *potentiam*, “power”) and do not return even after admonition, they are truly to be condemned before the Church as apostates by a sentence of anathema.

The same applies to those whose hair was cut by their parents, or who, after losing their parents, voluntarily devoted themselves to religion, but afterward assumed secular clothing. When seized by a priest, they are to be recalled to the religious life after first performing penance. If they cannot return, they are truly to be subjected as apostates to a sentence of anathema.

This rule is also to be observed concerning widows, consecrated virgins, and female penitents who have put on the habit of a religious woman and afterward either changed their clothing or entered into marriage.

### LVI. Concerning the Distinction between Secular Widows and Religious Widows

There are two kinds of widows: secular and religious. Secular widows are those who still intend to marry and have not laid aside lay clothing. Religious widows are those who, having already changed their secular dress, have appeared in religious attire before a priest or the Church.

If these women enter into marriage, according to the Apostle they will not be without condemnation, because, after first vowing themselves to God, they have afterward abandoned their commitment to chastity.

### LVII. Concerning the Distinction among Jews: Those Who Are Not to Be Compelled and Those Who Are to Be Compelled to Believe

Concerning the Jews, the holy synod has decreed this: henceforth no one is to use force to compel anyone to believe. “God has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” For such people are not to be saved unwillingly but willingly, so that the form of justice may remain unimpaired. Just as a human being perished by obeying the serpent through the will of his own free choice, so every human being is saved by believing through the conversion of his own mind when called by God’s grace.

Therefore they are to be persuaded to convert, not driven to it by force, but encouraged through the power of free will.

Those who were previously compelled to become Christians, as happened in the time of the most religious ruler King Sisebut, since it is now established that they have been joined to the divine sacraments, have received the grace of baptism, have been anointed with chrism, and have shared in the Lord’s body and blood, must also be compelled to retain the faith they received, whether by force or necessity, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed and the faith they accepted be regarded as worthless and contemptible.

### LVIII. Concerning Those Who Provide Gifts and Favor to Jews against the Faith of Christ

The greed of some is so great that, in seeking it, they have, in the words of the Apostle, even strayed from the faith [Variant: “strayed” (*erraverunt*) for “may have strayed” (*erraverint*)]. For up to now many priests and laymen, receiving gifts from Jews, have fostered their perfidy by their protection. Such people are rightly known to belong to the body of Antichrist, because they act against Christ.

Therefore, if henceforth any bishop, cleric, or secular person provides them support against the Christian faith, whether by gift or favor, he shall truly be made anathema as a profane and sacrilegious person and shall be excluded from the Catholic Church and the kingdom of God. For it is right that the person who becomes a patron of Christ’s enemies be separated from the body of Christ.

### LIX. Concerning Jews Who Were Formerly Christians and Later Returned to Their Former Rite

Many who were formerly brought to the Christian faith from Judaism are now known not only to have practiced Jewish rites while blaspheming Christ, but also to have presumed to perform the abominable act of circumcision.

Concerning these persons, after consultation with our most pious and most religious ruler, our lord King Sisenand, this holy council has decreed that such transgressors, corrected by episcopal authority, be recalled to the practice of Christian doctrine, so that those whom their own will does not reform may be restrained by priestly discipline.

Those whom they have circumcised are to be separated from their parents’ association if they are their children; if they are slaves, they are to be handed over to freedom in compensation for the injury done to their bodies.

### LX. Concerning the Children of Jews: That They Are to Be Separated from Their Parents and Assigned to Christians
Judaean sons and daughters, so that they may no longer be entangled in their parents’ error [Note: [Col. 0380D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., *errors*.], we decree that they are to be separated from their parents’ association and assigned either to monasteries or to Christian men and women who fear God, so that under their way of life they may learn the practice of the faith and, being trained toward what is better, may advance both in conduct and in faith.

### LXI. Concerning the faithful children of Jews, that they should not become exiles from their possessions because of their parents’ transgression

If baptized Jews afterward become transgressors against Christ and are condemned by any punishment, their faithful children ought not to be excluded from their property, because, as it is written: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”

### LXII. Concerning baptized Jews who associate with unbelieving Jews

[Col. 0381A]

The company of the wicked often corrupts even the good; how much more those who are inclined toward vices? Therefore, let there henceforth be no communion between Hebrews who have been transferred to the Christian faith and those who still remain in the former rite, lest they perhaps be overthrown by sharing in their company. Accordingly, whoever from among those who have been baptized does not henceforth avoid the company of unbelievers shall be handed over to Christians, while those others shall be assigned to public executions.

### LXIII. Concerning the marriages of Christians and Jews

Jews who have Christian women as wives are to be admonished by the bishop of that city that, if they wish to remain with them, they should become Christians. But if, after being admonished, they refuse, they are to be separated, because an unbeliever cannot remain in the union of one who has already been transferred to the Christian faith. The children born from such unions, moreover, are to follow the faith and status of their mother. Likewise, those born of unbelieving women and faithful Christian men are to follow the Christian religion, not Jewish superstition.

### LXIV. Concerning converted Jews who afterward transgress, that they are not to be admitted as witnesses

A person cannot be faithful toward human beings who has proved faithless toward God [Note: [Col. 0381D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, *T. 1, 2*, *unfaithful*.]. Therefore, Jews who were once made Christians and have now transgressed against faith in Christ ought not to be admitted to give testimony, even though they profess themselves Christians; for just as they are suspect in the faith of Christ, so they are considered doubtful in human testimony. Their testimony, therefore, must be invalidated, since they are taught to be false in faith; nor should those be believed who reject from themselves faith in the truth.

### LXV. That Jews are not to hold public offices

At the command of our lord and most excellent king Sisenand, this holy council decreed that Jews, or those who come from the Jews, should in no way seek public offices, because on this pretext they inflict injury upon Christians. Therefore, the provincial judges, together with their priests, are to suspend illicit petitions fraudulently obtained [Note: [Col. 0381D] In the remaining witnesses, except A., *relictas* (“left behind”).] and must not permit them to exercise public offices. If any judge permits this, excommunication is to be pronounced against him as against a sacrilegious person, and the one who has obtained office by stealth is to be assigned to public execution.

### LXVI. That Jews are not to possess Christian slaves

[Col. 0381D]

By decree of the most glorious prince, this holy council determined that Jews may not possess Christian slaves, purchase Christian slaves, or obtain them through anyone’s gift; for it is impious that members of Christ should serve the ministers of Antichrist. If Jews henceforth presume to possess Christian male or female slaves, those slaves, removed from their dominion, are to receive their freedom from the prince.

### LXVII. Concerning the freedmen of the Church

If those who distribute nothing from their possessions to the poor of Christ will be condemned in the future by the voice of the eternal Judge, how much more those who take away from the poor what they did not give? Therefore, let bishops who have contributed nothing of their own to the Church of Christ fear this divine sentence, and let them not presume to make free persons from the Church’s households to their own condemnation. For it is impious that one who has not contributed his property to the churches of Christ should inflict harm and intend to alienate the Church’s right. Accordingly, the succeeding bishop shall restore such freedmen to the right of the Church without any opposition, because it was not equity but wrongdoing that released them.

### LXVIII. Concerning the proper regulation of the Church’s manumitted persons

If a bishop wishes to manumit a slave belonging to the Church without retaining the Church’s ecclesiastical protection, he shall offer before the council of the Church over which he presides twice the value of the person’s merit and property, with the priests subscribing to the exchange [Col. 0382B], so that the decision of the one making the exchange may be found valid and just. For then he will be able to grant free manumission without the Church’s protection, once he has acquired for his own right the person whom he intends to hand over to freedom [Note: [Col. 0382D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, *because*.].

Such a freedman, however, is to be denied permission to bring an accusation or give testimony against the Church to whose right he belonged. If he presumes to do so, it is decreed that, while the exchange remains in force, he be recalled into servitude to his own church, which he attempts to injure.

### LXIX. That freedmen from the Church’s household may be made free by priests in compensation for property acquired

The agreement of the whole council determined that priests who either leave their own property to the Church, or, possessing nothing, nevertheless acquire estates or households for their churches, may manumit some persons from the households of that same Church in proportion to the value of the property contributed, as the ancient canons have decreed. In such a way, they are to remain free persons, together with their property and descendants, under the protection of the Church, carrying out the duties imposed upon them as far as they are able.

### LXX. Concerning the declaration of the Church’s freedmen

The Church’s freedmen, because their patroness never dies, must never depart from the protection of that same Church, nor may their descendants do so, as the earlier canons have decreed. And lest their freedom fail to appear in future offspring, and their descendants, relying on natural free status, withdraw themselves from the Church’s protection, it is necessary that both the freedmen themselves and those born from them make a declaration to their bishop, by which they acknowledge that they have been made free from the Church’s household and that they will not abandon its protection, but will offer it service and obedience according to their ability.

### LXXI. Concerning the Church’s freedmen who abandon its protection

The Church’s freedmen who, departing from its protection, have attached themselves to whatever persons, if they refuse to return after being admonished, are to have their manumission annulled, because through the contempt of disobedience they are held liable for an act of ingratitude.

### LXXII. Concerning freedmen commended to the Church’s protection

Freedmen who have been manumitted by any persons and entrusted to the Church’s protection are, as the rules established by the ancient Fathers have prescribed [Col. 0383A], to be protected by priestly defense from anyone’s insolence, whether in the condition of freedom which they are known to possess or in the property which they are known to have.

### LXXIII. Concerning the proper regulation of freedmen who may attain ecclesiastical honors

All who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from them are freely admitted to the clerical order, provided they are without crime, because they are known to have been released by direct manumission. But those who have been manumitted while retaining an obligation of service, because they are still bound in servitude to their patron, are in no way to be promoted to the ecclesiastical order, lest, whenever their masters wish, the clerics become slaves.

### LXXIV. Concerning the Church’s freedmen who are to be promoted to the priesthood

[Col. 0383B]

It is permitted to appoint priests and deacons from the Church’s households throughout the parishes, provided that uprightness of life and probity of conduct commend them. They are, however, to receive the freedom of their status by being manumitted beforehand, and only afterward are they to advance to ecclesiastical honors. For it is irreligious that those who receive the dignity of sacred orders should remain bound by servitude.

Whatever has been granted to such persons through freedom, or has become due to them by succession, or has been bestowed upon them in any way by anyone, they may not transfer in any respect to outsiders; rather, after their death, everything is to belong to the right of the Church from which they were manumitted. Like the other freedmen of the Church, they are also denied access to bringing accusations or giving testimony against the Church [Col. 0383C]. If they attempt this, let them not only lose the benefit of freedom but also the rank of honor which they earned not through the dignity of their nature but through the necessity of the time [Note: [Col. 0383D] Ae., B. R., *of the time of necessity*.].

### LXXV. Concerning the admonition of the people not to offend against princes; concerning the election of princes; concerning the admonition of princes as to how they should judge; and concerning the curse of Suintila, his wife and offspring, and likewise of his brother Geila and their possessions

After certain regulations of ecclesiastical order and decrees pertaining to the discipline of some persons, the final judgment which we, all the priests, must issue under God the Judge is this pontifical decree, for the strength of our kings and the stability of the Gothic people: for, as it is reported, among many peoples there exists such great treachery of mind that they refuse to keep the faith promised by oath to their kings. They feign with their mouths a profession of the oath while retaining the wickedness of treachery in their minds; they swear to their kings and violate the faith which they promise. Nor do they fear that book of God’s judgment by which a curse and many threats of punishments are brought upon those who swear falsely in God’s name.

What hope, then, will such peoples have when laboring against enemies? What faith can thereafter be trusted with other nations in peace? What treaty will remain inviolate? What sworn pledge toward enemies will endure, when they do not preserve the faith sworn to their own kings? For who is so mad as to cut off his own head with his own hand? They, as is well known, forgetful of their salvation, kill themselves with their own hand, turning their strength against themselves and their own kings. And while the Lord says, “Do not touch my anointed,” and David says, “Who,” he asks, “will stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be innocent?” they neither fear perjury nor hesitate to inflict destruction upon their kings.

Faith in a pact is given to enemies and is not violated; if faith is valuable in war, how much more must it be preserved among one’s own people? It is sacrilege if peoples violate the faith promised to their kings, because by this not only is a treaty transgressed among them, but also God is offended, in whose name the promise itself is made.

That is why heavenly anger has so altered many kingdoms of the earth that, through the wickedness of their faith and conduct, one was separated from another [Col. 0384B]. We therefore must beware of the fall of such peoples, lest we likewise be struck by a sudden blow and punished with a cruel penalty. For if God did not spare the angels who transgressed against him and who lost their heavenly dwelling through disobedience—whence he says through Isaiah, “My sword is drunk in heaven”—how much more must we fear the destruction of our salvation, lest through unfaithfulness we perish by the same sword of the enraged God?

If we wish to avoid divine anger and desire to move his severity toward mercy, let us preserve toward God the practice and fear of religion, and let us guard until death the faith and pledge promised toward our princes. Let there not be in us, as in certain peoples, the impious subtlety of unfaithfulness, the treachery of a deceitful mind, the wickedness of perjury, or the abominable schemes of conspiracies. Let no one seize the kingdom by presumption; let no one stir up mutual seditions among citizens; let no one plot the destruction of kings. Rather, when a prince has died in peace, let the leaders of the whole people, together with the priests, establish his successor to the kingdom by common counsel, so that, while the harmony of unity is maintained among us, no division of country and people may arise through force or ambition.

But if this admonition does not correct our minds and in no way lead our hearts to the common good, hear our sentence: Whoever from among us or from all the peoples of Spain, by any conspiracy or design, violates the oath of his faith which he has promised for the stability of the country and the Gothic people or for the preservation of the king’s safety; or attacks the king with death; or strips him of royal power; or by tyrannical presumption usurps the height of royal authority—let him be anathema in the sight of God the Father and the angels, and let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church which he has profaned by perjury and alien from every assembly of Christians, together with all the companions of his impiety, because it is fitting that one punishment hold liable those whom the same error has found entangled.

We repeat this a second time, saying: Whoever henceforth from among us or from all the peoples of Spain, by any plan or design, violates the oath of his faith which he has promised for the stability of the country and the Gothic people or for the preservation of the king’s safety; or attacks the king with death; or strips him of royal power; or by tyrannical presumption usurps the height of royal authority—let him be anathema in the sight of Christ and his apostles, and let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church which he has profaned by perjury and alien from every fellowship of Christians, and let him be held condemned in God’s future judgment together with his associates [Note: [Col. 0385D] In the remaining witnesses, except A., *fellow-associates*.], because it is fitting that those who join themselves to such persons should themselves be held liable to share in their condemnation.

This we proclaim a third time, saying: Whoever henceforth from among us or from all the peoples of Spain, by any intention or design, violates the oath of his faith which he has promised for the country’s safety, for the stability of the Gothic people, or for the security of royal power; or attacks the king with death; or strips him of royal power; or by tyrannical presumption usurps the height of royal authority—let him be anathema in the sight of the Holy Spirit and the martyrs of Christ, and let him be made an outsider from the Catholic Church of Christ which he has profaned by perjury and alien from every communion of Christians. Let him have no share among the righteous, but let him be condemned with the devil and his angels to eternal punishments, together with those who strive by the same conspiracy, so that an equal punishment of destruction may bind those whom a wicked alliance unites in ruin. Therefore, if this sentence, repeated for the third time, pleases all of you who are present, confirm it by the agreement of your voices.

The entire clergy and people said: “Whoever presumes to act against this definition of yours—anathema maranatha, that is, destruction at the coming of the Lord—let him, both he and his associates, have a share with Judas Iscariot.” Amen.

Therefore, we priests ourselves admonish the whole Church of Christ and the people, so that this dreadful and so often repeated sentence may condemn none of us in the present or eternal judgment. Rather, by guarding the faith promised toward our most glorious lord, King Sisenand, and serving him with sincere devotion, may we not only move the mercy of divine compassion toward ourselves but also deserve to receive the favor of the aforesaid prince.
