We also humbly beseech you, the king who are present and the princes of succeeding ages, that, being moderate and gentle toward your subjects, you govern with justice and piety the peoples entrusted to you by God, and render a good return to Christ the Giver who established you. Reign in humility of heart with zeal for good works, and let none of you alone pronounce judgment in cases involving persons or property. Rather, by public agreement with the governors, let the guilt of offenders be revealed through an open judgment, while gentleness toward you remains unharmed, so that you may prevail over them more by indulgence than by severity. Thus, while all these things are preserved by your pious governance with God as author, may kings rejoice in their peoples, peoples in their kings, and God in both.

We solemnly promulgate this sentence concerning future kings: If any of them, contrary to reverence for the laws, exercises over the peoples a most savage power through proud domination and royal arrogance, in wickedness, crime, or greed [Note: [Col. 0385D] B. R., E. 4, *inflated*.], let him be condemned by the sentence of anathema from Christ the Lord, and let him suffer separation from God and judgment because he presumed to act wickedly and turn the kingdom toward destruction.

Concerning Suintila, who, fearing his own crimes, deprived himself of the kingdom and stripped himself of the insignia of power, we have decreed this with the counsel of the people: Neither him nor his wife, because of the evils they committed, nor their children shall we ever associate with our unity, nor shall we at any time promote them to the honors from which they were cast down on account of their iniquity [Col. 0386B]. Just as they are considered outsiders from the dignity of the kingdom, so they are to remain excluded from possession of the goods which they had drained from the resources of the wretched, except insofar as they may have received anything through the mercy of our most merciful prince.

Likewise, we have resolved that Geila, the aforesaid Suintila’s brother by blood and crime, who was firm neither in the bond of brotherhood nor in preserving the faith promised to our most glorious lord, should, together with his wife, be separated from the fellowship of the people and from our association, just like those mentioned above. Nor are they to be restored to the possessions which they had increased through iniquity, except insofar as they may have obtained anything through the mercy of our most clement prince, whose grace enriches the good with the rewards of gifts and does not exclude the wicked from his generosity.

[Col. 0386C] Glory and honor, moreover, be to almighty God [Note: [Col. 0385D] In the remaining witnesses, except A. and E. 3, *to our God*.], in whose name we have assembled. After this, may peace, salvation, and long life strengthen our most pious and Christ-loving lord, King Sisenand, whose devotion summoned us to this health-giving decree. May the glory of Christ protect his kingdom and that of the Gothic people in the Catholic faith, in years and merits; may the grace of the Most High God protect him to the extreme of old age; and after the glory of the present kingdom, may he pass into the eternal kingdom [Note: [Col. 0385D] T. 2, *for the glory of the present kingdom*.], so that he who faithfully rules within this age may reign without end, by the favor of him who is King of kings and Lord of lords [Note: [Col. 0386D] Ae., *of those who rule*.], with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

When the matters set out above had thus been defined, with the agreement of the most religious prince, it was then resolved, with nothing preventing it, that none of us should violate what had been established, but that everything should be preserved by sound counsel. Since these things agree with the advancement of the Church and of our souls, we also confirm by our own signatures that they should remain [Note: [Col. 0386D] A. and E. 3 add: *and all subscribed*.].

I. I, Isidore, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Seville, in the name of Christ, have subscribed these statutes.

II. I, Sclua [Note: [Col. 0386D] In the others, except A., *Isclua*.], metropolitan bishop of the Church of Narbonne, in the name of Christ, have subscribed.

[Col. 0387A] III. I, Stephen, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Mérida, in the name of Christ, have subscribed.

IV. I, Justus, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Toledo, in the name of Christ, have subscribed.

# THE FIFTIETH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO

Twenty-four bishops, held in the era [Note: [Col. 0389D] From B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2. In A. and the others, *era* 674.] 664, in the first year of our lord King Chintila.

[Col. 0389]

[Col. 0389B] At the city of Toledo, we priests of the Lord from various provinces of Spain, who have assembled in one fellowship of peace in the basilica of the holy martyr Leocadia [Note: [Col. 0389D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, *confessor*.], offer thanksgiving to almighty God for his great mercy, by whose will we have come together in this harmony. We pray for the beginning of the reign of our glorious prince, King Chintila [Note: [Col. 0390D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, *Chintila*.], whose safety and prosperity move us to implore heavenly mercy. He entered into the midst of our assembly with the nobles and elders of his palace, humbly commended himself to the prayers of all, and by holy exhortation compelled his faithful subjects to do likewise. By divine inspiration he put forward this institution, which we establish by his command and by our decree.

### I. Concerning the institution of new litanies

[Col. 0389C] Namely, throughout the entire kingdom granted to him by God, this distinctive and proper religious observance is to be maintained at all times: beginning on the Ides of December, litanies are to be celebrated everywhere for three days each year in succession, and pardon for sins is to be sought through tears. If Sunday intervenes, they are to be celebrated in the following week. For since, with iniquity abounding and charity failing, wickedness is prolonged to such an extent that new crimes are committed, this new custom also should arise, one that may become our purification before the eyes of almighty God.

### II. Concerning the preservation of the kings’ safety and the defense of the present princes’ offspring

We must provide with the greatest vigilance and profound religious care that the evils which are constantly committed despite prohibition may be eradicated through carefully attentive ecclesiastical discipline. For it is not written without purpose: “Strike the pestilent man, and the fool will become wiser.”

Therefore, since experience teaches us that, under the weight of sins, what we ought especially to avoid almost always and frequently comes to pass, and that we violate through recklessness what we promise with the divine sacraments to guard, what is repeatedly found transgressed must frequently be restrained.

But lest those who succeed envy their predecessors and those who follow them envy those before them, so that everything may remain quiet and peaceful, this is the sentence jointly considered and presented by our council: while everything provided and written in the universal and great synod concerning the safety and welfare of princes is preserved, these additional provisions are also to be guarded:

Namely, that toward all the descendants of our prince, King Chintila, affection be maintained with every kindness and firmness, and that a reasonable means of defense be supplied, so that they may not be unjustly deprived of possessions rightly provided for them, or of those secured by the worthy provision of their parents, or of their rightful property. No one is to offer them illicit or contrived causes for harming them, nor are they to be harassed in any way or by any means with affection disregarded. For such license makes princes suspect to their subjects and subjects greedy for the possessions of princes.

Therefore, lest these provisions be violated and so that greed, the root of all evils, may be removed, we call to witness all who are present, absent, or to come in future times, before God and his angels: if anyone violates or despises our warning and by any contrivance attempts maliciously to harass them or harm them in any respect, let him be anathema in the assembly of all Christians and condemned by heavenly judgment. Let him be reproachable to all Catholics and abominable to the holy angels appointed to God’s service; let him be destroyed in this age and condemned in the future, because he refused to consent to such a righteous provision.

### III. Concerning the rejection of persons who are forbidden to attain the kingdom

For unfamiliar and new illnesses it is fitting to find a new remedy. Therefore, since the thoughtless minds of certain persons, incapable of understanding themselves, whom neither origin ennobles nor virtue adorns, casually think that they may lawfully reach the heights of royal power [Note: [Col. 0390D] In the remaining witnesses, except A. and E. 3, *of royal majesty*], our sentence concerning this matter is issued with divine invocation:

Whoever has contemplated such things, whom neither the election of all advances nor the nobility of the Gothic people draws to this summit of honor, is to be deprived of the fellowship of Catholics and condemned by divine anathema.

### IV. Concerning those who flatter themselves with hope of the kingdom while the king is still alive

Since it is both contrary to religion and plainly superstitious for anyone to think unlawfully about future events, investigate the fate of princes, and make provision for himself in the future, when it is written, “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power,” we decree by this decision that whoever is found to have investigated such matters and, while the prince is alive, looked toward another because of hope of a future kingdom, or for that reason drawn others to himself, is to be expelled from the assembly of Catholics by sentence of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0391D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, G., *repelled*.].

### V. Concerning those who presume to curse princes

We also decide by salutary deliberation concerning the pestilential behavior of human beings that no one is to heap curses upon a prince. For it is written by the lawgiver: “You shall not curse the prince of your people.” If anyone does so, let him be punished by ecclesiastical excommunication. For if those who curse will not possess the kingdom of God, how much more must such a person be expelled from the Church, since he is found to violate a divine sentence?

### VI. That the faithful servants of kings should not be deprived by the successors to the kingdom of the property due to them as the reward of their service

[Col. 0391C]

By a similar foresight, our sentence is given concerning the faithful servants of kings [Note: [Col. 0391D] Ae., *of our kings, by the counsel of the most religious prince*.]: whoever survives the princes must suffer no loss in possessions lawfully acquired through resources expended or through the generosity of the prince [Note: [Col. 0392D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, *and in accordance with the generosity*.]. For if the merit of the faithful is disturbed freely and unjustly, no one will wish to offer prompt and faithful service, when everything is wavering in uncertainty and the danger of the future is feared. Rather, the prince’s piety ought to provide protection for their safety and possessions. Others are encouraged by examples toward the same end, when the faithful are not defrauded of their reward.

### VII. That, at the celebration of all councils, the synod of Toledo held in the time of Sisenand should be clearly announced aloud to all for its own preservation

[Col. 0391D]

Because of the ease with which wicked minds forget and memory fails, this most sacred synod decrees that at every council of the bishops of Spain, the decree of the universal council established for the safety of our princes must be proclaimed aloud in the public synod after all other matters have been completed. Thus, by frequent repetition to their ears, the minds of the wicked may be terrified and corrected—minds which are led toward transgression by both forgetfulness and ease.

### VIII. Concerning the indulgence reserved to princes for offenders

[Col. 0392A]

In all the matters we have set forth, we reserve to the prince the power of indulgence in the faults of offenders, so that, according to the measure of his goodness and piety, once he has discerned the amendment of their minds, he may grant pardon for their faults.

### IX. Concerning the favor granted to the prince by the acclamation of the council

Bringing all these matters to an end and giving them force by our subscription, we render glory and praise to almighty God as far as mortal human strength permits. After this, we give thanks to our most excellent and glorious prince, King Chintila [398], whose ardor of faith, zeal for good intention, and harmony of unity have granted us confidence in charity.

May the Lord grant him triumph over his enemies and joy in blessedness. May he guard him with continual protection and fortify him with the most secure vigilance of his good will. May his kingdom remain for ever and ever. Amen.

I, Eugenius, by the mercy of God metropolitan bishop of the province of Carthage of the Church of Toledo—assenting to these common decrees—have subscribed.  
[Note: [Col. 0392D] The names of the bishops do not preserve the same order or position in all manuscripts.]

399 In the name of the Lord, Flavius Chintila, king.  
[Note: [Col. 0393] This confirmation of the council by Chintila is taken from Ae., since it is absent from the others.]

[Col. 0393B]

Since the care of a good ruler strives with every vigilance to provide for the welfare of his country and people, it is especially not fruitless when by his own diligence he also appeases divine clemency. Therefore, when bishops from various provinces had been assembled in the city of Toledo at the urging of our mildness, our earnest exhortation was that, at a suitable time, this observance of religion should be established through their decision, so that from the day of the Ides of December, according to what their holiness decreed, litanies should be celebrated throughout all the provinces of our kingdom with every devotion.

Therefore, favoring with royal authority so sacred an election, which is to be embraced with every desire, and confirming whatever was defined in that same synod, we decree:

That during the prescribed three days, according to what the decree of the most reverend men contains, every Christian soul should render to the Lord of heaven satisfaction through humility, and for the crimes and scandals by which, as the devil rages, we are daily ensnared, should offer fitting service through tears and fasts.

Nevertheless, so that the judgment of the aforesaid Fathers may become more certainly known to you, we order it to be appended below. By our commands we further enact that those whose care watches over our country in any matter—that is, the judgment of both the nobles and counts [Col. 0394B], as well as the chief concern of the other orders—should ensure that during these days every condition, age, and sex should be entirely free from all disturbance or any conduct of business, so that, devoted to holy leisure, they may become more worthy before God and obtain heavenly mercy by imploring it.

Therefore we entrust to the diligence of the priests the task of warning everyone of this command of ours.

Given on the day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of our reign, successfully, at Toledo.

LI. THE SIXTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, OF FORTY-EIGHT BISHOPS  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: universally assembled bishops, successfully, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.]

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393C] When we, the bishops of Spain and Gaul, had assembled in response to the salutary exhortations of the most orthodox and glorious king Chintila, and had taken our appointed seats in the praetorium of Toledo, in the church of the holy martyr Leocadia [Note: [Col. 0394D] B. R., confessor. E. 4, T. 1, 2, virgin.], on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the second year of the aforesaid ruler and victor in Christ, in the era 676 [Note: [Col. 0394D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: era 666], we first enact this decree of faith.

I. On the fullness of the Catholic faith

When, first of all, we had offered prayers to the almighty Lord for the crown of grace represented by so numerous a gathering of brothers, nothing better or more salutary occupied all our minds than that, following the custom of a universal synod, after completing the solemn prayer, we should pour forth with our tongues what we had pondered in our minds, and utter with our mouths what we believed in our hearts, approving the heavenly saying: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” which, according to the prophet, the Lord made brief upon the earth. Therefore, let confession come forth from the abundance of our heart, so that the tongue, as interpreter, may pour outward in confession the faith that everyone’s mind inwardly bears.

Accordingly, we believe and confess the most holy and almighty Trinity: the Father, Son [Col. 0394C], and Holy Spirit, one God alone but not solitary, of one essence, one power, one authority, one majesty, and one nature; distinct inseparably in persons, undivided essentially in the substance of the Godhead, creator of all creatures.

The Father is unbegotten, uncreated, the source and origin of all divinity. The Son was begotten from the Father timelessly, before every creature, without beginning, not created [G., nor]. For neither did the Father ever exist without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. Yet the Son is God from God the Father, not the Father God from God the Son; the Father is the Son’s Father, not God from the Son. The Son, however, is the Father’s Son and God from the Father, in every respect coequal with the Father, true God from true God.

The Holy Spirit, however, is neither begotten nor created, but proceeds from the Father and the Son, being the Spirit of both. [Col. 0394D] Thus they are substantially one, because one proceeds from both. In this Trinity the unity of substance is so great that it lacks plurality and retains equality; the person in each is neither less than in all nor greater in all than in each.

Of these three divine persons, therefore, we confess that only the Son, for the redemption of the human race and for releasing the debts of sins that we had contracted originally through Adam’s disobedience and through our own free will, came forth from the Father’s hidden and secret sanctuary [Col. 0395A] and assumed a sinless man from the holy ever-virgin Mary, so that the same Son of God the Father might be the Son of man: perfect God and perfect man; so that man and God might be one Christ in two natures, one in person, lest a quaternity be added to the Trinity if Christ had a double person.

Therefore, in person he is inseparably distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit, but in nature from the man he assumed. Likewise, with that same man he exists as one person, and with the Father and the Holy Spirit as one nature. As we have said, from two natures and one person there is one Lord Jesus Christ: in the form of God, equal to the Father; in the form of a servant, lesser than the Father. Hence his voice in the psalm: [Col. 0395B] “From my mother’s womb you are my God.”

Thus, born from God without a mother and born from a virgin without a father, he alone—the Word—became flesh and dwelt among us [Ae., “whose”]. And although the whole Trinity cooperated in forming the man who was assumed, since the works of the Trinity are inseparable, nevertheless he alone assumed a man in the singularity of his person, not in the unity of the divine nature—assuming what properly belongs to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity. For if he had confused one nature, that of man and that of God, into the other, the whole Trinity would have assumed a body, since it is established that the Trinity has one nature, though not one person.

This Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, sent by the Father, assuming what he was not and not losing what he was, inviolable in what was his own and mortal in what was ours, came into this world to save sinners [Col. 0395C] and justify believers. Performing miracles, he was handed over on account of our offenses; he died for our expiation; he rose again for our justification. By his bruising we were healed; by his death we were reconciled to God the Father; by his resurrection we have been raised again. We also await him as the one who will come at the end of the ages and, in his most equitable judgment, repay the just with rewards and the impious with punishments.

We also believe that the Catholic Church, spotless in works and without wrinkle in faith, is his body, and that it will possess a kingdom with its head, almighty Christ Jesus, after this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body immortality, so that God may be all in all.

By this faith hearts are purified; by this faith heresies are uprooted. In this faith the whole Church, already established in the heavenly kingdom and dwelling in the present age, rejoices. There is no salvation in any other faith, for no other name has been given under heaven to human beings by which we must be saved.

II. On the observance of the litanies

We receive with great reverence and veneration the devotion of our most religious ruler and the decree of our fellow priests, established in the first year of his reign and now evidently celebrated annually throughout his entire kingdom; and we have resolved to strengthen it also by our assent.

Accordingly, by the universal authority of the council we decree that the days of the litanies established in the aforesaid synod shall be held with every observance and celebrated with the greatest solemnity at the same time each year at which they were ordered to be observed, so that our expiation for the sins in which we have until now been entangled together may stand before the eyes of almighty God.

III. On the protection of the faith of the Jews

The unbending perfidy of the Jews now appears at last to have been bent by heavenly mercy and power. From this it is clear that the most excellent and Christian ruler, inflamed by the fervor of faith through the inspiration of the supreme God, has chosen, together with the priests of his kingdom, to eradicate their transgressions and superstitions completely; nor does he permit anyone who is not Catholic to dwell in his kingdom.

For this fervor of faith we give thanks to almighty God, the King of heaven, because he created so illustrious a soul and filled it with his wisdom. May he grant him long life in the present age and eternal glory in the future.

But we must determine this with provident care and very vigilant diligence: that his zeal and our labor may not at some time grow cold and melt away in future generations. Therefore, with heart and mouth in agreement with him, we promulgate a judgment pleasing to God; and, together with the consent of his nobles and distinguished men, after deliberation we enact:

That whoever in future times obtains the summit of the kingdom shall not ascend the royal throne before he has promised, among the other conditions of his oath, that he will not permit them to violate this Catholic faith; and that, in no way favoring their perfidy or, through neglect or desire, being enticed to do so, he shall not provide an opening for transgression to those rushing headlong into unbelief. What has been acquired with such great effort in our time must remain inviolate in the future. For good is undertaken in vain if its continuance is not foreseen [Note: [Col. 0395D] Ae., T. 1, 2, “foreseen beforehand.” G., “provided for.”].

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0396D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, “Thus”], after he has accessed the government of the kingdom in the manner prescribed above, if he himself proves to be a violator of this promise, let him be anathema, Maranatha, in the sight of the eternal God, and let him become food for eternal fire. Together with him, let all priests or other Christians who have been entangled in his error be struck by condemnation.

We decree these things in the present while confirming what was written about the Jews in the universal synod of the past, because we know that everything necessary that could have been written for their salvation was provided for in that synod [Col. 0396D]. Therefore we judge that what was then decreed shall remain in force.

IV. On the condemnation of clerics who obtain ecclesiastical orders through money

Although we know that the shoots of depravity, repeatedly springing up, have very often been condemned by the just severity of the Fathers, nevertheless, since they are again seen to flourish with frequent roots, we enact that they be cut out at the root with the sharper vigor of justice, according to what is written in the earlier canons: anathema upon the giver and the receiver.

Therefore, whoever imitates Simon and becomes an author of the simoniacal heresy, obtaining the ranks of ecclesiastical orders not through dignity of character but by the expenditure of gifts, and acquiring them through offerings—although neither rational order nor any dignity of character commends him—shall in no way be permitted to attain the highest sacred orders.

But if he has attained them, he shall be condemned, deprived of communion together with his ordainers and deprived of his own possessions [Ae., orders], because [Note: [Col. 0397D] From the word “because” to the end of the canon, all the other manuscripts lack the text except A.] it is recognized that they accepted the tonsure not for the love of God but out of ambition for honor.

V. On clerical stipends, so that they may not be alienated from the right of the Church

It often happens that the remoteness of time obscures the condition of one’s origin. Therefore, making provision, we decree that whoever among the clergy or any other persons receives a stipend from the possessions of any bishop’s Church through that bishop’s generosity [Col. 0397B] must write a declaration under the name of a precarious grant, so that prolonged possession may not prejudice the Church.

Whatever he has received for use, he must cultivate profitably, so that the property belonging to divine right may not be neglected for any reason, and so that the clergy may be able to receive support from the church they serve. If any of them refuses to do this, he shall appear to deprive himself of his stipend.

VI. On consecrated men and women who transgress their sacred profession

The course toward pleasure is easy, and nature imitates vices. Therefore, whoever among men or women has once put on, or shall put on, a religious habit voluntarily—whether a man has been or is devoted to the ecclesiastical choir, or a woman has been or is attached to a monastery of virgins—if either sex violates the profession, the offender shall be forced against his or her will to return to the former state: the man shall be tonsured, and the girl shall be restored to the monastery.

If, however, under any protection, they wish to remain deserters, they shall be held, by priestly judgment, as exiles from the Christian community, so that no communication whatsoever may be shared with them.

Widows likewise, as the universal synod established long ago, shall be condemned by the foregoing judgment if they desert their profession or habit.

VII. On transgressing penitents

Although earlier councils have never been silent about such great crimes [Note: [Col. 0398D] In the others, except A. and E. 3: “such great crimes”], reason nevertheless demands that things repeated through frequent transgression be condemned by frequent judgment. Therefore, since there is such perversity among human beings [Col. 0397D] that those whom the profession of penance, under a religious habit, brings or has brought to the hand of the priest for the remission of sins are again recalled by renewed wickedness to the filth of their former life, the holy synod decrees for this reason:

If any freeborn men or women have lived under the name of penance in a religious habit, but afterward have grown their hair, put on secular clothing, and returned or shall return to what they had abandoned, they shall be seized by the bishop of the city in whose territory they converted and again, against their will, be subjected to the laws of penance in monasteries.

If this should be difficult because of the power of some person, then, as the decrees of the ancient canons established, they shall be regarded as excommunicated until they return to the order they abandoned; and so shall those who, after warning or prohibition, have communicated with them.

The priest to whom they are known to belong, if through any gift, favor [Col. 0398A], or negligence he has refused to admonish them—either to receive them when they return or to cast them out of the Church when they persist in contempt—shall be punished by the same judgment until a sentence concerning their correction has been issued by him.

VIII. That certain penitents may be restored to their former marriages

It is the judgment of the ancient and most holy Father, Pope Leo, that a person who, placed in the age of adolescence, has resorted to the remedy of penance while fearing the danger of death, if married and perhaps incontinent, should return to the former marriage lest he afterward fall into adultery, until with the maturity of time he can attain a state of continence.

We judge the same equally concerning men and women—not as a general and legally binding command, but as a concession granted by us because of human frailty—subject only to this condition: if the person who is not bound by the laws of penance dies before returning by mutual consent to continence, the survivor may not again enter a marital embrace.

But if the life of the one who did not receive the blessing of penance continues, let that person marry, if unable to remain continent, and enjoy the companionship of another spouse. We have plainly decreed this equally for both sexes, with the provision, namely, that in all these matters the priest’s decision must be awaited, so that, according to what he discerns regarding the person’s past life, he may impose the rule of continence, absolution, or strictness.

IX. On the professions and obedience of the Church’s freedmen

It often happens through the passage of time that the condition of one’s origin is not apparent. Hence it was already decreed in a canon of an earlier universal council that the freedmen of the Church should make their profession, declaring that they had been manumitted from the households of the Church and would never abandon the service of the Church.

We add this provision as well: whenever a priest has completed the course of his life [Col. 0398D] and departed from this life, as soon as his successor has arrived, all his church’s freedmen, or those descended from them, must publicly present their documents before everyone to the bishop who has succeeded him and renew their professions in the presence of the Church, so that they may obtain the strength of their status and the Church may not lack their obedience.

But if they either neglect to disclose the documents of their freedom within a year of the new bishop’s ordination or refuse to renew their professions, those documents shall remain void and worthless, and they shall be returned to their origin as perpetual slaves.

406 X. On the offspring of the Church’s freedmen, so that they may not be permitted to wander away from the Church, even for their upbringing

[Col. 0399A]

It is fitting that those whose parents received the title of freedom from the households of the Church should be brought up within the Church to which they owe service, for the patrons are dishonored if, while they are neglected, the offspring of the manumitted are given to others for education.

Therefore, we decree that bishops should take them into the service of instruction without prejudice to their status, so that they may render the service they owe and suffer no diminution of their freedom. Those who attempt to act otherwise than our judgment has decreed, we order the bishops to bring back against their will for this very purpose.

But if their parents should refuse to give them to their own bishops and adopt other patrons for themselves [Col. 0399B], let them be struck by the law concerning ungrateful freedmen.

XI. That no one be condemned without a legitimate accuser

It is fitting that the life of the innocent not be stained by the ruin brought by accusers. Therefore, whoever is accused by anyone shall not be delivered to punishment before the accuser has been produced and the judgments of the laws and canons have been sought, so that if the person is found unworthy to accuse, judgment may not be rendered on the basis of that accusation—except where the case concerns the life of the royal majesty.

XII. On those who flee to the enemies

The audacity of depraved minds often seeks refuge with enemies, either through malicious thoughts or because of guilt [Col. 0399C]. Therefore, whoever proves to be the perpetrator of such acts, striving to defend the adversaries and bringing losses of property upon his country or people, shall, after being brought under the power of the ruler and the nation, be excommunicated and confined under the laws of a lengthy penance.

But if, remembering his evil beforehand, he should flee for refuge to a church, royal mercy shall be preserved toward him through the intercession of the priests and out of reverence for the place, together with justice.

XIII. On honoring the chief men of the palace

Those who are honored in the palace with the dignity and reverence or favor appropriate to their merit shall receive in every respect respectful honor from their juniors. They, in turn, shall embrace their inferiors with affection and instruct them by the example of usefulness.

XIV. On rewards granted to the kings’ faithful servants

[Col. 0399D]

To defraud the faithful of their reward is not only inhuman but also unjust. Since the merit of faithfulness, in divine as well as human matters, must not be regarded with ingratitude, it seems fitting that by priestly judgment we should provide for the king’s faithful servants.

Therefore, as the holy council decreed in the first year of our most serene ruler, all who have obeyed the ruler’s wishes or commands with faithful service and sincere devotion, and who have devoted their entire intention to guarding and watching over his safety, shall not be unjustly removed by his successors from either their dignity or their former possessions.

Even now, their position shall be regulated according to the ruler’s discretion and for the benefit of each, as he sees them to be necessary for the country [Col. 0400A]. Kindness shall be shown them in such a way that the power of favor remains in other matters as well, so that they may enjoy all things justly acquired in such a manner that they retain the free choice of leaving them to their descendants or bestowing them upon whomever they wish.

But if anyone has proved disloyal toward the royal person or useless in the responsibilities entrusted to him before our most pious lord Chintila, king, let such regulation remain in the hand of his clemency and at the discretion of his power. For it is impious to call into doubt the power of one to whom the governance of all has evidently been entrusted by heavenly judgment.

If, after his departure, anyone is found to have been disloyal to his life, let him lose whatever property he possessed through the king’s generosity; it shall be confiscated and distributed to the faithful.

XV. On property granted to churches, so that it may remain under their ownership

Since it is established that we have rendered excellent assistance to those who worthily serve rulers and offer them faithful service, by decreeing that possessions lawfully acquired from rulers should remain undivided under their ownership, it is equitable—and especially so—that we should apply suitable care to the possessions of the churches of God.

Therefore, whatever property has been or shall be lawfully granted to the churches of God by rulers, or whatever has been or shall be lawfully conferred upon them under any title by any other person, we order to remain so firmly under their ownership that it may in no way be removed by any circumstance or at any time [Col. 0400C].

For just as we have judged the faithful services of human beings not to be unworthy of gratitude, so possessions granted to churches—which properly are the nourishment of the poor—should remain undisturbed under their ownership as the reward of those who make the offering.

XVI. On the safety of the royal offspring and the affection to be shown them

Just as the insolence of wicked kings is always hateful and detestable to their subjects, so the prudent usefulness of good rulers becomes beloved among their peoples. 408 Therefore, what Christian could endure, or look upon with patience, the king’s children or descendants being stripped of their possessions or deprived of their dignities?

To prevent this, since our general judgment concerning the ruler’s sons is being promulgated, we openly issue decrees concerning the offspring of the present excellent and most glorious ruler, King Chintila [Col. 0400D]:

The whole of his kingdom shall preserve what the synod held in this church in the preceding year established concerning all his descendants. That is, his sons shall be shown kindly and steadfast affection, and wherever the opportunity of the place requires it, they shall be provided with proper means of defense, lest they be deprived through any cunning scheme of property lawfully expended, of what was secured through the dignity of their parents, of what was granted by the ruler’s generosity or by the expenditure of anyone else, or even of what is owed to them by right of ownership.

Nor shall anyone be given grounds for injuring them through any contrivance of plotting. For it is fitting that, since we possess security under his rule, we should grant peace to his descendants by decree of the council.

Finally, the benefits of our ruler toward us are so numerous that it would take too long to recount them individually. He, with God as author, gave us peace; he restored charity to us as though it had been captive; through his aid we enjoy tranquility; through his generosity we have been enriched; through the remedy of his goodness he spared the guilty and raised up the upright. If we wished to respond to his benefits with worthy benefits, we would not possess resources equal to so great a task, however much our will might suffice.

XVII. On those who, while the king lives, make provision for a future kingdom for themselves or others, and on persons forbidden to accede to the kingdom

Although a judgment concerning this matter was promulgated in the earlier council held in the first year of our glorious ruler, it pleases us to repeat what must be guarded [Col. 0401B].

Therefore, while the king’s life endures, no one shall, by any action or plan, make provision for a king for himself against the welfare and, beyond doubt, the will of the living king—whether a layman of whatever rank, one consecrated to the episcopate, presbyterate, or diaconate, or one devoted to the other offices of the clergy. No one shall, through flattery or persuasion arising from this hope, draw others to himself or himself yield to another.

For Christians must regard it as wicked and utterly detestable to look ahead to unlawful future arrangements and, ignorant of the course of their own life, to dispose of what is to come.

If anyone has already considered such matters through some wicked deliberation with anyone else, priestly moderation grants him this: he may disclose the matter without delay to the ears of the present ruler and thereby obtain pardon. But if through obstinate deliberation he refuses to reveal his schemes [Col. 0401C], let him be punished with the worst anathema.

When the king has died, no one shall assume the kingdom with tyrannical presumption. No one tonsured under a religious habit, shamefully shaven, of servile origin, or a man of foreign nation shall be advanced to the summit of the kingdom, unless he is Gothic by birth and worthy in character [Note: [Col. 0401D] In the others, except A. and E. 3: “be approved.”]. The violator of this most sacred command shall be struck with perpetual anathema.

XVIII. On protecting the rulers’ lives and on the defense that succeeding kings must provide for preceding kings

It is already established that the preceding universal synod made provision for the safety of our rulers. But we wish to repeat what was rightly enacted and strengthen what was salutarily ordered with fitting authority.

Therefore, we testify before God and the entire order of angels, before the choir of prophets and apostles and all martyrs, before the whole Catholic Church and the assembly of Christians:

Let no one aim at the king’s destruction; let no one assail the ruler’s life with murder; let no one deprive him of the government of the kingdom; let no one usurp the summit of the kingdom for himself with tyrannical presumption; let no one by any contrivance join his hand to the hand of conspirators against him.

[Col. 0402A] If anyone among our people should, through reckless audacity, presume to do any of these things, struck by divine anathema, let him be condemned by eternal judgment, with no place left for any remedy.

But the one who has obtained his throne, if he wishes to be cleansed from so great a crime, must avenge his death as though it were the death of his own father, with the strength of the entire Gothic kingdom consenting to aid in that defense.

If, however, through sluggish care and lesser zeal they refuse to avenge so dreadful a crime, let all of them, according to our judgment, become a reproach to other nations.

XIX. On the thanksgiving offered to God and the ruler at the confirmation of the council

When all these matters had been properly arranged and deliberated through lengthy discussion, we return blessing, glory, and honor to the invisible Father, author of all lights [Col. 0402B], and in preserving these things we implore the help of his assistance, asking that he grant strength to our constitutions by his power and render human weakness so effective in this arrangement that it may not prove transgressive.

We therefore confirm all the foregoing in our subscription, without prejudice to the authority of the ancient canons, and we give thanks to our most Christian and glorious ruler, Chintila [Note: [Col. 0401D] T. 1, 2, “to our ruler Chintila”], our king and prince, through whose initiative and earnestness we have been summoned together, whose will has proved acceptable [Note: [Col. 0401D] Ae., “ready.” B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G., “acceptable”] and whose arrangement has been religious.

May the Lord grant him, as the best of rulers, lasting triumph in the present age, an eternal kingdom among the portion of the just, and happy years. May he himself, blessed, enjoy long-lasting happiness and everywhere be fortified by the protection of the divine right hand.

I [Note: [Col. 0401D] In Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, the pronoun “I” is placed before the bishops’ names], Sclua [Note: [Col. 0401D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1: “Sclua, though unworthy, bishop of the Church of Narbonne, have subscribed to these constitutions issued by us” [Col. 0402D]. LII. THE SEVENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, OF THIRTY BISHOPS, HELD IN THE FIFTH YEAR, DURING THE REIGN OF OUR MOST CLEMENT LORD, KING CHINDASVIND, ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER, IN THE ERA 684

[Col. 0403]

I. On refugee and treacherous clerics or laymen

[Col. 0403C]

In the name of the holy Trinity, since our assembly at the city of Toledo had convened concerning certain ecclesiastical disciplines, both through our devotion and through the zeal of the most serene and Christ-loving King Chindasvind, it seemed fitting, by mutual deliberation, to decree [Col. 0403D] what, if carefully preserved, will—as we trust—prove exceedingly beneficial both to those now living and to future generations. For it is always of the greatest importance to provide for whatever is judged advantageous either to ecclesiastical morals or to the public welfare, without which we cannot live in tranquility.

For although there exist so many constitutions of the canons that they could suffice for every correction, if anyone would willingly attend to them, nevertheless, just as the clarity of a light shines all the more brightly the more diligently and frequently it is handled, so it contributes greatly to the amendment of many when, while what has been established is recalled to memory through fraternal deliberation, those matters are added which either seem to be lacking or are judged properly to require establishment.

For who is unaware of how many unlawful acts have thus far been committed by tyrants and refugees who transferred themselves into foreign regions, and how often their abominable arrogance has been displayed—acts which would bring about the diminution of the fatherland and impose unceasing labor upon the Gothic army? This might perhaps sometimes seem to us a tolerable result of the madness of laymen; yet what is more astonishing is that, even worse, so many are sometimes driven headlong into this presumption under the pretext of religion, so that, if the matter should in any way remain unpunished, it would be a grave disgrace to us. This must be corrected promptly by both secular law and ecclesiastical discipline.

Therefore it has now pleased us to define by unanimous decision:

Whoever, established in the clerical order from the highest rank to the lowest, transfers himself for any reason into the territory of another people, so that thereafter, in his pride, he appears to seek either his return or anything else; or whoever, on this pretext, has planned or in any way carried out anything that could specifically harm, or might be done against, the Gothic people, the fatherland, or the king; and likewise whoever is found to have been privy to such persons and is known to have supplied them either advice or assistance, whether in seeking flight to a foreign people, in persisting in the evils they had begun, in inflicting any injury upon the Gothic people, the fatherland, or the ruler after their flight, or in advising them that they would persist in the same wickedness—that person shall unquestionably be deprived of every degree of his honor, so that another may immediately and permanently receive the place which he had served to govern.

The transgressor himself, however, placed under penance, if, remembering the evil he has committed, he repents most rightly up to the day of his death, is to be granted communion only at the very end of his life. If, before the time of his end arrives, any priest—even at the command of the ruler—should agree to communicate with him, that priest, having become a participant in his crime, shall be anathema forever and shall be condemned with him by a similar sentence. For no priest ought in this matter to give assent to the ruler’s authority, lest he appear either to incur perjury or—God forbid—lest, if any ruler who is a betrayer of the Catholic faith should arise, that same priest be compelled, either through the ruler’s favor or through fear, to return from the light of right belief into darkness.

For thus none of the provisions set forth above ought ever to be annulled by the commands or threats of rulers. We know that nearly all the priests of Spain, all the nobles, judges, and other men of the palace establishment have sworn, and that it was long ago decreed by law, that no refugee or traitor who is found to have acted against the Gothic people, the fatherland, or the king, or to have transferred himself into the association of another people, should in any way be restored to possession of his property—unless perhaps the ruler should wish to bestow something out of humanity upon such persons. Even then, however, he shall have the power to grant the traitor no more than a twentieth part of his property, from whatever possessions the king may choose.

Moreover, because the perversity of certain clerics sometimes raises them to such levity that, abandoning the gravity of their order and forgetting the oath they had promised to keep to the reigning ruler, they rashly consent to the elevation of another, this license ought entirely to be abolished and utterly uprooted from our fellowship. Thus, if any layman should at any time, within the boundaries of the Gothic fatherland, attempt in his pride [Note: [Col. 0405D] The remaining witnesses, except A. and E. 3, read *superveniens* (“arriving/coming upon”).] to seize the summit of kingship, and any cleric should give him assistance or favor, and, through the power of his offense, this man who appears to be acting proudly should succeed in attaining the same ambition for kingship, then, from that day or time onward, the bishop or cleric of whatever order who has entangled himself in such a crime must remain excommunicated forever.

Nevertheless, if, through the wickedness of the ruler to whom he unjustly consented, the priests’ persistent efforts should be unable to suspend him from communion, then, at least, if he should survive and be found alive after the death of that same king, whoever has agreed to grant him the grace of communion—apart from at the very end of his life, provided that he has been proved to have repented legitimately—shall be subject to the correction of the foregoing anathema.

Meanwhile, reason has persuaded us to decree by synodal constitution concerning this matter that any layman who is subsequently found guilty under the aforesaid provisions—that is, by transferring himself into foreign parts in hostility to the people, the fatherland, or royal power, or by offering assistance to such persons—shall not only, as has been said, be deprived of all ownership of his property, but, condemned also to perpetual excommunication, shall never be granted communion except at the end of his life, unless the remedy of his communion, or that of the persons whom we have specified above, should otherwise be obtained from the ruler through the supplication of priests.

For if anyone—something that absolutely ought not to happen—is found wickedly to speak in disparagement or insult of the ruler, or to intend or consent to the king’s death or deposition, we indeed judge him worthy of such excommunication. Whether communion should nevertheless at some time be granted to him, we leave to the ruler’s mercy to determine; for without doubt it belongs to his authority to temper the faults of his subjects by a judgment of mercy and justice.

We admonish the most merciful rulers, and unanimously beseech them by the ineffable sacrament of the divine name, never, without a just priestly supplication where it is necessary, to suspend the sentence of this excommunication against traitorous clerics or laymen who transfer themselves into foreign parts or give their consent to such acts, through any rashness whatsoever. For what could appear to provide more prudently for their interests, if the rulers themselves preserve the form of this constitution and compel it to be fulfilled by all their subjects?

But if anyone should deem these enactments accursed, let him be anathema; and let whoever of the kings hereafter should believe or permit the authority of this canon to be violated in any respect always stand guilty before the Lord as a betrayer of the Catholic faith.

## II. Concerning the occurrence of illness among clerics performing ministry

Nothing is presumptuously attempted against the order’s established condition [Note: [Col. 0405D] The remaining witnesses, except A., E. 3, and T. 2, have [Col. 0406D] *statutum* (“established decree”).], nor are matters held in the highest veneration dissolved by even the least act of presumption, since it is recognized that what has been ordered to be done is interrupted only for this purpose: lest, through the onset of illness, nature be deprived of the strength of health. Thus provision is made not only for human weakness but also, in abundance, for the honor of God’s ministries, while care is taken diligently to avoid the danger of offense.

We therefore judge it fitting that, when the holy mysteries are being consecrated by priests at the time of Mass, if any illness should occur that makes it impossible to complete the ministry of the consecration already begun, it should be permissible for a bishop or another presbyter to complete the consecration of the office already begun. For, in order to supplement the mysteries that have been initiated, nothing is appropriate except the completed blessing of either the priest who began or the priest who follows; for they cannot be regarded as perfected unless they are completed in the proper order of perfection.

For since we are all one in Christ, diversity creates nothing contrary where the unity of faith displays the efficacy of prosperity. Let the clerics of every order likewise have no doubt that this provision has been granted to them, but, as stated above, let others willingly succeed those who preceded them for the completion of the rite.

Nevertheless, lest what is provided because of bodily illness be turned into a danger of presumption, no one may celebrate Mass after taking even the smallest amount of food or drink; and no minister or priest who has begun the imperfect rites may presume altogether to abandon them without an evident onset of illness. Whoever should presume to violate these provisions shall suffer the sentence of excommunication.

## III. Concerning the funeral rites of a dying bishop

[Col. 0407B] Matters appropriate to propriety are often left uncompleted through the negligence of certain persons [Note: [Col. 0407D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: *impleri* (“to be completed/fulfilled”), for *compleri*.]. Therefore, since it is known what dignity is preserved in the funeral rites of a dying bishop through the canonical tradition of ancient custom, we add only this: if any priest, after being summoned according to the statutes of the Council of Valencia to come for the burial of the body of a deceased bishop, should delay through sluggish unwillingness, then, if the clergy of the deceased bishop appeal against him before the synod or the metropolitan bishop, he shall have absolutely no permission either to celebrate Mass or to receive communion for the period of one year.

Presbyters and other clerics, moreover, who hold a higher place of honor in the same church whose priest has died, if they are found slow to summon the bishop, whether concerning the funeral rites of one already dead or of a bishop who is about to die immediately, or if they are proved to neglect this through any disturbance of mind, shall be assigned to penance in monasteries for the space of an entire year.

## IV. Concerning the exactions imposed upon the churches of the province of Gallaecia

Among the other matters which it was fitting for us to settle by common agreement, it was also appropriate to examine most carefully the complaints of the parish presbyters of the province of Gallaecia [Note: [Col. 0407D] T. 1, 2: *decernere* (“to decree”), for *discernere* (“to examine/discern”).], which, as we have learned, necessity finally compelled them to bring before a public inquiry against the rapacity of their bishops.

For, as a clear investigation has revealed, these bishops, burdening the parish churches with indiscriminate administration and frequently becoming excessive in their exactions, are shown to have brought certain basilicas almost to the point of complete exhaustion of their utmost resources.

Therefore, lest what has plainly been presumed in a disorderly manner up to now occur hereafter, no bishop of the aforesaid province shall demand that more than two solidi be delivered to him annually from each basilica of his diocese, in accordance with the Council of Braga; the basilicas of monasteries, however, are exempt from this payment [B. R.: *autem* (“but”), for *tamen* (“however”)] [Note: [Col. 0407D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: *impensione* (“contribution/payment”), for *pensione*.].

When the bishop visits the diocese, moreover, he must not become burdensome to anyone through excessive numbers, nor may his entourage ever exceed the number of fifty [Note: [Col. 0407D] All the manuscripts read *quinquagenarium*; we judge the passage corrupt and conjecture that perhaps *quinarium* was intended.] conveyances [Col. 0408A], nor shall he have permission to remain more than one day at each basilica.

Whoever of those bishops should presume to act otherwise than we decree shall unquestionably be subject to canonical correction, by which transgressors of synodal constitutions ought to be punished according to the edicts of the ancient Fathers.

## V. Concerning honorable recluses and vagrants

We observe that certain persons, ignorant of or forgetful of the traditions of the Fathers, have fallen into such great negligence that, through their detestable practice, those things which were legitimately established are seen to have been almost abolished. For when the unlearned desire to teach, what else do they show than that they are afflicted by the error of ignorance?

And because, relying upon a backward course, they place presumption in teaching before the zeal of learning, it is evident that they seek not the highest usefulness but serve a depraved course of action.

Therefore, decreeing such matters out of just severity, we command by appropriate judgment that those whom an ambition for holy life keeps enclosed in their own cells, and whom both the merits of that same holy purpose assist and integrity adorn, are to remain at peace, secure through God’s help and protected by our favor.

But those whom sloth has driven into such a purpose, not knowledge of wisdom; those whom no dignity of life adorns, but whom—what is worse—ignorance defiles and detestable conduct disgraces: we decree that they are to be removed from these cells and from the places where they are either said to wander or are kept enclosed. They are to be assigned without exception to monasteries by the bishops or heads of monasteries from whose congregation they came or in whose vicinity they reside, so that there, meditating upon the teaching of the holy order, they may first learn what has been established by the Fathers, and afterward be able to teach what they have acquired through holy meditation. Only then, if they have become fruitful in doctrine and holy works, let them hasten toward the highest virtue, imbued with the practice of holy purpose.

Henceforth, whoever decides to come to this holy purpose shall not be permitted to attain it in any other way, nor shall they be able to obtain it beforehand, unless they have first been established in monasteries and, according to the holy rules of monasteries, have been more fully instructed and have been able to merit both the dignity of an honorable life and knowledge of holy doctrine.

As for those whom the utmost madness has so seized that they are known to wander in uncertain places and, dishonorable through the depravity of their conduct, to possess absolutely neither stability of residence nor integrity of mind [Col. 0408D], whoever finds them wandering, whether priest or minister, shall assign them for correction to the Fathers of monasteries, if this can be done [Note: [Col. 0408D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “or, if it is permissible, let him reform them in their own places with their own superiors in the monastery; or, if that is difficult…”], or, if it is difficult, shall bend them to be instructed under the force of his own authority, solely for the sake of an honorable life.

## VI. Concerning neighboring bishops who are to reside in the royal city

It has also pleased us that, out of reverence for the ruler, for the honor of the royal see, and for the consolation of the metropolitan of that city, the bishops neighboring the city of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0408D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U.: “of the see.”] should, according to the instruction they have received from that same bishop, reside in the same city for one month each year, except that the harvest and vintage holidays are to be exempted.

We, however, unanimously offering thanks to immortal God and to the glorious ruler Chindasvind, on whose account we have assembled in this city with holy devotion, earnestly and desirously beseech that the holy Catholic Church may always be enriched with faith and peace, and that, together with the prosperity of the present kingdom, future rewards of joy may also be granted to the aforesaid ruler—through him by whose gift the one God lives and is glorified in the Trinity, throughout the ages of ages. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0409D] B. R.: “is glorified through infinite ages of ages. Amen.”]
