# LIII. The Eighth Council of Toledo of Fifty-Two Bishops, Celebrated in the Royal City on the Seventeenth Day before the Kalends of January, in the Era 691, in the Fifth Year of Reccesvinth, the Orthodox and Glorious King, Pre-eminent in the True Dignity of Mercy [Note: [Col. 0411] T., U., G.: “conspicuous.”]

[Col. 0411]

[Col. 0411A] 421–422 When the divine ordering of his will had gathered us all together, by the most serene command of that same ruler, into a sacred synodal assembly in the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, at last the long-desired and welcome day of joy arrived, delightful and pleasant, received with all the more eager a desire by our hearts as it had been sought by the innermost feelings of those yearning for the remedy of salvation.

And when, according to custom, each of us had occupied the seat proper to him in his order and awaited the outcome of the matter with calm attention, the most serene ruler appeared, filled with devout religion and glorious with the highest title of praise. Presenting himself inclined before our assembly so that we might commend him to the almighty Lord in our prayers, he exhorted us with attentive and very sweet words, giving thanks [Col. 0411B] to the God of hosts that, in fulfilling the decree of his command, we had been gathered together into one council.

But when we recognized how piously humble was the will of his holy soul, and saw the height of such sublime glory bending itself still more sublimely, we were inflamed with such exultation for the glory of God that, joyful, we rendered to him the thanks and honor due, both humbly and with bowed heads. Yet the more the order of humility had exalted the ruler, the more sublimely the examples of the most sacred ruler’s character instructed us in the exercises of supreme virtue and in the form of our religion.

Then, after praises had been offered to God for the outcome of mutual unity, he addressed us at length with the grace of tranquility, saying:

“Although the supreme author of all things raised me to the seat of the kingdom during the times of my lord and father of blessed memory and made me a participant in his glory, now, however, since he has attained the rest of the eternal dwellings, the divine power has entirely subjected to me the rights of the whole government which he transferred and left in my charge.

“Therefore, since the salvation of the members is the concern of the head, and the happiness of peoples is nothing other than the gentleness of rulers, I have gladly resolved to disclose openly before you, who are present, the deliberation of my wishes and to present the actions of my endeavors with sincerity.

“But because an eager heart pours itself out toward the fulfillment of its promises and, though weary, does not submit itself to the burdens of delay through sluggishness, I have compressed a long exposition into a brief summary. Whatever I could have spread before the assembly through extended speech, I have decided to offer entirely, scattered by the pen throughout the folded pages of this volume, to your holiness [Col. 0411D]. I exhort you with earnest prayer and deliberation to attend closely to whatever is written there, examine it with discerning zeal, and concerning whatever in it may prove pleasing to God, let the sacred oracle of your mouth report it to us.”

Thereafter, having received the volume offered to us, we cried out while giving thanks to the Lord: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

After the blessed joy of this exultation and the hymn of heavenly glory, we blessed the same sacred ruler. Then, when the volume had been opened [Note: [Col. 0411] Ae., T. 1, U.: “with the volume wrapped”; B. R., E. 4, 2: “with the wrapping of the volume.”], we found the following matters woven therein.

In the name of the Lord, Flavius Reccesvinthus, king, to the most reverend Fathers resident in this holy synod:

Holding, through the wondrous gift of the Holy Spirit, the firm and well-instructed rule of my faith, and humbly bowing my heart before the diadem of glory in his honor, I rejoice to hear that all the kings of the earth serve and obey God. Behold, reverend Fathers, exalted above me in the highest honor of veneration: I come before you, summoning the testimony of your blessedness in favor of my gentleness, and bowing myself before the fearful nods of almighty God in testimony of your vision. With joyful heart I render him abundant thanks, because in his merciful will he has deigned, at the command of our exalted authority, to lead you into the desired assembly of this holy congregation. I trust that both for me and for you, throughout the present sequence of time and the length of future ages, the reward of his grace will be present, since you demonstrate by coming together a unanimous and religious affection for concord, and have hastened openly to recognize how pious is my desire in governing peoples.

Now, since a brief address cannot contain the excess of a long discourse, you will find written in the sequence of this volume—and, when it has been read again, will understand beforehand—what I know concerning the holy faith, which I have learned as having descended from heaven through the mouths of the holy apostles and the Fathers who followed them, as well as what I have resolved to make known concerning the matters to come for which I have judged it right to assemble this gathering of your congregation. May the gravity of your blessedness promptly and mercifully give effect to everything that the authority of our greatness has impressed upon its text, just as the serenity of our gentleness commends these matters to you for fulfillment.

Beginning, therefore, my address with a definition of the holy faith, I shall attach the other matters that must be disclosed in what follows, as though building upon the solidity of a rock, so that, when I come to construct the edifice of my work, I may lay its subsequent parts more securely because I have placed the first ones more fittingly and firmly. Thus let your reverence have before you what it does not doubt that it knows: I possess, truly know, and most firmly retain, from a pure heart and a good conscience, the true, holy, and sincere rule of the orthodox faith; and I embrace, venerate, and love it just as apostolic tradition handed it down, just as the holy Synod of Nicaea established it, just as the gathering of the holy Fathers at Constantinople defined it, just as the unity of the first assembly at Ephesus affirmed it, and just as the definition of the Council of Chalcedon set it forth.

I preserve this faith with the faithful; I invite the unbelieving to it for salvation [B. R.: “I invite”]; I govern subject peoples within it; I instruct my own peoples to hold it; I proclaim it to foreign peoples, so that, glorifying God in it, I may attain the happiness of the supreme divinity during the time of mortal life, and may receive from him an inheritance of glory in the land of the living.

Behold, most reverend Fathers: as far as the truth of the holy faith is concerned, your honor has judged that I have fully unfolded the titles of its confession from the whole of my soul. I now consider it especially necessary for me to strive to join the practices of holy action to the fellowship of this same true faith, lest we possess it either dead without works, or in such a way that it falls dishonorably from the dignity evident in its fullness, while Scripture does not remain silent concerning certain people who say that they know God but deny him by their deeds.

Therefore, so that we may possess this faith more fully—faith founded upon that stone which the builders indeed rejected, but which was made by the Lord into the cornerstone, and which is wondrous in our eyes—and may be adorned more fittingly with its insignia, attend to the fruit of what work and the increase of what action we wish and hasten to associate and join with the studies of this holy faith.

We recall that in former times you and the whole people swore that anyone, whatever his rank or dignity, who was discovered either to have conceived or carried out anything harmful toward the death of the king and the destruction of the Gothic people and homeland would, condemned by the severity of an irrevocable sentence, nowhere deserve the remedy of pardon or receive any assistance whatsoever from clemency.

But now, since this is judged grievous and burdensome, when it is understood that this sentence is met by serious opposition from deeds of piety, and thus the pledge of condemnation is retained in its entirety, lest any avenue be opened against the piety which, as the Apostle proclaims, is useful for all things, I entrust this matter to your sacred judgments in confidence, to be examined and settled by your decisions.

It will therefore be yours, with divine compassion inspiring you, to regulate the measure of both dangers in such a way that neither the condition of the oath may hold the guilty bound, nor the vengeance of impiety treat them inhumanely. Let the form of your judgment instruct us so that I may neither keep subject peoples submissive in profanations nor grieve that they have been crushed by the bonds of impiety.

After this address to the assembly, I join the matters of business that follow and likewise ask you to attend to them.

We decree, bearing witness before your entire body by the coequal, coeternal, and inseparable Trinity of the supreme divinity, and by the mysteries of that sacrament which true faith proclaims throughout the whole world: that the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary for the salvation of the world; and by the coming of that same Jesus Christ, Son of God and our Lord, by whom the impious are to be destroyed and by whose kingdom the saints are to be glorified.

Whatever matters arising from anyone’s complaint are brought to your hearing, settle them with the strength of justice, mercifully and with the tempering of compassion, most justly and with our concurrence. In the judgments of the laws, where they stand corrupted or appear to have been inserted in excess or improperly, arrange, with the consent of our serenity, only those provisions that accord with sincere justice and the sufficiency of the cases. Bring certain obscure and doubtful canons into the daylight of clear understanding. Concerning all cases and the status of every order that may be brought before you, strive to establish them in the most just, pious, and temperate manner, in harmony with the rules of the Fathers, so that I, longing for the fruit of good works, may receive a share among the blessed; and so that you, because you fulfill God’s will and do not despise me when I implore you, may be received into the kingdom of eternal blessedness, and may be granted to remain forever attached to the vision of God’s delight.

You also, illustrious men whom ancient custom has established as attending this holy synod from the palatine office, whom distinguished nobility has honored and the experience of equity has appointed as rulers of the peoples—whom I embrace as partners in government, faithful in adversity, and energetic in prosperity; through whom justice fulfills the laws, compassion bends the laws, and the moderation of equity, against the strictness of the laws, draws forth the temperance of the law—I adjure and solemnly entreat you, by that whole wondrous and unique sacrament of the one holy faith by which I have adjured the venerable assembly of all the holy Fathers, to direct your minds toward so just a formula of truth and discernment [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except A. and E. 3, “of the whole” (cunctae)], so that, turning your mental gaze in no other direction than the consensus of the present Fathers and holy men, you may diligently, modestly, and with every worthy application complete whatever you recognize to be close to innocence, near to justice, not alien to piety, or pleasing to God alone.

Know that, in fulfilling these salutary wishes of mine, you show yourselves beloved by God; and, in strengthening the edicts of your decrees by the exhibition of your favor, I show that I too, together with you, shall be pleasing to God.

To all of you collectively—both the suitable ministers of divine worship and the governors properly chosen from the royal court, bound by the adjuration of the divine name—I add the true and sincere promise of my consent: whatever you choose, with our agreement, to decree or fulfill as close to justice, piety, and salutary discernment, I shall complete in all respects with God’s favor, and shall protect and defend it by royal authority against every kind of dispute and complaint.

After those matters that have been shown to belong to the domestic rule of the faith, the holy eagerness of your blessed assembly demands another matter from it. I bring forward, at the boundary of this separate section, a cause that is judged foreign to our doctrine. Although Christ desires to win it through me, he does not fail to recognize it as hostile to him until he openly obtains what he ardently desires: I mean, of course, the Jews and their life and practices. I know that the land of my kingdom alone remains polluted by the contagion of this plague. For although almighty God has utterly uprooted all heresies from this region, this one disgrace of sacrilege is recognized as remaining, which either the persistence of our devotion must correct or the vengeance of his punishment destroy.

Among these people I see some retaining, through the error of an ancient tradition, the rights of unbelief; others, cleansed by the washing of holy baptism, have fallen back into the error of apostasy, so that the profanation of blasphemy is found more detestable in them than in those who are not yet known to have been purified by the water of sacred regeneration.

For this struggle of good intention [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except A., “action” (actionis)] and gain for the true faith, I beseech the reverence of your blessedness, and by the tenor of the fearful oath already mentioned I solemnly charge you: without any favor, without any acceptance of persons or partiality toward them, command that whatever concerns the true faith and true honor of the Lord and my Redeemer Jesus Christ [Note: In the others, except A. and E. 3, “love” (amorem) instead of “honor” (honorem)] be dealt with by a sentence pleasing to God and to my faith, ardently and most truthfully. Thus, just as divine mercy has given me the governance of the faithful, with whom it recognizes that it is glorified by me, so may it grant me also to attain the gain of the unbelieving, among whom I may rejoice that the good of his will is brought about and his venerable kingdom has come.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth year, happily, of the glory of our reign.

In the name of the Lord, I, Flavius Reccesvinthus, king, have subscribed with my own hand this deliberation of my faith and good will.

## I.

When the page of the volume [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except A. and E. 3, “of every” (omni)] had been reread [Note: E. 4: “reported”] and completed, after we had glorified God for hearing the profession of the king’s faith and for the disposition of his good will, we immediately turned our attention to conducting the remaining business and began the judgment at once.

Then, at the beginning of the first account, a discussion of the true faith presented itself to us. As we began by speaking of it first, let us take the beginning of our solidity from the place where we received the beginning of sacred birth, so that, with a strong sentence placed at the start of our affirmations, whatever subsequently arises from the conduct of the matters under discussion may be able to stand with an even stronger sequence of decrees.

Therefore, with the whole strength of our minds, we both profess and proclaim that we hold the true profession and true rule of the one holy faith; and we ceaselessly preach and declare it to all for acceptance and retention with full deliberation, just as it is taught by what was shown by the holy apostles, just as it is proved by the orthodox exposition of the Fathers who followed them, and just as it is recognized as most truly confirmed in those holy synodal acts in which the insane error of Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, and Eutyches is both clearly exposed and utterly uprooted. Finally, just as we profess and recite it with one voice in the sacred solemnities of the Mass:

> We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible;
>
> and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth;
>
> who for us and for our salvation descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, made man from the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there [B. R.: “again”] in glory to judge the living and the dead, and whose kingdom shall have no end;
>
> and we believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets;
>
> in one catholic and apostolic Church;
>
> we confess one baptism for the remission of sins;
>
> we await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

This rule of the holy faith does not now admit an opening for discussion because it is known to have been sufficiently expounded by the holy teachers, and because the business of the cases pressing upon us draws us toward other matters that must be carried out.

## II.

At the beginning of the second discussion there arose a matter as difficult as it was grave. A debate was opened concerning refugees and traitors, and it was investigated with considerable effort whether the sentence imposed upon those condemned could be tempered.

But when the sequence of the conditions to which, not long before, the devastation of war had compelled us to swear because of their danger was recited to our hearing, we found that such a dense web of obligation was present there that the knot of its stains seemed not so much to have prohibited transgressions as to have closed up the very entrails of compassion.

For there was something that troubled us on both sides: lest the holy name be profaned, and lest the practice of mercy perish. What caused fear was not absent from the profanation of God’s name, and what caused distress was present in the prohibition of piety. While the two dangers opposed one another against the sentence that had been issued, we were caught in uncertainty on the divided path of the contending parties, along which the judgment was hastening toward separation.

But when the encounter with difficulty had thrown itself obliquely across the steps of our discussion, we finally abandoned the peril of haste and, amid the crash of sobs and showers of tears, turned both our words and our hearts to God, who is the fountain of compassion.

> Breathe upon us, Holy Spirit, and guide us into the harbor of your will, once the waves of our ignorance have been calmed. For behold, we have reached the sandbanks of danger upon the shore of our course, and, amid the wreck-producing obstacles confronting us, we do not see, with attentive consideration, where we should spread the sails of our judgment.
>
> But breathe upon us again, Holy Spirit, and grant us, by your gift, to know what you command and, with your help, to be able to fulfill what you command. By searching, enlighten what we do not know; by helping, accomplish what we fear to fulfill.
>
> If, then, resting in you and casting away the fears of wandering waves, you command us to arrange the commerce of peace, let us begin those things that may be brought to the glory of your omnipotence and, with your assent, granted for human salvation.

Not long ago, when the tumultuous revolt of certain refugees was repeatedly bringing devastation upon the lands and inflicting scandals upon the peoples together with destruction—so greatly that no one’s effort could bring back the bands of captives or repair the desolations of the land shaken by such a plague—it was demanded by the force of the necessity that had arisen rather than by a considered judicial decision that we swear the most severe oaths against those men and against others very much like them.

That we swore is shown by the condition of the oath, through the testimony of the divine name; and the authority of sacred Scripture presses upon us so that it cannot be undone. For it is written in Exodus:

> “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold innocent the one who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain.”

Likewise in Leviticus:

> “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God: I am the Lord.”

But the severity of the pressures inflicted can and should be relieved. This is suggested by the horror of the bonds and lamentations and commended by the commands of that same divine authority. For, according to the old translation, the Lord rebukes certain people through Isaiah with severe reproach, saying:

> “Woe to the sons of desertion, says the Lord. You have made a plan, but not through me, and an agreement, but not by my spirit, adding sin upon sin.”

Likewise Jeremiah says:

> “Our iniquities have turned these things aside, and our sins have removed good things from us, because impious men have been found among my people. They set snares to scatter men and caught them. As a snare standing full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.”

And through Micah:

> “Alas for me, my soul, because the faithful man has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among humankind. All are judged in blood; each one afflicts his neighbor with affliction. They prepare their hands for evil.”

Isaiah instructs us concerning beneficence, which is more pleasing to divine eyes in proportion as it is found to be more excellent, saying:

> “Loosen the bonds of wickedness; undo the bundles that oppress.”

Paul, the chosen vessel, likewise says:

> “Piety is useful for all things.”

And James:

> “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy; but mercy triumphs over judgment.”

John likewise:

> “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life remaining in him.”

And Truth himself says:

> “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you”;  
> and again: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; but if you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.”

Behold, on both sides there are the commands of the Lord’s order, supported by the firmest guarantee. Therefore, because they have been set forth through the utterance of the divine mouth, they will remain established by eternal law in every respect.

What then? Shall we say that the justice of an oath and the peace of mercy contradict one another, when it is written:

> “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced one another”?

Or, because the collapse of disputes spreads itself through contention, shall we say that the assertion of one side is not to be fulfilled at all? Why does the assertion of the other side threaten immediate loss? And because the keeping of the oath does not temper a vengeance to be feared, will the savagery of impiety therefore produce a death that must be abhorred? Far from it.

For if, in the public records of oaths—God forbid—an unlawful or evil condition had been imposed by anyone, one that compelled him either to cut the throat of his father or to commit rape against a most sacred virgin, would it not be more tolerable to reject the promises of a foolish pledge than, by keeping useless promises, to fulfill the measure of dreadful crimes?

If this were so, how could obedience to a single command be believed to be a fountain of piety when it poured out streams of vengeance [Note: A. and the remaining witnesses: “thorns” (tribulos)]? Or what kind of observance of sacred law would that be which committed sacrilegious wrongdoing? What measure of equity would it appear to have, if from the safeguard of one command there arose a savage horror of slaughter?

But we are not now contending in such a way that, once the divisions of disputes have been stirred up, we ourselves become involved in the contests of contention. There is truly peace in both sides of what we say, because the Holy Spirit so regulates the course of our journey that he excludes nothing deviant from his own arrangement.

Therefore, with full voice, fuller faith, and the fullest intention, we proclaim—and likewise proclaim and desire throughout the whole community of the holy Church—that the name of the one supreme divinity must not be taken through any profanation, profaned improperly by any sacrilege of perjury, or touched anywhere by any transaction of deceit.

For if, as Truth bears witness, swearing altogether is prohibited in order to avoid the profanation of perjury, when it is said, “Let your speech be: YES, YES; NO, NO; whatever is more than these is from evil,” how will it be unpunished to profane voluntarily the name of such great glory, when the faith prescribed in it is recognized to have perished? Or how will the treaties of peace be bound among nations if the agreements of oaths are not preserved with more sacred integrity?

Indeed, everything that enters into a peace treaty stands more securely when an oath strengthens it; everything that reconciles the hearts of friends endures more firmly when the bonds of an oath bind them; and everything that a witness confirms is established more truly when the addition of an oath affirms it. If the witness should fail, the declaration of an oath alone reveals the faith of the innocent.

For this reason, so that the divine will might disclose to human movements what it willed, lest fragile uncertainty hold as doubtful what the promise of inviolate truth expressed, the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying:

> “I am the Lord, and there is no other; by myself I have sworn.”

If, therefore, vows confirmed by so great an ordinance must be kept, who could assert that these things, which are alien to truth, should be violated sacrilegiously?

The living commands of sacred authority will therefore stand and must in no way be rashly profaned through empty violation. Yet, lest the oaths that have been given seem to have closed our hearts so completely against compassion that the inner parts of our souls conceive no indulgence from an affection for mercy, we open the bosom of mercy while maintaining the established bonds of the oath. We judge that mercy must be shown to all with a devotion pleasing to God, so that neither the safeguard of the oath may hold us guilty nor inhumanity make us detestable.

Each person ought, with whatever aid he can provide, to meet the ruin of the wretched and, by relieving another’s vengeance, remove God’s vengeance from himself. For the one who drives adversity away from the afflicted offers prosperity to the Lord.

Thus Job, before experiencing suffering, offering aid to those who suffered and remembering it in the patience of his own suffering, weaves a catalogue of his virtues and says among other things:

> “The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Once I wept over the one who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”

Hence Solomon also says:

> “Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction.”

Instructed by these decrees of sacred authority, it is clear that we have not profaned the holy name, since our preaching emphatically indicates that it must in no way be profaned. And, opening wide the inner depths of indulgence, although those condemned by the profession of their own mouths would scarcely deserve to be absolved, according to what is written:

> “Your blood is upon your own head, for your mouth has spoken against you”;  
> and again: “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned,”

nevertheless, out of regard for piety, we open a way of pardon and extend mercy.

We are compelled to temper the harsh and bloody sentence of this promise especially for the following reason: although both evils must be guarded against with the greatest care, if the necessity of danger compels us to violate one of them, we ought to undo the one that is known to bind us with the lesser obligation.

Let us investigate, with the pious sharpness of reason, which of these is lighter and which more serious. When we are compelled to commit perjury, we offend the Creator but stain only ourselves. When, however, we fulfill harmful promises, we both arrogantly despise God’s commands and harm our neighbors with impious cruelty, and we ourselves are slaughtered by the more cruel sword of death. There we are struck by a double weapon of guilt; here we are slaughtered three times over.

It remains, therefore, that our sentence proceed where the way of mercy has opened. This is so acceptable to the Lord that he desires it more than venerable sacrifices, as he himself says:

> “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”

With this permission of indulgence granted, we place the work of mercy in the power of the glorious prince. Since God has opened to him an avenue of compassion, may he himself also not deny the remedies of piety. Let these be moderated by royal discernment in such a way that mercy may in some measure be granted to those men, while through them the people or homeland nowhere suffers any danger or loss. It is sufficient that this matter be tempered under the protection of mercy.

For the rest, whatever oaths have been exacted up to now, or may hereafter be exacted, for the safety of the royal power or the protection of the people and homeland, we decree that they must be observed inviolably, with every care and vigilance, entirely released from the religious obligation of mutilation of limbs and the penalty of death [Note: In the others, except A., “confinement” (religatione) instead of “religious obligation” (religione)].

But lest the crafty wickedness of depraved minds someday summon us to the guilt of perjury and claim that this sentence comes from the rule of the holy faith, we have taken care to join to this discussion both the oracles of divine authority and the assertions of the Fathers who preceded us.

For the nature of the supreme God, immutable and always existing in the same way, is often read in the sacred writings to have changed his promises and tempered his sentence out of mercy. Although he is impassible and immutable, established in the firmest divinity, nevertheless both his oaths and his repentance are frequently read of him, concealed beneath sacred mysteries.

For God to swear is not at all to overturn what he has ordained concerning himself; to repent is, when he wills, to change those same ordinances. Thus he says through Jeremiah:

> “Suddenly I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot, destroy, and scatter it. If that nation repents of its evil against which I have spoken, I too shall repent of the evil that I had thought to do to it.”

And through Ezekiel:

> “If I say to the righteous man that he shall live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses will be consigned to oblivion, and in the iniquity that he has committed he shall die in it. But if I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin, he shall live and shall not die.”

If, then, our conversion changes the divine sentence in this way, why should the abundant tears or distress of the wretched not temper so harsh a vengeance through mercy? For this reason, too, the vengeance promised to the Israelite people is often suspended, and the destruction of the Ninevites is calmed by a change in the divine sentence.

But Ambrose, a distinguished author renowned for his title of praise, speaks in his first book *On Duties* as follows concerning a case of this kind:

> “It is also against duty sometimes to fulfill a promise, yet to keep an oath, as in the case of Herod, who swore that he would give the daughter of Herodias whatever she asked, and granted the death of John so as not to deny his promise. What shall I say of Jephthah, who sacrificed the daughter who first met him as he returned victorious, in order to fulfill the vow he had promised, that he would offer to God whatever first came out to meet him? It would have been better not to promise anything of this kind than to fulfill a promise by parricide.”

Likewise, in his third book:

> “The affection must therefore be pure and sincere, so that each person may speak plainly, possess his vessel in holiness, and not lead his brother astray by verbal deception; let him promise nothing dishonorable. And if he has promised it, it is more tolerable not to fulfill the promise than to do what is shameful.
>
> “Often many bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath, and, although they themselves recognize that what they promised ought not to have been promised, nevertheless, out of regard for the oath, they do what they pledged—as we wrote above concerning Herod, who shamefully promised a reward to a dancing girl and cruelly paid it. Shameful is the promise that a kingdom should be given for a dance; cruel is the gift by which the death of a prophet is granted out of reverence for an oath. How much more tolerable would such perjury have been than the oath?”

And, discussing Jephthah shortly afterward, he says:

> “Miserable is the necessity that is discharged by parricide. It is better not to vow than to vow what the one to whom it is promised would not wish to be paid.”

And a little later:

> “Not all promises, therefore, are always to be fulfilled. Finally, the Lord himself, as Scripture indicates, frequently changes his sentence.”

The most holy man Augustine, cautious through the sharpness of his investigation, outstanding in the art of discovery, fluent in the abundance of his assertions, graceful in the flower of eloquence, and fruitful in the harvest of wisdom, says the following in his writings:

> “There are altogether two kinds of lies in which there is no great guilt; yet they are not without guilt, whether we are joking or whether we lie about what we have promised” [Note: Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2: “or lie to our neighbors.” U., G.: “or lie to our neighbor about what we have promised.”].
>
> “The first, when joking, is not therefore most harmful because it does not deceive: the person to whom it is said knows that it was said as a joke. The second is milder because it retains some benevolence.”

The same author says:

> “Let truth not take away mercy, nor mercy impede truth. For if, on account of truth or of a truth that is seemingly rigid, you forget mercy, you will not walk in the way of the Lord, in which mercy and truth have met one another.”

The blessed Pope Gregory, worthy of honor both for his books and for his merits, and rightly preferred to almost all others in ethical exposition, says in his *Moral Works*:

> “Since this Behemoth binds with such inexplicable knots that the mind, often brought into uncertainty, is more tightly bound by guilt precisely where it strives to free itself from guilt, it is rightly said: ‘The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.’
>
> “For the arguments of his machinations are drawn together as if to release, but are entangled all the more in order to hold fast. Yet there is something that can usefully be done to destroy his deceptions: when the mind is caught between lesser and greater sins, if no avenue of escape without sin is entirely open, the lesser must always be chosen. For one who is enclosed on every side by the circuit of walls so that he cannot escape throws himself into flight wherever he finds the shorter wall.”

Isidore, also, the distinguished teacher of our age, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him but not inferior in learning, and—what is greater—most learned at the end of the ages, and to be named with reverence, says in the second book of his *Sentences* concerning such a matter:

> “An oath by which evil is rashly promised is not to be kept, as when someone promises an adulteress perpetual fidelity to remain with her. For it is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to persist in the disgrace of fornication.”

Likewise, in his *Synonyms*:

> “Break faith with evil promises; change your decision concerning a shameful vow; do not do what you have rashly vowed. A promise is impious when it is fulfilled by crime.”

Let this brief preface from the sacred writings and the principal authors suffice. Whoever seeks these matters by reading them more attentively will be able to gather many more examples. But those for whom these things are not sufficient should take silence from this point onward with shame, since we desire to be anathema to Christ for our brothers rather than to persist in cruel wrongdoing.

## III.

In the address concerning the third matter we grieved over the most pernicious vows of later generations, contrary to the admonitions of the Fathers who preceded them. For the more frequently those earlier Fathers prohibited harmful practices, the more earnestly these later people do not cease to perpetrate what was forbidden. Thus, by contradiction, what ought to have been utterly extinguished does not cease to attack; and what, cut off by so many decrees, could have withered, flourishes again like the head of the Lernaean [Note: In the others, except A.: “hydra,” instead of “Lernaean”]—as the stories tell.

Finally, what must be said without great sorrow: very many are found wishing to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit, at the cost of their own ruin, when they give a cheap reward in order to attain the lofty summit of the pontifical order, forgetting Peter’s words to Simon:

> “May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money.”

Therefore, since this evil is customary and has often been cut away by the sword of the Fathers, we too apply the remaining heated iron to this cancerous wound, decreeing absolutely that anyone henceforth discovered to have offered any reward in order to obtain the dignity of the priesthood shall know that from that very moment he is condemned by the disgrace of anathema and excluded from receiving the body and blood of Christ, since it is clear that he committed this execrable crime against Christ.

If anyone should be found who accuses him, the man who obtained this order through the acceptance of gifts shall be deprived of the rank of the honor he received and confined in a monastery under perpetual penance. Those who accepted gifts on this account, if they are clerics, shall be punished by the loss of their honor; but if they are laymen, they shall be condemned by perpetual anathema.

### IV

At the fourth session, the fall of the episcopal dignity confronted us; compelled first to lament it and then to make provision, we have proceeded in due order. For since Christ, according to the mystery of the flesh he assumed, deigned to be the head of his Church, it is rightly seen that the bishops’ office is performed as the eyes among his members. For they govern and administer, from the more exalted height of their orders, the multitudes of the peoples subject to them. Therefore, the more they become leaders of those who follow, the more they ought to shine with the light of their merits.

Accordingly, all bishops, among the adornments of their other virtues, ought to strive especially for purity of body, so that their hearers may be moved to seek purity by the fact that their teachers are not defiled by impurity. If, therefore, bishops should henceforth be discovered polluting themselves with abominable offenses with any women and associating with them in familiar intimacy, let them know that they will be punished by the irrevocable judgment of the Fathers, that is, deprived both of the dignity of their office and of their rank…

### V

By the impetus of the fifth action, it came to the sacred hearing of the entire council that certain priests and ministers, forgetting the ancient enactments of their predecessors, were defiling themselves through the unclean association and abominable contamination of wives or of women of any kind. Through the obstinacy of a most wicked heart, they opposed both the sacred Scriptures and the regulations of the Fathers, not even commending carefully to memory what is written: “Be holy, for I also am holy, says the Lord”; and that apostolic injunction: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” namely, fornication and impurity, evil desire and greed. The more stubborn [B. R., “more pernicious”] the practice of evils is, the more severe the decrees must be by which it is opposed.

Therefore, in particular condemnation of the disgrace of this offense, the holy council defines that all bishops should diligently see to it that the same matter is investigated among their own clergy, and when they have been able to discover it with complete certainty, should bind all such persons by an agreement of this kind [Col. 0423B], so that they never again commit such abominable acts.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] In the others, except A., *distringant*.]

The women associated with them in this disgrace, whether free or enslaved, must be separated from them in every possible way or, in any event, sold, so that every avenue by which they might return to the accomplices [B. R., *consocios*, “partners”] of their crime may henceforth be denied them. Those men, however, if they cannot be restrained by any means, must be assigned to monasteries until the end of their lives and remain entirely subject to the disciplines of penance.

### VI

In the course of the sixth discussion, the marked offense of certain men conscious of wrongdoing became evident. For it was reported to us that certain subdeacons, after attaining the rank of this sacred order, were not only defiling themselves with bodily impurity, although it is written, “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord,” but also—what it is unlawful even to say—were joining themselves to new wives. They asserted that this was lawful for them because they knew that they had not received a blessing from the bishop.

Therefore, with every veil of excuse torn away, we command that the following be observed: when these same subdeacons are ordained, they are to receive from the bishop, together with the vessels of the ministry, a blessing, as antiquity is known to have handed down in certain churches and as sacred custom is shown to support when it has been promulgated; and all the impurity and familiarity of women must be completely removed from them. If thereafter they are wounded by this offense, they shall immediately be confined in monasteries under the burdens of penance until the end of their lives.

### VII

With the advance of the seventh assertion, both an immodest course of action and a base and detestable presumption came before our assembly. For we know that certain men, whether through the circumstances of necessity or through fear of dangers, attained the offices of ecclesiastical dignities; and, since they testify that they did not wish this to happen to them when those offices were imposed upon them, they therefore attempt to despise them and return to their former marriages and ways of life, wickedly violating heavenly laws while eagerly gaping after worldly allurements.

Concerning this, we must understand that the summit of episcopal eminence has rightly been judged to be the highest of all sacred offices, since it forbade other priests to perform the following: the consecration of God’s temples, the blessing of chrism, [Note: [Col. 0424D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “by divine command.”] [Col. 0424A] and the institution of sacred orders. These remain efficaciously ordained insofar as they are conferred most excellently; and they are uniquely bestowed by them insofar as their performance is reserved for that same supreme dignity. [Note: [Col. 0423D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “let them be separated and handed over to a monastery, so that henceforth.”] How, then, can one who has received these things reject them from himself, when he knows that none other than bishops alone can confer them, and that what they have bound no one else can loose, nor what they have loosed be bound again by anyone?

For Truth says to Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” Therefore, what is known to have become sacred by the authority both of divine command [Note: [Col. 0424D] From E. 4, T. 1, 2. In A. and the others: “otherwise.”] and of apostolic tradition can in no way ever be profaned. Rather, just as the holy chrism once conferred and the honor of the altar cannot be torn away, [Col. 0424B] so also the dignity of sacred honors, which is held to be equal and allied to these, once received on whatever occasion, shall remain entirely unshaken.

To eradicate at the root the useless argument of this crafty contrivance, let them reasonably understand that the following objection is made against them: the inestimable gift of holy baptism is bestowed always and often not only upon those unwilling to receive it, but also—what is more—upon those who do not know what they are receiving; yet no one is permitted to profane it. If it is objected here that those who are shown to receive this sacrament are not yet capable of reason, let them be entirely silent on this point. For if adults do not unpunishedly abandon what children receive either unknowingly or unwillingly, how much less is it fitting to violate what, to avert the danger of death or punishments, is recognized as having come about through the hidden dispensation of God? [Col. 0424C]

Let the shameless supporters of such desires therefore withdraw; and although they received unwillingly what they did not deserve to possess, let them nevertheless willingly retain for this reason the heavenly reward which they obtained unwillingly on account of an earthly necessity, so that at last, against their will, they may desire to love the good things which they appear voluntarily and sluggishly to oppose.

But if, after this perpetual ordinance has been promulgated, anyone does not sincerely remain attached to sacred observances, and, casting away from himself the grace he received, attempts to return to marriage and the customs of the world—or is found to have returned—then, immediately deprived of every dignity of ecclesiastical rank, he shall truly be regarded as an apostate and be entirely excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church and from the fellowship of the faithful [437]. He shall be shut up in the enclosure of a monastery under penance for as long as he lives.

### VIII

In the course of the eighth discussion, we found certain men devoted to divine offices so full of the great dullness of ignorance that they were not even proved to be adequately instructed in the orders in which they exercise their daily functions. Therefore it is carefully established and decreed that henceforth no one of any ecclesiastical dignity may receive a rank unless he perfectly knows the entire Psalter, or the complete supplement of the customary canticles and hymns, or the rite of baptizing.

Those who already hold the dignity of their offices but are afflicted by the blindness of this ignorance must either voluntarily undertake to learn what is necessary or be compelled by their superiors, against their will, to undertake reading exercises.

### IX

At the prompting of the ninth consideration, the dreadful gluttony of voracious men was exposed. Since it is not restrained by the bridle of moderation, it is judged to oppose religion. For Scripture says: “He who despises small things will gradually fall into great ones.” These men rage with such expenditure of shameful indulgence that they seem to despise heavenly things and almost the highest matters.

For since the days of Lent are assigned as the tenth part of the entire year, consecrated to the offering of the Lord’s fast—and since, through them, the condition of the human race is most salutarily cleansed, when a person who is to believe is brought to this religious observance from the four regions of the world, and, formed from the four elements, is suitably afflicted four times ten on account of the transgression of the Decalogue—those men, rashly despising all these things, neither restrain their gluttonous appetite nor, what is worse, profane the paschal festivals by consuming illicit foods.

Therefore such foods are forbidden to them with the greatest severity. Whoever, without unavoidable necessity, evident weakness caused by illness, or the incapacity of age, presumes to eat meat during the days of Lent shall not only be guilty with respect to the Lord’s resurrection but shall also be excluded from the holy communion of that day. This shall be added to his punishment: for the remainder of that year he shall abstain from all eating of meat, because he forgot the discipline of abstinence during the sacred days.

Those, however, whom age bends, illness weakens, or necessity constrains must not presume to violate what is forbidden until they have received permission from a priest.

### X

By agreement in the tenth conference, we have seen that sufficient opposition has been offered, both by the law of the glorious prince and by the decree of this holy synod, to the troublesome actions which careful investigation has shown to oppose piety, and to the license of misgovernment which gentleness has proved that it resisted. Thus the Holy Spirit breathed through both definitions into the hearts of mortals, so that by the life-giving breath of its words it might thereafter burn out every frenzy of wickedly desiring minds [438].

For the definitions themselves established that, since the incomprehensible and unknowable nature of divine piety joined itself to the condition of mortals in the union of the person, in the mystery of human redemption, we too must uproot and cut away completely from the members of this head both the evil of unbelief and desire, which is the root of all evils, and greed, which is found to be the service of idols, by the same fire, the same sword, and every means.

Henceforth, therefore, rulers are to be appointed to the glory of the kingdom in such a way that they are chosen either in the royal city or in the place where the prince has died, with the complete consent of the bishops and the chief men of the palace—not from outside, not through the conspiracy of a few, and not through the seditious tumult of rustic peoples.

They shall be defenders of the Catholic faith, defending it both from the Jewish unbelief which threatens it and from the injury of all heresies. They shall be modest in their actions, judgments, and lives. In distributing resources they shall be more sparing than expansive, so that they neither exact nor intend to exact from their subjects any levy by force or faction under the pretext of Scripture or of any decrees whatsoever. In the goods acquired through offerings of the greatest gratitude, they shall not look to the rights of their own advantage but shall provide for their country and people. Of the resources gathered by them, they shall claim for themselves only those portions which the authority of the prince has assigned.

Whatever they leave unregulated, their successors shall inherit as glory [Note: [Col. 0425D] All witnesses except A. and E. 3 read: “their own successors”]; their own property, acquired most justly before the kingdom, shall be taken by their sons or heirs according to the right of proximity. As for the inheritance or gift of relatives, even if left unregulated, it shall pass first only to sons or heirs, and thereafter to relatives.

Thus, in all their actions, conduct, and possessions, the authority of the aforesaid law shall prevail, so that it may remain unshaken forever. No one shall receive the summit of the kingdom before declaring by an oath that he will fulfill that law in every respect. Showing reverence to this law and to the episcopal decree not only in the future but also at present, we decree that whoever chooses to be a detractor rather than a venerator of that decree and law, whether he is a religious or a layman, shall not only be punished by ecclesiastical excommunication but shall also be deprived of the dignity of his rank.

### XI

In the matter of the eleventh occasion, we gave perpetual support to the universal decrees, knowing that God always relieves the distress of the oppressed through many opposing judgments, and that, just as he permits the hardships of punishments to be inflicted when the wickedness of men demands it, so, whenever he wills, he alleviates the burdens of oppression.

For this reason the decrees of the preceding Fathers rightly judged that a synodal assembly should be held in order to uproot contention and quarrels at the root, so that disputes prolonged by differing judgments might find an end there where the Holy Spirit has gathered the universal assembly.

Therefore, set on fire by this Holy Spirit, we unanimously and fully decree that henceforth no one shall be able to stir up disturbances with impunity or overturn the general statutes. Whatever has been or shall be written as a definition of universal authority concerning matters of faith and ecclesiastical affairs—whether in past acts, present enactments, or future decrees—no one shall henceforth dare contradict, no one presume to assail, and no one strive not to fulfill.

If, therefore, anyone, out of religious profession, proves disobedient, murmuring, a destroyer, or envious toward these decrees, rather than becoming their gracious supporter, let him mourn that he has been punished by the loss both of his honor and of holy communion.

When any holy synod is being held, or when something is being peacefully defined among the bishops [Note: [Col. 0426D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “bishops.” U., G.: “bishops and laymen.”], if a few should happen to disagree through ignorance or contempt [Col. 0427A] [Note: [Col. 0427D] E. 4, T. 1: “contention.”], let them either yield, when admonished, to the judgment of the majority, or depart from their assembly with the disgrace of confusion and suffer the sentence of excommunication for a year.

### XII

In the twelfth matter, which is final and last, the cause of the Jews’ abominable and unspeakable unbelief became manifest to our assembly through the most devout supplication of the sacred prince. We judged that it should be placed at the end of the decrees because we lament that this same people, brought back by the oracles of divine sanction on account of its offense, has been placed from the head at the rear.

But since Christ died for them as well as for us, according to what he himself said, “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel,” we deemed it necessary to devote the greatest care to those for whom Christ did not disdain to lay down his soul. Therefore, most devotedly supporting the princely clemency—which for this reason prefers that the summit of its kingdom be made firm by the Lord if it gains the lost multitudes for the Catholic faith, judging it unworthy that a prince of orthodox faith should rule sacrilegious people or pollute the people of the faithful through association with unbelievers—we decree nothing else concerning them according to our judgment than that the decrees of the Council of Toledo, which was assembled in the time of King Sisenand of divine memory, be fulfilled by us and by our successors with every diligence. Whoever wishes to dissent from the judgment of that synod must know that he will truly be condemned as a sacrilegious person.

The inseparable name of the divine Trinity, just as by wondrous inspiration it marked out the beginnings of our deliberations [Col. 0427C], so by a sublime conclusion brings them to completion, now accomplishing them, so that our having set forth these matters may be attributed to the one from whom our beginning came.

Therefore we give glory and honor to that same holy and indivisible Trinity, which granted us both to speak from itself and to complete in itself what was spoken; which, at the end of the ages, restored the remedies of piety and dissolved the bonds of fetters through the bestowal of graces.

Salvation and blessing from the Lord of hosts upon the most serene and most glorious prince Reccesvinth; thanksgiving and the fullness of reverence from all of us together to that most merciful prince, the gracious giver of good things, whose benevolent persistence in prayer God has brought to fulfillment; whose [Note: [Col. 0428D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, “disposition.”] most devout disposition removed the destructive causes of oppression; in whose times may he grant justice to flourish and abundant mercy to overflow; and to him may he grant, after the times of the present age, an enduring crown in recompense together with all the saints.

We all commend this entire series of our decrees, flowing from the fountain of right faith, piety, and justice, most earnestly before God and his holy angels, and to all the orthodox, now and in the future. We earnestly beseech them to fulfill it reverently and defend it graciously against its enemies [Ae., earnestly]. May the vengeance of divine severity come upon those who despise it; but may overflowing mercy, perpetual peace, and eternal glory be granted to those who observe it.

By the force and authority of this judgment and decree, we decree that the series of our enactments which we issued in the name of our most serene lord, King Reccesvinth, concerning the properties acquired under any title by his father of divine memory, shall stand in full force.

Finally, we confirm with equal strength the law which that most merciful prince issued to restrain the dreadful greed of princes, and by equal judgment we define that it be observed in every respect throughout future times. Moreover, lest either of these perish through the silence of time or the forgetfulness of antiquity, we have decreed that both be attached to this constitution of ours and commended to the memory of all, so that they may never remain separated from all the rules established above.

If anyone should perhaps attempt to overturn the other judgments of our decrees known to have been enacted by this holy synod, or negligently fail to fulfill them, or at some time wish to violate them, let him be anathema by the judgment of almighty God.

To our God alone be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## From the illustrious men of the palace establishment

Hodoagrus, count of the Chamberlains and duke. Offilo, count of the Chamberlains and duke. Adulfus, count of the Scancii and duke. Babilo, count and nobleman. Astaldus, count and nobleman. Ataulfus, count. Ella, count and duke. [Col. 0430A] Paulus, count of the Notaries. Evantius, count of the Scancii. Euredus, count and nobleman. Riquira, count of the Patrimony. Afrila, count of the Scancii. Wenedarius, count of the Scancii and duke. Fandila, count of the Scancii and duke. Cumefrendus, count of the Spatharii. Froila, count and nobleman.
