# Decree of the universal judgment issued in the name of the prince

To restore what has been broken, to raise up what had fallen, and to make what had collapsed stand again is both an accustomed reward and the fullness of completed perfection. For if it is fitting that the care of equals and neighbors should oppose the weight of a ruin that strikes them down, how much greater is the guilt of superiors who incur the danger of negligence if they do not use the burden of excommunication, insofar as they are able, to lift up the peoples entrusted to them?

We must therefore hasten, amid the throngs of colliding ruins, to rescue those who have been struck down, so that from this time onward the accursed oppression may no longer possess the strength to do harm, and every oppressed person may know that the sacred remedies of the holy sanction have been conferred upon him.

When, therefore, as the times of harsh domination passed, grievous power raised itself up, and the authority of the ruler did not establish the laws of governance among subject peoples but rather the destruction of punishment, we saw that the condition of the subjects was not strengthened according to the order of the ruler but cast down by the weight of power. For arrogant heights had drawn the laws into a two-faced division of movement: either the stern law raged in punishments, or the voluntary law offered favor in plunder. As a result, mournful spirits were not nourished by hope of benefit but were afflicted by endurance in calamity.

Accordingly, now that restoration confronts us, not only does reason itself compel us to depart from this course, but the very disturbance of affairs drives us, so that from the concordant deliberation of all minds there may emerge that sentence of judgment which both properly puts an end to unlawful attempts and legally provides protection for the salvation of the peoples.

For we have seen certain kings, after attaining the glory of the kingdom, heap up profit for their own property by weakening the resources of their peoples. Forgetting that they were called to rule for the sake of defense, they turned defense into devastation, although they ought to have driven devastation away through defense. They added the still graver offense of assigning what they appeared to acquire not to the honor or glory of the kingdom, but of preferring to confuse it with their own right, as though by debt decreeing that these things should be transmitted to the posterity of their children.

Why, then, do they attempt to draw into the bosom of private ownership what they plainly received solely through the imperial dignity? Or by what license do they place in the chamber of their private right what is plainly known to have been acquired for the public good? For could the arrival of peoples or the consideration of resources have come to them unless they had been raised to the heights of glory? Or could they have been enriched by the accumulation of resources from their equals unless they had been elevated over their subjects by the glorious summit?

Certainly [Ae., T. 1, 2: “however”], all the members of the entire people, while subject, direct the attentive gaze of due regard toward the principal head; from him they look for a remedy in their affairs, to whom they assign a census sometimes as a gift and sometimes as a debt. Therefore the royal order proves that everything is owed to it precisely because it recognizes that it governs everything, and it rightly defends what has been acquired as belonging to no one else but itself. It does not doubt that these things are owed not to the person but to the power of the ruler.

For laws make the king, not the person, since his standing is not established by his mediocrity but by the honor of his exalted position. Therefore let what is owed to honor serve honor, and let what kings accumulate be left to the kingdom. Since the glory of the kingdom adorns them, let them also not diminish but embellish the glory of the kingdom.

Henceforth, kings established in the exercise of rule shall have attentive hearts in governing, modest actions in acting, just judgments in deciding, ready hearts in sparing, restrained zeal in acquiring, and sincere intentions in preserving. They shall retain the glory of the kingdom with happiness to the extent that they preserve the laws of government with gentleness and direct them with equity, the reward promised by the declaration [T. 2, “of affection”].

Lest it be thought that this has not proceeded from the source of reason, it is fitting to disclose the clearest form of the action, so that the integrity of truth may have us as suitable defenders from the moment when the quality of the action has preserved itself by its own evidence.

For behold, we have found and lamented that many men, both from the lesser and the greater persons of our people, have hitherto fallen in such a way that, once their ruin is recognized, we can consider nothing other than the judgments of divine permission. We see that the spoils of their houses, together with the wealth and estates of their powers, have been utterly emptied, and that they have not been transferred either as useful resources to the treasury or as a salutary remedy to the offices of the palace.

Because this defect has arisen from both sides—since the judgment of the courts struck down those who had been adjudged, and no one arose to be enriched from their goods in their place—it is almost judged that this matter established not discipline in the order but deficiency among the people. The greater loss to the common welfare was then added: both what the force of the judgments had taken away from those condemned and what any kind of revenue had gathered through the process of confiscation had all been enclosed by the entire greatness of the princes’ property in the bosom of its own reception.

Thus, with only the principal belly filled, all the members of the entire people, emptied of their resources, languished through deficiency. Hence it happened that neither the lesser could obtain support nor the greater dignity, because while the strength of a single power occupied the greatest resources, the condition of the entire people could legally defend not even the smallest portion.

Accordingly, together with the entire palace establishment, and with the assembly of the greater and lesser men, we—all the bishops, priests, and all who serve in sacred orders—unanimously decree and desire that every accumulation of property, whether in all living and nonliving things, immovable or movable, in body or appearance, form or kind, which is found to have been increased by King Chindasvinth of glorious memory from the day on which he is known to have ascended the kingdom, in whatever manner it may have arisen, shall pass into the perpetual power of our most serene and merciful lord, Prince Reccesvinth, and be permanently assigned to his right.

It shall not be held by inheritance from a parent but possessed through royal succession, so that each person may receive what is justly owed to him, while the prince’s will may employ whatever remains for the relief of the subjects. The only exceptions are those things which the aforementioned prince Chindasvinth of divine memory is seen to have possessed before the kingdom, whether from his own property or from acquisitions made with complete justice.

In all these matters, his sons, together with our glorious lord King Reccesvinth, shall retain both free division and possession in complete peace. Likewise, all the properties which the aforesaid prince is seen to have justly granted or left to his sons or to anyone else from lawful revenues shall remain unshaken in their right.

The truth of this matter shall be preserved as follows: since the gracious will of our glorious lord King Reccesvinth decrees that what is most justly owed to each person be restored, no one shall raise a charge of seizure or demand compensation for losses, because it had been established that certain things had been unjustly taken from his father of glorious memory.

# Law issued in the same council by the glorious Prince Reccesvinth
In the name of the Lord, Flavius Reccesvinthus, king.

Earthly eminence is then shown to seek lofty things more healthfully when it is seen, through pious compassion, to benefit the welfare of those nearby; hence it commonly happens that one gains more advantage from another’s welfare than from one’s own utility. For when the welfare of many is considered, a greater sum of profit is obtained; but when one seeks private advantage for oneself, it is not enough to gain the rewards of a single benefit. Hence the welfare of those who are governed is likewise only that which does not enclose its limits within private volition, but which protects the boundaries of the whole community by a law of common prosperity.

Therefore, lest a salutary order seem to be secured by imperial words rather than by deeds, from the height of our position we incline our tranquil gaze toward the petitions of the suppliants, so that salutary compassion may derive its benefit from the place where the crowds of the people have obtained the result of their supplication. Since, then, throughout the preceding course of time the immoderate greed of rulers had readily spread itself into the despoiling of peoples, and grievous suffering had increased the assessment of their private property, at last, through the breath of heavenly regard, it was divinely inspired in us that, since we had given laws of reverence to our subjects, we should also impose upon the excesses of rulers a restraint of moderation.

Accordingly, with sincere deliberation of gentleness, for ourselves as well as for all the successors who will come after our glory, with God’s help we establish a law and promulgate a decree of lasting observance: no king, under any impulse, movement, or faction of his, shall so extort, or arrange to have extorted, documents concerning any property owed to another that anyone may be unjustly and unwillingly deprived of ownership of the property owed to him.

But if, by someone’s very willing consent, he has received anything from anyone’s property, or has gained something in return for an evident payment, the condition of the consent and of what was provided shall be recorded openly in the same document. Through this, either the ruler’s coercion or the fraud of the donor may be exposed with complete clarity. If it becomes clear that the document was exacted from an unwilling person, either the ruler’s wickedness must repent and annul what it wrongly contracted, or, certainly, after his death, the very properties must without delay be restored to the person from whom the document was exacted or to his heirs.

Those properties, however, which, with every argument of coercion excluded, have passed directly into the ruler’s power shall remain permanently in his ownership; and whatever that same ruler wishes to arrange concerning those properties shall lie within the discretion of his power.

But so that the truthfulness of the facts may strengthen the entire force of this proceeding, whenever documents concerning any properties have been drawn up in the ruler’s name, the witnesses who have subscribed to that same document shall immediately be carefully questioned by persons whom the ruler chooses, to discover whether they have learned in any way of any indication either of the ruler’s coercion or of fraud by the person who drew up the document. Thus the sequence of the document will either remain validly made or, if invalidly produced, will disappear.

The same procedure shall also be observed concerning lands, vineyards, and dependants, if any arrangement has been made merely before witnesses, without the text of a document.

Concerning all properties acquired by rulers from the time of King Suinthila up to the present, or which may thereafter be acquired, whatever a ruler may perhaps have left or may leave unregulated, since they are shown to have been acquired for the summit of the kingdom, we decree that they belong equally to the successor of the kingdom, with this power granted to him: he shall be free to do whatever he chooses with them.

But in those properties which came to that ruler either from his parents’ goods or through successions from any of his nearest relatives, the rights of inheritance shall be open to that ruler and his sons—or, if he has no sons, also to his legitimate heirs—in the same way as they are known to be open to others by law or succession.

If it becomes clear that something from the property of any parents or near relatives came into his ownership not only by succession but also by any gift or by any kind of contract, and if it happens that these things are left unregulated, the entire acquisition shall belong specifically not to the successor of the kingdom but to the sons or heirs of the person who acquired it.

For concerning those properties which that same ruler is known to have possessed before becoming king, either from his own property or from property most justly acquired, he shall have irrevocable power either to do with them whatever he wishes, or, certainly, full succession in them shall be open to his sons. If he has no sons, his legitimate heirs may enter upon the inheritance of whatever he leaves unregulated.

The provision of this law shall be observed only in the affairs of rulers, and shall remain perpetually valid, so that no one may ascend the royal throne before promising under the bond of an oath that he will fulfill this law in every respect.

But whoever is shown to have attained the heights of kingship either through rebellious crowds or through hidden machinations against public dignity shall immediately, together with all who have so impiously consented to him, be made anathema and lose the communion of Christians. He shall be struck by such a dreadful punishment that every worshipper of the divine order who presumes to communicate with him shall perish under a similar condemnation and waste away in punishment.

Moreover, if anyone from the palace administration wishes maliciously to tear apart the provisions of this law by disparaging them, or is discovered either muttering silently or openly resisting and declaring that they should at some time be annulled, he shall immediately be stripped of all associations and offices of palatine dignity, lose half of all his property, and, confined to the place assigned to him, remain excluded from the society of the entire palace. A religious person who involves himself in the same offence shall likewise suffer the loss of his property.

## LIV. Ninth Council of Toledo, of sixteen bishops, happily held in the seventh year of the reign of our most serene and clement lord Reccesvinthus, king, in the Era 693.

[Column 0433]

When, in accordance with the edict of a canonical decision, we had gathered together, with the Lord’s favor, in the city of Toledo, in the basilica of Saint Mary ever-virgin, for the holding of a council after the Kalends of November in the seventh year of the most glorious ruler Reccesvinthus, we decreed by common decision that the chapters which were not at all contained in the ancient canons should be promulgated by an equal judgment and joined to the ancient rules, where they should remain forever and be preserved with every reverence.

But since one cannot rightly judge subjects who has not first disciplined himself by the standard of justice, it seemed fitting and expedient to us first to impose a limit upon our own offences and thus correct the errors of our subjects. For the beginnings of judgments are then directed better when the life of the judges has first been ordered; and the form of judgment is fulfilled all the more properly when equity among the judges is placed before the beginnings of legal proceedings. The beginning of equity must therefore be initiated by judges, so that the perfection of law may more suitably shape the boundary of cases.

### I. That bishops shall take nothing away from Church property, and how the nearest relatives of church-founders shall exercise their care.

The whole of ecclesiastical property, just as it grants the contributor a remedy of pardon, so properly brings loss upon the fraudulent person. Therefore, no priest or minister shall take anything from Church property which the faithful have donated in any place, or attach it to his own right or to the unity of his own see.

For just as the devotion of each person gratefully offered a vow to God, so it determined that the fullness of the vows should be preserved in the place where they were offered. If the gifts are kept there, the grace of the offerer remains; but if they are frustrated, ruin threatens the defrauder.

Yet, so that greater security may be established in this matter, the worthy sons or grandsons and the more honorable relatives of the person who built or endowed the church shall be permitted to exercise this good-intentioned vigilance: if they foresee that a priest or minister is defrauding the church of any of the donated property, they shall either restrain him through an honorable admonition and agreement, or report the matter to the bishop or judge for correction.

If the bishop attempts such things, they shall make the matter known to his metropolitan; if the metropolitan does so, they shall not delay informing the king.

Those heirs themselves, however, may not assert authority over the same property as though it were their own right, introduce robbery or fraud, or presume any violence. They shall apply themselves only to salutary vigilance, so that a harmful action may not go unpunished, but a salutary recompense may be taken either as a fine or in some share.

If anyone thereafter wishes to violate these instructions, he shall restore what he wrongly seized with humiliation and shall undergo a sentence of excommunication for one year.

### II. That church-founders shall retain care of their churches as long as they live, and shall themselves choose the ministers who will serve there.

Since it is often customary for even things that are not owed to be extorted by entreaty and supplication, and in a certain sense by the force of grief, how much more ought things sought both according to the order of law and through compassionate sorrow to be granted without hindrance?

Since, therefore, it is commonly known that parish churches or holy monasteries sometimes fall into dreadful ruin through the insolence or negligence of certain bishops, so that the builders suffer greater sorrow from this than the joy which their labor had produced in constructing them, we decree with pious compassion that, for as long as the founders of those churches remain alive in this world, they shall be permitted to exercise careful concern for those places and to bear their principal responsibility. They themselves shall present suitable rectors to the bishops for ordination in those basilicas.

If they cannot perhaps find such persons, then the bishop of the place shall, with their consent, appoint those whom he has judged pleasing to God to serve in the sacred offices.

But if the bishop presumes to ordain rectors there while disregarding those founders, he shall know both that his ordination is invalid and that, to his own shame, others whom the founders themselves have chosen as worthy shall be ordained in their place.

### III. If anything is said to be given from church property as payment, the reason for the payment shall be ascertained.

If a priest or minister grants anything from the property of his church to anyone under the pretext of payment, he shall clearly set out in the text of the instrument the reason for the payment, so that it may thereby become known either that the transaction was justly concluded or that the hidden and improper fraud may appear.

Otherwise, any document subsequently drawn up concerning this matter shall have no validity.

### IV. What division shall be made between the Church and the heirs of a priest concerning acquired property.

Priests, or whoever they may be to whom the care of ecclesiastical property has been entrusted, shall arrange for instruments to be drawn up in the name of the church over which they preside for whatever they purchase during the period of their administration, if they have little or nothing of their own property. For it is not fitting that a church which received an outsider should make him rich in another’s property while he retains a defrauder in his own.

Those, however, who are known to possess an adequate amount of their own property shall, from everything they are seen to have acquired after the day of their ordination—whether no documents or some documents have been drawn up—have the acquisition divided by equal right between the church and the heirs of the deceased, after the claims of both his own property and ecclesiastical property have been balanced. If the quantity of either side has grown larger by a greater accumulation of its own property, it shall receive the larger portion in the division.

If any of the aforesaid priests or ministers, for his own advantage, friendship, payment, or in any other manner, or through the text of a document, has deserved to receive something contributed by anyone, it may not be counted among ecclesiastical properties. Whatever he wishes to do with it thereafter shall lie within his own discretion.

But if, after his death, this property should perhaps remain unregulated, the church over which he presided or in which he served shall claim it for itself in perpetuity.

### V. If a bishop establishes a monastery or enriches a parish church, what portion of church property he may contribute.

To provide for a good cause is both considered a support for the present life and understood to await the reward of eternal recompense.

Therefore, if any bishop should wish to build a monastery in his diocese and decide to enrich it from the property of the church over which he presides, he shall not give there more than a fiftieth part, so that, with this equitable moderation preserved, he may provide suitable assistance to the recipient without inflicting serious losses upon the one from whom he takes.

A church which is not organized according to monastic rules, or which he wishes to endow for his own burial, may receive there no more than a hundredth part of the revenues of the church over which he presides. This precaution must nevertheless be preserved: he shall choose only one of these two portions to be given.

### VI. That a bishop may grant the third of the ecclesiastical property owed to him to whichever church he chooses.

Since it is very well known from earlier enactments what portion of the property of parish churches is to be granted to a bishop, we have fittingly judged that it should be decreed as follows: if a bishop decides to grant the third which he knows to be owed to him from the same property by ancestral sanction, either to that church whose property it is shown to be or to another church of his choice, this shall be permitted and his decision shall possess irrevocable force.

### VII. That the heirs of a deceased priest shall not presume to enter upon his property outside the established procedure.

[Column 0437A]

The relatives of a deceased bishop shall presume to take nothing from his property without the knowledge of the metropolitan. If the person who has died was a metropolitan, his heir shall await either his successor or a council, lest, once license to enter upon an inheritance has been granted indiscriminately, a full account of Church property not be rendered or fraud not be found to have been committed. [Note: A omits *non* (“not”) before “be found.”]

If the deceased was a presbyter or deacon, his heirs may not enter upon his property without the knowledge of his bishop.

Anyone thereafter found to be a transgressor shall, for what he has entered upon without awaiting this procedure, be subjected to the penalty of the law for unlawful seizure.

### VIII. That the years concerning documents unjustly made by priests or ministers shall be reckoned after their death.

[Column 0437B]

If a priest or minister, while appearing to administer the governance of churches, is found to have made any disposition concerning Church property contrary to the most holy sanctions of the Fathers, the reckoning shall not proceed from the day on which he decreed such things by writing, but from the time when it is established that, by dying, he left such dispositions completed.

For the life of one who judges invalidly can never extend to the period of thirty years, since the status of contracts did not take its beginning from the origin of equity.

### IX. How much benefit a bishop may take from the church whose priest he has buried.

Many, while greedily longing for what they ought not to seize, either fail to fulfill the work of compassion properly or mingle improper losses with compassion itself.

Therefore, lest the work of mercy be further turned into execrable crime, we decree by common decision that, when a bishop happens to die, the bishop who comes to bury his body, after the treasures and interiors of the houses have been inventoried, may not attempt to take more than a pound of gold from the property of the deceased church, if that church was wealthy, in whatever things he wishes, excepting the ornaments of the church, and only with the grace of the offerers.

If it was poorer in property, he may lawfully take half a pound for himself. For no principle would permit even this seizure, unless antiquity, moved by consideration for the injury of the priest who had been buried, had preserved it as a custom.

Moreover, the person who made the inventory shall ensure that a brief account of the inventoried property, faithfully reported, is sent to the metropolitan. The metropolitan, however, shall presume to take absolutely nothing from the same church of the deceased, but shall provide only the care of salvation that belongs to him.

### X. On the condemnation of children proven to have been begotten by priests and ministers.

[Note: In the other manuscripts, apart from A, “up to this point” is omitted.]

Although many judgments of the Fathers have hitherto been issued concerning the incontinent conduct of the clerical order, and correction of their morals could in no way be brought into effect, they prolonged the judgment upon the offences committed to such an extent that punishment was imposed not only upon the perpetrators of crimes but also upon the offspring of the condemned.

Therefore, if from this time anyone from a bishop down to a subdeacon, while holding an ecclesiastical rank, should beget children through a detestable union either with a slave woman or with a free woman, those from whom the children are proven to have been begotten shall be condemned by canonical censure. The offspring born from such pollution shall not only never receive the inheritance of their parents, but shall also remain in perpetual servitude to the church whose priest or minister they were born to disgrace.

### XI. That bishops must grant freedom to clerical slaves.

Those who are summoned from the households of the Church by their bishops to serve in the clergy must receive the gift of freedom from them. If they become distinguished by the merits of an honorable life, only then shall they undertake higher offices. Those whom an incorrigible fault has stained with disgrace shall be bound in the chain of their condition by perpetual servitude.

### XII. That, after the death of a priest, the period of years concerning freedom granted to slaves must be reckoned.

If a priest wishes to grant freedom to the slaves of the Church, the period of years shall not be reckoned from the day on which his document was made, but from the time when it is more truly established that the person who made the document has died.

### XIII. That those born from the Church’s freedmen and from free persons shall not withdraw from the Church’s service.

We have often seen the patron Church harassed by the offences of its freedmen, and have been compelled to grieve under a twofold weariness: on the one hand, because the authority of freedom is despised through the arrogance of the one who resists; on the other, because the freedom of the arrogant is forced to relapse into the condition of servitude.

Although many sanctions of diverse constitution have already issued from the rules of the Fathers concerning this matter, we have nevertheless perceived that a further complement, suitable to the fullness of the matter, must still be added.

Therefore, just as the revered sanction of the laws has judged, the nobility of the whole class must be preserved, so that no foreign mixture may stain what its own nobility has adorned throughout. Accordingly, by a general judgment, all freedmen and freedwomen of the churches and their descendants are forbidden to enter into marriage either with free Romans or with Goths.

[Note: Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U. read *causa conjunctionis* (“for the reason of union”) for *causa connubii* (“for the reason of marriage”).]

If this should ever be found to have happened, the offspring born from such intermixture shall never deserve the right of an unwarranted dignity, nor shall it ever be released from the service of the Church whose gift is known to have earned them the benefit of freedom.

### XIV. That if the Church’s freedmen do not wish to return to it, all their property shall be assigned to the Church’s ownership.

[Note: Ae., B. R. read *quibuslibet personis ingenuis copulari* (“to be joined to any free persons”) for *aut Gothis aut Romanis ingenuis copulari* (“to be joined either to Goths or to free Romans”).]

If it happens that anyone from the Church’s freedmen or their descendants joins himself, contrary to the ancient and current rules of the Fathers, either to Goths or to free Romans, neither they nor their offspring shall be permitted to withdraw from the Church’s protection. They must either be compelled to return to the service owed to it, or, if they refuse to return, whatever their parents or they themselves have acquired from the Church or are seen to have acquired under its protection shall, at the insistence of the bishop, be restored to the control of their own Church.

### XV. On the service and discipline of the Church’s freedmen.

The Church’s freedmen and their descendants shall provide ready and sincere service to the same basilica from which they earned the grace of freedom. Just as they shall contribute to this service, according to their ability, what useful free persons provide, so likewise, in the correction of offences, they shall endure what useless free persons endure.

### XVI. That the Church’s freedmen may transfer nothing of their property into another’s ownership.

The Church’s freedmen and their descendants may not, by any transaction whatsoever, transfer into another’s ownership anything from all the property which they are known to hold by right of the Church.

If they should perhaps wish to sell any of it, they shall suitably offer it for purchase to the priest of that Church; they may dispose of the prices of those properties as they wish or retain them. For we absolutely do not permit the value of any part of their property to pass into the ownership of another party.

They shall, however, have completely open access to sell or donate whatever they wish to their own sons or relatives who have been subjected to the same Church either in service or under its protection.

### XVII. That baptized Jews shall celebrate feast days with the bishops.

Baptized Jews, wherever they may live at other times, shall nevertheless, on the principal feasts consecrated according to the sequence of the New Testament and on those days which they formerly judged, by the sanction of the Old Law, to be solemn for themselves, celebrate in cities and public assemblies with the chief priests of God. Thus both the bishop may approve their conduct and faith, and the truth may preserve them.

Anyone who violates this edict shall, as his age permits, be subjected either to scourging or to fasting.

When everything belonging to the rule of honesty had been brought together in fraternal discussion, we offered thanks to the immortal Lord alone, by whose wondrous ordering we deserved to be gathered into this assembly of holy congregation, so that our common deliberation might reveal our prosperity and an equal decision assign concord.

We beseech his abundant mercy to grant our most serene [Note: E. 4, T. 1: “most reverend”] lord and beloved in Christ, the glorious ruler Reccesvinthus, such happiness in the present life that after a long span of time he may grant him the glory of angelic blessedness; and so to make us always rejoice in his happiness that he may raise us, having received our reward, into the land of the living.

Thereafter, while most healthfully retaining the order of antiquity, after your fraternity has learned the reckoning of the feast of Easter, let it know that in the coming year it is to gather in this city, with the Lord’s favor, on the day of the Kalends of November, for the holding of a council, so that, through a similar discussion, we may either decree whatever we foresee to be appropriate or rejoice in an assembly devoted solely to peace.

This holy council was completed on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, happily in the seventh year of the reign of our most serene and clement lord Reccesvinthus, king, in the Era 693.

## LV. Tenth Council of Toledo, of twenty bishops, held on the day of the Kalends of December, in the eighth year of the glorious and most religious lord Reccesvinthus, ruler, in the Era 694.

[Column 0439]

Divine grace granted us spiritual rejoicing when it allowed us both to meet frequently for salutary discipline and to assemble for the desired pursuits of peaceful resolutions.

Therefore, having gathered both in harmony of mind and in an assembly at one place, we gave thanks to the invisible God and to the glorious lord of all things, King Reccesvinthus, by whose most sacred desire, while preserving the holy tradition of the Fathers, we were able to unite in a sacred assembly. We establish that the rules appended below, issued by a concordant decision, shall remain fixed by eternal law.

### I. On the celebration of the feast of the Lord’s Mother

Although nothing contrary to the sincerity of faith arises from diversity, and no variety tears apart the unity of catholic discipline, there is nevertheless something which, unless it is preserved by unity of time, both produces division within undivided unity and cannot remain established in the unity of the sacraments.

Hence, unless we celebrate the feast of Easter on one day, we fall into the error of the Jews. Hence, unless after the resurrection of God we await the coming of the Holy Spirit at the appointed time, both according to the defined number of days and according to the time itself, we cannot be filled with the gift of that Spirit; for if it lacks the number belonging to fullness, it may also lack the sacramental mystery.

Hence, the sacred feast of the Lord’s Nativity, on which the Word clearly came forth from the virginal womb made flesh, undoubtedly preserves the course of time and represents the moment of a particular day.

If, then, the days of the Nativity and death of this incarnate Word are held to be so fixed, without alteration, that throughout the entire world they are celebrated concordantly by every Church without variation, why should the feast of his glorious Mother not likewise be observed everywhere on the same day and honored in the same way?

For it is found in many parts of Spain that the feast of this holy Virgin is not celebrated on one day throughout the cycles of all the years. People, led astray by variations of time, are shown, while following diversity, not to possess unity of celebration.

Since, therefore, the same feast cannot fittingly be celebrated on the day when the angel is found to have announced the conception of the Word to the Virgin both in words and through miracles—for at times the days of Lent or the feast of Easter fall upon it, during which, as has been guarded by the ancient rule, it is not appropriate to celebrate anything concerning the solemnities of the saints—and since it is also not appropriate at that time to proclaim the incarnation of the Word in celebrations, when it is established that the same Word, after the death of the flesh, is raised by the glory of the resurrection, it is sanctioned by a special constitution that the day of his mother shall also be celebrated most solemnly and gloriously before the eighth day on which the Lord was born.

For equal honor requires that just as the dignity of the days following the Son’s Nativity follows upon it, so the sacred solemnity of the same number of days should follow the feast of the Mother.

For what is the feast of the Mother except the incarnation of the Word? This must surely be solemn in the same way as the Nativity of that same Word.

[Note: From Ae., T. 1, 2. A and the other witnesses read *utique debet* (“it surely must”) for *utique ita debet esse solemne* (“it surely ought thus to be solemn”).]

This does not appear to have been instituted without the example of a fitting custom, which is known to be observed in various parts of the world. For this practice is known to be maintained in many churches distant from us both in space and in land.

Therefore, so that everything doubtful may henceforth be removed, the solemnity of the Lord’s Mother shall in every respect be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, and the Nativity of her Son, our Savior, shall be solemnly observed by all on the eighth day before those same Kalends, as is customary.

### II. On not violating oaths given for the safety of the king

[Column 0442A]

The harmful pressure of frequent troubles could indeed be disregarded with the gravity appropriate to its magnitude. But because slipping frivolity easily inclines empty hearts toward precipices, honorable vigilance rightly hastens to restrain what habitual practice does not take care to avoid.

Since both certain decrees of our fathers and legal enactments have taken precautions that no one should attempt to plot anything adverse against the safety of the rulers, the people, or the fatherland, this one matter is now specifically put forward for observance: if anyone among religious persons, from a bishop down to a cleric of the lowest order or a monk, is found to have violated, with profane intent, general oaths given for the safety of the king, the people, or the fatherland, he shall immediately be deprived of his own dignity and be excluded from his position and honor.

Only this concession of mercy shall be preserved: the supreme power shall possess the right and permission to grant him either his position, or his honor, or both.

### III. That laypeople must not be permitted to command religious persons

Because this difficult matter has come to the hearing of universal reverence, we are not unjustly compelled to eradicate it by a harsher censure.

We have learned that certain bishops have so forgotten the command of the prince of the apostles—“Feed the flock that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly, not as lording it over the clergy but becoming an example to the flock”—that they often appoint as superiors over certain monasteries and parish churches either persons of their own family or participants in their favor.

In this way they provide them with dishonorable advantages, so that they may be granted either what the proper order required them to give to their own bishop or what the violence of a delegated exactor could have assigned to seize.

Accordingly, it pleases everyone that such a practice be annulled in the present and not carried out in the future. For if any bishop thereafter attempts, with the audacity of wicked presumption, to grant such profitable advantages to persons bound to him by blood relationship or favor, both what has been ordered shall be reduced to nothing and the person who appointed him shall suffer a year-long sentence of excommunication.

Whatever may perhaps have been taken away shall be restored twofold by the person who took it.

### IV. On the profession and clothing of religious widows

By the Spirit of God we can rightly say with the holy apostle that we are not ignorant of Satan’s devices, since we are driven to burn with zeal for the house of God.

We see that the destructive force of fraud has grown so strong in the pursuit of such deceptions that some judge the primitive constitution of the Fathers to be mocked, while others think the new intention of the judges has been deceived.

For certain widows are found concealing themselves behind various excuses to such an extent that they flatter themselves [editorial correction: *blandiantur* (“they flatter themselves”) for *blandiant*] that they are not bound by the Fathers’ complete institution of religion.

Therefore, while the ancient rules remain unshaken, this is added by the oracle of a new sanction: a widow who wishes to undertake the profession of holy religion shall make to the priest or minister either to whom she has come or who has come to her a written profession marked by her sign or subscription. It shall declare that she wishes to observe continence and embrace the religious life, and to preserve this perpetually and inviolate.

Then, having received from the priest or minister suitable clothing for religious use, whether resting in a bed or remaining in any other place, she shall use it without hesitation.

The garment must not be conspicuous for a different color or a different cut, unless it is religious and above suspicion, free both from variations of color and from differences of style, so that without any suspicion of transgression it remains suitable only for the use of holy religion and appropriate to her sex as a testimony of chastity.

Moreover, so that nothing may thereafter be called into doubt, from the beginning of the religion she has undertaken she shall cover her head with a purple- or black-colored cloak. Thus, when she has placed there the sign of demonstrable holiness, where no observer’s sight can be deceived, no attempt of detestable presumption shall be ventured.

### V. On removing the excuses of widows who follow the transgression of religion

All women who are proven to have previously been clothed in religious dress shall gain nothing by any objection offered in their defense, even if they wish to conceal themselves behind various or cunning arguments of deceit. Rather, holier discipline shall hold and support them, bound by the sacred sanctions.

They shall be admonished by the authority of the priest to return voluntarily. If they refuse to return, they shall be restored to religious dress at the priest’s command, and, when returned to monasteries, shall be struck by an appropriate sentence of excommunication.

The same procedure shall also remain in force for the condemnation of those who had not received from a priest or minister any garment of religious sanctity, but who nevertheless either put on such a garment themselves or consented to be dressed in clothing which observers would believe to be religious. If they are subsequently shown, by clear indications or testimony, to have been seen wearing it before the Church, a priest, or suitable witnesses, the same rule shall apply.

All these women, whether entering religion for the first time or taking up a renewed conversion after transgression, shall, as stated above, cover their heads with a cloak and produce a written profession, committed to writing and confirmed, by which they are not thereafter permitted to fall back into the audacity of violation.

Those among all these women who are found to have placed either their intention or their clothing in transgression shall both suffer the sentence of excommunication and, after changing their clothing again, remain confined in monasteries under the hardships of severe penance until they close the final day of their lives.

### VI. Concerning those who, while still of tender age, have kept religious dress before their parents
Because up to this point the effect of lax administration has at times caused the decree of an honorable constitution to be altered, when what is held by the authority of an indissoluble sanction is thought to be capable of being dissolved without order, it is therefore fitting that whatever has arisen incidentally from uncertainty should be plainly rejected, so that henceforth nothing may remain wavering in doubt. Accordingly, if, at any age below maturity, either parent—or both parents—has given sons or daughters, whether male or female, the tonsure of religion or the clothing proper to religion, and, even if they accepted it unwillingly or unknowingly, the parents did not immediately renounce it when they saw it upon their children, but permitted those same children to retain such things either in their presence or before the church and publicly in the assembly, those children shall never thereafter be permitted to return to secular dress. Rather, once it has been established that they have at some time possessed the tonsure or religious clothing, they shall immediately be recalled to the religious way of life and clothing, and shall be compelled to serve under the perpetual strictness of this observance.

Parents, however, may have permission to dedicate their children to religion only until the children’s tenth year of age. Afterward, whether it is with the parents’ consent or by a solitary vow of their own devotion, it shall be lawful for the children to assume the religious way of life. Whoever is discovered to have committed a transgression, whether by abolishing the tonsure or by assuming secular clothing, shall receive the censure of excommunication and shall remain always attached to religion.

### VII. [Note: This seventh canon is absent from A., Ae., E. 3, U., and G. It has been taken from B. R., with the variant readings of the others, in which the following admonition is prefixed to the canon: “Therefore, we have taken care to insert below the laws of the seventh aggression, which have been consigned to oblivion, since it is evident to all that they must be observed.”] Let no one from among the priests, Levites, or the Catholic community dare to sell Christian slaves to Jews or Gentiles.

A matter of exceedingly monstrous and unspeakable conduct, brought forward as the subject of the seventh deliberation, has now come before our holy council. Many priests and Levites, who have been assigned the office of sacred ministry, devotion, and the advancement of the governance of the holy Church, prefer to imitate the crowd of wicked people rather than adhere to the commands of the holy Fathers. Thus even those who ought to redeem intend to carry out sales of people whom they know to have been redeemed by the blood of Christ, doing so in such a way that those oppressed by the ownership of their purchasers are converted to the rite of Judaism. Thus an execrable commerce takes place where, by God’s favor, a holy assembly has been ordered to be present.

For the canons of the Fathers forbade that any Jew should presume to possess marriages or servants from the Christian community; rather, marriages and servants attached to the holy faith should, with God’s favor, adhere exclusively to it, as the prophet says: “He makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house.”

Indeed, they do not even consider first what the Lord commanded through Moses, saying: “If anyone steals a person [more correctly, ‘has stolen a person’] and sells him, and is convicted, he shall surely be put to death.” And again: “If you redeem your Hebrew brother, he shall serve you for seven years, and you shall permit him to depart free”—which we undoubtedly know is fulfilled by them.

What could be worse, or more precipitous, than this? Those whom we know to be persecutors of God prefer to fulfill the commands granted to them in such a way that they remain in no respect avoided. How much more, then, is it fitting for us, who rejoice that we have been redeemed at the price of the sacred blood, to observe all the commandments?

What, therefore, does that priest or Levite, or indeed every athlete of Christ, wish to claim for himself, when he does not wish to imitate our Lord and Redeemer, according to what he himself said through the prophets:

“You priests and Levites, bring the altar of the Lord God of Israel to the place prepared for it. Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do everything diligently. Lift up the sacrifice and come into his presence, and worship the Lord in holy splendor.”

And elsewhere:

“Your perfection and your doctrine belong to your holy man, O Lord, that he may place incense in your wrath and burnt offerings upon your altar.”

And this:

“The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. He walked directing his course in peace, and turned many away from iniquity.”

David also says:

“Your priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with righteousness, and your holy ones shall rejoice. Blessing I shall bless her widow; I shall satisfy her poor with bread. Her priests shall be clothed with salvation, and her holy ones shall exult with rejoicing.”

The Lord and Savior himself also commanded this to his apostles, saying:

“Go throughout the whole world and preach the Gospel of the kingdom, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Cast out demons, cure the lame, cleanse lepers, raise the dead.”

And again:

“Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so. Amen, I say to you: he will appoint him over all his possessions.”

He also said to Peter:

“Simon Peter, if you love me, feed my sheep.”

Accordingly, the apostles, dwelling together in unity, sold their own possessions and property. They did not overthrow the souls of the believers; rather, they distributed them to each of the faithful according to need.

The blessed Peter likewise admonishes this, saying:

“Feed the flock of God that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly according to God, not for the sake of shameful gain but freely, so that when the chief Shepherd appears, you may receive the unfading crown of glory.”

Paul also says to Titus:

“Be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in faith, in charity, and in chastity, so that your progress may be manifest to all.”

For whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, we have all been given to drink of one Spirit in Christ, and he handed himself over for us, becoming accursed for us so that the blessing of Abraham might come to be in us.

James speaks as follows:

“Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself undefiled from this world.”

Let anyone who is a follower of that interminable whirlpool of testimony now say whether any of the holy apostles, or anyone from the whole crowd of believers whom the Lord called, ever sold a human being, while the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what had been lost.”

Hear also Zacchaeus saying to the Lord:

“Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.”

The apostles, and the entire company of holy martyrs and confessors, fulfilled these examples and indicated that we must fulfill them, as the apostle Paul says:

“Be imitators of me, as I too am Christ’s in all things” [I Tim. IV, 12].

With what face, and with what conscience, then, can anyone who imitates that earlier betrayer presume, after committing such wicked deeds against the Lord God, to offer libations or to receive the sacred mysteries of communion that have been granted to us for the cleansing of our sins, when the Lord says:

“It is not permitted to put it into the treasury, because it is the price of blood”?

“Corbona” [T. 1, 2: “Corban”] is the secret treasury of our hearts [T. 1: “of our sins”], in which we receive the holy body. We must especially guard ourselves against such commerce, lest our minds be defiled and we rush headlong, with the betrayer Judas and blinded hearts, into the words of the Lord:

“Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed into the hands of sinners. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

This was spoken not only concerning Judas, but concerning all who serve such commerce. They too will be condemned on the day of judgment: those who were sold through them fell into Jewish heresy, or will suffer evils even in the present age, according to the prophetic word:

“Behold, the fury of the Lord goes forth; a storm rushing forth will settle upon the head of the wicked.”

And again:

“For prophet and priest have been polluted, and in my house I have found their wickedness, says the Lord. Therefore their way shall be like slippery ground in darkness; they shall be driven and fall upon it. For I shall bring evils upon them, the year of their visitation, says the Lord.”

And through Isaiah:

“I have given my people into your hand. You showed them no mercy; you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. Descend into the dust; sit, be silent, and enter into darkness. Evil shall come upon you and you shall not know it, and calamity shall suddenly rush upon you which you will not be able to expiate.”

And again the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.”

And this:

“Beware of those who devour widows’ houses while pretending to make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.”

And again:

“Do not extort from anyone or accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages.”

For if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea.

Thus also in the Acts of the Apostles we read that the Lord said:

“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

Had Saul ascended into heaven so that the Lord might endure his persecution there? Rather, because the Lord dwells in his servants, this sentence was pronounced, as he himself says:

“Whoever despises you despises me; and whoever despises me despises him who sent me.”

And this:

“Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

He had also said earlier through the prophet:

“This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.”

And in the Gospel:

“For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?”

Behold, the householder planted a vineyard—that is, the Church—and leased it to cultivators—that is, to priests. When, therefore, the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those cultivators? “He will destroy those wicked men miserably and lease the vineyard to other cultivators who will render its fruits to him in their seasons.”

For he himself says:

“Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come.”

But if that wicked servant says in his heart, “My master is delaying his coming,” and begins to strike his fellow servants and maidservants, while eating and drinking with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know [Note: E. 4, T. 1, 2: “does not recognize”], and will send the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

If anyone attempts to do such things after this definition, let him know that he will be made an outsider to the Church and struck with punishment like Judas by both present and future judgment, since he has preferred once again to provoke the Lord to anger by the price of betrayal.

With the mercy of God assisting us, and with the religious will of the most glorious prince Reccesvinth adhering to us, now that these matters have been most fittingly bound together and joined in peace, from the innermost depths of our hearts we give glory and honor to the one eternal and immortal God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. By his gift we acknowledge that we have been granted the ability to care promptly for the condition of his Church and to arrange the laws appropriate to sacred governance. From him we ask and desire that, as the life of our most sacred prince is extended through happy days and his health remains perpetually endowed with every glory, he may also grant us to arrange the government of his Church, which we have undertaken, with equity, to govern it with vigilance, and to preserve it in peace, so that after enduring the dangers of this world we may be able to reach the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.
