### Decree [Note: This decree is absent from B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, [Col. 0448D] U., and G. In Ae. it is entered not here but at the end of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo.] concerning Bishop Potamius, issued at the same council

We might have taken up the resonant flute of song in fraternal joy, because divine mercy had summoned our assembly to the pursuit of concord, and we had come together to reject the sadness of life, since by the restoration of discipline we seemed to have renewed the rules of the Fathers. But, struck more grievously, we take up a lament instead of the cymbal and sing a funeral instead of a song. Groaning with the lamentations of Jeremiah, we say:

“The joy of our heart has been dissolved; our chorus has been turned into mourning.”

Therefore we see that woe is before us, because we see that the crown of our head has fallen, when something so noble has collapsed into the lowest place after standing at so lofty a height of sanctity.

For while we were discussing ecclesiastical rules in the peace of God, a letter of confused confession and a subscription requiring abolition was brought before our assembly. Bishop Potamius of the Church of Braga had written it concerning his own deeds and words in separate articles. When it was opened, the contents of the page that ought to be erased and the letters that ought to be abolished reported knowledge of matters that should be lamented with tears rather than words.

Then, after assembling the bishops of God alone and in secret, we had the aforesaid bishop brought before us. Addressing him with sobs, and more through our sighs than our words, we presented to him the writing that disclosed his disgrace and our confusion. He took it, read it again, and, when we asked whether the statement was the work and writing of his own hand, immediately asserted that the act was his, that the words were from his own mouth, and that the writing was the work of his own fingers, as he recognized while rereading it.

Again, invoking him under the testimony of the divine name, we earnestly adjured him that, if he had not voluntarily spoken a lie about himself or if he had narrated such things because he had been terrified by the exercise of some violence, he should report the truth. Then, in a mournful voice, with eyes wet from weeping and amid the crash of sobs, he cried out under oath by the name of the one God that he confessed these evils about himself as true and that no violence had compelled him to make this confession. He further declared that he had voluntarily abandoned the governance of his Church for nearly nine months and had shut himself up in a kind of prison to do penance for the crime he had committed.

When we learned through his faithful confession that he had defiled himself by so great a sexual offense with a woman, and although ancient paternal tradition had decreed according to the sacred rules that he should be cast down from his honor, we nevertheless, preserving the laws of mercy, did not remove from him the title of honor that he had already removed from himself by confessing his crime. Rather, by authoritative decision we decreed that he should serve perpetual penance in duties and hardships. We judged that, through the harsh and thorny solitude of penance, he might eventually reach a dwelling of refreshment more surely than if, left amid the spaciousness of his pleasures, he were cast down into eternal damnation.

Then, by the common election of all of us, we appointed the venerable Fructuosus, bishop of the Church of Dumium, to hold the reins of governance of the Church of Braga. He was to assume the government of the entire metropolitan province of Galicia, of all its bishops, peoples, and assemblies, and of all care for the souls and property of the Church of Braga; and he was to arrange and preserve everything in such a way that he would glorify our Lord through the uprightness of his work and provide us with joy over the safety of that Church.

Since it is fitting to look ahead to the future, lest some disturbance of litigation arise in a peaceful state, our vigilance has taken care to attach to this decree the sentence of the Fathers that condemns the aforesaid Bishop Potamius for his transgression.

Nor did we think it foreign to the usefulness of the Church to write this, brothers, so that you might know that whoever, while under the order of the diaconate, presbyterate, or episcopate, says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the offices just mentioned, whether he is guilty through true confession or through a false lie. For he cannot be absolved in these matters if he has declared of himself what would be punished if said of another, since anyone who becomes the cause of death to himself is a greater murderer.

Many other sentences could indeed have been attached to this decree, ordering that the aforesaid Bishop Potamius be cast out with the most severe strictness. But from among them all we preferred to set down this sentence, lest, if we repeated the entire edicts of condemnation, we might appear to be authors of the gravest vengeance.

This decree was made on the day of the Kalends of December, in the eighth year, happily, of the reign of our most glorious lord, King Reccesvinth. All the priests of the aforesaid council have firmly enacted this.

### Another decree [Note: This decree is absent from B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., and G. In Ae. it is entered at the end of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo.]

To discover what is just through vivid deliberations is proved by experience to belong to those who judge, and the fuller summit of just judgment is found thereby. Accordingly, directing both the intention of our minds and the efforts of our mouths toward the hearing of the case brought before us, a testament of the glorious-memory holy Martin, bishop of the Church of Braga, was presented to us in the assembly of the holy council directly from our glorious lord King Reccesvinth, through the illustrious man Wamba. This Martin also appears to have built the monastery of Dumium. Once the testament had been opened, what the most blessed man had decreed became clear to our examination.

When the testament had been reread in the presence of the whole assembly, we discovered that it had been sent to us by the aforesaid prince for the following reason: the holy man of glorious memory had decreed that, as kings succeeded one another in due order, the provisions of that testament should remain entrusted to them for its fulfillment.

Then the testament of Ricchimirus, bishop of the aforesaid Church of Dumium, was brought before us. He had decreed in it what should be done with his possessions in that Church, and it was to be resolved by truthful examination. When it had been read, we learned that its author had set out various conditions in it. Among them he had attempted to bind one condition with a firm restriction: he assigned that tax revenues and the prices of crops should be distributed annually to the poor without any reduction, leaving nothing, without deliberation, that could serve the uses of the Church through some act of generosity.

Then, from the voice of a party representing the Church of Dumium, it was added that the bishop Ricchimirus, when dying, had ordered every item of every kind, type, and material that he had found inside the house of that Church for domestic use at the time of his ordination—and everything that he himself had been able to have made and brought in through the work of artisans of both sexes from the Church’s households, or that he appeared to have acquired through his own provision—to be distributed to the poor. He had ordered certain things to be sold at so low a price that the sale of those goods should be considered loss rather than commerce.

It was also reported that he had emancipated certain freedmen from the households of that Church and had given them, together with other persons belonging to him, more than five hundred slaves of both sexes.

When these losses had thus become known, and because all the resources within the household had been so indiscreetly given away that nothing remained for the dignity of the Church, although no pressing necessity of the poor existed that could have justified such exact distribution under the holy law, and because it was evident that nothing had been given in exchange for those freedmen according to canonical sanction, nor was anything seen to have been left to the Church in compensation for the slaves and other goods bestowed upon those same freedmen, and because he had even transferred his own property in the name of the poor in such a way that no ecclesiastical use could derive any remedy from it, we were led, both by consideration of reason and by the decree of the paternal sanctions, to invalidate the provisions of the testament, though not in every respect, with reasonable moderation.

That is: since ecclesiastical property is recognized to have been subjected to losses of such magnitude through the damages inflicted by the aforesaid Bishop Ricchimirus, all his property that he left bound to the name of the poor shall serve the Church of Dumium in its entirety until the entire loss that it suffered in the household goods can be more clearly repaired. Once the loss has been fully restored, the provisions of the testament shall be observed as they were decreed.

As for the freedmen who were made from the households of the Church, and all the property known to have been bestowed upon them or their people in the form of slaves and other chattels, we leave everything to be arranged at the discretion of our venerable brother Fructuosus, bishop. Since the evident order of the Fathers renders these matters void, let his moderation bring this case to mercy, so that neither the paternal rule is exceeded by excessive leniency nor mercy is extinguished by severity. According to the merit of those who serve, let him either withdraw or grant the rewards of freedom and the gifts of property.

This decree was issued on the day of the Kalends of December, in the eighth year, happily, of the reign of our glorious lord King Reccesvinth.

Eugenius, unworthy metropolitan bishop of the Church of the see of Toledo, and the other priests mentioned above, write this decree of our judgment.

## THE FIFTY-SIXTH COUNCIL: THE ELEVENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, OF SEVENTEEN BISHOPS, HELD IN THE FOURTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF THE GLORIOUS PRINCE WAMBA, ON THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF NOVEMBER, IN THE ERA 723

[Col. 0451]

In the name of the holy Trinity, when the priests of the province of Carthage had gathered together in the city of Toledo, in the see of the blessed virgin Mary, mother of the Lord, in the fourth year of the most excellent and religious prince Wamba, on the seventh day before the Ides of November, there came upon us a votive occasion of joy and a day of exceedingly desired rejoicing. On it we were granted both to behold together and to mourn what tears we owed to the Lord because of the past.

For until now we had been unstable amid the filth of a declining age, because the long succession of years, deprived of the light of councils, had not so much increased vices as implanted ignorance, the mother of all errors, in idle minds. We saw how the cauldron of Babylonian confusion, once kindled, now turned away the times of councils and now entangled the priests of the Lord in loosened morals. For they followed the invitations of the purple-clad prostitute, because the discipline of ecclesiastical assemblies was absent; and there was no one to correct the factions of those who were in error, since the divine word had been banished. And because there was no command to assemble the bishops, the worse way of life grew still worse.

At last, divine clemency looked down upon us from on high and presented itself both to the needs of our age and to our salvation, preparing for our times the mind of a religious prince, at once devoted and instructed. Through the resolve of his fervent concern, the light of the councils was renewed and shone forth, and mutual charity stirred each side to correct and instruct their morals. The religious prince’s encouragement also gave us the opportunity to assemble, and discipline suitable for correction was prepared, so that we who, after the passage of eighteen years of decline, had at last deserved to be gathered into one assembly might, by a special grace, apply remedies for our illnesses.

For this number is not foreign to salvation. Thus that woman in the Gospel, bent over for eighteen years and bearing the figure of the whole human race, was restored by the Savior to her former health under the sacramental significance of this number.

Therefore, since the condition of our order had remained bent for so many years, because no definition of councils joined us and no assembly of ecclesiastical order united us, we were at last summoned by the command of the divine will and the order of the religious prince and assembled in the city of Toledo.

When we had been seated in the appropriate places in the church of the blessed virgin Mary, among the other matters arranged below in an orderly sequence of chapters, we began our discussion from no other point than the purity of our faith. Since this is always the first path of salvation for those being initiated into the blessed life, it might also become the preliminary foundation of our institutions and instructions.

Accordingly, embracing the admonitions concerning the sacred mystery of this instruction given by the holy Fathers of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—through which the false gatherings [perhaps: “assemblies”] of heretics are destroyed from their very roots and the clear splendor of the Catholic faith is made evident—we determined, by the common and mutual judgment of our minds, that we should endeavor to recite this very rule of our faith to one another individually and in turn, in simple words.

Thus, whatever the memory of reading had supplied to each of us over the course of three days concerning such questions was to be set down, as it came to mind or memory, in a simple style and with every sober brevity. Yet the account of the mystery itself was to begin purely and clearly from the beginning and then proceed to its remaining parts, containing no lines of obscurity and no rules of unusual expression. Its sole quality was to be the clear purity of its language, capable of expressing the evident meaning of its sense. In this way, the simple exchange of words would make us more practiced in understanding than instruction conveyed through condensed reading.

For it is truly fitting that the priests of God know the mystery of so great a matter in such a way that they are not carried away by the surface of words as by something unknown, but are found instructed in sound understanding; so that, especially in discussing the mystery of this holy Trinity, clarity rather than eloquence may make them discerning.

Thus, through the gift of divine grace, it came to pass that, according to the wish of our mutual decision, the promise was demonstrated in action. What the tongue of the presiding metropolitan poured forth on the first day was repeated individually and collectively by the voice of all of us on the third day.

This, then, is the tenor of our faith, which flowed forth abundantly from its beginning and shone forth gloriously when uttered by its several members:

We confess and believe that the holy and ineffable Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is naturally one God, of one substance, one nature, and likewise one majesty and power. We profess the Father to be neither begotten nor created, but unbegotten; for he derives his origin from no one, from whom the Son received birth and the Holy Spirit procession. He himself, therefore, is the fountain and origin of the whole divinity. He is also the Father of his own essence, who ineffably begot the Son from his ineffable substance; yet he did not beget anything other than what he himself is: God from God, light from light. From him, therefore, is all fatherhood in heaven and on earth.

We acknowledge also that the Son was born from the substance of the Father, without beginning, before the ages [Ae., T. 2: begotten], yet was not made, because neither has the Father ever existed without the Son, nor the Son at any time without the Father. Nevertheless, the Father is not from the Son as the Son is from the Father, because the Father did not receive generation from the Son, but the Son from the Father. The Son, therefore, is God from the Father; the Father, however, is God but not from the Son. The Father is indeed the Father of the Son, but not God from the Son; the other is the Son of the Father and God from the Father. Yet the Son is equal in every respect to God the Father, because he neither began nor ceased at any time to be born. He is also believed to be of one substance with the Father; for this reason he is called *homoousios* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father. For *homos* in Greek means “one,” while *ousia* means “substance”; joined together, the two signify “one substance.” For the Son must not be believed to have been begotten or born from nothing or from some other substance, but from the Father’s womb—that is, from his substance. The Father, therefore, is everlasting, and the Son is everlasting. But if the Father has always been, he has always had a Son to whom he was Father. For this reason we confess that the Son was born from the Father without beginning. We do not call this same Son of God, because he was begotten from the Father, a severed fragment of nature; rather, we assert that the perfect Father begot the perfect Son, without diminution and without division, because it belongs to divinity alone not to have an unequal Son.

This Son is by nature the Son of God, not by adoption. God the Father must not be believed to have begotten him either by will or by necessity, because no necessity has any place in God, nor does will precede wisdom. We believe also that the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Trinity, is one God with and equal to God the Father and the Son, of one substance and likewise of one nature. Yet he was neither begotten nor created, but proceeds from both and is the Spirit of both. This Holy Spirit is believed to be neither unbegotten nor begotten, lest, if we call him unbegotten, we should speak of two fathers, or, if begotten, appear to proclaim two sons. Nevertheless, he is called neither the Spirit of the Father alone nor of the Son alone, but simultaneously the Spirit of the Father and the Son. For he does not proceed from the Father into the Son, nor from the Son to sanctify creation; rather, he is shown to have proceeded simultaneously from both, because he is recognized as the love—or holiness—of both. This Holy Spirit, therefore, is believed to have been sent by both, just as the Son was, but is not considered inferior to the Father and the Son, just as the Son, because of the flesh he assumed, testifies that he is inferior to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This is the account handed down concerning the holy Trinity, which ought to be called and believed not “threefold” but “Trinity.” Nor can it properly be said that there is a Trinity in one God, but rather that one God is Trinity. In the relative names of the persons, the Father is referred to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to both. Although these are called three persons relatively, one nature or substance is nevertheless believed. Nor do we proclaim three substances as we do three persons, but one substance and three persons. For what the Father is, he is not in relation to himself but to the Son; and what the Son is, he is not in relation to himself but to the Father. Similarly, the Holy Spirit is related not to himself but to the Father and the Son, in that he is proclaimed the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

Likewise, when we say “God,” the term is not said in relation to something else, as “Father” is said in relation to the Son, or “Son” in relation to the Father, or “Holy Spirit” in relation to the Father and the Son; rather, “God” is said specifically in relation to himself. For even if we are questioned about each individual person, we must confess that each is God. Thus one speaks individually of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, yet there are not three Gods but one God.

Likewise, the Father is individually called almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty; yet there are not three almighty beings but one almighty, just as one light and one principle are proclaimed. Thus each person individually is confessed and believed to be fully God, while all three persons together are one God: one, undivided, and equal divinity, majesty, or power. It is neither diminished in the individual persons nor increased in the three, because each person has nothing less when individually called God, nor anything more when all three persons are declared to be one God.

This holy Trinity, therefore, which is the one true God, neither withdraws from number nor is comprehended by number. For number is discerned in the relation of the persons, but in the substance of the divinity what is numbered cannot be comprehended. Thus the three persons disclose number only in that they are related to one another, and lack number in that each is what it is in itself. For this reason we believe that what is said in the sacred writings applies to it: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number.”

Nor, because we have said that these three persons are one God, may we say that the Father is the same as the Son, or that the Son is the one who is the Father, or that the one who is the Holy Spirit is either the Father or the Son. For the Father is not himself the Son, nor is the Son himself the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit himself either the Father or the Son. Nevertheless, the Father is the same as the Son, the Son the same as the Father, and the Father and the Son the same as the Holy Spirit—that is, one God in nature.

When we say that the Father is not the same as the Son, this refers to the distinction of the persons. But when we say that the Father is the same as the Son, that the Son is the same as the Father, and that the Holy Spirit is the same as the Father and the Son, this is shown to refer to the nature or substance in which God exists, because they are one in substance. We distinguish the persons, but do not separate the divinity. We therefore acknowledge the Trinity in the distinction of the persons, and profess unity because of the nature or substance.

These three, therefore, are one in nature, not in person. Yet these three persons must not be considered separable, since none is believed ever to have existed or acted before another, after another, or without another. For they are found to be inseparable both in what they are and in what they do. We believe that there was no interval of time between the Father who generates, the Son who is generated, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds—no time in which the begetter preceded the begotten, the begotten was absent from the begetter, or the proceeding Spirit appeared later than the Father or the Son. For this reason this Trinity is both proclaimed and believed to be inseparable and undivided.

These three persons, therefore, are called such according to what the elders define [T. 1: defined], so that they may be recognized, not separated. For if we attend to what Holy Scripture says about Wisdom—“She is the splendor of eternal light”—then, just as we see splendor inseparably adhering to light, so we confess that the Son cannot be separated from the Father. Thus we neither confuse the three persons of one and inseparable nature, nor in any way proclaim them separable. Indeed, the Trinity itself has deigned to show this clearly to us, so that even in those names by which it wished the persons to be recognized individually [Ae., B. R., T. 2: all], it does not permit one to be understood without the other. For the Father is not known without the Son, nor is the Son found without the Father.

The relation expressed by the personal name itself forbids the persons to be separated: even when it does not name them together, it implies them together. No one can hear any one of these names without being compelled to understand the other as well.

Although these three are one and one is three, each person nevertheless retains his own property: the Father has eternity without birth; the Son has eternity with birth; and the Holy Spirit has procession without birth.

Of these three persons, we believe that only the person of the Son, for the redemption of the human race, assumed a true human being without sin from the holy and immaculate virgin Mary. From her he was begotten in a new order and through a new birth. It was a new order because he who was invisible in divinity was shown to be visible in the flesh. It was a new birth because her untouched virginity knew no male intercourse and, made fruitful through the Holy Spirit, supplied the material of flesh. The virgin’s childbirth can be established neither by reason nor demonstrated by example: if it can be established by reason, it is not marvelous; if by example, it will not be unique.

Nor must the Holy Spirit be believed to be the Father of the Son because Mary conceived when overshadowed by that same Holy Spirit, lest we appear to assert two fathers of the Son, which it is certainly impious to say. In this marvelous conception, when Wisdom was building a house for herself, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Yet the Word itself was not so changed and transformed into flesh that he ceased to be God who had willed to become human. Rather, the Word became flesh in such a way that there was present not only the Word of God and human flesh, but also a rational human soul. The whole is called God because of God and human because of the human being.

In this Son of God we believe there to be two natures, one divine and the other human. He united them in himself in such a way, in the one person of Christ, that neither the divinity can ever be separated from the humanity nor the humanity from the divinity. Thus perfect God and perfect human being are one Christ in the unity of person.

Yet, because we have said that there are two natures in the Son, we will not consequently claim that there are two persons in him, lest—God forbid—a quaternity appear in place of the Trinity. God the Word did not assume a human person but a human nature; in his eternal divine person he assumed the temporal substance of flesh.

Likewise, although we believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be of one substance, we do not say that the virgin Mary gave birth to the unity of this Trinity, but only to the Son, who alone assumed our nature in the unity of his person.

The incarnation of this Son of God must also be believed to have been accomplished by the whole Trinity, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable. Nevertheless, only the Son assumed the form of a servant in the singularity of his person, not in the unity of the divine nature; he assumed it in what is proper to the Son, not in what is common to the Trinity. This form was joined to him for the unity of person—that is, so that the Son of God and the son of man might be one Christ.

Likewise, this same Christ exists in these two natures and three substances: that of the Word, which is to be referred to the essence of God alone, and those of body and soul, which belong to the true human being. He therefore has in himself a twofold substance, the divinity that is his and the humanity that is ours.

Yet, in that he proceeded by birth from God the Father without beginning, he is understood to be born only, neither made nor predestined. In that, however, he was born from the virgin Mary, he must be believed to have been born, made, and predestined. Both of his generations are marvelous: from the Father before the ages he was begotten without a mother, and at the end of the ages he was generated from his mother without a father.

Yet, in that he is God, he created Mary; in that he is human, he was created by Mary. He is both the father of Mary his mother and her son.

Likewise, in that he is God, he is equal to the Father; in that he is human, he is less than the Father. He must also be believed to be both greater and less than himself. In the form of God, the Son himself is greater than himself because of the humanity he assumed, in relation to which the divinity is greater. In the form of a servant, he is less than himself—that is, in his humanity, which is regarded as less than the divinity. For just as, because of the flesh he assumed, he is regarded as less not only than the Father but also than himself, so, according to the divinity that is equal to the Father, both he and the Father are greater than the human being whom the person of the Son alone assumed.

Likewise, when it is asked whether the Son could be equal to and less than the Holy Spirit in the same way that he is believed to be at one time equal to and at another time less than the Father, we answer: according to the form of God, he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit; according to the form of a servant, he is less than both the Father and the Holy Spirit. For neither the Holy Spirit nor God the Father, but only the person of the Son, assumed flesh, through which he is believed to be less than those two persons.

This Son is believed to be inseparably distinct in person from God the Father and the Holy Spirit, but distinct from the human being by the assumed nature; likewise, he exists as one person with the human being, but in the nature or substance of divinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, the Son must be believed to have been sent not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what he himself says through the prophet: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” He is also understood to have been sent by himself, because the will and the operation of the whole Trinity are recognized as inseparable.

He who before the ages was called the Only-begotten was made, in time, the Firstborn: Only-begotten because of the substance of the divinity, Firstborn because of the nature of the flesh he assumed. In this assumed human form, according to evangelical truth, he was conceived without sin and is believed to have died without sin. He alone was made sin for us—that is, a sacrifice for our sins—and, while preserving his divinity, endured the passion itself for our transgressions. Condemned to death, he underwent true death in the flesh upon the cross; on the third day, by his own power, he was raised and rose from the tomb.

**[Note: [Col. 0457D] From the words “By this example,” a folio is missing in E. 3.]**

By this example of our Head, therefore, we confess that there will be a true resurrection of the flesh of all the dead. We do not believe that we shall rise in an airy or any other kind of flesh, as some deluded people claim, but in this flesh in which we live, stand, and move.

After completing and fulfilling the example of this holy resurrection, our same Lord and Savior, ascending, returned to the Father’s seat, from which he had never departed in his divinity. There, seated at the right hand of the Father, he is awaited at the end of the ages as judge of all the living and the dead. From there he will come with all the saints to render judgment and repay each person the due reward of his own deeds, according to what each has done while in the body, whether good or evil.

We believe that the catholic Church, purchased at the price of his blood, will reign with him forever. Within her bosom we are established, and we believe and confess one baptism for the remission of all sins. Under this faith we also truly believe in the resurrection of the dead and look forward to the joys of the age to come. This alone must we pray and request: that, when the judgment has been completed and concluded and the Son has handed the kingdom over to God the Father, he may make us participants in his kingdom, so that through this faith by which we cling to him we may reign with him without end.

This is the faith of our confession, set forth through which the doctrine of all heretics is destroyed, through which the hearts of the faithful are cleansed, and through which one also approaches God gloriously. Having, during a three-day fast, continually brought up and savored its most holy taste through repeated discussion, we proceeded to the matters that were to be decided on the following day.

## 476. I. On condemning those who mock or make a disturbance in the council

**[Note: [Col. 0458D] In the remainder, except A. and E. 3: “Lest the council be disturbed by uproar.”]**

The priests of the Lord, seated in the place of blessing, ought not to be interrupted by disorderly or indiscriminate voices, driven away by any disturbances, or agitated by vain stories or laughter. Worse still, they must not pour forth tumultuous voices in obstinate quarrels. For, as the Apostle says, if anyone thinks he is religious but does not restrain his tongue and deceives his own heart, his religion is vain. For he forfeits his worship of justice when the tumultuous crowd of those who interrupt confuses the silence of judgment, as the prophet says: “The worship of justice will be silence.”

Whatever is done in the discussions of those seated or brought forward by the accusing party must therefore be presented in language of such great gentleness that neither contentious voices disturb the hearing nor tumult weaken the strength of those judging. Whoever in the gathering of the council believes that the foregoing provisions may be violated and disturbs the council by uproar, insults, or laughter contrary to these prohibitions shall, according to the decree of divine law—“Cast out the mocker, and strife will depart with him”—be dragged away with every disgrace of confusion, withdraw from the common assembly, and undergo a sentence of excommunication for three days.

## II. The metropolitan must not cease instructing those in neighboring districts

**[Col. 0458B]**

The higher the position one occupies at the exalted summit, the more necessary it is that one surpass others in the grace of one’s merits, so that the one who presides over individuals may be individually adorned with the eminence of holiness. He must always have the sword of truth in his mouth and the effectiveness of light in his deeds, so that, according to Paul, he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it.

We must therefore carefully consider the rank of our order and the manner of governance we have undertaken, so that those who have accepted the office of preaching may not be deprived of divine reading by any cares. For the minds of certain bishops are so shut off from the grace of reading by the leisure of torpor that the silent herald cannot find what teaching he should offer to the flocks entrusted to him.

The greater must therefore always be urged not to allow those whom they protect under their governance to perish from hunger for the word of God. Thus metropolitans must watch over those in neighboring districts and all who are devoted to ecclesiastical orders; and those in neighboring districts must likewise watch over the religious communities entrusted to them, so that the ignorant may be instructed in the traditions of divine law. Each superior should continually seek out his subjects, either joyfully recognizing their progress or instructing their ignorance without arrogance.

It therefore pleased us to define the following concerning such matters, in accordance with the statutes of the Council of Toledo: they must either voluntarily undertake the necessary diligence to learn thoroughly, or be compelled by their superiors, against their will, to engage in the exercises of reading.

## III. That differing forms of worship must not be maintained within one province

Concerning those who, contrary to the Apostle’s will, are carried about by every wind of doctrine, this holy council decrees that, compelled by the authority of the metropolitan see, the bishops and rulers of the churches of each province shall maintain one and the same manner of singing that they have learned to be established in the metropolitan see. They must not allow themselves to be separated from the metropolitan see by any diversity in any order or office.

For it is just that each person should receive the rules of his instruction from the place from which he received the consecration of his honor, so that, according to the decrees of the elders, the see that is the mother of each person’s sacerdotal dignity may also be the teacher of ecclesiastical order.

Abbots may retain the offices granted to them, which they are to perform regularly according to the will of their bishop. But they may not celebrate the other public offices—that is, Vespers, Matins, or Mass—in any manner different from that of the principal church.

Whoever proves to be a violator of these decrees shall remain with the metropolitan for six months, deprived of communion and subject to the discipline of penance, so that before him he may wash away with tears the guilt of his former transgression and diligently learn the necessary rule of the offices.

Under this rule of discipline, therefore, the metropolitan must bind not only the bishops or priests of his entire province, but the other bishops as well must compel the rulers of the churches subject to them to obey these regulations.

## IV. On discord among priests

Just as everyone who loves his brother is from God, so everyone who hates his neighbor is from the devil. For it is love alone that distinguishes and proves from whom one has been born, as John says: “By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed: everyone who does not do justice is not from God, nor does he love his brother, because this is the proclamation that you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.” A little later he says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.”

Behold, the one who separates himself from fraternal fellowship is rightly shown to be a murderer. Even if he does not move his hand to kill, nevertheless, because he is harsh in forgiving, he is already regarded by God as a murderer: the other lives, while this man is already proved to be a killer.

Since the blessed Apostle Paul agrees with these commands in corresponding preaching, saying, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger, and do not give place to the devil,” reports have reached us that certain priests have allowed their discord to swell into such obstinacy that not only does the setting sun fail to recall them from anger, but even the passage of many years does not incline them toward the good of charity. In their hearts Christ, the sun of justice, has so gone down that they can scarcely return to the light of charity.

We therefore decree that, according to the definition of the ancient canon, the offerings of these and similar quarrelsome brothers are in no way to be received. Concerning the persons of those who are at discord, however, we specifically prescribe that, before true reconciliation binds them together, none of them may approach the altar of the Lord or receive the grace of holy communion. Instead, they shall compensate through penance for twice the period during which they served discord.

But if one of them, while the other shows contempt, hastens toward the satisfaction of charity, he is to be received as a peacemaker within the Church from the time when he is shown to have hastened toward reconciliation [Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: received]. Nevertheless, the foregoing sentence is preserved, so that each person must pay in penitential satisfaction twice the time he spent in anger.

## V. On restraining the excesses of priests

The life of bishops must not be disturbed by outbursts of emotion, for it is exceedingly unworthy that those who are called the throne [Note: [Col. 0460D] In the others, except A.: “thrones”] of God should be shaken by a slight impulse, and that those who ought to be the ark of justice should themselves become a seedbed of litigation and plunder.

When, therefore, will such people be irreproachable, according to the Apostle, when they not only do reprehensible things but commit things that are rather deadly and accursed? For reports have reached us concerning certain priests that, setting aside all the gravity of the sacerdotal order, they anticipate the hearing of judgment in a fury and, through the excess of a single dishonorable impulse, undertake matters for which they ought to have endured the judgments of equity.

While they flatter themselves with the height of their honor, they avoid exercising patience. Those who ought steadfastly to have preserved the position of truth suddenly change their religious purpose and, in precipitate fury, anticipate judgment. Thus, where it was fitting for them to await the hearing of judgment, they act through preemption, from which they are put to shame by their presumptions.

Such men are either to be punished equally by financial penalty and excommunication, or, with the settlement of property matters omitted, are to be cured solely through the satisfaction of penance. Those who are supported by the resources of their own property, or who are known already to have transferred their property in the name of the church over which they preside [Ae., T. 2: transferred], if either personally or through subordinates or anyone else they seize the property of others, or commit any act of presumption or killing, whether concerning fiscal property or property belonging to anyone whatsoever, must make restitution, according to the laws of the most excellent ruler, for whatever they seized or presumed upon, from their own resources. For the excess contrary to religion, by which they dishonorably appeared before judgment, they are to be punished by two weeks of excommunication.

Those, however, who both engage in such excesses and appear to possess no property must be treated with great discernment, so that they neither redeem unlawful ventures with the resources of the churches nor remain entirely exempt from punishment. For it is not just that the churches over which they preside should suffer loss on account of the wicked acts of priests, so that satisfaction for the excesses of such men should be exacted from the churches, since the Church instructs her ministers not toward litigation but toward honorable conduct.

We therefore decree concerning those who, possessing no property of their own, have committed acts of seizure against anyone or inflicted killing or any act of presumption upon any persons: they must not, through any degradation of their status, be handed over to the servitude of human beings. Rather, according to the degree of presumption shown by each offender, he shall be subjected to the laws of penance. That is, if someone is proved to have committed an act of presumption involving ten solidi, he shall be cleansed by twenty days of penitential satisfaction. Whether he has committed an excess involving a lesser or greater sum, he shall always repay it by a correspondingly doubled satisfaction of penance.

We refer the slaves of the churches who are known to have committed such excesses to be heard according to secular laws. Let this suffice concerning excess in general.

Pursuing the order of particular cases: if any bishop has defiled the wife, daughter, granddaughter, or any other female relation of a magnate by adultery through any fraud or cunning, he shall both lose the rank of his own honor and undergo a perpetual sentence of excommunication under exile and banishment. Nevertheless, toward the end of his life he is to be aided by the remedy of communion.

The same sentence shall also be deserved by those who have either intentionally committed homicide or are seen to have inflicted it—whether through killing or through any injury whatsoever—upon palace officials, noble persons, or any women or girls of higher rank. Accordingly, in accordance with the institutions of secular laws, they must either suffer retaliation, or surrender of their persons must be made, or proscription imposed upon them.

## VI. Priests may not mutilate the limbs of anyone in the households of the Church, nor judge anything deserving of death

Those who are entrusted with handling the sacraments of the Lord may not exercise judgment involving blood. Therefore such excesses must be strictly prohibited, lest, driven by impulses of indiscriminate presumption, they presume either to judge by their own sentence what deserves death or personally inflict, or order to be inflicted, any mutilation of limbs upon any persons.

If anyone, forgetful of these commands, does such a thing either against members of his own church household or against any other persons, he shall be deprived of the honor of the order he has received and held bound in a perpetual prison of condemnation. Nevertheless, communion is not to be denied him when he departs this life, because of the mercy of the Lord, who does not desire the death of the sinner but that he should turn and live.

## VII. What discernment must belong to the rulers of churches, lest through undisciplined correction they incur the charge of homicide

**[Col. 0461C]**

Since, according to the command of ancient teaching, benevolence ought to accomplish more in correcting people than severity, exhortation more than agitation, and love more than power, it has been reported to us that certain brothers, pursuing their subjects more out of the spite of hatred than from a desire for correction, suddenly inflict indiscriminate death while pretending to apply spiritual correction to them. They do this when they cast out people unheard and punish them under penance through secret judgments.

Henceforth, therefore, let it not be permitted to perverse intentions to pretend what they fabricate. Whenever any subject must be corrected, the matter must either be dealt with publicly by the priest’s discipline, or, if the rulers prefer another procedure, the nature of the crime and the measure of penance must be determined privately with the testimony of two or three spiritual brothers.

If a private judgment should determine that the offender deserves exile or confinement, the measure of penance that the priest has imposed upon the transgressor before the three brothers must be recorded by the personal signature of the one who pronounced the sentence. Thus transgressors will not, without testimony, suffer the destruction of their lives, nor will rulers be ashamed of being accused of killing anyone.

## VIII. No reward may be accepted for the divine sacraments

Whatever is granted through the bestowal of invisible grace must in no way be sold for monetary profit or any kind of reward, as the Lord says: “Freely you have received; freely give.”

Therefore, if anyone thereafter established in an ecclesiastical order voluntarily accepts any rewards or payments offered for baptizing and signing the faithful, for the bestowal of chrism, or for promotions through the ranks, then, if such a thing is perpetrated by subordinates with the knowledge of the bishop of the place, that bishop shall be subjected to excommunication for two months, because he both concealed known evils and failed to apply the necessary correction.

But if any of his subordinates, without his knowledge, believes that he may accept anything for the matters mentioned above, then, if he is a priest, he shall be punished by three months of excommunication; if a deacon, by four months. A subdeacon or cleric who serves these desires must be punished both with an appropriate beating and with the due sentence of excommunication.

## IX. What must be observed so that no one becomes a bishop through payment, and by what sentence one is to be punished if, after receiving the honor, he is discovered to have been ordained through payment

Many judgments of the Fathers have been issued concerning this matter, namely, that no one should think the priceless grace of the Holy Spirit can be acquired through gifts or presents. But, as must be said with profound sorrow, the more frequently this matter has been prohibited by decrees, the more it is known to have been repeated through new frauds. Those who strive to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit at such a price either advance the time of their ordination through a gift, or, after receiving the honor, deliver to their agents the promised reward of disgraceful profit.

Therefore, so that the opportunity for these and similar schemes may henceforth be cut off, this holy synod has decreed that, when anyone approaches the altar of the Lord to receive the episcopal dignity, he shall bind himself by an oath that, for the consecration of the honor being conferred upon him, he has not given, nor will ever arrange to give, any reward to any person. Thus either, free from this contagion, he shall receive the consecration of leadership, or, openly marked as implicated in this crime, he shall not approach the honor he sought to purchase before the Church.

Those whom it is thereafter established to have been ordained to leadership through payment are, as true simoniacs, to be separated from the Church under the prescribed laws of penance. That is, they are to be banished into exile for two years, restrained by a fitting sentence of satisfaction or excommunication, and instructed to seek and restore through tears the rank of honor they had purchased with rewards.

If worthy penitential satisfaction commends them, then, once the period of penance imposed upon them has been completed, they are to be restored not only to communion but also to their position and to all the offices of the order from which they had been separated.

## X. All bishops and rulers of churches, at the time of their ordination, must promise under surety that they will live with the utmost justice

Although everyone devoted to the sacred orders is bound by canonical regulations, it is nevertheless expedient that those whom ecclesiastical discipline advances to the ranks of promotion should pledge the vows of their promise under surety. For what one promises individually is usually feared more than what is contained within a general obligation.

Therefore this holy council has decreed that no one approaching the ecclesiastical ranks may receive the consecration of honor until, by binding himself to his agreement [E. 4, T. 1: notation], he promises that, while preserving the catholic faith with sincere devotion of heart, he must live justly and piously; that in none of his works will he contradict the canonical regulations; and that in every respect he will render the due honor and reverent obedience to each person superior to him, in accordance with the decree of the blessed Pope Leo: “Let one who knows that he has been placed over some people not be troubled that someone has been placed over him, but let him also render the obedience that he demands.”

A penalty, however, according to the custom of ecclesiastical practice, must both be inserted into the pledges of such persons and be paid by those who become transgressors.

## XI. On clarifying the ancient canon which prescribes that, if anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from a priest, he is to be expelled as a sacrilegious person
Since nothing in the divine canon ought to be confused, doubtful, or even indistinct, the canon of the First Council of Toledo was brought before our assembly for consideration. It commands that if anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from a priest, he is to be expelled as a sacrilegious person. No distinction of intentions was added there, although an unbeliever may do such a thing unbelievingly, while a believer may confidently receive what natural necessity does not allow him [Col. 0463C] to swallow.

For human weakness, weighed down at the very approach of death by an overwhelming burden of thirst, is often so oppressed that it cannot be refreshed by the intake of any food, but can scarcely be sustained by the pleasure of drinking an equal amount of liquid. We have also seen this at the death of many who, desiring as the fulfillment of their wishes the sacramental Communion as viaticum, rejected the Eucharist given to them by a priest—not because they did this through unbelief, but because, apart from drinking the Lord’s cup, they were unable to swallow the Eucharist delivered to them. Therefore, those who have done such things not through unbelief but through necessity must not be separated from the body of the Church, especially when no suspicion of erroneous faith is entertained concerning them.

It therefore seemed good to define that this should neither harm the believer nor remain unpunished in the unbeliever. Accordingly, if any believer [Col. 0463D], compelled by any unavoidable illness, rejects the Eucharist he has received, he is in no way to be subjected to ecclesiastical condemnation. Likewise, no punitive judgment shall censure those who do such things during childhood, or who, placed in any form of mental derangement, appear not to know what they have done. But whoever, whether among believers or unbelievers, casts away the Lord’s body without the unavoidable illness just mentioned: if he is a believer, let him be deprived of Communion perpetually; if an unbeliever, let him both be subjected to scourging and be sent into perpetual exile. If any one of them should afterwards lament such an offense with a fitting satisfaction of penance, it shall be lawful to restore him to his former Communion after five years.

## XII. That a penitent at the threshold of death should not be long withheld from reconciliation, and that the offering of one who dies penitent but unreconciled should be received by the Church

[Col. 0464A]

One who performs penance in the danger of death must not be kept long from the grace of reconciliation. Rather, if the danger of death is certainly pressing, then, once penance has been accepted through the laying on of hands, reconciliation must immediately be granted, lest the sick person depart from human affairs before receiving the gift of reconciliation. Thus, if death, hastened by force, should carry him away from the present life while he has been cut off [Ae.: “cut off beforehand”] from the members of the Church—though he had not yet deserved to be reconciled—the survivors might somehow seem to be afflicted with perpetual grief.

Therefore, in accordance with the decree of Pope Leo, for those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the assistance of penance and immediately thereafter reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because we can impose neither measures nor times upon the mercy of God.

But concerning those who, having received penance, depart from this life before they are reconciled: although differing prescriptions are found concerning this matter, we have nevertheless decided to follow the judgment of those who, numerous in number, have decreed more humanely regarding such persons, so that their memory may be commended in the churches and an offering dedicated for their spirits may be accepted.

## XIII. Concerning priests who appear to fall while being afflicted

[Col. 0464C]

It has rightly been established by the rules of our forefathers that those entangled in demonic or similar afflictions may not handle the sacred ministries. Accordingly, with rational agreement to this precept, we have jointly defined that none of those who are seized by demons and thrown to the ground, or who are carried away by attacks of affliction in any manner, may dare to minister at the sacred altars or intrude unexamined upon the divine sacraments.

This excludes those who, afflicted by various bodily ailments but without such forms of affliction, are demonstrably thrown to the ground. Even these, however, shall be suspended from the order and place of their office until, after the space of one year, the bishop’s discernment finds them to be free from demonic attacks.

## XIV. That those who sing to the Lord and offer sacrifice should always have appointed assistance behind them

[Col. 0464D]

Taking constant precautions against that saying of the divine oracle which is written, “Woe to the one who is alone, for when he falls he has no one to lift him up,” we must take the greatest care and guard against the possibility that, during the hours and times when the Lord is sung to or sacrifice is offered, some harmful illness or any bodily disorder may befall an individual engaged alone in the divine offices—an illness that might suddenly cause the body to collapse or confuse the mind through derangement or terror.

Therefore, to prevent such occurrences, we have deemed it necessary to establish that, wherever the availability of time, place, or clergy permits, whoever sings to God and offers sacrifice should always have behind him an assistant from the neighboring clergy, so that if, by some chance, the person who approaches to perform the offices is disturbed or thrown to the ground, he may always have at his back someone who can carry out his duties fearlessly.

## XV. Concerning the establishment of a fixed time for holding the council

After everything that has been promulgated in this council for the correction of our order had been completed, it seemed good to define that, in obedience to the institutions of our fathers, every year we should come together with devoted zeal to celebrate the council at the metropolitan see, at the time determined by the prince or the metropolitan. We must not be absent on the pretext of any demands whatsoever; rather, on the appointed day, when all the bishops of the province have assembled at the metropolitan see, the council shall be celebrated under God’s protection.

Any bishop who, except for an unavoidable cause or necessity, absents himself from the council that is to be held shall be punished by excommunication for one year. If thereafter a year passes without the council being celebrated, all the bishops of the province of Upper Carthage shall collectively remain subject to the sentence of the earlier censure—that is, if, with no power of the prince preventing them, they have not assembled to celebrate the council solely through the inclination of their own will.

## XVI. Concerning the rendering of thanks at the completion of the council

Having therefore added the final signature of our hand to these constitutions of ours, which we believe necessarily ought to be decreed, we render glory and honor to our immortal God and Lord, who has made us joyful through the assembly in which we see one another, who has opened our mouths in confession of his praise, and who has also brought the decrees of this council of ours to an honorable conclusion.

After this, we rendered thanksgiving to our religious lord and beloved prince, King Wamba, by whose command we were gathered and through whose initiative we were assembled. As a new restorer of ecclesiastical discipline in our age, he not only intends to restore the neglected order of councils, but has also established that they be celebrated at annual intervals, so that, coming together eagerly each year for the mutual correction of morals, we may, in accordance with the prophet’s prediction, bind up what has been broken among us and restore what has been cast away.

May the Lord therefore grant that same prince, in return for his desire for this sacred undertaking, to pass the course of his present life in peace and, after many years, to come to him in peace with his sins forgiven. May he thus enjoy happy times here and, blessed together with all over whom he rules, come to Christ without confusion. Since through him the crown of our order is restored for the better, may he receive the crown of the future kingdom, reigning with Christ forever and ever in the land of the living. Amen.
