# THE FIFTY-SEVENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO

Held on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the era 719, in the first year of our orthodox and most serene lord, King Ervigius

[Col. 0467]

[Col. 0467A] 487–488 When, by the glorious command of the aforesaid prince, we had been gathered into one assembly and were seated in the basilica of the holy Apostles in our appointed places, that same illustrious [Note: [Col. 0467D] In the other witnesses, except A. and U., “most merciful”] prince appeared before us, filled with humility and distinguished by the clear practice of piety. Presenting himself to our assembly as submissive and devoted, he first entrusted himself to the prayers of all the priests for their assistance. Then he offered abundant thanks to almighty God for the gathering of the entire council, because they had fulfilled the desire of his glorious command that they should be present together and had renewed themselves with the joy of seeing one another again. Then he added and addressed the entire council as follows:

“Most holy Fathers, there is no doubt that the excellent assistance of councils comes to the aid of a falling world, if what must be corrected is undertaken with dutiful zeal. Therefore, I do not think it is unknown to your fatherhood by what evils the earth is oppressed and by what blows it is struck as the days succeed one another.

“Since we are certain that the earth endures the ruin of afflictions because of contempt for the divine commandments—for the Lord says through the prophet, ‘Therefore the earth shall mourn, and everyone who dwells in it shall grow weak’—it is necessary that, because by the mouth of our Savior and Lord you are shown to be the salt of the earth, salvation should gain profit through you, through whom it receives the sacrament of regeneration. Thus, through the diligence of your definition, cleansed of every pollution and freed [Note: [Col. 0467D] E. 4, T. 1, 2: ‘liberated’] from the plague of weakness, it may be fruitful in the increase of every good.

“Now, because whatever sound reasoning permits me still to say, and whatever is suitable to be narrated to your ears, is either removed from memory by an interruption of cares or cut short by weariness with prolonged speech, behold: read through the matters of my devotion, briefly gathered and set down in this volume; having read them, examine them; having examined them, determine them in polished and decreed judgments of the headings. Thus, may the sound discernment of your definitions, pure and pleasing to God, both adorn the beginnings of our kingdom with an outpouring of justice and restrain the errors of the peoples with a worthy severity of judgment. For it is written: ‘Justice exalts a nation; sin makes peoples wretched.’”

Then, having received the volume from the glorious prince, we returned abundant thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ for so salutary an exhortation and again blessed the glorious prince. After that most serene prince had departed, we found the following matters of integrity written in the aforesaid volume [Note: [Col. 0468D] B. R., E., 4, T. 1, 2: “we discovered”]:

## In the name of the Lord, Flavius Ervigius, king, to the most holy Fathers sitting in this holy synod

[Col. 0468A]

“Behold, most reverend Fathers and honorable priests of the heavenly ministries: sincerely holding firm to the soundness of the holy faith and embracing it with genuine devotion of heart, I call upon the most powerful testimony of your fatherhood as an aid to our salvation. Since, with God’s favor, we believe that we have undertaken the kingdom for the salvation of the land and the lifting up of the peoples, may we be assisted by the counsels of your holiness.

“Although the beginnings of our elevation are not unknown to your fatherhood through an account worthy of belief—how, preceded by the clear disposition of divine judgments, I ascended the throne of kingship and received the sacred anointing of the kingdom—you will now be able to learn this more fully from the report of the documents and to make it public through the judgments of your promulgation. Just as the assembly of your holiness has discovered that the beginnings of our kingdom were divinely ordained, so may it bestow upon them the consolation of its prayers and the nourishment of its salutary counsels, so that, just as I hold the kingdom I have received with your approval, it may likewise enjoy consecration through the definitions of your blessings. In this way, the multitude of your assembled order may somehow appear as a renewal of our rule.

“And because the Lord commands in the Gospel, saying, ‘Amen, I say to you: if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatsoever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven,’ for this reason I appeal to the venerable assembly of your fatherhood with an outpouring of tears, so that through the zeal of your governance the earth may be cleansed of the pollution of wickedness.

“Rise, I beg you, rise! Untie the knots of the guilty; correct the dishonorable conduct of transgressors; exercise the discipline of zeal against the faithless; extinguish the biting attacks of the proud; assist those crushed beneath oppression; and—what is more than all these things—uproot from the foundations the plague of the Jews, which is always breaking out anew into madness. Examine also with every soundness of judgment the laws that have recently been promulgated by our glory against the faithlessness of those same Jews. Add to those laws an unshaken force of authority, and promulgate the judgments gathered together concerning the excesses of those faithless people.

“For we must take great care lest so many rules of the ancient canons, which were promulgated against their errors even with anathema, make us liable for their crimes, if, in the times of our kingdom, the structure of those same canons should pass away dissolved—especially if, God forbid, the establishment of that law should cease during the times of our serenity, by which the lord of blessed memory and our predecessor, King Sisebut, bound all his successors under the perpetual censure of a curse: any king who permitted a Christian slave to serve or wait upon a Jew.

“After this, I also bring before your God-pleasing minds for correction the matter which the command of our predecessor sanctioned by promulgated law: that anyone who failed to advance with the army on campaign, or who fled from the army, should irrevocably lose the testimony of his rank. While this institution of severity has proceeded in ordered fashion throughout the whole of Spain, it has subjected nearly half the people to perpetual disrepute. Thus, because in certain villages, territories, or districts the inhabitants of those places have been degraded by the plague of this infamy, since they possess no permission to testify, the authority of truth itself appears to have utterly perished. In this way the land is worn down by a twofold evil: it is branded by the reproachful designation of its peoples and deprived of assistance in discovering the truth.

“Therefore, although the mildness of our glory intends to temper this law, your fatherhood’s judgment most devotedly desires that those who had lost the title of their rank through it should be clothed again with the clear testimony of their former nobility. Thus our glory may neither apply its office to cruelty nor allow so harsh a command to press the land beneath the lasting yoke of infamy.

“I also generally beseech you to correct, by the judgment of your unanimity, whatever in the laws of our glory appears absurd or contrary to justice.

“As for the remaining causes and matters which are suitable to be confirmed by a new institution, write them down in titles of evident judgments [Note: [Col. 0469D] B. R., E. 4, U.: ‘formed’], so that, since the religious governors of the provinces and the leaders of the most illustrious orders throughout Spain are present, they may, after learning in advance the judgments of your promulgation while standing before you, carry them out in the broad lands entrusted to them with the unimpeded diligence of their judgments, to the extent that, being present here, they have received clear institutions from your mouth.

“I appeal collectively to all of you—to you, most holy Fathers, and to you, illustrious men of the royal court, whom our elevation has chosen to participate in this holy council—by the testimony of the divine name and by the terrifying day of future judgment, that without any acceptance of persons or favor, without any scruple of malicious contempt or zeal for subverting the truth, you examine with sound scrutiny of words whatever presents itself to your minds for hearing, and approve it with still sounder judgment. Thus, after the causes have first been considered, the integrity of your order may establish a discerning arrangement of titles.

“In this way, when love of equity has made you fervent in expediting matters, the effectiveness of your just works may also bind you eternally to God, so that, rejoicing in your good deeds, I may both gain profit in the present life and enjoy with you the everlasting joys of the heavenly dwellings.

“Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, happily in the first year of the reign of our serenity and tranquility, at our seat in Toledo.”

## In the name of the Lord, Flavius the glorious Ervigius, king

[Note: [Col. 0469D] This confirmation of the council is not found here, but at the end of the council in B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., and G.]

“A great salvation is secured for the peoples and for the kingdom of our nation if these synodal decrees of the proceedings, just as they were enacted through the pious devotion of our purpose, are likewise confirmed by the powerful and unshakable pronouncement of our law, so that what has been issued by the venerable Fathers and the illustrious senior officials of our palace, at the command of our most serene majesty and in a considered drafting of titles, may be defended from its opponents by the edict of this present law of ours.

“For this is the very definition of the canons, recorded under the following order of titles:”

## 491 I. Concerning the acknowledged and confirmed deliberation on the Holy Trinity and the prior selection of the sovereign dignity

[Col. 0470B]

In the name of our glorious lord King Ervigius, on the first day of the synod, when all the bishops and senior officials of the palace were seated, an exposition concerning the Holy Trinity was first undertaken—not one that might be revealed as defined in a novel style of writing, but one that would show itself plainly to sluggish minds in simpler words, with the reading always preceding what the following explanation would disclose.

Together believing and teaching whatever the evangelical and apostolic tradition has established, whatever the holy Synod of Nicaea has decreed, whatever the assembled council of the Fathers at Constantinople has promulgated, whatever the definition of the assembly at Ephesus has taught, and whatever the promulgation of the Council of Chalcedon has also defined, just as we have received this mystery expounded and handed down to us in the documents of many other catholic Fathers, and just as we also proclaim it in the solemn celebrations of the Mass with clear voices of confession:

“We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousios* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth.

“For us and for our salvation he came down and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became man. He suffered under Pontius Pilate and was buried; on the third day he rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

“We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets.

“In one catholic and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the forgiveness of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.”

After the peaceful efforts of these acclamations of the holy faith [Note: [Col. 0470D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U.: “expositions”], a salutary knowledge first presented itself for recognition by our minds. It bound the hearts of all with such ardor of love as that same knowledge showed itself worthy of being known beforehand in the assembly of the general council.

For the evidence of Scripture, which makes these matters known, teaches us under what peace and order the most serene prince Ervigius ascended to the height of the kingdom and received the power of ruling through the sacred anointing. In it are also recognized the penance undertaken by the preceding prince Wamba and the transfer of the honor of the kingdom to the name of this our prince.

For when Prince Wamba was held by the event of an unavoidable necessity, after undertaking the required religious observance and receiving the venerable sign of the sacred tonsure, he immediately, through a written declaration of his decision, chose this illustrious lord of ours, Ervigius, to reign after him and to be anointed with priestly blessing.

We saw and together clearly perceived, by the illuminating sight of mutual recognition, the documents of this previously mentioned sequence: namely, a record authenticated by the hand of the senior officials of the palace, before whom the preceding prince acquired both the religious observance and the venerable sign of the sacred tonsure; also the written declaration issued by that same man, in which he desired that our glorious lord Ervigius become king after him; and another document of the aforesaid man addressed to our honorable and most holy brother Julianus, bishop of the see of Toledo, in which he both hoped and instructed him to anoint the aforesaid lord of ours, Ervigius, as king with every requisite diligence and to celebrate his anointing with the utmost care.

In these documents, both the signature of that same Prince Wamba became clear to us and the entire evidence confirming those documents showed itself openly.

When all these documents had been approved and read, it seemed entirely fitting to our assembly that the confirmation of all of us should be added to the aforesaid written declarations, so that he who had been foreknown in the hidden judgments of God as destined to reign beforehand might now, in the manifest time, be consecrated by the definitions of all the priests.

Therefore, with the people’s hand released from every bond of the oath by which it had remained bound to the aforesaid man Wamba while he still held the kingdom, let it follow this sole and most serene prince Ervigius in free service and devoted obedience. Divine judgment chose him beforehand for the kingdom, the preceding prince appointed him as his successor, and, beyond this, the affection of the entire people sought him out.

Accordingly, with these matters known and foreseen, our aforesaid prince, King Ervigius, must be served under the God of heaven with pious devotion and obeyed with the readiest will. Whatever benefits his safety and whatever serves the interests of his people and of his homeland must be undertaken and pursued.

Therefore, from now on, whoever arrogantly raises his voice against his safety, incites slaughter, or seeks any opportunity whatsoever to injure him shall no longer be free from the sentence of anathema or secure from the vengeance of divine punishment.

## 493 II. Concerning those who receive penance without perceiving it

[Col. 0472A]

Often those to whom the Lord’s mercy comes to their aid even against their will appear ungrateful for the benefits of God. They abuse the grace of the giver, through which they could have attained the abolition of their crime by making good use of it. They often attack what they ought to have honored and reject from themselves, through profane arguments, the gift of grace granted to them, which they ought to have embraced with their highest desires.

For we have often seen many people who, while still in a condition of health, desired the final fruit of penance, and who then, through the extremity of illness, lost the natural capacity for speaking and understanding to such an extent that they seemed to have no concern for their salvation and were not seen to breathe after their former devotion.

Nevertheless, moved by fraternal compassion for their condition, the brotherhood accepted their needs in faith, so that the final viaticum might be granted to them and they might not appear to pass from the world without the fruit of penance.

If, perhaps through God’s regard, they should be restored to their former health, they then undertake empty guarantees and abominable objections by which they remove from themselves the venerable sign of the tonsure and cast off the religious habit. They assert with the utmost shamelessness that they are not bound by any rules of ecclesiastical discipline under this vow, because they themselves neither asked for penance nor received it while conscious.

Their brazen shamelessness and obstinate defiance would never say such things if they remembered how they came to life through the grace of holy baptism. For the life of little children, subject to original sin and judged incapable, because of their age, of discerning or desiring anything except through the pledge of the faithful, receives the sacrament of baptism. They themselves are unable to seek it through any understanding or exercise of discernment.

Therefore, just as baptism, which is received by unwitting little children without any contempt, solely through the faith of those close to them, is received, so also the gift of penance, which comes upon those who are unaware, must be observed inviolably and without any resistance by those who have received it.

If anyone, having received penance in any manner, violates this synodal institution, he shall be struck as a true transgressor by the rules of the Fathers. We do not, however, by establishing this, absolve priests so that they may dare indiscriminately and freely to extend the gift of penance to those who do not ask for it. Rather, we exclude from returning to the military belt those who, in whatever manner, have received penance.

A priest, however, who rashly grants penance to someone who neither perceives nor requests it, and who cannot prove that he was invited to do so by the exhortations of the person who received penance, whether through signs of his hands or through any other evident indications, shall be subjected to a sentence of excommunication for one year.

## 494 III. Concerning the reception of the guilty and their Communion with the Church

We have seen and lamented that some from among the guilty were received into the favor of princes while being excluded from the fellowship of the bishops. This deplorable evil arises from the fact that the license of the prince, where he more freely arranges to be absolved, binds others there, and those whom he appears to receive into his own fellowship he chooses to separate from the fellowship and peace of the Church, so that those who dine with him alone are deprived of the fellowship of the priests.

Therefore, since the remission of those who act against the king, the people, or the homeland is, according to the definitions of the ancient canons, placed solely in the power of the king, against whom they are known to have offended, from now on the fellowship of the priests shall in no way abstain from such persons. Those whom the royal power has either received into the favor of its kindness or made participants at its table, the assembly of priests and peoples must also receive into ecclesiastical fellowship, so that one whom the piety of the prince has already accepted may not be regarded as a stranger by the priests of God.

## IV. That in places where there has been no bishop, a bishop should never be ordained
[Col. 0473B] What else is it than to oppose the institutions of our forebears and tear down the decrees of the holy Fathers, except to sever the bond of the fellowship of Christ and, by the license of usurped presumption, to shatter the order of the entire Church?

Accordingly, while our venerable and most holy brother Stephen, bishop of the see of Mérida, was prosecuting the matter, a recent act of presumption presented itself for our consideration—one to be uprooted by the judgment of our whole communion in proportion to the private audacity with which it was known to have been perpetrated. For he said that he had been compelled by the violence of the ruler to establish a new episcopal ordination at the monastery of the little village of Aquis, where the venerable body of the most holy confessor Pimennius rests with due honor.

And because, through indiscriminate and excessively ready consent, he had obeyed the unjust orders of the ruler Wamba [Col. 0473C] and introduced there a new and unjust predesignation of an episcopal see, although canonical institution wholly rejects such an act, the same man, prostrating himself on the ground, sought pardon through the remedy of our instruction and asked that our judgment should determine what ought most properly to be done concerning the person who had been ordained there.

But because we knew—indeed, we all knew—that the aforesaid ruler, acting on the counsel of levity, had not only ordered that a bishop be made at the aforesaid place of Aquis, but had also determined with his customary obstinacy that he should ordain a bishop in the suburban district of Toledo, in the praetorian church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and likewise do the same in other villages and little settlements, we therefore ordered that the provisions of the canons concerning such an insolent [Col. 0473D] license of disturbance be brought forward for consideration.

The following materials, arranged in order, were then read:

First, from the Epistle of Paul, where he commands his disciple Titus to appoint bishops throughout the cities.

Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, title VIII, where, among other things, it is commanded that two bishops must not appear to be in one city.

Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, title LVI, where it says: “Bishops ought not to be ordained in villages and little settlements,” and so forth.

Likewise, from the Second Council of Africa, title V, where it says: “Let a diocese that has never had a bishop not have one.”

Bishop Felix of Selemsita [Note: [Col. 0473] B. R., E. 4: *Selemselitanus*. T. 1: *Scelemselitanus*. T. 2: *Silensitanus*.] said:

“Even if this is pleasing to your holiness, I submit that dioceses which have never had bishops should not have them, while a diocese that once had one should have its own. It is for your holiness, in accordance with this statement, to judge what ought to be done.”

Bishop Geneclius said:

“If the submission of our brother and fellow bishop Felix is acceptable, let it be confirmed by all.”

All the bishops said: “It is acceptable, it is acceptable.”

Likewise, from the Third Council of Africa, chapter XLII, where it says: “Let the people who have always been subject to a diocese not receive another bishop.”

For Bishop Epigonius said, among other things:

“I say that a people which has always been subject to a diocese and has never had its own bishop ought not to receive another ruler. Therefore, if this which I have stated pleases the entire most holy assembly, let it be confirmed.”

[Col. 0474B] Bishop Aurelius said:

“I do not oppose the submission of our brother and fellow priest; rather, I declare that I have done this and shall continue to do it.”

Likewise, from the Council of Sardica, where, among other things, it is commanded:

“Permission must not be granted indiscriminately. For if some village or small city, which is adequately served by one presbyter, suddenly wishes to have a bishop ordained for itself, so that the name and authority of a bishop may be cheapened, they must not invite a bishop from another province to ordain one for them.”

Likewise, concerning the sentence against those who perform such ordinations, or against those who are ordained contrary to these canonical institutions, from the Council of Tauritania, title II, where it says:

“It was also decided that, for perpetual discipline, the sequence of proceedings should be recorded concerning what the holy synod decreed about the bishops Octavius, Ursio, Remigius, and Treferius, who were said to have incurred a certain odium of usurpation in the ordination of priests. It appears that this much was granted to them: that, having been admonished by this authority, they should thereafter attempt to usurp nothing, since they defended themselves in this matter with the excuse that they had not previously been summoned.

“Therefore the synod judged that if anyone henceforth acts against the institutions of the forebears, he should know that the person ordained will be deprived of the honor of the priesthood, while the one who ordained him will retain no authority whatsoever either in ordinations or in councils. This sentence will prevail not only against the bishops mentioned above, but also against all who, deceived by a similar error, have carried out such ordinations.”

Applying the effect of a pious work to these exceptionally firm regulations, we determined by common definition that henceforth no episcopal see should remain in the aforesaid village of Aquis, nor should a bishop ever again be established there.

Nevertheless, Cuniuldus, who appears to have been instituted there as bishop contrary to the decrees of the forebears, will not be punished by any canonical sentence for his condemnation, because he was established and ordained there not through ambition but through the ruler’s compulsion. We therefore grant him this humane remedy: that he be transferred to another see when any bishop dies. The aforesaid place, thereafter to remain under monastic discipline, shall no longer rely on episcopal privilege, but shall be wholly subject to the rule of an abbot, as it has been until now.

[Col. 0475A] Furthermore, establishing a general edict for the future: if anyone attempts to act against these apostolic commands or these canonical prohibitions by arranging for a bishop to be chosen and made in places where there has never been a bishop, let him be anathema in the presence of almighty God. Moreover, both the one who ordains and the one who is ordained shall lose the rank of his order, because he has dared to tear down not only the decrees of the ancient Fathers but also the apostolic institutions.

## V. Concerning the most shameful practice of certain priests who do not communicate in the sacrifices they themselves have offered to God

It has been reported to us that certain priests do not receive the grace of holy communion as many times as they appear to offer sacrifices in one day. Rather, if they offer several sacrifices to God themselves on one day, they abstain from communion at all the offerings and receive the grace of holy communion only at the offering of the final sacrifice—as though they were not guilty of that true and singular sacrifice as many times as they ceased to partake of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For behold, the Apostle says: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?” If, therefore, those who eat the sacrifices are participants in the altar, it is certain that those who sacrifice but do not eat are guilty with respect to the Lord’s sacrament.

Therefore, any priest who thereafter approaches the divine altar to offer a sacrifice and abstains from communion shall know that he is excluded for one year from the very grace of communion from which he improperly deprived himself. For what sort of sacrifice will that be in which the one who sacrifices is himself not known to have participated?

Thus this must be observed in every respect: as often as the one who sacrifices immolates the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord upon the altar, so often must he present himself as a participant in the reception of Christ’s body and blood.

## VI. Concerning the authority granted to the bishop of Toledo by the general synod, so that bishops of another province may be ordained in the royal city with the ruler’s assent

It also occurred to us that this matter should be settled by mutual deliberation: in certain cities, when their own bishops die and the ordination of a successor is long delayed, considerable offense against the divine offices and harmful loss of ecclesiastical property are created.

For when the speed of messengers is obstructed by the great distances extending far and wide across the lands, it may be impossible either for the death of the bishop to become known to the royal hearing or for the ruler’s free choice of the deceased bishop’s successor to be awaited. Difficulty often arises for our order from the reporting of such matters, and for the royal authority as well, when an injurious necessity delays our consultation concerning the replacement of bishops.

Accordingly, all the bishops of Spain and Gaul [Note: [Col. 0475D] In E. 4, T. 1, and T. 2, the words “and Gaul” are absent.] agreed that, without prejudice to the privilege of each province, it should henceforth be lawful for the bishop of Toledo, in whatever provinces, to install as bishops in the existing sees those whom the royal authority has chosen and whom the judgment of the aforesaid bishop of Toledo has judged worthy, and, when bishops die, to choose their successors.

This condition shall nevertheless apply: whoever has been ordained must, within three months after the time of his ordination, go to appear before his own metropolitan, so that, instructed by his authority and discipline, he may properly hold the governance of the see entrusted to him.

If, through indolence or any form of neglect, he exceeds the limits of the appointed period and is unable to present himself before the eyes of his metropolitan, he shall know that he is excommunicated in every respect, except if he proves that he was prevented by royal command.

This formula of definition was also approved for observance concerning the other rulers of churches, just as concerning bishops.

## VII. Concerning the acceptance of the testimony of persons who lost the right to testify under the law enacted concerning the advancement of the army

[Col. 0476B]

All discipline ought to correct subjects in such a way that it does not appear to remove the hope of pardon or impose the yoke of subjugation utterly, but always applies the remedy of moderation.

And because our lord and ruler Wamba enacted that law which was recorded concerning the advance of the army, and because the gentleness of our ruler and lord Ervig has resolved to moderate it, this holy council, with our glorious and most religious ruler Ervig consenting, has deemed it necessary to define that those who lost the dignity of giving testimony under the aforesaid law may, once their former dignity has been restored, pursue the cases appropriate to lawful action.

Thus, bearing again the title customary to their nobility, they may obtain permission to testify lawfully concerning whatever past matters they wish to testify about [Col. 0476C], and they shall not be barred by any prohibition from the judges.

We add this qualification: if they wished to testify about past matters but were rejected solely because of the disrepute attached to this matter, they may now seek through their testimony what they could have sought concerning the past, provided only that it is clear that, at the time when they were summoned to give testimony concerning the past, they had not been disqualified under the provisions of the aforesaid law and bore no other criminal charge, or that those who rejected them clearly prove that thirty years had already elapsed when they were brought forward to testify.

## VIII. Concerning those who abandon their wives after a divorce

The Lord’s command is that, except on account of fornication, a wife must not be dismissed by her husband.

Therefore, whoever abandons his wife for any reason short of the aforesaid criminal fault, since he has resolved to separate what God joined together, shall remain deprived of ecclesiastical communion and alien from the assembly of all Christians until he returns to the companionship of his abandoned wife and sincerely embraces and cherishes the part of his own body according to the honorable law of marriage.

Those, however, who, after being admonished once, twice, and even three times by a priest to correct themselves, refuse to return to the dear companionship of their wives will, by their own merits, separate themselves from the office of palatine dignity. Moreover, as long as they remain in their fault, they shall lose the recognition of noble dignity, because they have handed their own flesh over to the sword of separation.

## IX. Concerning the confirmation of the laws promulgated against the wickedness of the Jews, according to the prefixed order of their titles, which are enumerated in the same canon

[Col. 0477A]

Concerning the Jews’ accursed faithlessness, we have carefully reread the laws recently issued by the glorious ruler under distinct title-headings, and we have approved their provisions with a correspondingly weighty judgment.

And because they were issued according to the judgment of proper reason and approved by synodal investigation, they shall henceforth be upheld against their offenses under an irrevocable judicial order. That is:

The law concerning the recollection of the ancient laws promulgated against the transgressions of the Jews, and concerning their renewed confirmation.

Likewise, concerning those who blaspheme the holy Trinity.

Likewise, that Jews must not withdraw themselves, their children, or their servants from the grace of baptism.

Likewise, that Jews must not celebrate Passover in their customary manner or practice circumcision of the flesh, and that they must not turn any Christian away from the faith of Christ.

Likewise, that Jews must not presume to celebrate Sabbaths or the other festivals of their rite in their customary manner.

Likewise, that every Jew must cease from work on Sundays and on the aforementioned days.

Likewise, that Jews must not judge foods according to their customary practice.

Likewise, that Jews must not contract marriages within the proximity of their blood relationship, and that they must not dare to marry without the blessing of a priest.

Likewise, that Jews, insulting our religion, must not dare to defend their sect, and that, when fleeing from the faith, they must not transfer themselves elsewhere, nor may anyone receive those who are fleeing.

Likewise, that no Christian may accept from a Jew any gift contrary to the faith of Christ.

[Col. 0477C] Likewise, that Jews must not dare to read those books which the Christian faith rejects.

Likewise, that Christian slaves must not serve or attach themselves to Jews.

Likewise, concerning the case of a Jew who declares himself to be a Christian and therefore refuses to dismiss from his service a Christian slave.

Likewise, concerning the declaration of the Jews: how each person, coming to the faith, must write down a written statement of his profession.

Likewise, concerning the conditions to which Jews must swear before those who, coming from their number to the faith, have submitted their professions.

Likewise, concerning the Christian slaves of Jews who have not revealed that they are Christians, and concerning those who disclose them.

Likewise, that Jews, having received authority from anyone, must not dare, outside the royal ordinance, to command, punish, or constrain any Christian.

Likewise, that Jewish slaves who have not yet been converted, if they hasten to the grace of Christ, must be granted freedom.

Likewise, that Jews must not, in an administrative capacity under the authority of Christian stewards and agents, dare to govern a Christian household, and concerning the penalties of those who have entrusted such arrangements to them.

Likewise, that a Jew coming from other provinces or territories belonging to the jurisdiction of our kingdom must not delay presenting himself to the bishop or priest of the place, and concerning what should altogether be observed in this matter.

Likewise, how the gathering of Jews before the bishop must take place on the appointed days.

Likewise, that whoever has a Jew serving him must not dare to retain him when the priest demands it.

Likewise, that the entire responsibility for disciplining the Jews must belong to the priests alone.

[Col. 0478A] Likewise, concerning the penalties of priests or judges who delay fulfilling the provisions of the laws established against the Jews.

Likewise, that judges must not presume to judge anything concerning the offenses of the faithless without the priests’ assent.

Likewise, that bishops are then considered free from liability for damages when their presbyters do not refer to them for correction those matters which the presbyters themselves have failed to correct.

Likewise, concerning the power of mercy preserved for rulers in the case of those who have truly converted to the faith of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0477D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, and T. 2: *reservata* (“preserved”).]

Likewise, that all bishops must deliver this book, issued concerning the errors of the Jews, to the Jews belonging to them, and must deposit their professions and conditions in the archives of the Church.

The promulgation of all these laws, as it has been approved by synodal judgment, so also by the general definition of us all, shall henceforth be enforced against their offenses.

## X. Concerning those who flee for refuge to a church

For those who seek a church because of any fear or terror, this holy council, with the consent and command alike of our most glorious lord Ervig, has defined that no one may dare to drag away those taking refuge in a church or remaining there, or inflict any injury, damage, or plunder upon those residing in the holy place.

Rather, those who seek the church shall have every right to advance thirty paces from the church doors. Within those thirty paces, the protection of each church shall be maintained throughout the entire circuit.

This condition shall nevertheless apply: those who flee to it must not in any way be concealed in houses belonging to outsiders or situated far from the church. Within the measure of these thirty paces they shall have access to advance without the shelter of external houses, so that they may fulfill the needs of nature in proper places and not be held by any necessity of circumstance, having entrusted themselves to be protected by the Lord’s enclosures.

But if anyone attempts to violate this decree, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical excommunication and shall be struck by the sentence of royal severity.

As for those who have fled for refuge to the church, if, in accordance with the institutions of the ancient canons, they have returned the required guarantees to those pursuing them, and the priest of that church has not dragged them away from the church doors, then either the priest must seek out their flight if they have escaped, or, according to the ruler’s choice, such priests must be subjected to a sentence for the damages.

## XI. Concerning worshipers of idols

[Col. 0478D]

The Lord’s commands include the following:

“You shall not make a carved image or any likeness of what is in heaven above or on earth below, or of what is in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not adore or worship them.”

Likewise:

“Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone.”

Likewise:

“A man or woman who does evil in the sight of the Lord your God and transgresses his covenant, going to serve foreign gods and adoring them—the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which I have not commanded—and this is reported to you, and after hearing it you investigate carefully and discover that it is true, and that this abomination has been committed in Israel, you shall lead the man or woman who committed this most wicked deed to the gates of your city, and they shall be overwhelmed with stones.”

Applying these commands of the Lord not for vengeance but to terrify offenders, we do not promulgate death by this sentence. Rather, we admonish worshipers of idols, venerators of stones, kindlers of torches, and those who cultivate the sacred places of springs or trees, so that they may recognize that they voluntarily subject themselves to death who appear to sacrifice to the devil.

For the devil is called by the name “Death,” as it is written concerning him: “And his name was Death.” Accordingly, every sacrilege of idolatry, or whatever it may be that is contrary to the holy faith, in which foolish people submit themselves to captivity by serving demonic cults, must be eradicated and cut down through the diligence of priests or judges when discovered.

Those who resort to such an abomination shall be restrained with beatings and, loaded with chains, handed over to their masters, provided that their masters promise under oath that they will guard them so carefully that thereafter they will not be permitted to commit such wickedness.

But if their masters do not wish to accept such guilty persons under their responsibility, they must be presented by those who restrained them before the royal presence, so that the ruler’s authority may retain free power to dispose of such people.

Their masters, however, who, after being informed of the errors of such slaves, delay punishing them, shall both undergo the sentence of excommunication and know that they have lost their rights over the slave whom they refuse to restrain.

If free persons should become entangled in these errors, they shall be struck by a perpetual sentence of excommunication and punished with harsher exile.

## XII. Concerning the fixed time at which the council ought to be celebrated

[Col. 0479C]

It has pleased this venerable council that, according to the institutions of the earlier canons, the bishops of each province shall gather every year in whatever province they are to celebrate the council on the Kalends of November.

Whoever delays coming on the aforesaid Kalends of November for the celebration of the synod shall be subject to the due excommunication.

## XIII. Conclusion of the definitions, in which thanks are returned to God and prayer is offered for the ruler

Having set forth all these synodal proceedings, which we have completed with an honorable conclusion of decrees, we attach perpetual force to them by the subscription of our hands. In them we give glory and honor to immortal [Col. 0479D] God and our Lord, by whose inspiration both the judgment of our decision prevailed and the integrity of the cases reached an honorable conclusion.

We ask the inexpressible name of his holy Trinity and the glorious majesty of his ineffable power to grant our most serene lord and most beloved ruler Ervig—by whose command we have deserved to be summoned to this assembly—the ability to rule mercifully, reign successfully, receive the fruit of mercy, obtain the reward of justice, and win the triumph of piety, so that here he may always appear as an unconquered victor over his enemies and, after the long courses of this age, may reach the kingdom of eternal [Col. 0480A] life to be crowned together with all his people, through God and Savior Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified as one God in the Trinity, forever and ever. [Note: [Col. 0479D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, and T. 2 read: *te praestante Deo . . . vivis et gloriaris* (“with you, God, granting it . . . you live and are glorified”).] Amen.

This holy council was completed on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the first and fortunate year of the reign of our most serene and most merciful lord, King Ervig; in the era 719.

When all these synodal proceedings had been decreed and completed, we have shown them the reverence due to honor and have taken care to attach to them the evident force of our authority.

Therefore, from the present day and time—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of February in the first year of our reign—no one shall dare to despise these synodal constitutions, nor shall anyone pass them over. No one shall dare to tear down the rights of these constitutions; no violator shall overturn these decrees; no unlawful actor or contemptuous person shall withdraw the force of these institutions from them.

Rather, throughout all the provinces of our kingdom, these canonical institutions, enacted in the days of our glory, shall prevail with the height of their due authority and, through the irrevocable exercise of judgment, shall be held in force in all the provinces of our kingdom according to the manner in which they have been established.

If anyone despises these institutions, let him know that he will be condemned by the sentence against the contemptuous: namely, that, according to the will of our glory, he shall depart excommunicated from our assembly and, in addition, shall lose a tenth part of his property, to be added to the treasury.

But if he possesses nothing from which he can pay the aforesaid composition, he must be flogged with fifty blows without any defamation of his person.

This law was issued in confirmation of the council at Toledo on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fortunate first year of the reign of our glory.

In the name of the Lord, I, Flavius Ervig, king, have subscribed this edict of our law, promulgated in confirmation of this council.

## Decree of our most pious and glorious ruler, King Gundemar

[Note: [Col. 0481D] This decree is absent from B. R., E. 4, T. 1, T. 2, U., and G. If it is permissible to conjecture why it is inserted here, perhaps there is no other reason than that its subject matter and teaching appear to belong to number six, or the sixth canon, of the preceding council; the same should be said of the following constitution of the Carthaginian priests.]

Flavius Gundemar, king, to our venerable Fathers, the Carthaginian priests.

Although the care of our kingdom appears to be most ready in arranging and governing the affairs of the human race, our majesty is then adorned with the more glorious renown of virtues when matters pertaining to the order of Divinity and religion are arranged with the equity of the straightest path. We know that by this our piety not only obtains the title of a long-lasting temporal empire but also acquires the glory of eternal merits.

For certain former rulers, through the delays of earlier times, took for themselves a certain license of usurpation in ecclesiastical disciplines contrary to the authority of the canons. Thus, some bishops of the province of Carthage did not hesitate, contrary to the judgment of canonical authority, to advance indiscriminately and freely into the episcopal office men of unexamined character, through certain brotherhoods and conspiracies, against the authority of the metropolitan Church, and to despise this dignity of the aforesaid Church, elevated by the throne of our empire, disturbing the truth of ecclesiastical order and abusing the authority of that see, as declared by the ancient judgment of the canons.

We shall by no means permit this to happen any longer or ever again. Rather, in accordance with the ancient authority of the synodal council, we demonstrate that the bishop of the see of the Church of Toledo possesses the honor of primacy throughout all the churches of the province of Carthage, and that among his fellow bishops he excels both in the dignity of honor and in title, in accordance with what the ancient canonical tradition has established and the old authority has permitted concerning metropolitans in each province.

Nor do we permit the province of Carthage to be divided, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, under the uncertain rule of two metropolitans, thereby giving rise to a variety of schisms through which the faith would be overturned and unity divided. Rather, just as this see is endowed with the ancient honor of its own name and with the devotion of our imperial rule, so also let it prevail in the dignity of the Church of the entire province and excel in authority.

As for what was long ago recorded by the venerable bishop Euphemius, with the subscription of his hand, in the general synod of the Council of Toledo—namely, that Toledo is the metropolitan see of the province of Carpetania—we correct the judgment arising from that ignorance, [Col. 0483B] knowing beyond doubt that the region of Carpetania is not a province but a part of the province of Carthage, as the ancient records of events also make clear.

Because it is one and the same province, we decree that, just as Baetica, Lusitania, Tarraconensis, and the other provinces belonging to the administration of our kingdom are known, according to the ancient decrees of the Fathers, to have individual metropolitans, so also the province of Carthage shall venerate one and the same metropolitan—whom the ancient synodal authority declares—and honor him as primate and supreme bishop among all his fellow provincials.

Nothing further shall be done in contempt of that same bishop, such as the proud presumption of arrogant priests has hitherto attempted.

Indeed, through this edict of our authority [Col. 0483C] we henceforth provide a rule of conduct and a law of religion and innocence. We do not thereafter permit similar things to be done by bishops through disordered license. But, through our clemency, with regard to past negligence, we both grant pardon out of consideration for piety and offer the assistance of indulgence.

Although it is a grave fault to have transgressed up to now, nevertheless a greater and inexpiable censure will bind those liable who thereafter attempt to violate this decree of ours, proceeding from the authority of the ancient Fathers, by rash presumption. If henceforth any of the Carthaginian priests despises the honor of that same Church, having obtained pardon for his offense he will undoubtedly undergo, as a disobedient person, both the sentence of degradation or ecclesiastical excommunication and the censure of our severity.

For, as we arrange such matters in the divine churches, we faithfully believe that the kingdom of our empire is governed by the divine helm, just as we, inflamed by zeal for ordered worship and justice, strive to correct these matters and intend to persevere in doing so forever.

I, Flavius Gundemar, king, have subscribed with my own hand the constitution of this edict in confirmation of the honor of the holy Church of Toledo.

I, Isidore, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Seville in the province of Baetica, when I had come to the city of Toledo for the royal reception, after learning of these constitutions, gave my assent and subscribed.

## Constitution of the Carthaginian priests in the city of Toledo before the most holy bishop of that same Church

**[Note: This constitution is absent from B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U, and G.]**

When we had assembled together for the religion and faith that we owe to Christ, it seemed good to us—so that nothing further absurd or unlawful might arise among us—to promulgate, after mutual consultation, a most just judgment, [Col. 0485A] by which the order and discipline of ecclesiastical dignity might clearly be evident among us and the harmony of fraternal peace be recognized.

Therefore, having observed that such an arrangement was necessary for the advancement of our order, by common election we decided that a judgment formed with prudent deliberation was appropriate. We acknowledge that the see of this holy Church of Toledo possesses the authority of the metropolitan name and surpasses our churches both in the power of its honor and in its merits. Its primacy, indeed, is not newly chosen by the assent of our consultation, but is declared already to have existed by the synodal judgment of the ancient Fathers, specifically in the form of the council that is recorded as having been held before Saint Montanus, bishop, in that same city.

Accordingly, celebrating our decision through the definition of an informed consultation, [Col. 0485B] we have decreed that no one henceforth among the priests of the same province shall, through empty and perverse reasoning, resist or presume to despise the primacy of this holy Church of Toledo; nor shall anyone, through obstinate zeal for schisms, advance any person to the highest ranks of the priestly insignia by removing the authority of this see from us, as has hitherto been done.

Thus we solemnly promise this Church, both on our own behalf and that of our successors, an honor of dignity such as the most blessed Fathers decreed in the statutes of the holy councils for metropolitan churches. We likewise promise faithfully to preserve the observance of this reverence, and we wish our successors throughout the limits of succeeding ages to maintain its honor with diligent care.

But whoever among us or among our successors transgresses these statutes, let him be anathema to our Lord Jesus Christ, be cast down from the priestly dignity, and be condemned by the sentence of perpetual excommunication.

This constitution of the priests was made in the city of Toledo on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the first year of the reign of the most pious and glorious King Gundemar, in the era 648.

Protogenes, bishop of the holy Church of Segontia, subscribed this profession of our decree for its confirmation.
