## Petition of your servant Sesuldus

I bring my lowliness to the memory of your holiness, and I earnestly petition that you often command prayers for the lowliness of your servant. Furthermore, I bring to the attention of your holiness the following: your servants, through your humble lord Emilanus, agreed that, by the will of God and of yourself, he should exercise the priesthood in your Church. Since no one of such standing, or better, is found in that diocese, they sent their petitions to the lord on his behalf, so that, if God grants the lord an opportunity, you may order him to come, in order that through your hands this matter may be completed, as well as another matter that is still pending, and that we, desiring this from the lord, may be made joyful by your countenance.

If, however, your foresight has determined otherwise, direct your ordination to whomever you wish, so that he may complete your purpose and your order remain unharmed.

## Another petition of your own servant Sunilanus

We bring to the attention of your holiness that, by God’s choice, all your priests and all the sons of the Church, assembling together, asked me through your humble lord Emilanus that, by the ordination of God and of yourself, he be appointed bishop in the Church of the city of Mentesa.

Since humility adorns him together with holiness, and his lineage makes him illustrious, your little client petitions that, if God grants your blessedness an opportunity to restore your churches, you not disdain to come even to your most humble servants, so that the election of your servants may be completed by your sacred hands.

If, however, some circumstance of the world should befall your excellence, order whomever you command among your brothers to write, so that he may fulfill your orders and your Church may no longer remain in desolation.

Thus may your excellence receive the grace of Christ without end.

## Another petition of Ermegildus to John and his servants

[Col. 0486D]

Through Sesuldus, your blessedness was informed on behalf of your humble lord Emilanus that, if it should be pleasing to God and to the lord, he be appointed bishop in the ecclesiastical order. We, your servants, likewise petition that, if God grants the lord an opportunity, you may order that he be admitted to this dignity here, so that it may be completed through your hands.

But if—which God forbid—some worldly circumstance should befall the lord, we petition that your holiness make known to your lord whom you wish, so that your person may complete the election of your servants. Thus may you receive the reward of eternal life.

# LVIII. The Thirteenth Council of Toledo

**Era 721, in the fourth year of the reign of the most excellent prince Ervig**

**[Col. 0487] [Note: This council is absent from A. and E. 3. It has been taken from Codex B. R., with the variant readings of the other witnesses.]**

[Col. 0487A] Having been brought together by the impulse of unblemished charity, restored to one another by the sight of our faces, and, with God’s favor, assembled together in one company—namely, in the Church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul—in the fourth year of the reign of the serene prince Ervig, on the day before the Nones of November, in the era 721, when each of us had taken his appointed seat, that same prince appeared, supported by the full ardor of faith and adorned with the grace of humility.

Commending to the synodal assembly the wishes of his deliberation, and asking that they pray for him most earnestly to the Lord, he addressed the council at sufficient length, exhorting it especially to sanction through the clarity of its deliberations those matters that accord with ecclesiastical discipline and those suitable for correcting morals.

Then he entrusted to the synodal assembly, for confirmation, the religious wishes of his clemency by which he had determined that the miserable should be aided. He offered the holy bishops a document, entreating and imploring them together that whatever more elegantly had been gathered there through the sprinkling of the pen should be arranged under the authority of the synod according to the order of headings.

Then, having received the document from the prince, we gave glory to God and blessed the same glorious prince. After that prince had completed the presentation of his wishes, he departed graciously from the council’s assembly. After the ruler’s departure, we found the following written in the binding of that document.

## In the name of the Lord, Flavius Ervig, king, to the most holy Fathers seated in this holy synod

[Col. 0487C] Behold, most holy bishops, to be honored for your religious piety, and most diligent followers of divine worship: before the reverence of your assembly I prostrate myself, humble and devoted; I stand bowed before you, ready to assent. First I offer abundant thanks to the Father of lights for the gathering of your assembly; then I commit the concerns of my wishes to be settled by your judgments.

For it is not lawful for anyone, even when the undertaking is good, to act without counsel, since it is greatly beneficial to have done good things with the counsel of good men. Therefore, to conclude my wishes in a brief exhortation—wishes in which I delight to exercise remedies of piety—I disclose them for recognition to the understanding of your fatherhoods.

Yet, lest they escape the memory through some forgetfulness, and lest an interval withdraw them from the proper report of my concerns, receive them recorded in the folding of this document.

First, I ought to make known to you my desire to spare the miserable: we are attempting to restore to the embrace of our fellowship that part of our body which was torn away through tyranny. For you know well what sentence of vengeance was imposed in the time of blessed memory, under our predecessor King Wamba, upon those who profaned their country and, together with a certain Paul, assumed tyranny; by the universal edict of judgment they lost their testimony and were deprived of their property. We have resolved to receive these men into the fellowship of our society and to restore to them the property that may lawfully be restored.

We also wish to establish a limit concerning accused persons, by the most just investigation—[Note: [Col. 0488D] Ae., E. 4, T. 1, 2, *perquisitionis*, “inquiry.”]—so that, whether religious or lay, no one driven forward by the zeal of some accusation is suppressed by hidden frauds or violence, nor violently compelled to give a deposition, but is judged in the common examination of all. According to the tenor of his public deposition, he shall either suffer the due penalties of condemnation if found culpable, or, if innocent, be shown to be so when the judgment of all has confirmed his innocence.

For what shall I now say concerning the exactions of fiscal taxes, whose arrears have grown into such great accumulations of debt [Col. 0488B] that, if they are ordered to be exacted in full, the condition of the peoples will be utterly overthrown and, in the crash of their destruction, the earth itself will feel the final ruin of its own collapse?

Therefore, desiring our glory to bestow abundant remedies of clemency upon such persons—both private and fiscal servants—our gentleness has released them from all tax exactions that remain outstanding from former times up to the first year of our highness, and has established by the writing of our own authority that these exactions are to be remitted to them. Our clemency has also chosen that these acts of authority be reread to your holy assembly.

I shall add one further matter. It is always horrifying to our wishes and detestable to our minds when the condition of freedmen or even slaves is made equal to nobility and thereby degrades the standing of our people. Therefore it pleases the minds of our glory that, except for fiscal slaves or freedmen, once the license of this evil presumption has been removed, no one from the servile condition—whether slave or freedman—shall thereafter pass into palace offices.

If anyone does so, let him know without doubt that he must be returned to serve the person from whom he took the origin of his condition or received the title of his freedom.

Having presented these explanations of my wishes, I ask that you extend the strong assistance of your fatherhoods. For it is clearer than daylight that whatever the sacred assembly of bishops decrees must be observed and, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, remain established for all eternity.

Therefore I appeal and earnestly implore the whole body of your fatherhoods, together with the nobility of the eminent men who have been selected from the service of the royal court to sit with you in this holy synod. By that ineffable sacrament of the Holy Trinity I adjure you to ensure that whatever is brought before you for judgment or reconsideration—both what has been said by us and whatever else is introduced for your hearing—you settle with the full force of justice tempered by mercy.

[Col. 0489A] Thus, with the judgment of your entire unanimity subject in every respect to the rules of the preceding Fathers, may it proceed from no other source than that of truth. In this way, may you promptly apply the solid authority of deliberation to the matters already mentioned, and discuss the other matters still necessary for carrying out the disciplines of ecclesiastical rule and for settling disputes; and may you record what has been settled with more religious diligence.

Then, while you scatter salutary teaching among the peoples, may you gain Christ the Lord as the reward of justice. Thus, while you preach and we fulfill what is pleasing in the divine eyes, may both parties receive in this age ineffable joy from the profit of souls, and in the future an unshaken reward from attaining eternity. [Note: T. 1, 2: *proventione*, “attainment” or “acquisition,” instead of *perventione*.]

Given on the day before the Nones of November, in the fourth year of the reign of our glory, happily, in the name of God, at Toledo.

After the necessary introduction of the institutions of the document placed before us had been read, the beginning of our discourse first concerned the faith of the Holy Trinity. We jointly professed and believed those things that the Gospels hand down and the apostolic decrees establish concerning this Holy Trinity, just as the Council of Nicaea explained this sacrament of piety, just as the definition of Constantinople sanctioned it, and as the evident teaching of the first council of Ephesus and of Chalcedon established it, in accordance with the elaborated profession of the holy Creed, which is proclaimed openly by the voice of all the faithful during the solemnities of the Mass.

## Creed of the Council of Nicaea

[Col. 0489C] We believe in one God, the Father almighty, etc.

After arranging the structure of this holy faith, we built the framework of the other matters that followed upon it as upon a most solid rock, so that they might endure with the same unshakable firmness with which they had been built perpetually upon the foundation of the true faith.

Accordingly, we have issued by common agreement these judgments that, at the prince’s urging, we received for enactment; and we decree that they must be observed with the eternal force of reverence.

## I. On restoring the testimony of dignity to those whom the profanation of infidelity drew, together with Paul, into the fellowship of tyranny

It is always a praiseworthy sign to engage in matters that begin from piety and are tempered through the very heart of piety. For, as the Apostle says, piety is useful for all things. By the admirable gift of this virtue, the heart of our glorious and most religious prince, kindled with divine fire, decreed and chose that all the bishops of Spain, gathered into one assembly, should determine those measures that would remove the burdens of oppression and abundantly provide help for the fallen.

At the beginning of these proceedings, therefore, with our most religious lord King Ervig urging and commanding it, it came before us to decree that all whom the once-criminal conspiracy of Paul drew into treachery against the people and the fatherland, and stripped of the status of honorable legal standing, should be restored to their former state of dignity. Henceforth no judicial chain should impede them on this account; rather, all should assume the honor of their noble stock and their own nobility, without bearing any disgrace from their former infidelity.

We decree that this same rule be observed concerning their sons who are reported to have been born after their parents committed the aforementioned crime of profanation, and likewise concerning all others who, from the time of King Chintila, of blessed memory, down to the present have been stained with a similar mark of infamy.

Since it is useless to free someone from servitude while he is oppressed by dispossession, the clemency of our exalted prince also ordered this to be added: that our assembled body should define the means by which those restored to the testimony of dignity might be suitably supported by resources.

Therefore, forming a judgment consonant with his wishes, we have chosen that whatever of their property was neither granted to anyone nor given as a stipend, but merely applied to the rights of the fisc, each person should without hesitation receive back by royal authority whatever had been his own, and should dispose of what he had recovered according to the freedom of his own judgment.

But whatever from their goods was granted to anyone by royal generosity or given as a stipend shall remain permanently under the right of those to whom it was granted.

If anyone therefore chooses to alter this judgment of piety, which we formed at the direction of the aforesaid glorious prince, and attempts to overthrow so great a structure of mercy, let him be anathema by the judgment of almighty God.

## II. Concerning accused priests, palace magnates, and *gardingui*, and the safeguards of justice under which they ought to be examined

[Col. 0490C] In the course of our second consultation, a matter arose before our assembly that was worthy of tears and must be driven away by the weight of synodal judgment in proportion to the immense slaughter and ruin it has brought upon the peoples.

For in the passage of former times we have seen—and mourned—the fall of many from the office of the palace order. Violent depositions cast them down from honor, and the judicial action of royal factions subjected them either to death or perpetual disgrace.

Desiring to abolish this intolerable evil and dreadful act of impiety, the mind of our religious prince introduced it for reconsideration by the general judgment of all the bishops and established that it should be restrained by the authority of avenging synodal power.

Therefore, decreeing a judgment appropriate to his devotion, we have established this in common: henceforth no one from the rank of the palace order or from the assembly of the holy religion shall, through royal cunning, the prompting of profane power, or the opposition of the malicious will of any persons, be removed from the honor of his order or from service in the royal household without a clear and evident indication of his guilt.

He shall not previously be bound with chains, subjected to interrogation, tormented by any kind of torture or scourging, deprived of his property, committed to prison custody, or dismissed by the use of unjust pretexts on either side, thereby extracting from him a forced, secret, or fraudulent deposition.

Rather, the accused person, retaining his rank and having first experienced nothing harmful from the chapters mentioned above, shall be brought before the public examination of priests, elders, and also *gardingui*, and shall be investigated with the utmost justice. If found liable, he shall suffer the legal penalties for the fault discovered; if innocent, he shall appear to be so when the judgment of all has confirmed him innocent.

Those, however, who are known to remain in places from which suspicion of harmful refuge may arise, or those whom it is more necessary to guard because of disturbance in the land, must remain under free custody, without any harm from bonds or injury. Nevertheless, with every terror removed, they must be kept under watchful and diligent custody, so that the time when they ought to be judged may in no way be fraudulently delayed, causing them to appear to have given their deposition unwillingly after being separated for a very long time from their wives, relatives, and property.

Even if such a deposition should be given—[Note: Ae., E. 4, T. 1, 2 add *et si*, “and if”]—it shall have no force at all. Instead, in accordance with the preceding order, only that shall be accepted as true which is shown by general judgment to have proceeded from his mouth.

The same procedure shall also be observed concerning the persons of other freeborn men who have not been attached to palace offices but nevertheless appear to bear the title of freeborn dignity. Even if they are beaten by the prince with blows of the whip for minor offenses, as commonly happens, they shall not on that account lose their testimony or be deprived of the property due to them.

If anything concerning the crime of infidelity is brought against them, they shall be judged according to the same procedure set forth above.

If any king henceforth rashly neglects to observe this synodal decree—which, as we trust, has been promulgated by the divine Spirit—or maliciously chooses to bypass it, so that any person among those specified is condemned otherwise than has been stated, or is killed through the cunning of accumulated malice, or, after being deposed, is deprived of the place of his order, let that king, together with all who willingly consented to him, be avenged by perpetual anathema in the sight of God the almighty Father, his only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, and let him be consigned to be burned in divine or eternal fires.

Moreover, whatever is done against this rule of our judgment concerning any person, or whatever is adjudged concerning the property of an accused person, shall have no force, so that the person judged otherwise than we decree may neither lose the dignity of his testimony nor be deprived of the profit of his own property.

By saying these and similar things, we do not remove from princes the power of domestic correction. For, specifically concerning those laymen whom the guilt of infidelity does not bind, but who are found either sluggish in the duty of their service or troublesome in the actions entrusted to them—[Note: E. 4: *mendaces*, “liars,” instead of *mordaces*, “troublesome”]—or rather negligent, it shall be lawful for the prince to correct such persons without any disgrace to them, damage to their property, or alteration of their service, and to replace them in the duties entrusted to them with others whom he prefers.

## III. On the prince’s remission of taxes among the people

The royal generosity, spread far and wide, came before our assembly for recognition in the course of this glorious third matter brought to our attention. Just as it proceeded from the pure spring of royal provision, so it ought to be confirmed by the sanction of the synod.

Therefore, the concern of our religious prince King Ervig, extending everywhere throughout the whole circumference of his people, advancing in a manner from virtue to virtue and ascending, as it were, by steps toward better things, decreed through the authority of royal writing that every tax from previous years up to the first year of his reign, which remains outstanding among private or fiscal populations, should be released under the sanction of perpetual remission.

He ordered only those amounts from these taxes to be presented to the public treasuries that were shown to have been collected but not paid in.

Admiring this benefit of piety, we not only add our force to his glorious definition, but also decree that whoever acts against it shall be subjected to perpetual excommunication.

## IV. On securing the king’s offspring

[Col. 0492B]

The glorious actions of the preceding day, through which the royal piety showed itself exceptional by the annotation of three chapters, compel the reverence of our assembly to promulgate something capable both of returning a beneficent favor to royal piety and of benefiting the royal offspring in the future.

For salutary foresight is always useful; indeed, whatever pertains to true salvation is always useful. Therefore, moved by pious solicitude, we have chosen to promulgate a decree of defense for the royal offspring and to extend protection into the future, since we have been unable to repay his paternal benefactions with equivalent gifts.

Concerning our prince King Ervig, whose provisionally peaceful rule governs us, whose affection cherishes us, and whose rewards we enjoy, it is fitting that we define this. He restored the lost honor of freedom to those who had profaned it; he decreed the manner in which the accused should be examined with the utmost justice; and he preserved the land of his own people unharmed by the enemy and raised it through the remission of many taxes.

Therefore, since we perceive so many benefits that he has bestowed upon the peoples of his nation, it is right that we extend at least to his children strong aids of protection for the future.

We therefore charge all priests and princes, present and absent, and those who will follow in future times, as well as persons of every honor or order, before God and his holy angels, that no one seek unjust opportunities to harm his descendants or his glorious wife, Queen Liuvigoto, nor those who are known to be joined to the sons or daughters of his glory, nor those who are not yet joined to them but are soon to be joined.

Let no one, secretly or publicly, direct against them malicious designs by which they might be cast down. Let no one kill them with a sword or by any harmful conspiracy. Let no one offer counsel or action by which they might be unjustly deposed or stripped of their possessions. Let no one unjustly impose upon them the violent mark of tonsure. Let no one presume to alter the clothing of his glorious wife, his daughters, or his daughters-in-law contrary to custom. Let no one, apart from evident evidence of guilt, cause them to be banished into exile or inflict upon their bodies any mutilation or injury from scourging.

Thus, together with all those mentioned above, may none of his glorious posterity throughout the future suffer an unjust mark of injury or experience loss of property.

But if any person, whatever his order or honor, refusing to accept this judgment of ours, should at any time attack or choose to overthrow the sons or daughters of his glory, together with his serene wife Queen Liuvigoto or all those mentioned above, without a just cause belonging to their own case; or should, by his own decision, consent that they be unjustly stripped of property due to them or overthrown by any deceit or contrivance, let him be avenged by eternal anathema and condemned by the judgment of the future tribunal.

## V. That after the prince’s death no one dare take his surviving wife in marriage or join himself to her in adultery

It is an execrable crime and a work of utterly habitual iniquity, after kings have died, to seek the royal bed of their surviving wife and defile it with horrifying stains of pollution.

For which Christian could endure calmly that the wife of a deceased king should afterward enter another marriage or be subjected to the lust of a succeeding prince, so that she who was mistress of the people should afterward become a prostitute of disgrace, and she who had been joined to the royal dignity through royal beds should be cast away as disgraced by the adulteries or marriages of those whom she had once ruled?

What, then, if princes die? Do they leave behind parts of their bodies that must be dishonored? Or because Christian kings pass to heavenly joys, are their wives therefore to be delivered over to insult in this world?

Therefore, what is fittingly to be held in honor must never be dishonored. No one, then, shall be permitted to take a surviving queen in marriage or defile her through disgraceful arrangements. This shall not be lawful for succeeding kings, nor shall it be permitted to any human being.

If anyone should presume to do such a thing—whether by joining the surviving queen to himself in marriage after the death of the departed prince or by contaminating her with adulterous pollution—whether he be a king or any other person who presumes to violate the judgment of this sanction, let him be excluded from the fellowship of all Christians and handed over to be burned in sulfurous fires with the devil.

Therefore, whoever presumes to tear away or erase the sanction of this institution of ours, let his name be erased and blotted out from the book of life, so that he may suffer the infernal penalties of judgment, since he has devoted these decrees of decency to violation.

## VI. That, except for fiscal slaves or freedmen, no one from any servile condition or among freedmen may henceforth at any time enter palace service

A shameful burden of servile origin often darkens a raised noble lineage. It both disgraces those who are noble by making them equal and frequently brings upon masters the stigma of treachery.

For we know that many slaves or freedmen, often by royal command, have been brought into palace service. Yet, desiring to attain the elevation of honor that their obscured origin denied them, once they had been made equal to their masters through the palace service they received, they attacked the lives of their masters with exceptional violence. And—what is wicked to say—even those who obtain the benefit of freedom from their masters themselves become, by royal command, torturers of their own masters.

Why should we now recall, through the historical narrative of earlier and ancient times, the disasters in which the obscure condition of servitude, often concealing the downfall of its own masters, caused both the kingdom and the masters to totter?

Therefore, at the urging and command of the aforesaid most glorious prince, the assembly of our body has established this for observance: except for fiscal slaves or freedmen, no slave or freedman of any kind shall henceforth ever be permitted to enter palace service. Nor shall they at any time be admitted to become administrators or agents of fiscal places or of royal property.

Instead, thereafter each slave or freedman, truly remembering the condition of his origin, shall benefit by remaining an exile from the palace order in such a way that he neither harms his masters or their posterity nor becomes their equal.

If in the future any freedman or slave, or all his future offspring, should enter the offices mentioned above after this judgment of our sanction, he shall in every way be handed over to serve or be subject to the person from whom he derived either the origin of his servitude or the title of his freedom.

## VII. Concerning those who presume, because of the occurrence of quarrels, to strip altars or remove the lights of the Church

“Woe to those who do the work of the Lord deceitfully and negligently,” says the prophetic word. If woe comes upon those who perform the work of the Lord carelessly, what punishment will those deserve who, through malice, withdraw the worship of divine service from the altars of Christ?

We mean those who, confused by the deceitfulness of an obstinate mind, whenever some grievance arising from quarrels with their brothers wounds them, are immediately seized by insane rashness: they strip the altars, remove their sacred vestments, take away the lights, and, through malice, withdraw the worship of the divine sacrifices. What they cannot avenge upon human beings, they inflict upon God—what is worse, they inflict an injury upon God.

Therefore, if someone is bound by the guilt of homicide because of such hatred toward a brother, what punishment will he deserve for contempt of God? For, in accordance with the divine word’s rebuke: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased for him; but if someone sins against God, who will pray for him?”

That sentence of the Lord by which the malice of priests is struck down will readily be applied to the excesses of such priests. For it says: “Those who honor me, I will honor; but those who despise me shall be held without honor.”

Therefore, if any priest or minister, moved by any cause of grief or bitterness, presumes henceforth to strip the divine altar of its sacred vestments, or to wrap it in any other garment of mourning; or if he removes from the temple of God the customary services of the sacred lights, orders them extinguished, or introduces any form of mourning into the temple of God; and, what is worse, nourishes an occasion by which the customary services may be absent from the temples of the Lord or the singular offering of the sacrifice may appear in any way diminished—unless satisfaction through true repentance before the metropolitan has previously cleansed him—let him know that, condemned to perpetual disgrace, he will be deprived both of the dignity and honor of his place, according to the Lord’s sentence stated above.

Excluded from this sentence of punishment, without doubt, are those persons who happened to do such things because they feared contamination of the sacred orders or the overthrow of the holy faith, or because they were enduring hostility or siege, or because they feared the sentence of divine judgments. In their action, the humility by which God is appeased is more clearly shown than the deceitfulness of inward labor.

## VIII. That, when summoned by the metropolitan, no one from the neighboring regions may disdain to come to the place where he is invited

If Christ commands that every brother be obeyed generally to such an extent that, even if we are compelled to travel a thousand paces, we fulfill the vows of obedience, and even carry this out with a twofold duty of charity, how much more must one obey a superior?

The Apostle commanded them to obey in such a way that they might not in any respect seem to be saddened by a brother’s disobedience.

It often happens that neighboring priests, summoned by a prince or metropolitan for the sake of someone’s salvation or for necessary consultation, delay coming and employ various excuses by which they neglect to fulfill what they are commanded. From this arise difficulty for the orders and contempt for superiors.

Therefore, if any bishop, admonished by his prince or metropolitan, delays coming on the day appointed for him, within a reasonable period designated for his arrival—whether for the celebration of the principal festivals, namely Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord; whether for the business of cases; whether for the consecration of bishops; or for any of the prince’s appointments—except in the unavoidable necessity of illness that can be proven by suitable witnesses, let him know that he will be punished with excommunication for his contempt.

This does not apply if, apart from the chapters specified above, an extraordinary violence of floods or storms prevents him from reaching the appointed day. Even this, however, must be established by suitable witnesses.

The bishops who, after being admonished by the metropolitan, delay correcting and restraining the complaints of disputes that have arisen against them shall likewise deserve to receive this sentence. The same applies if, when admonished to come to the judgment of the principal see, they either refuse to hasten there themselves or neglect to send their sureties, duly instructed according to law.

## IX. On confirming the Twelfth Council of Toledo, held in the first year of the reign of the most glorious King Ervig

[Col. 0495D]

Although, by the unanimous judgment of our agreement, the acts of the twelfth Council of Toledo—held in this royal city in the first year of the glorious prince Ervig—were enacted and arranged, nevertheless now, with the renewed assent of our unshakable definition, we decree that those same acts, as they were enacted and written, shall endure for all eternity, and we confirm them with the strength of complete solidity, according to the order of the chapters proved to have been written in those acts, namely:

On the acknowledged and confirmed prior election to the supreme dignity in the name of our glorious lord, King Ervig. Likewise: On those who receive penance without perceiving it [Note: E. 4, T. I: “not consenting.”]. Likewise: On the reception or communion of the guilty in the Church. Likewise: That in places where there has never been a bishop, no bishop should ever be ordained. Likewise: On the most shameful practice of certain priests who do not communicate in the sacrifices offered to God by themselves. Likewise: On the authority granted to the bishop of Toledo by the general synod, so that bishops of another province may be ordained in the royal city with the consent of the princes. Likewise: On the accepted testimony of persons who, under the law enacted concerning the advancement of the army, had lost the right to give testimony. Likewise: On those who abandon their wives after a divorce has taken place. Likewise: On the confirmation of the laws promulgated against the wickedness of the Jews [Col. 0496B], according to the established order of their titles, numbered 521 in that same canon. Likewise: On those who flee for refuge to a church. Likewise: On the worshipers of idols. Likewise: On the prohibition concerning the fixed time at which the council ought to be celebrated. Likewise: The conclusion of the definitions, in which thanks are rendered to God and prayer is offered for the prince: namely, establishing that whoever presumes to act against the decrees of the aforesaid chapters shall be struck both by the sentence of ecclesiastical excommunication and shall be held liable under that law of the glorious prince which was enacted in confirmation of this same council.

## X. Whether those who receive penance while constituted in the priesthood may minister

On the necessary occasion of the discussion on the third day, it seemed right to us to investigate the institution established by the ancient Fathers concerning the rules for penitents. For our most holy brother Gaudentius, bishop of the see of Valeria, worthy of our reverence, had come through a representative sent to the council in his place and had approached the reverence of our assembly, informing the holy synodal gathering that, overcome by excessive ill health, he had been subjected by the laying on of hands to the laws of penance. But whether, after receiving penance, he was permitted to handle the mysteries prescribed by his order or to perform the customary duties of his office, he preferred to be assured by the synodal answers of the council.

Then, after the canonical writings concerning this matter had been brought together, this holy synod defined that, once reconciliation had been granted, he should retain the duties of his customary order. For if the rules of the preceding Fathers permit those who receive penance in the danger of death, and who confess no manifest crimes concerning themselves—provided that they nevertheless display uprightness of conduct—to advance to ecclesiastical ranks, how much more should those who receive penance while constituted in the priesthood not be withdrawn from the duty of their order [Note: Here a negative particle is missing, unless I am mistaken. EDIT.], provided that they have not themselves marked themselves out by their own confession of mortal crimes?

For since every priest knows that he is permitted to sacrifice only when he is free from evil deeds, by what reasoning should one who receives the remedy of penance, which is given for the remission of sin, withdraw himself from the divine sacrifices? Penance is received for this purpose: both to wash away sin and not to permit a person to repeat the filth of sin [Col. 0497A] [Note: Ae.: “not to permit it to be repeated at all.”]. Therefore, whoever trusts that his sins have been forgiven through the penance he has received, why should he not confidently approach the altar of the Lord, or why should he not dare to resume the duties of his order, when this is permitted to no one except one who abstains from sins?

Indeed, when we receive penance, we strive to reform ourselves according to the likeness of our Creator. The reformation itself, therefore, is the medicine by which transgressions are erased. If this medicine is taken, the soul is rightly reformed for its Creator, and the worship of sacrificing to God is also rightly assumed, because in it the likeness of the Creator is recognized. But if the medicine of penance, which is received for the remission of sins, is withdrawn, one does not in any way attain the likeness of the Maker.

For penance, as has been said, is received as a remedy for sin [Col. 0497B], while the priesthood is retained for the sake of purity, so that the priest’s life may flourish in the fruit of good works in such a way that he may both extinguish within himself the passions of transgression and, through his preaching, powerfully destroy the reign of sin in others.

What harm, then, will it do to such a priest, living as we have described, if after receiving the laws of penance he offers loaves of propitiation at the divine altars [E. 4: “loaves of offering”]? Or should the gift of penance, which is made a remedy for sin, be turned into a prohibition of the sacrament? The precepts of penance, therefore, will nowhere deprive anyone of the heavenly rights. A penitent ought to abstain from sins and likewise from the tumult of worldly affairs, but he ought not to withdraw himself from those things that appear holy and supreme—things which, when performed, bring greater expiation than they bring defilement by contamination.

For it is written: “A priest shall not approach any dead person”; that is, he must not pollute himself by involvement in mortal crimes. God did not say that a priest should not dare to approach holy things, concerning which he had commanded that a priest should in no way go out from the holy places, but rather that he should not dare to touch works of death. Therefore, everything that defiles must be driven away from every priest, and everything that cleanses must be practiced.

With these matters thus established by reasonable ruling [Ae.: “by reasonable discourse”], this holy synod defined that, while the sanction of the ancient canons remains in force, whatever bishops or priests henceforth receive the gift of penance through the laying on of hands, and have not marked themselves out by a confession of mortal crimes, must not abandon the right to retain their governance [Col. 0497D], but, after receiving reconciliation through the metropolitan according to the custom of penitents, must perform the customary duties of their order and the other sacraments of the mysteries entrusted to them.

Only this must be observed: if someone is found to have been condemned for offenses before receiving penance and not yet reconciled, or if, while receiving penance itself, he says that he has become involved in mortal acts, then, according to the judgment of the metropolitan, he ought to abstain from the duties mentioned above. But if, as has been said, while undergoing the reception of penance, he declares that he has committed no mortal crime, yet conceals within the chambers of his heart something he is ashamed to confess to others, he should know that authority concerning himself has been granted to him, so that, according to the confidence of his conscience, whether he dares or does not dare to sacrifice to God, he may proceed by the power of his own judgment [Col. 0498A] 523 rather than by permission granted through our judgment.

## XI. That no one should receive another’s fleeing cleric or monk

Many judgments of the preceding Fathers have been issued concerning this chapter, in which it has been established by repeated prohibition that no one should dare to entice another’s cleric, receive a fugitive, conceal him, or ordain him. But because, as iniquity increases and charity grows cold, neither honor is heeded nor greed restrained, action must be taken so that an evident sentence of condemnation may restrain those whom an unpunished admonition does not correct.

It was therefore agreed that no one should receive another’s presbyter, abbot, minister, subdeacon, or any cleric whatsoever, or even a wandering and fugitive monk; no one should persuade him to flee, provide a hiding place for his flight, show him hospitality while keeping or retaining him, or devise, by shameful obstruction, pretexts by which he might hide elsewhere as though the person sheltering him were unaware. For in all such cases not only is honor disgraced, but the brotherhood is also pierced by the repeated bitterness of sorrows [Note: From the remaining witnesses, except B. R., which has “is confused.”].

If someone says that he received another’s cleric with a simple intention and did not know that he was a fugitive, then the evident purity of his innocence must be demonstrated by presenting the person he received to the judge within eight days, according to the sanction of the laws, and by returning that fugitive within the period established by law to the place from which he had wandered away in flight.

Therefore, whoever among bishops, priests, ministers [Col. 0498C], or other religious persons violates the sanction of this institution of ours—if the receiver is a bishop, and returns the person he received, together with whatever belongings he was able to have, without delay to the person from whom he had wandered—must nevertheless know that, as a true sacrilegious person and transgressor of the paternal institution, he will remain excommunicated and removed from his duties for as long as he happened to detain under his authority the person who fled.

But if the transgressor of this institution of ours is a presbyter, deacon, or any other religious person, then, after returning the person he received together with the property owed to him, he alone shall be held under the discipline of penance for an entire year under the authority of the person whose fugitive he is shown to have received.

Those who have nevertheless shown hospitality to such persons must know that they are to be prosecuted and bound by the same and similar legal penalty [Col. 0498D] by which the law warns that receivers of fugitives are to be bound.

Those, however, who maintain that this act was committed through the rashness of their predecessors shall be held free from the sentence of this punishment only if, within two months from the time of their ordination, they make public the fugitive’s hiding place and return his person to his master [524].

Those who receive persons who, out of necessity in their cases, flee from neighboring bishops and other heads of churches to their metropolitan cannot be condemned as receivers of fugitives, since such persons are permitted to seek refuge—especially if they keep them openly and warn them that, at the claimant’s summons, they must appear with those against whom they have brought actions [Col. 0499A].

## XII. That persons who have gone to their metropolitan to present their cases should not be excommunicated by their own bishop

Any cleric or monk who has a case against his own bishop and goes to his metropolitan to bring an action must not be condemned beforehand by his own bishop with a sentence of excommunication before it can be established through the judgment of his metropolitan whether he deserves excommunication.

If any bishop pronounces a sentence of excommunication against such persons before judgment [Note: Ae., 4, E. T. 1, 2: “has imposed beforehand”], he must know that, once those whom he has bound have been completely absolved, that sentence will be turned back upon himself.

This is also to be observed among metropolitans: if someone oppressed by his own metropolitan brings his case to the metropolitan of another province so that the burden of his distress may be examined [Ae., T. 2: “has transferred”], or if someone unheard by two metropolitans goes to present his case to royal hearings, and for this reason his own bishop appears to impose the yoke of excommunication upon him, this alone must be observed: if it happened that a person had first received excommunication before passing from his own bishop to another, he is to be held excommunicated before the one whose judgment he sought until it is ascertained, in response to the objections of his excommunicator, whether he was bound justly or unjustly.

## XIII. On the rendering of thanks, which are paid to God and the prince after the completion of the council

To all these synodal institutions, therefore, we add the strength of our subscription, and, under divine terror, consecrate what we have decreed to perpetual memory. We give glory and honor together to our immortal God, by whose inspiration all things that are salutarily accomplished are brought about.

To the most invincible and most religious prince, King Ervig, we also render manifold expressions of thanks, by whose most merciful command we have assembled in one gathering [525]. May desirable and blessed peace be his. May he pass his days happily through a longer span of life, and, after the scepters of an earthly kingdom, may he reach the heavenly kingdoms to be crowned, through Jesus Christ our Lord, God and Savior, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God in the Trinity, lives and is glorified forever and ever. Amen.

## A great reward of piety

A great reward of piety consists in removing the burdens of oppression, because that sacrifice of perfect mercy is always approved before the eyes of God by which relief is brought to the wretched, and through which salvation is introduced into the land because human oppression is relieved.

It is indeed a salutary judgment among peoples when affairs are governed in such a way that neither heedless exaction burdens the populations nor indiscriminate remission causes the condition of the nation to perish. The times of our glory, therefore, must be seasoned with the benefits of mercy, so that, while God spares us, we too may appear to spare the populations.

Desiring, therefore, to offer a votive sacrifice of my heart to my almighty God, in the divine name we extend this decree and benefit to all the populations of our kingdom, both privately owned and fiscally owned slaves, men and women subject to tributary exaction, residing in the province of Gaul or Galicia and in all the provinces of Spain:

Whatever from the account of tribute in past years, up to the first year of our clemency, you appear to owe to the public treasuries, know that it has all been granted to you in full. Thus, whatever from the account of tributes remains outstanding against you up to the aforesaid first year of our glory, you are to regard as wholly given to you by our serenity, so that henceforth you need fear no public exaction on account of past years [Col. 0503A].

This condition is nevertheless preserved: whatever was exacted in past years but was not brought into our fisc must be paid into the public treasury by those who exacted it. If they delay and neglect to pay it immediately, they shall pay that same amount fourfold, together with the disciplinary penalty, according to what our gentleness shall decree.

Certainly, if any duke, count, tiuphadus, treasurer, steward, or anyone else exercising public office has not exacted each year in full the tributes entrusted to him for collection, or has retained the amounts collected, and has neglected to bring them immediately into the public treasuries, he shall by every means enter the tributes themselves, doubled, into the public account from his own property.

We establish this by a special and clear decision of our serenity: none of the aforesaid counts, tiuphadi, vicars, treasurers, or any persons exercising public office may presume to demand from any of you—who are granted the relaxation of our gentleness—any exaction whatsoever on account of this act of mercy. If any one of them takes anything from you for such a reason, accepts from others anything offered to him, or presumes in any way to diminish anything on these grounds, he shall restore fourfold everything he has received to whomever our clemency shall designate [Col. 0503B].

As for the lands or vineyards that any of the aforesaid persons exercising public office has taken or received from you, private or fiscal populations, for the same tribute, each collector shall count against himself the dry and liquid produce he collected from them in past years toward that tribute, and he shall not delay restoring the lands or vineyards themselves to you, from whose legal possession they were taken.

For it is fitting that what is produced by the sincerity of this act of our mercy should be carried out by all without the spur of anyone’s exaction.

Issued at Toledo on the Kalends of November, in the fortunate fourth year of our reign.

## Law issued in confirmation of the council

In the name of the Lord, Flavius Ervig, king.

The eminent authority of a synod is at once venerable and awe-inspiring. It is conducted through the gift of the Holy Spirit to such an extent that, from the diversity of many minds and hearts, it appears to have made one heart and one soul, while the multitude of assembled bishops neither disagrees in its judgment, nor brings forward differing objections through rivalry, nor forms one judgment other than that of the whole body.

Therefore, reverently venerating and earnestly honoring the august gathering of the synodal council, in whose midst the presence of the Holy Spirit promised to dwell, we bring to the knowledge of all what was arranged by their mouth at the urging of our glory. We mean the acts of the synodal council known to have been completed in the city of Toledo in the fourth year of our reign. So that the evident substance of these institutions may become known to everyone without delay, we have selected the following items to be specially recorded here.

The first canon is therefore: On the restoration of the testimony of the dignity of those whom the profanation of infidelity drew, together with Patro, into partnership in tyranny; our majesty decrees that these men, together with their sons, be restored by this edict of our law both to the testimony of their former nobility and to the property they received through the force of our authority [Col. 0504A].

The second title is likewise: On accused priests, and also on palace nobles and gardingi, concerning the judicial safeguards under which they ought to be examined. Our gentleness has decreed, in accordance with the provisions of the canon itself, that they not be subjected to any form of torture before a public inquiry; but all who are henceforth accused shall unquestionably be judged according to the sanction of the aforesaid chapter.

Accordingly, we decree that this must be specially observed: whatever has been done against this rule or the institution of the aforesaid canon, whether against anyone’s person or concerning the property of an accused person, or whatever has been judged concerning it, shall have no force whatsoever according to the provisions of the aforesaid canon [Col. 0504B]. Thus no person may be judged otherwise than we decree, nor lose the dignity of his testimony or be deprived of the profit of his own property.

The third canon is: On the principal remission of tributes among the people [530]. By the authority and exhortation of our glory, it has been established that all tribute from past years up to the first year of our reign, whatever remains outstanding among private or fiscal populations, must be released by the sanction of perpetual absolution. Only those amounts are to be presented to the public treasuries which are shown to have been exacted but not paid in.

The fourth canon follows: On the protection of offspring, which the entire gathering of priests and also of elders chose to establish with willing and eager resolve.

The fifth canon follows: That, after the prince has died, no one may dare to take his surviving wife either in marriage or in adultery [Col. 0504C].

The sixth canon follows: That, except for fiscal slaves or fiscal freedmen, no one from the servile class or from the freedmen shall henceforth pass into the palatine office. If they do so, they must by every means be reduced, by the edict of the present law, to the yoke of their former servitude, so that they may be handed over to serve either their masters, if those masters survive, or their masters’ relatives, to whom succession from the deceased is owed by law.

After this comes the seventh canon: On those who presume, because of the occurrence of quarrels, to strip altars or remove the lights of a church.

The eighth canon follows: That no one, when admonished by his metropolitan, should refuse to come from neighboring places to the place where he is summoned.

The ninth canon follows [Col. 0504D]: On the confirmation of the twelfth Council of Toledo, which took place in the first year of our glory.

The tenth canon is added to this, in which the following is determined by special judgment: Whether those who receive penance while constituted in the priesthood may minister.

The eleventh canon is also recorded: That no one should receive another’s fleeing cleric or monk.

The twelfth canon is written after these: On persons who are not to be excommunicated by their own bishop when they have gone to their metropolitan to present their cases.

The final, thirteenth canon follows after this: On the rendering of thanks, which are paid to God and the prince after the completion of the council.

We decree that all the synodal institutions and decrees set forth above are to be observed from the present day and time, with every care and vigilance, throughout all the provinces of our kingdom, so that they may both attain the evident height of strong authority and remain permanently established in an enduring order of force.

Therefore, by the proclamation of this sacred law, we generally prohibit and command all religious persons and laypeople living under the rule of our kingdom alike: no one may despise the aforesaid synodal acts; no one may dare to pass over or tear them down; no person known to these constitutions may dissolve the rights established by them; and no unknown person may seek to excuse himself by alleging his ignorance [Col. 0505A]. For from the aforesaid day and time, and by the force of their due authority, they shall possess power, and the entire body of people shall be bound by the rules of their institutions.

If anyone becomes a violator of this law of ours and does not instead preserve what has been set forth above, he shall both receive prolonged excommunication under ecclesiastical discipline and lose a tenth part of his property, to be joined to the fiscal treasury.

If he possesses no means from which he can pay the aforesaid composition, he must be beaten with fifty blows without any disgrace to his person [Col. 0506A] 532.

We have therefore subscribed this decree of our law, known to have been promulgated in confirmation of this sacred council, with the writing of our glorious hand, and we bind to it perpetual validity for everlasting memory.

Law issued in confirmation of the council at Toledo, on the Ides of November, in the era 721, and, in the name of God, in the fortunate fourth year of the reign of our glory.

# LIX. FOURTEENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO

[Note: This council is absent from A., Ae., E. 3. It has been taken from B. R., with the variant readings of the others.]

Of seventeen bishops, held in the fifth year of the reign of Ervig.

## I. On the preliminary announcement of the assembled council and the report of the royal edict by which the synod was ordered to be held

When the most serene and illustrious prince, the glorious Ervig, a true lover of the faith, indeed a beloved son of the Church of Christ, mindful of his promise, ordered all of us to assemble together by the vigorous and invincible command of his majesty in order to refute the pernicious doctrine of Apollinaris, about which he had been informed by the Roman bishop, he issued this special edict:

Since, as was fitting for the treatment of so great a matter, the incursion of various adversities did not permit a general council to be held, councils should at least be held after being assembled by provinces. First, a synod should be held here in the royal city; afterward, a separate council should be held in each province. Whatever the other bishops of the principal sees learned through the reports of their representatives concerning what had been done here in the Council of Toledo, they themselves should subsequently observe through the separate councils of their provinces.

Thus the acts of our council would be entirely common to all of them, since they had been issued by them and confirmed by them while they were present; indeed, they had decreed that they should be confirmed through their legates. In this way there would be one and indivisible synodal edict of all the bishops of Spain throughout Spain and Gaul, since it would have been promulgated with the assent of all the metropolitans.

Accordingly, we, the bishops of the province of Carthage, in the year mentioned above, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, taking our seats in the aforesaid church according to the proper order, retracing the course of this matter and the affairs of the whole business [Col. 0505D], to which we had been invited by letters from the Roman see, began in this open and common voice:

## II. On the beginning of the report, by which the council began to mention the synodal acts and the letter of the Roman pontiff

A clear report fills all the peoples of Spain: as the sequence of passing time unfolded, the synodal acts were brought to our assembly through the bearer of the Roman bishop. From them we learned that, at Constantinople, through the mediation of Constantine, the pious and religious prince, a great and exalted gathering of bishops had destroyed the doctrine of Apollinaris.

Together with these acts, we also received the invitation and the deliberative letter of Leo, bishop of ancient Rome, through which the entire order of the acts and the acts of the various orders were clearly revealed to our understanding as they had been enacted.

In the course of that glorious letter [Note: E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “gracious”], all the bishops of Spain were invited [533] so that the aforesaid synodal institutions, which he had sent, might also remain supported by the authority of our strength and might be publicly disseminated by us among all who reside under the rule of Spain.

## III. On the twofold adversity by which a general council could not be held

This entire presentation of the matter was indeed submitted to us under the pressing force of a hostile season. Not only had the whole land, gripped by winter frost, hardened beneath an immense mass of icy snow, but this occurred at a time when it was already clear that we had been released from the nearby general council.

Hindered by this twofold obstacle opposing the matter, we were then unable to assemble again in general. The recent completion of the council had already returned us diminished to our own sees, while the adversity of the stormy season did not permit us, scattered as we were, to gather together again.

Although during that period the assembly of all the bishops of Spain could not be gathered together in general, nevertheless, dispersed among our sees and localities [Col. 0506D], we undertook to examine the aforesaid rules of the acts, read through what we had undertaken, and approved in them the orthodox sense, the unblemished statement of doctrine, and the style of apostolic tradition concerning the difference between the two natures of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, in whom a twofold will and operation is proclaimed.

## IV. On the responses of our party

It therefore pleased us, at that time, while satisfying the Roman pontiff through the responses of our apologetic defense, to confirm those same acts and to express the sense of our faith through the purest clarification of words.

And because there, concerning this twofold will and operation of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, many true things are set forth copiously and clearly—things that have already been sent to the Roman party through legates from Spain—it remains for us now to carry out this task:

In accordance with the special decree of the canons, by which a general council is ordered to assemble for matters of the faith, both sets of acts must be determined by synodal examination and supported by the authority of the separate councils. Thus, in accordance with the edict of the aforesaid glorious prince, once a council has been assembled in each province of his kingdom, and the synodal matters have again been sifted through examination or approved by the common judgment of all the councils, the aforesaid synodal acts, and likewise the responses of our party, may reach the knowledge of everyone through the individual councils of the provinces of Spain and may pass, through salutary publication, into the knowledge of the peoples.

## V. On the renewed examination of the aforementioned council
By the common judgment of all, therefore, it is now agreed that, since we have not been able to assemble all the bishops of Spain together in a single gathering, we should at least celebrate councils separately in the distinct provinces, so that the acts of the aforesaid synod or the responses of our party may at last be refined by a worthy judgment of their soundness and illumined by the commendable style of a synodal statement.

Accordingly, first, all of us, the bishops of the province of Carthage [Col. 0507C], compared the aforesaid acts with the ancient councils, judging with equal accord, while the vicars of the most reverend and exalted bishops of the principal sees were also assisting us—namely, Cyprian of the province of Tarraconensis, Sunifred of Narbonensis, Stephen of Emerita, Julian of Bracara, and Floresindus of Hispalis. We approved those same acts anew, since they are entirely consonant with those synodal decrees and principal authorities, and in agreement with the faith of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, while being so closely united with Chalcedon that they appear to have been issued or excerpted in its very words, since almost the whole substance of its preceding formulation seems to have been drawn from them.

## VI. On the honor conferred upon the aforesaid council

[Col. 0507D]

And therefore the acts of the aforesaid council shall stand as venerable and acceptable to us to the extent that they do not depart from the councils mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0507D] E. 4, T. 1, 2, U.: “depart” (discedunt), instead of “withdraw” (disciscunt).], indeed, to the extent that they appear to agree with them. Those matters that possess the dignity and merit of their proper rank shall therefore have their proper place. Accordingly, we decree that these acts be appended to those councils, whose authority supports them and by whose authority we approve them.

## VII. On the place and order in which the aforesaid council ought now to be placed

After the Council of Chalcedon, therefore, this council is to be placed with the honor, place, and order due to it, so that the honor of its place and order may correspond to the glorious theme with which it shines.

## VIII. Address to the entire structure of the Church concerning the two inseparable and perfect natures of Christ

[Col. 0508A]

But now we, to whom the divine voice commands that we speak to the heart of Jerusalem, admonish the flock of Christ entrusted to us, and proclaim to all who hasten toward the harbor of eternal life, gathering the matter into a very brief definition, that in the one person of Christ, the Son of God, they should recognize the individual properties of two natures as remaining, just as undivided and inseparable, so also unconfused and unchangeable: one belonging to deity, the other to humanity; one by which he was begotten from God the Father, the other by which he was born from the Virgin Mary.

Therefore each of his births is complete, each is perfect: he possesses nothing deficient in his deity, and he assumes nothing imperfect from his humanity. He is not divided by a doubling of natures, nor is [Col. 0508B] his person doubled; rather, fully God and fully human, without any sin, he is one Christ in the singularity of his person.

Thus, remaining one in both natures, he shines forth in the signs of divinity and is subject to the sufferings of humanity. For one was not begotten from the Father and another from the Mother, although he was born in one manner from the Father and in another manner from the Mother. Yet he himself, undivided but one and the same in both kinds of nature, is both the Son of God and the Son of man. He himself lives while dying; he himself dies while living; he himself suffers while impassible; he himself is not subject to suffering. He neither succumbs in his deity nor withdraws in his humanity from suffering.

From the nature of his deity he possesses the inability to die; from the substance of his humanity he possesses both the will and the ability to die. From the one nature he is regarded as immortal; from the other he is dissolved by the condition of mortals. In the eternal will of his deity he possesses the disposition by which he would assume the humanity that was taken up; in the will of the humanity that was assumed he possesses the disposition by which the human will would be subject to God.

Hence he also says to the Father: “Father, not my will but yours be done,” showing, evidently, one will of the deity by which the human being was assumed, and another will of the human being by which God must be obeyed.

## IX. On the wills and operations of Christ’s two natures

And therefore, in accordance with the difference between these two natures, the properties of two inseparable wills and operations must likewise be proclaimed.

## X. On avoiding the disputes of heretics, and on believing rather than examining what is supreme

Knowing, therefore, that this alone is the confession of faith [Col. 0508D] that conquers hell and surpasses Tartarus—for concerning this faith the Lord said, “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it”—we say to everyone, we cry out to everyone, that we beware of the traps of heretics and flee the poisons of their cancerous doctrine. Let us not prepare, through those expressions by which Christ’s assumption of humanity is affirmed, the snares of empty questions for ourselves, questions by which those desirous of empty glory dare to examine what is supreme.

For divine matters are not to be examined but believed; God does not command us to examine him but to believe. Let us therefore believe, not in our own senses, but in the indubitable doctrines of the ancient councils already set forth above.

If anyone, therefore, [Col. 0509A] diminishes anything of divinity in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the womb of the Virgin Mary, or removes anything from the humanity he assumed—except only the law of sin—and does not most sincerely believe that he is true God and perfect man, subsisting in one person, let him be anathema.

## XI. On the common judgment by which the responses of our party were confirmed

Those apologetic responses of our defense, therefore, which were issued for the confirmation of these matters, for the instruction of many and for the benefit of ecclesiastical discipline, we confirm with a similar force of honor and reverence, and we decree that they shall remain in the place of decretal letters.

## XII. On giving thanks to God for the council that has been completed

[Col. 0509B]

Giving glory in these matters to God alone, almighty, living, and true, reigning in the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—by whose gift, represented to one another through our presence and gladdened by fraternal fellowship, we have been made abundantly effective in the fulfillment of spiritual vows, we ask of the immensity of his glory that it grant our glorious prince, King Ervigius, under whose peace the peace of the Church is preserved, a long span of time in the flourishing continuance of his kingdom, so that after this present life he may come to reign with us in the kingdom of future glory, through our God, whose kingdom endures for ever and ever. Amen.

The council was completed on Sunday, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the year stated above.

[Col. 0509C]
