# LX. THE FIFTEENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, OF SIXTY-ONE BISHOPS, HELD IN THE FIRST YEAR OF THE MOST SERENE AND ORTHODOX PRINCE EGICA, ON THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY, IN THE ERA 726

[Col. 0509]

[Col. 0509D]

At the city of Toledo, in the praetorian church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the bishops of Spain and Gaul having assembled, while the charity poured out among them showed itself as each sat in the sight of the others, and the rendering of thanks to God resounded in alternating voices, the same most serene prince Egica appeared, exalted in the tranquil dignity of his devotion and praiseworthy in the bowed inclination of his majesty. Placed in the midst of the bishops and prostrate upon the ground, he commended himself to the prayers of God’s priests.

Then [E. 4, T. 1, 2: *deinde* (“then”), instead of *dein* (“thereupon”)], rising and addressing the council with an adequate exhortation [E. 4: *exoratione* (“with a prayer”), instead of *exhortatione* (“with an exhortation”)], he handed the priests of God a written volume containing the intentions of his majesty, to be read aloud:

“Behold,” he said, “most blessed Fathers: everything that either burdensome circumlocution prevented me from saying to you, or ordinary speech perhaps does not permit me to explain, I have here gathered into a brief style; here I have inserted it in a clear statement. I ask you to attend to these matters, examine them, and pronounce upon them the unshakable sanction of your deliberation.”

Then we received the volume presented by the king, and, giving glory to God, blessed that same prince. After he had departed, we found the following written in the folded volume mentioned above.

[539]

## In the name of the Lord. Flavius Egica, king, to the most reverend Fathers seated in this holy synod

Behold, most exalted Fathers and bishops whom I must honor by heavenly right: as I approach the splendid assembly of your order, I am lifted up by that greater power of joys, by which I do not doubt that the Lord Jesus Christ is placed among you. Trusting his words, in which he says, “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I shall be in the midst of them,” I am carried forward with such confidence in this hope that whatever your judgment shall decree, I shall believe to have originated only at his prompting.

Therefore I shall not be ashamed to open there the bosom of my heart, from which streams of healing flow abundantly. Attend now to the source from which the heart of our serenity boils over, and to the causes by which the distress of my troubled breast is constricted with grief.

First of all, I must say that, having inherited the royal dignity of our divine father and father-in-law, I feel myself entangled in a double net of oaths. Thus, if I preserve one of these obligations with careful observance, I nevertheless seem to have fallen into the charge of perjury through the other.

For that same divine father-in-law of ours, the prince Ervigius, among the other conditions by which he bound me through a heedless and unavoidable oath when he chose that his glorious daughter should be joined to me, imposed upon me the obligation of an oath of every kind: in every matter concerning his sons, I was to devote myself so completely that their causes might reach victory, and whatever he commanded me for any cause, I was to fulfill his orders in every respect.

While I was making this promise to the aforesaid prince under the security of an oath, he imposed upon me, at the time of his death, another obligation and compelled me to undertake another course of action: namely, that I should not assume the kingdom until I had first bound myself with the strict bonds of oaths, so that I would not deny justice to the peoples entrusted to me.

These things were done, and they are shown to have been bound by specific ties of conditions. I have sent to your fatherhood for consideration the unavoidable and contradictory sequence of these two conditions: both those which he demanded from me for the protection of his sons and those which he arranged to demand from me for the prior designation of the kingdom. I ask that, confirmed in the kingdom by your blessings, I may remain firmly established in it, and that, instructed by the rules of your sanction, I may recognize the path by which I can walk with measured steps through the danger of perjury.

For I shall not be able to escape the mark of perjury if, either by defending the offspring of the aforesaid prince against justice, I fail to render the truth to the peoples, or, by zealously pursuing the affairs of the peoples for the sake of truth, I fail to fulfill toward his sons the promises I have made.

In addition to this, there is, as is reported, the severity of his acts of oppression against many: men whom he unjustly deprived of their property and honor, whom he entangled in servitude under his own authority after stripping them of their noble status, whom he subdued by torture, and whom he crushed by violent judgments. Against all these matters, this further complaint is raised: that he compelled the entire people of his kingdom to swear an oath for the protection of his sons, and thereby, as it were, closed every avenue by which anyone might protest.

Occupied by all these cries of oppression and by the wasting tumult of anxiety, and desiring to escape the danger of this peril, I entrust these matters to your judgment and to your decisions, with that confidence by which I do not doubt that God is near to you.

I also desire that the other complaints of the cases and the remaining proceedings of the litigants that may present themselves to your assembly for resolution be quieted by your judgments. I solemnly charge all of you—the sacred bishops honored by heavenly right, as well as the noble and illustrious men of the royal court—by that ineffable and undivided mystery of the Holy Trinity, by the precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the dread day of the future judgment, that in all these matters mentioned above you direct your faithful conscience upon them, rejecting every acceptance of gifts or favor.

In examining all the complaints and cases, therefore, devote yourselves in such a way that you do not depart in any respect from the path of justice. Then, while your judgments, directed by the unbending summit of equity, commend themselves in the sight of the Lord, both gain from your admonition may come to me and the desired joy arising from your emulation of just judgments may come to you.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

After we had learned and read through the contents of this volume, the first matter that presented itself in due order was that, consecrating the first fruits of our spirit to the Lord, we should begin the opening of our deliberation with the solidity of the holy faith.

Therefore, professing in a pious confession the holy faith defined by the Fathers, just as the Council of Nicaea established it, just as the assembly of the Fathers at Constantinople promulgated it, as the tradition of the Council of Ephesus under the presidency of Cyril delivered it, and as the Council of Chalcedon likewise declared it, we proclaim that it must be held by all in this manner, and, as we profess, we recite the Creed handed down by the Fathers:

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, [Col. 0512D] true God from true God, begotten, not made, homoousion with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us and for our salvation came down, and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary and became man; who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom shall have no end.

We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets; in one catholic and apostolic Church; we confess one baptism for the remission of sins; we await [Col. 0513A] the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

After this rule of pious confession had been uttered in devout voices, we immediately turned to examine those chapters for the defense of which, two years earlier, Pope Benedict of blessed memory had admonished us through the message of his letters. He had not, however, taken care to record them in his own writings, but had instructed that they be set down by our messenger verbally. A sufficient and appropriate response had already been given to him concerning this in that same year.

Yet now, rereading more carefully the record made by our messenger, we found that in the book of our response concerning the faith, which we had sent through Peter, regional agent of the Roman Church, the first chapter had appeared to the aforesaid pope to have been imprudently stated by us. There we had said, according to the divine essence: “Will begot will, just as wisdom begot wisdom.”

Passing over these words in a careless rush through his reading, that man supposed that we had used these very nouns—that is, “will” and “wisdom”—not according to essence, but either according to relation or according to a comparison with the human mind. Therefore, in his written record, he seemed to admonish us in these terms:

“By the natural order we understand that the word derives its origin from the mind, as do reason and will; and these cannot be reversed, so that one might say that, just as word and will proceed from the mind, so the mind proceeds from word or will.”

From this comparison, it appeared to the Roman pontiff that “will from will” could not be said. We, however, did not speak according to this comparison with the human mind, nor according to relation, but according to essence, when we said: “Will from will, just as wisdom from wisdom.”

For in God, to be is the same as to will, and to will is the same as to know or be wise—something that cannot be said of a human being. In a human being, what he is apart from willing is one thing, and willing even without knowing or being wise is another. But it is not so in God, because his nature is simple. Therefore, for him to be is the same as to will and the same as to be wise.

Accordingly, whoever is capable of understanding that we spoke of “will from will” according to essence has not troubled himself with the question proposed in this way. This is also clear to those who carefully and intelligently read the work mentioned above concerning our response and faith, where the statement of blessed Athanasius, inserted there, declares that we ought to hold precisely this view. He says:

“We retain this judgment of religious belief concerning God: we do not believe that his will is one thing and his nature another.”

If, then, according to what this teacher says, we ought to hold that God’s will is not one thing and his nature another, then his will is the same as his nature, and his nature is the same as his substance or essence.

The Son of God, therefore, was born from the essence of the Father: essence from essence, just as nature from nature and substance from substance. Yet one cannot speak of two essences, two natures, or two substances, but only of one essence, nature, and substance. This is like light from light—not two lights but one light; essence from essence—not two essences but one essence; nature from nature—not two natures but one nature; and likewise will from will—not two wills but one will, because God’s will is not something other than his nature, as has already been confirmed above by the teaching of Athanasius.

Consequently, whatever is said of God according to essence appears to belong in common to each of the persons, such as wisdom and strength and the other attributes. For the Father can be called wisdom, and the Son can be called wisdom; the Father can also be called strength, and the Son can be called strength.

This cannot in any way be said according to that comparison with the human mind. For example, if the mind is taken as signifying the person of the Father, the Word, proceeding as it were from the mind, is understood as the Son, and the will proceeding from the mind and the Word signifies the Holy Spirit. Yet it does not follow that the mind, which is placed as a sign of the Father, can be said to belong to the Son or the Holy Spirit; or that the Word, which signifies the Son alone, can be compared with the Father or the Holy Spirit; or that the will, which is understood as the person of the Holy Spirit, can be said to belong to the person of the Father or the Son.

Rather, the individual terms correspond individually according to the comparison with the human mind, so that each thing said of one of them is not said at all of another. Likewise, when the Father is named by a relational term, he is not the same as the Son; when the Son is named, he is not the same as the Holy Spirit; nor is the Holy Spirit the same as the Father or the Son.

Accordingly, those names that are taken comparatively from human beings are spoken according to a comparison with the human mind so that, in some fashion, human weakness may be stirred to contemplate the ineffable mystery of the divine Trinity.

We were therefore thought to have said, according to this comparison, “will from will,” which is plainly absurd to say or to understand. Consequently, one rule applies when something is said of God according to essence, and another when something is pronounced of him according to a comparison with the human mind.

Accordingly, agreeing with and following the judgment of the eminent teacher Augustine, we said according to the essence of the divine Trinity: “Will from will,” just as he himself declares in the fifteenth book of *The Trinity of God*, saying:

“Better, as I think, one says ‘counsel from counsel’ and ‘will from will,’ just as ‘substance from substance’ and ‘wisdom from wisdom.’”

Here every wise person plainly understands that we did not err, but that they were perhaps misled by a careless reading, because what we had said according to essence they thought had been stated according to a comparison with the human mind.

## A clear statement of the lord Julian concerning the three substances remaining in Christ
As we proceed to reconsider the second chapter also, in which that same pope thought that we had imprudently declared that three substances are to be confessed in Christ, the Son of God, we shall not be ashamed to defend what is true; perhaps this will cause some people to be ashamed to be ignorant of what is true. [Variant: E. 4, T. 1, 2 read *ita forsitan* (“thus perhaps”).] For who does not know that every human being consists of two substances, namely soul and body? Concerning these the Apostle speaks expressly, saying: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.” So too that man, thirsting for God, cried out in the psalm: “My soul thirsts for you,” he says, “and how greatly my flesh does also.” There are many other passages as well that declare that a human being consists of two substances.

Against this rule, however, we likewise find in the Scriptures that sometimes flesh alone is named and the whole human being is understood, or that soul alone is named and the perfection of the whole human being is recognized. Therefore, when the divine nature has been joined to human nature, three substances may be called proper substances, and two may be called tropically. But it is one thing when the whole human being is expressed properly, and another when the whole is understood from a part. For there is a certain mode of expression frequently found in the divine Scriptures by which the whole is signified from a part; among grammarians this figure is also called synecdoche.

Thus it is written in the book of Genesis, according to this tropical expression signifying the whole from a part: “Man was made into a living soul,” although the human being consists not only of soul but also of flesh. Similarly, the whole is understood from a part where the substance of the soul is omitted and only the substance of flesh is named, as it is written in the psalm: “All flesh shall come to you,” although every human being consists not only of flesh but also of soul. Nevertheless, when flesh alone is named, the whole human being is understood, just as the whole human being is understood when soul alone is named.

In Exodus also, wishing in the same way for human beings to be understood as the whole from a part, Scripture says: “Seventy souls entered Egypt with Jacob,” although those seventy souls did not enter there without their bodies. He too wished the whole human being to be understood by the name “flesh” when he said: “And in my flesh I shall see God,” although bodies will rise again not without their souls.

Behold, by the customary usage of sacred Scripture we have proved both that a human being is properly called by the very substances of which he consists and that, tropically, the whole human being can be understood from a part. If you seek fault, neither can he be said to have erred who expressed the whole human being by naming flesh and soul, since divine Scripture proves that both expressions may be made without blame.

And yet, since we now hold it proved that neither one usage nor the other is to be blamed, we must ask which expression is more suitable for understanding the whole human being and, with every obscurity removed, is also clearer: the one that names flesh alone and silently wishes the soul to be understood, or the one that expresses soul and flesh and thereby states the whole. To make this more evident, some examples must be set forth.

Behold, according to the aforesaid tropical mode of expression, which is called synecdoche, by which either the part is understood from the whole or the whole from the part, we find written in the Psalms concerning the plagues of Egypt: “He sent among them the dog-fly”; and likewise: “He spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar.” Scripture wished by this kind of expression not singularity but plurality to be understood in the case of flies and locusts. For it was not one fly or one locust, but a multitude of flies and locusts, that filled Egypt.

Now, if someone among us were to say in our manner, “God sent flies, locusts, and caterpillars into Egypt,” using the plural number—which is certainly true—could any accusation fall upon this expression, which confesses plurality, so that it might be said not to be true that a multitude of locusts filled Egypt? The same is true of the passage where the people cried out to Moses, saying: “Pray to the Lord that he may take away the serpent from us,” although that people was suffering not from the trouble of one serpent but of many serpents.

The Apostle speaks in this same manner in the passage where he says: “For by works of the law no flesh shall be justified,” as though he were saying “no human being,” wishing the whole human being to be understood from the part, namely flesh.

So also, when it is written of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Gospel: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” flesh alone is named, so that the soul too might there be silently understood according to the aforementioned mode of expression, by which the whole human being is taken from a part. This rule of expression was also frequently observed by the Fathers.

Thus blessed Cyril, in the book called *Scholia*, says:

“How, then, the Word became flesh must be considered. First, divine Scripture frequently names flesh and, as though from a part of the whole living being, conveys the meaning of the whole; and at times it does the same from the soul alone. For it is written: ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God.’ And the divine Paul himself says: ‘I did not consult flesh and blood.’ The high priest Moses also addressed those who were of Israel: ‘In seventy-five souls your fathers went down into Egypt.’ But you must not therefore say that naked souls without flesh went down into Egypt, nor again that God granted his salvation in souls, bodies, and flesh alone. Therefore, whenever we hear that the Word became flesh, let us understand a human being composed of soul and body,” and so forth.

Likewise Saint Augustine, in the book *Questions against the Apollinarists*, says:

“If wherever flesh has been named and soul has been left unmentioned it must be understood that the soul is not believed to be there, then those of whom it was said, ‘And all flesh shall see the salvation of God,’ did not have souls; nor did those of whom it is said in the psalm, ‘Hear my prayers; all flesh shall come to you’; nor those of whom it is said in the Gospel, ‘As you have given him authority over all flesh, so that everything you have given him may not perish but have eternal life.’ From this it is understood that human beings are accustomed to be signified by the naming of flesh alone, so that according to this mode of expression the statement ‘The Word became flesh’ may also be understood to mean nothing other than ‘The Word became a human being.’ For just as, when the part is named, the whole is often understood from the soul alone, as in the statement ‘So many souls went down into Egypt,’ so again, when the part is named, the human being is understood from flesh alone.”

Again, in the book *Enchiridion* he says:

“‘The Word became flesh’: divinity assumed flesh; divinity was not changed into flesh. Here we must understand ‘flesh’ as ‘human being,’ the expression signifying the whole from a part, as it is said: ‘For by works of the law no flesh shall be justified,’ that is, no human being.”

Therefore this is the complete judgment drawn by the Fathers from the usage of the Scriptures: whenever any one substance of the human being assumed in Christ is named as the whole from a part, the other is immediately understood there as well. For even if one is left unmentioned according to this figure and the other is named, nevertheless both are understood.

Let no one, then, when he hears that the whole human being can be understood from a part, say that we ought not to confess three substances in Christ, since by this mode of expression one thing is necessarily understood from the other. There is therefore no difference whether one substance of the human being is named tropically or two are named properly, since both forms of expression permit and require us to understand and confess that the human being assumed by God exists in two substances. Consequently, whoever has learned this reasoning with full understanding will not hesitate to confess three substances in Christ.

But when these Fathers confess, not tropically but properly, that the whole human being was assumed by Christ, they expressed it in their treatises as follows.

Blessed Cyril, in the aforementioned book called *Scholia*, speaks as follows, where he clearly establishes the truth of Christ’s three substances by means of a figure from the Old Testament:

“Thus, when the Word God had been united to true humanity, the substances nevertheless remained unconfused. According to God’s will, a holy tabernacle was erected through the desert, and in it Emmanuel was represented in many ways. Almighty God therefore said to the divine Moses: ‘You shall make an ark of the testimony from imperishable wood, two and a half cubits in length and a cubit and a half in height; and you shall overlay it with pure gold; inside and outside you shall overlay it.’

“Now the imperishable wood is a figure of the incorruptible body, for cedar is imperishable; but the gold, as a material more precious than the others, indicates to us the majesty of the divine substance. Consider, therefore: since the whole ark was overlaid with pure gold, both outside and inside, God the Word had indeed been united to the holy flesh, and this, I think, is what it means that the ark was overlaid with gold on the outside. But that he also made the rational soul dwelling in the body his own is shown by the fact that he commanded the ark to be overlaid with gold inside as well.

“That the natures, or substances, remained unconfused we know from this: the gold laid upon the wood remained what it was, and the wood was indeed adorned with the splendor of gold; yet it did not cease to be wood.”

Likewise Saint Augustine, expressing the same point in the book *On the Trinity of God*, says:

“Human nature could be joined to God in such a way that from two substances there would be one person, and consequently now from three: God, soul, and flesh.”

Since the holy Fathers teach us these things and point out both rules of expression to us, let those who judge without favor toward either party at last see and recognize which position can be the safer: whether that which confesses in Christ, the Son of God, one substance of the Word and another substance of the human being, understanding the human being as the whole from a part; or that which properly confesses that the whole human being was united to the Word of God in two substances.

In the former position, which wishes the human being to be understood as a whole from a part, the deceit of heretics can lie concealed: by naming one of these substances, someone may suppress the other, and thus what he does not confess with his mouth he may not confess in his heart. Such was Apollinaris, who denied that the Lord Jesus possessed a human soul, and Manichaeus, who denied the reality of the body assumed in Christ.

In our confession, however, where, after the substance of the Word has first been stated, we expressly confess the two substances of the human being in the one person of Christ, no fraudulent deceit can arise or even be suspected, since the whole human being assumed by God is proclaimed openly.

The safer position, therefore, is the one that states the whole rather than the one that suppresses something; and what is said properly is clearer than what is formed by a restricted tropical expression.

[Note: B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: *firmatur* (“is strengthened”) instead of *formatur* (“is formed”).]

But perhaps we alone say this, without proving it by the judgment of our predecessors. Let us therefore, if it pleases you, call Augustine as judge and hear which position he declares to be more secure against heretics. Thus he says in his treatise on the Creed:

“Heretics lay snares for the Lord’s temporal dispensation in many ways; but whoever holds the catholic faith, so as to believe that the whole human being was assumed by the Word of God—that is, body, soul, and spirit—is sufficiently protected against them.”

Behold: the spiritual man, considering both matters spiritually, has delivered his judgment and fixed his decision, declaring that position more secure and safer which defends against heretics the whole human being assumed by the Word of God in two substances, flesh and soul.

But perhaps someone may say that here three elements of the human being have been named: body, soul, and spirit. Three are indeed mentioned, but they are two, as the same teacher demonstrates in the aforesaid treatise on the Creed. He says:

“There are three things of which a human being consists: spirit, soul, and body. These are again said to be two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit; for a certain part of that same rational faculty, which beasts do not possess, is called spirit.”

He also explains this clearly in his letter to Peter, showing that spirit and soul are both one and are understood to belong to one substance. For he says that soul and spirit are two things according to the statement: “You have delivered my soul from my spirit”; and that both belong to human nature, so that the whole human being is spirit, soul, and body. Yet sometimes these two are named together under the name “soul,” as in the statement: “And man was made into a living soul”; for there the spirit too is understood.

Likewise, sometimes both are called by the name “spirit,” as in the statement: “And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit,” where the soul too must necessarily be understood; and both are one and belong to one substance.

Accordingly, it is not soul and spirit but soul and body that are the two distinct substances of the human being, which are also said to be different.

Therefore, in the work on our faith already mentioned, responding to the heresy of the Apollinarists, we spoke of three substances in Christ. We show that our predecessors taught the same, honoring and following the judgment of that distinguished teacher, the bishop of the see of Hispalis, who discussed in his books *On the Difference of Christ’s Nature and Ours* and said:

“We subsist from two substances, namely body and soul; he from three, namely the Word, body, and soul. Hence he is proclaimed both perfect man and perfect God.”

These, then, are a few examples drawn from the Fathers, so that we might briefly demonstrate what is relevant. Whoever seeks these matters more intently by further reading will be able to gather many more.

But if someone, with shameless arrogance, refuses to yield even to these Fathers and insolently asks from what sources they drew these statements, let him at least believe the evangelical utterances by which Christ himself declares that these three substances are present in him.

For when he was asked by the Jews, “Who are you?” he replied: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you.” Behold, you have one substance, that of divinity, and the two substances of the human being remain.

To show that he had assumed true human flesh, he offered himself to be touched by the disciples, saying: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” Behold, the substance of human flesh is expressed.

Likewise, to show that he had assumed the substance of a human soul, he said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again.”

Behold, we all confess with one voice and proclaim with a settled declaration that three substances—namely divinity and humanity—were united without confusion and inseparably in the one person of Christ. In accordance with the Council of Chalcedon, we confess that the same Lord Jesus Christ is perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity, true God and true man; the same consisting of a rational soul and a body; according to divinity, of one nature with the Father; according to humanity, the same of one nature with us, like us in all things except sin; begotten before the ages from the Father according to divinity, but in these last days, for us and for our salvation, the same begotten according to humanity from Mary the Virgin, the Mother of God; one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the distinction of the natures in no way being abolished because of the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and the two coming together in one person and one status; not divided or separated into two persons, but one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ.

If anyone after this, instead of accepting instruction, should oppose himself to the reasoning that has been given, he will incur the condemnation of the council mentioned above.

As we examine the third and fourth chapters, we have shown that we drew not only their meaning but almost their very words from the books of blessed Ambrose and Fulgentius. We know that the aforementioned men taught these doctrines. Since the churches of God throughout the world count them among their celebrated teachers, we must not be angry with them but rather yield to them, because whatever is thought against them is perceived to depart from the rule of right faith.

Moreover, when we were urged to make the four particular chapters solidly grounded, we presented to that party, nearly two years ago, a book containing our response, in which we had gathered the catholic teaching of the Fathers and made clear what had been said by which teacher.

If, after this, they disagree even with the doctrines of the Fathers themselves from which these statements were taken, there is no longer any point in contending with them. Clinging directly to the footsteps of our predecessors, our response will, by divine judgment, be exalted among lovers of truth, even if ignorant rivals judge it unlearned.

Having thus completed these matters concerning the profession of the holy faith, we turn to examine the sequence of those conditions by whose bonds the aforementioned prince had declared himself bound.

For at the time when Ervig, the prince of blessed memory, substituted our present lord, King Egica, for himself in marriage to his daughter, he first bound him with these obligations. Accordingly, proclaiming them clearly and having first examined the text of those same conditions, we found there certain impossible bonds of oath attached, so difficult that the mind of the one who swore would scarcely be free from their binding even if it were removed from the cares and anxieties of the kingdom.

Among the other clauses of the interwoven obligations, their evident connection was expressed in these words:

“With regard to my relatives, your sons, whom you appear to have begotten by your glorious wife, my lady Queen Liuvigoto, I promise to present and to be to them as a dear friend, in sincere affection of mind and without deceitful guile; and I promise to live with them in affection, tenderness, and charity throughout all the days of my life, so that at no time, for any matter, arrangement, or occasion whatsoever, may I trouble or harass either them or any one of them. Nor will I henceforth retain or devise any grief or malice in my heart or mind against them, nor nourish any occasion or pretext by which either your aforesaid servant and my betrothed, or your aforementioned sons, who have been begotten by your most merciful wife, my lady Queen Liuvigoto, may be disturbed or harassed, whether greatly or slightly, except for the most just causes whose legal truth may become clear to me. In such cases I reserve to myself the freedom to investigate them with an affection of charity toward those same relatives.

“Nevertheless, I shall never withdraw from the most ready affection and charity toward them. For in their causes, whether they themselves have them against any persons or anyone should bring a matter against them, I shall rise up and take action on behalf of your sons, with the full intention of my mind, for as long as I live, insofar as I am able and God grants me the power, as though it were for my own cause, so that they may suffer no loss or destruction whatsoever, and so that their affairs, with God’s help, through my attention, action, and prosecution, may swiftly reach their conclusion,” and so forth.

Having read these conditions, which Ervig, the prince of blessed memory, had exacted from our present prince solely for the protection of his sons, other conditions arising from a common obligation now present themselves for reconsideration. To these conditions the aforementioned prince Egica, after ascending to the kingdom, rendered the vows of his oaths to God when he promised to administer justice to the peoples and swore by the testimony of an oath that he would injure no one contrary to justice.

The first sequence of those conditions, therefore, appears to be greatly opposed to these second conditions. [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except A, the reading is *pertractanda* (“to be considered”).]

How, indeed, will he rise up to plead the cause of his relatives and grant the palm of justice to those contending against them if he himself defends his judgment against them, or if, as he swore, he is himself the one bringing the case? Who will be expected to bring the judgment to an end? Or how will he keep the oaths given to the peoples, so that he does not oppress anyone contrary to justice, as he promised, if he provides such extensive assistance and protection to his relatives while their affairs appear to reach a conclusion through his own prosecution?

For, as has already been said above, it is clear that the aforementioned prince swore that their affairs should reach a conclusion through his own attention and prosecution.

Thus, as we observed the prince bound by the obligations of both parties, we understood that both promises could not be fulfilled without blame by the same person at the same time. Yet, if the matter is carefully considered, he is shown to have been released from those first conditions when he was compelled to swear these second conditions to the peoples, since both were completed by one and the same author of compulsion.

Accordingly, after weighing the claims of both conditions and considering them through the common deliberation of all, we found that in the conditions to which our prince is known first to have sworn to his father-in-law, only the advantages of private right had been considered; whereas in these conditions the vows of honorable right had been promised.

There, before the kingdom, fidelity was exacted for the protection of one household; here, after the accession to the kingdom, blameless vows were promised for the governance of the peoples. There, private affection was extended for the defense of sons; here, general concern for the fatherland and nation is promised. That oath, perhaps offensive to many, would benefit only one household; whereas this one, preserving a general commitment to equity in every individual case, will give no party the destruction of truth.

What, then, follows from the just conclusion of the dispute between the two? Surely the safety of the few must not be the destruction of the many; nor should the advantage of a private matter have as much force as the general relief of the peoples. Far be it from us.

Since, therefore, that oath considered the preference of private persons, whereas this one provides general protection for the peoples, let divine judgment disclose which of the two ought rather to be observed. For it is written in the Proverbs of Solomon: “To show partiality in judgment is not good.” Christ likewise says in the Gospel: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment.” And the Apostle Paul specifically establishes the principle for these matters: “Let us not seek what is useful for ourselves, but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved.”

It is now evident what, in salutary piety, outweighs the two. Therefore, the promises sworn for the welfare of the fatherland will remain inviolate more than those promised solely for the advantage of one household.

We do not say this in such a way that the promises previously sworn on behalf of the relatives are entirely destroyed. Rather, the same affection must be preserved toward both peoples and relatives: something unified, breathing the grace of unity, must divide neither, but reconcile them.

For both cannot be preserved separately on an equal scale of observance. If the fidelity promised to the relatives is maintained, what was promised to the peoples will perish; and again, if the sacred pledges given to God on behalf of the peoples are kept inviolate, the benefits promised to the relatives will undoubtedly be denied. The fulfillment of one side cannot occur without the loss of the other.

What, then? Must both promises of the oaths be dissolved because each cannot be carried out without fault independently of the other? Far be it from us. One must therefore be transferred into the other and brought under a single rule, so that the vows of the lesser party may be joined to those of the greater, and the affection of protection that was privately promised to the father-in-law and his relatives may be preserved in a general form toward the peoples.

This is not so that the promised fidelity on either side may suffer loss, but so that, joined and transferred into one another, they may together gain the benefit of protection.

Therefore, through the Spirit of God, we declare and establish this judgment, with him speaking in us who promised that he would be present in the midst of those gathered in his name.

Thus the holy synod chose that our prince, King Egica, should be released from the bonds of the oath by which he had previously sworn to his father-in-law, in such a way that he should either direct his relatives according to the rule governing the peoples or take the peoples into the just protection owed to his relatives. Treating both as though they were the children of one father and one family, and summoning both into one affection, he must neither interpose the favor of the peoples in the just affairs of his relatives nor again attempt to favor his relatives in the complaints of the peoples.

The same fidelity must be preserved in the affairs both of the peoples and of the relatives. He must not choose to treat his relatives with a different affection from the peoples, so that, walking on the straight path of equity in the kingdom bestowed upon him from heaven, he may neither incur the stain of profanation toward either side nor close the inward organs of compassion against either party.

A second matter for reconsideration was then brought before our assembly, concerning those conditions which the aforementioned prince Ervig compelled the peoples of his entire kingdom to swear for the protection of his sons.

After examining and considering them for a very long time, we found nothing there opposed to equity and nothing contrary to piety. Only opportunities for malice are cut off; the access to just cases is not excluded. The one thing specifically promised there to be observed is what the Lord commands generally of every Christian: namely, that malice be avoided, innocence be preserved undefiled, the intention to harm be frustrated, and a lawful and just case be admitted.

If this is observed according to the common law for all, the royal offspring will be preserved unharmed from injury, and truth will be restored to the peoples without the profanation of perjury.

For it was not sworn there that no one should assist those bringing a case against his sons, or that no one should obtain a judgment of equity against them. The aforementioned prince not only granted each person access to present his own case judicially, but also permitted any crimes committed by his sons, should any occur, to be punished according to the laws.

What, therefore, was not sworn there, yet is shamelessly asserted to have been sworn, did not summon the peoples into the crime of perjury, since it is not seen to be bound by the wording of the conditions. We must not restrain what we do not find to have been restrained in those conditions.

Nevertheless, malice must be abandoned and appropriate cases must be pursued. Nor should attention be paid to the imprudent loquacity of certain people, who shamelessly attempt to assert that only those who appear to have brought their own cases are free from the crime of perjury, whereas those who undertake to judge such cases or assist such proceedings on behalf of equity are entangled in an inexpiable crime of profanation.

They say these things, making more noise through contentiousness than through reason, evidently unaware that, if access to judging had been denied there, access to presenting a case would also have been denied. But the person who admitted a just case did not wish to cut off judgment of the equity that had been presented; nor did the person who admitted the one bringing the case deprive the judges of the power to judge justly.

It is therefore a great expression of folly to think or speak in this way. On the contrary, throughout almost the entire sequence of divine Scripture, judges are more strongly commanded to judge justly than peoples are commanded to present their cases. Scripture says: “Judge justly, sons of men,” and it does not add: “Present your cases justly, sons of men.”

Since it admonished judges to judge justly, did it therefore forbid the peoples to present their cases? Did it therefore say nothing about presenting cases? Is a form of judgment constructed concerning one who is thought to be mute and without a case presented?

Therefore, neither judgments can exist without cases being brought nor cases without judges, so that either the judge would be absent from the person bringing the case or the person bringing the case would in some way be absent from the judge.

Accordingly, the conditions themselves, in which neither truth has been cut off nor the inner organs of piety severed, will not condemn either those who present cases justly to the sacrilege of perjury or those who judge justly to the guilt of profanation.

Having thus given our reasoning, we conclude that no one is bound by the aforementioned sequence of conditions as culpable if, after rejecting malice, he brings before judges for judgment a case owed to him against the party of the aforementioned prince Ervig of pious memory; nor is anyone culpable who accepts the mandates of such persons, or any witness, informer, or advocate who gives testimony, or the judges themselves who justly bring such cases to a conclusion, or even those who simply support the party possessing justice, hastening rather to relieve the wretched than taking pleasure in being harmful to any party.

For it is written: “Piety is useful for all things.” Nor should one cease from the work of mercy, since that covenant did not forbid it. Since access to justice is not denied there, it follows that piety must not be denied either. For he does not fully love justice who does not extend piety to his neighbor.

Thus, preserving the affection of unshaken piety, we have chosen to observe that apostolic command which expressly says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

[Note: B. R.: *enim* (“for”) instead of *atque* (“and”); from this word onward a folio is missing, containing the remaining material pertaining to this council and the beginning of the following one.]

Having established this reasoning, and after the persons and the claims of each individual had been released and distinguished, we admitted the cases themselves that were to be brought against the party of the aforementioned prince Ervig of pious memory or against his sons. We determined that the justice designated by the laws and canons should remain unshaken among the judges, both for those bringing charges and for those responding.

Having completed these matters, which were concluded with a peaceful settlement, we give glory and honor to God alone, asking his most abundant mercy that his strength and power may loosen the bonds of our minds and grant our prince Egica, the glorious lover of Christ, happily [the text has *felicem* for *felix*] to retain the scepter of the kingdom, to direct the course of a happier life, and to maintain a long-lasting rule over the peoples in peace—he who grants this, who is the King of all kings and whose kingdom endures forever and ever. Amen.

## Law in confirmation of the general council, in the first year of the reign of our glorious prince Egica

Favoring the distinguished synodal acts of our time, by which we have drawn an abundance of sacred teaching concerning the faith and have learned that the chain of an indissoluble oath has been broken, we decree by a law promulgated for this purpose that the very things established with the unshakable force of the canons shall be observed by everyone with the greatest care and diligence.

But if anyone should wish to oppose these same decisions, he shall be fined a tenth part of his property and shall moreover be struck by the sentence of excommunication.

I, Julian, metropolitan bishop of the royal city, have subscribed these canonical statutes [Col. 0524C]. I, Suniefredus, bishop of the see of Narbonne, have subscribed these canonical statutes.

[Note: [Col. 0523D] E. 4, T. 1, 2 add *metropolitan bishop of the see*; in the same manuscripts the dignity of metropolitan is likewise assigned to the four bishops who follow. It should also be observed that the episcopal subscriptions do not preserve the same order in all manuscripts.]
