# SIXTY-FIRST: THE SIXTEENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO

Sixty-one bishops. Era 731.

[Col. 0527] [Note: [Col. 0527D] Everything preceding the canons in this council is absent from A. and Ae. It has been taken from Codex B. R., with the variant readings of the other manuscripts. In E. 3 this entire council is missing.]

[Col. 0527A] In the sixth year of the illustrious and orthodox lord and our prince Egica, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the era 731, when our assembly of unanimity had gathered and was meeting in the Praetorian Basilica, namely that of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and each of us, according to custom and in accordance with the time of his ordination, was seated in his proper place, we first rendered to the Lord, with the deepest devotion, the due offerings of thanksgiving for the fact that he had permitted us to be enlightened by the sight of one another and had established us in mutual peace by cherishing us with the kiss of concord. With our hearts and voices poured out together, we offered him the murmuring of our prayers, asking that, just as he had made us rejoice through the giving of mutual kisses, so he might establish in the faith, fortify with the extension of justice, enrich with abundant peace, support with the bestowal of mercy, and strengthen with the power of his might the most serene and religious prince Egica, whose command had brought together the assembly of our brotherhood; so that, renowned for the gifts of long life, he might hold the reins of the kingdom entrusted to him with prudent moderation, and rule the peoples committed to him kindly, govern them equitably, and regulate them according to the command of piety.

When these acts of the most ready devotion had been completed, our numerous assembly began to pour forth a mutual exchange concerning spiritual matters; and it awaited the outcome of the proceedings with the utmost gentleness.

As these matters were being conducted with attention, that same most excellent prince, relying upon the protection of holy purpose, filled with religion and renowned for the distinction of his most diligent labors, entered our assembly. Inclining the crown of his glorious head in a reverent vow, he judged that he should commend himself to the Lord through our prayers, bringing in his own hands a volume for us to open, in which the vows of his devotion and the desires of his pious deliberation had been set down in most gracious writing. Exhorting all collectively with the sweetly flowing utterances of his mouth, he said:

“Behold, most reverent priests of divine worship, whatever I was bound to communicate to your sacred minds by the utterance of my own mouth, and whatever an extensive address might have expressed through a lengthy outpouring of speech, I have arranged here briefly and in summary with a running pen. Therefore, having first tasted these words attentively, consider them with eager minds; and whatever is contained here, as well as anything else that may present itself for hearing to your most reverent assembly, bring to completion through the fairest definitions of your judgments, and decree that it shall endure through the firmest writing of your decisions.”

Our unanimity received the volume from him and blessed the same prince. When he had departed from our midst, we opened the contents of that volume, whose text is set out below in the following sequence.

## In the name of the Lord, Flavius Egica, king, to the most holy Fathers seated in this holy synod

[Col. 0528A]

“Most blessed Fathers, the glorious exaltation of our serenity knows that the efforts of synodal convocations oppose the ruin of a wavering age and provide the faithful peoples with the appropriate discipline of a salutary life. Therefore, moved by the devotion of orthodox faith and made happier by your desirable assembly, I render thanks and offerings of praise to the King of heaven, because the awaited gathering of your assembly has most devotedly obeyed the commands of our order and has granted us the desired joys of seeing one another.

Accordingly, standing before you and earnestly asking that heavenly clemency support me through your prayers, I address the whole of your holiness with Christian devotion of mind: since you stand in worthy contemplation of the holy Catholic Church, be supporters of my vows and, through the merits of your pontificate, prepare for me greater assistance in governing the peoples and bring me the nourishment of wholesome counsel. Thus, supported by the aid of your holiness, I may complete the course of my reign in peace and rule the people subject to me with pious and prudent moderation.

For I desire that you be present in this holy council in such a manner that the grace of the Holy Spirit, irradiating your hearts, may be among you, so that, with him as teacher, you may hold and preserve those things through which divine assistance may always come both to me, who am burdened above all others by many sins, and to the whole people entrusted to my rule.

How greatly the earth is daily scourged by evils that provoke God’s indignation, and by how many blows it wastes away through the crimes of the faithless, I do not think is unknown to your fatherhood. But since we undoubtedly believe that, through our transgression of God’s commandments, we receive what our deeds deserve, as the Lord says through the prophet, ‘Therefore the earth shall mourn, and everyone who dwells in it shall grow weak,’ it is most fitting that, through you, who by the proclamation of the divine voice are the salt of the earth, it should obtain the help of salvation.

Therefore I exhort the venerable whole of your holiness: first, let the rectitude of the life-giving faith, which through true belief is spread and extended throughout the entire world, be proclaimed in the words of your deliberation, be held once it has been truthfully preached, and, once retained, be preserved undefiled in the secret place of your heart.

Next, since we have learned that many basilicas of God, established in scattered places throughout your parishes, are assigned to the administration of a single priest, while the sacrifices offered to the Lord are not celebrated in them regularly, and they are left abandoned and are known to be roofless or half-ruined, record specifically in your canons that every church, however poor, which is able to possess ten dependents [*mancipia*], ought to be governed under the care of its own priest; but if it has fewer, it shall belong to the priest of another church.

For when, as we have said, very many basilicas are reduced to the responsibility of one person, the result is only that they remain deprived of care and that the proper order of sacred worship is maintained only with difficulty. This is not merely a fault among the priests of God; it also provides the unbelieving Jews with an occasion for ridicule. They say that their synagogues were indeed forbidden and destroyed, but that nothing has been accomplished by this prohibition, since they see the basilicas of Christians becoming worse than their own.

With regard also to their repair, your assembly should decree that each bishop diligently ensure that they are canonically restored from one-third of the revenues of the parish basilicas. If he does not wish to obtain that third, it must nevertheless be arranged that the priest of the ruined church repair the basilica entrusted to him. In the canon, establish a clear measure of discipline specifying how any negligent bishop is to be condemned if he neglects to fulfill the prescribed order for renewing the temples of God.

Let your honor also promulgate this: no bishop shall touch the rights of parish churches in order to provide the requisitions demanded by the king, nor shall he dare to exact from them any requisitions or transport services. Instead, he shall furnish the royal authority the customary services of requisition from the estates belonging to his own see, and he shall presume to give nothing from the property of those parish churches as a stipend for any purpose. If he does so, let him know that he is to be excommunicated for a period of two months.

[Col. 0529C] In the meantime, you must make it your particular concern that, wherever you find idolatry or various errors of diabolical superstition, or learn of them through any report, you rise as true worshipers of Christ, together with the judges, as quickly as possible to destroy such a crime. Whatever you find being brought to those same idols by peasants or by any other persons, you shall transfer in its entirety for distribution among the neighboring churches.

For the eradication of this crime, also insert such an edict in your regulations that any bishop who permits such wickedness to be practiced, or delays immediately abolishing it once it has been practiced in his diocese, shall be driven from his office and remain bound for the course of one year under the lament of penance. Another person, appointed there by royal choice, shall meanwhile be installed who can preserve the order of this institution and open for the Christian people the path of good conduct; afterward the bishop shall return to the order of his own see.

But, what is more important than these matters, in your zeal for God root out entirely the perfidy of the Jews of both sexes, so that the force of our laws—those previously issued because of their perfidy as well as those enacted in the present time—may remain fully upheld, and so that the excesses [E. 4, T. 1, 2: *accesses*] of their wickedness may perish through the sanction of those same laws. Likewise, in accordance with the edict of our new law, let none of those Jews who persist in their perfidy approach the *cataplus* [trading place or marketplace] for the conduct of any business, nor dare to engage in any commerce with Christians. Thus you may rightly say with the prophet: ‘Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies?’

But if, from these Hebrews or from their wives and children, anyone should henceforth be found converted to the rule of the Catholic faith with complete devotion—renouncing entirely the errors of ancestral transgression, all ceremonies, and every sect of parental rites—let that person remain stripped of every burden of public service which, previously appointed while in error, he was accustomed to discharge for the public utilities. In the case of the other unbelievers, however, let the obligation of payment be imposed upon them, since the unspeakable obstinacy of their ancestry still holds them fast.

Among the other matters, decree also that the shameful crime of men who engage in sexual relations with males be eradicated. Their dreadful conduct both stains the grace of an honorable life and provokes the wrath of the heavenly Avenger.

And since many of the faithless, devoted to the buskin of pride, are recognized as seeking royal eminence not from God but solely through the swelling of vainglory, whoever henceforth among the palatine officials, whatever his rank or honor, attempts to plot the death of the king, the destruction of the Gothic people and homeland, or tries to stir up any disturbance within the boundaries of Spain, both he himself and all his posterity shall be expelled from every palace office and shall forever serve the fisc under the burden of tribute. Moreover, he shall lose all his own possessions, which our royal clemency may freely grant to whomever it wishes.

Bring back to the clear light of truth everything that is found corrupted in the canons or in the edicts of the laws, or that plainly appears to have been inserted superfluously or improperly, with the consent of our serenity assisting you. Beyond doubt, reserve those provisions of the laws which, from the time of our predecessor of divine memory, our lord King Chindaswinth, down to the time of our lord Wamba, are known to have been drawn up according to reason and to pertain to sincere justice or the adequate conduct of affairs.

Let the various affairs of the peoples, and the other deeds of criminal men contrary to the holy faith, be brought to an end through your canonical and legal examination and judgment in such a way that justice is not passed over and the severity of the laws does not intrude in every case. Thus, when the love of Christ has made you fervent in all these things and the chain of equity has bound you together, you will remain conspicuous not only in this age through the gift of holiness, but you will also flourish forever in eternal rewards.

For I believe that I, together with the people entrusted to me, am then cleansed from sins by the Lord, when the examination of your judgment in the investigation of cases has preceded in such a manner that it deviates from the path of truth in no respect.

This alone we adjure you, honorable priests of God, and all the illustrious elders of the royal court whom the command of our serenity or a timely occasion has caused to be present at this council: by the inseparable power of almighty God, when the aforesaid matters that arise for hearing before your assembly are being settled, let no respect of persons or acceptance of gifts intervene, let no favor insert itself, and let no negligence born of tepidity obstruct the promulgation of the justice that is God’s.

Rather, settling the disputes of the cases with the pure balance of examination and setting the just judgments of God before your eyes, strive to reveal equity to each party, so that through this you may obtain for our gentleness the rewards of recompense awaited from God, be honorable before us because of the uprightness of your judgment, and always prevail before God through the grace of good works.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year, happily, of the reign of our gentleness, at Toledo.”

After the volume had been opened and we had carefully examined each part of its contents, the hidden places of our hearts boiled over with an immense mass of joy. Therefore, with minds made more fervent, we gladly strengthen the hymns of our songs in praise of our God, because he has made the inmost heart of our most religious and orthodox prince so fervent with the fire of his love that he considered it fitting to exhort the entire college of our assembly with the wisest and most salutary breathings of his mouth.

He most kindly admonished us that, like worthy watchmen, we should bring the ship of the Church of God—which, by heavenly dispensation, we have undertaken to steer amid the whirlpools of this vast sea—safely to the harbor of complete salvation by the steering-oars of salutary rowing, and devote ourselves daily to its defense, watching and keeping the night watches over the flocks entrusted to us.

Thus indeed, with the trumpets of spiritual words sounding and with the members’ joints sound [T. 1, 2: *compages*, “frameworks”], lest it, weighed down by the torpor of security, fall into the snare of various downfalls, we must continually provide it with salutary protections. To the weakened limbs, wounded as they are by various injuries of illness, we must apply suitable medicines, so that the aged ulcers may more easily be torn out by the roots and they may obtain the remedies of the desired salvation.

But now, since we see that none of us is capable of fulfilling these things without the assistance of the all-powerful Trinity, we therefore judge it sufficiently evident and necessary that, since one believes with the heart unto justice, while confession with the mouth is made unto salvation, we should proclaim by the confession of our own mouth the mystery of that Holy Trinity, which is one God, from whom we ought to ask that we may deserve to become worthy shepherds of his Church. And, as with mortal mouths, we should prelude the insignia of his praises as far as he himself commands, so that all the definitions issued by our devotion may remain unshaken, set upon the firmest foundation, and supported by the strength of justice, enduring through infinite ages.

[Col. 0531D] We believe and confess the undivided Trinity to be the creator and sustainer of all creatures, which are contained within the threefold structure of things: namely, the Father, who is the fountain and origin of the whole divinity; the Son, who is the full image of God because the Father’s glory is unitedly expressed in him, ineffably begotten from the Father’s inmost being before the beginning of all ages; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds without any beginning from the Father and the Son. These three, although distinguished by the distinction of their persons, are nevertheless never separated in the majesty of their power: indeed, their divinity is shown to possess inseparable equality. Yet although the Father begot the Son, the Son is therefore not the same person as the Father, nor is the Father himself the Son, [Col. 0532A] nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son, 563 but he is solely the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also coequal with the Father and the Son.

In this holy Trinity it is in no way fitting to believe that anything is created, servile, or enslaved, nor is it proper to suppose that anything is adventitious or introduced from outside, as though something had at some time happened to it that it plainly had not previously possessed. Accordingly, we confess in the Catholic faith that God the Father is omnipotent, that the Son likewise is God omnipotent, and that the Holy Spirit also is God omnipotent. Yet we do not believe in three Gods or three omnipotent beings, but with the unshaken truth of faith we believe in one God alone: one in nature, one in essence, one in omnipotence, one in majesty, and one in power.

Although no separability can be found among these persons in what pertains to themselves, nevertheless, in what pertains to distinction, there are certain things that can belong more particularly to each individual person: namely, that the Father derives his origin from no one; that the Son exists through the Father’s begetting; and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the union of the Father and the Son. But is the Son, because he was begotten from the omnipotence of the Father, or the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, therefore to be thought to have existed at some time when the Father was without the Son, or when the Begetter and the Begotten existed without the substance of the Holy Spirit? Far be it.

Rather, just as the Father is believed to be without beginning, so the Son is revered, and so also the Holy Spirit is truthfully confessed. Yet, just as the Father is believed by everyone to derive the origin of his existence from no one, so the Son and the Holy Spirit are not to be thought to exist from themselves. Rather, the Son, God, is from the Father, God—not the Father, God, from the Son, God—nor are the Father or the Son to be thought to have received their origin from the Holy Spirit without blame, since he himself is believed to have proceeded without beginning from the Father and the Son, without any stain of unbelief.

Therefore, in the mystery of this holy Trinity nothing is to be believed to be earlier or later, because there was never a time when the Father subsisted without the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor when the Son reigned with the Father without the Holy Spirit. In saying these things, we neither confuse the properties of the persons nor separate the unity of substance. Nothing in this same holy Trinity should be believed to be greater or lesser, nor anything imperfect or changeable. For the Father is perfect, the Son is perfect, and the Holy Spirit is perfect; the Father is immutable, the Son is immutable, and the Holy Spirit is immutable. For it was neither fitting nor acceptable to believe that a mutable and imperfect Son was born from the immutable and perfect Father.

Accordingly, there are certain things that ought to be confessed without distinction in this holy Trinity. In what pertains to themselves, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be believed without distinction as one God—the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit. But insofar as what is relative is concerned, the property of the three persons must be proclaimed distinctly, as the Evangelist declares: “Go, teach all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

That is called relative which refers one person to another. For when “Father” is said, the person of the Son is nevertheless indicated, [Col. 0533A] and when “Son” is said, the Father is without doubt shown to be present in relation to him. But since the designation “Holy Spirit” does not signify the whole Trinity, but the third person who exists in the Trinity, it is by no means equally clear how, in a relative sense, he refers to the person of the Father and the Son. For although we say “the Holy Spirit of the Father,” we do not correspondingly say “the Father of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Son be understood to be the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, in other designations by which the person of that same Holy Spirit is signified, he is recognized as belonging to the relative category.

Accordingly, we understand the gift to be specifically the Holy Spirit, who is known to be the third person in the holy Trinity, because he is bestowed by the Father and the Son, with whom the faithful believe him to be in every respect of one essence. Therefore, when “the gift of the giver” and “the giver of the gift” are said, the relative character is unquestionably made clear. The same must rightly be believed concerning the designation “Holy Spirit” itself.

Finally, because we have thus far arranged in confession the mystery of the holy Trinity—not as fully as we ought, but insofar as he himself has granted us to do so—we shall now set forth, in the sequence that follows, which person of that Trinity assumed flesh. Although the works of the Trinity are inseparable, we nevertheless faithfully confess, not only by faith of heart but also by profession of mouth, that it was not the whole unity that assumed flesh, but the Son of God alone. He was begotten before the ages from the substance of God the Father and, at the end of the ages, was born from the Virgin Mary, as the Gospel bears witness when it says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among [Col. 0533C] us.”

For the archangel Gabriel, sent from heaven to the Virgin Mary, said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Emmanuel.” When Mary, as Saint Ambrose says, neither refusing belief nor declining the duty, but rather offering her devotion and promising obedience, and not doubting that it would happen but asking about the manner in which it would happen, said to him, “How will this happen, since I have not known a man?”, the angel replied to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

When this angelic oracle says that the Holy Spirit would come upon her and foretells that the power of the Most High—who is the Son of God the Father—would overshadow her, it shows that the whole Trinity cooperated in the flesh of that same Son. Just as this Virgin preserved the modesty of virginity before conception, so after childbirth she experienced no violation of her integrity: for she conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and after childbirth retained without interruption the modesty of incorruption.

The mystery of this conception or birth, because according to the prophetic oracle something new was created upon the earth, so that a woman alone and uniquely, without intercourse with a man, would enclose a man within her, cannot be comprehended by any reasoning or expressed by the utterance of any mouth. For this reason John the Baptist solemnly confesses: “Behold, he who comes after me was made before me, whose shoe-latchet I am not worthy to loose.” It is as though he were saying: “I cannot loose the shoe-latchet of the divinity that has been shod, which is the bond of the mystery, because I am wholly unable to investigate how the Word was embodied in a virginal womb, or how that same Word, having become flesh, exists as an animate being.”

For this reason the most eminent Father Augustine said: “If a reason is sought here, it is no longer wonderful; if an example is demanded, it will not be unique.” The Son of God himself, begotten from the unbegotten Father—true from the true, perfect from the perfect, one from the one, whole from the whole—God without beginning, plainly assumed a perfect human being from holy and inviolate Mary, ever virgin.

And just as we ascribe to him the perfection of humanity, so also we believe that he possesses two wills: one of his divinity and another of our humanity. This is made most clearly evident by the words of our Redeemer in the oracles of the four Evangelists. Thus he said: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” And again: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me,” along with the other passages which, if we chose to gather them from all the books of the holy Scriptures, we would seem to weave, on the loom of our speech, a fabric of immeasurable length.

By these declarations he also shows that he referred his own will to the humanity he assumed, and the Father’s will to the divinity in which he is one and equal with the Father. For insofar as the unity of divinity is concerned, the Father does not have one will and the Son another; there is one will wherever one divinity persists. But insofar as the nature of the humanity assumed is concerned, there is one will of his divinity and another of our humanity.

Therefore, when he says, “Not as I will, but as you will,” he plainly shows that he did not will that what he was expressing through the affection of his humanity should happen, but that which he had descended to earth to accomplish by the Father’s will. Yet the will of that Father is in no way contrary to the will of the Son, because those who possess one divinity cannot possess different wills. And where no difference can occur in nature, nevertheless 566 various things are generally enumerated.

Accordingly, although the term “will,” through the comparative likeness of the Trinity—where memory, understanding, and will are spoken of—is referred to the person of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, insofar as it is said of itself, it is predicated substantially. For the Father is will, the Son is will, and the Holy Spirit is will, just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. Many other similar expressions are likewise unquestionably spoken according to substance by those who are true worshipers of the Catholic faith.

And just as it is Catholic to say “God from God, light from light, illumination from illumination,” so true faith rightly asserts that will is from will, just as wisdom is from wisdom and essence from essence. And just as God the Father begot God the Son, so the Father, will, begot the Son, will.

Thus, although according to essence the Father is will, the Son is will, and the Holy Spirit is will, nevertheless they are not to be believed to be one according to the relative category. For one is the Father, who is referred to the Son; another is the Son, who is referred to the Father; and another is the Holy Spirit, who, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, is referred to the Father and the Son—not another thing, but another person. For those who are one in being according to the nature of divinity possess a particular property in the distinction of their persons.

Accordingly, the same Son of God, who, although he was rich, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, while the nature of his divinity remained incapable of suffering, willingly suffered in the substance of the humanity he assumed and endured the harsh punishment of the first death for us. Though he remained free from the guilt of any sin, he willingly ascended the cross, about to die for our sins. Though he had no taint of flesh and blood, in his flesh he endured for us scourges, blows, spitting, and a crown of thorns; and by the outpouring of his blood he washed the whole world from its filth.

And lest the second death have power over God’s elect, he struck and utterly destroyed it with the dart of his invulnerable divinity, as the prophet says: “O death, I shall be your death.” He penetrated Tartarus in his soul and, with the bite of his power, rescued the souls of the saints whom the enemy held bound there, so that the prophetic oracle might be fulfilled: “O hell, I shall be your sting.”

On the dawn of the third day, having truly resumed the same flesh in which he had died, he appeared to the eyes of his disciples and comforted [printed reading: *solatus est*, “comforted”] their hearts, shaken by immense fear, by the manifestation of his presence. In the presence of the assembled angels and believers, he returned to his native seat, where he now sits at the right hand of the Father, just as he truly rose from the dead. From there, at the end of the age, he will come to separate the righteous from sinners by the exercise of judicial power, restoring to the saints the crown due for their good deeds, but assigning the wicked the fire-breathing punishment of endless condemnation.

By his resurrection he gives us an example: just as he who gives us life rose alive from the dead after two days, on the third day, so let us believe without hesitation that we too shall rise at the end of this age—not in the shadow of an airy or phantasmal vision, as the reprehensible opinion of certain people teaches, but in the true substance of the flesh in which we now are and live.

At the time of judgment, standing before Christ and his holy angels, each person will give an account of his own bodily deeds, according to what he has done, whether good or evil, and will receive from him either the kingdom of unending blessedness for his own acts or the destruction of everlasting condemnation for his crimes.

Washed in the water of baptism and redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, the holy Catholic Church of this faith—whose faith bears no wrinkle and whose works bear no mark of stain—is endowed with eminent distinctions, is renowned for virtues [T. 2: *claruit*, “has shone forth”], and sparkles, filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Together with Jesus Christ our Lord, her head, whose body she is beyond all doubt, she will reign forever.

But all those who do not now belong to her or who shall not belong to her, who have departed from her or shall depart from her, or who, through the evil of unbelief, deny that sins can be forgiven within her—unless they return to her through the aid of repentance and do not believe, without any stain of doubt, what the Nicene Synod decreed should be observed, what the assembly at Constantinople established should be venerated, what the authority of the First Council of Ephesus sanctioned should be embraced, and what the unanimity of the holy fathers at Chalcedon and of the other councils, as well as the decrees of all venerable Fathers who lived rightly in sound faith, commands to be preserved—will be punished by the sentence of everlasting condemnation and, at the end of the age, will be burned with the devil and his companions in fiery furnaces.

Having disclosed the mystery of the holy faith by the confession of our mouth, let us now bend the attention of our unanimity toward the chapters necessary for regulating ecclesiastical discipline and correcting the conduct of those who err; and let us define in decreed chapters what is appropriate.

## I. On the perfidy of the Jews

[Note: [Col. 0535D] From this title onward, Codices A and Ae begin writing.]

Although numerous judgments and laws promulgated by the ancient Fathers shine forth in condemnation of the perfidy of the Jews, nevertheless, because—as the prophetic oracle declares concerning their hardness—the sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus on a diamond claw, they have become harder than stone and persist in the blindness of their obstinacy. It is sufficiently evident that the wall of the Catholic Church is repeatedly battered by the engines of their unbelief, so that they may either at last be corrected against their will or be forcefully crushed [E. 4: “be forcefully crushed by the stylus”; T. 1, 2: “be forcefully crushed by the stylus”], destined to perish forever under the Lord’s judgment.

For it is the praiseworthy practice of experienced physicians to hasten with greater diligence, by the art of healing, to the aid of the sick who suffer from the afflictions of various diseases, until they receive the remedy of health. Indeed, since the fervent intention and ready devotion of our most glorious and Christ-loving prince Egica seek to apply the skill of this admirable remedy to them, so that they may either be converted to the faith or, if they persist in their perfidy, be continually punished by sharper goads, therefore, at his exhortation and command alike, our assembly of unanimity has chosen that whatever the judgments or laws of those who preceded us in the Catholic faith are known to contain for crushing their perfidy shall be most diligently carried out among them by all elders [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “priests.”] and all who hold judicial office. What we now establish shall likewise be preserved with the most fervent commitment.

Thus, whoever among them converts to Christ with wholehearted intention and preserves the Catholic faith without any taint of unbelief shall remain secure and exempt from every levy that they have customarily paid to the most sacred treasury, together with whatever possessions they may have. But those who persist in their unbelief shall pay that same contribution in full for public purposes.

Those who have been converted from their error shall devote themselves only to their own affairs, like the other freeborn, and, conducting their business, shall as true worshipers of Christ carry out whatever the prince commands them to provide for public assessments. For the order of equity demands that those who are adorned by the faith of Christ be regarded by everyone [Note: B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “by all people.”] as noble and honorable.

We confirm that law which, in the aforesaid chapters, our lord Prince Egica recently issued for crushing their obstinacy, and by the decree of this constitution we judge it to possess inviolable [Note: B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “unshakable.”] force.

## II. On the worshipers of idols

It is most plainly evident that the enemy of the human race, as the Apostle relates, runs roaring throughout the world, seeking whom he may devour. By various tricks of his deception he ensnares very many foolish people in his traps and never ceases to deceive them. Although the Lord commands, “You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above [Col. 0537B] or on earth beneath,” and so forth; and again, “You shall not make an idol or a graven image, nor set up pillars, nor place a conspicuous stone in your land to worship it”; and again, “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone,” they, deceived by various persuasions, become worshipers of idols: venerators of stones, kindlers of torches, cultivators of the sacred places of springs or trees, augurs or enchanters, and practitioners of many other things too lengthy to enumerate.

Since that enemy is neither their creator, nor their Lord, nor their redeemer, it is supremely fitting that the rulers of the Churches of God diligently strive to remove from his possession those whom the same enemy has subjected [B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “had subjected”] to himself through various sacrileges by his evil persuasion, and restore them to their creator.

Because many decrees of the holy Fathers concerning the eradication of such sacrileges shine forth in various councils, we examined them with vigilant discernment and weighed their ordinances with measured gravity. Since they rest upon the fullness of due reason, we establish and decree, with the consent and most fervent command of our most religious lord King Egica, that all bishops and priests, as well as those who preside over the adjudication of legal cases, keep careful watch.

Whenever, in any place, they find people venerating or performing the sacrileges mentioned above—or any others prohibited by divine law or restrained by the ordinances of the holy Fathers—whatever their race or condition, they must not delay immediately in correcting and eradicating them according to the tenor of the aforesaid judgments. Moreover, whatever has been offered in that place of sacrilege shall be presented forever in the neighboring churches, in the presence of those who had believed that it should be dedicated by this sacrilegious vow. [Col. 0537D]

If, however, a bishop, priest, or judge to whom that place belongs, already knowing of a manifest and fully proven act of sacrilege, neglects to correct it with ardent zeal, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his office and placed under penance for the space of one year. He shall later return to his office, with the provision that, during the same period in which he has been removed from his office, the prince shall specifically appoint someone in his place who, full of the fear of the Lord and inflamed with spiritual zeal like Phinehas, shall, together with the judges joined to him, as we have said, utterly eradicate the sacrilege they discover and restrain the Lord’s anger from the whole people.

But if anyone obstructs priests or judges in defense of such persons, so that they neither correct these practices as they ought nor eradicate them as is proper, and if he does not instead join them as an investigator, avenger, or eradicator of so great a crime, let him be anathema in the sight of the undivided Trinity. Moreover, if he is a noble person, let him pay three pounds of gold to the most sacred treasury; if he is of lower rank, he shall be beaten with a hundred lashes, disgracefully shorn, and half of his possessions shall be applied to the resources of the treasury.

## III. On sodomites

Just as purity of heart and body brings human beings close to God, so the practice of incestuous pollution makes them strangers to God. And just as, in the past, it handed over the peoples of Sodom—who had committed an appalling and utterly detestable deed—to be burned by fire descending from heaven, so the fire of eternal condemnation will consume those devoted to such impurities, as the Lord speaks through the prophet: “The garment mixed with blood shall be for burning, and food for the fire.”

But since this deadly act and the evil of sodomitical conduct are seen to have wounded many, we, all together, burning with the zeal of the Lord to eradicate the habit of this most shameful offense, decree that those who have been perpetrators of this wicked act, who have allowed themselves to become entangled in these disgraceful practices, and who have committed this abomination against nature, males upon males [printed reading: *operaverint*; corrected reading: *operati fuerint*, “have committed”], shall suffer the following penalty.

If the offender is a bishop, priest, or deacon, he shall be cast down from the rank of his office and remain struck by the condemnation of perpetual exile. If persons of any other order, rank, or condition are found entangled in the offenses of another kind of pollution, they shall likewise be struck by the sentence of the law enacted concerning such matters, excluded from the entire company of Christians, beaten with a hundred lashes, disgracefully shorn, and consigned to perpetual exile.

Unless fitting satisfaction through penance permits both those who are seen to have dishonored the practice of religion and the other persons of whatever rank, as we have said, to receive the body and blood of Christ at the end of their lives, or unless they return to the fellowship of Christians, they shall know that, on the day of their death, they will neither be restored to communion according to the ordinances of the canons nor admitted to the assembly of Catholics.

## IV. On those who despair

Priestly discipline must without doubt be promulgated for this purpose: both to cut away ingrained vices with the extremely sharp sickle of penance and to excise completely, through the effort of severe treatment, the ulcer that has suddenly arisen in the joints of the members, wounding and spreading.

For the contagion of despair has become so deeply rooted in certain people that, when they have been punished for some negligence or by the judgment of discipline, or when they have been confined under the satisfaction of penance for the purification of their crime, they prefer, because of the distress of despair, either to kill themselves by hanging from a noose or to destroy themselves by the sword or other deadly means. Unless some opportunity presents itself, the devil nevertheless completes his will in them.

Therefore, wishing to put an end to this most wicked persuasion and provide a suitable remedy for such an illness, our sacred united assembly decrees that whoever, having been caught in such traps, escapes an attempt at self-destruction shall remain wholly excluded for two months both from the fellowship of Catholics and from the body and sacred blood of Christ. For it is necessary that, through the discipline of penance, the person who was attempting in despair to join his soul to the devil be restored to his former hope and salvation.

## V. On the repair of churches and various other matters

[Col. 0539B]

Although in the past the judgments of the holy Fathers concerning various matters shine forth, nevertheless those things that suit the present time and order must now also be established by regulated law. For just as antiquity issued many decrees concerning pressing circumstances, so it is appropriate that our present age establish what needs to be done concerning the matters that arise.

Accordingly, the disordered practice of certain priests was brought before our assembly: they oppress their parishes beyond measure with various exactions or forced services, while many churches remain abandoned. Therefore, the unity of our assembly decrees and establishes that, if bishops choose to demand the thirds that the ancient canons have determined should be taken from their parishes, the bishops themselves shall repair the ruined churches. If, however, they prefer to relinquish those thirds, the cultivators of those same churches shall undertake their repair under the care and supervision of their bishop.

If all the churches are either intact or those that had been ruined have been repaired, each bishop shall have complete freedom, if he wishes to obtain the thirds owed to him according to the ordinances of the ancient canons. This is provided, however, that, beyond those thirds, no bishop shall exact anything from parish churches for royal requisitions, nor shall anyone presume to take anything from the estates of those churches as a stipend.

We have also decided that this must necessarily be established: several churches must not be entrusted to one priest. A single priest cannot discharge the office throughout all the churches, attend to the people with priestly authority, or provide the churches’ property with the necessary care. The rule is to be as follows: a church that has up to ten dependents shall have a priest assigned to it; a church with fewer than ten dependents shall be joined to other churches.

If any bishop disregards this institution of ours and thereafter presumes to violate it, he shall know that he will be punished by excommunication for two months, with the provision that, after returning from the prohibition of excommunication to the place of his office, he shall diligently fulfill all the sanctions of this canon in every respect.

## VI. On offering an entire and carefully prepared oblation in the sacrifice

[Col. 0540A]

Although many judgments of the holy Fathers who preceded us in the holy faith have issued concerning necessary matters, nevertheless, because even now many practices are known to occur beyond what is proper, we considered it necessary to put an end to illicit presumption.

For it has been brought to the knowledge of our assembly that in certain regions of Spain some priests, partly entangled in ignorance and partly provoked by reckless presumption, do not offer clean loaves carefully prepared for the sacrifice upon the Lord’s table. Instead, as necessity or personal inclination may impel each one, they remove a small round piece from bread prepared for their own use and offer it upon the altar with wine and water as a sacred offering. This practice is nowhere found to have been performed in the history of sacred authority.

For the Gospel truth says through Matthew: “While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, and broke it.” Likewise through Mark: “As they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them.” Again through Luke: “Having taken bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them.” The Apostle likewise says: “The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’”

Finally, what else is indicated except that, taking an entire loaf and breaking it after blessing it, he handed it over in pieces for each of the disciples to receive? He also clearly taught that we should do this afterward, indicating that every morsel is bread, but not every loaf is a morsel. Hence, when he wished to indicate his betrayer, he said later: “It is the one to whom I shall give the piece of bread.”

Therefore, since the words of the Redeemer testify that he took an entire loaf, not a piece, and, after blessing it, broke it and gave it in pieces to his disciples, and since the Apostle Paul likewise relates that he took bread and, giving thanks, broke it, as well as that Christ fed the crowd with five broken loaves, what else does he teach us except that we should take an entire loaf and place it upon the table of his altar to be blessed, not a piece of bread? We plainly understand that our Head did not do the latter.

For if a human being takes the greatest care to preserve the necessities of his life, how much more ought he to provide with the utmost diligence the proper dignity for the sacred worship of God? Therefore, wishing to put an end to this recklessness or ignorance, our assembly of unanimity has decided that bread is not to be placed upon the Lord’s altar to be sanctified by priestly blessing except when it is whole, clean, and carefully prepared.

It should not be excessively large, but only a small offering, according to the custom maintained by the Church. Its remnants should either be preserved more easily for safekeeping in a small container without any damage, or, if it is necessary to consume them, they should neither weigh down the stomach of the person who consumes them with the burden of heavy stuffing nor become merely food for digestion, but should refresh the soul with spiritual nourishment. In this way, those who consume them shall observe the ordinances of the ancient canons.

Therefore, whoever presumes to violate this decree of ours shall be subject to the punishment of divine judgment and remain excluded from communion for the space of one year.

## VII. On the publication of the council

A great correction of the people’s conduct is achieved when the acts of synods, whenever they are held, are published in the bishops’ own parishes through their report. Therefore, with complete unanimity, we decree that whenever a council is held in any province, each bishop shall, within six months, by his admonitions, not delay to assemble all abbots, priests, deacons, and clerics, as well as the entire assembly of the city in which he is known to preside, and also the whole people of his diocese.

Thus, in their presence, everything disclosed concerning what was done or defined in the council during that year shall be made fully known in public. Indeed, the severity of the wicked is eradicated when the canonical ordinances that must be observed are brought by every means to their knowledge. In such a way, no one may dare to contradict what has been established in past acts or present decrees; no one may presume to oppose it; and no one may strive not to fulfill it.

If anyone believes these provisions should be slighted, chooses to despise them, or, swollen with disobedience, full of murmuring, inflamed by envy, and engaged in destructive criticism, acts against them rather than becoming a willing and benevolent supporter of the same definitions, he shall remain punished by a sentence of excommunication for a period of two months.

## VIII. On the protection of the royal offspring
When the endeavors of holy action and the vows of fervent intention, spread far and wide, are openly evident to all through the prince’s beneficent acts and shine more brightly than daylight before the eyes of the holy Catholic Church, they compel our assembly to bring forth some provision conducive to salvation and to promulgate something appropriate or expedient for the sake of requital to his offspring. Thus we may appear both to return some measure of beneficent assistance in return for his paternal beneficence and to fortify his descendants with the necessary protection and defense of pious guardianship.

For our most glorious and serene lord, King Egica, inflamed by the fire of the most fervent love of Christ and engaged in the work of holy action, following that prophetic oracle, “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away over your enemies?”—as a true worshiper of Christ, he earnestly resolves to crush the perfidy of Christ’s enemies. He plans to strengthen the condition of the Church of God through vigilant diligence; he displays himself as generous toward the holy basilicas of God; he remits the burdens of tribute to the peoples with discerning moderation [Note: [Col. 0541] In B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: *submittit* (“reduces”). In A.: *submittit*. In Ae.: omitted.]; he is accustomed to forgive those who act with malicious obstinacy against him, with most welcome generosity of spirit and with the persistent attention of pious mercy; and, according to the prophet, he restores many who have been broken, freeing them from every burden and reforming them into a condition of liberty. He also excels by exercising himself in various pursuits of holy life.

Therefore, since our unanimity cannot find anything else by which it might suitably respond to so many and such great benefits that he strives, with manifold devotion, to extend to the Church of God and to the peoples of his nation, it decrees and establishes, with salutary foresight—which is always useful, indeed whatever truly pertains to salvation is always useful—that, as we have said, we promulgate strong aids of protection for his sons in the future. We call to witness that Name before which all things heavenly and earthly bend the knee, and we charge all priests and princes, present and absent, and those who will follow in future times, as well as persons of whatever rank or order, that no one in the future seek unjust occasions to injure his descendants or those who are known to be joined to the sons or daughters of his royal majesty, or those who are not yet joined to them but may perhaps be joined to them. Let no one secretly or publicly direct against them malicious designs by which they might be dispossessed. Let no one kill them by the sword or by any harmful faction. Let no one provide counsel or assistance by which they might be unjustly overthrown or stripped of their possessions. Let no one unjustly impose upon them the violent mark of tonsure. Let no one presume to change the clothing of his daughters or daughters-in-law contrary to established order. Let no one, except upon clear evidence of guilt, cause them to be banished into exile or inflict upon their bodies the injury of any mutilation or scourging.

Finally, although the provisions stated above have been arranged with the greatest justice, nevertheless, because the devotion of our same glorious lord shines forth so readily that these measures themselves cannot fully repay him with the gratitude owed, it is most salutary for our whole assembly to add the following: throughout all the cities and places belonging to the dominion of his kingdom in which episcopal sees are known to exist, and likewise throughout the dioceses of those bishops, except on the day of the Lord’s Passion, when the altars remain stripped and no one is permitted to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass on that day, on every other day during which our same lord remains alive, let offerings of sacrifice be dedicated to the Lord on his behalf, on behalf of all his sons and daughters, on behalf of those already joined to them by matrimonial right and those still to be joined, and on behalf of their grandchildren and all their relatives; let vows of pious prayer be discharged, and let them be commended with thanksgiving to the heavenly Majesty. Let good desires for them increase daily; let the efforts of their adversaries be shattered by the power of His right hand; let pardon and grace be granted to them from His mercy, so that, protected by the defense of His power, they may escape the snares of the ancient enemy and, abounding in charity and length of life, may deserve, after their passing, to enter the heavenly dwellings.

## IX. Concerning Bishop Sisbertus

Just as the highest and most conspicuous good is to cling lovingly and faithfully to the heavenly Majesty and to offer obedience to his commands with vows that continually grow, so, after God, it is a consequent good for kings, chosen by Him as His vicars by lawful right, that each person preserve the faith he has promised with an unwavering intention of heart and devise nothing harmful against them on any occasion, nor determine anything more wicked. The Lord says: “Do not touch my anointed”; and David says again: “For who will stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and remain innocent?” Again, threatening a certain man, he says: “Why did you not fear to stretch out your hand to kill the Lord’s anointed?”

Therefore it is entirely appropriate that a pledge made to princes be preserved without any stain of deceit, and that the faith rendered to them not be violated by any factions or schemes of wickedness. For if a bare promise of words is violated on any pretext, it is judged a criminal offense; how much more, then, if the faith promised to kings under the attestation of an oath is not feared to be profaned? There is indeed a very reprehensible obstinacy of certain secular persons and, worse still, of priests: they scorn to observe the faith promised under oath to their princes and obscure the promise of their oath with verbal deceit, while they retain the perversity of faithlessness hidden in their hearts. Yet it is written: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain”; and again: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God: I am the Lord”; and once more: “Cursed is everyone who swears falsely by the name of his God.” Nevertheless, such men do not fear to violate the faith they promised under oath, nor do they in any way fear to betray the promise of their oath.

Therefore, since Sisbertus, bishop of the see of Toledo, was found implicated in such schemes—because he resolved not only to deprive our most serene lord King Egica of his kingdom but also, together with Frogellus, Theodemirus, Liuvilane, Liuvigotone, Thecla, and the others, to kill him, and planned to bring disturbance and destruction upon his people and homeland—and since by the decree of our council he has already been deprived both of office and of rank, our college, assembled in common through this canonical sanction, decrees that this decree of our union, which we have also decided must be joined to these synodical definitions, shall stand strengthened with its full force and possess unshakable strength forever.

Sisbertus himself, however, for his violation of his oath and for the plotting of so great a crime, is to be punished according to the institution of the ancient canons, which prescribe that whoever is found to have done such things and, while the prince is alive, to have directed his attention toward another in hope of obtaining the kingdom, is to be expelled from the assembly of Catholics by a sentence of excommunication, deprived at once of honor and office, stripped of all his possessions, and confined in perpetual exile, with everything reduced to the power of the aforesaid prince. Thus, according to the decrees of those same ancient canons, he is to receive communion only at the end of his life, unless the royal mercy should decide to absolve him earlier.

Likewise, any other religious persons, whatever their order or rank, who are subsequently found to have acted or resolved in such a manner against the prince are to be punished by censure.

## X. Concerning Those Who Have Profaned Their Oath

Just as an ulcer that spreads greatly through the body is cured only by stronger medicines or by the sword, so the obstinacy of the faithless, which cannot otherwise be restrained, must be punished by harsher sentences. For although the Lord’s sanction declares: “The father shall not die for the sons, nor the sons for the fathers, but each shall die for his own sin”; and again: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son,” nevertheless, because the violation of oaths has grown greatly [Note: [Col. 0543D] In B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: *valide* (“forcefully” or “strongly”).] and the savage practice of plotting against our princes has spread widely—so that a prince is either killed by various forms of violence or deprived of the dignity of the kingdom—and because this cannot be restrained except by stricter censure, we therefore decree by this ordinance of ours that anyone in the future, whatever his rank or order, who plots anything against the death or deposition of the king, who considers him worthy to be attacked by any harm, or who attempts to disturb his people or homeland by any factions or schemes, shall remain, together with all his descendants, deprived of every dignity of the palatine order and bound under perpetual servitude to the power of the fisc.

Only this power is reserved to our glorious prince Egica: if he should at some time wish to release, through a vow of pious mercy, either those who have already been judged canonically and legally for their faithlessness or those who subsequently depart from the oath of their faith and endeavor to do or plot anything harmful against our aforesaid prince, the authority to do so shall remain entirely with him.

And since their possessions have come into the dominion of our same lord by just and lawful means, and since some of them, by the grant of that same prince, have deserved to be received by the Church of God, by the offspring of our same lord, or by many others in proportion to their service, we therefore establish and decree that at no time shall their sons, who are known or will be known to have been profaners of their oaths, or their subsequent descendants, dare to intend harm against those persons, nor attempt in any way to take those possessions away from them.

Finally, as we have stated, we have taken care to promulgate this most severe sentence of our decree, so that anyone who does not fear his own destruction may at least fear the ruin of his sons and of all his descendants. If any of the succeeding kings delays in observing or fulfilling all the definitions of this constitution of ours, may his entire line of descent perish under perpetual condemnation; moreover, by divine judgment, may he be deprived in this present age of all possessions and honor, and, when Christ judges, may he arrive with the devil and his companions at the destruction of Gehenna.

To this definition of ours we join certain necessary material from an ancient canon, and together we proclaim it in the very words in which, as we have said, antiquity set it forth, saying:

Whoever, therefore, from among us or from among all the peoples of Spain [Note: [Col. 0545D] B. R., E. 4, U, G.: *Ecclesiae* (“Church”). Everything following from this word to the end of this council is absent in A. and Ae.; in those witnesses the following marginal note appears at [Col. 0546D]: “In the Fourth Synod of Toledo you will find these things, of sixty-six bishops.” It has been taken from B. R., with variant readings from the other witnesses.], by any conspiracy or design, violates the oath of his faith which he promised for the welfare of the homeland and the Gothic people or for the preservation of the king’s safety, or wishes to attack our glorious prince Egica, or succeeding princes, with death, or attempts to strip them of royal power, or chooses through tyrannical presumption to usurp the height of the kingdom, let him be anathema in the sight of God the Father and the angels. Let him be made a stranger to the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, and alien from every assembly of Christians, together with all the companions of his impiety; for it is fitting that one punishment hold subject those whom a similar error is found to have entangled.

This we repeat a second time, saying:

Whoever henceforth, from among us or from among all the peoples of Spain, by any plan or design, violates the oath of his faith which he promised for the welfare of the homeland and the Gothic people or for the preservation of the king’s safety, or wishes to attack our aforesaid prince, or succeeding princes, with death, or attempts to strip them of royal power, or chooses through tyrannical presumption to usurp the height of the kingdom, let him be anathema in the sight of Christ and his apostles. Let him be made a stranger to the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, and alien from every fellowship of Christians, and let him be held condemned at the future judgment together with his accomplices; for it is right that those who associate themselves with such persons should themselves be held liable to share in their condemnation.

This also we acclaim a third time, saying:

Whoever henceforth, from among us or from among all the peoples of Spain, by any reflection or design, violates the oath of his faith which he promised for the salvation of the homeland and the Gothic people or for the preservation of royal power, or wishes to attack our often-mentioned prince, or succeeding princes, with death, or attempts to strip them of royal power, or chooses through tyrannical presumption to usurp the height of the kingdom, let him be anathema in the sight of the Holy Spirit and the martyrs of Christ. Let him be made a stranger to the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, and alien from every communion of Christians. Let him have no share among the just, but let him be condemned with the devil and his angels to eternal punishments, together with those who strive by the same conspiracy, so that equal punishment may bind those whom a wicked partnership unites in destruction.

And therefore, if this sentence, repeated for the third time, pleases all of you who are present, confirm it by the agreement of your voices.

All the priests of God, the elders of the palace, the clergy, and the entire people said:

“Whoever presumes to act against this definition of yours, let him be anathema Maranatha—that is, destruction at the coming of the Lord—and let both he and his companions have a share with Judas Iscariot.”

## XI. Concerning Thanksgiving

[Col. 0546A]

When all the matters that necessarily had to be defined for ecclesiastical discipline, as well as the remaining matters brought before our assembly for direction, had been completed and concluded, we render to the omnipotent and indivisible Trinity the due of ineffable thanks, offer vows of praise, and proclaim the insignia of His glory with the entire devotion of our minds. We do this because, by His wondrous ordering, He has deemed us worthy not only to be gathered into this assembly of holy congregation and to be comforted by the sight of one another, but also has enabled us to speak from Him and has fulfilled in Himself what was spoken.

We earnestly implore His mercy: just as He has made us sweet-speaking through the kiss of mutual peace, laid out the beginnings of our definitions, and brought them to completion by perfecting them with sublime consummation, so may He protect our most serene and pious lord King Egica, by whose command and exhortation we have been gathered here, with the shield of saving defense; may He fortify him with the standard of faith; and may He lead him, together with the people and homeland entrusted to him, along the way of His will. Thus may he prosper happily through the lengthened courses of the present age and, after the journey of this life, rich in the abundance of pious action, may he reach Christ crowned with those whom he now governs.

## Decree of Judgment Issued by All

The approved and venerable history of the Acts of the Apostles relates that, after Judas had been condemned for the crime of betrayal, the Holy Spirit did not descend upon the remaining eleven by a heavenly visitation until Matthias had been unanimously chosen as an apostle in his place. This was because the number eleven signifies transgression of the commandments.

And because Sisbertus, bishop of the see of Toledo, has been marked by his crime and is acknowledged to have been cut off from our body, it is therefore most necessary for our number to take care that another be substituted in his place, so that our body may be restored to the perfection due to it, just as the perfect number is known to have been completed through Matthias.

And because the apostles, acting as ambassadors of the heavenly Majesty, testified, saying, “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life”—an odor of life unto life for those who took care to offer obedience to their commands, but an odor of death unto death for those who nevertheless despised their admonitions—therefore, since the aforesaid Sisbertus, bishop of the see of Toledo, did not choose, through humility, to submit himself to their saving admonitions, so that he might govern the Church of God in the proper order, instruct it with humility, and invite it to the heavenly kingdoms by salutary examples, but, striking himself with a two-edged sword—namely, pride and perjury—wished not only to deprive our glorious lord King Egica of his kingdom but also to destroy him by inflicting death, it is not fitting for us to begin the council before he has first been punished by canonical and legal censure and another has been substituted in his place to occupy the chair of the see of Toledo.

For this reason, when we had all assembled together, the same Bishop Sisbertus was brought before our assembly and openly confessed, in his own words, the plot of his faithlessness. Therefore, through the form of this decree of ours, we depose the aforesaid Sisbertus from the episcopal order and honor, according to the ancient edict of synodical sanction and the decree of law promulgated concerning such matters; we decree that, excommunicated from receiving the body and blood of Christ, he remain in perpetual exile, receiving communion in every respect only at the end of his life, unless the princely mercy, with priestly consent, should choose to absolve him.

[Col. 0547B] Therefore, since, with the Lord’s favor, the council must be begun as quickly as possible according to the choice and authority of our repeatedly mentioned lord, by which in the past he ordered our venerable brother Felix, bishop of the see of Hispalis, to undertake the due care of the aforesaid see of Toledo, reserving him to be confirmed there afterward by our decree, we, with the consent of the clergy and people belonging to the often-mentioned see of Toledo, canonically transfer our venerable brother Bishop Felix from the see of Hispalis, which he has governed until now, to the see of Toledo.

In that same see of Hispalis we substitute our brother Faustinus, bishop of the see of Braga; and we appoint Felix, prelate of the Church of Porto, as bishop of the aforesaid see of Braga. By perpetual sanction we confirm each of them in the aforesaid sees, so that each may instruct the Church he receives through pious preaching, adorn it with holy morals, and edify it by examples of blessed life. Thus, gathered together in remarkable unanimity and made one body, with them sitting alongside us in the synodical assembly, may we deserve to have the Holy Spirit descend upon us as upon the twelve apostles, so that, inflamed by His fire and imbued with His teaching, we may promulgate with complete justice those things that pertain to ecclesiastical discipline and to restraining the morals of wicked people, and may sing praises to the Most High with devout minds.

We decree that this decree of our college is to be joined to the synodical acts that we are to define in the council, and we determine that it shall there obtain its proper place.

## Law Issued in Confirmation of the Council

The synodical assembly and the numerous gathering of priests are judged all the more venerable by everyone, and are seen to be all the more awe-inspiring, because it is beyond doubt that the undivided Trinity is present in the midst of their assembly, as the holy Gospel testifies: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

Therefore, since it has been made known that the omnipotence of the heavenly Majesty is present in their midst, what else can be said except that whatever is uttered by their mouths is brought about by His inspiration—He who has confessed that He will dwell among them? Accordingly, our glorious serenity has reverently received what their unanimity has brought forth, indeed what the Holy Spirit has proclaimed through their mouths; it embraces it lovingly and, through this decree of our law, determines that it shall remain firm forever. It establishes that it shall stand with unshakable authority and decrees that it shall possess complete force.

Specifically, from this day and moment onward, with all vigilance, all diligence, and every care, let everything defined in this synod for ecclesiastical discipline or benefit, and everything issued for the correction of wicked morals, be observed by all throughout every province of our kingdom and be kept without any scruple or opposition of controversy.

And because, when the devastation of the inguinal plague broke out, the bishops belonging to the see of Narbonne were not gathered in this holy synod, we therefore establish and command by this law of our gentleness that all bishops belonging to the diocese of that see assemble in the city of Narbonne with their metropolitan, and, after carefully reading all the chapters of this council, come forward to subscribe them in due order.

If anyone, therefore, presumes to violate the constitutions of these definitions, attempts to disparage them, or tries with deplorable audacity to oppose them, he shall be struck by a sentence excluding him from ecclesiastical communion and shall be fined a fourth part of his possessions [E. 4, T. 1, 2: “a fifth part”].

In the name of the Lord, Flavius, the glorious King Egica, to all the most holy Fathers residing in this holy synod:

Behold, most holy Fathers in Christ and faithful leaders of the people in apostolic doctrine: I confidently urge the united body of your synodical assembly with this exhortation, that you afford us the religious aid of your holiness and render the counsel for our enactment which is awaited in every respect.

For the devotion of our often-glorious serenity is most ready, and the most devoted fullness of a pure will burns to live among the people entrusted to me with those affections, to adhere to those acts of piety, and to maintain the work of government by an increase of mercy, through which our times, shaken by no assaults of adversity and impeded by no civil or foreign disturbances, may flourish in the gift of peace and continue heaped with the bounty of our mercy. And let those whom perhaps the action of wicked faithlessness entangles, if it be lawful, be raised from punishment by the arm of piety through regard for our clemency, so that, by sparing them, I may make heavenly mercy favorable to me and the condition of my people and homeland may not, God forbid, collapse any further through falls into ruin.

But as much as we endeavor to remit the penalty of offences, so much does the transgression of the profaners work against it, and it is undermined by repeated ventures of treachery. Therefore, whether I grant pardon to offences or impose penalties proportionate to their deeds, the anxious mind of our serenity is troubled because the very remission of offences is often turned to the contrary as wickedness increases, while even then the vices are not repressed which ought to have been brought to an end by an easy effort of correction.

You yourselves should plainly consider in this holy council—and already earlier you have learned by credible report of the downfall of very many persons—how daily I suffer the ruin of my security through the impious efforts of faithless men and of so many enemies, and how great disturbances have been insolently stirred up in the homeland. By the treachery of these criminals, who have been discovered faithless both in former times and now, we are compelled to consult the whole body of your assembly as to what it is fitting for our serenity to do concerning the excesses of those who are known to have offended against me in former times or even now: whether they should be punished canonically and legally by fitting sentences, or whether, by sparing them, the penalties due for their offences should remain unpunished. Let this be determined with especial care by the most salutary enactment of your unanimity [E. 4, T. 1, 2: *humanitatis* (“humaneness”)], with that freedom reserved in every way to our majesty or to our successor kings: if anyone hereafter should attempt to act against royal power, our people, or our homeland, his wickedness must be sharply restrained according to the canonical sentence issued in a council during the time of our predecessor, Lord King Sisenand, concerning such persons, or according to the sentence of the law. Provided only that, as we have said, your salutary reply may become clear to our minds, so that by zeal for correction the transgression of those who err against me may be amended.

For it is also fitting that this be ruled by the text of your decree: because our predecessor, the lord King Wamba of blessed memory, at the very beginning of his reign, contrary to the custom of Theudemund the *spatarius*’s lineage or rank, at the instigation of Festus, formerly bishop of Emerita, appointed him, by the impulse of royal authority alone, to perform the office of *numerarius* in that same city of Emerita—an office which he is known to have carried out contrary to reason for the space of one year. Since he was unable to resist the authority of the people, suspend that office by the edict of your council from Theudemund and all his posterity, so that neither he nor any of his descendants may ever be troubled in any way on this account until the end of the age.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the sixth prosperous year of our reign, in the name of God, at our seat of Toledo.

When he had finished this address from his sacred mouth, he received a blessing from our midst and departed. Then each of us, remaining seated in his place, ordered that the volume itself be opened, and we undertook to consider the necessary matters through mutual discussion.

# Sixty-Second Council: The Seventeenth Council of Toledo

Held in the seventh year of the reign of our most religious and serene lord King Egica, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, in the Era 732.

[Note: This council is absent from A., Ae., and E. 3. It has been taken from Codex B. R., together with the variant readings of the other acts.]

[Col. 0551]

When many bishops of Spain and Gaul had assembled in the church of the glorious virgin and confessor of Christ, Saint Leocadia, which is in the suburb of Toledo, where her holy body rests, and when we had taken our seats in the places assigned to us, the same most glorious prince appeared, inflamed by the fervor of holy devotion and filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Standing in our midst, he bowed his illustrious head, asked to be blessed by us, and desired to be commended to the Lord by the outpouring of our prayers.

When these things had been done, as is customary, he presented us with a volume in his own hand, saying:

“Behold, most holy and reverend priestly college of the Catholic Church, and honorable priesthood faithful to divine doctrine; and you, illustrious ornament of the royal court, together with the numerous assembly of distinguished men whom our highness has ordered to take part in this honorable gathering. Since it would be quite lengthy to recount to you in person those matters necessary for the interests of our kingdom and for our people and homeland, I therefore hand over this volume, because it is known to contain everything that our gentleness ought to make known to your minds for accomplishment. At the same time I command and exhort you by Him who said, ‘Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I shall also be in the midst of them,’ that you carefully consider, with serious and mature counsel, what this volume contains, as well as any other matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline or the affairs of various cases that may present themselves for hearing to your venerable assembly, and that you bring them to the most just and firm conclusion by the decrees of your judgments.”

When he had finished this address from his sacred mouth, he received a blessing from our midst and departed. Then each of us, remaining seated in his place, ordered that the volume itself be opened, and we undertook to consider the necessary matters through mutual discussion.

In the name of the Lord, Flavius Egica, king, to the most holy Fathers sitting in this holy synod:

The ardor of mind and the many flames with which the sublimity of our serenity burns and seethes, kindled by love for holy religion, can be expressed neither in a lengthy account of words nor recorded in the written word; for inasmuch as the Christian faith shines with the ineffable comparison of spiritual virtues, so far does the brevity of our understanding still fall short of recounting its mysteries.
