Yet although we cannot reach the abyss of its depth, let the great devotion of our clemency nevertheless recognize how we exhort your holiness, seated in this holy synod, first to discuss its mystery in spiritual decrees and to proclaim the doctrines of your apostolic order, so that the hearts of the faithful, illumined by an incomparable star, may pass onward, and the hearts of unbelievers likewise may be turned by the steps of their minds from darkness to light.

Finally, concerning the impious Jews dwelling within the boundaries of our kingdom, we set forth the following—something we express not without very great sorrow. Deceived from the beginning by the error of their ancestral rites, they have denied the name of Christ with incredible perversity and have until now mocked the same saving faith with their impious arguments. For it is certain, and a true proclamation has been openly circulated throughout almost the whole world, that the boundaries of Spain have always flourished in the fullness of faith. Hence the highest reason compels us to resist them with firm resolve, since in some parts of the world they are said to have risen up against their Christian rulers, while many are known to have been slain by Christian kings through the just judgment of God. This is especially so because recently, through manifest confessions, we discovered beyond doubt that these men had consulted other Hebrews in overseas regions, so that they might act unanimously against the Christian people, awaiting the time of their own destruction and considering how they might corrupt the rule of the Christian faith itself. This will also become clear from the very confessions that are to be disclosed to your ears.

From the beginning of our rule, such was the intention of our clemency concerning their conversion that we not only endeavored by various persuasions to draw them to the faith of Christ, but also, by decree of our tranquility, allowed them to receive Christian slaves whom they had previously lost, in accordance with the law, because of their faithlessness—solely so that, through the purpose of true conversion [E. 4, *conversationis*, “conduct/way of life”], their faithlessness of heart might be driven far away and the Church, as a mother, might receive them as adopted children.

Yet although, through the text of their pledge [E. 4, *causationis*], supported by the attestation of an oath, they promised this, they did not ultimately fulfill their promises; rather, they were found to have undoubtedly continued their customary rites and ceremonies. And because, by command of the divine will, they were reserved to be corrected during the time of our kingdom, our tranquility has judged it necessary that, through a general assembly of you and our nobles, their wickedness be restrained as quickly as possible. With Christ’s help, their wickedness may then be immediately uprooted, the Christian name may prevail, and the faith of Christ may shine forth without limit—lest it appear that such great faithlessness is opposed only when their hostility is recognized as attacking the Catholic Church.

Therefore, in order that such a dire perversity of unbelief may be conquered and perish, let them either be restrained by synodal correction from the error inherited from their ancestors, or, if your unanimous judgment so decides, remain cut down by the sickle of justice. Let the canonical judgment of your assembly openly establish what ought to be done concerning them and all their possessions, and let the sanction of our law decree that this remain permanently in force. The only Hebrews reserved for the present are those who are known to dwell within the boundaries of the province of Gaul or to belong to the government of that region. Since, as a result of mounting offenses, foreign invasion, and the devastation of the groin-plague, that province is recognized to have been widely depopulated, let them remain there with all their possessions under the protection of the duke of that land and unhesitatingly provide service for the public good. In this way, according to the rule of the holy faith, let them amend their lives as true worshipers of Christ and drive every error of their native unbelief from their hearts.

But if from now on they are discovered, even to a small degree, to be corrupters of the holy faith, they shall immediately be removed from that land and punished in every respect by the same judgment as their aforesaid kinsmen.

Truth also does not permit us to remain silent about the madness of certain priests who dare to celebrate Masses before the sacred altar of God for living persons on behalf of the dead. While intending to harm others, they become murderers of themselves and bring about the destruction of their own souls, as it is written: “The lying mouth kills the soul.” While they commit such abominations under the impulse of a certain envy or malice, one thing is clear: they both lie to God and bend the priestly order into a crooked bow. If they do not fear offering such a lie to the Lord as a sacrifice, what else will they be afraid to say falsely?

We read that the apostle Peter said to Ananias—I remember: “Why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings but to God.” We entrust the elimination of so great a crime to your council, so that your canonical rule may decree that those who are discovered to have committed such acts, those from whom they sought advice about perpetrating this wickedness, and thereafter all who fall into such an error are to be punished. Thus, feeling the correction they have brought upon themselves, they may repent of their evil deeds, and your judgment may display a special example of prohibition, so that such things may not be committed by others thereafter.

With these matters thus set forth, we entrust to your prudence, in the fear of God, the disputes of the peoples that have been brought to your ears, so that, since “the multitude of the wise is the health of the world,” no occasion may exist capable of dulling the sharpness of your minds in proclaiming justice, and no place may be given to favoritism to conceal the light of truth. Thus may the pronouncement of your judgments shine with the light of equity, extend due justice to the peoples, and contribute to the abundance of our reward.

We also most earnestly desire that the following be calmed through your prayers to the Lord: since the enemy of the human race never ceases eagerly to snatch some of our people toward perdition—so that, because of their own crime, they may be seen to fall, God forbid, not through any burden imposed by our authority—after this council has been completed, take care to celebrate special litanies for three days with contrite hearts. Continue the same three-day fasts in each month until the end of this year. For since we have never wished anyone whom the heavenly mercy has subjected to our rule to perish, nor do we seek to destroy anyone further, but greatly rejoice in the condition of our people and our homeland, may they at least through the prayers of your blessedness remove from their hearts the goads of the snares that they prepare daily against our glory, and remain toward our serenity in the pure sincerity of faith. Thus may they rejoice that they have been raised up from the fall of their predecessors, and may our glory, enriched with them by the gift of peace and charity, offer unceasing vows of thanks to Christ the Lord.

## On the Rule of the Holy Faith

Necessary order demands that, according to the decree of Paul, the chosen vessel, the kingdom of God be sought before the beginning of every matter, so that what is to be undertaken afterward may, with the Lord’s assistance, be brought to the most just conclusion. Accordingly, we have recognized it as appropriate to disclose with our own mouth and openly recount from the outpouring of our heart the mystery of the holy faith, which is the unshakable foundation of our salvation. Therefore, believing and confessing what the glorious confession has proclaimed in all holy councils and in the pronouncements of the holy Fathers, we also set forth, in the confession of our mouth, the sequence of the Creed, which contains the sacraments of the entire holy faith.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousios* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth. For us and for our salvation he descended and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit; he was made human from the virgin Mary; he suffered under Pontius Pilate; he was buried; on the third day he rose again; he ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of the Father; he will come again in glory [T. 1, 2, “thereafter”] to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets; in one Catholic and apostolic Church; we confess one baptism for the remission of sins; we await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

Having disclosed and completed this profession of our belief, as the assembly of the holy Fathers has promulgated it, we turn the article of our decree to the matters that are to be undertaken next.

### I. On the three days at the beginning of the council, during which nothing else is ordered to be done except matters of faith and other spiritual concerns, with no secular business interposed

The number three, inasmuch as it possesses a beginning, middle, and end, appears to signify the likeness of the Trinity. Therefore, since a multitude of priests is accustomed to assemble in the name of the Holy Trinity for the holding of a synod, we believe it fitting to establish at the beginning of the entire assembly that, over the course of three days accompanied by fasting, a discussion be held among them concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity, other spiritual matters, and the correction of the conduct of priests, with no secular person present. Thus, while disputes concerning written cases are conducted for three days under the fear of the divine name, the business of other cases may be carried out without impediment through the aid of that same Holy Trinity.

### II. On closing the doors of the baptistery at the beginning of Lent

Although at the beginning of Lent the mystery of baptism is generally closed, nevertheless, as the order of ecclesiastical custom requires, the doors of the baptistery must be closed on that same day by episcopal hand and sealed with the bishop’s ring [T. 1, 2, “marked”], and they must not be opened in any way until the solemnity of the Lord’s Supper. This is so that, through the episcopal seal, it may be shown throughout the world that during these days baptism and sanctification may not be performed, except in the event of the gravest necessity.

When the doors are opened again, they must likewise be marked with episcopal observance, so that the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection may be shown to be open: through it an entrance to life was made for humanity, so that the person buried with Christ through baptism may rise with him in the glory of God.

Because this holy custom is not at all observed or performed by bishops in certain churches, we therefore decree and establish by this judgment that it be observed by all the bishops of Spain and Gaul. On the aforesaid day, namely the beginning of Lent, the doors of the holy baptistery are to be closed at the completion of the praises, and sealed by the bishops with the impression of their rings. They must not be opened except at the celebration of the Lord’s Supper, when, according to customary practice, the altars are stripped of their coverings.

For it is an improper thing that, during the aforementioned days of Lent, access should be open to everyone in the place where the appointed mystery is not permitted to be performed.

### III. On the washing of the feet to be performed on the Lord’s Supper

The mystery is seen to be sufficiently pleasing and acceptable to God if the minds of those who worship Christ strive to be his imitators by following his example, since the Lord says: “Whoever serves me must follow me.” Therefore, since our Lord and Redeemer did not disdain to wash the feet of his disciples with water, as the evangelist testifies—“Jesus rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, saying: ‘If I, Lord and teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet’”—why should we, imbued with the performance of this pious action, not be his most devoted followers in imitation of his example?

Yet although the example of this holy action shines brightly, partly through negligence and partly through custom, in certain churches the priests do not wash the feet of the brethren during the celebration of the Lord’s Supper. They offer no excuse other than the custom of tradition, although Truth rebukingly says: “Why do you transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” Likewise, the most excellent teacher and unconquered martyr Cyprian says:

“In vain do those who are defeated by reason oppose custom to us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit ought not to be followed in spiritual matters.”

Therefore, while the example of truth shines more clearly than daylight, while his dreadful words of rebuke stand forth, and while the judgment of this eminent teacher instructs us that truth is greater than custom, they vainly oppose custom to us without reason.

Although it may be considered suitable for this washing of the feet to take place at any time, nevertheless it must be observed with particular care on the very day on which it was performed by Christ. Accordingly, this holy synod decrees and establishes that henceforth this solemnity may not be celebrated otherwise throughout the churches of Spain and Gaul than by each bishop or priest striving to wash the feet of his subjects according to this most sacred example.

If any priest delays fulfilling this decree of ours, let him know that he will be deprived of the reception of holy Communion for a period of two months.

### IV. On the sacred ministries and ornaments of the churches

The reprehensible will and disastrous recklessness of certain priests not only hand over the sacred altar ministries entrusted to them, and the other ornaments of the Church, to others for misuse in their wicked deeds, but, what is worse, do not hesitate to appropriate them for their own use and consumption.

Although the judgment of the ancient Fathers concerning such persons, who sacrilegiously destroy merely sacred vessels, has already been promulgated in earlier times, our assembly henceforth establishes in common that no priest may attempt to break up, sell, or waste anything—not only from the sacred ministries but also from all the ornaments of the Church—for his own use or according to his own wishes.

If any priest attempts to violate this institution of ours, let him lose the rank of his own honor according to the ancient provisions of the canons. Branded as a sacrilegious person with perpetual infamy, let him remain excluded from the reception of holy Communion throughout all the days of his life, except at the final hour of his life. Moreover, if the offender possesses property of his own, whatever he appears to have wasted from the same sacred ministries or ornaments of the Church, he himself or his estate shall be compelled to restore in full to that church.

### V. On those who maliciously dare to celebrate a Mass for the dead on behalf of the living

While the Holy Spirit, through the mouths of his saints, has commanded the human race by every means to avoid falsehood, as Solomon says: “Do not tell a lie against your brother, nor do likewise to your friend”; and again: “The lying mouth kills the soul,” many priests who ought to be preachers of truth, and from whose mouths the whole body of the people ought to seek the law of truth, according to Solomon, who says, “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0557D] The text is Malachi, chapter II, verse 7], nevertheless, obstructed by guilt and wounded by the deceit of hostility, do not fear to speak falsely to human beings, nor do they shrink from perpetrating the same deed before God in the holy basilicas above the Lord’s altar.

For they strive to celebrate for living people, with deceitful intent, the Mass promulgated for the repose of the dead—not for any other reason than that the person for whom the sacrifice is offered may, through the intervention of that most sacred offering, incur the danger of death and destruction. What has been given to all as a remedy for salvation, they perversely seek to make a cause of ruin for certain people.

Therefore, our unanimous assembly has chosen that if any priest is thereafter discovered to have committed such acts, he shall be deposed from the rank of his order. Both that priest and the person who is judged to have incited him to perform such deeds shall be confined in the prison of perpetual exile, and, except at the final hour of life, the reception of holy Communion shall be denied them throughout all the days of their lives—the Communion which they believed they had fraudulently tasted through their wicked endeavor.

### VI. On the days of the litanies to be celebrated throughout the twelve months

Although the institution of the ancient Fathers decreed that vows of litanies should be fulfilled throughout the entire year, during the course of each month, it did not specifically establish for what causes this was to be done. Nevertheless, because, with the cooperation of the adversary of the human race, a widespread habit of wandering astray and violating oaths has grown up, therefore, in accordance with the evangelist who says, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation,” we establish and decree in common that henceforth throughout the whole year, in all twelve months and throughout all the provinces of Spain and Gaul, exomologesis shall be celebrated with increasing vows:

- for the condition of the Church of God;
- for the safety of our ruler;
- for the salvation of the people;
- for the forgiveness of every sin; and
- for the expulsion of the devil from the hearts of all the faithful.

Thus, when the almighty Lord has seen the general affliction, may he mercifully forgive all sins and drive far from the souls of all the incitements of the raging devil.

### VII. On safeguarding the royal consort and offspring

When the activity of those in high station and their devotion to holy religion spread themselves through various deeds of pious action, they acquire benefit for themselves from virtue and provide an incentive for good conduct to their subjects. Thus, for what they have done well they receive a reward from God, and for having incited others to goodness they rejoice to have immediately received an equivalent recompense.

Therefore, when the sovereign majesty performs such deeds, it is clear that the holy Church should extend to him a reciprocal reward, since he strives to adorn that Church with just works. In this way he may become increasingly prompt in doing good, and the minds of his subjects may likewise be strengthened by a freely offered example.

Accordingly, because our religious and most glorious ruler, King Egica, burning with zeal for the Lord God of hosts, has attacked the enemies of the true faith—those who by various actions preferred to overthrow the state of Catholic belief and, by profaning their oaths, preferred to preserve the rites of their ceremonies contrary to their promise—he is rightly seen to have struck them with fitting vengeance, following the straight path of judgment, so that he might avenge the injury done to the cross of Christ, preserve the condition of the entire holy Church, and provide the necessary defenses for his people and homeland.

Therefore, for so many and such great benefits, which he intends to extend both to the holy Church and to his people and homeland, and desiring in some measure to repay this ruler with a pious recompense, through the sanction of this decree we proclaim and, by the inviolable sacrament of the undivided Trinity, we summon and solemnly charge all persons, both those now living and those who shall succeed in future times, of whatever order or class:

If it should ever happen that the glorious lady Queen Cixilo, after many long and happier years of our most serene ruler Egica have passed, should remain religiously a widow and should have sweet offspring by him, let no one, driven by the bite of envy, moved by the goad of hatred, or impelled by the prompting of diabolical deceit, attempt to rise up against them.

Let no one, without evidence of manifest guilt, seek through the most subtle investigations any opportunities for harm against them. Let no one oppress their lives with unjust vexations of any kind, nor torment them with deprivations. Let no one impose upon their sons or daughters, against their will, the religious habit, consign them to prisons of exile, or torture them with blows of the lash, thereby depriving them of their dignity and removing possession of their property from them outside the proper order of justice.

Rather, supported by the aid of peace and tranquility, let them possess with undisturbed right whatever succession the lawfully inherited property of their parents has given them, as well as whatever our most merciful lord may have chosen to confer upon them through official grants, and whatever they may have justly acquired. Let them have unrestricted permission to judge concerning these possessions as they wish.

For it ought to appear necessary to everyone that they be fortified by priestly pronouncements and made entirely secure by their decrees. If at any time they should be left destitute, they shall remain under the protection of the priests according to the force of canonical decree.

Therefore, if anyone chooses to violate this decree of piety, believes that it should be invalidated, or attempts in any way to violate it, let him be condemned by the punishment of perpetual anathema, erased from the heavenly register, and bound with the devil and his companions by harsher punishments.

### VIII. On the condemnation of the Jews

Just as the uprightness of the faithful ought to be rewarded with a great gift of generosity [T. 2, “donation”], so the perversity of unbelievers fittingly ought to be struck by the strongest sword of judgment. For it is just that those within the faith be raised up more abundantly, while its adversaries are condemned more harshly, so that the former may advance more greatly with the Lord’s support and the latter may perish through resistance to God.

And because the Jewish people are known to be deeply stained by the mark of sacrilege, bloodied by the shedding of Christ’s blood, and polluted many times by the profanation of oaths, it is necessary, in proportion to the abundance of their crimes, that they mourn having incurred a grave loss through punishment. By their other crimes they preferred not only to disturb the state of the Church but also, with tyrannical audacity, attempted to bring ruin upon the homeland and the whole people, rejoicing as though they had found their opportunity to inflict various massacres upon Catholics.

Therefore, this cruel and astounding presumption must be uprooted by a still more cruel punishment, and judgment must rage against them in such an ordered manner that what is known to have been wickedly determined may be punished in every respect.

For this reason, while in this holy synod we were carefully directing our steps through the paths of other cases, the conspiracy of those same unbelievers suddenly reached the hearing of our assembly: not only had they stained, by observing their own rites contrary to their promise, the tunic of faith with which holy mother Church clothed them through the water of sacred baptism, but they had also preferred, as stated above, to usurp the pinnacle of the kingdom through conspiracy.

Since our assembly learned this evil deed fully from their own confessions, we decree by the judgment of this decree that they be struck by an irrevocable sentence: by the command of our most pious and religious ruler, Egica, who, inflamed with zeal for the Lord and compelled by ardor for the holy faith, desires not only to avenge the injury done to the cross of Christ but also to uproot more harshly the destruction of his people and homeland which they had determined to inflict upon him, they shall be stripped of all their possessions. Their property shall be joined to the resources of the treasury, and the persons of those treacherous men, together with their wives, children, and remaining descendants, shall be removed from their own places and subjected throughout all the provinces of Spain to perpetual servitude, distributed to serve wherever he orders them. They shall remain scattered everywhere, and, so long as they persist in the obstinacy of their unbelief, no opportunity shall in any way be given them to return to the status of free persons, since they have been marked by the numerous and exact stain of their crimes.

Nevertheless, we decree that, according to the choice of our ruler, some Christian slaves belonging to those same Jews shall be selected. From the value of their property they shall receive whatever the aforementioned lord of ours has chosen to confer upon them through official grants or letters of emancipation. Whatever taxes or public dues those Jews are seen to have paid hitherto, the aforesaid slaves chosen by our ruler must pay in full, without any excuse.

Finally, those who have received the same Jews as gifts from the aforementioned lord of ours shall draw up such an agreement in the name of his glory that they will not permit them in any way to celebrate or observe the ceremonies of their rites, or to imitate any paths of their ancestral faithlessness.

We also decree that, from their seventh year onward, their children of either sex are to have no dwelling or association with their parents. Their new masters, who have received them, shall entrust them to the care of most faithful Christians, on the following condition: the boys shall be joined in marriage to Christian women, and the girls likewise to Christian men. Neither their parents, as we have said, nor their children shall have any license whatsoever to observe the ceremonies of Jewish superstition or to repeat the paths of their unbelief on any occasion.

## On the Giving of Thanks

When, with God’s favor, everything pertaining to the order of sacred instruction and to other affairs has been completed and brought to an end, we pour forth ineffable thanks to the same King of all, the immeasurably glorious Lord; we sound melodious harmonies and sing before him the vows of hymns in continual rejoicing, because he has gathered our entire assembly together under the fear of his name and has made us present to one another through mutual sight.

We earnestly pray to his omnipotence with tireless petitions that he grant our orthodox and most religious ruler Egica a long life of prosperous times, direct his steps along the paths of his will, and grant him to govern piously the ranks of the peoples entrusted to him, arrange them with prudent moderation, and support them with the mouth of mercy. Thus, after the vast course of time, may he deign to transfer him from a temporal kingdom to an eternal kingdom enriched by his most pious deeds, there to be joined forever with the inhabitants of heaven—he by whose command and authority we are known to have been gathered for this assembly of peace.

## Law Issued in Confirmation of the Council

It is judged most fitting and beneficial for our people and homeland, and useful for the whole Church, that what has been defined by synodal assembly be confirmed by a royal enactment. Therefore, by this enactment of law, the clemency of our serenity decrees that the judgments of all the chapters known to have been promulgated in this holy synod possess the strength of the firmest stability. They are as follows:

- On the three days at the beginning of the council during which nothing else is ordered to be done except matters of faith and other spiritual concerns, with no secular business interposed;
- On closing the doors of the baptistery at the beginning of Lent;
- On the washing of the feet to be performed on the Lord’s Supper;
- On the sacred ministries and ornaments of the churches;
- On those who maliciously dare to celebrate Masses for the dead on behalf of the living;
- On the days of the litanies to be celebrated throughout the twelve months;
- On safeguarding the royal consort and offspring;
- On the condemnation of the Jews.

Whoever, of whatever class, person, or order, believes that the decrees of all these constitutions ought to be violated, refuses to observe them, or neglects to honor them shall remain condemned forever, according to the laws of the preceding councils promulgated in confirmation of them, whether by excommunication or by punishment.

## LXIII. The First Council of Braga, of Eight Bishops, Held in the Era 599, in the Third Year of King Ariamir [Note: [Col. 0561D] Ae., T. 2: Argemiri; this name is written in that form thereafter], on the Kalends of May

[Col. 0561]

When the bishops of the province of Gallaecia [U., “Gaul”—an apparent textual variant], namely Lucretius, Andrew, Martinus, Cottus, Ildericus, Lucetius, Timothy, and Maliosus, had assembled at the command of the aforementioned most glorious King Ariamir in the metropolitan church of the same province, Braga, with the bishops sitting together, the priests also present, and the ministers and the entire clergy standing by, Lucretius, bishop of the aforementioned metropolitan church, said:

“It has been a long time, most holy brothers, since, according to the institutions of the venerable canons and the decrees of Catholic and apostolic discipline, we have desired that a priestly assembly be held among us. Such an assembly is not only appropriate for ecclesiastical rules and orders, but also always produces a stable harmony of fraternal charity, when priests gathered together in the name of the Lord seek from one another, in a saving discussion, those things which, according to apostolic teaching, preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

“Now, therefore, since our most glorious and most pious son, with the Lord’s favor, has granted us the desired day of this gathering by royal command, and we have assembled and taken our seats together, let us first, if it pleases you, inquire into the institutions of the Catholic faith; then let the institutions of the holy Fathers be made known after the canons have been reviewed; finally, let certain matters pertaining to the service of God and the clerical office be examined with greater care. In this way, if anything is perhaps held among us as uncertain or disputed through negligence arising from ignorance, through the carelessness of a long passage of time, or through various causes, it may be brought back, as is fitting, to one rule of reason and truth.”

All the bishops said:

“Your blessedness’s proposal is just. For this very reason we have assembled, so that some useful ecclesiastical arrangement may be provided for us.”

Bishop Lucretius said:

“Let us therefore first set forth [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: *conferamus*, ‘let us discuss’] the established points of the faith, as was said above. Although long ago the contagion of the Priscillianist heresy was detected and condemned in the provinces of Spain, nevertheless, lest anyone still be infected by some pestilence of that error, either through ignorance or through deception by certain apocryphal writings, as often happens, let it be declared more clearly to ignorant people who, established at the very edge of the world and in the remotest regions of this province, have encountered little or almost no knowledge of sound instruction.

“I believe that your blessed fraternity knows that, at the time when the most impious poisons of the Priscillianist sect were spreading through these regions, the most blessed Pope Leo of the city of Rome, who was approximately the fortieth successor of the apostle Peter, sent his writings against the impious sect of Priscillian to the synod of Gallaecia through Turibius, the notary of his see.

“Moreover, the bishops of Tarragona and Carthage, together with those of Lusitania and Baetica, having held a council among themselves, drew up a rule of faith against the Priscillianist heresy with certain chapters and sent it to Balconius, then bishop of this Church of Braga. Since we have here before us a copy of that prescribed faith together with its chapters, let it be read, if it pleases your reverence, for the instruction of the ignorant.”

All the bishops said:

“The reading of these chapters is extremely necessary, so that, when the ancient statutes of the holy Fathers are disclosed to the simpler among us, they may recognize the fabrications of the Priscillianist heresy, long ago abominated and condemned by the see of the blessed apostle Peter.”

The copy of the faith was read together with its chapters, which were not inserted into these proceedings in order to avoid prolixity.

After the reading of the chapters, all the bishops said:

“Although the reading of these chapters has rightly been judged necessary, nevertheless let the abominable matters be declared more clearly and simply, with the chapters now set forth placed before them, so that even the less learned may understand and so that the fabrications of Priscillian’s error, long ago rejected under the sentence of anathema, may be condemned. Whoever—whether cleric, monk, or layperson—is discovered still to hold or defend anything of this kind shall immediately be cut off from the body of the Catholic Church as a truly rotten limb, lest either his association inflict the stain of his perversity upon those who rightly believe, or the orthodox be further burdened with reproach because of their association with such people.”

## The chapters proposed and reread against the Priscillianist heresy contain the following

### I

If anyone does not confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons of one substance, virtue, and power, as the Catholic and apostolic Church teaches, but says that there is only one solitary person, so that he himself is the Father who is the Son, and he himself is also the Paraclete Spirit, as Sabellius and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

## II. If anyone introduces, outside the Holy Trinity, certain other names of divinity—saying that within the divinity itself there is a Trinity of the Trinity, as the Gnostics and Priscillian said—let him be anathema.

## III. If anyone says that the Son of God, our Lord, did not exist before he was born of the Virgin, as Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0563D] **IV.** If anyone does not truly honor the Nativity of Christ according to the flesh, but pretends to honor it by fasting on that very day and on the Lord’s Day, because he did not believe that Christ was born in the true nature of a human being, as Cerdon, Marcion, Mani, and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**V.** If anyone believes that human souls or angels came into existence from God’s substance, as Mani and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**VI.** If anyone says that human souls sinned previously in a heavenly dwelling and, on account of this, were cast down into human bodies on earth, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**VII.** If anyone says that the devil was not previously a good angel made by God, nor that his nature was God’s workmanship, [Col. 0564A] but says that he emerged from chaos and darkness and has no author of his own, but is himself the beginning and substance of evil, as Mani and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**VIII.** If anyone believes that the devil made certain creatures in the world, and that the devil himself, by his own authority, produces thunder and lightning, storms and droughts, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**IX.** If anyone believes that human souls and bodies are bound by the stars of fate, as the pagans and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**X.** If anyone believes that the twelve signs of the stars, which astrologers customarily observe, are distributed individually among the members of the soul or body and says that they are assigned the names of the patriarchs, as Priscillian says, [Col. 0564B] let him be anathema. 601

**XI.** If anyone condemns human marriages and shudders at the procreation of offspring, as Mani and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XII.** If anyone says that the formation of the human body is a fabrication of the devil, and says that conceptions in mothers’ wombs are shaped by the works of demons—and therefore does not believe in the resurrection of the flesh—as Mani and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XIII.** If anyone says that the creation of all flesh is not God’s workmanship but that of wicked angels, as Mani and Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

**XIV.** If anyone considers the fleshly foods which God gave for human use unclean, and abstains from them not for the affliction of his body but as though considering them impurity, so that he does not even taste cooked vegetables prepared with meat, as Mani and Priscillian said [Note: [Col. 0563D] Ae., B. R., E. 3, U., G.: *docuerunt* (“taught”).], let him be anathema.

**XV.** If any cleric or monk, apart from his mother, sister, aunt, or women joined to him by close blood relationship, keeps other women with him as though adopted and lives with them, as the sect of Priscillian taught, let him be anathema.

**XVI.** If anyone on the Thursday of Easter, which is called the Lord’s Supper, does not hold the proper liturgy in church after the ninth hour while fasting, but, according to the sect of Priscillian, celebrates that day’s feast from the third hour through memorial liturgies for the dead after breaking his fast, let him be anathema.

**XVII.** If anyone reads the Scriptures which Priscillian corrupted according to his own error, or the treatises of Dictinius which Dictinius himself wrote before his conversion, or any writings of heretics which they fabricated under the names of patriarchs, prophets, or apostles in agreement with their own error, and follows or defends their impious fabrications, let him be anathema.

After these chapters had been proposed and reread, Bishop Lucretius said:

“Since those things which Catholics ought to abominate and condemn have now been declared more plainly and openly even to the uninformed, I consider it necessary, if it seems good to your fraternity, that the regulations of the holy Fathers should next be made known to us by reviewing the ancient canons. Even if not all of them, at least some of those pertaining to the instruction of clerical discipline [Col. 0565A] should be reread.”

All the bishops said:

“We approve this statement, and it is fitting that those ecclesiastical regulations which perhaps have been abolished through negligence should be heard and observed by us according to the rule of the holy canons.”

The canons of both general and local synods were reread from the Codex before the council. 602 After their reading, Bishop Lucretius said:

“From this very reading of the canons, let your holy fraternity recognize that not only in general councils but also in local ones, priests assembled together established by common agreement whatever was suited to ecclesiastical order, and, according to the needs of each matter, made provision by following the apostolic teaching that says: ‘Test what is good and hold fast to it.’ If, therefore, it pleases your charity, since there are certain practices of ecclesiastical discipline which, especially in this remote part of the province, vary—not through contentiousness, God forbid, but rather, as we have said, through negligence or ignorance—let us establish certain chapters among ourselves, so that whatever is not observed by us in one manner may be brought altogether to a single form.”

All the bishops said:

“We consider it necessary and very useful that those practices which among each of us are retained through varied and disordered custom should, by God’s grace and our concord, be celebrated in one unified observance. Therefore, whether the matter in which we appear to differ is great or small, let it be brought, as has been said, to one form by chapters reasonably established—especially since, concerning certain [Note: [Col. 0565D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: *caeteris* (“other matters”).] matters, we possess instruction from the apostolic see [Col. 0565C], which was sent from the very chair of blessed Peter in response to a question once addressed by your predecessor of venerable memory, Profuturus.”

Bishop Lucretius said:

“Your fraternity has rightly recalled [Note: [Col. 0565D] In the remaining witnesses, except A., the reading is *terminata* (‘settled’ or ‘completed’).], on the authority of the apostolic see, that instruction which, although it became known at the same time that it was sent, should nevertheless, for the firmness of its testimony and the instruction of many, be reread before all these persons, if it pleases your unanimity, since it is at hand.”

All the bishops said:

“It is right that, since mention has been made of this authority, those present should hear what its teaching is.” [Note: [Col. 0565D] Ae.: “They said: ‘It is approved and right.’”]

The authority of the apostolic see addressed to Bishop Profuturus was reread; because of its length, it has not been inserted into these proceedings. After it had been read, Bishop Lucretius [Col. 0565D] said:

“It is now more clearly evident that apostolic teaching assists us. Therefore, as your fraternity has stated, if anything varies through ignorance among certain persons [Note: [Col. 0566D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: *varia habetur* (“is found to vary”).], let it be bound to a uniform rule of concord by chapters prescribed among us.”

Accordingly, chapters were proposed and reread, containing the following:

## I. On one order of psalmody

[Note: [Col. 0566D] These headings are depicted in the margin in A. and Ae.; they are absent from the other witnesses.]

It pleased everyone by common agreement that one and the same order of psalmody should be maintained in the morning and evening offices, and that monastic customs should not be mixed with the ecclesiastical rule through different and private practices. [Col. 0566A]

## II. On solemn days

It likewise pleased everyone that, during the vigils or liturgies of solemn days, all should read the same readings in church, and not different ones.

## III. On the greeting: “The Lord be with you”

It likewise pleased everyone that bishops and presbyters should greet the people not in different ways but in one manner, saying: “The Lord be with you,” as it is read in the Book of Ruth, so that the people may respond: “And with your spirit.” The whole East retains this practice as handed down by the apostles, and not as Priscillianist perversity has altered it.

## IV. On the order of the liturgies

It likewise pleased everyone that the liturgies be celebrated by all according to the same order, the written order which Profuturus, formerly bishop of this metropolitan church, received from the authority of the apostolic see. [Col. 0566B]

## V. On the order of baptism

It likewise pleased everyone that no one omit the order of baptism which the metropolitan Church of Braga previously observed, and which the aforesaid Profuturus, to remove the doubts of some, received in writing from the bishops and sent to him from the see of blessed Peter the Apostle.

## VI. On the primacy of the bishop

It likewise pleased everyone that, while the primacy of the metropolitan bishop is preserved, the other bishops should, according to the time of their ordination, yield one another places of precedence in seating.

## VII. On ecclesiastical property

[Col. 0566C] It likewise pleased everyone that ecclesiastical property be divided into three equal portions: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, and the third for the repair or the lights of the church. From this portion, the archpresbyter or archdeacon administering it shall render an account to the bishop.

## VIII. On ordaining another person’s cleric

It likewise pleased everyone that no bishop presume to ordain another bishop’s cleric, as the ancient canons have also forbidden, unless perhaps he has received a document bearing that bishop’s seal.

604

## IX. On the deacon’s orarium

It likewise pleased everyone that, since in some churches of this province deacons wear oraria concealed beneath their tunics, so that they appear to differ in nothing from subdeacons, from now on they should wear the orarium placed over the shoulder, as is proper. [Col. 0566D]

## X. On the vessels of the altars

It likewise pleased everyone that no one among the readers be permitted to carry the sacred vessels of the altar, except those who have been ordained subdeacons by the bishop.

## XI. On the readers of the church

It likewise pleased everyone that readers should not sing psalms in church dressed in secular clothing, nor let their hair fall in the manner of pagans.

## XII. On the canonical Scriptures

It likewise pleased everyone that, apart from the Psalms or the canonical Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, nothing composed poetically should be sung in church, as the holy canons also prescribe. [Col. 0567A]

## XIII. Where all communicate

It likewise pleased everyone that laypeople, men or women, be forbidden to enter the sanctuary of the altar in order to receive Communion; only clerics may do so, as the ancient canons have also established.

## XIV. On vegetables and meat

It likewise pleased everyone that any member of the clergy who does not eat meat be compelled, to remove suspicion of Priscillianist heresy, at least to taste cooked vegetables prepared with meat. If they refuse, then, according to what the holy Fathers established long ago concerning such persons, they must, on account of suspicion of this heresy, be removed from office in every way after excommunication. [Col. 0567B]

## XV. On the author of excommunication

It likewise pleased everyone that no one presume to associate with those who have been excommunicated for heresy or for any crime, as the ancient statutes of the canons also contain. Whoever voluntarily despises these statutes will hand himself over to another’s condemnation.

## XVI. On those who kill themselves

It likewise pleased everyone that no commemoration be made in the offering for those who inflict violent death upon themselves, whether by sword, poison, throwing themselves from a height, hanging, or any other means; nor should their corpses be escorted to burial with psalms. 605 For many have arrogated this to themselves through ignorance. The same was decreed concerning those who are punished for their crimes. [Col. 0567C]

## XVII. On deceased catechumens

It likewise pleased everyone that, for catechumens who die without the redemption of baptism, neither a commemoration in the offering nor the office of psalmody be provided in the same manner, for this too has been assumed through ignorance.

## XVIII. On the bodies of the dead

It likewise pleased everyone that the bodies of the dead be buried in no way within the basilica of the saints. If necessity requires it, burial outside, near the wall of the basilica, is not so objectionable. For if cities retain this most firm privilege even now—that in no way may the body of any dead person be buried within the circuit of the walls—how much more ought the reverence due to venerable martyrs to secure this?

## XIX. On the blessing of chrism

[Col. 0567D]

It likewise pleased everyone that if, after this prohibition, any presbyter dares to bless chrism or to consecrate a church or altar, he be removed from office, for the ancient canons have also forbidden this.

## XX. On the status of the laity

It likewise pleased everyone that no layman come to the rank of priesthood before first learning ecclesiastical discipline for a full year in the office of reader or subdeacon, and that, thus instructed through the successive ranks, he come to the priesthood. For it is highly blameworthy that one who has not yet learned should presume to teach, especially since this was also forbidden by the ancient regulations of the Fathers. [Col. 0568A]

## XXI. On the collection of the faithful

It likewise pleased everyone that whatever is offered from the contributions of the faithful, whether during the feast of martyrs or at commemorations of the dead, be faithfully collected by one of the clerics and, at an appointed time, distributed among all the clerics either once or twice a year. 606 For considerable discord arises from this inequality if each person, in his own week, claims for himself whatever has been offered. [Col. 0568B]

## XXII. On the prescriptions of the ancient canons

It likewise pleased everyone that no one dare disregard any of the prescriptions of the ancient canons which have now been recited in the council. If anyone, as though rebellious, transgresses them, he must be degraded from his office.

After the chapters had been reread, Bishop Lucretius said:

“Since, with the Lord’s assistance, we have decreed by unanimous and fitting deliberation those matters which pertain to the steadfastness of the catholic and orthodox faith and those which pertain to the office of ecclesiastical order, it now remains for each of us to strive to teach and instruct his own diocese in all that has been beneficially established through God’s grace. If any one of us, in his parishes, after learning the decrees of this council, finds either a cleric or a monk resisting this sound teaching, or perceives that someone still harbors some error of the Priscillianist sect, and does not immediately cast him out of the church as excommunicated and anathematized, so that none of the faithful dares share food with such a person, let him know that the one who receives such a person is subject both to fraternal excommunication and, beyond doubt, to divine judgment.”

All the bishops said:

“Whatever has been decreed by us, united through God’s grace in common agreement, must be observed with the utmost vigilance, so that the approved constitution may possess lasting firmness. For this reason, let each person subscribe these proceedings with his own hand.” The subscriptions of the bishops followed.

I, Lucretius, bishop, have subscribed. [Col. 0568D]  
I, Andreas, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Martinus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Cortus [U.: *Cortus*], bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Ildericus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Lucetius, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Timotheus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Maliosus [T. 2: *Meliosus*; U., G.: *Maliciosus*], bishop, have subscribed.

# LXIV. The Second Council of Braga, of Twelve Bishops, Held in the Second Year of King Miro, on the Kalends of June, in the Era 610

[Col. 0569]

[Col. 0569A] 607–608 When the bishops of the province of Galicia, from both the synod of Braga and that of Lugo, had assembled together with their metropolitans in the metropolitan church of Braga at the command of the aforesaid king—namely Martinus, Nitigis [Note: [Col. 0569D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1: *Nitigisis*; E. 5: *Nitigisus*; T. 2: *Nitigisius*; so also below.], Remisol, Andreas, Lucretius, Adoricus, Witimer, Sardinarius, Viator, Anila, Polemius, Mahiloc—and these bishops were seated together with the entire clergy present, Martinus, bishop of the Church of Braga, said:

“We believe, most holy brothers, that it has come about through God’s inspiration that, by the arrangement of our lord, the most glorious son and king, we should assemble as one from both councils, so that we may rejoice not only in seeing one another but also discuss together those matters which pertain to ecclesiastical order and discipline. For it is written in the Gospels, the Lord saying: ‘Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I shall be in their midst.’” [Col. 0569B]

Nitigis, bishop of the Church of Lugo, said:

“Nothing else can be believed except that those matters which pertain to the benefit of our souls can both be begun and completed through divine inspiration. Therefore, since we are all unanimous and think the same thing in the Lord, we desire to recognize whatever is brought forward that pertains to our instruction.”

Bishop Martinus said:

“We suppose that your blessedness remembers that when the first council of bishops was assembled in the Church of Braga, after many matters had been confirmed for the concord of the true faith, we also established certain things containing the orderly discernment of the holy canons. So that their usefulness may be recalled more clearly to memory, let that very letter be reread in your presence, if it pleases you.”

All the bishops said:

“It ought by every means to be recited in the hearing of all who are standing here.”

After the chapters had therefore been recited—because of their length they have not been inserted in these proceedings—Bishop Martinus said:

“These matters which have just been recited, which at that time seemed to us either varied, doubtful, or disordered, have, with God’s help, been set straight and now possess their firmness immutably. But those matters which did not then come to mind, or which it was burdensome to introduce all at once in that first council, now seem necessary to bring to the attention of your holy charity, with the particular purpose that, once examined by a special inquiry, they may be purified.

“For the holy Fathers and our predecessors, gathered from everywhere into general synods for the unity of the true faith, acted in this way: at Nicaea, 318 against Arius; at Constantinople, 150 against Macedonius; at Ephesus, 200 against Nestorius; and at Chalcedon, 630 against Eutyches. Or they convened special synods throughout their respective provinces to cut away contemptuous conduct or correct the negligence of some, and, as the occurrence of faults or whatever kind of excess required, they wrote, through the Spirit of God among them, defined judgments of the canons for each matter. We ought to read, understand, and retain them [Ae.: *retinere*, “retain”].

“And since, by Christ’s grace assisting us, there is no doubt in this province concerning the unity and soundness of the faith, we must now attend more particularly to this: if anything reprehensible is perhaps found among us outside apostolic discipline through ignorance or negligence, let us, turning to the testimonies of the holy Scriptures or the regulations of the ancient canons, and applying common [Col. 0570B] agreement, correct by reasonable judgment everything that displeases us.

“And first, if it pleases you, after rereading the commands of blessed Peter the Apostle, which he clearly wrote in his letter as a rule for priests, let us hasten without hesitation to amend whatever appears to be done by us otherwise than the prince of the apostles taught, lest, while we preach to others, we ourselves should be found rejected and condemned by that divine saying: ‘But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you.’”

All the bishops said:

“We desire to hear the letter of the Apostle Peter at the place where he teaches priests.”

Then, when the book had been brought, the following was read from the same letter:

“Elders, I exhort as a fellow elder: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, watching over it, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for the sake of sordid gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy [Note: [Col. 0570D] T. 1: *in clericis* (“over clerics”); T. 2: *in clero* (“over the clergy”).], but becoming a model for the flock from the heart, so that when the chief Shepherd appears you may receive the unfading crown of glory.”

After these words had been reread, all the bishops said:

“Having learned what has been recited from the letter of blessed Peter the Apostle, we desire, with God’s grace assisting us, to obey the divine commands and imitate in all things the model of the apostolic letter which has been read to us. Let us not, God forbid, be condemned by divine judgment because we walk disorderly in some matters, but, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, let us deserve to share in their rest and, together with them, receive that unfading crown of glory which has been promised.

“For this reason, we all together ask your charity to append below these proceedings all these matters, briefly included in individual chapters, explaining how they ought to be corrected. Once they have been carefully reread and more clearly brought to the knowledge of all our people, let each person subscribe with his own hand for their correction and confirmation, so that these decrees for the perfection of episcopal office may benefit not only us but also our successors.”

## I. That the bishop should travel through his diocese, and that the catechumens should be taught the Creed twenty days before Easter

It pleased all the bishops, and they agreed, that as bishops travel through the individual churches of their dioceses, they should first examine the clergy concerning how they observe the order of baptism and of the liturgies, and how each of the offices is performed. If they find everything correct, thanks be to God; but if not, they must teach the uninformed and prescribe by every means that, as the ancient canons command, twenty days before baptism the catechumens should undertake the purification of exorcism. During these twenty days the catechumens must be specially taught the Creed, namely: “I believe in God the Father Almighty.”

After the bishops have examined or taught their clergy in these matters, they should on another day summon the people of that church and teach them to avoid the errors of idols and various crimes—that is, murder, adultery, perjury, false testimony, and the remaining deadly sins—and not to do to another what they do not wish done to themselves. They should teach them to believe in the resurrection of all human beings and the day of judgment, on which each person will receive according to his works. Then the bishop should depart from that church and proceed to another. [Col. 0571B]

## II. That the bishop traveling through his diocese should accept only two solidi, should not demand a third part of the offerings, and that the clergy should not be compelled in a servile manner

[Col. 0571C] It pleased everyone that none of the bishops, when traveling through his dioceses, should take anything from the churches apart from the honor due to his see, namely two solidi, nor demand a third part of any offering of the people in the parish churches. Instead, that third part should be reserved for the lights or repair of the church, so that an account of it may be rendered to the bishop each year. For if the bishop takes that third part, he has taken away the church’s light and sacred roofs.

Likewise, it was decreed that parish clergy should not be compelled in a servile manner to perform certain works for the bishop, because it is written: “Nor domineering by force over the clergy.”

## III. That the bishop should accept no advantage in the ordination of clerics

[Col. 0571D] It pleased everyone that bishops accept no gifts for the ordinations of clerics. Rather, as it is written, “You have received freely from God’s gracious gift; give freely,” and God’s grace and the laying on of hands must not be sold for any price. For the ancient decree of the Fathers established the following concerning ecclesiastical ordinations: “Anathema to the giver and to the receiver.”

Because some persons, overwhelmed by many crimes and unworthily ministering at the holy altar, obtain this not through the testimony of good works but through an outpouring of gifts, clerics must therefore be ordained not through the favor of gifts but first through careful examination and then through the testimony of many.

## IV. That the bishop should accept nothing for chrism

It pleased everyone that, concerning the small amount of balsam which is blessed and given through the churches for the sacrament of baptism—for which three *tremisses* are customarily demanded—nothing further should be required, lest we appear damnably to sell what is consecrated through the invocation of the Holy Spirit for the salvation of souls, just as Simon Magus sought to purchase God’s gift with money. [Col. 0572A]

## V. That the bishop should demand nothing for the consecration of a basilica

It pleased everyone that whenever bishops are invited by one of the faithful to consecrate churches, they should not demand a gift from the founder as though it were owed. If the founder himself offers something from his own vow, it should not be refused; but if poverty or necessity holds him back, nothing should be demanded from him.

Each bishop must remember this alone: he should not dedicate a church or basilica until he has first received confirmation, through a deed of donation, of the basilica’s endowment and the provision for its service. For it is no slight recklessness if a church is consecrated like a private house without lights or without support for those who will serve there. [Col. 0572B]

## VI. That an oratory built for profit on someone’s land should not be consecrated

It pleased everyone that if anyone builds a basilica not out of devotion to the faith but out of greedy desire for profit, so that whatever is collected there from the people’s offerings may be divided equally with the clerics because he himself built the basilica on his own land—a practice said still to occur in certain places—then this must henceforth be observed: no bishop should assent to so abominable an intention as to dare consecrate a basilica founded not for the patronage of the saints but rather under a tributary condition. [Col. 0572C]

## VII. That no one should accept a reward for those baptized

It pleased everyone that each bishop should prescribe throughout his churches that, if those who present their infants for baptism voluntarily offer something as part of their vow, it should be accepted from them. But if, because of the necessity of poverty, they have nothing to offer, no pledge should be taken from them by force by the clerics.

For many poor people, fearing this, hold back their children from baptism. If, while delaying, their children should happen to depart this life without the grace of baptism, their loss must be required of those who, fearing the seizure of their possessions [Note: [Col. 0571D] So in the text, perhaps for *exspoliationem* (“plundering”). EDIT.], held themselves back from the grace of baptism.

## VIII. That anyone who accuses a cleric and cannot prove it should be excommunicated

[Col. 0572D] It pleased everyone that if anyone brings an accusation of fornication against a cleric, two or three witnesses should be required of him according to the command of the Apostle Paul. If he cannot prove by the witnesses he produces what he has said, the accuser should receive the excommunication intended for the accused.

## IX. That Easter should be announced each year by the metropolitan to the bishops

It pleased everyone that, after all matters had been arranged in the council of priests, this should by every means be observed: the metropolitan bishop should announce the Easter of the coming year, specifying on what calendar date or on what lunar day it ought to be celebrated. 612 The other bishops and the remaining clergy should note this in a brief memorandum and each announce it in his own church to the assembled people, after the Gospel reading, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, so that no one may be unaware of the beginning of Lent.

At its beginning, the neighboring churches should assemble and, for three days, celebrate litanies while walking with psalms through the basilicas of the saints. On the third day, after liturgies have been celebrated at the ninth or tenth hour, they should dismiss the people and instruct them to observe the fasts of Lent. At the middle of Lent, they should present infants to be baptized, twenty days before baptism, for the purification of exorcism. [Col. 0573A]

## X. That a presbyter should not hold a liturgy for the dead after eating

It pleased everyone that, since we have recently learned that certain presbyters remain in the audacity of this presumption, corrupted either by the folly of a recently assumed error or at least by the stench of the old Priscillianist heresy, so that they have dared to consecrate the offering at a liturgy for the dead even after drinking wine, the following should be observed by an explicit admonition of the prescribed judgment: if, after this edict of ours, any presbyter is again found in this madness—that is, if he consecrates the offering at the altar not while fasting but after having already taken any food—he shall immediately be deprived of his office and deposed by his own bishop. [Col. 0573B]

After these matters had been recorded, it pleased everyone, for the confirmation of their observance, that each person should subscribe with his own hand. It was agreed that if anyone wished to transgress the limit of any of these chapters and return to disordered customs, he should be corrected by the rebuke of the entire council and recognize that the severest judgment concerning the degradation of his order threatens him. [Col. 0573C]

I, Martinus, bishop of the metropolitan Church of Braga, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Remisol, bishop of the Church of Beja, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Lucetius, bishop of the Church of Coimbra, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Adoricus, bishop of the Church of Idanha, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Sardinarius, bishop of the Church of Lamego, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Viator, bishop of the Church of Meñtesa, have subscribed these proceedings.

[Col. 0573D] **From the synod of Lugo.**

I, Nitigis, bishop of the metropolitan Church of Lugo [Note: [Col. 0573D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “of the Church of Lugo”], have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Andreas, bishop of the Church of Iria [U., G.: *Herenensis*], have subscribed these proceedings. 613  
I, Witimer, bishop of the Church of Ourense, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Polimius, bishop of the Church of Astorga, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Anila, bishop of the Church of Tui, have subscribed these proceedings.  
I, Mahiloc, bishop of the Church of Britonia, have subscribed these proceedings.

[Col. 0574A] **Chapters, or canons, excerpted or revised from the synods of the ancient Eastern Fathers by the venerable Bishop Martinus or by the entire Council of Braga: headings in which he restored the judgments concerning clerics separately and those concerning laypeople separately, so that everything which translators rendered more obscurely from Greek into Latin, or which the negligence of scribes had corrupted or altered, might be contained in this one place in a simpler and more corrected form, so that whoever wishes to know about a particular chapter may find it more quickly.**

To the most blessed Lord and brother in Christ, Nitigis, worthy of the honor of the apostolic see, bishop, and to the entire council of the Church of Lugo, Martinus, bishop, sends greetings:

The holy canons which were established in the regions of the East by the ancient Fathers were first written in the Greek language and later, in the course of time, translated into Latin. [Col. 0574B] Since it is difficult for something to be transferred more simply from one language into another, and since it also happens that over so many years scribes, whether failing to understand or falling asleep, omit many things, certain matters in these canons consequently appear obscure to simpler readers.

Therefore it seemed appropriate that I should restore with every diligence, in a simpler and more corrected form, both what the translators expressed obscurely and what the scribes altered. I have observed this principle first: that those matters pertaining to bishops or the entire clergy should be written together in one section, and likewise those pertaining to laypeople should be gathered together, so that whoever wishes to know about a particular chapter may find it more quickly.

## I. On the election of a bishop

[Col. 0574C] The people must not make the election of those who are called to the priesthood; the judgment belongs to the bishops, so that they themselves may test the person who is to be ordained, whether he has been instructed in speech, faith, and spiritual life.

## II. On the ordination of a bishop

A bishop ought above all to be appointed by the entire council. But if this is difficult either because of necessity or because of the length of the journey, three should be gathered from among all, and the subscriptions of all, present or absent, should be obtained; only then should the ordination take place. Authority in this matter throughout the entire province belongs to the metropolitan.

## III. On annulling an ordination performed in the absence of the metropolitan

A bishop ought not to be ordained without the counsel and presence of the metropolitan bishop. All the priests who are in the province ought to be present, and he must summon them by his letter. If all attend, so much the better; but if this is difficult, the greater number ought to attend. Those who do not assemble should make their presence known through letters of their own, and the bishop’s ordination ought then to take place with the consent of all.

If anything is done otherwise than has been determined by us, we decree that such an ordination shall have no force. But if the bishop’s ordination has been carried out according to the canons and someone, out of malice, opposes it in some respect, the agreement of the majority shall prevail.

## IV. On the primacy of the metropolitan

[Col. 0575A]

Throughout the individual provinces, each bishop ought to recognize the primacy of the metropolitan bishop and to accept his oversight. The other bishops should do nothing without him, according to what is contained in the canon established long ago by our Fathers. For this reason, the metropolitan bishop should presume to undertake nothing on his own without the counsel of the others.

## V. On one who, through ambition, wishes to exercise clerical office by moving from a lesser city to a greater

If anyone is found to be ambitious in any matter—whether a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—he must not move from a lesser city to a greater one. If anyone obstinately resists these decrees of the great council, the action must be entirely annulled, [Col. 0575B] and he must be restored again to his own Church, in which he had previously been appointed bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

## VI. On not changing a parish
A bishop may not transfer from his own parish to another, nor enter it on his own initiative, whether invited or compelled by a bishop; rather, he must remain in the place in which he was ordained by God, and in the Church that he received by lot, according to the ordinance of the ancient canons.

### VII. On presumption concerning another diocese

If any bishop, not summoned by written request from the metropolitan [615] bishop or from those who are with him, comes from one province into another, but presumptuously intrudes and behaves improperly in ordaining and appointing clerics who do not belong to him, everything that he has appointed shall be void and empty [Col. 0575C]. He himself shall be excommunicated as deserving rebuke and rejected by the holy council.

### VIII. On not appointing a successor bishop

A bishop may not, before the end of his life, appoint another as his successor in his own place. If anyone attempts to usurp this right, such an appointment shall be invalid. It must therefore be done only with the counsel and judgment of the bishops who, after the predecessor’s death, have authority to ordain whomever they judge worthy.

### IX. On intruding into a vacant church

If any bishop, seizing a vacant church that has no bishop, rushes in and takes possession of its people without the council of the entire order—even if the people whom he has led astray desire him—he must be regarded as alien to the Church [Col. 0575D]. By a complete and perfect council we mean one in which the metropolitan bishop is present.

### X. On a bishop prevented by necessity from taking possession of his see

If a bishop has been ordained because of a dispute among the people or for some other reason, and through no fault of his own has not gone to the parish assigned to him, he shall receive only the honor of the priesthood and must presume to claim nothing from the goods of the Church in which he has been appointed. He shall await what the holy council wishes to judge concerning him.

### XI. On a bishop who despises his office

If a bishop ordained by a bishop is unwilling to exercise the priesthood and does not consent to go to the Church entrusted to him [Col. 0576A], he must be excommunicated immediately [Ae., at once]. If, however, he despises it after being compelled, the holy council shall determine what it approves concerning him.

### XII. On a seditious bishop

If a bishop has been ordained but does not wish to accept the very parish in which he was appointed, instead wishing to be ordained elsewhere, and uses force and stirs up seditions against those who ordained him, he must be removed from his dignity. If he wishes to remain in his former rank of presbyter, he should not be forbidden to retain the degree he held. But if he resists, he must also be deposed from the dignity of the presbyterate by his own ordaining bishop.

[616]

### XIII. On disagreement in judgment

[Col. 0576B] If a bishop is being judged in some cases of accusation [B. R., T. 1, 2, “charges”], and he sees that the bishops who are in the province disagree among themselves in judgment, so that some appear to justify the one being judged while others condemn him, the holy council has decreed the following for resolving this disagreement: another metropolitan bishop from a neighboring province shall be summoned, so that through him what accords with the correct canon may be confirmed.

### XIV. On a bishop’s presumption regarding Church property

If any bishop, compelled by no necessity of ecclesiastical business, presumes to sell something from ecclesiastical property without the knowledge of the clergy—or, where there happens to be no presbyter, [the printed reading is elliptical]—he shall be compelled to restore those goods to the particular Church to which they belong. In the judgment of the bishops [Col. 0576C], after being heard, he shall be deposed and deprived of his dignity as guilty of theft or robbery.

### XV. On administering Church property

What belongs to the Church must be preserved for the Church with every diligence, a good conscience, and faith in God, who sees and judges all things. It must therefore be administered with the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the entire people and congregation of souls have also been entrusted.

What belongs to the Church must be made known to the conscience of those who are around the bishops—the presbyters and deacons—so that all of them may know what is the Church’s own property. Thus, if a bishop should die, none of the things belonging to the Church can remain hidden from them, and in no way can those things be diminished or lost.

Nor should the bishop’s own property be subjected to harassment on account of the Church’s property. It is worthy, truly, and just before God and human beings that a bishop may leave his own possessions to whomever he wishes, and that neither the Church should suffer loss nor the bishop be condemned on account of Church property, or, after his death, be brought into lawsuits or reproach concerning matters that do not belong to him.

### XVI. On distributing Church property

A bishop shall have authority over Church property so that he may distribute it to those in need. He must share what is necessary with all reverence and fear of God. If, however, he himself or the brothers who are with him should lack something, they must in no way suffer want, according to the holy Apostle, who says: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content.”

But if a bishop wishes to appropriate Church property for his own purposes and, without the counsel of the presbyters or deacons, improperly handles the Church’s revenues or the produce of its fields, or gives authority to his brothers, sons, or any relatives so that Church property may secretly be harmed through them, he must be held accountable to the council [617].

The same applies if a bishop, or the presbyters or deacons who are with him, are accused of gathering into their own bosoms what comes to the Church from revenues or from any other activity, while defrauding the poor and wearing them down with hunger. They must be rebuked according to what the holy council has determined [Col. 0577A].

### XVII. On those who sell anything from the vessels used in the Church’s ministry

[Col. 0577B] If any presbyter or deacon is found to have sold something belonging to the Church’s sacred ministry, because he has committed sacrilege, it has been resolved that he shall not hold ecclesiastical office. Nevertheless, it shall be left to the bishop’s judgment whether he is worthy or unworthy to be restored to his rank, since on many occasions this very offense—defiling something from the most holy altar—has been remitted by the bishop’s authority.

### XVIII. On holding a synod

For the sake of ecclesiastical affairs and the resolution of disputes, it has been rightly decided that a council shall be held twice a year in each province. The metropolitan bishop shall summon [Note: [Col. 0577D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, “convoke”] all the bishops of the province, so that at these councils all presbyters, deacons, and those whose cases have been examined in their council may proceed to a just [Col. 0577C] judgment. If any bishops, presbyters, or deacons are clearly found to be at fault, they shall be excommunicated according to due process, for as long as the common agreement has determined that a milder sentence should be given concerning them.

No bishop may hold councils on his own authority, except those to whom metropolitan sees have been entrusted.

### XIX. On a bishop who refuses to come to the synod

Bishops summoned to the council may not be detained; they must go, and concerning matters that pertain to the benefit of the Church or of the others, they must either teach if they know, or be taught if they do not know.
