For if, apart from illness, anyone despises the summons and refuses to go, he shall be guilty before the council of the brethren.

### XX. On the proper age for ordaining presbyters

[Col. 0577D] If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he must under no circumstances be ordained presbyter, even if he is very worthy, because the Lord himself was baptized in his thirtieth year and then began to teach. Therefore, the one who is to be ordained must be kept until this lawful age [618].

### XXI. On eunuchs made so by others and on those who cut off their own natural organs

If anyone has had his natural organs cut off by physicians because of an illness, and likewise those who have been castrated by barbarians or foolish people [Note: [Col. 0577D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “or by foolish masters”], and if they appear worthy in character, this canon permits them to be promoted to clerical office [Col. 0578A].

But if a healthy person, not through the discipline of religion and abstinence but by cutting away the body fashioned by God, has castrated himself, thinking that he could amputate his carnal desires from himself, we decree that he is not to be admitted to any clerical office. If he had already been promoted to the clerical order [Note: [Col. 0578D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., G., “the clergy”], he shall be prohibited from his ministry and deposed.

### XXII. On neophytes

A neophyte who has recently been baptized, even if he is already of lawful age, may not immediately be promoted to an ecclesiastical order, because he must first be taught what he may teach and be tested for a long time after baptism, so that, having been well proved, he may come to the clergy according to the Apostle’s command: “Not a neophyte, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil” [Col. 0578B].

If, in the time that follows, he is overcome by a grave sin and this is established by two or three witnesses, he shall be deposed from his rank and cease from the clergy. If anyone presumes to act against this rule, he shall be expelled from the clergy as an opponent of the great council.

### XXIII. On not admitting a penitent to the clergy

A penitent may be assigned among the doorkeepers, or first among the readers if necessity or custom requires it, but he may not read the Gospels or the Apostle. Those who were ordained earlier shall be counted among the subdeacons, but they may not lay on hands or touch sacred things.

By “penitent” we mean one who, after baptism, has been reconciled to the divine altar after performing public penance in sackcloth for homicide, various crimes, or very grave sins.

### XXIV. On those ordained presbyters or deacons without examination

[Col. 0578C] If any presbyters or deacons have been ordained without examination, or if, when examined, they concealed their criminal sins and after ordination were exposed by others, they shall be expelled from the clergy [619]. The same rule shall be observed concerning the entire clerical order, for the holy and catholic Church will defend what is irreproachable in itself.

### XXV. On presbyters or deacons denounced after ordination

If a presbyter sinned before ordination and after ordination confesses that he had previously gone astray, he shall not offer the sacrifice, but shall bear the name of presbyter only for the sake of religion. If he did not confess it himself but was publicly convicted by another [Col. 0578D], he shall not even have the authority to bear the name of presbyter.

The same must be observed concerning deacons: if the deacon himself confesses, he shall receive the order of subdeacon.

### XXVI. On those who marry widows or divorced women, or who are involved in evil counsels

If anyone marries a widow or a woman divorced by another man, he shall not be admitted to the clergy; or, if he has slipped in, he shall be deposed.

Likewise, if after baptism he has been involved in homicide, whether by deed, command, counsel, or consent, and has entered the clergy by some deception, he shall be deposed and shall receive communion only at the end of his life.

### XXVII. On clerics who commit fornication

[Col. 0579A] If any presbyter or deacon has committed fornication or adultery, he shall be expelled and shall perform penance.

### XXVIII. On those whose wives commit adultery

If anyone’s wife is caught in adultery, such a man must in no way be brought into ecclesiastical ministry. If the wife of a cleric commits adultery after his ordination [Note: [Col. 0579D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, “has committed adultery”], he must dismiss her; but if he wishes to remain with her, he shall be excluded from the ministry.

### XXIX. On the widows of clerics

If a widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon takes another husband, no cleric and no religious woman shall eat with her; no one shall communicate with her. Only when she is dying shall the sacrament be given to her [Note: [Col. 0579D] In the others, except A., “let the sacraments assist her”].

### XXX. On the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon

[Col. 0579B] If she has been dedicated and takes a husband, and her father or mother receives her affectionately, they shall be excluded from communion. The father must know that he will have to answer for the matter before the council [620].

The woman herself shall not be admitted to communion unless, after her husband’s death, she has performed penance. But if, while he is alive, she separates from him and performs penance or requests communion [Note: [Col. 0579D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., “and repents or asks”], she shall receive communion when she is failing at the end of her life.

### XXXI. On a dedicated woman who sins or marries

A dedicated woman who sins is not to be received into the Church unless she ceases to sin and, after ceasing, performs suitable penance for ten years and receives communion. Before she is admitted to prayer in the Church, she may not attend the banquet of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, the woman who received her shall likewise be regarded as having incurred abstention [Col. 0579C]; the corrupter shall also be bound by the same penalty.

A woman who takes a husband shall not be admitted to penance unless she has lived chastely while that husband was still alive, or after he has departed this life.

### XXXII. On women introduced as adopted companions

No bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the clergy may have permission to admit to himself some woman as though she were an adopted daughter, sister, or mother, except perhaps a true sister by full kinship, or the sister of his father or mother, and only those persons who are free from every evil suspicion.

Likewise, we forbid religious women the familiarity and companionship of unrelated laymen, and of those who are neither subject to the fear of God [Col. 0579D] nor maintain the discipline of continence.

### XXXIII. On not receiving wandering clerics and on invalidating the ordination of one ordained by another bishop without his own bishop’s consent

If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the clergy, being under censure, withdraws from his own Church, he must under no circumstances be received into another [Note: [Col. 0580D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, “received into another Church”], but must be compelled in every way to return to his own Church.

If he persists in pride and refuses to return, he shall be excommunicated and expelled. If any bishop dares to ordain him into his own Church, without the consent of the bishop from whom he withdrew, his ordination shall be declared void [Col. 0580A].

### XXXIV. On clerical deserters

If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the clergy abandons his own Church, goes to another Church, and remains there for a long time, he shall never serve in the clergy [621].

If his bishop admonishes him to return to his own parish and he refuses, he shall be deposed from his office wherever he is, so that he may never return to his former rank because of the sin of disorder.

If another bishop receives him while aware of his offence, that bishop himself must, without further rebuke, be excluded from the common council, so that he may no longer violate the ecclesiastical canon.

### XXXV. On importunate clerics

[Col. 0580B] If any excommunicated bishop, presbyter, or deacon complains that he was unjustly condemned by the council, he shall return to a greater council of bishops and, awaiting their investigation and judgment, set forth whatever just causes he thinks he has.

But if he despises this and, by harassing the palace, wishes to trouble the ears of the rulers, he will be able to obtain no pardon and will have no hope of future reconciliation.

### XXXVI. On clearing a suspicion of heresy

If any bishop, or any presbyter or deacon belonging to a bishop, has fallen into the opinion of some heresy and for this reason has been excommunicated, no bishop may receive him into communion unless, first presenting in the common council a written statement of his faith, he satisfies everyone [Col. 0580C] and thereby maintains his acquittal free and clear.

The same decree shall apply to lay believers if they have been accused of holding some heretical opinion.

### XXXVII. On excommunicated clerics

If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been excommunicated by the council and, after excommunication, presumes—whether that bishop, presbyter, or deacon—to make an offering, or to conduct a morning or evening sacrifice as though he were exercising his office as before, he may not have hope of reconciliation in any other council [Note: [Col. 0580D] E. 4, T. 1, 2, “in any council”], nor may he ever be restored.

All who communicate with him shall also be rejected by the Church [Col. 0580D], especially those who knew that he had been deposed. But if he persists in disturbing and stirring up the Church through external authority, he must be expelled from the entire people as a seditious person.

### XXXVIII. On presbyters not attending second marriages

A presbyter ought not to go as a guest to a second marriage [Note: [Col. 0580D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., “become one”], because those who enter into second marriages seek penance. How can that man be a presbyter who attends such a marriage for the sake of the banquet? [622]

### XXXIX. On those chosen for the diaconate

If anyone is chosen for the ministry of the diaconate, and, when called to accept marriage, declares that he cannot remain chaste, he shall not be ordained. If he remains silent at his ordination, is ordained, and later desires marriage, he shall be excluded from the ministry and shall be removed from the clergy.

### XL. A deacon may not sit without being ordered to do so

[Note: [Col. 0581D] This and the following titles of the canons are taken from Toledan codices, since they are lacking in A.]

A deacon may not sit before a presbyter unless ordered to do so by the presbyter.

### XLI. No one may touch the sacred vessels

No one may touch the sacred vessels, except that a subdeacon or acolyte may touch the Lord’s vessels in the sacristy [Note: [Col. 0581D] B. R., T. 1, 2, “sacrarium”] [Col. 0581B].

### XLII. Women may not enter the sacristy

Women may not enter the sacristy [Note: [Col. 0582D] B. R., “sacrarium”].

### XLIII. If a reader marries another man’s widow

If a reader takes another man’s widow as his wife, he shall remain in the readership; or, if necessity should require it, he may become a subdeacon, but nothing higher. The same applies if he has married twice.

### XLIV. If a subdeacon takes a second wife

If a subdeacon takes a second wife, he shall be counted among the readers or doorkeepers, so that he may not read the Apostle.

### XLV. A reader may not ascend the pulpit

No one may sing or read from the pulpit except those who have been ordained readers by a presbyter [Note: [Col. 0582D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, U., “by a bishop”].

### XLVI. On those bound by a condition not being ordained without the consent of their patrons

[Col. 0581C] If anyone is bound by a servile tribute or by some condition to the patronage of any household, he is not to be ordained a cleric unless he has been of proven life and the patron’s consent has been given [Note: [Col. 0582D] E. 3, U., “agreement”].

### XLVII. On not receiving another person’s slaves into the clergy

If anyone, in the name of religion, teaches another person’s slave to despise his master and withdraw from his service, he shall be severely rebuked in every way [623].

### XLVIII. On not celebrating the birthdays of martyrs during Lent

The birthdays of martyrs may not be celebrated during Lent. Offerings may be made in their memory only on Saturday and Sunday. Nor may birthdays [Col. 0581D] or weddings be celebrated during Lent.

### XLIX. Infants are not to be received for baptism before three weeks before Easter

No one may be received for baptism before two weeks before Easter, but only before three weeks; and during these days those who are to be baptized must learn the creed and recite it to the bishop or presbyter on the Thursday of the final week.

### L. On not breaking the fast on the Thursday of Easter week

The fast may not be broken on the Thursday of the final week, thereby dishonoring the whole of Lent [Col. 0582A]. Rather, let them abstain sincerely and complete the whole of Lent using more austere foods.

### LI. On preparing the chrism

At all times bishops may prepare chrism and send it throughout their dioceses. For the purpose of conveying the chrism, a deacon or subdeacon from each Church shall be sent to the bishop before Easter Day.

### LII. A presbyter may not chrism in the presence of the bishop

A presbyter, when the bishop is present, may not sign infants unless the bishop has specifically commanded him to do so.

### LIII. A presbyter may not enter the baptistery before the bishop

A presbyter may not enter the baptistery before the bishop, but only together with the bishop, unless the bishop is absent or ill [Col. 0582B].

### LIV. On baptizing pregnant women

If any pregnant woman desires to receive the grace of baptism, she shall have the power to do so whenever she wishes. For the mother shares nothing of this matter with the infant who is to be born, and therefore each person’s own will must be shown in the confession of faith.

### LV. What ought to be offered on the altar

Nothing else ought to be offered in the sanctuary [624] except bread, wine, and water, which are blessed as a type of Christ, because while he hung upon the cross, blood and water flowed from his body. These three are one in Christ Jesus; this is the offering and sacrifice of God for a pleasing fragrance.

### LVI. On visiting presbyters

Visiting presbyters may not offer or minister among the people in the presence of the bishop or the city’s presbyter, unless these are absent [Col. 0582C].

### LVII. On not fasting or kneeling on Sunday, and likewise during the fifty days

If any presbyter, because of public penance received from a priest, or because of some necessity, fasts on Sunday under a religious pretext, as the Manichaeans do, let him be anathema.

Likewise, in accordance with the ancient canon handed down by the apostles, it has been resolved that throughout all Sundays and all the days of Easter up to Pentecost we shall not perform our prayers prostrate or bowed down, but with our faces raised toward the Lord. For on these days we celebrate the joy of the Lord’s resurrection.

### LVIII. On not tasting meat beforehand and not treating it as accursed

[Col. 0582D] If anyone abstains from meat not as a discipline of abstinence but because he regards it as accursed, the holy council has resolved that he should taste it, and then, if he wishes, abstain.

But if he rejects it so completely that he will not even taste vegetables cooked with meat, he shall be deposed from the clerical order as disobedient and as one who has not removed the suspicion of heresy from himself.

### LIX. On priests and clerics not practicing incantations or magical bindings

Clerics may not be practitioners of incantations or make magical bindings [Col. 0583A], which are a binding of souls. If anyone does these things, he shall be expelled from the Church.

### LX. Priests and clerics may not attend spectacles

Priests and clerics may not watch any spectacles at weddings or banquets. Before entering such spectacles, they must rise and withdraw from the place.

### LXI. Banquets may not be made from collected offerings

Priests and clerics, and likewise religious laypeople, may not hold banquets from collected offerings.

### LXII. On interest and profits from business

If anyone, having forgotten the fear of the Lord and the holy Scripture, which says, “Who has not given his money at interest,” after learning this decree of the great [Col. 0583B] council, lends at interest and exacts hundredths, or seeks shameful profits from any business, or obtains increases through buying or selling various kinds of wine, grain, or any other thing, he shall be deposed from his rank and regarded as excluded from the clergy [625].

### LXIII. On clerics who do not come to morning and evening services

If any presbyter, deacon, or any cleric assigned to a church is within the city or in any place where there is a church, and does not gather at the church for the daily service of psalmody at the morning or evening hours, he shall be deposed from the clergy, unless, after being disciplined, he wishes to obtain pardon from the bishop through satisfaction.

### LXIV. Clerics may not be absent from the Church on Sunday

[Col. 0583C] No cleric may be absent from the Church on Sunday. He must attend the solemn celebrations of the Mass and the fast.

### LXV. Clerics may not eat before the third hour, or approach or leave the table without a hymn

Clerics and religious laypeople ought not to begin banquets before the sacred third hour of the day. Clerics may never eat bread unless a hymn has been recited, and after the meal they must give thanks to God the Creator.

### LXVI. On cutting the hair of clerics and their prescribed clothing

Clerics ought not to grow their hair and minister in that condition, but must have their heads shorn, their ears exposed, and, following Aaron, must wear a full-length garment, so that they may be in prescribed attire [Col. 0583D].

### LXVII. Poetic psalms may not be recited in the Church, nor apocryphal books read

Composed and popular psalms ought not to be recited in the Church, nor should books outside the canon be read, except the canonical books of the New and Old Testaments.

### LXVIII. Masses may not be held over the monuments of the dead

Clerics who are ignorant or presumptuous may not carry out ministries [T. 2, “mysteries”] or distribute sacraments over monuments in the open field. Rather, an offering for the dead is to be made either in the Church or in the basilica where the relics of the martyrs have been deposited [Col. 0584A] [626].

### LXIX. Christians may not carry meals to monuments

Christians may not carry meals to the tombs of the dead or offer sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0583D] Ae., B. R., T. 1, 2, “and sacrifice from the things of the dead”] to God on behalf of the dead.

### LXX. Catholic clerics and laypeople may not receive *eulogiae* from heretics or pray with them or with schismatics

Catholic clerics and laypeople may not receive *eulogiae* from heretics, because they are curses rather than blessings. Nor may they pray either with heretics or with schismatics.

### LXXI. Christians may not observe various superstitions

[Col. 0584B] If anyone, following pagan custom, brings diviners and sorcerers into his house, as though they might drive out evil, discover magical practices, or perform pagan purifications, he shall perform penance for five years.

### LXXII. Christians may not maintain pagan traditions or observe the course of the moon or stars

Christians may not maintain the traditions of the pagans, observe or worship the elements, follow the course of the moon or stars, or heed the empty deception of signs when building a house, cultivating crops, planting trees, or arranging marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God.”

### LXXIII. The Kalends may not be observed

[Col. 0584C] No one may practice the wicked observances of the Kalends, devote himself to pagan leisure, or wreath houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All such observance belongs to paganism.

### LXXIV. Medicinal herbs may not be gathered with any ritual observance

When gathering medicinal herbs, no one may practice any ritual observances or incantations, except with the divine creed or the Lord’s Prayer, so that only God, the Creator and Lord of all, may be honored.

### LXXV. Christian women may not observe anything in their spinning and weaving

[627] Christian women may not observe any superstition in their spinning and weaving, but must invoke the Lord as helper, who gave them the wisdom to weave [Col. 0584D].

### LXXVI. On adulterers

If any man’s wife commits adultery, or if any man attacks another man’s wife, they shall perform penance for seven years.

### LXXVII. On fornicator women and those who cause abortions

If a woman commits fornication and kills the infant born from it, or if she attempts to cause an abortion and kill what has been conceived, or works to prevent conception, whether from adultery or from a legitimate marriage, earlier canons decreed that such women should receive communion only at the point of death.

We, however, out of mercy, judge that such women, and those who are accomplices in their crimes, should perform penance for ten years [Col. 0585A].

### LXXVIII. On voluntary and involuntary homicide

If anyone voluntarily commits homicide, he shall remain perpetually subject at the door of the Catholic Church and shall receive communion at the end of his life.

If anyone commits homicide not voluntarily but by accident, the earlier canon ordered seven years of penance, while the second canon prescribed five years.

### LXXIX. On a woman who marries two brothers, or a man who has two sisters

If a woman has two brothers as husbands, or a man has two sisters as wives, they shall abstain from communion until death. At the point of death, however, communion shall be given to them out of mercy.

If they survive after receiving communion and recover from their illness [Col. 0585B], they shall perform full penance for the appointed period.

### LXXX. On those who enter into multiple marriages

If anyone has been joined in many marriages, he shall perform penance. The conduct and faith of the penitent shorten the period.

### LXXXI. On those who have intercourse with animals

If anyone, before the age of twenty, sins through intercourse with any animal, he shall remain in humility for fifteen years at the door of the Church. After these years, he shall perform penance for another five years, being admitted only to communion in prayer [Note: [Col. 0585C] Ae., B. R., U., “received for another five years only into the communion of prayer”; G., “for another fifteen years,” [Col. 0586C] etc.], and thus receive the grace of the sacrament.

Others must be questioned about what sort of life he has led in penance, and thus he may obtain the mercy of communion.

If anyone, after reaching the age of twenty and having a wife, falls into this sin, he shall remain in humility for twenty-five years. Afterward, having communicated only in prayers for five years, he shall receive the sacrament [Col. 0586A].

If anyone has also exceeded this measure, he shall receive the sacrament at the point of death. Such persons ought to pray among those possessed by demons.

### LXXXII. On those who persist in sins until the end of life and seek communion at the point of death

If anyone, departing from the body, asks for the final and necessary viaticum of communion, it must not be denied him.

If, however, having received communion while in despair, he again becomes healthy, he shall be a participant only in prayer; he shall not receive the sacrament until he has completed the appointed period of penance.

Those who are at the point of death and desire to receive the sacrament ought to receive it with the bishop’s consideration and examination.

### LXXXIII. On those who, entering the Church, abstain from the sacrament through excessive dissipation

[Col. 0586B] If anyone, while inside the Church of God, does not listen to the sacred Scriptures because he is chatting, and through his dissipation turns away from sacramental communion and avoids the established rule of discipline in observing the mysteries, we decree that such a person must be expelled from the Catholic Church until he performs penance and shows the fruit of his penance, so that, after receiving communion, he may merit pardon [Note: [Col. 0586C] B. R., T. 1, 2, G., “his pardon, imploring that he may be able to…”].

### LXXXIV. On the excommunicated

No one may communicate with the excommunicated, enter their houses, or pray with them. Nor may one who has been separated from one Church be received into another.

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any ecclesiastical person communicates with an excommunicated person, he shall be excommunicated as one who disturbs the entire ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0586C].

## LXV. Third Council of Braga, held in the fourth year of the most glorious Lord our King Wamba, Era 713

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585C] 629–630 Having been suitably gathered together in the city of Braga through the divine Spirit, we have assembled to deliberate on the matters that are done perversely within the Church of God [Col. 0585D], so that, with the assistance of him who said, “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I shall be in the midst of them,” we may rise with one mind and with equal zeal of devotion and uproot errors that have been wrongly maintained.

For when synodal action had brought us together in one place, and we had taken our appointed seats, we first began to discuss the sacrament of the holy faith: namely, that nothing should be held concerning this most sacred sacrament of faith either through the vanity of disputants or through the ignorance of the simple that might lead to error.

Thus, when all of us examined ourselves in the true faith as in a mirror, and found ourselves unharmed in it because no storm of schismatic error had defiled any of us, but the true and simple apostolic preaching showed us to be sound in this sacrament, we gave thanks to almighty God.

Nevertheless, by recalling the very words and judgments of our rule of faith [Col. 0586C], we unfolded it again—the rule that we know was declared in the assembly of the Council of Nicaea.

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, [Col. 0586D] maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth; who for us and for our salvation descended, and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit, made man from the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there [B. R., *again*] will come in glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom will have no end. We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, who with the [Col. 0587A] Father and the Son is to be worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets; in one catholic and apostolic Church. We confess one baptism for the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 0587D] T. 1, 2: “for the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and life.”]; we await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

After this confession of the holy faith, the manifest and varied error of all our people was brought to our attention—an error that must be restrained by as much disciplinary skill as the perversity with which it is demonstrably admitted. For some were reported to offer milk instead of wine in the Lord’s sacrifices, and, instead of wine, a bunch of grapes; they also believe that the Eucharist, soaked in wine, ought to be presented to the people as the completion of Communion. And, worse than all these things, some priests place food for themselves in the Lord’s vessels and presume to eat from them. Some [Col. 0587B] priests were also reported to dare to celebrate Mass without oraria, contrary to the order of ecclesiastical custom, and, on solemn [Note: [Col. 0588D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “solemnities.”] occasions of martyrs, to hang relics around their necks and believe that they should be carried in litters only by deacons dressed in white. [Col. 0587C] There is also the matter that many priests live with women without witnesses, and that some of them subject their honored brothers to indiscriminate beatings; likewise, some, seized by the greed of Simon, release those whom they are about to ordain under a bond, so that after they have been ordained they may collect the money promised by them. There is also the matter that they wear out the church’s household in their own labors, causing loss to the possessions of the Lord. So that all these matters may not appear to have been set forth confusedly, we believe they should be appended under distinct headings.

## I. That, all superstitious opinions having been rejected, only bread and wine mixed with water be offered in the sacrifice

Since every crime and sin is wiped away by sacrifices offered to God, what will thereafter be given to the Lord for the expiation of offenses when error is committed in the very offering of the sacrifice? For we have heard that some, held by schismatic ambition, contrary to divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; others present to the people the Eucharist dipped in wine as the completion of Communion; and some offer not wine expressed from grapes in the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice, but give the people bunches of grapes to share. How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic [Col. 0587D] teaching, and how opposed to ecclesiastical custom, will not be difficult to prove from the very source of truth from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments themselves proceeded. For when the teacher of truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples, we know that he blessed not milk but bread alone and the chalice under this sacrament. For evangelical truth says: “Jesus took bread and the chalice, and, blessing them, gave them to his disciples.” Therefore let milk cease to be offered in sacrifice, because the clear and evident example of evangelical truth has shone forth, permitting nothing other than bread and wine to be offered.

[Col. 0588A] But as for the fact that they give the people the Eucharist dipped in wine as the completion of Communion, this too receives no testimony from the Gospel, where he commended his body and blood to the apostles; for the commendation of the bread separately and of the chalice separately is recorded. For we do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to anyone else, except only to that disciple whom the dipped morsel from the Master revealed to be the betrayer—not that it signified the institution of this sacrament.

[Col. 0588A] As for the people’s receiving from an unpressed bunch of grapes—that is, from grape berries alone—this is altogether a grave confusion. For the Lord’s chalice, as a certain teacher explains, ought to be offered mixed with wine and water, because we see the people signified in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, [Col. 0588B] the people are united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and attached to him in whom it has believed. This union and conjunction of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s chalice that the mixture cannot be separated.

For if anyone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to exist without us; but if there is water alone, the people begin to exist without Christ. Therefore, when a bunch of grapes alone is offered, in which only the efficacy of wine is represented, the sacrament of our salvation—which is signified through the water—is neglected. For the Lord’s chalice cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed together.

And therefore, since a very great and manifold judgment on this matter has already proceeded from the elders, whose devotion toward God has abundantly explained the efficacy of these sacraments and most truthfully declared their institutions, [Col. 0588C] every such error and presumption must henceforth cease, lest the disordered structure of the perverse weaken the established truth. Therefore from now on no one may offer anything else in the divine sacrifices except, according to the decisions of the ancient councils, bread alone and a chalice mixed with wine and water. Whoever thereafter acts otherwise than has been commanded shall abstain from offering sacrifice until, corrected by the lawful satisfaction of penance, he returns to the duty of the rank he has lost.

## II. That vessels consecrated to the Lord must not serve human uses

Every care and every effort must be taken lest those who appear to hold a position of governance be seen to inflict insult upon the heavenly sacraments. For—something judged horrifying to hear and execrable to see—we have been informed that certain priests, [Col. 0588D] rushing headlong in sacrilegious presumption, take the Lord’s vessels for their own uses and place food in them so that they may eat from them.

We are both astonished and grieve at this evil, and, grieving, are astonished: that human presumption should prepare a meal for itself there where it is known to have invoked the Holy Spirit; that, gorged with the eating of meat, it should take food there where it appears to have celebrated divine mysteries; and that in the vessels in which it received the sacrament of so great a matter for the expiation of sins, it should satisfy the desire of its mockery.

Therefore, from now on, any person who knowingly transfers divine vessels or ministries to his own uses, or chooses to eat from them or take a drink for himself from them, [Col. 0589A] shall suffer the loss of his rank or office. This is to be understood as follows: if he is a layman, he shall be condemned to perpetual excommunication; but if he is a religious, he shall be deposed from office. Under this same sentence of condemnation shall also be held those who knowingly transfer ecclesiastical ornaments, veils, or any other garments and utensils to their own uses, or decide that they are to be sold or given to others [Note: [Col. 0589D] In the remaining witnesses, except A., “given away.”].

## III. That a priest must not dare to celebrate Mass without an orarium

Since we know that ancient ecclesiastical institution has prescribed that every priest, when he is ordained, be wrapped around both shoulders with an orarium—so that he who is commanded to stand undisturbed amid prosperity and adversity may always appear surrounded on both sides by the adornment of virtues—for what reason should he not assume at the time of the sacrifice [Col. 0589B] what he does not doubt he received in the sacrament?

Accordingly, it is entirely fitting that what each person received in the consecration of his honor he should retain in the offering or reception of his salvation: namely, when a priest approaches the solemn celebrations of Mass, whether he is about to offer sacrifice to God himself or to receive the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he must approach only with an orarium wrapped around both shoulders, just as he is recognized to have been consecrated at the time of his ordination. Thus, pressing the neck and both shoulders with one and the same orarium, he shall bear the sign of the cross upon his breast. But if anyone acts otherwise, he shall be subject to the due excommunication.

## IV. That priests or any members of the clergy must not live with women without witnesses

[Col. 0589C]

Although the ancient institution of the canons has issued comprehensive and manifold disciplines and regulations concerning such presumption, we nevertheless, wishing to remove every opportunity for fornication, decree with every authority that this must be observed: no priest, nor anyone at all from the clergy, without an honorable and suitable witness—except his mother alone—may presume to associate secretly with any women, not only with women outside the family, but not even with sisters or female relatives. This is so that no unmarried man, through the license afforded by sisters or female relatives, may become excessively familiar for the perpetration of a crime. Therefore, let the transgressor of this command know that he must submit to the laws of penance for six months.

## V. Concerning the condemned presumption of certain bishops who, proceeding to church on the festivals of martyrs with relics hung around their necks, are carried in litters by deacons dressed in white

[Col. 0589D]

It is indeed a good thing for priests to handle divine mysteries, but great care must be taken lest anyone twist this to the use of his own perversity, when he ought to have pleased God alone by the goodness of his conscience. For it is written: “Woe to those who do the work of the Lord deceitfully and negligently.”

Since the detestable presumption of certain bishops was brought before our assembly for judgment, we learned that some bishops, when they were about to proceed to church on the solemnities of martyrs, placed relics around their necks; and, so that they might swell with the glory of greater pomp among men, [Col. 0590A] levites dressed in white carried them in litters, as though the bishops themselves were the ark of the relics.

This detestable presumption must be abolished in every respect, lest, under the appearance of holiness, simulated vanity alone prevail if the reverence proper to each order does not recognize its own measure. Therefore, let the ancient and solemn custom in this matter be observed: on every feast day, let the ark of the Lord with the relics be carried on the shoulders not by bishops but by levites, since we know that in the ancient law this burden was both imposed upon and commanded for them.

But if a bishop should choose to carry the relics himself, he will not himself be carried by deacons in a litter. Rather, proceeding on foot together with the people, he shall carry the holy relics of God [Col. 0590B] to the gatherings of the holy churches. Whoever knowingly delays fulfilling these regulations shall abstain from offering sacrifice for as long as he remains in this fault.

## VI. Concerning the proper discipline of honored subordinates

Since the blessed Apostle commands that one rebuke, exhort, or reprove with all patience and teaching, we know that certain brothers rage against their honored subordinates with beatings as severe as those that the persons of robbers might deserve. Therefore, those who have already merited ecclesiastical rank—that is, presbyters, abbots, or levites—must not be subjected to any beatings, except for graver and mortal offenses.

For it is not fitting that every prelate should indiscriminately subject his honored members to beatings and pain, as he wishes and whenever he pleases. Otherwise, while he strikes subordinate [Col. 0590C] members carelessly, he may himself withdraw from them the reverence due to him, in accordance with what a certain wise man said: “One who is corrected gently displays reverence toward the one correcting him; but through the harshness of excessive reproof he neither accepts the reproof nor receives salvation.” [B. R., T. 1, 2: “lightly.”]

Therefore, if anyone, elated by the license of the power he has received and moved by malice, believes that the aforesaid honored subordinates should be beaten beyond what has been stated, he shall suffer a sentence of excommunication and exile corresponding to the manner of the beatings he inflicted.

## VII. That honor must not be sold through promises of gifts

Since it is not fitting that the gift of the Holy Spirit be purchased with money, although on this matter the disciplines of the ancient canons remain both numerous and varied, nevertheless, because what is presumed without interruption must be restrained more frequently, we therefore establish the formula of this new regulation and decree that whoever, in order to confer upon anyone the rank of priesthood, has accepted any gift or any promise of a gift before that person is ordained—or, even after he has been ordained, has presumed to be rewarded in some way for this very thing—whether the giver or the recipient, shall, according to the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon, suffer the loss of his rank.

## VIII. That the rulers of the Church must not devote more labor to their own affairs than to ecclesiastical rights

It is not fitting for the rulers of the Church to be energetic in their own affairs and negligent in ecclesiastical matters. For it is reported that some priests wear out the church’s households in their own labors, increasing the profit of their private property while fostering loss to the possessions of the Lord.

Therefore, whoever under this neglect delays laboring for divine property must be restrained by a special decree. If he has increased the profit or labor of his private property from ecclesiastical possessions or gains, and thereby has shown neglect of labor toward ecclesiastical property or brought about its diminution or loss, he shall restore in full from his own possessions whatever diminution he caused to the church’s property—namely, from the possessions and resources by which he is convicted of having increased his own labors.

But if he has spent anything for the benefit of the Church or its property, or has suffered any loss or diminution, and can prove this, the whole amount shall be restored to him from the possessions of that same Church, for whose benefit he is shown to have spent it.

Therefore we give thanks to almighty God. [636] After these matters, may there be peace, safety, and long life for our most devout and Christ-loving lord, King Wamba, whose devotion summoned us to this salutary decree. We ask divine mercy that the glory of Christ [Col. 0592A] may strengthen his kingdom until the extremity of old age, through him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and is glorified as one God in the Trinity forever and ever.

Leodegisus [Note: [Col. 0591B] B. R., E. 4, T. 1: “Leodegisius”; T. 2: “Leodecisius.”], bishop in the name of Christ, surnamed Julianus, have reread and subscribed to these constitutions according to what, with my holy fellow bishops who subscribed with me, pleased us by the inspiration of God. Genitivus, bishop of the Church of Tui, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. Froaricus, bishop of the Church of Porto, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. Isidorus, bishop of the Church of Astorga, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. [Col. 0592B] Bela, bishop of the Church of Britonia, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. Hilarius [Note: [Col. 0592B] Ae., B. R., E. 3, 4, T. 1, 2: “Alarius”; U.: “Alaricus.”], bishop of the Church of Ourense, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. Rectogenes, bishop of the Church of Lugo, was present at these constitutions and subscribed. Ildulfus, who is surnamed Felix, bishop of the Church of Iria, was present at these constitutions and subscribed.

## LXVI. First Council of Seville. Letter of the Bishops Sent to Bishop Pegasius

[Col. 0591]

[Col. 0591C] To the holy lord and most beloved brother Pegasius, a bishop reverently honored by us: Leander, Joannes, Agapius, Stephanus, Basilius, Velatus, Sinticius, and Petrus, bishops, who were present together in the city of Seville, send greetings to your holiness in the devotion of charity and beseech the Lord, who may deem us worthy to rejoice in your well-being and presence.

## I. Concerning the Church’s slaves manumitted by a bishop

Meanwhile, while we were seated in the church of Holy Jerusalem at Seville, your deacons brought before us a brief register of the Church’s slaves whom your predecessor, Bishop Gaudentius of holy memory, appeared to have freed. We not only reread there those whom he had freed, but also reviewed those whom he had given to his relatives from the Church’s household, recorded in the same register. Concerning this matter, we consulted the provisions of the canons to determine whether such liberation or transfer could be valid.

We found in a canon that if a bishop has left his own property to others and not to the Church—except to sons and grandsons—whatever he has given or sold from the Church’s possessions, or transferred from the Church in any manner, is to be regarded as invalid.

Therefore, if your Church does not possess the property of your predecessor, Bishop Gaudentius, those whom he made free have not been lawfully freed. But if his property serves as compensation for your Church, let them remain entirely free. For if, as has been said, he did not make the provision from his own property, he ought certainly not to have inflicted loss upon the Church.

Accordingly, with one accord we all declare, thinking more humanely than severely, that those whom it is established were freed under such a condition should remain as dependents under the right of the Church, and should leave their peculium not to other persons but only to their sons. Their sons and grandsons likewise, together with their peculium, while remaining as dependents under the right of the Church, may not transfer anything belonging to them to an outsider. But if any of them dies without an heir, their peculium shall benefit the holy Church.

## II. Concerning the Church’s slaves given by a bishop to his relatives

As for the slaves whom the aforesaid bishop removed from the right of the Church and gave to his relatives, if he did not compensate the Church for them with equivalent property of his own, let your Church receive them without any opposition. This rule shall be observed not only by your Church—that is, the Church of Écija—but also by any persons who throughout the province of Baetica have passed out of the Church’s legal ownership under such a condition or circumstance; they shall be subject to the same judgment.

For it is harsh and irreligious that a bishop who lives on ecclesiastical revenues, and does not at all contribute his own property to the Church’s gains, should deprive others’ offerings of ecclesiastical ownership.

## III. Concerning clerics who live with women

Among other matters, know that we have defined the following for the removal of blemishes from the clergy: certain bishops, failing to observe the recently issued decree of the Council of Toledo, are insufficiently attentive to their subordinates. Therefore it has pleased us that, if presbyters, deacons, or clerics, after being admonished by their priest, do not remove from themselves the companionship of outside women or the familiarity of female servants, the judges, with the will and permission of the bishop, shall seize those same women and appropriate them as their own gain, so that, while the priest is unable to suppress this vice, judicial power may restrain it.

The judges must nevertheless give an oath to the bishops that they will not restore the women to the clerics by any means. If they restore them, the judges themselves shall be struck by a sentence of excommunication. Those women, separated by the priest according to the earlier canons [T. 2: “by the priests”], shall be sold [Note: [Col. 0593B] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2: “separated by the priest and handed over to a monastery of women vowed to God to serve there. These regulations…” In A. and the remaining witnesses, the words “be sold and” are perhaps absent.] and their price distributed to the needy.

We have subscribed these regulations with our own hand. Given to your holiness on the day before the Nones of November, in the fifth year of the reign of our most glorious lord King Reccared, in the era 628 [Note: [Col. 0594B] B. R., E. 4, T. 1: “era 627.”].

Leander, bishop of the holy Church of Seville, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Joannes, bishop of the Church of Cabra, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Agapius, bishop of the Church of Córdoba, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Stephanus, bishop of the Church of Elvira, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Basilius, bishop of the Church of Elipla, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Velatus, bishop of the Church of Tucci, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Sinticius, bishop of the Church of Italica, confirmed and subscribed this constitution. Petrus, bishop of the Church of Guadix, confirmed and subscribed this constitution.

## LXVII. Second Council of Seville, Held on the Ides of November in the Ninth Year of the Reign of the Most Glorious Prince Sisebut, Era 657

[Col. 0593]

[639] ## I. Concerning the complaints of Teudulfus, bishop of the Church of Málaga, against the other bishops concerning certain parishes

[Col. 0593B]

[Col. 0593C] In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ: Isidorus, Bisinnus, Rufinus, Fulgentius, Cambra, Fidentius, Teudulfus, and Honorius, bishops, who have assembled together in the city of Seville for certain ecclesiastical matters.

While we were therefore seated in the secretariat of the most holy Jerusalem of the Church of Seville, with the distinguished men Sisisclus, administrator of public affairs, and Suanilanus, administrator [Note: [Col. 0593D] From Ae., E. 3, 4, U., G. In A.: “administrator.” In B. R., T. 1, 2: “agent.”] of fiscal affairs, standing present [Note: [Col. 0593D] T. 1: “being present”; T. 2: “standing by.”], and with the most devout assembly of clerics in attendance, at the first session a petition was presented to us by Teudulfus, bishop of the Church of Málaga. He asserted that the ancient parish of that same city had been severed during the danger of former military hostility, and that part of it was being retained by the Churches of the cities of Écija, Elvira, and Cabra.

On this matter it pleased us that every parish which could prove that its Church had retained it under its ancient jurisdiction before the military hostility should be restored to it by privilege. For just as, under the law of the world, ancient possession is restored by right of return to those whom barbarian ferocity carried away under the compulsion of captivity, so the Church shall recover the parish that it formerly retained, together with its possessions, whether they are possessed by other Churches or have been transferred into anyone’s possession. A limitation based on the passage of time must not be raised where the necessity of hostility is involved.

## II. Concerning the complaints of the bishops Fulgentius and Honorius regarding certain parishes

[Col. 0594B]

[Col. 0594C] At the second inquiry, a dispute was examined between our aforesaid brothers Fulgentius, bishop of Écija, and Honorius, bishop of Córdoba, concerning the parish of a basilica, which one of them asserted was in Celtici [Note: From Ae., B. R., E. 3, 4. In A.: “Celsici.” In T. 1, 2: “Celestici.” In U., G.: “Altici.”], while the other asserted that it was in Regina. And because a boundary dispute has hitherto been claimed between the two parties, although its ancient possession would bring no prejudice to the law, and so that our judgment might not continue to call the matter between them into doubt, the synodal decrees were read after the canons had been produced. Their authority warns that greed must be restrained so that no one may usurp another’s boundaries.

For this reason it pleased us that inspectors be sent between the two parties, so that, if a boundary marked by ancient signs should show that the basilica lies in the diocese of the possessor, perpetual ownership shall belong to the Church whose rightful possession it is. But if a legitimate boundary does not enclose that same basilica, and the prescription of so long a time is proved to have been raised, the appeal of the bishop reclaiming it shall not prevail, because the objection of thirty years imposes silence upon him. For this is also commanded by the edicts of secular princes and decreed by the authority of the Roman bishops.

But if, within the limits of the thirty-year period, the basilica is found to have been unjustly retained outside the boundaries of another, it shall without delay be restored to the right of the bishop reclaiming it.

## III. That fugitive clerics be restored to their bishops

At the third determination, a petition was presented to us by our most reverend brother Cambra, bishop of Italica, concerning a certain cleric named Spassandus, who, abandoning the worship of his own Church, in which he had been dedicated from the beginning of his infancy, went over to the Church of Córdoba. We decided that, if nothing was alleged against him beyond the proposed delay, he should be restored to his own bishop.

For it is written in the law of the world concerning agricultural tenants that wherever someone has begun to be, there he must remain. Likewise, the decree of the canons prescribes concerning clerics who labor in the field of the Church that they must remain where they began. Therefore it pleased us that if any cleric, abandoning the ministries of his own Church, transfers himself to another, the priest under whom he has come shall compel him to be returned to the Church in which he previously lived.

But whoever receives him and does not immediately choose, without any attempt at exception, to send him back to his own Church must know that he is deprived of communion until he restores him. The cleric who has deserted should be stripped of the belt of his honor and rank and entrusted for a time to a monastery; afterward he should be recalled to the ministry of the ecclesiastical order. For license in such wanderings cannot be abolished unless, for the sake of correction, disciplinary censure follows upon them.

## IV. That bigamists not be promoted to the presbyterate or diaconate

At the fourth session it was announced to us that certain unlawful ordinations had recently taken place in the Church of Écija, so that some husbands of widows were consecrated to the ministry of levites. It is fitting that these men be recalled from the rank they received and that those found to have been instituted contrary to divine and ecclesiastical laws not be promoted further to the ministry of the diaconate.

## V. That a presbyter must not presume to ordain a deacon or presbyter

At the fifth inquiry, a report by Anianus, a deacon of the Church of Cabra, brought to our attention certain clerics of that Church. While one was being consecrated to the presbyterate and two to the ministry of levites, their bishop is said to have been afflicted by an illness of the eyes and merely laid his hand upon them, while a certain presbyter gave them a blessing contrary to ecclesiastical order.

Although he could have been accused and condemned at the present judgment for the audacity of so great a presumption, had he not been overtaken by the summons of death while still in the body, now that he has been left to divine judgment he cannot be accused before a human court. But those who remain, and who received from him not the title of consecration but rather a declaration of disgrace [Note: [Col. 0595D] Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, U., G.: “an encomium”; T. 2: “a eulogy.”], must not be allowed to exercise such usurpation again. We have therefore decreed that, after being deposed from the rank of the priestly or levitical order which they perversely obtained, they should suffer an equitable judgment [Possibly: “be rejected.”]. Such men are rightly judged fit for removal, because they are found to have been improperly instituted.

## VI. Concerning presbyters or deacons not to be deposed by one bishop alone

At the sixth session we discovered that Fragitanus, a presbyter of the Church of Córdoba, had once been unjustly expelled by his bishop and condemned to exile despite his innocence. We restored him to his rank and, against such presumption, decreed again that, in accordance with the synodal judgment of the ancient Fathers, none of us may dare to expel any presbyter or deacon without the examination of a council.

For there are many who condemn people without investigation by tyrannical power rather than canonical authority; and just as they elevate some through the favor of affection, so, moved by hatred and envy, they humble others and condemn, at the slightest breath of opinion, those whose crime they have not established.

A bishop alone can give honor to presbyters [Note: [Col. 0595D] In the remaining witnesses, except A.: “priests.”] and ministers; he cannot alone take it away. For if those who in the world have obtained the honor of freedom from their masters are not returned to the bond of slavery unless they have been publicly accused before praetors in a tribunal [Note: [Col. 0595D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “before praetors and governors in a tribunal”] and court, how much more is this true of those who, consecrated to the divine altars, are adorned with ecclesiastical honor?

They certainly cannot be condemned by one person or, by the judgment of one, be stripped of the privileges of their honor. Rather, they must be presented to synodal judgment, and what the canon has prescribed concerning them must be determined.

## VII. Concerning what is forbidden to presbyters in the ecclesiastical sacraments

At the seventh inquiry it was reported to us that the once-venerable Agapius, bishop of the see of Córdoba [Note: Ae., B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “of the city.”], frequently sent presbyters who, in the absence of the bishop, would erect altars and consecrate basilicas. It is not surprising that a man ignorant of ecclesiastical disciplines and transferred immediately from secular military service [Col. 0596C] to the priestly ministry should have commanded this.

Therefore, lest such permission be usurped by us again, it was necessary to establish by common judgment that, just as the consecration of altars is unlawful for a presbyter, so is their establishment. For in the divine Scriptures, when the Lord commanded, Moses alone erected the altar in the Tabernacle of God, and he alone anointed it—indeed because he was the high priest of God—as it is written of him: “Moses and Aaron among his priests.”

Therefore, presbyters, who bear the figure of the sons of Aaron, must not presume to undertake what was commanded only to the chief priests, whose type Moses and Aaron represented. Although the administration of many ministries is shared by them and by bishops, they must nevertheless recognize that certain things are forbidden to them by the authority of the ancient law and certain others by newer ecclesiastical regulations: the consecration of presbyters, deacons, and virgins; the establishment, blessing, or anointing of an altar.

They must know, moreover, that they are not permitted to consecrate a church or altar, to confer the Paraclete Spirit through the imposition of hands upon the faithful who have been baptized or converted from heresies, to prepare the chrism, or to sign the foreheads of the baptized with chrism. Nor may they publicly reconcile any penitent during Mass or send *formatae*—official letters of ecclesiastical commendation—to anyone.

All these things are unlawful for presbyters because they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. The canons prescribe that these things belong exclusively to bishops, so that through this both the distinction of ranks and the height of the dignity of the high priest may be demonstrated.

Nor is it permitted for presbyters to enter the baptistery in the presence of a bishop, to baptize or sign an infant while the bishop is present, to reconcile penitents without the command of their bishop, to celebrate the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ in his presence, or, while he is present, to teach, bless, or greet the people, or indeed to exhort the congregation.

## X. Concerning monasteries not to be dismantled
In the tenth action, at the request of the fathers of the monasteries, we unanimously decreed that the monasteries recently founded in the province of Baetica, like those that are ancient, should remain firmly established in immovable and unshaken stability. [Col. 0598A] But if—God forbid—anyone of our priests, or of those who succeed us, should attempt to strip any monastery by force of covetousness, or to tear it down or dissolve it under some pretense of fraud, let him remain accursed and excluded from the kingdom of God. Nor shall the goodness of faith or works profit for salvation the man who has destroyed the path of so great and so salutary a way of life.

Moreover, let all the bishops of the province of Baetica assembled together suspend that same sacrilegious destroyer and subverter from communion [Note: [Col. 0597D] B. R., T. 1. 2, U., G., “that destroyer of the sacred assembly.”], and let them restore the monastery that was torn down, together with its possessions, so that what one man impiously overturned, all may piously rebuild.

### XI. That the Monasteries of Virgins Are to Be Protected by Monks

In the eleventh action, by common agreement we decreed that the monasteries of virgins founded in the province of Baetica [Note: [Col. 0598D] In the remaining witnesses, apart from A., “founded in Baetica or everywhere.”] [Col. 0598B] should be governed under the administration and protection of monks.

For we then provide salutary care for virgins dedicated to Christ when we appoint spiritual fathers for them, by whose governance they may not only be protected but also built up by instruction. Nevertheless, this precaution shall be observed concerning the monks: kept away from their private quarters, they shall not be granted familiar access even as far as the vestibule. Nor shall the abbot, or the man appointed over them, be permitted to speak with the virgins of Christ about anything pertaining to the formation of their conduct apart from the woman who presides over them. Nor ought he frequently to speak with them in the presence of the woman who presides alone, but under the testimony of two or three sisters, so that the visit is rare and the conversation altogether brief.

For let it be far from us to wish monks to be familiar with the virgins of Christ—something that it is even impious to say. Rather, in accordance with what the commands of rules and canons enjoin, we appoint them as their governors only when they are kept far apart and completely separated. We decree that one monk of proven character be chosen, whose responsibility it shall be to supervise their rural or urban estates, construct buildings, and provide whatever else the needs of the monastery require, so that the servants of Christ, concerned only for the welfare of their souls, may live for divine worship alone and devote themselves to their religious duties.

The man appointed by the abbot must, however, be approved by the judgment of his bishop. The women, moreover, shall make garments for those same monasteries from which they expect protection, and from those same monasteries, as stated above, shall again receive the fruits of their labor and the support of administration.

But if any persons either despise this regulation of the monasteries or neglect it through any kind of negligence and indolence, let them know that their tepidity and pride are to be punished by the sentence of excommunication. [Col. 0598C–D]

### XII. On a Certain Bishop of the Acephali

In the twelfth action there came to us a certain Syrian, as he himself claimed, a bishop from the sect of the Acephali, denying the distinct properties of the two natures in Christ and asserting that the divinity was passible. When the confusion of so great an error had become evident to our understanding, we brought forward testimonies concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and recited the judgments of the holy Fathers. Then, with every form of exhortation, we invited him, in priestly moderation, to the uprightness of the true faith. He obstinately resisted communion despite salutary admonitions through many and prolonged disputations; but at last, instructed by divine grace, he renounced his own heresy before all who were present. He confessed two natures and one person in one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, believing that the nature of the divinity is impassible and that he assumed the weaknesses of suffering and the cross in his humanity alone.

Thus converted and received, he produced a profession of the faith he had embraced, confirmed by a solemn oath, and appeared cleansed of all his errors. Rejoicing in this according to its worth, we gave thanks to Christ because divine grace had brought him from the perversity of heresy to the uprightness of the faith. We pray that, remaining in the faith of Christ, he may be preserved in purity and deepest devotion. [Col. 0599A–B]

### XIII. On the Two Natures and One Person in Christ

In the thirteenth action, that is, in the final exposition, we thought it necessary to set forth briefly a refutation of those same heretics who, in their madness, confuse the two natures of Christ after the union and assert that the substance of the divinity in him is passible. Against their blasphemies, we must demonstrate the distinct property of the two natures in the one person of Christ and make clear that his suffering was endured in the assumption of humanity alone, so that, if some foolish persons have been deceived by the error of this ignorance, they may come to their senses when they read these things and firmly hold the truth of the right faith.

For undoubtedly there are many [Note: [Col. 0599D] T. 1, 2: “there are foolish persons who.”] who, in the words of the Apostle, “having itching ears,” turn their hearing away from the truth [Col. 0599C] and turn instead to fables.

Therefore, as the undefiled faith and holy Church of God teaches, we confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was timelessly born from God the Father, and temporally brought forth as man from the womb of the glorious Virgin Mary. For this reason he possesses two natures in one subsisting person: the nature of divinity, in which he was begotten before the ages, and the nature of humanity, in which he was brought forth in the last days; in the former existing according to the form of God, in the latter according to the form of a servant; in the former remaining equal to the Father, in the latter, without sin, resembling our condition; in the former invisible, in the latter visible; in the former inviolable, in the latter passible; in the former unable to die, in the latter having assumed death.

The distinction of these two natures must first be drawn from the writings of the Law, then from the pages of the prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles, so that we may establish what we assert not by arguments but by examples from Scripture.

The Law demonstrates both natures in the one and the same person of our Savior [Note: [Col. 0599D] Ae.: “of Christ”]. It demonstrates the divine nature when the Lord says to Moses: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you”; “observe him and listen to his voice, because my name is in him” [Note: [Col. 0599D] In T. 2, added by a later hand between the lines: [Col. 0600D] “and he will guard you on the way and bring you into the place that I have prepared; observe him.”]. It demonstrates the human nature when the same Lord says to Abraham: “In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed”—that is, in the flesh of Christ, which descended from the stock of Abraham.

The prophet in the Psalms shows both natures under the one and the same person of Christ: the divine nature in the words, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”; the human nature in the words, “And he became man in her, and the Most High himself founded her”; the divine nature in, “My heart has uttered a good word”; the human nature in, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.”

The prophecy in Proverbs likewise declares both natures under the one and the same person of Christ: the divine nature in, “Before the hills he begot me”; the human nature in, “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways”; the divine nature in, “The abysses did not yet exist, and I had already been conceived”; the human nature in, “Wisdom built herself a house”—namely, the temple of his body, in which the Son of God would dwell, when the Word became flesh. [Col. 0600A–B]

The prophecy in Isaiah demonstrates both natures under the one and the same person of Christ: the nature of divinity in, “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth? says the Lord”; the nature of humanity in, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son”; the divinity in, “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One”; the humanity in, “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together”; the humanity in, “A child is born to us”; the divinity in, “A Son is given to us.”

The child who was born refers to Christ according to the nature of the humanity he assumed, because he became man; but the Son who was given refers to the divinity, because he is the Son of God. To show that there is one person in both natures, he added concerning the child born and the Son given: “His name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel, Mighty God, Father of the coming age.”

In the Gospel too there is, in one and the same Christ, an indication of the divine nature: “I and the Father are one”; and an intimation of the human nature: “The Father is greater than I.” Again, an indication of the divine nature: “I am the truth and the life”; and an intimation of the human nature: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” Again, an indication of the divine nature: “All things were made through him”; and an intimation of the human nature: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father.” [Col. 0600C]

The Apostle Paul likewise expresses the nature of divinity in the one and the same Christ when he says: “He is the firstborn of every creature; he is before all things, and all things consist in him.” He declares the nature of humanity when he says: “He is the head of the body, the Church.” And elsewhere: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

By saying, “Although he was in the form of God,” he showed in him the nature of divine majesty; by adding, “He took the form of a servant,” he signified in him the nature of human lowliness. Again he says: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich.” When he says, “Although he was rich,” the glory of the divine nature is revealed; when he adds, “He became poor,” the subjection of human weakness is demonstrated. [Col. 0600D]

At the very beginning of the apostolic creed, the distinction of the two natures in the one and the same person of Christ is shown: the divinity from the Father in the words, “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our God and Lord”; the humanity from his mother in the addition, “Born of the Holy Spirit from the womb of the Virgin Mary.” [Col. 0601A]

Behold, from both Testaments there are two natures in Christ: one of divinity and the other of humanity. These two together made one person, because there is one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

Now, concerning the passion of this same Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, which he endured in his humanity alone and not in his divinity, the authority of the Law and the prophets, as cited above, as well as the preaching of the Gospels and the Apostles, must be brought forward.

The Law speaks in this way of the passion of Christ’s body: “He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape.” What is the cloak here, what is the robe, except the flesh of Christ adorned with the blood of his passion? For this alone endured the insults of the cross; the majesty of the divine nature experienced no injury. [Col. 0601B]

The prophet likewise asserts in the Psalms that Christ’s passion was in the flesh alone: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones.” Here the injury is understood not of the divinity but only of the crucified body. In the mention of the limbs, only the flesh, hung and fastened to the wood by nails, is declared, as it is also read in Jeremiah: “Come, let us cast wood into his bread”—that is, the cross into his body.

For the divinity could not be hung upon wood; only the humanity was fastened to the cross and hung there. Elsewhere, the flesh is likewise shown to have endured the persistence of death when he says: “My flesh shall rest in hope.” This is because only in Christ did the material flesh, having died through the frailty of death, look toward the hope of its resurrection, which it would receive without corruption, as he adds: “Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” [Col. 0601C]

Solomon, in the Song of Songs, proclaims the passion of Christ’s flesh in this way: “My hands,” he says, “dripped with myrrh, and my fingers with a drop of myrrh.” Here it is specifically shown that only the flesh of Christ was fastened to the stake in his hands and fingers, as it is read in Psalm 118: “Fasten my flesh with the nails of your fear.” [Col. 0601D]

Isaiah foretold that Christ, in the humanity in which he appeared, endured the injury of the passion in this way: “A man,” he says, “in affliction and knowing how to bear infirmity; truly he himself bore our sicknesses and carried our pains.” Who is “he himself,” except certainly the man? For the nature of God could not suffer or fail in him; rather, the man in him bore suffering and death, in whom death itself has its condition.

When the same prophet had said of him, “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” he added: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” What did he wish to show here by the red cloak and garment except the passion of Christ’s flesh, stained with the blood of the cross? Hence, in the passion itself, Christ is clothed in a scarlet cloak, so that the image of blood might be shown only in the flesh. [Col. 0602A]

Jeremiah likewise says that Christ offered only his body to suffering: “I was not rebellious,” he says, “nor did I contradict; I gave my body to those who struck me.” He did not say “the divinity,” which does not know how to endure suffering. Again: “I gave my back to whips and my cheeks to blows.” This too refers to the endurance of the flesh, not to an injury of the divinity.

And Zechariah says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.” Whom else could he unquestionably mean but the man whom the Jews crucified, and whom they will see judging in the flesh?

Behold, the passion of Christ’s body has been proclaimed from the Law and the prophets. Let us proceed from there to the Gospels. There let us seek Christ, the Son of God, bearing in the flesh alone the illnesses of suffering and the injury of the cross, when he himself speaks to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.”

All this was said of Christ according to the human being, and pertains not to the substance of the divinity but to the nature of the flesh. This is also taught in what follows, when the Jews say to Christ: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” And Jesus said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He said this about the temple of his body. For in his passion, when rebuking the betrayer, he said: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” Whom does he ask whether the betrayer is handing over, except the man? [Note: [Col. 0601D] B. R., T. 1, 2: “the man”; and they seized him.] It was the man whom they also seized, not the divinity, which, blinded by unbelief, they could not recognize. [Col. 0602B–C]

The blessed Apostle Paul likewise asserts that Christ endured the cross in the man alone: “As man,” he says, “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” He therefore says “as man,” so that by the designation “man” the distinction of the passible nature might be indicated.

Confirming this, he says elsewhere: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me? He is not weak, but powerful among you.” [Note: [Col. 0601D] In the remaining witnesses, apart from A.: “but his word is powerful in you.”] For although he was crucified in our weakness, he lives by the power of God.

Christ therefore suffered and died, but from our weakness; he lives, however, impassible and immortal, by his own power, which is so great that in itself it neither receives suffering nor admits death. [Col. 0602D]

Peter too, the foremost of the Apostles, proclaims that the punishment of Christ’s cross was completed in the body alone: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by his bruises we were healed.” A little later he says: “Christ therefore having suffered in the flesh.” Thus, if Christ suffered in the flesh, he was crucified not according to God but according to man. [Col. 0603A]

It has therefore become entirely clear concerning the Son of God that his suffering and death belonged only to the body, not to the divinity. These things are alien to God, as the prophet testifies concerning him: “The eternal God, the Lord who created the ends of the earth, shall not labor or grow faint.” And the psalmist says: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.” [Note: [Col. 0603A] T. 1, 2: “and”; U., “the psalmist.”]

In Christ, the humanity alone bore all the weaknesses: the flesh had the cries of infancy, not the divinity; the flesh was wrapped in swaddling clothes, not the deity; the flesh received nourishment; the flesh passed through the changes of the ages. For the fact that he grew weary, hungered, slept, wept, was sorrowful when close to his passion, and finally endured the passion itself and the condition of death—all this pertains to the weakness of the humanity, not to the incomprehensible substance of the divinity.

For Christ is one: God and man, Word and flesh. But from that by which he is God he has immortality; from that by which he is man he endured suffering; from that by which he is flesh he died; and from that by which he is the Word he is eternal.
