Nor can the one who is equal in power to the Father’s nature be passible in his divinity. The Father is therefore dishonored when the nature of the divinity is believed to be passible in the Son.

For if the substance of the Father and the Son is one, then, just as the Father is immortal, so also is the Son. And if “I and the Father are one,” then, just as there is no death in the Father, so neither is there death in the Son of God. And if the statement “Everything that the Father has is mine” is true, then the Father’s immortality is shared with the Son.

When the Apostle says concerning the ignorance of unbelievers, “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory,” he does not mean that the Lord of glory was crucified in such a way that the nature of the divinity appears passible. Rather, because Christ is one in both natures, the Lord of glory is said to have suffered according to the form of the man he assumed.

Conversely, the statement, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man,” is made even though no one descended from heaven except the Son of God, who had not yet become the Son of Man. [Col. 0603B]

Because of the unity of the person, therefore, things proper to God are also referred to the man in Christ, and things belonging to man are ascribed to the divinity. Thus, although suffering and dying belong not to the divinity but to the flesh, nevertheless, because of the unity of the person, God himself, born of a virgin, suffering and dead, is proclaimed—but through the weakness of our flesh, not through the power of his divinity.

When the same Apostle says, “For while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son,” the Son of God is called dead in the same way that martyrs are said to have suffered and died, although their souls were not killed in the suffering of the body, as the Word of Truth testifies: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” [Col. 0603C–D]

Here we must recognize that, if the souls of martyrs cannot be extinguished when their bodies have been slain by punishments, how could God, the creator of souls, suffer the destruction of death through the cross of the flesh?

This is also declared more clearly elsewhere, when the same Son of God says: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again.” If the divinity itself had died, I ask: who took up that soul again? It is therefore foolish to apply the passion of the cross to the divine nature, rather than only to the created and human nature.

The flesh alone felt the destruction of the cross; the flesh alone endured the spear; the flesh alone poured forth blood and water; it alone died; it alone was placed in the tomb; it alone was raised from the tomb on the third day. It was also glorified and ascended into heaven, and in it he will come as judge, in the glory of the Father, to judge the living and the dead. [Note: [Col. 0603D] In the remaining witnesses, apart from A.: “to judge the living and the dead.”] [Col. 0604A]

After bringing forward the testimonies of the New and Old Testaments, in which the two natures of Christ have been revealed in one subsisting person, and in which his passion appeared to have been completed in the man alone, it was then necessary to append the judgments of the holy Fathers who shone with great glory in the sacred writings. Thus their tradition too would make entirely clear that our Lord Jesus Christ subsists in two natures and one person, and that he assumed death and suffering in the flesh alone.

Saint Hilary, in his exposition of the Epistle to Timothy, speaks as follows:

“For when Scripture says ‘the man Christ,’ when it says ‘Christ died,’ and when it says ‘the Word became flesh,’ the sentence must not be stripped of its proper explanations by the deceitfulness of the reader. For where it says ‘the man Christ,’ the mediator between God and human beings, man from God, comes first: the two are one, and he is mediator between man and God through the confession in himself of both natures. Where it says ‘Christ died,’ it adds: ‘who rose again, who is at the right hand of God.’ In his death there is the weakness of our flesh; in his resurrection, his power; in the agreement, the dignity of God.” [Note: [Col. 0604D] B. R., E. 4, T. 1, 2, U., G.: “the power of his power in agreement.”]

Saint Ambrose likewise asserts in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke:

“Christ ascended not his own cross but ours, and that death was not the death of the divinity but of the man.”

A little later he says:

“For Christ is all, and in Christ are all things, although Christ works in each particular thing; nevertheless, the flesh dies so that it may rise again.”

Again, in the same book, explaining among other things, he says:

“My soul is sorrowful”; and elsewhere: “Now my soul is deeply troubled.” Therefore it is not the one who assumes that is troubled, but the one who is assumed; the soul is subject to passions, while the divinity is free. Finally, “the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” It is the soul, not he himself, that is sorrowful. Wisdom is not sorrowful, nor the divine substance, but the soul. He assumed my body; he did not deceive me, so that one thing would be and another appear.

Saint Athanasius, in the treatise he wrote on the Nativity of Christ, says:

“Let our faith, dearly beloved brothers, rest in this; let our entire salvation and life consist in this: that we believe that the Son of God, God, was first begotten invisibly and impassibly by God the Father before all the ages; then, according to the man, was born from the Virgin Mary; and that, according to this man, he suffered, died, was buried, rose again, and ascended from the underworld into heaven.”

Again, in his exposition On the Faith, he says:

“The Word is born from the Virgin Mary, receiving an animate body; but the Word was not enclosed by the flesh, rather, in the flesh and above the flesh. As God, he was foreknowing, the power of God, the truth of God; but he suffered as a human being, while the Word of God is impassible. In the passion, the man dies so that he may give life to the first-formed human being who had fallen through disobedience.”

Saint Gregory, writing to Cledonius, says:

“For there are two natures in Christ, God and man, but not two sons or two gods.”

Again, in his sermon On the Son, he says:

“With one brief rule I advise you: attribute the higher things to the divinity and to that nature which is shown to be superior to passions and to the body; attribute the lower things to the human nature, which was assumed from the portion of our weakness.”

Again, in his fourth book Against Eunomius:

“And lest anyone apply the suffering of the cross to the incorruptible nature of the divinity, he corrects such an error more clearly by calling the mediator himself between God and human beings both man and God, so that, when two things are said of one, what is fitting may be understood concerning each: impassibility concerning the divinity, and the dispensation of suffering concerning the humanity.”

Saint Basil, in his fourth book Against Eunomius, writes as follows:

“What is meant by ‘The Lord created me,’ and ‘Before all the hills he begot me’? We must understand that ‘he begot’ refers to the Son of God, while ‘he created’ refers to that part by which he is in the form of a servant, so that he might show both natures in one person.” [Col. 0605A–B]

Saint Cyril, in his First Letter to Succensus, says:

“Therefore, as far as understanding and the vision of the soul’s eyes are concerned, we say that, in considering how the Only-Begotten became incarnate, there are two natures; but we confess one Son, one Christ, God and Lord, the Word incarnate and made man.”

Again, in his Second Letter to the same Succensus, he says:

“Since Christ is one and the only Son, the same person is God and man, perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity. We do not say that the Only-Begotten Son of God, insofar as he is understood and is God, suffered in his own nature; rather, we say that the earthly nature suffered.

“For it is necessarily required that both be preserved in the one true Son: that he not suffer according to the divinity, yet that the same person be said to have suffered according to the humanity. For it was his flesh that suffered.”

The same writer, in his exposition of Leviticus, says among other things:

“Consider again in these things the entire mystery of our Savior and the cleansing that takes place through holy baptism. For he commands two living and clean birds to be taken, so that you may understand that, through the birds, the heavenly man and God are to be divided into two natures as far as reason is concerned, with what is appropriate assigned to each.”

Saint Augustine, in the Extracts, says:

“For in that assumption neither of the two was changed into the other or transformed into it. The divinity was not changed into a creature so as to cease to be divinity, nor was the creature changed into divinity so as to cease to be a creature.

“For if the substance of the man had been changed into divinity—which God forbid that we should believe—it would have augmented the divinity with something; but far be it from us to suppose that the ineffable and incomprehensible fullness receives augmentation. Therefore each nature of the Son of God remains, and there is one person.”

Again, in his work Against Maximus:

“If, then, you attend to the distinctions of the natures, the Son of God descended from heaven, and the son of man was crucified. If you attend to the unity of the person, the son of man descended from heaven, and the Son of God was crucified on earth.”

The same writer says shortly afterward:

“Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day. Where would he rise except in that which was able to fall? There he rose where he died. Seek death in the Word: it could never have existed there. Seek death in the soul: it was never there. Seek death in the flesh: plainly, it was there; and it was there because death was real.”

A little later:

“What do you marvel at? Certainly Christ is life. Why did life die? Neither the soul died, nor the Word died; the flesh died. Why? So that death might die in it.”

Again, in his exposition of the Evangelist John:

“Who, then, is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? The same Jesus Christ, but in the form of a servant.”

The blessed Leo, bishop of the apostolic see, says in the letter he wrote to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople:

“While the property of both natures is therefore preserved and both come together into one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity. In order to pay the debt imposed by our condition, the inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that the one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, could die in one respect and could not die in the other.

“Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true man, true God was born, wholly in his own things and wholly in ours.”

A little later:

“He who, remaining in the form of God, made man, became man in the form of a servant. Each nature retains its property without defect; and just as the form of a servant does not take away the form of God, so the form of God does not diminish the form of a servant.”

Again, a little later:

“Each form acts, in communion with the other, according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles; the other submits to injuries. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the glory of the Father, so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race.”

Saint Fulgentius, in the book he wrote On the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, says among other things:

“I therefore say to you, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, that we must confess our Lord Jesus Christ in two unconfused natures—that is, the nature of divinity and the nature of humanity—in one person or substance.”

The same writer says afterward:

“If anyone, therefore, is unwilling or hesitates to believe and proclaim that in our Lord Jesus Christ there are either two natures or one person, or if anyone is unwilling to confess that he is both God and man—that is, the Word incarnate, truly born from the Virgin Mary for our salvation—he is condemned and shown to be an outsider to the Catholic faith, since he resists the sacrament of human redemption with thankless unbelief.”

A little later:

“Therefore the Word made flesh is one and complete Christ, one from both and in both—that is, in the human and divine nature. In him the glory of both natures subsists from the very beginning [Note: [Col. 0605] Ae., B. R., E. 4: “persists”; T. 1, 2, U., G.: “persists.”] in such a way that, whether anyone removes humanity from Christ’s divinity or takes divinity away from his humanity, he dissolves Christ through sacrilegious unbelief and blasphemous teaching.”

Again, a little later:

“Christ suffered for us in the flesh, he who alone was born from God the Father as impassible God. We truly believe that this same Christ, the Son of God, tasted death for us in the flesh, while the immortality of his divinity remained unharmed.”

And again afterward:

“But because there is not one God and another man, but the same one Christ is God and man, it follows that the same Christ who is God is the one who assumed death in his flesh, and the same Christ who is man is the one who destroyed death through his divinity. For the same Christ, the Son of God, who could not die in his divinity, died in the flesh, which immortal God assumed as mortal; and the same Christ, the Son of God, rose again after dying in the flesh, because, having died in the flesh, he did not lose the immortality of his divinity.”

Hence, after his resurrection, just as he demonstrated in himself the solidity of true flesh through real scars and the real eating of fish and honey, so, entering while the doors were closed, he showed in himself the true power of eternal divinity, so that it might be recognized both that the weakness of Christ when dying was natural and that, when he rose, natural majesty was present in the same person. [Col. 0607A–B]

These teachings, which have been set forth both in the words of divine Scripture and in those of the holy Fathers, we have briefly inserted into our decrees, demonstrating the twofold nature of flesh and divinity in the one person of our Lord and Savior, and also that the same person suffered in the nature belonging to the body, but did not suffer in the nature belonging to the divinity.

Having therefore reached this conclusion by unanimous agreement in three secretariats, we appended our individual signatures in confirmation of it. [Col. 0608A]

I, Isidore, bishop of the Church of Seville, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Bisinus, bishop of the Church of Eliberis, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Rufinus, bishop of the Church of Asidona, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Fulgentius, bishop of the Church of Astigi, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Cambra, bishop of the Church of Italica, have subscribed in the name of Christ. [Col. 0608B]

I, John, bishop of the Church of Egabra, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Fidentius, bishop of the Church of Tucci, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Theudulfus, bishop of the Church of Málaga, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Church of Córdoba, have subscribed in the name of Christ.

## LXVIII. First Council of Barcelona

[Note: [Col. 0607] This council is absent from the remaining codices except Ae., from which it has been taken.]

[Col. 0607]

When the holy bishops had assembled at Barcelona in the name of God—namely, Sergius the metropolitan; Nibridius of Barcelona; Casontius of Emporiae; Andreas of Lérida; Stafilius of Girona; John of Zaragoza; and Asellus of Tortosa—they established the following regulations.

I. That Psalm 50 be recited before the canticle.

II. That the blessing be given to the faithful at morning prayer just as at vespers.

III. That no cleric grow his hair long or shave his beard.

IV. That a deacon under no circumstances sit in the company of presbyters.

V. That, when the bishop is present, the presbyters collect the prayers in due order. [Col. 0607C–D]

VI. That male penitents, with their heads tonsured and wearing religious dress, spend the time of their lives in fasts and supplications.

VII. That penitents not attend banquets or engage in business involving giving and receiving, but should live frugally in their own homes.

VIII. Concerning those who ask for penance during illness and receive it from a priest: if they later recover, they shall live the life of penitents, without the laying on of hands, separated from communion for as long as their priest approves their life as worthy.

IX. We command that those who are suffering illness receive the viatic blessing.

X. Concerning monks, we prescribe that what the Council of Chalcedon established be observed.

### Concerning the Barcelonan Fisc
To the most exalted and magnificent lords, sons or brothers, the tax officials Artemius and all the bishops bringing the fiscal payment to the city of Barcelona:

Since, by the election of our lord, son, and brother Scipio, count of the Patrimony, in the seventh prosperous year of our glorious lord King Reccared, you were elected to the office of tax official in the city of Barcelona, province of Tarraconensis, and since, as is customary, you requested from us an assessment concerning the territories that we have been accustomed to administer, therefore, by the tenor of this assessment of ours, we have decreed that both you and your agents or assistants must exact from the people, for one canonical modius, [Col. 0608D] eight siliquae, namely, and one siliqua for your labor, and four siliquae for unavoidable losses, 657 or among the prices of commodities, making fourteen siliquae in all. In the matter of barley, which, according to our definition, as we have said, both you and your assistants and agents are to exact, let them presume neither to exact nor to take anything more.

If anyone should be unwilling to comply with our assessment, or should fail to arrange to bring to you in kind what was agreed for you, let him arrange to bring his fiscal payment. But if anything has been over-exacted by your agents beyond what the tenor of this assessment of ours specifies, you must order it to be corrected and restored to those from whom it was wrongly taken. 658

[Col. 0609A] We who have agreed to this assessment have subscribed it below with our own hands. This assessment was made on the day before the Nones of November, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord.

Artemius, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed our assessment.

[Col. 0610A] Sophronius, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed our assessment.

Galanus, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed our assessment.

Joannes, bishop, in the name of Christ, have subscribed our assessment.

# LXIX. The Second Council of Barcelona

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609A] [Note: [Col. 0609] [Col. 0609] This note is printed at the foot of column 609, but its callout letter, a, does not appear in the text. This council is absent from the other codices except Ae.] Under the leadership of the Lord Jesus Christ, on the Kalends of November, in the fourteenth prosperous year of the reign of our most Christian and most devout lord King Reccared, the bishops of the province of Tarraconensis had assembled in the city of Barcelona, in the church of the Holy Cross. This holy synod chose to establish the following:

[Col. 0609B] **I.** When clerics are advanced to ecclesiastical offices, let nothing be sought from any bishop or from his clergy, whether for the conferring of a blessing, the subdiaconate, the diaconate, or the presbyterate, or under the name of an offering; remembering that edict of the Lord Jesus which says: “You received freely; give freely.”

**II.** It has likewise been established under a similar condition that, when chrism is given to diocesan presbyters for confirming neophytes, nothing is to be accepted as payment for the liquid, lest the grace of God, made subject to the price of a blessing, join a simoniacal destruction to those who buy and sell it.

**III.** The holy synod has also established and renewed this provision for observance in all things: according to the constitutions of the ancient canons and the synodal letters admonishing the bishops, henceforth no layman may aspire or be advanced to the highest priesthood, once the time prescribed by the canons has been disregarded, whether through sacred royal authority, through the consent of the clergy or people, or through the election and assent of bishops. Rather, after he has ascended through the ecclesiastical grades during the periods prescribed by the canons, laboring in spiritual work and accompanied by the support of a proven life, he may be advanced to the highest priesthood by the Lord’s authority, if his life has proved equal to the dignity.

This is to be done, however, in such a way that, after two or three men chosen by the consent of the clergy and people have been presented to the judgment of the metropolitan and his fellow bishops, the one whom the lot, with the bishops’ fast preceding and Christ the Lord determining, has indicated shall receive the fullness of the consecratory blessing. Otherwise—God forbid that such a thing be presumed—the deposition from their proper honor shall follow both those who ordain and those who are ordained.

[Col. 0610A] **IV.** We likewise decree with equal consideration that, if a virgin, of her own will, casting aside lay clothing and dressed in the manner of the devoted, promises to preserve chastity, or if men or women of either sex, having sought and received from a priest the blessing of penance, voluntarily turn to earthly marriage, or if women violently abducted refuse to separate themselves from the violator of their chastity, both parties are to be expelled from the thresholds of the churches and separated from the communion of all Catholics in such a way that absolutely no consolation of conversation is left to them.

Asiaticus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the metropolitan city of Tarraconensis, was present at these constitutions, agreed, and subscribed. In the name of Christ, Ugnus, bishop of Barcelona, subscribed this agreement. Simplicius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Urgel, agreeing with this constitution, subscribed. 659 In the name of Christ, Aquilinus, bishop of the Church of Ausona, agreeing with this constitution, subscribed. [Col. 0610C] Julianus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Tortosa, agreeing, subscribed. Mumius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Calahorra, agreeing, subscribed. Galanus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Ampurias, assenting to these constitutions, subscribed. Froisclus, bishop of the Church of Tortosa, assenting, subscribed. 660 Joannes, the sinner from Gerunda, assenting to these constitutions, subscribed. Maximus, minister of the Church of Zaragoza, assenting to these constitutions, subscribed. Amelius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Lleida, assenting to these constitutions, subscribed. [Col. 0610D] Ilergius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Egara, subscribed these constitutions.

# LXX. The Council of Narbonne

[Note: [Col. 0609] This council is absent from the remaining codices except Ae.]

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609D] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fourth prosperous year of the reign of the most glorious lord King Reccared, we, Migetius, Sedatius, Benenatus, Boetius, Pelagius, Tigridius, Agripinus, and Sergis, bishops of the province of Gaul, desiring with fear of God to observe the councils of the holy ancient Fathers and their decrees, assembled together in the city of Narbonne, according to what the holy synod, through the arrangement of our most glorious lord King Reccared, had concluded in the city of Toledo, on the Kalends of November, with God’s favor.

We caused to be recapitulated and brought to memory in the present times of our lord, under prefaces, certain matters that had been justly and devoutly issued but had not been supplemented through the power of patronage; and, by common deliberation, we chose to write down and append to the canons whatever still appeared necessary for the rule and discipline of the Catholic faith, as the tenor of the chapters that follow clearly declares.

**I.** It has been regularly defined that no cleric shall wear purple garments, which pertain to worldly ostentation rather than to the dignity of religious persons. Just as devotion exists in the mind, so it must also be displayed in the body, because purple is chiefly owed to laymen endowed with power, not to religious persons. Whoever fails to observe this is to be restrained as a transgressor of the law.

[Col. 0611B] **II.** It has therefore been defined that, in the order of psalm-singing, “Glory” shall be said to almighty God after every psalm. With the longer psalms, longer pauses shall be made as appropriate, and at every pause the Glory of the Trinity shall be sung to the Lord.

**III.** This too has been settled according to the judgment of the ancient canons: no cleric, subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter shall sit in the streets, nor indeed stand in the streets and mingle in various conversations. Whoever presumes to do so is to be entirely removed from office and condemned; if he does not amend, he is also to be deprived both of communion and of office.

**IV.** Every person, whether freeborn or enslaved, Goth, Roman, Syrian, Greek, or Jew, shall do no work on Sunday, nor shall oxen be yoked, except if necessity for changing or altering something should arise. Whoever presumes to do so, if freeborn, shall pay six solidi to the count of the city; if enslaved, shall receive one hundred lashes.

**V.** In accordance with the most holy Council of Nicaea, no gatherings or conspiracies of clerics shall be held, such as laymen were accustomed to arrange under the protection of a patron. Nor shall anyone of a lower rank, being arrogant, rebuke or insult his senior. If anyone, disregarding so just an order of discipline, dares to do so, let him be corrected with the harshest severity, so that, withdrawing from life under the name of penance—that is, for one year in a monastery—he may learn to cast off the pride with which he is puffed up, which is the devil, and learn humility, since through it he was deemed worthy to taste death.

[Col. 0611D] **VI.** In accordance with the decrees of the ancient orthodox councils, the brotherhood decrees that whenever a cleric or a distinguished person from a city is found guilty and assigned to a monastery, the abbot who has been mentioned 661 shall deal with the person sent to him just as the bishop has ordered through an explicit correction. Otherwise, if the abbot chooses to act differently, he shall be suspended for a period of time as a corrective measure, because the person is sent for this reason: to be corrected, not to be indiscriminately stuffed with various dishes.

**VII.** Whoever among the clergy, from the highest to the lowest, is found to act, deliberate, or attempt anything contrary to the welfare of the holy Church shall rightly be deposed, because he is shown to have no knowledge of preserving the faith.

**VIII.** If any cleric, subdeacon, deacon, [Col. 0612A] or presbyter takes anything from the possessions or house of the Church without the knowledge of the bishop, or commits fraud, he shall not only restore, under every disgrace and constraint, what he has done, but also shall not be allowed to remain in that church where he is seen to have committed the fraud. He shall lie under penance for two years, and, when he has mourned his deed, shall return to office.

**IX.** Above all, it has been decreed that Jews may not escort a body by singing, but, according to their ancient custom and practice, shall escort and lay down the body. If they presume to do otherwise, they shall pay six ounces of gold to the count of the city.

**X.** This has been especially defined: no cleric shall dare to despise the ordination of his bishop, but wherever he has been ordained, he must walk with gratitude [Col. 0612B] and obedience and perform whatever has been enjoined. If, under the boot of pride, he neglects to fulfill this, he shall be deprived not only of his stipend but also of communion for one year.

**XI.** Henceforth no bishop may ordain as deacon or presbyter anyone ignorant of letters. If any such persons have been ordained, they shall be compelled to learn. But if a deacon or presbyter is uneducated in letters and delays through negligence in reading or performing his office, and is not ready for all things in the church, he is to be deprived of his stipend and bent down until, once bowed, he fulfills and defends what he is known to be, or what he will be, in the Church of God. If he has not been trained to read, and if he persists in negligence and does not wish to advance, let him be sent to a monastery, because he cannot edify the people except by reading.

[Col. 0612C] **XII.** We have chosen that these matters be especially observed and maintained for fear of God and according to the manner of canonical discipline: while Mass is being celebrated, no presbyter or deacon, unless prevented by illness, shall dare to leave the altar before Mass is completed; nor shall a deacon, subdeacon, or even lector presume to remove his white vestment before Mass is finished. Whoever fails to fulfill these provisions: presbyters are to be rebuked so that they return; deacons are to be condemned and deprived of their stipends; and the others are to be punished with the strictest discipline.

**XIII.** This has been settled regularly, according to the earlier 662 canonical statutes: both the subdeacon and the doorkeeper, as well as the others serving the holy Church, shall fulfill their customary service without any negligence and shall raise the curtains for their seniors at the doors. Those who disdain to do and complete this are to be rebuked verbally if they are subdeacons; if they do not amend, they are to be deprived of their stipends; the others are to be restrained by lashes.

[Col. 0612D] **XIV.** We have chosen to conclude and maintain this for the extension of the discipline of the Catholic faith: if men or women diviners, whom they call *caragios* and *sorticularii*, are found in the house of any Goth, Roman, Syrian, Greek, or Jew, or if anyone henceforth dares to consult them about their vain incantations and is unwilling to make this publicly known, for what he has presumed he shall not only be suspended from the Church but shall also pay six ounces of gold to the count of the city. Those, however, who are filled with such wickedness and practice lots and divinations and lead the people astray by transgressing, wherever they are found, whether they are free men, enslaved men, or female slaves, shall be publicly beaten with the greatest severity and sold, and their prices shall be distributed to the poor.

**XV.** It has come to our attention that certain people of the Catholic faith, in an accursed rite, honor Thursday, which is called the day of Jupiter, and do no work. Abominating and condemning this practice out of fear of God, we decree that whoever, apart from the festivals that fall on that day, dares to take this day off and do no work shall, if freeborn, man or woman, be expelled from the Church and placed under penance for one year, satisfying God through almsgiving and weeping so that the Lord may forgive him or her. If the person is enslaved, male or female, after being corrected with one hundred lashes, he or she shall be handed over to the master, who shall not permit them to observe such practices again.

Migetius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Catholic Church of Narbonne, [Col. 0614A] have reread and subscribed these constitutions, according to what, with God inspiring us, pleased us together with our brothers.

Sedatius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Catholic Church of Béziers, was present at and subscribed these constitutions.

Boetius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Maguelonne, was present at and subscribed these constitutions.

Pelagius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Nîmes, was present at and subscribed these constitutions.

Tigridius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Agde, was present at and subscribed these constitutions.

[Col. 0614B] Sergis, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Carcassonne, was present at and subscribed these constitutions.

Agripinus, from the city of Lodève, bishop in the name of Christ, was present at and subscribed these constitutions.

# LXXI. The Council of Huesca, Held in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of Our Most Glorious Lord King Reccared

[Note: [Col. 0613] This council is absent from the other codices except Ae.]

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613B] 663–664. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, when we had all assembled together in the council at Huesca, this holy synod chose to establish that, once each year, every one of us should order all the abbots of the monasteries and the presbyters and deacons of his diocese to assemble at the place chosen by the bishop; that he should set forth for all the rule for conducting their lives; and that he should admonish everyone to remain under ecclesiastical rules until their reputation for thrift, sobriety, and truthful chastity had been commended by the testimony of honorable men.

It is also appropriate that each of us be concerned about this matter, so that we may investigate with careful inquiry whether the life of the presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and [Col. 0614B] clerics is modest and chaste. If, God forbid, rumor should report anything evil about anyone, everything is to be investigated with the greatest discernment through a true and most certain examination of the clerics, or of male scribes, or indeed of those women about whom rumor circulates, and also through various indications from which signs of adulterers are customarily suspected with certainty. This is to be done so that no one is branded under the shadow of falsehood, nor is an admitted crime concealed through excuses, while they chatter that they cannot be refuted by public proof, but demonstrate through the testimony of honorable clerics that they have lived a proven life.

# LXXII. The Council of Egara

[Note: [Col. 0613] This council is absent from the remaining codices except Ae.]

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613D] In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, on the day of the Ides of January, in the third prosperous year of the reign of our most glorious lord King Sisebut, the bishops of the province of Tarraconensis assembled at Egara. This holy synod established that the provision which had formerly been established in the thirteenth year of the reign of Reccared, of blessed memory, in the Council of Huesca, but had not been written down, should be confirmed and remain valid forever; and that everything written concerning the chastity of presbyters and the clerics below them should, in the same form, be examined at all times concerning all the bishops, with such diligence and care that, with the Lord’s help and assistance, no opportunity for blame—God forbid—might ever steal upon the concern for such a life.

Eusebius, I subscribed. [Col. 0614D] Mumius, I subscribed. Joannes, I subscribed. Maximus, I subscribed. Emilia, I subscribed. Rufinus, I subscribed. Ursus, I subscribed. Vincentius, I subscribed. Stephanus, I subscribed. Pompedius, I subscribed. Sinthasius, I subscribed. Justus, I subscribed. Maximus the presbyter, acting in the place of my lord Bishop Stephanus, I subscribed. Fructuosus, deacon in the name of Christ, acting in the place of my lord Bishop Gomarellus, I subscribed.

# LXXIII. The Emeritan Council of Twelve Bishops, Held on the Eighth Day before the Ides of November, in the Eighteenth Year of the Most Serene and Most Devout King Reccesvinth, Era 704

[Note: [Col. 0615D] This council is absent from A., Ae., and E. 3. It has been taken from Codex B. R., with the variant readings of the others.]

[Col. 0615]

[Col. 0615A] 665–666. All the bishops of the province of Lusitania having assembled in the name of the Lord and sitting in the church of Holy Jerusalem, which is in the city of Emerita, known to be the capital of this province and remaining dedicated under that principal name, we began, with God’s help, according to the order of our earlier canons.

First, as is customary, we rendered due praises to almighty God, by whose gift and grace we have been united. Then we offered thanksgiving to our most serene and most merciful prince and lord, King Reccesvinth, praying for divine mercy: may the one who granted him the power of kingship also grant him the happiness of life with peaceful tranquility, and may he make him victorious over his enemies, so that, with grace favoring him, he may subject the necks of his enemies to his authority; [Col. 0615B] thus may he possess the present life in tranquility for long ages and, after many cycles of years, obtain the joys of blessedness through the ages that shall never end. And since he retains a holy concern for secular matters and rightly orders ecclesiastical affairs with a mind attentive through divine grace, may the ineffable grace of almighty God assist him, remaining near to those who seek it.

## I. On the Formation of the Faith and Its Order

According to the rule of the earlier Fathers, which has been handed down to us in holiness and through whose instruction the holy Catholic Church of God possesses the progress of faith, although it is remembered in very many councils, it must nevertheless not be neglected by us. For this is the first path of a council, and unless it has been properly constructed, the means of proceeding to anything else is unsuitable. Therefore, since we confess ourselves firm in the faith and profess it perpetually, it is fitting that we set forth our belief in this holy council.

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, *homoousion* with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth; who for us and for our salvation came down and was made incarnate by the Holy Spirit, became man from the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, [Col. 0615D] was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom shall have no end; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets; in one Catholic and apostolic Church; we confess one baptism for the remission of sins; we await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0616D] E. 4, T. 1, 2: “our Lord Jesus.”]

This is our faith and this is our holy belief. Whoever worthily holds it shall receive a fitting reward at the time of judgment; whoever departs from it and does not wish to remain in this faith shall suffer the punishments of eternal torment with the devil. Let us therefore pray to almighty God that this sincere belief may confer upon us his divine benefits, that his holy mercy may forgive us all our sins in the present age, and that, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, he may place us at his right hand to be justified. If anyone does not believe or does not confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in the Trinity, let him be anathema.

## II. On Preserving the Order of the Evening Office

Just as there is unanimity among us in the holy faith, so there ought to be the highest attentiveness concerning the holy service of God. Therefore, just as in other churches, in the evening, after the light has been offered, the evening office is first recited before the sound on feast days, so it must also be observed by us in our churches. If anyone does not preserve this order in his church and does not instruct all those belonging to him to perform this good work, when this has reached the ears of the metropolitan and the matter has been proved, let him know that he is to be struck by a sentence of excommunication.

## III. What Is to Be Observed When the King Goes Out with the Army for the Security and Salvation of the King, the People, or the Homeland

[Col. 0616C]

As much as reason, with God’s help, has discovered that a rule of uprightness must be established in ecclesiastical order, so much is it necessary to devise and arrange what ought to bring prosperity to our most merciful lord King Reccesvinth and to his faithful people or homeland. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0616D] E. 4, T. 1, 2: “this holy council established.”] the holy council has established that whenever a cause makes him go forth against his enemies, each of us shall maintain this order in his church: every day, through good arrangement, a sacrifice shall be offered to almighty God for the safety of him, his faithful people, and his army, and the assistance of divine power shall be sought, so that salvation may be granted to all by the Lord and victory may be granted to him by almighty God.

This order is to be maintained for as long as he remains away, with divine help, until he returns to his seat. Whoever delays fulfilling the measure of this provision shall know that he is excommunicated by his metropolitan.

## IV. How a Metropolitan Is to Make an Agreement with His Suffragans, or Suffragans with Their Metropolitan

[Col. 0617A]

After the belief of our faith had been made manifest, we took care to insert those matters that establish uprightness in the holy Church. Our assembly of unanimity therefore took care to insert this provision: when a metropolitan has been ordained bishop in the Church of God, he shall make an agreement in the name of his provincial [Note: [Col. 0617D] E. 4, T. 1, 2: “comprovincial”] bishops that he will live chastely, soberly, and rightly.

Similarly, when neighboring bishops have been ordained in the churches over which they are able to preside, they shall make an agreement in the name of their metropolitan bishop that they will live chastely, rightly, and soberly. If, according to the judgment of the canons, some have been ordained by the will of the metropolitan and through his letter of instruction, by royal command, by another metropolitan, when they come to their own metropolitan after their ordination, they shall not delay making such an agreement. If they delay, each one shall know that he is excommunicated for as long as he fails to fulfill the order of good discipline.

## V. That a Bishop Send to the Council, on His Own Behalf, Not a Deacon but Either an Archpresbyter or a Presbyter

According to the order of the canons, when a council has been chosen to meet by the will of the metropolitan and by royal command, all neighboring bishops ought to be present together, and no excuse ought to be advanced against such a matter. If it should happen that one of the brothers is detained by illness and unable to come, or receives a royal command to undertake some duty that prevents him from attending the council, whatever has occurred he must faithfully report to his metropolitan in a letter signed in his own hand, so that afterward he may not offer any excuse.

For his own person, however, he shall send no one other than his archpresbyter; or, if the archpresbyter is unable, a suitable presbyter whose dignity is evident together with his prudence. He shall sit among the presbyters behind the bishops, know what has been done in the council, and subscribe it. For our assembly considers it unjust that any bishop should send a deacon in his place. Since the deacon appears to be junior to the presbyters, he is in no way permitted to sit with the bishops in the council.

[Col. 0617D] Therefore, whichever presbyter he chooses to send, he shall send him instructed according to the requirements of the matter, and with him his authorized representative, equipped according to the order of the law. Thus, if anything is brought forward in the council against that bishop, the petitioner may receive an answer from the one whom he sent, and the justice that has been arranged may afterward suffer no delay.

## VI. How a Bishop, After Receiving an Admonition, Is to Come to His Metropolitan

We believe that it is pleasing to God when, for the sake of good work, we impose a fitting rule in the holy Church. Therefore our brotherhood decided that, just as primatial reverence is commanded by synodal rule to be shown to the metropolitan bishop, so these admonitions must also be observed by his provincial bishops. By common deliberation we judge, and establish that the order of this decision is to be observed, that whenever a provincial bishop receives an admonition from his metropolitan to celebrate the feast days of the Nativity of the Lord and Easter with him, he shall make no excuse for coming to him.

If he should be detained by illness, or be unable to come into his presence because of excessive severity of the weather, he must send a letter signed in his own hand, in which the cause of this matter is stated with complete truth. But if the person who received the admonition is healthy and delays coming, he shall not be released without excommunication.

## VII. How the Council Is to Be Held According to the Institutions of the Earlier Canons

[Col. 0618B]

The ancient canons decreed that a council should be held once each year wherever the metropolitan bishop chose, and in that holy rule it remains established that provincial bishops, when admonished by their metropolitan, must be present at the appointed place and time. This matter is not conducted outside the royal will.

There are some who receive the admonition of their metropolitan and the royal command for this purpose but utterly fail to fulfill what is ordered. The judgments of the ancient canons command that such persons be excommunicated until the time of the coming council; yet, although they are struck by the penalty of excommunication, nothing is imposed upon them that they ought to fear.

It pleased this holy synod [Col. 0618C] that whichever bishop, after being admonished, delays coming to the council shall perform the period of excommunication there, wherever the metropolitan chooses, together with those who were present. His cell and the property belonging to him shall be governed, for as long as he is under penance, by the diligence and concern of the metropolitan, because this has been chosen so that under penance he may learn what he refused to fulfill through willing obedience.

When he returns to his cell, therefore, he shall find the property belonging to his Church in its proper condition.

## VIII. What Has Been Ordered Concerning Bishops Who Have a Dispute with One Another over Dioceses

It is known to almost everyone how divine grace, which holds the heart of our most serene [Note: [Col. 0618D] E. 4, T. 1, 2: “our most serene and most merciful lord.”] lord and prince, King Reccesvinth, in its hand and turns it wherever it wishes, moved his mind toward piety when the most holy man Orontius, bishop of blessed memory, made a request. The king restored and brought back the boundaries of this province of Lusitania, together with its bishops and their dioceses, to the name of the province and to this metropolitan see, according to the judgment of the earlier canons.

After these matters had been restored to this metropolis according to the same rule, by synodal decree and the formula of judgment, with the confirmation of his clemency, and after, by the command of the prince and through the Lord’s mercy, we had assembled together in the holy council, one of them, Selua, bishop of the holy Church of Egitania, appealed to the holy synod because Justus, bishop of the Church of Salamanca, retained the diocese that was owed to him. He also added that he should recover from him what had been possessed from his diocese by the metropolitan of Gallaecia, even though a long time had passed, since these things had been owed to his parish.

But since the ancient canons establish that, if any bishop in one province has possessed part of another bishop’s diocese for thirty years, he shall retain it undisturbed, we judged it just that, since he has not yet held thirty years from the time when he was restored to the metropolitan province, and since he has recovered what he had not possessed for a very long time, and since thirty years have not yet been completed for the other party in this matter, just as the former has returned to the diocese owed to him, so the one who is claiming the diocese owed to him should, by order of the metropolitan and together with his brothers, recover it through his *sajo*. The following condition is imposed: inspectors shall be sent in the presence of the metropolitan, who shall examine the dioceses themselves through clear signs, so that each person may receive and possess what is owed to him.

[Col. 0619B] Agreements that have been made most justly between bishops through peaceful deliberation according to canonical rule are, in all respects, to be observed. It is also established for all bishops that they must guard their own dioceses well and must not permit any brother to usurp them. If the period of thirty years should elapse through their will or negligence, the diocese shall in no way be returned.

## IX. What a Presbyter Must Observe When He Is Ordered to Give Holy Chrism to Presbyters

This judgment remains agreed upon by all of us and is to be properly observed in our province. It has pleased us that whenever anyone has received from a bishop, with authority, holy chrism to distribute to presbyters at the appropriate time, he shall not presume to take or demand anything from them as a benefit. Likewise, the presbyters who administer God’s holy baptism to infants shall not presume to take anything for such a grace from their parents.

If anyone offers something out of goodwill, it may be gratefully accepted; nevertheless, as we have said, nothing is to be taken on any pretext. If anyone fails to preserve the order of this judgment and presumes to transgress it, he shall remain excommunicated under penance for three months.

671 **X. That Every Bishop Established within This Province Have an Archpresbyter, Archdeacon, and Chief Clerk in His Church**

By common deliberation we decree that all of us bishops established within our province must each have in our cathedral churches an archpresbyter, an archdeacon, and a chief clerk; for this is a holy order and is to be observed by us in all respects. Therefore it pleased this great synod that whoever attains this office must show humility and the highest reverence toward his bishop, so that none of them may in any way incur the arrogance of pride, but each may remain kindly in the order in which he has been established and maintain the dignity of his office in all respects.

If any of them fails to preserve the order of his rank and delays fulfilling what his bishop has commanded him for the sake of this office, he shall know that, according to the evident circumstances of the case, he is to be punished by the penalty of excommunication.

## XI. That Every Presbyter, Abbot, or Deacon Maintain Humility and the Highest Reverence toward His Bishop

[Col. 0620A]

It has come to the attention of this holy council that presbyters, abbots, and deacons are disobedient to their bishop. It has also been reported that, when any of the presbyters or abbots of their churches obtain absolution from bishops who are departing this life, they do not show their own bishop the obedience due to him and the proper reverence; and that those who have been granted permission by canonical judgment to visit their parish are instead subjected to insult and slander. Therefore it has pleased this holy council that due honor be shown to the bishop by presbyters, abbots, and even deacons alike, so that he may not appear to suffer insult from anyone. Whenever it happens that he visits his parish according to canonical judgment [Col. 0620B], they are to receive him worthily and, according to what they possess or what circumstances permit, prepare for him whatever is necessary.

We therefore establish that this is to be observed in every respect: no presbyter or deacon may, without the will and permission of his bishop, conduct secular lawsuits [Note: [Col. 0619D] Except B. R., which has *curas* (“cares,” “duties”).] or settle public injunctions. If anyone wishes to transgress the order of this chapter, let him know that he is to be struck by a sentence of excommunication.

### XII. That a bishop may make those presbyters and deacons of his parish whom he approves cathedral clergy for himself

If the ruling of the preceding canons rightly maintains this order—that a bishop should request and receive from another bishop a cleric for ordination whenever he has need—why should he not bring to his principal church and retain those whom he has found worthy in his own diocese for the service of God and for his assistance? For this reason our unanimity has chosen the following: if any bishop of our province wishes to make presbyters and deacons from among his parish clergy cathedral clergy for himself in his principal church, he shall have full permission to do so.

Those who have been transferred, however, must maintain the humility due toward their bishop and must be held and honored in the cathedral church with the same honor and reverence as those who are known to have been ordained there. Although they may receive something from their own bishop by proper obedience as a stipend, they must not remain strangers to the churches in which they were previously consecrated or to their property. Instead, by episcopal decision, another presbyter is to be appointed under the direction of that presbyter, to perform the holy office; and, at the discretion of the former presbyter, he is to be reasonably supplied with food and clothing, so that he does not suffer want [Col. 0620D]. Or, if the one who is appointed asks his own presbyter for a stipend, he is to receive as much as the dignity of his office requires him to have. To the clerics whom he gives him for service, he is to provide whatever is necessary, with due discretion.

If anyone delays to fulfill the order of this ruling, let him know that, as circumstances permit, he is to be excommunicated.

### XIII. That a bishop may honor and enrich from the Church’s property any member of his clergy whom he sees advancing toward good progress

A considerable congregation of clergy is gathered in the holy Church of God [Col. 0621A]. Some show no small dedication to the holy service of God, while many are not led toward good progress by the pride of slothfulness. Therefore this holy council has decreed that whenever a bishop sees anyone advancing toward good progress, he shall have the power, with good intention, to venerate, love, and honor him, and to grant him whatever he wishes from the Church’s property. This practice gives greater grace to those already great and encourages the lesser to strive toward what is better.

Whatever he grants to the good through grace, they are to possess as a legal right, so that they may both experience the benefit of it and increase the property dedicated to God. But if they fail, through their lukewarmness, to bring what they have received to fruitful use, or if loss becomes evident, the bishop shall have permission, without prejudice to the rights of the Church [Col. 0621B], to reclaim the property as his own.

### XIV. That the money offered in the Church of God is to be collected faithfully and divided faithfully

In the holy Church of God, on feast days, according to custom and as the reward of communion, we know that money is contributed by the faithful. For this reason it has pleased the holy council to establish this rule of justice: since the whole clergy share a common labor in the holy ministry, all should receive a return from it according to their merit.

We decree that the following is to be observed in our churches and cities: whatever money is offered by the faithful in the Church is to remain faithfully collected and preserved, and is to be faithfully presented to the bishop, so that it may then be divided into three equal parts. One part is to belong to the bishop; the second is to be received by the presbyters and deacons serving there [Col. 0621C], who are to divide it among themselves as dignity and rank require; the third is to be assigned to the subdeacons and clerics, and is to be distributed individually by the chief clerk according to the diligence he observes in their service.

A similar arrangement is to be observed concerning the parish presbyters in the churches entrusted to them by God.

### XV. That bishops and presbyters may not, without judicial examination, destroy members of the Church’s household for serious offenses condemned by the law

If royal piety, for the safety of its subjects, has deigned to establish decrees through its laws, why should holy religion, through the order of a holy council, not have regulations concerning matters that must altogether be guarded against? Therefore it has pleased this holy council that every episcopal authority restrain its anger [Col. 0621D] and that, for any offense whatsoever, no one presume on his own authority to cut off or remove any bodily member of anyone belonging to the Church’s household.

If such a fault should arise, the judge of the city is to be summoned, and the alleged act is to be brought before his examination. Since it is entirely just that a bishop should not inflict the most savage vengeance, whatever the judge establishes as more truly proven is to be corrected through the severity of discipline, without disgraceful shaving of the head. The person who has committed an evil condemned gravely by the laws is either to remain, having been handed over by his bishop to his faithful [people], or the bishop shall have permission to expel him if he wishes.

Likewise, because we have learned that some presbyters, when illness approaches, accuse members of their own Church’s household, saying that certain persons among them have practiced sorcery against them, and torture and injure them by their own authority and with great impiety, we have decided that this too is to be corrected through the justice of this ruling. We therefore decree that if a presbyter says that he has suffered such things, he must bring the matter to the ears of his bishop. The bishop, appointing good men from his own side, is to order a judge to investigate it; and if the cause of such a crime is discovered, they are to refer the matter for the bishop’s judgment. Once a sentence has proceeded from his mouth, the evil is to remain eradicated, so that no one else may presume to do such a thing.

If anyone fails to observe the order of this ruling, he is to be struck by a sentence of excommunication and expelled from the clergy.

### XVI. That a bishop may not take a third from parish churches

[Col. 0622B]

Divine grace has arranged well that each church should possess whatever has been contributed by the faithful. In very ancient canons it had been decreed that a bishop should receive a third from parish churches, although what belongs to him can fully suffice for him. It has pleased this holy council that no bishop of the province of Lusitania exceed the limit of this ruling or presume to take a third from any parish church. Rather, whatever he might have obtained from it is to be used entirely for the repair of those basilicas.

All the presbyters mentioned above who have the means are to please their bishop by taking care to repair the churches entrusted to them [Col. 0622C]. If they delay to do so, they are to be compelled by their bishop, as reason permits, to repair properly the churches entrusted to them. Churches, however, that possess no worldly resources are to be repaired through episcopal care, attention, and provision, as reason permits.

### XVII. That after the death of a bishop none of his subjects may speak ill of him

Since, by divine grace, episcopal authority is established in the holy Church of God, it is fitting that, just as a bishop is held in the highest honor and goodness during life, so after death there should be no defamation of him. For this reason our assembly has issued this ruling and commands that it remain firm in every respect.

We therefore decree that no subject may defame a deceased bishop [Col. 0622D], disparage him, or speak any evil of him. If anyone thereafter presumes to do such things:

- If he is a presbyter, he is to remain confined by his bishop under penance for three months.
- If he is a deacon, for five months.
- If he is a subdeacon, cleric, or any religious person of a higher rank—for it is evident that some among these are already to be venerated for their good conduct—for nine months.
- If they are persons of the lowest rank, light-hearted people and persons still of very little standing, they are to be struck with fifty lashes by order of the bishop.
- If he is a layman, even though freeborn, but raised in the household of the Church and endowed with property belonging to the Church for the sake of his status, he is to be struck by a sentence of excommunication for such an offense, according to what his status requires.
- If someone belongs to the Church’s household, since there are degrees of rank even among them, and if he is a person of higher standing who possesses dignity, he is to remain excommunicated by his bishop for six months.
- A person of lower or lowest standing is to receive the discipline merited by him, according to the sentence issued by his bishop.

For it is fitting that, for one to whom honor was shown during life, the spur of defamation should be removed after death.

### XVIII. That parish presbyters should, according to their means, make and retain clerics from their Church’s household

Whatever is unanimously and properly arranged in the holy Church of God must remain guarded by parish presbyters. There are some who possess the resources of their churches in abundance, yet show no concern for having clerics [Col. 0623B] with whom they may render the proper services of praise to almighty God.

Therefore this holy synod has decreed that all parish presbyters, according to the strength they perceive themselves to possess in the resources entrusted to them by God, are to make clerics for themselves from their Church’s household. They are to nurture them with good will so that they may both perform the holy office worthily and remain fit for their service.

These clerics are to receive food and clothing through the presbyter’s administration, and they must be faithful to God, to their presbyter, and to the interests of the Church. If they prove useless, they are to be punished by disciplinary correction, according to the fault that becomes evident.

If any presbyter fails to observe and fulfill this ruling, he is to be corrected by his bishop so that he may fully observe what has been rightly commanded.

### XIX. That a presbyter entrusted with several churches should intend to offer a sacrifice to God in each one on every Sunday

[Col. 0623C]

Many churches are established in the parishes, and these, having been built by the faithful, appear to possess little or nothing of their resources. Thus, by priestly decree, several have been entrusted to one presbyter. Care must therefore be taken that, when poverty intervenes, the order of the Mass is not neglected there.

Accordingly, with salutary deliberation, we decree that for each church in which a presbyter has been ordered by his bishop’s arrangement to preside, he is to arrange to offer the sacrifice to God on each Sunday. During the time of Mass, the names of those by whom the churches are known to have been built, or who appear or are known to have contributed something to these holy churches, are to be recited, if they are still living in the body, before the altar [Col. 0623D]. If they have departed or passed from this light, their names are to be recited in due order with the faithful departed.

If a presbyter neglects to fulfill this institution, once such a matter has reached the ears of his bishop through anyone, that presbyter is to be struck by a sentence of excommunication.

### XX. How bishops are to make freedmen, and how freedmen are never to depart from the Church’s protection

In the order of the preceding canons it has been established how bishops are to make freedmen from the Church’s household. Many priests, insofar as divine grace has granted them the means, possess enough to fulfill the canonical order and thus make freedmen; but many who possess nothing presume to come to this grace and make freedmen in this manner.

The canonical rule does not command such persons to be established as freedmen. It often happens that, after their manumitter has departed from this light, a successor appears who either takes no account of the Church’s household or, through goodwill or negligence, allows those who were made free by one who offered nothing to the Church to claim for a long time that they are freedmen. They conceal their instruments of freedom so thoroughly that they cause trouble for the bishop who seeks to investigate the matter.

No permission is granted for such persons to do this. Since they were unable to do so lawfully, they must never depart from the service of the Church, nor can they remain free on account of these matters.

The institutions of the holy canons are not to be rejected, and we add new provisions to those that ought to be fulfilled. It has pleased this holy synod that anyone who has been made a freedman properly and according to canonical rule is to remain free, but neither he nor his descendants may ever depart from the Church’s protection.

Whoever has been made a freedman contrary to what the canonical order demands, even if a long period of time is found in the text of his written instrument, since he has never been seen to have departed from the Church’s service—and since canonical judgment commands that such freedom be rescinded—is to remain, together with all his descendants, in the service of the holy Church, to which they remain bound by their true origin.

We decree that those are to be established fully in freedom who have been or are made free by bishops who are known, through the text of their written instruments, to have contributed very substantial property of their own to the holy Church over which they preside [Col. 0624C]. Even though these persons are ordered to be established securely, they are in no way to depart from the protection of the holy Church.

If it should happen that they or their children are joined in marriage to freeborn persons, and at some point their descendants wish to despise the Church’s protection—from whose household they are demonstrably descended by true origin—then, if they derive their origin from those freedmen who are ordered by canonical judgment to remain established, they are to retain the name of their status and never lose the Church’s protection.

But if they are found to derive their origin from those whom the canonical rule does not command to be free, then, however much time may have passed, provided their origin is established, they are nevertheless to be returned to the rights of the holy Church to which they belong.

Freedmen, however, made from the Church’s household, and their descendants born from them, if they are found to have concealed or hidden their own freedom or that of their parents, and, when warned by the bishop, have delayed to produce it, are to be returned to the Church’s service once their origin has been established, as we have already said, by a lawful witness. The bishop is to hold them according to what he decides.

This rule is also to be observed by presbyters who, with the consent of their bishop, wish according to canonical rule to make free persons from the household of their Church.

### XXI. How it is to remain established what a bishop wishes to grant from his Church’s property to his friends, servants, or freedmen

It must not be thought that we act against canonical rule when we establish what ought to be observed concerning ecclesiastical property [Col. 0625A]. Although canonical judgment has its own order concerning what a bishop must observe with regard to Church property, it is nevertheless appropriate that, wherever a bishop has brought about good progress, a measure established by his successor should be maintained.

It has pleased this holy council that, if a bishop is found to have contributed a great deal from his own property to the Church over which he presides, and if he is found to have given anything from the property of his Church to his friends, servants, freedmen, or any other persons, then, if what he has recorded in the name of his Church is shown to be three times as much or considerably more, what he distributed to the persons listed above is to remain firm. His successor may not violate the will of his predecessor.

If ecclesiastical cases have also been entrusted to these persons, and they are seen to have made progress in the Church’s affairs by pursuing them faithfully, they are to receive the reward of their labor. Whatever they acquire in this way—since it is clear that they conduct their entrusted business not without benefit to the Church—whatever they bring to completion with faith and good intention, and whatever is shown to have been restored through them to the Church’s rights, they are to receive as their tenth from movable property. For immovable property they are to receive worthy compensation from the bishop. Nevertheless, whatever they or their descendants, or those to whom they wish to grant it, have earned, they are to possess perpetually.

If any bishop, acting contrary to the order of this ruling, wishes to violate what his predecessor did, let him lose his voice and fulfill the penalty imposed by the written instrument that was made; moreover, let him remain excommunicated from the brotherhood [Col. 0625C], so that he may amend the matter of his excess.

### XXII. How the person who does not observe the ruling of this canon is to be excommunicated

Since, with divine grace assisting us, we have accomplished in this holy council [678] what is required for the proper order of the Church, we have imposed a manner of precaution in certain rulings. But because some matters are not confined by a specific rule, we establish through this decree that every bishop, presbyter, and person of lower rank must fear the following.

Whoever delays to observe the institutions of this canonical rule—however great he may appear, or however clearly he recognizes himself to be of middle or lower rank—must know beyond doubt that, as the matter permits, he is to be excommunicated by the metropolitan bishop together with his neighboring bishops who have observed the order of the rulings set out above [Col. 0625D].

### XXIII. Confirmation of this council

After we had set forth the belief of our faith and arranged in order, as best we could, the matters that proved necessary [Col. 0626A], we rendered due praises to our Creator and Lord, whom we believe to be Triune in unity and whom we venerate as One in Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—glorifying the name of such majesty, who deigned to show us the way of righteousness.

Then we offered thanks to our most serene, most devout, orthodox, and most merciful lord, King Reccesvinth, whose vigilance governs secular affairs with the highest piety and more fully orders ecclesiastical affairs through the divine wisdom granted to him.

May the Lord himself, whose Trinity we venerate and confess, grant increase from the faith of his Church and grant to priests, ministers, and the whole clergy the remedies pleasing to him, so that they may serve him worthily. May he grant our most merciful prince, King Reccesvinth, a happy life and still happier joys to possess in the present age and, thereafter, in the everlasting kingdom. May he deign to grant the same to all who believe in him, so that, when he wishes to reveal the time of his judgment, the Lord and our Redeemer may grant everlasting remedy to all. He remains one God in Trinity with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. To him belong honor, glory, power, and dominion, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Proficius, by the mercy of God bishop of the metropolitan holy Church of the province of Lusitania, have subscribed with my own hand to these synodal acts established with my fellow bishops.

I, Sclua, bishop of the Church of the city of Egiditana [Note: [Col. 0625D] T. 1, 2: *Igiditanae*.], belonging to the metropolitan Church of Emerita, have likewise subscribed to these institutions established by us with my archbishop Proficius [Col. 0626C].

Adeodatus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the holy Church of Pax, likewise.

Asphalius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the holy Church of Abila, likewise.

Theoderic, in the name of Christ, bishop of the holy Church of Olyssipo, likewise.

Theodisclus, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Lameco, likewise.

Justus, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Salamanca, likewise.

Cantaber, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Conimbriga, likewise.

[Col. 0626D] Donatus, in the name of Christ, bishop of the holy Church of Caurium, likewise.

Exarnus, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Oxonoba, likewise.

Petrus, by the mercy of God bishop of the Church of Elbora, likewise.

Aloarius, unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Calabria, likewise.

# Decretal Letters

[Col. 0627]

## Here begins the collection of the decretal letters of twenty bishops: Damasus, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Flavian, Peter, Hilary, Simplicius, Acacius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, John, Vigilius, and Gregory

[Note: [Col. 0627B] In Aem.: “Here follow certain decrees of the Roman bishops concerning the ecclesiastical rule of faith.”] (C)

## I. Letter of Pope Damasus to Paulinus, Bishop of Antioch

[Col. 0627A]

Damasus to his most beloved brother Paulinus.

I had sent written communications to you through my son Vitalis, leaving everything to your will and judgment; and through the presbyter Petronius I had indicated that, when he was at the point of departing, I had been moved to some extent. Therefore, lest any scruple remain with you [Note: [Col. 0627B] Bibl. Reg., Ger., Tol. 1; Alv. and the remaining witnesses: *scripulus*.], and lest your pleasing caution perhaps delay those who wished to be joined to the Church, dearest brother, we have sent the confession of faith—not so much to you, who share his faith and communion [Note: [Col. 0628B] Bibl. Reg.: *comunicationique*.], as to those who, by subscribing to it [Note: [Col. 0628B] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Tol. 1; the remaining witnesses: *scribentes*.], may wish through you to be joined to us.

Therefore, if the aforesaid son of mine, Vitalis, and those who are with him wish to be joined to you, they must first subscribe, in that undertaking, to the confession of faith established at Nicaea by the pious will of the Fathers.

### I. That Christ assumed a complete human being without sin

[Col. 0627B]

Moreover, since no one can apply medicine to future wounds, that heresy must be eradicated which is said to have later sprung up in the East. That is, it must be confessed that the Word himself, the Wisdom, the Son of God, assumed a human body, a soul, and a faculty of understanding—namely, the complete Adam—and, to speak more explicitly, our entire former human being without sin [Col. 0628A].

For just as, when we confess that he assumed a human body, we do not immediately add to him the human passions of vices, so also, when we say that he assumed a human soul and faculty of understanding, we do not immediately say that he was subject to the sin of human thoughts.

### II. That Christ is one: begotten before the ages from the Father and born in time from the Virgin

But if anyone says that the Word acted in the Lord’s flesh in place of a human faculty of understanding, the Catholic Church anathematizes him. It also anathematizes those who confess two sons in the Savior: one before the incarnation and another after he assumed flesh from the Virgin, and who do not confess the same Son of God both before and afterward [Col. 0628B].

Anyone who wishes to subscribe to this letter, provided that he has already subscribed to the ecclesiastical canons—which you know very well—and to the faith of Nicaea, you should receive without any ambiguity. This is not because you could not propose the very things to which we have subscribed to those who are subscribing, but because our agreement gives you a free example for receiving them.

## II. Another letter of the same Pope Damasus to the same Paulinus

[Col. 0627]

### I. On the condemnation of certain heretics

[Col. 0627C]

After the Council of Nicaea, which was later assembled in the city of Rome, the Catholic bishops added a statement concerning the Holy Spirit. Since this error later became widespread, so that certain people dared with sacrilegious speech to say that the Holy Spirit was made through the Son, we anathematize those who do not proclaim with complete freedom that he is of one power and one substance with the Father and the Son.

We also anathematize those who follow the error of Sabellius, saying that the Father is the same person as the Son. We anathematize Arius and Eunomius, who with equal impiety, though in different language, assert that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures. We anathematize the Macedonians, who, coming from the stock of Arius, changed not their perfidy but their name. We anathematize Photinus, who renews the heresy of Ebion and confesses the Lord Jesus Christ as existing only from Mary. We anathematize those who assert two sons: one before the ages and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin [Col. 0629A].

We anathematize those who say that, in place of a rational [Note: [Col. 0629C] Ger. has *rationabili*, “rational”; likewise below.] and intelligible human soul, the Word of God acted in human flesh, when the Son himself is the Word of God. He was not in his body in place of a rational and intelligible soul, but for ours: that is, he assumed and saved a rational and intelligible soul without sin.

We anathematize those who contend that the true Son of God will be separated from the Father in substance and end through extension or collection.

If anyone does not say that the Father is always, the Son always, and the Holy Spirit always, let him be anathema.
