If anyone does not say that the Son was born from the Father—that is, from his divine substance—let him be anathema.

[Col. 0629B] If anyone does not say that the Word of the Lord, the Son of God, is God, that he can do all things, knows all things, and is equal to the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that, when the Son of God was established in the flesh and was on earth, he was not in heaven with the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that, in the passion of the cross, the Son of God as God endured suffering, and not the flesh with the soul with which he had clothed himself and had assumed the form of a servant, as Scripture says, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that Christ, in the flesh that he assumed, sits at the right hand of the Father and will come in that flesh to judge the living and the dead, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, just as the Son is from the divine substance, and that he is true God [Col. 0629C], let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit can do all things, knows all things, and is everywhere, like the Son and the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the Holy Spirit will make or has been made through the Son, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father made all things through the Son and the Holy Spirit—that is, visible and invisible things—let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one divinity, power, majesty, might, glory, dominion, kingdom, will, and truth, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that there are three true persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—equal, ever-living, containing all visible and invisible things, possessing all power, judging all things, giving life to all things, making all things, and saving all things, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be adored by every creature, just as the Son and the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone has a sound understanding concerning the Father and the Son but does not hold a right understanding concerning the Holy Spirit, he will be a heretic. For all heretics who think wrongly concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the perfidy of the Jews and the Gentiles.

### II. On the unity of the Trinity

If anyone allows God the Father, God his Son, and the Lord the Holy Spirit to be called “gods,” and not “God,” on account of the one divinity and power that we believe and know to belong to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; or if, removing the Son or the Holy Spirit, he should think [Note: [Col. 0629C] Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3: *existimet*.] or believe that God the Father alone is to be called or believed to be one God, let him be anathema [Col. 0630B].

We say this especially against the Jews: the name “gods” has been applied and given by God to angels and holy human beings. But concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, on account of their one and equal divinity, Scripture reveals and indicates to us not the name “gods,” but “God.” Thus we believe that we are baptized only in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and not in the names of archangels or angels, as heretics, Jews, or foolish Gentiles do.

This, therefore, is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we unquestionably believe that in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is one true and only divinity, power, majesty, and the same substance.

### III. On priests who have migrated from their own churches to other churches

[Note: [Col. 0630C] This paragraph is absent from the printed editions.]

As for those priests who have migrated from one church to another, let us hold them separated from our communion until they return to the cities in which they were first established. But if, when one has migrated elsewhere, another has been ordained in his place while he is still alive, then the one who abandoned his city is to remain deprived of the dignity of the priesthood until his successor rests in the Lord.

## III. Letter of Pope Siricius to Eumerius, Bishop of Tarragona: On Arians not being rebaptized

(C)

[Col. 0629]

[Col. 0629C]

Siricius to Eumerius, Bishop of Tarragona, greetings.

I found, after I had been established in the very see of our predecessor Damasus of holy memory, the report that your fraternity had sent to him [Aem.: *precationem*, “prayer”]. When we read it with particular care in the gathering of the brethren, we found in it as many matters deserving blame and correction [Col. 0630C] as we would have wished to find worthy of praise.

Since it was necessary for us to succeed to the labors and cares of the one to whose honor [Note: [Col. 0629] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Tol. 1: *cujus*.] we have succeeded through God’s grace, after first conveying, as was proper, an indication of my promotion, we do not refuse to give an appropriate answer to each of your questions, insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist us. For, in view of the responsibility of our office, it is not for us to dissemble; silence is not liberty for those upon whom, more than upon all others, the zeal of the Christian religion rests [Note: [Col. 0631D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, T. 1, 2, Ger., Urg.: “it is not permissible for us to be silent.”].

We bear the burdens of all who are burdened. Indeed, blessed Peter the Apostle bears them in us; and, as we trust [Note: [Col. 0631D] Aem., Esc. 3, Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1; the remaining witnesses: *quae*.], he protects and guards us in all things as heirs of his ministry.

### I. That Arians are not to be rebaptized by Catholics

[Note: [Col. 0632D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Tol. 1, 2: “not to be baptized again.”]

At the very beginning of your letter you reported that many baptized by the impious Arians are hastening to the Catholic faith, and that some of our brethren wish to baptize these people again. This is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it, the canons oppose it, and the general decrees sent to the provinces by my predecessor Liberius of venerable memory, after the Council of Ariminum had been annulled, prohibit it.

We unite such persons with the Catholic assembly, as has been established in the synod, together with the Novatians and other heretics, through the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and the imposition of the bishop’s hand. The whole East and West likewise observe this practice [Note: [Col. 0632D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3: “henceforth.”]. You, too, must not thereafter deviate from this path, if you do not wish to be separated from our collegial body by synodal judgment.

### II. That baptism is not to be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost

Next comes the question of the time for baptism: an unacceptable confusion, requiring correction, according to which each person acts as he pleases. Our fellow priests, we say this with distress, presume to do this not by reason of any authoritative rule but through sheer rashness, so that freely and indiscriminately countless multitudes, as you report, receive the mystery of baptism on the birthdays of Christ, on the feast of his manifestation, and also on the festivals of the Apostles and martyrs.

Yet the Lord’s Easter, together with its Pentecost, specially claims this privilege for itself both among us and among all churches. On these days alone during the year is it fitting that the general sacraments of baptism be given to those who come to the faith—only to the chosen who have enrolled their names forty days or more beforehand and have been purified by exorcisms, daily prayers, and fasts—so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: when the old leaven has been cleansed out, the new dough should begin to be made.

Thus, just as we say that Easter reverence must in no respect be diminished, so we wish the sacred water of baptism to come to the aid of infants who, because of their age, are not yet able to speak, and of those for whom it is necessary in any emergency, with all possible speed. Otherwise it would threaten the destruction of our souls if, when those who desire it are denied the saving font, each person should depart from this age and lose both the kingdom and life.

Those who encounter the peril of shipwreck, the attack of enemies, the uncertainty of a siege, or the despair of any bodily illness, and who ask to be aided by this one resource of faith, are to receive, at the very moment when they ask, the reward of the regeneration they seek [Col. 0632A].

Let the error in this matter now be sufficient.

From this point onward, let all priests who do not wish to be separated from the solidity of the apostolic rock observe the rule stated above—the rock upon which Christ built the universal Church.

### III. On Separating Apostates from the Church

It has also been reported that certain Christians have passed over into apostasy—an act which it is impious even to name—and have been polluted by the worship of idols and the contamination of sacrifices. We command that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they had formerly been redeemed through rebirth. And if at some time they should come to their senses and turn to lamentation, they must do penance for as long as they live, and at the very end of their life the grace of reconciliation is to be granted them, because, as the Lord teaches, we do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live.

### IV. That It Is Not Permitted to Take Another Man’s Betrothed as a Wife

You have inquired concerning the nuptial veiling, whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another. We absolutely forbid this, because that blessing which the priest bestows upon women about to marry is, among the faithful, tantamount to a sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

### V. On Those Who Have Not at All Kept the Penance They Accepted

In the case of those about whom your affection has rightly believed the apostolic see should be consulted—those who, after performing penance, like dogs and swine returning to their former vomit and wallowing places, have again desired the military belt, frivolous pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations, and whose avowed lack of self-restraint has been revealed by children begotten after their absolution [Note: [Col. 0632D] Aem., Bibl. R., Esc. 3, 4: *prodiderunt* (“they have revealed”).]—since they no longer have the remedy of doing penance, we have decided the following: they are to be joined to the faithful within the church only in prayer; they may attend the celebrations of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve to do so; but they are to be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table. Thus corrected at least by this severity, they may punish their own offenses within themselves and provide an example to others, so that they may be drawn away from shameful desires.

Nevertheless, since they have fallen through carnal weakness, we wish them to be strengthened by the gift of viaticum through the grace of communion when they begin to depart to the Lord. We decree that the same rule is to be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such pollutions.

### VI. On Monks and Virgins Who Do Not Keep Their Vow

Moreover, you report that certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their commitment to holiness, have sunk into such great wantonness that at first, secretly and as though under the pretext of monasteries, they joined themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious [Col. 0633A] contamination; afterward, driven headlong by despair of conscience, they openly fathered children from their illicit embraces. Both public laws and ecclesiastical rights condemn this.

We therefore command that these immodest and detestable persons be expelled from the company of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches, so that, shut away in their prisons and bewailing such a great crime in continual lamentation, they may be purified and refined by the cleansing fire of repentance. Thus, at least at death, through the grace of communion, forgiveness may come to their aid solely out of regard for mercy.

### VII. On Incontinent Ministers

Let us now come to the most sacred orders of the clergy. Your affection informs us that, to the injury of venerable religion, they have been so trampled upon and thrown into confusion throughout your provinces [Col. 0633B] that we must say with the voice of Jeremiah: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes” [Note: [Col. 0633D] Aem.: “to my eyelids”] “that I may weep for this people day and night?”

If the blessed prophet said that his tears were not sufficient for lamenting the sins of the people, how deeply must we be struck with grief when we are compelled to mourn the crimes of those who belong to our own body—those for whom, according to blessed Paul, daily urgency and concern for all the churches continually press upon us? “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not burned?”

But we have learned that very many [Note: [Col. 0633D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Tol. 1, Urg., Ger.: *enim* (“for”).] priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods of consecrated service, have fathered offspring both from their own wives and from shameful intercourse [Col. 0633C], and have defended their crime by this argument: that in the Old Testament the power of begetting children is recorded as having been granted to priests and ministers.

Let whoever he may be who follows lust and teaches vice now tell me whether he thinks that, in the law of Moses, the reins of lust were everywhere loosened by God for the sacred orders [Note: [Col. 0633D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Tol. 1: [lacuna], “because”; the reading is uncertain]. Why, then, does he warn those entrusted with the holy of holies, saying: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” [Note: [Col. 0633D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Ger., Urg., Tol.: [lacuna]; [Col. 0634D] “because I also …”]? Why, moreover, were priests ordered to live far from their own homes in the temple for the year of their service? Clearly, for this reason: so that they could not have sexual relations even with their wives, and, shining with integrity of conscience, might offer to God an acceptable gift.

After their period of service had been completed, the use of a wife had been permitted to them solely for the sake of succession, because no one from any tribe other than Levi had been commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry. Hence the Lord Jesus, when he had enlightened us by his coming, declares in the Gospel that he came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it.

Therefore he wished the Church, whose bridegroom he is, to radiate the form of chastity with splendor, so that on the day of judgment, when he comes again, he might find her without stain or wrinkle, as he established through his Apostle. By an unbreakable law all priests and Levites are bound by these decrees, so that from the day of our ordination we dedicate both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity, provided that in all things we please our God by the sacrifices we offer daily: “Those who are in the flesh,” says the chosen vessel, “cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” And where could God’s holy Spirit dwell, unless in holy bodies, as we read?

Since, as your holiness has reported, some of those about whom we speak lament that they fell through ignorance, we declare that mercy is not to be denied them on this condition: without any increase in honor, they are to remain for as long as they live in the office in which they were discovered, provided that thereafter they strive to show themselves continent [Col. 0634B].

Those, however, who rely upon the excuse of an illicit privilege, claiming that this was granted to them by the ancient law, should know that, by the authority of the apostolic see, they have been deprived of every ecclesiastical honor of which they made unworthy use. They can never again touch the venerable mysteries from which they deprived themselves while they gazed greedily upon shameful desires.

And because present examples warn us to take precautions for the future: if any bishop, priest, or deacon should henceforth be found to be such—which we do not desire—let him understand that we have now closed against him every avenue of indulgence. Wounds that have not responded to the medicine of soothing remedies must necessarily be cut out with the sword.

### VIII. What Sort of Men Should Advance to the Clerical Office

We have also learned that men of unexamined life, some of whom have even had numerous marriages, freely and without restraint aspire, as each chooses, to the aforementioned [Note: [Col. 0634D] Aem., Esc. 3: [lacuna], “private”] dignities. We attribute this not so much to those who attain them through immoderate ambition as specifically to the metropolitan bishops, who, by conniving at forbidden attempts, despise, insofar as lies within them, the commands of our God.

To say nothing of what makes us sigh more deeply, where is that which our God established through the law given by Moses, saying: “My priests shall marry once”? And elsewhere: “A priest shall take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not a divorced woman, not a prostitute” [Note: [Col. 0634D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Ger., Urg., Tol. 1, 2: “priests … [lacuna] … may take”]. Following this, the Apostle, who changed from persecutor into preacher, commanded that both a priest and a deacon should be the husband of one wife.

The bishops of your regions disregard all these matters as though they had been established in the opposite sense. Since we must not neglect such usurpations [Note: [Col. 0634D] Bibl., Reg., Esc. 3: [lacuna], “usurpation”], lest the just voice of the indignant Lord rebuke us—“You saw a thief and ran with him, and you joined your portion with adulterers”—we issue a general decree concerning what all churches must henceforth follow and what they must avoid.

### IX. On the Conduct of Clerics

Whoever from childhood has devoted himself to the service of the Church must be baptized before the years of puberty and associated with the ministry of the readers. From the beginning of adolescence until his thirtieth year, if he has lived commendably, he must be content with one wife only—the woman whom he received as a virgin through the common priestly blessing [Note: [Col. 0635D] Esc. 3, Urg.: [lacuna], “whom he may have received”—and serve as acolyte or subdeacon. Afterward he may advance to the rank of deacon, if he has first proved himself worthy by leading the way in continence. If he has served there commendably for more than five years, he shall appropriately attain the presbyterate. Thereafter, after ten years, he may obtain the episcopal see, provided that during these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.

### X. On Those Who Convert to the Sacred Service at an Advanced Age

But whoever, already advanced in age, is impelled by conversion to a better way of life and hastens to pass from the laity into the sacred service will obtain the fruit of his desire only if, from the time of his baptism, he is immediately associated with the number of readers or exorcists—provided that it is established that he has had, or has, one wife, and that he received her as a virgin.

Once he has been initiated, after completing two years he shall serve for another five years as acolyte or subdeacon. Then, if during these periods he has been judged worthy, he shall be promoted to the office of deacon. Thereafter, with the passage of time, he may rightly obtain the presbyterate or the episcopate, if the election of clergy and people calls him to it.

### XI. On Clerics Who Enter a Second Marriage and Are Therefore to Be Deposed

Any cleric who takes either a widow or, certainly, a woman in a second marriage shall immediately be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity [Note: [Col. 0635D] All witnesses except Alv., in which [lacuna], “ecclesiastical”]. Only lay communion shall be granted to him, and he may retain it only if afterward he commits nothing of the kind that would cause him to lose it.

### XII. On the Women Who May Live with Clerics

We permit no women to live in the homes of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely on account of necessary relationships.

### XIII. On the Promotion of Monks to the Clergy

We both desire and command that monks whose seriousness of character and holy formation in life and faith commend them be added to the offices of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0635D] All witnesses except Alvend., in which [lacuna], “and those whom”]. Those who are worthy and are under thirty years of age are to be promoted through the minor orders, advancing through each grade, and thus are to reach the insignia of the diaconate or presbyterate through ordination at a mature age. They are not to leap directly to the summit of the episcopate unless they have observed, in these matters, the same periods that we prescribed above for each dignity.

### XIV. That Clerics Are Not to Receive Penance through the Laying on of a Priest’s Hand

It was also fitting for us to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever attain clerical honor. For although they may have been cleansed from the contamination of every sin, those who were formerly vessels of vice ought not to receive any instruments for administering the sacraments [Note: [Col. 0635D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Cer., Tol. 1: “who had been”; Esc. 4: “who had been”].

### XV. On Penitents, Bigamists, and Husbands of Widows, Who Are Not to Be Admitted to the Clerical Order [Note: [Col. 0635D] Esc. 3: [lacuna], “to be admitted to the clerical order”]

Since ignorance is offered as the sole excuse for all these matters that incur censure—and for the time being we must mercifully forgive this solely out of regard for compassion—whoever, as a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a widow, has improperly and unsuitably entered the sacred service [Note: [Col. 0636D] Esc. 3, Bibl. Reg.: “has entered”] should understand that we grant him pardon on this condition: he must reckon it a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion removed, he remains permanently in the order in which he is found.

Henceforth the chief priests of all the provinces should know [Note: [Col. 0636D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Ger., Urgel., Tol. 1, 2: [lacuna], “bishops”] that if they presume to admit anyone of this sort to the sacred orders, an appropriate judgment will be issued by the apostolic see both concerning them and concerning the status of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and our prohibitions.

I believe, dearest brother, that we have explained all the matters that were arranged for complaint and have given sufficient answers, insofar as I think, to each of the cases concerning which you reported through our son, the presbyter Bassianus, to the Roman Church, as to the head of your body.

Now we urge your fraternal spirit more and more to preserve the canons and hold fast to the decretal decisions, so that you may cause what we have written in reply to your consultations to be brought to the knowledge of all our fellow bishops—not only those established in your diocese, but also all the Carthaginians, Baeticans, Lusitanians, and Galicians, as well as those who border on you in the neighboring provinces on every side [Note: [Col. 0636D] All witnesses except Alv., in which [lacuna], “serve alongside”]. Send them, under cover of your letters, the matters that we have settled by a salutary ordinance.

Although no priest of the Lord is free to be ignorant of the venerable determinations of the apostolic see or of the canons, it may nevertheless be more useful and very glorious for your affection, given the antiquity of your priesthood, [Note: [Col. 0636D] All manuscripts except Alv.: *utiliter* (“usefully”).] if what has been written generally to you in particular is brought, through your united diligence, to the knowledge of all our brothers. Thus both the measures salutarily established by us—not rashly, but prudently, with the greatest caution and deliberation—may remain inviolate [Col. 0637A], and access may be closed to every future excuse, an access that will no longer be able to stand open before us [Col. 0638A].

Given on the third day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto.

## IV. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE SIRICIUS, SENT THROUGH VARIOUS BISHOPS, AGAINST THE HERETIC JOVINIAN AND HIS ASSOCIATES, WHO ARE TO BE REMOVED FROM THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH (C)

[Col. 0637]

I would always wish, dearest brothers, to announce to you the joys of your sincerity in love and peace, so that, as letters passed between us, each of us might in turn be strengthened by news of your well-being.

But because the ancient enemy does not allow us to remain at peace, free from his attacks—the enemy who was a liar from the beginning, hostile to truth, the rival of mankind, who deceived himself beforehand in order to deceive man, the adversary of chastity, the teacher of lust, who feeds upon cruelties and must be punished by abstinence—he hates fasts when his ministers preach against them, saying that they are superfluous, having no hope concerning the future, struck down by the Apostle’s sentence: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

O unhappy boldness! O desperate cunning of the mind! The previously unknown speech of the heretics was already creeping through the Church like a cancer, so that, taking possession of the whole breast, it might hurl the entire person into death. And unless the Lord of Hosts had broken the snare they had prepared [Note: [Col. 0637D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Ger., Urg., Tol. 1: [lacuna], “had broken”], the spectacle of so great an evil and the exposure of its hypocrisy would have dragged many simple hearts into ruin, because the human mind is easily led toward the worse part, preferring to walk along the broad road rather than to travel laboriously on the narrow way.

For this reason it was entirely necessary, my beloved, to report to your conscience what has taken place here, lest the ignorance of any priest allow the Church to be defiled by the contagion of the worst men who invade it under a religious name. As it is written, the Lord says: “Many will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits.”

These are the men who cunningly boast of being Christians, so that, walking under the veil of a pious name, they enter the house of prayer and pour forth the speech of a serpent-like argument. They shoot in the darkness at those who are upright in heart and, turning them away from Catholic truth, lead them in devilish fashion into the madness of their doctrine and defraud the simplicity of the sheep.

We have learned and tested the wickedness of many heresies from apostolic times until now [Col. 0637D–0638A]. But never have such dogs wearied the mystery of the Church with their barking as these sudden enemies who have burst forth now. Polluted by the doctrine of perfidy, they have revealed by the fruits of their words whose disciples they are.

For whereas other heretics, misunderstanding divine institutions, have proposed to themselves individual kinds of questions in order to tear apart and rend them, these men, having no wedding garment, wound Catholics and, as I have said, pervert the continence of the New and Old Testaments. Through a devilish, seductive, and counterfeit manner of speaking, they have already begun to lay waste to certain Christians and join them to their madness. Keeping within themselves the poison of their wickedness, they have publicly revealed their blasphemies to the elect by a rash written declaration, and, driven on by the frenzy of a desperate mind, have published them everywhere in favor of the Gentiles.

But faithful Christian men, excellent in lineage and distinguished in religion, suddenly brought a horrifying document to my humility, so that, once exposed by priestly judgment as contrary to divine law, its contents might be destroyed by a special sentence.

We do not reject the vows of marriage; we have accepted them, and we participate in their veiling. But we count virgins devoted to God with greater honor.

A presbyteral investigation was therefore held, and it became clear that this doctrine was contrary to our teaching, that is, to Christian law. Following the apostolic command, since they were announcing something other than what we had received, the unanimous judgment of all our presbyters and deacons, as well as of the entire clergy, was that Jovinian, Auxentius, Genialis, Gemninator, Felix, Plotinus [Note: [Col. 0637D] Bibl. Reg.: Photinus], Martianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus—who were found to be the authors of a new heresy and blasphemy—should, by divine sentence and our judgment, remain perpetually condemned outside the Church [Note: [Col. 0638D] In all manuscripts: [lacuna], *remanere* (“to remain”); perhaps *remanerent* (“they should remain”), as in the printed editions.]

Since I have no doubt that your holiness will preserve this decision, I have sent these writings through my brothers and fellow presbyters Crescent, Leopard, and Alexander, who are able to fulfill this most religious service of faith with a fervent spirit [Col. 0638D].

## V. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE SIRICIUS, SENT THROUGH VARIOUS BISHOPS [Note: [Col. 0637D] Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Urg.: *constituta* (“issued/established”).]: THAT NO UNWORTHY MAN SHOULD BECOME A BISHOP (C)

[Col. 0637]

Pope Siricius [Note: [Col. 0638D] Tolet. 2: “Pope Siricius to the orthodox bishops.”] to the orthodox bishops throughout the various provinces.

When we consider the fear of divine judgment, dearest brothers, and that after this life each person will receive according to what he has done [Col. 0639A] [Note: [Col. 0639D] In all witnesses except Alv.: [lacuna], “according to how”], it was not permitted to remain silent about what gives rise to complaint; necessity commanded us to speak. The prophet says: “Raise your voice like a trumpet.” And if I, whose concern is for all the churches, remain silent [Note: [Col. 0639D] All except Alv.: [lacuna], “if I make myself unlike them”], I will hear the Lord saying: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own traditions” [Note: [Col. 0639D] Aem.: “You rejected”].

For what else is it to reject the commandment of God than to take greater pleasure in establishing new things through private counsel and human judgment?

### I. Who Should Be Promoted to the Ecclesiastical Order

It has reached the awareness of the apostolic see that certain men presume against the ecclesiastical canon and wish to introduce their own new observances, neglecting the foundation and building upon sand, although matters have been so ordered by our predecessors that they ought not to be violated even by a slight whisper. The Lord says: “You shall not move the boundary stones that your fathers established.”

The holy Apostle Paul also, preacher of the New and Old Testaments, in whom Christ spoke, gives this warning: “Stand firm and hold to your traditions” [Note: [Col. 0639D] Aem.: “the traditions which”; Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4: [lacuna] [Col. 0640D], “our”] “which you learned, either by word or by letter.”

Therefore your sincerity sees that great care and diligent concern must be exercised in the sacred ministries and in the ordinations of your priests. Finally, he says to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others.”

This is mentioned so that, after examination has been made, the man called forward to receive the highest priesthood may be commended both for the probity of his character and for his ecclesiastical labor: approved by judgment, not by favor; received in truth, not through personal influence; exercising the apostolic order, not acting through hasty [Col. 0639C] will.

Concerning this, my beloved, letters of this kind previously went to your sincerity [Note: [Col. 0640D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Esc. 3: “converged”], confirmed by the subscription of many brothers and fellow priests and by your own, so that the disposition of the ecclesiastical canon, which was established and confirmed at Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0640D] Aem., Esc. 3, 4, Ger., Tol. 1: [lacuna], “discussed”], might remain firmly grounded by its own authority.

Men of the sort whom apostolic authority commands are to be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical order—not those whom ambition now attempts to seize: namely, curiales, or men who formerly boasted of being bound by the belt of secular military service. After they have exulted in worldly pomp, desired to serve in public affairs, or managed worldly concerns, they frequently thrust themselves forward, aided by the hands of certain men and supported by the favor of their relatives, so that they may become bishops although, through tradition and evangelical discipline, they cannot be.

How often has this matter been contested with the greatest force! Yet nothing of this kind could be chosen unless reason compelled it, even if those to be ordained must come from far away so that they may be judged worthy and approved both by the people and by us [Note: [Col. 0640D] From the following number, leaves are missing in Esc. 3].

### II. That the Priesthood Is Not to Be Given to Unknown Men

How can it be tolerated that people refuse to assist with expenses passing strangers—whether they pretend to be monks or truly are what they call themselves—men whose way of life and baptism we cannot know, whose faith is unknown and untested—but hasten immediately to make them deacons, ordain them priests, or, what is more serious, appoint them bishops?

Among such men, it is considered more worthwhile to give money to a passerby than a priesthood to one who is unknown. From this they are lifted up into pride; from this they quickly fall into perfidy, because, as strangers throughout the ecclesiastical world, they do not claim to have learned the true faith.

### III. That Neophytes or Laymen Are Not to Become Priests

Certainly this too ought not to have been omitted: on one or two occasions the necessity created by heretics has introduced the practice, and it has begun to be presumed lawful as though authorized by statute, contrary to apostolic commands—that a neophyte or layman who has held no ecclesiastical office should carelessly be ordained either priest or deacon. It is as though they were better than the Apostles, whose command they dare to alter, and as though one who has not learned should now be compelled to teach.

Is no cleric found suitable? Is there no one among the deacons or other clergy who is considered worthy of the priesthood, so that a layman must be demanded to the condemnation of the Church?

I exhort, warn, and proclaim that this must not happen. Since we have one faith, we must also have one mind in tradition, proving ourselves unanimous and harmonious, peaceful in Christ, and charitable in apostolic observances.

Therefore, by the Father, his Only-Begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the Trinity of one divinity, I appeal to you that our Catholic faith and discipline may remain in these matters. Let no one ordain as though ordinations were earthly acts, since the priesthood is heavenly, so that the glory of its dignity may remain with the faithful and no accusation may be brought against it hereafter before the tribunal of Christ.

## VI. LETTER OF POPE INNOCENT TO DECENTIUS, BISHOP (C)

[Col. 0639]

Innocentius sends greetings to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium [Note: [Col. 0639] Aem., Bibl. Reg.; in the remaining witnesses: *Euqubrino* (“bishop of Euqubium”).].

If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed Apostles, there would be no diversity or variation in the orders themselves or in the consecrations. But since each person judges that what seems right to him, rather than what was handed down, must be observed, different things appear to be held or celebrated in different places and churches. This creates scandal among the people, who, because they do not know that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, think either that these practices are unsuitable for themselves or for the Church, or that disagreement has been introduced by the Apostles or apostolic men.

Who does not know, or who does not perceive, that what was handed down by the chief of the Apostles, Peter, to the Roman Church and has been preserved until now must be observed by all? Nothing should be added or introduced that lacks authority or seems to take its example from elsewhere, especially since it is clear that throughout Italy, Gaul [Note: [Col. 0641D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4: “the Gauls”], the Spains, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one founded churches except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter or his successors established as priests.

Let them read, if they find or read that another of the Apostles taught in these provinces. If they do not read this because they find it nowhere [Aem.: *invenitur* (“is found”), rather than *inveniunt* (“they find”)], they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves. It is beyond doubt that they received their beginning from her [Note: [Col. 0641D] Gerund: [lacuna], “from whom they received this beginning”], lest, while they devote themselves to foreign assertions [Note: [Col. 0641D] Aem., Bibl. R., Esc. 4, T. 1; in the others the word “assertions” is absent], they appear to omit the source of their institutions.

There is no doubt that your affection has often come to the city and met with us in the church, and that you learned what custom we observe both in consecrating the mysteries and in conducting the other sacred rites. I would consider that sufficient for the instruction or reformation of your Church, if I were certain that your predecessors had observed nothing less or otherwise. But since you have said that we should be consulted about certain matters, we answer—not because we believe that you are ignorant of anything, but so that you may instruct your own people with greater authority, or admonish those who deviate from the institutions of the Roman Church, or not delay to identify them, so that we may know who introduces novelties or thinks that the custom of a Church other than the Roman Church must be observed.

### I. On Giving the Kiss of Peace after the Completion of the Mysteries

You state that certain persons command the people to give the peace before the mysteries have been completed, or that priests give it to one another at that point. But after everything that I ought not to disclose has been completed, peace must be announced as necessary. Through it, it is shown that the people have given their consent to everything enacted in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that all has been completed is demonstrated by the seal of the peace that concludes the rite.

### II. On Not Reciting Names before the Priest’s Prayer

As for the recitation of names before the priest offers the prayer and commends in his prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, you yourself, in your prudence, will recognize how superfluous this is. You name in advance the one whose sacrifice you have not yet offered to God, although nothing is unknown to him.

The offerings must therefore first be commended, and then the names of those to whom they belong must be announced, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other matters that we mention beforehand in order to open a way for the prayers that will follow in the mysteries themselves [Ae.: *ministeriis* (“ministries”), for *mysteriis* (“mysteries”)].

### III. That the Baptized May Be Signed Only by Bishops

As for signing infants, it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop. For although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the highest rank of the episcopate. That this belongs solely to bishops—that they should sign or impart the Spirit, the Paraclete—is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which states that Peter and John were sent to give the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized.

For priests, whether they baptize outside the presence of a bishop or in the bishop’s presence, may anoint the baptized with chrism, but with chrism consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs solely to bishops when they impart the Spirit, the Paraclete. I cannot state the actual words, lest I seem to disclose rather than answer the consultation.

### IV. That One Should Properly Fast Every Saturday

The clearest reasoning demonstrates that one ought to fast on Saturday. If we celebrate the Lord’s Day because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—not only at Easter but also throughout each weekly cycle, repeatedly observing an image of that day—and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s passion, we must not pass over Saturday, which appears to have been enclosed within that period between grief and joy.

For it is certainly established that during those two days the Apostles were both in mourning and hidden because of fear of the Jews. It is beyond doubt that they fasted so rigorously during those two days that the tradition of the Church holds that the mysteries are not celebrated at all during them.

This practice must certainly be maintained each week because the commemoration of that day must always be observed. If they think that one should fast on only one Saturday and only once, then Sunday and Friday will likewise be celebrated only once, at Easter. But if the image of Sunday and Friday is to be renewed each week, it is foolish to observe the custom of the two days while omitting Saturday, since it has the same cause as Friday, namely, that on Friday the Lord suffered and descended to the underworld, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding two-day grief.

We therefore do not deny that one should fast on Friday; rather, we say that this must also be done on Saturday, because both days imposed grief upon the Apostles and upon those who followed Christ. On Sunday they were gladdened, and they wished not only that it should be the most festive day itself but also that it should be observed repeatedly throughout all the weeks [Note: [Col. 0642D] Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Ger., Urgel., Tol. 2: [lacuna], “they judged”].

### V. On Sending the Fermentum to the City’s Priests

As for the *fermentum* that we send on Sunday to the titular churches, you wished to consult us unnecessarily, since all our churches are established within the city. Their priests cannot meet with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them. Therefore they receive from us, through the acolytes, the *fermentum* that we have prepared, so that on that day in particular they will not consider themselves separated from our communion.

I do not think that this ought to be done through outlying parishes, because the mysteries need not be carried over a long distance. Nor do we send them to priests established in various cemeteries, since those priests possess the right and the authority to consecrate the mysteries themselves.

### VI. On Baptized Persons Possessed by Evil Spirits

Your affection has asked concerning baptized persons who afterward are seized by a demon, or by some intervening defect or sin, whether they may or should be signed by priests or deacons. This may not be done unless a bishop commands it. They must not be subjected to the laying on of hands at all unless the bishop has granted authority for this to be carried out.

For it to be done, it belongs to the bishop to order that hands be laid upon them either by a priest or by other clerics. For how could this be accomplished without great difficulty, so that a person possessed by an evil spirit who lives far away might be brought to the bishop, when, if such a case occurs to him on a journey, he can neither easily be carried to the bishop nor taken back home?

### VII. On Penitents
Of penitents, however, who are doing penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones, the custom of the Roman Church shows that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released from penance on the Thursday before Easter. As for assessing the gravity of offenses, it belongs to the priest to judge, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession, and to the tears and weeping of the one correcting his ways, and then order him to be released when he sees that a fitting satisfaction has been made. Certainly, if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before the time of Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.

## VIII. Concerning the Epistle of Saint James the Apostle, in which prayer for the sick is commanded

[Col. 0644A]

Since your Belovedness wished to consult me about this matter, as about the others, my son the deacon Caelestinus also added in his letter that your Belovedness had cited the passage written in the Epistle of the blessed apostle James:

> “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters [Note: [Col. 0643C] The Royal Library, Toledo 1: “the presbyters of the church, and,” etc.] and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has been in sins, they will be forgiven him.”

There is no doubt that this must be understood as referring to faithful sick people, who may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism. Once this has been prepared by the bishop, not only priests but also all Christians are permitted to use it, in their own need or that of their own people, for anointing.

Moreover, we see that the addition concerning the bishop is superfluous, as though there were uncertainty about something which it is beyond doubt that presbyters may do. For this reason it was said to the presbyters: bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot go to all the sick. Nevertheless, if a bishop is able, or considers someone worthy of a visit from him, he may without hesitation both bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one who prepares the chrism itself.

This cannot, however, be poured out upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For if the other sacraments are denied to them, how can it be thought that one kind may be granted? Thus, dearest brother, we have taken care to respond as best we could to all the matters about which your Belovedness wished us to give an explanation, so that your Church may be able to observe and preserve the Roman custom from which it derives its origin. As for the remaining matters, which it was not lawful to commit to writing, when you are present we shall be able to state them in response to your questions.

It will also belong to the power of the Lord to arrange that you may rightly instruct both your Church and our clergy, who under your episcopate serve in the divine offices, and that you may provide others with a model which they ought to imitate.

Issued on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Palladius [Note: [Col. 0644C] Toledo 1: “Palladius for the fifth time.”].

## VII. Letter of the same Pope Innocent to Victoricus, Bishop of Rouen (C)

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643D] Innocent sends greetings to Victoricus, bishop of Rouen.

### 13

Although, dearest brother, on account of the merit and honor of the priesthood in which you are especially distinguished, the rules for ecclesiastical conduct and teaching are familiar to you, and although there is nothing in the sacred readings which could seem unknown to you, nevertheless, since you earnestly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church, I have readily accommodated myself to your wishes and sent attached to my letter a set of rules for life and approved conduct. Through them, the peoples of your region may learn by what principles and rules the Christian life ought to be ordered in each person’s calling, and what order is maintained in the churches of the city of Rome.

It will be your Belovedness’s duty diligently to commend this book of rules, as a kind of instructional and admonitory work, among the neighboring peoples and to our fellow priests who preside over their own churches in those regions, so that through assiduous instruction they may come to know our practices and shape the conduct of those who flock to the faith. Either they will recognize their purpose from this suitable instruction of ours, or, if anything is still lacking, they will easily be able to supply it through good imitation.

I shall therefore begin, with the help of God and of the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ had their beginning, so that, since many matters have often arisen which in some cases were not merely matters but crimes, from now on each priest may be concerned to exercise such care in his church as the blessed apostle Paul proclaims: that such a church should be presented to God without spot or wrinkle, lest our conscience be stained and violated by the breath of any diseased sheep.

[Col. 0645A] On behalf, therefore, of those who, through ignorance or laziness, do not maintain ecclesiastical discipline and presume to undertake many things which ought not to be attempted, you rightly requested that in those regions the form maintained by the Roman Church should be observed—not because any new commands are being imposed, but because we desire that all should observe what the laziness of some has neglected, although these matters have been established by apostolic and patristic tradition.

For it is written to the Thessalonians, at the admonition of the apostle Paul:

> “Stand firm and hold fast to our traditions, which I delivered to you, whether by word or by letter.”

Certainly, this ought to exercise your mind most seriously: that you may be found secure before God’s presence from every stain of this world. For from the one to whom much has been entrusted, more is demanded, with the interest of punishments. Therefore, since we are compelled to give an account not only for ourselves but also for Christ’s people, we must instruct the people in the Lord’s discipline.

You assert that there have been certain men who, failing to uphold the statutes of their predecessors, have violated the Church’s chastity through their presumption, following the favor of the people and not fearing God’s judgment. Therefore, lest by our silence we seem to give them our consent—since the Lord says through the prophet, “You saw a thief and ran with him” [Note: [Col. 0645D] In the Royal Library manuscript. In the others: “you ran together with him”]—these are the matters which, with regard to divine judgment, it is useful for every Catholic [Note: [Col. 0645D] In the others, except Alv., Urg., and Ger., which have: “of all Catholics.”] bishop henceforth to guard.

### I. That bishops are not to be ordained without the metropolitan’s knowledge

First, no one should dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan. For a judgment is sound when confirmed by the decision of many. Nor should one bishop presume to ordain a bishop, lest the benefit appear to have been granted secretly. The Council of Nicaea also established this.

### II. Concerning those who after baptism have taken up the belt of secular military service

If anyone, after the remission of sins, has worn the belt of secular military service, he must not be admitted to the clergy at all.

### III. Concerning clerical cases which, if not settled in the province, are to be determined by the Apostolic See

If any cases or disputes arise among clergy, whether of the higher or lower order, judgment is to be concluded, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, by assembling the bishops of that province. No one may—without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, whose reverence must be preserved in every case—abandon the priests who govern God’s churches in those provinces and flee to other provinces.

If anyone should presume to do so, all are to judge him removed from clerical office and liable for the wrongs he has committed. If more serious cases have arisen, they are to be referred to the Apostolic See after episcopal judgment, as ancient custom requires.

### IV. Concerning the wives of clergy: that they be joined to virgins and not marry a second wife

[Col. 0646A]

A cleric must not marry a widow, because it is written: “Let a priest take a virgin as his wife, not a widow or a rejected woman.” Since he strives through his labor and the uprightness of his life to attain the priesthood, he must take care lest, hindered by this impediment, he be unable to attain it.

### V. That if a layman has married a widow, he is not to become a cleric

If anyone, even as a layman, has married a widow, whether before or after baptism, he is not to be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same fault. In baptism sins are forgiven; the union with a wife already taken is not dissolved.

### VI. That one who has married a second wife is not to be a cleric

Nor is one who has married a second wife to become a cleric, because it is written: “The husband of one wife”; and again: “Let my priests marry only once.”

And lest anyone think that, if a man took a wife before baptism, and after her departure from this world married another, he could say that the first marriage had been dissolved in baptism, he is greatly mistaken about the rule. In baptism sins are forgiven; the number of wives taken is not abolished. Indeed, a wife is taken in accordance with the precept of the law, to such an extent that the parents of the human race, when they were joined in Paradise, were blessed by the Lord himself; and Solomon says: “A wife will be prepared for a man by God.” The practice of the Church itself also shows that all priests must observe this form.

For it is exceedingly absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not counted after baptism, since the blessing imposed by the priest upon those marrying is shown to have preserved, rather than supplied an occasion for wrongdoing, the form of the law established by God from ancient times. But if a wife taken before baptism is not thought to count, then neither should children begotten before baptism be regarded as children.

### VII. That no bishop should presume to ordain another church’s cleric

No one is to presume to ordain a cleric from another church unless that cleric’s bishop, prevailed upon by petitions, wishes to grant permission. The Council of Nicaea also appears to contain this provision. Therefore, a cleric rejected by his own church is not to be received by another church.

### VIII. That those who come from the Novatians or Montenses are not to be rebaptized

Those who come from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received only through the laying on of hands, because, although baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in Christ’s name—except those who, after passing over from us to them, have perhaps been rebaptized. If such people, having come to their senses and considering their downfall, prefer to return, they are to be admitted after a long penitential satisfaction.

### IX. That priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with women

Furthermore, the Church must maintain in every way what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites not have intercourse with their wives [Note: [Col. 0646D] Escorial 4: “not have intercourse with them.”], because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry.

For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.” In ancient times, if priests did not leave the temple during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, and did not even touch their own homes, although the use of a wife had been permitted to them for the succession of offspring—for no one from another tribe, or anyone except from the seed of Aaron, had been commanded to approach the priesthood—how much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession, and no day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the ministry of baptism?

For if the blessed apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer”—and he certainly commanded this to laypeople—then priests, whose constant duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, must much more always abstain from such intercourse.

If someone has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit believe that he can be heard, when it is said: “Everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

Perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written: “The husband of one wife.” But he did not say that a man should remain in the desire to beget children; he said it with regard to future continence. For he did not exclude those who were physically intact when he said: “I wish that all were as I am.” And he makes this clearer by saying: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit.”

### X. That a monk who becomes a cleric must preserve his way of life

[Col. 0647C]

Concerning monks who have remained for a long time [Note: [Col. 0647D] The Royal Library, Toledo 1 and 2: “who, dwelling for a long time.” In the others: “who, remaining.”] in monasteries and later attain the clerical order: they must not abandon their former way of life.

Either, as he was in the monastery, he ought not to lose, when placed in a better rank, what he long preserved; or, if he was corrupted and later baptized, and while residing in a monastery wishes to enter the clerical order, he absolutely cannot have a wife [Note: [Col. 0647D] Aemilianus: “he will absolutely not have a wife.”], because, having previously been corrupted, he cannot already be blessed together with a bride [Note: [Col. 0648D] The Royal Library and Escorial 4: “he will be able.”].

This form is to be observed among clerics, especially since the ancient rule holds that anyone who had been corrupted and was later baptized, if he wished to become a cleric, was to promise that he would never marry a wife.

### XI. That a cleric is not to be made from among curiales, because he is compelled to perform duties devised by the devil

[Col. 0647D]

Moreover, some of our brothers frequently strive to make clerics of curiales or of men occupied with public functions. Later, when the emperor orders something concerning their recall, greater sorrow arises than gratitude. For it is clear that such men, even in the very duties imposed upon them, perform entertainments which were undoubtedly devised by the devil, and either preside over or participate in theatrical games and public spectacles.

Certainly, the anxiety and sorrow of the brothers—which we have often endured in the emperor’s presence—serve as an example. You yourself, when you were with us, recognized how often we pleaded on behalf of these men, since not only lower clerics from among the curiales but also men already established in the priesthood were subjected to great pressure to be returned.

### XII. Concerning consecrated virgins who have fallen

Those who have spiritually married Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or are secretly corrupted, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless those to whom they joined themselves have departed this life.

For if this principle is observed concerning laymen, so that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is considered an adulteress and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of them has died, how much more must it be maintained concerning a woman who had previously joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward chose to pass over to human marriage?

### XIII. Concerning unveiled virgins who have gone astray

Those who have not yet been consecrated by the sacred veil but had promised to remain in the purpose of virginity—even though they were not veiled—if they should perhaps marry, are to be permitted to perform penance for some time, because their promise was held by God.

For if among human beings a good-faith contract is ordinarily not dissolved for any reason whatsoever, how much more must a promise which they made with God not be dissolved without punishment? If the apostle Paul said that women who departed from their purpose of widowhood incurred condemnation because they had invalidated their first faith, how much more do virgins incur it when they have failed entirely to keep faith with their agreement?

If, then, this rule is guarded with full vigilance by all God’s priests, ambition will cease, discord will be quieted, heresies and schisms will not arise, and the devil will find no opportunity to rage. Rather, unanimity will remain; every iniquity will be overcome and trampled down [Note: [Col. 0648D] In the others except Alv., which has: “every iniquity of man.”]; truth will blaze with spiritual fervor; the peace proclaimed by lips will be preserved in the mind; and the apostle’s command will be fulfilled, that we should remain of one mind, thinking one thing in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through rivalry or empty glory, and pleasing not human beings but our God and Savior, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus and Aristo.

## VIII. Letter of Pope Innocent to Exuperius, Bishop of Toulouse (C)

[Col. 0647]

[Col. 0647D] Innocent sends greetings to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse.

When you consulted me, dearest brother, about what opinion I held concerning each of the matters you proposed, I responded, to the extent of my understanding, with what seemed appropriate: what a teachable reason persuaded us ought to be followed, what the authority of reading showed, or what the preserved sequence of events demonstrated.

Indeed, your Belovedness, following the practice of prudent men, preferred to refer to the Apostolic See what ought to be observed concerning doubtful matters, rather than by presumptuous usurpation to obtain from each matter whatever seemed right to you. Why should we think it more shameful to learn something than to be completely ignorant?

I myself also acquire the capacity for learning through discussion [Note: [Col. 0649D] Perhaps *docilitas* (“teachability”); but all the manuscripts read *docibilitas*.], when, after examining the arguments, I am compelled to respond to the matters proposed. Thus it happens that the person asked to teach always learns something. I shall therefore set out each matter and append the response.

### I. Concerning the incontinence of priests and Levites

You proposed what ought to be observed concerning those placed in the ministry of the diaconate or the office of the presbyterate whom children born to them have revealed to be, or to have been, incontinent.

Concerning these matters there is both the discipline of the divine laws and the clear admonitions of the blessed bishop Siricius of venerable memory [Note: [Col. 0649D] Escorial 4: “of Pope Siricius.”]: that those placed in such offices who are incontinent should be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and should not be admitted to a ministry which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

There is a very ancient authority of sacred law, observed from the beginning: priests were commanded to dwell in the temple during the year of their service, so that, serving at the sacred offerings, they might claim the divine mysteries as men pure and cleansed from every stain. Nor is it lawful to admit to the sacrifices those who engage in carnal intercourse even with their wives, because it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

The use of a wife had been permitted to them for the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe had been commanded to approach the priesthood. How much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession, and no day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the ministry of baptism?

For if the blessed Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer”—and he certainly commanded this to laypeople—then priests, whose constant duty is to pray and offer sacrifice, must much more always abstain from such intercourse.

If someone has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit believe that he can be heard, when it is said: “Everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

Perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written: “The husband of one wife.” He did not say this of someone who was to remain in the desire to beget children, but with regard to future continence. Nor did the one who said, “I wish that all were as I am,” exclude those who were physically intact. And he makes this clearer by saying: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit”; and he spoke of one who had children, not of one who was begetting them.

But that other opinion is plainly different and contrary. If it is found that the form of ecclesiastical life and discipline which Bishop Siricius communicated to the provinces did not reach certain men, their ignorance will be forgiven, provided that from now on they begin entirely to abstain. They are to retain the ranks in which they are found, so that they may not rise to higher ones. It should count as a benefit to them that they do not lose the very position they retain.

But if some are found to have known the form of life sent by Siricius and nevertheless not to have immediately rejected their lustful desires, they must be removed in every way, since, after receiving the admonition, they judged pleasure preferable.

### II. Concerning those who, having devoted themselves to the pleasures of incontinence after baptism, seek penance at the end of life

[Col. 0650B]

It was also asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of incontinence and at the very end of life seek both penance and restoration to communion.

The earlier practice was stricter; the later one, with mercy intervening, is more lenient. The earlier custom held that penance should be granted but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times, it was rightly feared that the granting of communion might make people secure about reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling; therefore communion was denied, while penance was granted, so that everything would not be entirely refused. The circumstances of the time made forgiveness more severe.

But after our Lord restored peace to his churches, once the terror had been driven away [Note: [Col. 0650D] In the others except Alv., which has: “once the error had been driven away.”], it seemed right that communion should be given to those departing this life—both as a kind of viaticum for those setting out because of the Lord’s mercy, and lest we seem, like the heretical Novatians, to follow their harshness and severity in denying pardon.

Communion is therefore granted together with final penance, so that people of this kind, even at their last moments, may, with the permission of our Savior, be rescued from eternal destruction.

### III. Concerning administrators

It was also asked about those who, after baptism, served as administrators and either merely exercised torture or even pronounced a capital sentence.

We read that nothing was defined concerning them by our predecessors. They remembered, however, that powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that such an avenger had been appointed as God’s minister. How, then, could they condemn an act which they saw had been permitted by the Lord as its author?

Therefore, concerning these men, we maintain the practice observed up to now, lest we either overturn discipline or appear to act against the Lord’s authority. All their actions will be preserved for them when an account is rendered [Note: [Col. 0650D] In the other manuscripts, except Alv. and Escorial 3: “all the things which have been done will be preserved for them when an account is rendered.”].

### IV. That men do not remain with adulterous wives

It was also desired to know why men who are communicants do not remain with adulterous wives, while wives of adulterous men appear to remain in the marital union.

In this matter Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not receive punishment; men, however, more freely report adulterous wives to priests. Therefore communion is denied to women when their crime has been exposed. In the case of men, when the offense remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicions; he will certainly be removed if his crime is revealed.

Since the case is therefore equal, when proof is lacking, the basis for punishment sometimes remains inactive.

### V. That those who dictate petitions or criminal charges are considered immune

You also wished to inquire whether those who dictate petitions are granted permission—after the regeneration of baptism, certainly—to ask rulers for someone’s death or for bloodshed as punishment for a crime.

Rulers never grant such a request without an investigation; rather, they always refer the alleged offenses or crimes to judges, so that punishment may be imposed after the case has been examined. When these matters have been assigned to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case. While the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the person who dictated the petition will remain immune.

### VI. That those who, after a divorce, have endured separation and then entered another marriage are shown to be adulterers

[Col. 0651C] Your Belovedness also asked about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves to another in marriage; it is evident that they are adulterers on both sides.

Those who, while their wife was still alive—even though the marriage might appear to have been dissolved—hastened to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Indeed, even the persons joined to them appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel:

> “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; likewise, whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

Therefore all such persons are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful. Concerning their parents or relatives, however, nothing of this kind can be established unless they are found to have encouraged the unlawful union.

### VII. Which books are to be received into the canon

A brief list appended here will show which books are received into the canon of the Holy Scriptures. These, then, are the matters which you wished to have set forth in reply to your request:

The five books of Moses—that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—as well as Joshua son of Nun, Judges, and the four books of Kings, together with Ruth; the sixteen books of the prophets; the five books of Solomon; and the Psalter.

Also among the historical books: one book of Job, one of Tobit, one of Esther, one of Judith, two of Maccabees, two of Ezra, and two of Chronicles.

Also of the New Testament: four books of the Gospels; fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul; three Epistles of John; two Epistles of Peter; the Epistle of Jude; the Epistle of James; the Acts of the Apostles; and the Apocalypse of John.

As for the remaining writings, whether under the name of Matthias [Toledo 2: “Matthew”] or of James the Less, or under the names of Peter [Note: [Col. 0652C] In Alv. these words are absent: “of Peter and John, which were written by a certain Leucius.”] and John, which were written by a certain Leucius, or under the name of Andrew, which were written by the philosophers Xenocaris and Leonidas, or under the name of Thomas—and any others of this kind—you should know that they are not merely to be rejected but also to be condemned.

Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and of Anthemius.

## IX. Letter of Innocent to Bishop Felix (C)

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651C] Innocent to Felix, bishop of Nocera [Toledo 1: “of Nuceria.”].

I cannot but admire that your Belovedness follows the practices of our predecessors and refers to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, everything which can admit some doubt, so that the Apostolic See, having been consulted, may pronounce from those very doubtful matters something certain to be done. We have gladly received this, and we approve your Belovedness as mindful of the canons.

You wrote that, through the fervor of faith in which you are strong and through your love for the holy people, you have either restored God’s churches or built new ones, but that among them you do not have clerics, while some men are mutilated [Note: [Col. 0651] In certain manuscripts, “murcos”; in others, “mucros.” It appears to be an error in all of them for “mutilos,” as is clear from what follows], and some are twice-married.

At this we were astonished that a prudent man wished to consult us about matters which are clearly established for everyone by sound reasoning. Therefore we do not speak to you as though you were ignorant, but say that perhaps, being occupied with other matters, you have forgotten this.

### I. If someone has deliberately amputated part of his body, he cannot be a cleric; if it happened unwillingly, he can

[Col. 0652C]

If anyone deliberately cuts off part of any finger from himself, the canons do not admit him to the clergy. But if this happened to someone accidentally, while he was attending to farm work or, while doing something, struck himself unintentionally, the canons command that such men be made clerics and, if they are found among the clergy, not be expelled.

In the former cases, the will is judged, since it was the cause that led them to cut themselves with iron; plainly, others could not hesitate to do the same. In the latter cases, however, the accident deserved pardon.

### II. That the twice-married cannot be admitted to the clergy

There should have been no need to consult about the twice-married, since the apostle’s reading is clear: “the husband of one wife” is to be admitted to the priesthood or the clergy—and even that wife must have been a virgin when he took her.

If a woman had previously had a husband, even if he has died, and afterward was joined to a cleric, the cleric who took her cannot be a cleric, because the law has stipulated that a priest may not have a widow or a rejected woman as his wife.

### III. That certain laymen cannot be admitted to the clergy [Note: [Col. 0653B] Aemilianus, Royal Library, Escorial 4, Urgell, Gerona, Toledo 1 and 2: “ought not to be admitted.”]

Your Religiousness consulted us about which laymen the canons forbid to be ordained. It is certain that the ecclesiastical rules contain this provision, but it has not been defined in such a way that it applies to all laymen.

For men cannot be born clerics rather than made so; instead, categories have been designated from which men cannot reach the clergy. These include anyone who has conducted legal cases—that is, acted as a petitioner—and anyone who has served as an administrator.

Concerning curiales, the reason is clear: even if men of this kind are found who ought to become clerics, they are nevertheless frequently summoned back to the curia. They must therefore be avoided because of the trouble which the Church often suffers on their account.

### IV. Which laymen can become clerics. Here a concubine is expressly prohibited

The laymen who were baptized while having wives, and who have conducted themselves in such a way that their reputation does not waver in any respect—so that from the time they were baptized they have either remained attached to clerics or stayed in monasteries—are not forbidden to be chosen for the clerical lot, provided that they have known neither a concubine nor a mistress and have been vigilant in every good work.

### V. Concerning the periods to be spent in the orders of the clergy

This is to be done in such a way that the periods established by our predecessors are observed for them. A lector must not quickly become an acolyte, an acolyte quickly a deacon, or a deacon quickly a priest. They must remain for a long time in the lesser offices, and their life and service must alike be tested, so that they may later come to the priesthood after having earned merit through their periods of service, and may not seize what an approved life deserves to receive.

Since it has therefore been shown by a clear definition who ought to be admitted and who rejected, from among those whom your Dignity sees cannot be rejected you must choose those whom you will make clerics. For if we wish to grant neither favor nor benefit to human beings, we can find men whose appointment will bring us neither guilt nor shame.

## X. Letter of Innocent to Bishops Maximus and Severus. Concerning those who have begotten children while in the presbyterate, so that they are to be removed from office (C)

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653B] Innocent to Maximus and Severus, bishops among the Britii [Note: [Col. 0653C] The Royal Library: “among the Briacii.” Toledo 1: “among the Bruttii.”].

### 20

The standard of the ecclesiastical canons ought to be unknown to no priest, for it is sufficiently disgraceful for a bishop not to know these matters—especially since religious laymen know them and consider that they must be observed.

Recently, the attached text of the petition shows what complaint our son Maximilianus, acting in this matter, brought forward. Moved by zeal for faith and discipline, he does not tolerate the Church’s being polluted by unworthy presbyters whom he asserts have fathered children while in the presbyterate. I would explain that this is not permitted, if I did not know that your Prudence possesses knowledge of the whole law.

Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the substance of the attached petition, you will order those accused of having committed such acts to be brought forward.
