After the charges made against those presbyters have been investigated, if they can be convicted, they are to be removed from priestly office, because those who are not holy cannot touch holy things, and they must be made strangers to the ministry which they have polluted by living unlawfully.

We are astonished that bishops conceal such conduct, so that they may be judged either to connive at it or not to know that it is unlawful.

## XI. Letter of Innocent to Agapitus and the Other Bishops. That no one can be admitted to the clergy after penance (C)

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653D] Innocent to Agapitus, Macedonius, and Marinus, bishops in Apulia.

Many reports from different sources and highly trustworthy communications have stated that, throughout the province, many things contrary to the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of our predecessors are being usurped. These matters could easily be cut away if bishops were not found to be responsible for them—bishops who, while trying to win favor either with friends or through acts of service, violate religion and corrupt the orders.

Thus it happens that all sorts of unworthy men receive ecclesiastical honors and are admitted to the clergy, although they do not deserve even a respectable place among the laity. As has now been shown to us in a petition, a certain Modestus, entangled in many crimes and said on account of them even to have performed penance, has not only been made a cleric—which is not permitted—but is also striving toward the summit of the episcopate, although the canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices.

Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the substance of the petition, order him to be brought before you, so that, if he is truly found to be as the petition asserts, he may be removed not only from his ambition but also from clerical office.

# XII. LETTER OF POPE INNOCENT TO RUFUS AND GERONTIUS, AND THE OTHER BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT MACEDONIA

Concerning Bubalius and Taurianus, condemned by the provincial bishops, whose judgment the Apostolic See undertook to reconsider. (C)

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655A] Innocent to Rufus, Gerontius, Sophronius [Note: [Col. 0655B] Ger., Urg., Sophronianus.], Flavianus [Note: [Col. 0655B] From the other witnesses, except Alv., which has Alavianus.], Macedonius, Prosdochius [Note: [Col. 0655B] From Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Urg., Ger. In Alv., Prosdocus. In Tol. 1, Prosdicius. In Tol. 2, Prostocius.] and Aristeus [Note: [Col. 0656B] From the others, except Alv., which has Arisacus.], bishops established throughout Macedonia.

**21.** The delay of our fellow bishops Maximianus and Eumenius [Note: [Col. 0656B] Tol. 1, Eugenius. Tol. 2, Emenius.]—or rather, the urgency of the times—has caused you to renew your complaint about Bubalius and Taurianus, and has caused us once again to rise up against men utterly ruined. But, as far as I can, I shall seek a concise summary of such great evils, and shall briefly review what I have observed in the volume of your letters.

It ought not to have seemed burdensome to your most devout minds that any judgment should be reconsidered, because truth, repeatedly challenged, shines forth more brilliantly into the light, and destruction, recalled to judgment, is condemned more gravely and without repentance. For it is a divine fruit, dearest brothers, that justice should be examined again and again. Yet I see that what moved your minds was this: Bubalius, often exposed in many deceptions, had produced copies of forged letters as though they had come from us, although, given the man’s customary conduct, nothing he might bring forward now appeared entirely worthy of belief.

But let every murmur about such a matter now be silenced, and let the very breath of the convicted devil be suppressed. We have appended to these letters the earlier ones that we sent through the bishops mentioned above; in them the full judgment of our thoughts has been set out so clearly that, when you reread them, you will not thereafter repeat anything ambiguous or anything requiring further inquiry in this case.

Send this little page of ours also to the bishops of Crete, so that they may know most fully what has been pronounced concerning Bubalius, Taurianus, and the others, and so that those who are worthy of admonition may take care to avoid such men, lest they suffer the same fate. [Col. 0656B]

# XIII. LETTER OF POPE INNOCENT TO FLORENTIUS, BISHOP OF TIBUR, CONCERNING THE BOUNDARIES NOT TO BE TRANSFERRED

(C)

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655B] Innocent to Florentius, bishop of Tibur.

**22.** Divine Scripture cries out not once but repeatedly that the boundaries established by the Fathers ought not to be moved, because it is sacrilege for one person to invade what another has always possessed. Our brother and fellow bishop Ursus asserts that you have done this.

For he has complained with grief that you invaded the parish of Nomentum, or Faciliense, which had belonged by ancestral right to his diocese, and celebrated divine services there without consulting him or his knowledge. If this is true, know that you have incurred no light offense. Therefore, if you wish to avoid the odium of so great an usurpation, it is fitting that, admonished by our letter, you abstain.

Certainly, if you believe that anything supports your claim of justice, you must appear after the venerable days of Easter, with everything intact and remaining in its former condition, so that you may respond to the claims mentioned above and, with the ancient authorities placed before us, we may inquire what antiquity or truth establishes. [Col. 0656C]

# XIV. LETTER OF POPE INNOCENT TO PROBUS

If a man’s wife has been taken captive and he has taken another wife, when the first returns the second woman must be dismissed. (C)

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655C] Innocent to Probus.

The upheaval caused by the barbarian storm brought disorder upon the legal arrangements; and the attack of captivity would have blemished the well-ordered marriage between Fortunius and Ursa, had not the sacred provisions of religion intervened.

For while the aforementioned woman Ursa was being held in captivity, the said Fortunius is known to have entered into another marriage with Restituta. But, by the Lord’s favor, Ursa returned and approached us; and, with no one denying it, she made it fully clear that she was the wife of the aforementioned man.

Accordingly, illustrious lord and deservedly honored son, with the Catholic faith supporting us, we have determined that the marriage founded first by divine grace was the true marriage, and that the union with the second woman, while the first was alive and had not been expelled by divorce, could in no way be legitimate. [Col. 0656D]

# XV. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO AURELIUS AND AUGUSTINE, AFRICAN BISHOPS

A salutary letter full of charity. (C)

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657A] Innocent to Aurelius and Augustine, bishops.

**23.** Most beloved brothers and fellow presbyters, that return visit ought not to have been empty of the service owed by our office. For it seems almost natural and fitting to us to greet those who are most dear to us with a greeting of affection.

Therefore, most beloved, we desire that your brotherhood rejoice in the Lord, and we ask you to offer to God prayers equal to ours on our behalf; for, as you well know, by our shared and reciprocal prayers we accomplish more than by prayers that are solitary or private. [Col. 0658A]

# XVI. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO THE SAME AURELIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

Concerning Easter. (C)

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657A] The service of our charity is interrupted by no interval, even if no written page carries any letters. Spiritual grace lives reciprocally in our hearts and nourishes our love; and the fellowship itself of the priesthood sustains it.

Take care, therefore, as is fitting, to preserve the unity of the Church [Note: [Col. 0657B] In the printed editions: “Why, then, is it unworthy that the unity of the Church should be preserved?”], and let us all together both think and proclaim the same things, dearest brother.

I have therefore written this letter concerning the date of Easter in the other—that is, the coming—year. Since the moon will be nearly at the sixteenth day on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April (for it is not anything less), and likewise the twenty-third day will fall on the fourth day before those same Kalends, I judged that the Paschal feast should be celebrated on the eleventh day before the aforementioned Kalends, since we know that Easter has never before been celebrated on the twenty-third day of the moon.

I have set out and declared the substance of my judgment. It will now be for your prudence, my brother and associate, together with our like-minded fellow priests, to reconsider this very matter in a most devout synod [Col. 0658B] [Note: [Col. 0658B] In Urg., “to discuss.” Thus *retractare* here means “to discuss again.”], so that, if nothing results contrary to our arrangement, you may write to us fully and openly, and we may prescribe in advance, as is customary, the Paschal day that has been decided upon, to be observed at its proper time.

Although I know that you will most willingly receive the fellow presbyter Archidamus in your customary manner, nevertheless, out of an abundance of caution, I ask you to be willing to have him among your own people.

# XVII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO THE SAME AURELIUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

That no one should be made a bishop contrary to the order of the canons. (C)

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657C] Innocent to his most beloved brother Aurelius.

**24.** Your brotherhood knows well with what indignity and distress I read or hear that the Church, and especially its bishops, are being mistreated; and I cannot find words adequate to so great a grief, while hands are easily laid upon men and the highest priest is bound through negligence.

Behold, a public complaint has arisen, and it has always made the reverence owed by all a matter of dread. Thus clerics nourished and honored in ecclesiastical teaching are rejected within the altars of Christ; thus they are passed over, as though it were sacrilege to reach primacy through the proper order.

For when men entangled in worldly bonds, actions, or habits are abruptly admitted to so great a college of priests, those from whom the choice ought to have been made appear to be despised, while those who break in contrary to order are admitted improperly rather than chosen.

How wretched it is that one should become a teacher who was never a disciple; that one should become the highest priest who never served in any rank of the priesthood! Read again the letters of the prefects, and see what things concerning the eminent powers are recorded in writing, whether falsely or as established fact.

We have indeed ourselves lost—lost, I say—the reverence due to holiness, since we make high priests as though this were some utterly worthless thing, so that it now begins to be condemned in public pronouncements as though it were something harmful.

Dearest brother, I ask that you send these writings to be read aloud throughout all the African Churches, and join to them the letters of the prefects that we have appended [Note: [Col. 0657D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Urg., Ger., “of the prefects.”], so that counsel may be taken concerning those things that are unjustly praised, and judgment rendered if anything of this kind can be proved. Thus past evils, if shown to have been committed, may be restrained with appropriate severity, and provision may be made for the future, lest the holiness of the Church, wearied by our negligence, lose the privileges it has acquired through venerable men. [Col. 0658D]

May God keep you safe.

Given on the second day before the Nones of June, in the consulship of Julius IV and Palladius V.

# XVIII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO JULIANA, A NOBLEWOMAN

An exhortation. (C)

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659A] It is manifest to all that you are a singular member of your Church, an embodiment of the greatness of its religion, and that you are held by us in the highest reverence.

For, at the very height of nobility, you devote to the Church a devotion **more noble** [25], obeying Christ’s commandments with a more joyful recognition of him, and exulting in faith rather than boasting of the splendor of so great a lineage.

It is the mark of supreme virtue to conquer the glory of the flesh, and of great grace in Christ to surpass nobility by one’s conduct, deservedly illustrious lady and daughter.

Therefore, dearest daughter, being assured of this, strive to illuminate all the periods of this life, whatever they may be, with eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may make you more illustrious for himself throughout the ages. [Col. 0660A]

# XIX. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO THE PRESBYTER BONIFACIUS

Concerning the Church of Antioch. (C)

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659B] Innocent to the presbyter Bonifacius.

The Church of Antioch, which the blessed apostle Peter honored with his presence before he came to the city of Rome, did not long endure to remain estranged from that Church, its sister, the Roman Church.

For, after sending envoys, it asked for and obtained peace in such a way that it received the Evagrians in the orders and places they had received through the unimpaired ordination conferred upon them by Memoratus, and gathered and united together in one body both the clerics and the laypeople of John, of holy memory.

My brother Alexander, the bishop of that city, promised that, even if someone should later come to them from us or from elsewhere by a subsequent ordination, he would receive him without controversy, and that he would recite the name of Bishop Memoratus among the bishops who are at rest.

Know, dearest brother, that we have given our hands to this arrangement and received them into our own heart, lest members that had sought healing should remain for a long time alienated from the whole body.

My son, the deacon Paulus, bearer of this letter, will be able to recount to your affection everything that was done in due order, so that you may share our common joy and inform those who have been accustomed to intervene on behalf of Atticus. [Col. 0660B]

# XX. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

Concerning peace. (C)

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659C] Innocent to Bishop Alexander.

**26.** You will learn from a repetition of the events themselves how welcome, devout, and necessary the embassy sent to us from your holiness, dearest brother, has been [Note: [Col. 0659] From the other witnesses, except Alv. and Esc. 4, which have: “you know.”].

For our fellow presbyter Cassianus wished this little document of our friendship to be written through our fellow presbyter Paulus, the deacon Nicolaus, and the subdeacon Petrus, our sons, as the first fruits of our peace.

I therefore greet both your brotherhood in Christ, which is joined to me, and the whole Church that thinks rightly with you. And, as you do, I ask that you address us by letter more frequently and gladden us more often with news of your well-being. For, as I trust, the Lord will grant us to make up for all the losses of the past through the most loving conversation of letters. [Col. 0660C]

# XXI. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO BISHOP MAXIMIANUS

Concerning Atticus, bishop of Constantinople. (C)

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659D] Innocent to Bishop Maximianus.

We are surprised that you ask us for writings addressed to Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, both by your own representation and by the petition submitted below, although you have produced no letters sent either to us or, in any event, to our synod.

Nor should you consider that what was granted after careful examination to those who made petitions ought to be granted to one who has not petitioned. Communion that has been suspended is restored to one who demonstrates that the causes by which it occurred have now been cleared away and who declares that the conditions of peace have been fulfilled.

But, as I said, Atticus has been unwilling either to state or demonstrate, by sending any of his people, that this has been completed, either among you or among us; whereas our brother and fellow bishop Alexander of the Church of Antioch both pursued and confirmed this through a worthy embassy.

You were good enough to be present at all these proceedings, and you learned how I examined individually every point in our earlier writings concerning the case of our most blessed former bishop John, so that all the things those writings had shown with sufficient clarity—that everything which ought to have been done at Antioch had been completed—might be established.

Having embraced their peace, we gave it our faith and showed to all, by a great and direct path, the same peace that you await—provided only that they eventually show that they themselves have done or completed, in their proper place, the things that were examined and completed, and that they solemnly request, through an embassy sent for this purpose, that communion be restored to them as it was to these others.

We therefore await both the declaration of the aforementioned man concerning the fulfillment of all the conditions that we have set out at different times and his request for communion, so that we may rightly restore it to one who both requests it and proves himself worthy of it, dearest brother. For long ago you received from us a very full letter concerning all these matters. [Col. 0661A]

# XXII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

Concerning peace. (C)

[Col. 0661]

[Col. 0661B] Innocent to Alexander, bishop of Antioch.

The grace of apostolic favor has shone upon us with the great splendor of peace, and has cast such light and joy upon the faithful that, while giving the greatest praises to God, we acknowledge that we owe him still greater ones.

We have been made joyful by God all the more because, after examining every aspect of your brotherhood’s actions, we have learned that everything was conducted with such devotion and patience that in all things we praised the Lord.

We see that success was granted to your labors for this reason: because, being a lover of peace with such great virtue, you sought the peace you desired, found it, and preserved it with the greatest charity—toward everyone, but especially toward those who had once been reckoned under the name of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius.

I regard my vows as fulfilled when the cleansing of the ancient blemish is prolonged through your times and your merits. I also judged that those of the same name who had acquired the merits of the clerical office in Italy should retain the grace of the peace they had received.

And because our fellow presbyter Cassianus said that it would be pleasing to your graciousness if, by my advice, they were judged to hold the clerical order in your city, I have decided, out of regard for your goodwill and because of the promises of the aforementioned man, that they should be numbered among the other priests and ministers who are in the city, dearest brother. [Col. 0662B]

I learned with pleasure, moreover, that the bishops Helpidius and Pappus had recovered their Churches without dispute. I examined the proceedings with great care, as the documents appended below testify, to determine whether all the conditions had been fulfilled in the case of the blessed and truly God-worthy priest John.

When, point by point, the envoys’ testimony acknowledged that everything had been fulfilled according to our desire, I gave thanks to the Lord and received your Church into communion. Thus I shall report that the fellow disciples of the Apostolic See were the first to give the others a way to peace; and, once you are firmly established in that peace, the kindness of the Lord Christ will embrace and strengthen both you and us, so that henceforth no slight irritation or shame from any small dispute may disturb it.

Since we received the writings of Bishop Acacius when they were submitted together with yours, we did not wish him—who had once been suspended by us—to be rejected through any injury to you. Nevertheless, as you will graciously take care to reread what we established in the proceedings, you will see what must be observed concerning his person. If, in every respect, he asks to be united with your counsels and such holy actions, let the old man, through your favor and our judgment, receive the extension of communion and of the letters of grace from us. [Col. 0662C]

Twenty bishops of Italy signed.

# XXIII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO THE SAME MAN

(C)

[Col. 0661]

[Col. 0661D] Innocent to Bishop Alexander.

**28. I.** The burden and honor imposed upon us by your brotherhood has introduced matters requiring necessary discussion, so that we may respond to your letter or memorandum as the grace of the Holy Spirit grants.

Accordingly, as we review the authority of the Council of Nicaea—which expresses the single mind of all the priests throughout the world—we find that what it determined concerning the Church of Antioch must be observed by all the faithful, not to say by all priests. We recognize that the aforementioned Church was established over its own diocese, not over some other province.

From this we understand that this was attributed to it not so much because of the magnificence of the city as because it is shown to be the first apostolic see: there the Christian religion received its name; there it merited that the most celebrated gathering of the apostles should take place; and it would not yield to the see of the city of Rome except that Rome merited this in passing, while Antioch rejoices that what was received there was completed in its own midst.

Therefore, dearest brother, we think that, just as you ordain the metropolitans by your singular authority, so you should not allow the other bishops to be created without your permission and knowledge. You should properly observe this arrangement: you should judge that those who are far away are to be ordained by letters issued to those who now ordain them solely at their own discretion. But if you consider those nearby, you should appoint them to come to the laying on of hands by your grace. For those whose greatest care awaits you ought especially to merit your judgment. [Col. 0662D]

## II. That there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops according to the imperial arrangements

[Col. 0663A]

As to your question whether, when provinces are divided by imperial judgment so that there are two metropolises, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be appointed, it has not truly seemed right that the Church of God should be altered according to the shifting necessities of worldly affairs, or suffer honors and divisions that the emperor has judged should be made for his own purposes.

Therefore, metropolitan bishops ought to be counted according to the former custom of the provinces.

You assert that the Cyprians, once harassed by the power of Arian impiety, did not observe the Nicene canons in ordaining bishops for themselves, and that they still presume to ordain at their own discretion, consulting no one.

For this reason we urge them to take care to think in accordance with the Catholic faith of the canons [Col. 0663B] and to share one judgment with the other provinces, so that it may be evident that they too, like all the Churches, are governed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## III. That the clerics of the Arians are not to be received into their offices, although the Church confirms their baptism, which is acknowledged to be Catholic

Moreover, as for the Arians and the other plagues of this kind: since we receive their laypeople who have been converted to the Lord under the appearance of repentance and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands, it does not seem that we should receive their clerics with the dignity of the priesthood or of any ministry.

For we allow only their baptism to be valid—a baptism, certainly, performed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and we do not think that they possess the Holy Spirit through that baptism and those mysteries. When their leaders defected from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit that they had received.

Nor can they bestow the fullness that operates especially in ordinations—fullness that, rather than through faith, I should say they lost through the treachery of their impiety.

How can we regard as worthy of Christ’s honors the profane priests of those whose imperfect laypeople, as I have said, we receive under the appearance of repentance in order to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit?

Therefore, let your gravity bring this to the knowledge of your fellow bishops or, if possible, of the synod, or at least by having these letters read aloud, so that what you yourself have so necessarily asked about, and what we have answered so carefully, may be observed by the common agreement and zeal of all. [Col. 0664B]

# XXIV. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO ACACIUS, BISHOP OF BEROEA

Concerning Saint John, bishop of Constantinople. (C)

[Col. 0663]

[Col. 0663C] **29.** We have judged that your brotherhood rejoiced at the letters concerning the clerics and peoples of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius having been received, and concerning the restoration of our fellow bishops Helpidius and Pappus. We have seen that, setting aside every dispute, you have at last begun to cherish the grace of the peace received.

Therefore we have sent these letters to your unanimity so that they may be delivered to our distinguished brother and fellow bishop Alexander. If every hostility and every rivalry concerning both the name of the holy and admirable bishop John and all who share in the same communion has departed from your mind, receive these letters of our fellowship, dearest brother—provided that, before our mediator, the beloved Alexander, you confess in your own voice, as is fitting for one who shares communion, all the things established here in the proceedings.

For just as the cause of unity and charity is venerable to us, so it remains watchful lest anything crooked or incomplete be found to remain in anyone. [Col. 0664C]

# XXV. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO LAURENTIUS, BISHOP OF SINIUM

Concerning the Bonosiacs, who are to be compared with the Jews. (C)

[Col. 0663]

[Col. 0663D] Innocent to Laurentius, bishop of Sinium.

Having read the letters of your affection, we long wondered that heretics following the poisons of Photinus not only exist within the territory of your affection but also publicly prepare meeting places for themselves on certain estates, although, in a world almost wholly explored, nowhere are so many reported to dwell as among you [Note: [Col. 0663D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., “have chosen to dwell.”].

Marcus, the author of their wicked teaching, expelled from the City some time ago, has been carried away by such great audacity that he claims the first place among them.

But so that they may no longer have the opportunity to rage or drag the souls of the simple and the country people with themselves into the Gehenna to which they are destined, action has been taken against them by the defenders of our Church, so that they may be expelled. For they deny that Christ God was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; therefore, with the Jews, who denied his divinity and continue even now to deny it, let them share in condemnation.

It is your responsibility, dearest brother, to carry out the commands given with no less zeal, lest through your inaction you lose the people entrusted to you and begin to render an account to God for those who have been lost. [Col. 0664D]

At an earlier time—if I remember correctly—I sent letters of this kind both to your affection and to our brothers and fellow bishops Rufus and the others concerning the clerics of Naxos: namely, those who asserted that, before the condemnation of Bonosus, they had been ordained by him as both presbyters and deacons.

I instructed that, if they wished to abandon and condemn his error and be joined to the Church, they should be willingly received, lest perhaps those who were worthy of recovering salvation should perish in that same error.

But now, while I am staying in the city of Ravenna because of the frequent needs of the Roman people, Germanus, who claims to be a presbyter, and Lupentius, who says that he is a deacon, having undertaken what was almost an embassy on behalf of many such men, eagerly expressed their own distress by pouring out prayers.

They asserted that they still possessed churches located in the parishes of your affection, but that they had not been able to obtain your communion, for the following reason: a certain man named Rusticius had received the presbyterate through a repeated ordination.

This creates no small impediment, since either they grieve that such a man is retained in the Church, or he thinks that another ought to sin in the same way in which he recognizes that sin was committed against himself.

Although my letters mentioned above contain a fuller treatment of the same matter, we have nevertheless thought it necessary to admonish your brotherhood again: if it is truly established that certain men ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation later wished—or now wish—to return, we judge that they should be received.

This is especially so since the men mentioned above assert that they were ordained so long ago that the man of holy memory, Cornelius, bishop of the city of Sirmium, as well as our brother Nicetas and several others, were present; and they affirm that they possessed the offices they mention.

Therefore, dearest brother, if their assertion is found credible, you should not hesitate to receive those whom you have allowed for so long to retain the Churches entrusted to them. [Col. 0666B]

# XXVI. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO RUFUS AND EUSEBIUS AND THE OTHER BISHOPS

(C)

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665B] Innocent sends greetings in the Lord to Rufus, Eusebius, the other Macedonian bishops, and the deacons.

I was filled with great joy when, after the dangers of the whole world, so to speak, Vitalis the archdeacon, the bearer of your letter, arrived among us, having been sent from those regions to us.

When we saw him, we immediately asked him, as was fitting, about your condition. But when we found that you were faring as desired, we gave abundant thanks to our God, who deigns both to protect you, his servants who serve at his altars [Note: [Col. 0665D] From the other witnesses except Alv., which has “at his altar.”], in adversity and graciously to govern you in prosperity.

When he had delivered the letters, I ordered them to be read at once. I saw that many things had been set down in them that would cause astonishment in our minds and make us doubt considerably whether we should understand them otherwise or whether they had been written exactly as they sounded.

After having them read repeatedly, I realized that an injury was being done to the Apostolic See, to which the report had been sent as though to the head of the Churches, since its judgment was still being left in doubt. Therefore, concerning matters about which I remember having written some time ago, your repeated inquiry now compels me to restate the position with clearer arguments. [Col. 0665D]

## I. That if a priest or anyone from the clergy takes a widow or a divorced woman as his wife, he loses his office

I have learned that those who are said to have taken widows as wives were not only made clerics but even attained the episcopal insignia, although no one is unaware that this is contrary to the command of the law.

For when Moses the lawgiver declares: “Let a priest take a virgin as his wife,” and so that this command should not be thought ambiguous he adds: “Not a widow nor a divorced woman.”

Against this command, supported by divine authority, no defense based on another mandate can be brought except your custom, which, as you yourselves admit, was established through ignorance—or, to put it more modestly, not through apostolic tradition and sound reasoning.

But let your affection know that we, and all the Churches throughout East and West, wholly reject this practice and do not admit such men even to the lowest place in the ecclesiastical order; and, if they are found, we remove them. [Col. 0666C]

## II. That if a catechumen had a wife who has already died and, after baptism, took another, he cannot be a cleric

Next it is asserted that a man who, while a catechumen, had and lost a wife ought not to be called a bigamist if, after baptism, he took another; rather, the woman joined to the new man is said to be the first, because that marriage, together with the other sins, was washed away through the sacrament of baptism.

But if this is said of one wife, then certainly, if he had three wives while he was in the old man, the woman who is fourth after baptism will, according to this interpretation, be his first. She too will receive the name of virgin, although she was taken as his fourth wife.

Who, then, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says that a priest ought to be “the husband of one wife”? [Note: [Col. 0666D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1, Urgel., Ger., “who.”]

It is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man has been washed away. Tell me—speaking with your permission—are only crimes forgiven in baptism, or also those things that are fulfilled according to the Lord’s commands and God’s institutions?

Is taking a wife a crime, or is it not a crime? If it is a crime, then, let me say this with the pardon already mentioned, the author is at fault who, in order that crimes might be committed, blessed them in paradise when he himself joined them together.

But if it is not a crime—because what God has joined it is sacrilege to call a crime—and Solomon added, “For a wife is prepared for a man by God,” how can we believe that what is recorded as having been completed by God’s authority was forgiven among crimes?

What is judged concerning the children of such men? Surely they are not to be admitted to a share in the inheritance because they were born from a woman who was a wife before baptism? Are they to be called either natural children or bastards, because, as you seem to think, no marriage is legitimate except the one entered into after baptism?

When the Lord himself was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, and explained that this ought not to be done, he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no man separate.”

And lest anyone think that he was speaking about those marriages entered into after baptism, let them remember that he was questioned by Jews and gave this answer to Jews.

I ask—and I ask anxiously—whether the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and later became a believer is one and the same wife, if he fathered children by her while he was a catechumen and later had other children with her when he was among the faithful [Note: [Col. 0667D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1, 2, “when he was a believer.”]. Are they to be called brothers, or, after their father’s death, are they not to have a share in the division of the inheritance, because spiritual regeneration is thought to have taken away from them the name of children?

Since it is absurd to think and judge this way, what reason is there to defend this evil and boast of an empty opinion rather than prove it by some authority [Note: [Col. 0667D] In the others, except Alv. and Esc. 4, “strengthen.”], when what the law commanded and God joined cannot be counted among sins?

Suppose a catechumen devoted himself to virtues, pursued humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued those destined for death by whatever means, abhorred adultery, and maintained chastity. I ask whether, after he became a believer, he loses these things because baptism is thought to remove everything done by the old man.

Let us consider the Gentile Cornelius, whose prayers and almsgiving were seen in a revelation by Peter himself. Were these things taken away from him through baptism, on account of which baptism appears to have been granted to him?

If this is believed, trust me, there is serious error. For whatever has been done well and preserved according to the legal commands cannot be lost to those who performed it.

Therefore, the union of marriage, because it is completed by God’s command, cannot be called a sin. And what is not a sin must not be dissolved among sins. It will thus remain wholly valid to judge that the name of the earlier wife cannot be abolished, since it was not dismissed as a sin but was completed according to God’s will. [Col. 0667D]

## III. That clerics ordained by heretics are not to be admitted

We have come to the third question, which because of its difficulty requires a longer discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have a wounded head through that laying on of hands.

Where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that health may be restored; and the health that follows a wound cannot exist without a scar.

Therefore, where the remedy of repentance is necessary, we decree that the honor of ordination cannot have a place.

For, as it is written, “Whatever the unclean person touches will be unclean” [Note: [Col. 0667D] From Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1, Urg. The others have: [Col. 0668D] “Whoever touches what is unclean will be unclean.” Tol. 2: “Whoever touches what is unclean will be unclean.”]; how can that be bestowed upon him which purity and cleanness customarily receive?

But, on the other hand, it is asserted that one who has lost an honor cannot give an honor, and that the other person received nothing, because there was nothing in the giver that he could receive.

We agree, and it is true: certainly, he could not give what he did not possess. But he did give the condemnation that he possessed through the wicked laying on of hands; and I cannot discover how one who has become a partner of the condemned should be able to receive honor.

Yet it is said that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every defect that had been inflicted by the defective one. [Col. 0668B]

## IV. That crimes or defects should not rightly be believed to be removed in ordinations

If this is so, then let sacrilegious men, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be brought to ordination, since crimes or defects are thought to be removed by the blessing of ordination.

Let there be no place for repentance, since ordination can provide what prolonged satisfaction is accustomed to provide.

But the law of our Church is that, for those coming from the heretics who have nevertheless been baptized there, we grant only lay communion through the laying on of hands, and do not promote any of them, even to the slightest degree, to the honor of the clergy.

## V. That those ordained by Bonosus the heretic were received so that scandal might not remain in the Church
[Col. 0668C] But those who have passed from the Catholic faith to heresy, and who ought to be received only through penance, among you not only do not perform penance, but are even heaped with honors. Yet the considered judgment of our former brother Anisius and of the other bishops was this: those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received as ordained, provided that they did not remain with him, lest no small scandal should arise. We have, I think, overcome the ambiguities.

Therefore, what was established as a remedy and because of the exigency of the time plainly did not exist at the beginning; rather, there existed the ancient rules which the Roman Church, handed down by the apostles or by apostolic men, observes and commands to be observed by those accustomed to heed her. But the necessity of the time urgently [Col. 0668D] demanded that this be done. Therefore, whatever necessity discovered as a remedy, once the necessity has ceased, must likewise cease, because one thing is the legitimate order and another is the usurpation which present circumstances compel for a time.

But the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done in the case of the Novatians. First, that canon instituted by the Fathers must be set forth, so that we may perceive either what they understood or how they understood and commanded it. “Concerning those,” it says, “who call themselves Cathars—that is, the Pure—and who sometimes come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.” I can say, however, that this command concerns only the Novatians and does not apply to the clergy of other heresies. For if they had defined this concerning all, they would have added that those returning from the Novatians and other heretics were to be received into their own order. If that were so, even what was said especially concerning the Paulianists could be confirmed: those coming from them are ordered to be baptized anew. Surely, when they command that all who return from heretics be baptized on the example of the Paulianists, will all who return from heretics have to be baptized in this same manner? Since no one would dare to do that, reason itself shows that the command concerns those people alone.

Finally, Peter and John complete by the mere laying on of hands those whom the evangelist Philip had rightly baptized. But those whom the apostle Paul found to have been baptized with John’s baptism, and whom he asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit, when they confessed that they had not even heard of that name, he ordered to be baptized. You see, therefore, that those rightly baptized cannot be baptized again with that gift, whereas it is foreseen to be necessary that those washed only with water in another manner be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is read with clear demonstration that this command was given concerning the Novatians alone. The reason why it was distinguished between these two heresies is plainly shown by the fact that the Paulianists do not baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, nor has any question ever arisen among them concerning the unity of the divine power—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And therefore, of all the separated groups, this one alone was selected as the one to which they believed this concession should be granted, because they committed no offense in the sacrament of the Father, Son, and Holy [Col. 0669C] Spirit.

But if someone passing from the Catholic faith to heresy, or a believer returning to apostasy, should repent and wish to return, could he by the same reasoning be permitted into the clergy, whose offense could be erased only through lengthy penance? The canons themselves do not permit him, even after penance, to become a cleric by their authority.

It is therefore clear that those who passed from the Catholic faith to the condemned Bonosus, and who allowed or desired themselves to be ordained by him, ought not to have received the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination. They abandoned the common judgment of all the churches and chose to follow Bonosus’s peculiar error.

Yet it is clear that many were subjected to force, dragged there unwillingly, and ordained by him despite their resistance. Let whoever believes this tell me: if he was not present after Bonosus’s ordination when Bonosus celebrated the sacraments; if he did not participate in his communion; if he departed immediately from that most wicked assembly and returned to the Church—such a man may have some appearance of an excuse.

But those who returned to the Church after a year or a month, we understand to have gone to him because they knew that, on account of their vices, they could not be admitted to ordination in the Catholic Church. They therefore went to one who was indiscriminately and without any examination performing illicit ordinations, believing that through this institution they could find a place in the Catholic Church, a place of which they had previously despaired.

Now I ask about what remains: what do you judge concerning one who returned after a month or more, while admitting that he had been ordained a presbyter by Bonosus, if he did not celebrate the sacraments, if he did not distribute them to the people, and if he did not complete the Masses according to custom? I ask you to state your judgment more openly.

In short, those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of having usurped a dignity: they claimed for themselves the authority to celebrate the sacraments and thought themselves to be what had not been granted to them by any regular procedure.

## VI. That the sin of the people in the Church is customarily allowed to pass unpunished

Your Affection therefore clearly sees that such matters have hitherto been allowed to pass, and observe that, as you say, necessity certainly dictated that one should not presume to disturb churches already established in peace. Rather, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd sins, because punishment cannot be inflicted upon everyone on account of their number, the matter customarily passes unpunished. I therefore say that what happened earlier must be left to God’s judgment, while henceforth the greatest care must be taken to prevent such things.

## VII. That something was secretly obtained from the Apostolic See, and that it changed its judgment for the better when it rescinded the condemnation of Photinus

I shall now come to the greatest matter, as though to a certain central theme: Photinus, and what is anxious and most difficult for me, namely, to reconsider the judgments of my predecessors. Something rather serious had previously been decreed concerning him, in whatever manner—as you yourselves also remember. But since you assert and demonstrate that this was obtained from this See through a false report and extracted by intrigue, and since the matter has returned to a salutary condition, we now grant you this pardon, after the condemnation, in the apostolic manner, insofar as you press for it. We consider it harsher than any hardship not to consent to such strong assertions by you, who are so good and so dear to us.

Therefore, dearest brothers, in accordance with your approval, judgment, and petition, regard Photinus as a bishop. It is permitted to establish matters in the way you request; and, having attained your wish through your labor and testimony, receive our judgment, which has been turned toward what is better.

Likewise, do not expect Eustathius—so frequently approved by me—to be stripped of the dignity of the diaconate. I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation; but I do not gladly admit anything directed against his head, even if it must be done. To the one to whom you extend your hand, I extend mine with you; to the one to whom I extend mine, extend yours with me.

For this is the apostolic kindness declared toward the Corinthians: that good people should always follow without distinction a judgment brought back and forth in one spirit. I confess that this matter first commends me favorably to Eustathius the deacon: he has neither spoken anything against the faith nor admitted anyone who did so, and I have found no crime committed by him deserving death, whether ever alleged or fabricated.

If he is sound in these matters, yet in some way does not possess an amiable manner of life, he should be regarded as less loved for the time being, not as an enemy to be handed over eternally to the devil. I know that amid those rivalries and storms he held views differing from the efforts of many—I do not say what sort of efforts—and that, although the circumstances and calamities on this side have themselves been corrected, the correction of the deacons Dizonianus and Ciriacus has still not been able to revive among you.  
[Note: In the other witnesses, except Alv., “subdeacons” is read instead of “deacons.”]

I ask you to restrain him and the aforementioned men, and all whose minds you see engaged in unjust rivalries, so that he, remaining unimpaired among us and restored among you together with his associates, may deserve and discern genuine peace through charity.

Therefore, let charity meet all of you, individually and collectively, and may it rejoice perpetually in the Lord, joined with you by those bonds which Christ in no way dissolves.

# XXVII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE INNOCENT TO ALL THE BISHOPS IN TOULOUSE (C)

[Col. 0671]

Innocent sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops assembled in the synod of Toulouse, his dearest brothers.

## I. On the rebuke of the Spaniards who appoint clerics irregularly

[Col. 0671B]

Often excessive concern kept me anxious about the dissensions and schisms of the churches, since rumor reports that this evil, spreading more widely through Spain, is advancing by stages of separation. A necessary moment has now arisen when so great a correction can no longer be postponed and an appropriate remedy must be provided.

For we know that the Hispanic bishops celebrate ordinations through the fault of a corrupt custom. Something ought to have been established concerning this according to the traditions of our predecessors, unless we had considered that we might thereby stir up very numerous disturbances in the churches. We therefore rebuke their action in such a way that, because of the number of those who must be corrected, we do not call into question what has been done in any manner whatsoever, but rather leave it to God’s judgment.

## II. That advocates, curials, and those devoted to military service are not to be admitted to the clergy

[Col. 0671C]

How many men do we find to have been admitted to the priesthood from among those who, after receiving the grace of baptism, practiced in the courts and adopted the stubbornness required for winning cases? Rufinus and Gregory are said to be among their number.

How many have come from military service—men who, while obeying authorities, necessarily carried out severe commands? How many from the curial order—men who, while obeying officials, did what was commanded them? How many who celebrated pleasures and public entertainments for the people have attained the honor of the highest priesthood?

None of all these ought even to have reached membership in the clerical order. If we ordered each case to be investigated individually, we would introduce considerable disturbances or scandals into the Spanish provinces, which we desire to heal, through the very endeavor of correction. For this reason we think these matters should rather be allowed to pass. But so that similar things may not be committed henceforth, your Affection must take care that at least now a necessary end be imposed upon so great a usurpation, with the following provision:

## III. That all who have been ordained in this manner are to be deposed together with their ordainers

[Note: In the manuscripts, the number three in the heading forms part of this paragraph.]

After this, if anyone attempts to enter either the ecclesiastical order or the priesthood itself contrary to the canonical forms, he shall be deprived, together with his ordainers, of the order and honor in which he is found.

And although the Nicene rules are known to you, dearest brothers, according to which you determine by judgment how ordinations are to be carried out, I have thought it necessary to insert a portion of the provisions concerning ordinations, and according to it ordinations are to be celebrated in the future, so that no one may be left free to interpret the matter otherwise. First, let the prohibitions be arranged.

## IV. A reminder of the Council of Nicaea, in which the foregoing practices are prohibited

No one who has served in the army after baptism is to be admitted to the clerical order; nor those who have practiced law after receiving baptism; nor those who, after receiving God’s grace, have administered public offices.

Nor may anyone from the curial order enter the ecclesiastical order if, after baptism, he has either worn the crown of office, or held what is called a priesthood, or celebrated public spectacles. This too must be guarded against in the case of curials: that those who have come from the curial order should at some time be reclaimed by their own curiae, as we frequently see happening. All these things, rationally prohibited, must be observed in every possible way.

## V. What kind of men are to be chosen for the clerical order

The clear rule shows what kind of men are to be chosen for the clerical order: those who were baptized from early childhood and joined to the office of readers; or, if they are older, those who, after receiving God’s grace, immediately devoted themselves to the ecclesiastical orders.

And if they have had wives, it must be investigated whether they took a virgin as wife, because it is written in the Old Testament: “Let the priest take a virgin as wife”; and elsewhere: “Let my priests marry only once.” Nor is a man who has had two wives to be admitted, since the apostle Paul says: “The husband of one wife.”

## VI. That a cleric is not to be made from one who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism

Nor should that argument be admitted which some advance in defense of their perverse error, asserting that everything prior to baptism is remitted. They do not understand that in this matter only sins are remitted in baptism, and that the number of wives is not abolished.  
[Note: In Alv., the reading is: “In baptism, original sins.”]

For if, as it is written, a wife is prepared by God for a man; if “what God has joined, let no man separate”; and if the very founders of the human race are blessed by God at their origin, how can it be believed that such things can be remitted among sins?

If, according to those who believe this, it is true, then all the righteousness performed by catechumens before baptism will be taken away through baptism. Let no one, therefore, think or admit anything of this sort against the Apostle; rather, let him understand faithfully that “the husband of one wife” is designated (nominatum), whether before baptism  
[Note: In the other witnesses, except Alv., “counted” (numeratum) is read instead of “designated” (nominatum).]  
or after baptism.

For if a wife taken before baptism is not counted, neither can the children born from her be counted among one’s children. Your prudence will better judge how absurd and alien this is.

Therefore, let no one be permitted to interpret the divine Scriptures otherwise than right reason allows, lest, while some prepare unlawful remedies for themselves as an excuse, they be judged both to have corrupted the law and to have overturned the rules.

Rather, those things must be maintained which the sequence of the divine Scriptures contains and which the priests have established by useful reasoning.

Farewell, dearest brothers.

# XXVIII. LETTER OF THE DECRETALS OF POPE ZOSIMUS TO HESYCHIUS, BISHOP OF SALONA (C)

[Col. 0673]

[Col. 0673B] Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings to Hesychius, bishop of Salona.

Your Affection demands a decree from the Apostolic See in which the decrees of the Fathers concur, and you report that some from the community of monks—whose solitude is greater than any crowd—and also some laymen are hastening to the priesthood.

## I. That monks and laymen are not to reach the highest priesthood except through the ecclesiastical grades

This has specifically been prohibited both under our predecessors and recently by us, in letters sent to Gaul and Spain, regions in which this presumption is common, although Africa too is not exempt from this admonition of ours.

No one, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, who has not been instructed in ecclesiastical discipline in due order and trained through the approved passage of time in divine service, should presume to aspire to the highest priesthood. Thus not only should ambition in such a person be regarded as ineffective, but his ordainers should also lose the order which, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, they believed could be presumed upon without due order.

We therefore wonder that the statutes of the Apostolic See have not been conveyed to your Affection. We praise your steadfast purpose, dearest brother. Nothing else was to be expected from your judgment as bishop, grounded in ancient authority, than that, stationed in the forefront of the faith, you should oppose such ambitions in accordance with the commands of the Fathers.

Therefore, if anything—though we do not think so—is believed to have been lacking in authority, we supply it. Resist such ordinations; resist the proud and the arrogance that is approaching. The commands of the Fathers are with you; the authority of the Apostolic See is with you.

For if secular offices confer the principal place not upon those who have entered merely the threshold of service but upon those examined through many grades and tested periods of time, who could be found so arrogant and shameless as to desire immediately to become a commander in the heavenly army—which must be weighed with greater care and tested like gold through repeated fires—when he has not previously been a recruit and wishes to teach before learning?

Let him first become accustomed, in the Lord’s camp, to the rudiments of divine service in the grade of reader. Let it not seem beneath him to become, in order, an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon, not by a leap but at the times established by the ordination of the elders.

Then let such a man approach the dignity of the presbyterate that both his age fulfills the title and the previous periods of service testify to the merit of his uprightness. From there he ought rightly to hope for the place of highest bishop.

This is caused by the excessive leniency of our fellow priests, who seek the pomp of a multitude and think that some dignity is acquired for themselves from this crowd. Hence, even in places where there is solitude, a numerous popular following is found everywhere among such men, while they desire to extend parishes or bestow divine orders upon those to whom they can provide nothing else. This must always be subject to strict judgment.

For everything great is rare.

## II. That anyone who disregards the prohibitions will be subject to the penalty of his grade

Accordingly, so that we should not detract from the merits of your Affection, we have directed these writings especially to you. They will come to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops, not only those who are in that province but also those attached to the neighboring provinces of your Affection.

Let anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the Apostolic See, has neglected this know that such matters must be punished with greater severity, so that he may have no doubt that his position will not remain secure if he thinks that after so many prohibitions this can be attempted with impunity. Whatever is so often usurped after having been prohibited is done in a spirit of contempt.

## III. What periods of time are prescribed for each of the clerical grades

The following periods must be observed for the individual grades.

If someone gives his name to ecclesiastical service from childhood, he is to remain continuously among the readers until his twentieth year. If he comes later, already an adult or advanced in age, yet desires immediately after baptism to devote himself to divine service, he is to remain for five years either among the readers or among the exorcists.

From then on he is to serve four years as an acolyte or subdeacon, and thus, if he deserves it, approach the blessing of the diaconate. In that order he must remain for five years if he has conducted himself blamelessly.

Then, with the periods of service granted through all these grades supporting him, and with the proofs of his own faith thus given, he may merit the priesthood. From that position, if a life devoted more diligently to good conduct leads him there, he ought to hope for the highest pontificate.

This law must nevertheless be observed: neither a man with two wives, nor the husband of a widow, nor a penitent may be admitted to these grades.

Indeed, defenders of the Church who come from the laity must also be bound by the foregoing observance if they deserve to belong to the clerical order.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March  
[Note: In all the manuscripts except Alv., Esc. 3, and Ger., “the ninth” is read instead of “the eighth.”]  
during the consulship of our lords Honorius, consul for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, consul for the eighth time, both Augusti.

# XXIX. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ZOSIMUS TO THE CLERGY OF RAVENNA (C)

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675B] Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna.

From the report of our brother Archidamus  
[Note: Bibl. Reg. reads “Archiami”; Tol. 2, “Arciamini.”]  
the presbyter, we have learned how you were received and what you did, and also how those were received who, with an audacity whose source I do not know, wished to go to the imperial court against us and contrary to the canons.

To them we had formerly sent the letters we now issue, replying to the letters which they had sent abusively. But since, as defendants, they could not remain in their own—that is, in our—Roman Church with our fellow presbyters  
[Note: In all the witnesses except Alv., “be commemorated” is read instead of “remain.”]  
we have sent these letters to you, to be delivered to them. In them we decreed that the aforementioned disturbers had been alienated from the communion of our Apostolic See and had received the judgment approved by our subscription.  
[Note: Tol. 2 reads: “had received our approved judgment.”]

As for those who wished to lend their assent to this unrestrained action and plan, it is for your Charity to judge how they are to be regarded. You must charge them with this: that they attempted boldly to run counter to the commands of the canons and to become rebels, as was not fitting for presbyters.

But we warn you that you must remain vigilant, lest any audacity break forth from those whom the holy and apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized.  
[Note: This passage appears mutilated in the manuscripts. In some, the word “knows” is absent; in others, “the holy and apostolic Church” is absent; in some, only “holy and” is absent; in the remaining witnesses, “suscitet” is written instead of “sancta et.” The reading here has therefore been drawn from all of them.]

As for those who joined themselves to their association, when you have returned we shall consider, with better counsel, what we ought to do.

# XXX. LETTER OF POPE BONIFACE TO HONORIUS AUGUSTUS: A PETITION OF THE SAME POPE THAT THE EMPEROR ESTABLISH THAT NO PONTIFF SHALL EVER BE ORDAINED IN THE CITY OF ROME THROUGH CANVASSING (C)

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675C] Boniface, bishop, to Honorius Augustus.

The care owed to my Church, to which our God has assigned my priesthood while you govern human affairs, constrains me not to fail to appear before the ears of the most Christian prince concerning its affairs, although I am still detained by bodily illness, because of the assemblies stirred up by all the priests, clergy, and Christian people. For if anything should happen contrary to what is proper, it will appear that not you—who arrange all things with just moderation—but we, through our silent negligence, have allowed something capable of overturning the peace of the city and the tranquility of the Church.

Since, with the Lord’s favor, you preside over human affairs as a worshiper of divine religion, it will be our fault if, under your glory—which is certainly always more ready to favor divine matters—the firm and stable right that has prevailed through so many years, even under emperors who were bound by no concern for our religion, is not preserved. I speak confidently of what is lawful: under the rule of your clemency, let what is unlawful be feared.

The Church itself, most Christian emperor, addresses your devotion in my words but with her own reverent affection. Christ our Lord, the faithful ruler and governor of your empire, has betrothed her to himself alone and preserves her as an untouched virgin, so that you may not allow the waves of plotting storms to crash against her or her tranquil face to be disturbed by the swelling of an unfamiliar tempest, most glorious and most tranquil Emperor Augustus.

Therefore, the Church, betrothed to him alone yet also your mother, appeals to your piety through the embassy which she has entrusted to her priests. She recalls past and present matters to you, under your religious rule: my people—now yours—have grown as faithful to God as to you, the Christian prince.

For behold, amid the very mysteries and prayers which she offers for the welfare of your empire, with holy Peter as witness, before whom and concerning whose See the matter is at issue, she cries out with anxious words for the preservation of religion. She mingles petition with prayer, lest the tempter, having torn them away, draw them into various courses and separate them from their accustomed worship.

She would be distressed by many things, most Christian prince, unless she were secure with you concerning her affairs and had prevailed in the suppression of idols and the correction of heretics, with your faith and divine worship flourishing together with your empire.

She finds refuge in your gentle spirit, joined to reverence for her religion, since whatever benefits her you do and confer upon my most proven brothers and fellow priests, whom I send as legates, together with all who constitute the Church. We ask that, when they pursue the cause of sacred religion in the city of your gentleness, you unite with them in the spirit in which we petition and provide perpetually for the welfare of the universal Church.

Given on the Kalends of July.

# XXXI. RESCRIPT OF HONORIUS AUGUSTUS TO POPE BONIFACE, IN WHICH HE ESTABLISHES THAT, IF TWO BISHOPS ARE AGAIN ORDAINED AT ROME, BOTH ARE TO BE EXPELLED FROM THE CITY (C)

[Col. 0677]

[Col. 0677B] Victor Honorius, illustrious victor, ever Augustus, to the holy and venerable Boniface, pope of the city of Rome.

We received the writings of Your Blessedness with the congratulation owed to your dignity. After reading them, we gave the greatest thanks to almighty God, because we learned that your holiness, after a long illness, had been restored to the health you desired.

Therefore, we mark our joy by the testimony of sacred letters to the reverent and venerable men, and we ask that your Apostolate deign to offer, in daily prayers, its devotion and its prayers for the health and empire of us.

Know that our piety was especially pleased by the fact that your holiness is concerned about the disturbance of the churches or the people, a disturbance which our clemency believes has been sufficiently guarded against so that it cannot occur in any way.  
[Note: In Alv. the words “which your holiness is concerned about” are absent; they have been supplied from the other manuscripts.]

Finally, at the proclamation of Your Blessedness, we wish this to come to the knowledge of all the clergy: if anything should happen by human fortune to your religious office—which we do not wish—everyone must know that ambition is to cease. And if two men should happen to be ordained through unlawful audacity and rivalry, neither of them is to become a priest at all. Only the one whom divine judgment and the consent of all shall choose from the number of the clergy by a new ordination is to remain in the Apostolic See.

Therefore, all must observe this, preserving a tranquil mind and peaceful spirits in response to our serene admonition. Let no one attempt anything through seditious conspiracies, since it is certain that the efforts of neither party will benefit it.

# XXXII. LETTER OF POPE BONIFACE TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL: ON MAXIMUS, A BISHOP ACCUSED OF VARIOUS CRIMES (C)

[Col. 0677]

[Col. 0677C] Boniface, bishop, to Patroclus, Remigius, Maximus, Hilary, Severus, Valerius, Julian, Castorius, Leontius, Constantine, John, Montanus, Marinus, Mauricius, and the other bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

The clergy of the city of Valence came before us, presenting in a written petition crimes which they assert Maximus committed, with the entire province as witness. They state that, although jurisdiction had repeatedly been delegated and judgments established, he had always evaded them and had not hastened forward in confidence of conscience so that, if innocent, he might be cleared after everything had been examined. We have learned of these repeated decrees also from the contents of your documents.

By contrast, he has proved these charges against himself. To refute them—although they were innumerable—my predecessors delegated provincial jurisdiction. He is also said to have avoided the assemblies and to have been entirely unwilling to appear. No one doubts that a guilty man evades judgment in the same way that an innocent man seeks it in order to be acquitted.

But the cunning evasion of those who think matters should be handled by crafty schemes will never acquire the name of innocence. Anyone who thinks he can evade judgment through delays confesses everything. Yet the man so described will eventually come forward; it will not benefit him to have hidden and evaded judgment so often, since his own acts and whatever offenses are charged against him, if true, pursue him.

I ought even now to have rendered a sentence worthy of the acts of which he is accused before our judgment, since by repeatedly avoiding investigation and a decreed judgment he thought he could mock it. But lest anyone perhaps judge the matter premature, and lest he say that nothing had been reserved for the absent man, although we had sought him, we preferred to postpone the matter by granting an interval of time. His accusers also asserted that Maximus, confident regarding their intentions and character, committed acts deserving condemnation all the more readily the longer he delayed appearing before the appointed tribunal.

They accuse him of having long ago defiled his mind with the shameful sect of the Manichaeans, wrapped in their darkness, in such a way that he cannot cleanse himself; as proof of the charge they produce synodal records and state that, enveloped on every side in crimes, he had no regard for his own spiritual health.

They further allege that, through his madness and insane recklessness, he came before the tribunals of secular judges and was subjected to judicial torture—something most shameful even in a lowly person—and that he was condemned for homicide, producing the official records as evidence.

They complain with the deepest grief that, after committing such and so many offenses, this man still claims the name of bishop in his hiding places, to the disgrace of his own city, and wishes to pollute the holy name by claiming it for himself.

Therefore, dearest brothers, because he refused to present himself so that he might be heard, and so that, perhaps convicted by the clergy who accuse him, he might at last, when brought before an episcopal judgment, receive the appropriate sentence of a fitting pronouncement—although, once these matters have been made known to him, what loss can there be for one of this title who is said never to have possessed priestly shame and not to have guarded his office even for a short time?—we granted a delay.

We decreed that judgment should take place within your province and that a synod should be assembled before the day of the Kalends of November. If he wishes to attend, let him answer the charges in person, provided that he has confidence; if he neglects to attend, let his absence not win him a postponement of the sentence.  
[Note: From these words Esc. 3 continues the text.]

For it is manifest that a man confesses a crime when, although a judgment has been granted and repeatedly delegated for his acquittal, he does not use the opportunity to clear himself. It makes no difference whether all that has been alleged is proved in a hearing held in his presence, since his repeated absence itself is clearly an act equivalent to confession.  
[Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 2, and Urg. read “as a compression” instead of “as a confession.”]

We shall send letters throughout all the provinces, so that he cannot plead ignorance as an excuse. He must be compelled to come to the province and there be brought before the established judgment.

Whatever your Charity decides concerning this matter, once it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority, as is fitting.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of Monaxius, a man of illustrious rank, consul for the eleventh time.  
[Note: The other witnesses, except Alv., read: “Nona XI vicies consule” (a materially uncertain reading).]

# XXXIII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE BONIFACE TO HILARY, BISHOP OF NARBONNE: THAT IN EACH PROVINCE NO ONE IS TO BE ORDAINED BISHOP IN CONTEMPT OF THE METROPOLITAN (C)

[Col. 0679]

[Col. 0679B] Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne.

Difficult indeed [Bibl. Reg., “with the greatest difficulty”] do we lend credence to complaints whose intent strikes at the priests of the Lord, especially when they say that they have attempted something contrary to the statutes of the Fathers; but, as now, the multitude of accusers frequently supports these complaints. For behold, as your Charity recognizes, the clerical order of the Lutubensis Church [Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Tol. 1, Urg., Ger.; Alv., Esc. 4, Tol. 2: “Lugdunensis”], or the people subject to it, have sent their petitions or tears to us, as far as can be understood, with great sorrow, saying that our fellow bishop Patroclus, without any petition from them, had appointed some unknown person in place of the deceased bishop, in [the other manuscripts except Alv.: “from”] a different province, after bypassing the metropolitan, contrary to the rules of the Fathers. We can by no means endure this patiently, since it is fitting that we be careful guardians of the paternal enactments. No one, surely, is unaware of the decree of the Council of Nicaea, which commanded the following—in order to set down its very words: “In each province, the metropolitans ought individually to possess jurisdiction, and no one ought to have two provinces subject to him.” Since it is impossible to believe otherwise, they judged, with the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that this should be observed by them.

Therefore, dearest brother, if matters stand thus and the boundary of your province encloses the aforesaid Church, summoned by our authority—and indeed you ought to do this voluntarily—having regard to the wishes and will of those who petition, approach the same place where such an ordination is said to have taken place, fortified by the right of the metropolitan [Aem. and Bibl. Reg.; in the others: “having been admonished”] and relying upon our commands. Understand that, according to the rules of the Fathers, whatever must be done has been entrusted to your judgment by us, so that, when everything has been completed, whatever you decide may become known to the Apostolic See through your report, since it is clear that the administration of the entire province has been committed to you.

42 Let none of them, therefore, boldly and rashly overstep his boundary, nor let anyone, to the insult of those others, defend in his own district what does not appear to have been granted to him. Let the presumption of those who extend the limit of their dignity beyond what is permitted cease, restrained by our authority. We say this so that your Charity may recognize how carefully we observe the prescriptions of the canons: our own constitution likewise determines that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of our lords Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the tenth time.

## XXXIV. Letter of the same Pope Celestine to the Bishops of Gaul (C)

[Col. 0679]

[Col. 0679D] Celestine to his most beloved brothers Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, Fillacius, and the other bishops of Gaul: greetings.

The words of the apostolic command are that we ought to be without offense among Jews and Gentiles. Every Christian guards this with the full strength of his soul. Since this is so, considerable danger may remain before God for one who refuses to extend this even to the faithful. For how much these things distress us—things which, when done by Christian leaders, strike Christian hearts—the Lord’s saying in the Gospel bears witness. For the Savior himself says that it would be better for one who causes scandal to be submerged in the depths of the sea; and therefore let us consider what punishment already awaits one for whom we read that such a penalty would be better.

### I. Concerning Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain priests of Gaul of being followers of Pelagius

Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our Lord is worthy of praise, have reported to us that certain priests there—I do not know who they are—are being permitted so much liberty to pursue the dissension of the churches that, bringing undisciplined questions into public discussion, they persistently preach, as they say, things opposed to the truth. But we more justly attribute the blame to your Charity, since they have the opportunity to dispute above you. We read that a disciple is not above his teacher; that is, no one ought to claim a doctrine for himself as an injury to his teachers. We know that you yourselves have been appointed by our God to teach, since, as the Apostle says, the third place within the church has been assigned to you [Esc. 3: “since the Apostle says”]. What hope is there where the teachers are silent and those who, if this is so, were not their disciples are speaking? I fear that silence here may amount to connivance. I fear that those who allow them to speak in this manner are themselves speaking even more strongly. In such cases silence is not free from suspicion, since the truth would intervene if falsehood were displeasing; for the matter rightly concerns us if we foster error by our silence.

Therefore let such men be corrected; let it not be free to them to use speech according to their own will. If matters stand thus, let novelty cease to assail antiquity; let disturbance cease to trouble the peace of the Churches. They often attempt to drown in shipwreck those whom a secure anchorage makes safe while they stand within the harbor. Secure indeed is the station of all whose footprints do not shift as they advance in perfect steps. The aforesaid men have appealed to the Apostolic See, complaining to us of this very disturbance that is being attempted. Hold, dearest brothers, this discussion for the peace of the Catholic people. Let them know that, if indeed they are counted as members of the presbyterate, they are subject to you. Let all who teach wrongly know that it is more fitting for them to learn increasingly than to teach. For what are you doing in the churches if they hold the supreme authority to preach?
