Unless perhaps this objection stands in the way: that some who have recently been admitted from the company of the laity into our college, not by authority and not yet by reason, do not know what they ought to claim for themselves [“e.” in the others].

Much has already been said on these matters, at the time when we sent our written reply to our brother Tuens [Tol. 2, Urg.: “Tuendus”]. Nevertheless, repeating the warning again and again, we admonish you: let such men be forbidden [Bibl. Reg.; in the others: “let them avoid”] to labor throughout the lands at sowing anything other than what our farmer has commanded. Yet we cannot be surprised that they now dare to attempt these things against the living, since they also strive to scatter the memory of brothers who have fallen asleep.

### II. A remarkable [Aem., Esc. 3, Tol. 1, 2, Urg., Ger.: “wondrous”] declaration of praise concerning the holy bishop Augustine

[Col. 0682A]

We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our [Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1: “holy”] communion on account of his life and merits; nor has even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever touched him. We remember that he was once of such great learning that, even among the best teachers, he was always regarded as such by my predecessors. Everyone therefore formed a good judgment of him in common, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all [Bibl. Reg. and Esc. 3; in the others: “in communion”]. Hence such men must be resisted, whom we see growing in wickedness.

It is impious for religious souls to suffer this; and since, through their affliction, they are our members, it is fitting that we too should be afflicted. Nevertheless, blessedness awaits all who are proved to endure persecution for righteousness [Aem., Esc. 3, 4, Tol. 1, 2, Urg., Ger.: “for the sake of righteousness”; B. R.: “through righteousness”]. What the Lord promises them in the future, the following passage declares. It is not the cause of those alone who are acting, when the universal Church is struck by any novelty. Let us understand that these same things which displease us also displease you. We shall be able to demonstrate this only when, after silence has been imposed upon the wicked, complaint about such a matter has ceased in the future. May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.

### III. Authorities of the bishops of the Apostolic See from earlier times concerning the grace of God

[Editorial note: The material that follows from this point appears to have been written and appended by someone other than Celestine. Some testify that it was composed by Prosper.]

Since some who glory in the Catholic name, lingering in the condemned opinions or perversity or ignorance of heretics, presume to oppose devout disputants—and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, nevertheless speak against our teachers as though they had exceeded the necessary measure—and profess that they follow and approve only what the most holy See of blessed Peter has decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through its bishops, it was therefore necessary to inquire carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their times, and what they determined ought to be believed concerning the grace of God against the most harmful defenders of free will.

We therefore also joined to these certain pronouncements of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops made their own when they approved them. Thus, so that those who have doubts about any matter may be more fully instructed, we disclose the constitutions of the holy Fathers in a concise catalogue. If anyone is not excessively contentious [in the other manuscripts except Alv.: “least”], let him recognize that the connection of all these discussions depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no reason for contradiction remains for him if, with Catholics, he believes and says:

### IV. That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ

Pope Innocent, of blessed memory, pronounced that in Adam’s transgression all human beings lost their natural capacity and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that fall through free will unless the grace of a merciful God has raised him up. He says in his letter to the Council of Carthage:

“For when that man suffered the loss of free will, using his goods too rashly, he fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression. He found nothing by which he could rise from it thereafter; and, deceived forever in his freedom, he would have lain crushed beneath that ruin, unless the coming of Christ had afterward raised him up by his grace. Through the purification of the new birth, Christ cleansed every past fault by the washing of baptism.”

### V. That no one is good by his own powers except through participation in the One who alone is good

No one is good by himself unless the One who alone is good grants participation in himself. The judgment of that same pontiff declares this in the same writings:

“After this, are we to judge the minds of those people to be sound who think that what makes them good is owed to themselves, and do not consider the One whose grace they receive daily, while they confidently believe that they can achieve so much without him?” [Aem., Esc. 3, Tol. 1; in the others: “without any one.”]

### VI. That unless we are continually aided by God’s grace, we cannot avoid the devil’s snares

No one, even after being renewed by the grace of baptism, is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he has received perseverance in a good way of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same pages:

“For although that One redeemed the human being from past sins, nevertheless, knowing that he could sin again, he preserved and supplied many remedies by which he could correct him afterward as well. Unless we rely upon and trust in these remedies, we can in no way overcome human errors. For it is necessary that, by the help of the One through whom we conquered, we should not again be conquered when he does not help us.”

### VII. That through Christ we make good use of free will

The same teacher proclaims in a letter to the Council of Milevis that no one uses free will well except through Christ, saying:

“Consider at last, O perverse teaching of minds of the greatest gravity, that this freedom so deceived the first human being that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell into the presumption of transgression. He could not be rescued from this unless the providence of regeneration, through the coming of Christ the Lord, restored to him the former condition of freedom” [in the others, except Alv.: “had formed.”].

### VIII. That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God

All the zeal, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any other reason than that which he himself has given. The authoritative rule of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us to this judgment when, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

“But we have referred everything to the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise.”

The African bishops venerated this speech, shining with the light of the most sincere truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man:

“But what you placed in the letter that you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Yet we have done this at God’s prompting,’ and so forth, we understood in this sense: that, passing swiftly by as though with the sword of truth, you cut down those who exalt the freedom of human will against God’s assistance. For what did you do by so free a will as to refer everything to the awareness of our humility? Yet you rightly and wisely saw, and truthfully and confidently declared, that this had been [Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4: “is”] done at God’s prompting. This is so because the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself, through paternal inspirations, moves the hearts of his children to do something good. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Thus we do not find that our will is absent, yet in every individual movement of human will toward good we do not hesitate to acknowledge that his assistance is more powerful.”

### IX. That every holy thought and movement of a pious will is from God

God works in human hearts, or in free will itself, in such a way that every holy thought, pious plan, and movement of a good will is from God, because through him we can do something good, while without him we can do nothing. The same teacher instructed us in this confession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole city about the dispensation of divine grace, he said:

“What time, then, intervenes in which we do not need his assistance? In all our actions, circumstances, thoughts, and movements, we must pray for him as helper and protector. For it is arrogant for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.’ And as he himself says again: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.’ And again: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me.’”

### X. That God’s grace not only forgives sins but also helps prevent their commission and enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, merely with ease, as though it could be fulfilled with greater difficulty without God’s grace

We also embrace as properly belonging to the Apostolic See what was established among the decrees of the Council of Carthage. In its third canon it was defined that whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the forgiveness of sins already committed, and not also as assistance so that they may not be committed, is to be anathema.

Again, in the fourth canon: whoever says that God’s grace through Jesus Christ helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what to avoid, but that through it we are not also granted the ability to love and to accomplish what we have learned ought to be done, is to be anathema [in Alv.: “but that it is not granted to us through it.”].

Since the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up,” it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have Christ’s grace for that which puffs us up, but not for that which builds us up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do and loving in order to do it, so that, as love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. Just as it is written of God, “He teaches human beings knowledge,” so it is also written, “Love is from God.”

Likewise, in the fifth canon: whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason—that what we are commanded to do by free will we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily, is to be anathema. For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments: “There he did not say, ‘Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,’ but he said, ‘Without me you can do nothing.’”

### XI. That, apart from the decrees of the Apostolic See, all the prayers of Christ’s Church resound with the grace by which the human race is restored from eternal condemnation

Besides these inviolable decrees of the most blessed Apostolic See, by which the most devout Fathers taught us, after casting down the pride of a destructive novelty, to refer both the beginnings of a good will, the growth of worthy endeavors, and perseverance in them to the grace of Christ, let us also consider the solemn prayers of the priests. Handed down from the apostles, these are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in every Catholic Church, so that the law of prayer establishes the law of belief.

When the leaders of holy peoples perform their delegated ministry, they plead the cause of the human race before divine mercy. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith be given to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed love; that remedies of repentance may be granted to those who have fallen; and, finally, that the heavenly halls of mercy may be opened to catechumens who have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration.

The effects of these very matters show that they are not requested from the Lord perfunctorily or in vain. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, transferring them, rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of his beloved Son, and making them vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. It is so clearly understood that all this is the work of God that thanksgiving and confession of praise are always rendered to God, who accomplishes it, for the illumination or correction of such people.

### XII. That God’s grace is also attested by the established purification of those to be baptized, when unclean spirits are driven [Bibl. Reg.: “expelled”] from them through exorcisms and insufflations

[Col. 0686A]

We do not contemplate without purpose what the holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young adults come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the fountain of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them through the exorcisms and insufflations of the clergy. Then it is truly shown how the prince of this world is cast out, how the strong man is first bound, and afterward his vessels are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor, who leads captivity captive and gives gifts to human beings.

Strengthened, therefore, by these ecclesiastical rules and by documents drawn from divine authority, with the Lord’s assistance, we profess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and virtues by which, from the beginning of faith, one strives toward him. 46 We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through which it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

By this assistance and gift of God free will is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes luminous, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes prudent. God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes our merits to be his gifts, and for what he has bestowed he will grant eternal rewards. He acts within us so that we both will and do what he wills. Nor does he permit the gifts he has given us to lie idle within us; they are to be exercised, not neglected, so that we may also be coworkers with God’s grace. If we see anything in us growing weak through our own negligence, let us hasten anxiously back to him who heals all our diseases and redeems our life from destruction [Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. 1, Ger.: “our soul”], and to whom we say each day: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

### XIII. That deeper questions are neither to be despised nor asserted absolutely

As for the deeper and more difficult parts of the questions that arise, which those who opposed the heretics treated at greater length: just as we do not dare to despise them, so we do not consider it necessary to establish them. For, in confessing the grace of God, from whose work and gracious favor nothing at all ought to be removed, we believe it sufficient to accept whatever the writings of the Apostolic See have taught us according to the rules set out above, so that we may in no way regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the stated judgments.

Here ends the discussion of the grace of God and free choice of the will.

## XXXIV. Letter of the same Pope Celestine to the Bishops of Gaul (C)

[Col. 0685]

[Col. 0685D] Celestine to all the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne and Narbonne: greetings in the Lord.

We should certainly have wished to rejoice in the ordering of your Churches in such a way that we might congratulate you on progress rather than grieve over anything admitted contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. Beneficial things reach us for our joy, while wrongdoing pierces us with the thorns of sorrow. Nor can we remain silent when the impulse of our office urges us to recall some people from unlawful acts—we who have been appointed by God as watchmen—so that, demonstrating the diligence of our vigilance, we may cut away what must be restrained and establish what must be observed. And although special care does not fail even concerning distant places, but extends everywhere that the name of God is preached, matters attempted by the authority of a new presumption for the overturning of the rules do not escape our notice.

### I. That priests and clerics should not minister in church clothed in a shoulder-cloth and girded about the loins

For we have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve a superstitious style of dress rather than purity of mind or faith. It is not surprising that those who did not grow up within the Church act contrary to ecclesiastical custom; they have come by another path and brought into the Church practices that belonged to another way of life.

Clothed in a shoulder-cloth and girded around the loins [Bibl. Reg.: “with the loins”; Esc. 4: “and girded over the loins”], they believe that they will fulfill the faith of Scripture not spiritually but literally. If these commands were given so that they should be observed in this manner, why are the things that follow not likewise performed—why are burning lamps not held in the hands together with a staff? These things have their own mystery, and to those who understand them they are so clear that they should be observed according to the more appropriate symbolism. The girding of the loins signifies chastity; the staff, pastoral governance; and the burning lamps, the radiance of good works, concerning which it is said: “In this way let your works shine.”

Perhaps those who live in remote places and dwell far from others have this form of dress, following custom rather than reason. But why should this clothing be introduced into the Gallican churches, so that the custom of so many years and so many bishops should be changed into another form of dress? We must be distinguished from the people and from others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by outward adornment. For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the Fathers in order to make room for needless superstitions.

We must not therefore lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful toward other things; they should be taught rather than mocked. The commandments should not be imposed upon their eyes but poured into their minds. There were indeed many things that we could [Esc. 4: “can”] say concerning ecclesiastical discipline or explain by the reason inherent in the matter itself, but we are being drawn away from them to other matters.

### II. That final repentance must be denied to no one

We have learned that repentance is being denied to the dying, and that the requests of those who, at the time of their death, desire this remedy for their souls are not being granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to dispense with God’s mercy, as though he could not assist anyone who runs to him at any time, and free a person endangered beneath the weight of sins by the very burden from which he desires to be released.

What else, I ask, is this than adding death to one who is dying, and killing his soul by cruelty so that it cannot be absolved, when God is most ready to come to his aid and, inviting repentance, promises:

“The sinner,” he says, “on whatever day he turns, his sins will not be charged against him”; and again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn and live.”

Whoever, therefore, denies repentance even at the time of death deprives a person of salvation and despairs of God’s mercy, since he does not believe that God can suffice to help the dying even in a single moment. The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the repentance of one hour had not helped him. While suffering punishment, he repented, and through the profession of a single statement he earned, by God’s promise, a dwelling in paradise.

True conversion to God in those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the disposition of the mind rather than by the amount of time, as the prophet asserts in this way: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.” Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, repentance must not be denied at any time to one who requests it, since he binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things will be revealed.

### III. That the episcopal office should be reached through the ecclesiastical orders

We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain men have been ordained bishops who had not been formed through any ecclesiastical orders before attaining the summit of such dignity. This usurpation contradicts the decrees of the Fathers, and the one who acknowledges having done this has done so even though the episcopate ought to be reached through those stages for which provision has so frequently been made, so that those initiated in the lesser offices may be strengthened for the greater.

Anyone who desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned. Every institution of life confirms itself by this principle in relation to the goal toward which it tends. One who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through each stage of service cannot attain the rank and merit of that service. Is the priesthood alone among these, I ask, of less value, since it is granted more easily even though it is fulfilled with greater difficulty?

But now it is not enough to ordain laymen, whom no order permits to become such; men whose crimes are known far and wide throughout almost all the provinces are also being ordained bishops. Daniel, recently reported to us from the eastern regions, was accused by the entire monastery of virgins over which he had presided, through heinous charges. Many disgraceful acts were alleged against him. He was sought out to discover in what part of the world he was hiding, so that, if he trusted in his innocence, he would not avoid the judgment requested against him. Our instructions were sent through our subdeacon Fortunatus to the bishop of Arles, so that Daniel might be brought to episcopal judgment.

Burdened by such weighty testimonies and assailed by such an accusation of crimes, stained, as is said, by incest with sacred virgins, he is reported to have been ordained bishop. The written accusations are kept in our archives, and we have also sent copies of them to you. At the very time when, by letters sent from us, he was being summoned to answer the charge, he insinuated himself into the dignity of the episcopate. May no injury be done to the sacred name. It is easier to suppose that the ordainer himself lost this dignity by conferring it upon such a man than that the ordained man should obtain it. The one who believed him worthy to be made a bishop will be associated with the convicted man, since he made him his associate by granting him the episcopate; for whoever ordains such men shows what kind of person he himself is.

Since these matters have now been brought forward, and since many of you know the statutes of the Apostolic See [Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. 1, 2, Urg.: “have known”], your fraternity should hasten to recall everything to the rule of discipline through our admonitions, as you have spent some time with us.

### IV. That each province must be content with its own metropolitan

First, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, each province must be content with its own metropolitan, as the provisions contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establish; no priest should be given an opportunity for usurpation to the injury of another. Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him. Let no one presume anything in another’s province; nor should foreign and unknown clerics, who have not previously been known there, be placed over those who have earned the good testimony of their fellow citizens in their own churches, lest an institution of some new kind appear to have been established from which bishops are made.

### V. That no one should be ordained bishop against the will of the clergy or people

Let no bishop be given against the will of the people. The consent and desire of the clergy, people, and order must be sought. Someone from another Church may then be chosen if no one worthy can be found among the clergy of the very city for which a bishop is to be ordained—a circumstance we do not believe can occur. First, the local candidates must be rejected, so that someone from another church may rightly be preferred.

Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has spent his entire life through all the offices. Let no one intrude upon another’s service; nor let one person dare to claim for himself the reward owed to another. Let the clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being overburdened, and let them not fear to reject those outsiders whom they recognize as being thrust upon them. They must have the proper reward and the freedom to judge the one who is to govern them.

### VI. That unlawful ordinations must be avoided

Unlawful ordinations must also be avoided. No layman, no bigamist, no man who is or has been the husband of a widow may be ordained; rather, one who is blameless, of the sort chosen by the Apostle, must be appointed. Through Moses the Lord commanded: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife.” The Apostle follows and completes this, speaking by the same Spirit, by saying that a bishop must be consecrated as the husband of one wife.

Priests must therefore be chosen according to this standard, and if any unlawful ordinations have been carried out, they must be removed. They cannot stand, nor will they be able to evade our investigation, even if those who have attained office by another route think they can remain hidden, so that no reverence for religion may be darkened by obscurity.

Let there be no empty boasting among those clothed in the pallium; let those who are bishops follow episcopal custom. Daniel, as we have said, believed that he could evade his accusation by the honor of the episcopate and reached such a height by concealing himself from his accusers. He must know that, for the present, he is separated from the assembly of your holiness; if he knows that he has confidence in his conscience, he ought to submit himself to our judgment.

As for the priest of the Church of Marseilles, who is said—an unspeakable thing—to have rejoiced in such a way at the death of his brother that he went to meet this man, who arrived stained with his brother’s blood, intending to share a portion with him, we delegate him to your college for examination.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus.

## XXXV. Letter of the same Celestine to the Bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria (C)

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689C] Celestine to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria.

49 ### I. That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons

No priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons or to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what matter worthy of respect will remain among us if the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken at the pleasure of certain people, with license granted to the populace?

### II. That bishops should not be ordained from the laity, with the clergy of the churches disregarded
We have heard that certain cities assigned to particular governors wish to obtain bishops for themselves from among the laity, and consider so lofty an office so cheap that they think we can confer it upon men who have served not God but the world. In doing this, they judge badly not only of their own clergy, whom they hold in contempt, but also most wickedly of us, whom they believe capable of such an act. They would never dare this if the opinion of certain persons there did not connive in agreement with them. Thus decrees issued so frequently achieve nothing, since this matter is ignored as though nothing had ever been written about it. What advantage is there in clerics having served through the several ranks and spent their whole lives in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to preside over them are sought from among the laity—men who, free from worldly affairs and ignorant of the whole ecclesiastical order, seek by a reckless leap to cross over into another’s honor [Note: [Col. 0689D] In the other manuscripts, except Alv.: “by a reckless leap they seek another’s order”] with immoderate ambition, and to pass into another way of life after trampling underfoot the reverence due to ecclesiastical discipline?

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we guard the helm of our law—that is, of the canons—we must oppose such persons. By these letters we admonish your fraternity [Note: [Col. 0690D] More correctly, “your fraternities,” since the address is made to several persons], so that no one may admit a layman to the clerical order or allow something to be done that will deceive him and generate for himself grounds on which he may become liable under the established decrees.

### III. That the people must be instructed, not followed

The people must be instructed, not followed. If they are ignorant, we must remind them what is permitted and what is not permitted [Col. 0691A], not give our consent to them. Whoever attempts to undertake what is forbidden will find that the censure of the apostolic see will by no means be lacking. For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must necessarily punish with a severity suited to the regulations. [Col. 0692A] We therefore wish this to be made known throughout all the churches that lack their own governors, so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope, may deceive himself.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius.

## XXXVI. LETTER OF POPE LEO AGAINST EUTYCHES, ABBOT OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He dared to declare that the Word and the flesh had one nature, although it is established that we confess one person in the Lord Jesus Christ in two natures, namely, that of God and that of man. (C)

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691B] Leo, bishop, sends greetings in Christ to his dearest son, the presbyter Eutyches.

### 50

You have brought to our attention, in a letter from your affection, that the Nestorian heresy was again sprouting through the efforts of certain persons. We reply that we have approved your concern in this matter, since the statement we have received is an indication of your mind. From this we do not doubt that the Lord, the author of the catholic faith, will be present with you in all things. But when we have been able to learn more fully through whose wickedness this has occurred, we must, with the Lord’s help, take care that the impious and long-condemned poison may be utterly destroyed.

May God keep you safe and sound, dearest son.

## XXXVII. LETTER OF POPE LEO TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

In which he asks why Eutyches, who held an opinion contrary to the catholic faith, had been separated by him from communion with the Church. (C)

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691C] Leo to his dearest brother Flavian.

When the most Christian and most merciful emperor, anxious for the peace of the catholic Church, sent us a written account concerning those who have caused an uproar of disturbance among you, we are surprised that your fraternity was able to keep silent about the nature of that scandal instead of taking care that your report should first inform us, lest we be unable to establish the truth of what had occurred.

For we have received a petition from the presbyter Eutyches, who complains that he was deprived of communion unjustly, at the accusation of the bishop Eusebius. He especially testifies that he was present when summoned and did not refuse to appear, to such an extent that he asserts that at the very hearing he presented a written appeal, yet it was not accepted. For this reason, he says, he was compelled to post written protests in the city of Constantinople. In view of these circumstances, we still do not understand by what justice he was separated from communion with the Church.

But, considering the case, we wish to know the reason for your action, and we wish the entire matter to be brought to our attention. For we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, can decide nothing concerning anyone to the prejudice of either party while the facts remain unknown, before we have truthfully heard everything that was done.

Therefore let your fraternity inform us through a person especially suitable and qualified, with the fullest possible report, what novelty contrary to the ancient faith has arisen that deserved to be punished by a more severe judgment. For both the Church’s discipline and the faith of the most religious prince impose upon us a great concern for Christian peace, so that, once dissensions have been cut away, the catholic faith may be preserved inviolate; and so that those who defend what is perverse may be recalled from error, while those whose faith has been proved may be strengthened by our authority.

Nor can any difficulty be raised in this matter, since the aforesaid presbyter has declared in his own petition that he is prepared to correct anything found in him deserving reproach. In such cases it is especially fitting to ensure that both charity is preserved and truth defended without the uproar of disputation, dearest brother.

Therefore, since your affection sees that we are necessarily concerned about so important a matter, let it hasten to indicate everything to us as fully and clearly as possible—as it ought to have done earlier—so that we may not be misled by any ambiguity among the assertions of the parties, and so that a disagreement, which ought to be abolished at its beginning, may not be nourished. For, with God inspiring us, reverence remains in our heart, lest the constitutions of the venerable Fathers, divinely strengthened and pertaining to the solidity of the faith, be violated by anyone’s perverse interpretation.

May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother.

## RESPONSE OF FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO LEO, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME (C)

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693A] Flavian sends eternal greetings in the Lord to the most blessed lord, his beloved father Leo.

### I. Concerning the snares of the deceitful enemy

Nothing restrains the devil’s poisons or holds back his deadly arrows. Flying about above and below, he seeks those whom he may kill, whom he may separate, whom he may devour. For this reason we must remain vigilant and devote ourselves to prayer and to God, so that we may be able to avoid foolish investigations.

It is fitting to follow our Fathers and not alter the perpetual definition of those whose rule, according to the Scriptures, we have learned [Note: [Col. 0693C] In the others, except Alv.: “nor”]. Therefore, setting aside lamentations and tears—for a cleric living under my authority was attacked by a savage demon, and I could neither free him nor remove him from such a wolf, although I was prepared to lay down my life for him—I shall now begin to recount how he was snatched away, how he recoiled from the divine purpose and ran to the one accustomed to destroy, turning aside from the commands of the Fathers and despising their decrees.

### II. Concerning the fraudulent cunning of heretics

There are certain people who signify sheep by their clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. We must recognize them by their fruits. At first sight they seem to belong to our number, but they do not belong to our number; for if they belonged to our number, they would have remained with us. When they begin to embrace impiety, what was hidden within them is revealed, and all their deceit becomes manifest to everyone [Note: [Col. 0693C] In the others, except Alv.: “becomes manifest to everyone”].

There are found among them people weak in faith and ignorant of the divine readings, and these men plunge them with themselves into perdition, scattering and reviling the teachings of the Fathers and abandoning the holy Scriptures to their own destruction. We must foresee such people and beware of them greatly, lest some who are occupied with their wickedness fall from their steadfastness. For they have sharpened their tongue like serpents and have poison on their lips like asps; concerning them the prophet cried out.

### III. Concerning the blasphemies of Eutyches

Such a man as Eutyches has emerged among us, formerly a presbyter [Col. 0694A] and archimandrite. He appeared to hold the teaching of our religion and professed it, but he confirmed the impiety of Nestorius and girded himself to fight on Nestorius’s behalf in the struggle that had been prepared against Nestorius.

He attempted to tear away the exposition of the faith made by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers against Nestorius and those like him, to which all had assented. In doing so he revived the ancient sect of the impious Valentinus and Apollinaris, and he did not fear the command of the true God, who said: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be fastened around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea.”

He cast aside all shame and shook off the garment of unbelief that he had worn. In the holy synod he persistently asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ ought not to be confessed as being from two natures after the assumption of humanity, since we recognize him as being of one substance and one person. Nor, he said, does the Lord’s flesh subsist as coessential with us, as having been assumed from us and united to God the Word according to substance.

He did say that the Virgin who bore him according to the flesh was coessential [Note: [Col. 0694C] More correctly, “consubstantial”; although the manuscripts understand “coessential” in the same sense] with us; but he maintained that the Lord himself had not assumed from her flesh coessential with us. Rather, he said, the Lord’s body is not indeed the body of a man, though it is a human body that comes from the Virgin. In this he held opinions contrary to the expositions of all the Fathers.

### IV. Concerning his entirely just excommunication

But, to avoid making the letter long by saying too much, we formerly sent to your blessedness an account of everything we did. [Col. 0694C] In that letter we explained that he had also been stripped of the presbyterate, since he had been caught in this way; we ordered that he should have no association with the monasteries; and we excluded him from our communion.

Your holiness, having learned what was done concerning him, should make his impiety known to all the bishops living under your blessedness, lest some, not knowing what he held, should communicate with him either by letter or by some other association as though he were orthodox.

## XXXVIII. LETTER OF LEO TO BISHOP FLAVIAN

Against the perfidy of Eutyches. (C)

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693D] Leo to his dearest brother Flavian [Note: [Col. 0693D] Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4: “father”].

### 53

After reading the letter of your affection [Note: [Col. 0694D] In the others, except Alv.: “After reading your affection’s letter”], which we are surprised was so late, and after reviewing the sequence of the episcopal proceedings, we have at last learned what scandal occurred among you and what had arisen against the integrity of the faith. What previously seemed hidden has now been opened and revealed to us.

### I. That ignorance of the holy Scriptures made Eutyches a heretic

[Col. 0694D]

In these matters Eutyches, who seemed honorable by reason of the name of presbyter, is shown to be very imprudent and exceedingly ignorant, so that what the prophet said may also be applied to him: “He refused to understand so that he might do good; he meditated iniquity on his bed.” For what is more iniquitous than to hold impious opinions and refuse to yield to those wiser and more learned?

Those who, when impeded by some obstacle from recognizing the truth, turn not to the prophetic utterances, not to the apostolic letters, not to the evangelical authorities, but to themselves, fall into this folly. They therefore become teachers of error because they were not disciples of the truth.

For what learning from the sacred pages of the New and Old Testament did the man acquire who did not even comprehend the beginnings of the creed itself? What is proclaimed throughout the whole world by the voice of all the regenerate is still not grasped in the heart of this old man.

### II. Against those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons

Since he did not know what he ought to believe concerning the incarnation of the Word of God [Col. 0695B], and was unwilling to labor over the breadth of the holy Scriptures in order to gain the light of understanding, he should at least have received with attentive hearing that common and undivided confession [Note: [Col. 0695D] From Aem. and Bibl. Reg. In the others: “distinct”] which the whole body of the faithful professes: that they believe in God the Father Almighty and in Jesus Christ, his Son, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.

By these three statements nearly all the devices of the heretics are destroyed. For when God is believed to be both Almighty and Father, the Son is shown to be co-eternal with him, differing from the Father in that he is God from God, Almighty from Almighty, born from the eternal one as co-eternal—not later in time, not inferior in power, not unlike in glory, not divided in essence.

The same eternal Only-begotten of the eternal Begetter was born from the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary. This temporal birth diminished nothing and contributed nothing to that divine and eternal birth; rather, it wholly devoted itself to restoring the human being who had been deceived, so that it might conquer death and destroy by its power the devil who held dominion over death.

For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he, whom neither sin could defile nor death hold captive, assumed our nature and made it his own. He was conceived from the Holy Spirit within the womb of his virgin mother, who bore him while preserving her virginity, just as she conceived him while preserving her virginity.

But if he could not draw sincere understanding from this most pure source of the Christian faith because, through his own blindness, he darkened for himself the radiance of evident truth, he should at least have submitted himself to evangelical teaching, where Matthew says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”

He should also have sought instruction from apostolic preaching and, reading in the Epistle to the Romans, have found: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

He should also have directed pious attention to the prophetic pages and found God’s promise to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.” And, so that he might not doubt the particular identity of this seed, he should have followed the Apostle, who says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ.

He should also have grasped inwardly the preaching of Isaiah, who says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.” He should likewise have read faithfully the words of the same prophet: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose authority is upon his shoulders, and his name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come.” [Note: [Col. 0695D] In the others, except Alv.: “they shall call”]

Nor, speaking deceitfully, should he have said that the Word became flesh in such a way that Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, possessed the form of a man but did not possess the reality of a body from his mother.

Or perhaps he thought that our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our nature because the angel sent to blessed Mary said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.” Did he therefore think that, because the Virgin’s conception was a work of God, the flesh conceived did not come from the nature of the one who conceived?

But we must not understand that uniquely wonderful and wonderfully unique birth in such a way that, through the novelty of creation, the particularity of the human race was removed. The Holy Spirit gave the Virgin fertility; but the reality of the body was taken from a body. As Wisdom built a house for itself, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—that is, in the flesh which he assumed from a human being and which the spirit of rational life [Note: [Col. 0696D] Esc. 4, Urg., Ger.: “rational”] animated.

### III. Against those who dare to assert that the divinity of the Only-begotten Son was passible

[Col. 0696C]

Thus, while the distinct property of each nature was preserved and both came together in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, and mortality by eternity. In order to discharge the debt imposed by our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that the one and same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, could both suffer death in one respect and could not suffer death in the other.

In the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, the true God was born—wholly in what was his own, wholly in what was ours. By “ours” we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he assumed in order to restore it. Those things which the deceiver introduced and the deceived human being admitted left no trace in the Savior. Nor, because he shared in the weakness of human beings, was he therefore a participant in our sins.

He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, increasing what was human without diminishing what was divine. For that self-emptying by which the invisible made himself visible, and the Creator and Lord of all things willed to become one of mortal beings, was an inclination of mercy, not a loss of power.

Accordingly, the one who, remaining in the form of God, made the human being was himself made human in the form of a servant. Each nature retains its property without defect; and just as the form of God did not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant did not diminish the form of God.

For, since the devil gloried that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts and stripped of the endowment of immortality, and had undergone the harsh sentence of death—and since he found a certain consolation in his own evils through the fellowship of the transgressor—and that God too, justice demanding it, had changed his own sentence concerning the human being whom he had created with such honor, there was need for the dispensation of a hidden plan. Thus the unchangeable God, whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness, would complete the first dispensation of his mercy toward us through a more concealed mystery, and the human being, driven into guilt by the devil’s wicked cunning contrary to God’s purpose, would not perish.

### IV. Against those who argue for a blending or confusion of Christ’s two natures

[Col. 0697B]

The Son of God therefore enters these lowly conditions of the world, descending from his heavenly seat but not departing from the Father’s glory, generated in a new order and by a new birth.

In a new order, because the invisible in what was his own became visible in what was ours; the incomprehensible willed to be comprehended; he who existed before the ages began to exist in time; the Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, the immensity of his majesty being veiled; and God, impassible, did not disdain to be a passible human being and to be subject to the laws of death.

He was generated by a new birth because inviolate virginity knew no desire and supplied the material of flesh. From the Lord’s mother he assumed nature, not guilt. Nor, in the Lord Jesus Christ born from the Virgin’s womb, is our nature unlike his merely because his birth is wondrous.

For the one who is true God is also true man; and there is no falsehood in this unity, since within it are both the humility of humanity and the loftiness of divinity. Just as God is not changed by mercy, so humanity is not consumed by dignity.

Each form acts in communion with the other according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles; the other submits to injuries. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father’s glory, so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race.

For one and the same person is truly the Son of God and truly the Son of man: God by virtue of what was in the beginning—the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; man by virtue of the fact that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. God by virtue of the fact that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; man by virtue of the fact that he was made from a woman, made under the law.

The birth of the flesh is a manifestation of human nature; the Virgin’s delivery is an indication of divine power. The infancy of the little child is shown by the lowliness of the cradle, while the greatness of the Most High is declared by the voices of angels. He resembles the beginnings of human life—the one whom Herod wickedly attempts to kill—yet he is Lord of all, whom the Magi rejoice humbly to adore.

When he came to the baptism of his forerunner John, lest it remain hidden that divinity was concealed beneath the veil of flesh, the Father’s voice thundered from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” The one whom the devil’s cunning tempts as a human being is served by angelic ministries as God.

To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is plainly human. But to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves, to give the Samaritan woman living water whose drink would ensure that she would never thirst again, to walk with feet that did not sink upon the sea’s surface, and to subdue the rising waves by rebuking the storm is unmistakably divine.

Thus, to pass over many things, it is not of the same nature to weep for a dead friend from compassionate affection and, by a command of the voice, to raise that same friend alive after removing the barrier of a four-day burial; nor to hang upon a cross and to make all the elements tremble when daylight had been turned into night; nor to be pierced with nails and to open the gate of paradise to the faithful thief.

Likewise, it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one,” and to say, “The Father is greater than I.” Although there is one person of God and man in the Lord Jesus Christ, one thing is the source of what is common to both in humiliation, and another is the source of what is common to both in glory. From us comes his humanity, by which he is lower than the Father; from the Father comes his divinity, by which he is equal with the Father.

### V. Against those who madly assert that the form of a servant which he assumed from us is heavenly or of some other substance

Because of this unity of person in both natures, the Son of man is therefore read as having descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin from whom he was born. Conversely, the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in the divinity itself, by which the Only-begotten is co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, but in the weakness of human nature.

Thus we all confess, even in the creed, that the Only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty.”

When our Lord and Savior himself was instructing the faith of his disciples through his questions, he said: “Who do people say the Son of man is?” When they had recounted the various opinions of others [Bibl. Reg.: “divided opinions”], he said: “But who do you say that I am?”—that is, who am I, who am the Son of man and whom you see in the form of a servant and in the reality of flesh? Who do you say that I am?

Then blessed Peter, divinely inspired and destined through his confession to precede all the nations, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

And rightly was he pronounced blessed by the Lord, and drew both the solidity of virtue and of name from the principal Rock. Through the Father’s revelation he confessed the same person to be both the Son of God and the Christ, because accepting either one without the other did not lead to salvation. It was equally dangerous to believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was God alone without a human being, or a human being alone without God.

After the Lord’s resurrection—which certainly belonged to a true human being, since the one raised was not other than the one who had been crucified and died—what else was accomplished during the delay of forty days than that the integrity of our faith should be cleansed of every darkness?

For he conversed with the disciples, lived with them, ate with them, and allowed himself to be handled with careful and inquisitive touch by those whom doubt had unsettled. For this reason he also entered to the disciples through closed doors, gave them the Holy Spirit by his breath, and, after granting the light of understanding, opened to them the hidden things of the holy Scriptures.

Again, he showed the wound in his side, the marks of the nails, and all the signs of his very recent passion, saying: “See my hands and my feet, because I am he. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” Thus it might be recognized that the distinct property of the divine and human nature remained indivisible in him, and we might know that the Word is not the same as the flesh, while confessing one Son of God and confessing both the Word and the flesh.

Eutyches must therefore be considered exceedingly empty of this mystery of faith. He recognized neither our nature in the Only-begotten Son of God through the humility of mortality nor through the glory of the resurrection. Nor did he fear the judgment of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, who says: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that separates Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist.”

For what does it mean to separate Jesus except to separate the human nature from him and to empty, through the most shameless fabrications, the mystery through which alone we have been saved?

Since he is confused concerning the nature of Christ’s body [Bibl. Reg.: “being confused”], it is necessary that he should also go astray concerning his passion through the same blindness. If he does not consider the Lord’s cross false and does not doubt that the punishment undertaken for the world’s salvation was real, let him recognize whose death he believes in and whose flesh he acknowledges. Let him not deny that the human being whose suffering he recognizes belonged to our body, since denial of true flesh is also denial of bodily suffering.

If, therefore, he has accepted the Christian faith and has not turned his hearing away from the preaching of the Gospel, let him see what nature hung, pierced by nails, upon the wood of the cross. When the side of the crucified man was opened by the soldier’s lance, let him understand from where blood and water flowed, so that the Church of God might be regenerated both by the washing and by the cup.

Let him also hear the blessed apostle Peter preaching that sanctification takes place through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. Let him not read casually the words of the same apostle: “Knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable silver and gold from your futile conduct inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ.”

Let him not resist the testimony of the blessed apostle John, who says: “The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin.” And again: “This is the victory that has conquered the world, our faith; and who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is truth. For there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and the three are one”—the Spirit, that is, of sanctification; the blood, of redemption; and the water, of baptism.

These three are one and remain indivisible; none of them is separated from its connection with the others. For the catholic Church lives by this faith and advances by it: in the Lord Jesus Christ, humanity is not believed without true divinity, nor divinity without true humanity.

### VI. Against those who absurdly maintain that the Lord had two natures before the union but invent one nature after the union

When, in response to the examination by your assembly, Eutyches answered, saying, “I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature,” I am astonished that so absurd and perverse a profession was not rebuked by any reprimand from the judges, and that so foolish a statement was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard.

For it is just as impious to say that the Only-begotten Son of God existed from two natures before the incarnation as it is blasphemous to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there is in him a single nature.

Therefore, lest Eutyches judge that this was stated correctly [Esc. 4: “certainly”] or tolerably merely because it was not refuted by any sentence of yours, we admonish the diligence of your affection, dearest brother, that if, through the inspiration of God’s mercy, the case is brought to satisfaction, the imprudence of this ignorant man may through you be cleansed even of this stain in his understanding.

As the sequence of the proceedings revealed, he had indeed begun to withdraw from his own position when, compelled by your judgment, he professed that he was saying what he had not previously said and assented to a faith from which he had earlier been alien. But when he refused to consent to the impious doctrine by anathematizing it, your fraternity understood that he remained in his own perfidy and was worthy to receive a judgment of condemnation.

If he truly and usefully grieves over this, and at least late recognizes how rightly episcopal authority was moved [Note: [Col. 0699] In the others, except Alv.: “would recognize”], or if he condemns by spoken words and a personal subscription everything that he has wrongly believed, no amount of mercy toward one who has corrected himself will be blameworthy. For our Lord is the true good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and came to save human beings, not to destroy them. He wishes us to imitate his compassion, so that justice may restrain sinners but mercy may not reject those who have turned back.

For true faith is defended most fruitfully when a false opinion is condemned even by its own adherents [Note: [Col. 0699] In the others, except Alv.: “Then indeed faith is defended most fruitfully”].

To carry out the whole case piously and faithfully, we have sent our brothers, Bishop Julian and the presbyter Renatus, together with our son, the deacon Hilary [Bibl. Reg.: “Hilarius”], as our representatives. We have associated with them our notary Dulcitius, whose faithfulness has often been tested, trusting that divine assistance will be present, so that the man who had gone astray may be saved once he has condemned the perversity of his own understanding.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most distinguished men Asterius and Protogenes, in the year 486 of the era.

## XXXIX. LETTER OF PETER, BISHOP OF RAVENNA [Note: [Col. 0701B] Esc. 4, Tol. 1, Narbonensis], TO THE PRESBYTER EUTYCHES

In which he responds to his errors with an appropriate example. (C)

[Col. 0701]

[Col. 0701A] Peter, bishop, to his beloved and deservedly honored son, the presbyter Eutyches.

I read your sorrowful letter with sorrow, and with the grief it deserved I passed through your mournful writing. Just as the peace of the churches, the harmony of the priests, and the tranquility of the people make us rejoice with heavenly joy, so fraternal disagreement afflicts and casts us down—especially when it arises from such causes.

Human laws put an end to human disputes after thirty years [Col. 0701B]. The generation of Christ, which divine law declares to be ineffable, is now, after so many ages, being subjected to rash disputation. You know what Origen, the investigator of beginnings, encountered, and how Nestorius fell when disputing about the natures.

The Magi confess Jesus as Lord in the cradle by their mystical gifts, while priests, with a lamentable question, inquire who he is who was born from the Holy Spirit in a virginal birth. When Jesus cried in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaimed, “Glory to God in the highest.” And now, when every knee bows at the name of Jesus—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—the question of his origin is stirred up.

We, brother, say with the Apostle: “Although we have known Jesus according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way.” Nor can we offensively repeat the matter, since we are commanded to give honor, render fear, and await rather than investigate the one whom we confess as judge.

This is my response in every respect, brother, to your letter.

## XL. LETTER OF POPE LEO TO THE SYNOD OF EPHESUS

In which he urges the assembled bishops to condemn the blasphemies of Eutyches. (C)

[Col. 0701]

[Col. 0701C] Leo, bishop, to the holy synod assembled at Ephesus.

The faith of the most merciful prince, knowing that it pertains greatly to his glory if no seed of error should arise within the Catholic Church, paid this reverence to the divine ordinances: he applied the authority of the apostolic see to bring about their holy purpose, as though he desired the blessed Peter himself to declare what was praised in his confession, when the Lord said, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” The disciples indeed recalled various opinions of different people. But when they were asked what they themselves believed, the prince of the apostles embraced the fullness of faith in a brief statement: “You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.” That is: “You who truly are the son of man are likewise truly the Son of the living God: you, I say, are true in divinity, true in flesh, and, while the distinct properties of both natures remain intact, one in both.”

If Eutyches had believed this intelligently and vigorously, he would by no means have strayed from this path of faith, for which the Lord answered Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” But one is exceedingly alien to the structure of this building if he does not grasp the confession of blessed Peter and contradicts Christ’s Gospel, showing that he has never had any zeal for recognizing [Esc. 4: acknowledging] the truth, and that he was regarded as honorable in vain, since he adorned the gray hairs of old age with no authority of heart.

But since the care even of such people must not be neglected, and since the most Christian emperor wished an episcopal council to be held in a pious and religious manner, so that every error might be abolished by fuller judgment, I sent our brothers Bishop Julian, the presbyter Renatus, and my son Hilary the deacon [Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4: Hilarius], together with Dulcitius the notary, whose faith has been tested by us. They are to attend the holy assembly of your brotherhood in my place and, together with you, establish by common judgment what will be pleasing to the Lord. That is, first, after the baneful error has been condemned, the matter of restoring the man who imprudently erred is also to be considered—provided that, embracing the doctrine of truth, he condemns fully and openly, by his own voice and signature, the heretical opinions by which his ignorance had been entangled. He also professed this in the statement he sent to us, promising that in all things he would follow our judgment.

After receiving the letter of our brother and fellow bishop Flavian, we wrote back to him more fully concerning what he seemed to have reported to us, so that, once this error—which appeared to have been born—had been abolished, there might be throughout the whole world one faith and one identical confession, and so that “in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asterius and Protogenes, in the era stated above.

## XLI. LETTER OF POPE LEO TO THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS

Concerning the second Synod of Ephesus, in which the heresy of Eutyches was assisted by the perverse understanding of certain bishops; hence he urges the same Augustus not to allow the establishment of the ancient faith to be violated by them until the priests of the whole world have been assembled. (C)

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703A] Leo, bishop, and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome, to Augustus Theodosius.

59. In the letters of Your Clemency, which some time ago you sent to the see of the blessed apostle Peter out of love for the Catholic faith, you gave us such confidence that you would defend truth and peace that, in a matter so simple and so well fortified, we thought nothing harmful could arise—especially since those sent to the episcopal council which you ordered to be held at Ephesus were so well instructed that, if the Alexandrian bishop had permitted the writings they brought to the holy synod and to Bishop Flavian to be read to the ears of the bishops, the uproar of all disputes [Note: Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. I, Ger.: “assemblies” (congregationum)] would have been silenced by the clearest manifestation of the pure faith which we have received and hold as divinely inspired. Then neither ignorance would continue to rave, nor rivalry find an opportunity to do harm.

But while private causes were being pursued under the pretext of religion, the impiety of a few committed an act that would wound the entire Church. For we learned—not through an uncertain report, but from our deacon Hilary, a most faithful narrator of what occurred [Col. 0703D: Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4: Hilario]—who barely escaped lest he be forced to subscribe by violence, that very many priests had assembled at the synod. Their number would certainly have benefited the deliberation and judgment if the man who claimed the chief place for himself had been willing to preserve priestly moderation, so that, as custom requires, after everyone had freely expressed his opinion, what accorded with the faith and assisted those in error might be established by a calm and impartial examination.

But we have learned that not all who had assembled were present at the judgment itself. Some were rejected [Bibl. Reg.: expelled], while others were admitted—men who, at the will of the aforesaid priest, surrendered their hands to impious subscriptions, knowing that their own position would suffer if they did not do what was commanded. He issued such a judgment that, while one man was being attacked, the whole Church was assailed. Our representatives, sent from the apostolic see, saw this to be so impious and contrary to the Catholic faith that no oppression could compel them to consent. They steadfastly protested in that synod, as was proper, that the apostolic see would in no way accept what was being established, since truly the entire sacrament of the Christian faith would—God forbid—be cut away from the age of Your Piety unless this most wicked crime, exceeding every sacrilege, were abolished.

Since the devil’s wickedness subtly deceives the unwary, and so mocks the imprudence of certain people through a likeness of piety that it persuades them to accept harmful things as beneficial, remove, we beg you, from the conscience of Your Piety the danger to religion and faith. Grant in divine matters the same equity of your laws that is granted in secular affairs, so that human presumption may not do violence to Christ’s Gospel.

Behold, most Christian and venerable emperor: together with my fellow priests I fulfill toward the reverence due to Your Clemency the duty of sincere love, desiring that you please God in all things—God for whom the Church prays on your behalf, lest we be judged guilty of silence before the Lord’s tribunal. We beseech you before the inseparable Trinity of the one Godhead, which is injured by such an act, since it is itself the guardian and author of your imperial power, and before the holy angels of Christ, to order that everything remain in the condition in which it was before any judgment, until a larger number of priests from the whole world has assembled. Do not permit yourselves to be burdened by another’s sin, for—we must say this—we fear that the indignation of the one whose religion is being shattered may be provoked.

Keep before your eyes, and reverently behold with the full attention of your mind, the glory of blessed Peter, the crowns shared with him by all the apostles, and the palms of all the martyrs. They had no other reason for suffering than the confession of true divinity and true humanity in Christ. Since a few imprudent people now impiously oppose this sacrament, all the churches of our parts and all the priests appeal to Your Gentleness with sighs and tears, asking you to order a general synod to be held within Italy, since our representatives faithfully protested and Bishop Flavian gave them a written appeal. Let it either remove or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further remains doubtful in faith or divided in charity.

The bishops of the Eastern provinces should of course assemble; if any of them, overcome by threats and injuries, have strayed from the path of truth, let them be restored completely through salutary remedies. Let those whose case is more difficult, if they accept better counsel, not depart [Urg., Ger.: withdraw] from the unity of the Church. That this must necessarily be sought after an appeal has been lodged is attested by the decrees of the Council held at Nicaea, which were established by the priests of the whole world and are appended below.

In accordance with your custom and that of your parents, favor the Catholics; grant freedom to defend the faith—a freedom which, with due regard for Your Clemency, no force and no worldly terror can take away. Since we are acting for the cause of the Church and the stability and welfare of your rule [Note: Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Tol. 1, 2, Ger.: “the established order of your reign” (statutum regni vestri)], so that you may possess your provinces in peaceful security, defend the Church’s unshaken condition against the heretics, so that the right hand of Christ may also defend your empire.

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asterius and Protogenes, in the era stated above.

## XLII. LETTER OF POPE LEO TO THE AUGUSTA PULCHERIA

Against the second Synod of Ephesus, so that its errors might be reconsidered in another synod. (C)

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705A] Leo, bishop, and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome, to Augusta Pulcheria.

61. If the letters sent concerning the faith to Your Piety had reached you through our clerics, it is certain that, with the Lord assisting you, you could have provided a sure remedy for the matters [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4: “these matters” (his rebus)] done against the faith. When have you ever failed priests, or Christian religion, or faith? But since those who were sent were unable to reach Your Gentleness to such an extent that only one of them, our deacon Hilary, returned to us by fleeing [Aem., Esc. 4: Hilarius], we judged that the writings had to be sent again. To make our petitions more effective, we have appended copies of the very writings that did not reach Your Clemency, entreating you with more urgent appeals: the more bitter the actions are which, from your royal position, you are bound to oppose, the greater the glory with which you should care for the religion in which you excel, lest the integrity of the Catholic faith be violated by any occasion of human dispute.

For what was believed to require remedy through the peace-restoring measures of the synod assembled at Ephesus has advanced not only to still greater damage to peace, but—what is most grievous—even to the destruction of the faith itself by which we are Christians. Those who were sent, one of whom, fleeing the violence of the Alexandrian bishop who claimed everything for himself, faithfully reported to us the sequence of events, protested in the synod, as was proper, that the actions carried out by force and fear could not prejudice the sacraments of the Church or the creed instituted by the apostles. Nor could they be separated by any injury from the faith which they had brought, fully expounded and arranged, from the see of the blessed apostle Peter to the holy synod [Note: In the other witnesses, except Alv., “prepared” instead of “fully expounded”].

When the bishops requested that this faith be read aloud, its recitation was not admitted. Thus, once the faith that crowned patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs had been removed, the birth according to the flesh of Jesus Christ our Lord and the confession of his true death and resurrection would—horrifying even to say—be dissolved. We therefore wrote about this matter, as best we could, to the most glorious prince and, above all, to a Christian prince. We appended copies of his letter as well, so that he would not allow the faith in which he reigns, reborn by God’s grace, to be corrupted by any novelty.

Bishop Flavian remains in communion with all of us, and no principle permits what has been done—without consideration of justice and against the entire discipline of the canons—to be regarded as valid. Moreover, the synod of Ephesus did not remove the scandal of dissension but increased it. Therefore, concerning a council to be held within Italy, let a place and time be established, with all complaints and prejudgments of both parties suspended, so that everything that produced offense may be reconsidered more carefully. Let the priests who were forced by powerlessness to subscribe return to the peace of Christ without injury to the faith or insult to religion, and let the errors alone be removed.

To obtain this, may your piety, whose faith is fully approved by us and which has always assisted the labors of the Church, deign to support our petition before the most merciful prince—or the embassy entrusted to you by the blessed apostle Peter—so that, before this civil and deadly war grows strong within the Church, he may, with God’s help, grant the opportunity for restoring unity, knowing that whatever his benevolent disposition grants to Catholic freedom will benefit the strength of his empire.

Given on the third day before the Ides of October [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, 4, Tol. 1, 2: the fourth day before the Ides], in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asterius and Protogenes, in the era stated above.

## XLIII. LETTER OF POPE LEO TO THE AUGUSTA PULCHERIA (C)

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705C] Leo, bishop, to Augusta Pulcheria.

Your letter has caused me to rejoice and exult greatly in the Lord. It clearly shows how much you love the Catholic faith and how much you detest heretical error. For it is a most impious heresy and hostile to the Gospel of Truth: it strives not to injure some portion of Christianity, but to tear out the very foundations of the Christian religion. It denies that the eternal Son of the eternal Father took true flesh of our nature from the womb of the blessed Virgin Mother, and it strikes with condemnation those who could not be led away from the evangelical and apostolic faith by any error. It also falsely claims to hold the faith of the Synod of Nicaea, although it is clear that he is alien to it, most glorious Augusta.

Therefore, because divine protection does not abandon its Church—the Lord saying, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age”—the Spirit of God, at the same time and through the same work, has kindled both the concern of Your Clemency and the care of our heart, so that we might desire the same remedies for both of us. What I previously requested I now ask even more urgently, with greater confidence in making my appeal, after receiving the support of your venerable exhortation. I hope that God’s mercy will be present, so that, with Your Clemency cooperating, the disease of this baneful error may be removed, and whatever can salutarily be done through his inspiration and help may be accomplished to the praise of your faith.

For human affairs cannot otherwise be secure unless both royal and priestly authority defend what pertains to the divine confession.
