Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Augustus Valentinian for the seventh time and the most illustrious man Avienus, in the era 488.

## XLIV. EXHORTATORY LETTER OF LEO TO THE PRESBYTERS MARTIN AND FAUSTUS

Concerning the condemnation of the second Council of Ephesus. (C)

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707A] Leo, bishop, to the presbyters Martin and Faustus.

63. There is no doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual endeavors: he assists the actions of those whose minds he stimulates. This has clearly appeared to us through present experience. For, despite the great distances between separated regions, our hearts have reached one decision: that what you desired from us should reach you at the time when your letters [Possibly more correctly: “our letters” (nostrae), rather than “your letters” (vestrae)] were being sent—provided that our writings could be delivered to Your Love. They were sent not only with the authority of the apostolic see but also with the unanimity of the holy synod, which had assembled here in large numbers, so that it might be evident how great a concern we have for the whole Church.

We have exhorted the minds of all the faithful and requested the protection of the most merciful princes for the defense of the faith. We do not doubt that their pious and Catholic minds will provide their assistance and authority to just petitions, so that, with the Lord’s help, the pernicious heresy—long ago condemned by the authority of the holy Fathers, but recently wrongly supported at Ephesus—may be removed.

Meanwhile, let Your Love do everything possible so that all the children of the Church may know what we preach against the impious doctrine according to the evangelical and apostolic teaching. Although we have written fully what has always been and remains the judgment of Catholics, we have now added no small measure of exhortation to strengthen everyone’s minds.

I remember that I preside over the Church under the name of him whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith destroys all heresies, but especially attacks the impiety of the present error. I understand that I may do nothing else than devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is under attack.

Lest our writings have been unable to reach you through some occasion of negligence, we have now decided to send copies of them, so that the preaching of the faith we defend may in no way be withheld from your knowledge.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Augustus Valentinian for the seventh time and the most illustrious man Avienus, in the era stated above.

## XLV. LETTER OF POPE LEO TO THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS

In which he writes that he should acknowledge what is preached concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, and that a universal council should be held in Italy. (C)

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707C] Leo, bishop, to Augustus Theodosius.

64. In all the letters of Your Piety, amid those anxieties which we endure on behalf of the faith, you have given us the greatest hope of security by commending the Council of Nicaea. Indeed, as you have often now written, you do not permit the priests of the Lord to deviate from it.

But lest I appear to have done anything prejudicial to the defense of the Catholic faith, I thought it unwise for the moment to write rashly in either direction concerning the ordination of the man who has begun to preside over the Church of Constantinople. This was not a denial of affection, but an expectation of a manifestation of Catholic truth. May Your Clemency bear this patiently, I ask, so that, when he has shown himself toward the Catholic faith as we desire, we may rejoice more fully and securely in his sincerity.

Lest any sinister suspicion trouble him concerning our disposition, I remove the cause of the entire difficulty. I demand nothing that seems either arduous or doubtful; I invite him only to what no Catholic would reject. Those who have shone before us throughout the world, whether in Greek or Latin, in preaching Catholic truth are well known and manifest. Some even in our own age have joined their knowledge and teaching to theirs, and from their writings an equal and manifold instruction is produced. Just as this instruction destroyed the Nestorian heresy, so it will cut off the error that is now sprouting again.

Let him therefore carefully reread what faith concerning the Lord’s Incarnation was preserved and always preached in the same manner by the holy Fathers. When he sees that the letter of holy memory Cyril, bishop of Alexandria—which he sent to correct and heal Nestorius, refuting his perverse preaching and setting out more clearly the faith of the Nicene definition, and which the archives of the apostolic see received from him—agrees with the thought of those who preceded him, let him also review the acts of the Council of Ephesus. In them, against the impiety of Nestorius, testimonies of Catholic priests concerning the Lord’s Incarnation were inserted and attached by holy memory Cyril.

Let him not disdain to read my letter as well; he will find that it agrees in every respect with the piety of the Fathers. When he learns that this is sought and desired from him for his own benefit, let him wholeheartedly consent to the judgments of the Catholics, and declare to the apostolic see, before all the clergy and the entire people, a sincere profession of the common faith by an entirely unambiguous subscription, so that it may be published to all the priests and Churches of the Lord. Then, with the world pacified through one faith, we may all say what the angels sang when the Savior was born from the Virgin Mary: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

Since we and our blessed Fathers, whose teaching we both venerate and follow, stand in harmony in one faith—as the bishops of all the provinces testify—may the most devoted faith of Your Clemency act so that writings from the bishop of Constantinople, such as those of an approved and Catholic priest ought to be, may reach us as soon as possible. They must clearly and plainly declare that if anyone believes or asserts anything concerning the Incarnation of the Word of God other than what all Catholics and I profess and declare, he should exclude that person from his communion, so that we may rightly extend to him fraternal love in Christ.

So that the effect of these salutary concerns may be brought about more swiftly and fully, with the Lord’s help and through the faith of Your Clemency, I have sent to Your Piety my brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, as well as the presbyters Basilius and Senator, whose devotion has been tested by me. Through them, and through the written instructions we have sent, you may graciously recognize what form our faith takes. If the bishop of Constantinople wholeheartedly consents to the same confession, we may rejoice securely, as is fitting, in ecclesiastical peace, and nothing ambiguous will appear to remain for us to struggle over through perhaps needless suspicions.

But if some disagree with the purity of our faith and with the authority of the Fathers, may Your Clemency grant a universal council within Italy, as the synod that assembled at Rome for this very reason asks together with me. Then all who have fallen through ignorance or fear may assemble and receive the remedies of correction, and no one may any longer mention the Council of Nicaea in such a way as to be found contrary to its faith. This will benefit both the universal Church and your empire, if one God, one faith, and one sacrament of human salvation are held in one confession throughout the whole world.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Augustus Valentinian VII and the most illustrious man Avienus, in the era stated above.

## XLVI. LETTER OF LEO TO THE AUGUSTA PULCHERIA

Concerning what he requested above from Augustus Theodosius. (C)

[Col. 0709]

[Col. 0709B] Leo, bishop, to Augusta Pulcheria.

I rejoice in the faith of Your Clemency, because you graciously devote religious zeal to renewing ecclesiastical peace, which appears to have been disturbed by the dissensions of certain people. This is especially due to your glory: once all the scandals that the enemy had stirred up against the Catholic faith have been removed, there should be one identical confession of truth throughout the whole world. It will be restored more easily and securely if no seeds and no traces of perverse opinions are left behind.

Nevertheless, I must not pass over what belongs to my responsibility: namely, I must acknowledge what is held concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God by the bishop of Constantinople, especially since difficult events preceded his ordination and he ought to have sent us writings of such a kind as would clearly show him to be free from the contamination of this error that recently emerged.

Desiring therefore to have secure concord with him and to extend to him the grace of fraternal love, I have so far delayed writing to him—not denying affection, but awaiting a manifestation of Catholic truth. What I ask is simple and unambiguous: without the labor of lengthy arrangements, let him assent to the letter of holy memory Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, which he himself had sent to Nestorius, in which he both refuted Nestorius’s error and expounded the faith of the Nicene definition; or let him consent to my letter sent to Bishop Flavian of holy memory.

After carefully examining these, let the bishop of Constantinople unhesitatingly acknowledge that he must reject what, in ignorant folly, he dared to define against the pure and unique faith, since my confession and that of the holy Fathers concerning the Lord’s Incarnation agree in every respect and are one. If anyone thinks this should not be followed, he will cut himself off from the structure of Catholic unity, although we desire that everything be restored to its proper state.

To obtain the salutary arrangements more swiftly, I have sent my brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, as well as the presbyters Basilius and Senator, most approved men. They are to offer Your Clemency the form of faith which we preach according to the teaching of the venerable Fathers and, removing the circumlocutions by which truth is usually obscured, show what the approved priests of the entire world have defended concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God.

After divine grace, it is fitting that they be assisted by the holy aid of Your Piety, lest an imprudent course proceed to the disturbance of the whole Church, since, once correction has been applied, all ought to return to harmony in one confession. If some perhaps disagree with it, may Your Clemency order that a universal council of priests be held within Italy, so that, once the art of deception has been removed, it may at last become clear, through deeper deliberation, what must be restrained or healed.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Augustus Valentinian VII and the most illustrious man Avienus.

## XLVII. LETTER OF LEO TO FAUSTUS AND MARTIN [Note: Esc. 4, Tol. 1: Martianum . . . . . . . Martiano] AND THE OTHER PRESBYTERS (C)

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711A] Leo, bishop, to the presbyters and archimandrites Faustus, Martin, Peter, Manuel, Job, Antiochus, Abraham [Note: Esc. 4, Tol. 1, 2: Abraam. Illo; Theodoro], Theodore, Pientius, Eusebius, Elpidius, Paul, Asterius, and Carosus, and to James, deacon and archimandrite.

The cause of the faith, in which Christian salvation consists, compels me to labor with great anxiety, fearing that the perversity which ought to have been cut off at its beginnings may, with the passage of time, become both more persistent and more widespread. For although the most merciful emperor sent us writings showing his concern for the peace of the universal Church, the bishop of Constantinople himself, and those who consecrated him, told us nothing about errors that had been suppressed or renounced beyond what concerned the ordination of the new bishop. It was as though no scandal or offense had arisen in that Church, or as though the merit of the one ordained did not chiefly have to be demonstrated by showing that he taught nothing contrary to the understanding of Catholics.

Lest, as often happens between distant regions, examinations of the truth be prolonged by excessive delays, we sent to the most pious prince our brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, as well as the presbyters Basilius and Senator, most approved men, with sufficient instruction from the authorities of the Fathers. Dearest brothers, we desire that they be assisted in every respect by your diligence and concern, so that the impiety which, in blind audacity, has advanced toward deadly precipices may no longer have power to deceive the simple. We wish even those who have fallen through ignorance or been led astray by error to be assisted through remedies of correction and a more profound medicine.

Therefore, you who are justified by faith, who love Catholic truth, and who have been taught by the Holy Spirit concerning the unique sacrament of human salvation, cooperate with us. Act with as much devotion as you can so that, with falsehood destroyed and the solidity of the faith defended, we may enjoy God’s peace securely throughout the whole world [Note: Aem.: “act throughout with this purpose”].

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Augustus Valentinian for the sixth time and the most illustrious man Avienus.

## XLVIII. LETTER OF LEO TO THE AUGUSTA PULCHERIA

In which he thanks her for destroying the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies by defending the faith. (C)

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711B] Leo, bishop, to Augusta Pulcheria.

67. What we have always presumed concerning the holy mind of Your Piety, we have learned fully through experience: although the Christian faith was attacked by the diverse plots of the wicked, it could not be disturbed while you were present and prepared by the Lord for its defense.

God does not abandon either the sacrament of his mercy or the merit of your labor. Some time ago you drove the insidious enemy of holy religion from the very entrails of the Church, when Nestorian impiety could not defend its heresy, because it did not deceive the servant and disciple of truth, despite the amount of poison that the painted lies of that loquacious man would pour into simple minds.

From this struggle of virtues it came about that, through your vigilance, what the devil had contrived through Eutyches did not remain hidden. Those who had chosen for themselves separate portions of a twofold impiety fell by the single strength of the Catholic faith.

This is therefore your second victory over the destroyed error of Eutyches. If he had possessed any soundness of heart, he could long ago have avoided it, since it had already been struck down in its authors and overthrown in the past, lest he attempt to stir up renewed fires from buried ashes and pass into the company of those whose example he had followed, most glorious Augusta.

It is therefore a pleasure to exult with joy and offer worthy vows to God for the prosperity of Your Clemency, since throughout all the regions of the world in which the Gospel of the Lord is preached he has already bestowed upon you both a double palm and a double crown.

Let Your Clemency therefore know that the entire Roman Church greatly rejoices in all the works of your faith: both because you assisted our embassy with every pious affection, and because you restored Catholic priests who had been unjustly expelled from their churches, and because you caused the remains of holy memory Flavian, an innocent and Catholic priest, to be brought back with due honor to the Church over which he had rightly presided.

In all these things the increase of your glory is multiplied, since you both venerate the saints according to their merits and desire thorns and thistles to be removed from the Lord’s field.

We have learned through the reports both of our representatives and of my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, whom you graciously deign to attest, that certain bishops among those who appear to have consented to impious actions are seeking reconciliation and desiring communion with the Catholics. We therefore grant effect to their desires in such a way that, once they have corrected their conduct and condemned by their own subscription what was wrongly done, communion may be granted through the shared care of our representatives and the aforesaid bishop, for the sake of peace. Both things belong to Christian devotion: that truth should justly restrain the obstinate, and that charity should not reject the converted.

Since we know how much Your Gentleness graciously devotes itself to Catholic priests, we have taken care to inform you that my brother and fellow bishop Eusebius lives with us and shares our communion. We commend to you the Church of which he is bishop, and which, it is said, is being devastated by the man unjustly alleged to have been substituted for him.

We also ask this of Your Piety, though we do not doubt that you will do it of your own accord: that you extend the favor due to them both to my brother and fellow bishop Julian and to the Constantinopolitan clerics who faithfully adhered to Bishop Flavian of holy memory.

Through our representatives we have instructed Your Piety concerning everything that ought to be done or arranged.

Given on the Ides of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius, in the era 489.

## XLIX. LETTER OF LEO TO ANATOLIUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE (C)

[Col. 0713]

[Col. 0713A] Leo, bishop, to Bishop Anatolius.

### I. His faith approved by the writings he sent

68. Let us rejoice in the Lord and glory in the gift of his grace, because, as we have learned from the letters of Your Love and from the report of our brothers whom we had sent to Constantinople, you show yourself to be a follower of evangelical instruction. Thus, from the approved faith of a priest, we rightly presume that the entire Church entrusted to you will have neither the wrinkle of any error nor the stain of any blemish, as the Apostle says: “For I have betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ.”

For the Church is the virgin, bride of one man, Christ. She does not allow herself to be defiled by any error, so that throughout the world there may be for us the integrity of one chaste communion. In this communion we embrace the fellowship of Your Love, and we approve the sequence of the acts we have received, duly fortified, as was proper, by the necessary subscriptions.

Therefore, so that the mind of Your Love might be strengthened by our personal greetings, we sent our sons, the presbyter Carterius and the deacons Patricius and Asclepiades, who had brought your writings to us [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “the writings subscribed”], with our letters after the venerable day of the Paschal feast. We informed you that, as we said above, we rejoice in the peace of the Church of Constantinople, for which we have always maintained such care that we do not wish it to be violated by any deception of heretics.

### II. Those who fell into heresy through fear are to be received if they have converted
Concerning the brothers whom we have learned, both from their letters and from the report of our legates, to desire our communion, because they regret that, in opposition to power and terrors, they did not maintain steadfastness but lent their consent to another’s crime—since fear had so shaken them that, in the condemnation of a catholic and innocent bishop and in the acceptance of detestable depravity, they served with trembling obedience—we approve what was established in the presence and through the agency of our representatives: that, for the time being, they should be content with the communion of their own Churches. But, in consultation with our legates whom we sent and whom we wished to share your concern, let it be arranged that those who, with full acts of satisfaction, condemn their evil deeds, and choose rather to accuse themselves than to defend themselves, may rejoice in the unity of our peace and communion; yet only after they have first condemned, with a fitting anathema, whatever was accepted against the catholic faith.

For otherwise, in the Church of God, which is the body of Christ, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true Pontiff reconciles us in the reality of our nature, and the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us. Although he is seated at the right hand of the Father, he nevertheless performs the sacrament of propitiation in that same flesh which he took from the Virgin, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God and who also intercedes for us.” Nor can our kindness be reproached in any respect when we receive those whom we have grieved to find deceived, once they have made satisfaction. The grace of our communion, therefore, must neither be harshly denied nor granted rashly: for just as it is wholly an act of piety to restore the Lord’s charity to the oppressed, so it is just that everything be charged to the authors of the disturbance.

### III. That the names of heretics are not to be recited at the sacred altar

As for the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius, which are not to be recited at the sacred altar, your Dilection should observe what our representatives stationed there said must be done—something that does not conflict with the honoring of the memory of Saint Flavian and does not turn the hearts of the Christian people away from your Grace. For it is exceedingly unjust and incongruous that those who persecuted innocent and catholic men should be indiscriminately mingled with the names of the saints, when, by refusing to abandon the condemned impiety, they themselves condemn themselves through their depravity, 69 and ought either to be struck down for their perfidy or to labor for pardon.

### IV. Commendation of Bishop Julian and of those clerics who remained faithful to Bishop Flavian

We also wish our brother and fellow bishop Julian, and the clerics who faithfully adhered to Flavian of holy memory, to adhere to your Dilection, so that they may recognize him as present with them in you, since we know that he lives before our Lord through the merits of his faith [Note: Esc. 4: “through faith or merit.”].

We also wish your Dilection to know that our brother and fellow bishop Eusebius, who endured many dangers and labors for the sake of the faith, is meanwhile staying with us and continuing now in our communion. We wish his Church to be protected through your care, so that nothing may be lost in his absence and no one may presume to prejudice him in any matter, until he reaches you with the written communication from us.

And so that either our affection or that of the entire Christian people toward you may be increased, we wish what we have written to your Dilection to become known to everyone,  so that those who serve our God may rejoice in the peace of the apostolic see, which has been confirmed through you. Concerning the remaining matters and persons, your Dilection will be more fully instructed by the letters which you will receive through our representatives.

## L. LETTER OF LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

In this letter he congratulates him on the preservation of the catholic faith. (C)

### [Col. 0715] Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian

Although I previously wrote to Your Piety through the clerics of Constantinople, I nevertheless received great cause for congratulation when I received the letters of Your Clemency through the illustrious prefect of the City, my son Tatianus, because I recognized in you the most zealous devotion to ecclesiastical peace. To this holy desire a fitting justice corresponds: that the state of religion which you wish to exist may also be the state of your realm. For among Christian rulers [Note: Esc. 4: “our Christian rulers.”], when concord is strengthened by the Spirit of God, a twofold confidence is fortified throughout the world, because the progress of charity and faith renders the power of both arms unconquerable. Thus, with God propitiated by one confession, both heretical falsehood and barbarian hostility may together be destroyed, most glorious Emperor.

With hope of heavenly assistance therefore increased through imperial friendship, I venture more confidently to urge Your Piety, for the sake of the sacrament of human salvation, not to allow anyone’s shameless and insolent cunning to make inquiry as though it were uncertain what must be followed. Since it is not permissible to disagree even in a single word from evangelical and apostolic teaching, or to think about the divine Scriptures otherwise than the blessed apostles and our fathers learned and taught, undisciplined and impious questions are now at last being stirred up—questions which the Holy Spirit, through the disciples of truth, long ago extinguished as soon as the devil aroused them in minds prepared for such proceedings.

It is exceedingly unjust that, through the folly of a few, we should be recalled to conjectural opinions and the battles of carnal disputation, as though the matter had been reopened for debate: whether Eutyches thought impiously, and whether Dioscorus judged perversely—the man who allowed himself to condemn Flavian of holy memory and caused the simpler-minded to stumble, so that they might be rolled into the same ruin. Since, as we have learned, many of these have already turned to the remedies of satisfaction and are asking pardon for their irresolute fear, the question is not what faith must be held, but how their petitions should be answered.

Accordingly, through the legation which, God willing, will soon reach Your Clemency, fuller and more timely advice will be offered to your most pious concern, which you deign to have for convening a synod, concerning everything that I judge relevant to the advantage of the case.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of the illustrious man Adelphius.

## LI. LETTER OF LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

In this letter, among other matters, he congratulates the emperor, defender of the catholic faith. (C)

### [Col. 0715] Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian

Both Your Letters, which I received with reverence, and my fellow bishops returning from Constantinople have given me great confidence in writing to Your Clemency. They have shown, not merely by assertions in words but by the actual results of their works, that divine protection is active in you for the defense of the catholic faith. Through this protection not only the condition of the Church but also the strength of your empire is secured, so that you may rightly expect the protection of the one whose truth you honor, glorious Emperor.

For the title of your courage and the fruit of your piety consist in this: that the integrity of my brother Anatolius might be made manifest more quickly; that the revived defender of an error once condemned might have no place in the Church of Christ; that catholic bishops whom the persecution of heretics recently failed to corrupt might be recalled from unjust exiles; and that, when the relics of Flavian of blessed memory had been received with fitting honor, his condemner might acknowledge his own impiety. I trust that other distinguished crowns of victory will also be added to this, so that, just as the Church of Constantinople rejoices in having recovered the liberty of apostolic faith, all the provinces of your realm may likewise glory in having been cleansed from the contagion of the devil’s doctrine.

As I indicated in my previous letters, I have sent my brothers Bishop Lucentius [Note: In all the manuscripts, “Lucensis.” Nevertheless, because the correct name of this bishop is established as Lucentius both in the following letter and in the printed editions and from history, we have not hesitated to write “Lucentius.”] and the presbyter Basilius, who can discharge the duties of my concern. I commend them in every matter that must be undertaken to the favor of Your Piety.

For from the letters of my brother Anatolius and from the report of our representatives I have learned that many of those who, at Ephesus, compelled by the faction of Dioscorus, gave their consent to detestable decrees, are asking pardon for their inconstancy and seeking catholic communion through the satisfaction of correction. The conversion of such men ought not to be neglected, since they are known to have fallen into these things not through their own judgment but through the impulse of an evil usurper, and did not possess freedom of decision in the matter.

Therefore, lest a longer delay weary the desires of those who are repenting, or careless ease rashly and indiscriminately receive certain persons, it has been enjoined upon those sent by the apostolic see that, with the bishop of Constantinople summoned to share in their deliberation, neither the contagions of pestilence be admitted nor the remedies of health be denied. This diligence will, with the Lord’s help, achieve a swift result in correcting everything wickedly done, if Your Piety deigns to lend its aid to the restoration of ecclesiastical peace, so that, while you reign, you may merit to possess the kingdom of God within you, and so that no falsehood may violate the catholic faith, no heresy disturb it, and no one be permitted to abandon evangelical doctrine while enjoying sacerdotal honor.

As Your Clemency recalls, we ourselves also requested that a synod be held. But the necessity of the present time in no way permits the priests of all the provinces to assemble, because those provinces from which they must chiefly be summoned are being troubled by war and do not allow them to depart from their Churches. Therefore, when security has been restored more firmly, with the Lord’s favor, let Your Clemency order that this matter be reserved for a more suitable time. Those whom we have sent will be able to explain this matter more fully, among others, before Your Piety [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4: “I sent.”].

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Adelphius.

## LII. LETTER OF LEO TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

Concerning those who become involved in the errors of heretics through fear or willingness, so that they may be received by the Church through satisfaction, and concerning the names of heretics not being recited at the altar. (C)

### [Col. 0717] Leo, bishop, to Bishop Anatolius

Although I hope that your Dilection is devoted to every good work, nevertheless, so that your diligence might become more effective, it was necessary and appropriate, as we promised, to send my brothers Bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius. Your Dilection should cooperate with them, so that in matters concerning the state of the universal Church nothing may be done doubtfully or sluggishly. While you sit together, having been entrusted with the execution of our decision, everything can be conducted with such moderation that neither the claims of benevolence nor those of justice are neglected, but that divine judgment is considered in every matter without respect of persons.

To ensure that they can preserve this with proper observance, the integrity of the catholic faith must first be maintained. Since the way that leads to life is narrow and difficult in every respect, one must not deviate from its path either to the left or to the right. And since evangelical and apostolic faith overthrows every error—casting down Nestorius on one side and striking down Eutyches and his associates on the other—remember that this rule must be observed:

Those who, as we have learned through your Dilection’s report, are grieved that at that synod—which could neither bear nor deserve the name of synod, and in which Dioscorus displayed his malevolence and Juvenal his ignorance—they were compelled by fear and overcome by terror to consent to the most criminal judgment, and who desire to obtain catholic communion, should receive fraternal peace upon making satisfaction. They must first condemn Eutyches with his doctrine and his associates by an anathema of execration, through unequivocal professions.

As for those who sinned more gravely in this matter, and who on that account claimed for themselves the higher place in the same unhappy synod, so as to burden the simplicity of humble brothers with the prejudices of their arrogance: if they should perhaps come to their senses and, ceasing to defend their action, turn toward condemning their own error, then, if a satisfaction is offered that does not appear rejectable, the matter should be reserved for the more mature counsels of the apostolic see, so that, after everything has been examined and weighed, it may be judged what should be determined concerning their own acknowledgments. Nor, as we have already written, should the name of any such person be recited at the altar in the Church over which the Lord wished you to preside, until the course of proceedings shows what ought to be decided concerning them.

As for the memorandum submitted to us by your clerics, it was not necessary to include in letters what we thought about it, since it was sufficient to entrust everything to the legates; through their report you will be more carefully instructed about all matters.

Therefore, dearest brother, strive to carry out faithfully and effectively, together with these brothers whom we have chosen as suitable agents in so great an affair, whatever is appropriate for the Church of God. The very nature of the case and the hope of divine assistance encourage you to do so, especially since the faith of the most clement rulers is so holy and their devotion so religious that in them we experience not only Christian but also sacerdotal affection. In accordance with the piety by which they glory in being servants of God, they will graciously receive all your suggestions that may benefit the catholic faith, so that through their work Christian peace may be restored and impious error abolished.

If anything further must be deliberated, let a report be sent to us promptly, so that, after the character of the cases has been considered, our concern may determine what must be observed.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Adelphius.

## LIII. LETTER OF LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

Concerning the legation sent in his place to Constantinople for the holding of the Council of Chalcedon. (C)

### [Col. 0717] Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian

I had indeed requested Your Most Glorious Clemency to order that the synod which you judge necessary for restoring peace to the Eastern Church, and which we too have requested, be postponed for a while to a more suitable time, so that those bishops whom fear of hostility detains might assemble with minds freer from every disturbance.

But because you piously place divine affairs before human concerns, and reasonably and religiously believe that it will benefit the strength of your realm if there is no disagreement among the minds of priests and no discord in the preaching of the Gospel, I too do not resist your arrangements, desiring that the catholic faith—which can only be one—may be firmly established in the hearts of all.

From its integrity both Nestorius formerly and Eutyches now have strayed by different paths but with an equal impiety. Their convictions must be utterly abhorred, for they drew them from the foul pools of diabolical falsehood against the pure fountain of the true light.

The earlier synod of Ephesus therefore rightly and justly condemned Nestorius together with his doctrine; and whoever persists in that error cannot belong to the hope of any remedy. But the later gathering in the aforementioned city I cannot call a council, since it is clear that it was conducted for the overthrow of the faith. Your Clemency, about to assist the catholic faithful through love of truth, will annul it by determining otherwise, most glorious Emperor.

Therefore, by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the author and ruler of your realm, I implore and beseech Your Clemency not to allow the faith preached by our blessed Fathers as handed down to them from the apostles to be reconsidered in the present synod as though it were doubtful. Do not allow what was once condemned by the authority of our ancestors to be revived through renewed attempts. Rather, order that the decrees of the ancient Council of Nicaea remain in force, with the interpretation of heretics removed.

Nor should you believe that I am absent from that council, as Your Clemency desired, since in my brothers whom I have sent—namely, Bishops Paschasinus [Note: Aem., Esc. 4, Tol. 1: “Paschasius.”] and Lucentius, the presbyters Boniface and Basilius, and also my brother Julian, whom I wished to join them—my presence too must be regarded as present. With Christ’s help, I trust that they will act so that decisions pleasing to our Lord may be made, with the support of Your Piety’s zeal, which serves both peace and the guardianship of religion and truth.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the illustrious man Adelphius, in the era noted above [Note: Esc. 4: “Era 489.”].

## LIV. LETTER OF LEO TO THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON

In this letter, through his legates, he exhorts the priests of God to arrange everything according to the sacred Scriptures. (C)

### [Col. 0719] Leo, bishop, to the holy synod assembled at Chalcedon

Dearest brothers, because of the charity of our common fellowship I had wished all the priests of the Lord to remain steadfast in one devotion to the catholic faith, and no one to be corrupted by favor or fear of secular powers or to depart from the way of truth.

But since many things often occur that can produce repentance, and God’s mercy surpasses the faults of sinners, and punishment is therefore delayed so that correction may have a place, the deeply religious counsel of the most clement emperor must be embraced. He wished your holy fraternity to assemble for the destruction of the devil’s snares and the restoration of ecclesiastical peace, while preserving the right and honor of the blessed Apostle Peter. Indeed, he invited us by letters to offer our presence to the venerable synod, although neither the necessity of the time nor any established custom permitted this.

Nevertheless, through these brothers—Bishops Paschasinus [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1: “Paschasius.”] and Lucentius, and the presbyters Boniface and Basilius—who have been sent by the apostolic see, let your fraternity regard me as presiding over your synod, not as though my presence were separated from you. I am now present in my representatives, and for a long time I have not been absent from the preaching of the catholic faith. Since you cannot be ignorant of what we believe from ancient tradition, you cannot doubt what I desire.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let the empty unbelief of those who err, which rashly disputes against the faith inspired by God, be utterly rejected and fall silent. Let no one defend what it is not permissible to believe, since, according to evangelical authorities, prophetic voices, and apostolic teaching, the pious and sincere confession concerning the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ has been fully and clearly declared in the letters that we sent to Flavian, bishop of blessed memory.

Since we know that the condition of many Churches was disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that many bishops, because they refused to receive heresy, were expelled from their sees and carried into exile, while others were substituted in the place of those who survived, let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds. Let no one be deprived of his own so that another may use what belongs to him. If, as we desire, all abandon error, no one’s honor ought to perish; rather, the rightful possession of those who labored for the faith must be restored to them with all its privileges.

The specific decrees of the earlier synod of Ephesus, over which the bishop Cyril of holy memory then presided, must remain in force against Nestorius, lest the impiety condemned at that time flatter itself in any respect merely because Eutyches is struck down by a just execration. For the purity of faith and doctrine which we preach in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers condemns and persecutes equally the depravity of Nestorianism and of Eutychianism, together with their authors.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the illustrious man Adelphius.

## LV. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

In this letter he congratulates him on his faith and on what was done at the Council of Chalcedon concerning Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, who at that council wished, contrary to the decrees of Nicaea, to subject the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch to himself through ambition. (C)

### [Col. 0721] Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian

By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the entire catholic Church have been multiplied, when, through the holy and glorious zeal of Your Clemency, the most pernicious error was extinguished, so that our labor might more swiftly reach the desired result—a result which a principality serving God had assisted by both faith and power.

For although, by the power of the Holy Spirit, liberty of the Gospel had to be defended amid every kind of dissension through the service of the apostolic see, the grace of God appeared still more clearly. It granted the world this: that, in the victory of truth, only the authors of the violated faith should perish, while the Church’s integrity was restored to her.

The war which the enemy of our peace had stirred up was so happily broken by the Lord’s right hand fighting for us that, with Christ triumphant, there was one victory for all priests, and, when the light of truth shone forth, only the darkness of error and its defenders were driven away.

For just as, at the very resurrection of the Lord, much security was added for strengthening the beginnings of faith when certain apostles doubted the bodily reality of the Lord Jesus Christ, and by seeing and touching the marks of the nails and the wound of the spear, examining them in their uncertainty, removed uncertainty from everyone through their own doubt, so now also, while the unbelief of certain persons is refuted, the hearts of all who hesitate have been strengthened. What brought blindness to some has advanced all others toward illumination.

Your Clemency rightly and justly rejoices in this work, since you faithfully and properly took care that the snares of the devil should not harm the Churches of the East, but that more effective sacrifices might everywhere be offered to propitiate God, when, through the mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, the confession of peoples, priests, and kings alike became one, most glorious son and most clement Augustus.

When the matters for which the assembly of priests was convened had been settled with a good and desirable outcome, I am astonished and grieved that the spirit of ambition should again disturb the peace of the universal Church, restored by God. Although my brother Anatolius seems necessarily to have provided for himself by abandoning the error of those who ordained him and passing, through salutary correction, into assent [Bibl. Reg.: sensum, “understanding”] to the catholic faith, he nevertheless ought to have taken care that what he is known to have obtained through your benefaction should not be disturbed by any depraved desire.

We, for our part, keeping in view your faith and intervention, and observing that the beginnings of his consecration were unstable according to its authors, wished to be more lenient toward him than strict, so that we might soothe, by applying remedies, all the disturbances which had been stirred up through the devil’s activity. These measures ought to have made him modest rather than immoderate.

Even if he had been lawfully and solemnly ordained with outstanding merits and the best judgment, he could nevertheless receive no assistance against the reverence due to the canons of the Fathers, against the decrees of the Holy Spirit, or against the examples of antiquity.

I speak before a Christian and truly religious, truly orthodox ruler: Bishop Anatolius greatly diminishes his own merit if he desires to increase it by unlawful advancement. Let the city of Constantinople possess, as we desire, its own glory, and, under the protection of God’s right hand, enjoy Your Clemency’s rule for a long time. But secular matters have one order and divine matters another; and no structure will be stable except upon that rock which the Lord placed as its foundation. He who covets what is not due to him loses what is his own.

Let what has already been granted be sufficient: with the help of Your Piety and the assent of my favor, he obtained the episcopate of so great a city. Let him not despise the royal city, which he cannot make an apostolic see, and let him not hope in any way that he can be increased through offenses against others. For the privileges of the Churches established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Council of Nicaea can be shaken by no wickedness and changed by no novelty.

In faithfully carrying out this work, with Christ’s help, I must show persevering service, because an administration has been entrusted to me, and guilt will extend to me if, God forbid, the rules of the sanctions of the Fathers—established at the Council of Nicaea for the governance of the entire Church under the instruction of the Spirit of God—are violated while I connive, and if the will of one brother proves more important to me than the common good of the entire household of the Lord.

Therefore, knowing that Your Glorious Clemency is devoted to ecclesiastical concord and offers a most pious agreement to whatever serves peaceful unity, I ask and earnestly beseech you to withhold your consent from the wicked attempts opposed to Christian unity and peace, and to restrain with salutary firmness my brother Anatolius’s desire, which, if he persists, will harm him himself.

Let him not, in desiring things hostile to your glory and your reign, wish to be greater than his predecessors, but let him be free to shine with as many virtues as he can. He will share in those virtues only if he wishes to be adorned more by charity than stretched out by ambition.

He ought never to have received this conception of wicked desire in the secret chamber of his heart. But when my brothers and fellow bishops who were present in my place opposed it, he should at least have abandoned his unlawful desire because of their resistance. Both the letters of Your Piety and his own writings make clear that the legates of the apostolic see resisted, as was proper, with the most just opposition; thus the presumption, which did not restrain itself even when rebuked, was all the more inexcusable.

It is therefore consistent with your faith and glory that, just as heresy was destroyed through God’s action by you, so every ambition should also be blunted. Do what is both Christian integrity and royal duty: let the aforesaid bishop obey the Fathers and consult the interests of peace. Let him not suppose that he was permitted to do what he rashly presumed to do against the decrees of the canons—namely, to ordain a bishop for the Church of Antioch without any precedent. We refrained from reopening this matter out of love for the restoration of the faith and zeal for peace.

Let him therefore refrain from violating ecclesiastical rules and avoid unlawful excesses, lest, while he attacks peace, he cut himself off from the universal Church. I would rather love him acting irreproachably than see him persist in this presumption, which could separate him from everyone.

My brother and fellow bishop Lucianus, who brought me the letters of Your Clemency together with my son Basilius the deacon, fulfilled the duties of the legation entrusted to him with complete devotion. He should not be judged to have failed in the affair; rather, the cause itself failed him.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. 1, Ger.: “June.”], in the consulship of the illustrious man Herculanus, in the era 490.

## LVI. LETTER OF LEO TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

In this letter he first praises the same bishop for his faith at the Council of Chalcedon; then he rebukes him because he had wished, contrary to the Council of Nicaea, to subject the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch to himself. (C)

### [Col. 0723] [Note: [Col. 0723D] This note is printed at the foot of column 723, but its callout letter, “a,” does not appear in the text. Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Ger., Tol. 1: “they are frequent.”]

### Leo, bishop, to Bishop Anatolius

76 Since, as we desired, the light of evangelical truth has been manifested through God’s grace and the night of the most pernicious error has been driven away from the universal Church, let us rejoice ineffably in the Lord. The labor of the administration entrusted to us has reached its desired result, as the text of your letter also declares: that, according to apostolic teaching, we should all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among us, but that we be perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment.

We congratulate your Dilection on sharing in the devotion to this work, so that your diligence might benefit the correction of abuses and you might purify yourself from every participation in those who deviate. Since your predecessor, Flavian of blessed memory, was expelled because of his defense of catholic truth, it was not without reason believed that those who ordained you appeared to have consecrated someone like themselves, contrary to the decrees of the holy canons.

But God’s mercy was present, directing and strengthening you in this matter, so that you might make good use of evil beginnings and show that your advancement came not from human judgment but from God’s gracious favor. This must truly be understood in that way if you do not lose the grace of this divine gift through another offense.

A catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought to be entangled in no error and violated by no desire. For Holy Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your own will.” One must resist the many enticements and vanities of this world in order to obtain the integrity of true self-restraint. Its first blemish is pride, the beginning of transgression and the origin of sin.

A mind greedy for power knows neither how to abstain from what is forbidden nor how to rejoice in what is permitted. Through an unordered and perverse advance, the excesses of unpunished transgressions increase, and faults multiply—faults that were tolerated because of the effort to restore the faith and the love of concord.

After those beginnings of your ordination that were not without blame, and after the consecration of the bishop of Antioch, which you claimed for yourself contrary to canonical rule, I grieve that your Dilection has also fallen into this: that you attempted to violate the most sacred constitutions of the Nicene canons, as though this time had conveniently presented itself to you because the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of the second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of the third dignity, so that, with these places subjected to your authority, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their own honor.

You have been carried forward by such unheard-of and never-before-attempted excesses that you drag the holy synod, which was assembled through the zeal of the most Christian emperor solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the catholic faith, into an occasion for ambition. You pressure it to grant you its acquiescence, as though what the multitude had illicitly desired could not be refuted, and as though the condition of the Nicene canons, established by the truly holy Spirit, could ever be dissolved in any respect [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except Alv. and Urg., the reading is voluit (“desired”)].

Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the multiplication of assemblies. Let no larger number of priests dare to compare itself with or place itself above those three hundred and eighteen, since the Council of Nicaea was consecrated by such a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more, whatever differs from their constitution is entirely devoid of authority [Note: In the other witnesses except Alv., the reading is atque (“and”)].

These things, therefore, are exceedingly wicked and exceedingly perverse, since they are found to contradict the most sacred canons. 77 This proud exaltation tends toward the disturbance of the entire Church. It wished to misuse the synodal council in such a way that the brothers summoned only for the matter of the faith and having completed the definition of the case that required attention would be led, either by corruption or by terror, to consent to it.

For this reason our brothers sent from the apostolic see, who presided over the synod in my place, reasonably and firmly opposed the unlawful attempts, openly protesting that a presumption of reprehensible novelty should not rise against the institutions of Nicaea.

There can be no doubt about their opposition, since in your letter you yourself complain about them, saying that they wished to obstruct your efforts. By writing this, you in fact commend many of them to me. But you accuse yourself because you refused to obey them while plotting unlawful things, seeking excessively what ought not to be granted and unhealthily desiring what was opposed—things that will never be able to obtain the consent of any of us.

Far be it from my conscience that so wicked a desire should be aided by my efforts. Rather, may it be overthrown by my work and by that of all who do not think lofty thoughts but consent to the humble.

The holy and venerable Fathers who, in the city of Nicaea, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety, established laws of ecclesiastical canons destined to endure until the end of the world—laws that live among us and throughout the whole world in their decrees, and if anything anywhere is presumed contrary to what they established, is annulled without delay—ordained that what has been instituted generally for perpetual benefit should not be altered by any change, and that what has been established for the common good should not be drawn toward private advantage. While the boundaries established by the Fathers remain fixed, let no one reach into another’s right [Note: [Col. 0725D] Bibl. Reg., “let no one unjustly invade another’s right”], but within his own proper and lawful limits, let each exercise himself, as he is able, in the breadth of charity. The bishop of Constantinople can acquire very abundant fruits of this charity if he strives more through the virtue of humility than if he is puffed up by a spirit of ambition.

Do not, brother, be high-minded, but fear, and cease to trouble the most devout ears of Christian princes with wicked petitions. I am certain that you will please them more by modesty than by arrogance. For the written decision made by certain bishops sixty years ago, as you boast, and never transmitted by your predecessors to the knowledge of the apostolic see, lends no support whatever to your attempt to prevail. To that see, whose former fallen and long-collapsed condition you have now wished to apply late and useless remedies, you have sought to extract from the brethren an appearance of consent which their exhausted sense of shame might furnish you to their own injury.

Remember what the Lord threatens the one who causes one of the little ones to stumble, and wisely understand what judgment of God you will have to face, since you do not fear to bring scandal upon so many churches and so many priests. I confess that I am so bound by love for the whole brotherhood that I will agree with no one at all in matters which he demands against it. You can clearly recognize that I oppose your desire with a kindly intention, so that by sounder counsel you may restrain yourself from disturbing the universal Church.

Let not the rights of provincial primacies be overthrown, nor let metropolitan bishops be deprived of privileges established in ancient times. Let nothing be lost from the dignity that belongs to the see of Alexandria, which it earned through the holy evangelist Mark, the blessed Peter’s disciple; and, while Dioscorus falls through the obstinacy of his impiety, let not the splendor of so great a Church be obscured by alien darkness.

Let the Church of Antioch also, in which the Christian name first arose through the preaching of the blessed apostle Peter, remain in the order established by the Fathers, and, placed in the third rank, never make itself inferior. For sees are one thing, and those who preside over them another; and the integrity of each is a great honor to it. Since this integrity does not lose its proper adornments in any place, how much more glorious can it be in the magnificence of the city of Constantinople if, through your observance and defense of the canons of the Fathers, many priests have an example of uprightness?

Writing these things to you, brother, I exhort and admonish you in the Lord that, having laid aside the desire for ambition, you should rather burn with the spirit of charity and be adorned with its virtues, making progress according to apostolic teaching. For charity is patient and kind; it is not jealous, it does not act wrongly, it is not puffed up, it is not ambitious, and it does not seek its own interests. Therefore, if charity does not seek what is its own, how greatly does the one sin who covets what belongs to another?

I wish you to refrain entirely from such things, and to remember the sentence that says: “Hold fast what you hold, lest another receive your crown” [Note: [Col. 0725D] Aem., “lest anyone receive it”]. For if you seek what is not granted you, you will yourself deprive yourself, by your own action and judgment, of the peace of the universal Church.

My brother and fellow bishop Lucian [Note: [Col. 0726D] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “our”], and my son Basil the deacon, diligently attended, insofar as it lay within them, to the matters you had entrusted to them; but justice denied their action its effect [Note: [Col. 0726D] Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. 1, 2, “injustice”].

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculanus.

## LVII. LETTER OF LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

In which he thanks him because peace has been restored to the Catholic Church through the Council of Chalcedon. (C)

[Col. 0725]

[Col. 0725D] Leo, bishop, to the emperor Marcian.

### 78

There is in all the letters of Your Clemency much that gives me cause for rejoicing, since I perceive that, through the great mercy of divine providence, it has been granted to human affairs that you deign, with most devout zeal, to assist the ecclesiastical peace which is preserved only through unity in the preaching of the Gospel, so that the glory of your faith may increase not only through the welfare of the state but also through the advancement of religion, most glorious Augustus.

Therefore I offer ineffable thanks to God, who, foreseeing the scandals of heretics that were to arise, placed you at the summit of imperial power, so that, for the salvation of the whole world, both royal authority and priestly diligence might be active. Since it has been accomplished chiefly through your work that, by the synodal council and the condemnation of the defenders of impious doctrine, sacrilegious error has lost all its strength, it belongs to the palm of that same devotion that the evil which has been crushed in its leaders should also be destroyed in whatever remnants remain.

Your Clemency considers that this can more easily be accomplished if it is made known throughout all the churches that the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon have pleased the apostolic see. There was indeed no reason for doubt about this, since the agreement of all subscribed to the faith that was sent to me according to the form of apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers. Through my brother, Bishop Lucian, I sent writings to your glory and to the bishop of Constantinople which clearly showed that I approved what had been defined concerning the Catholic faith in the aforesaid synod.

But because in those same letters I had reproved the things wrongly attempted on the occasion of the synod, the aforesaid bishop preferred to conceal my congratulation rather than publish his own ambition. Yet great confidence has been bestowed upon me by God working through you, because you have indicated, in the words of Your Piety, that you approved my observance concerning the preservation of the canons of the Fathers. My joy is rightly doubled when I learn that it is most pleasing to you both that the faith of Nicaea should retain its firmness and that the privileges of the churches should remain unimpaired.

Although Your Piety said nothing concerning the splendid work of your faith, I nevertheless indicate that I learned through Julian, a bishop and my brother, specially honored by you and by me, how piously you deigned both to restrain and to instruct the minds of the ignorant monks by your reply. If divine mercy has not wholly abandoned them, let them perceive that they have learned both what they should believe and what they should fear.

Since in every way obedience must be given to your piety and most religious will, I have gladly added my own judgment to the synodal decrees which pleased me concerning the confirmation of the Catholic faith and the condemnation of heretics. May Your Clemency deign to order that this judgment be brought to the knowledge of all priests and churches.

I believe and hope that the grace of God will be present, and will grant so holy a concern of so great a ruler the fullest fruit of its desire, so that, with every occasion for dissent cut away, peace and truth may reign everywhere through apostolic teaching.

Let Your Clemency know that I have especially entrusted my brother, Bishop Julian, with this task: whatever he proves to pertain there to the preservation of the faith, he is to report confidently to Your Piety in my name. For I am certain that, with God’s help, you are sufficient for correcting or defending all these matters.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Apilio [Note: [Col. 0728C] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. 1, Opilio; Ger., Opilione], in the year 411 of the era.

## LVIII. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

Concerning Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, that he should preserve the decrees of his predecessors; and he asks the emperor to send to the Church of Alexandria the letter addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, translated into the Greek language. (C)

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727D] Leo, bishop, to the emperor Marcian.

You have demonstrated, also in the letters brought by my brother and fellow bishop Nestorius, the purity of the Christian faith with which Your Clemency shines, extending to my brother Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, a most just favor, by which he would be made wholly acceptable to me. For anyone to whom Your Piety deigns to give testimony would unquestionably be worthy of approval, even if he were silent.

There is the additional grace that he is also known through his own speech, and that he is a sincere preacher of Catholic doctrine is made clear by his own profession. Therefore, with the fullest affection, I embrace the love of my orthodox brother, and I give thanks to God who, having removed the man who wished to oppose the Gospel and to dissent from the understanding of the holy Fathers, has provided the Church of Alexandria with such a priest—one who agrees in faith and life with its former rulers.

Since he openly professes with all his heart that he embraces the letter which I sent to Flavian of blessed memory against the impious Eutyches, what else does he show himself to be than a disciple of the apostles? For the doctrine of truth remains in its own light, and what is one and divine cannot be different.

I therefore replied to the aforesaid brother as I ought, and admonished him to persevere in his holy zeal. He will undoubtedly be more steadfast if he is also strengthened by the exhortations of Your Clemency. Let him not be frightened by the ignorant dissent of certain persons whom ignorance, through the instigation of a few heretics, has made liable to error. Let what they cannot attain through their own negligence be opportunely brought to their hearing.

And lest the aforesaid man appear to introduce novelties and assert opinions of his own, let the writings of the venerable Fathers who presided over that Church be reread, and let them learn what the blessed Athanasius, what Theophilus, what Cyril, and what the other Eastern teachers thought concerning the incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0729B] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “let them recognize”].

Let them not be deceived by errors sprouting again, errors that were long ago struck down by the power of the Gospel—for nearly all the heresies that have arisen at different times have deviated from the Gospel because they did not understand the mystery of Christ’s bodily birth, passion [Note: [Col. 0729B] From this word leaves are missing in Esc. 4], and resurrection.

We could labor less in refuting heretics if falsehoods destroyed by antiquity did not now disturb inexperienced minds. But, as I have said, the best method of instruction here is that the lines of the Fathers’ teaching should become known to the ears of the people and clergy of Alexandria; and if there are some who despise our writings, at least let them acquiesce in those who agree with us in apostolic understanding.

I shall greatly rejoice in the devotion of my fellow priest in this work, and shall always take pleasure in his unanimity, because fraternal peace is preserved only in one confession of faith.

Since the crafty wickedness of certain heretics is reported to have falsified my letter which I gave to Flavian of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0729B] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Tol. 1, 2: “which I gave to Flavian of blessed memory”], in order that, by changing certain words or syllables, they might claim that I supported the Nestorian error [Note: “receptor,” that is, one who receives or accepts me; Bibl. Reg., “acceptor”], I beseech Your Venerable Clemency to order that the same letter, through my brother Bishop Julian or through those whom Your Piety selects as suitable for this work [Note: [Col. 0730B] Bibl. Reg., “selects”], be translated fully and carefully into the Greek language and conveyed by a trustworthy messenger under the impression of your seal. It should be delivered to the Alexandrian judges, who are to have it read to the clergy and people of that city together with the preaching of the aforesaid bishops, with which my writings also agree.

Thus they may recognize that they must no longer be deceived by the fraud of deceitful men, and may be proved to be sincere disciples of the apostolic see, in which neither Eutyches nor Nestorius has any place, because the universal Church has condemned them, just as it has condemned the other heretics.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studius [Note: [Col. 0730B] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “Stueno”; and in Tol. 2, “Stadio”], in the year 462 of the era.

## LIX. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

In which he writes to him concerning the exile of Eutyches, asking that he be transferred to more remote places, because where he had been placed he was still teaching wicked doctrines. (C)

[Col. 0729]

[Col. 0729C] Leo, bishop, to the emperor Marcian.

What repeated experience has very often taught, namely, that Your Holy Piety’s zeal for the Christian religion perseveres and grows through glorious increases, is confirmed by your faith; and this faith of Your Clemency consoles and strengthens not only me but all the priests of the Lord, since in a most Christian ruler we experience priestly concern.

If the priests of the Eastern regions strive to imitate this concern, neither peace nor the Christian faith will suffer any scandal. Since the bishop of Constantinople is instructed by the present example of Your Clemency toward every advance in piety, if he faithfully obeys your exhortations, he has in me a sincere disposition of favor [Note: [Col. 0729D] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “a sincere disposition”], provided only that he fulfills in his heart what he promises in words.

But if he deliberately chooses what displeases God and Your Piety, then, without detracting from the reverence due to your gentleness, I shall act with all and for all, with your support as well, against the arrogant man with greater freedom and firmness. As must often be said, most glorious emperor, I would rather have him perfected in holy deeds through fraternal charity.

Since you gladly receive my suggestions concerning the tranquility of the Catholic faith, learn from the report of my brother and fellow bishop Julian what has been made known to me: that the impious Eutyches is indeed in exile according to his merits, but that in the very place of his condemnation he is pouring forth, with increasing desperation, many poisonous blasphemies against Catholic integrity, and vomiting forth with greater shamelessness what the whole world abhorred and condemned in him, so that he may deceive the innocent.

I therefore consider it entirely reasonable that Your Clemency should order him to be transferred to more distant and more secluded places. As for his monastery established at Constantinople, where its inhabitants, the monks, must be strengthened more frequently and more fully in evangelical and apostolic teaching, I think it will be beneficial if the man said to be placed over that monastery does not withdraw from the companionship of your honored Julian, the bishop whom I appointed to be there as a watchman for the faith. Through his constant visitation, the spiritual progress of the servants of God who dwell there may be increased.

I rejoice that Your Piety received my petition concerning the feast of Easter in such a way that you immediately sent an agent of the state to Alexandria to remove the error which the decree of Theophilus of holy memory appears to introduce. Concerning this matter, just as you deign to write, order me to know whatever is brought to the attention of Your Piety, so that, concerning the observance which may not be different, the universal Church may recognize what must above all be held.

I ask what I know to be fitting for Your Clemency: protect especially, against every ambush, those whom you know to please both me and Your Gentleness because of their love of the faith, so that the bishop of Constantinople may not have the power to harm them.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studius [Note: [Col. 0731] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “Stueno”; in Tol. 2, “Stadio”], in the year stated above.

## LX. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THE EMPEROR LEO AUGUSTUS

Concerning the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches and their deserved anathema. (C)

[Col. 0731]

[Col. 0731A] Leo, bishop, to the emperor Leo Augustus.

I remember promising, venerable emperor, that in the matter of the faith—concerning which I know Your Clemency to be devoutly concerned—I would send a fuller statement of my humility. With the Lord’s help, I now fulfill that promise on a suitable occasion, so that useful instruction, as I judge, may not be lacking to the holy zeal of Your Piety.

Although I know that Your Clemency has no need of human instruction, and that you have drawn the purest teaching from the abundance of the Holy Spirit, it is nevertheless my duty both to make clear what you understand and to proclaim what you believe, so that the fire which the Lord, when he came, sent upon the earth may, stirred by repeated meditation, grow warm until it burns, and be inflamed until it gives light.

For the Eutychian heresy has attempted to bring great darkness upon the regions of the East and has tried to turn the eyes of the ignorant away from that light which, as the Gospel says, shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. Although Eutyches himself has fallen back into his own blindness, what failed in the author now grows virulent again in his disciples.

Within no long interval of time, the Catholic faith—which is singular and true, and to which nothing can be added or taken away—was attacked by two enemies. Nestorius arose first, and Eutyches second. They wished to bring into the Church of God two heresies opposed to each other, so that each might rightly be condemned by the preachers of truth, because what both men held through varied falsehood was exceedingly mad and sacrilegious.

Let Nestorius, therefore, be anathematized. He believed that the blessed virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being, thereby making one person of the flesh and another of the deity. He did not understand one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but separately and distinctly proclaimed one Son of God and another son of man.

Yet while that unchangeable essence of the Word remains—an essence that is timeless and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit—it was in such a manner that the Word became flesh within the virgin’s womb that, through the ineffable mystery, in one conception and one birth, the same virgin was both the handmaid of the Lord and his mother according to the truth of both natures.

Elizabeth also understood this, as the evangelist Luke declares, and said: “And why is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

Let Eutyches also be struck by the same anathema. Having been carried through the impious errors of the ancient heretics, he chose the third doctrine of Apollinaris, so that, by denying the reality of human flesh and soul, he might assert that our whole Lord Jesus Christ was of one nature, as though the deity of the Word itself had changed into flesh and soul. Thus conception and birth, nourishment and growth, crucifixion and death, burial and resurrection, ascension into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father—from which he will come to judge the living and the dead—would have belonged only to the divine essence, which receives none of these things in itself without the reality of flesh.

For the nature of the Only-Begotten is the nature of the Father; it is also the nature of the Holy Spirit. It is at once impassible and unchangeable: the indivisible unity and consubstantial equality of the eternal Trinity.

Therefore, if an Eutychian departs from the perversity of Apollinaris, lest he be convicted of believing the deity to be passible and mortal, yet dares to say that the incarnate Word—that is, the Word and the flesh—has one nature [Note: [Col. 0731D] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., “to pronounce”], he plainly passes into the madness of Valentinus and Manichaeus. He believes, in a fictitious manner, that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, performed everything, and that no human body was in him, but that only a phantasmal appearance of a body was visible to the eyes of those who looked upon him.

Since the Catholic faith has long rejected these impious falsehoods, and since the sacrileges of other assertions have already been condemned by the concordant judgments of the blessed Fathers throughout the world, there is no doubt that we proclaim and defend the same faith which the holy Council of Nicaea confirmed, saying:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, Only-Begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate and became human, suffered [Note: [Col. 0731D] Esc. 3, “suffered under Pontius Pilate”], and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.”

In this confession it is most clearly contained what we also confess and believe concerning the Lord’s incarnation: that, for the restoration of the human race to salvation, he did not bring true flesh belonging to our weakness down from heaven with him, but assumed it in the womb of the virgin mother [Note: [Col. 0732D] In certain codices, the following title is inserted between this and the next paragraph: “That in the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ a twofold nature, of deity and humanity, must be affirmed”].

[Col. 0733A] Therefore, whoever is so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that, from the time of the incarnation, he denies the reality of human flesh in the Word of God, let him show on what grounds he claims for himself the Christian name, and in what way he agrees with the Gospel of truth. Was flesh without deity, or deity without flesh, born from the blessed Virgin?

For just as it cannot be denied, as the evangelist says, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” so it cannot be denied, as the blessed apostle Paul proclaims, that “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.”

But what reconciliation could there be by which God would be reconciled to the human race unless the mediator between God and humanity assumed the cause of all? And how could he fulfill the truth of mediation unless he who is equal to the Father in the form of God became a participant in our condition in the form of a servant, so that the bond of death contracted through one transgression might be dissolved by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death?

The shedding of Christ’s blood for the unjust was so rich as a price that, if the whole multitude of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would remain held by the bonds of the devil, because, as the Apostle says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.”

And although those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn to righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the debt of slavery.

What hope, then, do those leave themselves in the protection of this mystery who deny the reality of a human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed.
