Who is it, as the Apostle says, “who gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma”? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal High Priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

Although the death of many saints has been precious in the sight of the Lord, the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful arose examples of endurance, not gifts of righteousness.

For each person’s death was singular, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end. Only one among the children of humanity, our Lord Jesus Christ, truly the spotless Lamb, existed in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised.

Concerning them he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.”

For true faith justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous. It draws human beings into participation in his humanity and obtains salvation in him in whom alone a human being finds himself innocent. Through the grace of God, humanity is free to glory in the power of the one who, in the lowliness of our flesh, engaged the enemy of the human race and granted his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

Therefore, although in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and human being, there is one person of the Word and the flesh, which inseparably and indivisibly possesses actions common to both, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood. Through the contemplation of sincere faith, it must be discerned toward what the lowliness of the flesh is raised and toward what the height of the deity inclines; what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither conceive nor give birth; and without the reality of flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not lie there.

Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not adore the child revealed by the guiding star; and without the reality of flesh, the child would not be ordered to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.

Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him”; and without the reality of flesh, John would not testify, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not occur; and without the reality of flesh, food would not be necessary for one who was fasting, nor sleep for one who was weary.

Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father; and without the reality of flesh, he would not likewise say that the Father was greater than he. Catholic faith embraces and defends both, believing, according to the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, that the one Christ, the Son of the living God, is both human and the Word.

Although, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the virgin’s womb, there was never any division between the two forms, and although through all bodily growth the actions of the entire period belonged to one person, we nevertheless do not confuse by any mixture the things done inseparably. Rather, from the character of the actions we perceive what belongs to which form.

Let these hypocrites, therefore, who refuse to receive the light of truth with blind minds, say in what form Christ the Lord of majesty was fastened to the wood of the cross. What was it that lay in the tomb? When the stone of the monument had been rolled away, what flesh rose on the third day? In what form did he rebuke certain disciples after his resurrection and refute the hesitation of those who doubted when he said:

“Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have”?

And to the apostle Thomas:

“Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and my feet, and do not be unbelieving but believing.”

By this manifestation of his body he was already destroying the lies of the heretics, so that the whole Church, which was to be instructed in the teachings of Christ, would not doubt that it must believe what the apostles had received to proclaim.

But if, in the midst of so great a light of truth, heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness, let them show from where they promise themselves the hope of eternal life, to which no one can attain except through the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ.

For, as the blessed apostle Peter says: “There is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved,” nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a ransom for all.

And as the blessed apostle Paul proclaims, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.

Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

Since, then, the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and in him there is altogether one and the same person of true deity and true humanity, we understand the exaltation by which, as the Teacher of the Gentiles says, God exalted him and gave him the name that surpasses every name to belong to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification.

For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction in essence, no difference in majesty; nor had anything departed from the Word through the mystery of the incarnation that would have to be restored to him as a gift from the Father. But the form of a servant, through which the impassible deity fulfilled the sacrament of great piety, is the humility of humanity raised up into the glory of divine power. In such unity, from the very conception in the Virgin, deity and humanity were joined together that neither divine things were done without the human, nor human things without God.

Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who is eternally equal to God is said to have been exalted, because, with the unity of the person remaining inseparable, one and the same is wholly the Son of man because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of the one deity he shares with the Father. For whatever Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which what it did not possess was bestowed. For according to the power of his deity, the Son also possesses without distinction everything that the Father has; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself likewise bestowed in the form of God.

For according to the form of God, he and the Father are one; but according to the form of a servant, he did not come to do his own will but the will of him who sent him. According to the form of God, just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself. According to the form of a servant, his soul is sorrowful even unto death. According to the form of God, he is known to have bestowed life upon the dead. And he himself is, as the Apostle proclaims, both rich and poor: rich, because, as the Evangelist says:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

But poor, because for our sake the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

And what is his self-emptying, or what is his poverty, except the taking on of the form of a servant, through which, while the majesty of the Word was veiled, the dispensation of human redemption was accomplished? For since the original bonds of our captivity could not be loosed unless there existed a man of our race and of our nature, whom the sentence of sin did not hold, and who would erase the deadly bond with his spotless blood, as had been divinely ordained from the beginning, so, when the fullness of the predetermined time had come, it was accomplished that the promise, signified in many ways, should attain the long-awaited fulfillment, and that what had always been announced by continuous testimonies could not remain uncertain.

But the impiety of the heretics reveals that they are involved in great sacrilege when, under the pretext of honoring the deity, they deny the truth of human flesh in Christ, and think it should be devoutly believed that what saves is not true in our Savior. For in this way, according to the promise [the source reads: *secundum - promissionem*] extending through all the ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ, so that unless the Word had deigned to become flesh, no flesh could have been saved.

For the entire sacrament of the Christian faith is disfigured by a great darkness, as the heretics wish, if the light of truth is thought to have lain concealed beneath the lie of a phantom. Therefore no Christian should be ashamed of the truth of our body in Christ, because all the apostles and the disciples of the apostles, and all the distinguished teachers of the Churches who were worthy to attain either the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession, shone in the light of this faith, proclaiming everywhere with harmonious judgments that in the Lord Jesus Christ one person of deity and flesh must be confessed.

But by what likeness of reasoning, by what passage of the divine books, does heretical impiety think itself supported when it denies the truth of Christ’s body, although neither the Law has ceased to testify to it, nor prophecy to announce it beforehand, nor the Gospels to teach it, nor Christ himself to demonstrate it? Let them search through the entire sequence of the Scriptures—not in order to obscure the true light, but to flee their own darkness—and throughout all the ages they will find the truth shining forth, so that they may see that this great and marvelous sacrament was believed from the beginning and completed at the end.

Since no part of the sacred writings is silent concerning it, it is enough to set forth certain harmonious signs of the truth, by which the diligence of faith may be directed into the most splendid breadth and, in the sincere light of understanding, may discern this: Christians should not be ashamed of the Son of God, who unceasingly professes himself the Son of man and a man, but should glory in him with the utmost steadfastness.

So that your Piety may recognize that we agree with the preaching of the venerable Fathers, I have thought that some of their statements ought to be appended to this discourse. If you deign to attend to them after they have been read, you will find that we proclaim nothing other than what our holy Fathers taught throughout the world, and that no one differs from them except impious heretics.

Having briefly touched on these matters, therefore, most glorious and venerable Emperor, recognize that our preaching too is united with the faith divinely inspired in you, and that in no respect do we differ from evangelical and apostolic teaching or from the creed of the Catholic confession. For, as the blessed Apostle Paul teaches, great is the sacrament of piety:

> He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.

What, then, is more useful to your salvation, or more fitting for your piety, than that by your imperial ordinance you should provide for the peace of the Churches of the Lord, defend God’s gifts in all who are subject to you, and in no way allow the ministers of the devil, through the devil’s envy, to rage to the destruction of anyone? Thus, having excelled in a temporal kingdom in this age, you may deserve to reign with Christ eternally.

[Note: In certain manuscripts, between this and the following paragraph is written: “There follow hereafter testimonies excerpted from the books of the Catholic Fathers concerning the matter written above, collected by Pope Leo and addressed to Emperor Leo.”]

## Testimonies of the Holy Fathers

### Saint Hilary, Bishop and Confessor of Poitiers

From Book Two *On the Faith*, among other passages:

> This, then, is the one immovable foundation, this is the one blessed rock of faith confessed by the mouth of Peter: “You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God”—a confession sustaining as many proofs of truth as questions of perversity and accusations of unbelief may raise. The rest belongs to the dispensation of the Father’s will. The Virgin, the birth, and the body, and afterward the cross, death, the underworld, and our salvation: these are the work of God. For the Son of God was born of a virgin and of the Holy Spirit for the sake of the human race, the Holy Spirit himself ministering to him in this work, while he—that is, God—overshadowed it with his own power and established for himself the beginnings and origins of a body, [Note: Tol. 2, Ger.: “consecrated.”] so that, having become man from a virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh; and through the fellowship of this union, the body of the whole human race might be sanctified in him. Thus, just as all were established in him through his willing to be corporeal, so he himself might again be extended into all through what is invisible in him.
>
> Therefore the image of the invisible God did not reject the humiliation of human origin, and through conception, birth, crying, and the cradle he passed through all the indignities of our nature. What, then, worthy of such an act of condescension will be returned by us? The one Only-Begotten God, whose origin from God cannot be told, grows within the body of a holy Virgin in the form of a human body. He who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth; and he at whose voice archangels and angels tremble, and heaven, earth, and all the elements of this world are shaken, is heard crying like an infant.
>
> He who is invisible and incomprehensible, whom sight, sense, and touch cannot govern, is wrapped in swaddling clothes. If anyone recalls these things as unworthy of God, he will confess himself subject to a far greater benefit, since these things accord so little with the majesty of God. He did not need to become man, through whom man was made; but we needed God to become flesh and dwell among us—that is, through assuming one flesh, to dwell within the whole of flesh.
>
> His humility is our nobility; his humiliation is our honor. What he is—God abiding in the flesh—we, in turn, renewed from the flesh, are in God.

The same author, in Book Nine, among other passages:

> Clearly he does not know his own life who does not know Christ Jesus to be true God and likewise true man; and it is a matter of the same danger either to deny Christ Jesus as the Spirit who is God or as flesh of our body. “Therefore everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.”
>
> This was spoken by the Word made flesh, and the man Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, was teaching. He himself was constituted mediator for the salvation of the Church; and by that very sacrament of mediation between God and human beings, he exists as one, since in him, from the natures united into one, the same reality belongs to both natures. Yet neither nature is lacking in either, lest perhaps God should cease to be man by being born, and man should not again be God by remaining so.
>
> This, then, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess the Word and flesh; neither to be ignorant that God is man, nor to ignore that the flesh is the Word.

The same author, in the same book, among other passages:

> The Only-Begotten God, therefore, born man from a virgin, and destined, in the fullness of time, to raise man in himself to God, followed throughout the pattern of the Gospel’s language, so that he might teach that he should be believed to be the Son of God and might urge that he be proclaimed the son of man. As man, he spoke and did all that belongs to God; then, as God, he spoke and did all that belongs to man. Yet in that very discourse concerning both kinds, he never spoke except with an indication both of man and of God.

Elsewhere in the same little book, among other passages:

> Here, then, heretics find an opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant: they falsely claim that what was spoken by him according to man was spoken according to the weakness of the divine nature. And because one and the same person speaks everything that he speaks, they insist that he spoke everything about himself.
>
> We certainly do not deny that all this utterance belongs to him who remains in his own nature. But since Jesus Christ is both man and God, and neither, when he was man, was he then for the first time God, nor, when he was man, was he not also God, nor, after becoming man, was he, while in God, not wholly man and wholly God, the mystery of his sayings must be one and the same as that of his nature.
>
> When, therefore, in time you distinguish man from God in him, distinguish also the speech of God and of man according to time. And when you confess God and man in time, judge also the words of God and of man according to time. But when from man and God you again understand the time of the whole man and now the whole God, apply whatever was said for the demonstration of that time to the appropriate time.
>
> Thus, when one thing is God before man, another is man and God, and another is the whole man and the whole God after man, do not confuse the sacrament of the dispensation according to its times and kinds. For according to the quality of the kinds and natures, it was necessary that his speech in the sacrament of man should be one kind before he was born, another while he was still destined to die, and another once he was eternal.
>
> Jesus Christ, therefore, remaining what he is, and born man of our body, spoke for our sake according to the custom of our nature, yet did not omit that he belongs to his own nature, which is God. For although in birth, passion, and death he accomplished the reality of our nature, he nevertheless performed all these realities by the power of his own nature.

And the rest.

Elsewhere in the same book, among other passages:

> Do you see how God and man are proclaimed, so that death is attributed to man, but the raising of the flesh to God? Not, however, as though one is he who died and another he through whom the dead man rises. For Christ died with the flesh stripped away, and again the same Christ, stripping himself of flesh, raises Christ from the dead. Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of man in the death. And although both things were accomplished according to their respective natures, remember that the one Christ Jesus is he who is both.

A little later:

> These things, then, had to be demonstrated by me briefly, so that we might remember that the form of both natures is treated in the Lord Jesus Christ, because he who, remaining in the form of God, assumed the form of a servant did not in any way lose his divinity.

[Col. 0739B]

### Saint Athanasius, Bishop and Confessor of the Church of Alexandria

To Epictetus, Bishop of Corinth:

> How, then, did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt? The Lord who proceeded from the Virgin Mary is indeed, in substance and nature, the Son of God; but what he is according to the flesh is from the seed of David and from the flesh of holy Mary.

### Saint Ambrose, Bishop and Confessor of the Church of Milan

From Book Two *On the Faith*, which he sent to the Emperor Gratian, among other passages:

> Therefore, when we read that the Lord of majesty was crucified, let us not think that he was crucified in his own majesty, but because the same one is God and the same one is man—God through divinity, man through the assumption of flesh. Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, is said to have been crucified because, sharing in both natures, that is, the human and the divine, he underwent suffering in the nature of man. Thus the Lord of majesty who suffered and the Son of man who descended from heaven, as it is written, are indiscriminately said to be one and the same.

Elsewhere in the same book, among other passages:

> Let empty disputes about words, then, be silent, because, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of power. Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh. The Son of God speaks as one in both, because both natures are in the same one; and although the same person speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner.
>
> Consider in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of man. As God, he speaks divine things, because he is the Word; as man, he says human things, because he spoke in that substance.

From the same author’s book *On the Incarnation of the Lord Against the Apollinarists*:

> But while we refute these people, others arise who say that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one nature. What underworld has vomited forth such sacrilege? The Arians are now more tolerable, since through these people the strength of their perfidy grows, so that they may assert with greater insistence that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of one substance, because these people have attempted to say that the Lord’s divinity and flesh are of one substance.

Further on:

> These people frequently declare to me that they hold the teaching of the Council of Nicaea. But in that teaching our Fathers said not that the flesh, but that the Word of God, is of one substance with the Father; and they confessed that the Word proceeded from the Father’s substance, but that the flesh was from the Virgin. How, then, is the name of the Council of Nicaea invoked as a pretext, and new doctrines introduced that our ancestors never held?

And the rest.

The same author, to Bishop Sabinus, among other passages:

> Therefore the Apostle beautifully used a repetition of the same word when he said of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”
>
> What does “in the form of God” mean except in the fullness of deity, in that expression of divine perfection? Therefore, since he was in the fullness of divinity, he emptied himself and took on the fullness of human nature and perfection. Just as nothing was lacking in God, so nothing was lacking for the completion of man, so that he might be perfect in both forms.
>
> Hence David also says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.”
>
> The Apollinarist is trapped and has nowhere to turn; he is enclosed in his own nets. For he himself had said: “He took the form of a servant,” not “the servant spoke.” I ask again, then: What does “in the form of God” mean? He answered: “In the nature of God.” For, says the Apostle, there are those who are not gods by nature.
>
> I ask: What does “taking the form of a servant” mean? Without doubt, the perfection of human nature and condition, as I said, so that he might be in the likeness of human beings. And he aptly said not “the likeness of flesh” but “the likeness of human beings,” because he was the same in flesh; but because he alone was without sin, while every human being is in sin, he appeared in human form.
>
> Hence the prophet also says: “And he is a man, and who knows him?” A man according to the flesh, but beyond man through divine action.
>
> Finally, when he touched the leper, he appeared to be a man; but he was beyond man when he cleansed him. And when he wept over Lazarus who had died, he wept over the dead man as a man; but he was beyond man when he commanded the dead man bound to come out on his feet. He appeared to be a man when he hung on the cross; but he was beyond man when, after the tombs had been opened, he raised the dead.

### Saint Augustine, Bishop of the Church of Hippo

To Dardanus, among other passages:

> Do not doubt, therefore, that the man Christ is now there, from where he will come. Recall this carefully and hold faithfully to the Christian confession: he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there and nowhere else to judge the living and the dead. The angelic voice bears witness to this, saying that he was seen going into heaven—that is, in the same form and substance of flesh to which he certainly gave immortality without taking away its nature.

The same author, in his letter to Volusianus, among other passages: [Note: In the others, except Alv., “Valerianum.”]

> Now he appeared as mediator between God and human beings in such a way that, joining both natures in the unity of one person, he both exalted what was customary by what was extraordinary and tempered what was extraordinary by what was customary.

The same author, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, among other passages:

> What, then, heretic? Since Christ is God and man, he speaks as man, and you bring accusations against God? He commends the human nature in himself; do you dare to deform the divine nature in him?

And again, further on:

> Let us recognize the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet taken together they are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. For just as one man consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man. Accordingly, Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh.
>
> We confess Christ in all these things and Christ in each of them. Who, then, is he through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus—but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus—but in the form of a servant.

The same author, as above:

> Who was not abandoned in the underworld? Christ Jesus—but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb for three days, destined to rise? Christ Jesus—but in the flesh alone. Christ is therefore named in each of these particulars; yet all these things together belong not to two or three, but to one Christ.
>
> Therefore he said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father.” For human nature should rejoice because it was assumed by the Only-Begotten Word in such a way that [Note: *Bibl. Reg.*: “our mortal nature might be established immortal in heaven”] it was established immortal in heaven; and thus earth was exalted, so that incorruptible dust might sit at the right hand of the Father.

### Saint John, Bishop and Confessor of Constantinople

From the homily *On the Cross and the Robber*:

> Let us see why he will come with the cross. Clearly, so that those who crucified him may feel the blindness of their madness, and therefore the sign of their madness is carried. Hence the prophet says: “Then the tribes of the earth will mourn when they see the accuser and recognize their sin.”
>
> And what is surprising if he will come bearing the cross, when the wounds of his body themselves also show it? For then, he says, “they will see him whom they pierced.”
>
> And just as after the resurrection he wished to refute Thomas’s disbelief, showed him the places of the nails, displayed the wounds of his side, and said, “Put your hand here, and see that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me having,” so then also he will show the wounds and display the cross, to show that he is the one who had been crucified.

The same author, from the homily *On the Lord’s Ascension*:

> For just as, when two people are separated by a quarrel, one person placed between them dissolves the dispute and discord of those who are contending, so Christ also acted. God was justly angry with us, and we despised him while he was angry; we avoided the merciful Lord. Christ placed himself between us, joined the two natures, and himself endured the punishment that threatened us.

The same author, in the same homily, among other passages:

> Christ therefore offered the first fruits of our nature to the Father. The Father marveled at the gift that had been offered, because such dignity offered it and no stain defiled what was offered. For he received the offering with his own hands, made it share in his own seat, and, what is more, placed it at his right hand.
>
> Let us recognize who it is that heard: “Sit at my right hand”; what nature it is to which he said: “Be a sharer of my seat.” It is that nature which heard: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

The same author, in the same homily, among other passages:

> What language shall I use, what words shall I find to say it? I cannot discover them. Nature that is fragile, nature that is despised and shown to be inferior to all things, has conquered all things, surpassed all things, and today has deserved to be found higher than all things.
>
> Today the angels have begun to receive what they had long desired; today the archangels have been able to behold what they had long wished to see: our nature shining with immortal glory in the Lord’s seat.

### Saint Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria

From the Easter letter that he sent throughout Egypt:

> The witness to this is the one who says: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless”; and the prophets, imploring Christ’s help, say: “Lord, incline the heavens and come down”—not so that he might change the place in which all things are, but so that for our salvation he might assume flesh of human frailty.
>
> The Apostle Paul joins in the same song: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that we might be enriched by his poverty.” He came to earth, but, having come forth from the Virgin’s womb, which he sanctified, he appeared as man, confirming by his dispensation the interpretation of his name, Emmanuel—that is, “God with us.” In a marvelous manner he began to be what we are and did not cease to be what he was, assuming our nature in such a way that he did not lose what he himself was.
>
> For although John writes, “The Word became flesh”—that is, in other words, “God became man”—the Word was not changed into flesh, because he never ceased to be God. To him the Holy Spirit also says, “But you are the same,” and the Father bears witness from heaven and says, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Thus, even after becoming man, he is said in our confession to remain what he was before he became man, while Paul proclaims the same thing with us: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
>
> By saying “the same,” he shows that Christ did not change his former nature or diminish the riches of his divinity, because, having become poor for our sake, he had assumed the complete likeness of our condition.

The same author, in another Easter letter against Origen, among other passages:

> The one Son, mediator between the Father and us, neither lost his equality with the Father nor was separated from our fellowship. The invisible God and visible man, hidden in the form of a servant [*Bibl. Reg.*: “in the form of a servant”], and the Lord of glory, is confirmed by the confession of believers.
>
> For the Father will not deprive him of the name of his nature after he became man and poor for our sake, nor did he call him by another name when he was baptized in the Jordan, but called him the Only-Begotten Son: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
>
> Nor was our likeness changed into the nature of divinity, nor was divinity changed into the likeness of our nature.

### Saint Gregory, Bishop of Nazianzus

From the homily *On the Epiphany*, among other passages:

> When God, therefore, had proceeded from the Virgin in the human nature he had assumed, existing as one from two mutually contrary things, flesh and spirit, one element is assumed into God, while the other bestows the grace of deity.

Further on:

> He was indeed sent, but as man, for his nature was twofold. Hence he also became weary from the journey, hence he hungered and thirsted, became sorrowful, and wept according to the law of the human body.

### Saint Basil, Bishop of Cappadocia

> When, therefore, we see certain things in Christ so human that they seem in no way different from the common frailty of mortals, and others so divine that they belong to no one else except that ineffable nature of deity, the narrowness of the human intellect is held back. Struck by the stupor of such great wonder, it does not know where to turn, what to hold, or where to direct itself.
>
> If it thinks him a man, it sees him returning from the dead after conquering the kingdom of death, bearing away its spoils. Therefore he must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same person the truth of both natures may be demonstrated in such a way that neither anything unworthy or improper is thought about that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, are the things that happened judged to have been deceived by false appearances.

### Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria

> He was called man, although by nature he is God, the Word of God the Father, because in the same way as we he shared in blood and flesh. For he appeared on earth without losing what he was, but assuming the nature of humanity in its complete reality.

The same author, in the book called *Scholia* [Note: In certain manuscripts, *Golia*; in others, *Colia*: an error in all of them]:

> He is therefore one and the same: before the incarnation, true God; and in humanity he remained what he was, is, and will be. We must not distinguish one Lord Jesus Christ as man separately and as God separately, but we say that Jesus Christ is one and the same, not ignoring the differences of the natures but preserving them unconfused among themselves.

The same author, as above:

> For it is clearly understood as though one thing dwells in another—that is, the divine nature in the human nature—without suffering mixture or change, so that it would become what it was not. For whatever is said to dwell in another does not itself become like that in which it dwells; rather, one thing is understood to be in another.
>
> But in the person of the Word, the diversity of the natures indicates only the distinction between them for us. One Christ is understood from both. Therefore he says that the Word dwelt in us, preserving the lack of confusion, as I said above. For he knows that there is one Only-Begotten Son, made flesh and man.

The same author, in the work addressed to Nestorius:

> The holy and great synod says, therefore, that he who was naturally born from God the Father, the Only-Begotten Son, true God from true God, light from light, through whom and with whom the Father made all things—this same one descended, became incarnate and man, suffered, rose on the third day, and again ascended into heaven.

[Col. 0743D]

We ought to follow these words; we ought to obey these doctrines, considering what it means that the Word of God became incarnate and became man. For we do not say that the nature of God was changed or transformed into flesh, nor that it was transformed entirely into a man composed of soul and body. Rather, we say that the Word joined to himself flesh animated by a rational soul and became man substantially, ineffably, and irreproachably, and was also called the Son of man—not by bare will alone, nor by the assumption of a person alone, but because different natures came together into one.

Yet one Christ and Son came from both, the difference between the natures not being emptied or removed by the union, but because divinity and humanity together made for us one Lord, Christ, and Son through that mysterious and ineffable union into unity. Thus he who was born from the Father before all ages is also said to have been carnally begotten from a woman [Urg.: “from a mother”]—not because his divine nature took its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor because he himself needed to be born a second time after the birth he had from the Father. For it is foolish and senseless to say that he who is coeternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to exist.

Rather, because for our sake and for our salvation he joined a human nature to himself and proceeded from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born carnally. For a common man was not first born from the holy Virgin, and only afterward did the Word dwell in him; rather, in the very womb and virginal uterus he joined himself to the flesh, underwent carnal generation, and made the birth of his flesh his own birth.

Thus we say that he suffered and rose again—not because God the Word suffered in his own nature or received the piercing of nails or other wounds, for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering, but because the body that became his own suffered. Therefore he himself is said to have suffered all these things for us. For God, who could not suffer, was present in the body that suffered.

In the same way we understand his death. The Word of God, life and giver of life, is naturally immortal and incorruptible; but because, according to Paul’s words, his own body by the grace of God tasted death for everyone, he himself is therefore said to have suffered death for us—not because he experienced death in himself, insofar as his nature is concerned [Note: *Bibl. Reg.*: “not because he himself experienced death”], for it is madness either to say or to think this, but because, as we said above, his flesh tasted death.

In the same way, when his flesh rose, we speak of his resurrection—not because it had fallen into corruption, far from it, but because his body rose. Thus we confess one Christ and Lord, not worshiping a man together with the Word, as though a kind of division were introduced, but worshiping one and the same, because his body is not alien to the Word, with whom it also sits beside the Father.

Nor do we say this as though two sons were sitting beside the Father, but one Son with the flesh through unity. For if we choose to understand such a substantial union as either impassible or somehow dishonorable, we fall into the claim that there are two sons. It is necessary to distinguish and say that a man was honored separately by the title of Son, and again that the Word, who is from God both in name and in truth, is the Son of God; but we must not distinguish one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons.

For this does not support the right rule of faith, even though some people assert some kind of union of persons. Scripture did not say that the Word of God assumed the person of a man for himself, but that he became flesh. This means that the Word of God, like us, shared in flesh and blood, made our body properly his own, and proceeded as man from a woman—not casting away or laying aside either his deity or that birth which he had from the Father, but remaining, even in the assumption of flesh, Lord of what he was.

The rule of right faith proclaims this everywhere; we find that the holy Fathers held this meaning. For this reason they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin *Theotocon*—“God-bearer”—not because the nature and deity of the Word took its beginning from the holy Virgin, but because from her was born that sacred body, animated by a rational soul, to which the Word of God was substantially united and which is said to have been born carnally.

## LXI. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THURIBIUS, BISHOP OF ASTORGA (C)

[Col. 0745]

[Col. 0745B]

Leo, bishop, to Thuribius, bishop: greetings.

### 90

How commendably you are moved on behalf of the truth of the catholic faith, and how conscientiously you devote the ministry of pastoral office to the Lord’s flock, is demonstrated by the letter of your fraternity delivered to us by your deacon. In it you have taken care to make known to us what disease of error has broken out in your regions from the remnants of the ancient pestilence. For both the wording of your letter, the sequence of your memorandum, and the text of your little treatise declare that the foulest sewer of the Priscillianists has begun to boil up again among you.

There is no kind of filth in the minds of impious people that has not flowed together into this doctrine. For they have mixed together for themselves a manifold dregs from every kind of earthly opinion, so that they alone might drink whole whatever others had tasted in part. Finally, if all the heresies that arose before Priscillian’s time are examined more carefully, scarcely any error will be found from which that impiety did not draw its contagion. Not content to receive the falsehoods of those who, under Christ’s name, deviated from Christ’s Gospel, it also plunged itself into the darkness of paganism, placing the faith of religion and the rule of morals under the power of demons and the influence of the stars through the profane secrets of magical arts and the empty lies of astrologers.

If this may both be believed and taught, neither reward will be due to virtues nor punishment to vices, and all decrees—not only of human laws but also of divine ordinances—will be dissolved. For there can be no judgment concerning good or evil actions if a fatal necessity impels the mind’s movement in either direction, and whatever human beings do belongs not to human beings but to the stars.

To this madness also belongs that monstrous division of the whole human body among the twelve signs of heaven, as though different powers presided over different parts, and as though the creature whom God made in his own image were subject to the stars to the same degree that its limbs are joined together.

Our fathers, in whose time this unspeakable heresy burst forth, rightly labored urgently throughout the world to drive this impious fury from the entire Church. Even the rulers of the world so detested this sacrilegious insanity that they struck down its author, together with many of his disciples, by the sword of the public laws. For they saw that every concern for morality would be removed, every marital bond dissolved, and divine and human law alike overthrown if people of this profession were permitted to live anywhere.

This severity long benefited ecclesiastical leniency. Although the Church, content with priestly judgment, avoids bloody vengeance, it is nevertheless assisted by the strict enactments of Christian rulers, since those who fear bodily punishment sometimes have recourse to a spiritual remedy.

But after hostile invasion occupied many provinces and the storms of war blocked the execution of the laws; after travel among the priests of God became difficult and assemblies began to be rare, secret treachery found freedom amid the public disorder and was encouraged to overturn many minds by the very evils by which it ought to have been corrected.

And what portion of the peoples there is free from this plague, when, as your love indicates, even the hearts of certain priests have been corrupted by this deadly disease? Those through whom falsehood was believed to be suppressed and truth defended have themselves subjected the Gospel of Christ to Priscillian’s doctrine, so that, under the names of prophets and apostles, the piety of the sacred books is twisted to profane meanings, and what is preached is not what the Holy Spirit taught but what the devil’s servant inserted.

Therefore, since your love, with as much faithful diligence as possible, has gathered the opinions once condemned into sixteen chapters, we too shall review everything briefly, lest any of these blasphemies appear either tolerable or doubtful.

### 91. I. Against the Priscillianists, who distinguish the holy Trinity not by persons but only by names

[Col. 0746D]

[Note: From this word Esc. 4 resumes.]

In the first chapter it is shown how impiously they think about the divine Trinity: they assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as though the same God were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit. They say that there is not one who begot, another who was begotten, and another who proceeds from both, but that a singular unity is to be understood in three names, not in three persons.

They took this form of blasphemy from the opinion of Sabellius, whose disciples are rightly called Patripassians, “those who say that the Father suffered.” For if the Son himself is also the Father, then the Son’s cross is the Father’s passion, and whatever the Son endured in the form of a servant through obedience to the Father, the Father himself endured in his entirety.

This is plainly contrary to the catholic faith, which confesses the Trinity of the Godhead as *homoousios*—consubstantial—believing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be undivided without confusion, eternal without succession in time, and equal without distinction, because unity in the Trinity is fulfilled not by the same person but by the same essence.

### II. Against the claim that they believe the Lord God existed as the Father

In the second chapter their inept and empty invention is exposed concerning certain processions of powers from God, which supposedly began to exist and which God’s own essence preceded.

In this they also support the error of the Arians, who say that the Father is prior to the Son because there was a time when he existed without the Son, and that he began to be Father when he begot the Son. But just as the catholic Church detests the Arians, so too does it detest those who think that what is of God’s own essence was ever lacking in God, whom it is impious to describe as either changeable or progressive. For what is increased changes just as what is diminished changes.

### III. Against the claim that Christ is called the Only-Begotten because he alone was born from a virgin

The statement of the third chapter indicates that these same impious people assert that the Son of God is called the Only-Begotten because he alone was born from a virgin.

They would certainly not dare to say this unless they had drunk the poison of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who said that the Lord Jesus Christ did not exist before he was born from the virgin Mary.

[Note: In the other witnesses, except Alv., “our Lord Jesus.”]

If, however, they intend something else according to their own understanding, and do not grant Christ a beginning from his mother, they must assert that the Son of God is not one alone but that others too were begotten from the supreme Father, of whom this one alone was born from a woman and is therefore called the Only-Begotten, because none of the other sons of God assumed this condition of birth.

However they turn, therefore, they rush into the abyss of great impiety: either they want the Lord Christ to have his beginning from his mother, or they deny that he is the Only-Begotten of God the Father. Yet the one born from his mother was God the Word, and no one was begotten from the Father except the Word.

### IV. On the Lord’s Nativity, on which the Priscillianists observed fasts

The fourth chapter contains the claim that, although the catholic Church venerates Christ’s Nativity according to his assumption of true humanity—because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—these people do not truly honor it but merely pretend to do so. They fast on that day, just as they do on the Lord’s Day, which is the day of Christ’s resurrection.

They do this because they do not believe that the Lord Christ was born in a true human nature. Instead, following the doctrine of Cerdo and Marcion and agreeing in every respect with their kindred, the Manichaeans, they wish it to appear that what was displayed was a kind of illusion and was not real.

When the Manichaeans were exposed and convicted in our investigation, it was found that they observe the Lord’s Day—which the resurrection of our Savior consecrated for us—as a day of mournful fasting. They devote this abstinence, as was revealed, to reverence for the sun alone, so that in every respect they would be discordant from the unity of our faith, and so that the day we celebrate with joy would be spent by them in affliction.

It is therefore fitting that the enemies of Christ’s cross and resurrection should receive the sentence corresponding to the doctrine they have chosen.

### V. Against the claim that the human soul is of divine substance

The fifth chapter reports that they assert the human soul to be of divine substance and that the nature of our condition does not differ from the nature of its Creator.

The catholic faith condemns this impiety, which flows from the opinion of certain philosophers and of the Manichaeans. It knows that no created thing is so exalted or distinguished that God himself is its nature. For what is from him is what he is; nothing else is so except the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Apart from the one consubstantial, eternal, and unchangeable divinity of the supreme Trinity, there is nothing among all created things that was not created from nothing at its beginning. Nor is whatever excels among creatures God; nor, if something is great and wondrous, is it therefore identical with the one who alone performs great wonders.

No human being is truth, wisdom, or justice, but many participate in truth, wisdom, and justice. God alone, however, is in need of no participation.

[Note: Urg. and Ger. read “is in need of no participation.” The others read “is unworthy of no participation,” which is certainly absurd. The scribes of the codices apparently read and wrote *indignus* for *indiguus* through carelessness or ignorance, with the letter *u* changed into *n*, a highly plausible explanation.]

Whatever is worthily understood of him, however imperfectly, is not a quality but an essence. For nothing is added to the unchangeable and nothing is taken away, because what he is—always eternal—is always proper to him. Remaining within himself, therefore, he renews all things and receives nothing that he himself has not given.

They are exceedingly proud and exceedingly blind, then, when they say that the human soul is of divine substance. They do not understand that they are saying nothing other than that the Lord is changeable and that he himself suffers whatever can be inflicted upon his nature.

### VI. Against the claim that the devil is from himself or from chaos and possesses a nature of his own

The sixth statement indicates that they say the devil was never good and that his nature is not God’s workmanship, but that he emerged from chaos and darkness. Thus, supposedly, he has no author of his own, but is himself the beginning and substance of all evil.

The true faith—which is catholic—confesses that the substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, is good, and that evil has no nature.

[Note: Bibl. Reg. reads “your” rather than “our.”] God, who is the Creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good. Thus even the devil would have been good if he had remained in what he was made.

But because he used his natural excellence badly and did not stand in the truth, he did not pass into an opposite substance. Rather, he departed from the supreme good to which he ought to have adhered.

[Note: The other witnesses, except Alv. and Esc. 3, read “he separated himself.”]

So too these people, who make such assertions, rush from truth into falsehood and accuse nature in the very matter in which they voluntarily transgress and are condemned for their own willing perversity. This will indeed be evil for them, but evil itself will not be a substance; it will be the punishment of a substance.

### VII. Against the claim that marriage and the procreation of children are sin

The seventh point concerns their condemnation of marriage and their horror of the procreation of those who are born. Here, as in nearly everything, they agree with the profanation of the Manichaeans. Their practices show that they detest marital intercourse because there is no freedom for shameful conduct where the modesty of marriage and the hope of offspring are preserved.

### VIII. Against the claim that human bodies are the devil’s creations and are formed by demons in the womb

The eighth of their doctrines is that the fashioning of human bodies is the devil’s creation and that the seeds of conception are shaped by the work of demons in women’s wombs.

For this reason they say that the resurrection of the flesh is not to be believed, since the body’s composition is supposedly incompatible with the dignity of the soul.

This falsehood is undoubtedly the devil’s work, and the other monstrous inventions of their opinions are also fabrications of demons. Demons do not form human beings in women’s wombs; they manufacture such errors in the hearts of heretics.

[Note: From this word onward, leaves are missing in Esc. 4.]

The catholic faith long ago detected and condemned this most filthy poison, proceeding especially from the fountain of Manichaean impiety.

[Note: Bibl. Reg. reads “rebuked.”]

### IX. Against the claim that the children of promise are conceived from the Holy Spirit

The ninth statement makes clear that they say the children of promise are indeed born from women but are conceived from the Holy Spirit, so that offspring born from the seed of the flesh might not appear to belong to God’s creation.

This is contrary and opposed to the catholic faith, which confesses that every human being, in the substance of body and soul, is formed and animated by the Creator of the universe within the mother’s womb. The contagion of sin and mortality does remain—the contagion that passes into offspring from the first parent—but through the sacrament of regeneration, by which the children of promise are reborn through the Holy Spirit, they are reborn not in the womb of flesh but in the power of baptism.

Thus David, who was certainly a child of promise, says to the Lord: “Your hands made me and fashioned me.”

And the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you.”

### X. Against the belief that souls sin in the heavens and receive either a good or an evil lot in this world according to the quality of their sin

The tenth chapter reports that they assert that the souls inserted into human bodies formerly existed in a body and sinned in a heavenly dwelling. For this reason, they say, they fell from the heights to lower regions, encountered rulers of differing qualities, and were confined by aerial and stellar powers in different bodies, with differing lots and unequal conditions. Thus whatever occurs variously and unequally in this life is supposed to arise from preceding causes.

They have woven this impious fable for themselves from the errors of many others.

But the catholic faith cuts all such people away from the body of its unity, steadfastly and truthfully proclaiming

[Note: Aem. and Bibl. Reg. read “these people” (*hos*) rather than “all such people” (*eos*).] that human souls did not exist before they were breathed into their own bodies, and that they are incorporated by no one other than God the Maker, who is the Creator both of the souls themselves and of the bodies.

Because the entire offspring of the human race has been corrupted through the transgression of the first human being, no one can be freed from the condition of the old humanity except through the sacrament of Christ’s Baptism. In it there is no distinction among the reborn, as the Apostle says: “All who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

What, then, have the courses of the stars to do here? What have the fictions of fate to do here? What have the changeable condition and restless diversity of worldly affairs to do here?

Behold: the grace of God has made so many unequal people equal. If they remain faithful amid all the labors of this life, they cannot be wretched, saying in every temptation the apostolic words: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us.”

Therefore the Church, which is Christ’s body, fears nothing from the inequalities of the world, because it desires nothing from temporal goods. Nor does it fear being weighed down by the empty tumult of invented destinies, since it knows that it is increased through endurance of tribulations.

### XI. Against the claim that human souls are bound to the fatal stars

Their eleventh blasphemy is the belief that both human souls and bodies are bound to the fatal stars.

Through this madness they must become entangled in all the errors of the pagans, worshiping the stars that they think favorable to themselves and striving to appease those that are hostile.

No place in the catholic Church exists for those who pursue such practices, since anyone who gives himself over to such beliefs has wholly departed from Christ’s body.

### XII. Against the claim that the parts of the soul are assigned to some powers and the members of the body to others

The twelfth point among these teachings is that they assign the parts of the soul to certain powers and the members of the body to others. They establish the qualities of inner rulers under the names of the patriarchs, and oppose to them, in turn, the stellar signs to whose power they subject the bodies.

In all this they entangle themselves in an inextricable error, refusing to hear the Apostle’s words: “See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him dwells the whole fullness of divinity bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

And again: “Let no one deceive you, wishing to do so through humility and the religion of angels, dwelling on things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections, grows with the growth of God.”

What need is there, then, to admit into the heart what the Law did not teach, what prophecy did not sing, what the truth of the Gospel did not proclaim, and what apostolic teaching did not hand down?

But these things are hidden from the minds of those about whom the Apostle speaks when he says: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, having itching ears, they will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires. They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables.”

Let those who dare either to teach or to believe such things have nothing in common with us. They strive by every means to establish that the substance of the flesh is excluded from the work of the resurrection, and thus they dissolve the entire sacrament of Christ’s incarnation, because it would have been unworthy for the whole human being to be assumed if it were unworthy for the whole human being to be liberated.

[Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1 and 2 read “dwells within.”]

[Note: Bibl. Reg. reads “rely upon.”]

### XIII. Against the claim that the names of the patriarchs are distributed among the individual members of the body

[Note: All codices except Alv. read “they describe.”]

The thirteenth point is their claim that the whole body of the canonical Scriptures is to be understood under the names of the patriarchs, because the twelve powers that bring about the reformation of the inner human being are indicated by these names. Without this knowledge, they say, no soul can attain reformation into the substance from which it came.

But Christian wisdom holds this impious vanity in contempt. It knows that the nature of the true Godhead is inviolate and unchangeable, whereas the soul—whether living in the body or separated from the body—is subject to many sufferings.

If it were of divine essence, it could suffer no adversity. Thus, ineffably, the Creator is one thing and the creature another. He is always the same and is changed by no variation; the creature, however, is changeable even when it has not changed, because it can possess, as a gift and not as its own, that it should not be changed.

[Note: Aem. reads “given” (*datum*) for “bestowed” (*donatum*).]

### XIV. Against the claim that the twelve signs observed by astrologers are distributed throughout the entire body

In the fourteenth chapter they are said to hold that the condition of the body is subject to the power of the stars and signs according to its earthly quality.

For this reason, they say, many things are found in the sacred books that pertain to the outward human being, so that within Scripture itself there is a kind of conflict between the divine and earthly natures: one thing belongs to the rulers of souls and another to the creators of bodies.

These fables are expounded in order to affirm that the soul is of divine substance and to persuade people that the flesh is of an evil nature. They also profess that the world itself, together with its elements, is not the work of the good God but the creation of an evil author.

To cloak these sacrileges of their falsehoods with respectable titles, they have violated nearly all the divine utterances by inserting their wicked interpretations.

### XV. On the apocryphal writings of these same Priscillianists

[Col. 0752A]

The fifteenth chapter complains about this matter and rightly detests the devilish presumption. We have learned of it through the testimony of truthful witnesses and have found many of their thoroughly corrupted books bearing the titles of canonical writings.

For how could they deceive the simple unless they first smeared their poisoned cups with a kind of honey, so that the deadly contents to come would not be perceived as wholly unpleasant?

Care must therefore be taken, and priestly diligence must provide above all, that falsified books—and those at variance with the sincere truth—be used in no reading.

[Note: Aem. reads “false” (*falsi*) for “falsified” (*falsati*).]

Apocryphal writings, which under the names of the apostles contain a seedbed of many falsehoods, must not merely be prohibited; they must be completely removed and burned in the fire. Although some things in them may seem to bear an appearance of piety, they are never free from poisons. Through the enticements of their stories they secretly contrive to ensnare those seduced by marvelous narratives in the traps of whatever error.

Therefore, if any bishop fails to prohibit people from keeping apocryphal books in their homes, or permits books corrupted by Priscillian’s adulterating revision to be read in the Church under the name of canonical books, he must know that he is to be judged a heretic. For anyone who does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error.

### XVI. Corrections concerning the book of Dictinius

Finally, the sixteenth chapter justly complains that the treatises of Dictinius, which he composed according to Priscillian’s doctrine, were read by many with veneration. If they think that anything should be attributed to Dictinius’s memory, they ought rather to love his restoration than his fall.

They are not reading Dictinius but Priscillian, approving what he taught while in error, not what he chose after correction.

Let no one presume to do this with impunity, nor let anyone who uses writings condemned not only by the catholic Church but also by their own author be counted among Catholics.

Let it not be free for the perverse to pretend what they invent, nor let them evade the decrees of the imperial laws under the covering of the Christian name. For this reason they approach the catholic Church with such great division in their hearts: they make their own as many as they can, while pretending to be ours in order to escape the severity of the laws.

The Priscillianists do this, and so do the Manichaeans. Their hearts are so closely allied that, although they differ in name alone, they are found united in their sacrileges. The Manichaeans reject the Old Testament, while these people pretend to accept it; nevertheless, the intention of both tends toward one end. What the former attack by rejecting, the latter corrupt by imposing.

In their execrable mysteries—whose greater impurity makes them more carefully conceal them—there is altogether one crime, one obscenity, and a similar shamefulness. Although we blush to speak of it, we investigated it with the most diligent inquiries and, after it had been disclosed by the confession of the Manichaeans who had been arrested, caused it to become publicly known.

There can be no doubt about what was revealed in our court, which was attended not only by a very large number of priests but also by distinguished men, including part of the senate and the people. The facts sent now to your love demonstrate that it was disclosed by the mouths of those who had committed every crime.

What was formerly discovered and widely publicized about the most abominable crime of the Manichaeans has also been discovered and widely publicized concerning the most incestuous practice of the Priscillianists. Since they are equal in every respect in the impiety of their beliefs, they cannot differ in their sacred rites.

Having therefore reviewed everything contained in the sequence of the little treatise, from which the form of your memorandum does not differ, we have, as I think, sufficiently shown what judgment we hold concerning what your fraternity reported to us, and how intolerable it is if the hearts of certain priests either consent to such profane errors or, to put it more mildly, fail to resist them.

With what conscience do they claim the honor bestowed upon them, when they do not labor for the souls entrusted to them? Beasts rush in, and they do not close the sheepfolds; thieves lie in wait, and they do not set guards; diseases multiply, and they provide no remedies.

When they add to this their refusal to agree with those who act more diligently, and evade anathematizing by their signatures impieties long condemned throughout the world, what do they want understood about themselves except that they belong not to the number of the brethren but to the party of the enemies?

As for what you wrote at the end of your familiar letter, I am astonished that the understanding of any Catholic should be troubled by it, as though it were uncertain whether, when Christ descended to hell, his flesh rested in the tomb. Just as it truly died and was buried, so it truly rose again on the third day.

The Lord himself had announced this when he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The evangelist adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

David had also foretold the truth of this matter, speaking in the person of the Lord our Savior and saying: “Moreover, my flesh shall rest in hope; for you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption.”

By these words it was plainly shown that Christ’s flesh truly rested after burial and did not undergo corruption, because, swiftly vivified by the return of the soul, it rose again.

It is exceedingly impious not to believe this, and there is no doubt that such disbelief belongs to the teaching of Mani and Priscillian. With sacrilegious understanding they pretend to confess Christ while removing the reality of his incarnation, death, and resurrection.

Let an episcopal council therefore be held among you, and let the priests of the neighboring provinces gather at a place convenient for all, so that, in accordance with our replies to your questions, a full investigation may determine whether any bishops are contaminated by the contagion of this heresy. [Note: The other witnesses, except Alv., read “heresy” (*haereseos*).] They must certainly be separated from communion if they are unwilling to condemn this most unspeakable sect in all the perversity of its doctrines.

For it is entirely intolerable that anyone who has undertaken the office of preaching the faith should dare to argue against the Gospel of Christ, against apostolic teaching, and against the creed of the universal Church.

What sort of disciples will there be where such teachers instruct? What religion will the people have, and what salvation will the populace possess, where the sanctity of modesty is removed contrary to human society, the bond of marriage is taken away, the propagation of offspring is restrained, the nature of the flesh is condemned, the Trinity of the Godhead is denied contrary to the true worship of God, the distinct properties of the persons are confused, divine essence is attributed to human souls, and those same souls are enclosed in flesh at the devil’s discretion?

The Son of God is proclaimed Only-Begotten because of what was born from the Virgin, not because of what was begotten from the Father.

[Note: From this point onward, Esc. 4 begins again.]

At the same time, he is asserted to be neither the true offspring of God nor the true birth from the Virgin, so that through a false passion and an unreal death even a deceptive resurrection of the flesh taken up from the tomb may be believed.

They use the catholic name in vain who do not resist these impieties. Can those who are able to believe such things patiently listen to them?

We have therefore sent letters to our brothers and fellow bishops in Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Gallaecia, and have summoned them to a council of a general synod.

It will be the responsibility of your love to convey the authority of our decision to the bishops of the provinces mentioned above. But if any should oppose the holding of a general council—which God forbid—let at least the priests of Gallaecia assemble together. Our brothers Idacius and Coeponius will oversee their gathering, with your joined diligence, so that a remedy for such great wounds may be brought as quickly as possible, even through a provincial assembly.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Callipius [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 4, Tol. 1, Ger. read “Gallipius”] and Ardabur.

## LXII. Letter of the same Leo to the bishops established throughout Italy

Concerning the fact that very many Manichaeans were expelled from the city of Rome through Pope Leo’s vigilance. (C)

[Note: Aem. reads “from the City” (*ab Urbe*).]

[Col. 0753]

[Col. 0753D] Leo sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy.

We call you, dearest brothers, into partnership in our concern, so that with pastoral vigilance you may care more diligently for the flocks entrusted to you, lest any opportunity be granted to the devil’s cunning.

The disease that, through the mercy of the Lord’s revelation, is driven away from our sheep by our care must not proceed through the Churches of your sees while you remain uninformed and have not yet been warned about what is happening. Otherwise it may find secret tunnels and hiding places among you, so that what is extinguished by us in the City may be planted among you with dark roots.

Our investigation discovered very many followers and teachers of Manichaean impiety in the City; vigilance exposed them, and authority and discipline restrained them. Those whom we could correct, we corrected. We compelled them publicly in the church, by confession and by the subscription of their own hands, to condemn Mani together with his preaching and practices. After they had confessed the abyss of their impiety, we lifted them from it by granting them penance.

Some, however, had plunged themselves so deeply that no remedy provided by those assisting them could reach them. Subjected to the laws, according to the enactments of the Christian rulers, they were sent into perpetual exile by public judges, so that they would not contaminate the holy flock with their contagion.

We also displayed before the eyes of the Christian people, with definite clarity, everything profane or shameful that they possess both in their Scriptures and in their secret traditions, so that the people might know what to reject and avoid. Even the man who was said to be their bishop, after we detained him, disclosed the disgraceful things he maintained in their mysteries, as the record of the proceedings will be able to teach you.

For your instruction we have also sent the proceedings themselves. Once you have read them, you will be able to learn everything we discovered. Since we have learned that some of those whom a more serious guilt prevented from being absolved have fled, we have sent this letter to your love through our acolyte, so that your holiness, made more fully informed, may act with greater vigilance and caution. Take care that nowhere men of Manichaean perversity find an opportunity to harm your peoples or find teachers of this sacrilege.

[Note: Bibl. Reg. reads “of the Manichaeans” (*Manichaeorum*) for “Manichaean” (*Manichaeae*).]

We cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way than by pursuing with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are destroyers and destroyed, and by cutting them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely.

Therefore I exhort, entreat, and admonish your love to remain vigilant, with the concern you ought to have and can exercise, in searching for them, lest they find anywhere an opportunity to conceal themselves.

Just as the diligent person who carefully accomplishes what benefits the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of diligence, so no one who refuses to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will be able to excuse himself before the Lord’s tribunal for the guilt of his negligence.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Theodosius, for the eighteenth time, and Albinus.

## LXIII. Letter of the same Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily (C)

[Col. 0755]

[Col. 0755C] Leo sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.

We are stirred by divine commands and apostolic admonitions to watch tirelessly and zealously over the condition of all the Churches. If anything anywhere is found liable to reproach, we must promptly recall it either from the ignorance of inexperience or from the presumption of unauthorized usurpation.

The command of the Lord’s voice admonished the most blessed Apostle Peter and, through a threefold repetition, instructed him with a mystical sanction to feed Christ’s sheep as one who loves Christ. We therefore appeal, out of reverence for the very see over which we preside through the abundance of divine grace, that we avoid as far as possible the danger of negligence.

Otherwise the profession of the chief Apostle, by which he testified that he was a lover of the Lord, might not be found in us, because one who negligently feeds the flock so often entrusted to him is shown not to love the chief Shepherd.

[Note: In the other witnesses, except Alv. and Esc. 3, it reads *habere* (“to have”).]

### I. That the celebration of baptism is prohibited on the day of the Epiphany
Since, then, while I am fraternally concerned about the actions of your charity, it has become known to me through reliable indications that you differ from the custom of apostolic institution in what is primary among the Church’s sacraments—so that the sacrament of baptism is celebrated more frequently on the day of Epiphany than during the Paschal season—I am astonished that you or your predecessors could have adopted so irrational an innovation, imagining that there was no difference between the day on which Christ was adored by the Magi and the day on which Christ rose from the dead, thus confusing the mystery of the two seasons. You could never have fallen into this fault if you had received the rule of all observance from the source from which you received the honor of your consecration, and if the see of blessed Peter the Apostle, which is the sacerdotal mother of your dignity, had been the teacher of ecclesiastical reason. A departure from its rules could have been tolerated with less equanimity [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., the reading is *volorari* (materially uncertain)] if no admonitory rebuke of ours had preceded it. But now, because correction is not despaired of, gentleness must be preserved. Although an excuse that pleads ignorance is scarcely tolerable in priests, we nevertheless prefer both to temper the necessary censure and to instruct you by the clearest reasoning of truth.

**98 II. That all the mysteries of salvation were arranged for us in due order through the incarnation of our Lord.**

The restoration of the human race was indeed always immutably foreordained in God’s eternal plan; but the temporal order of the events to be accomplished through Jesus Christ our Lord took its beginning in the incarnation of the Word. Thus there is one time when, at the angel’s announcement, the blessed Virgin Mary believed that she would conceive through the Holy Spirit and conceived; another when, with her virgin integrity preserved, the child was born and announced to the shepherds amid the rejoicing of the heavenly ministers [Note: In this word, *exsultante* (“rejoicing”), Codex Escorial 4 ends.]; another when the infant was circumcised; another when the legal offering was presented for him; another when the three Magi, stirred by the brightness of the new star, came from the East to Bethlehem and honored the child by worshiping him and offering mystical gifts.

Nor are the days the same on which he was withdrawn from the impious Herod by the divinely ordered journey into Egypt, or on which, after the persecutor’s death, he was called back from Egypt to Galilee [Note: Escorial 3: “was recalled.”]. Amid these various dispensations, bodily growth also advances: the Lord grows, as the Evangelist testifies, in the progress of age and grace. On the day of Passover [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Escorial 3, Tol. 1 and 2 read *dies* (“days”).] he came with his parents into the temple of Jerusalem; and when he was absent from the company of those returning, he was found sitting among the elders and disputing among the astonished teachers. In response to their question about why he had remained, he said: “Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s temple?”—signifying that he was the Son of him whose temple it was.
