But when, in more mature years, he sought the baptism of his precursor John, in order to declare his divinity more openly, what ambiguity about it remained, when, after the Lord Jesus had been baptized, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained, and the Father’s voice was heard from heaven saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased”?

We have touched briefly on all these matters, as far as we could, so that your charity may know that all the days of Christ were consecrated by innumerable manifestations of power, and that the mysteries of the sacraments shone forth in all his actions. Yet these things are announced in one way by signs and fulfilled in another through realities; nor does everything recorded among the works of the Savior belong to the time of baptism. For if we were to honor indiscriminately even those things that we know were accomplished by the Lord after the washing of blessed John, all seasons would have to be counted as assigned to festivals, because all are filled with miracles.

But because the Spirit of wisdom and understanding so instructed the apostles and the teachers of the whole Church that, in Christian observance, he allowed nothing disordered and nothing confused, the reasons for the solemnities must be distinguished, and in all the institutions of our fathers and leaders a reasonable discrimination must be preserved. For we are not one flock and one shepherd unless, as the Apostle says, we all say the same thing: “Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment.”

**III. That in baptism death occurs through the killing of sin; that the threefold immersion imitates three-day burial; and that being lifted from the waters is like resurrection from the tomb.**

Although both what pertains to Christ’s humility and what pertains to his glory converge in one and the same person, and everything in him that belongs to divine power and human weakness tends toward our restoration, nevertheless it is specifically in the death of the Crucified One and in his resurrection from the dead that the power of baptism creates a new creature from the old, so that both the death of Christ and his life may operate in those who are reborn.

As blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as the Lord rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with him in resurrection”—and so forth, along with the other matters that the Teacher of the Gentiles discussed at greater length in order to commend the mystery of baptism.

It was therefore apparent, through the spirit of this teaching, that the day and season had been chosen for the rebirth and adoption of the children of humanity as children of God in which, through the likeness and form of the mystery, what is performed in the members might correspond to what was accomplished in the Head himself: in the rule of baptism, death intervenes through the killing of sin; the threefold immersion imitates a three-day burial; and being lifted from the waters is like the rising of one who comes forth from the tomb.

The very character of the rite therefore teaches that the proper day for the general celebration of grace is the day on which the power of the gift and the form of the action are adorned. For confirmation of this, it is especially significant that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after rising from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the leaders of the churches were represented—both the form and the authority to baptize, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” He could certainly have instructed them in this even before his passion, unless he specifically wished it to be understood that the grace of regeneration began with his resurrection.

To this observance is also added the solemnity consecrated by Pentecost through the coming of the Holy Spirit, which depends upon the Paschal feast. While other festivals belong to other days, this one always occurs on the same day that is distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection, extending, as it were, the hand of assisting grace, so that those whom illness, the length of the journey, or the difficulty of navigation has unwillingly prevented from reaching the day of Easter, or whom any other necessities have impeded, may obtain through the gift of the Holy Spirit the fulfillment of their desire.

For the Only-Begotten Son of God did not wish there to be any difference between himself and the Holy Spirit in the faith of believers or in the power of works, because there is no diversity in nature. He said: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth.” And again: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.” And again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth.” Since, then, Christ is truth, and the Holy Spirit is truth, and the name “Paraclete” properly belongs to both, the festival is not dissimilar where there is one sacrament.

**IV. That blessed Peter the Apostle baptized three thousand men on the day of Pentecost.**

We prove that we should preserve this practice not by our own persuasion but by a sufficiently authoritative apostolic example, following blessed Peter the Apostle, who on the very day when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit filled the whole number of believers consecrated three thousand people, converted by his preaching, through the washing of baptism.

Holy Scripture, which contains the Acts of the Apostles, teaches this in a faithful account, saying: “When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles: ‘What shall we do, men and brothers?’ Peter said to them: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God will call.’”

He testified and exhorted them with many other words, saying: “Save yourselves from this perverse generation.” Therefore those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day.

**V. That these two seasons—that is, Easter and Pentecost—have been lawfully appointed by the Roman pontiff for baptism.**

Since it is therefore most clearly evident that the two seasons of which we have spoken are the proper seasons for the chosen to be baptized in the Church, we admonish your charity not to mix any other days into this observance.

**VI. That at every time those who are threatened by the necessity of death—that is, by illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck—ought to be baptized.**

Although there are other festivals as well to which much reverence is owed in honor of God, the exception belonging to the mystical rationale of the principal and greatest sacrament must nevertheless be preserved: this is not a prohibition of the permission by which aid is given through baptism to those in danger at whatever time.

We defer the free wishes of those who are safe and living in the security of peace to these two festivals, joined and related to one another, in such a way that in danger of death, in the peril of siege, in the distress of persecution, and in fear of shipwreck, we deny no one, at any time, this unique protection of true salvation.

If anyone thinks that the festival of Epiphany, which in its proper order must be venerated with due honor, has the privilege of baptism because some believe that on that same day the Lord approached the baptism of Saint John, let him know that the grace of that baptism was different and its rationale different, and that it did not belong to the same power by which those who are reborn through the Holy Spirit are born—of whom it is said: “They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”

The Lord, needing no forgiveness of sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, nevertheless wished to be baptized just as he wished to be circumcised and to have an offering of purification presented for him, so that he who had been made from a woman, as the Apostle says, might also become subject to the law—which he had not come to abolish but to fulfill and bring to completion—as the blessed Apostle proclaims, saying: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

He established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, he taught that he was the beginning; and he then sanctioned the power of regeneration when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side [Note: In the other witnesses, except Alva, the reading is: “when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side.” Ger. reads: “streamed forth.”].

For just as the Old Testament was a testimony to the New, and the law was given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ [Note: In all witnesses except Alva and Urg., *ergo* (“therefore”)]; so various sacrifices prefigured one offering, and the slaughter of many lambs came to an end in the immolation of him of whom it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

Likewise, John was not Christ but Christ’s forerunner; he was not the bridegroom but the bridegroom’s friend. He was so faithful, seeking not his own things but those of Jesus Christ, that he declared himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandals, since he baptized with water for repentance, whereas Christ would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire—a baptism possessing a twofold power, both restoring life and consuming sins.

Since, then, dearest brothers, there are so many and such great testimonies by which, once all ambiguity has been removed, you clearly recognize that, according to apostolic rule, those who are to be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching must observe only two seasons—that is, Easter and Pentecost—we announce this to your charity, so that you may no longer depart in any excess from the apostolic institutions. For after this, it cannot remain unpunished if anyone believes that the apostolic rules may be neglected in any respect.

**VII. That three bishops from Sicily, every year, must come without fail to Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October, to be joined in synod.**

Therefore, first of all, for the preservation of the most harmonious unity, we require this: since the holy Fathers have most beneficially established that there ought to be two assemblies each year, three of you must come unfailingly to Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October, so as to be joined in a fraternal council. For, with God’s grace assisting, it will more easily be possible to ensure that no scandals and no errors arise in the churches of Christ, when everything must always be discussed collectively in the presence of the blessed Apostle Peter, so that all his constitutions and canonical decrees may remain inviolate among all the priests of the Lord.

We wish these matters, which by the Lord’s inspiration we believe ought to be brought to your attention, to reach your knowledge through our brothers and fellow bishops Vacillus and Paschasinus [Note: Tol. 1 and 2: “Paschasius.”]. Through their report we shall learn how reverently the institutions of the apostolic see are observed by you [Note: A leaf is missing in Escorial 3.].

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Calapodius and Ardabur.

# LXIV. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO ALL THE BISHOPS. (C)

[Col. 0761]

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Campania and Picenum, or Tuscany, and throughout all the provinces.

Just as the well-ordered condition of the churches brings us joy, so we are distressed by no slight sorrow whenever we learn that something has been attempted or committed against the provisions of the canons and ecclesiastical discipline. If we do not cut away such things with the vigilance we ought to exercise, we cannot excuse ourselves before him who wished us to be watchmen, allowing the sincere body of the Church—which we ought to guard pure from every stain—to be defiled by the wicked contagion of those who seek advancement, when the structure of its members itself fails to cohere through dissimulation.

**I. That no bishop should presume to promote another’s slave to clerical office.**

People are admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order who possess no dignity of birth and no dignity of character to support them. Those who could not obtain freedom from their masters are advanced to the height of the priesthood, as though servile status could receive this honor; and one who has not yet been able to prove himself to his master is believed capable of being approved by God.

There is therefore a twofold guilt in this matter: both the sacred ministry is polluted by the degradation of such an association, and the rights of masters are violated insofar as this concerns the rashness of illicit usurpation. Therefore, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from such men. We wish them to abstain not only from these but also from those who are bound by an original status or by some other condition, unless perhaps the request or consent of those who claim some power over them has been given.

Anyone who is to be enrolled in divine service ought to be free from the claims of others, so that he may not be withdrawn by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, in which his name is enrolled.

**II. That those promoted to the priesthood who are husbands of widows or who have contracted numerous marriages must be excluded from all ecclesiastical offices.**

We have learned both from the Apostle’s teaching and from divine instruction and the rules of the canons what dignity of birth and character ought to belong to each person who is to be associated with the ministry of the sacred altar. Yet we find that many of our brothers have departed from these rules and completely strayed from them.

It is established that husbands of widows have attained the priesthood, and that some men who had contracted numerous marriages and lived with excessive freedom in every respect had been admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order, contrary to the blessed Apostle’s declaration concerning such men: “The husband of one wife”; and contrary to the command of the ancient law, which says and prescribes: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated.”

Therefore, by the authority of the apostolic see, we order that all such men who have been admitted be excluded from ecclesiastical offices and from the priestly name. They cannot claim for themselves what they were not capable of receiving because of the very impediment that stood in their way. We claim special responsibility for examining this matter, so that any offenses committed in these matters may perhaps be corrected, that they may not be committed thereafter, and that no excuse may arise from ignorance—although a priest could never legitimately be ignorant of what has been defined by the rules of the canons.

We have therefore sent these written instructions to your provinces through our brothers and fellow bishops Innocentius, Legitimus, and Segetius, so that what is known to have grown up wrongly may be uprooted from the roots [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg.: “is known,” rather than “is recognized”], and so that no weeds may corrupt the Lord’s harvest. For those things that are sound will produce abundant fruit only if what habitually destroys the growing crop is cut away with greater diligence.

**III. That not only clerics but also lay Christians must not exact interest.**

Nor did we think this matter should be passed over: some, seized by a shameful desire for profit, practice lending at interest and wish to grow rich through usury. We grieve that this occurs not merely among those established in clerical office but even among laymen who desire to be called Christians. We decree that harsher punishment be imposed on those who have been convicted, so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Ger., Tol. 1 and 2: *Non* (“not”); the remaining witnesses also read *Non*.].

**IV. That a cleric must not practice lending at interest either in his own name or in another’s.**

We also thought it necessary to warn you that, just as no cleric may practice usury in his own name, so no one may attempt to practice it in another’s name. It is an unbecoming crime to devote one’s own wrongdoing to another’s advantage.

The only “interest” that we ought to seek and practice is this: that we may be able to receive from the Lord what we mercifully give here, for he will repay it many times over and it will remain forever.

**V. That if any priest acts contrary to these prohibitions, he must be removed from his office.**

Our admonition therefore declares that if any of our brothers attempts to act contrary to these regulations [Note: Urg. and Ger.: *constituta venerit vel venire tentaverit* (“has contravened the enactments or will attempt to do so”).] and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not share in our communion, since he refused to be a companion in discipline [Note: Codex Escorial 3 resumes with these words: “Our admonition therefore.”].

So that nothing may perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command your charity to preserve all the decretal constitutions both of blessed Innocentius [Note: In all witnesses except Alva: “of blessed memory”] and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons. If anyone despises them, he must know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Maximus II and Paterius.

# LXV. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO BISHOP JANUARIUS. That a cleric of any order who abandons the Catholic Church and joins himself to heretical communion, if he returns to the Church, must remain without promotion in the rank in which he was. (C)

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia.

Having read the letters of your fraternity, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we knew formerly, and we congratulate you because you diligently carry out pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flocks, lest the wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep tear apart even the innocent with the ferocity of beasts [Note: In the other witnesses, except Alva: “bestial ferocity”], and lest they not only make no progress through correction themselves but also corrupt what is sound.

To prevent this from being achieved by viperous deceit, we thought it necessary to admonish your charity, making it clear that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics and schismatics, and has in some way defiled himself with the contagion of heretical communion [Note: In the other witnesses, except Alva: “contagion”], is received back into Catholic communion without promotion, after legitimate satisfaction.

It is most salutary and full of the benefit of spiritual medicine that, whether they are presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order, those who wish to appear corrected and seek to return to the Catholic faith—which they previously lost—must first confess without ambiguity that they condemn both their own errors and the authors of those errors. Thus, once their corrupt opinions have also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope remains for them, and no member of the Church can be violated by association with such men, since their own profession will have begun to oppose them in every respect [Note: Bibl. Reg.: “confession” rather than “profession.”].

Concerning such men, we also order that the following canonical constitution be observed: they should regard it as a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion removed, they remain permanently in the order in which they are found—provided they have not been defiled by a second baptism.

He incurs no slight offense before God who judges that such men should be promoted to sacred orders. If promotion is granted only after rigorous examination to those who are blameless, much less should it be permitted to those under suspicion.

Therefore, let your charity, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our dispositions and ensure that the measures laudably proposed and beneficially ordered for the safety of the whole Church are carried out carefully and promptly.

Your charity should not doubt that, if—which we do not expect—those things that we decree for the preservation of the canons and the integrity of the faith should be neglected, we shall be moved to act with greater severity. For the faults of those in the lower orders ought to be attributed to no one more than to negligent and careless rulers, who often nurture a great pestilence while avoiding the application of the necessary medicine.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Alipius and Ardabur.

# LXVI. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO RUSTICUS, BISHOP OF NARBONNE. (C)

Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne.

I received with pleasure the letters of your fraternity, which your archdeacon Hermes delivered. They contained a variety of matters joined together and were extensive, but they were not so burdensome to the patience of the reader that anything in them was omitted amid the many concerns arising on every side [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1 and 2, Urg., Ger.: “intervening.” The other witnesses: “non-intervening.”].

Having grasped the whole structure of your discourse and reviewed the proceedings completed in the examination of bishops and other distinguished persons, we have understood that the priests Sabinianus and Leo lacked confidence in their case, and that they have no just complaint, since they voluntarily withdrew from the disputes they had begun.

As to the form and measure of justice that you ought to maintain toward them, I leave the matter to your moderation. I nevertheless urge you, in the spirit of charity, to apply spiritual medicine to the sick; and, as Scripture says, “Do not be excessively just.” Deal more gently with those who seem, through zeal for chastity, to have exceeded the proper measure of punishment, lest the devil, who deceived adulterers, rejoice over the avengers of adultery.

I am astonished that your charity should be so disturbed by the adversity of scandals arising on every occasion that you say you prefer release from the labors of the episcopate and would rather spend your life in silence and leisure than remain in the responsibilities entrusted to you.

But the Lord says: “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end.” From what, then, does blessed perseverance arise, if not from the virtue of patience? For, according to apostolic teaching, all who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution. Persecution must not be reckoned only as what is inflicted against Christian piety by sword, fire, or any kind of punishment. The ferocity of persecution is also supplied by dissimilarity of character, by the insolence of the disobedient, and by the arrows of malicious tongues.

Since these conflicts always strike all the members, and no part of the devout is free from them, so that neither leisure nor labor is without danger, who will guide a ship amid the waves of the sea if the helmsman withdraws? Who will guard the sheep from the ambushes of wolves if the shepherd’s care does not keep watch? Finally, who will resist robbers and thieves if love of repose draws away from his vigilant duty the watchman stationed at the lookout for observation? [Note: The word *obsistet* (“will resist”), absent in Alva, is supplied from Codex Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1, Urg., and Ger. Aem. reads *resistet* (“will withstand”).]

Therefore one must remain at the work entrusted to him and at the labor undertaken. Justice must be upheld steadfastly and mercy must be offered kindly. Let sins be hated, not human beings. Let the arrogant be corrected, the weak be tolerated; and whatever in sins must be punished more severely should not be punished with the spirit of one who rages but of one who heals.

And if more severe tribulation should weigh upon us, let us not be so terrified as though that adversity had to be resisted by our own strength. Christ is both our counsel and our strength, so that without him we can do nothing, but through him we can do all things. He strengthens the preachers of the Gospel and ministers of the sacraments, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.” And again: “I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In this world you will have tribulation; but take courage, because I have conquered the world.”

Since these promises are without doubt clear, we must not weaken them through any scandals, lest we appear ungrateful toward God’s choice, whose helps are as powerful as his promises are true.

As for the consultations of your charity, which your archdeacon brought separately in writing, it would have been more appropriate to inquire into the matter among those present if you had given us the opportunity to see you. Since some of the questions seem to exceed the proper form of an inquiry, I understand that they are more suited to conversation than to writing. For just as some matters cannot be overturned by any reasoning, so many others must be tempered either in consideration of age or because of the necessity of circumstances, always preserving this condition: in matters that are doubtful or obscure, we must know that we should follow what is found to be contrary neither to the evangelical precepts nor to the decrees of the holy Fathers.

**I. That those are not to be regarded as bishops whom neither the clergy elected, nor the people sought, nor the provincial bishops consecrated. Nevertheless, if clerics are ordained by such pseudo-bishops, their ordination may be valid.**

No reasoning permits those to be counted among the bishops who have been elected neither by clerics, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan. Since a dispute about an improperly received honor often arises, who could doubt that it must not be attributed to these men when it is not shown to have been conferred?

But if some clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches that belonged to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be held valid, so that they may remain in those churches. Otherwise, the consecration must be regarded as void, since it was established neither in the proper place nor supported by proper authority.

**II. That presbyters or deacons who have fallen into some crime cannot obtain the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands.**

It is contrary to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated in the dignity of the presbyterate or in the rank of the diaconate should receive, for some crime of theirs, the remedy of repentance through the laying on of hands. This undoubtedly descends from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest sins, who will pray for him?”

Therefore, such fallen men must seek private withdrawal in order to merit God’s mercy; there, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.

**III. That deacons, like bishops and presbyters, must abstain from conjugal relations, but must not repudiate their marriages.**

The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. While they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully marry wives and beget children. But when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them became unlawful.

Therefore, so that what is carnal may become a spiritual marriage, they ought neither to dismiss their wives nor to have them except as though they did not have them [Aem.: “having them”], so that the love of marriage is preserved while the acts of marriage cease.

**IV. That a wife is one thing and a concubine another; and that no one should err if he gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine.**

Not every woman joined to a man is his wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The bonds of marriage are legitimate among the freeborn and among equals, and this was established by the Lord long before the beginnings of Roman law.

Therefore, a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another. For this reason the Apostle, to display the distinction between these persons, cites testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.”

Since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage in whom the nuptial mystery is not found.

Therefore, if a cleric of any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he had given her to a married man, unless perhaps that woman is seen to have been made free, lawfully endowed with a dowry, and honored by a public marriage [Note: In the other witnesses, except Alva: “honest.”].

Women joined to men by paternal decision are free from guilt if the women whom those men kept were not married to them, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Escorial 3, Tol. 1 and 2, Ger.: “joined.”].

**V. That it is not a duplication of marriage when, after dismissing a slave woman, a wife is taken.**

To cast a slave woman away from one’s bed and take a wife of established free birth is not a duplication of marriage but an advance in respectability.

The negligence of such men should indeed be censured, but they should not be utterly despaired of, so that, stirred by frequent exhortations, they may faithfully carry out what they have necessarily sought. No one should be despaired of while he remains in this body, because sometimes what is postponed through lack of confidence in one’s age is completed through more mature deliberation.

**VI. Concerning communion for those who were deprived of it and have died.**

Their case must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the deaths of such persons were postponed until the remedy of communion. We, however, cannot give communion after death to those with whom we did not communicate while they were alive.

**VII. Concerning those who delay doing penance.**

This delay may arise not from contempt for the remedy but from a serious fear of committing a graver offense. Therefore, when the delayed penance is sought more earnestly, it must not be denied, so that the wounded soul may reach the medicine of pardon by whatever means.

**VIII. That one who asks forgiveness for illicit acts ought also to abstain from many licit things.**

It is one thing to demand back what is justly owed, and another to renounce what is one’s own out of love for perfection. But a person asking forgiveness for illicit acts ought also to abstain from many licit things, as the Apostle says: “Everything is permitted, but not everything is beneficial.”

Therefore, if a penitent has a case that he perhaps ought not to neglect, it is better for him to seek an ecclesiastical judgment than a secular one.

**IX. That it is not fitting for a penitent to engage in profit-seeking commerce.**

The character of profit either excuses or condemns the merchant, because there is both honorable gain and shameful gain. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for a penitent to endure losses than to become entangled in the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transaction between seller and buyer.

**X. That it is not fitting to return to secular military service after penance.**

It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after performing penance, since the Apostle says: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs.” Therefore, a person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service [Note: In the other witnesses, except Alva and Urg.: “human military service.”] is not free from the snares of the devil.

### XI. That if a young man undertook penance because of some pressing danger, and does not remain continent, he may be supported by the remedy of a wife

[Col. 0767C]

If a man in adolescence undertook penance because of the danger of death or captivity, and afterward, fearing a lapse into youthful incontinence, chose marital intercourse so as not to incur the crime of fornication, he seems to have done something venial, provided that he had intercourse with no woman at all except his wife. In this matter, however, we are not establishing a rule, but judging what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has undertaken penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.

### XII. That if anyone abandons the monastic profession, he must be cleansed by public penitential satisfaction

106 A monk’s profession, undertaken by his own judgment and will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what one has vowed to God, one ought also to render. Therefore, whoever, having abandoned the profession of solitude, has turned to military service or marriage [Esc. 3, *provolutus*: “has rushed headlong”] must be cleansed by public penitential satisfaction. [Col. 0768A] For although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the better choice is a transgression.

### XIII. That girls who, not under compulsion but of their own will, have undertaken the profession of virginity sin when they marry, even if they have not yet been consecrated

Girls who, not compelled by parental authority but by their own spontaneous judgment, have undertaken the profession and habit of virginity, if they afterward choose marriage, violate their commitment, even if the grace of consecration has not yet been bestowed upon them—for they certainly would not have been deprived of that gift had they remained in their profession.

### XIV. Concerning those who have already been consecrated, if they marry afterward

There can be no doubt that a great crime is committed where both the profession is abandoned and consecration is violated. For if human agreements cannot be trampled with impunity, what will become of those who have violated the covenant of the divine sacrament?

### XV. Concerning those who doubt whether they have been baptized: they must be baptized

If there are no indications among relatives or members of the household, nor among clergy or neighbors, by which it can be shown that those in question were baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they perish openly. In such cases, reason does not permit what is not shown to have been done to be regarded as repeated. Those, however, who can remember that they came to church with their parents may recall whether they received what was given to them by their parents. But if even this is beyond their memory, they should be given what is unknown to have been given, [Col. 0768C] because where careful piety is present, there is no rashness of presumption.

### XVI. That those who acknowledge that they were baptized but do not know in which faith [Note: [Col. 0768D] In the remaining witnesses, except Alv., *fide*: “in what faith.”] should be received through the laying on of hands

Those about whom you have written—who know that they were baptized but profess that they do not know of what faith those who baptized them were—are not to be baptized, since in some manner they received the form of baptism. Rather, through the laying on of hands, by the power of the Holy Spirit—which they could not have received from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.

### XVII. Concerning the baptized who afterward partook of Gentile banquets and sacrificial foods

Those who merely took part in a Gentile banquet and ate sacrificial foods may be cleansed by fasting and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from food offered to idols, they may be able to share in the sacraments of Christ. But if they either worshiped idols or defiled themselves with murder or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

## LXVII. Letter 67 of the same Leo to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (C)

[Col. 0767]

[Col. 0767D] Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

107 How great are the responsibilities entrusted to your Fraternity by the authority of the most blessed apostle Peter, and with what favor on our part they have also been committed to you: if you perceived this with sound judgment and weighed it by a just assessment, we could rejoice greatly in the devotion with which you discharge the solicitude imposed upon you. For just as my predecessors delegated their authority to your predecessors, so I too, following the example of those before me, have entrusted to your affection the functions of my governance, so that, becoming an imitator of our gentleness, you might assist in the care which, by divine institution, we principally owe to all the churches, and might in a manner extend the presence of our visitation to provinces distant from us. From a continuous and suitably placed vantage point, it would thus be easy for you to recognize what matters you should settle through your own diligence and what you should reserve for our judgment.

For since it was open to you to suspend the greater affairs and the more difficult outcomes of cases while awaiting our decision, you had neither reason nor necessity to deviate into something exceeding your measure. You have an abundance of our admonitory letters, by which we have often instructed you concerning moderation in all actions, so that through exhortations of charity you might call the churches of Christ entrusted to you toward the health of obedience. For although among negligent or sluggish brothers there are often matters which ought to be corrected with greater authority, correction must nevertheless be applied in such a way that affection is always preserved. Thus the blessed apostle Paul, instructing Timothy in ecclesiastical governance, says: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity.”

If this moderation is owed by apostolic institution to all the lesser members, how much more must it be rendered without offense to our brothers and fellow bishops? And although matters sometimes arise that deserve reproach in priestly persons, benevolence accomplishes more toward those who are to be corrected than severity, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power. But those who seek what is their own and not what belongs to Christ Jesus easily depart from this rule; and while they seek rather to dominate their subjects than to advise them, honor pleases, pride puffs up, and what was provided for concord turns toward harm.

That we are compelled to say this does not arise from a small grief of mind. I feel myself, in a certain sense, drawn into blame when I learn that you have departed excessively from the rules handed down to you. Even if you were careless of your own reputation [Note: [Col. 0769D] In the remaining witnesses except Alv. and Esc. 3, *errasses*: “had gone astray”], you ought at least to have spared my reputation, lest actions undertaken solely by your judgment appear to have been carried out by ours. Let your Fraternity reread our pages and run through all the letters sent to your predecessors by the bishops of the apostolic see; you will find, either from me or from my predecessors, that what we have learned you presumed to do had been otherwise prescribed.

Our brother Atticus, metropolitan bishop of Old Epirus, came to us with the bishops of his province and complained in a tearful statement of the most undeserved affliction he had suffered, in the presence of your deacons. Since they offered no response against his complaints and tears, they showed that the matters brought before us were not without credibility. Your letters, which those same deacons brought, were also read. They stated that Brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica and had confirmed his consent by a written declaration, so that we could understand nothing other than that his coming and the document he had written concerning his promise of obedience had resulted from his own judgment and voluntary devotion. Yet the mention of that document revealed an injury.

It was not necessary to bind in writing one who had already demonstrated his obedience by the service of his voluntary arrival. Thus the words of your letter provided testimony for the complaints mentioned above, and by what was not concealed, what had been covered in silence was laid bare: namely, that the prefecture of Illyricum had been enlisted and the highest authority among worldly offices stirred up against an innocent bishop, so that, with a terrifying execution [Note: [Col. 0769D] In the remaining witnesses except Alv. and Esc. 3, *excusatione*: “excuse”] sent out, which was to bring all public offices to bear in carrying out the command, a priest was dragged from the sacred sanctuaries of the Church, charged with no crime, even a false one [Note: [Col. 0770D] In the others except Alv., *persimulatus*: “falsely accused”]. No respite was granted him on account of the burden of illness or the severity of winter; instead, he was compelled to travel a rough road, full of dangers and blocked by impassable snows. The labor and danger were so great that some of those who accompanied the bishop are said to have collapsed.

I am greatly astonished, dearest brother, and also deeply grieved, that you were able to become so fiercely and violently agitated against a man about whom you had reported nothing more than that, having been summoned, he delayed appearing [Note: [Col. 0770D] In the others except Alv., *deberet*: “ought to delay”] and pleaded illness—especially since, even if he had deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited what I would write in response to your inquiries.

But, as I see, you judged well of my character, and very accurately foresaw how civilly I would respond in order to preserve priestly concord. Therefore you hastened to carry out your impulses without delay, lest, once you had received letters in which our moderation prescribed something else, you should no longer have the freedom to do what you did.

Or had some crime become known to you, and was the metropolitan bishop burdened by the weight of a new accusation? But you yourself confirm that this was foreign to him by bringing no charge against him. Even if he had committed something grave and intolerable, our judgment ought to have been awaited, so that you would decide nothing beforehand without learning what pleased us [Note: [Col. 0770D] In the others except Alv., *agnosceres*: “you might learn”]. For we have entrusted our functions to your affection in such a way that you have been called to share the responsibility, not to possess the fullness of power.

Therefore, just as the things you have piously managed greatly rejoice us, so the things wrongly carried out distress us excessively. After the experience of so many cases, it is necessary to look ahead more carefully and take precautions more diligently, so that through the spirit of charity [Col. 0771A] and peace every source of scandal may be removed from the churches of the Lord entrusted to you—your episcopal dignity indeed remaining preeminent in those provinces, but every excess of usurpation being cut away.

### I. That the rights of metropolitans be preserved

Therefore, in accordance with the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose care is extended through our delegation by your Fraternity, retain unimpaired the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor presumption.

### II. That metropolitans ordain as bishops neither laymen, nor bigamists, nor husbands of widows, but irreproachable men

[Col. 0771B]

In cities whose rulers have died, this procedure is to be observed in substituting bishops: the man to be ordained, even if supported by testimony of a good life, must not be a layman, a neophyte, or the husband of a second wife, nor even one who has or has had only one wife but has married a widow. The choice of priests is so eminent that practices which are not counted as blame in other members of the Church are nevertheless considered illicit in them.

### III. That subdeacons be denied carnal marriage

For although those outside the clerical order have free choice to devote themselves to marriage and the begetting of children, nevertheless, in order to display perfect [Aem., *perfectae*: “of perfect”] purity of continence, even subdeacons are not granted carnal marriage, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who have none may remain unmarried. If this is worthy of observance in this order, which is fourth from the highest, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third orders, lest anyone be judged suitable for Levitical, presbyteral, or episcopal dignity who has not yet been shown to have restrained himself from sexual pleasure [Note: [Col. 0771D] In all witnesses except Alv. and Esc. 3, *luxuriae*: “lust”]?

### IV. That no one be ordained bishop against the will of the people [Note: [Col. 0771D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Tol. 1, 2: *antistes*: “bishop”]

When, therefore, the election of the chief priest is under consideration, the man whom the clergy and people have unanimously requested by common consent is to be preferred to all others. If, however, their votes should happen to be divided among different persons, the metropolitan’s judgment is to prefer one to the other [Note: [Col. 0771D] In all witnesses except Alv. and Urg., *is alter*: “the other is”] who is supported by greater zeal and greater merits—provided that no one is ordained against the will and without the request of the people, lest an unwilling people either despise or hate a bishop whom it did not desire, and become less devout than is fitting because it was not permitted to have the man it wanted.

### V. That the metropolitan of Epirus report to the bishop of Thessalonica concerning the man whom he is going to ordain bishop, and that the provincial bishops likewise report concerning the elected metropolitan

[Col. 0772A]

Concerning the person to be consecrated as bishop, and concerning the consent of the clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop is to report to your Fraternity and inform you of what has been approved in the province, so that your authority may also confirm the ordination when it is properly celebrated. Your authority should introduce no delay or difficulty into sound arrangements, lest the Lord’s flocks remain too long without the care of shepherds.

When a metropolitan has died and another must be substituted in his place, the provincial bishops must assemble in the metropolitan city. After the wishes of all the clergy and citizens have been examined, the best man is to be chosen from among the presbyters or deacons of that church. The provincial priests are to report his name to your knowledge, and are to fulfill the wishes of those who requested him once they learn that what pleased them has also pleased you. For just as we do not wish just elections to be wearied by any delays, so we permit nothing to be presumed without your knowledge.

### VI. That two provincial councils of bishops be held each year, and that if a difficult matter arises and is not settled by the judgment of the bishop of Thessalonica, it be referred to the Roman bishop

Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers salutarily established: namely, that two assemblies be held each year, in which judgment is given concerning all the complaints that commonly arise among the various orders of the Church. If, however, a matter concerning greater offenses should arise between those who preside—God forbid—and it cannot be settled by provincial examination, the metropolitan is to inform your Fraternity of the entire nature of the case. If the matter is not resolved by your judgment after the parties have appeared before you, whatever it may be is to be transferred to our judgment.

### VII. That if a bishop, abandoning his own city, seeks a greater see out of ambition, he may obtain neither that see nor retain his own [Note: [Col. 0772D] In the others except Alv., *carere debebit*: “he will have to lose”]

If a bishop, disdaining the modesty of his own city’s administration, has sought the administration of a more renowned place and has transferred himself by whatever means to a greater people, let him indeed be expelled from the foreign see, but let him also lose his own. Thus he will preside neither over those whom he coveted through greed nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries [Note: [Col. 0772D] In the others except Alv. and Esc. 3, *quisquis*: “whoever”], and let no one seek to enlarge himself beyond the measure of his own right.

### VIII. That no one presume to entice or retain another’s cleric without the consent of his bishop

Let no one receive another’s cleric, or entice him, against the will of his own bishop, unless perhaps an agreement of charity has been reached between the one giving and the one receiving him [Note: [Col. 0772D] From Urg. and Ger. In Alv., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Tol. 1, *explicito*: “explicit”; Aem., *exemplo*: “by example”]. For he is guilty of grave injury who dares to allure or retain from a brother’s Church what is more useful or more precious.

Therefore, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan is to compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. If he has gone farther away, he is to be recalled by the authority of your command, so that no opportunity may be left either to greed or ambition.

### IX. That moderation be maintained by the bishop of Thessalonica in summoning provincial bishops, lest under this pretext priestly honor be subjected to insults; and that no more than two bishops from each province, approved by the metropolitans, be sent

In summoning bishops to you, we wish you to be most moderate, lest you appear to take pride in fraternal injuries under the pretext of greater diligence [Note: [Col. 0773C] From Bibl. Reg., Urg., and Ger. In Alv. and Tol. 1, 2: *fraternis in gloriam videaris injuriis*: “you appear to glory in fraternal injuries.” Aem. and Esc. 3: *fraternis gloriam videaris*: “you appear to glory in fraternal…”]. Therefore, if some greater cause should arise for which it is reasonable [Col. 0773B] and necessary to summon a fraternal assembly, it is sufficient for two bishops from each province, whom the metropolitans judge should be sent, to come to your Fraternity.

### X. That bishops not remain more than fifteen days beyond the appointed time of the council, and that if contention arises among them concerning the matter, everything be disclosed to the Roman bishop in an official record, so that he may order what pleases God

Those who have assembled are not to be delayed beyond fifteen days from the appointed time. If, however, in the matter which you have judged should be discussed and settled with the brothers, their opinions differ from your own, everything is to be reported to us with the testimony of the official proceedings, so that, once ambiguities have been removed, what pleases God may be decreed [Col. 0773C].

Toward this end we direct all our concern and care: that nothing pertaining to the unity of concord or the preservation of discipline be violated by disagreement or neglected through sluggishness. I therefore exhort and admonish you, dearest brother, and those of our brothers who are offended by your excesses—although not all have the same grounds for complaint—not to disturb through contention what has been piously ordered and salutarily arranged [Col. 0774A].

Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another; and, as the Apostle says: “Let each of us please his neighbor for the good, to build him up.” For the structure of our unity cannot be firm unless the bond of charity binds us together in inseparable solidity. Just as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.

The connection of the whole body produces one health and one beauty. This connection indeed requires unanimity throughout the body, but above all it demands concord among priests. Although their dignity is not equal, their general order is one; for even among the most blessed apostles there was, despite a similarity of honor, a certain distinction of power. Though the election of all was equal, one was nevertheless given precedence over the others.

From this pattern also arose the distinction among bishops, and provision was made by a great ordinance so that no one might claim everything for himself. Instead, in each province there would be individual bishops whose judgment would have first place among their brothers. Again, certain bishops established in the greater cities would undertake a broader responsibility, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one see of the Father [Note: [Col. 0774C] Aem., Tol. 1, 2, *patriae*: “of the fatherland”; in the printed editions, *Petri*: “of Peter”], and nothing anywhere would disagree with its head.

Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over some people should not resent having someone placed over him. He should render the obedience that he requires from others, and just as he does not wish to bear the burden of a heavy load, so he should not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon another.

For we are disciples of the humble and gentle Teacher, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.” How can we experience this unless we also observe what the same Lord says: “The one who is greater among you shall be your servant; but whoever exalts himself [Note: [Col. 0774C] In the others except Alv., *exaltaverit*: “has exalted himself”] shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted”?

## LXVIII. Letter 68 of the same Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia (C)

[Col. 0773]

[Col. 0773D] Leo, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

111 My son Adeodatus, a deacon of our see, having returned to us, reported that your affection had requested from us the authority of the apostolic see concerning matters which appear to present considerable difficulty of judgment. But, in view of the necessities of the present time, care must be applied so that the wounds inflicted by the hostility of the enemy may be healed above all through the concern of religion.

### I. That women who had married other men while their husbands were captive must be joined to their former husbands when those husbands return from captivity, so that each may recover what belongs to him

You report that through the calamity of war and the gravest assaults of hostility certain marriages have been so divided that, when the husbands were led into captivity, their wives remained abandoned. These women thought that their own husbands had either been killed or would never be freed from their masters’ power, and, compelled by their isolation, entered into the marriages of other men.

Now that, with the Lord’s help, circumstances have turned for the better, some of those who were thought to have perished have returned. Your charity therefore rightly appears uncertain what instruction should be given by us concerning women who have been joined to other men. But since we know that it is written that a woman is joined to a man by God, and since we again recognize the command that what God has joined, man must not separate, we must believe that the bonds of lawful marriage are to be restored. Once the evils brought by hostility have been removed, each person must be restored to what he or she lawfully possessed; every effort must be made so that each may recover what is his or her own.

### II. That the man who appears to have taken in marriage the wife of a captive is not to be judged culpable

Nor should the man who assumed the position of a husband believed already dead be judged culpable or treated as an invader of another’s right. In this way many things belonging to those who were led into captivity could pass into another’s legal possession, and yet it is entirely just that, when those same people return, their property be restored to them. If this is rightly observed with slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in restoring marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored by the remedy of peace?

### III. That if the husbands returning from captivity are not offended by their wives’ conduct and wish to receive them back in marriage, they have full freedom to do so

Therefore, if husbands returning after a long captivity continue so steadfast in affection for their wives that they desire them to return to their marital union, what necessity brought about is to be set aside and judged blameless, and what fidelity demands is to be restored.

### IV. That if the women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious

But if some women have been so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to remain attached to them rather than return to their lawful union, they are rightly to be censured, even to the point of being deprived of ecclesiastical communion. For they inexcusably chose the contamination of sin, showing that, because of their lack of continence, they preferred what a just remission could have expiated.

Let marriages therefore return to their former state through voluntary restoration, and let what the condition of necessity extorted never be turned into a reproach for evil will. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection established by God are rightly to be praised.

### V. That penance is to be granted to captives who were compelled by terror or hunger, not by religious veneration, to eat sacrificial foods

[Col. 0775D]

Concerning those Christians who are said to have been defiled by sacrificial foods among the people by whom they had been taken captive, we believe that this too must be answered to your charity: they are to be cleansed by penitential satisfaction, which is to be measured not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart [Aem., “contrition”]. Whether terror forced this upon them or hunger persuaded them, the fault should without hesitation be pardoned, since such food was eaten out of fear or necessity, not out of religious veneration.

### VI. That those who were compelled by force or fear to submit to a repetition of baptism are to be assisted by the remedy of penance, with careful consideration also given to old age, dangers, illnesses, and other necessities

Those about whom your affection likewise judged that we should be consulted—who were compelled by fear or led astray by error into repeating baptism, and now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—are to be treated with this moderation: they are not to be restored to fellowship with us and the unity of communion except through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

The period of their penance is to be moderated according to your judgment, depending on how devoted you perceive the hearts of the converts to be. At the same time, you are to take account of the condition of old age and to consider the necessities arising from every kind of danger or illness. If anyone is so gravely afflicted that, while still doing penance, his salvation is despaired of, priestly care must come to his aid by granting the grace of communion [Note: [Col. 0775D] Urg., Ger., “through priestly order and care”].

### VII. That those baptized by heretics be strengthened by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone

[Col. 0776C]

Those who received baptism from heretics, if they had not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone through the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism, without the power of sanctification. As you know, we proclaim that this rule is to be observed in all the churches: the washing once begun must not be violated by repetition. The Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism.” Its washing must not be profaned by repetition; instead, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that they may receive from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

You are to circulate this letter of ours, which we have sent in response to the consultation of your Fraternity [Note: [Col. 0776D] From Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1, Ger.; in the others, “consolation of your Fraternity”], to all your brother and fellow-provincial bishops, so that the authority issued may benefit the observance of all.

## LXIX. Letter 69 of the same Leo to the African bishops (C)

[Col. 0775]

[Col. 0775D] Leo sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Africa.

113

### I. That unlawful persons not be promoted to the episcopate
When a more frequent report was circulating among you that certain practices had been unlawfully usurped in the ordination of priests, the reasonableness of pastoral concern [Col. 0776D] requires that, in accordance with the solicitude which by divine institution we owe to the universal Church, we should take care to ascertain the truth of the matter. Entrusting the responsibility for our concern to our brother and fellow priest Potentius, we commanded him to investigate what the truth was concerning those bishops whose election was being reported as culpable, and to inform us faithfully of everything [Col. 0777A]. Since he has now fully disclosed all the facts and has sincerely revealed to us under what sort and what kind of rulers a portion of Christ’s people in the districts of the province of Caesarea is being held, it was necessary for us, by letters sent to you, to express the grief of our heart, with which we burn on account of the dangers threatening the Lord’s flocks. We are astonished that, under the pretext of unsettled times or through the presumption of ambition, popular tumult should have had such force among you that the pastoral dignity and governance of the Church were entrusted to persons who were unworthy and far removed from priestly merit. This is not to care for the peoples but to harm them; it is not to provide governance but to increase danger.

For the integrity of those who preside is the salvation of those subject to them, and wherever obedience is secure, [Col. 0777B] there the form of sound doctrine is preserved. Yet a principate which sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if it does not offend by its morals and conduct, is nevertheless pernicious because of the example set by its very beginning; and it is difficult for those things to reach a good end which were begun with an evil beginning.

If, then, in every rank of the Church it must be prudently and intelligently ensured that nothing disordered or out of place exists in the Lord’s house, how much more must care be taken that there be no error in the election of him who is placed above all the ranks? For the condition and order of the entire household will totter if what is required in the body is not found in the head.

Where is that command of the blessed apostle Paul, issued through the Spirit of God, by which the whole company of Christ’s priests is instructed in the person of Timothy, and [Col. 0777C] each one of us is accordingly told: “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others”? What does “Lay hands quickly on no one” mean except that one must not confer priestly honor upon those who have not been tested—before the age of maturity, before the time of examination, before the merit of labor, before experience of discipline? And what does “share in the sins of others” mean except to become the sort of ordainer that the person who has not deserved to be ordained is?

For just as the one who carefully exercises sound judgment in choosing a priest gains the fruit of a good work for himself, so the one who raises an unworthy person to the fellowship of his dignity inflicts serious harm upon himself. What is contained in the general regulations must not be set aside in anyone’s case, nor should that honor be considered legitimate which has been conferred through transgression.

For since the Apostle says, among the rules governing election, that a bishop is to be ordained who is known to have been or to be “the husband of one wife,” this command has always been regarded as so sacred that the same condition was understood to apply to the woman chosen as the priest’s wife: she must not previously have experienced marriage with another man before marrying the one who had had no other wife.

Who, then, would dare to conceal what is done as an offense against so great a sacrament, when even the provisions of the law did not fail to address this great and venerable mystery, explicitly defining that a priest should take a virgin and should not know the marriage-bed of another husband—the woman who is to become the wife of the bishop?

Even then, the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church [Col. 0778A] was being represented in priests, so that, since the man is the head of the woman, the bride of the Word might learn to know no other man than Christ, who rightly chose one, loves one, and joins no other to himself in companionship. If, therefore, this form of priestly marriages was observed even in the Old Testament, how much more, now that grace has been revealed, ought we who are established under it to obey the apostolic commands? Thus, however distinguished by good morals and adorned with holy works a man may be found, he must nevertheless by no means rise to the rank of deacon, the honor of presbyter, or the summit of the episcopate if it is established either that he himself was not the husband of one wife or that his wife had not been the wife of one man.

But when the Apostle warns and says, “Let these also first be tested, and then let them serve,” what else should we understand [Col. 0778B] except that in these promotions we must consider not only the privileges of marriage but also the merits of labor? We must not entrust pastoral office either to those inexperienced from baptism or to those suddenly converted from secular activity, since it ought to be judged from their progress through all the ranks of Christian service whether greater responsibilities can be entrusted to each one.

Accordingly, when the venerable enactments of the blessed Fathers spoke about the election of priests, they judged those finally suitable for sacred administration whose entire life, from childhood’s beginnings to more advanced years, had passed through the disciplines of ecclesiastical service. In this way a person’s earlier life would provide testimony, and there could be no doubt about the advancement of one who, for his many labors, chaste morals, and vigorous conduct, deserved the reward of a higher [Col. 0778C] position.

If it is unworthy to attain worldly honors without the support of time and without the merit of labor, and if those whose proofs of integrity do not support them are customarily branded as ambitious, how careful and prudent must be the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities, lest the apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in any respect, and the governance of the Lord’s Church be entrusted to those ignorant of legitimate institutions and unaware of all humility! Such persons do not wish to rise by advancement from the lowest ranks but want to have their beginning from the highest, although it is extremely unjust and absurd that the inexperienced should be preferred to teachers, the new to the old, and the untrained to those who have earned their standing.

In a great house, as the Apostle said, there must be different vessels: some of gold and silver, but others of wood [Col. 0778D] and clay. Their service, however, is assigned according to the quality of their material, and the use of the valuable is not the same as that of the inferior. Everything will be disordered if clay vessels are preferred to golden ones, and wooden vessels to silver ones.

Just as the forms of those people who as yet shine with no virtues are represented by the wooden and clay vessels, so without doubt those who, through the long fire of instruction and the furnace of prolonged labor, have been refined and have deserved to be tested gold and pure silver are represented by the golden and silver vessels. If they receive no reward for their devotion, all obedience is dissolved and every order is disturbed, while in the Church those who have undergone no ministry obtain, through the perverse judgment of the electors, a principate to which they have no right.

Since among you [Col. 0779A] either popular enthusiasm or the ambition of the proud has had such force that we recognize not only laymen but also husbands of second wives and husbands of widows as having been advanced to pastoral office, do not the circumstances most plainly require that we cleanse by stricter judgment the Churches in which these things have been committed, and that fitting severity be directed not only against such prelates but also against those who ordained them?

But on one side gentleness born of clemency surrounds us, and on the other the discipline of justice. Since “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” we are compelled, in accordance with the pastoral concern of the apostolic see, to temper our sentence in such a way that, having weighed the measure of the offenses—which plainly are not all of one kind—we may define some as in some fashion tolerable and cut off others completely.

For we do not permit those who have entered into second marriages [Col. 0779B] or joined themselves in marriage to widows to remain in the priesthood; and we decree that, with much greater reason, the man who is simultaneously the husband of two wives, or the man who is reported to have married another after being dismissed by his first wife, must be deprived of his honor.

As for the others whose advancement incurs this sole ground of reproach—that they were elected from among the laity to episcopal office [Bibl. Reg.: selected]—and who cannot be blameworthy merely because they have a wife, we permit them to retain the priesthood they have undertaken. In doing so, we do not prejudice the statutes of the apostolic see, nor the decrees of our predecessors or of ourselves, by which it has salutarily been established that no layman, however supported by popular votes, should ascend to the first or second rank in the Church, or even to the third, before reaching the requisite merit through legitimate [Col. 0779C] stages of advancement.

What is now tolerable in some measure cannot later remain unpunished if anyone presumes to usurp what we wholly forbid, because the remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor will we henceforth allow what could in some way be conceded to be committed with impunity.

[Note: [Col. 0780C] In the other copies, apart from Alv., this letter is more extensive in the collated text.]

## II. Concerning Donatus, bishop of the Novatians, and Maximus, formerly a Donatist

We wish Donatus of Salacina, converted from the Novatian party together with his people, as we have learned, to preside over the Lord’s flock in such a way that he remember to send us a statement of his faith [Col. 0780A], in which he condemns the error of Novatian doctrine and confesses the Catholic truth in full.

We do not exclude Maximus, although he was improperly ordained from the laity, from the episcopal dignity which he acquired by whatever means, provided that he is no longer a Donatist and has separated himself from the spirit of schismatic perversity. He must, however, demonstrate by a statement issued to us that he is Catholic [Note: [Col. 0779C] In the others, except Alv., “declare.”].

## III. Concerning Aggarus [Note: [Col. 0779C] From the other copies; in Alv., “Accarus.”] and Tiberianus, who were ordained from the laity

With regard to Aggarus and Tiberianus, whose case differs from that of the other men ordained from the laity in this respect—that violent disturbances and savage seditions are said to have attended their ordination—we entrust everything to your judgment, so that, once the reliability of the investigation conducted among you has been reported, we may know what ought to be decided concerning the persons mentioned above [Col. 0780B].

## IV. Concerning sacred virgins who suffered barbarian violence [Note: [Col. 0780C] From the others; except Alv., where it reads “who endured.”]

Those servants of God who lost the integrity of their chastity through barbarian oppression will be more praiseworthy in humility and modesty if they do not dare to compare themselves with undefiled virgins. Although every sin arises from the will, and the mind, unwilling, may not have been polluted by the corruption of the flesh, it will nevertheless harm them less if they grieve that they lost bodily what they were able not to admit in their minds.

## V. Concerning the preservation of the canonical statutes

Since, therefore, you see that your affection has been fully instructed concerning everything contained in the report of our brother Potentius [Col. 0780C], it remains for you to receive his salutary exhortations with united obedience. Do nothing through contention, but, unanimous in every effort of devotion, serve the divine and apostolic constitutions, and in no respect permit the devout decrees of the canons to be violated.

For what we have now relaxed after consideration of particular cases must henceforth be guarded according to the ancient rules, lest what we have conceded for a time in pious leniency we later punish with just retribution.

## LXX. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THEODORE, BISHOP OF FOROJULIUM. That penance and communion are not to be denied to those at the point of death. (C)

[Col. 0779]

[Col. 0779D] Leo to Theodore, bishop of Forojulium, greetings.

The proper course of your solicitude should indeed have been first to confer with your metropolitan concerning the matter which seemed to require inquiry; and, if he too did not know what your affection did not know, you should have sought instruction together. For in matters that pertain to general observance, nothing ought to be investigated without the primates. But I shall not leave unspoken how the uncertainty of one seeking advice is to be instructed, or what rule the Church maintains concerning the condition of penitents [Col. 0780D].

The manifold mercy of God so comes to the aid of human falls that the hope of eternal life is restored not only through the grace of baptism, but also through the remedy of penance, so that those who had violated the gifts of regeneration, condemning themselves by their own judgment, might attain remission of their crimes. Thus the aids of divine goodness have been ordered so that God’s indulgence cannot be obtained except through the supplications of priests. For the Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus the Lord, entrusted this power to the rulers of the Church: that they should both impose the discipline of penance upon those who confess, and admit those cleansed by this salutary satisfaction to communion in the sacraments through the door of reconciliation.

The Savior himself, certainly, intervenes unceasingly in this work and is never absent from them: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age”; so that, if anything is accomplished through our service in good order and with a welcome result, we should not doubt that it has been granted to us through the Holy Spirit. But if any of those for whom we beseech the Lord, intercepted by whatever obstacle, falls short of the gift of present indulgence and, before reaching the appointed remedies, ends this temporal life by the condition of humanity [Col. 0781B], he cannot obtain when stripped of the flesh what he did not receive while remaining in the body.

Nor is it necessary for us to examine the merit and deeds of those who have died, since our Lord, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his justice what he did not permit the priestly ministry to accomplish. He wills his power to be feared, so that this fear may benefit all, and no one may fail to fear what happens to certain lukewarm or negligent persons. For it is very useful and necessary that the liability of sins be loosed by priestly supplication before the last day.

But for those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressing urgency of danger, seek the aid of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because we can neither set measures nor determine times for God’s mercy, with whom true conversion suffers no delay of pardon. The Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When, having turned, you groan, then you shall be saved”; and elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified”; likewise: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” [Col. 0782A]

Therefore, in dispensing God’s gifts we ought not to be difficult, nor neglect the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very desire to repent is conceived through God’s inspiration.
