The Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God give them repentance, that they may come to their senses from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will.” Therefore every Christian ought to pass judgment on his own conscience, so that he does not defer turning to the Lord from day to day, nor set for himself the time of satisfaction at the end of his life—a time which human ignorance perilously restricts—so that he reserves himself for the uncertain space of a few hours. Though he can merit indulgence through fuller satisfaction, he chooses the narrowness of that time, in which scarcely may either the penitent’s confession or the priest’s reconciliation find room [Col. 0782B].

Thus assistance must be given even to the necessity of such persons, so that neither the exercise of penance nor the grace of communion may be denied them, if they are proved to seek it, even after loss of the use of speech, by signs of an unimpaired mind. But if they have been so weighed down by some illness that they cannot indicate in the priest’s presence what they were requesting shortly before, the testimony of faithful persons standing by ought to assist them, so that they may nevertheless receive together the benefit both of penance and of reconciliation, while preserving the rule of the canons concerning those persons who have sinned against the Lord by departing from the faith [Note: [Col. 0781] From Aem., Bibl. Reg., Ger., and Urg. In the others: “by departing from the Lord’s faith.”].

Brother, you will make these things, which I have answered to your affectionate inquiry so that nothing contrary may be done under the excuse of ignorance, known to your metropolitan [Col. 0782C], so that, if there are perhaps any brothers who formerly thought these matters doubtful, through him all that has been written to you may become known. Given on the third day before the Ides of June [Tol. 2: July], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculaneus.

## LXXI. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO LEO, BISHOP OF RAVENNA. (C)

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781C] Leo to Leo, bishop of Ravenna, greetings.

We have indeed often strengthened the wavering hearts of our brethren amid the uncertainty of various questions [Col. 0781D], as the Spirit of God instructed us, deriving a form of response either from the teaching of the sacred Scriptures or from the rules of the Fathers. But recently in a synod a new and previously unheard-of kind of consultation arose.

### I. Concerning little children who came into captivity and do not remember the grace of baptism

For, at the suggestion of certain brethren, we learned that some captives, returning in freedom to their homes, who had come into captivity at an age at which they could have no firm knowledge of anything, seek the remedy of baptism; but they cannot remember, through their infantile awareness, whether they received the sacraments of that mystery before. Thus, under this uncertainty of hidden recollection, their souls are brought into danger, while, under the appearance of caution, a grace is denied them which is not bestowed because it is thought to have been bestowed [Col. 0782C–D].

Although the fear of certain brethren not without reason hesitated to confer upon such persons the sacraments of the Lord’s mystery, we received, as we have said, in the synodal assembly a formulation of this consultation. We wish it to be examined more diligently and considered with careful reasoning according to each person’s judgment, so that, once the matter has been understood, we may more certainly attain the truth through the agreement of many. Yet frequent agreement of the brethren also confirmed those things which came into our mind by divine inspiration.

First of all, therefore, we must take care that, while observing a certain appearance of caution, we do not incur the loss of souls needing regeneration. For who is so given over to his suspicions as to determine as true that which, with the Lord’s manifestation absent, he conjectures from an ambiguous opinion? Therefore, when neither the person who desires regeneration remembers that he was baptized [Col. 0783A], nor can another who does not know him to have been consecrated attest it concerning him, there is nothing by which sin can creep in, since in this respect of conscience neither he who is consecrated is guilty nor he who consecrates.

We know, indeed, that it is an inexpiable crime whenever, in accordance with the practices of heretics condemned by the holy Fathers, someone is compelled to undergo twice the washing that is granted once to those needing regeneration; for apostolic teaching protests, teaching us one Godhead in unity, one confession in faith, one sacrament in baptism. But in this case no such thing is feared, because what is wholly unknown to have been done cannot incur the charge of repetition.

And therefore, whenever such a person occurs, first investigate by careful examination and over a long time—unless perhaps the final end is imminent—whether absolutely no one can aid by testimony the ignorance of one who does not know [Col. 0783B; 0784A]. When it has been established that the person who needs the sacrament of baptism is vainly prevented by suspicion alone, let him approach without fear to obtain the grace of which he knows no trace in himself. Nor should we fear to open to him the door of salvation, which he is never shown to have entered before.

### II. That one baptized by heretics is to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands

But if it has been established that anyone was baptized by heretics, the sacrament of regeneration is by no means to be repeated for him. Rather, only what was lacking there is to be conferred, so that through the episcopal laying on of hands he may receive the power of the Holy Spirit. Dearest brother, we wish this matter to come generally to the knowledge of all of you, lest, while people fear more than is right, God’s mercy be denied to those who desire salvation. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the Emperor Majorian.

## LXXII. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO DIOSCORUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA. (C)

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783B] Leo to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, greetings.

You will be able to recognize how much affection of the Lord’s charity we bestow upon your affection from the fact that we hasten to establish your beginnings more firmly, lest anything seem lacking to your charity for perfection, since, as we have proved, the merits of spiritual grace support you. Therefore paternal and fraternal communication ought to be most welcome to your holiness and received by you in the manner in which you understand it to proceed from us [Col. 0783C]. For we ought to think and act as one, so that, as we read, it may be proved that in us too there is one heart and one soul.

For since the most blessed Peter received apostolic primacy from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0783D] Aem.: “received apostolic power from the Lord.”], and the Roman Church remains in his institutions, it is wicked to believe that his holy disciple Mark, who first governed the Church of Alexandria, formed the ordinances of his traditions according to different rules. Without doubt, from the same fountain of grace, there was one spirit of disciple and master, and one who was ordained could not hand on anything other than what he received from his ordainer. Therefore we do not permit, when we confess ourselves to be of one body and one faith, that we differ in anything or that the ordinances of master and disciple should appear different.

### I. Concerning the ordination of a presbyter or deacon: that it be celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, on the Lord’s Day

[Col. 0783D]

Therefore we wish you also to preserve what we know was observed by our Fathers with more devoted care: that priestly or levitical ordination should not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but that the beginning after the sabbath day, of the night which dawns into the first day of the week, should be chosen. In these, the sacred blessing is to be conferred upon those to be consecrated while they are fasting, and by persons who are fasting. The same observance will apply [Note: [Col. 0783D] From the other copies except Alv., in which: “applies.”] if it is celebrated on the very morning of the Lord’s Day, with the sabbath fast continued [Col. 0784B]. For that time does not depart from the beginning of the preceding night, which, as is also made clear in the Lord’s Passover, unquestionably belongs to the day of resurrection.

For apart from the authority of custom, which we know comes from apostolic teaching, sacred Scripture also shows that, when the apostles, by command of the Holy Spirit, sent Paul and Barnabas to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles, they laid hands on them while fasting and praying, so that we may understand [Col. 0784C] with how great devotion on the part of both those giving and those receiving it must be ensured that the sacrament of so great a blessing is not seen to be performed negligently.

Therefore you will devoutly and laudably follow the custom of apostolic institutions if you yourself preserve this form of ordaining priests throughout the Churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside: so that blessing may never be conferred on those to be consecrated except on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, whose beginning is known to be assigned from the evening of the sabbath. That day is consecrated by so great mysteries of divine dispensations that whatever more outstanding has been established by the Lord has been accomplished in the dignity of this day. On this day the world took its beginning; on this day, by Christ’s resurrection, death received destruction and life received its beginning; on this day the apostles receive from the Lord the trumpet of the Gospel to preach to all nations [Col. 0784D], and receive the sacrament of regeneration to bring into the whole world. On this day, as the blessed evangelist John testifies, when the disciples had assembled together and the doors were shut, the Lord entered to them, breathed upon them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain [Note: [Col. 0784D] From the other copies except Alv. and Esc. 3, which read: “detain,” “detained.”], they are retained.” Finally, on this day the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord came upon the apostles, so that, a certain heavenly rule having been indicated and handed down, we may know that the mysteries of priestly blessings are to be celebrated by us on that day [Col. 0785A], on which all gifts of graces are bestowed by deliberate counsel.

### II. Concerning festivals: if one celebration is insufficient for the people, there is to be no hesitation in repeating the sacrifice

Moreover, so that our observance may agree in all things, we also wish this to be preserved: when a more solemn festival has summoned a larger assembly of people and so great a multitude of believers gathers that one basilica cannot receive them all at once, the offering of the sacrifice is without hesitation to be repeated. Otherwise, if only those who arrived first are admitted to this devotion, those who flocked together afterward seem not to have been received. It is full of piety and reason that, whenever the presence of a new body of people has filled the basilica in which the service is conducted, a further sacrifice should be offered [Col. 0786A].

Some part of the people must be deprived of its devotion if, keeping the custom of only one Mass, only those can offer the sacrifice who assembled in the first part of the day. We therefore earnestly and affectionately admonish your affection that your care also should not neglect what has become established in our custom from the pattern of paternal tradition, so that we may agree with one another in all things in faith and actions. For this reason we gave this letter to be carried to your fraternity by our returning son Possidonius the presbyter, who has often taken part in our processions and ordinations and, having been sent to us so often, has learned what we maintain in all matters by apostolic authority. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July.

## LXXIII. LETTER OF THE SAME LEO TO THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT CAMPANIA. (C)

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785B] Leo to all bishops throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum, greetings.

### I. That the regeneration of baptism is not to be given at every time, except at Easter and Pentecost, and if a dangerous illness supervenes

I am moved by great indignation and deeply distressed because I have learned that some among you have so forgotten the apostolic tradition and are so intent on pursuing their own error that, apart from the paschal feast [Note: [Col. 0786D] From Aem. In the others: “festive.”], to which alone the solemnity of Pentecost is comparable, they dare to claim for themselves the right of baptism—not because any necessity of human weakness compels them, but solely by the license of undisciplined judgment. They celebrate the mysteries of regeneration on the birthdays of martyrs, whose death is to be honored otherwise than the day of the Lord’s passion; and, without any instruction in spiritual preparations, they so hand over the sacrament to the untrained and ignorant [Col. 0785C] that, in renewing them, neither ecclesiastical teaching, nor the laying on of hands in exorcisms, nor the very fasts by which the old man is destroyed, accomplish anything. And in so many mysteries of human salvation no exception is made for that day on which the very gift of rebirth was established.

We therefore admonish you, and we declare not without danger to the standing of those who do this, that this presumption must cease and that you confer this supreme and most powerful grace of God upon those who desire and believe only on the days of Easter and Pentecost. Yet at every time consideration must remain for grave necessities and dangers, according to which help ought to be given, lest weakness, constrained by mortal condition, be deprived of necessary deliverance. While, as we have previously said [Col. 0785D], the reverence of only the two festivals is preserved, it is necessary, because of many dangers, to take care [Col. 0786B] lest regeneration be denied by the priests of the Lord to anyone in desperate illness, in an enemy attack, or in fear of shipwreck. But if anyone, after this prohibition, is discovered in the same usurpation, he will incur a punishment worthy of his obstinacy, because he has shown himself to have pursued shameful gain rather than religious worship.

### II. Concerning the penance of the faithful: that their confession is not made public

I also order by every means to be removed that presumption contrary to the apostolic rule, which I recently learned is committed by some through unlawful usurpation: namely, concerning the penance sought by the faithful, that a written declaration concerning the kind of each individual’s sins should not be publicly read from documents, since it is sufficient that the guilt of consciences be made known to priests alone through secret confession [Col. 0786C].

Although the fullness of faith which, because of fear of God, is not ashamed before men may appear praiseworthy, nevertheless, because not everyone’s sins are such that those who seek penance need not fear to disclose them, this reprehensible custom must be removed, lest many be excluded from the remedies of penance while they either are ashamed or fear that their deeds may be disclosed to their enemies, by whom they can be struck under a legal provision. For that confession is sufficient which is offered first to God and then also to the priest, who approaches as a suppliant for the sins of penitents. Then more people can be stirred to penance if the conscience of the confessor is not made public to the ears of the people. Given on the second day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of Ricimer.

## LXXIV. SYNODAL DECREE OF POPE HILARY. (C)

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785D] In the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Basiliscus [Aem., Urg.: Basilicus] and Hermenericus [Col. 0786D], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the basilica of Saint Mary, Pope Hilary was seated [Note: [Col. 0787C] In the other copies, except Alv., Tol. 1 and 2: “the venerable Pope being seated.”] with fifty bishops; all the presbyters were also seated, and the deacons stood by. Hilary, bishop of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said:

### I. The enactments of the canons are to be observed

Since the religious assembly, gathered by the Holy Spirit, urges us to consider with more diligent care certain matters necessary for ecclesiastical discipline, if it pleases the brethren, let us, with the Lord’s help, establish for all time the matters that pertain to the rule of ordinations according to the precepts of divine law and the enactments of the Nicene canons. Thus no one may lawfully, without danger to his standing, violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see, lest we, who administer the offices of the most mighty priesthood [Col. 0787B], be charged with blame for such transgressions if we are found negligent in God’s causes. For we remember how we ought to fear the Lord’s threats concerning the negligence of priests: one who enjoys greater honor sins with greater guilt, and the loftiness of dignities makes the vices of sinners more grievous.

### II. That a bigamist, or the husband of a widow or of a woman who has been defiled, is not to enter ecclesiastical ranks

Therefore, first of all, care must be taken that no one who has not taken a virgin as wife aspire to the sacred [Aem.: priestly] ranks, as has previously been prescribed in the records. Likewise, anyone who has entered into the marriage of a second wife contrary to the apostolic precepts must be excluded.

### III. That penitents, the illiterate, and those who, through loss or cutting off of limbs, have some deficiency, are not to come to higher orders

[Col. 0787C]

Those ignorant of letters, those who have suffered any bodily loss, and those who are among the penitents must likewise not dare to aspire to sacred orders. Whoever has been the consecrator of any such person shall himself undo his deed.

### IV. That things unlawfully ordained by a bishop or his predecessor are to be corrected by the one who remains

But whatever unlawful thing anyone has committed, or has found admitted by his predecessors, he shall condemn if he wishes to avoid danger to himself [Col. 0788A]. For in no respect do we wish to exceed the severity of retribution. But whoever has sinned in God’s causes through obstinacy or any transgression will himself find whatever he has not cut off in any matter.

That this may henceforth be observed more firmly, if it pleases you, furnish all your own decisions and subscriptions, so that unlawful access may be closed off by synodal judgment. All the bishops said six times: “These things we both confirm and teach.” They said eight times: “These things must be maintained; these things must be observed.” They said five times: “We give thanks for your teaching.” They said ten times: “We ask that these things be observed forever.” They said fifteen times: “Through Saint Peter we desire that these things be observed forever.” They said eight times: “May this presumption never occur.” [Note: [Col. 0787C] This passage has been taken from the manuscripts Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1 and 2, Urg., and Ger., since it is lacking in the others.] They said ten times: “Whoever violates these things will find in himself the censure of excommunication” [Note: [Col. 0788C] These words, “the censure of excommunication,” are absent in Alv., Aem., Esc. 3, and Ger. They have been taken from the other manuscripts.]. Then silence having been made, Hilary the bishop said:

### V. That no bishop is to choose a successor for himself
Moreover, brothers, as has reached us through letters sent from Spain with a reliable report, new and unheard-of seeds of perversity are continually springing up in certain places. Indeed, some people regard the episcopate—which is granted only on the basis of preceding merits—not as a divine gift but as an hereditary advantage, and believe that, like perishable and mortal possessions, the priesthood too can be transferred by way of legacy or testamentary right. For many priests, when placed at the point of death, are said to designate others to be substituted in their place under specified names [Col. 0788C], so that a legitimate election is not awaited, but rather the consent of the people, supposedly won over by the deceased, is obtained. You judge how serious this is; and therefore, if it seems good, let us also remove this license generally from the Churches, lest—shameful as it is to say it—anyone think that he owes to a human being what belongs to God. But so that what has been reported to us may also come to your knowledge, let the writings of the Spanish bishops and of our fellow bishops, our brothers, be read. The notary Paul recited them, and it was decreed that priests make no further presumption of this kind.

# LXXV. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE HILARY TO ASCANIUS AND TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF TARRACONA. (C)

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787D] To his most beloved brothers Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarracona, Hilary, bishop.

122 After we received the letter of your affection, in which you requested that the presumptions of Silvanus, bishop of the Church of Calagurris, be restrained, and again sought to have the excessively unlawful petitions of the people of Barcelona confirmed, it is clear to us that letters from the leading men and landholders [Note: In the remaining witnesses, except Alv. and Esc. 3, “of bishops”] of the cities of Turiassus, Cascantum, [Col. 0788D] Calagurris, Varegia [In the printed editions, Virgilia], Tritium, Legio, and Birovesca [In the printed editions, Civitas], together with the subscriptions of various persons, were brought to us. Through these letters they excused what your complaint had brought forward against Silvanus. Yet their defense likewise did not lack the most just grounds for censure, because it became clear that priests had been ordained in certain cities without the knowledge of our metropolitan brother and fellow bishop Ascanius [Note: In the others, except Alv., “father” instead of “brother.”]. Therefore, since we saw that everything reported by either side was confused by perversity, having considered the necessity of the times, we decree on this basis that what was done should be remitted, so that henceforth nothing be attempted against the sentence of the blessed Apostle, and nothing against the decrees of the canons of Nicaea.

## I. That no bishop be ordained without the consent of the metropolitan.

This, then, we first wish to be observed according to the regulations of those same Fathers: that no bishop whatsoever be consecrated without the knowledge and consent of the metropolitan brother Ascanius, because the ancient order has maintained this, and the holy authority of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers defined it [Col. 0789B]. Whoever stretches out his hands against it confesses himself unworthy of the fellowship of those whose commands he has resisted.

## II. That no bishop, abandoning his own Church, transfer to another.

In contempt of these provisions, that other rule too is despised through an arrogant spirit, by which it is forbidden that anyone presume to leave his own Church and transfer to another [Note: In the others, except Alv., “another” is supplied]. Bishop Irenaeus is attempting to permit this through most shameful connivance—and, what is more grievous, with you asserting it—although you seek by our authority to strengthen those whom you demonstrate to be inflamed with great indignation over unlawful matters. Therefore, when your letters had been read in the assembly of the brothers whom the celebration of my birthday had gathered, you will learn from the tenor of the proceedings which we likewise sent what sentence has been issued concerning the ordination of bishops according to the provisions of the canons or the decrees of my predecessors [Col. 0789C].

## III. That Irenaeus, removed from Barcelona, return to his own Church.

Accordingly, with Bishop Irenaeus removed from the Church of Barcelona and sent back to his own, and with the desires that seek through ignorance of ecclesiastical laws to obtain what is not permitted quieted by priestly moderation, a bishop is to be ordained for the people of Barcelona immediately from their own clergy—such a one as you, Brother Ascanius, ought especially to choose and are properly entitled to consecrate [Col. 0790A]. Otherwise, should something else perhaps be done, our command will rebuke your name with the greatest severity, since we would have learned that something had been admitted to the injury of God, from whom the grace of priestly dignities comes in a special way; nor should episcopal honor be regarded as an hereditary right, since it is bestowed upon us solely by the kindness of our God.

## IV. Concerning the removal of bishops who were illicitly ordained, and that there not be two bishops in one Church.

We therefore confirm the bishops now ordained—who, although advanced without your knowledge, deserved to be removed together with those responsible for them—on this condition: that none of them has been the husband of a widow or entered into the marriage and vows of a second wife, just as the legal enactments also command when they say: “Let a priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated.” Likewise, according to what the blessed Apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, did not leave unspoken in his own instruction concerning those who desire to become priests, saying: “The husband of one wife.” You ought, dearest brothers, to be so formed by the force of this sentence that, among the other things which must be guarded against, you especially strive to preserve these requirements, which you know were commanded before all else.

Among these provisions it must also be ensured that there not be two priests at the same time in one Church; that no one ignorant of letters, or lacking any part of his limbs, or one of the penitents, be permitted at all to approach the sacred mystery. Nor should you think the petitions of the people so powerful that, when you wish to comply with them, you abandon the will of our God, which forbids sinning. His indignation is aroused all the more seriously by this, because his kindness is offended when unlawful acts are committed by those who are interpreters of reconciliation [Col. 0790C].

## V. Concerning the condemnation of Irenaeus if he did not return to his own Church.

But so that everything may be corrected according to what has been written [Note: Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Urg., Ger.: “which we have written”], we have sent this present letter through the arrival of the subdeacon Trajan. If Bishop Irenaeus neglects to return to his own Church after laying aside his insolent ambition—a return that will be granted to him not by judicial sentence but by humaneness—let him know that he must be removed from the fellowship of bishops. May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brothers.

# LXXVI. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE HILARY TO THE SAME ASCANIUS, BISHOP OF TARRACONA. Concerning the matters written above. (C)

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789D] To his most beloved brother Ascanius, Hilary, bishop.

We must not be forgetful of the divine grace toward us, which through the mercy of its favor has raised us to the summit of the priesthood for this purpose: that, clinging to its commands and established, as it were, upon a watchtower of its priesthood, we may prohibit what is unlawful and teach what must be followed. Therefore, by the letter sent through our subdeacon Trajan [Col. 0790D], we admonish you that what has been badly done be corrected.

We are greatly astonished that your affection not only failed to repel the petitions of the people of Barcelona with any authority, but even requested, by letters sent to us, that their perverse desire be carried through, introducing at the beginning of your letter a mention of the council, as though the excesses of guilt were diminished by the multitude of the ignorant [Col. 0791A]. Even if each person had reported himself together with you under the designation of his own name and the brothers had individually supplied their own subscriptions, your affection would nevertheless have been touching the very heart of the matter that displeases us, because, in view of the position and honor owed to you, the other priests ought to have been taught by you, not followed by you.

Therefore, as I indicated in a general letter, let Irenaeus return to his own Church, and let a bishop be consecrated immediately for the people of Barcelona from their own clergy, provided that the provisions of the canons and the apostolic commands agree with him. Although those priests who were ordained without the knowledge and consent of your affection ought to have been removed together with those responsible for them, nevertheless, so that we may not decree anything harsh in so great a necessity, we wish those who have become bishops to remain in this position, provided that they are not found liable under the apostolic commands and the statutes of the holy Fathers [Col. 0791B], and provided that henceforth nothing contrary to ecclesiastical discipline is perpetrated, as has occurred until now [Col. 0792A].

It is your responsibility, dearest brother, to preserve the authority properly belonging to you, and not merely to withhold consent from unlawful acts, but also to restrain everything that you find being done against the rule. Above all, compel Irenaeus to return to his own Church—something we decree solely out of humaneness. He ought rather to return voluntarily if he fears being separated from the fellowship of the priesthood. Two bishops must not be permitted to belong to one Church. We have delegated the execution of this matter, with greater expediency, to the diligence of the aforesaid subdeacon, whom our authority has also caused to travel to Spain for the preservation of the Church’s discipline. May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brother.

# LXXVII. DECREES OF POPE SIMPLICIUS SENT TO ZENO, BISHOP OF HISPALIS. Concerning the apostolic see’s delegated authority. (C)

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791B] To his most beloved brother Zeno, Simplicius.

From the report of many we have learned that your affection, through the fervor of the Holy Spirit, so acts as the helmsman of the ecclesiastical ship that, with God as its author, it suffers no loss from shipwreck. Therefore, rejoicing in such indications, we consider it fitting that you be strengthened by the delegated authority of our see [Col. 0792B]. Armed with its force, you must in no way permit the decrees of apostolic instruction or the boundaries established by the holy Fathers to be overstepped, since he deserves to be heaped with a worthy reward of honor through whom divine worship is known to have increased in those regions. May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brother.

# LXXVIII. LETTER OF ACACIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO SIMPLICIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME. (C)

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791C] To the holy lord Father and archbishop Simplicius, Acacius.

125 You continually exhort us to bear, according to the Apostle, the concern of all the Churches, although we are voluntarily watchful and take the lead; and you too customarily demonstrate divine zeal by seeking more certain information concerning the condition of the Church of Alexandria, so that in accordance with the paternal canons you may undertake this task with most devout labor, shedding sweat for these matters, as has always been approved.

But Christ our God, who works all things together for good for those who love him, taking his place within our thoughts and recognizing that we have one and the same mind in these matters and the same concern for his glory, himself accomplished the entire victory, making us partners with the most tranquil emperor. He removed from human life Timothy, our predecessor, who breathed storms and, as it appeared, disturbed ecclesiastical tranquility, saying to him: “Be silent and hold your peace.” He also dispersed Peter, who had risen from Alexandria in a similar storm, and, with the Holy Spirit blowing, turned him into perpetual flight, as one of those long ago condemned.

For, as has been found in our archives—and from your own archives, if you deign to inquire, you will be able to learn what was subsequently reported concerning this same matter by the bishop of Alexandria to Rome and reciprocally—the aforesaid Peter, being a son of the night and appearing alien to the radiant works of the day, found darkness, suitable for carrying out robbery, entirely cooperating with him. In the middle of the night, while the corpse of the man who had overturned the paternal canons still lay unburied, he crept into the see, as he himself supposed, with only one person present, and that person a partner in his madness, so that for this reason he might be subjected to greater punishments. Nor did what he hoped for come to pass.

That man, judging himself—at least in some small measure—never appeared anywhere at all. Timothy, however, guardian of the paternal canons, who follows the example of David’s gentleness, enduring patiently to the end and restored by Christ to his own authority, rejoices in the honor of his own see. He receives the voices of his spiritual children and awaits the grace of healing, honored in himself with multiplied honor by Christ, the prince of priests; for his sake he has bound upon himself the crown of endurance [Col. 0792D].

Therefore let your Beatitude pray attentively for the most Christian emperor and for us ourselves; nothing is omitted that pertains to the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline. I and those who are with me salute in Christ the entire brotherhood that is with you. And in another hand: “In the Lord, pray for us, most righteous father.”

# LXXIX. LETTER OF FELIX TO THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT SICILY. (C)

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793A] To all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Sicily, Felix sends greetings in the Lord.

126 How fiercely the devil’s cunning raged against the Christian people in the regions of Africa, and how far it advanced through manifold deception, so that it plunged not only the unwary populace but even the priests themselves into the depths of death—there is no part of the world that has not groaned over it, no land that has remained unaware. Therefore, placed in great sorrow, we cannot conceal the peril of the souls who are perishing and whose salvation will be demanded from us. Consequently, an appropriate remedy must be applied to wounds of this kind, lest an untimely readiness to cure benefit nothing those seized by the deadly disease, while a calamity treated too slowly brings the guilt of illegitimate treatment alike upon the wounded and upon those who treat them.

## I. Concerning those who regretted having been rebaptized but afterward refused to do penance.

[Col. 0793B]

First, therefore, the confession and person of anyone who comes to you seeking a remedy must be carefully examined, so that an appropriate medicine may be supplied. In the case of one who, wishing to make satisfaction to God through penance, legitimately regrets having been rebaptized, it must be investigated whether he joined in this crime or approached it under compulsion. He must know that the deceiver deceives himself, and that by our leniency nothing is taken away from the judgment of the tribunal on high, before which those things are valid that are pious, true, and just. The circumstances of necessity must be handled one way, and those of intention another.

The case of one who was perhaps enticed by payment to bring about his own ruin is worse. For the enemy left nothing untried. To prevent him from rejoicing in his capture, those who have been entangled must be rescued, and the hunter’s snare must be crushed, so that the unfeignedly lamenting lapsed person may return to the hall he had abandoned through both the moderation of justice and the compunction of piety [Col. 0793C].

Let him perhaps neither be ashamed nor reluctant to obey the prescribed periods of fasting and lamentation, or to submit to other commands of salutary observance, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud. If someone seeks to be raised upright in Christ, let him lie prostrate because of his own fall. Through the ministry of our arrangement—which it is fitting for your affection to follow, and which no one has the right either to wish or to be able to surpass—let us handle with priestly firmness and humaneness the cases both of one who, contrary to apostolic teaching, gave himself over to the repetition of baptism, and of one who cunningly thought that his own consent could be excused by some arguments [Col. 0793D]. Thus, with the help of the Lord our Judge, the faith—which, unless it is one, is no faith at all—may be restored in them to salvation without the offense of our haste.

For when the satisfaction of the sinner is prolonged by us, his mind is found purer for pardon, not apart from our praise and joy. Therefore remember that we hold this judgment concerning such matters: while discrimination among sinners is preserved, not all who have fallen are to be weighed on the same scale, since the one entrusted with the discipline of the Lord’s house must be required to pay the price of a greater correction.

## II. Concerning priests or deacons who, in falling to heretics, submitted themselves to baptism.

[Col. 0794A]

Thus, beginning with the highest ranks of the Church, we decree the following concerning those who are known to have been bishops, priests, or deacons, and who, whether perhaps willingly or under compulsion, clearly suffered the loss of that one and saving washing, and stripped off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of the honor they had received. Since it is clear that no one could come to a second immersion unless he had openly denied that he was a Christian and professed himself to be a pagan, this is generally to be regarded as execrable in all persons; but in bishops, priests, and deacons it is proven horrifying even to hear or to say it.

Yet because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful and wills that no one perish, if they come to their senses, it will be appropriate for them to lie in penance until the day of their death. They must not participate at all in prayer—not merely in the prayer of the faithful, but not even in that of the catechumens—and at death lay communion is to be restored to them. The care of a most approved priest must investigate or carry out this matter with greater diligence [Col. 0794B].

## III. Concerning those who impiously submitted themselves to be rebaptized.

Concerning clerics and monks, maidens dedicated to God, and secular persons, we command that the following rule be observed, which the Council of Nicaea established for those who have fallen or did fall: namely, that those who, under no necessity and through no fear or danger, impiously gave themselves to be rebaptized, if they nevertheless repent from the heart, are to remain for three years among the hearers; for seven years they are to remain among the penitents under the hands of priests; and for two years they are in every way not to be permitted to offer oblations, but only to join the people in prayer, nor are they to be ashamed to submit their necks to God [Col. 0794C].

If, however, since they are mortal, the end of life begins to press upon them within the limits of the prescribed period, aid must be given to the one who implores it. Whether by the bishop who imposed the penance, or by one who has nevertheless confirmed that it was imposed, or similarly by a priest, viaticum must not be denied to the person departing from this world.

## IV. Concerning those who were rebaptized through ignorance due to their age.

To children—who are so called from childhood because they are still underage—and likewise to clerics, laypersons, or similar maidens, for whom ignorance is supported by their age [Col. 0794D], communion is to be restored after they have been held for a time under the laying on of hands. Their penance is not to be awaited, since the censure of discipline has exempted them from punishment.

This has been prudently established by us so that those who retain more or less of the contagion of earthly defilement on the road to life, while they are still in penance, may not perhaps commit further acts requiring penance. But if, before the appointed time of penance, someone who had received the grace of communion recovers—though the physicians had given up hope or the signs of death had plainly appeared—let us observe what the canons of Nicaea ordained: that such a person be counted among those who communicate only in prayer [Col. 0795A], until the period of time assigned to him has been completed.

Nor do we pass over our catechumens who were baptized under such a profession, because the case is not different, as the same holy canons ordained, from that of one who in any manner has renounced Christ, whom he once confessed. Let them remain for three years among the hearers; afterward let them be permitted to pray with the catechumens through the laying on of hands, so that they may receive the grace of communion in the Catholic Church. The sole exceptions are bishops, priests, and deacons, whom, as we have already said, are to be reconciled only at the time of their death.

As for the others—that is, clerics, monks, and laypersons of either sex—who are found to have undergone a repetition of baptism under compulsion and danger [Note: In the others, except Alv., “who may have happened upon it”], or who have said, by some contrivance, that they were not bound by the guilt of this crime [Col. 0795B], we decree that penance last for three years and that they be received into fellowship in the sacrament through the laying on of hands.

## V. Concerning those baptized or rebaptized by heretics, that they not attain ecclesiastical service.

With this rule observed in every respect: those who, at any age, have been baptized or rebaptized anywhere other than in the Catholic Church must never be permitted to enter ecclesiastical service. It ought to be sufficient for them that they have been received into the number of Catholics [Col. 0796A], since anyone who wishes to do so—or any bishop who has not removed one whom he knows to have intruded into the clerical ministry from among such persons—will be seen to bear judgment concerning their order and communion.

## VI. That penitents not be received by other bishops.

Above all, care must be taken and every precaution provided, lest any of our brother bishops and fellow bishops—or even priests—receive in another person’s city or diocese a penitent, or one placed under the hand of a priest, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or priest; nor should anyone receive such a person in a priest’s parish or in a bishop’s city. If this is neglected through some concealment, the guilt also touches the clerics who reside in places where this matter has been insufficiently attended to [Col. 0796B].

Now that these matters have been properly arranged and brought to the knowledge of your Churches through your deliberation, it is fitting that you obey them. Although nothing may seem lacking for the restoration of souls, nevertheless, if something new is revealed to anyone—something that may have escaped us—let him confidently make it known, according to the blessed Apostle Paul, while the one who spoke first is silent [128], because the Holy Spirit inspires where he wills, especially when his own affairs are being handled. Nor will we be reluctant to hear, nor arrogantly reject anything that has been omitted, but will order it reasonably. May God keep you, most beloved brothers [Note: Bibl. Reg.: “May God keep you safe and unharmed”].

# LXXX. LETTER OF THE SAME FELIX TO ACACIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Concerning the condemnation of his daring to communicate with heretics. (C)

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795C] Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Acacius.

You are found liable for many transgressions, and have often acted in contempt of the venerable Council of Nicaea. You have rashly claimed the rights of provinces belonging to others. You thought that heretics and usurpers, those ordained by heretics, and those whom you yourself had condemned and had insisted must be condemned by the apostolic see, were not merely to be received into your house, but even placed over other Churches—something that could not be done even with Catholics—or promoted to honors they did not deserve.

John bears witness to this: although he had not been received by the Catholics at Apamea and had been driven from Antioch, you placed him over the people of Tyre. Also Humerius, who had then been removed from the diaconate and deprived of the designation of the Christian name, was advanced by you to the office of the presbyterate [Col. 0795D].

And as though these things seemed small to you, you extended your daring and arrogance against the very truth of apostolic teaching, so that Peter—whom you yourself had reported as condemned by my predecessor of holy memory, as the attached documents attest—might, with your connivance, again invade the see of the blessed Evangelist. After driving out the orthodox bishops and clerics, he indisputably ordained persons like himself, and, having expelled the man who had been regularly established there, held the Church captive.

His person is so pleasing to you, and his ministers so acceptable, that you are now shown to be afflicting many orthodox bishops and clerics who are coming to Constantinople [Col. 0796C], supporting his representatives, and believing that the same Peter—who anathematized the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and violated the burial of Timothy of holy memory, as messengers have again recently reported to us—should be excused through Mesena and Vitalis. Nor did you cease to praise him and extol him with many commendations, to the point of claiming that his condemnation, which you had previously reported, was not true.

You persist so greatly in defending this perverse man that you allowed certain bishops—now deprived of honor and communion—Vitalis and Mesena, whom we had specifically sent for his expulsion, to be handed over to custody after their documents had been taken away. You then had them brought out to the procession held by you with the heretics and, as their declarations made clear, dragged them into communion with the heretics and with you, disregarding the embassy that ought to have been preserved even by the law of nations, and bribing them with rewards. Thus, to the injury of the blessed Apostle Peter, from whose see they had departed, you not only caused them to return ineffective but also displayed them as opponents of everything that had been commanded [Col. 0796D].

In deceiving them, you exposed your wickedness; and, not daring to answer at the apostolic see according to the canons to the libel of my brother and fellow bishop John, who attacked you with the gravest accusations, you confirmed the charges [Col. 0797A] 129. You also judged Felix, our most faithful defender, unworthy of your sight when necessity had caused him to follow later. He testified that persons whom we know to be heretics were also communicating with you through letters.

For what else are those who, after the death of Timothy of holy memory, return to the Church under Peter, or those who have handed themselves over to him from among the Catholics, than what Peter had been judged to be by the universal Church and by you? Therefore, with those whom you willingly embrace, accept your share in the sentence now issued, which, through your defender of the Church, we have declared to you: recognize that you have been separated from priestly honor and Catholic communion, as well as from the number of the faithful; that the name and office of the priestly ministry have been taken from you; that you have been condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority exercised through us; and that you will never be released from the bonds of anathema.

# LXXXI. LETTER OF POPE FELIX TO ZENO, BISHOP [Note: Aem.: “to Zeno, bishop of Hispalis.”] (C)

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797A] To his most beloved brother Zeno, Felix.

Our son, the most distinguished man Terentianus [Aem., Esc. 3: Terentius], recently coming to Italy, proved himself an exceptional herald of your affection and made you known as a man so overflowing with the grace of Christ that, amid the storms of the world, you appeared as the Church’s outstanding helmsman [Col. 0797B].

Therefore, dearest brother, when he was returning to the province and earnestly requested that our letter be sent to your affection, we gladly agreed. We wished both to address an exhortation worthy of God to a bishop and especially wished this to be done through the man by whose praises you had been brought to our attention.

Although the man mentioned above has affirmed that your brotherhood is endowed in every respect with holy works and already possessed much confidence in your benevolence, it is nevertheless right that he obtain what he greatly desired: so that one who was formerly pleasing to your mind may, through regard for us, become still more acceptable, and may at the same time be cherished with maternal and priestly consolation and find, through pastoral piety, protection during his pilgrimage. Beyond doubt, this will also be proved by the affection of your dignity: our conversation, through which you are greatly refreshed, has been of no small value to your sincerity [Col. 0798B]. May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest brother.

# LXXXII. GENERAL DECREE OF POPE GELASIUS (C)

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797C] To all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium [Note: From Ger. In the others, “Brities”; correctly, “Bruttium.”], and Sicily, Gelasius.

130 ## I. Concerning ecclesiastical institutions arranged with moderation according to the circumstances of the time.

We are constrained by the necessary ordering of circumstances and bound by the governance of the apostolic see to weigh the decrees of the paternal canons and measure the commands of our former bishops and predecessors in such a way that, after careful consideration, we moderate as far as possible whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the Churches. In this way we will neither appear entirely to exceed the form of the ancient rules, nor fail to restore the offices of the clerical service, which the incursions of war and famine have so consumed throughout various parts of Italy that, as we have learned from the frequent report of our brother and fellow bishop John, priest of the Church of Ravenna, the service of ministers is altogether failing in many Churches.

Unless the intervals fixed in ancient times for ecclesiastical advancement are relaxed for a little while, those Churches, utterly deprived of sacred orders, cannot be administered; and in very many places, because of the lack of suitable assistance, the saving help needed for redeeming souls is absent. We would also be bound by great guilt if, under the pressure of so great a danger, we did not provide some remedy.

## II. That where no urgent necessity exists, the decrees of the Fathers be preserved inviolate.

Therefore, while the ancient provisions remain in force because of their venerable authority, and where no difficulty of circumstances or times presses, they ought properly to be observed. For Churches that are either entirely deprived of ministers or so stripped of sufficient service that they cannot supply divine gifts to the congregations belonging to them, we grant that the intervals for both instituting and providing clerical service may be arranged in this way [Col. 0798C].

## III. That when clerics are lacking, they be chosen from among monks.

If someone trained in a religious way of life and in monastic disciplines comes to clerical office, his life in the preceding periods must first be investigated [Col. 0798D]: whether he is proved to be stained by no serious crime; whether he has perhaps not had a second wife and is not shown to have taken one abandoned by her husband; whether he has perhaps not performed public penance; whether he appears to be impaired in no part of his body; whether he is not subject to servile or hereditary condition; whether he is also proved to be free from the bonds of the municipal curia; and whether he has acquired literacy, without which he perhaps could not even fulfill the office of doorkeeper.

If he is supported by all the qualifications just mentioned [Note: Aem., Urg., Ger.: “the qualifications mentioned above”], let him immediately become a reader or notary, or at least a defender; after three months, let him become an acolyte, especially if his age also supports this [Col. 0799A]. In the sixth month let him receive the title of subdeacon; and, if he is of modest conduct and honorable intention, in the ninth month let him become a deacon; and when the year is complete, let him be a priest.

Nevertheless, the devotion voluntarily undertaken in the holy purpose is said to have supplied to him whatever the intervening periods of years would have contributed.

## IV. How much time is to be observed if laypersons are chosen for the clergy.

If someone from among the laity is to be added to ecclesiastical offices, it is fitting to examine such a person in each of the matters set out above with all the greater care, in proportion to the difference known to exist between secular and religious life. For the appropriate ministries of the Church must be restored, not imposed upon persons of inappropriate merit. And the more someone may be suitable for sacred service, the more carefully his training must be sought, in proportion to the time removed from that in which these attainments ought to have been acquired.

He must be shown to possess in his character the integrity that a longer habit has not supplied. Otherwise, on the pretext of remedying the clerical shortage, we might be judged to have introduced defects into divine worship rather than to have provided for the needs of a legitimate community. For such promotions, beyond the one-year limits, we nevertheless substitute six months, since, as has been said, it is fitting to distinguish between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from the way of life of the laity.

We have believed this concession should be granted only to the extent that those Churches in which, through the devastation of wars, no ministries at all or only a few have remained may be renewed. Once these have been restored, with God’s favor [Col. 0799C], the ancient form of the paternal canons must be preserved in appointing persons to the ecclesiastical grades. Under no circumstances should the fact that provision is being made as a remedy for an accidental deficiency prevail against them, since this is not being proposed as a new law contrary to the decrees of the ancients.

The other Churches, which have not been devastated by a similar disaster, must abstain from taking advantage of this occasion and should maintain the former rule in making ordinations. Thus, moved all the more by this opportunity, we more earnestly entrust observance of the venerable canons, admonishing the consciences of persons at each grade not to strive to break out into unlawful excesses [Col. 0799D].

## V. Concerning bigamists and other persons who are in no way to be admitted to the clerical ministry.

Let no bishop presume that he may assign to divine service bigamists, or those who have married women abandoned by other husbands, or persons who have undergone penance, or those without letters, or those impaired in body, or persons subject to servile condition, or those entangled in the bonds of the curia or of public affairs, or those examined indiscriminately without awaiting an appropriate period of time. Nor should they attempt, according to their own inclination, to invade the rights of others without the proper disposition and command of the apostolic see [Col. 0799D].

## VI. That new basilicas not be dedicated without the bishop’s command.

No one should dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without requesting, according to custom, the appropriate commands. Bishops must not strive to claim for themselves clerics belonging to another’s authority.

## VII. That no charges be demanded for baptizing and confirming the faithful.

Let them set no charges for baptizing and confirming the faithful, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions, since we are commanded to give freely what we have received freely. Therefore they must not attempt to demand anything at all from the persons mentioned above, lest, deterred by poverty or turned back by indignation, they disdain to approach the means of their redemption. Let them be certain that those discovered to have committed prohibited acts, or who have not rather corrected their offenses of their own accord, will suffer the danger of losing their own honor [Col. 0800A].

## VIII. Concerning priests, that they presume nothing against bishops.

We therefore prohibit presbyters also from extending themselves beyond their proper measure, or audaciously assuming for themselves what belongs to episcopal dignity: they are not to seize for themselves the authority to prepare chrism or to administer episcopal confirmation [Col. 0800B]; nor, when any bishop is present, unless perhaps ordered to do so, are they to presume that they have the freedom either to offer prayer or to perform sacred action; nor, in his presence, unless ordered, are they to presume either to sit or to handle the venerable mysteries. Let them remember that they are in no way permitted to claim the right of making a subdeacon or acolyte without the chief bishop. Let them have no doubt that, if they undertake on their own initiative anything specifically pertaining to episcopal ministry, they will immediately be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of sacred communion. We decree that this must occur if such transgression is established with their bishop’s testimony; nor will their own bishop be free from the guilt of connivance and from punishment if he has failed to discipline those acting immoderately [Col. 0800C].

### IX. That deacons observe their proper measure according to the decrees of the Fathers

We likewise establish that deacons observe their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the scope assigned by the ancestral canons. They are not to apply wholly to their own ministry anything that antiquity decreed properly to belong to the higher orders. They are not to presume to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless extreme necessity should compel them to undertake the aforesaid offices when those ministers are far away; this is something that is also generally permitted to Christian laypeople.

### X. That deacons may not sit in the presbyterium

These men are not to sit in the presbyterium when divine worship is being celebrated or any ecclesiastical proceeding is taking place. They have no right to exercise the privilege of distributing the sacred body in the presence of a bishop or presbyter, except when those ministers are absent. [Col. 0800D]

### XI. That the Apostolic See preserves the ancestral canons with devout and pious zeal

Since we too earnestly strive to observe the decrees of the venerable enactments, and believe that even those provisions which may perhaps seem to be relaxed for the sake of some useful advantage may be relaxed without detriment to those decrees; since we desire that nothing rashly be permitted to us against the reverence due to salutary rules; and since the Apostolic See, with the Lord’s favor, devoutly and piously endeavors to uphold in all these matters what has been established by the ancestral canons: it is most unworthy that any bishop or member of the lower orders should reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both following and teaching. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord has established the principate over the entire Church, as Scripture says: “Order love in me”; and again: “Let all things be done with order”; and once more, as the Psalmist proclaims: “Encircle Zion and embrace her; recount it in her towers; set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her steps, so that you may recount them to the next generation; for this is our God forever, and he himself will rule us unto the ages.”

This is undoubtedly he who is proclaimed in the exaltation of ecclesiastical dignities, and in whose strength hearts must be set by good works; with the ranks duly apportioned, our God and ruler is to be proclaimed to all Christian peoples. Here no one should think that anything has been diminished for him, since nothing is lost from the perfection of any rank, and, by consistently retaining what has been bestowed through heavenly dispensation, God is made known to us all alike and is granted to be our ruler. For even if something is conceded in respect of the length of time, it is compensated by the vigorous diligence added through one’s conduct, provided that what was to be completed over a prolonged period of life is now contained in one’s established way of life—so long as those things do not stealthily intrude, in any form, which, if found to be present, would rightly prove the person unworthy of the clerical insignia.

And although at times those things may be tolerated which, if the integrity of the others is assured, cannot by themselves cause harm, nevertheless those things must be especially guarded against which cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement. If the consideration of circumstances and times, or regard for an expedited provision, excuses even those matters which are sometimes believed to be indulgible without harm, how much more must those matters remain wholly unimpaired which no necessity and absolutely no ecclesiastical advantage compels us to alter? [Col. 0801C]

### XII. That no one presume to baptize except at Easter or Pentecost, except those whom extreme illness has compelled

Let no one presume to baptize indiscriminately at any time other than the paschal feast and the venerable sacrament of Pentecost, except only in the event of the onset of a most serious illness, when there is fear that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart overtaken by death without the remedy of salvation. [Col. 0801D]

### XIII. Concerning the ordinations of presbyters and deacons, to be celebrated at appointed times

They must not perform the ordinations of presbyters and deacons except at the appointed times and on the appointed days: that is, during the fast of the fourth month, of the seventh and of the tenth, and also at the beginning of Lent and on the middle day of Lent; they should know that these ordinations are to be celebrated toward evening during the Saturday fast. For no reason of convenience should anyone place either a presbyter or a deacon before those who were ordained before them.

### XIV. When sacred virgins are to be veiled

They are not to place the sacred veil upon consecrated virgins except at the Epiphany, during the paschal white-robed days [Aem., “during the paschal days”], or on the festivals of the apostles; unless perhaps, as was said concerning baptism, it is not to be denied to those afflicted by serious illness who petition for it, lest they depart from this world without receiving this gift. [Col. 0802A]

### XV. That widows are not to be veiled

No bishop is to attempt to veil widows, since what neither divine authority delegates nor the form of the canons prescribes must not be usurped at all. Ecclesiastical assistance is to be provided to them in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed.

### XVI. That slaves are not to be received into the clergy or monasteries under pretext of religion

The presumption behind a widespread complaint must also be avoided: nearly everyone complains that slaves or persons bound by birth, fleeing the rights of their masters and their property, are indiscriminately admitted—sometimes with the connivance of bishops—either to monasteries under the pretext of religious life or into ecclesiastical service [Col. 0802B]. This evil must be removed by every means, lest, through the institution of the Christian name, another’s property appear to be seized or public discipline overturned. In particular, it is not fitting that the dignity of clerical ministry itself be stained by this obligation, and that it be compelled to quarrel over the status and condition of those serving in it, or, God forbid, appear liable to such a charge.

After these persons have been appropriately forbidden by careful prohibition, any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or any of those known to preside over monasteries, who keeps such persons with him rather than restoring them to their patrons, or thereafter thinks to assign them either to ecclesiastical service or to religious communities—unless they have first been released by the will of their masters under written testimony, or granted through a lawful transaction—must not doubt that he will incur danger to his own honor and communion if anyone’s truthful complaint brings this matter before us. For, according to the blessed Apostle, great care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed. [Col. 0802C]

### XVII. That clerics are not to pursue dishonorable business dealings or shameful profits

It followed that we should not pass over those matters recently reported to us from the region of Picenum: namely, that very many clerics are intent on dishonorable business dealings and shameful profits [Col. 0802D], seeing without any shame the Gospel reading in which the Lord himself is said to have driven the traders from the temple with whips; and failing to recall the Apostle’s words: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business.” They also disregard with deaf ears the Psalmist David singing: “For I have not known business dealings; I will enter into the strongholds of the Lord.”

Accordingly, let them know that they must henceforth abstain from such disgraceful profits and cease from every scheme or desire for any kind of business dealing; otherwise, whatever rank they hold, they must immediately be compelled to withdraw from clerical duties. For the house of God must be and be called a house of prayer, lest it rather be a workshop of commerce and a den of robbers.

### XVIII. That no one ignorant of letters or impaired in any part of the body is to be promoted to the clergy

[Col. 0803A]

We have also learned that illiterate persons and those impaired in some part of the body are being brought into ecclesiastical service without any consideration. Both ancient tradition and the old practice of the Apostolic See reject this, since one who lacks literacy cannot be suitable for sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective is to be offered to God. Henceforth, therefore, such cases must be avoided by every means, and no such person is to be received into the clergy.

If any such persons have previously been admitted, whether through their own rashness or through the negligence of those presiding, let them remain in the positions in which they have been placed, so that they may never seize any advancement; and let them consider it sufficient that, out of excessive compassion, this very permission has been granted to them.

### XIX. Concerning those who mutilate themselves

[Col. 0803B]

With regard to those who mutilate themselves, the ancestral canons have clearly laid down what must be followed, and it is sufficient to insert their wording. For they say that those who perpetrate such acts, as soon as they have been recognized, must be excluded from clerical office. We must observe this in every respect, since no one is permitted to judge otherwise than according to those provisions established by the memorable rule.

### XX. Concerning criminals, that they are not to be promoted to the clergy

We have also discovered that persons entangled in certain horrifying crimes, with all discernment set aside, not only fail to undergo the necessary penance for atrocious deeds, but, without any correction having followed at all, strive for divine ministry and honor [Note: [Col. 0803D] In the others, except Alv., *conscendere* (“to ascend”).]. Others, already established in the orders, are not expelled even when committing serious crimes [Col. 0803C], although the Apostle says that hands must not be laid upon anyone hastily and that one must not share in the sins of others. The venerable enactments of our predecessors likewise declare that, even if such persons have perhaps slipped in, those previously guilty, once detected, must be expelled, and that those who have forgotten their sacred profession and betrayed their holy purpose must unquestionably be removed.

### XXI. That those possessed by demons or entangled in other afflictions may not handle the sacred ministries

We have found illicit practices breaking out to such an extent that the most sacred ministries are entrusted to persons possessed by demons or entangled in similar afflictions. If something of their own necessity should befall those engaged in this work, who could have confidence concerning the salvation of the faithful, when he sees the very ministers of healing afflicted by such great calamity? Therefore they must necessarily be removed, lest scandal be generated for any of the weak, for whom Christ died.

Finally, if divine holy law has by no means permitted a person wounded in body or disabled to touch sacred things, how much less is it fitting that those struck down in mind—what is worse—should be dispensers of the heavenly gift? [Col. 0803D]

### XXII. That those who join themselves to sacred virgins and enter into incestuous unions may not communicate unless they have performed public penance

We have learned that certain men rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after their dedication to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. It is right that such men be immediately thrust away from sacred communion and not be received at all unless through public and approved penance; nevertheless, if they have repented, the viaticum is not to be denied them as they depart from this world. [Col. 0804A]

### XXIII. That widows, as stated above, are not to be veiled; but if they violate their professed continence after changing their resolve, they themselves must render an account to the Lord

We have already stated at length and sufficiently that widows are not to be veiled under any blessing. If, however, of their own will and with changeable minds they trample upon the chastity they previously professed in marriage, it will be their concern, and their danger, with what satisfaction they ought to appease God, since, according to the Apostle, they have made their first faith void.

For just as, if they were perhaps unable to remain continent, they were not at all forbidden to marry, according to the Apostle, so, after deliberation with themselves, they ought to keep the pledge of chastity promised to God. We, however, must impose no snare upon such women, but set before them only exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render an account to God on their behalf.

For care must be taken regarding what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies about their conduct and actions. We pass over a fuller explanation, lest the unstable sex appear to be not so much deterred as admonished. [Col. 0804B]

### XXIV. That second marriages are not denied to laypeople, although they are by no means permitted afterward to enter the clergy

Just as laypeople are permitted to enter into second marriages, so no one is permitted after them to enter the clerical college. For one thing is the permission generally granted to human weakness, and another must be the life dedicated to the service of divine matters. [Col. 0804C]

### XXV. That if anyone receives a deserter from his own church and advances him to some dignity, he is to undergo the sentence established by the canons

Whoever deserts his own church and, without any existing cause, thinks that he ought to transfer to another, if he is rashly received and promoted, will not escape the provisions established by the revered canons for such presumptuous persons—nor will the person who received and advanced him.

### XXVI. Concerning laypeople or monks who are ordained for payment, so that the crime of Simon Magus may involve both giver and receiver

Concerning monks and laypeople, the earlier part of this directive dealt more fully with what, and to what extent, has been granted by the necessity of circumstances and times, and with how, where no necessity is shown to exist, the ancient institution alone must be observed [Col. 0804D].

Those who are established to have purchased sacred dignity with money despite being unworthy in merit must be barred once convicted; those who commit such a crime should not do so without danger. For the condemnation of Simon, as sacred Scripture testifies, involves both the giver and the receiver.

### XXVII. That no basilica is to be dedicated under the name of the dead

Although the consecration of holy places was briefly covered above, it has also been disclosed to us that some presume, without a command of the Apostolic See, to consecrate churches or oratories that have been built. We have been moved by an even more detestable report: that buildings constructed under the name of various dead persons—and, so it is said, not even of the faithful—are being boldly established for sacred purposes.

Since these matters are so bitter and so harsh that our hearing can scarcely endure them, if a genuine and firm Christian concern exists in those involved, let the matters be investigated with greater strictness, and let those by whom they were committed be identified. For just as, while the names remain hidden in this atrocity, there is no one against whom the appropriate sentence can be pronounced, so, when the person whom the enormity of so great a crime demands has been exposed by clear evidence, he will in no way escape punishment. [Col. 0805A]

### XXVIII. Concerning women, that they are not to minister at the sacred altars or presume to undertake anything assigned to men’s offices

[Col. 0805B]

We have heard with no small indignation that divine matters have fallen into such contempt that women are said to minister at the sacred altars and to perform for a sex to which it does not belong everything assigned exclusively to the service of men.

Yet the whole guilt, liability, and crime of all the offenses we have individually touched upon falls upon those priests who either commit these acts or, by failing to publicize those who commit them, show that they favor their depraved excesses—if indeed those who strive so to overthrow the religious office entrusted to them that, without any regard for Christian rule, they rush headlong toward every perversion and profanation are still to be called priests.

Since it is written, “Whoever despises little things will gradually fall,” what should be thought of such men who, overwhelmed by immense and manifold heaps of depravity, have produced a great collapse through many kinds of aggression—a collapse that appears not only to bury them themselves but, unless they are healed, to bring deadly ruin upon all the churches?

Those who have dared to practice these things, and likewise those who have hitherto remained silent despite knowing them, must not doubt that they lie under the loss of their own honor unless they hasten with all possible speed to ensure that these deadly wounds are healed by appropriate medicine.

By what manner do they preserve the rights of bishops when they disregard what has been entrusted to episcopal vigilance to such an extent that they instead carry out works opposed to the house of God over which they preside? Let them consider how much they could accomplish before God if they attended only to what is fitting; then let them see what they deserve when they zealously pursue the opposite.

It is as though this were more truly the rule by which the churches ought to be governed: that whatever is hostile to ecclesiastical regulations should be perpetrated, even though every bishop, if he knew the canons, ought to maintain them in inviolate guardianship. And if perhaps he did not know them, he ought confidently to have sought advice. Thus no excuse at all comes to the aid of the ignorant, since the one who did not know proposed to preserve what he did know, yet, being ignorant, did not take care to learn what he was doing. [Col. 0806A]

### XXIX. Concerning the revenues [Note: [Col. 0805D] In the others, except Alv., *haereditatibus* (“inheritances”).] of the church and the offerings of the faithful, so that they are to be divided into four portions

Four portions, both from revenue and from the offerings of the faithful, are to be made, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as was long ago reasonably decreed: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the buildings.

Concerning these portions, just as it will be the priest’s responsibility to pay the full stated amount to the ministers of the church, so the cleric must know that he is not to demand insolently anything beyond the sum assigned to him.

The restoration of the holy places is to demonstrate clearly that what has been assigned to ecclesiastical buildings has truly been devoted to this work. For it is impious if, while sacred buildings are left neglected, a bishop converts to his own profit the expenses designated for them.

Likewise, although he may appear to show that he has dispensed the portion assigned to the poor according to divine accounting, nevertheless, in accordance with what is written—“so that they may see our good works and glorify the Father who is in heaven”—it must also be proclaimed through present testimony and not be concealed from the praises of good reputation. [Col. 0806B–C]

### XXX. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who acts against these provisions is to incur the danger of losing his honor

Therefore, no cleric should think himself immune from this offense if, upon seeing a bishop, presbyter, or deacon transgress in those matters which we have set forth as salutarily to be followed, he fails immediately to bring the matter to our ears, provided that suitable evidence is produced, so that punishment may be inflicted upon the transgressor and the others forbidden to offend.
