Every bishop will in every way be a destroyer of his order and honor if he thinks these matters should be suppressed from any cleric or from the hearing of the whole Church. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Praesidius [Note: [Col. 0806D] In the others, except Alv., *Presieno*.]

## LXXXIII. LETTER OF THE SAME POPE GELASIUS TO THE BISHOPS IN SICILY (C)

[Col. 0805]

Gelasius, bishop of the Roman Church, to the beloved brothers, united with me in the love of Christ, the bishops established in Sicily.

### I. On the proper administration of the affairs of the Church by bishops

The authority of our predecessors has established that bishops should have the power to administer the resources of the Church, but in such a way that they must distribute the allowances of widows, orphans, and the poor, as well as those of the clergy. We decree that the bishops be given what has hitherto been established; let them claim the remainder for themselves, so that, as we said earlier, they may be able to give generously to travelers and captives. [Col. 0806D]

### II. Concerning the thirty-year limitation

It has also seemed good to add that, if—God forbid—church property, and likewise dioceses possessed by certain bishops, should claim by legal right for themselves what the thirty-year law has foreclosed [the transmitted syntax is uncertain], the authority of our sons, the emperors, has likewise decreed that no one may appeal after thirty years concerning a matter excluded by the time prescribed by the laws. Given on the Ides of May, in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Praesidius. [Col. 0807A–0808A]

## LXXXIV. LETTER OF POPE ANASTASIUS OF THE CITY OF ROME TO THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS, SENT FOR THE PEACE OF THE CHURCHES (C)

[Col. 0807]

Anastasius, bishop, to the most glorious and most merciful son, Anastasius Augustus.

I announce the beginning of my pontificate, with peace first offered to the peoples. Thereafter, on behalf of the catholic faith, I approach your humble piety as a petitioner. In this I trust that divine favor has first drawn near to me: that the agreement between my name and that of your august majesty undoubtedly provides assistance, so that, just as the exalted title of your piety shines throughout all nations and across the whole world, so, through the ministry of my humility, the see of blessed Peter may, as it always has, hold in the universal Church the principate assigned to it by the Lord God.

Nor, while your serenity is governing the commonwealth, should that garment of the Savior, woven from above throughout its entirety, suffer longer the uncertainty of an evil fate because of one dead man. It alone could not be brought into pieces for the sake of its integrity. Even in private life you possessed such devotion to sincere religion that, as the most certain report has proclaimed, no one, even among the foremost priests, is said to have observed the rules established by the holy Fathers of the Church more faithfully than you [Note: [Col. 0807] In all witnesses except Alv., *quoniam studium* (“because of the devotion”).]. We trust that this holy devotion has grown together with the majesty of the empire. [Col. 0807B–C]

### I. That he acts as an ambassador for Christ while pleading for the peace of the Church

We therefore act as ambassadors for Christ, so that you may not suffer those men to be publicly named because of offense or scandal whose merits or deeds cannot be hidden from that Judge in whose judgment they now stand. Nor can rash presumption intrude there while still in a mortal body, where not only confession makes the merits of each person evident, but even the secret of silence itself cannot remain hidden.

For both our predecessor, Pope Felix, and Acacius are certainly there, where each person, under so great a Judge, cannot lose the quality of his merit.

### II. That judgment must not rashly be passed on those who have already departed to the Lord

[Col. 0807D]

Since the most blessed Apostle Paul warns us not to create an offense in the Church by attempting to judge those who have already departed—something we cannot do—let your tranquility know that this must be observed.

For he says concerning those who presume to judge matters belonging solely to the Lord:

> “None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For Christ rose from the dead for this purpose, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of us shall render an account to God. Let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or an offense before your brother.”

The blessed Apostle therefore warns us not to presume to pass judgment on those concerning whom no one can judge more truly or better than God, nor should anyone arrogate rash acts to himself in this matter, thereby disrupting the peace and unity of the Church.

For it is also said in the Book of Kings: “Not as God sees does man see, because man sees the face, but God sees the heart.” Likewise, in the First Book of Chronicles: “And now, Solomon, know the God of your fathers and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing soul, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every thought.” Likewise, in Ezekiel: “Thus says the Lord: This is what you have said, house of Israel, and I know the thoughts of your spirit.” Hence it is also said of the Lord as judge in the Gospel: “But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” [Col. 0808A–C]

### III. That the name of Acacius is specifically to be suppressed in the Church

We therefore ask your clemency that the name of Acacius specifically be suppressed, for he has stirred up very great scandal and offense in the Church. Let it be suppressed by specific designation, since, as we have said, although the merit of each priest cannot be hidden from that Judge in the general company of priests, he alone knows what must be assigned to each according to the evaluation of his merits, and to him alone even thoughts are manifest.

As for the many excesses and presumptions of Acacius, lest it seem burdensome to your clemency for us to recount them individually, we have given our brothers and fellow bishops Cresconius and Germanus, whom we sent to your serenity, a full account of each of Acacius’s cases and of what kind of man he was, for your clemency to examine particularly, if your piety should wish to investigate the matter more closely.

Thus, in accordance with your divine wisdom, you may clearly see that the sentence proceeded against such an Acacius not from pride or arrogance on the part of the Apostolic See, but—so far as we can judge outside that judgment which alone cannot err—from certain crimes and, above all, from zeal for divine things, which compelled it. [Col. 0808D]

### IV. That contention must be avoided with the greatest care

We, however, humbly beseeching you, do not wish controversy to remain in the Church, since contention must rather be avoided, as it is said in Proverbs: “Contention arouses hatred.” But friendship protects all who do not contend.

The Apostle likewise says to the Corinthians: “Since there are jealousies and contentions among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” Again, to the Philippians:

> “If there is therefore any consolation in Christ, any encouragement of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and compassion, complete my joy by all saying the same thing and having the same love, doing nothing through contention or vain glory, but in humility of mind considering one another superior to yourselves, not each looking to his own interests, but to those of others.” [Col. 0809A]

### V. That the emperor should urge the Alexandrians to return to sincere faith and catholic peace

[Col. 0809B]

I especially impress this upon your serenity, most glorious and most merciful son Augustus: when the case of the Alexandrians has been laid open to your most pious ears, use your authority, wisdom, and divine admonitions to make them return to sincere and catholic faith.

If you also command this, we shall renew for those who know it what must be held in the catholic religion according to the definitions of the Fathers and the teaching of all the priests who have flourished in the Church, transmitting it to their memory; and for those who do not know it, we shall offer it for learning, as our duty requires, so that no arrogance or perversity of human minds may be heard beyond these things.

### VI. The emperor is admonished to obey the provisions of the Apostolic See

[Col. 0809C]

For the love of your empire and for the blessedness that the kingdom may attain, we proclaim in the exercise of our apostolic office that obedience must be given to our admonitions, just as is fitting and as the Holy Spirit says [Note: [Col. 0809D] In the Bibliothèque Royale witness; in the others, *dicat* (“may he say”), perhaps *dictat* (“dictates”), as in the printed editions.], so that all good things may come to your commonwealth, as is promised in Exodus:

> “If you hear the voice of the Lord your God and do what pleases him in his sight, obey his commandments and observe all his justice, I will not bring upon you any of the infirmity that I brought upon the Egyptians. For I am the Lord who heals you.”

And there again the most powerful trumpet is sounded:

> “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and observe the commandments of the Lord your God and his statutes that I command you?”

May your piety not disdain me when I repeatedly offer these reminders, keeping before your eyes the Lord’s words in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me, and whoever despises me despises him who sent me.”

The Apostle, likewise singing in harmony with our Savior, says: “Therefore, whoever despises these things despises not a human being but God, who has given his Holy Spirit among us” [Ger., *accinens* (“joining in song”), rather than *concinens* (“singing in harmony”)].

The breast of your clemency is the sanctuary of public happiness, so that, through your diligence—you whom he has commanded to preside on earth as his vicar—the Gospel and apostolic commandments may not be resisted with hard arrogance, but what is salutary may be fulfilled through obedience. [Col. 0809D–0810A]

### VII. That no portion of injury touches those whom Acacius baptized or ordained after his condemnation

According to the custom of the catholic Church, let your most sacred breast recognize that no portion of injury arising from the name of Acacius touches any of those whom Acacius baptized or whom he ordained as priests or levites according to the canons, so that the grace of the sacrament perhaps conveyed through an unworthy man may not appear less secure.

For baptism, whether it was administered outside the Church, or by an adulterer or a thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift. The voice that sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution, as it declares and says: “This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire.”

If the visible rays of this sun, when they pass through the most foul places, are not stained by any pollution from contact, how much more is the power of the one who made this visible sun untouched by any unworthiness of his minister?

Judas, too, though he was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles in accordance with the dignity entrusted to him, did not cause the benefits given through an unworthy man to suffer any loss. The Lord himself declares this in unmistakable words:

> “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Whatever they say, do; but do not do what they do, for they say and do not do.”

Whatever, therefore, any minister in the Church appears to accomplish in his office for the advancement of human beings is wholly contained in the effect produced by divine action. Paul, the one through whom Christ speaks, affirms this:

> “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

God therefore does not ask who or what kind of person preaches; indeed, he confirms that even the envious preach Christ well. The devil himself was deceived by this evil, and by this very means he does not cease to bring about his own downfall. [Col. 0810B–C]

### VIII. That evil men, by administering good things, harm only themselves and do not stain the sacraments of the Church
Therefore, this man—whose name, as we have said, ought to be passed over in silence—by administering good things wickedly harmed only himself. For the inviolable sacrament that was given to others through him obtained the perfection of its power.

But if anyone’s excessively inquisitive suspicion goes so far that they imagine that, after the judgment pronounced by Pope Felix, the sacraments in which Acacius usurped authority were afterward administered ineffectively, and consequently fear that those who received the mysteries conferred either in consecrations or in baptism may seem to have received divine gifts invalidly, let them remember that the foregoing reasoning prevails in this matter as well. For he did this only after having assumed the name of the priesthood unlawfully; and since the mysteries retained their power, the guilty person did not thereby harm others.

For to him applied what is sung in David’s trumpet:

> “Nevertheless God crushed the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins.”

For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others. The whole authority of the heavenly Scriptures bears witness to this, as it is also said through the Holy Spirit in the prophet:

> “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house.”

Therefore, since the condemned man had claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head. It was not the people who thirsted for his house in the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0811A] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, Ger., “ministries”], who were excluded; rather, only that soul which had sinned was, by a just judgment, properly liable. The abundant instruction of the Scriptures everywhere testifies to this.

Therefore, setting aside the interests or devices of men who are still placed in this present frailty, and in accordance with our prayers, offer to our God one catholic and apostolic Church by your imperial exertion and authority. For this alone will enable you to triumph without end, not only on earth but also in heaven [Note: [Col. 0811] In the others, except Alv.: “that you may triumph”].

**Subscription.** May almighty God preserve your kingdom and your welfare by perpetual protection, most glorious, most clement, and ever Augustus.

## LXXXV. POPE SYMMACHUS’S LETTER TO CAESARIUS, BISHOP (C)

[Col. 0811]

[Col. 0811B] Symmachus to his dearest brother Caesarius.

Equity urges us gladly to grant the request of your fraternal charity concerning each of the matters that you ask to have granted by the Apostolic See; this is not at variance with the caution and provision of the Fathers. And although ecclesiastical rules cover nearly everything, we nevertheless do not consider it superfluous to repeat matters that have often been prohibited.

### I. That Church property not be alienated, but be granted only for the use of clerics, monks, or pilgrims

We do not permit possessions that anyone has given or left at the disposal of a particular church to be alienated under any title or transferred under any pretext, unless perhaps they are granted to clerics because of their meritorious rank, to monasteries out of regard for religion, or certainly to pilgrims if necessity should require generosity—yet in such a way that they enjoy these things not perpetually but only temporarily.

### II. That no one receive ecclesiastical office through payment

We strongly admonish that those who try to approach the priesthood not by God’s grace but by promising beforehand ecclesiastical property be deprived of the fulfillment of such desires. Those who do not restrain themselves from such an intention should know that, by the penalties of the canons, they will unquestionably not easily be permitted to approach the priesthood. For degrees and periods have been established by which they ought to aspire to this dignity: whoever is promoted without the prescribed procedure does not easily escape offense, and no one can obtain the judgment of election without prior testing.

### III. That abductors of widows or virgins be expelled from communion with the Church

[Col. 0811D]

We detest abductors of widows or virgins because of the enormity of so great a crime, pursuing especially fiercely those who have attempted to join sacred virgins to their marriage either willingly or against their will. Because of the atrocity of so abominable a crime, we order that such men be suspended from communion.

### IV. That widows or professed virgins not marry thereafter

We do not permit widows to pass to marriage if they have remained for a long time in a religious commitment with persevering observance. Similarly, we prohibit virgins from marrying if they have spent many years of their lives in monasteries.

### V. That no one approach the episcopate through canvassing or bribery

No one, therefore, is to be permitted to approach the honor of the episcopate through canvassing or bribery. Since such misconduct is censured even in secular life, who doubts that it brings disgrace upon religious persons and those who serve God?

A person desiring the episcopate must not, with money given, employ powerful persons as supporters. He must not compel clerics or citizens, by fear of any kind, to subscribe to a decree made for him, nor encourage them by any rewards. No one is to draw up a decree without the presence of the visitor, whose testimony can establish the unanimity of the clergy and citizens.

We therefore exhort all the faithful to observe these provisions with devoted minds, out of regard for catholic religion and the peace of the Churches. For there is no doubt that, according to the venerable canons, those who violate such prohibitions incur the loss of their own communion. Nevertheless, we wish these matters to be brought to the knowledge of all the bishops [Note: [Col. 0811] In the others, except Alv., “to be offered”; perhaps “to be brought”].

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. [Col. 0812D] Given on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of the illustrious Probus.

## LXXXVI. POPE HORMISDAS’S LETTER TO THE EMPEROR JUSTIN [Note: [Col. 0811D] Aem., “Justinian . . . . . . Justinian”] (C)

[Col. 0811]

[Col. 0811D] Hormisdas the bishop sends greetings to his most glorious and clement son Justin.

Among the matters pertaining to the unity of the Church, for whose sake God chose your Clemency for the imperial office, you included in your letter, venerable Emperor—whose concern for the faith you demonstrate in many ways—that the petitions of certain persons should be appended for presentation to my humble self. Through these I might learn what question had arisen, or might give a response appropriate to religious knowledge for removing the scope of the consultation that had been proposed.

I read everything with the concern that was proper. Although I could have been sufficient for a full response if I had written back only what had been defined by the authorities, nevertheless, in order to reward the devotion of your religious purpose, I did not think that I should withhold the service of my own words as well.

### I. Against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches

What did the paternal teaching fail to address when the poisons of Nestorius and Eutyches emerged? The synodical decrees, in agreement with their inventors, pressed nearly all the impieties into one condemnation together with the authors of such detestable doctrines. Once the seeds of such dreadful unbelief had been cut off, no room remained for believing either that Christ our Lord existed without the reality of flesh, or that the same Christ did not emerge from the undefiled fertility of his mother’s womb both God and man.

The one, by denying the dispensation through which we were saved, rendered it ineffective insofar as he could; the other, with an opposing opinion but similar impiety, excluded divine power from true humanity in the same Lord Jesus Christ. The former did not remember that Christ displayed his flesh for touching; the latter did not remember the Gospel’s statement that the Word became flesh [Note: [Col. 0813D] In the others, except Alv., “teaching”], although the Lord’s voice ought continually to have sounded in his ears:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

These matters have often been included in the judgments of many of our predecessors. Yet your Clemency, venerable Emperor, although they have already been stated, will not be able to regard their repetition as tedious [Note: [Col. 0813D] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Esc. 3, “to recognize”]; nor are we ashamed to rehearse what was proclaimed by our predecessors. For it is impossible that there should be diversity of preaching where there is one form of truth; nor will it rightly be judged irrelevant if we agree in doctrine with those with whom we agree in faith.

Let the synodical decrees and the constitutions of blessed Pope Leo, which accord with the sacred faith, be recalled to the pious ears of your gentleness. You will find in them the same things that you review in ours. What more, then, can any inquisitive investigator seek after that fountain of the faithful’s ordinances—provided that he preserves the boundaries of the faith? Nothing is needed either to add to what is complete or to distinguish what is perfect, unless someone perhaps prefers to doubt rather than believe, to quarrel rather than know, and to follow uncertainties rather than preserve the decrees.

### II. The mystery of the Trinity: what is signified by “person” and what by “substance”

[Col. 0813D]

For if God is Trinity—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and God is one, as the Lawgiver expressly says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God,” then anyone who holds otherwise must either divide the divinity into many parts or, in a particular way, attribute suffering to the very essence of the Trinity. And—far be this from the minds of the faithful—this would mean either introducing several gods in the manner of profane paganism or transferring sensible punishment to a nature that is free from every kind of suffering.

The holy Trinity is one. It is not multiplied by number, it does not increase by addition, and neither can it be comprehended by the intellect nor can what God is be separated by distinction. Who, then, would attempt to impose a profane division upon that secret, eternal, and impenetrable substance—which no nature, even among invisible creatures, has been able to investigate—and reduce the mysteries of the divine mystery to the reckoning of human custom?

Let us adore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Trinity’s substance, distinct without division, incomprehensible and indescribable. Although reason may admit number with respect to the persons, unity nevertheless does not forfeit the distinction of the essence. Yet we must preserve what is proper to the divine nature and what is proper to each person, so that neither the singularity of divinity is denied to the persons nor what is proper to the names is transferred to the essence [Note: [Col. 0814D] From Aem. In the others: “the essence, yet so”].

Great, holy, and incomprehensible is the mystery of the Trinity: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity. Nevertheless, it is known that it is proper to the Father to beget the Son; proper to the Son of God to be born from the Father, equal to the Father; and proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son, under the one substance of the Godhead.

### III. The divinity and humanity of the Lord Jesus Christ

It is also proper to the Son that, according to what is written, “in the last times the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Thus, within the womb of the holy virgin Mary, the mother of the Lord, the two natures were united without any confusion, so that he who before the ages was the Son of God became the Son of Man and was born in time as man. He was born without opening his mother’s womb and, by the power of his divinity, did not violate his mother’s virginity.

It was wholly fitting to the mystery of God’s birth that he should preserve childbirth without corruption, who caused conception to occur without seed—preserving what he was from the Father and displaying what he received from his mother. For while lying in a manger he was seen in heaven; wrapped in swaddling clothes he was worshiped by the Magi; born among animals he was announced by angels; scarcely beyond infancy, he proclaimed a mysterious teaching without a teacher; amid the beginnings of childhood he performed signs of heavenly powers.

He is the same God and man—not, as unbelievers say, under the introduction of a fourth person, but the very Son of God, the same God and man, at once power and weakness, humility and majesty, redeeming and sold, placed upon the cross and bestowing the kingdoms of heaven. He was so subject to our weakness that he could be killed, yet so mighty in power that death could not consume him. He was buried insofar as he willed to be born a man, and insofar as he was like the Father he rose again. He suffered wounds and was the Savior of the sick; he was one among the dead and the giver of life; descending to the underworld and yet not departing from the Father’s embrace.

Therefore, the soul which he laid down according to the common condition he soon took up again through his singular virtue and wondrous power.

To show that these things are so and must admit no doubt—that is, lest our God Jesus Christ be thought not to be God amid the works of his passion, or lest, being thought God alone, he be not also believed to be man amid the astonishing works of his wondrous powers—he instructed us by the example of two apostles. Peter’s faith declares that Christ our Lord is God; Thomas’s doubt declares that he is man.

For what purpose would he have wished his disciples to inquire who people said he was, unless, when Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he intended to confess that this had not been disclosed by flesh and blood, but revealed by God the Father’s inspiration, and that through the testimony of this praised response the faith of the revealed truth might be made manifest?

What purpose would there have been in Thomas’s being absent from the others after the Lord’s resurrection, or in his being the only one to doubt, unless it was so that the world might believe what the doubting disciple had examined? By allowing himself to be touched by the hands of one man, he made it possible for the whole body of the faithful to recognize what he was.

Doubt, therefore, was not introduced to condemn the disciple but to instruct posterity.

Or what else should we expect from the fact that the same Lord inserted into his conversation with Cleopas and another disciple, as they traveled toward Emmaus, what they were saying about him? Although they had learned of the Lord’s resurrection from the women who had first come to the tomb, he nevertheless, in order through their doubt to give firmness of belief to future ages, began with Moses and all the prophets and interpreted the Scriptures to show that Christ had to suffer and in this way enter into his glory. Thus he demonstrated that in him there was both human nature through suffering and divine nature through glory.

These matters are indicated by numerous examples in the sacred Scriptures. Nor should they be presented to your religious conscience, venerable Emperor, as though they were unknown. The faith itself, which you constantly assert, gives you this gift: it implants in your mind both love for it and the knowledge by which it may be defended more diligently.

Nevertheless, it belongs to the dispensation entrusted to me that I too should not remain silent about what is known even to the knowledgeable, so that as the preaching of Catholics succeeds itself through the changing ages, what is asserted without fail may be believed without end.

I could discuss at greater length the matters pertaining to the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the union in him of two natures without confusion, according to the definitions of the ancients, if I had to dispute against those who disagree with these things. But since both the synodical constitutions and the teachings of blessed Pope Leo are in everyone’s hands, I have thought it more appropriate to touch briefly upon a few points than to unfold everything.

For now, it is enough to recognize and guard the distinction and essence in such a way that it is understood what concerns the person and what we ought to attribute to the substance. Those who ignorantly fail to understand these things, or conceal them through cunning impiety, omit what is proper to the Son and thereby lay snares for the unity of the Trinity. But if what has been proclaimed is held fixed with strong roots, then neither will anyone depart from the tradition of the Fathers nor will questions fail to be met firmly.

## LXXXVII. LETTER OF THE EMPEROR JUSTIN TO POPE HORMISDAS (C)

[Col. 0815]

[Col. 0815C] The Emperor Justin to Hormisdas, most holy and blessed archbishop of the venerable city of Rome and patriarch.

Know, most religious Father, that what had long been sought with the greatest efforts has been accomplished for us and brought to light. Before those whom you sent have arrived, know that John, the most blessed bishop of New Rome, together with his clergy, agrees with you, differing in no ambiguity and divided by no discord.

Know that he signed the libellus which you had indicated was to be offered and which conforms to the council of the most holy Fathers. All eagerly hasten to accept the wishes both of your see and of the see of Constantinople, illuminated by the brilliant splendor of truth; all hasten most willingly, delighted by the clear path.

They follow the most holy decisions of the Fathers and the most approved laws, affirming the decrees of those councils that held the straight path and correcting those who wandered uncertainly. The matter is brought together in this: that they too should worship the unity of the undivided Trinity with unity of mind.

It has been denied that remembrance should henceforth be made during the divine mysteries, according to the tenor of the libellus mentioned above, of Acacius, once bishop of this royal city and a transgressor, and likewise of the other priests who either first acted against the apostolic decrees or became successors in error and were never corrected by repentance until their final day.

Since all our regions must be admonished to imitate the example of the imperial city, we have judged that the imperial commands should be sent everywhere. We burn with such zeal for religion and desire with such devotion the peace of the catholic faith that our state may be rewarded from heaven with peace and that heavenly protection may be secured for my subjects.

For what could be found more pleasing, more just, or more illustrious than that those whom the same kingdom contains and the worship of the same faith illumines should not contend over different things, but, united in the same understanding, venerate institutions established not by human judgment but by the Spirit of divine providence? [Note: [Col. 0815D] In the others, except Alv., “illumines”].

Therefore, may the holiness of your religion pray that divine assistance may grant that what is being pursued through vigilant effort for the concord of the Churches and the catholic faith may be preserved forever by the constant help of God.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of May at Constantinople.

## LXXXVIII. LETTER OR LIBELLUS OF FAITH OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TRANSLATED FROM GREEK INTO LATIN AND SENT TO THE HOLY POPE HORMISDAS OF THE CITY OF ROME, IN WHICH HE ANATHEMATIZES NESTORIUS, EUTYCHES, AND THE BLASPHEMIES OF THE OTHER HERETICS (C)

[Col. 0817]

[Col. 0817A] When I received the letters of your holiness in Christ, dearest brother, through Gratus, the illustrious count, and now through Germanus and John, most reverend bishops, Felix and Dioscorus, most holy deacons, and Blandus the presbyter [Bibl. Reg., “bishop”], I rejoiced at the spiritual charity of your holiness: that you seek the unity of the most holy churches of God according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers and hasten, for the love of Christ, to drive the destroyers from the rational flocks.

Know with certainty, therefore, most holy Father, that in everything I agree with you in the truth, as I wrote to you, and that I too, because I love peace, reject all the heretics rejected by you.

For I accept that the most holy churches of God—that is, your elder Rome and this new Rome—are one; and I declare that the see of the Apostle Peter and that of this imperial city are one.

I assent to everything enacted by the four most holy synods—Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—concerning the confirmation of the faith and the state of the Church, and I do not tolerate any wavering concerning their rightly made judgments. I know that those who attempt or strive to disturb even a single point of what has been established have fallen away from the holy universal and apostolic Church of God.

Using your rightly spoken words, I declare in this present writing that the first condition of salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no way to depart from the tradition of the Fathers, because the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be set aside when he says:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

The effects of events prove what has been said, because inviolable catholic religion has always been preserved in the apostolic see.

Therefore, desiring not to fall away from this faith and following in everything the constitutions of the Fathers, we anathematize all heresies, especially the heretic Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by blessed Pope Celestine of the city of Rome and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

Together with him we also anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, condemned in the holy synod of Chalcedon, which we venerate and follow and embrace, since it proclaimed the apostolic faith in accordance with the holy Synod of Nicaea.

Together with these we anathematize Timothy the parricide, surnamed Aelurus, and condemn in like manner his disciple and his follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria.

We likewise anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, who became their accomplice and follower, as well as those who continued in communion and participation with them. For whoever embraces the communion of any one of them receives a similar judgment of condemnation along with them.

In the same way, condemning Peter of Antioch, we anathematize him together with his followers and all those listed above as his associates.

Therefore, we approve and embrace all the letters of blessed Leo, pope of the city of Rome, which he wrote concerning the right faith.

Accordingly, as we have said, following the Apostolic See in everything, we preach all that has been decreed by it. For this reason I hope that I shall be in one communion [Note: [Col. 0817C] From Bibl. Reg. In the others, “communication”] with you, which the Apostolic See proclaims, in which there is the complete integrity and perfect solidity of the Christian religion.

We promise that in time to come the names of those who have been separated from communion with the catholic Church—that is, those who do not agree in everything with the Apostolic See—will not be recited among the sacred mysteries.

But if I should ever attempt to depart from my profession in any respect, I declare by my own condemnation that I am their companion and share their fate.

I have signed this profession with my own hand and sent it by letter to you, holy and most blessed brother Hormisdas, pope of great Rome, through the aforesaid Germanus and John, venerable bishops, Felix and Dioscorus, deacons, and Blandus, presbyter.

And in another hand:

John, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, consenting in this profession of mine to all the matters stated above, have signed them, being sound in the Lord. Pray for us, most holy and blessed brother.

Given in the month of March, on the twenty-eighth day, in the twelfth indiction, during the consulship of the lord Justin, august prince, and Heraclius, illustrious men. Era 557.

## LXXXIX. LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF ILLICITANA [Note: [Col. 0817D] In the printed editions, “Melicitana” or “Miletopolitana”], IN WHICH, WRITING TO HIM ABOUT THE COMMUNION OF THE CHURCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE, HE CONGRATULATES HIM (C)

[Col. 0817]

[Col. 0817D] We do not wish our wishes to be unknown to your charity, lest one who shared in our anxiety should be excluded from the fruit of our joy.

Therefore, through letters of communication and through the instructions that we gave to our legates, we inform you that the Church of Constantinople has returned to communion with us, by the Lord’s favor, and that the entire sequence of our commands has been completed.

So that perfect joy concerning this matter might reach your affection more fully, we have entrusted to be sent together copies of the libellus of our brother and fellow priest John, bishop of Constantinople, and of the sacred letters of Justin, most clement prince of the East. We also report that very many bishops throughout the eastern regions have acted in the same way.

It remains for us to pray that the divinity, entreated by our fitting petitions, may grant that we too may rejoice in the restoration of the other churches.

You will take care to bring what we have considered it important to report to the knowledge of those priests who are near your fraternity, so that they too may not cease with us to give thanks for the accomplishment of so great a matter through the gifts of heavenly mercy.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

## XC. LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO THE SAME JOHN, BISHOP, CONCERNING THE INSTRUCTIONS SENT AND THE AUTHORITY DELEGATED (C)

[Col. 0819]

[Col. 0819A] Hormisdas to his dearest brother John.

Your charity has done something appropriate to charity and faith by informing us in a letter of your arrival in Italy and showing what a high degree of religious devotion is in you.

Would that the joy of your presence had been granted to us for the fuller satisfaction of our affection, so that we might rejoice in enjoying conversation with one whom we have embraced so deeply through letters [Note: [Col. 0819C] In the others, except Alv., “eloquence”]. Nevertheless, dearest brother, you have demonstrated with what devotion you venerate the Christian faith, since you desire to preserve without any transgression the matters pertaining to the rules of the Fathers and to catholic commands. You hope that, once the general regulations established for the churches of Spain have been extended, we may enact ecclesiastical disciplines appropriate to matters that are either neglected or treated irreligiously.

We have embraced these desires and have granted your request. For what is sweeter to us than to speak with the faithful, or more fitting to God than to recall those who have strayed from error?

Therefore, greeting you in the charity that unites us, we inform you through your deacon Cassian that we have sent general regulations. In them we have either suitably declared what ought to be observed according to the canons or sufficiently instructed you concerning the precautions that ought to be taken regarding those who come from the Greek clergy.

The appended instructions concerning the case itself will also teach you from the ecclesiastical archives, so that, recognizing the care of the Apostolic See, which keeps watch according to the rules of the Fathers, you may show that, through hatred of the condemned, you love the fellowship of the faithful.

Since, through your charity’s communication, this path of providence has been opened to us, we reward your concern. While preserving the privileges of the metropolitans, we delegate to you the authority of the Apostolic See to this extent: you are to keep watch and report to us, through your communication, whether the matters pertaining to the canons and recently commanded by us are being observed, or whether anything concerning ecclesiastical affairs occurs that deserves to be reported.

It will be the object of your effort and concern to show yourself in the matters entrusted to you in such a way that you imitate the faith and integrity of the one whose care you undertake.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of the illustrious Agapitus. Era 555.

## XCI. LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SPAIN (C)

[Col. 0819]

[Col. 0819C] Hormisdas to all his dearest brothers, the bishops established throughout both Spains.

Blessed be the Trinity, our God, who, through his mercy, has spread the peace and tranquility of the Roman state throughout all its regions and has also granted us the means of showing charity toward one another. Thus, those whom the firmness of faith unites may also be joined by the desired joy of conversation; and, while through the service of letters we reach you, we may stir your hearts to religious worship through apostolic admonitions and, while rendering what is almost a debt of our office, display our complete devotion toward God.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us join constant and humble prayers, and let us beseech our Lord with tears of mouth and heart, asking through continual supplication that in teaching and in works we may cling to him whose members we desire to be, and that we may never turn aside from that path which is Christ by a wandering road, lest we be justly abandoned by him whom we impiously abandon.

This can come about for us with the help of heavenly favor if we observe the apostolic teachings and the commands of the Fathers. For our Lord says:

> “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Although these words could suffice as a general statement, so that we might avoid errors and preserve catholic decrees, nevertheless, since it has been made known to us through the communication of our brother and fellow bishop John that certain things are being presumed contrary to the reverence due to the canons, I thought that general regulations should be issued. In this way I would avoid the danger that threatens teachers because of silence, and, pierced by the prophetic voice that says, “Speak; do not remain silent,” I would set forth what is necessary.

### I. On ordaining priests according to the provisions of the canons

When priests are ordained, you must consider what has been prescribed and defined by the Fathers [Bibl. Reg., “established”; Esc. 3, “pre-established”]. Just as Christ is the head of the Church and priests are Christ’s vicars, so evident care must be exercised in choosing them.

Those who must preside over people who need correction ought to be irreproachable, and nothing should be lacking in the character of one in whose hands lies the summit and substance of religious discipline. Let each person estimate the value of the Lord’s flock, so that he may know what merit is appropriate in the shepherd who is to be appointed.

This will happen if the rank of the priesthood is not transferred indiscriminately from laymen by some kind of sudden leap. The person to whom the helm of the Church is entrusted ought to demonstrate his way of life through long testing.

We do not deny that there are ways of life among laymen that please God; but faithful institutions seek proven soldiers for themselves. A person ought to learn before teaching and ought rather to provide others with an example of religious conduct from himself than to receive such an example from them.

The person who must pray for the people ought to be more upright than the people. Religious worship should be handed down through long observance so that it may shine forth, and a person should serve for a long time in clerical duties, being trained by them, so that, when brought to the summit of the venerable rank, he may show what fruit humility produces [Note: [Col. 0821D] In the others, except Alv., “may be practiced.” Esc. 3, “may be held”].

It was neither insignificant nor meaningless that, even among the ancients, only men of the Levitical line were brought to the holy altars, lest someone unfit should approach sacred worship indiscriminately, with merit despised for the sake of money or presumption.

That prerogative of families has passed to the institutions of worshipers: now education takes the place of birth. What birth gave them, training must give us. Nature gave them to the tabernacle; discipline brings us forth for the altars.

Nor do we merely prohibit the consecration of laymen; no penitent either may aspire as a profane violator to such a rank. Let forgiveness be enough for one who seeks it. With what conscience can a man absolve the guilty when he knows that he himself confessed his sins before the people as witnesses? Who will venerate as a bishop one whom he saw lying prostrate only a short while before? He who bears the stain of a pitiable crime does not possess the radiant dignity of the priesthood.

### II. That no payment be accepted for the episcopate

We join this matter to what was said earlier, lest a blessing conferred by the laying on of hands—which is believed to come from God—be purchased for a price. It should be kept before one’s eyes that Simon, who wished to buy the Holy Spirit with money, was struck by the apostle’s condemnation.

Who, then, would not consider what he sold to be vile? The election of priests to be ordained must preserve this reverence, so that in the grave responsibility for peoples the judgment may be believed to be God’s. For God is present where there is simple consent without corruption.

Nor do we omit this aspect of our concern and admonition: the man who himself, free from the crime of purchase, initiates a priest through the mystical blessing must not consider himself free of guilt if he willingly or under compulsion consents to the will of another who has purchased it.

What does it profit him not to be polluted by his own error if he gives consent to another’s error? Without doubt, both the man who has his own sin and the man who follows another’s sin act against the commands. The mind resists desire in vain if it has not also resisted fear.

With God’s help, provision can more easily be made against these things if the privileges established by the holy Fathers for metropolitans remain in force; if metropolitans preserve their proper order with respect to their dioceses with the reverence that is fitting, so that neither arrogance diminishes the bishops nor contempt depreciates those who render obedience.

If these matters are held firm in works and in hearts as they are read in the Scriptures, there will be no seeds of rivalry and no sources of discord [Note: [Col. 0822D] In the others, except Alv., “there will in no way be”]. Rather, while charity reigns, people will live under that peace which God promised and granted to us.

### III. On holding a council every year
Because of this, the Fathers, stirred by that providence with which the Holy Spirit has deigned to prick the consciences of his worshipers, taught that councils ought to be held twice a year in each parish, so that, gathered together in accordance with the principles of salutary instruction, they might deliberate collectively on matters requiring ecclesiastical consideration—or, if everything stands according to their desire, praise God with united voices, who grants what is desired.

For it is difficult that anyone’s heart should be so hardened by wicked thoughts that he would allow blameworthy things to be done by him, when he knows that he must undergo the judgment of a council. Let them always have their loins girded for this journey, knowing that they must render an account of their actions. Let them be restrained from illicit things by fear, and those whom fear cannot restrain, by shame.

But concerning assembling, it is known that the holy canons have definitively prescribed that it take place twice a year; and, if possible, this ought to be observed inviolably. But if either the necessities of the times or emerging circumstances do not permit this to be fulfilled, we command that they assemble at least once—although this falls short of what is permitted—without any excuse.

These things, dearest brothers, and the other matters contained in the regulations of the Fathers, let us meditate upon unceasingly with our lips and in our hearts [Esc. 3: “your hearts”], and, as it is written, let us recount them to our children. Let us meditate upon them while sitting in the house, walking on the road, sleeping, and rising, because blessed before the Lord is the one who meditates on his law day and night.

The Teacher of the nations likewise followed this principle in instructing his disciple, admonishing him: “Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them,” adding the full instruction: “Pay attention to yourself and to the teaching.” For if we devote ourselves without interruption to the instruction of the faithful, we are separated from vices, since devoted care for God’s work leaves no room for human error.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, under Agapetus, a most illustrious man, as prince. Year 556.

## XCII. LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO THE SAME BISHOPS OF HISPANIA

In it he sends them the profession of John, bishop of Constantinople, concerning Eastern clerics who have sought communion with them. (C)

[Col. 0823]

### To his dearest brothers, all the bishops established in Hispania, Hormisdas.

Among the matters which our brother and fellow bishop John brought to our attention out of zeal for ecclesiastical usefulness, he also, from his devotion to the Catholic faith and his reverence for the apostolic see, sought advice about the procedure by which holy communion ought to be granted to those coming from the Greek clergy. This concerned, of course, the case of Acacius, condemned by our predecessors for communion with heretics; those who do not separate themselves from his contagion are likewise excluded from our communion.

We praise the proposal of this man, who burns with such zeal for the faith and for apostolic institutions, that he would not allow anyone, even through ignorance, to be plunged into the mire of another’s error. Such care is worthy of the faithful: they should always keep watch with anxious devotion and preserve themselves blameless from every perversity. For this is the innocence of faith: to foresee that it cannot err even by accident.

Therefore, both to satisfy the praiseworthy desires of the aforesaid man and mindful, as we ought to be, of our duty, we have also taken documents from the archives of the Church and sent them to your council for the instruction of the whole body. From these, learning more fully what was done, you may separate yourselves from every association with those who err.

For the sentence was not pronounced out of personal hatred, but against impious transgressors, by God’s inspiration. In this matter we have ceased neither from preaching nor from entreaty: we have pleaded with the prince and admonished priests and peoples, so that the transgressors, once absolved, might turn back to the true faith through love of God and fear of judgment. But their pitiable obstinacy persists, and the deadly poisons cannot be overcome by any means, since the evil seed, having fixed its roots, continues to grow toward what is worse.

Therefore, dearest brothers, properly instructed in every respect, preserve yourselves as the Church of God and rejoice together with the Apostle. We have sent a libellus under which, if anyone from the Eastern clergy seeks your communion, he may be admitted to it—just as, according to the same profession, it is already established that many from Thrace, Scythia, and the regions of Illyricum, as well as from Old Epirus, and also many from Syria, have been received, rejoicing to come together in what is right and to have abandoned what is astray.

Accordingly, we command again that every care and every concern remain vigilant.

[Note: [Col. 0823] In Aem. and the Royal Library manuscript: “under reiteration.” In Alv., Esc. 3, Urg., and Ger.: “under stealthy seizure.” Tol. 1: “under a pledge.” Tol. 2: “under trembling.”]

There is now no place for ignorance. Let no one use the excuse of former simplicity. For one who sins knowingly, confession is necessary: whoever does not persist on the path once it has been shown to him must ascribe the errors to himself.

Boniface, notary of the holy Roman Church, carries out copies of the libellus issued from the archives.

[Col. 0824A]

The first salvation is to preserve the rule of the true faith and in no respect to deviate from the decrees of the Fathers. And because the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over—“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”—and because what was said is proved by the effects of events, since the Catholic religion has always been preserved without stain in the apostolic see:

Desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize every heresy, especially the heretic Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by the blessed Pope Celestine of the city of Rome and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

Likewise, we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, condemned at the holy synod which we follow and embrace, the Council of Chalcedon, which, following the holy Council of Nicaea, proclaimed the apostolic faith.

We detest also Timothy the parricide, surnamed Aelurus, as well as his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria.

We also condemn and anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, condemned by the apostolic see, and those who were his accomplices and followers, or who have remained in association with their communion. For since Acacius joined himself to their communion, he rightly deserved a sentence of condemnation like theirs.

We likewise condemn Peter of Antioch with his followers and with all those mentioned above.

[Col. 0824C]

We receive and approve all the letters of the blessed Pope Leo which he wrote concerning the Christian religion, as we have already said, following the apostolic see in all things and proclaiming all its decrees.

Therefore I hope that I may deserve to be in one communion with you, which the apostolic see proclaims, in which there is the complete, truthful, and perfect solidity of the Christian religion. I promise that the names of those separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not consent to the apostolic see—will not be recited among the sacred mysteries.

But if I should attempt to deviate in anything from my profession, I declare by my own judgment that I am an accomplice of those whom I have condemned.

I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it to you, Hormisdas, holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome.

## XCIII. LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE (C)

[Col. 0825]

### To his dearest brother Epiphanius, bishop, Hormisdas.

I have been filled with great joy because, concerning the peace of the Church, I have learned from the testimony of my legates also of the zeal of the most holy emperor and of your affection, such as you indicated in your letter. From this it is clearly proclaimed as evidence of heavenly mercy that worldly rulers join the cause of the faith with the ordering of the state, and that the leaders of the churches, mindful of the duty belonging to their administration, carry it out.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] From Tol. 1. In some manuscripts: “are exercised”; in others, corruptly, “are exercised” with an altered spelling.]

After the storms of discord, the Christian religion needed such leaders—leaders who, by prudent arrangement, would suppress the tempests, restore peace, long driven into exile, once the storm had been dispelled, and, extending examples of their purpose into future ages, show without hesitation what their successors should write about them and what later generations, for their own imitation, might do if it pleased God.

Let us bless the Lord, dearest brother, that this has been granted in our days, and let us strive with all the strength of our prayers and cares so that what has been well begun with God’s help may, with his assistance, be completed in every respect.

For it is to be hoped that the remaining members, still divided, will hasten to the joining of the body, and that the lesser will not differ from the greater. Since your affection urges me to this with Christian charity, what invites must be followed, and what it counsels us to love must be embraced.

Since we already share a similar concern for the faith, through religious patience we hope for an equal reward from the accomplishment of a good work. For we must not yield to difficulties. Faith is not wearied by hardships, nor does one ascend to the heights of heaven by an easy path, nor does anyone deserve a reward without the exercise of labor.

Therefore, so that we do not grow weary in doing good, we are specially admonished, as the psalmist also bears witness: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times.” For it is not the beginning of labor that customarily receives the reward of recompense, but its completion.

Therefore, taking up an equal zeal of concern, since we share one fellowship in communion and belief, just as we rejoice together in the Lord over the Constantinopolitan Church’s reconciliation with the apostolic see, so let us also care, as you affectionately urge, for the restoration of the others—first of all so that we may preserve our faith and integrity unstained by every contagion.

For you know, most holy brother, what bonds preserve ecclesiastical harmony, what protect us from the snares of heretics, and through what means the authority of the canons is also maintained. When these things have been preserved in their full strength with every vigilance, remedies should be granted to those who hope for them.

For the order of ecclesiastical regulations and the very form of justice require that rational medicine not be denied kindly and faithfully to those who hope for it. Nor is anyone so remote from humanity that unwary simplicity would not incline him away from the strictness of rigor.

But so that you may carry this out carefully and without complaint or blemish of any error, dearest brother, you ought in this matter to put on my person, knowing—as was said above—what must be done and what must be avoided in such cases. Foresee everything in such a way that you do not doubt that an account of this administration must be rendered to God.

Nevertheless, those whom you admit into communion must either be declared to us by your letters as having been joined to you, or be commended to us through the apostolic see; and the contents of the libelli they have presented must also be included.

In this way we shall both absolve the errors of Severus and his accomplices or others like them, and not allow those who could have been healed to suffer loss. We have entrusted this to you particularly, transferring our burdens to your diligence, because you have already given no small evidence of resistance to heretics; and there should be no doubt about one who has been properly examined.

At the same time, take up the remedy of medicine and gird yourself with the authority of justice. Show such humanity toward those who plead that you exclude from those for whom provision and care are being given for the restoration of the Church both those who persist in the contagion of heresy and those who feign innocence and agree only in words with our people. For it is not fitting to temper ecclesiastical discipline toward such people.

The good of mercy will not have been bestowed for the needs of those who ought to be helped if it is indiscriminately shared by the good and the wicked.

And because your affection thought it necessary in your letter to mention what should be done concerning the Jerusalemites, whose profession has also been conveyed to us in part, we judged it necessary either to receive what was written or to respond with what was appropriate.

If they observe the decrees of the holy Fathers, if they venerate those foundations of the faith, let them not depart from what was defined through them by the arrangement of the Holy Spirit. For either those definitions are perfect as they stand and require no addition, or they are fully sound and therefore must not be changed.

Through them all the poisons of the heretics have been suppressed. Nor did the Council of Chalcedon omit anything useful that any diligence could have devised. It either made the doctrines of those who preceded it clearer or confirmed them by renewed authority.

It undertook a particular struggle against Nestorius and Eutyches: the one separated the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ from the flesh and therefore avoided confessing holy Mary as the Mother of God; the other rejected the truth of the Lord’s flesh.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is the same Son of God and the same Son of man, one person in two natures, divine and fleshly, with the natures not confused by their union. He is not a fourth person added to the Trinity; rather, he himself, the Son of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.

Therefore we also confess one—and indivisible—essence of the Trinity [Bibl. Reg.: “also one”], while nevertheless knowing that each person retains its own property. For we confess one person of the Father, one person of the Son of God together with the assumed flesh, and one person of the Holy Spirit. We designate the persons by their properties and confess, through the unity of essence, the inseparable mystery of the Trinity.

For there can be no doubt that the Word of God assumed human nature through flesh within the Virgin’s womb, nor that afterward he was divided from himself within the womb by a union of the natures. For just as in him humanity was not brought forth without God, so on the cross the impassible divinity was not separated from the suffering of the flesh.

The Virgin’s birth, her undefiled fertility, the unique resurrection from the dead, and the ascension into heaven make this clear.

If they preserve these things as they were established by the Fathers, let them believe and not go beyond what was defined. Those who turn aside from this path spread over themselves the cloud of doubt.

But to contentious people we must answer with the apostolic statement: “We have no such custom, nor the Church of God.”

I have stated these things briefly because it is not appropriate to debate repeatedly matters defined according to the faith, and because an argument addressed to those already instructed is almost superfluous—especially since I have touched on these matters at some length in my letter to the most clement prince.

Since we have responded concerning the profession of the Jerusalemites, we judged it appropriate to add this also for their salvation: if they desire unity with the apostolic communion, let them indicate their profession in writing, as they presented it to our legates stationed at Constantinople; or let them send it to us through their own representatives, or hand it over to your fraternity. It must nevertheless be written in the same form, as we have said, and conveyed to us in every respect under your supervision.

Concerning the Thessalonians, whose legates came to us through the arrangement of the son of our most clement and faithful prince, we want you to know that the entire matter is to be handled according to what pleases our Lord Jesus Christ, under our direction.

If they complete what is required, we have been content to write that the necessary arrangements should be made through our brother and fellow bishop, the venerable John, and through our sons Heraclius the presbyter and Constantine the deacon, men most worthy of ecclesiastical honor in matters pertaining to the case.

We have rejoiced to find in a man of our own order equal merit and a religious purpose, together with wisdom corresponding to the commission entrusted to him and conduct corresponding to it. For it is a thing of prayer and full of joy that those whom a share in a common duty has brought together should be found worthy according to a just assessment.

## XCIV. LETTER OF HORMISDAS TO SALUSTIUS, BISHOP OF HISPALIS

Concerning the delegated authority over the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania. (C)

[Col. 0827]

### To his dearest brother Salustius, Hormisdas.

[Col. 0827C]

Having received the conversations conveyed in your brotherly and welcome congratulation, by which the indication of your twofold well-being—supported by bodily health together with spiritual duties—has brought us joy, we have perceived that it is fitting to disclose in words the joy which we hold in our mind.

For you have given evidence of a good bishop, both by doing what deserves praise and by not delaying to make it known. We have taken an indication of our own judgment from your election, since we have learned that you voluntarily performed what we command others to do.

We pray that all may acknowledge the divine benefits, and we have sent these instruments of ecclesiastical peace to you out of zeal. You received our wishes with faithful understanding and immediately fulfilled them with devotion to your duty, making known to all the brothers what you had recognized, through heavenly grace, as beneficial to everyone.

Therefore, since so many merits of pious concern and labor support you, we are now pleased confidently to entrust to you what clearly belongs to the care of our office: that, for provinces separated by such great distance, you may both represent us and apply the protection of the regulations of the Fathers.

Accordingly, with the present authority, we entrust our vicariate to you throughout the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania, without prejudice to the privileges which antiquity has decreed for metropolitan bishops. By this participation in the ministry we increase your dignity and lighten our own watchfulness through the remedy of the same administration.

Although you do not need to be instructed about each matter, since we have already proved that you preserve everything with caution, it is nevertheless usually more agreeable when a path is shown to those who are to travel and the form of the assigned task is displayed to those who are to labor.

Therefore we command that the paternal regulations and the decrees defined by the holy councils be observed by all. In these matters we show your vigilance and concern through a brotherly exhortation. When these are guarded with the reverence they deserve, they leave no room for guilt or obstacle to holy observance.

There what is lawful and unlawful has been prescribed; there is what is forbidden, which no one should dare to pursue; there is what is permitted, and what a mind pleasing to God ought to undertake.

Whenever the religious cause requires a general council, let all the brothers assemble at your summons. If any of them is troubled by a dispute over a particular matter, restrain the quarrels that have arisen among them, determining the contests after they have been examined according to the sacred laws.

Whatever you prescribe there for the faith and the ancient decrees, whether through prudent arrangement or by confirming it with the authority of our person, let the whole matter reach our knowledge through a report that gives an informed account.

In this way both our spirit will enjoy the charity of the duty entrusted to you and yours will enjoy the security of what you have received.

May God preserve you safe, dearest brother.

## XCV. RESCRIPT OF POPE HORMISDAS SENT TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF BAETICA (C)

[Col. 0827]

### To his dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica, Hormisdas, bishop.

[Col. 0829A]

What can be so sweet to one who is concerned as learning from you those things that I desire? What is so fitting for religious institutions as for priests to preserve among themselves the peace which, in accordance with their duty, they must announce to others?

I confess that I received with complete joy what you indicated to me in your letter concerning the affection existing among you and the peace of the churches. Whatever I could have urged or advised has been voluntarily brought before me.

May God confirm what he works in us, and may he, in the mercy by which he redeemed us, make easy the things he commands to be done for the salvation of souls.

But in response to such good news, we too return news worthy of religious messengers. Whatever has been done concerning the Easterners whom, as we previously indicated in the letters you sent, we had long ago recalled to the unity and body of the Church through the help of our God, we now communicate to you again through repeated reports.

Immediately after the return of our representatives from the Easterners, a delegation was sent. It had firm hopes and sought definite counsel. But we shall make a summary of what had to be said, sending you instead the responses we gave, so as to inform you directly. In this way neither opinion nor error may claim anything on account of the great distance of the lands, since holding to the truth itself is sufficient for knowledge of the facts.

As for the contents of your letter, your desires should indeed have been explained more fully, so that, after everything had been considered, an answer appropriate to the matter could be given. But because you mentioned in the same letter the ancient privileges and paternal statutes, we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Salustius concerning this matter. We also indicate briefly to you what was expressed more fully there: we do not wish to tear down privileges granted to us, and we judge nothing more fitting for the faith than that what the Fathers decreed should be preserved in its honor.

May God preserve you safe, dearest brothers.

## XCVI. LETTER OF POPE VIGILIUS TO PROFUTURUS, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0829D] In printed editions: “Eutherium … Eutherio.”]

[Col. 0829]

### To his dearest brother Profuturus, Vigilius.

We gladly received the letters of your affection addressed to us, filled with the concern of Catholic inquiry. We bless the mercy of our God because he deigns to provide shepherds such as you for his sheep in the farthest regions of the world—shepherds through whom they may abound in salutary pastures and be preserved from the rapacity of the wicked wolf, so that they may not fall into his ambushes.

Thus it is certain that the grace of the promised blessedness follows you, since the perfection of heavenly doctrines is sought from you with such praiseworthy inquiry. For it is written: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart.”

Therefore, dearest brother, considering the purpose of your consultation with our whole mind, we trust that this also proceeds from you: you strive to hold to the rule of the Catholic faith in the same footsteps in which you recognize it to have been founded in the apostolic see.

Although their sound has gone forth throughout the whole world and their words have been extended to the ends of the earth, so that the hearts of your affection have shown themselves faithful to Christ, nevertheless, if anything in the Church entrusted by God’s help to your governance has not yet become clear in the full light, you return to the same source from which salutary water had flowed there.

For this reason we have embraced your request with the charity it deserves: you wished our response to confirm those matters concerning which, as you said, observance among them was uncertain. Therefore, greeting your affection in the Lord, we have thought it appropriate to instruct you concerning each point about what the authority of the apostolic see holds according to Catholic discipline, adding certain chapters from the sacred regulations.

### I. Concerning the Priscillianists who abstain from eating meat

First, concerning those whom you indicated to be polluted by the vices of the Priscillian heresy: with a holy and fitting detestation for Catholic religion, you should judge and reprove those who, under the pretext of simulated abstinence, appear to withdraw themselves from eating meat in such a way that they are shown to do this out of a spirit of execration rather than devotion.

Since in this matter they are proved to resemble the most wicked Manichaeans, they have rightly been prohibited from this superstition under threat of anathema by the venerable decrees of the Fathers. They must not believe that any food has been polluted by contact with meat, because among all the things which divine mercy has granted for human nourishment, nothing is judged unclean by Catholics.

Thus the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, admonishes Titus, saying: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being detestable and unbelieving, disqualified for every good work.”

Similarly, in another passage he preached to Timothy concerning the avoidance of errors of this kind, saying: “In later times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, who forbid marriage and abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth, because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.”

Accordingly, the venerable decrees of the Fathers, which they follow, specifically judged that those were to be condemned who, while abstaining from meat, also believed that those things were to be avoided [Bibl. Reg.: “condemned”] which appeared to have been mixed with meat.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself gave this warning, saying: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—this is what defiles a person.”

Therefore, we neither reject abstinence that is pleasing to God nor receive into our fellowship those who execrate the Lord’s creation.

### II. Concerning triple immersion

Regarding the solemn completion of the baptism of those being reborn through triple immersion, your affection will clearly recognize below what the apostolic authority has either decreed or observed.

We judge it to be a novel error, however, that, although all Catholics customarily say at the end of the psalms, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” some, as you report, remove one connecting syllable and try to diminish the complete expression of the Trinity, saying: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, the Holy Spirit.”

Although reason itself clearly teaches us that, by removing one syllable, they in a certain way indicate that the person of the Son and that of the Holy Spirit are one, nevertheless the voice of the Lord Jesus Christ is sufficient to convict such error. In indicating that baptism should be celebrated through invocation of the Trinity, he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Since he did not say “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, the Holy Spirit,” but commanded that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit be named with equal distinctions, it is evident that those who wish to subtract anything from this confession depart entirely from the Lord’s teaching.

Therefore, let your affection in every way drive such people back to the path of the correct confession. If they persist in error, they cannot be our associates.

### III. Concerning those who are baptized again by the Arians

Concerning those who, after receiving the grace of saving baptism, were baptized again among the Arians and thereby plunged into the death of a deep abyss, we have taken from our archives and sent below the chapters containing what the decrees of our predecessors judged concerning them according to their several orders and ages, since these matters have been arranged in multiple ways.

Nevertheless, your affection should observe this especially: since this wickedness arose among the nations from many sins, it should be left to the judgment of your fraternity and of the other bishops in their dioceses whether, if the character and contrition of the penitent’s devotion are approved, the person may also be near the remedy of indulgence.

Their reconciliation, however, is not effected by that imposition of hands which takes place through invocation of the Holy Spirit, but by that which acquires the fruits of repentance and is completed by restoration to holy communion.

### IV. What is to be observed concerning the restoration of churches in their buildings or their dedication

Concerning the restoration of any church that had been destroyed [Note: [Col. 0831D] From the other witnesses, except Alv., which has “buildings”], and whether the solemnity of consecration should be repeated in a place where there were no sanctuaries [Note: [Col. 0831D] Aem., the Royal Library manuscript, Esc. 3, Ger., Tol. 1 and 2: “should be renewed”], we judge that it causes no difficulty if no exorcised water is sprinkled there. For we know that the consecration of any church in which no sanctuaries are placed consists only in the celebration of Mass.

Therefore, if any basilica of the saints has been renewed even from its foundations, there is no doubt that, once the solemnity of Mass has been celebrated in it, the sanctification of the entire consecration will be completed.

But if the sanctuaries it possessed have been removed, it should receive the reverence of sanctification again through their replacement and the solemnity of Mass.
