### V. Concerning the feast of Easter, the order of prayers, and the solemnity of Mass

Know that, if God wills, we shall celebrate the coming Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

We also indicate that at no time and on no feast do we have a different order of prayers in the celebration of Masses, but always consecrate the offerings made to God according to the same form.

Whenever the feast of Easter, the Lord’s Ascension, Pentecost, the Epiphany, or one of God’s saints is to be celebrated, we add the individual chapters appropriate to those days. Through them we make commemoration of the holy solemnity or of those whose birthdays we celebrate; we continue everything else according to the customary order.

For this reason we have also sent below the text of the canonical prayer, which, by God’s favor, we received from apostolic tradition. And so that your affection may know at which points we connect material appropriate to particular feasts, we have added the prayers of Easter Day as well.

Having answered the inquiry of your fraternity in these matters, we earnestly beseech our God, as far as we are able, to multiply the gifts of his grace in all the churches of the Catholic religion and among all whom he makes faithful to himself, and to deign to render all his peoples immune from every ambush of the spiritual and fleshly enemy.

We also announce that, as you hoped, we have sent to your affection sacred relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs, trusting that your faith will henceforth be more fully aided by their merits.

### VI. That baptism must be administered in the name of the Trinity

If any bishop or presbyter, in accordance with the Lord’s command, does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but either in one person of the Trinity, or in two, or in three Fathers, or in three Sons, or in three Paracletes, let him be cast out of the Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] Printed editions add a paragraph asserting that the Roman Church is the mother and teacher of all churches; it is absent from all our manuscripts.]

## XCVII. LETTER OF POPE GREGORY TO LEANDER, BISHOP OF HISPALIS

Concerning single immersion in baptism. (C)

[Col. 0831]

### To the most reverend and holy brother Leander, bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0833A]

I would have wished to respond to your letters with complete attention, unless the labor of pastoral care so exhausted me that I find it more fitting to weep than to say anything. Your reverence will also perceive this attentively in the very text of my letter, when I speak carelessly to one whom I love intensely.

For I am so shaken here in this place of the world by such great waves that I am utterly unable to steer toward harbor the old and rotten ship which, by the hidden administration of God, I have undertaken to govern.

Now waves rush against it from the front; now foaming masses of the swollen sea rise from the side; now a storm pursues it from behind. Amid all these circumstances, confused, I am forced now to direct the helm against the very adversity, now, by bending the side of the ship, to avoid the threats of the waves obliquely.

I groan because I perceive that, while I am negligent, the bilge of vices is increasing, and, while the storm beats violently against it, the rotten planks already sound as though shipwreck were imminent.

Weeping, I remember that I have lost the calm shore of my repose, and, sighing, I behold the land which nevertheless I cannot hold against the opposing winds of circumstances.

Therefore, dearest brother, if you love me, extend to me the hand of your prayer amid these waves, so that, by helping me in my labor, you may in turn become stronger in your own labors through the reward you receive.

I cannot express adequately in words the joy I feel at learning that our common son, the most glorious King Reccared, has turned to the Catholic faith with wholly sincere devotion. When you describe his character to me in your letters, you have made me love even one whom I do not know.

But since you know the snares of the ancient enemy, and know that he prepares a harsher war against victors, your holiness must now watch over this same son of ours with greater diligence, so that he may complete what he has begun well and not exalt himself over his perfected good works; so that he may hold the faith he has learned also through the merits of his life, and show by his works that he is a citizen of the eternal kingdom, so that after the passage of many years he may pass from one kingdom to another.

[Col. 0834A] Concerning the triple immersion in baptism, no truer answer can be given than what you yourselves have understood: because there is one faith, the differing custom of the holy Church causes no harm. We, however, by immersing three times, signify the sacramental mysteries of the three-day burial, so that when the infant is raised from the waters for the third time [157], the resurrection after the period of three days may be expressed. But if someone should think that this is also done out of the highest reverence for the Trinity, that too presents no obstacle: to immerse the one being baptized once in the waters cannot be reprehensible, since, while there is one substance in three subsistences, it cannot in any way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, when in the three immersions the Trinity of the persons can be signified, and in the single immersion the unity of the Godhead.

But if until now the infant has been immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the Godhead, and while doing what they used to do they boast that they have overcome your custom. To your most beloved fraternity I have sent books, whose contents I have listed below. As for the material that had been written in the exposition of blessed Job and that you write should be sent to you: because I had sent it through homilies, in words and ideas that were somewhat unfinished, I have nevertheless taken pains to convert it into the form of books, which are still now being copied by scribes. And if the urgency of the bearer of this letter had not constrained me, I would have wished to send you everything without any omission, especially since I wrote this very work for your reverence, so that I might seem to have labored in my work for the one whom I love above all others.

Moreover, if you learn that you have been granted time away from ecclesiastical duties, you know what must now be done. Although absent in body, I always see you as present to me, because I carry the image of your face impressed within my heart. May God preserve you unharmed, my sweetest [Bibl. Reg., most beloved] and most reverend brother.

## XCVIII. LETTER OF THE SAME GREGORY TO THE SAME BISHOP LEANDER, CONCERNING THE BOOKS SENT, THE *PASTORAL RULE* AND THE EXPOSITION OF BLESSED JOB. (C)

[Col. 0833]

[Col. 0833D] Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother Leander, bishop.

How ardently I long to see you, since you love me deeply, you can read in the tablets of your heart. But because I cannot see you, separated as you are from me by so great a distance of lands, I did the one thing that charity toward you suggested: I sent to your holiness, with our common son Probinus the presbyter who is coming, the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, which I wrote at the beginning of my episcopate, and the books that you knew I had composed some time ago as an exposition of blessed Job.

[Col. 0834D] I did not, however, send the books of the third and fourth parts of that work, because I had only copies of those same parts, which I have already given to monasteries. Let your holiness read through these carefully, and weep over my sins still more carefully, lest it be counted as a heavier fault for me that I seem to know what I fail to do. How heavily I am oppressed in this Church by the tumult of so many affairs will be made known to your charity by the brevity of my letter, since I speak so little to one whom I love more than all others. May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend brother.

[Note: [Col. 0833] This subscription is taken from Cod. Bibl. Reg. and Esc. 3, since it is absent from the others.]

## XCIX. LETTER OF THE SAME GREGORY TO THE SAME PRIEST LEANDER, CONCERNING THE PALLIUM SENT FROM THE SEE OF BLESSED PETER THE APOSTLE. (C)

[Col. 0835]

[Col. 0835A] Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother Leander, bishop.

I received a letter from your holiness, written with the pen of pure charity. For the tongue had been dipped in the heart before pouring onto the page what it wrote. When it was read, good and wise men were present, whose hearts were immediately moved to compunction. Each began to draw you into his own heart with the hand of love, because in that letter it was not possible merely to hear the sweetness of your mind but to see it. Each was kindled and filled with wonder, and the very fire of those listening showed what ardor had burned in the one who spoke. Unless flames first burn within themselves, they do not set another alight. Thus we saw how greatly your mind had burned with charity, since it kindled others in this way.

They did not know your life at all, which I always recall with profound reverence, but the greatness of your heart was revealed to them through the humility of your speech. Yet that letter of yours says that my life is worthy of imitation by all. But since it is not so, let it be so because it is said, lest one who is not accustomed to lying become a liar. On this subject I shall briefly repeat the words of a certain good woman: “Do not call me Naomi,” that is, “beautiful”; “call me Mara,” that is, “bitter,” because I am full of bitterness.

For, good man, I am not today the one whom you knew. I confess that, while advancing greatly outwardly, I have fallen inwardly, and I fear that I belong to the number of those of whom it is written: “You cast them down when they were lifted up.” For the one who advances in honors but falls in character is cast down when he is lifted up [159]. Following the ways of my head, I had resolved above all to be “the reproach of men and the rejected of the people,” and to run in the lot of the one of whom the Psalmist again says: “You have placed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears,” so that I might rise inwardly all the more truly as I lay more humbly outwardly in the valley of tears.

But now burdensome honor weighs me down greatly: innumerable cares resound around me, and whenever the mind gathers itself toward God, they tear it apart by their assaults, as though by swords. There is no rest of heart; it lies prostrate in the depths, crushed beneath the weight of its own thoughts. The wing of contemplation lifts it to higher things either very rarely or not at all. The ignorant mind grows numb, and, nearly reduced to stupor by the temporal cares barking around it, is forced now to engage in earthly affairs, now even to administer matters that are carnal. At times, compelled by weariness, it is forced to arrange even certain things with guilt.

Why say more? Overcome by its own weight, it sweats blood. If guilt were not reckoned under the name of blood, the Psalmist would not say: “Deliver me from bloods.” When we join guilt to guilt, we also fulfill what was said through another prophet: “Blood has touched blood.” Blood is said to touch blood when one guilt is added to another, so that the heap of iniquity may multiply.

Amid all this I beseech almighty God: hold me, escaped from the waves of disturbance, by the hand of your prayer. I was sailing, as it were, with a favorable wind when I was leading a tranquil life in the monastery; but suddenly a storm arose in violent movements, seized me in its turmoil, and I lost the prosperity of my voyage, because, having lost my quiet, I suffered shipwreck of mind. Behold, I am now tossed among the waves, and I seek the plank of your intercession, so that I, who did not deserve to reach port safely in an intact ship, may at least be brought back to shore after my losses upon a plank.

As for the trouble of gout, your holiness writes that you are afflicted by it; I too have been severely worn down by its continual pain. But consolation will be easy if, amid the scourges that we suffer, we recall to mind the sins that we have committed. We shall then see that these are not scourges but gifts, if we who sinned through the pleasure of the flesh are pricked by pain of the flesh.

Moreover, from the blessing of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have sent you a pallium, to be used only for the solemn celebrations of Mass. Having sent it, I ought certainly to have admonished you how you should live; but I suppress my words, because your conduct surpasses words.

May almighty God guard you by his protection and lead you to the homeland of heavenly reward through an abundant harvest of souls. How greatly I am weighed down by responsibilities and weakness is shown by the brevity of the letter, in which I say little even to one whom I love greatly. May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend brother.

[Note: [Col. 0835C] Leaves are missing in Bibl. Reg.]

[Note: [Col. 0836C] Aem., Esc., Tol. 1, 2, Ger.: “the brevity of the letter bears witness.”]

## C. THE ABOVE LETTER TO RECCARED, KING OF THE GOTHS. (C)

[Col. 0835]

[Col. 0835D] Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the most glorious and most excellent son Reccared, king of the Goths and Suebi.

### I. Praise of the same ruler, because through him the Gothic people was converted to the Catholic faith

I cannot express in words, most excellent man, how much I delight in your work and your life. In these days I have learned of the power of a miracle wrought through your excellence: the entire Gothic people has been transferred from the error of the Arian heresy to the solidity of the true faith. I long to exclaim with the prophet: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” What heart, even if made of stone, upon learning of so great a deed would not immediately melt into praise of almighty God and love for your excellence?

I confess that I often tell my assembled sons what has been accomplished through you, and that I often delight in wondering at it together with them. These things frequently even stir me against myself, because I, sluggish and useless, am then tormented in idle inactivity when kings are laboring in the gathering of souls for the profit of the heavenly homeland. What, then, shall I say at that dreadful examination when the Judge comes, if I arrive there empty, while your excellence leads behind you the flocks of the faithful whom you have now drawn to the grace of the true faith through diligent and continual preaching?

Yet, good man, I have great consolation in this as a gift from God: the holy work that I do not possess in myself, I love in you; and while I rejoice with great exultation over your deeds, what is yours through labor becomes mine through charity.

Therefore, concerning the conversion of the Goths, in your work and our rejoicing, I desire to exclaim with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.” For we, as I believe, are all the more indebted to almighty God in thanksgiving, since, although we have done nothing with you, by rejoicing together in your work we are nevertheless participants in it.

### II. Concerning the gifts sent by the aforesaid ruler to blessed Peter the apostle

How gladly blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, received the gifts of your excellence, our entire life clearly testifies. For it is written: “The vows of the righteous are pleasing.” In the judgment of almighty God, it is not what is given that is considered, but by whom it is given. Hence it is written: “God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but he did not look upon Cain and his gifts.” Since he was going to say that the Lord looked upon the gifts, he carefully prefaced this by saying that he looked upon Abel. From this it is plainly shown that it was not the offerer who pleased because of the gifts, but the gifts because of the offerer.

You therefore show how pleasing your offering is, since, before giving gold, you first gave the gifts of souls through the conversion of the people subjected to you. As for the report that the abbots sent to carry your offering to blessed Peter the apostle were worn out by the sea and returned to Spain from the very journey, your gifts were not rejected—they later arrived—but the steadfastness of those who had been sent was tested, to see whether they knew how to overcome dangers encountered through holy desire and not grow weary in mind amid bodily fatigue. Adversity placed before good vows is a test of virtue, not a judgment of rejection.

For who does not know how prosperous it was that blessed Paul the apostle was coming to Italy to preach, and yet, while coming, suffered shipwreck, while the ship of his heart remained intact amid the waves of the sea?

### III. Concerning his ordinance against the Jews, which was not corrupted by their gold

Moreover, I declare that this has increased the praises of God through your work, as I learned from the account of my beloved son Probinus the presbyter: when your excellence issued a certain ordinance against the perfidy of the Jews, those against whom it had been issued attempted to bend the rectitude of your mind by offering a sum of money. Your excellence despised it and, seeking to please almighty God, preferred innocence to gold.

In this matter the deed of King David comes to mind. When his attendants had brought him the water he desired from the cistern of Bethlehem, which lay among enemy troops, he immediately said: “Far be it from me to drink the blood of righteous men.” Because he poured it out and refused to drink it, it is written: “He offered it as a libation to the Lord.” If water despised by an armed king was turned into a sacrifice to God, let us consider what kind of sacrifice the king offered to almighty God who, for love of him, refused to accept not water but gold. Therefore, most excellent son, I shall say confidently: you made a libation of gold to the Lord, since you refused to possess it against him.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] From this word onward, Codex Bibl. Reg. begins again.]

### IV. That rulers should possess humility of heart

These things are great and must be attributed to the praise of almighty God [Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 2: “to the praises”]. Yet amid them the snares of the ancient enemy must be avoided with vigilant care. The greater the gifts he sees in people, the more subtly he seeks to take them away. Robbers on the road do not seek out empty travelers, but those carrying vessels of gold or silver. The present life is indeed a road, and each person must beware the spirits lying in wait all the more carefully as the gifts he carries are greater.

Therefore your excellence must guard above all the humility of heart, and then purity of body, in the midst of this great gift received through the conversion of the people subjected to you [Aem., “first”]. Since it is written: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted,” it is plainly evident that the one who truly loves high things is the one who does not sever his mind from the root of humility.

Often the evil spirit, in order to destroy good things that he previously did not wish to oppose, comes to the mind of the one who performed them after the work has been completed, and shakes it with silent thoughts through certain praises of its own. Thus the deceived mind marvels at how great are the things it has done. While it is lifted up by hidden swelling within itself, it is deprived of the grace of the one who granted the gift.

Hence, through the prophet’s voice, it is said against the proud soul: “Trusting in your beauty, you have played the harlot in your own name.” For the soul’s trusting in its beauty means presuming upon a righteous deed in itself; it plays the harlot in its own name when, in what it has rightly done, it does not seek to spread the praise of its Creator but seeks the glory of its own reputation.

Again, it is written through the prophet: “The more beautiful you are, descend.” For the soul descends from the place where it is more beautiful when, through the splendor of virtue by which it ought to have been exalted before God, it falls from his grace through its own pride.

What, then, must be done in these matters except that, whenever the evil spirit brings back to us the good things we have done in order to lift up our mind, we should always recall our sins to mind, so that we may recognize that what we have done by sinning is truly ours, while, when we turn away from sins, we recognize the gifts to be those of almighty God alone [Note: [Col. 0839C] In the printed editions, the following paragraph is arranged differently from the manuscripts.]

Some time ago your most beloved excellence, through a certain young man from Naples, had instructed me to write to the most devout emperor so that he might seek in the archive the agreements that had once been issued between the prince Justinian of pious memory and the laws of your kingdom, in order that from them I might determine what ought to be preserved for you.

Two things, however, strongly prevented me from doing this. First, the archive was burned in a sudden fire during the time of the aforesaid prince Justinian of pious memory, so that scarcely any document from his period remained at all. Second, no one should be told to seek within himself documents that are against you and then produce them publicly on my behalf.

For this reason I urge your excellence to arrange what accords with your character and diligently carry out whatever pertains to peace, so that the years of your kingdom may be remembered with great praise through long cycles of time.

Moreover, we have received, among the gifts of your excellence sent to the poor of blessed Peter the apostle, three hundred cowls (*cucullae*). We pray as earnestly as we can that you may have as protector on the dreadful day of judgment the one whose poor you have protected by your generosity in clothing. The necessity of the ship prevented us from sending our man to your excellence at this time, since no one can be found who is able to depart from these regions for the shores of Spain.

### V. That rulers should devote themselves to bodily chastity

Purity of body must also be guarded through diligent good action, according to the voice of the preaching Apostle [Note: [Col. 0839C] Codex Esc. 3 ends at this word]: “You are the temple of God, which is holy.” He says again: “This is the will of God, your sanctification.” Showing what sanctification he meant, he immediately added: “That you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passions of desire.”

### VI. That rulers should be moderate and gentle toward their subjects

[Col. 0840A]

The very reins of government must also be tempered toward subjects with great moderation, lest power creep into the mind. A kingdom is governed well when the glory of ruling does not rule the mind. Care must also be taken that anger does not creep in and cause everything that is permitted to be done too quickly. For anger, even when it pursues the faults of offenders, must not go before the mind as its mistress, but must serve behind reason’s back like a handmaid, coming forward when commanded. Once it has possessed the mind, it considers even what it does cruelly to be just.

Hence it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God.” Again it is said: “Let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak and slow to anger” [Aem., “to wrath”].

I do not doubt that, with God as author, you observe all these things. But since an occasion for admonition has arisen, I furtively attach myself to your good actions [Note: [Col. 0840C] Aem., Bibl. Reg., Tol. 2: “actions,” and so subsequently], so that what you do without being admonished you may, when an admonisher is also added, no longer do by yourselves alone.

May almighty God protect you in all your actions by the extension of his heavenly arm, and grant you both the prosperity of the present life and, after many cycles of years, eternal joys.

### VII. Concerning the key from the body of blessed Peter, the cross of the Lord that was sent, and the pallium sent to blessed Leander the bishop

We have sent a small key from the most sacred body of blessed Peter the apostle as his blessing. It contains iron enclosed from his chains, so that what bound his neck for martyrdom may loose yours from every sin [Aem., “absolve you from every sin”].

We have also given the bearer of this letter a cross to offer you. It contains wood from the Lord’s cross and hairs of blessed John the Baptist, so that through the intercession of his Forerunner you may always have consolation from our Savior.

To our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Leander we have sent a pallium from the see of blessed Peter the apostle, which we owed both to ancient custom, to your character, and to his goodness and dignity.

## CI. THE ROMAN COUNCIL HELD IN THE TIME OF GREGORY THE FIRST, POPE. (C)

[Col. 0839]

[Note: [Col. 0839] This council is absent from Cod. Bibl. Reg., Tol. 1, 2, Urg., and Ger.]

[Col. 0839D] While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever, in the time of the most devout emperors Maurice, Tiberius, and Theodosius, in the thirteenth year, the thirteenth indiction, on the fifth day of the month of July, Pope Gregory, seated before the most sacred body of blessed Peter the apostle with all the bishops and presbyters of the Roman Church, with the deacons and the entire clergy standing by, said:

In this holy Roman Church, which divine providence has willed me to govern, a very blameworthy custom has for some time arisen: certain singers are chosen for the ministry of the sacred altar and, having been established in the order of deacons, devote themselves to vocal melody, although they ought to be free for the work of preaching and the pursuit of almsgiving. Consequently, it often happens that, while a pleasing voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a suitable life is neglected, and the singer-minister spurs God by his conduct while delighting the people with his voice.

Therefore, by the present decree I establish that in this see the ministers of the sacred altar must not sing, but are to perform only the duty of reading the Gospel during the solemn celebrations of Mass. I decree that the psalms and the other readings be delivered by subdeacons or, if necessity requires, by the lower orders. If anyone attempts to act against this decree of mine, let him be anathema.

And all replied: Let him be anathema.

### SECOND CHAPTER

A shameful custom, wrapped in the torpor of indiscretion, has arisen: lay boys and secular persons attend upon the pontiffs of this see in the private services of the bedchamber. Since the life of the shepherd ought always to be an example to his disciples, clerics often do not know what the life of their pontiff is like in private, while secular boys, as has been said, do know it.

Therefore, by the present decree I establish that certain men selected from among the clergy or even the monks should attend upon the pontifical bedchamber in its service. The one who holds the place of governance should have such witnesses, so that those who derive an example of progress from their careful observation may see his conduct in private. If anyone acts against this decree of mine, he will endanger his position.

[Note: [Col. 0841A] In the printed editions this council is written at much greater length.]

## CII. INSTRUCTION OF SAINT GREGORY, POPE OF ROME, GIVEN TO THE RECTORS OF SICILY. (C)

[Col. 0841]

[Col. 0841B] Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Peter the subdeacon.

As you go to Sicily, you must constantly reread the capitulary that I gave you, so that you may take the greatest care concerning the bishops: they must not become involved in secular causes except insofar as the necessity of defending the poor compels them. As for the matters concerning monks or clerics contained in the same capitulary, I do not think they should now be raised; but let your experience guard these matters with as much care as my desire can be fulfilled through them.

Moreover, it has come to me that from the time of the defensor Antoninus until now, during this decade, many people have suffered certain acts of violence from the Roman Church. Some openly complain that their boundaries have been violently invaded, their slaves taken away, and even their movable property removed by force and without any judicial process.

In all these matters I want your experience to be intensely vigilant. Whatever you find to have been violently taken away during this decade, or unjustly retained under the name of the Church, restore it, by the authority of this present instruction of mine, to the one whose property you discover it to be. Nor should the person who suffered violence be forced to come to me and undertake the labor of so long a journey, since it cannot be established here with me whether he is speaking the truth.

Therefore, considering the majesty of the Judge who is to come, restore everything offered with sin, knowing that you bring me great profit if you gather a reward rather than riches.

We have learned that many people complain about slaves they have lost, saying that if perhaps a slave, fleeing from his master, declared himself to be under ecclesiastical jurisdiction, the rectors of the Church immediately treated him as a slave belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction. They did this without any judicial process, defending the slave’s statement by force. This displeases me as much as it departs from the judgment of truth.

Therefore, I want your experience to correct without delay whatever it discovers to have been done in this way. Other slaves as well, if any are now held under ecclesiastical jurisdiction, ought to be restored before judgment, just as they were taken away without judgment; and if anything legitimately belongs to the holy Church in them, then their possessors ought to be summoned by due legal action.

Correct all these matters irrevocably. For then you will truly be a soldier of blessed Peter the apostle if, in his affairs, you maintain the guardianship of truth even without partiality toward him. But if you see that anything can justly belong to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, beware of ever attempting to defend it by force, especially since I have established by decree, with the imposition of an anathema, that no titles are ever to be imposed by our Church upon urban or rural estates. Whatever belongs by reason to the poor must also be defended by reason, lest, while a good matter is handled badly, what is justly claimed from us be condemned before almighty God as unjust.

Let noble laymen, or the glorious man Perfectus, love you for your humility and not shrink from you because of pride. Yet when you recognize that they are perhaps acting unjustly against any of the poor, immediately turn humility into firmness, so that you may always be submissive to them when they act well and opposed to them when they act badly. Do this in such a way that neither your humility is slack nor your authority rigid, so that rectitude may season your humility and humility make your rectitude gracious.

Moreover, since it was customary for bishops to gather for the birthday of the pontiff, forbid them to come on the day of my ordination, because this empty superfluity does not please me. But if they must assemble, let them assemble on the feast of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that they may offer thanks to him from whose generosity they are shepherds.

## CIII. DECRETAL ISSUED IN THE CITY OF ROME BY POPE HORMISDAS: WHAT THE UNIVERSAL CATHOLIC CHURCH RECEIVES CONCERNING THE DIVINE SCRIPTURES, AND WHAT IT MUST AVOID THEREAFTER. (C)

[Col. 0843]

### I. The order of the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments

[Col. 0843A]

The order of the Old Testament that the holy and catholic Roman Church receives and venerates is as follows: one book of Genesis; one book of Exodus; one book of Leviticus; one book of Numbers; one book of Deuteronomy; one book of Joshua; one book of Judges; one book of Ruth; four books of Kings; two books of Chronicles; one book of the one hundred and fifty Psalms; three books of Solomon, namely Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; also one book of Wisdom and one book of Ecclesiasticus.

Likewise, the order of the prophets:

One book of Isaiah; one book of Jeremiah with his *Cinoth*, that is, his Lamentations; one book of Ezekiel; one book of Daniel; one book of Hosea; one book of Amos; one book of Micah; one book of Joel; one book of Obadiah; one book of Jonah; one book of Nahum; one book of Habakkuk; one book of Zephaniah; one book of Haggai; one book of Zechariah; one book of Malachi.

Likewise, the order of the histories [Note: [Col. 0843D] This order of the histories is absent from Alv., although it is found in the other manuscripts]:

One book of Job; one book of Tobit; one book of Ezra; one book of Esther; one book of Judith; two books of Maccabees.

Likewise, the order of the Scriptures of the New [Note: [Col. 0843D] From Aem. In Bibl. Reg.: “of the New and Eternal Testament.” In the others, incorrectly: “of the New and Old Testament.”] Testament:

Four books of the Gospels: one according to Matthew; one according to Mark; one according to Luke; one according to John. Also one book of the Acts of the Apostles; fourteen letters of the apostle Paul: one letter to the Romans; two letters to the Corinthians; one letter to the Ephesians; two letters to the Thessalonians; one letter to the Galatians; one letter to the Philippians; one letter to the Colossians; two letters to Timothy; one letter to Titus; one letter to Philemon; one letter to the Hebrews.

Also seven canonical letters: two letters of the apostle Peter; one letter of the apostle James; three letters of the apostle John; one letter of the apostle Jude Zelotes [Note: [Col. 0844D] Codex Bibl. Reg. is mutilated at the end up to this point.]

Also one book of the Apocalypse of John.

### II. The number of apostolic sees

After all the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures that we have listed above, through which the Catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, we thought it should also be made known that, although all the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church has been placed before the other Churches not by synodal decrees, but has held the primacy by the evangelical utterance of our Lord and Savior, saying: “You are Peter,” “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

There was also added the fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, who was crowned with a glorious death together with Peter in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero—not at different times, as the heretics babble, but at one time and on the same day—striving in martyrdom. By their suffering they consecrated the holy Roman Church mentioned above to Christ the Lord, and they placed it before all the other cities in the whole world by their presence and venerable triumph.

[Col. 0844B] The first see, therefore, is the Roman Church of the apostle Peter, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind [Note: [Col. 0844D] In the others, except Alv.: “of this kind”].

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, he preached the word of truth there and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third see, likewise, is honorably held at Antioch in the name of the most blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before coming to Rome, and there the name of the new people, Christians, first arose.

### III. The decrees of the holy councils

Although no one can lay another foundation apart from that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus, nevertheless, for holy edification, the Roman Church does not refuse to receive, in addition to those Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments that we have regularly listed above, the following as well:

The holy Council of Nicaea, consisting of three hundred and eighteen Fathers, under the auspices of the great Emperor Constantine, in which the heretic Arius was condemned;

the holy Council of Constantinople, consisting of one hundred and fifty Fathers, under the auspices of the elder Emperor Theodosius, in which the heretic Macedonius received his deserved condemnation;

the holy Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Coelestine, under the leadership of Cyril, bishop of the see of Alexandria, and Arcadius, the bishop sent from Italy;

the holy Council of Chalcedon, under the auspices of the Emperor Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian heresy and Eutyches, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices, were condemned.

We have also decreed that any councils instituted by holy Fathers up to the present, after the authority of these four, are both to be preserved and received.

### IV. The works of the holy Fathers that are received

What follows now concerns the works of the holy Fathers that are received in the Catholic Church.

The works of blessed Caecilius Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage.

Likewise, the works of blessed Gregory Nazianzen, bishop.

Likewise, the works of blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Likewise, the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

Likewise, the works of blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

[Col. 0845B] Likewise, the works of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

Likewise, the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Likewise, the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius [Ae., “of Hippo Regius”].

Likewise, the works of blessed Jerome, presbyter.

Likewise, the works of blessed Prosper, a most religious man.

Likewise, the letter of Pope Leo sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone disputes its text even to the extent of a single iota and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.

Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from fellowship with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in its communion to the final day of their lives, are to be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters that the most blessed popes, at various times, issued from the city of Rome in response to consultations from different Fathers are to be received reverently.

As for the acts of the holy martyrs, which shine with the manifold sufferings of torments and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions: what Catholic would doubt that they endured great things in their struggles and bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and assistance of God? And therefore, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to be excessive or less fitting than the order of events warrants, having been composed by unbelievers and unlearned persons—such as the passions of Quiricus and Julitta, Gregory, and others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. For this reason, as has been said, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church.

Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious contests, who are known to God more than to human beings.

Likewise, we receive with honor the Lives of the Fathers—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which, nevertheless, the most blessed Jerome wrote.

[Col. 0846A] Likewise, we have learned that the Acts of the blessed Sylvester, bishop of the Apostolic See, although the name of its author is unknown, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome; and, following this ancient practice, many Churches imitate it.

Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s Cross, and the other writing concerning the discovery of the head of the blessed John the Baptist, are indeed recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But since these writings have come into the hands of Catholics, the statement of the blessed apostle Paul must take precedence: “Test everything, and hold fast to what is good.”

Likewise, the most religious man Rufinus published many books of ecclesiastical composition and also interpreted several writings. But because the venerable Jerome criticized him on certain points concerning freedom of the will, we hold those views which we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held—not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom that often-mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we accept for reading certain minor works of Origen which the most blessed Jerome does not reject; but the rest, together with their author, we declare should be refused.

Likewise, the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea and the books of his Ecclesiastical History, although he showed tepidity in the first book of his narrative and later wrote one book in praise and defense of Origen the schismatic, we nevertheless do not declare wholly to be rejected, on account of their knowledge of particular matters, which is relevant to instruction.

[Col. 0846C] Likewise, we praise the most learned man Orosius, who arranged for us a history extremely necessary against the calumnies of the pagans and composed it with remarkable brevity.

Likewise, we esteem with distinguished praise the Paschal Work of the venerable man Sedulius, which he composed in heroic verse; nor do we disdain Juvencus’s laborious work, but rather admire it. All the remaining works written or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church by no means accepts. Of these, we believe that a few which have come to mind and which Catholics ought to avoid should be set forth below.

## V. Concerning minor works and information about apocryphal books that are not to be received

[Col. 0846D]

First of all, we confess that the Synod of Ariminum, convened by the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine, through the agency of the prefect Taurus, was then, is now, and shall be forever condemned. We also know that the Itinerary in the name of the apostle Peter, which is called that of Saint Clement, consisting of nine books, is apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of the apostle Andrew are apocryphal.

The ten-book Acts in the name of the apostle Thomas are apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of the apostle Peter are apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of the apostle Philip are apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Matthias are apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Barnabas are apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of James the Less are apocryphal.

[Col. 0847A] The Gospels in the name of the apostle Peter are apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Thomas, which the Manichaeans use, are apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Bartholomew are apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of the apostle Andrew are apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Lucian are apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Hesychius are apocryphal.

The Book of the Infancy of the Savior is apocryphal.

The Book of the Nativity of the Savior and of Mary, or of the midwife, is apocryphal.

The book called *The Shepherd* is apocryphal.

All the books produced by Leucius, the disciple of the devil, are apocryphal.

The book called *The Foundation* is apocryphal.

The book called *The Treasuries* is apocryphal.

[Col. 0847B] The book concerning the daughters of Adam, added to Genesis, is apocryphal.

The *Cento* concerning Christ, assembled from Virgilian verses, is apocryphal.

The book called *The Acts of Thecla and Paul* is apocryphal.

The book called *Nepos* is apocryphal.

The Book of Proverbs written by heretics and marked beforehand with the name of Saint Sixtus [Aemilianensis: Stephen] is apocryphal.

All these writings and similar ones, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata as well, Photinus and Bonosus, and those who fell away through similar error taught or wrote; likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinus, or Manichaeus, Faustus the African, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatian, Sabbatius, Callistus, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinianus, Pelagius, Julian of Celanum, Coelestius, Maximianus, Priscillian of Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the Cynic, Lampetius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter, and another Peter—one of whom disgraced Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, and also all the heresiarchs and their disciples, whether schismatics or otherwise, whose names we have not retained, are not merely rejected but have also been expelled from the entire Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church. We confess that they and the followers of their authors have been condemned forever under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

The Decretal issued by Pope Hormisdas ends here.

[Col. 0849]

# HISTORICAL-CRITICAL PREFACE TO THE TRUE AND GENUINE COLLECTION OF THE ANCIENT CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF SPAIN

First arranged, as is believed, by Saint Isidore, metropolitan of Seville and teacher of the Spains; subsequently enlarged in the following centuries by the Spanish Fathers; recovered from several manuscripts of venerable antiquity—namely, those of Toledo, the Escorial, Ripoll, Gerona, Córdoba, Urgell, and others—and corrected in accordance with their authority through the study and work of Andrés Burriel of the Society of Jesus.

By Charles de la Serna Santander. Brussels, 1800. (C)

## Charles de la Serna Santander sends greetings to the reader

[Col. 0849]

Nearly eight years have now elapsed since I resolved to make public the most excellent and genuine collection of the canons, arranged by Saint Isidore, metropolitan of Seville, which I possess copied from manuscripts of the finest quality. Accordingly, I had prepared for the press both the brief preface which I now present to you, benevolent reader, and the encomium of the most learned man Andrés Burriel, to be placed before the work. But the many and varied disturbances of the times, the tumults that arose, the dreadful wars, and the countless evils issuing from them—by which we are still overwhelmed—unwillingly compelled me to desist from what I had begun.

Now, however, having been informed by letter both that a new edition of the works of blessed Isidore is being prepared in Italy and that the ancient authority of the Spanish bishops, in accordance with the true discipline of the ancient Church, is being restored through the efforts of the Catholic king of Spain, Charles IV, I have thought that I might contribute somewhat to the execution of these undertakings by submitting to the press this preface of mine, whatever its worth, in which the blessed Isidore of Seville and especially the ancient canon law of the Church of Spain are discussed.

When, indeed, could it be more opportune to do this than when the ancient and true discipline of the Church is being restored? What could be more welcome or more pleasing to the Spanish prelates than for the Isidorian collection of canons—through which the Spanish Church once flourished in complete integrity, restored its morals, settled disputes that had arisen, and preserved the rights of the metropolitans inviolate even under the cruel and prolonged rule of the Moors—to be brought out of the darkness in which it has lain concealed for so many centuries and made known to men of learning?

Nor, as I think, will this brief preface be unwelcome to those who are preparing a new edition of the works of blessed Isidore in Italy. For from it they will readily recognize that more distinguished works of the bishop of Seville still lie hidden and unpublished. These must certainly be added to the works already published if a complete collection of his writings in every respect is desired to be gathered into a single corpus. Therefore the following works must necessarily be published together with the remaining works of the celebrated Isidore.

First: The common Latin version of the sacred books of the Bible, called the Gothic Bible [Note: See *Isidoriana*, chapter 77, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXI, where Arevalus discusses the question of the Bible learnedly. Editor.], revised by blessed Isidore, which we mentioned in numbers 62 and 63 of our preface. A very beautiful and extremely ancient manuscript of this version, perhaps written in the seventh century, is preserved in the library of the Church of Toledo.

Second: The true and genuine collection of the canons discussed here, arranged by Isidore himself.

Third: The ancient Isidorian, Toledan, or Mozarabic liturgy, which our Isidore revised for the use of the Church of Spain. For this reason, the most ancient manuscript copies preserved in the aforementioned library of the Church of Toledo should be consulted. We mentioned this liturgy in number 63, note 47.

[Note: The Isidorian liturgy will be contained in the two following volumes. Editor.]

Fourth: The *Book of Judgments*, in which the earliest laws of Spain are contained. As we observed in number 17, these laws have not yet been abrogated, and after the collection of the canons they are found inserted in almost all the ancient codices. For this work is believed to have been approved in the time of King Sisenand at the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which blessed Isidore presided, and to have been arranged in a new order by Isidore himself.

[Note: The learned Roman editor has clearly demonstrated that the *Book of Judgments* should not be attributed to blessed Isidore. See *Isidoriana*, chapter 92, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXI, where he clarifies this question. Editor.]

From what has been said, it is clear how much labor must be expended in preparing a new edition of Isidore and how much care the editors must devote to consulting and comparing the manuscripts, so that the remaining works of so great a writer may be brought to light with the utmost accuracy.

You have here, candid reader, an outline of our preface. Farewell.

# HISTORICAL-CRITICAL PREFACE

[Col. 0849]

## PROEM.—The labors of scholars in elucidating collections of canons

[Col. 0849]

### 1

After the tireless labors and vigils of so many most learned men in arranging and elucidating collections of canons; after the outstanding works in this field by Voellius and Justellus [Note: *Bibliotheca Juris canonici veteris*, in Greek and Latin, from the edition of Guillelmus Voellius and Henricus Justellus. Paris, 1661, 2 folio volumes.], Pithaeus [Note: *Codex canonum vetus Ecclesiae Romanae*, restored by Franciscus Pithaeus. Paris, from the Royal Press, 1787, folio.], Beveregius [Note: Guillelmus Beveregius’s *Synodicon*, or *Pandectae canonum apostolorum*, etc., in Greek and Latin. Oxford, Wels, 1672, 2 folio volumes.], and others, many will regard it as entirely useless to bring this new collection to light, and will think that we are carrying owls to Athens. For what, they will say, is new or worthy of the attention of learned men in this code of canons that has not been reprinted again and again in the other collections of canons and councils? What is there that could not be sought elsewhere? Especially since scarcely any public or private library exists today that does not possess one or another collection of canons containing all these materials, or at least the principal ones.

### 2

Although these considerations may seem plausible, nevertheless, moved by many reasons, I have resolved to make public this important collection, attributed with substantial arguments—as will be shown below—to blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, and capable of contributing greatly to the restoration of a purer discipline of the Church and to the observance of the ancient canons. I hope that all learned men who take pleasure in ecclesiastical antiquities and who will kindly read through this preface of mine, whatever its worth, will judge this decision fairly and favorably.

### 3

Indeed, even if other reasons were lacking, this one is not insignificant: this most precious codex, containing canons composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, has until now lain either wholly unknown or at least insufficiently known to the learned world—not without detriment to the Catholic Church, disgrace to Spain, and injury to the blessed bishop Isidore of Seville.

[Col. 0851C] ### 4

Moreover, no code of canons has ever existed, compiled under private or public authority, that can be compared with ours, whether one considers its extent, its arrangement and elegant disposition, or, more importantly, the canonical authority of the monuments contained in it. For you will encounter nothing in them that is not genuine and free from every stain of interpolation; nothing that would evade even the keenest scrutiny of critics with a properly discerning nose. As for the multitude of documents, besides the Greek and African canons, this codex also contains the Spanish and Gallican canons absent from the other ancient codices, together with more than one hundred letters of the Roman pontiffs. All of these have been arranged and ordered with excellent judgment.

### 5

I add, moreover, that I have considered it no small matter to vindicate Spain and her most illustrious teacher, Isidore, bishop of Seville, from calumnies. For although the Spanish Church could boast above all others of its outstanding and wholly uncorrupted collection of canons, through which it preserved the ancient discipline intact and restored it after its collapse—not only during the most prosperous times of the Gothic kings but also under the harsh and prolonged rule of a barbarian people, as will readily be clear to anyone from the Arabic codex described below, preserved in the celebrated Escorial library—nevertheless, for many centuries past, that is, from the time of Hincmar of Reims down to the present day, Spain herself and her teacher Isidore have been accused by many, through false denunciation, of being the fabricators of the collection forged by Isidore Mercator, filled with spurious and interpolated documents. Indeed, no Spaniard was found to undertake the defense of his homeland, although it would have been extremely easy for anyone, simply by exhibiting this codex—which the Spanish Church used into the thirteenth century and beyond—to make clear to the learned world that the author of that most corrupt collection was not Spanish and that no such collection had been composed in Spain.

### 6

Finally, so that it may be understood from this that the supreme authority of the Apostolic See, which the Spanish Church is shown always to have acknowledged from the documents of that same collection, does not rest in the least upon spurious or interpolated monuments of antiquity, the most illustrious Blasius long ago demonstrated, through many weighty arguments, that the false wares disseminated among the public by Isidore Mercator at the end of the eighth century or the beginning of the ninth favored the rights of bishops and metropolitans rather than those of the Roman Pontiff.

[Note: *Commentary of Charles Blasius on the collection of canons of Isidore Mercator*. Naples, 1760, quarto.]

### 7

Moved, therefore, by these considerations, we publish this most excellent Isidorian collection. In order that it may become better known, and that we may vindicate Spain herself and her outstanding teacher, Isidore of Seville, from the unjust accusation of having interpolated the ancient canons and decretals, we place before it this historical preface, divided into seven sections, whose plan in summary is as follows:

First, the manuscript codices of this collection preserved in various libraries are catalogued. An exact description of the principal codices is given in section 2; at its conclusion we provide information about the Arabic codex, truly singular and most distinguished. Section 3 then treats the origin and composition of this collection of the Church of Spain, preceded by a brief historical account of the principal ancient codices of canons. Fourth, the ancient codex used by the Spanish Church before the time of Isidore of Seville is discussed in outline. In section 5 it is established by the strongest arguments that blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, arranged this collection of canons for the use of the Spanish Church. From this most excellent collection the most corrupt compilation of Mercator flowed, as may be seen in section 6; yet it is shown that this compilation was assembled neither in Spain nor by Spaniards. Finally, the supreme authority of the Apostolic See acknowledged by the Spanish Fathers is demonstrated from the documents of the collection itself.

## § I. The numerous codices of this unpublished Isidorian collection are catalogued

### 8

Very many manuscript codices on parchment of this most excellent collection, arranged by blessed Isidore of Seville, written in Gothic and Lombardic letters during the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries, are carefully preserved in various public and private libraries of Spain and in the archives of its churches. For, besides those mentioned by the most celebrated and never sufficiently praised Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, in his letters to Juan Bautista Pérez—formerly a canon of the holy Church of Toledo and later bishop of Segorbe—written at Lérida on 13 July and 30 August 1576 [Note: They are extant, together with several other letters of learned men, at the end of the excellent work entitled *Censura de historias fabulosas*, published after the death of the most learned author Don Nicolás Antonio through the care and study of the celebrated Don Gregorio Mayans. Valencia, from the press of Antonio Bordazar, 1742, folio.], there are five other codices of the finest quality in the Royal Library of Madrid, brought there from the Escorial monastery by the distinguished Don Blas Nasarre, formerly director of that Royal Library. Among them two especially famous codices stand out, namely the Vigilanus and the Aemilianensis, whose description is given in the following section. Our Burriel was the first to identify another codex, presented to the Church of Palencia by the most learned King Alfonso, and he arranged for it to be transferred to the aforementioned Royal Library, where it now remains.

### 9

Two outstanding parchment codices of our collection are also preserved in the archive of the metropolitan Church of Toledo, which is filled with many other precious manuscripts relating to ecclesiastical and civil history and antiquity. The Church of Córdoba possesses one of its own. Two other very ancient codices exist in the archives of the Churches of Gerona [Note: The two Councils of Gerona which Hardouin arranged to have printed in his great royal collection, vol. XI, cols. 1671–1672, were copied from this Gerona codex by the noble Don José Taverner, canon of the Church of Barcelona.] and Urgell [Note: This codex was made more famous by the most learned Don Fernando de Mendoza. From it he copied the names of the priests who attended the Council of Elvira and had them printed in his most erudite *Commentary on the Council of Elvira*.]. The aforementioned Father Burriel transcribed their variant readings. He also had access to another extremely ancient codex, now preserved in the Royal Library of Madrid, which he named the Loayso-Carvajalean after its former owner, M. D. García Loaysa, archbishop of Toledo.

[Col. 0853C] ### 10

The most celebrated and entirely praiseworthy Pedro de Marca, archbishop of Paris, catalogued two other very ancient codices in the monastery of Ripoll among the Catalans. From these he copied the genuine Isidorian preface and inserted it into his own works.

### 11

That another codex of our collection once existed in the monastery of Cella Nova among the Galicians is demonstrated by a fragment of its table of contents published by the Reverend Father Enrique Flórez. It is truly regrettable that this codex was lost, for it contained the Eighteenth Council of Toledo, which many have sought in vain.

[Note: Flórez, *España sagrada*, vol. VI, pp. 233–234.]

[Col. 0854A] ### 12

At Alcalá, in the library of the major college founded by the celebrated Don Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, several manuscript copies are carefully preserved. The Imperial Library of Vienna possesses another outstanding and very ancient codex, transferred there from the Ambrosian Library of Milan. I have before my eyes an exact description of the codex written in the hand of Bernard Gentilotti, formerly director of that library.

It is indeed remarkable that, out of so many manuscript copies of the genuine Isidorian collection, this one Viennese codex alone should to this day be found pure and unmixed outside Spain. I say “pure,” because the manuscripts that the most learned Benedictine Father Coustant had access to in France he recognized as mixed with spurious materials drawn from Mercator’s collection and as interpolated.

[Note: *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, edited by Pierre Coustant. Paris, 1721, folio.]

### 13

Finally, omitting the other manuscript codices that are less well known or that lie hidden in various libraries while battling moths and cockroaches, I shall add by way of conclusion what Ambrosius de Morales, a most distinguished man and the most diligent investigator of Spanish antiquities, recorded concerning several others in his *Itinerary*, written in Spanish.

[Note: The account of this journey, revised from the autograph manuscript of the Escorial monastery, was published by the Reverend Father Enrique Flórez, who added his own notes and a Life of the author, under the title *Journey of Ambrosius de Morales*, etc. Madrid, Antonio Marín, 1765, folio.]

Morales traveled through the kingdoms of León and Galicia and the principality of Asturias at the command of Philip II, the great king of Spain, in order accurately to catalogue and describe the antiquities, mausoleums, cenotaphs, and manuscript codices hidden in the libraries of various churches and monasteries, and to commit his findings to writing.

[Note: This royal commission, dated at Madrid on 18 May, is found on pages 2 and 3 of the aforementioned *Itinerary*.]

[Col. 0854C] ### 14

This most learned man, in title IX, page 32, of the work mentioned above, where he discusses the monastery of Saint Zoilus at Carrión, describes a manuscript codex of our collection preserved there, in which the following is written:

> This book was begun on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the Spanish Era 986.

[Note: These are his words: “They have few books, but among them is one of councils which can and should rightly be highly esteemed. It is in Gothic script, and right at the beginning it has a depiction of the Holy Cross of Oviedo; then comes the ordinary inscription, which says, *The book of Theodemir the abbot*. Then, on another page, it says: ‘This book was begun on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the Era 986.’”]

That is, in the year of Christ 948.

He testifies that he saw another codex in the library of the monastery of Saint Facundus, of the Order of Saint Benedict, older than the Carrión codex, though some material was missing at its end.

[Note: I would believe that this Saint Facundus codex is the very one frequently cited by García Loaysa. *Councils of Spain*, pp. 4, 610, 719, and elsewhere.]

In the exceedingly rich library of the Church of Oviedo, containing manuscripts of every kind, he had in his hands an outstanding and very ancient codex of our collection written in large Gothic letters.

[Col. 0855A] He believes that this codex was brought there from the city of Toledo after it was captured by the Moors.

[Note: Page 94.]

Finally, besides the extremely ancient and everywhere damaged codex found in the monastery of Saint Peter of the Mountains, of the Order of Saint Benedict, which he mentions on page 174, he identified another very old codex preserved in the archives of the Church of Lugo. He arranged for it to be transferred to the celebrated Escorial library, where, unfortunately and to the great loss of learning, it was consumed by fire together with several other exceedingly precious manuscript codices in the lamentable and most dreadful fire of the Escorial library, which occurred in the year of our Lord 1671.

This celebrated codex of Lugo is frequently and honorably mentioned in the *Decree of Gratian* corrected by Gregory XIII. For, at the command of Cardinal de Quiroga, the copy transcribed from it by the most illustrious Don Juan Bautista Pérez, canon of Toledo and later bishop of Segorbe, and sent to Rome, brought considerable light to the correctors.

[Note: *Journey of Morales*, p. 104, note 2. There it is recorded with what persistence the Reverend Father Enrique Flórez unsuccessfully attempted to have the copy transcribed for him from the Roman manuscript.]

But enough has now been said about this matter. We must proceed to the description of the principal codices.

## § II. In which a description and account of the principal codices of our collection are presented

[Col. 0856A]

### 15

As I turn, therefore, to the description of the principal codices of our distinguished collection, it has seemed appropriate to me to begin with the Alveldensis, or Vigilanus, as the most outstanding.

### 16

This celebrated codex, called Vigilanus after the monk Vigila, who wrote it in the Spanish Era 1014, that is, in the year of Christ 976, and Alveldensis after the place where it was written—namely, in the monastery of Saint Martin of Albelda, of the Order of Saint Benedict, founded by Sancho, king of Navarre, and Queen Toda around the year of our Lord 924—was written in exceedingly beautiful Gothic letters and adorned with various images and ornaments, excellently painted in gold and colors.

[Note: Albelda is a small town situated two Spanish leagues from the city of Logroño.]

[Note: This extremely ancient monastery, where two hundred monks are said once to have lived, fell into ruin through the injury of time and was transferred from there to the Church of Santa María la Redonda near the city of Logroño. From its library, by order of King Philip II, this codex was brought to the Escorial monastery and from there transferred to the Royal Library of Madrid.]

[Col. 0856B] It consists of 421 parchment folios of the largest format. The first twenty contain various Latin trochaic verses and acrostics in which the scribe Vigila implores divine assistance, together with other minor works on the ecclesiastical calendar, the winds, the trees of consanguinity, and so forth. The codex of canons follows in this order.

[Note: This introductory work, entitled *Excerpta canonum*, is nothing other than an index of the subjects of this collection, arranged according to a very useful and excellent method and divided into ten books. Each book is prefaced by an index of titles; under each title are reported the canons of general and provincial councils, as well as sentences transcribed from the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, with the chapters and titles of the collection to which the reader is referred indicated. This is precisely the work that Cajetanus Cenni copied from Aguirre and published at Rome; mistakenly taking the index for the code itself, he grandly entitled it *Code of the Ancient Canons of the Church of Spain*.]
