[Col. 0857A] ### 17

Various minor works follow, as well as the *Book of Judgments*, or the laws of the Visigoths. Since all these lie outside our purpose, I pass them over. I shall add only this: these Visigothic laws, entitled *Book of Judgments* or *Forum Judicum*, are found inserted in almost all the codices of our collection, since together with the aforementioned collection they formed the corpus of the canon and civil law of Spain. Indeed, the *Book of Judgments* still remains in full force among the Spaniards, apart from a few provisions that have been abrogated.

This is what may be said about the Vigilanus codex. We must now speak of the Aemilianensis.

18. This outstanding codex, often praised by such eminent men as Ambrosius de Morales, Juan Vázquez del Mármol, Juan Bautista Pérez, José Moret, and others, took the name Aemilianensis from the place where it was written or where [Col. 0857B] it was formerly kept. By order of King Philip II it was first brought to the monastery of El Escorial and soon transferred to the royal library at Madrid. The priest Velasco, believed also to have been a monk of the monastery of Saint Emilian of Coculla [Note: The monastery called Saint Emilian of Coculla was, for its antiquity, wealth, and the extent and magnificence of its entire building, among the foremost in Spain.], of the Order of Saint Benedict, with the assistance of Bishop Sisebutus and Sisebutus his disciple, prepared this codex around the end of the tenth century. Whether one considers the form of its letters or the excellence and beauty of its illustrations and ornamentation, it is in no way inferior to the preceding Vigilian codex. It consists of 476 parchment folios of large format, of which the first twenty contain various preliminary works, several hexameter verses, illustrations, and ornamentation. The codex of canons follows in precisely the same order, [Col. 0857C] form, and method as that possessed by the Vigilian codex. It must nevertheless be noted that this Aemilian codex contains only thirteen Toledan councils, and that its appendix lacks the Council of Carpentras and the Third Council of Clermont. As in the Vigilian codex, 103 decretal letters are counted.

19. As for the antiquity of this codex, it must be noted that in the margin of the first page there is an inscription, somewhat effaced by use and age, which reads: “From Udam to the Era C, in which era the work of this codex was produced.”

For this reason many learned men believed that the codex was written in the year of the Lord 962; and indeed, if from the Spanish Era [Col. 0858A] M, or one thousand, one subtracts 38, the sum 962 remains. But this does not at all agree with the subscription placed at the end of the codex beside the images of Kings Urraca, Sancho, and Ramiro, where these words are read: “In the time of these kings and queen this work of the book was completed, the Era proceeding XXX……” From this it is plainly evident that the codex was written after the Spanish Era 1030, corresponding to the year of the Lord 992, but undoubtedly before Era 1040; otherwise, instead of XXX, the scribe would have written T or XI, according to the usage and practice of that period.

20. Opposite the images of Velasco the scribe, Sisebutus the bishop, and Sisebutus the disciple, there is a marginal inscription reading:

“Bishop Gisebutus, with the scribe Velasco, pr… together with Gisebutus … his disciple, produced … this book … so that their memory may always remain in blessing.”

21. Older and more accurate than these was the distinguished Hispalense codex, which perished, as stated above, in the disastrous fire of the monastery of El Escorial in the year of the Lord 1671, together with the extremely ancient Lucense codex. Ambrosius de Morales and Juan Vázquez del Mármol called this codex Hispalense because they believed that it had been written at Seville [Note: García de Loaysa took the Aemilian codex for the Hispalense, but incorrectly, since they are wholly different, as is readily apparent from their descriptions. Moreover, the Aemilian codex was written by the scribe Velasco, as stated above, after Spanish Era 1030. The Hispalense, however, more than fifty years older, was written by the deacon John in Era 949.]. But the most learned Andrés Burriel, led by stronger reasoning, named it the Ayalense after its former possessor, Martín de Ayala, archbishop of Valencia [Col. 0858C]. Here we present a description of this codex made by the most illustrious Juan Bautista Pérez, formerly a canon of the Church of Toledo and later bishop of Segorbe, transcribed from a manuscript codex in my possession:

> “A great treasure, O reader.

22. “Whoever you are, O reader, who have come upon this book, first pray earnestly for the soul of the most reverend lord Martín de Ayala, archbishop of Valencia. Since he was devoted to antiquity, he preserved this truly golden book in his library, half-destroyed through the injury of utterly ignorant men, so that it might not perish completely. Next, recognize what a treasure you hold in your hands, and strive, I beg you, so that through you this book may bring benefit to the Christian world and honor to your Spain. For you will scarcely believe, unless you have tested it, how greatly the materials have been corrupted from the time when Saint Isidore of Seville collected all the councils and the decretal letters of the pontiffs into one work down to the present day, while what was already uncorrected has been copied day by day in still more defective form. Yet a large part of these materials can easily be restored from this most ancient book, if anyone applies his mind to that task.

“But make the experiment yourself, and you will discover in the printed volumes of the councils countless passages in which certain words are read in place of others, words that wholly overturn the meaning of the passage; many canons of the councils and certain letters of the pontiffs are missing; and the subscriptions of the bishops themselves, which in most of the councils of Spain are either entirely or partly absent, you will see here set down fully and most faithfully. Yet these subscriptions are of the greatest importance for discovering the succession of bishops in our Spanish churches and for arranging the order [Col. 0859B] of the councils. That order of the Spanish councils which has until now been circulated in printed books—without bringing small disgrace upon the Spanish people—seems scarcely tolerable, since it is extremely disordered; but it can readily be corrected through your work from this codex, both by comparing the subscriptions of the councils with one another [Col. 0860A] and by reading the titles of the individual councils, which always have appended the era in which they were assembled, something you will rarely find in printed books.

23. “As for the antiquity of this codex, know that it was written in Era D.CCCC.XLVIIIJ, as you will find noted at its end before the degrees of affinity. That year was the nine-hundred-and-eleventh from the birth of the Lord. For it is most certain that the beginning of the Caesar’s Era preceded the birth of our Savior by thirty-eight years. This book was written by John the deacon for the benefit of a certain bishop, also named John, as can be seen in the margin of the Fifth Council of Carthage and likewise in the letter of Pope Leo to Leo Augustus.

24. “And so that you may see at a glance everything contained in this codex, we have appended a catalogue of its contents. In it you will observe that the councils are not arranged according to the succession of their years, but that all councils belonging to the same province are placed together; for you can easily determine the chronological succession for yourself from the appended era.”

[Col. 0859] The Council of Nicaea is missing together with the first quaternion [Note: The index of contents, entitled “Excerpts of Canons,” is also missing.]. The following five are present: the conclusion of the Council of Gangra; the complete Council of Sardica; the Council of Laodicea; the First Council of Constantinople, Era 318; the First Council of Ephesus; and the Council of Chalcedon, Era 488.

Thus far the Greek councils. The African Latin councils follow: the First Council of Carthage; the Second Council of Carthage, Era 428; the Third Council of Carthage, Era 435; the Fourth Council of Carthage, Era 435; the Fifth Council of Carthage, Era 438; the Sixth Council of Carthage, Era 457; the Seventh Council of Carthage, Era 457; and the Council of Milevis, Era 440.

Thus far the African councils. The Gallican councils now follow: the First Council of Arles; the Second Council of Arles; the Third Council of Arles, Era 461; the Council of Valence, Era 423; the Council of Turin; the Council of Riez, Era 477; the Council of Orange, Era 479; the Council of Vaison, Era 470; the Council of Agde, Era 543; and the First Council of Orléans.

Thus far the Gallican councils. The Spanish councils follow: the Council of Elvira, in the same period as Nicaea; the Council of Tarragona, Era 554; the Council of Girona, Era 555; the Council of Zaragoza; the Council of Lleida, Era 584; the Council of Valencia, Era 584; the First Council of Toledo; the Second Council of Toledo, Era 565; the Third Council of Toledo, Era 627; the Fourth Council of Toledo, Era 671; the Fifth Council of Toledo, Era 674; the Sixth Council of Toledo, Era 674; the Seventh Council of Toledo, Era 684; the Eighth Council of Toledo, Era 691; the Ninth Council of Toledo, Era 693; the Tenth Council of Toledo, Era 694; the Eleventh Council of Toledo, Era 713; the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, Era 721; the First Council of Braga, Era 599; the Second Council of Braga, Era 610; the First Council of Seville, Era 628; and the Second Council of Seville, Era 656.

Thus far the councils. The decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs follow, from Damasus through Gregory I: two letters of Damasus; three of Siricius; twenty-one of Innocent I; two of Zosimus; four of Boniface I; three of Celestine I; thirty-nine of Leo I; three of Hilary; two of Simplicius; three of Felix III; two of Gelasius I; one of Anastasius II; one of Symmachus; ten of Hormisdas; one of Vigilius; and four of Gregory I.

Decrees of the Roman See concerning books to be received and not to be received.

A table of blood relationships and relationships by marriage.

In this codex the Twelfth Council of Toledo is missing, although it is said to have been printed; in addition, four others are missing that have not yet been printed, namely the Fourteenth, Fifteenth, Sixteenth, and Seventeenth Councils of Toledo. The most reverend Lord Carranza, archbishop of Toledo, says that these are extant in the codex of the library of San Facundo.

[Col. 0859B] 25. Thus far Pérez. From this anyone will understand that learned men rightly mourn the loss of so distinguished a codex, although not a few excellent manuscript codices of the finest quality still survive. Among these the Girona codex holds no inferior place. We append here an account of its arrangement and a summary of its contents, omitting what does not pertain to the collection of canons:

[Col. 0861A] 26. Among learned men the Urgell codex is held in approximately the same esteem as the Girona codex, although it is both more emended and more accurate. It consists of 292 large-format parchment folios. In all other respects it agrees completely with the Girona codex; therefore it would be superfluous to provide a lengthy description of its contents. I will add only that the Excerpts of Canons, which, as stated above in note 25, are arranged according to the same method as in the Girona codex, contain only six of the ten books.

27. Nor should the very ancient Gothic codex be passed over in silence. It was named the Loayso-Carvajalean by its former possessor, García de Loaysa. This codex consists of 323 large-format parchment folios; yet it is defective and worn by age: several earlier folios are missing, [Col. 0861B] and consequently the Seventh Council of Carthage, together with everything preceding it, is absent. Although it displays the form and resemblance of the letters of the Vigilian and Aemilian codices, it is nevertheless believed to be older than they and to have been written in the ninth century. It contains only twelve Toledan councils; the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, as in the other codices, number 103.

28. We must now describe two codices of the Church of Toledo. From these, as being the most extensive and accurate, the most learned Andrés Burriel had the codex which we are publishing transcribed, and he compared it with several other codices of better quality. I omit the catalogue of contents, which may be seen prefixed to the Greek councils in our collection; [Col. 0861C] it would therefore be superfluous to reproduce it here.

29. The first and older codex, which we may call the Gothic Toledan, because it is carefully kept in the library of the Church of Toledo, shelf 15, no. 16, contains 315 large-format parchment folios. It shines with an elegant, rounded Gothic script arranged in three columns, each page being distinctly laid out from the beginning; accents are also very frequently added, the larger letters are varied with red pigment, and the entire vast work is marked by integrity, cleanliness, and an altogether most accurate sequence. On the margin of the first page, where the first book of the summary or index of contents begins—the work called the Excerpts of Canons—the following is written above and below in Gothic hand:

> “This book was begun on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in Era D.CCCC.LXXXVI.”

This era falls in the year of Christ 948. On the final page of the book, after the letter of Hormisdas concerning books to be received and not to be received, the following subscription is found, in which an interval of eighty-six years is noted:

[Col. 0862B]

> “This book ends: XXVII. Ides, Kalends of April, Era M.LXXII. Julian, an unworthy priest, wrote it in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Genesius the martyr, as a memorial, so that you may order prayers to the Lord for me, if God be for you.”

From this it appears that an error has entered either this inscription or the preceding one concerning the year in which this outstanding codex was copied.

30. The second codex, which we have chosen to call the Gothic Complutensian after the place where it was written, is kept in the same library of the Church of Toledo, shelf 15, no. 17. It too is written in an elegant script, though not so rounded, arranged throughout in two columns, each page being distinctly laid out. Its titles are decorated with red pigment and various colors. Although it does not equal the former in value, it must nevertheless be highly esteemed by fair-minded judges of such matters for its integrity, cleanliness, and the considerable diligence of its copyist. It is certainly less ancient than the Toledan codex, for it was written in Era 1133, which falls in the year of Christ 1095. But on that account it will not seem less worthy of esteem to learned men, since it is thereby made entirely clear that around the beginning of the twelfth century those abominable wares of Isidore Mercator were quite unknown to the Spanish people. [Col. 0863A] For if the copyist had known the work of Mercator, he would undoubtedly have preferred to copy it as the more extensive work rather than this codex. But more will be said about this in the sixth paragraph.

31. At the end of the codex, after the letter of Hormisdas concerning books to be received and not to be received, the following subscription is found, written in larger letters:

> “The book of the canons of the councils of the Holy Fathers is finished, or rather the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, successfully. Thanks be to God. Julian, an unworthy priest, wrote it. He whose it is, with God’s help, dwelling in Ulbalaga, which is situated above the praiseworthy plain. Wednesday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, Era T.C.XXXIII.
>
> “The number of folios of this book: 351.”

Between the lines, in smaller letters, one reads: “The number of folios of this book: 351.” In fact, to this day the codex has 348 usable parchment folios; without doubt the scribe also counted the blank folios.

32. Thus far concerning the more distinguished Latin codices. It remains for us to summarize what the most learned Michael Casiri relates about a truly rare and singular Arabic codex in the Arabic-Hispanic library at El Escorial. This highly praised scholar describes our codex under no. 1618 in volume I, page 541, of the aforementioned library, in these words:

> “A very ancient parchment codex, mutilated or effaced in some places by the passage of time itself, consisting of 435 folios. It was formerly written in Kufic letters by a certain priest named Vincent, as is clear from a note placed at the end of the eighth book. There Vincent himself declares that he collated this book and the preceding seven with other copies and corrected them according to their authority. You may nearly determine the age of the codex from another note of this kind, which is read at the end of the seventh book: ‘By divine assistance the seventh book was completed on Tuesday, the seventeenth day of October, in Spanish Era 1087, for the use, namely, of the most noble bishop John Daniel.’”

33. “As for the title of the work, although the codex bears none, since several folios are missing from its beginning, the true and genuine title plainly seems to be *Collection of the Sacred Canons for the Use of the Church of Spain*, both from the survey of the episcopal sees of Spain which it contains and from these words, found at the end of Book X: ‘And now let this be the end of Book X and of the final book of the COLLECTION OF THE SACRED CANONS.’”

34. And further:

> “It has therefore become clear and certain, both to me and to the most distinguished Juan de Santander, prefect of that same library, through comparison with the books mentioned above, whether printed or in manuscript, that we possess a collection of this kind in its entirety. It is consequently a complete, whole work, finished in every respect; whereas the codex published by Aguirre and Censius should be judged to be nothing other than the index of this collection, since it agrees exactly with its division into books, its sequence of titles, and the subjects of its contents.”

35. Thus far Casiri. Since they concern the same subject, I will add the following notes, which I have before me written in Arabic and Spanish by the hand of the most learned Juan de Santander, distinguished by every praise of discipline and erudition and formerly prefect of the royal library at Madrid. I present them here translated literally from Spanish into Latin, so that the character of the Arab-Spanish writer may become better known. [Col. 0864B] The notes are as follows.

> “At the end of the seventh book of the codex of canons, written in Arabic by Don Paulo Hoddar, the following subscription is read:
>
> “ ‘The seventh book was completed by the grace of God and with his help and assistance, on Tuesday, the fourteenth night before the completion of the month of October, in the year 1087 of the Era of Safar [Note: Safar, from the Hebrew *Saphardi*, as some believe, means Spain among the Arabs; hence this Arabic codex seems to have been written in the year of Christ 1049.]; the eighth book follows, with the blessing of God the helper, to whom may gratitude be rendered.’
>
> “This subscription is followed by four Arabic verses in which the copyist dedicates his work to Bishop Abd al-Malik in these words:
>
> “ ‘A book for Bishop Abd al-Malik, the generous protector, liberal in a time of barrenness and misery, sharp and effective in speech, the Phoenix of his age, learned, noble, kind, and discerning; through him God renews his blessings upon us and multiplies his protection over every creature. O, may God preserve him, while rain descends from the clouds upon the earth.’
>
> “At the end of the eighth book there is the following inscription:
>
> “ ‘I, Vincent, a sinful priest, the most humble servant of Christ, completed this eighth book of the sacred canons at the eighth hour of the morning, on the first Sunday of Lent, the day on which the story of the Samaritan woman is commemorated, from whom Christ our Lord asked water to drink at Jacob’s well. These things I have written, and I know truly that although my hand will at some time be consumed and reduced to nothing, what it has copied will remain. True delights are possessed only in eternal rest. As for hell—alas!—may its evils not prevail, and may God free me from its punishments, and grant that I may remain forever in his presence, which is delightful and sweet, just as are his rewards. Whoever reads these writings after my death, let him pray to God daily for my soul. O, may such a prayer be heard. Amen.’”

36. These are the notes; I omit the others as less necessary. From this same Arabic-written codex of the sacred canons it plainly appears how great, to use the words of the aforementioned Casiri, was once the love of sacred writings, how great the devotion to the Catholic faith and to ecclesiastical discipline among the Spanish people—whether it flourished amid the hardships of barbarian servitude or shone amid the darkness of Muslim blindness.

37. From the foregoing account of our collection and the description of its principal codices, it follows that no collection of canons has hitherto existed that does not readily yield to ours, whether one considers the number and authority of the monuments it contains or the excellence of its arrangement. As for its extent, everyone can see that it contains many councils, especially Gallican and Spanish councils absent from the other ancient collections, and also more numerous authentic and genuine decrees of the Roman pontiffs, which were either unknown to Dionysius Exiguus and the other collectors of canons who lived before the ninth century or were sought by them in vain.

[Col. 0865B] 38. If, however, one considers its method and the proper arrangement of its order, it will be evident at first glance to anyone that our collection surpasses the others. For the Greek, African, Gallican, and Spanish councils, together with the other monuments, have been arranged and disposed in it in such a way that anyone could easily enter councils celebrated at a later time into the distinguished collection without damaging its arrangement or reversing its order.

39. Nevertheless, this very extensive, most complete collection of canons, finished in every respect, in which the Spanish Church can boast above all others, was interpolated and corrupted by the fabricated wares of one Pseudo-Isidore’s rashness and audacity. It not only shamefully disgraced the honor of Spain, but also made the illustrious collector—namely, the celebrated Isidore, bishop of Seville—a false forger, though the Fathers gathered at the Eighth Council of Toledo deservedly honored him in these most laudatory words:

> “The distinguished teacher of our age, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last among his predecessors in age, not least in comparison of learning, and, what is more important, most learned in the faith of the ages and worthy to be named with reverence: Isidore.”

40. How much harm this same collection, which had preserved ecclesiastical discipline intact throughout the first eight centuries, suffered after being corrupted by the many fabrications and spurious decretals of the masked Isidore Mercator, and after being received for many centuries with general applause, perhaps solely because of the splendor of the name by which it appeared to be distinguished, is now universally understood; and learned commentaries on this subject, published by various authors, demonstrate it plainly. I therefore considered it superfluous to dwell at greater length on this matter. We shall address only those points that can scarcely be omitted for an explanation of the subject and that it will be necessary to state below in accordance with our argument.

## § III. The Origin and Composition of the Spanish Collection, with a Brief Discussion on that Occasion of the Ancient Collections of Canons

[Col. 0866A]

41. The rules of the councils, which the Greeks call *canons*, and the statutes of the Holy Fathers appear to have been established according to the same method and the same natural order as civil laws and regulations constituting the government of public affairs. Just as the human race, when it first gathered into society, began to be governed first by natural law, by the arrangements of heads of households, and by the counsels and example of princes and leaders; then, as wickedness and depravity increased, laws were enacted and written law emerged in order to cut away the vices arising from them, for the good of the commonwealth and for public and private security; so the holy Church of God was at first governed only by custom and example, by the commands, teaching, and preaching of the Holy Fathers and priests, without any written law. Later, however, when the ancient discipline was relaxed, the weakening of morals arose from it, abuses and corrupt practices were introduced into the Church, and bishops and ministers of God were compelled by their office to celebrate synods and councils. Through these they sought remedies suitable for curing such evils, restored the discipline that had collapsed, and provided the faithful and the priests themselves with an unimpaired way of life and the best form for administering the Church.

42. Once the rules and statutes established by the Fathers of the Church in these synods had been committed to writing and had grown into a considerable body, many learned men—whether priests or bishops themselves—gathered them into a single volume for the more convenient use of their studies. Once collected in this way, they subsequently came into use in the Churches. Although the faith of the entire Christian world is one and its doctrine wholly one, discipline nevertheless varies according to the character of peoples and the diversity of regions. For, as Saint Gregory says in his letter to Bishop Leander, in the one faith a diversity of custom does not harm the holy Church. This is also clearly demonstrated by the individual liturgies, rites, and ceremonies of the various Churches. It therefore came about that many Churches, according to the variety of their customs, possessed their own particular codices. In these, besides the canons of the general councils common to all Churches, they recorded the synods held by themselves and added the statutes of different Churches that they judged suitable to their own discipline [Note: Canons and councils, even general ones, were entered into a codex only by decree of a synod of the nation or kingdom, and thereby acquired the force of law. This is known to have been observed at least among the Spaniards. At the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, the Spanish bishops, invited by letters from Pope Leo II to receive and publish the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, decreed that it should be placed after the Council of Chalcedon with its due honor, place, and order.].

43. From this arose various collections of canons. Although they were arranged and ordered according to different methods at the discretion of their compilers, they nevertheless agreed with one another in the substance of their contents. Later they were corrupted by heretics opposed to the Catholic Church, who interpolated the opinions of the Holy Fathers and fabricated canons of councils. They carried this out with such skill and craft that afterward it was extremely difficult for learned men to distinguish the true from the false and the spurious from the genuine [Note: It has always been customary among heretics to adulterate the writings of the Holy Fathers and to disseminate false doctrine and impious teachings among the people under the name of illustrious men, so that in this way their writings might be read by Catholics more securely and without suspicion. Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, rightly expressed this for us in Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 12, in these words: “Such is the craftiness of heretics that they mix false things with true and evil things with good, and frequently insert the poison of their error into salutary things, so that they may more easily persuade people of the depravity of their perverse doctrine under the appearance of truth. Often heretics compose their statements under the name of Catholic teachers, so that they may be believed when read without question. Sometimes also, by hidden deceit, they insert their blasphemies into the books of our writers and corrupt true doctrine by adulterating it—either by adding what is impious or by removing what is pious.” Thus Isidore. Indeed, the charge of falsification seems properly attributable to those whose interest it was to corrupt the codices in order to defend a bad cause. Thus Felix of Urgel, as Hincmar of Reims testifies, was discovered to have tampered with the codex of Saint Hilary in the library of Charlemagne and, after corrupting the keeper of the books, to have written *Adoptatur* in place of *Adoratur*. See more in Germon, *On the Ancient Heretics Who Corrupted Sacred Codices*.].

44. An example of this kind of corruption is supplied by that most ancient collection called the *Canons of the Apostles*. The question of their authority has long been debated at great length among learned men. Some believe that all eighty-five canons commonly circulated were derived from the apostles themselves and promulgated through Saint Clement the pope, and they recognize the work as genuine. Others, on the contrary, entirely reject them as apocryphal or as having been adulterated by heretics. Others again, holding a kind of middle position, accept only fifty canons and reject the remaining thirty-five. In any event, this much is absolutely certain: these canons, marked with the name of the apostles, were commonly received by the Eastern Church and entered into its codex; they surpass the others in antiquity, and genuine traces of ancient discipline are contained in them. This perhaps was the reason why Dionysius Exiguus, omitting the rest, published the first fifty in Latin in his codex of canons.

45. But whether Clement himself, the Roman pontiff, or some other writer of the third century, as most have thought, collected these extremely ancient canons, since it is established that they were variously and deplorably interpolated and corrupted by heretics, Pope Gelasius rightly and deservedly declared them apocryphal at the Roman council held in the year of the Lord 494. For this reason our Isidore did not admit them into his pure and uncorrupted collection, as these words, found in the genuine preface of Isidore itself prefixed to the collection, plainly testify:

> “The canons that are called those of the apostles, since neither the Apostolic See receives them nor did the Holy Fathers give them their approval, because they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the apostles—although certain useful things are found in them—are nevertheless known to be devoid of canonical and apostolic authority, and assigned among the apocrypha [Note: We present here these words of the genuine preface, later interpolated by Pseudo-Isidore, transcribed from the first edition, published at Paris in 1524 under the care of Jacques Merlin: “Finally, because of their authority, we have placed before the other councils the canons called those of the apostles, although some call them apocryphal, since many receive them and the Holy Fathers have strengthened their opinions by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions.” From these words you may easily recognize Isidore the falsifier and impostor.].”

### 46

But indeed, that the Eastern Fathers had devoted attention to collecting canons and statutes from the earliest times of the Church seems evident from these very apostolic canons. And certainly that the Eastern Church possessed a collection of canons in the fifth century is demonstrated by the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, which was the fourth ecumenical council, celebrated in the year of our Lord 451. At that council the canons of the Councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople I were recited, arranged and ordered in one continuous numerical series, as appears from the acts themselves. In the fourth session, where Carosus and Dorotheus are discussed, the fourth and fifth canons of the Council of Antioch—“If any bishop deposed by a synod …”; “If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, etc.”—were read from a codex under numbers 83 and 84. Likewise, in the eleventh session, the sixteenth and seventeenth canons of that same Council of Antioch, listed under numbers 95 and 96, were reread by Leontius, bishop of Magnesia. [Note: See Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VI, cols. 437 and 692.]

### 47

From this you will easily understand that this collection of canons, received in the Eastern Church and arranged and ordered for its use, was the very collection which the Roman Church later embraced after Dionysius Exiguus rendered it into Latin at the beginning of the sixth century. For Dionysius’s own preface makes clear that he arranged the canons of all the councils up to the First Council of Constantinople in the same order in which they were found in the Greek original, and inserted them into his codex under one continuous series of 165 numbers. Here are his words:

> “We have arranged the canons of the Council of Nicaea and thereafter of all the councils, whether those held earlier or those held later, up to the Council of the 150 bishops who assembled at Constantinople, in numerical order—that is, from the first chapter through the 165th—just as they are found in the Greek original.”

### 48

Now, if you count twenty Nicene canons, twenty-five Ancyrean, fourteen Neocaesarean, twenty Gangran, and twenty-five Antiochene canons in one continuous numerical series, you will easily find that the fourth, fifth, sixteenth, and seventeenth Antiochene canons correspond exactly to the canons reread from the Greek codex at the Council of Chalcedon under numbers 83, 84, 95, and 96. Hence it is clear that Dionysius inserted into his collection, without any inversion of order, the Greek codex mentioned in the acts of the aforementioned Council of Chalcedon after rendering it into Latin.

### 49

Indeed, I readily persuade myself that this very collection of canons praised by the Council of Chalcedon was in use in the Roman Church in the time of Innocent I, notwithstanding the opinion of the most distinguished Peter de Marca, who maintains that until the time of this pope the Roman Church had received only the Nicene canons. He relies on a letter of that same Pope Innocent I addressed to the clergy of Constantinople. [Note: This letter is extant in Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 26.] In it these words are found:

> “As regards observance of the canons, we say that obedience is owed only to those which were defined at Nicaea. The Catholic Church ought to follow and acknowledge those canons alone. But if some bring forward others that disagree with the Nicene canons and are alleged to have been composed by heretics, they must be rejected by Catholic bishops. For what has been devised by heretics may not be added to Catholic rules. Indeed, they are perpetually striving to overturn the council of the Nicene Fathers. Therefore, we say not only that those canons must not be followed, but also that they must be utterly condemned together with heretical and schismatic doctrines, just as they were already condemned at the Council of Sardica by the bishops who preceded us.”

### 50

These very words, however, completely overturn the opinion of the highly esteemed Peter de Marca. Do they not clearly demonstrate that, besides the Nicene canons, the Council of Sardica—which Innocent praises—was also approved and received by the Roman Church? Indeed, who could bring himself to believe that the Council of Sardica, established by the agreement of approximately 300 bishops, and all the other most holy councils—at which, to use the words of blessed Agobard, bishop of Lyons, [Note: In the book *Against the Law of Gundobad*, p. 119 of vol. I of the works of Saint Agobard, in the edition of Baluze, Paris, 1666, octavo.] not merely two or three, but twenty, thirty, or more bishops had assembled to establish the discipline of the Church—bishops gathered not only in the name of the Lord but also endowed with faith, distinguished by wisdom, renowned for their life, revered for their holiness, and fearful through signs and miracles—could have been entirely unknown to or rejected by the Roman Church?

### 51

Moreover, in the words quoted above Innocent in no way asserts that the Catholic Church admits only the Nicene canons while rejecting the canons of the other holy councils. No one can attribute such a position to Innocent without doing him an injustice. Rather, he says that the Roman Church does not admit canons that dissent from or contradict the Nicene canons—that is, canons issued by Arian bishops seeking to overturn the council of the Nicene Fathers in their conventicles, or interpolated and corrupted by heretical men.

### 52

Finally, since the canons of the Council of Nicaea and of the other councils were listed in the codex under one continuous numerical series, as we observed above, might it not be said that Innocent intended to include under the name “Nicene” all the canons entered into the codex in a continuous series and thereby forming, as it were, a single body of text? Certainly, at first sight it will seem to everyone consistent with the truth that the very codex of canons praised at the Council of Chalcedon had already been embraced by the Roman Church from the fourth century onward.

### 53

Since this very collection of canons—the oldest of all those that have come down to us, if one excepts the so-called apostolic canons—was later translated into Latin by Dionysius Exiguus, disseminated throughout the West, and received by nearly all the Latin Churches, while the collections compiled by Theodore of Cyrus, John the Scholastic, and other authors, as well as the collection which Paschasius Quesnellus appended to the works of Saint Leo the Great, were passed over as collections of lesser importance, [Note: The most learned Dom Coustant, in his preface to the letters of the Roman pontiffs, pp. LXVII ff., completely overturns, by many very powerful arguments, the reasons by which Paschasius Quesnellus attempts to prove that this codex belonged to the Roman Church.] it will be necessary to say something about the Dionysian collection.

### 54

Dionysius, therefore, called Exiguus—some believe because of the smallness of his body, or, better, as common opinion holds, because of Christian humility [Note: No ancient writer has been found who asserts that Dionysius was called Exiguus because of the smallness of his body. Since ecclesiastical authors of that period, especially monks, customarily called themselves “the least” or “sinners” for the sake of Christian humility, common opinion holds that Dionysius called himself Exiguus out of modesty, a virtue with which he was endowed.]—was distinguished for the piety of his character and his learning. [Note: Cassiodorus, his contemporary, vividly describes the mind and character of Dionysius Exiguus in chapter 33 of *Divine Readings* in these words:

> “In our own time there was Dionysius, a monk, a Scythian by nation but wholly Roman in character, extremely learned in both languages. In his actions he rendered the justice he had read in the Lord’s books; he had examined and understood the Scriptures with such care that, whenever questioned on any subject, he was ready with a suitable answer without any delay. … In him great wisdom was joined with simplicity, learning with humility, and eloquence with restraint in speaking. … When Bishop Stephen of Salona requested him, from Greek exemplars he set forth the ecclesiastical canons with lucid clarity, being, as he was, plain and eloquent and endowed with great eloquence; today the Roman Church embraces them with the greatest acclaim. … He possessed such knowledge of Latin and Greek that, whenever he took up any Greek books, he could read through them in Latin without difficulty, and likewise read Latin books in Attic speech, so that one would think that what his mouth poured forth with unhindered speed had been written in that language.”)]

He was the first, according to Bede, to begin dating the Paschal cycles from the year of the Lord’s incarnation. [Note: In *On the Six Ages of the World*, under the year 4480.] At the beginning of the sixth century, at the request of Stephen, bishop of Salona, and also urged by a certain Laurence, as he himself testifies in his preface, [Note: Here are his words:

> “To my venerable lord and father in Christ, Stephen, bishop: Dionysius Exiguus sends greetings in the Lord. Although our dearest brother Laurence, by his continual and familiar exhortation, urged my littleness to translate the ecclesiastical rules from Greek—offended, I believe, by the confusion of the earlier translation—I nevertheless undertook the task out of regard for your blessedness.”

> See Labbe, *Councils*, vol. I.]

he prepared an outstanding collection of canons translated from Greek into Latin and divided it into two parts. In the first he inserted the first fifty apostolic canons; beneath these he placed the canons of the Councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople I, which, as stated above, he arranged in one continuous series of 165 numbers, just as they were found in the Greek codex. He then added the Chalcedonian, Sardican, and African canons, which close this first part of the codex.

### 55

In the second part he collected several decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo the Great, Gelasius, and Anastasius, and there Dionysius completed his work. For it is easily demonstrated that the decrees of Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, Hormisdas, and Gregory the Younger, which are found in more recent codices of Dionysius, were added by another compiler: Dionysius Exiguus flourished long before the time of Gregory the Younger.

### 56

These additions are believed to have been appended to the Dionysian codex by Pope Hadrian I; at least, it may be inferred that this was done at his command from the fact that the codex of canons presented by Pope Hadrian himself to Charlemagne at Rome toward the end of the eighth century contained the aforementioned decrees of Hilary, Simplicius, and the succeeding pontiffs down to Gregory the Younger. Moreover, among the many manuscript copies of the enlarged Dionysian codex preserved in the libraries of Gaul, the most learned Sirmond possessed one of great antiquity, copied in the year of Christ 805 and kept in Paris at the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It contained the preface or dedication of Pope Hadrian addressed to Charlemagne. [Note: This preface or dedication of Pope Hadrian is printed in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. VI, col. 1820, and in Hardouin, vol. III, col. 2033.]

### 57

This collection of canons may accordingly be called Hadrianic-Dionysian, [Note: It should be noted here that in some manuscript copies of this codex certain chapters are found that circulate under the name of Pope Hadrian, addressed to Angilramnus. These chapters, however, appear to have been excerpted by Angilramnus himself from fictitious pontifical letters in order to support his own case. It is plausible that Angilramnus, bishop of Metz, having perhaps been accused of some offense, employed this device in order to evade diocesan jurisdiction by appealing to the Apostolic See. A very ancient manuscript codex preserved in the library of Saint-Victor in Paris strongly supports this opinion. It bears the following title: “Here begin chapters collected from various councils and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, taken from Angilramnus, bishop of Metz, and Pope Hadrian.” See also the works of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, vol. II, p. 475, in Sirmond’s edition.] because it contained the pure Dionysian codex together with the additions of Pope Hadrian I. Although it includes the so-called Apostolic canons, rejected by Pope Gelasius at the Roman Council held in the year 494 and called into question by Dionysius Exiguus himself, [Note: “At the beginning, therefore, we translated from Greek the canons called apostolic; but because very many have not readily assented to them, we did not wish your holiness to be unaware of this.” Preface of Exiguus, in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. I.] it nevertheless enjoyed such renown in the West that, with almost universal approval, all the Latin Churches gradually received it.

### 58

There can scarcely be any doubt that the Gallican Church used this very codex of canons. For Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, referred to it as a pure codex containing the rules of ancient discipline in his disputes with Nicholas I concerning the judgment and execution of episcopal cases in a provincial council, notwithstanding appeals to the Apostolic See—appeals that had by then been introduced into ecclesiastical discipline through the fictitious decretals of Isidore Mercator. Cresconius, a bishop, compiled from this same codex a summary for the use of the African Church toward the end of the eighth century. [Note: Ferrandus, a Carthaginian deacon, had earlier prepared another abridgment of the canons for the use of that same African Church. But that abridgment was certainly not compiled from the Dionysian codex, as is evident from the fact that, besides using a Latin version older than the Dionysian one, it cites several African councils absent from the Dionysian codex.]

Finally, that the Church of Great Britain received this codex is clearly demonstrated by a letter of Leo IV addressed to the bishops of that Church:

> “The canons which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments are those of the Apostles, of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon, Sardica, Carthage, and Africa, together with the rules of the Roman pontiffs Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, and Simplicius. These are entirely the authorities by which bishops judge and by which bishops, together with clerics, are judged.”

[Note: This letter is extant in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VIII, col. 30, and in Hardouin, vol. V, col. 1.]

These words accurately describe the enlarged Dionysian codex, or the Hadrianic-Dionysian codex.

### 59

Some have believed that the use of this same codex prevailed in Spain, on the basis of these words found in the celebrated Third Council of Toledo:

> “Let the constitutions of all the councils remain in force, together also with the synodal letters of the holy Roman pontiffs,”

but this is mistaken, as we shall show in the following paragraph. Enough, however, has now been said about the ancient collections of canons. The present occasion requires us to say something about the composition of the genuine Isidorian collection.

### 60

Isidore, therefore, bishop of Seville, distinguished equally for learning and holiness of character, a man, to use the words of Ildephonsus of Toledo, endowed with both grace and intellect—for he achieved such an abundant and delightful richness in speaking that the astonishing fertility of his discourse turned his hearers to amazement, so that anyone who had heard him once would commend him only by hearing him repeatedly—following the example of Dionysius Exiguus but by a far superior method, arranged an extensive and wholly complete collection of canons, perfected in every respect and adapted to the use of the Spanish Church. He divided it into two parts, one embracing all the councils and the other the decretal letters. He subdivided the first part into four sections and ordered it with excellent judgment.

First, he placed before the work a very beautiful preface, later disfigured by the false Isidore. In it, as we observed above (no. 45), he rejects the so-called Apostolic canons as apocryphal. Then he placed the councils of Greece, beginning with the Council of Nicaea because of the authority of that great council, as he himself testifies in the preface in these words:

> “At the beginning of this volume we have placed the Council of Nicaea because of the authority of that same great council.”

He did not place these Greek councils in one continuous numerical series, as Dionysius had done, but distinguished each by its own chapters. Immediately afterward follow the Latin councils of Africa. In third place he arranged the Gallican councils, and finally placed beneath them the Spanish councils, which complete this first part of the collection.

By this arrangement, it was easy for anyone to add to the collection new councils celebrated after the time of Isidore of Seville, whether Greek or Latin, without reversing or disrupting its order, and to place each in its proper place and sequence.

### 61

Before we come to the later and final part of this collection, two matters must be observed here. First, at the beginning of the work, before the preface itself, there is placed an excellent index arranged according to the order of subjects, entitled *Excerpts from the Canons*. As we have already noted (note 19), Cajetan Cenni copied this index from Aguirre and published it at Rome; taking it for the codex itself, he gave it the imposing title *Codex of the Ancient Canons of the Spanish Church*. This is hardly surprising. For whether one considers its suitable and well-ordered division of books or its summary of titles formed from the canons of the councils and the rules of the decretal letters, one will immediately pronounce it a perfect and complete codex of canons. The most learned Dom Coustant judged it entirely such, although he correctly understood that it derived from our collection. Speaking of it in his preface to the letters of the Roman pontiffs, no. 150, he says:

> “Indeed, the Spaniards deserve this praise: in composing works of this kind they preceded Regino, Anselm, Burchard, Ivo, Gratian, and the other compilers of canons.”

### 62

Second, it should be noted that the Latin version of the Greek canons found in our collection is entirely different from the Dionysian version, and most scholars have believed it to be older than Dionysius Exiguus himself. At what time and by what author it was made remains unknown and insufficiently investigated. Nevertheless, I do not hesitate to adopt the view that blessed Isidore, who was by no means unskilled in Greek letters and was not inclined readily to swear by the words of others, prepared this translation by comparing Greek exemplars with the ancient Latin version, and perhaps with the Dionysian version itself. A substantial indication and argument for this is the Latin version of the sacred books, which Doctor Isidore himself revised, after the example of Saint Jerome, from Greek and Hebrew codices and from Jerome’s Vulgate version. If learned men carefully consider this method, they will undoubtedly conclude that the ancient Latin version of the Greek canons was either made by Isidore or at least corrected and restored by him.

[Note: Since the subject is the Latin version of the Greek canons, it is worthwhile to present here a brief dissertation on this topic by the most learned Matthaeus Aimerichus, copied from p. 102 of his *Specimen of Lost or Still Hidden Ancient Roman Literature*. I believe it will be especially welcome to readers because the work is not readily available.]

#### A Brief Dissertation on the General Councils Celebrated in the East

> “It is beyond doubt that several ecclesiastical councils held before and after Constantine the Great during the first four centuries of the Church are missing. It is likewise clear that not a few of those that survive are incomplete and mutilated, partly through the violence of time and the hatred of pagans toward Christian writings, partly through the negligence of scribes, and partly also through the wickedness of the heretics condemned by them.
>
> “Whether, however, the councils—especially the general synods celebrated in the East from the reign of Constantine the Great to Honorius—were conducted in Latin or in Greek seems to be a question that has been insufficiently discussed and even less thoroughly investigated. The common opinion holds that these Eastern councils were conducted in Greek and that everything in them was handled in Greek. This is because the largest part of the assembled Fathers were bishops of the Eastern Churches, where divine matters were conducted in Greek; because scarcely any ancient exemplars of these councils survive except Greek ones; and because the Latin versions derived from Greek exemplars are very recent and were produced by men learned in Greek and Latin.
>
> “I have not read that this opinion has been called into question, but the following considerations seem to me capable of being opposed to it.
>
> “1. Because, as a result of the many Roman colonies established in the East, the countless Romans dispersed throughout the eastern provinces in public offices, and especially the political decrees and administration of the Roman emperors, the Latin language had become the common, almost vernacular, language of the entire Roman Empire among persons of civilized education—especially after the right of Roman citizenship had been granted to all peoples subject to Roman rule.
>
> “2. Because the presidents of the general councils, or the legates sent by the Roman pontiff to preside over them, were for the most part Roman clerics, or clerics of the Western Church, which is called Latin. Latin, not Greek, was familiar to them, and they needed to understand clearly what was being done in the councils so that they could report it accurately to the absent Roman pontiff.
>
> “3. Because the general councils were attended either by the emperors themselves—as we know was the case with Constantine the Great at Nicaea and with other emperors at other councils—or at least by provincial governors together with civic magistrates, so that everything might proceed peacefully and nothing contrary to the laws of the empire might be decreed. This was also observed in the national councils of Spain in the time of the Goths. Kings attended the councils of Toledo; leading men, the nobles of the kingdom, accompanied the king and were present at the sessions of the Fathers. It was fitting, and consonant with the dignity both of the Roman Empire and of the Roman Church, that matters should be handled in the Latin or Roman language by learned men not unfamiliar with Roman speech.
>
> “4. Because Roman law forbade public business, especially judicial business, to be conducted in any language other than Latin. In the councils, however, both public and judicial business was conducted: the Fathers passed judgment on heretics and their errors and decreed many matters relating to religion, discipline, and the sacred public institutions of the empire.
>
> “5. Because Constantine the Great, in the Council of Nicaea, as Eusebius testifies in his *Life*, delivered a speech in Latin to the sacred assembly, that is, to the assembly of bishops gathered at Nicaea. This indicates that Latin speech was both understood and used there by the Fathers.
>
> “6. Because the acts of the councils had to be sent by the legates to the Roman pontiff at Rome, so that they might be examined by the council of the Western Fathers and by the Roman clergy and approved and confirmed by the subscription of the Roman pontiff. This was necessary for the council to be regarded as legitimate and for its decrees to be promulgated throughout the Churches of the world. For this purpose it was necessary that a Latin copy of the acts and definitions of the council be sent to Rome, so that, on the basis of this copy—perhaps after certain corrections had been made at Rome—the authentic Greek copy could later be issued. Nor was there little controversy at the Council of Nicaea over which Greek word corresponded to the Latin word *consubstantialis* and did not conflict with the Latin understanding and canonical definition. Finally, it is established that at the Council of Chalcedon, celebrated in the fifth century and attended by the Emperor Marcian, the letter of Leo was read in Latin and that Marcian first addressed the Fathers in Latin.
>
> “Nor are these considerations sufficiently overthrown by the arguments advanced above in favor of the common opinion. It is true that the greater part of the bishops who flocked to the general councils celebrated in the East were Greeks or Asiatics. But these men were educated, and at that time the Roman language was common among them, just as Greek had formerly been. For this reason Greeks and Asiatics were more than once appointed bishops of the Churches of the West, including the Roman Church, as is evident from the succession of the Roman pontiffs and of the bishops of other Western Churches. This would not have happened if they had not been educated in the Roman language and formed according to Roman customs.
>
> “It is likewise true that most of the copies of the councils that we possess in Latin were later revised and translated from Greek exemplars. But this by no means proves that Latin copies of those councils, and indeed original ones, did not once exist. It proves only that they, like many other ancient Latin monuments, were corrupted and lost through the incursions of barbarians into the provinces of the West and through the destruction of libraries and archives by fires occasioned by war. No one will deny that Latin copies of the Eastern councils were once kept in the archives of the Roman Church, even if those councils had been celebrated in Greek, Arabic, or Egyptian.
>
> “But enough on this subject. I submit these matters to the judgment of learned men, without despairing that at least some scholars, after weighing the arguments presented, may regard as probable what at first sight seems scarcely plausible because of the contrary opinion accepted through prejudice and without careful examination. ‘Truth,’ says Lucius Annaeus Seneca, ‘has not yet been fully possessed, and much of it has been left for posterity, since it belongs to all ages and all intellects.’ We must dare to call into examination matters accepted without much investigation, lest we be said to follow the opinions of others like sheep or swear by the statements of others, when the matter at issue would inflict no injury upon morals and no harm upon the rules of the Catholic faith.”

### 63

Some manuscript copies of the sacred Scriptures in the Latin version of Blessed Isidore are still preserved today, written in Gothic letters, in various libraries of Spain, especially the libraries of Toledo and the royal library at Madrid. The same fate befell this Latin version of the sacred Bible, apart from the prefaces published among the works of the aforementioned Isidore, as befell our collection of canons: it still lies unknown, deprived of the benefit of the printing press. May God grant that at last, together with the most ancient Mozarabic liturgy, arranged through the diligence of Isidore of Seville, it may emerge into the light from the archives of the Church of Toledo, with the assistance of learned Spaniards who cherish the honor of so great a doctor and the glory of the Spanish Church—which perhaps surpasses all others both in the antiquity of its sacred rites and in preserving the rules of a purer discipline.

[Note: This ancient liturgy of the Spanish Church, called Mozarabic, Muzarabic, Toledan, and Isidorian, and said to have descended from the Apostles through Saint Torquatus and his companions, the Roman Curia, perhaps envious of its antiquity, strove with all its might to extinguish in the eleventh century. As that century declined, after various and repeatedly renewed disputes, the Roman liturgical order was first introduced into the kingdom of Aragon and was later gradually spread throughout Spain. It unjustly antiquated the very ancient Mozarabic liturgy and would have erased it forever had not the most celebrated and immortal Cardinal Ximénez de Cisneros, having founded fourteen chaplaincies at Toledo—where six Mozarabic parishes still exist—restored it to some measure of its ancient splendor, out of religious zeal for ecclesiastical antiquity, by sending its missals and breviaries to the press. Pisa, Robles, Villegas, Aguirre, Pinius, Flores in vol. VI of the *Acta Sanctorum* for July, *España Sagrada*, vol. III, and others have written about this celebrated liturgy.]

### 64

With these matters noted, let us come to the second and later part of our collection. It contains 103 decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs Damasus, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Vigilius, and Gregory the Great, as we noted in the second paragraph of the description of the principal codices. A brief preface is placed before them, which in many words agrees with the preface of Dionysius Exiguus to the letters of the Roman pontiffs.

### 65

You therefore have, learned Reader, a brief account of the most illustrious collection of canons, prepared after the example of Dionysius Exiguus but by a far superior method and drawn from pure sources. That this collection was prepared by the holy Isidore, bishop of Seville, as we shall now demonstrate more fully, seems to be suggested by the facts themselves. Nevertheless, in order to proceed by a better path, we must first give a brief preliminary account of the codex of canons received in Spain before the time of Isidore, bishop of Seville.

## § IV. In which something is discussed concerning the ancient codex of the canons of the Spanish Church before the time of Isidore, bishop of Seville

### 66

That the Spaniards possessed their own codex of canons long before the time of Isidore, bishop of Seville, is known from the acts of the councils of Spain themselves. What that codex was, however, what canons it contained, and how they were arranged; by what author or authority it was collected—all this remains uncertain and insufficiently investigated.

Some believe that it was the collection called the Chapters of Martin of Braga, but this is not correct. That very brief collection was only a part, and indeed a small part, of the codex of the Spanish Church, as we shall show below. Others think that the codex of Dionysius Exiguus belonged not only to the use of the Gallican Church but also to that of the Spanish Church. In my judgment, however, it can easily be discovered from the acts of the councils of Spain themselves that neither collection was peculiar to the Spanish Church. To examine this matter clearly and establish our opinion more precisely, we must first see what the councils mentioned above teach us about it.

### 67

From the Second Council of Toledo, celebrated in the 565th year of the Spanish Era—that is, in the year of Christ 531—it is clear that not only the statutes of provincial synods but also the ancient decrees of the canons and the institutions of the Fathers were then in force in Spain. The words of that council are these:

> “When, by the will of the Lord, the presence of the holy bishops had assembled in the city of Toledo and mention had been made of the institutions of the Fathers and the decrees of the canons, it seemed good to us, gathered together as we were, that if anything had not been mentioned in the ancient canons, it should be established through salutary deliberation and careful consideration. But if anything had been decreed in earlier councils and had hitherto been neglected through the abuse of time, let it receive the correction of a renewed ordinance.”

[Note: Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 82.]

### 68

The same conclusion follows from the First Council of Braga, held thirty years after the aforementioned Second Council of Toledo. After the seventeen chapters established against the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, these words are read:

> “Bishop Lucretius said: Since those things which Catholics ought to abhor and condemn have been declared more clearly and openly even to those who are ignorant of them, I consider it necessary after this—if it seems good to your fraternity—that the institutions of the holy Fathers be made known to us by reviewing the ancient canons. Even if they are not all reread, at least some of them, especially those relating to the instruction of clerical discipline, should be reread.”
>
> “All the bishops said: What has been said is pleasing. … The canons both of general and of local synods were reread from the codex before the council.”

[Note: Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 119. This council is called the Second Council of Braga in Labbe’s collection. The council copied from Bernardo de Brito and published in vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 1507, was entitled the First Council of Braga; but this is incorrect. The council mentioned there is not genuine and is not found inserted in our manuscript codices.]

### 69

Then, in chapters XII, XIII, XIV, and XV prescribed by this same synod, the ancient decrees of the canons and the statutes of the holy Fathers are again cited in these words:

> “As the holy canons also prescribe.”
>
> “As the ancient statutes also contain,”

and so forth.

70. Moreover, that the general councils and the ancient canonical statutes mentioned in the aforesaid synod as having been read from the codex are precisely those contained in the ancient canonical codex of the Greek Church is confirmed by the Second Council of Braga, celebrated in the year of Christ 572. There Martin, the bishop, lists the general synods held at Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon [Col. 0878B]; he also recalls particular synods and the decisions of the canons written by the Spirit of God, which, he says, we ought to read, understand, and keep [Note: [Col. 0878D] Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 166.].

71. It is apparent that the ancient canonical codex of the Spanish Church contained not only the canons of general and local synods but also the decretal letters of the Roman prelates, from the fact that at the aforesaid First Council of Braga, after the chapters issued against the Priscillianists, the letter of Pope Vigilius to Profuturus was read:

“The authority of the apostolic see, formerly addressed to Profuturus the bishop, was reread; because of its length it has not been inserted in these proceedings” [Note: [Col. 0878D] Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 120.].

72. The same point is confirmed, indeed manifestly demonstrated, by the first canon of the celebrated Third Council of Toledo [Col. 0878C], which Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, attended. At that council, after the Arian heresy had been renounced, the entire nation of the Goths and Sueves, in the presence and with the testimony of the most glorious King Flavius Reccared, publicly embraced the true Catholic faith, which it had abandoned for 213 years. In the canon, or first chapter, of that council it is therefore decreed:

“Let the constitutions of all the councils remain in force, together with the synodical letters of the holy Roman prelates” [Note: [Col. 0878D] Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 217.].

73. Furthermore, it is clear that the canonical codex of the Spanish Church already contained, from the beginning of the sixth century, the councils of Gaul as well, from the Council of Tarragona, celebrated in the Spanish Era 554, corresponding to the year of Christ 516. There, canon 11, treating of monastic discipline, orders the statutes of the Gallican canons to be observed, in these words:

“Above all, the constitution of the Gallican canons concerning them having been observed” [Note: [Col. 0878D] Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 70.].

74. Finally, the Council of Lleida, held in the Spanish Era 584, orders that the following be observed concerning monks, namely, what had been established in the Council of Agde and the Council of Orléans. Here are its words, title III:

“Concerning monks, it was decided that what the Council of Agde or of Orléans is known to have decreed should be observed” [Note: [Col. 0879D] Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 96.].

75. Having established these points, let us turn to what can be determined concerning the ancient canonical codex of the Spanish Church.

First, from the aforesaid acts of the councils of Spain it will be immediately clear to anyone that the Spanish Church, even before Isidore’s time, possessed its own canonical codex. It contained not only the councils of Greece but also those of Gaul and Spain, as well as the decrees of the Roman prelates.

Indeed, the councils of Greece are rightly cited in most of the synods of Spain, especially in the Second Council of Braga, as stated above. That the councils of Gaul had been in use among the Spaniards from the beginning of the sixth century is clearly attested by the councils held at Tarragona and Lleida in the year of Christ 516 and 533. As for the letters of the Roman pontiffs, the aforesaid Third Council of Toledo plainly declares that the Spanish Church had received them.

76. It follows, secondly, that the chapters of Martin of Braga are not the most ancient canonical codex of the Spanish Church, as some have incorrectly believed. For, apart from the fact that these chapters contain no excerpt from the councils of Gaul or from the decrees of the Roman prelates, it is well established that Martin of Braga flourished nearly half a century after the Council of Tarragona. Indeed, the aforesaid chapters, which Martin himself had compiled chiefly from Greek synods during his journey through the East [Note: [Col. 0879D]

“Martin,” says Isidore in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 35, “the most holy bishop of the monastery of Dumium, sailing from the regions of the East, came to Galicia. There, after the Suevic peoples had been converted from Arian impiety to the Catholic faith, he established the rule of faith and holy religion, strengthened the churches, founded monasteries, and composed abundant instructions for pious formation. I myself read his book *On the Differences among the Four Virtues*, and another volume of letters, in which he urges the correction of life, conduct in the faith, perseverance in prayer, [Col. 0880D] and the distribution of alms, and above all the cultivation of every virtue and piety. He flourished under Theodemir, king of the Sueves, at the time when Justinian held the imperial power in the Roman state and Athanagild in Spain.”

Gregory of Tours’s *History* informs us that this Martin was a Pannonian by nationality. He presided over the monastery of Dumium, which he himself had founded, until approximately the year 563, when he became archbishop of Braga; he died around the year of Christ 585.]

were first read at the Second Council of Braga, held in the year 572, over which the aforesaid Martin presided, and were probably approved and received there. For it is chiefly from this circumstance that we infer that they were attached to the canonical codex from that time onward: in all the manuscript copies of our collection that have so far been found, they are consistently placed at the end of that same Second Council of Braga, as in their proper place and order; and in one or another codex they appear under the name of the Third Council of Braga.

Accordingly, it is plainly evident that these chapters of Martin, placed at the end of the Second Council of Braga, constituted only a part—and a very small part—of the canonical codex of the Spanish Church. Since they contain nothing, or almost nothing, excerpted from the councils of Gaul and Spain or from the decrees of the Roman prelates, while nearly all their chapters are taken from Greek and African synods, it must be concluded altogether that some have incorrectly called the chapters in question the canonical codex of the Spanish Church.

[Col. 0880A] 77. I do not hesitate to assert precisely the same concerning the canonical codex of Dionysius Exiguus. For from what has been said it will be clear to anyone that this codex was by no means in use among the Spaniards. The statutes of the councils of Gaul and Spain are lacking in it, although we have observed above that they were contained in the canonical codex of the Spanish Church.

78. Moreover, if the Spanish Church had embraced the aforesaid canonical collection of Dionysius, very many manuscript copies of it would undoubtedly have been preserved in the various libraries and ecclesiastical archives of Spain. Yet none can be seen there, although innumerable copies of the same collection—offered by Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne—are found in the libraries and archives of the monasteries of Gaul [Col. 0880B]. This is certainly not surprising: the codex enjoyed such authority among the Gauls that it was called simply, by its common and familiar name, “the Canonical Codex,” as the most learned Coustant correctly observed in the frequently cited preface to his *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 131.

79. And indeed, if the Spaniards used the canonical codex of Dionysius Exiguus, how did it happen that they wasted so much oil and labor in copying the numerous surviving manuscript copies of our very extensive Isidorian collection, written at various times, and in adorning them with so many embellishments, depicted in gold and colors through varied labor? To what end was this effort uselessly expended, when otherwise it would have been both much more useful and much easier for them to copy the very brief collection of Dionysius [Col. 0880C], adapted for the use of the Spanish Church? Yet if one were to travel throughout Spain, as far as it extends, one would find no manuscript copy of it written in Spain or by a Spanish hand.

80. Having observed and carefully weighed these matters, I hope that no one will deny that the chapters of Martin of Braga, and likewise the codex of Dionysius Exiguus, have incorrectly been accepted by some as the canonical codex of the Spanish Church.

Indeed, I do not hesitate to assert that the ancient canonical codex received in Spain before Isidore’s time—containing the councils of Greece, Gaul, and Spain, together with the decrees of the Roman prelates—was in reality none other than this, and did not differ in substance from our outstanding Isidorian collection [Col. 0880D]. For nowhere is there any codex, nor any canonical collection, that embraces all the materials so frequently mentioned in the councils of Spain; none, I say, that agrees entirely with their wording, except our own.

This collection, which at that time was confusedly arranged and put together without any method or order, was carefully revised and suitably reorganized before the middle of the seventh century by Isidore, bishop of Seville—perhaps following the example of Dionysius Exiguus, but by a far superior method. He prefixed to it a most beautiful preface and a new, excellently arranged table of contents, entitled *Excerpts of the Canons*. What has just been asserted is clearly demonstrated by substantial arguments in the following paragraph.

§ V. It is asserted that Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, compiled this canonical collection for the use of the Spanish Church.

81. I now undertake to establish by definite arguments that Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, took the ancient canonical codex of the Spanish Church—composed from the councils of Greece, Africa, Gaul, and Spain, as well as from the letters of the Roman prelates, but collected confusedly and without any principle of order, with all its contents mixed together—and arranged it during the middle of the seventh century in the form in which it now exists, organizing it according to a most excellent method.

82. For the clarification of this matter, it must first be stated that after the death of our Isidore, this outstanding canonical collection, arranged and composed by him with marvelous order, was often enlarged by the bishops of Spain, or by their command and authority, through councils celebrated at later times, especially Spanish councils, as commonly happens with such compilations.

The manuscript codices themselves of our aforesaid collection provide evidence of this [Col. 0881C]. Some of them still exist and contain nothing later than Blessed Isidore’s time; composed just as they had been by the author himself, they contain no council later than the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which our Isidore presided. Others, according to the period in which they were copied, contain more councils or acts. In some, thirteen, fifteen, or seventeen councils of Toledo are found inserted. Indeed, in the codex of the monastery of Cella Nova in Galicia, a fragment of whose index was published by Henry Flórez in volume VI of *Sacred Spain*, the Eighteenth Council of Toledo was contained.

83. Yet these acts of the councils, otherwise authentic, inserted into the canonical collection after the death of Saint Isidore do not at all prevent Isidore himself from being regarded as the author of the aforesaid collection [Col. 0881D]. For the method and excellent system of arrangement of that collection were so skillfully ordered that the councils of Spain, or any others that might subsequently be celebrated, could be added to the codex without reversing either its method or its order.

84. Just as the canonical collection of Dionysius Exiguus, although enlarged by Pope Hadrian or by his command and authority, is rightly attributed to Dionysius, and we call it the Dionysian codex—or, to use a more recent example [Col. 0882A], just as the historical dictionary consisting of ten large-format volumes circulates under the name of Louis Moréri, although it has been expanded tenfold and scarcely any genuine work of the author can be identified in it [Note: [Col. 0881D] The first edition of this work appeared at Lyon in 1674 in a single folio volume; the latest appeared at Paris in 1759 in ten folio volumes.]—so our outstanding collection, although enlarged by several councils of Toledo and certain others after the author’s death, is rightly to be attributed to Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, and called the Isidorian canonical collection, especially since these additions in no way overturn the substance or the system of order of the codex.

85. Moreover, that these additions were attached to the canonical collection by legitimate authority is demonstrated, among other things, by what was decreed by the Spanish prelates at the Ninth Council of Toledo, celebrated in the Spanish Era 693 [Col. 0882B], in these words:

“By common definition we have decreed that the chapters which are not at all found inserted in the ancient canons should be promulgated with equal authority and joined to the ancient rules, so that they may remain forever united with them and be preserved with every reverence” [Note: [Col. 0881D] Loaysa, *Councils of Spain*, p. 478.].

86.
