Likewise, Saint Julian, archbishop of Toledo, and the other prelates assembled at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, invited by Pope Leo II through a letter to receive the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, whose acts he had sent to them, and to promulgate it throughout the provinces of Spain with synodal authority, judged that nothing more honorable could be done in observance of that ecumenical synod than to decree by an established canon that it should be placed in the body of the canons after the Council of Chalcedon, in its proper place and with due honor:

“After the Council of Chalcedon,” says canon 7, “these matters are therefore to be placed with due honor, place, and order, so that to the one whose glorious theme they display they may be joined with the honor appropriate to their place and order.”

87. Led into error by these additions, the distinguished Coustant called the index of our outstanding collection—which, as has often been said, is entitled *Excerpts of the Canons*, although he recognized that it had been compiled from the collection itself—the ancient canonical codex of the Spanish Church, and declared that it had been composed after the year 693.

For when he had correctly understood from the description of the manuscript canonical codex sent to him by the illustrious Joseph de Taverner de Ardene, vicar general of the Church of Gerona and later its most worthy bishop [Col. 0882D], that the aforesaid codex contained nothing later than the Fourth Council of Toledo, whereas the index that Cardinal Aguirre had arranged to be printed in volume III of *Councils of Spain* cited the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, he inferred—incorrectly—that the index in question was entirely different from, and later than, our collection [Note: [Col. 0881D] Coustant, preface to the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, nos. 149–150.

It is not surprising, however, that the most learned Coustant judged in this way, since the eminent Cardinal Aguirre, who had repeatedly handled very many manuscript codices, and who himself copied the index from an old manuscript of Toledo, called it *The Book of the Canons of the Holy Fathers*. Indeed, he incorrectly conjectured that it might perhaps be the compendium of canons composed by the deacon Ferrandus [Col. 0883D]. Here are his words in the preface to volume III of *Councils of Spain*:

“Volume three begins with a most useful index of councils and canons, never previously, as far as we know, made public, which the Spanish Church used until approximately the year 700. Perhaps it is the very one that had been prepared much earlier by the deacon Ferrandus, at the beginning of the sixth century, under the title *Compendium of the Sacred Canons*. If I may say so, it is the same as that one; nevertheless, this is far more extensive, since it cites many councils and decrees of much later date. … Whoever may finally have first written it, it is exceedingly useful. See more below.”]

[Col. 0883A] 88. The most learned man would certainly have judged quite differently if he had been permitted to inspect the very many manuscript codices of the aforesaid collection that exist in Spain. He would have found that each codex has its own index prefixed to it, in which the canons and decisions are listed only from those documents contained in that codex.

For these indices were enlarged in the same way and according to the same principle as the codices themselves, so that in the index prefixed to a codex containing nothing beyond the Fourth Council of Toledo, one would search in vain for any citation later than that council. It is therefore not surprising that the index of canons published by the eminent Cardinal Aguirre at the beginning of volume III of *Councils of Spain* cites the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, since the old manuscript of the Church of Toledo from which the aforesaid Aguirre copied it contains seventeen councils of Toledo.

89. These are the points I wished to establish in advance against the objections of those who think that this canonical collection cannot at all be attributed to Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, because it mentions several councils celebrated after Isidore’s time. We must now discuss the matters that demonstrate that the aforesaid canonical collection was prepared by Blessed Isidore of Seville.

90. The first, and by no means insignificant, argument for this assertion is that in book VI, chapter 16, of the *Etymologies* of the same Blessed Isidore, the first and principal part of the genuine preface to our outstanding canonical collection is found copied almost word for word, as follows:

“Now the canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. In the preceding years, while persecution was raging, permission was scarcely given to instruct the peoples. Consequently Christianity was divided into various heresies, because the bishops were not permitted to assemble in one place except in the time of the emperor just mentioned. For he gave Christians permission to gather freely.

Under him also the holy Fathers from the whole world assembled at the Council of Nicaea and, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic faith, handed down the Creed following the apostles. Among the other councils, we know of four venerable synods that principally embrace the whole faith, like the four Gospels or the four rivers of Paradise.

The first of these, the Council of Nicaea, was held under the emperor Constantine Augustus by 318 bishops. In it the blasphemy of Arian faithlessness, which Arius had asserted concerning the inequality of the Holy Trinity, was condemned; and that God the Son is consubstantial with God the Father was defined by that holy synod in the Creed.

The second synod, of 150 Fathers, was assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius [Col. 0884A]. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and supplied the form of the Creed that the confession of all Greeks and Latins proclaims in the churches.

The third, the First Council of Ephesus, consisting of 200 bishops, was held under the younger Emperor Theodosius. It condemned Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, with a just anathema, showing that one person of the Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

The fourth, the Council of Chalcedon, consisting of 630 priests, was held under the emperor Marcian. There it condemned, by the single judgment of the Fathers, Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared one nature of the Word of God and the flesh; Dioscorus, an Alexandrian bishop and his defender; and Nestorius himself again, together with the other heretics [Col. 0884B]. The same synod proclaimed that Christ the Lord was born from the Virgin in such a way that we confess in him the substance of both the divine and the human nature.

These four are the principal synods, proclaiming the doctrine of the faith in its fullest form. But if there are any councils that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have enacted, they remain established with full force after the authority of these four. Their proceedings are contained in this body.”

91. Against this argument it may be objected that the final words, “whose proceedings are contained in this body,” which fit poorly in the books of the *Etymologies*—for no councils are found in those books—seem rather to indicate that this passage of the *Etymologies* [Col. 0884C] was copied from the preface of the canonical collection. Consequently, the aforesaid preface may have been composed by another author and published before Isidore wrote his books of the *Etymologies*. As is well known, Isidore often gathered into his work many excerpts from various books without naming their authors.

92. But these objections are of little weight. For the most learned Grial correctly observed in his remarks on Isidore’s works that Braulion, who edited the work left incomplete at its author’s death and divided it into twenty books, drew this chapter of the *Etymologies*, almost in its entirety, from the aforesaid preface prefixed to the canonical collection, as from a genuine product of Isidore.

We have already noted above that, perhaps in the same way, the prefaces to the books of the Old and New Testaments were copied from an old manuscript codex of the sacred biblical books in the Isidorian version and published among the works of Isidore [Col. 0884D].

93. Furthermore, since both the aforesaid preface to the canonical collection and the collection itself were compiled during the time of Isidore of Seville, as will be made clear below, it would indeed be absurd to attribute it to anyone other than Isidore himself. For no writer of that period in Spain was more distinguished or more learned than Isidore, to whom the work in question could be attributed [Col. 0885A].

94. Another extremely weighty argument that vindicates the canonical collection for Isidore of Seville, the distinguished doctor of the Spanish Church, is drawn from the fact that, although the Second Council of Constantinople—the Fifth Ecumenical Council—was celebrated before Isidore’s time, it is not mentioned in the preface and is not found inserted into the aforesaid canonical collection. The matter would certainly have been otherwise if the author of this collection had not been Isidore.

The reason is that our doctor, as can easily be discerned from his writings, did not hold a favorable view of the aforesaid Second Council of Constantinople. Indeed, he frequently attacks it sharply because it anathematized the Three Chapters against the authority, as he himself says, of the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0885B] [Note: [Col. 0885D] It would take too long to recount the history of the Three Chapters, from which arose the controversy that disturbed the peace of the Church for more than a century. The substance of the matter is this: In the year of Christ 449, Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, and Ibas, bishop of Edessa, were condemned at the assembly of Ephesus, from whose entrance they had been excluded, at the instigation and under the presidency of Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, a heretic and Eutychianist, and were expelled from their churches because Theodore had written against Cyril’s twelve anathemas. Ibas, moreover, had sent a letter of insufficiently Catholic character to Maris the Persian.

When this assembly of Ephesus had been overturned by the Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, held in 451, Theodore and Ibas, the bishops, were honorably restored to their churches [Col. 0886D]. In the period that followed, however, at the Second Council of Constantinople, the Fifth Ecumenical Council, held in 553, the Three Chapters were condemned: namely, the writings of Theodoret against Cyril, the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Maris the Persian, and the works of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia.

From this arose many serious disputes, because condemnation of these chapters seemed to undermine the authority of the Council of Chalcedon. It should also be noted that Pope Vigilius, with great steadfastness, repeatedly refused to approve the Second Council of Constantinople in opposition to the pressure and insistence of the emperor Justinian; moreover, very few Latin bishops attended the aforesaid council, contrary to what had been agreed.]

95. To clarify the matter, it is useful to hear Isidore himself on the subject:

“Emperor Justinian,” he says in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 31, “published certain books on the Incarnation of the Lord, which he also sent through the various provinces. He likewise composed a rescript against the Illyrian synod and against the African bishops, defenders of the Council of Chalcedon, through perverse zeal. In it he attempted to condemn the Three Chapters: namely, the statements of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; the writings of Theodoret; and the letter called that of Ibas, bishop of Edessa.”

96. Again, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 5762 from the creation of the world, he says:

“Justinian reigned for thirty-nine years. [Col. 0885C] Embracing the heresy of the Acephali, he compelled all the bishops in his kingdom to condemn the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon.”

97. The same Isidore explains what the heresy of the Acephali was in *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5, in these words:

“They are called Acephali, that is, ‘without a head,’ for none of them is found to have an author from whom they arose. These opponents of the Three Chapters of Chalcedon deny the particularity of the two substances in Christ and proclaim one nature in his person.”

98. The judgment of the distinguished doctor concerning the Three Chapters is also more plainly discerned in the aforesaid *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 4, where, speaking of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, he says:

“The bishops of the Acephali judged that he should be condemned after his death, together with the bishops Ibas and Theodoret, in prejudice to the Council of Chalcedon, under the compulsion of the emperor Justinian. [Col. 0886A] Yet it is established by the testimonies of distinguished men that he was a doctor of the most illustrious Church.”

99. Likewise, speaking of Bishop Facundus in chapter 32, he says:

“Facundus the African, bishop of the Church of Hermiana, wrote twelve books in defense of the Three Chapters. By the force of his style he showed that the aforesaid Three Chapters had been condemned as an attack upon the Apostolic faith and the Council of Chalcedon: namely, the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, addressed to Maris the Persian; Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; and the statements of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus.”

100. From so many statements of our Isidore it is plainly evident that he was strongly inclined to defend the Three Chapters and that he held an unfavorable view of the Second Council of Constantinople, the Fifth Ecumenical Council [Col. 0886B].

This explains why, in his preface, after the four general councils, he made no mention of the aforesaid Fifth Council of Constantinople, although it had already been held long before, and did not insert it into his canonical collection. The Spanish prelates adopted the same position. Assembled at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, they decreed that the Sixth Ecumenical Council should be placed after the Council of Chalcedon, with due honor, place, and order, without any mention of the Fifth.

Consequently, in all the manuscript codices of the Isidorian canonical collection that exist, even those written in the twelfth century, one finds absolutely no mention of the Second Council of Constantinople, the Fifth Ecumenical Council.

101. The temporal circumstances and place in which this outstanding canonical collection was compiled also provide an argument of no less weight for our case [Col. 0886C]. Since it is evident, as will become clear from what follows, that the aforesaid collection was prepared during the time of Isidore of Seville, in Spain, and for the use of the Spanish Church, there can scarcely be any doubt that, if any canonical collection is to be attributed to our Isidore, it is this very one under discussion.

102. Several passages of the preface itself clearly show that this canonical collection was arranged after the year of Christ 589. For the words of the aforesaid preface—

“But if there are any councils that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have enacted”

—appear to have been taken from the first canon of the Third Council of Toledo, celebrated in the year 589, where we read:

“Let nothing be done contrary to what the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have established as necessary to be done” [Col. 0886D].

103. Another passage of the same preface adds considerable force to this argument. It contains the following words concerning the Constantinopolitan Creed:

“Giving the form of the Creed more fully, which all Greece and Latin Christianity proclaim in the churches.”

Since the Constantinopolitan Creed referred to here first began to be sung in the churches of Spain after the decree of the Third Council of Toledo—where canon 2 orders that throughout all the churches of Spain and Galicia, according to the practice of the Eastern Churches, the Creed of the Council of Constantinople, that is, of the 150 bishops, should be recited, and that before the Lord’s Prayer it should be sung aloud by the people [Col. 0887B]—it necessarily follows that the aforesaid preface of our collection was written only after the Third Council of Toledo, that is, after the year of Christ 589.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Indeed, the aforesaid Creed is found inserted in the Isidorian mixed Missal, which is called Mozarabic, immediately before the Lord’s Prayer. It was sung, however, after the elevation, as appears from this rubric of the aforesaid Missal: “And let the priest elevate the Body of Christ, so that it may be seen by the people. And let the choir say the Creed, two by two, that is, in pairs.”]

104. It is shown not only by the preface but also by the canonical collection itself that it was arranged during the time of Isidore, bishop of Seville. Among the many manuscript codices of the aforesaid collection preserved in the libraries of Spain, none has so far been found that does not contain the Fourth Council of Toledo and the Second Council of Seville, over which our doctor presided. None, I say, lacks the decretal letters of Pope Gregory the Great, Isidore’s contemporary as a bishop.

There are nevertheless some in which nothing is found later than the aforesaid councils or the letters of Gregory the Great [Col. 0887C]. It is therefore clear that the canonical collection in question was prepared while Isidore was still alive.

105. So much concerning the time at which our canonical collection was compiled. As for the place, many considerations demonstrate that it was prepared in Spain and for the use of the Spanish Church. The following are especially decisive.

First, the words concerning the Constantinopolitan Creed that, as stated above, occur in the preface itself—“which all Greece and Latin Christianity proclaim in the churches”—clearly demonstrate that the author was Spanish. For at that time this Creed was sung in no churches other than those of Spain. Everyone knows, moreover, that the Gauls adopted this practice in the eighth century, and the Romans much later [Col. 0887D].

106. Second, the large number of manuscript codices of this canonical collection preserved chiefly in the various libraries of Spain supplies us with another effective argument for asserting that it was arranged for the use of the Spanish Church. If the matter were otherwise, copies of the aforesaid collection would undoubtedly be found in equal numbers among other nations [Col. 0888A].

Yet no genuinely pure copy can be seen outside Spain, except for the one which, as observed above, was transferred from the Ambrosian Library and is preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna. The copies that the most learned Coustant saw in Gaul are not pure, although they were undoubtedly copied from manuscript codices brought from Spain itself, perhaps at the time when the province of Narbonne was counted as part of the Spanish Church [Note: [Col. 0887D] The province of Narbonne remained under the rule of the Spanish kings until the beginning of the eighth century, that is, until the death of Roderic, the last Gothic king. It is clear from the subscriptions of the councils that the archbishop of Narbonne often and for long periods attended the Councils of Toledo. In the ancient division of the provinces of Spain, the following churches are said to have been subject to the metropolitan see of Narbonne: Béziers, Agde, Maguelone, Nîmes, Lodève, Carcassonne, Elne, and Toulouse.]

107. The third argument, by which it is easily demonstrated that this outstanding collection was composed both in Spain and for the use of the Spanish Church, is that the councils contained in the aforesaid collection—not only Spanish councils but also, remarkably, Greek, African, and Gallican councils—are dated according to the Spanish Era, in the following manner:

“The canons of the Council of Nicaea, Spanish Era 362.”

“The Chalcedonian Council begins, Spanish Era 489.”

“The Third Council of Carthage begins, Spanish Era 435.”

“The Third Council of Arles, Spanish Era 461.”

“The Council of Vaison, Spanish Era 480,” and so forth.

Everyone knows that this kind of dating was a distinctive practice of the Spaniards.

108. Finally, to omit other considerations, let this also be added in confirmation of our case: all the letters of the Roman prelates addressed to the Spaniards are contained in our collection. Indeed, the letters of Pope Hilary to Ascanio of Tarragona, of Simplicius and Felix to Zeno of Seville, of Hormisdas to John of Elche, and several others first saw the light in it, as is evident from the collection itself [Col. 0888C].

109. These, then, are the principal considerations that vindicate our collection of canons for blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, the most illustrious teacher of his age. This collection, truly worthy of so great a man, not only still lies unknown to the learned world, but—what is more lamentable—gave the disguised Isidore an opportunity, at the beginning of the ninth century, to fabricate that collection of canons which I should more accurately call a heap of spurious and interpolated documents, to the great detriment of the Catholic Church and the injury of Isidore’s name. We shall demonstrate in the following paragraph that this crime was committed neither in Spain nor by a Spaniard, but was rather conceived by Riculfus, bishop of Mainz—a proposition that, if not certain, is at least consistent with the truth.

## § VI. The utterly corrupt collection of canons of Isidore Mercator, which is shown to have been compiled neither in Spain nor by a Spaniard, is nevertheless asserted to have proceeded chiefly from the entirely pure Isidorian collection. Some remarks are also offered on the ancient discipline of the Spanish Church.

110. From the statutes of the ancient canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers contained in our distinguished Isidorian collection—by which the Spanish bishops preserved ecclesiastical discipline whole and inviolate through so many centuries—it will readily be clear to everyone that evocations, apostolic indults, immunities, reservations, and other abuses introduced by the new Pseudo-Isidorian law in the time of Charlemagne were completely unknown to the Spanish Church, since they were contrary to those canons contained in its body of canon law.

111. Indeed, in that ancient period bishops in Spain were ordained without the intervention or authority of the Apostolic See, with the prescribed consent or advice of the metropolitan bishop, according to the statutes of the canons, as is shown by the index of our collection. For the thirty-ninth title of the first book of the aforementioned index cites many items contained in the collection of canons to prove this; for example: Council of Nicaea, title 6; Council of Antioch, title 19; Council of Laodicea, title 12; Council of Riez, title 6; Letter of Innocent to Victorius, title 1; and many others. Yet nowhere in this index prefixed to the aforementioned collection will you find anything concerning the required confirmation of the Apostolic See in the ordination or election of bishops. Indeed, during the first thirteen centuries of the Spanish Church no one is found who sought to obtain such confirmation from the Apostolic See.

112. As regards election, it seems probable that, in accordance with the discipline of the universal Church, bishops in Spain were elected in the earliest period by the votes of the clergy and people. That custom was common to all Churches, as Bishop Anselm of Lucca testifies in these words [Note: In the second book Against Guibert the Antipope. It is found in the Library of the Fathers, vol. XI, p. 586, Cologne edition; or vol. XVIII, p. 606, Lyons edition.]:

> “Moreover, after those same apostles had departed, the Churches throughout the world inviolably preserved the custom handed down by them: when the bishop of any Church died, its clergy and people, after common deliberation, appointed as their pastor someone from their own clergy or from the clergy of another Church.”

113. It must nevertheless be admitted that the bishops and clergy had the principal role in these elections, and that bishops could be elected and ordained without the prior vote of the people. For the votes of the people did not constitute the election, since the bishops could reject even someone elected by the people, especially if the election had been conducted tumultuously. I would therefore readily believe that the election was made chiefly by the clergy, while the will of the people was merely customarily consulted. This appears to be attested by a letter of Pope Leo, written in the middle of the fifth century to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne:

> “No consideration permits those to be counted among the bishops who have been elected neither by the clergy nor desired by the people.”

This letter is found in our collection, no. 68.

Indeed, it is plain from the frequently mentioned index of our collection that the people or populace in Spain were excluded from such elections. For in title XXXVI of the first book, entitled “On the Election of Bishops,” these words are read: “That it is not permitted to the people to elect ministers of the altar.” That this statute was already in force in Spain from the time of Martin of Braga is clearly demonstrated by the chapters of Martin inserted into our collection. In their first title, on the election of a bishop, it is decreed:

> “It is not permitted for the people to conduct the election of those who are called to the priesthood; rather, the judgment belongs to the bishops, so that they themselves may examine whether the one who is to be ordained has been instructed in speech, faith, and spiritual life.”

114. Nevertheless, at a later time Christian princes intervened in these elections. This right seems to have been granted them by the Church for the purpose of enabling them, by their authority, to confirm and support elected bishops against the perverse quibbles of heretics. Whatever the case may be, it is established by canon 6 of the Twelfth Council of Toledo that, already in the seventh century, the kings of Spain possessed the unrestricted right to elect bishops [Note: The king referred his nomination to the national council for confirmation. Once this had been done, the confirmed bishop was required, within the fixed period prescribed by the canons after his ordination, to present himself before the metropolitan, so that, instructed by his discipline, he might worthily govern the reins of the see he had received. See the Councils of Tarragona, Toledo XII, and Toledo XVI.].

115. Moreover, supported by the ancient statutes of the canons and the rules of the holy Fathers, the Catholic Church preserved an entire and inviolate discipline through the first eight centuries and restored it, once it had declined, to its former splendor. As we have already observed, bishops were elected by the votes and consent of the clergy and by the suffrage of the people, and were confirmed and ordained by the metropolitan together with the comprovincial bishops, without any prior confirmation being required from the Roman pontiff. Clerics to serve in cathedral or parish churches were chosen by the bishops. Tithes and the offerings of the faithful, possessions, and other ecclesiastical goods were distributed according to the statutes of the individual Churches and the customs of the provinces. The bishops possessed full authority both over the secular clergy and over monks; as most vigilant guardians of the doctrines of the faith and of ecclesiastical discipline, they devoted themselves entirely to the observance of divine law, omitting nothing they judged necessary for the instruction of the people entrusted to them. They imposed public penance on sinners according to the nature of their crimes, and, like diligent heads of households, hastened to assist widows, orphans, and the poor [Note: “The authority of our bishops has established that bishops should possess the power to administer the resources of the Church, but in such a way that they must distribute the support of widows, orphans, and the poor, as well as the stipends of clerics.” Letter of Gelasius to the Sicilian bishops, title 7, which appears in our collection, no. 85.].

116. The translation of bishops from one see to another was strictly prohibited by the canons. Episcopal sees, however, whenever the welfare of the faithful or the advantage of the Church required new ones, were established by national synods.

117. As for judicial matters, the bishops exercised general jurisdiction throughout their dioceses and, with the advice of the clergy, decided cases by their own authority. Appeals from their judgments, however—especially when the case was serious—were made to the metropolitan bishop, who, together with the comprovincial bishops, issued the judgment. Thus clerics were judged by bishops, and bishops themselves by the metropolitan and the comprovincial bishops assembled in synod, according to the statutes of the canons.

118. When cases were of greater importance, or concerned the condition and welfare of the universal Church, they were referred to the Apostolic See as the head of the whole Church. The very clear words of Innocent I in his letter to Victorius, bishop of Rouen, title III, teach us this:

> “If,” he says, “more important cases should have been brought forward, they are to be referred to the Apostolic See after episcopal judgment, as ancient custom requires.”

[Note: This letter appears in our collection, no. 7.]

119. Accordingly, so that the Roman bishops might provide more easily and properly for Churches situated at a distance, from the beginning of the fifth century they appointed their apostolic vicars in various provinces as most vigilant guardians of the faith and ecclesiastical discipline. Thus Pope Innocent entrusted the judgment of cases in Illyricum to the Thessalonian bishops Anysius and Rufus. In Gaul, too, the bishops of Arles, and in Spain the bishops of Seville, acted in place of the Apostolic See. The examination of major cases was likewise entrusted to these vicars; they judged such cases together with two bishops from each province, selected for that purpose by the metropolitans. This is clearly demonstrated by the words of Pope Leo in his letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, title X:

> “Therefore, if any more serious case should arise on account of which it is reasonable and necessary to summon a fraternal assembly, it will be sufficient for two bishops from each province, whom the metropolitans deem suitable to send, to come to your fraternity.”

[Note: Apostolic vicars obtained this office not by virtue of a privilege of the see, but by virtue of their person—that is, according to the measure of their merits. Consequently, the Church of Seville wrongly claims primacy in Spain on the ground that the bishops Leander, Zeno, and Sallustius had exercised an apostolic vicariate. By the same reasoning, the Churches of Astorga and Elche could also claim primacy, since it is established that blessed Toribius, bishop of Astorga, and John of Elche were honored with the title and dignity of vicars.]

120. Those cases that could not be settled by the apostolic vicars or in provincial synods because of their difficulty were referred to the Apostolic See as the foster-mother of the faith and the true interpreter of the canons. The same Leo says in the same letter, title XI:

> “But if, in that matter which you have judged should be discussed and decided with the brethren, their opinion should differ from your will, let everything be referred to us with the testimony of the proceedings, so that, once ambiguities have been removed, what pleases God may be decreed.”

He had likewise given this prior instruction in title VII of the same letter:

> “And if, by chance, a case should arise among those who preside concerning grave sins—which God forbid—that cannot be settled by provincial examination, the metropolitan should take care to inform your fraternity of the entire character of the matter, so that, if the matter has not been resolved by your judgment when the parties are present, whatever it may be may be transferred to our examination.”

121. In a similar manner Gregory the Great, in a letter to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, by which he grants him his own authority, reserves to his judgment the more serious cases that Maximian could not settle:

> “But if perhaps there should be difficult matters that cannot at all be resolved by the judgment of your fraternity, let these alone demand our judgment, so that, relieved of minor matters, we may devote ourselves more effectively to the greater ones.”

122. Such, in summary, was the ecclesiastical discipline preserved in the Church during the first eight centuries and confirmed by the statutes of synods and holy Fathers. With the privileges proper to each person preserved according to divine institution, it flourished incorruptibly, while the individual provinces retained their respective rites and customs according to the diversity of their Churches, since these did not differ from the Catholic Church in the substance of faith and doctrine. For, as Saint Augustine says in his letter to Januarius, “whatever is not shown to be contrary either to the faith or to good morals is to be regarded indifferently and preserved for the sake of the fellowship of those among whom one lives.” And Saint Gregory, in his letter to Leander, bishop of Seville, which appears in our collection as number 99, says:

> “In one faith, differing custom does not injure the holy Church.”

123. This, then, was the external form of the government of the Church until the end of the eighth century, when, during the reign of Charlemagne, a new collection of canons appeared, bearing the name of Isidore Mercator or Peccator. It was filled with a great many documents—genuine, adulterated, and fictitious—and was so much larger than our genuine Isidorian collection that it embraced almost the whole of it in adulterated form. The most learned Coustant briefly describes how much harm this offspring of an impostor inflicted upon ecclesiastical discipline and what pernicious changes it introduced into canon law in his preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 157:

> “Hence the sinews of discipline were utterly weakened and broken; the rights of bishops were disturbed; the laws of judgments were removed, or at least afflicted in a wretched manner. Hence arose an immense harvest of discord, sedition, and litigation, which for so many centuries bore fruit to the disgrace of the Church and the offense of the faithful.”

124. This utterly corrupt collection of canons, from which the collections of Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and others, as well as Gratian’s Decree, proceeded, was brought from Spain and obtained by Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, who disseminated it far and wide throughout Gaul in a short time. Hincmar of Reims testifies to this in these words:

> “Because perhaps you thought that no one besides yourself possessed the same opinions or the very letters, you therefore believed that you could freely collect such things. It is a remarkable matter, since this land is full of those very opinions, just as it is full of the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, obtained after it had been brought from Spain; zealous in matters of this kind, as also in royal capitularies, he caused these regions to be filled from it.””

[Note: Works of Hincmar, edited by Sirmond, vol. II, p. 476.]

125. These words also clearly show that the book of collected letters brought from Spain had been compiled by a certain Isidore. Indeed, the same Hincmar asserts in his forty-eighth opusculum, no. 31, that the Isidore in question was the bishop of Seville. He says:

> “For it is written in a certain sermon, without the name of the excerptor, excerpted from the Deeds of Saint Sylvester, which Bishop Isidore of Seville collected together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman See, from Saint Clement up to blessed Gregory.”

[Note: Works of Hincmar, vol. II, p. 793.]

126. It must nevertheless be observed here that Hincmar of Reims in this passage was referring to Mercator’s spurious collection of canons, not to the genuine collection of Isidore of Seville. This is made perfectly clear by Hincmar’s own words: “which he collected together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman See from Saint Clement up to blessed Gregory.” For at that time no collection so extensive existed, apart from Mercator’s interpolated collection, that embraced so many decretal letters, from Saint Clement specifically to blessed Gregory.

127. The following words of the aforementioned Hincmar, in his treatise Against Hincmar of Lyon, chapter 24, make the same point even more clearly. Speaking there of Isidore’s book of collected letters, he says:

> “In its preface the same Isidore says concerning the canons of the Apostles that some call them apocryphal, that many accept them, and that the holy Fathers confirmed their judgments by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions.”

[Note: Works of Hincmar, vol. II, p. 477.]

These words are found nowhere except almost verbatim in the interpolated preface of the disguised Isidore [Note: See above, note 32, where we transcribed the very words of the disguised Isidore and compared them with those found in the genuine preface, so that the impostor might be more clearly recognized.].

128. Furthermore, if Hincmar of Reims had investigated the whole matter more carefully in his disputes against Hincmar of Lyon, consulted the bishops of Spain, or arranged for a copy to be made for him from the manuscript codices of the genuine Isidorian collection of canons, he would certainly have exposed the impostor. After recognizing the fabrication of the collected letters, he would have attacked Hincmar of Lyon and Nicholas I with better weapons and refuted them. Would that he had done so! For if the falsehood had been conquered at its very birth and the fraud suppressed, one can easily infer how much benefit would have resulted from this, even from the very disputes that for so many centuries so bitterly disturbed the peace of the Church [Note: In his disputes against Hincmar of Lyon and Nicholas I, Hincmar of Reims regarded the new Pseudo-Isidorian decretal letters as genuine. At that time, because of the lack of a developed critical method, nothing was known about their falsity. Therefore, in response to his opponents’ objections drawn from these fictitious letters, Hincmar replied only that the letters were not entered in the code of canons and consequently possessed neither authority nor the force of law.].

129. Moreover, from the aforementioned words of Hincmar of Reims some have conjectured that Mercator’s most disgraceful collection of canons was both composed in Spain and revised by Isidore, bishop of Seville. Since, as we have often stated, the Spanish Church possesses its own distinguished collection of canons—“the richest,” to use the words of the most learned Dom Coustant, “and all the more precious because in it you encounter nothing spurious, nothing not free from every stain of interpolation” [Note: Preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 156. This most learned man makes honorable mention of our collection of canons more than once, although he had not seen it, and had formed such a conjecture from an index alone, copied from a manuscript codex of the Church of Gerona and sent to him by the illustrious Dom Joseph de Taverner de Ardenne. In the aforementioned preface, no. 134, he says: “It must be admitted that no collection of canons has yet been made public that does not yield to it in the multitude and arrangement of its documents.” And again, in no. 140: “Moreover, as we have already observed, we have not yet had the opportunity to see any collection which, whether the multitude of its documents or the method of its arrangement is considered, can compete with the method and extent of this one.”]

—yet, instead of praise or honor, he accepted the injury of disgraceful falsity inflicted both upon himself and upon his own most illustrious teacher, without a single one among so many learned Spaniards arising to vindicate his native Church and its teacher Isidore from so unjust an accusation. Indeed, the most eminent Cardinal Aguirre, otherwise a most learned man, filled almost half of the first volume of his great collection of the councils of Spain with needless scholarship in order to assert that Mercator’s most corrupt collection had been composed in Spain and collected by Isidore, bishop of Seville. Moreover, although he admitted that the decretal letters attributed to the Roman bishops who preceded Pope Siricius had been interpolated, he nevertheless maintained that they possessed complete authority.

The error of so great a man, undoubtedly born of a preconceived opinion, is all the more astonishing because he had many manuscript codices of our genuine Isidorian collection at hand and had repeatedly examined them. Among them were two excellent Toledan codices, the index of which—entitled, as we have often observed, Extracts of the Canons—he had printed in the third volume of his great collection as though it were a codex of the Spanish Church. In reality, however, it is not a codex but an index of the contents of the codex from which it was copied. If he had properly investigated this matter, he would have understood that the absurd system, injurious to Isidore’s teaching, which he sought to establish with such zeal and such useless learning would collapse completely.

130. The delusion and preconceived opinion of this most learned man are especially apparent from the words found on page 2 of the third volume of the aforementioned great collection of the councils of Spain. He says:

> “It was necessary that, toward the end of the seventh century or the beginning of the eighth, that codex should have been extremely extensive and contained in a volume of enormous size, since it included all the councils celebrated up to that time, both general and national and provincial, as well as a great many decretal letters of the Roman bishops written over so many centuries, especially to the Spaniards.”

These words clearly demonstrate that the eminent Aguirre correctly judged and conjectured the extent of the codex from the index he published. But he was so blinded by his opinion that he failed to notice the very extensive codex he had before his eyes and from which he had copied the aforementioned index. I can scarcely express sufficient astonishment at this in so great a man, especially since he had handled that codex day and night and had repeatedly examined both the general, national, and provincial councils contained in it and the letters of the Roman bishops cited in the index. From this he could very easily have recognized that the little work he presented to us under the title Book of the Canons of the Holy Fathers was not a codex but an index of the contents of the genuine Isidorian codex of canons, consistently prefixed to all the manuscript codices that exist [Note: See above, note 58.].

131. Moreover, I do not hesitate to assert, with the utmost certainty, that the filthy collection of Mercator or Peccator, as will become clear from what follows, was composed neither in Spain nor by Spaniards, but was arranged by Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, or under his authority, and disseminated throughout the Frankish-Gallic empire. This is easily inferred from the aforementioned words of Hincmar of Reims. For the aforementioned Riculfus obtained from Spain a genuine Isidorian manuscript codex and gave it the name of the illustrious Isidore after interpolating it in an extraordinary manner with the fictitious decretal letters of which he possessed a store [Note: The following words of Benedict the Levite of the Church of Mainz appear to bear witness to this. In the preface to books five, six, and seven of the Capitularies he compiled, he says:

> “These things . . . which had been issued in various places and on various sheets, as well as in various synods and general assemblies, we found scattered about, and especially stored in the archive of the holy metropolitan Church of Mainz by Riculfus, metropolitan of that holy see, etc.”

Perhaps the letter of Pope Gregory was taken from the same archive. No earlier knowledge of it had existed, and it is said that Riculfus himself brought it to Worms. It is cited in book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 281, in these words:

> “For when we had held a general assembly at Worms, a letter of Pope Gregory was brought to us by Riculfus, metropolitan of Mainz, etc.”]

so that he might more easily deceive people and attract many by the splendor of so great a teacher.

132. On what occasion Riculfus may have conceived and carried out this notorious crime may perhaps be conjectured briefly. As the eighth century was drawing to a close, Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of Urgell, infected with the Nestorian heresy, sought to spread throughout Spain erroneous opinions concerning the Son of God by sending letters and books to every province, thereby aggravating the sufferings of the Spanish Church, which was already severely afflicted by the ferocity and domination of the Moors. Elipandus drew many to his side by the metropolitan authority he enjoyed. This was all the easier for him because at that time the Spanish bishops were unable, on account of Moorish rule, to celebrate councils according to the institutions of the Fathers. Nevertheless, there were most holy Spanish bishops who, both orally and in writing, condemned the impious error and its authors. Among these, the priest Beatus and Etherius, bishop of Osma, suppressed the impiety with powerful arguments committed to writing [Note: Among the opponents of the Felician heresy, the first place belongs to Alcuin, who composed seven books against Felix, written with the greatest elegance. Agobard also, the most holy bishop of Lyon, wrote one book against Felix on the occasion of a memorandum discovered after Felix’s death, in which he seemed to defend the impious error. It is found among his other works, edited by Stephen Baluze, Paris, 1666, 2 vols. in octavo.].

133. Finally, when the controversy had diminished and Felix had been condemned at the assembly held at Regensburg in the year 792, Elipandus sent a letter to Charlemagne in which, undertaking the defense of his error, he attacked Beatus fiercely and requested that the king not judge the matter alone but rather follow the judgment of many [Note: Elipandus’s letter to Charlemagne is found in Flórez, Sacred Spain, vol. V. This letter was written, as is characteristic of heretics, in a sharp and overly arrogant style. Among other statements expressed with insufficient reverence concerning King Charles, it contains these words: “Surely, do not reject alone the testimony of so many venerable Fathers concerning the adoption of Christ’s flesh . . . for it is said that by the terror of your power you convince many, not by justice.”].

134. Accordingly, Charlemagne, illustrious no less in letters than in arms and deeply devoted to sacred affairs, sent frequent embassies to the Roman pontiff for the benefit of the Catholic Church [Note: Consult the letter of Charlemagne himself to Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain, which is found in Hardouin’s Greatest Collection, vol. IV, col. 896.]. He also ordered a very full council to be held at Frankfurt in the year 794. After the matter had been examined, Felix and Elipandus were condemned for asserting adoption in the Son of God. Felix, deposed from his see by the judgment of the Fathers, ended the final day of his unhappy life at Lyon.

135. This religious dissension, which disturbed the peace of the Church for many years through the publication of numerous writings on both sides, was without doubt the reason for seeking out and bringing from Spain the work of Isidore, bishop of Seville. For Elipandus and Felix of Urgell, among the other authors of great renown whom they used to support or defend their error, repeatedly appealed to the authority of Isidore of Seville, so that their cause might gain greater favor under the name of so great a man [Note: Isidore of Seville is often praised in the writings of Elipandus. In a letter to Alcuin, found among Alcuin’s works and in Flórez, Sacred Spain, vol. V, p. 543, Elipandus praises Isidore in these words:

> “Blessed Isidore too, the radiance of the Church, the star of the West, the teacher of Spain, says in the book of the Etymologies: ‘He is called Only-Begotten according to the excellence of his divinity, because he has no brothers.’”]

136. From this it can easily be discerned how Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, obtained the codex of the canons of Isidore of Seville that had been brought from Spain. Hincmar of Reims’s words concerning the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Riculfus obtained after it had been brought from Spain, are to be understood in this sense: that is, Riculfus obtained from Spain the pure and unadulterated collection of canons of Isidore, that most illustrious teacher—a collection which, by ill fortune, Hincmar of Reims did not see, nor, because of the lack of a sounder critical method less developed in that age, did he conjecture it to be such. Riculfus then disseminated it far and wide throughout the Frankish-Gallic empire after it had been astonishingly interpolated and marvelously enlarged with very many fictitious documents, undoubtedly drawn from the aforementioned archive of the Church of Mainz.

This interpretation is fully confirmed by the Pseudo-Isidorian collection of canons itself, which was formed from our genuine Isidorian collection. For many things prove and clearly demonstrate that Isidore’s pure and unadulterated collection of canons served Mercator or Riculfus as the foundation on which he constructed his own.

137. The first argument for this assertion is that Riculfus included, at the beginning of his collection, the order for celebrating a council. Since this order appears in no work except the Hispanic manuscript codices, there can be no doubt that the impostor had in his possession a Spanish codex of the genuine collection from which he copied it. The Hispanic era, prefixed to most of the councils in our collection and likewise preserved by Pseudo-Isidore, adds considerable force to this argument. For this usage is observed nowhere in the world except Spain.

138. Furthermore, since the Pseudo-Isidorian preface to the councils is in reality nothing other than the genuine preface of Isidore of Seville itself—torn apart, interpolated, and rearranged according to the forger’s intention—does it not most clearly indicate the source from which it flowed? It contains these words:

> “Afterward, we placed the Nicene Synod, on account of the authority of that same great council. Next, we arranged the various councils of the Greeks and Latins, both those held earlier and those held later, distinguished according to the order of their numbers and times in their respective chapters, under the view of this volume. We also appended the remaining decrees of the Roman bishops up to Saint Gregory and certain letters of his, in which, by reason of the eminence of the Apostolic See, there is an authority equal to that of the councils.”

From where, I ask, did the impostor draw this? Was it not from the genuine preface of Isidore of Seville, where almost the very same words are found? Indeed, comparison of the two prefaces makes this clearer than daylight [Note: Here are the words of the genuine preface:

> “At the beginning of this volume we placed the Nicene Synod on account of the authority of that same great council. Next, we arranged the decrees of the various councils of the Greeks and Latins, both those held earlier and those held later, distinguished according to the order of their numbers and times in their respective chapters, under the view of this volume. We also appended the decrees of the Roman bishops, in which, by reason of the eminence of the Apostolic See, there is an authority equal to that of the councils.”

From this it can be seen that Pseudo-Isidore copied almost word for word the words of his preface from the genuine Isidorian preface, except for the phrase “At the beginning of this volume we placed the Nicene Synod,” in whose place he wrote, “Afterward, we placed the Nicene Synod,” and so forth. The reason is that the impostor placed the canons of the Apostles at the beginning of his compilation, whereas Isidore of Seville rejects them as apocryphal.]

139. Finally, the first part of our Isidorian, pure and unadulterated collection of canons—which includes the decrees of the councils of Greece, Africa, Gaul, and Spain—was appropriated by the disguised Isidore in such a way that he transcribed it in its entirety, preserving the order of the councils and the titles of the canons. More importantly, he preserved with the greatest fidelity the Latin translation of the Greek councils. This is the strongest possible argument for our assertion, and no one can offer anything solid against it. For either one must say that Isidore’s genuine and much older collection of canons proceeded from Mercator’s most corrupt and adulterated collection—which would be the height of absurdity—or one must frankly admit that the impostor formed his own collection from the Isidorian one.

140. We are now brought to the point at which we must briefly prove that the Pseudo-Isidorian collection of canons was composed neither in Spain nor by Spaniards. To clarify this matter, we must briefly touch upon the miseries and sufferings endured by the Spanish Church during the eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries.

[Col. 0898C] **141.** It is a well-known fact, fully recorded in the history of that period, with what lamentation and turmoil all Spain was filled when, at the beginning of the eighth century, the Moors invaded and the Gothic kingdom—which had stood in the greatest prosperity for more than three hundred years—was utterly destroyed by a barbarous and savage people. The Spaniards were everywhere slaughtered or reduced to cruel slavery; those who survived the disaster, fleeing servitude, scattered to various remote and hidden places. In the midst of so great an upheaval of both secular and sacred affairs, some ecclesiastical prelates went to Asturias, carrying with them the sacred relics of the saints and the books and writings of distinguished men that they had been able to collect. Others, concerned for the safety of the flock entrusted to them and reduced to slavery along with it, became participants in the same danger and, despising death—and what was worse than death—[Note: Regarding the destruction of basilicas, the insults to priests, and also the tribute which we pay monthly with great sorrow as no hardship; so that the swift relief of death is more expedient for us than the laborious ordeal of a most destitute life. Eulogius, book I of the *Memorial of the Saints*, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XV, Lyon edition.] [Col. 0898D] the barbarous cruelty of the Saracens, remained in their native places to offer consolation to the wretched and to defend their own fold from rapacious wolves. Let us therefore hear blessed Eulogius, designated bishop of the Church of Toledo, who suffered martyrdom at Córdoba and who himself witnessed these most miserable events and had a large share in them. In a letter to Wilesindus, bishop of Pamplona, preserved in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XV, p. 298, Lyon edition, this most holy prelate describes the savagery of the Moors in these words:

> “A tyrannical fury, savage against the Church of God, has overturned everything, laid waste to all things, and scattered the whole; it has shut bishops, priests, abbots, deacons, and the entire clergy, and all whom it was able to seize in that time, in prison, bound in chains, and plunged them, as though they were dead, into the subterranean caves of the world. Among them I, that sinner, your beloved friend, am held in chains, and together with all the others I endure the horrible filth of the prison-houses. It has deprived the Church of its sacred ministry, robbed it of its sanctuary, and alienated it from its office; and at this time we have neither offering, nor sacrifice, nor incense, nor a place for firstfruits where we may be able to appease the Lord, etc.”

**142.** In such a wretched condition of affairs and amid such lamentable ruin, the Spanish Church lay buried for more than three centuries, its basilicas destroyed, its bishops and priests thrown into prison or condemned to death, and the entire Christian people deprived of the sacred ministries.

[Note: It may be said that the captivity of the Spanish Church lasted 371 years—that is, from the year 714, when the Gothic kingdom was overthrown, until the capture of Toledo by King Alfonso in the year 1085. From that time onward, when the minds of the Christians were roused by the sweet name of liberty, the fortunes of the Moors began increasingly to decline and to sink into a worse condition.]

**143.** Since this was the state of affairs, and since throughout the entire period of captivity there was no communication or intercourse between the Spanish prelates and the Roman pontiffs—and since, in fact, no genuine decretal letter addressed to the Spaniards survives, except that of Pope Hadrian, which he wrote on the occasion of the error of Elipandus and Felix, condemned at the Council of Frankfurt—who could persuade himself that the Spaniard was the author of the decretal letters fabricated during this most unhappy period, or that they could have been forged in Spain? In the judgment of learned men, this has no credibility, especially when proper consideration is given to circumstances that strongly confirm the point: the scarcity of books preserved from the general destruction, and the interruption—or complete degeneration—of literary studies during such a cruel and prolonged captivity. For the Spaniards of that time, harassed by continuous war with the Moors and recognizing that liberty had to be recovered not by letters but by arms, abandoned their studies and devoted themselves entirely to warfare.

**144.** Furthermore, if, as is maintained, the pseudo-Isidorian mass of collected letters was fabricated in Spain, how did it happen that, after the diligent investigations of learned men in so many libraries and archives of this kingdom, not even one manuscript codex of such a compilation has yet been discovered? No one can deny that many copies of such a collection must already have been disseminated throughout the various provinces of Spain before the copy from which Riculphus of Mainz caused the Frankish-Gallic empire to be filled came into his hands. How, then, did it happen that all the immense volumes of this celebrated collection disappeared so completely that in the very place where they were first patched together not even a trace of a single copy is found?

But you will say that it is not surprising that, amid such universal confusion and misery and the constant wars, all the copies in Spain perished without exception. What then? The genuine Isidorian collection of canons, made and organized in Spain before the invasion of the Moors, was able to survive intact and unharmed the mournful destruction, wars, fires, and finally all the calamities with which this most noble kingdom was afflicted by the barbarians for more than three centuries; yet no trace remained of the pseudo-Isidorian jumble, compiled two centuries later and, moreover, at the time when Charlemagne possessed the most delightful province of Spain.

[Note: Catalonia is a province of Spain, part of Tarraconensis, whose capital is Barcelona, a most famous city, formerly exceedingly vigorous in the arts of war. Consult the learned work of Antoni Capmany entitled *Historical Memoirs concerning the Navy, Commerce, and Arts of Barcelona*, published at Madrid in 1779, in two quarto volumes.]

And while numerous manuscript copies of our pure and genuine collection, written in the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries, are still preserved in the libraries of Spain, not even a single leaf of the fictitious pseudo-Isidorian compilation exists that could at least indicate that it ever existed in this kingdom. Who could bring himself to believe that all the copies suddenly perished, even in their native place, as though deliberately?

The reason for their disappearance is plainly at hand: it is certain beyond doubt that the fictitious collection of pseudo-Isidorian letters was patched together neither in Spain nor by a Spaniard.

**145.** Indeed, it is demonstrated most clearly by the many manuscript codices of our genuine collection of canons, repeatedly cited and written in the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries, that the spurious collection of the disguised Isidore was either wholly unknown to the Spaniards until the twelfth century or was at least regarded by them as apocryphal and fictitious. For if the Spaniards had known pseudo-Isidore, they would unquestionably have copied his collection of canons rather than ours, since it was more extensive and enriched with a greater number of documents. Yet the outstanding codex of the Church of Toledo, written in the year 1133, clearly shows that the spurious wares of Mercator had not yet penetrated the interior of Spain at the beginning of the twelfth century.

Moreover, a letter of Innocent III addressed to Peter of Compostela declares that, at the beginning of the thirteenth century, they were still unknown in Spain. It contains these words:

> “You maintained by many arguments that the Council of Mérida is authentic, first because it is contained together with other councils in the book called the *Corpus of Canons*, which Pope Alexander approved as authentic by a formal decision.”

[Note: This letter is found in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VI, p. 511, and in Hardouin, vol. III, as well as elsewhere.]

Now the Council of Mérida mentioned here is included in our collection but does not appear in the pseudo-Isidorian compilation. Therefore our genuine Isidorian collection was still called the *Corpus of Canons of the Spanish Church* in the thirteenth century. Since no mention of Mercator’s spurious collection is found among the Spaniards, and no knowledge of it appears before the fifteenth century, one may reasonably conclude that the celebrated collection was completely unknown to the Spaniards before the invention of printing.

[Col. 0901B] **146.** From what has been observed thus far it is certain that the adulterated collection of pseudo-Isidore was fabricated neither in Spain nor by a Spaniard. Indeed, we have shown that Riculphus, bishop of Mainz, formed it from the genuine collection of canons of Isidore of Seville, together with notes and documents that had until then been unknown and were stored in his chest. In this way the words of Hincmar of Rheims—adequately explained, so far as we know, by no previous author—are made perfectly clear.

“Riculphus,” says Hincmar, “obtained a book of collected letters brought from Spain by Isidore, and caused the Frankish lands to be filled with it.” That is, Riculphus obtained from Spain—where numerous copies were preserved—a book of collected letters by Isidore, completely intact and free from every taint of interpolation; he then greatly enlarged and defiled it with many decretal letters, both fictitious and interpolated, disseminated it far and wide, and caused the Frankish-Gallic empire to be filled with it.

Thus it came about that the Spanish Church, and its distinguished teacher Isidore, bishop of Seville, suffered no small disgrace from the shameless audacity of one man, instead of receiving, as was fitting, praise and honor for their own collection, which was completely intact and outstanding.

**147.** Many have judged that Riculphus did this through an imprudent devotion toward the Apostolic See and through misguided zeal. Let it be so, if you will; nevertheless, the Roman Church, founded upon the rock of apostolic truth, has no need of lies,

> “nor of such aid, nor of such defenders.”

The Spaniards likewise had no need of such assistance to strengthen the authority of the Apostolic See, which they profess in their—I believe pure—code of canons by many arguments. In fact, the dignity of the letters of the Roman prelates was so great among them that those letters held authority in Spain no less than the decrees of councils. We shall demonstrate this in the following paragraph.

### § VII. It is asserted that the Spanish Church always acknowledged the authority of the Apostolic See, a fact proved both by the authority of documents and by events recorded in history.

[Col. 0902A]

**148.** Although the nearly unanimous opinion of learned men is that pseudo-Isidore, perhaps carried away by excessive zeal for the Apostolic See, assembled his collection of canons, fabricated new decretal letters, and interpolated genuine ones in order to enlarge the authority of the Roman prelates, the distinguished Blascus, in his learned commentary on the collection of canons of Isidore Mercator, demonstrates by several arguments that Mercator labored chiefly to safeguard the security of bishops and to enlarge their rights.

**149.** History teaches us that Angilramnus, bishop of Metz, was the first of all to use the new decretal letters in order to withdraw himself, under the protection of the Apostolic See, from the judgment of bishops. Rothadus, bishop of Soissons, and Hincmar, bishop of Laon, among others, later followed his example. For the Roman pontiffs, in receiving the appeals of bishops, were preparing for themselves nothing other than manifold cares and a heavier burden of affairs. Nevertheless, it must not be concealed that these privileges, fabricated by pseudo-Isidore as a defense and protection for bishops, were later often invoked to oppress those same bishops and, in good faith, were brought forward by the Roman pontiffs in support of their authority.

**150.** It is, however, completely certain that the primacy of the Roman See, derived by Christ to the apostle Peter and his successors, does not rest in the least upon lies or fictitious documents. For all the Churches have always acknowledged the supreme authority of the Apostolic See, as is most clearly testified by the consultations concerning difficult matters sent to that See from nearly the whole ecclesiastical world.

[Note: A rich witness to this is blessed Jerome, who says in a letter addressed to Ageruchia in the year 409:

> “Many years ago, when I was assisting Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, with the ecclesiastical records and responding to the consultations of the East and West, etc.”

Nor was the Roman See consulted only in the time of Pope Damasus. That it was consulted by other Churches from the very beginning of the nascent Church is demonstrated by the letter of Clement of Rome responding to the consultation of the Corinthians. Whatever the Roman prelates decided concerning such matters was regarded as a judgment already settled, as may be inferred from Saint Augustine’s Sermon 131 against the Pelagians:

> “For already two councils have sent to the Apostolic See concerning this matter; replies have also come from there. The case is finished.”]

Likewise, apostolic vicars were established in various regions to watch over the integrity of the faith and the observance of the sacred laws, and the works of the holy Fathers full of material on this subject testify to the same fact. To cite their testimonies here would be both superfluous and contrary to the purpose of this work.

**151.** Therefore, leaving aside what the most learned men have eloquently treated and asserted concerning the power of the Roman prelates over the Catholic Church, we shall speak here only of the authority of those same Roman pontiffs among the Spaniards. Documents incorporated into the Spanish collection of canons clearly testify that the prelates of the Spanish Church always acknowledged that authority.

**152.** A particularly clear testimony to the supreme dignity and primacy of the Apostolic See is provided by a letter of Pope Gelasius inserted into the celebrated Spanish collection under number 103. Its authority is all the greater because it was issued at a Roman council of seventy bishops. Thus, in the second title of the said letter, these words are read:

> “Although all the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church, set above the other Churches not by synodical constitutions but by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior, has obtained the primacy.”

**153.** The same point is confirmed by another letter of Pope Gelasius addressed to the bishops of Lucania, which is numbered eighty-four in our collection of canons:

> “It is sufficiently unworthy,” he says in title IX, “for anyone, whether among the pontiffs or among the subordinate orders, to reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both following and teaching; and it is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing there where the Lord placed the principate of the whole Church.”

**154.** Moreover, title 51 of the first book of the frequently cited index of our collection, entitled “On the Commissioned Vicariate of the Apostolic See,” in which apostolic vicars are discussed, declares plainly that the Spanish prelates acknowledged the supreme authority of the Apostolic See. For, to establish that the Spaniards accepted the vicariate commissioned by the Apostolic See, it cites the letters of Simplicius to Zeno of Seville and of Hormisdas to John, bishop of the Church of Elche. These are found inserted in our collection under numbers 79, 91, 95, and 96.

Indeed, the Roman prelates would certainly not have delegated their authority throughout Spain to Zeno and other bishops unless they had considered themselves placed over the Catholic Church and unless the Spanish prelates had acknowledged their supreme authority.

**155.** Someone might reply that not all the documents inserted into Isidore’s collection of canons, even if received and approved with the assent of the Spanish prelates, could have possessed the force of law. The reason would be that some of them appear to be contrary to the customs and discipline of the Spanish Church. An example is the very letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops of Lucania mentioned above, which, as we have already noted, is numbered eighty-four in our genuine collection. In title XXVII of that letter it is reproved that some presume, without the command of the Apostolic See, to consecrate churches or oratories that have been built, although among the Spaniards the right to consecrate churches existed without the permission or command of the Apostolic See; indeed, no bishop or priest of the Spanish Church is known ever to have sought permission from the Roman pontiff to consecrate sacred buildings.

But this objection, although it may at first sight appear plausible, has no force. The aforesaid letter of Pope Gelasius was written to the bishops of Churches subject to the Roman See not as to the head of the Church but as to their metropolitan. The Spanish prelates, understanding this correctly, admitted it into their collection of canons in this sense: just as the bishops of Churches subject to the Roman See as their metropolitan were not permitted to consecrate churches without the command of that See, so Spanish bishops could not consecrate basilicas without the consent and authorization of their metropolitan. For metropolitans possess the same power over their suffragan bishops that the Apostolic See possesses over the suburban Churches subject to it as their metropolitan.

**156.** The authority exercised among the Spanish prelates by the decrees of the Roman prelates is demonstrated both by the many letters of those same prelates admitted into the Spanish collection and by the fact that the Spanish prelates often testify to it in general and provincial councils.

At the First Council of Braga, held in the year 561, after mention had been made of Pope Leo’s letter to the synod of Galicia, the following is added concerning Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus:

> “Bishop Lucretius said: ‘Your fraternity has rightly recalled the authority of the Apostolic See . . . The authority of the Apostolic See once addressed to Bishop Profuturus has been reread.’”

The Spaniards’ religious observance in preserving the decrees of the Roman prelates is also most clearly declared by the first canon of the celebrated Third Council of Toledo, in these words:

> “Let the constitutions of all the councils remain in force, together with the synodical letters of the holy Roman prelates.”

Thus, after the Gothic people had renounced the perfidy of the Arian heresy, their first undertaking at this most holy council of all Spain appears to have been to signify their reverence, devotion, and obedience toward the Apostolic See. Later, with no less observance toward the Roman See, the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo decreed that the book of the Apocalypse should be received among the divine books, since, as they say, “the authority of many councils and the synodical decrees of the holy Roman prelates prescribe this.”

**157.** What more is needed? The genuine preface of blessed Isidore, placed before the councils of Greece in the celebrated Spanish collection of canons, clearly shows that the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs possessed among the Spaniards no less authority than the decrees of councils. The words of that preface are:

> “We also append the decrees of the Roman prelates, in which, because of the eminence of the Apostolic See, there exists an authority equal to that of councils.”

It would be difficult to say anything more precise or explicit concerning the dignity of the Apostolic See than these words.

**158.** Having therefore established the supreme authority of the Apostolic See over the Spanish Church by these documents, it remains for us to bring forward historical records that testify to the exercise of that See’s authority in Spain and declare the reciprocal intercourse maintained between the Spanish prelates and the Roman prelates. Before reviewing them, however, it seemed appropriate to offer a preliminary discussion of the falsity of the decretal letters fabricated as though they had been addressed to the bishops of Spain and falsely attributed to pontiffs who preceded Pope Siricius. The eminent Cardinal Aguirre, adopting a less accurate opinion, defended these decretals as genuine and admitted them into his great collection of the councils of Spain.

**159.** The first of these fabrications, in Aguirre, vol. I of the *Councils of Spain*, p. 163, is a letter of blessed Pope Anterus, bearing this title: “To our most dear brothers, the bishops established throughout the provinces of Baetica and Toledo.”

Apart from the many indications of falsity noted in this letter, the inscription itself presents a point of no small importance. In the time of Anterus—that is, in the year 238—the province of Toledo did not yet exist. Toledo, at that time certainly a less distinguished town, became a metropolis, according to the better opinion, only around the middle of the fifth century.

[Note: See Flórez, *Sacred Spain*, vol. V.]

Furthermore, the subject of the same letter, in which episcopal translations are discussed and declared lawful, exposes the impostor. Apart from the fact that it is improbable that Anterus, who scarcely completed a month of his pontificate, could have responded to a consultation from the Spaniards, the translation of bishops was so strictly prohibited by the canons that during the first six centuries of the Church we have no trace of such translations. The examples that the impostor adduces concerning the bishops Eusebius and Felix are fictitious and entirely unknown to ecclesiastical historians.

Indeed, concerning the strict observance of the ancient discipline in such matters, the letter of Pope Hilary to the bishops of Tarragona, numbered seventy-seven in our collection of canons, provides us with an excellent example, further confirming both the falsity of Anterus’s letter and the impostor’s shamelessness. In the year 465 the bishops of Tarragona humbly asked Pope Hilary by letter to confirm the transfer of Bishop Irenaeus, which they themselves had approved for a just cause. But Hilary, after consulting the Roman council, answered them with the utmost severity in these words:

> “In contempt of these, that provision too is despised by a proud spirit which provides that no one, after abandoning his own church, may presume to transfer to another. Bishop Irenaeus is attempting to do this, while you most shamefully connive and, more grievously still, give your approval; and you seek to strengthen it by our authority, although you show yourselves especially inflamed with great indignation against unlawful acts.”

[Col. 0905D] **160.** Finally, the words that the forger excerpted from Jerome, Gregory the Great, Isidore, and other authors much later than Anterus testify that this letter is spurious.

**161.** Learned men rightly regard as of equally defective credibility the letter of Pope Lucius addressed to the bishops of Gaul and Spain, which appears in the aforementioned Aguirre, vol. I of the *Councils of Spain*, p. 195. For, to omit other matters, it contains many things patched together from Pope Leo, Gregory the Great, and other documents later than Lucius.

[Note: Pope Lucius is believed to have occupied the Roman episcopate from 256 to 257.]

[Col. 0906A] **162.** Likewise, the letter of Pope Sixtus II, entitled “To our most beloved brothers established throughout the provinces of Spain,” is rightly counted among the spurious letters, because it contains many things contrary to the decrees of the sacred canons concerning the judgments of bishops and also includes statements copied from more recent authors. It appears in Aguirre, vol. I, p. 213.

**163.** Next, in the same Aguirre, vol. I, p. 218, there appears a letter of Pope Dionysius, who held the episcopate of the Roman See from the year of the Lord 261 to 273, addressed to a certain Bishop Severus. Its falsity is demonstrated by several features, but especially by the words concerning the Churches of the province of Córdoba. From where did the impostor derive the claim that Córdoba was a metropolis in the time of Pope Dionysius? We find Spain divided by the best authorities into five provinces: Carthaginensis, Baetica—with Córdoba in it—Lusitania, Tarraconensis, and Galicia. But concerning a province of Córdoba there is not a word.

The reason why the forger wrote this is obvious: in the time of pseudo-Isidore, Córdoba was most famous under Moorish rule and was the capital of the Cordoban kingdom. I omit the fact that, as usual, the compiler also inserts material directed against accusers of bishops.

[Col. 0906B] **164.** There is also, in the aforementioned Aguirre, vol.
