I, p. 221, a certain letter attributed to Pope Eutychianus and addressed to John and all the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica—though what could have been accomplished in so short a time, and what of the province of Córdoba? Nearly the entire letter consists of words taken from Hilary and Leo; for this reason, in the judgment of learned men, it is placed among the spurious letters.

[Note: Eutychianus held the episcopate of the Roman Church from the year of the Lord 275 to 284.]

**165.** Finally, in vol. II, p. 70, of the same Aguirre, there appears a letter of Pope Melchiades, believed to have occupied the See from the year of the Lord 311 to 314, addressed to Marinus, Benedictus, Leontius, and the other bishops of Spain. In it the impostor repeatedly recites the same claims concerning the judgments of bishops and appeals to the Roman See as in the preceding forged letters:

> “Do not judge bishops,” he says; “do not condemn them without the authority of this See. If you do so, your judgments will be void and you will be condemned.” And below: “But if any one of you sees himself oppressed, let him appeal to this See; let him return here, as has always been the established custom.”

I omit the other matters that prove this letter, attributed to Pope Melchiades, to be spurious.

[Col. 0906D] **166.** Thus far we have discussed the decretal letters found in Aguirre’s *Collection of the Councils of Spain*, attributed to the earliest Roman pontiffs who preceded Siricius, and judged by the most learned men to have been fabricated by pseudo-Isidore around the beginning of the ninth century. For if the aforesaid letters had truly been sent by such holy pontiffs to the provinces of Spain, they would not have lain unknown to the Fathers of the Spanish Church during the first eight centuries, nor would Isidore of Seville—who collected the letters of the Roman prelates, especially those addressed to the Spaniards, with the greatest diligence—have passed them over in silence.

But let us turn to the genuine documents, which clearly show that the Spanish Church was steadfast in preserving the force of ecclesiastical discipline, observed the Roman prelate with the greatest reverence, and often consulted him as supreme judge and head of the Catholic Church in difficult matters.

To proceed more correctly in reviewing these matters, we shall endeavor, as far as possible, to assign each one to its proper time.

**167.** In the year 258, Basilides, bishop of León, and Martial, bishop of Astorga, were accused as *libellatici* and of the crime of idolatry. By the judgment of a provincial synod they were expelled from their sees, and Felix and Sabinus were substituted in their places.

[Note: *Libellatici* were those who, by offering a gift or money, requested certificates from pagan magistrates so that they would not be compelled to sacrifice or approach the altars of the devil. Such Christians were branded with disgrace because they were ashamed to profess the Catholic faith. See Mendoza’s commentary on canon III of the Council of Elvira concerning this matter.]

Basilides, adding crime to crime, went to Rome and obtained from Pope Stephen—whether he knew the truth I do not know—through deception, admission back into communion. Returning to Spain, he attempted, by Stephen’s decision, to recover the episcopate into which Sabinus had been legitimately appointed.

The Spanish prelates, disturbed by this affair, consulted blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. After examining the matter in a council, he replied that everything had been done lawfully and canonically and that Sabinus’s duly performed ordination could not be rescinded, notwithstanding the judgment of Pope Stephen, who had been craftily deceived by Basilides:

> “Nor can he rescind,” Cyprian says, “a lawful ordination properly completed, because Basilides, after his crimes had been exposed and his conscience laid bare even by his own confession, went to Rome and deceived our colleague Stephen, who was far away and ignorant of the facts and of the concealed truth, so that he might solicit his unjust restoration to the episcopate from which he had been justly deposed.”

Saint Cyprian, Letter 68.

**168.** It is clear from this that the Spanish prelates reverently observed the authority of the Apostolic See. Otherwise they would not have been disturbed by the judgment of Pope Stephen, nor would they have consulted Cyprian of Carthage in Africa. Cyprian’s judgment also makes clear that one is not bound by the decision of a pontiff to whom an appeal has been made contrary to the provisions of the canons. The eventual outcome of this affair, however, is unknown.

**169.** In the year of the Lord 353, Pope Liberius warned Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, by letter concerning the lapse of Vincent, the legate who had subscribed to the condemnation of Saint Athanasius.

**170.** In the year 385, Siricius, bishop of the Roman See, replied in fifteen chapters or statutes to the consultation that Eumerius, bishop of Tarragona, had sent to Pope Damasus. These chapters discuss Arians converted to the Catholic faith, who are not to be rebaptized; apostates; penitents; monks; and clerics. This decretal letter of Siricius is numbered third in our collection.

**171.** Around the year 402, while Innocent I was governing the Roman Church, Hilary the bishop and Elpidius the priest, both Spaniards, went to Rome so that they might provide a remedy for the grave evils from which the Spanish Church was suffering: its peace had been disturbed, the provisions of the canons despised, and the rules of the holy Fathers disregarded.

After hearing their requests and carefully examining the matter, Innocent addressed a letter to the Fathers of the First Council of Toledo. Concerned for the integrity of the discipline of the ancient Church, he established in various chapters that bishops converted to the faith should be received into communion; that ordinations performed contrary to the provisions of the canons should in future be prohibited; and that the Nicene rules should be observed. Finally, he explained more fully which men were to be excluded from orders and which were to be chosen.

**172.** In the year 447, blessed Pope Leo I sent a celebrated letter to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, against the errors of the Priscillianists, which at that time were seriously disturbing the peace of the Spanish Church. In this letter he commands Turibius to summon a general council, or at least a provincial council, to apply an appropriate remedy to such great evils:

> “Let an episcopal council be held among you,” he says, “and let the priests of the neighboring provinces assemble at a place convenient for all.”

And below:

> “But if some persons, God forbid, should prevent a general council from being held, let at least the priests of Galicia assemble together.”

**173.** In the year 454, Pope Leo likewise warned the bishops of Gaul and Spain by letter concerning the day on which the Paschal solemnity was to be celebrated in the following year.

**174.** In the year 465, Ascanius of Tarragona and the other bishops of that province humbly complained by letter to Pope Hilary about Silvanus, bishop of Calahorra, because, contrary to the rules of the holy Fathers and the provisions of the canons, and disregarding their fraternal admonition, he was not ashamed to ordain bishops.

[Note: The Spanish prelates profess their reverence and supreme veneration toward the See of Peter in these words:

> “Even if there existed a necessity of ecclesiastical discipline, we ought truly to have sought that privilege of your See by which, after the keys of the kingdom had been received following the Savior’s resurrection, the singular preaching of blessed Peter looked toward the illumination of all throughout the world. Just as the primacy of his vicar stands preeminent, so it is to be feared and loved by all.”]

**175.** In the same year they wrote a second letter to the same Hilary, in which, as we have mentioned above, they humbly begged him to confirm by his authority the transfer of Bishop Irenaeus to the See of Barcelona, which they themselves had approved.

After these letters had been reread and examined at the Roman council, Hilary, writing back to Ascanius and the other bishops of the province of Tarragona, decreed the following statutes:

1. No bishop is to be ordained without the consent of the metropolitan.
2. No bishop is to leave his own church and transfer to another.
3. Irenaeus, removed from the See of Barcelona, is to return to his own.
4. Bishops who have been illicitly ordained are to be removed, and two bishops are not to be appointed in one church.
5. If Irenaeus does not return to his own church, he is to be removed from the fellowship of the bishops.

**176.** Around the year 480, Simplicius entrusted his authority to Zeno, prelate of the city of Seville, as is evident from the letter preserved in our collection under number 79.

177. Felix wrote to the same Zeno, bishop of Seville, around the year 484, a letter full of courtesy and honor, commending to him a certain Terentianus, a very distinguished man returning to Spain.

178. In the year 517, Hormisdas writes that he had gladly heard of John, bishop of the Church of Ilici, coming to Italy, and entrusts him with his authority, while nevertheless preserving the privileges of the metropolitans.

179. In the following years the same Hormisdas sent a decretal letter to the bishops established throughout Spain, in which the following provisions are laid down:

1. Priests are to be ordained according to the canons.
2. No payment is to be accepted for the episcopate.
3. A council is to be held every year.

[Col. 0909C]

He then wrote another letter to the same bishops, in which he congratulates them on the peace of the Church both in Spain and in the East, and sends them the profession of John, bishop of Constantinople.

180. Around the same time, the aforesaid Hormisdas appointed Sallustius, bishop of Seville, as Apostolic vicar throughout Baetica and Lusitania, and congratulated the bishops of Baetica on their peace and concord.

181. In the year 538, Pope Vigilius replied by letter to the consultations of Profuturus, bishop of Braga; in it he laid down various provisions chiefly concerning the errors of the Priscillianists. This letter of Vigilius—which, as stated above [Col. 0909D], was reread in the First Council of Braga—is found, together with the preceding letters of Hormisdas, in our collection, nos. 91 and 98.

182. In the year 589, when the Gothic people, in the presence of King Flavius Reccared, renounced the impiety of the Arians at the Third Council of Toledo and were converted to the Catholic faith, blessed Gregory sent Leander, bishop of Seville, a letter full of goodwill. In it he complains of the many labors of his pastoral care by which he was burdened; he rejoices exceedingly at King Reccared’s conversion; and he responds to a consultation concerning the threefold immersion in baptism. [Col. 0910A] Finally, he sends him the book of the *Pastoral Rule* and his *Exposition of Job*.

183. The same Gregory, writing back to the aforesaid Leander, sent him the pallium for use only at the solemn celebrations of Mass. He amicably complains of the great cares with which he was occupied and of the loss of the tranquility of monastic life. “For,” he says, “I seemed to be sailing with a favorable wind when I was leading a tranquil life in the monastery; but suddenly a storm arose with violent disturbances and carried me away in its upheaval, and I lost the prosperity of my journey, because, having lost the mind’s repose, I suffered shipwreck.”

184. Gregory also composed a letter to King Reccared, in which he praises him highly because through his agency the Gothic people had been converted to the Catholic faith, and because he had not altered the constitution which he had issued [Col. 0910B] against the Jews, although they offered him a large sum of money. The letter also concerns the gifts sent by Reccared himself to Saint Peter, and contains many other matters, especially pertaining to the instruction of rulers, which are exceedingly worthy of reading.

185. Around the same time, the aforesaid Gregory commended to Claudius, a minister of the king, a monk named Cyriacus by letter.

186. These, indeed, are the letters of blessed Gregory the Great inserted in our collection of canons. Those found in Aguirre’s *Maxima Collectio*, vol. II, pp. 409 ff., which deal with the case of a certain Januarius, bishop of Málaga, are rightly counted by highly learned men among the apocrypha. Indeed, the profound silence of the historians of Spain, especially of [Col. 0910C] blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, concerning this matter confirms the falsity of such letters. For it must be noted that Málaga, a city of the province of Baetica, was subject to Seville; and since at that time our Isidore was metropolitan of Baetica, he could not have been unaware of so notable a case involving his suffragan. Nor does it seem plausible that Gregory the Great would have judged the case of the bishop of Málaga against the discipline of the Church and the privileges of metropolitans, without consulting Isidore.

187. From the time of Gregory the Great until the pontificate of Leo II—that is, over the course of almost an entire century—we possess no letter, at least none that survives, sent by a Roman prelate to the Spanish Fathers. This will seem all the more remarkable [Col. 0910D] because, throughout this period, several most celebrated councils were held in Spain under its most holy metropolitans.

188. Finally, in the year 684, Pope Leo II sent the Spanish prelates the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, held at Constantinople under Pope Agatho against the Monothelites, who maintained that there is one will and only one operation in Christ, inviting them to disseminate throughout Spain, supported by canonical authority, the acts he had sent.

> **Note:** [Col. 0909D] Canon 2 of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo declares this in these words: “In the gracious course of whose letter, all the prelates of Spain were also invited to this end [Col. 0910D]: that the aforesaid synodal decrees which he had sent might remain supported by the authority [Col. 0911C] of our own firmness, and might be openly published to all who live under the rule of Spain.”

189. But when the acts of this Sixth Ecumenical Synod [Col. 0911A], together with the letters of the aforesaid Leo II written to King Ervig and to Count Simplicius, had been brought into Spain at the very time when the Thirteenth Council of Toledo had already been dismissed, it seemed exceedingly harsh to blessed Julian, metropolitan of the Church of Toledo, to summon the dismissed Fathers again while the severe cold of winter held them rigid. Therefore he endeavored to bring together the suffragan bishops along with the vicars of the metropolitan sees, so that they might meet in one assembly, approve the acts of the aforesaid Sixth Ecumenical Synod insofar as they did not depart from what had preceded it, and, once approved, publish them throughout Spain.

> **Note:** [Col. 0911D] Cardinal Baronius not only doubts the authenticity of these letters but also attempts to prove that they are spurious. Pagius, however, has already shown that he did so less correctly and with weaker arguments, in his discussion of the year 683, no. 8 and following. For the rest, I would readily believe that the aforesaid Baronius would have judged otherwise had he had the manuscript codices of our collection at hand. For that learned man would not have declared that the letters in question were different from those mentioned in the Fourteenth Council of Toledo on the grounds that, as he says, these letters state that what was sent to Spain was not the synodal acts themselves, but only the synod’s definition, the emperor’s edict, and the synodal acclamatory address—a very small part of the acts. In the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, however, the bishops testify that they received, together with Leo’s letters, the complete synodal proceedings. This argument collapses entirely from inspection of the manuscripts [Col. 0912C] of our collection alone, into which the Fathers of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo ordered these synodal acts to be entered. In the manuscripts in question, only the synod’s definition is present, which is the smallest part of the acts; and at its conclusion the aforesaid letters of Leo II are consistently found. Together with the synod’s definition, they are written [Col. 0912D] in a continuous series of numbers and form, as it were, a single body.

190. Meanwhile blessed Julian composed a short work entitled *Apology of the Faith* concerning the acts [Col. 0911B] of the aforesaid Sixth Ecumenical Synod. He sent it to Rome through Peter the *Regionarius*, who had brought these same synodal acts and the letters of Leo II into Spain, to Benedict II, who, after the death of Pope Leo, had assumed the headship of the Roman see.

191. This apologetic work of blessed Julian, which was reread at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, was decreed by the Fathers of that council to possess the same honor and reverence as the decretal letters, in these words:

> “Therefore, we confirm with a similar force of honor and reverence those apologetic responses of our defense which were issued for the confirmation of these matters, for the instruction of many and the benefit of ecclesiastical discipline; and we decree that they are [Col. 0911C] to remain in the place of decretal letters.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0912D] Fourteenth Council of Toledo, canon 11.

192. But when Benedict II, the Roman pontiff, indicated that certain passages in the aforesaid work of blessed Julian seemed to him to have been written with insufficient caution, especially those in which it asserts that there are three substances in Christ, the Fathers of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, displeased by this criticism, composed a fuller exposition of this doctrine, clearly explained and strengthened by testimonies of the holy Fathers, and inserted it into the acts of that council.

In their exposition of the doctrine of the three substances in Christ, the aforesaid Fathers [Col. 0912A] respond firmly and vigorously in these words:

> “Proceeding also to reconsider the second chapter, in which the same Pope thought that we had incautiously said that we profess three substances in Christ, the Son of God: just as we shall not be ashamed to defend what is true, so perhaps some will be ashamed to be ignorant of what is true.”

At the conclusion of this chapter, these no less forceful words are read:

> “But if, after these things, they disagree in any respect with the very doctrines of the Fathers from whom these statements were brought forth, there is no longer any need to contend with them. Rather, adhering directly to the footsteps of our ancestors, our response to the lovers of truth will be exalted through divine judgment, even if by ignorant adversaries it is judged unlearned.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0912D] Although these two expressions can be pronounced correctly and in a Catholic sense—“Christ consists of two substances” and “Christ consists of three substances”—the Fathers of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo judged the latter preferable. Since this manner of speaking is now unusual, however, it seemed to some insufficiently learned people to be opposed to the Catholic faith. Not long ago, certain half-learned persons judged that this same sound doctrine ought to be erased as alien to the Catholic faith, although it had been clearly and lucidly explained in the following stanza by the most learned and celebrated Spanish poet Lope de Vega:

> *Being three natures—*  
> *Body, Divinity, and Soul—*  
> *Composed in one person.*

193. These statements seemed to many somewhat harsher than was fitting for [Col. 0912B] the Spaniards’ respect toward the Roman prelate. Nevertheless, Benedict II did not consider himself offended by them; indeed, he piously accepted and approved the doctrine of the Toledo Fathers and, giving thanks, exclaimed, according to Roderic: “Your praise, O Lord, reaches to the ends of the earth.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0912D] Roderic, *Chronicle*, book III, chapter 13.

194. These are, in their entirety, the historical records concerning the dealings of the Roman prelates with the Spaniards that are found during the first eleven centuries of the Church. They declare that the supreme authority of the Apostolic See was acknowledged by the Spanish Fathers. Although [Col. 0912C] it is clear that the Spaniards were always devoted and conscientious observers of the discipline handed down by their ancestors, the foregoing nevertheless shows how religiously they followed the decrees of the Roman prelates and how greatly they regarded it as an honor to show themselves most observant toward the Roman See.

195. These, finally, are the matters I had to say concerning the true origin, formation, and excellence of Isidore of Seville’s genuine collection of canons—perhaps more than is suitable for a preface, but matters which I nevertheless judged useful so that it might be understood how unjustly Isidore, that most distinguished doctor of Spain, and Spain herself are accused by many of having fabricated the fictitious collection of Mercator. Rather, it must be acknowledged—as is evident from our collection—that the Church of Spain surpasses the others in preserving genuine records and rejecting false ones. For the canons of the Apostles, admitted into the canonical books of other Churches, including the Roman Church, are classified by our Spaniard among the apocrypha and rejected from the body of the canons.

196. Moreover, by many and not at all weak arguments, we have vindicated Spain and the Spaniards from the accusation that the decretal letters are false and interpolated. Indeed, we have demonstrated that the Spanish Church may rightly take pride both in other matters and especially in its collection of canons.

First, from the description given above of the principal manuscript codices of this Spanish collection of ours, it will be evident at first sight to anyone that it is both the most excellent and the most complete of all the ancient collections: in the abundance and authority of its records, and in the sound arrangement of its order, it easily surpasses all the others. Moreover, from the information concerning the Arabic codex it is not difficult to understand how conscientious the Spanish prelates were in preserving the canons, even under the harshest rule of a barbarous people.

197. We then discussed the ancient canonical codex of the Spanish Church, as well as the origin and development of our collection. We established, with arguments not to be rejected, that blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, compiled it perhaps following the example of Dionysius Exiguus, but by a method far superior.

198. By no weaker arguments we showed that the spurious collection of Pseudo-Isidore was fabricated neither in Spain nor by a Spaniard, but rather in the Franco-Gallic empire during the time of Charlemagne, by some impostor—perhaps an associate of Ricuffus of Mainz—constructed upon the foundation of the genuine Isidorian collection.

199. Finally, we established from the records of the Spanish collection itself that the Spanish Church always acknowledged the supreme authority of the Apostolic See. If anything has been said by me in this preface with insufficient caution, I wish it to be regarded as unsaid, and I submit everything to the Roman See, which I acknowledge and revere as the head of the Catholic Church.

## Volume back matter

[Col. 0913]

# INDEX OF THE MATTERS AND SUBJECTS CONTAINED IN THIS COLLECTION OF CANONS

The numbers correspond to those represented in the text in heavier type. (C)

[Col. 0913] **A**

**Abbot.** He is to show his bishop the utmost humility and reverence. Council of Mérida, 672. He is not to preside over two monasteries. Councils of Epaon, 262, and Agde, 241.

**Abbots.** They are to be under the authority of the bishops. First Council of Orléans, 248. [Col. 0913] They are not to receive monks belonging to another monastery. First Council of Orléans, 248. Individual abbots are forbidden to possess different cells or several monasteries. Council of Agde, 238. They are not to conduct sales without the bishop’s knowledge. Council of Agde, 241.

**Washing of the feet.** It is to be performed on the Lord’s Supper. Seventeenth Council of Toledo, 591.

**Abortion.** Those who cause an abortion, or destroy their newborn children, are to receive communion after seven years. Council of Elvira, 313.

**Acacius.** No share in the injury is to affect those baptized or ordained by him after his condemnation. Letter of Anastasius to the Emperor Anastasius, 138. His letter to Simplicius, 125. His name is specifically to be silenced in the church. Letter of Anastasius to the Emperor Anastasius, 137.

**Accuser.** In court, it must be investigated what sort of faith he possesses. Fourth Council of Carthage, 152. No one is to be condemned without a legitimate accuser. Sixth Council of Toledo, 406.

**Accusers.** Accusers of their brethren are to be deprived of communion. Second Council of Arles, 202. Slaves are not to be admitted for the accusation of clerics. Seventh Council of Carthage, 179. They are not to be heard in minor cases, but are to be examined in criminal cases. First Council of Vaison, 226. False accusers of their brethren are to be excommunicated until death. First Council of Arles, 196. Those implicated in crimes are not to accuse clerics. Second Council of Carthage, 122. Anyone who accuses a cleric and does not prove the charge is to be excommunicated. Second Council of Braga, 611. Those who falsely accuse priests or ministers are not to receive communion even at the end of life. Council of Elvira, 293. If they bring forward many charges and cannot prove the first matter they brought forward, they are no longer to be admitted to the others. Seventh Council of Carthage, 179.

**Acolytes.** How they are to be made or ordained. Fourth Council of Carthage, 142. See *Clerics*, *Cleric*, *Clergy*.

**Adulterer.** A man is judged such if, after a repudiation has intervened, he has undergone divorce and then entered into a marriage. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, bishop, 18.

**Adulteress.** Communion is denied to an adulterous wife. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, bishop, 17. The husband of an adulterous wife may not become a cleric. Council of Neocaesarea, 25.

**Adulterers.** They are to do penance for seven years. Council of Ancyra, 22, and Second Council of Braga, 627.

**Adultery.** Husbands who are aware of their wives’ adultery, if they do not leave them, are not to receive communion even at the end of life. Council of Elvira, 292. Married men or women who afterward fall into adultery are to do penance for five years. Council of Elvira, 292. Husbands are not to associate with adulterous wives. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, bishop, 17. See *Fornication*.

**Agape.** The agape of the brethren is not to be despised. Council of Gangra, 30. It is not permitted to hold an agape in churches. Council of Laodicea, 54.

**Aggarus.** Concerning Aggarus and Tiberianus, who were ordained from the laity. Letter of Leo to the Africans, 115.

**Alipius, bishop.** His response concerning the search for authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea. Sixth Council of Carthage, 161.

**Altar.** Concerning those who presume to strip altars or remove the lights of the church. Thirteenth Council of Toledo, 518. It is to be anointed and blessed. [Col. 0914] Council of Agde, 233. It is not to be anointed unless it is made of stone. Council of Epaon, 264. No one from among the readers may carry the sacred vessels of the altar. First Council of Braga, 604.

**The insane.** Whatever works of piety are appropriate are to be provided for those who are mentally deranged. Council of Orange, 220.

**Emperor Anastasius.** He is admonished to obey the constitutions of the Apostolic See. Letter of Anastasius to the Emperor Anastasius, 138. Pope Anastasius urges him to admonish the Alexandrian bishops to return to sincere faith and Catholic peace. Letter of Anastasius to the Emperor Anastasius, 138.

**Pope Anastasius.** Letter sent to the Emperor Anastasius for the peace of the Churches, 136.

**Anatolius.** His faith was approved by writings sent to Pope Leo, 68.

**Soul.** Those who say that the human soul is of the divine substance are to be condemned. Letter of Leo to Turibius of Astorga, 91. Those who believe that souls sin in the heavens and, according to the quality of their sin, receive either a good or a bad lot in this world are to be condemned. Letter of the same to the same, 93. Those who say that human souls are bound by the stars of fate are to be condemned. Letter of the same to the same, 93. Those who assign parts of the soul to one set of powers and bodily members to another are to be condemned. Letter of the same to the same, 93.

**Apostates.** They are to be separated from the Church. Letter of Siricius to Himerius, 4. Catholics who pass into heresy may, if they return, be admitted to communion after ten years of penance. Council of Elvira, 285. Faithful apostates may receive communion after ten years. Council of Elvira, 289. Those who have fallen away in faith are to do penance for two years. Council of Epaon, 264. Those who pass from the Catholic faith into heresy are to undergo two years of penance [Col. 0915], in addition to the penalties established by earlier canons. Council of Agde, 212. Those who, after baptism, sacrifice to idols are not to receive communion even at the end of life. Council of Elvira, 281. Those who return late are not to be received except through worthy penance. First Council of Arles, 197. If they have been converted, reconciliation is not to be denied them. Third Council of Carthage, 132. If they do not return, they are not to be admitted to clerical office. Second Council of Arles, 202.

**Arians.** What is to be observed concerning those who are rebaptized by Arians. Letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, 155. The churches of the Arians are to belong to the Catholic bishop in whose diocese they are located. Third Council of Toledo, 350.

**Asylum.** A cleric who drags away a slave or pupil taking refuge in a church is to do penance. Council of Lérida, 314. Concerning adulterers who take refuge in a church. First Council of Orléans, 245. Concerning thieves who take refuge in a church. Same council, 245. Concerning those who flee for refuge to a church. Twelfth Council of Toledo, 500. Concerning murderers who take refuge in a church. First Council of Orléans, 245. Concerning kidnappers who take refuge in a church. Same council, 245. Concerning slaves who take refuge in a church. Same council, 245. Freedmen are to be defended by the church in necessity. Council of Agde, 236. Freedmen who have been entrusted to the church are not to be oppressed. Council of Orange, 219. Slaves who flee for refuge to a church are not to be seized. Same council, ibid. Those who flee for refuge to a church are not to be handed over. Same council, ibid.

**Atticus, bishop of Constantinople.** His *formata* letter. Council of Chalcedon, 113. His letter to the Sixth Synod of Carthage. Sixth Council of Carthage, 168.

**Augurs.** They are to be separated from the church assembly. Fourth Council of Carthage, 151. Those who observe auguries are to be separated from the Church. Council of Agde, 238.

**Augustine (Saint), bishop.** His promise concerning the preservation of the Council of Nicaea. Sixth Council of Carthage, 163. A remarkable statement praising him. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 43.

**Aurelius, bishop.** His address to the Sixth Synod of Carthage. Sixth Council of Carthage, 159. His letter to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome. Sixth Council of Carthage, 165.

**Charioteers.** While they are driving, they are excommunicated. First Council of Arles, 195. They and pantomimes are to be received if they are converted. Council of Elvira, 291. As long as they practice their profession, they are to be separated from communion. Second Council of Arles, 202.

**Unleavened bread.** It is not to be received when sent by Jews. Council of Laodicea, 56.

**B**

**Ballematiae.** They are forbidden on the birthdays of the saints. Third Council of Toledo, 355.

**Baptism.** *The person to be baptized; the baptized person*, and so forth. It is to be conferred upon the sick who are no longer able to speak. Third Council of Carthage, 132. Concerning children who have fallen into captivity and do not remember receiving the grace of baptism. Letter of Leo to Leo, 117. Concerning threefold and single immersion in baptism. Fourth Council of Toledo, 367. Threefold immersion in baptism is not rejected. Letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, 155. Baptism is forbidden on the day of Epiphany. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily, 97. Baptism is to be conferred in the name of the Trinity. Letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, 156. Baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated. First Council of Carthage, 115. Baptism is not to be given to the dead. [Col. 0915] Third Council of Carthage, 127. Regeneration through baptism is not to be conferred at every time, but only at Easter and Pentecost, unless a dangerous illness has intervened. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Campania, 119. Infants are not to be admitted to baptism except during the three weeks before Easter. Second Council of Braga, 623. No one is to be admitted to baptism after the second week of Lent. Council of Laodicea, 56. Baptism is to be given only at Easter and the Nativity of the Lord. Council of Gerunda, 300. A presbyter or deacon who has suspended himself from the Eucharist on account of some offense may, in a case of necessity, confer baptism upon one who requests it. First Council of Orléans, 247. Baptism is not to be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost. Letter of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, 4. Those who, compelled by force or fear, have inclined their minds toward rebaptism are to be assisted by the remedy of penance. Letter of Leo to Nicetas, 112. Those who immediately after baptism present themselves for the clergy are not to be advanced immediately, but only at the appointed time, to the presbyterate or episcopate. Council of Nicaea, 1. That in baptism death may take place through the destruction of sin, and that the threefold immersion may imitate burial, while the raising from the waters may be like resurrection from the tomb. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily, 98. Two times, namely Easter and Pentecost, have been legitimately appointed by the Roman pontiff for baptizing. Letter of the same to the same, 99. Those to be baptized are to learn the Creed. Council of Laodicea, 57. Concerning the baptism of pregnant women. Council of Neocaesarea, 25, and Second Council of Braga, 623. Infants are to be baptized if absolutely certain witnesses cannot be found to testify that they have already been baptized. Fifth Council of Carthage, 156. No fees are to be demanded for baptizing and consigning the faithful. General Decree of Gelasius, 131. Those who are to be baptized are to give their names. Fourth Council of Carthage, 150. Those baptized by the Donatists, if they have been converted to the Church of God, are to be advanced to the ministry of the sacred altar. Second Council of Carthage, 138. The baptized are not to be confirmed except by bishops. Letter of Innocent to Decentius, 11. The baptized who die before receiving confirmation may be counted righteous in the faith in which they believed. Council of Elvira, 294. The baptized who afterward have taken part in the banquets of the gentiles and eaten sacrificial foods may be cleansed by fasts and the laying on of hands. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 106. One baptized by heretics is to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. Letter of Leo to Leo, 117. The clergy are to receive nothing for baptizing. Council of Elvira, 289. No one is to receive a reward for baptizing. Second Council of Braga, 611. The recently baptized are to live chastely. Fourth Council of Carthage, 151. Those baptized by heretics are to be strengthened solely through invocation of the Holy Spirit. Letter of Leo to Nicetas, 112. Those who are uncertain whether they have been baptized must be baptized. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 106. Those baptized during illness are not to be ordained. Council of Neocaesarea, 26. Those who acknowledge that they were baptized but do not know under what profession are to be received through the laying on of hands. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 106. Gentiles may be baptized in danger. Council of Elvira, 288. In necessity, the faithful are also to baptize. Same council, ibid. Those who come from the Novatians or Montanists are not to be rebaptized. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 14. No one is to omit the order of baptism. First Council of Braga, 603. No minister is to set out to baptize without chrism. Council of Orange, 219. Outside the Easter season or Pentecost, no one is to presume to baptize except those whom extreme illness has compelled. [Col. 0916] General Decree of Gelasius, 132. Children who have been rebaptized through ignorance of their age are to be kept for some time under the laying on of hands, and communion is then to be restored to them. Letter of Felix to the bishops throughout Sicily, 127. Those who have been baptized or rebaptized by heretics are not to attain ecclesiastical service. Letter of the same to the same, ibid. Those who come to the faith are to be baptized after two years. Council of Elvira, 288. Those baptized during illness, once they recover, are to be taught the Creed of the faith. Council of Laodicea, 57. Those pressed by the necessity of death—that is, by illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck—are to be baptized at any time. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily, 99. Those who are rebaptized are to pray among the catechumens for seven years. Council of Lérida, 314. Those rebaptized who regretted it and afterward refused to repent are to be questioned whether they joined in the deed or approached it under compulsion. Letter of Felix to the bishops throughout Sicily, 126. Those who impiously offered themselves for rebaptism are to remain among the penitents for seven years. Letter of the same to the same, 127. An infant one day old is to be baptized if in danger. Council of Gerunda, 300.

**Baptistery.** A presbyter may not enter the baptistery before the bishop. Second Council of Braga, 623. The doors of the holy baptistery are to be closed at the beginning of Lent by the bishop’s hand, with the completion of the episcopal praises. Seventeenth Council of Toledo, 591.

**Basilica.** Basilicas of heretics cannot be applied to sacred uses. Council of Epaon, 265. Basilicas are to remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are located. First Council of Orléans, 247. Basilicas built by laypeople are to be erected with the bishop’s approval. Council of Lérida, 313. To which bishop newly constructed basilicas belong. Fourth Council of Toledo, 378. No basilica built in the name of the dead is to be dedicated. General Decree of Gelasius, 134. New basilicas are not to be dedicated without the bishop’s authorization. Same decree, 131. If no body or relics of martyrs are proven to have been buried in them, they are to be demolished by the bishops. Fifth Council of Carthage, 158.

**Benedict the presbyter.** His letter to Peter the regional notary. Second Council of Constantinople, 14.

**Bigamists.** They are not to be admitted to clerical ministry. General Decree of Gelasius, 131. They are not to be advanced to the presbyterate or diaconate. Second Council of Seville, 611. A bigamist, or the husband of a widow or a corrupted woman, is not to approach the ecclesiastical orders. Decree of Hilary, 120. See *Digamists*.

**Pope Boniface.** His letter to the bishops of Gaul, concerning Maximus, a bishop accused of various crimes, 40. His letter to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, 41. His letter to Honorius Augustus, 38.

**Bonitiaci.** The Bonitiaci are to be received into the Church. Second Council of Arles, 201.

**Bonosus.** Those ordained by Bonosus the heretic are to be received. Letter of Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, 32.

**C**
### Chalice

The chalice is to be consecrated when the bread is consecrated. Council of Orange, 221.

### Canons

The Apostolic See preserves the paternal canons with pious and devoted zeal. General Decree of Gelasius, 132.

The provisions of the canons are to be observed. Decree of Hilary, 120.

On preserving the statutes of the canons. Letter of Leo to the Africans, 115.

They are to be observed. Council of Chalcedon, 98.

On the precepts of the ancient canons. Council of Braga I, 606.

### Canonical Women

It is not permitted for them to be established in the church as though they were ordained. Council of Laodicea, 52.

### Cantors

Those who sing and sacrifice to the Lord must always have appointed assistants after them. Council of Toledo XI, 484.

### Capitolium

The faithful are not to go up to the Capitol for the purpose of sacrificing. Council of Elvira, 291.

### Captives

Captives who have been compelled by terror or hunger, rather than by veneration, to eat sacrificial foods are to be granted penance. Letter of Leo to Nicetas, 112.

### Meats

On not tasting meats beforehand and not regarding them with abhorrence. Council of Braga II, 624.

On vegetables and meats. Council of Braga I, 604.

Those who condemn people for eating meat are to be anathematized. Council of Gangra, 29.

### Cataphrygians

If they flee to the Catholic Church, they are to be rebaptized. Council of Nicaea, 7.

If they convert to the Church, they are to be catechized and baptized. Council of Laodicea, 52.

### Female Catechumen

If she falls seriously ill, she is not to be deprived of baptism. Council of Elvira, 284.

### Catechumens

They are not to approach the baptistery. Council of Orange, 221.

Catechumens who have lapsed are to spend three years merely as hearers of the word. Council of Nicaea, 5.

For catechumens who die without receiving baptism’s redemption, neither commemoration in the offering nor the office of chanting psalms is to be provided. Council of Braga I, 605.

They are not to receive the blessing together with the faithful. Council of Orange, 221.

On catechumens who sin. Council of Neocaesarea, 25.

They are to hear the Gospels. Council of Orange, 221.

It is not permitted for clerical ordinations to take place in their presence. Council of Laodicea, 51.

Those who do not attend church may receive baptism. Council of Elvira, 289.

The sacrament is not to be given to them. Council of Carthage III, 127.

If they have had a deceased wife and, after baptism, have taken another, they are not to become clerics. Letter of Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, 31.

### Catholics

They are not to associate with the rebaptized. Council of Lérida, 315.

They are not to give their children for baptism to heretics. Council of Lérida, ibid.

They are not to be joined in marriage to heretics. Council of Agde, 243, and Council of Laodicea, 52.

They are not to enter those places which heretics call their martyr-shrines. Council of Laodicea, 52.

### Cases

On the distinction of cases. Council of Toledo IV, 377.

On the thirty-year period and the distinction of cases by provinces. Council of Toledo IV, 378.

In cases involving churches, executors or advocates are to be requested from the prince. Council of Milevis, 186.

### Legal Advocates

They are not to be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Innocent to the bishops in Toulouse, 34.

### Pope Celestine

His letter to the bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria, 49.

His letter to the bishops of Gaul, 42, 46.

### Candle

On blessing the candle and lamp during the vigils of Easter. Council of Toledo IV, 369.

### Chorepiscopi

They must be content with the care and governance of their own office, which they have undertaken. Council of Antioch, 45.

What their powers are. Council of Ancyra, 20.

### Chrism

On the blessing of chrism. Council of Braga I, 605.

On preparing chrism. Council of Braga II, 623.

It is not to be made by presbyters. Council of Carthage II, 121.

A presbyter may not sign infants with chrism while the bishop is present. [Col. 0917] Council of Braga II, 623.

Chrism is to be given after baptism. Council of Laodicea, 57.

No one except the bishop is to prepare chrism. Council of Toledo I, 326.

Presbyters may give chrism to heretics for the salvation of souls. Council of Epaon, 263.

When chrism is given to diocesan presbyters for confirming neophytes, nothing is to be accepted as payment for the liquid. Council of Barcelona II, 657.

### Christians

They are not to be gathered into assemblies of idolatry. Council of Laodicea, 55.

The banquets of Jews are forbidden to them. Council of Orléans II, 255.

When they go to weddings, they are not permitted either to sing or to dance. Council of Laodicea, 57.

They are not to marry Jews. Council of Clermont I, 269.

They are to avoid Jewish banquets. Council of Agde, 238.

They are not permitted to carry meals to tombs. Council of Braga II, 626.

They are not permitted to maintain pagan traditions or to observe the course of the moon or stars. Council of Braga II, ibid.

They are not permitted to attend to various superstitious observances. Council of Braga II, ibid.

None of them is permitted to bathe with women. Council of Laodicea, 55.

Those who eat with Jews are to be barred from communion. Council of Elvira, 289.

They ought not to observe the Sabbath. Council of Laodicea, 54.

If a Christian suffers tribulations for the Catholic faith, he is to be honored by the priests. Council of Carthage IV, 146.

### Christ

He became human without sin. Letter of Damasus to Paulinus, 1.

In time he was born from the Virgin. Letter of Damasus, ibid.

He is one, born before the ages from the Father. Letter of Damasus, ibid.

### The Belt of Secular Military Service

Whoever, after the remission of sins, has worn the belt of secular military service is not to be admitted to the clergy. Council of Telepte, 192.

### Clerics

They are in no way to be incited by the powerful of this world against their bishops. Council of Clermont I, 268.

Those deposed by their own bishop are not to appeal to the emperor. Council of Antioch, 45.

Those who withdraw from office are to be removed from it by the same authority. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

They are not to have access to virgins or widows except with fellow clerics, and never alone. Council of Carthage III, 131.

Accusers are to be excommunicated. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

They are not to undertake secular acts or procuratorships. Council of Carthage I, 117.

When invited to an agape, they are not to take portions away. Council of Laodicea, 54.

Those unable to work are to learn a craft and letters. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

Adulators are to be degraded from office. Council of Carthage IV, ibid.

They are not to come to the royal city without the permission of their bishop. Council of Chalcedon, 104.

Strangers are not to be received by one another. Council of Arles III, 204.

A stranger is not to be ordained in another’s church without the consent of his own bishop. Council of Nicaea, 6.

Clerics of another bishopric are not to be received. Council of Clermont I, 269.

Arians are not to be restored to their offices. Letter of Innocent to Alexander, 28.

They are not to grow their hair long or shave their beards. Council of Barcelona I, 655, and Carthage IV, 146.

They are not to be contractors or merchants. Council of Carthage III, 129.

Married men are not to become deacons unless they profess continence. Council of Orange, 222.

Those who despise the canons are to be deprived of honor. Council of Carthage I, 120.

Continence is commended to clerics and deacons. Council of Clermont I, 270.

The obstinate are to be deposed from their order. Council of Orléans II, 257.

The obstinate and those slow to perform their office are to be corrected by the bishops. Council of Agde, 229.

The obstinate and proud are to be restrained. Council of Carthage I, 118.

They are not to celebrate banquets of the sort commonly called *commissana*. [Col. 0918] Council of Laodicea, 58.

They are not to live with unrelated women. Council of Lérida, 315; Clermont I, 271; Clermont II, 273; Agde, 232; Carthage IV, 146.

They are not to live with unrelated men or women. Council of Carthage I, 116.

Condemnation of clerics who obtain ecclesiastical orders through money. Council of Toledo VI, 403.

On clerics who cohabit with women. Council of Seville I, 638.

On clerics who desert. Council of Braga II, 620, and Seville II, 640.

On excommunicated clerics. Council of Braga II, 621.

On clerics who consult magicians or soothsayers. Council of Toledo IV, 376.

On clerics who are excommunicated by their bishop through fault. Council of Turin, 210.

On clerics who rashly withdraw from the church. Council of Nicaea, 6.

On the conduct of clerics in receiving orders. Letter of Pope Siricius to Eumerius, 6.

On the conversion of clerics, so that they may be in one room. Council of Toledo IV, 375.

On their discipline and modesty. Council of Laodicea, 53.

On fornicator-clerics. Council of Braga II, 619.

On troublesome clerics. Council of Braga II, 621.

On ordained clerics who have lapsed. Council of Nicaea, 4.

On not receiving wandering clerics, and on invalidating the ordination of one ordained by another bishop without the consent of his own bishop. Council of Braga II, 620.

On the order in which deposed clerics are to be ordained again. Council of Toledo IV, 376.

On proven men who enter into a second marriage. Council of Orange, 222.

Digamous clerics are not to minister. Council of Agde, 229.

Those who disagree are to be brought to agreement by the bishop. Council of Carthage IV, 148.

Drunkenness is forbidden to clerics. Council of Agde, 238.

If their cases are not settled in the province, they are to be decided by the Apostolic See. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 14.

Their conspiracies are to be punished in synod. Council of Orléans II, 257.

Their stipends are not to be alienated from the right of the church. Council of Toledo IV, 403.

Their stipends are to be distributed according to merit. Council of Agde, 237.

And doorkeepers who associate with adulterous women are to be expelled from the clergy. Council of Tarragona, 297.

They are not to have children by concubines. Council of Orléans II, 254.

Excommunicated persons are to assert their innocence within the year of excommunication. Council of Carthage V, 157.

If persons excommunicated by their bishop go to another bishop, the latter ought not to grant them communion. Council of Sardica, 39.

They are not to have unrelated women in the house. Council of Elvira, 286.

Foreign clerics are not to linger at Thessalonica. Council of Sardica, 40.

Foreign clerics are not to minister without commendatory letters. Council of Chalcedon, 101.

Those convicted of false testimony are to be regarded as guilty of a capital crime. Council of Epaon, 263.

They are not to allow their sons to leave their authority unless the sons have been approved in age and character. Council of Carthage III, 129.

Usurers are to be excommunicated. Council of Arles I, 196.

They are to avoid the banquets and associations of heretics and schismatics. Council of Carthage IV, 149.

Honored adulterers are to be confined in a monastery for the whole of their lives. Council of Orléans II, 253.

Honored clerics who are discovered to have committed perjury are to be punished by two years of excommunication. Council of Orléans II, 254.

Honored clerics who commit theft or forgery are to be degraded from their order. Council of Orléans II, 253.

They are not to migrate to another city unless they have lost their own. Council of Chalcedon, 103.

They are not to receive communion in another church without letters from their bishop. Council of Carthage I, 117.

They are not to reside in another city. Council of Orléans II, [Col. 0919] 256.

They are not to remain in another city without necessity. Council of Carthage III, 132.

They are not to be ordained in another’s church. Council of Carthage I, 117.

The incontinent are not to be promoted. Council of Orange, 222.

Those caught demolishing tombs are to be assigned three years of penance. Council of Toledo IV, 380.

Freeborn clerics, on account of their religious office, are to be exempt from every public levy and labor. Council of Toledo IV, 380.

They are not to break out into mutual slaughter. Council of Lérida, 315.

Those who do not remain in their profession are not to enter secular honors. Council of Chalcedon, 100.

Those who sing during meals are to be rebuked most severely. Council of Carthage IV, 148.

The envious are not to be promoted. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

Jesters who use shameful words are to be withdrawn from office. Council of Agde, 243.

Clerics condemned by the judgment of bishops may not be defended by the churches over which they presided, or by anyone else. Council of Carthage V, 155.

The testimony of litigating clerics is not to be accepted without examination. Council of Carthage IV, 118.

Magicians and enchanters are to be expelled from the church. Council of Agde, 243.

They are not to be magicians or enchanters, nor make amulets. Council of Laodicea, 55.

Those given to abusive or cursing speech are to be compelled to ask forgiveness. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

Ministers are not to enter the sacristy. Council of Agde, 243.

They are not to give anything from their possessions to unbelievers. Council of Carthage III, 129.

They are not to receive penance through the laying on of a priest’s hand. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 7.

After the death of their bishop, they are not to seize property belonging to him. Council of Chalcedon, 104.

They are not to buy more cheaply or sell more dearly. Council of Tarragona, 295.

They are not permitted to lend at interest. Council of Carthage I, 119.

They are not permitted, either as clerics or as Catholic laymen, to receive *eulogiae* from heretics or to pray with them or with schismatics. Council of Braga II, 626.

They are not permitted to go to secular courts while bypassing the bishop. Council of Chalcedon, 100.

They are not permitted, after disregarding the bishop, to gather separately. Council of Antioch, 43.

They are not permitted to minister if they have been stripped of office. Council of Antioch, ibid.

They are not permitted to attend spectacles. Council of Laodicea, 57.

They are not permitted to receive interest or sixfold repayment. Council of Laodicea, 51.

They are not permitted to eat before the third hour, nor to approach or leave the table without a hymn. Council of Braga II, 625.

They are not permitted to absent themselves from church on the Lord’s Day. Council of Braga II, ibid.

They are not to minister wearing cloaks and girded about the loins. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 46.

Penance is not to be denied to clerics who desire it. Council of Orange, 219.

Clerics ought not to grow their hair long and then minister. Council of Braga II, 623.

They are not to be ordained unless all who are with them are faithful. Council of Carthage III, 130.

They are not to be merchants. Council of Orléans II, 259.

They are not to receive secular estates or legal cases. Council of Chalcedon, 98.

No one is to pursue dishonorable business or shameful profits. General Decree of Gelasius, 133.

No one is to make a cleric of someone bound to another without the consent of the owner or patron. Council of Toledo I, 324.

They are to avoid wedding banquets. Council of Agde, 238.

Those oppressed by a bishop are to appeal to synod. Council of Orléans II, 257.

Those ordained by heretics are not to be admitted. Letter of Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, 32.

Those who swear by creatures are to be rebuked most severely. Council of Carthage IV, 148.

They are not to be ordained for money. Council of Chalcedon, 98.

Traitors to their brothers, sacred vessels, or the Scriptures are to be removed from the clerical order with beatings. [Col. 0919] Council of Arles I, 196.

They are not to appeal to public courts. Council of Carthage III, 128.

What sort of men are to be chosen for the clerical order. Letter of Innocent to the bishops in Toulouse, 35.

Those deprived of office by their own bishops are not to be received by others. Council of Zaragoza I, 304.

Those absent from the church’s office on solemn days are to be suspended from communion for three years. Council of Agde, 242.

Those who dare to return again to the marriage bed are to be deposed from office. Council of Clermont II, 274.

Those who do not come to the offices of Matins and Vespers are to be deposed. Council of Braga II, 626.

Those who disdain to come to the office are to receive ecclesiastical discipline according to the bishop’s judgment. Council of Orléans I, 249.

Those who flee to secular authorities are to be expelled from communion with the same authorities. Council of Agde, 232.

Those who, under compulsion by others, have laid hands upon the sacrifices of idols are not to be barred from communion as though they were guilty. Council of Ancyra, 17.

Those who minister at the altar are to abstain from all blood. Council of Lérida, 311.

Those who have taken up arms are to be handed over to penance. Council of Toledo IV, 380.

Those who grow their hair long are to be tonsured by the archdeacon. Council of Agde, 234.

Those ordained contrary to the prohibition, or who have fathered children while in office, are not to be permitted to higher grades of orders. Council of Valence, 212.

Those who commit a capital crime are to be deposed from the honor of office, confined in a monastery, and there receive only lay communion for as long as they live. Council of Agde, 240.

If any cleric, from the highest to the lowest, is found to act, deliberate, or attempt anything against the welfare of Holy Church, he is rightly to be cast down. Council of Narbonne, 661.

Those who approach even their nearest blood relatives are to go with a witness. Council of Tarragona, 295.

Those who have sought a secular judgment from the prince are to be deprived of their proper honor. Council of Milevis, 187.

Those who seek the monastic profession are to be granted free entry by the bishop into monasteries. Council of Toledo IV, 381.

Those ordained while possessing nothing are to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, unless something has come to them personally through another’s generosity or through inheritance from their family. Council of Carthage III, 138.

Those who refuse to fulfill their office are not to be counted among the other canonical clerics. Council of Orléans II, 255.

Those who are found incontinent after receiving the diaconate are to be expelled from office. Council of Orange, 222.

Those who seek secular judges are to be excommunicated. Council of Toledo III, 351.

Those who depart without letters from their bishop are to be deprived of communion. Council of Agde, 240.

Those who have lent a solidus are to receive it back without interest. Council of Tarragona, 295.

What they possess from the church’s remuneration is not to be claimed as private property through the passage of time. Council of Epaon, 263.

When they are promoted to ecclesiastical offices, nothing is to be demanded for the blessing. Council of Barcelona II, 657.

When clerics are lacking, they are to be chosen from among the monks. General Decree of Gelasius, 130.

Buffoons are to be withdrawn from office. Council of Agde, 243.

Seditious men, usurers, and avengers of their own injuries are never to be ordained. Council of Carthage IV, 148.

If they have been ordained by pseudo-bishops, such an ordination may remain valid. Letter of Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, 104.

If they have gone to the emperor without letters from their bishop, they are to be deprived of communion. Council of Antioch, 45.

If they complain of the judgments of their bishops, neighboring bishops are to hear them. [Col. 0920] Council of Milevis, 187.

If they are at odds with one another, the bishop is to compel them to reconciliation. Council of Carthage IV, 144.

If they have been unjustly excommunicated, they may approach neighboring bishops. Council of Sardica, 39.

If they have undertaken monasteries, dioceses, or basilicas to be administered. Council of Orléans II, 257.

They are not to wander without commendatory letters. Council of Orléans II, 256.

Without the ordination of their bishop, they are not to presume to approach a public court. Council of Epaon, 262.

They are always to remain under the authority of the bishop in whose diocese they reside. Council of Chalcedon, 100.

They are not to enter taverns. Council of Carthage III, 131.

Those who receive interest or an increase are to be cast out of the clergy and regarded as strangers to the ecclesiastical order. Council of Nicaea, 6.

They are to take a virgin as wife and not marry a second time. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 14.

The wandering and disobedient are to be deprived of communion and honor. Council of Valence, 320.

The sale of women known to be joined to clerics. Council of Toledo IV, 380.

They are not to wear purple garments. Council of Narbonne, 659.

See *Clericus*, *Clerus*.

### Cleric

A rejected cleric is not to be admitted by another church. Council of Telepte, 192.

He is not to transfer to another church. Council of Toledo II, 330.

If he transfers elsewhere, he is to be excommunicated. Council of Arles I, 197.

No one is to receive an alien cleric or fugitive monk. Council of Toledo XIII, 523.

No one is to ordain an outsider. Council of Valence, 230.

One person is not to promote another’s cleric or receive one who has been rejected. Council of Valence, 211.

Anyone ordained contrary to the statutes is to be deprived of the office he has received. Council of Orléans II, 253.

If a cleric’s wife has sinned, he has power—apart from killing her—to discipline her, and he is not to eat with her. Council of Toledo I, 323.

A cleric of any order who comes late to church is to be deposed. Council of Toledo I, 323.

A man married to a widow is not to be admitted to the clerical order. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 7.

No one is to presume to ordain a cleric from another church. Council of Telepte, 192.

He is not to be given away by the prince from the fisc’s household. Council of Toledo III, 350.

If he is a schismatic, he is to fall from his own grade. Council of Carthage IV, 153.

A man with two wives is not to be ordained a cleric. Council of Orléans II, 253.

He is not to minister in two churches. Council of Chalcedon, 100.

Without consulting the bishop, he is not to go to a secular judge. Council of Agde, 236.

A younger man is not to be placed above an older man. Council of Agde, 235.

A layman is not to be ordained a cleric unless he has first undertaken religion. Council of Epaon, 266.

A cleric is not to take a woman—that is, a widow—as his wife. Council of Telepte, 192.

A mutilated man is not to become a cleric; if he mutilates himself voluntarily. Letter of Innocent to Felix, 19.

Neither a cleric is to drag a layman, nor a layman a cleric, before a secular court. Council of Orléans II, 260.

He is not to seek elegance in clothing or footwear. Council of Carthage IV, 146.

A presbyter or cleric is not permitted to sell or give away church property. Council of Agde, 234.

A man who has not undertaken the place to which he has been assigned is not to be a cleric. Council of Valence, 320.

He is not to be one who has taken a second wife. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 14.

No one is to be compelled to give testimony. Council of Carthage V, 155.

No one is to presume to entice or retain another’s cleric without the consent of his bishop. Letter of Leo to Anastasius, 109.

No cleric is to dare to despise the ordination of his bishop; rather, wherever he has been ordained, he ought to proceed with gratitude and obedience and carry out what has been assigned to him. Council of Narbonne, 661.

No cleric or deacon is to have an unrelated woman in his *solatium* or upper room. [Col. 0921] Council of Arles II, 199.

No cleric is to leave his bishop and transfer to another. Council of Toledo I, 324.

No cleric is to admit a woman into the storeroom or private chamber. Council of Agde, 233.

No cleric is to admit a girl into the storeroom or private chamber. Council of Arles II, 199.

No cleric is to leave his church for any reason. Council of Arles II, 201.

No cleric, subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter is to sit about in the streets. Council of Narbonne, 659.

Henceforth no one of whatever ecclesiastical dignity is to receive a grade who does not know completely the whole Psalter, or the usual canticles and hymns, or the full rite of baptism. Council of Toledo VIII, 437.

No bishop is to presume to ordain another bishop’s cleric unless he has received a document signed by that bishop. Council of Braga I, 603.

No one is to become a cleric who had a wife before baptism and another after baptism. Letter of Innocent to all the bishops in Toulouse, 35.

No one is to be ordained unless he has a reputable life. Council of Carthage III, 130.

No one is to be ordained a cleric before the thirtieth year of age. Council of Orléans II, 253.

No one is to travel abroad without the bishop’s order. Council of Laodicea, 56.

A cleric of any order who, after abandoning the Catholic Church, has joined heretical communion is, if he returns to the church, to remain in the grade he held, without promotion. Letter of Leo to Januarius, 102.

He is not to walk through streets and arcades. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

One tested for the faith and remaining steadfast in it ought to be honored with grades. Council of Carthage IV, 146.

However learned in the word of God, he is to seek his livelihood through a craft. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

Anyone who has acquired something from the generosity of the church he served and has been ordained to the highest priesthood of another city is to return what he received as a gift. Council of Epaon, 263.

Whoever, without the bishop’s knowledge, has taken anything from the possessions or house of the church, or has committed fraud, must not only restore it under constraint and with complete disgrace, but also ought not to remain in that church where he committed the fraud. Council of Narbonne, 661.

A cleric who thinks the bishop’s discipline toward him unjust should appeal to synod. Council of Carthage IV, 148.

He who breaks the fast is to be strictly restrained. Council of Carthage IV, ibid.

Whoever wishes to become a monk for the sake of license is to be excommunicated. Council of Zaragoza I, 304.

The husband of a remarried woman is not to be ordained a cleric. Council of Orléans II, 253.

If he is absent from vigils without bodily infirmity, he is to be excommunicated. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

If he transfers to another church, he ought not to remain there. Council of Antioch, 43.

If he enters a second marriage, he is to be deposed. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 6.

If he has stolen from the church, he is to be granted foreign communion. Council of Agde, 231.

If he communicates with an excommunicated person, he is to be excommunicated. Council of Carthage IV, 149.

If he is found guilty or, as an honored man, is assigned from the city to a monastery. Council of Narbonne, 660.

If, without necessity, he walks about at fairs or in the marketplace, he is to be degraded from his office. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

If he voluntarily harms the church, he is both to make satisfaction and to be excommunicated. Council of Agde, 235.

A cleric or monk is not permitted to travel without a letter from his bishop. Council of Agde, 237.

He ought not to travel without a letter. Council of Laodicea, 56.

A cleric of a higher place is not to attend the banquet of any heretical cleric. Council of Epaon, 263.

A foul-mouthed man is to be withdrawn from office. [Col. 0921] Council of Carthage IV, 148.

Wherever a man has first read, there he is to remain as a cleric. Council of Milevis, 186.

He is not to be a usurer. Council of Carthage III, 129.

He is not to receive interest. Council of Arles II, 201.

He is not to take a wife of another sect unless she has promised that she will come to the true faith. Council of Chalcedon, 101.

He is to prepare food and clothing for himself by craft or agriculture, without detriment to his office. Council of Carthage IV, 147.

See *Clerici*, *Clerus*.

### Clergy

Criminals are not to be promoted to the clergy. General Decree of Gelasius, 133.

Curials are not to be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Innocent to all the bishops in Toulouse, 34.

Laymen who are chosen for the clergy are to be observed for six months. General Decree, ibid., 130.

Laymen who have taken a widow or a divorced woman are not to be admitted to the clergy. Council of Gerunda, 301.

A layman is not to be ordained before the completion of a year of conversion. Council of Arles III, 203.

No one ignorant of letters or deficient in any part of the body is to be promoted to the clergy. General Decree of Gelasius, 133.

No bishop is to presume to promote another’s slave to clerical office. Letter of Leo to all the bishops, 101.

A penitent is not to be admitted to the clergy. Council of Braga II, 618.

Penitents, those ignorant of letters, and those lacking something through bodily defect or mutilation are not to enter the higher orders. Decree of Hilary, 121.

Who ought to attain the clerical office. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 6.

Those ordained contrary to the canons are to be deposed. Council of Lérida, 315.

Those who, through necessity or fear of danger, have obtained the offices of ecclesiastical dignity, and attempt to return to their former marriages and way of life, are to be deprived of every dignity of the ecclesiastical order and confined in the cloisters of a monastery under penance for the rest of their lives. Council of Toledo VIII, 436.

Those who have already merited ecclesiastical orders ought not to be subjected to blows except for graver and mortal faults. Council of Braga III, 634.

If an elderly man aspires to the clergy, he will obtain it only if, from the time he is baptized, he is immediately enrolled among the readers or exorcists. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 6.

Those baptized abroad are not to enter the clergy. Council of Elvira, 286.

A layman who has married a widow is not to be admitted to the clergy. Council of Telepte, 192.

Whoever, from bishop down to subdeacon, has fathered children through a detestable union is to be condemned by canonical judgment. Council of Toledo IX, 452.

Who are to be promoted to the ecclesiastical order. Letter of Siricius to various bishops, 9.

Anyone who, after baptism, has worn the belt of secular military service is not to be admitted to the clergy. Letter of Innocent to Victor, 13.

Anyone who, after the remission of sins, has worn the belt of secular military service is not to be admitted to the clergy. Council of Telepte, 192.

Those who do not receive public penance but only the viaticum are to be promoted to the clergy. Council of Gerunda, 301.

Those who cut themselves off from the clerical office are to be excluded. General Decree of Gelasius, 133, and Council of Arles II, 200.

Whoever receives a deserter from his own church and promotes him to some dignity is to undergo the sentence prescribed by the canons. General Decree of Gelasius, 134.

Second marriages are not to be denied to laymen, although they are in no way permitted to enter the clergy. General Decree, ibid.

Wherever each person is ordained, there he is to remain. Council of Arles I, 195.

See *Clerici*, *Clericus*.

### Cemeteries

Candles are not to be lit in cemeteries. Council of Elvira, 287.

Women are not to keep vigil in cemeteries. Council of Elvira, ibid. [Col. 0922]

### The Offering of the Faithful

If anything is offered from the contribution of the faithful, it is to be carefully collected by one of the clerics. Council of Braga I, 605.

### Communion

Communion is to be received in the basilicas of the martyrs. Council of Gangra, 32.

Communion is not to be denied to those who persist in sins until the end of life and seek communion at their departure. Council of Braga II, 628.

Laymen are not permitted to enter within the altar sanctuary. Council of Braga I, 604.

Laymen ought to receive communion on the days of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost. Council of Agde, 234.

It is not permitted to despise the communion of the Church. Council of Antioch, 42.

Whoever does not communicate in his own province is not to communicate in another either. Council of Milevis, 186.

Those who, upon entering the church, abstain from communion in the sacrament through excessive luxury are to be expelled from the Catholic Church until they perform penance. Council of Braga II, 628.

After giving the blessing to the people, the priests ought to communicate. Council of Toledo IV, 373.

Council of Chalcedon, 91.

Council of Constantinople I, 59; II, 63.

Council of Egar, 663.

Council of Elvira, 281.

Council of Mérida, 665.

Council of Epaon, 261.

Council of Ephesus, 79.

Council of Gangra, 27.

Council of Gerunda, 299.

Council of Seville I, 635; II, 639.

Council of Lérida, 311.

Council of Laodicea, 49.

Council of Milevis, 181.

Council of Narbonne, 659.

Council of Neocaesarea, 23.

Council of Nicaea, 1.

Council of Huesca, 663.

Council of Riez, 212.

Roman Council in the time of Pope Gregory I, 162.

Council of Sardica, 33.

Council of Tarragona, 295.

Council of Turin, 208.

Council of Telepte, 189.

Council of Toledo I, 321; II, 329; III, 338; IV, 363; V, 394; VI, 400; VII, 411; VIII, 421; IX, 447; X, 455; XI, 467; XII, 487; XIII, 509; XIV, 531; XV, 537; XVI, 557; XVII, 585.

Council of Valence, 206.

Council of Vallis, 317.

Council of Vaison I, 223; II, 227.

Two provincial councils of the bishops are to be held each year. Letter of Leo to Anastasius, 109.

The statutes of the councils and the decrees of the Roman bishops are to be observed. Council of Toledo III, 348.

The constitutions of the holy councils. Decree of Hormisdas, 165.

On the character of councils, and why or when they are held. Council of Toledo IV, 366.

They are to be held every year. Council of Carthage III, 126.

Rules of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, established at the First Council of Toledo by the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica, 326.

Everything enacted in councils is to be confirmed by the subscriptions of the bishops. Council of Carthage III, 139.

### Council

It is to be celebrated twice a year. Council of Antioch, 47, and Council of Riez, 216.

It is to be celebrated twice a year in each province. Council of Chalcedon, 103.

It ought to be celebrated every year on the Kalends of November. Council of Toledo XII, 501.

A metropolitan council is to be held every year in each metropolitan city. Council of Orléans II, 251.

Confirmation of the Twelfth Council of Toledo, held in the first year of the most glorious King Erwig. Council of Toledo XIII, 520.

The bishops of the same province who are summoned to the council are obliged to come. Council of Clermont II, 278.

Condemnation of the council’s mockers and noisy interrupters. Council of Toledo XI, 476.

On the twofold adversity by which a general council could not be held. Council of Toledo XIV, 533.

On the honor conferred upon the Fourteenth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XIV, 534.

On the beginning of the account, where the council began to mention the synodal acts and the letter of the Roman pontiff. Council of Toledo XIV, 532.

On the repeated discussion of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XIV, ibid.

On the place and order in which the Fourteenth Council of Toledo ought to be situated. Council of Toledo XIV, ibid.

On the prior mention of the assembled council and the report of the principal edict by which the synod was ordered to be held. Council of Toledo XIV, 531.

On the rendering of thanks to God for the completed council. Council of Toledo XIV, 536.

On the rendering of thanks offered to God and the prince after the completion of the council. Council of Toledo XIII, 524.

From Sicily, every year, three bishops are always to come without fail to Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October, to join the synod. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily, 100.

On holding a synod. Council of Braga II, 617.

On the three days at the beginning of the council during which nothing else is ordered to be done except matters of faith and other spiritual concerns, with no secular matter introduced. Council of Toledo XVII, 590.

Decree of the faith of the Sixth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo VI, 400.

The same decree of the Eleventh Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XI, 470.

The same decree of the Twelfth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XII, 491.

The same decree of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XV, 540.

The same decree of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XVI, 562.

The decree of the Council of Mérida. Council of Mérida, 665.

The day of the council is to be kept on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. Council of Carthage V, 156.

Letter or council from the city of Clermont addressed to King Theudebert, 271.

Copies of the Council of Nicaea sent on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. Council of Carthage VI, 166.

The formula according to which the holy synod is to be held in the name of God. Council of Toledo IV, 366.

In common cases of the Church, a general council is to be convened. Council of Milevis, 184.

The establishment of a fixed time at which the council is to be held. Council of Toledo XI, 484.

Law issued in confirmation of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XIII, 529.

Law issued in confirmation of the general council in the first year of the reign of the glorious Egica. Council of Toledo XV, 553.

Law in confirmation of the Seventeenth Council of Toledo. Council of Toledo XVII, 597.

The bishops are not to remain more than fifteen days beyond the time established for the council. Letter of Leo to Anastasius, 110.

It is to be celebrated every year. Letter of Hormisdas to the bishops throughout Spain, 148.

Profession of faith made at the Eighth Council of Toledo. Council.
eod., 427. Publication of the council must take place within six months. Council of Toledo XVI, 573.

Whatever has been established or shall be established in synod concerning matters of the faith and ecclesiastical affairs, let no one dare contradict. Council of Toledo VIII, 439.

How a council is to be held according to the institutions of the earlier canons. Council of Emerita, 669.

The rule of the holy faith of the seventeenth Council of Toledo. Council cited above, 590.

A report of thanksgiving for the completion of the eleventh Council of Toledo. Council cited above, 484.

The replies of the fathers of the fourteenth Council of Toledo to the Roman pontiff. Council cited above, 533.
