**Magistrates.** A magistrate, during the year in which he exercises the office of duumvir, shall abstain from the Church. Council of Elvira, 290.

**Sorcery.** Whoever kills a person by sorcery shall not receive communion even at the end of his life. Council of Elvira, 283.

**Slaves.** Concerning slaves of the Church manumitted by a bishop. Council of Seville I, 635. Concerning slaves of the Church transferred by a bishop to his relatives. Council of Seville I, 637. Slaves fleeing to the Church shall not be seized. Council of Orange, 219. Christian slaves who are held in Jewish service shall not be joined in marriage with Jews. Council of Orléans II, 255.

**Manumitted persons.** See *Freedmen*.

**The Virgin Mary.** The solemnity of the Lord’s mother shall in every way be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, and the Nativity of her Son, our Savior, on the eighth day before those same Kalends. Council of Toledo X, 456.

**Martyrs.** The birthdays of martyrs ought not to be celebrated during Lent, except on Saturday and Sunday. Council of Laodicea, 57. If no body or relics of martyrs are proved to be buried in basilicas, those basilicas shall be demolished by the bishops. Council of Carthage V, 158.

**False martyrs.** Whoever wishes to go to false martyrs shall be anathema. Council of Laodicea, 55.

**Marriage.** See *Marriage union*.

**Maximus.** Concerning Maximus and the Donatists. Letter of Leo to the Africans, 114.

**Maximus the Cynic philosopher.** The ordinations performed by him are annulled. Council of Constantinople I, 61.

**Prostitutes.** Pagan prostitutes, if they convert, shall be received. Council of Elvira, 288.

**Metropolis.** Whoever proves that his city was a metropolis shall hold the primacy. Council of Turin, 209.

**Metropolitan.** Concerning the primacy of the metropolitan. Council of Braga II, 614. There shall not be two, according to the imperial constitutions. Letter of Innocent to Alexander, 28. Their offices, honors, authority, and so forth. Council of Antioch, 44. No one may be a bishop who has been ordained contrary to the will and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop. Council of Nicaea, 3. He shall subscribe letters summoning a council. Council of Milevis, 185. The rights of metropolitans shall be preserved. Letter of Leo to Anastasius, 108. The metropolitan of Epirus shall refer to the bishop of Thessalonica the candidate whom he is about to ordain bishop; and likewise the provincial bishops shall refer an elected metropolitan. Letter of Leo to Anastasius, 109. When the metropolitan gives warning, no one from the neighboring regions shall refuse to come to the place where he is invited. Council of Toledo XIII, 519. The metropolitan must not cease instructing those from the neighboring regions. Council of Toledo XI, 476. The ordination of a metropolitan shall be performed by a metropolitan, with all the provincial bishops present if this can be done. Council of Orléans II, 251. How a metropolitan shall make an agreement with his neighbors, or the neighbors with their metropolitan. Council of Mérida, 667. There shall be only one in each province. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 48.

**Military service.** After penance, it is not fitting to return to secular military service. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 105. Those who cast away their weapons in peacetime shall be excommunicated. Council of Arles I, 195. Whoever, after the remission of sins, has taken up the belt of secular military service shall not be admitted to the clergy. Council of Telepte, 192.

**Sacred ministries.** No one may touch the sacred ministries. Council of Braga II, 622.

**Ministers.** They shall not withdraw from the doors. Council of Laodicea, 56. They may not give the bread or bless the chalice. Council of Laodicea, 54. They shall not use the stole, nor leave the doors. Council of Laodicea, ibid.

**Mass.** It shall be celebrated by those who are fasting. Council of Carthage III, 131. Before the Mass has been completed, the people shall not presume to leave. Council of Agde, 239. While Mass is being celebrated, no presbyter or deacon, unless prevented by illness, shall dare to leave the altar before the Mass is finished; nor shall the deacon presume to remove his alb. Council of Narbonne, 661. Those who maliciously dare to celebrate a Mass for the dead on behalf of the living shall be deposed from their rank. Council of Toledo XVII, 593. The Mass must be heard in its entirety. Council of Orléans II, 259. Masses shall be celebrated at the third hour only on the principal solemnities. Council of Orléans II, 255. A priest must not dare to celebrate Mass without a stole. Council of Braga III, 632. It is not permitted to hold Masses over the monuments of the dead. Council of Braga II, 625. A presbyter shall not celebrate a Mass for the dead after eating. Council of Braga I, 612. Once every superstitious opinion has been rejected, only bread and wine mixed with water shall be offered in the sacrifice. Council of Braga III, 630.

**Monks.** New cells or small monastic communities are prohibited without the bishop’s knowledge. Council of Epaon, 262. Concerning the honor due to monks. Council of Chalcedon, 99. The provision enacted by the Council of Chalcedon concerning monks shall be observed. Council of Barcelona I, 656. Monks shall be ordained as clerics with the abbot’s consent. Council of Lérida, 313. Monks must be subject to the bishop. Council of Chalcedon, 99. Monks shall not possess a stole or *zancas* (boots). Council of Orléans I, 248. Wandering monks shall not be ordained without testimony from their abbot. Council of Agde, 235. Wandering monks shall be recalled by their abbots into custody with the bishop’s assistance. Council of Orléans I, 248. Wandering monks shall be assigned penance in the same monastery from which they departed. Council of Toledo IV, 381. From a monk who presumes to possess anything privately, the abbots shall take away everything he has acquired. Council of Orléans I, 248. A monk sent somewhere shall not presume to perform clerical ministry. Council of Tarragona, 298. A monk shall be neither a merchant nor an agent. Council of Tarragona, ibid. A monk shall not be ordained a cleric without the consent and will of his abbot. Council of Agde, 236. A monk who marries shall never obtain ecclesiastical office. Council of Orléans I, 248. A monk shall not build a cell for himself without the permission of the bishop or abbot. Council of Orléans I, ibid. Monks may not withdraw from the community to solitary cells. Council of Agde, 238. He may not enter into marriage. Council of Chalcedon, 182. They shall not accept secular estates or lawsuits. Council of Chalcedon, 98. No abbot shall receive or retain a monk who is migrating to another monastery without the permission or consent of his own abbot. Council of Agde, 235. No one shall attain the highest priesthood except through the ecclesiastical grades. Letter of Zosimus to Hesychius, 36. No monk shall attempt to disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs, or receive another man’s slave without that man’s knowledge. Council of Chalcedon, 99. They shall not come to the royal city contrary to the will of their bishop. Council of Chalcedon, 104. The profession of monks. Council of Toledo IV, 380. How they are to be advanced to the clergy. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 7. If they have become clerics, they must preserve their way of life. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 15. If they do not preserve their way of life, communion shall be granted to them only at the point of death. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 5. If anyone abandons the monastic way of life, he shall be cleansed by public penitential satisfaction. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 105. A cleric or monk may not depart without a letter from his bishop. Council of Agde, 237.

**Monasteries.** No one shall build or establish a monastery or a house of prayer without the bishop’s knowledge. Council of Chalcedon, 99. Concerning the preservation of monasteries from destruction. Council of Seville II, 644. Secular hostels shall not be established. Council of Zaragoza III, 308. Monasteries for girls shall be built far from monks. Council of Agde, 236. Monasteries of virgins shall be defended by monks. Council of Seville II, 644. No one shall build a monastery without consulting the bishop. Council of Agde, 235. No one shall be permitted to enter a monastery of girls for any of their needs or services except women of proven character and mature age. Council of Epaon, 266. A monastery shall not be built without the bishop’s knowledge. Council of Agde, 241. Secular hostels shall not be established. Council of Chalcedon, 104. Girls who seek the monastery shall remain for a year in the clothing in which they entered. Council of Arvernus II, 278. Girls who seek the monastery, where they are not kept enclosed permanently, shall remain for three years in the clothing in which they entered, and afterward receive religious clothing. Council of Arvernus II, ibid. Things offered to a monastery shall not be taken away. Council of Lérida, 313.

**Montanus.** Bishop Montanus’s admonition to the clergy of Palencia concerning the chrism, the consecration of basilicas, and the sect of the Priscillianists, 332. Letter of Bishop Montanus to Thuribius, 335.

**Montanists.** Those coming from the Novatians or Montanists shall be received by the laying on of hands. Council of Telepte, 192.

**Women.** They shall not enter the altar area. Council of Laodicea, 56. They shall not presume to baptize. Council of Carthage IV, 152. A woman may not cut her hair. Council of Gangra, 31. They may not marry two brothers. Council of Nicaea, 23. Women ought not to assume men’s clothing for the sake of continence. Council of Gangra, 30. Concerning those women whom it is not fitting for clerics to associate with. Council of Toledo IV, 380. Concerning the removal of women from the companionship of clerics. Council of Toledo IV, 379. Concerning women living under the same roof. Council of Nicaea, 2. Concerning adopted women living under the same roof. Council of Braga II, 620. They shall not enter the sacristy. Council of Braga II, 622. A woman, however learned and holy, shall not dare to teach men. Council of Carthage IV, 152. Free women or slave women joined to priests and ministers in disgraceful conduct shall be separated from them or sold, and access to those privy to their crime shall be denied them. Council of Toledo VIII, 434. Christian women may not observe anything in wool-working. Council of Braga II, 627. No woman except an aunt, sister, maternal aunt, and so forth, shall live with clerics. Council of Nicaea, 2. See *Females*.

**Mute persons.** Those who suddenly become mute may receive baptism and penance. Council of Orange, 220.

## N

**Neophytes.** They may not immediately be advanced to an ecclesiastical order. Council of Braga II, 618. They shall not be ordained clerics. Council of Arles II, 199. They shall not be advanced to the priesthood. Council of Laodicea, 51. They shall not become priests. Letter of Siricius to various bishops, 10.

**Nestorius.** His blasphemies are condemned again. Letter of Hormisdas to the Emperor Justin, 141.

**Nestorius and Eutyches.** Their blasphemies, and the fitting anathema against them. Letter of Leo to Leo Augustus, 81.

**Council of Nicaea.** Its Acts, 1. Decree of the Sixth Council of Carthage requesting copies of the Council of Nicaea. Council of Carthage VI, 164.

**Names.** The names that are to be recited before the priest’s prayer shall not be recited. Letter of Innocent to Decentius, 11.

**Novatians.** They shall not be received before they condemn every heresy. Council of Laodicea, 51. Novatians shall not be received into communion. Council of Arles II, 200. If they flee to the Catholic Church, they shall be ordained and remain in the clergy; but beforehand they must confess that they will observe the statutes of the Catholic Church. Council of Nicaea, 4. Those coming from the Novatians or Montanists shall be received by the laying on of hands. Council of Telepte, 192.

**Marriage ceremonies.** Sacred ministries shall not be provided for the adornment of weddings. Council of Arvernus I, 269. Concerning those who have entered into several marriages. Council of Neocaesarea, 24. Weddings may not take place during Lent. Council of Laodicea, 57. Those who assert that marriage and procreation are sinful are condemned. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 92. If a woman, condemning marriage, wishes to leave her husband, let her be anathema. Council of Gangra, 31. If anyone has been joined in several marriages, let him do penance. Council of Braga II, 627. If anyone condemns marriage, let him be anathema. Council of Gangra, 29. One devoted to virginity ought not to curse marriage. Council of Gangra, 30. See *Marriage union*.

## O

**Offerings.** They shall not be sent to other parishes. Council of Laodicea, 52. Of the things offered on the altar, the bishop shall claim half for himself. Council of Orléans I, 247. No one shall give or receive offerings of produce except through the bishop or the person appointed by him for the relief of the poor. Council of Gangra, 30. An entire offering, carefully prepared, is to be offered in the sacrifice. Council of Toledo XVI, 572. Offerings of dissenting brothers shall be received neither in the sacristy nor in the treasury. Council of Carthage IV, 151. Offerings shall not be made in private houses by bishops or presbyters. Council of Laodicea, 58. Of those offerings made by the faithful on the altar of parish basilicas, one third shall be brought to the bishop. Council of Orléans I, 247. Money offered in the Church of God shall be divided. Council of Mérida, 673. Things offered by the faithful in parish basilicas shall remain under the bishop’s authority. Council of Mérida, ibid. Those who retain offerings made for the dead shall be excommunicated. Council of Vaison I, 245. Those who either deny offerings made for the dead to the churches or return them with difficulty shall be excommunicated. Council of Carthage IV, 151. Those who defraud the Church of their own offerings or those of their relatives shall be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor. Council of Agde, 231. What ought to be offered on the altar. Council of Braga II, 623. Priests and clerics may not hold banquets from things brought together or contributed. Council of Braga II, 624. Offerings belonging to churches shall not be taken away. Council of Arvernus II, 277. Offerings belonging to the Church shall not be retained. Council of Arvernus II, 258. Offerings of those who do not communicate are not to be accepted. Council of Elvira, 286. Offerings of penitents who have suddenly died shall be received. Council of Vaison I, 225. Communion shall be denied to pagan priests who have given only a gift to idols. Council of Elvira, 282.

**Stewards.** The appointment of stewards. Council of Toledo IV, 380. They shall not be appointed from among the laity. Council of Seville II, 643. All churches that have bishops shall have stewards from their own clergy. Council of Chalcedon, 165.

**Offertory.** During Lent, bread is to be offered only on Saturday and Sunday. Council of Laodicea, 57.

**Divine office.** A blessing shall be given to the faithful at Matins just as at Vespers. Council of Barcelona I, 655. Concerning the distinction of the doxology at the end of the responsories. Council of Toledo IV, 373. Concerning the hymn of the three boys, to be sung at all solemn Masses. Council of Toledo IV, 372. Concerning not refusing the singing of hymns. Council of Toledo IV, 371. Concerning not singing *alleluia* during Lent. Council of Toledo IV, 369. Concerning celebrating one order in the ministries or offices throughout all churches. Council of Toledo IV, 365. Concerning preserving the order of the evening office. Council of Mérida, 667. Bishops and presbyters shall greet the people in one manner, saying: “The Lord be with you.” Council of Braga I, 603. The Gospel shall be read after the Apostle. Council of Valladolid, 317. Apart from the Psalms or the canonical Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, nothing composed poetically shall be sung in the Church. Council of Braga I, 604. At the end of the Psalms, “Glory and honor to God” shall be said. Council of Toledo IV, 372. In all churches the Creed shall be recited on Sunday. Council of Toledo III, 348. In the orders of psalmody, “Glory” shall be said to almighty God after each psalm. Council of Narbonne, 659. The diversity of offices shall not be maintained within one province. Council of Toledo XI, 477. “Kyrie eleison” or “Sanctus” shall often be said. Council of Vaison II, 228. Laypeople who do not assemble in the city on the greater solemnities shall be deprived of communion for three years. Council of Agde, 242. The praises shall be said not immediately after the Apostle but after the Gospel. Council of Toledo IV, 371. Litanies shall be celebrated after Pentecost, from Thursday through Saturday. Council of Gerona, 299. The second litanies are to be performed on the Kalends of November. Council of Gerona, ibid. Masses shall be celebrated by everyone in the same order. Council of Braga I, 603. No professed woman or widow, in the priest’s absence, shall perform the priestly office or the lamp-lighting office in her own house. Council of Toledo I, 323. No citizen shall celebrate the greater festivals in the countryside. Council of Orléans I, 249. Every day, after Matins and Vespers, the Lord’s Prayer shall be said. Council of Gerona, 302. During vigils or Masses on solemn days, all shall read the same readings in the church, and not different ones. Council of Braga I, 603. The people shall not leave the Mass before the priest’s blessing. Council of Orléans I, 249. Prayers shall be said after the antiphons. Council of Agde, 236. The principal festivals shall be celebrated with the bishop in the city. Council of Arvernus I, 270. Psalm 50 shall be said before the canticle. Council of Barcelona I, 655. How homilies are to be recited by deacons. Council of Vaison II, 227. If anyone residing in the city has not attended church for three Sundays, he shall be subjected to abstinence for a short time. Council of Elvira, 285. “As it was in the beginning” shall be said. Council of Vaison II, 229. The greater solemnities shall be celebrated in the cities. Council of Agde, 234. The Creed shall be preached to the candidates eight days before Easter. Council of Agde, 233. Each province shall maintain one order in the Church’s office. Council of Gerona, 299. One and the same order of psalmody shall be maintained in the offices. Council of Braga I, 602.

**Stole.** Deacons shall appropriately use the stole placed over the shoulder. Council of Braga I, 604.

**Prayers.** They shall be celebrated at the hours of None and Vespers. Council of Laodicea, 53. The prayers of the Church ought not to be despised. Council of Gangra, 29. They shall not be made with heretics or schismatics. Council of Laodicea, 55. They shall not be said unless they have been approved in a council. Council of Milevis, 185. What order is to be observed in the prayer and communion of catechumens and the faithful. Council of Laodicea, 53. How they are to be directed. Council of Carthage III, 130.

**Oratory.** If anyone makes an oratory in his field for the sake of profit, it shall not be consecrated. Council of Braga II, 611.

**Holy orders.** Outside the knowledge of the apostolic see—that is, the primate—no one shall dare to ordain. Council of Telepte, 191. One must abstain from illicit ordinations. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 48. Orders shall be conferred on no one except in his own church. Council of Chalcedon, 99. After the death of a bishop, the ordination of another shall not be delayed. Council of Chalcedon, 104. At the ordination of bishops, at least three bishops shall assemble. Council of Carthage III, 133.

**Ornaments.** No priest shall attempt to break up, sell, or squander any church ornament for his own uses or desires. Council of Toledo XVII, 592.

**Kiss of peace.** It is to be given after the mysteries have been completed. Letter of Innocent to Decentius, p. 11.

**Doorkeepers.** How they are to be appointed. Council of Carthage IV, 142.

## P
### P

**Pallia.** On their use. Council of Gangra, 30. The bodies of the dead are not to be wrapped in pallia serving the church or the divine ministries. Council of Arvernus I, 268.

**Pantomimes.** If pantomimes convert, they are to be received. Council of Elvira, 291.

**Pope.** The pope’s name is to be recited in the church. Council of Vaison II, 229.

**Parish priests.** On an official booklet to be given to parish presbyters. Council of Toledo IV, 376. On the profession of parish presbyters. Council of Toledo IV, ibid.

**Parishes.** The resources of parishes. Council of Orléans II, 252. On not changing one’s parish. Council of Braga II, 614.

**Little children.** All are to be baptized for the remission of sins. Council of Milevis, 181.

**Easter.** On seeking among the bishops an announcement of Easter before Epiphany. Council of Toledo IV, 367. On celebrating the office on Good Friday. Council of Toledo IV, 369. On the festival of Easter, the order of prayers, and the solemnity of Masses. Letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, 155. The day of Easter is to be announced to everyone by subscription to the *formatae*. Council of Carthage V, 156. It is not permitted to celebrate Easter at a different time or with the Jews. Council of Antioch, 45. Every year Easter is to be announced to the bishops by the metropolitan. Council of Braga II, 615. Easter is to be celebrated on one and the same day and at one and the same time. Council of Arles I, 194, and Carthage IV, 148.

**Patriarchs.** Those who arrange the names of the patriarchs through the several members of the body are condemned. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 94.

**Paulianists.** Paulianists are to be baptized. [Col. 0942] Council of Arles II, 201. If they have fled to the Catholic Church, they are to be rebaptized. Council of Nicaea, 7.

**Paul.** On the testimony rendered concerning the dignity of those whom the profanation of unbelief drew, together with Paul, into fellowship in tyranny. Council of Toledo XIII, 513.

**The poor.** The poor and the elderly of the church are to be honored more than others. Council of Carthage IV, 150.

**Peace.** Those who, while quarreling with others, bind themselves by oath not to return to peace are to be excluded from communion for one year. Council of Lérida, 314. Those who do not return to peace because of hatred are to be excommunicated. Council of Agde, 236.

**Sin.** There is no one who can exist without sin. Council of Milevis, 183. The sin of the people ordinarily passes unpunished in the church. Letter of Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, 33.

**Money.** What is offered in the church of God is to be distributed faithfully. Council of Mérida, 673.

**Pelagians.** Their anathema. Council of Milevis, 181.

**Pentecost.** The day of Pentecost is to be celebrated by all. Council of Elvira, 288.

**Pilgrim.** No one is to be received without a letter. Council of Antioch, 44.

**Traitors.** A discussion concerning refugees and traitors. Council of Toledo VIII, 427.

**The apostle Peter.** Blessed Peter the Apostle baptized three thousand men on the day of Pentecost. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily, 99. — **Peter, bishop.** Letter of Peter of Ravenna to Eutyches, 57.

**Photinians.** Photinians and Paulianists are to be baptized. Council of Arles II, 201.

**The people.** A people that has never had a bishop is not to receive its own rulers. Council of Carthage III, 134.

**Penitent. Penitents.** If a young man has undertaken penance because of any pressing danger and does not remain continent, he may be sustained by the remedy of a wife. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 105. One placed at the point of death is not to be kept long from reconciliation. Council of Toledo XI, 483. It is not fitting for him to conduct any profitable business. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 105. One who asks forgiveness for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful ones. Letter of the same to the same, ibid. A penitent is to perform penance. Council of Toledo III, 351. However good he may be, a penitent is not to be ordained a cleric; if he has become a cleric through the bishop’s ignorance, he is to be deposed. Council of Carthage IV, 149. Penitents are not to be received by other bishops. Letter of Felix to the bishops throughout Sicily, 127. They are not to be admitted to the clerical order. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 7. They are not to be promoted to the priesthood. Council of Arles III, 204. On those who receive penance without feeling it. Council of Toledo XII, 493. The distinction among penitents. Council of Toledo IV, 381. They are not to attend banquets or engage in business dealings, whether giving or receiving, but are to lead a frugal life only in their own homes. Council of Barcelona I, 653. When placed in sickness, they are to receive the blessing of viaticum. Council of Barcelona I, 656. They are to carry out and bury the dead of the church. Council of Carthage IV, 150. More negligent penitents are to be received later. Council of Carthage IV, 149. Penitent clerics are not to be ordained. Council of Agde, 239. Those departing from this life are to be admitted to communion. Council of Orange, 219. Those who join themselves to another after the death of a spouse are to be kept from the thresholds of the church. Council of Arles II, 202. Those who are ill are to receive viaticum. Council of Carthage IV, 150. Those who have received viaticum in illness are not to consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands if they survive. [Col. 0943] Council of Carthage IV, 150. For certain penitents their former marriages are to be restored. Council of Toledo VI, 405. They are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. Letter of Innocent to Decentius, 12. Priests are to lay hands upon them. Council of Carthage IV, 150. They are always to kneel. Council of Carthage IV, ibid. If they have received penance from heretics, how they are to be received by the Church. Council of Milevis, 188. If they do not keep the penance they have received, they are to be excluded from communion. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 5. If they die where no assistance could be given them, their memory is to be commended in prayers and offerings. Council of Carthage IV, 150. If one requesting penance becomes speechless through illness, he is to receive penance. Council of Carthage IV, 149. Transgressors are to be placed unwillingly in monasteries; if this proves difficult, they are to be regarded as excommunicated until they return to the order from which they were dismissed. Council of Toledo IV, 404. Where they have received prayer, there they are to receive communion. Council of Arles I, 196. Men and widows or virgins who again transgress are to be recalled to penance by the bishop; and if, after being admonished, they do not return, they are to be condemned as apostates. Council of Toledo IV, 382. Men, with their heads tonsured and wearing religious clothing, are to spend the time of their lives in fasts and supplications. Council of Barcelona I, 655. Penance is to be imposed at the bishop’s discretion. Council of Carthage III, 132. Penance is not to be given to married persons except with their consent. Council of Arles II, 202. No one may give the blessing of penance to married converts except with the consent of both parties and once they have reached full age. Council of Orléans II, 258. On the penance of the faithful, so that their confession is not made public. Letter of Leo to the bishops throughout Campania, 120. Penance and communion are not to be denied to those who are at the point of death. Letter of the same to Theodore, 115. No one should presume to confer the blessing of penance upon young converts. Council of Orléans II, 258. Penance is to be denied to no one at the end of life. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 47. What has been deferred, when it has been sought more earnestly, is not to be denied. Letter of Leo to Rusticus, 105. How the older and how the younger are to receive penance. Council of Agde, 233. Whoever, after receiving and professing penance, returns to secular life is to be deprived of communion. Council of Epaon, 264. Those who, being in danger, receive penance in such a way that they publicly confess having committed some mortal sin cannot enter the clergy. Council of Gerunda, 302. Those who, being in danger, receive penance while confessing no manifest crimes may advance to ecclesiastical orders. Council of Gerunda, ibid. Those who ask for penance in illness and receive it from a priest, if they later recover, are to live the life of penitents, except for the laying on of hands. Council of Barcelona I, 655. Those who die while under penance are to be admitted. Council of Arles II, 260. Those who ask for penance are first to be tonsured if male, and first to change their clothing if female. Council of Toledo III, 351. Those who violate their penance are to be suspended from communion. Council of Orléans I, 246. Those who return to secular life after undertaking penance are to be punished by excommunication until death. Council of Orléans II, 258. The priest is to impose the laws of penance without respect of persons. Council of Carthage IV, 149.

**Pomp.** No one is to give his clothing for the adornment of secular pomp. Council of Elvira, 290.

**The people are to be taught, not followed.** [Col. 0943] Letter of Celestine to the bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria, 49. The people are not permitted to choose the ministers of the altar. Council of Laodicea, 52.

**Potamius.** Decree of the tenth Council of Toledo concerning Potamius, bishop, 464.

**Governors.** Governors are to communicate with the knowledge of their bishop, and likewise those who wish to administer public affairs. Council of Arles I, 195.

**Those who lapsed.** On those who lapsed during persecution. Council of Arles II, 200. On those who, overcome by punishments, were compelled to sacrifice. Council of Arles II, ibid.

**Prayers.** Unless they have been approved in a council, they are not to be recited. Council of Milevis, 185. How they are to be directed. Council of Carthage III, 130.

**Presbyter. Presbyters.** A presbyter is not to presume to give a blessing or penance in the church. Council of Agde, 239. He is not to prepare chrism. Council of Carthage III, 132. A stubborn or proud presbyter is to be admonished by six bishops. Council of Carthage I, 119. One overtaken by bodily sin, if he sinned before ordination, is not to offer. Council of Neocaesarea, 25. On the lawful age at which a presbyter is to be ordained. Council of Braga II, 617. On the offering of a married presbyter. Council of Gangra, 29. He is not to presume to ordain a deacon or presbyter. Council of Seville II, 641. He is to show the utmost humility and reverence toward his bishop. Council of Mérida, 672. He is to bless and confirm the neophyte. Council of Reggio, 215. He is not to reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop. Council of Carthage III, 132. He is to reconcile a penitent at the bishop’s command. Council of Carthage II, 122. What is to be observed if the holy chrism is ordered to be given to presbyters. Council of Mérida, 670. A presbyter is not to presume to ordain deacons or consecrate an altar. Council of Agde, 239. A presbyter under thirty years of age is absolutely not to be ordained. Council of Neocaesarea, 26. Whoever has held a diocese is to draw up a document in the name of the church. Council of Epaon, 261. If accused, how many bishops are to hear his case. Council of Carthage II, 128. If an excommunicated presbyter presumes to sacrifice, he is to be anathematized. Council of Carthage II, 123. If he celebrates the office without consulting the bishop, he is to be deprived of his rank. Council of Carthage II, 124. If he has been entrusted with several churches, he is to undertake to offer sacrifice to God in each one on each Sunday. Council of Mérida, 675. If he incurs guilt, he is to be heard by six bishops. Council of Carthage II, 124. A presbyter or deacon is to provide testimony concerning his life. Council of Toledo IV, 375. Presbyters of another region may offer in the presence of bishops or the city’s presbyters. Council of Neocaesarea, 26. They are to receive chrism from their own bishops. Council of Carthage IV, 145. They are not permitted to contract a second marriage. Council of Neocaesarea, 25. They ought not to enter or sit in tribunals before the bishop enters. Council of Laodicea, 38. On the distinction between presbyters and deacons, so that they may stand in the two choirs. Council of Toledo IV, 379. They are to make clerics for themselves from the household of their own church. Council of Mérida, 675. On those things forbidden to presbyters in ecclesiastical sacraments. Council of Seville II, 642. On those ordained presbyters or deacons without examination. Council of Braga II, 618. On presbyters and deacons who return to marital intercourse. Council of Agde, 232. On presbyters or deacons who are denounced after ordination. Council of Braga II, 619. On foreign presbyters. Council of Braga II, 624. In the presence of the bishop, presbyters are to gather the prayers in due order. Council of Barcelona I, [Col. 0944] 655. Those established in parishes are to receive younger readers into their homes with them. Council of Vaison II, 227. They are not to enter into second marriages. Council of Braga II, 621. The appointment of stewards. Council of Toledo IV, 380. Although excommunicated, they may give communion in an emergency. Council of Elvira, 287. Neither presbyters nor deacons are to be deposed by one bishop alone. Council of Seville II, 642. They are to presume nothing against bishops. General Decree of Gelasius, 131. They are not to despise meat as unclean. Council of Ancyra, 20. The ordination of a presbyter or deacon is to be celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, on Sunday. Letter of Leo to Dioscorus, 118. After ordination they are not to beget children. Council of Toledo I, 321. Presbyters and deacons are to be ordained at appointed times. General Decree of Gelasius, 132. Parish presbyters are to acquire in the church’s name whatever they purchase. Council of Agde, 240. The ecclesiastical order does not receive presbyters established without examination. Council of Nicaea, 4. The reconciliation of penitents is not to be performed by presbyters. Council of Carthage II, 121. Those converted from the Arian heresy to the holy Catholic Church are to be received into the clergy. Second Council of Zaragoza, 305. Those who, falling into heresy, have submitted themselves to baptism are to lie in penance until death. Letter of Felix to the bishops throughout Sicily, 126. How they are to be ordained. Council of Carthage IV, 141. The widow of a presbyter or deacon is not to join herself to another. Council of Orléans I, 247. If they sacrificed through fear of torture, they are to retain the honors of their own rank, but are not permitted to offer, preach to the people, or perform any priestly functions. Council of Ancyra, 17. They are not to depart without letters from their own bishop. Council of Epaon, 261. They are not permitted to take a wife. Council of Neocaesarea, 23.

**Primates.** Honor is to be paid to the primates of the palace. Council of Toledo VI, 406.

**Ruler. Rulers.** An admonition to the people not to commit offenses against rulers. Council of Toledo IV, 387. The protection of the rulers’ lives and the defense of preceding kings are to be undertaken by their successors. Council of Toledo VI, 409. The safeguarding of the kings’ welfare and the defense of the royal offspring. Council of Toledo V, 395. On the election of rulers. Council of Toledo VI, 387. On the protection of the royal offspring. Council of Toledo XVI, 573. On the protection of the king’s wife and offspring. Council of Toledo XVII, 594. On the protection of the king’s offspring. Council of Toledo XVIII, 516. When a ruler has died, no one is to dare to take his surviving wife either in marriage or in adultery. Council of Toledo XIII, 517. The ruler’s favor granted by the acclamation of the council. Council of Toledo V, 397. Those who, while the king is alive, make provision for a future kingdom either for themselves or for others are to be punished with the worst anathema. Council of Toledo VI, 408. Those who presume to curse rulers are to be punished by ecclesiastical excommunication. Council of Toledo V, 396. Those who flatter themselves with the prospect of kingship while the king is alive are to be expelled from the assembly of Catholics by sentence of excommunication. Council of Toledo V, ibid. Safety and affection are owed to the royal offspring. Council of Toledo VI, 407. The rulers’ indulgence is reserved for those who have done harm. Council of Toledo V, 397. Rulers are to be appointed for the glory of the kingdom in such a way that they are chosen, with the complete consent of the chief bishops and palace officials, either in the royal city or in the place where the ruler died—not from outside, nor through the conspiracy of a few, nor through the seditious tumult of rustic peoples. Council of Toledo VIII, 438. Oaths given for the king’s safety are not to be violated. Council of Toledo X, 457. Rulers are to devote themselves to bodily chastity. [Col. 0945] Letter of Gregory to Reccared, 161. Rulers are to possess humility of heart. Letter of the same to the same, 160. Rulers are to be moderate and gentle toward their subjects. Letter of the same to the same, 161. Rejection of persons who are forbidden to attain the kingdom. Council of Toledo V, 396. What is to be observed when the king goes forth with the army, for the condition and safety of the king, the people, or the country. Council of Mérida, 667. The king’s faithful servants are not to be deprived by the successors to the kingdom of the rights to their property as the reward for their service. Council of Toledo V, 397. Remuneration granted to the king’s faithful servants. Council of Toledo VI, 406.

**Priscillianists.** The apocryphal writings of the Priscillianists. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 94. The doctrine of the Priscillianists condemned. Council of Braga I, 599. Priscillianists who observe fasts on the Nativity of the Lord are condemned. Letter of Pope Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 91. Priscillianists who distinguish the Holy Trinity not by persons but only by names are condemned. Letter of the same to the same, ibid. Priscillianists who abstain from the use of meat are condemned. Letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, 154.

**Procreation.** See *Marriage*.

**Procurators.** They are not to be ordained unless they have previously rendered an account. Council of Carthage I, 117.

**Prosper and Hilary.** They accuse certain presbyters of Gaul, followers of Pelagius. Letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, 42.

**Proterius.** On Proterius, bishop of Alexandria. Letter of Leo to the Emperor Marcian, 79.

**Province.** It is by no means to be divided between two metropolitans. Council of Chalcedon, 101.

**Psalms.** Those composed by ignorant persons may not be recited in the church. Council of Laodicea, 58. They may not be mixed together indiscriminately. Council of Laodicea, 53. It is not permitted to recite poetic psalms in the church or to read apocryphal books, except only the canonical books of the New and Old Testament. Council of Braga II, 625. See *Divine Office*.

**Psalmists.** They are not to enter taverns. Council of Laodicea, 54. They ought not to wear the *orarium*. Council of Laodicea, ibid. How they are constituted. Council of Carthage IV, 142. Only canonical psalmists may sing psalms in the church. Council of Laodicea, 53.

**Girls.** Girls dedicated to God may not be joined in marriage. Council of Chalcedon, 102. Their blessing is not to be given by presbyters. Council of Carthage II, 121. If they have been betrothed, they cannot enter into the rights of marriage with another. Letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 4.

### Q

**Lent.** Lent is to be observed before the solemnity of Easter. Council of Orléans I, 249. The birthdays of martyrs are not to be celebrated during Lent. Council of Braga II, 623. The fast is not to be relaxed on the Thursday of the final week. Council of Laodicea, 57. On all days of Lent, including Saturday, fasting is to be observed. Council of Agde, 233.

**Quartodecimans.** They are not to be received until they condemn every heresy. Council of Laodicea, 51.

### R

**Abductors.** Abductors of widows or virgins are to be expelled from communion with the Church. Letter of Symmachus to Caesarius, 140. Those who seize wives for themselves, if they are clerics, are to fall from their own rank; if they are laymen, they are to be anathematized. Council of Chalcedon, 105. Abductors of consecrated virgins are to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion. Council of Orléans II, 236.

**Reccared.** Reccared’s confession of the faith of the Council of Chalcedon and of Nicaea at the Third Council of Toledo, 341. His constitution against the Jews, and that he was not corrupted by their gold. Letter of Gregory to Reccared, 160. On the gifts sent by the aforesaid ruler to the blessed apostle Peter. Letter of the same, ibid. Edict of King Reccared in confirmation of the Third Council of Toledo, 355.

**Reccesvinthus.** His profession of faith and the submission of the *tome* for the council’s deliberation. Council of Toledo VIII, 421. The law issued by him at the Eighth Council of Toledo concerning writings dealing with anything owed to another, their ownership, and the observance imposed by this king upon his successors. Council of Toledo VIII, 445.

**Refugees.** A discussion concerning refugees and traitors. Council of Toledo VIII, 427.

**Queen.** When the ruler has died, the surviving queen is immediately to lay aside secular clothing and be committed to a convent of virgins, where she is to remain. Third Council of Zaragoza, 310.

**Religious persons.** Laymen are not permitted to command religious persons. Council of Toledo X, 458. Those who, at a young age, maintained the religious habit before their parents are always to remain attached to the religious life. Council of Toledo X, 459. The superior who is to be placed over religious women is to be approved by the bishop. Council of Carthage IV, 152. The license of wandering religious persons is to be restrained by the bishops in whose assembly they are known to remain. Council of Toledo IV, 381. The bodies of religious persons are to be escorted only with psalm-singing. Council of Toledo III, 354.

**Relics.** Relics of the saints are not to be placed in rural oratories. Council of Epaon, 264. If relics are found anywhere that derive from the Arian heresy, they are to be tested by fire. Second Council of Zaragoza, 305.

**Ecclesiastical property.** See *Ecclesiastical matters*.

**Richimirus.** Decree of the Tenth Council of Toledo concerning Richimirus, bishop of the Church of Dumium. Council of Toledo X, 466.

### S

**Priest.** He is to abstain from his wife. Council of Carthage V, 155. He is not to be ordained before the age of thirty. Council of Arles III, 203. Before true reconciliation unites priests who are at odds, none of them may dare approach the Lord’s altar or receive the grace of holy communion. Council of Toledo XI, 477. A layman is not to advance to the priestly rank until he has first spent an entire year learning discipline in the office of reader or subdeacon. Council of Braga I, 605. No one is to be ignorant of the canons. Letter of Celestine to the bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria, 49. No one is to be made a priest unless he remains in the minor offices for the period designated by the Church. Letter of Innocent to Felix, 19. A priest’s body is never to be covered with the cloth used for the Lord’s body when he is carried to the tomb. Council of Arvernus I, 269. If he has lapsed, hands are not to be laid upon him as upon penitents or faithful laymen. Council of Carthage V, 157. If he has married a widow or a rejected woman, he is to lose his office. Letter of Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, 31. A usurer is to be removed from his office. Letter of Leo to all the bishops, 101. If he confesses some crime concerning himself, he is to be deposed. Council of Valencia, 207.

**Priests.** Those afflicted by a demon may not handle the sacred ministries. Council of Toledo XI, 483. They are not to use dogs for hunting or hawks. Council of Agde, 241. They are to live chastely with their wives. Council of Toledo III, 349. Married priests are not to have intercourse with their own wives. Council of Orléans II, [Col. 0946] 251. They ought not to have intercourse with women. Letter of Innocent to Victoricus, 14. On accused priests, and also palace nobles and *gardingi*, and the judicial safeguards under which they ought to be examined. Council of Toledo XIII, 514. On the chastity of priests. Council of Toledo IV, 374. On restraining the excesses of priests. Council of Toledo XI, 478. On the benefactions of priests. Council of Orléans II, 256. On the number of years at which priests and Levites are to be ordained. Council of Toledo IV, 374. On priests sending messengers to a foreign people. Council of Toledo IV, 376. Incontinent priests are to be deprived of every dignity. Council of Arvernus I, 270. They are to be ordained according to the provisions of the canons. Letter of Hormisdas to the bishops throughout Spain, 147. Priests associated in disgrace with women, whether free or enslaved, if they cannot be restrained at all, are to be assigned to monasteries until the end of their lives and remain subject to the discipline of penance. Council of Toledo VIII, 435. Priests or anyone from the clergy are not to live with women without testimony. Council of Braga III, 633. Priests are not permitted to inflict mutilation of limbs on anyone in the households of the churches, nor to judge anything punishable by death. Council of Toledo, 479. After a priest’s death, the number of years is to be reckoned for the freedom granted to slaves. Council of Toledo IX, 452. Those who have not overthrown idolatry are either to be regarded as sacrilegious or deprived of communion. Council of Arles II, 262. Whenever the celebrant sacrifices the body and blood of Jesus Christ on the altar, he is to present himself as a participant in the reception of Christ’s body and blood. Council of Toledo XII, 496. When the holy mysteries are consecrated by priests during Mass, if any illness occurs so that the ministry of the consecration begun cannot be completed, the bishop or another presbyter is free to carry out the consecration of the office already begun. Council of Toledo VI, 415. Pagan priests who are still sacrificing as catechumens are to be admitted to baptism after three years. Council of Elvira, 283. Pagan priests who no longer sacrifice are to receive communion after two years. Council of Elvira, 290. Pagan priests who have sacrificed after baptism are not to receive communion even at the end of life. Council of Elvira, 281. Communion is to be denied to pagan priests who have merely laid their hands on idols. Council of Elvira, 282. Writings unjustly prepared by priests or ministers are to have the number of years reckoned after their death. Council of Toledo IX, 451. They are to possess knowledge of the sacred Scriptures and the canons. Council of Toledo IV, 376. If they migrate from their own churches to others, they are to be kept from communion until they return. Letter of Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch, 2. If they are incontinent, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical honor. Letter of Innocent to Exuperius, 16, and letter of Siricius to Eumerius, 5. Whether those who are established in the priesthood and receive penance dare to minister. Council of Toledo XIII, 521. See *Presbyter, Presbyters*.

**Priesthood.** It is not to be given to unknown persons. Letter of Siricius to various bishops, 10. No layman may aspire to or be advanced to the highest priesthood, bypassing the period prescribed by the canons, whether through sacred royal authority, the consent of the clergy or people, or the election and approval of the bishops. Council of Barcelona II, 657. Whoever has been promoted to the priesthood, whether a widow’s husband or one with numerous marriages, is to be excluded from all ecclesiastical offices. Letter of Leo to all the bishops, 101. Whoever is discovered to have offered any reward in order to obtain the dignity of the priesthood is to be condemned with the reproach of anathema. Council of Toledo VIII, 433. How married men are to be promoted to the priesthood. Council of Arles II, 199. Husbands of repudiated women are not to be promoted to the priesthood. Council of Arles III, 204.

**Sacraments.** Wicked persons, by administering good things, harm only themselves and do not defile the Church’s sacraments. Letter of Anastasius to the Emperor Anastasius, 139. No reward is to be accepted for the divine sacraments. Council of Toledo XI, 480.

**Sacrifice.** Only bread and a chalice are to be offered in the sacrifice. Council of Carthage III, 131.

**Saints.** They truly say, “Forgive us our debts.” Council of Milevis, 184. — **The holy Fathers.** Where no urgent necessity exists, the decrees of the Fathers are to be observed. General Decree of Gelasius, 130.

**Nuns.** They are not to be veiled before the age of forty. Council of Agde, 234, and Council of Zaragoza I, 305. Religious girls are not to maintain familiarity with men. Council of Toledo I, 323.

**Stage performers.** If they convert, reconciliation is not to be denied them. Council of Carthage III, 132.

**Holy Scripture.** Nothing is to be read in the church except the sacred Scriptures. Council of Carthage III, 137.

**Apostolic See.** Outside the knowledge of the apostolic see—that is, of the primate—no one may presume to ordain. Council of Telepte, 191. The number of apostolic sees. Decree of Hormisdas, 164.

**Seditionaries.** Seditionaries are never to be ordained clerics. Council of Agde, 243.

**Seditious persons.** Those who have acted seditiously against churches or their worshipers, that is, priests, are to be separated from the Church of God. Council of Reggio, 216.

**The elderly.** They are to be honored. Council of Carthage IV, 150.

**Tombs.** The honor due to the tombs of martyrs. Council of Carthage I, 115.

**Slaves. Slave.** Slaves are not to be admitted as accusers of clerics. Council of Carthage VII, 179. Those who flee to a church are to be excused only from corporal punishments. Council of Epaon, 266. Masters are to forbid their slaves to practice idolatry. Council of Toledo III, 352. Sons begotten by clergy from bishop down to subdeacon are to remain perpetually in the service of the church whose minister’s disgrace gave them birth. Council of Toledo IX, 452. A slave ought not, on the pretext of religion, to despise his master. Council of Gangra, 29. No priest, Levite, or member of the Catholic community may dare to sell Christian slaves to Jews or pagans. Council of Toledo X, 460. Those who kill their slaves without a judge are to be excommunicated. Council of Agde, 242. Whoever kills his own slave without the judge’s knowledge is to expiate the shedding of blood by two years of excommunication. Council of Epaon, 265. Other people’s slaves are not to be received into the clergy. Council of Braga II, 622. How the slaves of the church are to be manumitted by the bishop. Council of Agde, 231. Fiscal slaves who build churches are to provide an endowment, and it is to be confirmed by the ruler. Council of Toledo III, 352. Slaves are not to be ordained. Council of Arvernus II, 274, and Orléans II, 259. Slaves are not to be received into the clergy or monasteries under the pretext of religion. General Decree of Gelasius, 132. The bishop may sell fugitive slaves of the church. Council of Agde, 239. A slave of the church manumitted by the bishop is never to depart from the church’s protection. Council of Toledo III, 350.

**Signs.** Those who distinguish the twelve signs observed by astrologers throughout the entire body are condemned. Letter of Pope Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 94.

**Simony.** No office of honor is to be sold in return for a promise of gifts. Council of Braga III, 634. No one is to obtain honor by means of rewards. Letter of Symmachus to Caesarius, 140. If laymen or monks are ordained for payment, let the crime of Simon Magus involve both the giver and the recipient. General Decree of Gelasius, 134.

**Simplicius.** Decrees of Pope Simplicius addressed to Zeno of Seville concerning the delegated authority of the apostolic see, 124.

**Pope Siricius.** His letter to various bishops against the heretic Jovinian, 8, 9. His letter to Eumerius of Tarragona, 3.

**Sisbertus.** On his condemnation. Council of Toledo XVI, 575.

**Sodomites.** The penance of those who have lived irrationally. Council of Ancyra, 21. If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is a sodomite, he is to be cast down from the rank of his own honor and remain struck by the sentence of perpetual exile; but if he is of any other order, rank, or station, such persons are to be excluded from the entire company of Christians. Council of Toledo XVI, 570.

**Divination.** Those who observe divinations or auguries are to be separated from the Church. Council of Agde, 238.

**Spectacles.** The sons of clerics are not to attend spectacles. Council of Carthage III, 129. Priests and clerics are not permitted to attend spectacles. Council of Braga II, 624.

**The Holy Spirit.** Those who say that the children of promise were conceived from the Holy Spirit are condemned. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 92.

**Betrothed persons.** How they are to be blessed. Council of Carthage IV, 143.

**Subdeacons.** Their ministries. Council of Laodicea, 53. No one from the rank of subdeacon upward is to live with a foreign woman. Council of Toledo II, 330. How they are appointed. Council of Carthage IV, 141. If a subdeacon takes a second wife, he is not to read the Apostle. Council of Braga II, 622. If, after his wife’s death, he takes another wife, he is to become a doorkeeper. Council of Toledo I, 322. Subdeacons defiled by sexual impurity or joined to new wives are to be confined in monasteries under the burdens of penance until the end of their lives. Council of Toledo VIII, 435. Both the subdeacon and the doorkeeper, as well as the others, are to perform the customary service of the holy church without any negligence and are to raise the curtains for their elders at the doors. Council of Narbonne, 662.

**Suicides.** No commemoration is to be made in the offering for those who inflict death upon themselves. Council of Braga I, 604. See *Homicides*.

**Suintilan.** The execration of Suintilan and his wife and offspring. Council of Toledo IV, 387.

**Superstition.** It is not permitted to gather medicinal herbs with any ritual observance. Council of Braga II, 626.

**Creed.** The Creed of faith issued at the great Council of Nicaea, 7. The Creed of the Council of Nicaea. Council of Constantinople II, 63. The Creed of the holy Fathers assembled at Constantinople. Council of Constantinople II, 65.

**Symmachus.** Letter to Caesarius, 139.

**Synod.** See *Councils* and *Council*.

### T

**Witnesses.** False witnesses are to be excluded according to the nature of the crime. Council of Elvira, 293. Which persons are not to be admitted as witnesses against clerics. Council of Carthage VII, 179. False witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion. Council of Agde, 237.

**Teudulfus.** On the complaints of Teudulfus, bishop of the Church of Málaga, against the other bishops concerning certain parishes. Council of Seville II, 639.

**Theatrical performers.** As long as they practice their profession, they are to be excommunicated. Council of Arles I, 195, and Arles II, 202.

**Tiberianus.** On Aggarus and Tiberianus, who were ordained from among the laity. Letter of Leo to the Africans, 115.

**Toledo.** Constitution of the Carthaginian priests in the city of Toledo before the most holy bishop of that same Church. Council of Toledo XII, 507.

**Tonsure.** On the form of tonsure to be maintained by all clerics or readers. Council of Toledo IV, 379.

**Translations.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon is not to pass from a smaller city to a larger one. Council of Braga II, 614. Transfers of bishops are not permitted. Council of Carthage III, 133.

**Tributes.** On the ruler’s remission of tributes among the people. Council of Toledo XIII, 515.

**The Most Holy Trinity.** It is to be believed and preached. Council of Carthage II, 121. On the mystery of the Trinity, and what is signified by “person” and what by “substance.” Decree of Hormisdas to the Emperor Justin, 141. The declaration and confession of its unity. Letter of Damasus to Paulinus, 2. Those who believe that the Lord God was the Father are condemned. Letter of Leo to Thuribius of Astorga, 91.

### U

**Avengers.** Those who avenge their own injuries are never to be ordained clerics. Council of Agde, 243.

**Usury.** A cleric is not to practice lending at interest either in his own name or in another’s. Letter of Leo to all the bishops, 101. Not only clerics but Christian laymen also ought not to exact interest. Letter of Leo to all the bishops, 101.

**Usurers.** A moneylender is to be deposed from his rank and regarded as excluded from the clergy. Council of Braga II, 624. Usurious clerics are to be degraded; lay usurers are to be expelled from the church. Council of Elvira, 285. They are never to be ordained clerics. Council of Agde, 243.

### V
### V

**Vagrants.** Vagrants are to be corrected. Council of Toledo VI, 417.

**Valentinian and Marcian.** Their edicts in confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon and condemnation of the heretics. Council of Chalcedon, 106, 107, 110.

**Sacred vessels.** Vessels consecrated to the Lord shall not be used for human purposes. Council of Braga III, 622.

**Sale.** The sale of ecclesiastical property made by a bishop without the subscription of the clergy shall be invalid. Council of Carthage IV, 145. Presbyters ought not to sell ecclesiastical property. Council of Ancyra, 21.

**Widows.** They shall not live with unrelated persons. Council of Carthage I, 116. A man married to a widow may not be admitted to the clerical order. Letter of Pope Siricius to Bishop Himerius, 2. Concerning those who marry widows or divorced women, or who have become involved in evil counsels. Council of Braga II, 619. Concerning the profession and dress of religious widows. [Col. 0949] Council of Toledo X, 458. Concerning the remote excuses of widows who follow a violation of religion. Council cited above, 459. Concerning the widows of clerics. Council of Braga II, 619. The distinction between secular widows and those living in religious communities. Council of Toledo IV, 382.

Widows shall not be veiled. Decree of Gelasius, general, 132. Widows shall not be veiled; but if, after professing continence, they trample it underfoot by changing their purpose, they themselves shall render an account before the Lord. Decree cited above, 134.

What kind of women are to be ordained for the ministry of baptism. Council of Carthage IV, 143. Those who are supported by the Church’s stipend ought to be continually engaged in the work of God. Council of Carthage IV, 152. If they appear in religious dress and afterward pass over to secular marriage, they shall incur condemnation. Council cited above, ibid. They shall be supported at the expense of the Church. Council cited above, ibid.

Widows or professed virgins who have vowed continence shall not marry thereafter. Letter of Symmachus to Caesar, 140. No one shall inflict violence upon widows on account of their chastity. Council of Toledo III, 350. Women who have professed widowhood before a bishop are bound to preserve it. Council of Orange, 222.

**Vigilius.** Letter to Bishop Profuturus, 154. [Col. 0949]

**Virgins. Virgin.** They shall not be consecrated before the age of twenty-five. Council of Carthage III, 127. Consecrated virgins who consent to live with their abductors shall be excluded from ecclesiastical communion. Council of Orléans II, 256. Concerning virgins who, under the pressure of necessity, are veiled before the age of twenty-five. Council of Milevis, 189. Concerning sacred virgins who have suffered barbarian violence. Letter of Pope Leo to the Africans, 115. Those who join themselves to sacred virgins and enter into incestuous unions cannot receive communion unless they have performed public penance. Decree of Gelasius, general, 134. How they are to be guarded. Council of Carthage III, 132.

Virgins under twenty-five may, under the pressure of necessity, be veiled. Council of Milevis, 189. Virgins shall not be veiled except at Epiphany, in the white garments of Easter, or on the birthdays of the apostles. Decree of Gelasius, general, 132. If they do not preserve their purpose, communion shall be denied them, except at the point of death. Letter of Siricius to Himerius, 5. Virgins or professed widows who have vowed continence shall not marry thereafter. Letter of Symmachus to Caesar, 140.

An un veiled virgin who goes astray shall be admitted to penance. [Col. 0950] Letter of Innocent to Victoricius, 15. If a consecrated virgin marries or is violated, she shall not be admitted to penance unless the man to whom she had joined herself has departed this life. Letter of the same to the same, ibid. How a religious virgin is to be dressed. Council of Carthage IV, 142.

**Virginity.** Let those who take pride in virginity be anathema. Council of Gangra, 30. Those who profess virginity, if they transgress, shall be reckoned among the twice-married. Council of Ancyra, 22.

**Vow.** Men and women who transgress their sacred commitment shall be condemned by the foregoing sentence. Council of Toledo VI, 404.

### X

**Xenodochium.** Concerning the preservation of the xenodochium at Lyon. Council of Auvergne II, 277.

### Z

**Pope Zosimus.** His letter to the clergy of Ravenna, 37. His letter to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, 36.

[Col. 0949]

For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption, VI, 23.

**Psalm XX.**—13. For you will set them as a back, V, 511.—32. The coming generation will be announced to the Lord, and the heavens will proclaim his righteousness to the people who will be born, whom the Lord made, VI, 102.

They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked upon me and observed me, VI, 46.—19. They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot, VI, 47.—28. All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, V, 355.—28 and 29. All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord . . . for the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and he himself will rule the nations, V, 313; VI, 66.

**Psalm XXVIII.**—1. Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams, V, 450.—2. Glory and honor to God, II, 559.—5. The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars, V, 540.

**Psalm XXIX.**—12 and 13. You turned my mourning into joy for me . . . so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with grief, V, 550.

**Psalm XXXI.**—1 and 2. Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, V, 331, 424; VI, 464.—4. I was turned into misery while the thorn was being fixed . . . for when I was silent, all my bones grew old while I cried out all day, VI, 223.—9. **Chapter I.**—Verse 8. “For the law is good, if someone uses it lawfully,” V, 307.

**Chapter II.**—1. “Therefore, first of all I ask that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions,” II, 559. —2. “Therefore I wish, first of all, that petitions and prayers be made . . . who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” V, 549. —3. “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” V, 549. —14. “The man was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression,” VI, 216.

**Chapter III.**—2. “A bishop must be blameless,” II, 562. —The same. “The husband of one wife,” VI, 420. —7. “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside,” V, 327. —8. “Deacons likewise must be blameless, certainly chaste, not double-tongued . . . and so let them minister, having no accusation,” VI, 428. —10. “Let them first be tested, and so let them minister, having no accusation,” II, 562. —15. “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth,” III, 346.

**Chapter IV.**—1 and following. “Some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error . . . which God created to be received,” V, 418.

**Chapter V.**—6. “But she who lives in luxury is dead while alive,” VI, 452. —9. “Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one man,” VI, 451. —11. “When they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made their first faith void,” VI, 451. —13. “At the same time they also learn to be idle, going around the houses,” VI, 451. —22. “Lay hands quickly on no one. Do not appoint a novice,” VI, 421. —23. “Use a little wine,” VI, 255. —24. “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but some they also follow,” VI, 612.

**Chapter VI.**—8. “Having . . . be content,” I, 68. —9. “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, and into the devil’s snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into destruction and perdition,” VII, 216. —10. “The root of all evils is greed; by desiring it, some have gone astray from the faith,” II, 571; VI, 249. —16. “Who alone possesses immortality,” III, 296.

## SECOND LETTER TO TIMOTHY

**Chapter II.**—Verse 2. “Entrust these things to faithful people who are able to teach others also,” VI, 331. —3. “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who approved him,” V, 469. —24. “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist the truth,” VII, 213.

**Chapter III.**—8. “Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, and these also resist the truth; people corrupted in mind, disqualified concerning the faith, but they will progress no further. Their madness will be manifest to all, as theirs also was,” V, 368. —12. “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution,” V, 521.

**Chapter IV.**—2. “Exhort with all patience and instruction,” VII, 213. —3. “Itching in their ears, they will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn to fables,” II, 526.

## TO TITUS

**Chapter I.**—Verses 5–7. “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains . . . For a bishop must be blameless,” VI, 426. —15. “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, because both their mind and their conscience are defiled,” VI, 256.

**Chapter II.**—3. “Not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, but using little, teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence,” VI, 451.

## TO THE HEBREWS

**Chapter I.**—Verse 14. “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” VI, 138.

**Chapter IV.**—13. “All things are naked and open to his eyes,” I, 68.

**Chapter V.**—14. “Solid food belongs to the mature,” V, 351.

**Chapter IX.**—17. “A testament is confirmed over the dead,” III, 200.

**Chapter XI.**—6. “Without faith no one can please God; for whatever is not from faith is sin,” VI, 192.

## THE LETTER OF JAMES

**Chapter I.**—Verse 8. “A double-minded person is unstable in all his ways,” V.

**Chapter II.**—10. “Whoever stumbles in one of these has become guilty of all. For the one who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Now if you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law,” VI, 612. —19. “For the demons also believe and tremble,” VI, 598. —20. “Faith without works is dead,” V, 106. —21. “Abraham our father was justified by works,” V, 107.

**Chapter III.**—8. “No human being can tame the tongue; it is a restless evil, full of deadly pain. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing,” VII, 213.

**Chapter IV.**—9. “Be wretched, mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow,” VI, 307.

**Chapter V.**—1. “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted; your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you,” VII, 216.

## FIRST LETTER OF PETER

**Chapter I.**—Verse 12. “Into which the angels of God desire to look,” VI, 138.

**Chapter II.**—5. “You are living stones, built into spiritual houses,” V, 401, 483. —9. “A holy people, a royal priesthood,” V, 509; VI, 416. —24. “He bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by his bruise we have been healed,” II, 530.

**Chapter IV.**—1. “Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh,” II, 530. —17. “Judgment must begin from the house of God,” VI, 260.

**Chapter V.**—5. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble,” V, 448.

## SECOND LETTER OF PETER

**Chapter II.**—Verse 4. “He did not spare the angels,” II, 576. —16. “He received a rebuke for his madness: a mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s foolishness,” V, 457.

**Chapter III.**—13. “A new man and a new earth,” V, 250.

## FIRST LETTER OF JOHN

**Chapter II.**—Verse 1. “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ,” III, 303. —27. “And may the anointing which you received from him remain in you; and you have no need for anyone to teach you about anything,” III, 310.

**Chapter IV.**—12. “No one has ever seen God,” III, 297.

## SECOND LETTER OF JOHN

**Chapter I.**—Verse 10. “If anyone comes to you bringing another doctrine, do not receive him, nor say ‘Hail’ to him,” VI, 568.

## THE LETTER OF JUDE

**Chapter I.**—Verse 5. “Jesus, after delivering the people from the land of Egypt, subsequently destroyed those who did not believe,” VI, 262.

## THE APOCALYPSE

**Chapter I.**—Verse 1. “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to disclose to his servants,” III, 248.

**Chapter II.**—6. “But you have this: that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans,” III, 352. —9. “Those who say they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan,” V, 499.

**Chapter III.**—19. “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline,” VI, 262.

**Chapter V.**—3. “No one was found in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, who could open the book and break its seals,” VI, 613.

**Chapter X.**—9 and 10. “Take the book and eat it; it will be sweet in my mouth, like honey, and bitter in my belly,” V, 253.

**Chapter XII.**—10. “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before our God day and night,” III, 378.

**Chapter XIX.**—10. “See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers. Worship God,” VI, 140 and 404.

**Chapter XXII.**—13. “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last,” III, 303.

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND WORDS CONTAINED IN THE SEVEN VOLUMES [Note: [Column XXIX] Of this edition, namely Arevalo’s. These seven volumes are contained in the three preceding volumes of the Patrologia: the first and second in our volume LXXXI; the third and fourth in our volume LXXXII; the fifth, sixth, and seventh in our volume LXXXIII. For the rest, we have preserved the title and pages of each volume—the latter represented in the text in heavier type—to which the index numbers correspond. EDITOR.] OF THE WORKS OF SAINT ISIDORE OF SEVILLE

The Roman numeral indicates the volume; the Arabic numeral, the page. Certain exotic words may be found in the Glossary in this volume VII, beginning on page 443. (C)
